Settings.A4: Yellow cells: human entries. Coding criteria: stage2_instructions.md.
Settings.G7:
Treatment: Difference in effective strike range between RX and CX, DR_t, measured in effective-range units ('sigmas' of Black-Scholes implied volatility) on day t. Continuous treatment.

Method: The paper runs a simple time-series regression of the end-of-day relative level of the replication volatility index to the corridor index, Z_t = RX_t/CX_t - 1, on the difference in their effective strike ranges, DR_t. This is a linear regression with Newey-West standard errors (20 lags), not a panel or FE design. The intended interpretation is causal/mechanistic: exogenous/idiosyncratic widening of the strike range used in RX raises RX relative to CX, holding option-price-based volatility concept fixed. Identification is descriptive-regression-based and relies on the authors' argument that DR_t reflects strike-range variation unrelated to underlying option prices/volatility rather than a formal quasi-experiment.

Identification: The identifying variation is day-to-day variation in the discrepancy between the effective strike ranges used by RX and CX. The authors argue this variation is idiosyncratic and unrelated to option prices/volatility, so a wider RX range mechanically inflates RX relative to CX. The main concern is that DR_t may still co-move with market conditions, but the paper interprets it as induced by truncation-rule noise rather than fundamentals.

Setting: Using a daily linear regression, the authors argue that idiosyncratic expansion of the effective strike range used in RX causes RX to rise relative to CX. They report Z_t = 0.0340 + 0.0089 DR_t with t-statistics 6.76 and 11.36 and adjusted R^2 = 67.2. Since the standard deviation of DR_t is 1.88, they state that a one-standard-deviation increase in the RX range 'inflates the value of RX relative to CX by an additional 1.7% (= 1.88·0.89%).' This is a supporting methodological result showing that incoherent truncation mechanically distorts VIX-style measures.

Main role: This regression supports the paper's methodological claim that random strike-range variation distorts VIX-style indices, but it is not the central substantive return-volatility dynamics result emphasized in the abstract and conclusions.
Settings.H7: Section 3.4 'Basic properties of the volatility indices,' regression displayed in text on PDF page 19.
Settings.N7: Section 3.4, printed pp. 2919-2920: daily OLS regression of Z_t = RX_t/CX_t - 1 on DR_t, the difference in effective strike-range widths, with Newey-West standard errors using 20 lags. Reported equation Z_t = 0.0340 + 0.0089 DR_t; the authors explicitly interpret an exogenous one-treatment-SD widening as inflating RX relative to CX by an additional 1.7%. Include the same-location alternative VIX*/CX regression reported in footnote 18: RX strike range proxies the VIX* range, using observations where RX and VIX* values are close; other VIX* observations excluded. Footnote reports almost identical results but no separate coefficient.
Settings.O7: Retain because p. 2920 explicitly attributes distortions to exogenous/idiosyncratic strike-range variation unrelated to option prices, rather than merely describing covariance. Supporting measurement result. Adjusted R-squared 67.2 is on a percent scale. DR SD=1.88 is treatment SD, not outcome SD; the 1.7% interpretation and construction of ratio-minus-one Y do not separately benchmark the focal slope against a mean/SD/level of that same Y. No qualifying comparison. Footnote 18 alternate outcome added as hy1.
Settings.G8:
Treatment: One-minute innovation in the corridor implied volatility index CX, measured as one-minute log return in CX; in tables/figures often grouped into sigma bins such as (-inf,-9), (-9,-6), ..., (6,9), (9,inf). Continuous underlying treatment, sometimes discretized by bins.

Method: The paper estimates the return-volatility relation by linear correlation/regression-style association between high-frequency CX innovations and contemporaneous S&P 500 return innovations, using one-minute returns sorted by volatility-jump size and illustrated with scatter plots and fitted regression lines. There is no quasi-experimental design; the authors interpret the contemporaneous association as informative about the effect of volatility jumps/innovations on returns and vice versa, including cojump behavior. This is a regression-adjustment/association design used with causal language about return-volatility asymmetry and cojumps.

Identification: The paper exploits high-frequency synchronization between an observable corridor implied volatility index and S&P 500 futures returns. Under the maintained argument that CX is a robust proxy for spot volatility innovations and that large discontinuities in CX reveal volatility jumps, contemporaneous high-frequency covariance/sorting identifies the sign and strength of the return-volatility interaction. Key assumptions are that CX innovations track spot volatility innovations without large measurement error and that contemporaneous alignment captures cojump behavior rather than stale quotes or truncation artifacts.

Setting: The authors interpret one-minute changes in CX as volatility innovations and show that larger positive volatility jumps are accompanied by negative equity returns and larger negative volatility jumps by positive equity returns. In Table 4, when CX returns are in (-9,-6) sigmas, the average contemporaneous S&P return is +2.20 sigmas (0.12%); for (6,9) sigmas it is -2.72 sigmas (-0.17%); for extreme CX jumps below -9 sigmas it is +3.32 sigmas (0.20%), and above +9 sigmas it is -4.38 sigmas (-0.40%). They conclude there is a pronounced negative monotone cojump relation and that negative volatility jumps are as substantively real as positive ones. This is one of the paper's main substantive results.

Main role: A central paper conclusion is that volatility jumps are common, symmetric, and cojump negatively with returns; this setting directly underlies that substantive claim in the abstract, Section 4.1, and conclusions.
Settings.H8: Section 4.1.2 'Empirical evidence on the volatility-price jump interaction,' Table 4 and top panels of Figure 5, PDF pages 24-25.
Settings.O8: Section 4.1.2, Table 4/Fig. 5, pp. 2924-2926: conditional mean returns, densities and a fitted scatterplot line document a contemporaneous negative association/cojump distribution. Authors conclude a negative monotone association, not a directional effect of an intervention in CX on equity returns. Model language about a causal effect is unsupported. Exclude as descriptive under the causal-setting gate, not because OLS is inherently inadmissible.
Settings.G9:
Treatment: One-minute log return of the S&P 500 futures, grouped by sigma categories such as (-inf,-6), (-6,-4), ..., (4,6), (6,inf). Continuous underlying treatment, discretized for reporting.

Method: The paper reverses the conditioning direction and studies the relation between large S&P 500 return innovations and contemporaneous CX innovations using grouped means, scatter plots, and smoothed conditional densities. This remains a high-frequency linear/associational design without FE or quasi-experimental variation, used to infer causal cojumping and leverage-type effects between returns and volatility.

Identification: Identification again comes from synchronized high-frequency observations. Large S&P futures returns are taken as revealing return shocks; contemporaneous CX movements proxy spot-volatility responses. The paper's interpretation relies on CX being a reliable volatility measure and on high-frequency timing being accurate enough that observed co-movements capture same-interval economic interaction rather than index-construction noise.

Setting: Conditioning on large S&P 500 returns, the paper finds mirror-image volatility responses in CX, which the authors interpret as strong inverse return-volatility cojumps. In Table 5, S&P returns below -6 sigmas are associated with average CX moves of +6.54 sigmas (1.49%), while S&P returns above +6 sigmas are associated with average CX moves of -6.32 sigmas (-1.13%). For medium-large return bins (-6,-4) and (4,6), the corresponding average CX moves are +3.70 sigmas (0.63%) and -3.61 sigmas (-0.59%). Figure 6 shows near mirror-image conditional CX densities for negative versus positive equity jumps. This supports the paper's central claim of a contemporaneous inverse cojumping relation between returns and volatility.

Main role: This reversed-direction cojump evidence is part of the core substantive conclusion that returns and volatility cojump negatively and that the leverage asymmetry applies broadly, not just in one tabulation direction.
Settings.H9: Section 4.1.2 'Empirical evidence on the volatility-price jump interaction,' Table 5 and Figure 6, PDF pages 25-26.
Settings.O9: Section 4.1.2, Table 5/Fig. 6, pp. 2926-2928: authors explicitly reverse the conditioning direction to describe volatility increments conditional on equity-return bins and conclude a contemporaneous inverse cojumping relation. Reversing the conditioning direction does not identify either causal direction. Conditional densities/group means are descriptive, not a separate causal treatment-response setting.
Settings.G10:
Treatment: Ten-minute log return of the S&P 500 futures (or equivalently, contemporaneous equity return innovation used in the leverage correlation). Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate the leverage effect as the high-frequency correlation between returns and implied-volatility innovations, motivated by a one-factor diffusive model in which this correlation identifies the leverage coefficient. Empirically they use local correlations of ten-minute log returns and average them over time to estimate integrated leverage. This is not an FE/DiD/RD design but a model-based regression/correlation estimator. The baseline estimates use CX with S&P 500 futures returns and no jump correction in the initial signature-plot exercise.

Identification: Under a one-factor diffusive approximation, implied volatility is a smooth monotone function of spot variance, so the instantaneous correlation between returns and implied-volatility innovations equals the leverage coefficient. The empirical design uses high-frequency synchronized ten-minute returns to mitigate the Epps effect and quote staleness. The main assumptions are that CX innovations closely track spot-volatility innovations, that ten-minute sampling avoids substantial attenuation from nonsynchronicity/microstructure noise, and that the one-factor mapping is a reasonable approximation for this baseline estimator.

Setting: Using local correlations of ten-minute S&P 500 futures returns and CX returns, the authors estimate a very strong negative leverage effect. The signature plot in Figure 7 shows the integrated leverage becomes stable below -0.80 for frequencies up to ten minutes, and the paper states there is a 'typical correlation between return and volatility innovations of about -0.85.' They interpret this as evidence that the contemporaneous return-volatility asymmetry is substantially stronger than in prior literature, with CX providing a cleaner proxy for spot volatility than VIX-style indices. This is a main empirical contribution of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions emphasize that the return-volatility asymmetry is much stronger than previously recognized and that CX reveals a typical correlation around -0.85. This is a central substantive result.
Settings.H10: Section 4.2.2 'The basic estimator for the leverage coefficient,' Figure 7, PDF pages 30-31.
Settings.O10: Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2, Eqs. (17)-(20), Fig. 7, pp. 2928-2931: leverage is explicitly defined as limiting contemporaneous return-spot-volatility CORRELATION; integrated leverage averages local correlations. One-factor assumptions identify this latent correlation from observable prices, not a directional causal response. Section 4.2 discusses alternative causal explanations without identifying between them. Exclude from causal settings; neither an OLS causal coefficient nor a causal outcome-SD effect.
Settings.G11:
Treatment: Ten-minute equity return innovation: primarily S&P 500 futures log return, with variants using bias-corrected futures returns and implied forward-price returns. Continuous treatment.

Method: This setting reports robustness estimates of the leverage correlation using ten-minute returns, varying whether large volatility innovations are excluded or retained, and using alternative return series (futures, bias-corrected futures, implied forward). The estimator remains a correlation/regression-style linear measure interpreted as the leverage effect. It is a substantive robustness analysis around the baseline leverage claim.

Identification: The same model-based identification as in the baseline leverage setting is used, but robustness is assessed by excluding increasingly large volatility innovations to test sensitivity to jumps and by alternative return measurements. The authors argue that near invariance of the estimated correlation across thresholds indicates the leverage asymmetry applies similarly to diffusive moves and jumps, and that attenuation from measurement choices is limited for CX.

Setting: Table 6 shows that the CX-based leverage estimate is extremely stable across jump cutoffs and return definitions, which the authors interpret as evidence that the return-volatility asymmetry applies to both diffusive and jump components. Using ten-minute futures returns, the CX correlation ranges from -0.814 when only 0-3 sigma volatility moves are kept to -0.832 when all moves are included; with Kalnina-Xiu bias correction it ranges from -0.817 to -0.835; with implied forward returns it ranges from -0.835 to -0.848. The authors contrast this stability with weaker, noisier VIX-style estimates and conclude that their strong negative leverage result is robust and central to the paper.

Main role: These robustness results materially support the central conclusion that the leverage effect is very negative and similar for diffusive and jump innovations; the paper highlights this robustness in the abstract and conclusions.
Settings.H11: Section 4.2.3 'Alternative estimates of the leverage coefficient,' Table 6, PDF page 31.
Settings.O11: Section 4.2.3, Table 6, p. 2932: jump-exclusion cutoffs, bias correction and alternative price series check robustness of the estimated contemporaneous leverage CORRELATION. They do not estimate a causal effect of equity-return treatment on volatility. Main scientific importance does not satisfy the causal-setting inclusion rule.
Settings.G12:
Treatment: Ten-minute S&P 500 futures log return innovation, paired with CX measures built from different option maturities: T1, T2, and categories C1 (7-21 days), C2 (22-35), C3 (36-49), and C4 (50+ days). Continuous treatment.

Method: The paper studies whether the estimated leverage effect varies with option maturity by computing CX from different maturity buckets and then estimating the same ten-minute return-volatility correlation. This is a robustness/heterogeneity exercise using the same linear correlation estimator, reported in a scatter plot and summary-statistics table across maturity groups.

Identification: The identifying argument is the same correlation-based leverage mapping, here stress-tested across different option tenors. If multiple volatility factors or maturity-specific measurement problems dominated, the estimated correlation would vary systematically with tenor. Similar estimates across intermediate maturities are interpreted as supporting the substantive leverage claim rather than a maturity-specific artifact.

Setting: Using CX indices computed from different option maturities, the paper finds leverage estimates remain strongly negative and broadly similar, suggesting the main leverage result is not driven by a particular tenor choice. Table 7 reports mean leverage estimates of -0.832 for constant maturity TM, -0.801 for T1, -0.836 for T2, and -0.791, -0.816, -0.838, and -0.829 for maturity buckets C1 through C4. The authors interpret the somewhat less negative estimates at very short maturities as likely noise from wider relative bid-ask spreads, not a substantive maturity effect.

Main role: This is an important robustness analysis for whether the leverage effect is a maturity artifact, but it is secondary to the main baseline leverage and cojump findings.
Settings.H12: Section 4.2.3 'Alternative estimates of the leverage coefficient,' Figure 8 and Table 7, PDF pages 32-34.
Settings.O12: Section 4.2.3, Fig. 8/Table 7, pp. 2933-2935: distribution of leverage-correlation estimates across option maturities is a measurement/robustness exercise, not a causally interpreted treatment-response estimator. The mean/SD rows summarize estimated correlations, not a focal causal effect paired with a same-outcome benchmark. Discussion of liquidity/noise is an explanation of estimator precision, not a separately identified maturity intervention.
Settings.G13:
Treatment: Level of the CX volatility index, interpreted as capturing market turbulence/uncertainty. Continuous, quoted in annualized percent (index level).

Method: The paper estimates time variation in the leverage effect by plotting centered 21-day moving averages of integrated leverage estimates against the concurrent CX index and discussing cyclicality. This is a rolling-window correlation/regression-style exercise, still based on ten-minute returns and the model-based interpretation of the correlation as leverage. No formal causal design beyond time-series association is used.

Identification: The authors use rolling estimates of the return-volatility correlation and relate them to the level of CX. The interpretation relies on the maintained view that CX is a real-time measure of market stress and that variation in the estimated correlation reflects genuine shifts in the leverage effect rather than changing measurement error. The main limitation is the short sample and absence of an external source of exogenous variation in market turbulence.

Setting: The paper concludes that the leverage effect becomes more negative when markets are turbulent. Figure 10 shows 21-day moving-average leverage estimates ranging roughly from -0.67 to -0.92, with the most negative values during the 2008 crisis and again during the 2010 European sovereign debt episode. Figure 11 shows a negative relation between leverage and CX. The authors interpret this as evidence that return-volatility asymmetry is countercyclical and intensifies when uncertainty rises, a central empirical message of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions emphasize significant time variation in the leverage effect, becoming more negative in turbulent markets. This setting directly supports that central conclusion.
Settings.H13: Section 4.2.4 'Time-variation in the leverage coefficient,' Figures 10 and 11, PDF pages 34-35.
Settings.O13: Section 4.2.4, Figs. 10-11, pp. 2935-2936: centered 21-day averages and scatterplots show the leverage correlation co-varies with CX. Authors state the short sample prevents firm conclusions and suggest association with risk pricing. No implemented directional causal regression or intervention in turbulence is established; the model invents an OLS treatment-effect setting from a descriptive time-series pattern.
Settings.G14:
Treatment: Use of a given volatility index measure during the flash crash, especially CX versus RX/VIX, in the stressed period after 13:30 CT on May 6, 2010. The substantive treatment is effectively the volatility measure's construction/robustness to strike-range instability; binary comparison in prose, but implemented through separate continuous return series.

Method: In the flash-crash illustration, the authors compare contemporaneous correlations of volatility-index returns with S&P 500 futures returns before and after 13:30 on May 6, 2010, using two- and ten-minute log returns. This is a descriptive time-series correlation exercise interpreted causally as evidence that CX, unlike VIX-style indices, continues to reflect true market stress/volatility conditions when market liquidity deteriorates. No formal experiment or identification design is used.

Identification: The argument exploits within-day comparison during a stress event when option-market liquidity and the VIX truncation rule generate unstable strike ranges. Because CX uses a coherent corridor, it should remain aligned with underlying returns if it better captures true volatility conditions. The evidence is the persistence of strong negative return-volatility correlation for CX when VIX/RX correlations collapse, interpreted as showing that CX avoids artificial index movements induced by truncation noise.

Setting: During the May 6, 2010 flash crash, the authors argue that CX provides a more accurate real-time gauge of market stress than VIX-style indices because it is robust to strike-range instability. Table 8 shows that before 13:30 the two-minute correlations with S&P 500 returns were -0.82 for CX, -0.78 for RX, and -0.65 for VIX; after 13:30 they were -0.74 for CX but only -0.21 for RX and -0.15 for VIX. At the ten-minute frequency, after 13:30 the correlations were -0.84 for CX, -0.65 for RX, and -0.43 for VIX. Combined with Figure 12's divergent index paths, the paper interprets this as evidence that VIX became distorted by liquidity-driven strike-range shifts while CX remained informative during market stress.

Main role: This is an illustrative application showing the practical usefulness of CX during extreme stress, important to the paper but secondary relative to the main findings on jumps and leverage.
Settings.H14: Section 4.3 'Volatility indices during periods of market stress: The flash crash,' Figure 12 and Table 8, PDF pages 36-38.
Settings.N14: Section 4.3, Fig. 12 and discussion, pp. 2937-2938: measurement-mechanism case study of how changing CBOE effective strike-range truncation distorts the VIX level during May 6, 2010. Authors reconstruct major VIX movements using the underlying option quotes and truncation rule, and compare with CX*, the corridor index scaled to match pre-13:30 VIX levels. The range varies continuously/nonbinarly; the 13:30 split is not a treated/post causal DiD design. VIX is reportedly downward biased by up to 5% during the crash and overvalued by 10%-15% subsequently relative to CX*.
Settings.O14: Other = formula-based index reconstruction and same-market measurement-counterfactual comparison, not OLS/IV/DiD. Retain only the explicit causal attribution of artificial index movements to strike-range truncation (p. 2938); Table 8 return correlations are supporting descriptive diagnostics, not the causal estimator. Main=1 because real-time robustness during market stress is a central abstract/introduction/conclusion claim. CX* is a scaled reference proxy, not observed true volatility; attribution depends on that maintained measurement argument. Comparisons use other_level, not a mean/SD benchmark.
Settings.G15:
Treatment: Bank AQR exposure at the lender level, measured as divergence in lender annual provisioning due to AQR divided by lender total assets, in percent. In this collapsed setup the regressor is the difference between average post-AQR exposure and average pre-AQR exposure for the lender in a firm-lender pair.

Method: Khwaja-Mian-style bank-lending-channel design implemented as linear OLS on a collapsed firm-lender panel. The authors collapse 3 pre-AQR years and 3 post-AQR years to the firm-lender level, and regress the change in log(1+loan amount) from pre to post on the bank's change in average AQR exposure, where exposure is divergence in provisions due to the RBI asset quality review normalized by bank total assets. Main specifications include firm fixed effects to compare different lenders within the same borrowing firm; some columns also add pre-AQR lender controls (size and capital adequacy ratio), and one robustness excludes bank-years under Prompt Corrective Action. Standard errors are clustered at the lender level. Identification is from within-firm cross-lender heterogeneity in exposure, with firm FE intended to absorb borrower credit demand shocks.

Identification: The endogeneity concern is that banks more exposed to AQR may lend to firms experiencing weaker loan demand. The authors argue that AQR occurred in a relatively stable macro period and, following Khwaja and Mian (2008), use within-firm variation across lenders in AQR exposure. Firm fixed effects absorb borrower-specific demand shocks common across lenders within a firm. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on firm FE and lender controls, cross-lender differences in post-versus-pre exposure within the same firm reflect bank credit supply effects rather than differential borrower demand. Remaining concerns include endogenous bank-firm matching and bank-level omitted shocks correlated with exposure.

Setting: Using a collapsed firm-lender specification with firm fixed effects, the authors interpret higher lender exposure to the Indian AQR as causing lower credit supply to the same borrower relative to less exposed lenders. In Table 5 panel A, the coefficient on Average lender exposure ranges from -3.4217 to -1.7493 depending on controls and exclusions. They state that a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure reduces lending by 24.76% in column 1 and by 23.87%, 15.57%, and 13.94% in subsequent specifications. This setting is central to the paper because it provides the main evidence that the bank cleanup, absent adequate recapitalization, contracted bank lending.

Main role: This is a core empirical design supporting the paper's central claim that AQR-induced undercapitalization reduced bank credit supply through the bank lending channel.
Settings.H15: Section 5.1.1 'The Khwaja Mian setup', Table 5 Panel A, columns 1-4 (PDF page 24; article p. 4155).
Settings.N15: Table 5, Panel A, columns 2-4 (article p. 4155): effect of the post-minus-pre change in average lender AQR exposure (additional provisions divided by lender assets) on the post-minus-pre difference in log(1+loan amount), at the firm-lender level, with identifying firm fixed effects. Columns 3-4 add pre-AQR lender controls; column 4 excludes PCA observations. Column 1 is a separate OLS setting h1.
Settings.O15: Approved split: retain identifying-FE columns 2-4 here; no-FE column 1 and its headline comparison are recorded under h1. Original model fields preserved.
Settings.G16:
Treatment: Annual lender exposure to AQR, measured as divergence in provisions assessed because of AQR divided by lender total assets, in percent, at the lender-year level.

Method: Annual firm-lender-year bank-lending-channel regression estimated by OLS. The dependent variable is log(1+loan amount) at the firm-lender-year level. The key regressor is annual lender exposure to AQR, defined as divergence in provisions due to AQR divided by bank total assets; exposure is zero pre-AQR and for nonbank lenders or bank-years without disclosed divergence. Specifications include firm×year fixed effects to absorb borrower demand shocks and, in some columns, lender fixed effects to absorb time-invariant lender heterogeneity. Additional relationship controls include loans completed, maximum loan tenure, and relationship length. Standard errors are clustered by firm or lender depending on column.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in lender exposure across lenders lending to the same firm in the same year. Firm×year fixed effects absorb any time-varying firm-level loan demand or firm shocks; lender fixed effects absorb time-invariant lender characteristics. The authors treat exposure as the bank-side shock generated by the cleanup's revealed divergence and subsequent provisioning. The key assumption is that, conditional on firm×year FE, lender FE, and relationship controls, differences in exposure across lenders within the same firm-year are unrelated to unobserved changes in borrower demand and instead shift credit supply.

Setting: In firm-lender-year regressions with firm×year fixed effects, and in some specifications lender fixed effects, the authors interpret higher AQR exposure as causing lower annual lending from a bank to a borrower. Table 5 panel B reports exposure coefficients of -0.3484, -0.2826, -0.2156, and -0.2899 across columns, corresponding to annual economic magnitudes of -4.01%, -3.25%, -2.48%, and -3.33% for a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure. These estimates are presented as confirming that the Indian AQR reduced loan supply through the bank lending channel even after flexibly absorbing firm-year demand shocks.

Main role: This is the paper's richer annual version of the main lending design and materially supports the headline conclusion that AQR exposure reduced bank loan supply.
Settings.H16: Section 5.1.2 'Analysis at the firm-lender-year level', Equation (1), Table 5 Panel B, columns 1-4 (PDF pages 24-25; article pp. 4155-4156).
Settings.G17:
Treatment: Annual lender AQR exposure, measured as divergence in provisions due to AQR divided by bank total assets, in percent, interacted with lagged zombie-firm indicators to estimate heterogeneous effects.

Method: Firm-lender-year OLS with firm×year and lender fixed effects, extending the annual lending specification by interacting annual lender AQR exposure with lagged zombie-firm indicators. The dependent variable is log(1+loan amount). Zombie status is measured in several ways (M1-M3 here): M1 based on interest coverage excluding related-party income being below one; M2 adds a below-median decline in fixed-assets-to-debt ratio during the forbearance period; M3 further adds above-median related-party-loans-to-debt tunneling. Some columns add relationship controls. Standard errors are clustered at the lender level.

Identification: The underlying identification follows the within-firm-year across-lender approach of the main annual lending design. Firm×year fixed effects absorb borrower demand and shocks; lender fixed effects absorb time-invariant lender propensities. Heterogeneity is identified by comparing how more exposed lenders alter lending to zombie versus non-zombie borrowers within the same firm-year environment. The paper argues that a positive interaction between exposure and zombie status indicates relative favoritism toward zombie firms, consistent with risk shifting rather than general risk aversion. Assumptions remain that zombie classification is meaningful and that no unobserved lender-borrower-year factor jointly drives exposure and relative zombie lending.

Setting: The authors estimate whether AQR-induced credit contraction differs for zombie borrowers. In Table 6, the main exposure coefficient remains negative, while the interaction of exposure with zombie indicators is positive and significant across M1-M3: 0.7216/0.7509 for M1, 1.1526/1.1863 for M2, and 1.1311/1.1247 for M3. They interpret this as zombie firms being less affected by the lending contraction; for M1, they state that a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure lowers lending by 6.2% overall but only about 1.2% for zombie firms because the interaction offsets about 80% of the main effect. This is central evidence for the paper's risk-shifting mechanism.

Main role: These results directly support a central substantive claim of the paper: undercapitalized banks risk-shift by comparatively preserving or increasing zombie lending while cutting overall credit.
Settings.H17: Section 5.2 'Impact on lending to zombie firms', Equation (2), Table 6 columns 1-6 (PDF pages 27-28; article pp. 4158-4159).
Settings.G18:
Treatment: Annual bank AQR exposure, measured as divergence in provisions due to AQR divided by bank total assets, in percent. In some columns it is interacted with a Public Bank dummy.

Method: Bank-year OLS with bank and year fixed effects estimating whether more AQR-exposed banks raise more capital. Dependent variables are additions to paid-up capital, additions to paid-up capital scaled by total assets, divergence-adjusted capital additions (capital raised minus additional provisions/divergence), and that divergence-adjusted measure scaled by assets. One specification interacts exposure with a public-bank dummy to distinguish government-owned from private banks. Standard errors are clustered at the bank level.

Identification: The design exploits within-bank changes over time in AQR exposure, controlling for bank fixed effects and common year shocks. The key endogeneity concern is that exposure may correlate with other bank-specific deteriorations that also affect capital raising. The authors interpret exposure as the shock from the cleanup's revealed hidden losses and examine whether higher exposure predicts more equity issuance. The identification assumption is that, conditional on bank and year FE, exposure variation captures the capital need induced by AQR rather than omitted concurrent bank shocks. Interaction with public-bank status is used to separate government recapitalization from private market recapitalization.

Setting: Using bank-year fixed-effects regressions, the paper asks whether banks exposed to AQR recapitalize after the cleanup. Table 8 shows that exposure is positively related to raw capital additions in column 1 (6,185.03), but this disappears for private banks once exposure is interacted with a Public Bank indicator in column 2; the interaction is 7,715.77, implying the positive association is driven by government-owned banks receiving state capital. More importantly, when the dependent variable nets out AQR divergence, coefficients are sharply negative: -23,335.41 in levels and -0.8141 scaled by assets, indicating capital raised falls short of the added provisions. The authors interpret this as evidence that market forces did not sufficiently recapitalize banks after cleanup, a central conclusion of the paper.

Main role: Whether cleanup induces recapitalization is a core question of the paper, and these regressions provide the direct evidence that market forces did not recapitalize affected banks sufficiently.
Settings.H18: Section 5.4 'Does cleanup lead to debt overhang?', Equation (3), Table 8 columns 1-6 (PDF pages 33-34; article pp. 4164-4165).
Settings.N18: Table 8, p. 4164: exposure × public-bank interactions appear in both columns 2 and 4, for capital additions and capital additions divided by assets, respectively. The remaining setting description is retained.
Settings.G19:
Treatment: Annual lender AQR exposure, measured as divergence in provisions due to AQR divided by total assets, in percent; heterogeneity estimated by interaction with contemporaneous lender capital adequacy ratio and zombie indicators.

Method: Firm-lender-year OLS with firm×year and lender fixed effects, examining heterogeneity in AQR lending effects by bank capital adequacy ratio (CAR). The dependent variable is log(1+loan amount). Core regressors are annual lender exposure, CAR, and their interaction; additional columns add Exposure×Zombie, CAR×Zombie, and triple interactions Exposure×CAR×Zombie for zombie measures M1-M3. Some columns include relationship controls. Standard errors are clustered at the lender level.

Identification: As in the main annual lending setup, identification uses within-firm-year cross-lender exposure variation with firm×year fixed effects absorbing borrower demand shocks and lender fixed effects absorbing time-invariant bank traits. Interactions with CAR test whether exposure effects are stronger for less capitalized banks. Triple interactions with zombie measures test whether the relative preservation of zombie lending is concentrated among low-CAR exposed banks. The crucial assumption is that conditional on these fixed effects and controls, differential responses by CAR reflect bank balance-sheet incentives rather than omitted lender-year shocks correlated with both CAR and lending choices.

Setting: The authors show that the effect of AQR exposure on lending depends on bank capitalization. In Table 9 columns 1-2, the interaction Exposure×CAR is positive and significant (about 0.233), implying that more highly capitalized banks cut lending less, so less capitalized banks reduce lending more. In columns 3-8, triple interactions Exposure×CAR×Zombie are negative and significant across zombie measures, such as -0.2752 for M1 and -0.3244 for M2, indicating that among exposed banks, lower-capital banks tilt relatively more toward zombie lending. These estimates are used to support the underinvestment and risk-shifting mechanisms central to the paper.

Main role: These regressions substantively support the paper's mechanism that undercapitalization drives underinvestment and risk shifting: less capitalized exposed banks cut lending more and favor zombie lending more.
Settings.H19: Section 5.4.1 'Banks with a lower capital adequacy ratio', Table 9 columns 1-8 (PDF pages 35-36; article pp. 4165-4166).
Settings.G20:
Treatment: Firms with High Exposure: indicator equal to one if a firm's weighted-average exposure to AQR, based on exposures of its lenders and pre-AQR lending weights, is above the median in a given year, and zero otherwise.

Method: Firm-year OLS with firm and year fixed effects assessing the effect of firm-level AQR exposure on borrowing and real outcomes. Firm exposure is a weighted average of all lender exposures in a year, using pre-AQR average loan amounts as weights; the treatment used in regressions is a dummy for whether a firm's exposure is above the sample median in a year. Controls include independent-director share, Big-4 auditor indicator, and SME status. Standard errors are clustered by firm.

Identification: The endogeneity concern is that firms more exposed to affected banks may differ systematically in time-varying investment opportunities or financing conditions. The authors use firm fixed effects to absorb time-invariant firm characteristics and year fixed effects for aggregate shocks, and define exposure using pre-AQR lender weights to reduce simultaneity from post-shock lender reshuffling. The causal interpretation assumes that conditional on firm and year FE and governance/auditor/SME controls, crossing the median of lender-based exposure captures exogenous tightening of external finance caused by bank AQR exposure.

Setting: At the firm-year level, the paper interprets high exposure to AQR-affected lenders as causing financing shortfalls and real contraction. In Table 10, highly exposed firms have 0.3848 lower log(1+borrowing), which the authors describe as about 38% lower overall borrowing; they find no significant replacement through related-party borrowing or new equity. Real outcomes also worsen: PP&E falls by 60.765, total fixed assets by 97.608, log fixed-asset additions by 0.0587, and stalled projects rise by 76.701. The paper states these magnitudes correspond to a 34% decline relative to average PP&E and a 12.2% increase relative to the average value of running projects. This setting is a main piece of evidence that the AQR cleanup adversely affected the real economy through firms.

Main role: These regressions are central to the paper's claim that the AQR-induced lending contraction had real effects on firms, reducing borrowing and investment and increasing stalled projects.
Settings.H20: Section 6.1 'Impact on firms' and Section 6.1.1 'Investment by firms', Equation (4), Table 10 columns 1-7 (PDF pages 37-38; article pp. 4168-4169).
Settings.N20: Table 10 / Equation (4), pp. 4167-4169: lender weights use pre-AQR average OUTSTANDING loan amounts, not new lending flows (Table 2, p. 4149; Section 4, p. 4154). Other treatment, FE and outcome definitions are retained.
Settings.O20: Table 10 col. 6: the log1p fixed-asset-additions coefficient is negative but not statistically significant at the table's reported levels. Comparison alignment and uncertain zero masses are coded separately rather than inferred.
Settings.G21:
Treatment: Bank AQR exposure at the lender level, measured as divergence in annual provisioning due to AQR divided by bank total assets, in percent; in this collapsed NBFC-borrower setup, the regressor is the change between average post- and pre-AQR exposure.

Method: Collapsed firm-lender OLS on the subsample of NBFCs/nonbanks as borrowers, mirroring the Khwaja-Mian bank-lending setup. The dependent variable is the post-minus-pre change in log(1+loan amount) from banks to NBFC borrowers. The key regressor is the bank's change in average post-versus-pre AQR exposure. Specifications include firm fixed effects, optional lender controls (pre-AQR bank size and CAR), and a robustness excluding Prompt Corrective Action bank-years. Standard errors are clustered at the lender level.

Identification: The identification parallels the main collapsed within-borrower lending design, here restricted to NBFC borrowers. Firm fixed effects compare different bank lenders to the same NBFC borrower, aiming to absorb NBFC-specific credit demand. The assumption is that, within an NBFC, differences across bank lenders in AQR exposure generate differential supply contractions in refinancing. Remaining concerns are analogous to the main setting: endogenous lender-borrower matching and omitted bank shocks correlated with exposure.

Setting: To test spillovers to shadow banks, the authors examine bank lending to NBFCs as borrowers. Table 11 reports negative coefficients on Average lender exposure ranging from -8.1644 to -2.7305, with economic significance from -50.65% to -18.49% depending on controls and exclusion of PCA bank-years. They interpret these estimates as evidence that AQR-exposed banks reduced refinancing to shadow banks, contributing to contagion beyond the directly regulated banking sector.

Main role: This is an important spillover analysis supporting the broader real-economy consequences, but it is secondary to the paper's main lending, capitalization, and firm-investment results.
Settings.H21: Section 6.2.1 'Impact on refinancing by banks', Table 11 columns 1-4 (PDF page 39; article p. 4170).
Settings.N21: Table 11, p. 4170, columns 2-4 only: nonbinary change in average bank AQR exposure affects the post-minus-pre difference in log(1+loans) to NBFC borrowers, using borrower firm FE; cols. 3-4 add pre-AQR lender controls, col. 4 excludes PCA observations. Column 1 has no FE and is separated into h2.
Settings.O21: Human_main=1: shadow-bank contagion is explicitly a central finding in the abstract (p. 4132), introduction (pp. 4135-4136), and conclusion (p. 4173); Section 6.2.1 / Table 11 supplies direct evidence. Economic-significance rows use treatment SD, not outcome benchmarks.
Settings.G22:
Treatment: District exposure to AQR measured either continuously as branch-weighted average bank exposure (using number of bank branches in the district as weights) or as a binary indicator High branch-weighted exposure equal to one if that district-year exposure is above the median.

Method: District-year OLS with district and year fixed effects relating district exposure to AQR to local economic activity proxies. District exposure is constructed as a branch-weighted average of banks' AQR exposure, using the number of branches in the district as weights; an alternative binary treatment indicates districts above the median branch-weighted exposure. Outcomes are growth in nighttime lights and growth in MNREGA wage payments. Standard errors are clustered by district.

Identification: Because AQR was nationwide, identification comes from cross-district heterogeneity in exposure based on branch presence of more exposed banks. District fixed effects absorb time-invariant local characteristics and year fixed effects absorb nationwide shocks. The causal interpretation assumes that, conditional on these fixed effects, differences in branch-weighted exposure reflect differential local tightening in credit supply caused by AQR rather than other coincident district-specific shocks correlated with exposed bank branch networks. The paper acknowledges data and measurement challenges and presents these as evidence on broader economic impact rather than the cleanest design in the paper.

Setting: At the district level, the authors link higher local exposure to AQR-affected bank branches to weaker economic activity. In Table 12, the continuous branch-weighted exposure measure is negatively associated with night-light growth (-0.1084) but falls just short of conventional significance, while the high-exposure dummy is significantly negative at -0.0154. For distress, branch-weighted exposure is positively associated with MNREGA wage growth (0.8810), and high branch-weighted exposure raises MNREGA wage growth by 0.0789, which the authors summarize as about 8% higher in highly exposed districts. These estimates are used to argue that AQR-induced credit contraction spilled over to regional growth and local distress.

Main role: These district-level results extend the main findings to aggregate real activity and local distress, supporting the paper's concluding claim that AQR adversely affected growth in exposed regions.
Settings.H22: Section 6.3 'Impact on the economy', Table 12 columns 1-4 (PDF page 40; article p. 4171).
Settings.N22: Table 12, p. 4171, columns 1 and 3 only: continuous branch-weighted district AQR exposure, using bank-branch counts as weights, affects growth in nighttime luminosity and growth in the district MNREGA wage bill. District and year FE; district-clustered inference. Coefficients -0.1084 and 0.8810. Binary high-exposure columns 2 and 4 are separated into h3.
Settings.O22: Replaces pooled binary=unknown with the known continuous treatment. Table 2, p. 4149, and Table 12 distinguish the continuous score from its above-median indicator. No qualifying mean/SD/level benchmark found for the continuous columns.
Settings.G23:
Treatment: Fundamental-to-market ranking: the lagged FM decile (1 to 10) assigned from sorting stocks on FE/ME at June of year t, where FE is estimated fundamental equity and ME is market equity. The estimand is the return effect of moving from low to high FM; coefficients are scaled to represent the annualized decile-10 minus decile-1 spread.

Method: The paper interprets cross-portfolio regressions of subsequent value-weighted portfolio returns on a single sorting-variable decile rank as estimating the return premium associated with a higher value signal. Portfolios are formed each June from 1973 to 2018 on deciles of FM = FE/ME, where FE is estimated out-of-sample from a firm-level VAR using accounting characteristics and then scaled by market equity. The reported coefficient is the slope from a pooled panel regression of portfolio returns on lagged portfolio deciles, multiplied by 9×12 so units correspond to an annualized high-minus-low decile spread. Inference uses Driscoll-Kraay standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and cross-portfolio correlation. This is a regression-adjustment design without an external quasi-experimental source of variation.

Identification: The paper treats cross-sectional variation in the estimated FM signal as revealing differences in long-term expected returns because FE is constructed as the present value of expected payouts under a common discount rate across firms. The identifying argument is valuation-based rather than quasi-experimental: firms with higher FE/ME should have higher expected subsequent returns, and sorting on FM should therefore predict realized returns. Endogeneity is not resolved by an external design; the claim relies on the maintained asset-pricing interpretation that FE better captures cash-flow fundamentals than BE and that out-of-sample VAR forecasts mitigate data-mining concerns.

Setting: Using univariate panel regressions of portfolio returns on FM deciles for 1-year holding-period portfolios, the paper reports that moving from the lowest to highest FM decile is associated with an 8.3% annualized return spread in the full sample (t = 4.50), 9.2% in 1973–1995, and 7.4% in 1996–2018. The authors interpret this as evidence that the fundamental-to-market ratio captures a strong and stable value premium. This setting is central to the paper’s argument that the apparent decline in the value premium is due to book equity becoming a worse proxy for fundamental equity rather than a true disappearance of the underlying premium.

Main role: A central claim of the paper is that the premium associated with FE/ME is strong and stable and that this undermines the apparent decline in the traditional value premium. The abstract, introduction, Figure 1, Table 5, and conclusion all emphasize this result.
Settings.H23: Table 6, Panel A, row FM, columns 'Univariate' for Full Sample / 1973 to 1995 / 1996 to 2018; Section 4.4; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G24:
Treatment: Lagged FM decile (1 to 10) constructed from FE/ME sorts, with the effect scaled to correspond to the annualized return difference between decile 10 and decile 1 for 5-year holding-period strategies.

Method: This setting uses the same pooled panel regression framework as s1 but for 5-year holding-period portfolio returns. Each reported coefficient is the average slope from five panel regressions using sorting signals dated t through t−4, multiplied by 9×12 to match an annualized high-minus-low decile spread. Portfolios are value-weighted and sorted on FM. Inference uses Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. The design remains regression adjustment rather than a quasi-experiment.

Identification: Identification again comes from cross-sectional differences in the FM signal, which the paper interprets as variation in long-term expected returns implied by the valuation identity and the estimated FE measure. The strategy assumes the out-of-sample VAR-based FE captures expected cash flows sufficiently well that FM primarily reflects discount-rate variation rather than omitted cash-flow components.

Setting: For 5-year holding-period portfolios, the univariate panel regressions show a 6.5% annualized full-sample FM spread (t = 4.37), with 7.9% in 1973–1995 and 5.0% in 1996–2018. The authors interpret this as evidence that the FM premium is not merely short-lived but remains economically important over longer horizons, reinforcing their core claim that the underlying value premium has not declined when measured with FE/ME.

Main role: The paper explicitly argues that FM captures long-term expected returns; the 5-year holding-period evidence is used to show persistence of the FM premium and is highlighted in the main text as corroborating the central claim.
Settings.H24: Table 6, Panel B, row FM, columns 'Univariate' for Full Sample / 1973 to 1995 / 1996 to 2018; Section 4.4; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G25:
Treatment: Primary focal treatment is the lagged BM decile (1 to 10), i.e., ranking on BE/ME. The specification conditions on FM decile to estimate the marginal return premium associated with BM beyond FM.

Method: The paper estimates pooled panel regressions of 1-year-ahead portfolio returns on both FM and BM decile ranks using the method of Gonçalves (2021). Twenty portfolios are used: ten formed on FM and ten on BM, and each portfolio is assigned average FM and BM deciles of the stocks it contains. Coefficients are multiplied by 9×12 to be comparable to an annualized high-minus-low spread. This is a multivariate regression-adjustment design used to assess whether FM subsumes BM in predicting returns.

Identification: The identifying variation is residual cross-portfolio variation in BM ranks after conditioning on FM ranks. The paper’s interpretation is that if BM predicts returns only through its correlation with the more fundamental FM signal, then controlling for FM should eliminate or materially weaken the BM premium. This remains an observational comparison relying on the valuation framework rather than exogenous variation.

Setting: In 1-year holding-period panel regressions including both FM and BM deciles, the paper finds that the BM premium falls to 3.6% annually in the full sample (t = 1.25), versus 4.3% in 1973–1995 (t = 0.91) and 1.5% in 1996–2018 (t = 0.36). The authors interpret these estimates as showing that the traditional book-to-market premium is statistically insignificant once the correlation between BM and FM is controlled for, so FM largely subsumes BM as a value signal.

Main role: A headline result in the introduction, abstract, Section 4.4, and conclusion is that FE/ME subsumes the BE/ME premium; this conditional BM analysis is key evidence for that claim.
Settings.H25: Table 6, Panel A, row BM, column [1] for Full Sample / 1973 to 1995 / 1996 to 2018; Section 4.4; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G26:
Treatment: Lagged BM decile (1 to 10), based on BE/ME, entered jointly with FM decile. The estimand is the annualized long-horizon return spread attributable to BM conditional on FM.

Method: This setting uses the same bivariate pooled panel regression framework as s3, but for 5-year holding-period portfolio returns. Coefficients are the average slope from five regressions using signals dated t through t−4 and are scaled by 9×12. The design evaluates whether BM has any marginal long-horizon predictive effect once FM is included.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in BM across portfolios holding FM constant in the multivariate panel regression. The causal interpretation relies on the maintained assumption that FM better isolates expected-return variation, so any remaining BM effect would represent marginal information not already contained in FM.

Setting: For 5-year holding-period strategies, the conditional BM coefficient is 2.8% in the full sample (t = 1.04), 4.5% in 1973–1995 (t = 0.92), and 0.2% in 1996–2018 (t = 0.06). The paper interprets these small and insignificant estimates as showing that BM does not add meaningful long-horizon return predictability once FM is controlled for.

Main role: The long-horizon conditional BM results reinforce the main claim that the BM premium is subsumed by FM and that the value premium decline is only apparent.
Settings.H26: Table 6, Panel B, row BM, column [1] for Full Sample / 1973 to 1995 / 1996 to 2018; Section 4.4; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G27:
Treatment: Lagged FM decile (1 to 10), based on FE/ME, entered jointly with BM decile. The coefficient measures the annualized return spread associated with FM after controlling for BE/ME ranking.

Method: This is the companion multivariate pooled panel regression to s3, with 1-year holding-period returns regressed on both FM and BM deciles. The focal treatment here is FM conditional on BM. The implementation uses 20 portfolios and average portfolio deciles as regressors, with coefficients scaled by 9×12 and Driscoll-Kraay inference.

Identification: The estimating variation is cross-portfolio variation in FM rank conditional on BM rank. The paper’s maintained assumption is that FM captures the relevant expected-return component while BM is a noisy proxy, so a strong conditional FM coefficient indicates that FE/ME contains independent pricing information beyond book-to-market.

Setting: With 1-year holding-period returns and both FM and BM in the regression, the FM premium is 8.7% annually in the full sample (t = 4.29), 7.8% in 1973–1995 (t = 1.95), and 8.7% in 1996–2018 (t = 3.47). The authors read this as evidence that the FM premium is robust to controlling for BM and remains stable across subsamples, supporting their claim that the underlying value premium has not declined.

Main role: Showing that FM remains strong after controlling for BM is one of the main empirical demonstrations that FE/ME subsumes the standard value signal.
Settings.H27: Table 6, Panel A, row FM, column [1] for Full Sample / 1973 to 1995 / 1996 to 2018; Section 4.4; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G28:
Treatment: Lagged FM decile (1 to 10), based on FE/ME, included jointly with BM decile. The coefficient maps to the annualized 5-year strategy spread from decile 1 to decile 10 in FM holding BM fixed.

Method: Same multivariate panel regression approach as s5, but using 5-year holding-period portfolio returns. The reported coefficient is the average across regressions using signals lagged t through t−4, scaled by 9×12. This estimates FM’s long-horizon return premium conditional on BM.

Identification: Identification relies on differences in FM ranks across portfolios net of BM ranks. The interpretation assumes FE/ME more closely maps into long-term expected returns than BE/ME, so the conditional FM coefficient captures the economically meaningful value effect.

Setting: For 5-year holding-period returns, FM remains strong after controlling for BM: 7.1% in the full sample (t = 3.42), 5.6% in 1973–1995 (t = 1.40), and 6.7% in 1996–2018 (t = 3.15). The paper uses this as further evidence that FE/ME, not BE/ME, captures the persistent value premium.

Main role: The long-horizon conditional FM results are emphasized to show persistence and to link FM to long-term expected returns, a central theoretical and empirical point of the paper.
Settings.H28: Table 6, Panel B, row FM, column [1] for Full Sample / 1973 to 1995 / 1996 to 2018; Section 4.4; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G29:
Treatment: Big-firm FM decile (FMBig), a 1–10 ranking on FE/ME formed using only firms above the NYSE median market equity. In the bivariate specification [1], FMBig is entered jointly with BMBig.

Method: The paper estimates univariate and bivariate pooled panel regressions of 1-year-ahead portfolio returns using size-split FM and BM deciles. Portfolios are formed separately among big firms and small firms, where size is based on the NYSE median market equity as in Fama and French (1993). Coefficients are annualized high-minus-low style spreads from portfolio-decile regressions with Driscoll-Kraay inference.

Identification: The paper uses cross-sectional return variation within the big-firm subsample to ask whether FM continues to predict returns after isolating the sample from small firms. The identifying argument is the same valuation-based one as in the main analysis, now applied within a size segment and with or without control for the corresponding big-firm BM signal.

Setting: Among big firms, the univariate FM premium is 6.4% in the full sample (t = 3.60), 7.8% in 1973–1995, and 5.0% in 1996–2018; controlling for big-firm BM yields 7.0%, 7.0%, and 6.7%, respectively. The paper interprets this as evidence that FE/ME predicts returns even among large firms and does not exhibit the pronounced decline seen for book-to-market.

Main role: These size-split analyses are robustness and heterogeneity checks supporting the broader claim that FM dominates BM across firm-size segments.
Settings.H29: Table 7, Panel A, row FMBig, columns Univariate and [1]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G30:
Treatment: Big-firm BM decile (BMBig), a 1–10 ranking on BE/ME among firms above the NYSE median market equity, estimated jointly with FMBig in specification [1].

Method: Using the size-split portfolio panel regression framework, the paper estimates the marginal BM premium among big firms, conditional on the corresponding FM signal. Portfolios are restricted to firms above the NYSE median market equity and coefficients are scaled to annualized high-minus-low spreads.

Identification: Cross-sectional variation in BMBig conditional on FMBig is used to test whether BM contains marginal pricing information within large firms. The strategy is observational and depends on the paper’s interpretation that FM more cleanly captures expected-return variation.

Setting: Among big firms, the univariate BM premium is 2.6% in the full sample (t = 1.16), 5.9% in 1973–1995, and −0.7% in 1996–2018; conditional on FMBig it is 2.9%, 3.1%, and 1.3%. The authors interpret these weak estimates as evidence that BM has little incremental ability to explain the value premium among large firms once FM is considered.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness analysis showing that BM is weak relative to FM in the large-firm segment.
Settings.H30: Table 7, Panel A, row BMBig, columns Univariate and [1]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G31:
Treatment: Small-firm FM decile (FMSmall), a 1–10 ranking on FE/ME formed only among firms below the NYSE median market equity. In specification [2], FMSmall is entered jointly with BMSmall.

Method: This setting uses the same size-split panel regression framework as s7–s8 but for small firms, defined as below the NYSE median market equity. Univariate and bivariate portfolio-decile regressions relate subsequent returns to the small-firm FM and BM rankings.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-small-firm cross-sectional variation in FM rank, with or without conditioning on small-firm BM rank. The interpretation again rests on the valuation identity and the assumption that FM is a better proxy for expected returns than BM.

Setting: Among small firms, the univariate FM premium is 8.7% in the full sample (t = 4.78), 9.9% in 1973–1995, and 7.5% in 1996–2018; conditional on BMSmall it is 8.4%, 2.5%, and 10.8%. The paper treats this as further evidence that FM predicts returns across size groups, though the early-sample conditional estimate is imprecise.

Main role: A supporting heterogeneity analysis showing FM’s strength among small firms as well.
Settings.H31: Table 7, Panel A, row FMSmall, columns Univariate and [2]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G32:
Treatment: Small-firm BM decile (BMSmall), a 1–10 ranking on BE/ME among firms below the NYSE median market equity, estimated jointly with FMSmall in specification [2].

Method: This is the small-firm counterpart to s8: pooled portfolio panel regressions of subsequent returns on the BMSmall decile with or without control for FMSmall. Coefficients are annualized high-minus-low style spreads.

Identification: Variation in BMSmall conditional on FMSmall is used to assess whether book-to-market adds independent pricing information within small firms. This remains a nonexperimental, valuation-based interpretation.

Setting: Among small firms, the univariate BM premium is 3.1% in the full sample (t = 1.26), 6.3% in 1973–1995, and −0.1% in 1996–2018; conditional on FMSmall it is 2.5%, 7.8%, and −0.2%. The authors note that although the early-sample conditional estimate is economically larger, BM remains statistically insignificant in both subsamples and does not overturn the dominance of FM.

Main role: This is a robustness result used to show BM weakens relative to FM even in the small-firm segment.
Settings.H32: Table 7, Panel A, row BMSmall, columns Univariate and [2]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G33:
Treatment: FMwithin decile, a 1–10 ranking based on within-industry deviations of FE/ME from the median FE/ME in the firm's Fama-French 48 industry. In specification [1], FMwithin is included jointly with FMacross.

Method: The paper decomposes FM into within-industry and across-industry components and runs pooled panel regressions of 1-year-ahead portfolio returns on deciles formed from these components. FMwithin is firm FM minus industry median FM; FMacross is the industry median FM. Portfolios are formed on these signals and coefficients are scaled annualized high-minus-low spreads.

Identification: The strategy exploits cross-sectional variation in industry-relative FM. By comparing firms with higher or lower FE/ME than peers within the same industry, the paper assesses whether the FM premium is a within-industry phenomenon versus an across-industry one. Interpretation remains observational.

Setting: The within-industry FM premium is 4.9% univariately in the full sample (t = 2.87), 7.7% in 1973–1995, and 2.2% in 1996–2018; controlling for the across-industry FM component raises the corresponding estimates to 8.7%, 9.4%, and 9.5%. The paper interprets this as evidence that FM’s predictive power has an important within-industry component but is not limited to it.

Main role: This is a supporting decomposition showing the channels through which FM predicts returns and how they differ from BM.
Settings.H33: Table 7, Panel B, row FMwithin, columns Univariate and [1]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G34:
Treatment: FMacross decile, a 1–10 ranking based on the industry-level median FE/ME in the firm's Fama-French 48 industry. In specification [1], FMacross is estimated jointly with FMwithin.

Method: This setting estimates the across-industry FM component’s association with returns using pooled portfolio-decile regressions. FMacross is the industry median FM, and specifications may include FMwithin as a control.

Identification: The design uses between-industry variation in industry median FM to assess whether industries with higher FE/ME earn higher subsequent returns. The interpretation assumes industry-level FM captures industry differences in long-term expected returns.

Setting: The across-industry FM premium is 4.4% univariately in the full sample (t = 2.53), 3.0% in 1973–1995, and 5.9% in 1996–2018; conditional on FMwithin it is 7.5%, 5.6%, and 11.0%. The authors interpret this as evidence that the FM premium also has an across-industry component, unlike BM.

Main role: This is a robustness/decomposition exercise used to show FM combines within- and across-industry information.
Settings.H34: Table 7, Panel B, row FMacross, columns Univariate and [1]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G35:
Treatment: BMwithin decile, a 1–10 ranking based on within-industry deviations of BE/ME from the industry median BE/ME. In specification [2], BMwithin is included jointly with BMacross.

Method: This setting applies the within/across-industry portfolio-decile regression framework to BM. BMwithin is firm BM minus industry median BM, and BMacross is the industry median BM. Returns are regressed on BMwithin deciles, with or without controlling for BMacross.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in BM relative to firms in the same industry. The paper interprets this as isolating the within-industry component of the value effect associated with book-to-market.

Setting: The within-industry BM premium is 5.4% univariately in the full sample (t = 2.60), 7.1% in 1973–1995, and 3.8% in 1996–2018; controlling for BMacross gives 6.3%, 8.2%, and 3.6%. The paper interprets this as showing that BM’s predictive content is concentrated within industries and weakens over time.

Main role: This decomposition supports the paper’s claim that BM is mainly a within-industry phenomenon and that its decline is tied to that component.
Settings.H35: Table 7, Panel B, row BMwithin, columns Univariate and [2]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G36:
Treatment: BMacross decile, a 1–10 ranking based on the industry-level median BE/ME in the firm's Fama-French 48 industry. In specification [2], BMacross is entered jointly with BMwithin.

Method: This setting is the across-industry BM counterpart to s13, estimating pooled panel regressions of returns on BMacross deciles, with or without BMwithin as a control. Coefficients are annualized spread equivalents.

Identification: The strategy uses between-industry differences in median BM to test for an across-industry value effect based on book-to-market. The interpretation is again observational and valuation-based.

Setting: The across-industry BM premium is only 0.3% univariately in the full sample (t = 0.17), 1.3% in 1973–1995, and −0.6% in 1996–2018; conditional on BMwithin it is 0.7%, 2.1%, and −0.3%. The paper interprets these near-zero estimates as showing that BM’s value effect is not meaningfully an across-industry phenomenon.

Main role: A supporting decomposition result showing that BM has little across-industry predictive power.
Settings.H36: Table 7, Panel B, row BMacross, columns Univariate and [2]; PDF p. 14.
Settings.G37:
Treatment: Alternative value-signal decile (1 to 10), where the signal is one of: BE/ME, BEint/ME, RE/ME, Y/ME, GP/ME, E/ME, PO/ME, fitted-value \u005chat{ME}/ME, or ICC. Each coefficient corresponds to the annualized high-minus-low spread implied by moving from the lowest to highest signal decile; in bivariate specifications the signal is conditioned on FM decile.

Method: The paper evaluates alternative value signals one at a time using pooled panel regressions of 1-year-ahead portfolio returns on the signal’s decile rank, and then in bivariate specifications including FM deciles. Signals include BE/ME, BEint/ME, RE/ME, Y/ME, GP/ME, E/ME, PO/ME, fitted-value M-hat/ME, and ICC. Coefficients are scaled by 9×12 and estimated with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. This is a family of regression-adjustment specifications comparing alternative return predictors to FM.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in each alternative value-signal ranking, either alone or net of FM. The paper’s argument is comparative: if alternative proxies for long-term cash-flow fundamentals were sufficient, their premia should remain stable and survive conditioning on FM. The observed weakening and subsumption are interpreted as evidence that FM better isolates expected-return variation.

Setting: Across alternative value signals in 1-year holding-period regressions, the paper finds that each signal’s return premium weakens in the late sample and tends to be reduced once FM is controlled for. Examples: BE/ME has a 4.2% full-sample univariate spread and 3.6% conditional on FM; BEint/ME has 6.7% univariately and 5.2% conditional on FM; Y/ME has 5.0% univariately and 6.4% conditional on FM but falls from 8.3% early to 1.6% late univariately; ICC has 5.1% univariately and 4.9% conditional on FM. The authors interpret this body of evidence as showing that alternative value signals also exhibit decline and are generally weaker than, and largely subsumed by, FM.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state that FE/ME captures the value premium better than several alternative value signals beyond BE/ME. These comparative regressions directly support that central contribution.
Settings.H37: Table 8, Panel A, all rows under 'Alternative Value Signals one at a Time'; Section 5.2; PDF p. 15.
Settings.G38:
Treatment: Alternative value-signal decile (1 to 10), where the signal is one of: BE/ME, BEint/ME, RE/ME, Y/ME, GP/ME, E/ME, PO/ME, fitted-value \u005chat{ME}/ME, or ICC; coefficients correspond to annualized long-horizon high-minus-low spreads, with optional control for FM decile.

Method: This setting repeats the alternative-value-signal comparison from s15 for 5-year holding-period returns. Each coefficient is the average slope from five panel regressions using current and up to four lagged sorting signals, scaled by 9×12. FM is included in bivariate specifications. Inference is Driscoll-Kraay.

Identification: Cross-sectional variation in alternative value-signal rankings is used to predict long-horizon returns, alone or conditional on FM. The paper interprets the long-horizon decline and FM subsumption as evidence against these alternative signals being stable measures of the true value effect.

Setting: For 5-year holding-period strategies, alternative value signals again weaken relative to FM. For example, BE/ME yields a 3.4% full-sample univariate spread and 2.8% conditional on FM; BEint/ME gives 5.2% univariately and 4.2% conditional on FM; ICC gives 4.3% univariately and 5.2% conditional on FM. Most signals show large early-to-late declines, and the paper emphasizes that these declines are at least as pronounced at long horizons, strengthening the case that FM is the more stable value signal.

Main role: These long-horizon comparisons are supporting evidence for the central claim that FM dominates alternative value signals, especially for long-term returns.
Settings.H38: Table 9, Panel A, all rows under 'Alternative Value Signals one at a Time'; Section 5.2; PDF p. 16.
Settings.G39:
Treatment: Portfolio decile rank on an alternative value signal, interacted with IEarly and ILate to allow different return slopes by subperiod; in the second specification FM decile is also included. The treatment is nonbinary and pooled across all non-FM alternative signals.

Method: The paper pools portfolios formed on all alternative value signals except FM and estimates panel regressions of returns on signal deciles interacted with early/late sample indicators, with and without a control for the FM decile. Year fixed effects are included via ayear in the regression. Coefficients are scaled by 9×12. This joint regression is used to gain statistical power when assessing whether alternative value signals collectively exhibit a declining premium and whether FM subsumes them.

Identification: The specification exploits pooled cross-portfolio variation across many alternative signals and allows separate early and late slopes. The interpretation is that if non-FM value proxies captured the true value effect, their average slope should remain stable and survive inclusion of FM. The late-sample collapse and attenuation with FM are read as evidence against that.

Setting: When all alternative value signals are analyzed jointly for 1-year holding periods, the pooled decile slope is 8.5% in the early sample and 1.7% in the late sample, a decline of −6.8% (t = −1.79). Once FM deciles are added, the FM coefficient is 16.4% (t = 3.63) and the early and late alternative-signal slopes shrink to 1.5% and −0.1%, respectively. The authors interpret this as pooled evidence that alternative value signals collectively show a declining premium that is subsumed by FM.

Main role: This joint specification is a supporting summary exercise used to reinforce the comparative claim that alternative value signals decline and are subsumed by FM.
Settings.H39: Table 8, Panel B, 'Alternative Value Signals Jointly'; Section 5.2; PDF p. 15.
Settings.G40:
Treatment: Portfolio decile rank on a pooled set of alternative non-FM value signals, interacted with early and late period indicators; FM decile is included in the second specification.

Method: This is the 5-year holding-period analogue of s17. Portfolios formed on all alternative value signals except FM are pooled, and returns are regressed on early/late interacted deciles with and without FM deciles. Coefficients are averages across five lag structures and are scaled by 9×12.

Identification: The pooled long-horizon regression uses cross-signal, cross-portfolio variation and subperiod interactions to test whether the average predictive slope of alternative value signals declines and whether FM explains it away. Interpretation remains comparative and observational.

Setting: For 5-year holding periods, the pooled alternative-signal decile slope is 7.7% in the early sample and 0.9% in the late sample, implying a −6.8% decline (t = −2.06). With FM included, the FM coefficient is 11.3% (t = 3.39) while the early and late pooled alternative-signal slopes are 2.4% and −0.3%. The paper interprets this as especially strong long-horizon evidence that FM dominates alternative value signals.

Main role: A supporting long-horizon pooled comparison reinforcing that the decline in non-FM value signals is stronger over long horizons and that FM dominates.
Settings.H40: Table 9, Panel B, 'Alternative Value Signals Jointly'; Section 5.2; PDF p. 16.
Settings.G41:
Treatment: Lagged BM decile (1 to 10), based on BE/ME, included in multivariate portfolio-return regressions with controls for Size, Inv, Prof, and/or Qual depending on specification [1]–[4].

Method: The paper runs pooled panel regressions of 1-year-ahead portfolio returns on BM deciles while controlling separately or jointly for other valuation-related portfolio deciles: size, investment, profitability, and quality. Portfolios are value-weighted, deciles are based on the respective signals, and coefficients are scaled by 9×12. These regressions assess the marginal BM effect after adjusting for other characteristics motivated by valuation identities and the quality-minus-junk literature.

Identification: The identifying variation is the cross-portfolio component of BM deciles orthogonal to the included control-signal deciles. The paper interprets these regressions through a valuation-identity lens: controlling for size, investment, profitability, and quality should partial out cash-flow-related components that contaminate BM. The resulting relative stability of the conditional BM effect is viewed as consistent with the broader FE/ME logic.

Setting: For 1-year holding periods, BM’s univariate premium is 4.2%, but conditional on Size and Inv it rises to 19.2%; with Size, Inv, and Prof it is 8.4%; with Quality alone it is 18.5%; and with all controls it remains economically large in some specifications. Across early and late samples, the paper emphasizes that BM’s conditional effect is more stable over time than the raw BM premium, supporting the idea that BM’s predictive content should be assessed controlling for other valuation effects.

Main role: This section connects the paper to prior literature and is important substantively, but it is framed as an extension rather than the core evidence for the main claim.
Settings.H41: Table 10, Panel A, row BM, columns [1]–[4]; Section 5.4; PDF p. 17.
Settings.G42:
Treatment: Lagged BM decile (1 to 10), based on BE/ME, included in multivariate 5-year holding-period portfolio-return regressions with Size, Inv, Prof, and/or Qual controls depending on specification [1]–[4].

Method: This is the 5-year holding-period analogue of s19. Pooled portfolio panel regressions relate long-horizon returns to BM deciles plus controls for size, investment, profitability, and/or quality. Each coefficient is the average slope across five lagged-signal regressions and is scaled by 9×12.

Identification: The strategy uses cross-portfolio variation in BM conditional on control-signal deciles to assess the long-horizon marginal BM effect. The interpretation is the same as s19 but focused on long-term returns, where the paper argues value investing is more naturally defined.

Setting: For 5-year holding periods, BM’s univariate premium is 3.4%, while conditional BM coefficients are 18.5% with Size and Inv controls, 6.5% with Size/Inv/Prof, 17.2% with Quality, and similarly large in some pooled-control specifications. The paper interprets these results as showing that BM’s conditional predictive effect is more stable over time than its raw premium, though FM remains the stronger single value signal.

Main role: A supporting extension linking the paper’s findings to long-horizon versions of the valuation-identity control literature.
Settings.H42: Table 11, Panel A, row BM, columns [1]–[4]; Section 5.4; PDF p. 21.
Settings.G43:
Treatment: Composite value-signal decile (1 to 10) based on ErIS or ErOOS combinations of BM with Size+Inv+Prof, with Qual, or with All controls. In bivariate specifications the composite-signal decile is entered jointly with FM decile.

Method: The paper constructs composite expected-return signals Er that combine BM with other valuation effects using coefficients from Fama-MacBeth regressions on cross-sectional quantiles of the component characteristics. It then estimates pooled panel regressions of 1-year-ahead portfolio returns on deciles of these composite signals, with and without FM deciles. Both in-sample (ErIS) and out-of-sample expanding-window (ErOOS) versions are analyzed. Coefficients are scaled annualized high-minus-low spreads.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in deciles of composite return-prediction signals designed to summarize BM plus other characteristics.
