The paper’s comparative interpretation is that if these composite signals captured the underlying value effect better than FM, they would be at least as strong, stable, and resistant to subsumption by FM. They are not.

Setting: For 1-year holding periods, composite Er signals formed from BM plus other characteristics predict returns but tend to decline over time and weaken when FM is included. For example, ErIS(BM+Size+Inv+Prof) has a 7.7% full-sample univariate premium and 6.8% conditional on FM, but falls from 13.6% early to 1.8% late; ErOOS(BM+All) has a 7.0% full-sample premium and 3.3% conditional on FM. The paper interprets these results as showing that even sophisticated combinations of BM with other valuation effects do not capture the value premium more robustly than FM.

Main role: This is a substantive extension addressing whether combining BM with other valuation effects can outperform FM; it supports the central claim by showing the answer is no.
Settings.H43: Table 10, Panel B, all rows under 'Value Signals Combining BM with Size, Investment, Profitability, and Quality'; Section 5.4; PDF p. 17.
Settings.G44:
Treatment: Composite value-signal decile (1 to 10) based on 5-year-horizon ErIS or ErOOS combinations of BM with Size+Inv+Prof, with Qual, or with All controls. In bivariate specifications, the composite decile is estimated jointly with FM decile.

Method: This is the 5-year holding-period version of s21. Composite ErIS and ErOOS signals combining BM with other valuation effects are used to form decile portfolios, and pooled panel regressions of long-horizon returns on those deciles are estimated, with and without FM deciles. Each coefficient is averaged across five lag structures and scaled by 9×12.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in composite expected-return-signal deciles across portfolios over long horizons, optionally net of FM. The interpretation is again comparative: FM is judged against other constructed value signals on strength, stability, and subsumption.

Setting: For 5-year holding periods, composite BM-based Er signals continue to predict returns but are generally weaker and less stable than FM. For instance, ErIS(BM+Size+Inv+Prof) has a 5.5% univariate premium and 5.3% conditional on FM, while ErOOS(BM+All) has a 5.0% univariate premium and 3.0% conditional on FM. The paper reads this as long-horizon evidence that FM remains the stronger and more stable single value signal.

Main role: A supporting long-horizon extension showing that composite BM-based signals still do not outperform FM in capturing the value premium.
Settings.H44: Table 11, Panel B, all rows under 'Value Signals Combining BM with Size, Investment, Profitability, and Quality'; Section 5.4; PDF p. 21.
Settings.G45:
Treatment: Assignment to the high versus low decile portfolio based on FM, BM, or BF sort at June. The principal focal contrast emphasized by the paper is high minus low FM versus high minus low BM.

Method: The paper reports value-weighted high-minus-low decile portfolio return contrasts from direct portfolio sorts on FM, BM, and BF over the full sample, early sample, late sample, and large-firm subsamples. These are group-mean comparisons rather than regression coefficients. Because the requested taxonomy prioritizes linear regression-type estimators and this implementation is a pure portfolio sort contrast rather than a regression, it is classified as Other. The paper interprets these return spreads as the causal/predictive effect of a higher value signal on subsequent returns.

Identification: The strategy is based on sorting firms by the value signal and comparing average subsequent returns of high- and low-signal portfolios. The interpretation relies on the asset-pricing premise that higher FM identifies firms with higher long-term expected returns. There is no exogenous treatment variation; this is a substantive predictive/causal interpretation from observational portfolio contrasts.

Setting: The paper’s main portfolio-sort evidence shows that the annual high-minus-low FM return spread is 8.5% for 1-year holding periods versus 5.9% for BM, and that FM is stable over time (8.8% early vs. 8.2% late) while BM declines sharply (10.3% early vs. 1.5% late). For 5-year holding periods, FM yields a 7.0% spread versus 4.7% for BM, again with much greater stability. The authors interpret these contrasts as the core evidence that the true value premium persists when measured with FE/ME and only appears to decline when measured with BE/ME.

Main role: Figure 1 and Table 5 are among the paper’s main headline exhibits. The abstract and introduction explicitly discuss the high-minus-low FM and BM spreads and their stability/decline.
Settings.H45: Figure 1; Table 5, Panels A–C; discussion in Introduction and Section 4.3; PDF pp. 2, 11–13.
Settings.G46:
Treatment: Three alternative continuous treatments, each in a separately reported decomposition column but used for the same causal purpose: (i) log percentage change in the share of nontraditional borrowers attending for-profit institutions and community colleges from 2006 to 2009; (ii) log percentage change in zip-code home prices from 2006 to 2009; and (iii) log percentage change in zip-code employment from 2006 to 2009. All are continuous changes, not binary switches.

Method: The authors run cross-sectional weighted OLS regressions at the zip-code level over Great Recession long differences. The dependent variable is the log change in student loan default rates from 2007 to 2010, and regressors are separately the log change in the share of nontraditional borrowers from 2006 to 2009, the log change in home prices from 2006 to 2009, or the log change in employment from 2006 to 2009. Zip codes are weighted by total student loan balances; standard errors are clustered at the zip-code level. The paper uses these elasticities in a Blinder-Oaxaca-style decomposition to interpret how much of the aggregate rise in defaults is explained by compositional shifts or home-price declines. This is regression adjustment rather than a stronger quasi-experimental design, and the authors are cautious that some evidence is descriptive rather than fully causal.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation across zip codes in changes in borrower composition, home prices, or employment over the Great Recession. The intended interpretation is that these shocks explain portions of the rise in defaults, but the paper does not claim a clean exogenous design here. Endogeneity concerns include omitted local shocks and compositional differences across places; the exercise is used as an accounting/decomposition framework rather than a fully causal design.

Setting: Using weighted zip-code-level long-difference regressions, the authors estimate that a 1% increase in the share of nontraditional borrowers is associated with a 0.3282% increase in student loan defaults, while a 1% increase in home prices is associated with a 0.4179% decrease in defaults; employment changes have essentially zero explanatory power. Combining these elasticities with observed aggregate changes, they conclude that shifts in borrower composition explain 29.3% and falling home prices explain 31.8% of the 18.9% rise in defaults during the Great Recession. Although not based on a strong quasi-experiment, this decomposition materially supports the paper’s central claim about why defaults rose.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that compositional shifts and home-price collapse each account for about 30% of the rise in student loan defaults; this decomposition is a central headline contribution.
Settings.N46: Restricted to Table 2 column 1 (Section 3, pp. 7-9): change in log share of nontraditional borrowers, 2006-2009, explaining change in log new student-loan default rate, 2007-2010. Zip-code weighted OLS, weighted by total student-loan balances; zip-code clustered standard errors. Coefficient 0.3282; reported composition change 16.9%; share of overall default increase explained 29.3%. Home-price and employment regressions split to h1 and h2.
Settings.O46: Distinct treatments require separate settings. Composition contribution is a headline result in the abstract. Decomposition does not establish exogenous treatment variation.
Settings.G47:
Treatment: Current regional home price, measured as the natural log of Zillow home prices in year t at the zip-code, county, or commuting-zone level. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate regional panel linear regressions relating next-year regional student loan default rates to current regional log home prices. Regions are alternatively zip codes, counties, or commuting zones. All specifications include region fixed effects and year fixed effects, with observations weighted by total student loan balances and standard errors clustered at the regional level. They also report analogous long-difference regional regressions in Panel A, but the core implemented identifying panel design in this location is a two-way fixed-effects panel at the regional level. The design aims to absorb time-invariant regional heterogeneity and common macro shocks while using within-region home-price changes over time.

Identification: Identification relies on within-region changes in home prices over 2006–2009, controlling for region fixed effects to absorb permanent differences across places and year fixed effects to absorb economy-wide shocks. The key concern is omitted time-varying regional shocks correlated with home prices and defaults; the authors partly address serial correlation by clustering at the regional level and compare results across broader regional aggregations.

Setting: At the regional level, the authors find that falling home prices are associated with higher subsequent student loan default rates. In the panel specifications with region and year fixed effects, a one-unit increase in log home prices reduces next-year default rates by 0.00614 at the zip-code level, 0.00639 at the county level, and 0.00728 at the commuting-zone level. These results support the paper’s claim that the home-price collapse contributed to the rise in defaults, but they are presented mainly as corroborating evidence before the preferred borrower-level analyses.

Main role: These regional results motivate and reinforce the main borrower-level findings, but the paper states that the individual borrower panel specification becomes its main specification for the rest of the paper.
Settings.H47: Section 4, Table 3 Panel B columns 1–3 (with related long-difference evidence in Panel A), PDF p. 10.
Settings.N47: Scope restricted to Table 3, Panel B, columns 1-3 (Section 4, pp. 9-10): annual regional panel regressions of the new student-loan default rate in year t+1 on log home prices in year t, with region and year fixed effects. Regions are zip codes, counties, or commuting zones; observations are weighted by total student-loan balances and standard errors clustered at the corresponding regional level. Home prices cover 2006-2009 and recorded defaults 2007-2010. Coefficients are -0.00614, -0.00639, and -0.00728, respectively. Panel A long-difference results are outside this setting.
Settings.O47: Region FE absorb time-invariant regional heterogeneity and year FE absorb common annual shocks. Regional clustering addresses within-region error dependence for inference; it does not eliminate omitted time-varying regional confounders. Supporting regional evidence preceding the main borrower-level Table 4. No qualifying outcome-benchmark comparison found for Panel B. The p. 10 footnote 10 conversion using the 3.6% default rate refers to the Panel A elasticity, not this setting; Panel A coverage is deferred.
Settings.G48:
Treatment: Zip-code home price in year t, measured as the natural log of Zillow home prices. Continuous treatment; home prices are lagged relative to the default outcome because defaults are recorded with about a one-year delay.

Method: This is the paper’s main borrower-level linear fixed-effects panel design. The dependent variable is an indicator for whether borrower i newly defaults in year t+1. The treatment is zip-code log home price in year t. Baseline regressions include year and zip-code fixed effects; robustness variants in the same table add controls (loan balance, borrowing duration, family income, school type, Pell grant aid), cluster at county rather than zip-code level, include cohort-year fixed effects, include zip-code×cohort-year fixed effects, or include individual borrower fixed effects. Observations are weighted by individual loan balances. The intended design uses within-zip or within-borrower variation in home prices over time to absorb unobserved heterogeneity in local conditions and borrower composition.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-zip-code or within-borrower changes in local home prices during the Great Recession, net of year effects and fixed differences across zip codes, cohorts, or individuals. The main endogeneity concern is that changing borrower composition or unobserved local shocks may coincide with home-price declines; the paper addresses this by adding cohort-year, zip-code×cohort-year, and individual fixed effects, plus controls. The interpretation still requires that remaining time-varying unobservables correlated with local home-price changes do not drive default changes.

Setting: Using borrower-level panel regressions, the paper finds that lower local home prices raise subsequent student loan default risk. In the baseline specification with zip-code and year fixed effects, the coefficient on log home price is -0.0113 (s.e. 0.00280), implying that a 1% decline in home prices is associated with a 0.0113 percentage point increase in new defaults. This estimate is stable when clustering at the county level, adding borrower and loan controls, using cohort-year or zip-code×cohort-year fixed effects, and using individual borrower fixed effects (coefficient -0.0107). This is a core causal setting supporting the paper’s main claim that the Great Recession home-price collapse increased student loan defaults.

Main role: The introduction explicitly says the borrower-level panel specification constitutes the paper’s main specification throughout the rest of the paper, and the abstract highlights the negative effect of falling home prices on defaults.
Settings.N48: Table 4 columns 1-3, 5 and 6, Section 4, pp. 10-11: continuous log zip-code home prices in year t explaining individual new default in t+1, weighted by individual loan balances. Columns 1-3 use zip-code and calendar-year FE; column 5 uses zip-code x repayment-cohort FE plus calendar-year FE; column 6 uses individual and calendar-year FE. Column 4 is split to h3 because it separately includes zip-code, repayment-cohort and calendar-year FE. Baseline coefficient -0.0113; the paper interprets a 1% home-price decline as a 0.0113 percentage-point rise in new defaults.
Settings.O48: An interacted zip-code x cohort FE set counts as one dimension, not two. Table 4 column 4 has three separately included FE dimensions and a borrower-composition identification rationale (p. 10), satisfying the project HDFE definition. No valid benchmark comparison found for the retained FE estimates.
Settings.G49:
Treatment: Zip-code log home price in year t. Continuous treatment, estimated separately by institution type (public four-year, private four-year, for-profit, community college) and by Barron’s selectivity category.

Method: The authors re-estimate their main borrower-level two-way fixed-effects panel regression separately within institution-type and selectivity subsamples. The dependent variable is an indicator for new default in year t+1; the treatment is zip-code log home price in year t. All specifications include year and zip-code fixed effects, are weighted by individual loan balances, and cluster standard errors at the zip-code level. This is a heterogeneity analysis of the main FE design, not a different identifying strategy.

Identification: Same borrower-level fixed-effects logic as the main specification, but identification is assessed within institution-type or selectivity subsamples to address concern that home-price effects merely reflect changing composition toward riskier institutions. The assumption is that within each subgroup, remaining within-zip changes in home prices are not confounded by omitted time-varying shocks specific to that subgroup.

Setting: When the main borrower-level FE regression is estimated separately by school type, falling home prices continue to predict higher default risk across public, private, for-profit, community-college, selective, and nonselective institutions. Estimated coefficients on log home price are -0.00764 for public four-year institutions, -0.00787 for private four-year institutions, -0.0377 for for-profit institutions, -0.0220 for community colleges, -0.0205 for nonselective institutions, and -0.00668 for selective institutions. These heterogeneity results support the claim that the home-price effect is not driven solely by compositional shifts into a particular institution sector.

Main role: These subsample analyses support the generality of the main home-price result across institution types and selectivity groups, but are secondary robustness/heterogeneity results.
Settings.G50:
Treatment: Zip-code log home price in year t. Continuous treatment, estimated separately for borrowers with annual labor earnings < $20,000, $20,000–$40,000, $40,000–$60,000, and > $60,000.

Method: The authors estimate variants of the main borrower-level fixed-effects panel separately by borrower labor-earnings groups to study the labor-market channel. The dependent variable remains a new-default indicator in year t+1; the treatment is zip-code log home price in year t. All specifications include year and zip-code fixed effects, weight observations by individual loan balances, and cluster at the zip-code level. This is a subgroup analysis of the core FE regression focused on effect heterogeneity by pre-existing individual labor earnings.

Identification: Identification comes from within-zip-code changes in home prices over time, separately within earnings bins. The authors interpret larger effects for low-income borrowers as evidence for a labor-market mechanism. The maintained assumption is that within each income group, unobserved time-varying shocks do not differentially correlate with home-price changes in a way that explains the pattern.

Setting: The home-price effect on default is concentrated among low- and middle-income borrowers. In regressions with year and zip-code fixed effects, the coefficient on log home price is -0.0176 for borrowers earning under $20,000, -0.0129 for those earning $20,000–$40,000, -0.0113 for those earning $40,000–$60,000, and an insignificant -0.00498 for borrowers earning above $60,000. The monotonic decline in sensitivity across income groups is a central piece of evidence that falling home prices raised defaults primarily through labor-market distress affecting lower-income jobs.

Main role: The labor-market channel is a central mechanism in the abstract and conclusion; this table provides key evidence that the home-price effect is concentrated among lower-income borrowers.
Settings.N50: Table 6 columns 1-4, Section 5.1, pp. 11-12: log zip-code home prices in year t explaining new borrower default in t+1, separately by individual labor-earnings bands shown in the table. Zip-code and year FE, individual loan-balance weights, zip-code clustered standard errors. Coefficients -0.0176, -0.0129, -0.0113 and -0.00498 (last not significant).
Settings.O50: Remove unsupported model claim that earnings groups are pre-existing/predetermined: the cited table and discussion do not establish a fixed pre-recession classification. Do not infer an exogenous low-income treatment from subgrouping. Central labor-market-channel evidence; no qualifying magnitude comparison found.
Settings.G51:
Treatment: Zip-code log home price in year t, measured using Zillow data. Continuous treatment, estimated within earnings subsamples.

Method: To test the labor-market channel more directly, the authors estimate borrower-level linear fixed-effects regressions where the dependent variable is an indicator for a large labor-earnings drop in year t. The treatment is zip-code log home price in year t, estimated separately by borrower labor-earnings groups. All specifications include year and zip-code fixed effects, weight by individual loan balances, and cluster at the zip-code level. The outcome is substantive here because the paper interprets home prices as affecting labor earnings, which then affect defaults.

Identification: The design uses within-zip changes in home prices over time to explain within-group changes in the probability of a large earnings drop, controlling for zip-code and year fixed effects. The key assumption is that conditional on these FE, local home-price changes capture shocks affecting labor-market outcomes rather than omitted confounders. The authors use this as mechanism evidence rather than a definitive exogenous design.

Setting: Falling home prices are associated with large declines in borrowers’ labor earnings, especially among low-income borrowers. The probability of a 50% or greater earnings drop is significantly related to lower home prices for borrowers earning under $20,000 (coefficient -0.0135) and $20,000–$40,000 (-0.0108), but not for higher-income groups (0.00682 and -0.000485). This pattern supports the paper’s central mechanism that home-price declines increased student loan defaults by damaging labor-market outcomes, particularly in low-income jobs.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that falling home prices impair labor earnings, especially for low-income jobs; this table provides direct mechanism evidence.
Settings.G52:
Treatment: Primary continuous treatment is zip-code log home price in year t; heterogeneity is by homeowner status measured as an indicator for paying mortgage interest in year t (Form 1098), which proxies for owning a home with a mortgage. The focal causal contrast is whether the home-price effect differs for homeowners versus renters.

Method: The authors augment the main borrower-level fixed-effects panel regression with homeowner status and its interaction with home prices to test a direct home-equity liquidity channel. The dependent variable is new default in year t+1. Regressors include log home price in year t, an indicator for whether the borrower pays mortgage interest in year t based on Form 1098, and Home price×Owner. Variants mirror the main table: county clustering, controls, cohort-year FE, zip-code×cohort-year FE, and individual FE. This is still a linear FE regression, now with interaction-based heterogeneity in treatment effects.

Identification: Identification uses within-zip or within-borrower changes in home prices, with the liquidity-channel test coming from differential sensitivity of defaults to home prices for homeowners relative to renters. The paper argues that only homeowners should be directly affected through home-equity borrowing capacity. Assumptions include comparable trends for homeowners and renters after conditioning on FE and controls, and accurate homeowner measurement; the authors discuss attenuation from missed outright owners or those without mortgages.

Setting: To test whether falling home prices raise defaults by constraining home-equity borrowing, the authors compare homeowners and renters in borrower-level FE regressions. Across all specifications, the interaction Home price×Owner is small and insignificant—for example, 0.000972 (s.e. 0.000882) in the baseline—while the main home-price effect remains about -0.0112. Homeowners have lower baseline default rates than renters, but their default sensitivity to home-price changes is not larger. The authors interpret this as evidence against a direct home equity-based liquidity channel.

Main role: Rejecting the direct home-equity liquidity channel is one of the central substantive conclusions highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.N52: Table 8 columns 1-3, 5 and 6, Section 5.2, pp. 13-14: continuous log home-price effect on new borrower default in t+1, with Owner and Home price x Owner testing heterogeneity. Owner indicates mortgage-interest payments reported on Form 1098, not all legal homeownership. Columns 1-3 use zip-code and calendar-year FE; column 5 uses zip-code x cohort FE plus year FE; column 6 uses individual plus year FE. Column 4 split to h4 (HDFE). Baseline home-price coefficient -0.0112 and interaction 0.000972 (insignificant). Loan-balance weighted linear regression.
Settings.O52: Focal treatment remains continuous home prices; a binary moderator does not make the price treatment binary. Small insignificant homeowner interactions are evidence of no detected differential sensitivity, not proof of identical effects. Owner level coefficients are conditional intercept differences, not unconditional homeowner default gaps. No qualifying outcome-benchmark comparison found.
Settings.G53:
Treatment: Zip-code log home price in year t, interacted with homeowner status and alternatively with labor earnings, total income, or family income. The substantive treatment remains the local home-price change, with heterogeneity by homeowner status conditional on resources.

Method: This is a robustness extension of the homeowner-interaction FE regression. The authors add controls for financial resources—either labor earnings, total income, or family income—and their interactions with home prices, alongside homeowner status and Home price×Owner. The dependent variable is new default in year t+1; the treatment remains log home price in year t, with interest in whether the homeowner interaction survives conditioning on resources. All specifications include year and zip-code fixed effects, are weighted by loan balances, and cluster at the zip-code level.

Identification: Same FE identification as in the homeowner-interaction setting, with added controls to compare homeowners and renters holding observed resources more constant. The relevant assumption is that these resource controls capture differential financial capacity that might otherwise confound the homeowner interaction.

Setting: After controlling for borrowers’ labor earnings, total income, or family income—and allowing the home-price effect to vary with those resources—the interaction between home prices and homeowner status remains tiny and insignificant. Meanwhile, the resource interactions have the predicted signs: higher resources reduce defaults and attenuate home-price sensitivity. These robustness checks reinforce the paper’s conclusion that the lack of stronger home-price sensitivity among homeowners is not simply due to homeowners having more financial resources than renters.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness check addressing whether homeowners’ greater resources mask liquidity effects; it supports, but does not independently carry, the main conclusion.
Settings.G54:
Treatment: Zip-code log home price in year t, interacted with homeowner status measured from Form 1098. Estimated separately for age groups (<30, 30–40, >40) and repayment cohorts (<2000, 2000–2005, >2005).

Method: The authors further re-estimate the homeowner-interaction FE regression in subsamples split by age and repayment cohort to assess measurement-error concerns in homeowner status. The dependent variable is new default in year t+1; regressors include log home price, homeowner status, and Home price×Owner. All specifications include year and zip-code fixed effects, are weighted by loan balances, and cluster at the zip-code level. This is a heterogeneity/robustness analysis of the liquidity-channel test.

Identification: The design again relies on within-zip variation in home prices, but examines whether the differential homeowner response appears in subgroups where owner measurement should be more accurate, such as younger likely first-time buyers or recent repayment cohorts. The authors argue that if attenuation from misclassification were driving null results, interaction effects should emerge in these cleaner subsamples.

Setting: Splitting the sample by age and repayment cohort does not reveal the stronger homeowner response predicted by a home-equity liquidity channel. In nearly all subsamples, the Home price×Owner interaction remains insignificant; the lone marginally significant estimate for borrowers under age 30 is positive rather than negative, implying homeowners are if anything less sensitive than renters. These results support the paper’s conclusion that measurement error in homeownership is unlikely to explain the null evidence on the liquidity channel.

Main role: This is a robustness test supporting the conclusion against the liquidity channel by checking whether mismeasured homeownership masks effects in younger or newer cohorts.
Settings.G55:
Treatment: IBR program exposure, operationalized primarily as eligibility for IBR in year t based on the means test 0.15 × (discretionary income) < payment under the standard 10-year plan, interacted with the post-2009 period and with local log home prices. Eligibility is binary; the post-policy dimension switches on after 2009. The paper interprets these interactions as the causal effect of the IBR program on default levels and on sensitivity to home-price shocks.

Method: The authors evaluate the 2009 Income Based Repayment (IBR) program using a triple-difference linear regression. The outcome is borrower default. Regressors include log home price, IBR-eligibility based on the statutory means test, a Post indicator for 2009 onward, and all two-way and three-way interactions among home price, IBR eligibility, and Post. Columns 1–3 include zip-code and year fixed effects; column 4 uses individual borrower fixed effects. Observations are weighted by loan balances and standard errors are clustered at the zip-code level. The design compares eligible versus ineligible borrowers, before versus after IBR introduction, and differentially across local home-price shocks. This is a conventional DDD/TWFE design, not a modern heterogeneous DiD estimator.

Identification: Identification comes from a difference-in-differences/triple-differences comparison of IBR-eligible versus ineligible borrowers before and after the 2009 rollout, while also comparing areas with different home-price shocks. The main assumptions are parallel trends between eligible and ineligible borrowers absent the policy, and no other contemporaneous shocks differentially affecting eligible borrowers exactly when IBR began. The paper supports this with pre-trend graphs and by showing that post-2009 improvements are driven by eligible borrowers who actually take up IBR. Borrower FE in one specification address time-invariant heterogeneity.

Setting: The triple-difference analysis indicates that the 2009 IBR program reduced student loan defaults and dampened their sensitivity to local home-price declines for eligible borrowers. In Table 11 column 2, IBR-eligible borrowers have higher baseline default rates (0.0425), but their relative default rate falls after IBR introduction (IBR eligible×Post = -0.0404) and their extra sensitivity to home-price shocks is attenuated after 2009 (Home price×IBR eligible×Post = 0.00314). These effects become stronger in a restricted sample and with individual borrower fixed effects, where IBR eligible×Post is -0.0707 and the triple interaction is 0.00513. This is a central policy result of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion state that IBR reduced defaults and reduced sensitivity to home-price fluctuations; this table is the core causal evidence for that claim.
Settings.H55: Section 6, Equation (2), Table 11 columns 1–4, PDF pp. 15–16.
Settings.N55: Restricted to Table 11 columns 2-4, Eq. (2), Section 6, pp. 15-17: conventional DiD/DDD for binary IBR eligibility under the means test, with Post equal to one beginning in 2009. Outcome is new borrower default in t+1; treatment years 2006-2011 and default years 2007-2012. Full interactions of log home price, eligibility and Post; zip-code plus calendar-year FE in columns 2-3, individual plus year FE in column 4. Individual loan-balance weights and zip-code clustered standard errors. Column 3 restricts to relatively high debt/discretionary-income borrowers. Column 1 is a separate FE specification (h5).
Settings.O55: Eligibility, not actual enrollment, defines exposure; no IV receipt effect is estimated. In column 2, eligibility x Post is -0.0404 and the triple interaction is 0.00314. With the triple interaction, the post-policy change in the eligibility gap at log price h is beta4 + beta6*h; -0.0404 alone is not an unconditional average program effect. Similarly beta2=0.0425 is not an unconditional baseline gap. Post includes 2009, not only years after 2009. Table heading Default_t conflicts with Eq. (2), text and reporting lag; use t+1. No qualifying benchmark comparison found. Fig. 6 substantive dynamic effects added as h6; do not treat selected take-up groups in Fig. 5 as randomized or IV receipt estimates.
Settings.G56:
Treatment: Time-t predictor variables for factor returns: change in FX volatility, change in CRB commodity price index, average forward discount of currencies against the US dollar, and change in the TED spread. These are continuous variables measured in their constructed time-series units; the setting groups these predictors because they are reported together in the same predictive-regression table.

Method: In-sample predictive OLS regressions relate next-month global currency factor returns (dollar factor or carry factor) to time-t predictor variables. Table 2 reports separate linear regressions using FX volatility, commodity returns, average forward discount, and TED spread, plus specifications including multiple predictors and a constant. Standard errors are Newey-West. The paper interprets coefficients as economically meaningful predictive effects of these variables on factor returns, but identification is purely observational time-series regression with no design-based source of exogenous variation; endogeneity and omitted-variable concerns remain.

Identification: The paper uses observed time-series variation in macro-financial predictors to explain subsequent factor returns. The intended causal/predictive interpretation is that higher volatility, commodity prices, or forward discounts affect subsequent dollar/carry factor returns. Identification rests on linear conditional expectation assumptions in observational time-series data and is not design-based; omitted shocks, reverse causality in broader macro conditions, and instability are potential concerns.

Setting: Using full-sample OLS predictive regressions, the authors argue that macro-financial variables help drive next-month currency factor returns. In Table 2, FX volatility loads negatively on dollar and especially carry factor returns; commodity returns load positively and strongly on both factors; average forward discount positively predicts the dollar factor; TED spread has little explanatory power. These results provide the empirical basis for the paper's DCF hedging forecasts but are supporting rather than final performance evidence.

Main role: These predictive regressions motivate the mechanism behind the proposed hedging strategy, but the paper's central claims concern out-of-sample portfolio and hedging performance rather than these in-sample coefficient estimates.
Settings.G57:
Treatment: Adoption of the DCF hedging framework instead of alternative hedging strategies for the currency exposure of an equal-weighted global equity portfolio from the perspective of a US investor. Operationally, treatment is the portfolio rule generating monthly hedge ratios from predicted currency returns and mean-variance optimization. The contrast is discrete at the strategy level.

Method: Out-of-sample portfolio evaluation of the paper's dynamic currency factor (DCF) hedging strategy for a US investor in an equal-weighted global equity portfolio. The strategy first estimates rolling 60-month bilateral currency betas on dollar and carry factors, then forecasts factor returns from expanding-window predictive regressions using average forward discount, FX volatility, and commodity returns, converts these into expected currency returns, and plugs them into a mean-variance optimizer with risk aversion gamma=3 and historical 60-month covariance estimates to choose monthly currency-specific hedge positions constrained between fully hedged and unhedged. The paper interprets differences in portfolio performance across hedging rules as the causal effect of using DCF hedging rather than alternative hedging frameworks on investor outcomes. This is a portfolio-construction/backtest design rather than a standard causal econometric estimator.

Identification: The paper's argument is that applying the DCF rule changes hedge positions and thereby changes ex post portfolio performance. Identification is by out-of-sample comparison of strategy-generated return paths over the same underlying portfolio and sample period, holding asset positions fixed while varying only the currency hedging rule. This is not based on exogenous assignment, so causal interpretation depends on treating the portfolio backtest as the relevant intervention comparison and assuming the out-of-sample implementation avoids in-sample overfitting sufficiently to inform the effect of adopting DCF hedging.

Setting: For a US investor holding an equal-weighted global equity portfolio, adopting the DCF hedging strategy rather than alternative currency hedging rules improves portfolio performance out of sample from January 1997 to July 2017. In Table 3 Panel A, the DCF-hedged portfolio has mean return 7.93%, standard deviation 15.3%, and Sharpe ratio 0.52, versus 4.92% and 0.27 when unhedged and 5.10% and 0.37 when fully hedged. The differences in Sharpe ratios relative to DCF are negative and statistically significant for all nine alternatives; CEQ is 4.40%, also statistically higher than every alternative. The authors interpret this as core evidence that exploiting factor-based currency return predictability causes superior equity-portfolio hedging performance.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that DCF hedging outperforms leading alternatives for global equity and bond portfolios across performance metrics; Table 3 is the core evidence for that claim.
Settings.H57: Section 5.3.1, Table 3 Panel A, PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G58:
Treatment: Adoption of the DCF hedging framework instead of alternative hedging strategies for the currency exposure of a GDP-weighted global equity portfolio from the perspective of a US investor. Strategy-level discrete intervention.

Method: Same out-of-sample DCF backtest design as s2, but applied to a GDP-weighted global equity portfolio for a US investor. Monthly DCF hedge ratios are generated from predicted factor returns, rolling factor betas, and mean-variance optimization, then compared against nine alternative hedging frameworks using portfolio performance metrics over the OOS period.

Identification: Identification is by out-of-sample strategy comparison with underlying asset weights fixed at GDP shares and only the currency hedging rule varied. The intended causal claim is the effect of adopting DCF hedging on portfolio performance. As in the main portfolio tests, this is a backtested intervention comparison rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Setting: For a GDP-weighted global equity portfolio, DCF hedging is also reported to improve out-of-sample performance relative to alternative hedging rules. Table 3 Panel B shows mean return 6.16%, standard deviation 15.3%, and Sharpe ratio 0.40 under DCF, versus 3.36% and 0.20 when unhedged and 4.51% and 0.31 when fully hedged. CEQ is 2.66%, the highest in the panel, and the paper notes that DCF yields consistently higher Sharpe and CEQ measures than each alternative framework, reinforcing the central claim's robustness to portfolio weighting.

Main role: The paper states that GDP-weighted equity results are qualitatively identical and support the central conclusion that DCF hedging outperforms alternatives.
Settings.H58: Section 5.3.1, Table 3 Panel B, PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G59:
Treatment: Adoption of DCF hedging instead of alternative currency hedging strategies for an equal-weighted global bond portfolio from the perspective of a US investor.

Method: Out-of-sample DCF backtest for a US investor holding an equal-weighted global bond portfolio. Hedge ratios are generated monthly using predicted currency returns from factor forecasts and mean-variance optimization, then portfolio outcomes are compared to nine alternative hedging frameworks in the same OOS sample.

Identification: The comparison holds the underlying bond portfolio constant and varies only the currency hedging rule. The paper interprets higher out-of-sample Sharpe and CEQ under DCF as the effect of adopting DCF hedging. As with other strategy comparisons, identification is from out-of-sample portfolio simulation rather than exogenous assignment.

Setting: For an equal-weighted global bond portfolio, DCF hedging is argued to causally improve investment performance relative to standard hedging rules. Table 4 Panel A reports DCF mean return 5.21%, standard deviation 6.81%, and Sharpe ratio 0.77, compared with a fully hedged portfolio Sharpe ratio of 0.54 and an unhedged Sharpe ratio of 0.25. CEQ is 4.52%, statistically higher than all alternatives, and investors would pay up to 3.05% per year to switch to DCF. The result is central because prior work often views full bond hedging as optimal, so DCF's outperformance is especially notable.

Main role: Bond-portfolio outperformance is highlighted repeatedly in the introduction and conclusion as a major result, especially because fully hedging bonds is often viewed as optimal in prior literature.
Settings.H59: Section 5.3.2, Table 4 Panel A, PDF pp. 14-15.
Settings.G60:
Treatment: Adoption of DCF hedging instead of alternative currency hedging strategies for a GDP-weighted global bond portfolio from the perspective of a US investor.

Method: Same out-of-sample DCF backtest design as s4, but applied to a GDP-weighted global bond portfolio for a US investor. Monthly mean-variance hedge choices derived from factor forecasts are compared to alternative hedging frameworks using portfolio performance statistics over the OOS period.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing out-of-sample returns of the same GDP-weighted global bond portfolio under different currency hedging rules. The causal language concerns the effect of the DCF intervention on portfolio performance, but the design remains a strategy backtest without external exogenous variation.

Setting: For a GDP-weighted global bond portfolio, DCF hedging again delivers the strongest reported performance. Table 4 Panel B shows mean return 4.16%, standard deviation 5.53%, and Sharpe ratio 0.75 under DCF, versus 2.69% and 0.64 for fully hedged and 1.54% and 0.18 for unhedged. CEQ equals 3.70%, higher than alternatives, and investors would pay up to 2.80% per year to adopt DCF. This supports the paper's broad claim that factor-based dynamic hedging improves both equity and bond portfolios.

Main role: GDP-weighted bond results are part of the paper's main demonstration that DCF hedging outperforms across equity and bond portfolios and different weighting schemes.
Settings.H60: Section 5.3.2, Table 4 Panel B, PDF p. 15.
Settings.G61:
Treatment: Choice of covariance matrix (or, in the 'Actual rets' column, actual future return vector) used inside the DCF mean-variance hedging algorithm. This is a discrete menu of alternative implementation rules rather than a scalar treatment.

Method: Robustness/extension analysis re-estimating the DCF strategy for US global equity and bond portfolios using alternative covariance-matrix constructions within the same mean-variance hedging framework. Compared methods include the baseline 60-month historical covariance, realized covariance from synchronized daily data, realized covariance with shrinkage, diagonal covariance, covariance using the following month's actual returns ('Actual covar'), and, separately, replacing expected currency returns with actual following-month returns ('Actual rets'). The paper interprets these comparisons as showing how better or different covariance information affects DCF hedging performance.

Identification: The paper varies the covariance input inside the DCF optimizer while keeping the overall strategy framework intact. The intended interpretation is the causal effect of improving or altering covariance measurement on portfolio performance. Identification comes from mechanical out-of-sample strategy comparison within the same portfolio sample; there is no external exogenous variation.

Setting: The covariance-matrix extension suggests that more sophisticated realized-covariance inputs do not improve DCF hedging performance, while perfect foresight about future expected returns would. In Table 5, for equal-weighted global equity portfolios, baseline historical-covariance DCF has Sharpe 0.52 versus 0.47 with realized covariance and 1.25 with actual future returns; for equal-weighted bond portfolios, baseline Sharpe is 0.77 versus 0.76 with realized covariance and 2.52 with actual future returns. The authors conclude that covariance estimation has only modest payoff, whereas better return forecasts are the main source of potential gains.

Main role: This is an extension/robustness exercise about implementation details of the DCF strategy, not the main demonstration against alternative hedging frameworks.
Settings.H61: Section 6.1, Table 5 Panels A-B, PDF p. 16.
Settings.G62:
Treatment: Adoption of DCF hedging instead of alternative currency hedging frameworks, now from the home-currency perspective of Germany, Japan, UK, Canada, Australia, Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, and New Zealand. Strategy-level discrete intervention.

Method: Extension evaluating DCF hedging from the perspective of non-US investors across G10 home countries for equal-weighted and GDP-weighted global equity and bond portfolios. The same DCF rule is implemented from each home-currency perspective and compared with the same set of alternative hedging frameworks using Sharpe ratios, CEQ returns, and performance fees.

Identification: The comparison varies the home-currency perspective and hedging rule while holding the portfolio backtest framework fixed. The intended causal interpretation is that adopting DCF hedging improves performance for investors outside the US as well. Identification again relies on out-of-sample simulated strategy comparisons rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Setting: The non-US investor extension argues that DCF hedging improves portfolio performance broadly across G10 investors. Table 6 reports that, for equal-weighted equity portfolios, DCF has the highest Sharpe ratio for 8 of 9 investors and the highest CEQ for 8 of 9; for bond portfolios, DCF usually ranks first or second. The paper summarizes that DCF delivers either the highest or second-highest Sharpe ratio and CEQ return in 95% of tests, supporting the claim that the strategy's benefits are not US-specific.

Main role: This supports the paper's claim of broad applicability but is framed as an extension beyond the baseline US-investor analysis.
Settings.H62: Section 6.2, Table 6 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 17-18.
Settings.G63:
Treatment: Choice of currency hedging strategy, especially DCF versus no hedge, full hedge, carry, value, momentum, UIP, random walk, interest-rate, and model-combination hedges, applied to global equity or bond portfolios.

Method: Extension decomposing the return consequences of alternative hedging strategies into average hedging return, forward-premium component, and exchange-rate component for global equity and bond portfolios under equal and GDP weights. The treatment is the choice of hedging rule, especially DCF versus alternatives, and the paper interprets the decomposition as evidence about the mechanism through which DCF affects returns.

Identification: The paper mechanically decomposes ex post hedging returns under alternative strategy rules to infer whether DCF's effect operates through timing exchange-rate movements or harvesting forward premia. The interpretation is causal with respect to the strategy rule, but the evidence is descriptive within an out-of-sample backtest rather than identified by exogenous variation.

Setting: The return decomposition suggests that DCF hedging raises portfolio returns mainly by timing exchange-rate movements rather than only by exploiting forward premia. In Table 7, for the equal-weighted global equity portfolio, DCF mean hedging return is 3.02%, of which 0.23 percentage points come from forward premia and 2.79 from the exchange-rate component; for the equal-weighted bond portfolio, the corresponding figures are 2.88%, 0.33, and 2.55. The authors interpret this as evidence that DCF's superior performance mainly comes from hedging currencies before they depreciate against the US dollar.

Main role: This is a mechanism decomposition explaining where DCF gains come from, not the main headline comparison of overall portfolio performance.
Settings.H63: Section 6.3.1, Table 7 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 18-19.
Settings.G64:
Treatment: Which source of DCF dynamics is allowed: full DCF, only time-varying factor betas with average factor returns, or predictable factor returns with constant betas. This is a discrete implementation choice.

Method: Extension comparing three versions of the DCF strategy: baseline DCF with time-varying factor betas and predictable factor returns; a 'Factor betas' version that shuts down factor-return predictability and uses historical average factor returns; and a 'Factor returns' version that keeps predictable factor returns but fixes betas at unconditional averages. The same portfolio backtest framework is applied to equal- and GDP-weighted global equity and bond portfolios.

Identification: The paper toggles components of the DCF algorithm while keeping the backtest environment fixed, interpreting changes in performance as the effect of those components. Identification comes from deterministic reimplementation of alternative strategy rules, not from exogenous variation.

Setting: The factor-beta versus factor-return comparison indicates that DCF's gains come mainly from forecasting factor returns, not from time-varying factor betas. In Table 8 for equal-weighted equity portfolios, baseline DCF Sharpe is 0.52 versus 0.31 for the 'Factor betas' version and 0.51 for the 'Factor returns' version; for equal-weighted bond portfolios, the corresponding values are 0.77, 0.29, and 0.77. CEQ differences show the same pattern. The authors conclude that the forecastable component of factor returns is the principal driver of DCF hedging gains.

Main role: This is an extension that isolates the mechanism behind DCF's success—factor return predictability versus time-varying betas—rather than the main portfolio result itself.
Settings.H64: Section 6.3.2, Table 8 Panels A-B, PDF p. 20.
Settings.G65:
Treatment: Choice of predictor set used to forecast factor returns inside the DCF hedging algorithm: full baseline predictor set versus Afd only, Com only, Vol only, Afd+Com, Afd+Vol, or Com+Vol.

Method: Further extension decomposing the contribution of specific predictor sets to DCF performance by re-estimating factor returns using subsets of the baseline predictors: average forward discount (Afd), commodity returns (Com), and FX volatility (Vol), singly or in pairs. The resulting DCF variants are evaluated in the same out-of-sample portfolio framework for equal- and GDP-weighted equity and bond portfolios.

Identification: The paper changes the predictor set used to generate DCF return forecasts and treats resulting performance differences as the effect of including those predictors. This is a model-component comparison inside the same backtesting environment rather than a design-based causal estimate.

Setting: The predictor-subset exercise indicates that commodity returns are the most economically important predictor behind DCF hedging gains, with average forward discount adding some value and FX volatility adding little incremental performance. Table 9 shows, for example, that in equal-weighted equity portfolios the full DCF Sharpe is 0.52, commodity-only yields 0.48, and Afd+Com yields 0.53; in equal-weighted bond portfolios the analogous values are 0.77, 0.67, and 0.78. The authors interpret this as evidence that factor-return predictability, especially through commodity returns, is the key mechanism behind DCF performance.

Main role: This is a mechanism-focused robustness exercise showing which predictors matter inside the DCF strategy, not the primary headline comparison to existing hedging rules.
Settings.H65: Section 6.3.2, Table 9 Panels A-B, PDF p. 21.
Settings.G66:
Treatment: Implementation of the DCF time-series currency trading rule: long foreign currency against the US dollar when expected currency return is positive and short when expected return is negative. At the portfolio level, go long all positive-signal currencies and short all negative-signal currencies.

Method: Out-of-sample evaluation of an independent DCF-based currency trading strategy rather than a hedging overlay. Expected bilateral currency returns are generated from the baseline DCF forecasting model, and a time-series signal rule goes long currencies with positive expected returns and short those with negative expected returns. Panel A of Table 10 reports bilateral and portfolio-level performance of these pure currency strategies.

Identification: The paper constructs pure currency positions from DCF-predicted returns and compares realized out-of-sample performance. The intended causal claim is that exploiting DCF-predicted currency returns in a separate portfolio raises risk-adjusted returns. Identification is from strategy backtesting rather than exogenous assignment.

Setting: The paper argues that a separate DCF currency portfolio can itself generate high risk-adjusted returns. Table 10 Panel A shows bilateral strategies with Sharpe ratios ranging from 0.13 for JPY to 0.85 for NZD, and the combined DCF time-series portfolio has mean return 5.78%, standard deviation 7.38%, and Sharpe ratio 0.78 with positive skewness 0.20. This is one of the paper's headline contributions beyond hedging: DCF forecasts can support a profitable standalone currency strategy.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly highlight that an independent DCF currency portfolio earns a high risk-adjusted return and provides diversification gains beyond carry, value, and momentum.
Settings.H66: Section 7, Table 10 Panel A and Fig. 3, PDF pp. 20-22.
Settings.G67:
Treatment: Adding the DCF time-series currency portfolio to a fully hedged global equity or global bond portfolio, rather than adding alternative currency strategies or holding only the fully hedged underlying portfolio.

Method: Out-of-sample portfolio-allocation exercise combining a fully hedged global equity or bond portfolio with alternative independent currency strategies, including carry, momentum, value, a style combination, and the DCF time-series portfolio. Table 10 Panel B compares resulting combined-portfolio performance metrics.

Identification: The paper compares the same fully hedged underlying portfolios with or without added currency strategies. The intended causal interpretation is the effect of adding the DCF time-series currency portfolio on overall investor performance. Identification is by out-of-sample strategy comparison in a portfolio simulation setting, not by external random or quasi-random assignment.

Setting: Adding the DCF time-series currency portfolio to a fully hedged global portfolio substantially improves diversification gains relative to adding standard currency styles. In Table 10 Panel B, the fully hedged global equity portfolio has Sharpe 0.37 and CEQ 2.19, while the same portfolio combined with the DCF time-series portfolio has Sharpe 0.70 and CEQ 7.30; for the fully hedged global bond portfolio, Sharpe rises from 0.54 to 0.97 and CEQ from 2.19 to 7.19. The implied performance fees to move from the fully hedged portfolio to the DCF-combined portfolio are about 5.6% per year. The paper interprets this as evidence that DCF provides superior diversification gains compared with carry, value, momentum, or style portfolios.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that the DCF independent currency portfolio delivers superior diversification gains relative to carry, value, and momentum strategies.
Settings.H67: Section 7, Table 10 Panel B, PDF pp. 20-22.
Settings.G68:
Treatment: Indicator Treat×Post for exposure to an exogenous reduction in analyst coverage after the closure/merger event. Treat equals 1 for affected firms; Post equals 1 after the coverage reduction. This is a binary treated-post exposure in a DiD design, not the number of analysts lost.

Method: Difference-in-differences regressions compare firms experiencing exogenous analyst-coverage reductions due to brokerage closures/mergers with matched control firms not experiencing reductions one year before/after the event. The baseline specification is linear with firm fixed effects and quarter fixed effects plus controls for log market capitalization, log book-to-market, and log leverage; standard errors are double-clustered by firm and quarter. Identification comes from closure/merger-driven analyst exits argued by Kelly and Ljungqvist (2012) and Hong and Kacperczyk (2010) to be unrelated to affected firms' prospects. The setting uses the matched sample of firms with five or fewer analysts pre-shock and studies earnings announcements two years before/after the shock.

Identification: The identifying variation is analyst coverage loss caused by brokerage closures and mergers, argued to arise from regulatory and business shocks to the equity research industry rather than from information about firm prospects. Treated firms are matched to control firms by industry, size, book-to-market, and pre-event bid-ask spread, and the DiD assumes parallel trends in market-efficiency measures absent treatment. Remaining concern is that treatment assignment may correlate with unobserved time-varying shocks, but the paper argues no predictive power for future earnings and later shows no pre-trends.

Setting: Using a matched-firm difference-in-differences design around brokerage closures and mergers that exogenously reduce analyst coverage, the paper estimates that market efficiency deteriorates for affected firms. In the specification with firm and quarter fixed effects, the price jump ratio rises by 0.051 for CAR[0,2]/CAR[-63,2], 0.049 for CAR[-1,2]/CAR[-63,2], and 0.057 for CAR[-2,2]/CAR[-63,2], implying less information is incorporated into prices before earnings announcements after analyst exits. This is a central causal result supporting the claim that sell-side analysts facilitate price discovery.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that exogenous analyst exits worsen market efficiency; this is one of the paper's four main findings and motivates the substitution role for hedge funds.
Settings.H68: Section 4.1, Eq. (1), Table 2 cols. (2), (4), (6), PDF pp. 322-324.
Settings.G69:
Treatment: Binary DiD exposure Treat×Post indicating a treated firm's post-reduction conference calls after exogenous analyst coverage loss.

Method: Difference-in-differences regressions examine whether exogenous coverage reductions affect hedge-fund participation in earnings conference calls. The linear probability and log-count specifications include firm fixed effects and, in preferred columns, quarter fixed effects, with controls for LnSize, LnBEME, LnLev, and Ret2mPrior; standard errors are double-clustered by firm and quarter. Treated firms are those with coverage reductions from brokerage closures/mergers, matched to untreated controls, over a two-year before/after window.

Identification: Identification relies on closure/merger-induced analyst exits as exogenous shocks to firms' information environment. The DiD compares changes in conference-call participation for treated firms relative to matched controls before and after coverage reductions. The key assumption is parallel trends in participation absent treatment; firm FE absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity and quarter FE absorb aggregate shocks.

Setting: The paper estimates that exogenous analyst exits cause hedge funds to increase information acquisition via earnings conference calls. In Table 3 panel A, the treated-post coefficient is about 0.051-0.052 for the participation indicator and 0.040 for log(1+number of hedge-fund analysts), implying a roughly 5.2 percentage point increase in the probability that hedge-fund analysts ask questions and a significant rise in hedge-fund analyst presence on calls after coverage reductions. This is a main causal result consistent with substitution between sophisticated investors and sell-side analysts.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly state that hedge funds scale up information acquisition after coverage reductions; conference-call participation is one of the paper's main information-acquisition channels.
Settings.H69: Section 4.2.1, Table 3 panel A, PDF pp. 323-325.
Settings.G70:
Treatment: Binary treated-post exposure indicating a firm after its exogenous analyst coverage reduction due to brokerage closure/merger.

Method: Difference-in-differences regressions study how exogenous analyst coverage reductions affect EDGAR search intensity by hedge funds. The dependent variable is log(EDGAR search volume + 1) by quarter for each firm, with firm and quarter fixed effects, controls for LnSize, LnBEME, LnLev, and Ret2mPrior, and double-clustered standard errors by firm and quarter. The design compares treated firms and matched controls two years before and after the reduction event, overall and by filing type.

Identification: The design uses exogenous variation in information environment from brokerage closures/mergers that reduce analyst coverage. Treated-control differences before and after the event identify the effect on hedge-fund information acquisition under the assumption of parallel trends. Firm FE absorb fixed cross-sectional differences in search demand; quarter FE absorb common time shocks. Remaining concerns include measurement error in IP matching and that EDGAR searches proxy rather than directly observe cognition.

Setting: The paper finds that hedge funds increase EDGAR-based information acquisition after exogenous coverage reductions. In Table 4 panel A, the treated-post coefficient is 0.187 for all filings, which the authors describe as an 18.7% increase in hedge-fund search volume for treated firms; coefficients by filing type range from 0.142 to 0.199 and are generally statistically significant. This is a main causal result showing that hedge funds substitute for lost sell-side information by collecting more information directly.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight increased information acquisition, especially EDGAR search volume from hedge-fund IP addresses, as a key main finding.
Settings.H70: Section 4.2.2, Eq. (2), Table 4 panel A, PDF pp. 324-326.
Settings.G71:
Treatment: Binary treated-post exposure from an exogenous analyst coverage reduction, interacted with continuous SUE to capture whether hedge-fund positions become more informative after treatment.

Method: Triple-difference-style linear DiD regression estimates whether exogenous analyst coverage reductions change the sensitivity of abnormal hedge-fund holdings to future standardized unexpected earnings (SUE). The specification includes firm and quarter fixed effects, all lower-order interactions among Treat, Post, and SUE, plus controls LnSize, LnBEME, LnLev, and Ret2mPrior; standard errors are double-clustered by firm and quarter. The outcome is abnormal hedge-fund holdings at the quarter end prior to the earnings announcement.

Identification: The identifying variation combines the exogenous information-environment shock (coverage reduction) with cross-sectional/temporal variation in future earnings surprises. Because SUE is not public when holdings are measured, a stronger post-treatment sensitivity of pre-announcement holdings to future SUE is interpreted as evidence of more informed trading by hedge funds. The causal piece is the exogenous shock to information environment; interpretation still relies on the assumption that no other contemporaneous treated-firm shock differentially changes the holdings-SUE relation relative to controls.

Setting: The paper estimates that exogenous analyst exits make hedge-fund holdings more predictive of future earnings news. In Table 5 column (3), the Treat × Post × SUE coefficient is 0.091, indicating that after coverage reductions abnormal hedge-fund holdings become more sensitive to future standardized unexpected earnings. The authors state that for a one-standard-deviation increase in SUE (4.32), the drop of one analyst leads to a 0.39 percentage point increase in abnormal hedge-fund holdings, consistent with more aggressive informed trading by hedge funds after the information shock.

Main role: A major contribution in the abstract and introduction is that hedge funds trade more aggressively on affected stocks after analyst exits and exploit increased information advantage; this is the main trading-behavior result.
Settings.H71: Section 4.3.1, Eq. (3), Table 5 cols. (1)-(3), PDF pp. 324-327.
Settings.G72:
Treatment: Binary treated-post exposure for affected firms after exogenous analyst coverage reduction; sample conditioned on hedge-fund purchases, large purchases, sales, or large sales inferred from changes in aggregate holdings.

Method: Difference-in-differences regressions estimate whether exogenous analyst coverage reductions change hedge-fund profitability on stocks they buy or sell. The sample is split by inferred trading direction based on changes in aggregate hedge-fund holdings from quarter t-1 to t and, separately, by large purchases/sales. Regressions include firm and quarter fixed effects, controls LnSize, LnBEME, LnLev, and Ret2mPrior, and double-clustered standard errors. The outcome is three-month abnormal stock return from quarter end t to t+1 benchmarked by corresponding DGTW portfolios.

Identification: The design compares post-vs-pre changes in future abnormal returns of stocks traded by hedge funds for treated versus matched control firms. Exogenous analyst exits create the information shock; higher post-treatment returns on purchased treated stocks are interpreted as evidence that hedge funds profit more from information advantage. This is not a direct causal design for hedge-fund trades themselves, but a causal interpretation of the treatment shock on profitability conditional on inferred trade direction.

Setting: The paper finds that exogenous analyst exits increase hedge-fund profitability on the affected stocks they buy. In Table 8 panel A, the Treat × Post coefficient is 2.530 percentage points for hedge-fund purchases and 3.731 percentage points for large hedge-fund purchases, while estimates for sales are near zero and insignificant. The result supports the paper's main claim that coverage reductions increase hedge funds' informational advantage and trading profits.

Main role: The abstract states that hedge funds earn higher abnormal returns on affected stocks after analyst exits; profitability is one of the core main findings.
Settings.H72: Section 4.3.3, Table 8 panel A, PDF pp. 330-331.
Settings.G73:
Treatment: Interaction of treated-post exposure with high hedge-fund participation D(HF++), where D(HF++) equals 1 if abnormal aggregate hedge-fund holdings are in the top quartile at that quarter-end. This is a binary high-participation contrast layered onto the binary coverage-reduction DiD.

Method: A triple-interaction difference-in-differences specification examines whether high hedge-fund participation mitigates the effect of exogenous analyst coverage reductions on price jump ratios. The regression includes firm fixed effects and, in preferred columns, quarter fixed effects; controls are LnSize, LnBEME, and LnLev; standard errors are double-clustered by firm and quarter. Hedge-fund participation is proxied by an indicator for abnormal aggregate hedge-fund holdings in the top quartile at the nearest quarter-end before earnings announcements.

Identification: The exogenous coverage reduction supplies treated-post variation; the analysis then compares whether the treatment effect differs when hedge-fund participation is high. The key coefficient is the triple interaction Treat×Post×D(HF++). Although the authors are careful that coverage reductions do not directly instrument hedge-fund participation, they interpret the result as evidence that sophisticated investors help restore efficiency after the exogenous information shock. Assumptions are that no other post-treatment factor correlated with high hedge-fund holdings differentially changes price jump ratios for treated firms relative to controls.

Setting: Conditional on high hedge-fund participation, the market-efficiency impairment from exogenous analyst exits is substantially reduced. In Table 9 with firm and quarter fixed effects, Treat × Post is 0.072, 0.082, and 0.084 for the three price-jump measures, but the triple interaction Treat × Post × D(HF++) is -0.109, -0.129, and -0.109. The authors report that the sum of these coefficients is statistically indistinguishable from zero, implying that when abnormal hedge-fund holdings are in the top quartile, the net worsening in price efficiency after coverage reductions disappears.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that hedge-fund participation mitigates the impairment of market efficiency caused by coverage reductions; this is one of the paper's headline findings.
Settings.G74:
Treatment: Interaction of treated-post exposure with high abnormal short interest D(SI++), where D(SI++) equals 1 if abnormal short interest is in the top quartile at that quarter. This is a binary high-short-selling contrast layered onto the binary coverage-reduction DiD.

Method: A triple-interaction difference-in-differences regression evaluates whether high short-selling activity mitigates the effect of exogenous analyst coverage reductions on price jump ratios. The specification parallels Table 9 but replaces high hedge-fund holdings with D(SI++), an indicator that abnormal short interest is in the top quartile at the nearest quarter-end before earnings announcements. Regressions include firm FE, optionally quarter FE, controls LnSize, LnBEME, and LnLev, and double clustering by firm and quarter.

Identification: Identification again relies on exogenous analyst coverage reductions. The triple interaction tests whether treated firms' post-shock efficiency deterioration is smaller when short-selling activity is high. The authors motivate short interest as a proxy because hedge funds account for much short selling, but this is not a direct causal design for short-selling activity itself. Interpretation assumes no other omitted factor jointly affected by coverage reductions and high short interest drives the relative mitigation.

Setting: As a robustness analysis, the paper shows that high short-selling activity also mitigates the decline in price efficiency after exogenous analyst exits. In Table 10 with firm and quarter fixed effects, Treat × Post is 0.074, 0.081, and 0.088 across the three price-jump measures, while Treat × Post × D(SI++) is -0.123, -0.151, and -0.137. The net effect under high short interest is statistically indistinguishable from zero, supporting the broader claim that sophisticated investors' trading helps restore market efficiency after analyst coverage falls.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness analysis extending the main hedge-fund-participation result to short sellers; it is not the primary headline result in abstract/introduction.
Settings.G75:
Treatment: Binary treated-post exposure from coverage reductions; in the mitigation specification the relevant treatment contrast is Treat×Post×D(HF++), where D(HF++) indicates top-quartile abnormal hedge-fund holdings at the prior quarter-end.

Method: Difference-in-differences regressions use variance-ratio-based efficiency measures as alternative outcomes. Panel A estimates the effect of exogenous analyst coverage reductions on |1 - VR(n,m)| with firm and quarter fixed effects, controls LnSize, LnBEME, LnLev, and Ret2mPrior, and double-clustered standard errors. Panel B adds a triple interaction with D(HF++) to test whether high hedge-fund participation mitigates the treatment effect. Variance ratios are computed from quote-midpoint returns over quarterly windows using overlapping observations.

Identification: The same exogenous closure/merger-driven analyst exits provide treatment variation. Panel A identifies whether coverage reductions worsen variance-ratio efficiency relative to matched controls. Panel B tests heterogeneity in that treatment effect by high hedge-fund participation. Assumptions mirror the earlier DiD settings: parallel trends in variance-ratio outcomes and no treated-specific confound correlated with high hedge-fund holdings in the mitigation specification.

Setting: Using variance-ratio measures of market efficiency, the paper finds the same causal pattern as with price jump ratios. In Table 11 panel A, Treat × Post is positive and significant across six variance-ratio deviations—for example 0.030 for |1-VR(1,10)| and 0.029 for |1-VR(1,20)|—indicating that market efficiency worsens after exogenous coverage reductions. In panel B, the triple interaction with high hedge-fund participation is negative—for example -0.027 for |1-VR(1,10)| and -0.031 for |1-VR(1,20)|—showing that high hedge-fund participation mitigates this deterioration. These are substantive robustness results reinforcing the paper's central mechanism.

Main role: These are alternative-outcome robustness checks for the main market-efficiency and hedge-fund-mitigation results rather than separate headline claims.
Settings.H75: Section 5.2, Table 11 panels A-B, PDF pp. 333-334.
Settings.G76:
Treatment: Binary treated-post exposure from exogenous coverage reductions, operationalized through its interaction with current log(M/A) to estimate changes in price informativeness; mitigation uses the additional binary high-hedge-fund-participation interaction D(HF++).

Method: Difference-in-differences regressions use Bai et al. (2016) price informativeness as an alternative market-efficiency metric. The linear model regresses future EBIT/assets on current log(market capitalization/assets) and its interactions with Treat, Post, and high hedge-fund participation D(HF++), with firm fixed effects and, in preferred columns, year fixed effects, plus controls LnSize, LnBEME, LnLev, and Ret2mPrior. The coefficient on Treat×Post×log(M/A) captures changes in price informativeness after coverage reductions, and the additional interaction with D(HF++) tests mitigation by hedge-fund participation.

Identification: Coverage reductions from brokerage closures/mergers provide exogenous shocks to firms' information environment. In the Bai et al. framework, price informativeness is the sensitivity of future earnings to current valuation ratios; thus a decline in the Treat×Post×log(M/A) coefficient after treatment indicates less informative prices. The additional interaction with D(HF++) tests whether this sensitivity falls less when hedge-fund participation is high. Identification again relies on DiD-style parallel trends in this slope absent treatment.

Setting: Using Bai et al.'s price informativeness approach, the paper finds that exogenous analyst exits reduce the ability of prices to predict future earnings and that hedge-fund participation offsets this decline. In Table 12, Treat × Post × log(M/A) is -0.014 in the preferred column (2), indicating lower price informativeness after coverage reductions. When high hedge-fund participation is added, Treat × Post × log(M/A) is -0.019 while Treat × Post × log(M/A) × D(HF++) is 0.028, implying that the decline in informativeness is significantly mitigated for high-participation stocks. This robustness analysis supports the central claim that sophisticated investors help restore market efficiency after analyst exits.

Main role: This is an alternative-measure robustness analysis confirming the main conclusions about market efficiency and hedge-fund mitigation.
Settings.H76: Section 5.2, Table 12 cols. (2) and (4), PDF pp. 334-335.
Settings.G77:
Treatment: Weekly futures excess return for a commodity, either contemporaneous R_{i,t} or lagged one-week return R_{i,t-1}, measured as front-month futures price change from Tuesday to Tuesday in decimal returns. In some specifications lagged position change Q_{i,t-1} is an additional regressor; the focal interpreted treatment is return variation.

Method: Weekly Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions relate trader net position changes to contemporaneous or lagged weekly futures returns across 26 commodities. The reported specification regresses net position change Q in week t on either contemporaneous return R_{i,t} or lagged return R_{i,t-1}, with lagged Q_{i,t-1} included in some specifications. The authors interpret the signs as evidence on trading style—commercials as contrarians and noncommercials as momentum traders—rather than as a causal return effect. No fixed effects are absorbed; identification is from cross-commodity covariance in weekly returns and positions. Remaining endogeneity is substantial because returns and trading are jointly determined, but the paper uses these regressions to support the causal narrative about who initiates trades and how trader demand affects prices.

Identification: The paper interprets cross-sectional associations between returns and trader position changes as evidence on who trades with or against price movements. Identification is not causal in a strict sense because contemporaneous returns and trading are jointly determined, and lagged returns may proxy for omitted signals. The maintained interpretation is behavioral: positive sensitivity of noncommercial Q to past returns reflects momentum demand, while negative sensitivity of commercial Q reflects contrarian liquidity provision.

Setting: Using weekly Fama-MacBeth regressions, the authors show that trader position changes move oppositely across trader types in response to returns: contemporaneously, the coefficient on R_{i,t} is -0.65 for commercials and 0.52 for noncommercials; with lagged returns, the coefficient on R_{i,t-1} is -0.21 for commercials and 0.23 for noncommercials (Table II). They interpret these patterns as commercials trading as contrarians and noncommercials as momentum traders. This is a supporting causal setting because it motivates the later claim that noncommercial trading shocks create liquidity demand that commercials absorb.
