Setting: The paper checks whether the effect of competition mentions on returns survives alternative samples and horizons. The 3+ minus 1 value-weighted alpha is 0.51% when excluding small stocks, 0.40% when excluding January, 0.41% outside recessions, 0.77% in 1995–2006, and 0.26% in 2007–2017; size-neutral alphas in the two subperiods are 0.84% and 0.43%, respectively. With longer holding horizons, the monthly alpha declines gradually from 0.39% at 3 months to 0.27% at 18 months but remains statistically significant. The authors interpret these results as showing a robust and persistent causal effect of competition mentions on future abnormal returns.

Main role: These are robustness checks that reinforce the stability of the main return result across samples and horizons but do not themselves introduce a new central claim.
Settings.H169: Section 7.1 "Sample splits and longer horizons," Table 14, PDF pages 32–33 (article pp. 4331–4332).
Settings.G170:
Treatment: C-Rank, a continuous network-based competition-mention rank derived from a PageRank-type algorithm on directed competition links, operationalized in reported estimates as High versus No mentions and High versus Low C-Rank portfolio contrasts.

Method: Alternative-treatment-measure portfolio-sort analysis using C-Rank, a PageRank-style competition-mention metric that overweights mentions made by firms that themselves receive more mentions. Each month the authors run a PageRank-type algorithm on the directed network of competition links from firms’ most recent annual reports to obtain firm-level C-Rank. Firms are sorted into four portfolios: No mentions, and among mentioned firms Low, Mid, and High C-Rank. They report single-sort and size-double-sort mean excess returns and six-factor alphas. This is an observational robustness design using an alternative mention measure.

Identification: The identifying logic mirrors the baseline return-sort design, but replaces simple mention count with a network-weighted measure intended to capture more informative mentions. The authors use similar return spreads under C-Rank to argue the baseline findings are not an artifact of the simple count measure. This remains observational.

Setting: Using a PageRank-style network measure of competition mention called C-Rank, the paper finds similar return predictability to the simple mention count. In the single sort, the High minus No-mentions portfolio has a six-factor alpha of 0.31% per month and High minus Low has 0.36%; in the size-double-sort, the corresponding alphas are 0.49% and 0.25%. The authors interpret this as evidence that the effect of competition mentions on future returns is robust to using a richer network-weighted treatment measure rather than a simple mention count.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis showing the main findings are similar under a more complex alternative mention metric.
Settings.H170: Section 7.2 "Alternative mention-based measure," Table 15 Panels A and B, PDF pages 34–35 (article pp. 4333–4334).
Settings.G171:
Treatment: Indicator for lender-quarter being just above rather than just below the zero EPS-surprise cutoff around analysts' consensus forecast at the earnings announcement; specifically, lenders that just meet/beat versus just miss the benchmark in the local window shown in Figure 1 panel A.

Method: The paper presents a sharp regression-discontinuity style estimate of lenders' 3-day cumulative market-adjusted stock return around earnings announcements as a function of lender EPS surprise relative to the zero-surprise cutoff. Treatment is eligibility/assignment to just beating rather than just missing the analyst consensus benchmark near zero EPS surprise, implemented as a local discontinuity in outcomes at the cutoff in Figure 1 panel A. The authors use this as diagnostic/motivating evidence that just beating the benchmark raises market value, thereby creating short-termism incentives. The running variable is lender EPS surprise in cents, cutoff at zero, and the reported effect compares lenders just to the right of zero (zero or +1 cent) with those just to the left (-1 or -2 cents).

Identification: Identification comes from local comparison of lender announcement returns for observations just above versus just below the zero EPS-surprise benchmark. The paper argues that the discontinuity in capital-market rewards at the benchmark reveals incentives to manipulate or behave myopically. The RD interpretation requires that other determinants of announcement returns vary smoothly through the cutoff and that local observations on either side are comparable, though the paper uses this mainly as diagnostic evidence rather than a full causal design for a substantive outcome.

Setting: Using a sharp RD around the zero EPS-surprise cutoff, the paper shows that lenders that just meet or beat analysts' consensus forecast receive higher announcement returns than lenders that just miss it. Figure 1 panel A reports a 0.69% discontinuity in the 3-day cumulative market-adjusted return for just-meet/beat relative to just-miss lenders. This result is used to support the premise that beating short-term earnings benchmarks yields capital-market benefits and therefore generates short-termism incentives, which motivates the paper's main enforcement analyses.

Main role: This is motivating/validation evidence for the short-termism measure rather than the paper's main spillover result about covenant enforcement and borrower outcomes.
Settings.H171: Figure 1, Panel A; Section 2.1 Economic framework; PDF pp. 3, 12
Settings.G172:
Treatment: Interaction treatment capturing whether a breaching borrower (Breach=1, covenant slack below zero) is matched to a short-termist lender (STLender=1, lender EPS surprise equals zero or +1 cent within the main two-cent window around analyst consensus). The focal causal contrast is incremental enforcement for breached loans when the lender has short-termism incentives.

Method: Baseline linear probability regressions at the loan package-quarter level estimate whether lender short-termism raises covenant enforcement when borrowers breach covenant thresholds. The core regressor is Breach × STLender, where STLender indicates lender-quarters with EPS surprise of 0 or +1 cent, and Breach indicates negative covenant slack. Specifications include quarter FE, industry×quarter FE, lender FE, and in the preferred specifications lender×quarter FE, plus controls for Slack, indicators for each cent of lender EPS surprise, loan characteristics, and borrower characteristics. Standard errors are double clustered by lender and borrower. The preferred design absorbs three FE dimensions/sets at once (quarter, industry×quarter, lender×quarter), and the authors explicitly argue these absorb time-varying lender heterogeneity, portfolio composition, and industry shocks.

Identification: The paper identifies from within-lender-time and within-industry-time variation in whether a lender is just meeting/beating its EPS benchmark, interacting that with whether the borrower is in breach of a covenant threshold. By controlling flexibly for lender EPS surprise bins, slack, borrower and loan observables, and especially industry×quarter and lender×quarter fixed effects, the authors aim to compare breaching and nonbreaching loans facing the same lender in the same quarter and in the same industry-time environment, attributing extra enforcement to lender short-termism incentives rather than borrower quality or macro conditions. The strategy still relies on selection-on-observables-plus-fixed-effects assumptions and on the claim that unobserved differences in borrower breach opportunities or manipulation are not systematically related to STLender; the paper presents appendices arguing STLender is uncorrelated with slack, breaches, borrower short-termism, and lender health.

Setting: The paper's main fixed-effects evidence shows that lenders facing short-term earnings benchmark pressure enforce covenant breaches more often. In Table 2, the coefficient on Breach × STLender ranges from 0.029 to 0.033 across specifications and is 0.032 in the preferred specification with controls and quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter fixed effects (PDF p. 17). The authors interpret this as a 3.2-percentage-point increase in enforcement for breached loans when the lender just meets or beats analysts' EPS forecast, which they describe as a 51.6% marginal effect relative to the 6.24% baseline enforcement rate in that column. This setting directly underpins the paper's core claim that lender short-termism spills over to borrowers through covenant enforcement.

Main role: This is the paper's central causal setting: the main claim is that lenders facing short-term earnings benchmarks enforce covenant breaches more aggressively.
Settings.H172: Equation (3); Table 2 columns 1-5; Section 2.3 Baseline results; PDF pp. 16-18
Settings.G173:
Treatment: Same binary interaction treatment as in the baseline: breaching loan-package-quarter observations exposed to a short-termist lender (Breach × STLender), where breach is alternatively measured from specific covenant types or in restricted samples to reduce measurement error.

Method: Robustness linear probability regressions for Enforcement on Breach × STLender using alternative constructions of covenant slack and breach status and restricted samples designed to reduce measurement error. All specifications are otherwise identical to the preferred Table 2 column 5 model, with controls and quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter FE, and double-clustered standard errors by lender and borrower. Panel A redefines Slack/Breach using standardized covenant types (Debt/EBITDA, current ratio, net worth, or combined). Panel B restricts the sample to loans without dynamic thresholds, without renegotiations, near first breach, or excluding never-breach loans.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same as in the main FE design, but the authors attempt to strengthen credibility by reducing measurement error in the constructed running variable Slack and in breach identification. By focusing on more standardized covenant definitions and samples less likely to involve changing thresholds or renegotiation, they argue any remaining estimate more cleanly captures the effect of lender short-termism on enforcement rather than artifacts of mismeasured breaches. Assumptions remain those of the baseline FE framework.

Setting: A battery of FE robustness tests shows that the main finding survives alternative constructions of covenant slack and restricted samples intended to limit measurement error. In Table 3 panel A, the preferred combined standardized-covenant specification yields a Breach × STLender coefficient of 0.048, implying a 4.8-percentage-point higher enforcement rate for short-termist lenders; other standardized covenant definitions produce estimates from 0.038 to 0.090. In Table 3 panel B, estimates remain positive and significant under restrictions excluding dynamic thresholds (0.035), renegotiated loans (0.065), observations after first breach (0.032), and never-breach loans (0.033). These results support the paper's main conclusion that short-termism increases covenant enforcement rather than arising from slack measurement error.

Main role: These robustness designs materially reinforce the central enforcement claim by showing it is not driven by slack measurement error or renegotiation-related mismeasurement.
Settings.H173: Table 3 Panels A and B; Section 2.4 Alternative measurement and robustness; PDF pp. 19-21
Settings.G174:
Treatment: Binary interaction treatment Breach × STLender, where STLender is alternatively defined using different EPS surprise bins around the analyst benchmark and estimated in wider EPS-surprise samples.

Method: Robustness FE regressions for Enforcement on Breach × STLender using alternative definitions of STLender and wider EPS-surprise windows around the benchmark. The specification matches the preferred Table 2 column 5 model with controls and quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter FE; standard errors double clustered by lender and borrower. Variants include 5-cent and 10-cent sample windows and STLender defined as exactly zero, 0-2 cents, 0-3 cents, or -1 to +3 cents.

Identification: The design continues to exploit within-lender and within-industry-time variation in benchmark pressure, but varies the coding of short-termist status to assess sensitivity to how benchmark-induced incentives are measured. The assumption is that if the effect is truly due to short-termism near earnings thresholds, it should persist across reasonable alternative definitions of just meeting/beating or narrowly missing the benchmark.

Setting: The paper shows that higher covenant enforcement by short-termist lenders is robust to alternative definitions of the short-termism treatment. In Table 4, the Breach × STLender coefficient is 0.026 in a [-5,5] sample with the baseline [0,1] treatment bin, 0.040 in a [-10,10] sample with the same bin, 0.038 when STLender is defined as exactly zero, 0.023 when defined as [0,2], 0.024 when defined as [0,3], and 0.027 when defined as [-1,3]. The authors interpret this as evidence that the main result does not hinge on a particular benchmark-window choice and continues to support the claim that lender short-termism raises covenant enforcement.

Main role: These robustness tests directly support the main enforcement result by showing it is not an artifact of one narrow STLender coding choice.
Settings.H174: Table 4; Section 2.4 Alternative measurement and robustness; PDF pp. 21-22
Settings.G175:
Treatment: Binary or continuous moderated treatment: the incremental effect of Breach × STLender when analyst forecast dispersion is low or analyst coverage is high. The focal treatment remains lender short-termism during borrower breach, interacted with benchmark precision/salience measures.

Method: FE triple-interaction regressions test whether the effect of lender short-termism on covenant enforcement is stronger when analyst benchmarks are more precise or salient. The underlying model is the preferred Table 2 column 5 specification, augmented with Breach × STLender × Disp, Breach × STLender × 1[Low Disp], Breach × STLender × Cov, or Breach × STLender × 1[High Cov]. Controls and FE include quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter fixed effects, with double clustering by lender and borrower.

Identification: The authors argue that if STLender captures benchmark-driven short-termism, then the enforcement response should be stronger when the relevant benchmark is more precise (low analyst forecast dispersion) or more salient (high analyst coverage). Identification is within the same FE framework as the main design, but on differential slopes by these moderator variables. Interpretation assumes the moderators do not proxy for omitted variables driving enforcement in a way not absorbed by the FE and controls.

Setting: Cross-sectional FE tests show that the benchmark-related enforcement effect is larger when analysts' forecasts are more precise or more salient. In Table 5, the triple interaction Breach × STLender × 1[Low Disp] is 0.073, implying short-termist lenders with low forecast dispersion enforce 7.3 percentage points more often, and Breach × STLender × 1[High Cov] is 0.080, implying 8.0 percentage points more enforcement for high-coverage lenders. These patterns are interpreted as validating the short-termism measure: lenders respond more strongly when the earnings benchmark is clearer or draws more attention.

Main role: These are internal-validity and mechanism-style heterogeneity tests validating the short-termism construct rather than standalone central claims.
Settings.H175: Table 5; Section 2.4 Alternative measurement and robustness / internal validity discussion; PDF pp. 23-24
Settings.G176:
Treatment: Alternative measures of lender short-termism or incentives to accelerate income recognition during borrower breach: ex ante manipulation likelihood (%manip), CEO near retirement, long-tenured CEO, low bank capital, or low bank liquidity. Treatments are continuous for %manip and binary for the others.

Method: Alternative-treatment FE regressions relate covenant enforcement to other measures of lender short-termism or income-acceleration incentives. Each regression interacts Breach with one alternative treatment: %manip (continuous ex ante structural manipulation likelihood), RetirementAge, LongTenure, LowCapital, or LowLiquidity. Specifications include controls and quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter FE, with double-clustered standard errors by lender and borrower.

Identification: Identification mirrors the main FE strategy but substitutes alternative treatment proxies for STLender. The logic is that if myopia or earnings pressure drives enforcement, other proxies for short horizons or regulatory pressure should also predict higher enforcement of breaches. Causal interpretation remains limited by possible omitted variables specific to each proxy, though the FE and controls absorb broad heterogeneity.

Setting: Using alternative measures of short-termism and income pressure, the paper finds similar increases in covenant enforcement. Table 6 shows that a 10-percentage-point increase in the ex ante manipulation likelihood %manip is associated with a 3.7-percentage-point higher enforcement rate; CEOs near retirement are associated with an 18.7-percentage-point increase; long-tenured CEOs with a 9.7-percentage-point increase; low-capital banks with a 10.0-percentage-point increase; and low-liquidity banks with a 4.7-percentage-point increase. These results corroborate the main interpretation that short-term incentives and income pressure increase lender enforcement.

Main role: These are corroborating analyses using alternative short-termism proxies and related motives, supporting but not replacing the main STLender design.
Settings.H176: Table 6; Section 2.4 Alternative measurement and robustness; PDF pp. 24-25
Settings.G177:
Treatment: ExAnteSTLender, an indicator equal to one if the lender's latent (pre-enforcement) EPS surprise is in the [-2,0) cent window, interpreted as ex ante incentive to manipulate earnings via covenant enforcement.

Method: Bank-quarter panel regressions estimate whether an ex ante short-termism measure based on the latent pre-enforcement EPS surprise distribution raises bank-level enforcement rates. Treatment is ExAnteSTLender, an indicator for latent EPS surprise in [-2,0). Outcomes are enforcement rates defined as fraction of all loans with material covenant violations or fraction of breached loans with material covenant violations. Specifications add quarter FE, lender FE, and bank controls; errors clustered by lender. Because the regressions include at most two FE dimensions (quarter and lender), this is standard FE rather than HDFE.

Identification: The paper constructs a latent EPS surprise distribution by removing the direct effects of enforcement on earnings and then compares lender-quarters just below versus just above the latent benchmark, focusing on banks with plausible ex ante incentive to manipulate. Identification comes from within-bank and within-quarter comparisons in a narrow window around latent zero surprise, assuming this latent measure better captures ex ante incentives and reduces concerns that realized STLender reflects omitted variables. Remaining concerns include modeling assumptions in constructing latent EPS.

Setting: Using a distinct bank-level FE design based on a latent pre-enforcement EPS distribution, the paper finds that ex ante short-termism incentives raise enforcement rates. In Table 7, ExAnteSTLender increases enforcement rates by about 0.037-0.044 when the denominator is all loans, and by 0.076-0.097 when the denominator is breached loans; in the most restrictive specifications the authors emphasize a 3.7-percentage-point increase relative to a 5.42% mean enforcement rate, or 69%. They interpret this as corroborating the main result with different identifying variation: banks that ex ante need enforcement income to hit EPS targets enforce more.

Main role: The paper highlights this as distinct identifying variation that corroborates the main result using ex ante incentives rather than realized surprise.
Settings.H177: Table 7; Section 2.4 final paragraphs on ex ante lender short-termism; PDF pp. 26-27
Settings.G178:
Treatment: Moderated lender short-termism during borrower breach, with moderators capturing alternative earnings management tools: share repurchases, changes in loan loss reserves, loan loss provisions, or large unrealized losses. The focal causal parameter is the triple interaction on incremental enforcement.

Method: FE triple-interaction regressions study whether covenant enforcement by short-termist lenders is stronger when other earnings-management tools are simultaneously available or being used. The underlying model is the preferred Table 2 column 5 specification, augmented with Breach × STLender × 1[Repurchase], Breach × STLender × LLR, Breach × STLender × LLP, or Breach × STLender × 1[LargeUnrealizedLoss]. Controls and FE include quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter FE; standard errors double clustered by lender and borrower.

Identification: Within the preferred FE design, the paper tests whether the short-termism effect is amplified when banks are using or constrained in other earnings-management channels. Interpretation assumes these moderators do not simply proxy for omitted, time-varying lender distress not already controlled for by FE and covariates. The causal claim is modest: benchmark-driven short-termism is stronger alongside other manipulation tools.

Setting: The paper finds that covenant enforcement is part of a broader portfolio of earnings-management tools used by short-termist lenders. In Table 8, the triple interaction Breach × STLender × 1[Repurchase] is 0.064, implying repurchasing short-termist lenders enforce 6.4 percentage points more. A one-standard-deviation decrease in loan loss reserve changes is associated with a 6.4-percentage-point higher enforcement rate, higher loan loss provisions reduce enforcement by 4.6 percentage points, and large unrealized losses are associated with a 13.9-percentage-point increase. These results support the mechanism that short-termist lenders opportunistically use covenant enforcement together with other income-management tools.

Main role: These are mechanism/complementarity tests showing covenant enforcement is part of a portfolio of earnings-management tools, not the central spillover claim itself.
Settings.H178: Table 8; Section 2.5 Cross-sectional heterogeneity in lender short-termism; PDF pp. 27-29
Settings.G179:
Treatment: Moderated treatment capturing short-termist lender exposure during borrower breach, interacted with executive pay-performance sensitivity (Delta), variable compensation, institutional ownership share, ownership concentration, or board experience. Some moderators are continuous, one binary.

Method: FE triple-interaction regressions examine how governance and managerial incentive structures moderate the effect of lender short-termism on covenant enforcement. The preferred Table 2 column 5 model is augmented with Breach × STLender × Delta, VariableCompensation, IO(%), OwnConcentration, or ExperiencedBoard. Controls and quarter, industry×quarter, lender, and lender×quarter FE are included; standard errors are double clustered by lender and borrower.

Identification: The same FE identification as the main enforcement design is used, while allowing the Breach × STLender effect to vary with managerial incentives and governance quality. The paper argues that if short-termism truly drives enforcement, stronger pay-performance sensitivity should amplify it and stronger governance should attenuate it. Interpretation assumes the governance variables do not capture omitted drivers of enforcement that survive the FE and controls.

Setting: Governance and compensation shape the enforcement response of short-termist lenders. In Table 9, one-standard-deviation higher Delta raises the short-termist enforcement effect by 3.6 percentage points, and higher variable compensation raises it by 2.1 percentage points. By contrast, stronger governance attenuates the effect: a 10-percentage-point increase in institutional ownership lowers enforcement by about 2.0 percentage points, more concentrated institutional ownership lowers it further, and experienced boards reduce it by 3.8 percentage points. The paper interprets this as evidence that managerial incentives amplify myopic enforcement while governance constrains it.

Main role: These are important heterogeneity and mechanism tests but support the central argument rather than constituting the core standalone result.
Settings.H179: Table 9; Section 2.5 Cross-sectional heterogeneity in lender short-termism; PDF pp. 29-31
Settings.G180:
Treatment: Binary interaction treatment Breach × STLender, indicating a breached loan matched to a short-termist lender, where short-termism is lender EPS surprise of 0 or +1 cent. The causal contrast is whether such exposure raises the chance the borrower switches lenders on its next loan.

Method: Loan package-quarter FE regressions estimate whether short-termist lender enforcement increases borrowers' propensity to switch lead arrangers on their next loan. The model is Equation (4) with outcome Switch, an indicator for changing lead arranger on the subsequent loan within a given horizon, and includes Slack, lender EPS surprise bins, loan and borrower controls, quarter FE, industry×quarter FE, lender FE, and lender×quarter FE in preferred specifications. Breach and Slack are based on the minimum slack in the prior four quarters to allow time for enforcement. Standard errors are double clustered by lender and borrower. Panel B varies the horizon from 1 to 5 years.

Identification: Using within-lender-quarter and within-industry-quarter variation, the paper compares future switching behavior for breached versus nonbreached loans depending on whether the current lender is short-termist. Extensive FE and controls are intended to absorb differences in lender-borrower matching and macro conditions. The interpretation assumes that, conditional on these controls and FE, the additional switching among breached borrowers with short-termist lenders reflects harsher enforcement and damaged relationship capital rather than omitted borrower demand for other lenders.

Setting: The paper finds that short-termist lender enforcement damages lending relationships by increasing future lender switching. In Table 10 panel A, the coefficient on Breach × STLender ranges from 0.026 to 0.048, and equals 0.046 in the preferred specification, implying a 4.6-percentage-point higher probability that the borrower uses a different lead arranger on its next loan. Panel B shows the effect is strongest at short horizons: 8.3 percentage points within 1 year, 4.6 within 2 years, and 3.0 within 5 years. The authors interpret this as evidence that short-termist lenders trade off relationship capital for short-run income.

Main role: Borrower switching is one of the paper's main consequences of short-termist enforcement and supports the core claim that lenders sacrifice relationship capital.
Settings.H180: Equation (4); Table 10 Panels A and B; Section 3.1.1 Relationship dynamics; PDF pp. 32-35
Settings.G181:
Treatment: Binary interaction treatment Breach × STLender: a breached borrower facing a short-termist lender. The parameter captures whether short-termist lenders renegotiate into higher spreads or amounts after breaches.

Method: Loan package-quarter FE regressions estimate the effect of short-termist lender enforcement on renegotiated loan terms. The model is Equation (4) with outcomes lnSpread and lnAmount, defined as differences in natural logs between the current loan and the renegotiated next loan's spread or amount. As in the switching regressions, Breach and Slack use the minimum slack in the prior four quarters, and specifications include controls, quarter FE, industry×quarter FE, lender FE, and lender×quarter FE; standard errors double clustered by lender and borrower.

Identification: The paper compares how loan terms change after covenant breaches depending on lender short-termism, conditioning on slack, observable loan and borrower characteristics, and extensive FE that absorb lender-time and industry-time shocks. The identifying assumption is that, absent short-termism-induced enforcement behavior, breached borrowers handled by the same lender in the same quarter would not face systematically different renegotiated terms. Remaining concerns include endogenous renegotiation selection and unobserved borrower demand shocks.

Setting: Short-termist lenders not only enforce more often but also extract tougher renegotiated terms. In Table 11 panel A, the preferred coefficient on Breach × STLender is 0.068, which the authors interpret as renegotiated loans having 6.8% higher spreads when the lender is short-termist. In panel B, the preferred coefficient is 0.155, implying 15.5% higher renegotiated loan amounts. The paper argues this pattern is consistent with lenders maximizing short-term fee and spread income rather than simply reducing exposure to troubled borrowers.

Main role: Renegotiated spreads and amounts are key substantive consequences showing how short-termist lenders extract income from borrowers.
Settings.H181: Equation (4); Table 11 Panels A and B; Section 3.1.2 Renegotiation; PDF pp. 33-36
Settings.G182:
Treatment: STLender indicator equal to one if the enforcing lender has EPS surprise of zero or +1 cent in the relevant quarter, zero otherwise.

Method: A small-sample fee regression estimates whether short-termist lenders charge higher waiver/amendment fees when covenant breaches are enforced. Outcome is fee in basis points, measured from manually collected borrower 8-K disclosures. Treatment is STLender. Specifications incrementally add year FE, industry×year FE, lender FE, and lender×year FE plus loan and borrower controls; heteroskedasticity-robust SE reported. Because the most restrictive model uses year, industry×year, lender, and lender×year FE but not the same HDFE discussion as main identification and with only one focal treatment, this is treated as standard FE robustness/supporting evidence.

Identification: The paper compares fees charged by short-termist versus other lenders after material covenant violations, controlling for observed loan and borrower characteristics and increasingly rich year/lender/industry FE. The causal interpretation is that lender short-termism raises the fees extracted conditional on an enforcement event. Selection into the small sample of disclosed fees and limited sample size remain important concerns.

Setting: In the subsample where waiver and amendment fees are observed from 8-K filings, short-termist lenders charge materially higher fees. Table B.7 reports fee differences from 18.29 to 53.18 bps across specifications; in the preferred specification with controls and industry×year and lender×year FE, the estimate is 51.75 bps. The paper interprets this as direct evidence that short-termist enforcement boosts contemporaneous lender income through fees.

Main role: This is supportive evidence on one mechanism—higher direct fees—rather than a main headline result.
Settings.H182: Appendix Table B.7; discussed in Section 3.1.2 Renegotiation; PDF pp. 36, 51
Settings.G183:
Treatment: Binary interaction treatment Breach × STLender, indicating a breached borrower currently matched to a short-termist lender. The treatment is interpreted as exposure to short-termist lender enforcement pressure during/after covenant breach.

Method: Loan package-quarter FE regressions estimate the effect of short-termist lender enforcement on borrower investment outcomes. The model is Equation (4) with outcomes Investment(%) and an indicator for large investment cuts, using the minimum slack in the prior four quarters. Investment is defined as quarterly growth in total investment, where total investment is capital expenditures plus R&D plus acquisitions; large-cut outcome equals one if investment falls by at least 20% quarter-over-quarter. Specifications include quarter FE, industry×quarter FE, lender FE, lender×quarter FE, borrower and loan controls, and double-clustered SE by lender and borrower.

Identification: The paper compares investment outcomes for covenant-breaching and nonbreaching borrowers depending on whether their lender is short-termist, with lender×quarter and industry×quarter FE absorbing lender-time and industry-time shocks and controls absorbing observed borrower and loan differences. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on these FE and controls, the extra decline in investment among breached borrowers with short-termist lenders reflects incremental enforcement and financing pressure rather than omitted borrower shocks. The paper discusses the usual concern that enforcement is endogenous to investment, but argues the relevant bias would require borrowers to manipulate breaches differentially by lender short-termism, for which it finds little evidence in appendices.

Setting: The paper finds that lender short-termism has real effects on borrower investment. In Table 12, the preferred specification shows Breach × STLender = -0.078 for investment growth, implying 7.8% lower investment for affected borrowers, and 0.041 for the probability of an investment cut larger than 20%, implying a 4.1-percentage-point higher chance of a large investment cut. These estimates support the paper's central claim that short-termist enforcement transmits myopic incentives from lenders to borrowers' real policies.

Main role: Real effects on borrower investment are among the paper's main substantive conclusions about spillovers from lender short-termism.
Settings.H183: Table 12 Panels A and B; Section 3.2 Real effects; PDF pp. 36-38
Settings.G184:
Treatment: Interaction treatment Enforcement × STLender: announced material covenant violation by a borrower whose lender is short-termist (EPS surprise 0 or +1 cent in the local window) versus announced violation with non-short-termist lender.

Method: Event-study style linear regressions estimate the market reaction to borrower announcements of material covenant violations, comparing announcements when the lender is short-termist versus not. The model is Equation (5): cumulative abnormal return over the 3-day window around the announcement on Enforcement, STLender, and Enforcement × STLender, controlling for borrower Slack and lender EPS surprise. No FE are reported in this equation. Abnormal return outcomes include raw returns, market-adjusted returns, market model, FF3, and FF3+momentum abnormal returns. The sample is restricted to disclosures within four quarters of the covenant breach and lender EPS surprise; results are shown for 2-cent and 10-cent EPS-surprise windows.

Identification: The paper attributes differences in announcement returns to whether the disclosing borrower's lender is short-termist, conditional on enforcement having occurred, borrower slack, and lender EPS surprise. This is a regression-adjustment/event-study design rather than a quasi-experiment. Identification requires that, conditional on the included controls and sample restrictions, material covenant violation announcements by borrowers with short-termist versus non-short-termist lenders differ primarily because of the lender's benchmark-driven enforcement rather than omitted information revealed at announcement.

Setting: Event-study regressions show that borrower announcements of material covenant violations are received more negatively when the lender is short-termist. In Table 13, the market reaction to an announcement for non-short-termist lenders is around -1.7% to -3.0% depending on the return model and window, while the incremental coefficient on Enforcement × STLender is between -0.9% and -1.7%. The paper interprets this as evidence that the market views the extra attention and tougher treatment from short-termist lenders as value-decreasing for borrower shareholders.

Main role: The more negative borrower market reaction is a central piece of evidence that short-termist lender attention is value-decreasing for borrower shareholders.
Settings.H184: Equation (5); Table 13; Section 3.3 Market reaction to violation announcements; PDF pp. 38-40
Settings.G185:
Treatment: STLender indicator equal to one if the bank just meets or beats its earnings benchmark (EPS surprise 0 or +1 cent) in that quarter, within the preferred [-2,2] cent window.

Method: Bank-quarter event-study regressions estimate long-run lender performance following earnings announcements for STLender banks. Equation (6) regresses 3-year cumulative abnormal returns from one day before the earnings announcement through 3 years after on STLender plus calendar-quarter fixed effects. Return outcomes include raw, market-adjusted, market model, FF3, and FF3+momentum measures. This is a linear regression/event-study design with quarter FE, not a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: The authors interpret lower long-run abnormal returns for STLender banks as evidence that actions taken to meet short-term benchmarks are costly in the long run. Identification is limited: this is essentially an event-study regression with quarter FE, so causal interpretation relies on the assumption that being a just-meet-or-beat bank near the benchmark captures myopic actions rather than persistent differences in bank quality or risk. The result is framed as supportive evidence consistent with costly short-termism.

Setting: The paper documents that banks just meeting or beating earnings benchmarks earn lower returns over the next three years, consistent with long-run costs of short-termist behavior. In Table 14 column 1, STLender coefficients across return models range from -0.039 to -0.082, meaning 3.9% to 8.2% lower long-run cumulative returns. The authors use this as broad evidence that the strategies banks use to hit short-term earnings targets, including excess covenant enforcement, are costly over the long run.

Main role: Long-run costs to lenders are one of the paper's major conclusions used to justify the 'short-termism' label and the tradeoff of short-run gains for long-run losses.
Settings.H185: Equation (6); Table 14 column 1; Section 3.5 Long-run costs for lenders; PDF pp. 42-44
Settings.G186:
Treatment: Interaction between STLender and the year-over-year change in covenant enforcement rate for the bank-quarter, with enforcement rate measured either by number of loans or loan amounts; the focal treatment is higher enforcement intensity when the bank is short-termist.

Method: Long-run lender event-study regressions augment the STLender specification with EnforcementRate and EnforcementRate × STLender to test whether using covenant enforcement to meet benchmarks is especially costly. Equation (7) regresses 3-year cumulative abnormal returns on STLender, year-over-year change in enforcement rate, and their interaction, with calendar-quarter fixed effects. EnforcementRate is defined alternatively using loan counts or loan amounts. Outcomes are the same five long-run return measures as in Table 14.

Identification: This regression-adjustment design relates long-run abnormal returns to changes in enforcement rates for STLender banks. The interaction coefficient is interpreted as the extra long-run cost of relying more on covenant enforcement as a benchmark-beating strategy. Identification is associational and depends on the assumption that conditional on STLender and quarter FE, variation in enforcement-rate changes is not driven by omitted determinants of long-run returns.

Setting: The paper further tests whether increasing covenant enforcement is an especially costly way for short-termist banks to meet earnings benchmarks. In Table 14, the interaction STLender × EnforcementRate is negative across all specifications: for example, -0.109 and -0.244 when enforcement rates are count-based, and -0.087 and -0.159 when amount-based, depending on the return model shown. Although not always statistically significant, the uniformly negative estimates are interpreted as evidence that using covenant enforcement to hit benchmarks is at least as costly, and possibly more costly, than other benchmark-beating tools.

Main role: This is a supporting test sharpening the long-run-cost mechanism by asking whether excess enforcement is especially costly relative to other benchmark-beating tools.
Settings.H186: Equation (7); Table 14 columns 2-5; Section 3.5 Long-run costs for lenders; PDF pp. 43-44
Settings.G187:
Treatment: Lagged state variables included jointly in linear predictive regressions. Treatments are continuous macro-finance variables: dividend yield (DY), default spread (DS), term spread (TS), three-month t-bill rate (RF), price-earnings ratio (PE), value spread (VS), Cochrane-Piazzesi bond factor (CP), and term-structure level factor (LVL). Units are those of the underlying financial variables/spreads as constructed from market and bond data; coding is continuous, not binary.

Method: The authors estimate unconditional linear predictive regressions of log consumption growth cumulated over horizons H=1, 2, and 4 quarters on lagged state variables for four benchmark state-variable models: Model 1 z=(DY, DS, TS), Model 2 z=(DY, DS, RF), Model 3 z=(TS, PE, VS), and Model 4 z=(DY, CP, LVL). The regressions are quarterly time-series OLS with Newey-West standard errors using H lags. The intended interpretation is that changes in lagged state variables predict future macro growth, which the paper treats as economically meaningful and as motivation for later asset-pricing tests, though the authors acknowledge unconditional predictability is modest.

Identification: Identification comes from time-series covariation between lagged state variables and future consumption growth in linear regressions. The paper interprets coefficients as predictive effects of state variables on macro growth, but there is no quasi-experimental source of variation; endogeneity/model misspecification remains possible. The assumptions are standard predictive-regression assumptions plus HAC inference for serial correlation from overlapping horizons.

Setting: In Table 1, the authors estimate unconditional OLS predictive regressions of future log consumption growth on lagged state variables. For example, in Model 1, DY positively predicts consumption growth while DS negatively predicts it, with adjusted R2 values from 7.11% at H=1 to 10.25% at H=4; in Model 2, DS is again negative while RF is near zero; Models 3 and 4 have weaker predictive content. These regressions are interpreted as evidence that state variables affect future macro growth, but the authors emphasize that unconditional specifications understate the economically relevant time variation central to the paper.

Main role: These regressions are motivational background rather than the paper's core contribution. The abstract and conclusion emphasize time-varying predictability and time-varying state-variable risk premia, not the unconditional predictive regressions themselves.
Settings.G188:
Treatment: The treatment is the rolling-window fitted conditional predictor of future consumption growth, a_t^H + b_t^H z_t, derived from lagged state variables in the four benchmark models z=(DY,DS,TS), (DY,DS,RF), (TS,PE,VS), and (DY,CP,LVL). This predictor is continuous and summarizes the time-varying relation between state variables and future consumption growth.

Method: The authors implement a two-stage rolling-window predictive regression design for consumption growth. First stage: over a backward-looking ten-year rolling window, they regress consumption growth on lagged state variables to estimate time-varying coefficients a_t^H and b_t^H. Second stage: they regress realized future consumption growth from t+1 to t+H on the first-stage fitted conditional expectation a_t^H + b_t^H z_t. Estimation is linear OLS in both stages; inference uses Newey-West and block-bootstrap standard errors to address serial correlation, overlapping horizons, and generated-regressor/errors-in-variables concerns. No forward-looking information is used when forecasting.

Identification: Identification relies on time-series variation in rolling estimated predictive relationships between lagged state variables and future consumption growth. The paper's argument is that these estimated coefficients proxy time-varying SDF/risk-aversion coefficients. Assumptions are that the backward-looking rolling regression captures economically meaningful variation rather than noise, that no look-ahead bias is present, and that bootstrap inference addresses generated-regressor uncertainty. This remains observational, not experimental.

Setting: The paper's first main empirical claim is that time-varying predictive relations between lagged state variables and future consumption growth materially improve macro-growth forecasts. In the second-stage regressions of Table 2, the coefficient d1 on the rolling fitted predictor is positive and significant across all four state-variable models and all horizons: at H=1 it ranges from 0.56 to 0.71, with R2 values from 17.30% to 26.80%; relative to unconditional models, the R2 improvement ranges from 10.86% to 25.14%. The authors interpret this as evidence that changes in state variables affect future consumption growth in a time-varying way, which underpins their later causal interpretation of time-varying risk premia.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight as a first main result that the relation between state variables and consumption growth is time-varying and that controlling for this substantially improves predictability. This two-stage setting is therefore central to the paper's argument.
Settings.H188: Section 3.2, Eqs. (6) and (7), Table 2, PDF pp. 7–8.
Settings.G189:
Treatment: Lagged time-varying predictive relation between each state variable and future consumption growth, measured by either (i) a dummy for positive rolling coefficient I(b_t,zk^H>0), (ii) a dummy for coefficient above the state variable's time-series median I(b_t,zk^H>median), or (iii) the raw rolling ten-year predictive coefficient b_t,zk^H from regressions of future consumption growth on lagged state variables. Treatment is continuous or binary depending on specification; the central pooled setting groups these closely related estimands reported together.

Method: The authors run pooled panel predictive regressions of annualized state-variable risk premia on lagged measures of the strength of each state's predictive relation with future consumption growth. The dependent variable is the H-quarter overlapping return to a state-variable risk-premium portfolio estimated from Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions; the key regressors are either an indicator for a positive rolling coefficient I(b_t,zk^H>0), an indicator for above-median rolling coefficient I(b_t,zk^H>median), or the raw rolling coefficient b_t,zk^H. Some specifications include state-variable fixed effects to absorb time-invariant differences in unconditional premia across the eight unique state variables. Inference uses Driscoll-Kraay and block-bootstrap standard errors.

Identification: Identification comes from within-state-variable and pooled time-series variation in lagged rolling predictive coefficients for macro growth. The authors argue that if a state variable's shocks become more informative about future consumption growth, ICAPM implies its risk price should rise. State-variable fixed effects absorb average differences across variables so identification in those columns is from time variation within variable. Key assumptions are that the rolling coefficients proxy time-varying risk aversion/SDF loadings and are not spurious; simulations are offered to argue size and power, but endogeneity remains observational.

Setting: Using pooled predictive regressions with state-variable fixed effects, the authors find that stronger lagged state-variable prediction of consumption growth raises subsequent state-variable risk premia. In Table 4, an above-median rolling coefficient raises annualized risk premia by 5.17% at H=1, 5.16% at H=2, and 6.31% at H=4; using the raw coefficient, a one-standard-deviation increase in b_t,zk implies roughly a 2.5% increase in quarterly-horizon and 3% increase in annual-horizon risk premia. The authors interpret this as core evidence that time variation in macro predictive content causally shifts the price of state-variable risk, consistent with the ICAPM.

Main role: This is the paper's central result: the abstract states that when a state variable predicts consumption strongly relative to its own history, its annualized risk premium increases by about 6% (0.4 in Sharpe ratio). Table 4 provides the core evidence.
Settings.G190:
Treatment: Joint treatment is the time-varying predictive coefficient between the state variable and future consumption growth and the conditional variance of that state variable, especially their interaction sigma^2_t,zk × b_t,zk (or the dummy interaction I(b_t,zk>0) × I(sigma^2_t,zk>median)). Both components are continuous in the main specification; the robustness dummy version is binary.

Method: The authors augment the pooled predictive regressions of state-variable risk premia with the interaction between the rolling consumption-growth predictive coefficient and the GARCH(1,1) conditional variance of each state variable. They estimate both a continuous specification using b_t,zk and standardized conditional variance sigma^2_t,zk, and a dummy specification using I(b_t,zk>0) and I(sigma^2_t,zk>median). Some specifications add state-variable fixed effects. Outcomes are annualized annual-horizon overlapping returns to state-variable risk-premium portfolios. Inference uses Driscoll-Kraay and block-bootstrap standard errors, and the authors emphasize predicted values in four cases (low/high b crossed with low/high variance).

Identification: Identification relies on pooled time-series variation in lagged rolling predictive coefficients and lagged estimated conditional variances of state variables. The ICAPM implies that the price of unit beta exposure should be larger in absolute value when the state variable is both more informative about future consumption and more volatile. State-variable fixed effects absorb unconditional cross-variable differences where included. Assumptions are that GARCH conditional variance captures relevant time-varying risk magnitude and that rolling coefficients capture time-varying risk aversion rather than noise; the design is observational.

Setting: At the annual horizon, the authors find that high conditional variance amplifies the effect of state variables' macro predictive content on their risk premia. In Table 5, predicted annualized risk premia rise monotonically from −4.36% when the predictive coefficient is low and variance high to +4.73% when both are high in the continuous specification; in the dummy specification the analogous values are −4.89% and +5.59%. The high-high minus low-high spread is 9.09% in the continuous specification and 10.49% in the dummy specification, and the interaction coefficient in the dummy model is 8.09%. The paper interprets this as evidence that variance causally magnifies time-varying state-variable risk premia, consistent with the ICAPM.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight as a second major result that time variation in risk premia is magnified when the conditional variance of the state variable is high, with premia around +5%/-5% in high-variance states versus +1%/-1% in low-variance states. Table 5 is therefore a core main-result setting.
Settings.G191:
Treatment: Joint treatment is a positive lagged rolling predictive relation between a state variable and future consumption growth, I(b_t,zk>0), interacted with high macro-uncertainty, I(sigma_t^2>median), where macro-uncertainty is the GARCH(1,1) conditional variance of consumption growth (two variants: controlling for state-variable predictability or based on demeaned consumption growth). Binary in the tabled main specification.

Method: The authors replace state-variable conditional variance with macro-uncertainty, proxied by the GARCH(1,1) conditional variance of consumption growth, in pooled predictive regressions of annualized annual state-variable risk premia. They estimate a dummy specification using I(b_t,zk>0), I(sigma_t^2>median) for macro-uncertainty, and their interaction; related tables in the Online Appendix also consider continuous specifications and fixed effects. Macro-uncertainty is measured either from residual consumption growth after conditioning on state variables or from demeaned consumption growth.

Identification: Identification comes from pooled time-series variation in lagged state-variable macro predictive content and lagged macro-uncertainty. The paper argues that if a state variable is bad news for future consumption, its risk premium should be larger when macro-uncertainty is high. This is an observational interaction design, relying on the validity of GARCH-based uncertainty measures and the rolling predictive coefficients as proxies for priced macro risk.

Setting: When the authors substitute macro-uncertainty for state-variable conditional variance, they find similar magnification of state-variable risk premia. In Table 6, with uncertainty measured as the conditional variance of consumption growth controlling for state-variable predictability, predicted annualized risk premia move from −4.87% in low-b/high-uncertainty periods to +4.51% in high-b/high-uncertainty periods; the high-high minus low-high difference is 9.38%. Using conditional variance of demeaned consumption growth gives nearly identical numbers, with a 9.30% spread. The authors interpret this as evidence that macro-uncertainty causally amplifies the pricing of state-variable risk.

Main role: This is an important supporting mechanism analysis showing that the relevant variance component is closely tied to macro-uncertainty, but the central conclusions in the abstract and conclusion remain the time-varying predictive relation and state-variable variance magnification.
Settings.G192:
Treatment: Joint treatment is the lagged rolling relation between each state variable and future consumption growth together with the conditional variance of that state variable and their interaction, as in Eq. (12). The specification examines the same treatment while partialling out benchmark factor-return exposures. Treatments are continuous in Panel A and binary indicators in Panel B.

Method: The authors re-estimate the annual-horizon pooled predictive regressions of time-varying state-variable risk premia while controlling for contemporaneous exposure to benchmark asset-pricing factors from the CAPM, Fama-French three-factor model, Carhart four-factor model, and Fama-French five-factor model. The dependent variable is the High-minus-Low state-variable risk premium from equal- or value-weighted quintile sorts on stock exposures to a given state variable. Regressors include the rolling macro predictive coefficient b_t,zk, the state-variable conditional variance sigma_t,zk^2, their interaction, and benchmark factor returns. They report predicted premia in four cases to assess how much of the original time-varying effect remains after factor controls.

Identification: Identification uses the same time-series variation in lagged macro predictive content and state-variable variance as earlier pooled regressions, now conditioning on benchmark factor returns to assess whether the conditional expected-return effect is distinct from standard factor exposures. The assumption is that contemporaneous factor controls isolate the portion of time-varying state-variable premia not explained by benchmark factors. This remains an observational linear projection exercise.

Setting: The paper shows that benchmark factors, especially the Fama-French factors, absorb much of the conditional expected-return effect associated with state-variable risk. In Table 8 without factor controls, the equal-weighted High-minus-Low spread between high-b/high-variance and low-b/high-variance cases is 7.20% in the continuous specification and 9.49% in the dummy specification; after FF5M controls, only 1.41% and 2.50% remain. For value-weighted portfolios, the analogous spreads fall from 6.10% and 5.58% with no controls to 2.43% and 2.37% with FF5M controls. The authors interpret this as evidence that benchmark factors contain much of the same conditional risk-premium variation as state-variable risk.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness and interpretation exercise: it shows whether benchmark factors subsume the paper's time-varying state-variable premia. It supports the broader interpretation but is not the first-order main result.
Settings.G193:
Treatment: Lagged time-varying relation between each state variable and future consumption growth, measured by I(b_t,zk>0), I(b_t,zk>median), raw b_t,zk, and in augmented specifications their interaction with the state variable's conditional variance sigma_t,zk^2. Treatment is binary in indicator specifications and continuous in raw-coefficient specifications.

Method: For each state variable, the authors first form a maximum-correlation mimicking portfolio by regressing realized annual state-variable risk premia on benchmark factor returns (SMB, HML, RMW, CMA, WML) and taking the fitted factor component. They then run pooled predictive regressions of these mimicking portfolio returns on the rolling macro predictive coefficient and, in augmented specifications, on the interaction between that coefficient and state-variable conditional variance. Some columns include state-variable fixed effects. This is a linear regression/predictive-regrerssion design on constructed outcomes rather than a quasi-experiment.

Identification: Identification uses time-series variation in rolling macro predictive coefficients and state-variable variances to predict returns on constructed benchmark-factor portfolios that best mimic realized state-variable premia. The logic is that if benchmark factors are ICAPM-relevant portfolios, their expected returns should vary with the same state-variable information. Assumptions are linear spanning and that the factor-mimicking portfolios capture the relevant component of benchmark-factor returns.

Setting: The authors find that portfolios of benchmark factors inherit the same conditional expected-return effects as state-variable risk premia. In Table 9 Panel A, with fixed effects, an above-median rolling coefficient raises equal-weighted mimicking-portfolio returns by 4.10% and value-weighted returns by 3.96%, while the raw coefficient implies about a 2.6% increase for a one-standard-deviation rise in b_t,zk. In Panel B, the high-high minus low-high spread is about 6.50% for equal-weighted mimicking portfolios and 6.26% for value-weighted portfolios in the fixed-effects continuous specification. The paper interprets this as evidence that benchmark factors causally contain the conditional expected-return effects of state-variable risk in an ICAPM.

Main role: This is an important extension showing that benchmark factors contain the same conditional expected-return effects as state-variable premia, but it is downstream from the main evidence on the state-variable premia themselves.
Settings.G194:
Treatment: Indicator for whether the household has negative home equity in month t, defined as current mortgage LTV > 100% (or equivalently household is 'underwater'). This is actual treatment receipt, instrumented by an indicator for SLTV > 100%. Binary treatment contrast.

Method: The paper’s core design is a linear 2SLS using a binary instrument for negative home equity. The endogenous treatment is a household-month indicator for actual current loan-to-value (LTV) exceeding 100% (negative home equity). The instrument is an indicator for synthetic LTV (SLTV) exceeding 100%, where SLTV is constructed from cohort-level median origination LTV, synthetic amortization, and MSA-level house-price changes so that identifying variation comes from the interaction of mortgage origination timing and location relative to other households financed by the same lender. Specifications include MSA×time fixed effects and origination-date×time fixed effects; in the main specification they also include household fixed effects. The intent is to absorb local time-varying demand shocks, nationwide cohort-time lending changes, and household time-invariant heterogeneity. Standard errors are clustered at the MSA level. The author emphasizes exclusion-restriction concerns: borrowers might differ by timing/location in unobserved sensitivity to local shocks, so the paper presents placebo and robustness evidence, but the estimator here is the main linear IV/2SLS design reported in Table IV columns (1) and (2).

Identification: Identification comes from plausibly exogenous variation in whether a household is pushed into negative equity by having purchased at a relatively favorable or unfavorable time within its MSA, compared with other borrowers from the same lender, while holding constant MSA×time shocks and origination-date×time nationwide cohort effects. The main endogeneity concerns are omitted local labor-demand shocks, changing lending standards, and reverse causality from income to equity. The synthetic instrument removes household-specific choices from current LTV, and the fixed effects are meant to absorb local shocks and nationwide lending/cohort changes. Causal interpretation requires that, conditional on these controls, SLTV affects income only through the increased probability of negative equity.

Setting: Using 2SLS with actual negative home equity (LTV>100%) instrumented by synthetic negative equity (SLTV>100%), the paper estimates that being underwater reduces household labor income. In Table IV, column (1), instrumented negative home equity lowers monthly deposits by $298.1 (s.e. 61.3), and in column (2) lowers normalized monthly deposits by 3.47 percentage points (s.e. 1.18), interpreted as a 3.47% decline in household labor supply/income. The identifying variation is mortgage purchase timing within location relative to neighbors, with MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. This is the paper’s main causal claim.

Main role: This is the paper’s central causal design and directly underlies the abstract’s headline claim that negative home equity causes a 2% to 6% reduction in household labor supply/income.
Settings.H194: Section III.B, Table IV columns (1) and (2), PDF pp. 2981-2983 (article pages 19-21 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G195:
Treatment: Indicator for actual negative home equity in the household-month, defined as current LTV > 100%, instrumented by an indicator for synthetic LTV > 100%.

Method: This is the same linear 2SLS design as the main specification, but reported as geographic robustness replacing MSA×time fixed effects with zip-code×time fixed effects to address within-MSA selection into neighborhoods that may differentially load on local demand shocks. The endogenous treatment is actual negative home equity (LTV>100%), instrumented by SLTV>100%. Household fixed effects and origination-date×time fixed effects are included. Standard errors are clustered at the MSA level.

Identification: The same purchase-timing-by-location instrument is used, but identification now conditions on finer zip×time shocks rather than MSA×time shocks. The strategy is to show that even comparing households within narrow local areas over time, the timing-based synthetic equity measure predicts negative equity and lower income only through the treatment. This addresses concern that earlier or later buyers chose different neighborhoods within an MSA that later had different labor-market shocks.

Setting: As a robustness test of the core IV design, the paper replaces MSA×time with zip×time fixed effects and still finds that instrumented negative home equity reduces household income. In Table IV column (3), the estimate is -3.77 on the normalized deposit outcome (s.e. 1.13), interpreted as a 3.77% decline in household labor supply/income. This supports the paper’s central conclusion by showing the effect is not driven by within-MSA neighborhood selection.

Main role: The paper uses this as a substantive robustness check supporting the central claim that the main IV estimate is not driven by selection within MSAs.
Settings.H195: Section III.B, Table IV column (3), PDF p. 2982 (article page 20 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G196:
Treatment: Indicator for actual negative home equity (current LTV > 100%) in the household-month, instrumented by a dummy for SLTV > 100%.

Method: This is the core linear 2SLS design with added flexible time-varying household-level controls: deciles of origination income and property value, original mortgage interest-rate buckets, and original credit-score bins, each interacted with time fixed effects. The endogenous treatment is LTV>100%, instrumented by SLTV>100%, with MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. The purpose is to address nonlinear selection on observables related to sensitivity to local demand shocks.

Identification: The same IV timing-location instrument identifies variation in negative home equity, while the added flexible controls allow households with different origination income, property values, rates, and credit scores to have different time paths. This is intended to rule out the possibility that the estimated income decline reflects nonlinear sorting of more shock-sensitive households into purchase timing cohorts rather than a causal effect of negative equity.

Setting: Adding rich nonparametric household-level controls to the main IV specification does not eliminate the effect of negative home equity on income. In Table IV column (4), instrumented negative home equity reduces normalized monthly deposits by 4.94 percentage points (s.e. 1.03), interpreted as a 4.9% decline in household labor supply/income. The result reinforces the paper’s central claim by showing robustness to flexible controls for origination characteristics.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis that the paper highlights as strengthening the causal interpretation of the main result.
Settings.H196: Section III.B, Table IV column (4), PDF p. 2982 (article page 20 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G197:
Treatment: Indicator for actual negative home equity (current LTV > 100%), instrumented by SLTV > 100%.

Method: This 2SLS robustness specification strengthens comparisons by including MSA×time×origination-year fixed effects instead of separate MSA×time and origination-date×time effects. The treatment remains actual negative home equity (LTV>100%), instrumented by SLTV>100%, with household fixed effects. Identification therefore comes from households buying within the same MSA and origination year but at different months. Standard errors are clustered at the MSA level.

Identification: By saturating with MSA×time×origination-year fixed effects, the design compares borrowers within the same local labor market and same purchase year, differing only in purchase timing within that year. This is meant to minimize concerns that different cohorts faced different lending standards or entered the labor market at very different times. The exclusion restriction is that within such narrow comparisons, the synthetic timing-based equity measure affects income only through negative home equity.

Setting: In a stringent within-MSA-year IV design, the paper finds that negative home equity still reduces income. Table IV column (5) reports that instrumented negative home equity lowers normalized monthly deposits by 2.20 percentage points (s.e. 0.89), interpreted as a 2.2% decline in household labor supply/income. This is a central robustness result because it aligns with the abstract’s claim that the estimates survive comparisons among households purchasing only months apart in the same market and year.

Main role: The abstract and text explicitly emphasize that results hold comparing purchases within the same year-MSA that differ by only a few months; this is one of the headline causal robustness claims.
Settings.H197: Section III.B, Table IV column (5), PDF pp. 2983-2984 (article pages 21-22 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G198:
Treatment: Indicator for actual negative home equity in the household-month, defined as current LTV > 100%, instrumented by synthetic LTV > 100%.

Method: This is the core linear 2SLS design estimated on the subsample of borrowers with outstanding student loans, adding MSA×time×graduation-year fixed effects (graduation year proxied by average student-loan origination date) instead of origination-date×time fixed effects. The treatment is actual negative home equity (LTV>100%), instrumented by SLTV>100%, with household fixed effects. This robustness is designed to control flexibly for time since entering the labor market.

Identification: The same timing-location-based instrument is used, but the control structure now allows flexible MSA×time heterogeneity by approximate college graduation year, intended to absorb differences in labor-market experience, age, and job duration that might be correlated with purchase timing and exposure to downturns. Identification assumes remaining variation in SLTV affects income only through negative equity.

Setting: On the student-loan subsample, after flexibly controlling for approximate labor-market entry timing using MSA×time×graduation-year fixed effects, instrumented negative home equity continues to reduce income. Table IV column (6) reports a -5.63 estimate (s.e. 2.97) on normalized monthly deposits, interpreted as a 5.6% decline in household labor supply/income. This supports the paper’s main conclusion by showing the result is not an artifact of differential labor-market experience across purchase-timing cohorts.

Main role: The paper uses this as an important robustness analysis to address labor-market-entry timing as an alternative explanation for the main causal result.
Settings.H198: Section III.B, Table IV column (6), PDF p. 2984 (article page 22 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G199:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 if the household’s synthetic loan-to-value ratio exceeds 100% (SLTV > 1), a timing-location based measure of exposure to negative-equity risk. Binary reduced-form treatment, not actual negative equity itself.

Method: This setting reports reduced-form/fixed-effects regressions rather than 2SLS. The treatment is the binary instrument itself, SLTV>100%, interpreted as plausibly exogenous exposure to negative-equity-inducing house-price movements based on purchase timing. Outcomes include current income measures and origination-period placebo outcomes. Specifications include two absorbed FE dimensions—MSA×time and origination-date×time—and no household fixed effects in Table II. These regressions are used to argue that the instrument predicts lower current income but not worse observable borrower characteristics at origination.

Identification: The identifying variation is again the timing-location component of synthetic LTV after controlling for MSA×time and origination-date×time. The point is not a final causal effect of actual negative equity, but evidence that the reduced-form instrument predicts current income and negative equity while not predicting observable ex ante borrower quality. This supports the plausibility of the exclusion restriction for the main IV design.

Setting: Table II presents reduced-form and placebo evidence for the paper’s identification strategy. Households with SLTV>100% are 0.623 more likely to have actual negative home equity (column 1), have 4.42 percentage points lower normalized monthly deposits (column 2), and $436.8 lower raw monthly deposits (column 3). By contrast, SLTV>100% does not significantly predict income at origination (-64.8), credit score (+1.03), or origination mortgage rate (-0.0003) in columns (4)-(6). These results are interpreted as supporting the causal IV design by showing a strong first stage and no observable ex ante selection on key borrower characteristics.

Main role: These are supporting reduced-form and placebo specifications used to validate the IV design rather than the paper’s final treatment-effect estimates.
Settings.H199: Section III.A, Table II columns (1)-(6), PDF pp. 2974-2976 (article pages 12-14 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G200:
Treatment: Indicator for SLTV > 100%, capturing exposure to negative-equity-inducing purchase timing by region and cohort. In column (6) this treatment is also interacted with demeaned monthly percent changes in aggregate MSA deposits.

Method: These are reduced-form/fixed-effects robustness and placebo regressions using the binary instrument SLTV>100% directly, with MSA×time, origination-date×time, and in columns (4)-(6) household fixed effects. Outcomes are difficult-to-observe origination characteristics and current income placebo outcomes. The aim is to test for selection on unobservables and nonlinear placebo patterns rather than estimate the final IV treatment effect.

Identification: The author uses the same timing-location variation in SLTV but asks whether it predicts hard-to-observe underwriting attributes at origination or current income when treatment is absent (positive-equity-only sample). The argument is that if the instrument merely captured households more sensitive to local shocks, it would continue to predict income even when no household actually has negative equity; the null placebo helps support the exclusion restriction.

Setting: Table III provides additional reduced-form validation. SLTV>100% does not significantly predict Alt-A status (0.0002), no-income-doc status (-0.004), or verified income at origination (-6.1) in columns (1)-(3). With household fixed effects, SLTV>100% predicts a 1.37 percentage point decline in normalized deposits in the full sample (column 4), but in the positive-equity placebo sample the estimate is 0.08 and insignificant (column 5); the interaction with aggregate MSA deposit changes is also insignificant in column (6). The paper interprets these patterns as evidence against selection on unobservables and in favor of a causal negative-equity channel.

Main role: These are supporting placebo and validation exercises used to bolster the exclusion restriction and nonlinear interpretation of the main IV design.
Settings.H200: Section III.A, Table III columns (1)-(6), PDF pp. 2976-2978 (article pages 14-16 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G201:
Treatment: Current household mortgage loan-to-value ratio categorized into 10-percentage-point LTV buckets; omitted category is 30% to 40% LTV. This is a nonbinary treatment measuring actual leverage/home equity status.

Method: This setting consists of within-household fixed-effects regressions of income on categorical actual current LTV buckets, controlling for MSA×time and origination-date×time fixed effects. The design is linear on the reported outcome and uses household fixed effects to absorb time-invariant heterogeneity, but it does not instrument LTV. The author interprets the pattern causally/informatively as evidence of nonlinear effects concentrated near negative home equity.

Identification: Identification comes from within-household changes in actual LTV over time after controlling for local time-varying shocks and cohort-time effects. The paper acknowledges endogeneity of actual LTV elsewhere, so this figure is not the cleanest causal estimate; instead it is used to show that declines in income appear only near or in negative equity, not across the full home-equity distribution. The causal argument relies on the fixed effects plus the nonlinear pattern being inconsistent with generic local demand shocks.

Setting: Figure 1 regresses normalized monthly deposits on actual current LTV buckets with household, MSA×time, and origination-date×time fixed effects. The reported pattern is that there is essentially no relationship between income and LTV at low leverage, but household income declines nonlinearly as LTV approaches and exceeds 100%, remaining low once households are underwater. The paper interprets this as evidence that the labor-supply effect is tied to negative home equity rather than smooth exposure to local house-price or labor-demand shocks.

Main role: This is a substantive supporting analysis used to show nonlinear effects of home equity on income, relevant to mechanism and identification, but not the paper’s headline estimator.
Settings.H201: Section III.A, Figure 1, PDF pp. 2978-2979 (article pages 16-17 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G202:
Treatment: Categorical buckets of MSA-level house price index changes since mortgage origination, in 10% bins; omitted category is HPI changes of 20% to 30%. In Panel B the same treatment is applied only among households with positive home equity.

Method: These are reduced-form fixed-effects regressions of normalized household income on categorical MSA-level house-price-index (HPI) change buckets since origination, with MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. Panel B repeats the same estimator only for households with positive home equity as a placebo. The treatment is nonbinary exposure to local house-price changes induced by purchase timing rather than actual negative equity.

Identification: The identifying variation is local HPI movement since origination interacted with origination timing, conditioned on MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. Because the house-price measure is area-level, it avoids household-specific mortgage choices. The author interprets the absence of income effects for positive-equity households as evidence that the results are not driven by generic local demand shocks correlated with house prices.

Setting: Figure 2 shows reduced-form income responses to local house-price changes. In Panel A, large adverse HPI changes are associated with lower normalized monthly deposits only when they are large enough to make negative equity likely; in Panel B, restricting to households with positive home equity, even large declines in home equity are not associated with lower income. The paper uses this nonlinear reduced form and placebo to support the claim that negative home equity, rather than house-price movements per se, lowers labor supply.

Main role: These figures are supporting reduced-form evidence used to visualize the nonlinear timing-location mechanism and a placebo absence of effects among positive-equity households.
Settings.H202: Section III.A, Figure 2 Panels A and B, PDF pp. 2979-2980 (article pages 17-18 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G203:
Treatment: Synthetic loan-to-value ratio categorized into 10% SLTV buckets. This is a nonbinary exposure based on timing of purchase, cohort median LTV, synthetic amortization, and local HPI changes.

Method: This figure reports nonlinear reduced-form fixed-effects regressions of two outcomes—actual negative home equity and normalized income—on categorical SLTV buckets. Regressions include MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. The treatment is nonbinary SLTV category, a timing-location-based exposure variable.
