This is a visualization of the first stage and reduced form rather than a 2SLS treatment-effect regression.

Identification: Variation in SLTV buckets comes from purchase timing and location after conditioning on local shocks, cohort-time effects, and household fixed effects. The key identifying argument is that if income declines emerge only where SLTV sharply raises the probability of actual negative equity, this supports the exclusion restriction and nonlinear treatment interpretation rather than generic sensitivity to house-price movements.

Setting: Figure 3 plots how both the probability of actual negative equity and normalized income vary with synthetic LTV. The paper reports no income change for large changes in SLTV when SLTV is low, but as SLTV approaches 100% the probability of negative equity rises and household income falls; once SLTV is high, income remains lower. This figure is used to show that the reduced form tracks the first stage around the negative-equity threshold, supporting the core causal interpretation.

Main role: This is supporting graphical evidence that the first stage and reduced form turn on at the negative-equity threshold, reinforcing the main IV interpretation.
Settings.H203: Section III.A, Figure 3, PDF pp. 2980-2981 (article pages 18-19 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G204:
Treatment: Indicator for actual negative home equity (current LTV > 100%), instrumented by SLTV > 100%.

Method: This setting contains IV robustness tests addressing whether measured income declines reflect households hiding or shifting deposits away from MyBank. Columns (1)-(3) of Table V use the main 2SLS design: treatment is actual negative home equity (LTV>100%), instrumented by SLTV>100%, with MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. Column (1) excludes observations with a 100% decline in deposits; column (2) excludes changes larger than 25%; column (3) uses a binary outcome for receiving Social Security/disability checks. These are linear IV specifications with clustered SEs at the MSA level.

Identification: The same timing-location IV identifies negative equity. The question here is whether the IV effect on observed MyBank deposits reflects true income/labor-supply changes or strategic reallocation of deposits away from the lender. Stability of the estimate when zero-deposit observations are removed, disappearance when only small changes are retained, and an increase in Social Security/disability receipt are interpreted as evidence for real extensive-margin labor-supply changes rather than mere deposit shifting.

Setting: Table V columns (1)-(3) suggest the main IV results are not driven by households hiding deposits from their lender. Excluding zero-deposit months, instrumented negative home equity still reduces normalized deposits by 3.35 percentage points (s.e. 1.12) in column (1). When large income changes are excluded, the estimate shrinks to -0.07 and is insignificant in column (2), which the paper interprets as evidence that effects are concentrated on large extensive-margin labor-income drops. Column (3) shows instrumented negative home equity raises the probability of receiving Social Security/disability checks by 0.91 percentage points (s.e. 0.32), consistent with reduced labor-force participation rather than deposit concealment.

Main role: These are supporting robustness analyses designed to rebut an alternative measurement explanation for the main findings.
Settings.H204: Section III.B, Table V columns (1)-(3), PDF pp. 2984-2986 (article pages 22-24 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G205:
Treatment: Nonbinary measure of the percentage of mortgages with negative home equity in the household’s estimated region×cohort×time cell (zip code × origination year × time), derived using mortgage timing/location rather than observed own LTV. In column (5), the sample is restricted to households whose mortgage is not serviced or owned by MyBank.

Method: These are reduced-form fixed-effects regressions on a broader sample of MyBank retail and credit-card customers with mortgages at any lender, where the author cannot observe actual LTV and therefore does not run 2SLS. The treatment is the percentage of mortgages in estimated zip-code×origination-year×time cells with negative home equity. Regressions include MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. Column (5) restricts to households whose mortgages are not serviced or owned by MyBank, directly addressing the deposit-hiding concern.

Identification: Identification comes from timing-location variation in the prevalence of negative equity across estimated local cohort-time cells, absorbing MSA×time, origination-date×time, and household fixed effects. Because MyBank is not the mortgage lender in column (5), borrowers have little incentive to hide income from MyBank, so a negative reduced-form relationship is interpreted as evidence against deposit-shifting as the mechanism behind the main results.

Setting: In a broader reduced-form sample where own mortgage LTV is unavailable, the paper still finds that greater exposure to negative equity lowers observed deposit income. Table V column (4) reports that a higher percentage of mortgages with negative equity in the household’s estimated region×cohort×time cell is associated with $48.8 lower monthly deposits (s.e. 10.4), and column (5) shows a $65.0 decline (s.e. 15.0) even when MyBank neither services nor owns the mortgage. The author interprets this as evidence that the main income effects are not driven by hiding deposits from MyBank.

Main role: This is a supporting reduced-form robustness exercise to show the observed deposit-income effects are not specific to households whose lender is MyBank.
Settings.H205: Section III.B, Table V columns (4) and (5), PDF pp. 2985-2986 (article pages 23-24 of supplied PDF).
Settings.G206:
Treatment: Exposure to a functioning Debt Recovery Tribunal in the firm's state/jurisdiction, implemented as event-time indicators DRT(t=0), DRT(t=+1), ..., relative to the year before DRT establishment. The underlying treatment is a binary switch from no DRT access to DRT access for all firms in the region once the tribunal is established.

Method: The main design is a staggered-adoption event-study difference-in-differences using the rollout of Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) across Indian states from 1994 to 2000. The authors estimate a fully saturated relative-time specification with indicators for years before and after DRT establishment in a firm's state, omitting the year immediately before establishment. Regressions include firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific linear time trends, and 100 size-percentile dummies; some columns additionally include lagged firm controls (profitability, cash, tangibility, interest coverage). Standard errors are clustered at the state level. Identification relies on parallel trends between early- and late-DRT states absent the reform, plus the claim that DRT timing was plausibly exogenous because the stagger arose from litigation and Supreme Court timing rather than state choice.

Identification: The identifying variation is across-state and over-time exposure to DRTs, which the paper argues reduced debt contract enforcement costs without changing the underlying law. Because individual states could not choose whether or when to establish DRTs, and the stagger was created by a legal challenge and subsequent Supreme Court ruling, the authors treat timing as plausibly exogenous. The key assumption is that absent DRTs, firms in early- and late-access states would have followed similar trends in financing outcomes; they support this with pre-trend/event-time evidence and appendix tests showing little relation between adoption timing and observable state or firm characteristics.

Setting: Using staggered DRT introduction as a quasi-experiment, the authors estimate that lower enforcement costs increase debt maturity and reduce trade credit. In Table 2 panel A, four years after DRT establishment, long-term debt/assets rises by 0.025, short-term debt/assets falls by 0.017, the short-term debt share of total debt (Short) falls by 0.066, and trade credit/assets falls by 0.010, relative to the year before DRT establishment. They explicitly interpret these as economically large: about 11.9% of the sample mean for long-term debt/assets, 11.3% for short-term debt/assets, 14.7% for Short, and 6.4% for trade credit/assets. This is the paper's central evidence that reducing debt contract enforcement costs shifts firms away from short-term debt and trade credit and toward longer-maturity financing.

Main role: This is the paper's core causal design. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all frame the paper as using staggered DRT introduction to estimate the causal effect of lower debt-enforcement costs on debt maturity and trade credit.
Settings.H206: Section 4.2, Equation (1), Figure 2, and Table 2 panel A, columns 1-8 (PDF pp. 15-23).
Settings.G207:
Treatment: Exposure to DRT implementation in the firm's state/jurisdiction, captured by event-time indicators relative to the year before DRT establishment. The treatment is binary access to a functioning DRT.

Method: The authors estimate linear panel regressions of log debt amounts on event-time indicators for DRT implementation, using firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific linear trends, and size dummies; some specifications also add lagged firm controls. Outcomes are transformed as log(1+level). Although the reform variation is still staggered over time and space, this table is framed as decomposing the mechanism behind the main result by asking whether the financing-mix changes reflect changes in the underlying amounts on firms' balance sheets. This is not a separate DiD contrast with treated×post; rather it is a fixed-effects event-time panel specification on transformed levels.

Identification: Identification again comes from within-firm changes around staggered DRT rollout, netting out firm fixed characteristics, common year shocks, and state-specific trends. The authors interpret DRT timing as exogenous due to the litigation-driven stagger, and use this setting to infer that lower enforcement costs causally changed the levels of long- and short-term borrowing and trade credit on the balance sheet.

Setting: In Table 2 panel B, the authors show that lower enforcement costs changed the amounts of financing on firms' balance sheets, not just financing shares. Four years after DRT implementation, log(1+long-term debt) rises by 0.224, log(1+short-term debt) falls by 0.193, and log(1+trade credit) falls by 0.067 in the controlled specifications. The text interprets these magnitudes as about a 22.1% increase in long-term debt, a 19.4% decrease in short-term debt, and a 7% decrease in trade credit relative to the year before DRT. This supports the paper's central claim that lower enforcement costs lengthen financing maturity and reduce reliance on trade credit through active balance-sheet adjustment.

Main role: The paper uses these regressions to show that the maturity-share results reflect active changes in debt amounts, not merely denominator effects. This materially supports the central financing-structure claim, though it is secondary to the scaled-outcome results.
Settings.H207: Section 4.2, Table 2 panel B, columns 1-6 (PDF pp. 23-24).
Settings.G208:
Treatment: Exposure to a functioning DRT in the firm's state/jurisdiction, measured by event-time dummies relative to the year before DRT establishment. Treatment is binary DRT access.

Method: The authors estimate the effect of DRT rollout on firms' number of banking relationships using nonlinear limited-dependent-variable models. Their preferred specification is a probit model for whether a firm has multiple banking relationships, using state fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific linear trends, and optionally firm controls; they omit firm fixed effects because of the incidental-parameters problem. They also report OLS and ordered logit variants with number of banks as the dependent variable. Because the implemented main estimator is probit/ordered logit rather than a linear model, this setting falls under Other.

Identification: The causal interpretation uses the same quasi-exogenous DRT timing as the financing-mix analyses. The argument is that improved enforcement lowers the need to maintain multiple banking relationships, especially in Diamond's framework. Identification assumes that absent DRT rollout, treated and later-treated states would have evolved similarly in firms' lender counts, after accounting for common year effects, state effects, and state trends.

Setting: Table 3 studies whether lower enforcement costs reduce firms' reliance on multiple lenders. Using a probit model, the authors find negative post-DRT coefficients, and interpret the DRT(t=+4) estimate as implying that the odds ratio of borrowing from multiple banks is 0.194 lower four years after DRT than in the year before. They translate this into a 9.1% decline relative to the sample mean odds ratio of 2.125. OLS and ordered-logit specifications for number of banks are reported as corroborating evidence. This directly supports the paper's central claim that better contract enforcement reduces the need for multiple banking relationships.

Main role: A reduction in the number of lenders is one of the paper's headline conclusions in the abstract and conclusion, and this table provides the direct evidence for that claim.
Settings.H208: Section 4.3, Table 3 (labeled 'Number of lenders' in the PDF scan), columns 1-4 (PDF pp. 24-26).
Settings.G209:
Treatment: Exposure to DRT implementation in the firm's state, with treatment effects allowed to differ by whether the firm had a single versus multiple banking relationships in the year before DRT. The focal treatment remains binary DRT access.

Method: This is a cross-sectional heterogeneity version of the staggered-adoption event-study DiD. The authors re-estimate equation (1) after interacting the DRT relative-time indicators with a pre-DRT indicator for Single versus Multiple banking relationships, and include interactions of Single with controls and fixed effects so that trends and covariate effects may differ by subsample. Regressions include firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific time trends, and controls. The sample is restricted to firms observed before DRT with nonmissing banking-relationship data.

Identification: Identification uses the same staggered DRT timing as the main design, but now asks whether treatment effects differ across firms classified ex ante by pre-DRT banking structure. The authors do not assume random assignment to multiple banking relationships; instead they interpret multiple lenders before DRT as an equilibrium marker of firms constrained by poor enforcement. The key assumption is that, absent DRT, differential trends between these ex ante groups are adequately handled by interactions with controls/fixed effects and the DiD structure.

Setting: The authors find that the maturity response to lower enforcement costs is concentrated among firms with multiple lenders before the reform. In Table 5 panel A, by year +4 after DRT, firms with multiple banking relationships have LongTermDebt/Assets higher by 0.052, ShortTermDebt/Assets lower by 0.021, and Short lower by 0.085, while firms with a single lender show no significant change. The text summarizes these as a 23.6% increase in long-term debt/assets relative to the multiple-lender subsample mean of 0.22 and a 13.3% decline in short-term debt/assets relative to its mean of 0.15. This is central evidence for the Diamond-style mechanism that short-term debt from multiple lenders substitutes for formal enforcement.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the debt-maturity response is confined to firms borrowing from multiple lenders before the reform. This is a core mechanism test tied directly to the paper's interpretation of Diamond (2004).
Settings.H209: Section 4.4.1, Table 5 panel A ('Cross-sectional tests, debt maturity: Multiple banking relationships') (PDF pp. 25-32).
Settings.G210:
Treatment: Exposure to DRT implementation in the firm's state, with heterogeneity by whether the firm had an abnormally short debt maturity structure before DRT. The treatment itself is binary DRT access.

Method: Another heterogeneity event-study DiD based on the staggered DRT rollout. The authors interact DRT relative-time dummies with an indicator for Abnormal debt maturity, defined ex ante as below-median industry-adjusted long-term debt/assets and above-median industry-adjusted short-term debt/assets in the year before DRT. They include firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific trends, controls, and compare coefficients across abnormal and non-abnormal firms.

Identification: The setting exploits staggered DRT timing but focuses on heterogeneous treatment effects across ex ante financing structures. The authors interpret abnormal short maturity before DRT as a proxy for firms especially constrained by weak enforcement. Identification assumes the DRT timing remains exogenous and that, absent the reform, abnormal and other firms would not differentially change in these outcomes in a way that mimics the estimated interactions after conditioning on fixed effects, controls, and trends.

Setting: Table 5 panel B shows that firms with abnormally short debt maturity before DRT drive the financing response. By year +4 after DRT, the abnormal group has LongTermDebt/Assets higher by 0.128, ShortTermDebt/Assets lower by 0.084, Short lower by 0.298, and TradeCredit/Assets lower by 0.035, while the non-abnormal group shows little change. The text highlights the trade-credit effect as a 21.9% decline relative to the abnormal-group mean of 0.16. These results support the paper's interpretation that DRTs particularly relaxed constraints for firms previously forced into unusually short-maturity and trade-credit-heavy financing structures.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the debt-maturity and trade-credit responses are stronger for firms with abnormally short maturity structures before the reform. This is a major cross-sectional mechanism result.
Settings.H210: Section 4.4.1, Table 5 panel B ('Cross-sectional tests, debt maturity: Abnormally short debt maturity') (PDF pp. 28-32).
Settings.G211:
Treatment: Exposure to DRT implementation in the firm's state, with heterogeneity by whether the firm is small or large based on pre-DRT tangible assets. The underlying treatment remains binary DRT access.

Method: This setting interacts the DRT event-time indicators with a pre-DRT size classification (small versus large firms) in the staggered-adoption event-study DiD. Regressions include firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific trends, and lagged controls. The paper defines large versus small using above/below median tangible assets in the year before DRT.

Identification: As in the main DiD, identification comes from the staggered DRT rollout, but treatment effects are allowed to differ by pre-DRT size. The paper argues that small firms may benefit more because implicit enforcement mechanisms are weaker for them. The causal interpretation assumes DRT timing is exogenous and that any differential trends by size are adequately handled by the interacted event-study design with controls and fixed effects.

Setting: The size-heterogeneity estimates in Table 5 panel C imply that smaller firms respond more strongly to lower enforcement costs. By year +4 after DRT, small firms show LongTermDebt/Assets higher by 0.033, ShortTermDebt/Assets lower by 0.028, Short lower by 0.112, and TradeCredit/Assets lower by 0.019, whereas large firms display weaker or insignificant changes in short-term debt and trade credit. The authors emphasize that the average small firm reduces trade credit by 9.4% relative to its sample mean and that Short declines by 21.9% relative to the small-firm mean of 0.51. This is a key substantive conclusion of the paper: formal enforcement improvements matter especially for smaller firms.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state that the increase in debt maturity and fall in trade credit are greater for smaller firms. This is a highlighted substantive heterogeneity result.
Settings.H211: Section 4.4.1, Table 5 panel C ('Cross-sectional tests, debt maturity: Firm size') (PDF pp. 29-32).
Settings.G212:
Treatment: Exposure to DRT implementation in the firm's state, with heterogeneous effects by abnormal pre-DRT maturity structure or firm size. The underlying treatment is binary DRT access.

Method: This is a nonlinear heterogeneity analysis of the effect of DRT rollout on banking relationships. The authors estimate probit models for the multiple-banks indicator, interacting DRT relative-time dummies with either Abnormal debt maturity or Small firms. Specifications include state fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific time trends, and controls, and are estimated on firms present before DRT. Because the implemented estimator is probit, the setting is classified as Other.

Identification: The same staggered DRT timing is used to identify changes in lender concentration, with interaction terms testing whether the response is stronger among firms presumed more constrained ex ante. The causal interpretation assumes exogenous DRT timing and appropriate comparison of abnormal versus other firms, and small versus large firms, after conditioning on fixed effects, trends, and controls.

Setting: In Table 7, the authors show that the shift toward fewer banking relationships is concentrated in firms with abnormally short maturity structures and in small firms. For abnormal firms, the DRT(t=+4) probit coefficient is -0.464 versus -0.104 for non-abnormal firms, and the text interprets this as a 0.36 reduction in the odds of borrowing from multiple versus single banks, or a 21.1% reduction relative to the sample mean odds ratio of 1.7. Small firms also show more negative post-DRT coefficients than large firms. These results support the mechanism that improved enforcement allows constrained firms to consolidate lenders.

Main role: These are supporting mechanism results extending the lender-count finding. They reinforce, but are not the primary basis for, the central claims about financing and asset structure.
Settings.H212: Section 4.4.2, Table 7 ('Cross-sectional tests, number of lenders'), columns 1-6 (PDF pp. 33-34).
Settings.G213:
Treatment: Exposure to positive or negative DRT implementation news, operationalized through regressions estimated on event-day abnormal returns and interacted via firm characteristics (Multiple and Abnormal) capturing expected treatment intensity. This is not a direct randomized treatment; the causal object is the stock-market response to DRT news for more affected firms.

Method: The authors run cross-sectional event-day regressions of firm abnormal stock returns on lagged firm characteristics indicating likely exposure to DRT benefits: Multiple lenders and Abnormal maturity structure. Abnormal returns are computed relative to benchmark portfolios formed daily on beta, size, and book-to-market quintiles. Regressions include day fixed effects, and standard errors are clustered by date. This is essentially an event-study regression adjustment linking news about DRT implementation to differential stock-price responses across firms.

Identification: Identification comes from narrow event windows around public news about DRT enactment or judicial decisions, under the standard event-study assumption that these dates contain unanticipated information about DRT likelihood and that differential abnormal returns across firms proxy differences in expected causal gains from the reform. By focusing on firms classified ex ante as Multiple or Abnormal and using benchmark-adjusted returns plus day fixed effects, the authors aim to isolate treatment-intensity differences rather than broad market movements.

Setting: Table 8 asks whether firms expected to benefit more from lower enforcement costs experienced larger stock-price reactions when DRT prospects changed. On positive DRT news days, firms with multiple lenders have abnormal returns about 0.43 percentage points higher in the (0,1) window, while on the negative-news day they fall by about 1.1 percentage points more. Firms with abnormally short maturity structures show a similar sign pattern. The authors interpret this as evidence that DRT implementation relaxed borrowing constraints and raised firm value especially for firms most exposed to weak enforcement.

Main role: The stock-return evidence is corroborative. It supports the interpretation that DRTs relaxed constraints for maximally exposed firms, but the main paper conclusions rest on balance-sheet outcomes.
Settings.H213: Section 4.5, Equation (2), Table 8 ('News about DRTs and stock returns'), columns 1-6 (PDF pp. 33-36).
Settings.G214:
Treatment: Exposure to a functioning DRT in the firm's state/jurisdiction, captured by event-time indicators; in heterogeneity specifications, effects differ by abnormal pre-DRT maturity or firm size. Treatment is binary DRT access.

Method: The authors estimate the effect of DRT rollout on asset maturity using the same staggered event-study DiD framework as equation (1), with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, state-specific linear trends, size dummies, and controls. They then interact DRT relative-time indicators with Abnormal maturity and Small/Large firm indicators to study heterogeneity. The outcome is the share of fixed assets in total assets.

Identification: Identification mirrors the main DiD strategy: staggered, plausibly exogenous DRT rollout is used to trace within-firm changes in asset composition relative to firms not yet exposed, while controlling for firm fixed effects, common time shocks, and state trends. The authors interpret DRTs as lowering enforcement costs and therefore enabling access to longer-term financing, which in turn allows firms to shift toward longer-maturity assets.

Setting: The asset-side results in Table 10 indicate that lower enforcement costs increase firms' asset maturity. In the full sample, FixedAssets/Assets rises gradually after DRT, reaching 0.015 by year +4. In the heterogeneous specifications, firms with abnormally short pre-DRT maturity and small firms respond most strongly; for example, the abnormal group reaches 0.038 by year +3 or +4, which the text interprets as an 8.8% increase relative to the mean fixed-asset share of 0.43. The introduction and conclusion summarize the average effect as about a 3.5% increase relative to the sample mean. This supports the paper's claim that better debt enforcement affects not only financing structure but also real asset structure.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly state that firms increase the proportion of long-term assets after reform. This is one of the paper's headline contributions on asset structure.
Settings.H214: Section 4.7, Table 10 ('Asset Structure'), columns 1-7; discussion in Section 4.7 and conclusion (PDF pp. 38-41).
Settings.G215:
Treatment: Joint treatment/exposure defined by (i) the lagged return of the producer country’s associated customer-country index, discretized into quintiles, and (ii) the producer firm’s lagged trade credit level, measured as accounts receivable divided by sales (accounts receivable turnover), discretized into terciles. The economically emphasized contrast is high-trade-credit versus low-trade-credit firms within the bottom or top customer-return quintile, and cross-quintile contrasts for a given trade-credit group. Both underlying variables are nonbinary multi-valued/discrete exposures rather than a simple binary treatment.

Method: The main empirical design is a pooled firm-month weighted least squares panel regression of producer-firm monthly stock returns on interactions between lagged customer-country return quintile indicators and lagged firm trade-credit tercile indicators. Firms are weighted by market capitalization relative to others in the same trade-credit group so coefficients can be interpreted as value-weighted portfolio returns. The fully controlled specification includes lagged firm characteristics and return controls—firm size rank within country-month, cash-to-assets, short-term debt-to-assets, net debt-to-assets, accounts receivable-to-sales, equity market value-to-book, a multinational dummy, lagged firm return, lagged customer-country index return, lagged domestic industry return, lagged country return, and contemporaneous world market return—plus industry and country fixed effects. Identification is not quasi-experimental; the authors interpret the interacted coefficients causally as the effect of trade-credit-linked customer-country return shocks on producer-firm returns, with FE and controls used to address confounding from firm, country, and industry heterogeneity.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from differences over time in customer-country lagged returns and differences across firms in trade credit intensity, interacted in firm-level return regressions. The endogeneity concern is that trade credit may proxy for other firm characteristics, risk exposures, financing conditions, industry composition, or country-level shocks that also predict returns. The paper argues for identification by controlling for extensive firm-, country-, industry-, and market-return covariates and by including country and industry fixed effects so that the remaining comparison is largely among firms within the same industry/country with differing trade credit exposure to the returns of their linked customer countries. The strategy still relies on the assumption that, conditional on controls and FE, the interaction of customer-country returns and firm trade credit is not driven by omitted variables correlated with future producer-firm returns.

Setting: In the baseline panel regressions, the authors interpret lagged customer-country stock returns as affecting subsequent producer-firm stock returns through trade credit links. In Table 3, within the bottom quintile of customer-country returns, low-trade-credit firms outperform high-trade-credit firms by about 1.176% per month without controls and 1.047% per month with controls, or 1.098% per month with country and industry fixed effects; they describe this as roughly 13–14% per year. Across customer-return quintiles, the top-minus-bottom spread for high-trade-credit firms is 1.349% per month with controls and 1.312% with fixed effects. These estimates are presented as evidence that trade credit is the channel generating cross-border return predictability.

Main role: This is the paper’s core empirical test of the main claim in the abstract and introduction: customer-country returns predict producer-firm returns more strongly for firms with high trade credit, and trade credit is the proximate channel behind cross-country return predictability.
Settings.H215: Section 4.1–4.2, Eq. (24), Table 3, especially 'With controls' and 'With fixed effects' columns (PDF pp. 602–604; Table 3 on PDF p. 603).
Settings.G216:
Treatment: Joint exposure given by lagged customer-country return quintile, lagged trade-credit tercile, and whether the firm has high foreign sales (top tercile of foreign sales to total sales within country). The emphasized treatment contrast is high- versus low-trade-credit among firms with high foreign sales, within customer-return quintiles, and corresponding across-quintile contrasts. This is nonbinary overall.

Method: This specification augments the baseline pooled firm-month WLS panel regression by interacting the customer-return quintile × trade-credit tercile indicators with a high-foreign-sales indicator. The same lagged firm-level controls, return controls, and in some columns country and industry fixed effects are included. The implemented estimator remains a linear weighted panel regression with FE. The purpose is to test whether the trade-credit channel operates more strongly for firms with greater international sales exposure, which the paper treats as sharpening identification of cross-border firm links.

Identification: The identification argument is that if trade credit truly transmits shocks across borders, the effect should be concentrated among producer firms with stronger foreign sales exposure. By interacting the main treatment with a high-foreign-sales indicator and keeping the extensive controls and FE from the baseline regression, the paper uses heterogeneity consistent with the mechanism as evidence against alternative explanations. Remaining assumptions are that high foreign sales do not simply proxy for omitted return predictors unrelated to the trade-credit channel after conditioning on controls and FE.

Setting: In Table 4, the authors interpret the stronger return predictability for high-foreign-sales firms as evidence that customer-country return movements affect producer-firm returns through international trade-credit links. Within the bottom customer-return quintile, the low-minus-high trade-credit spread is about 1.613% per month without fixed effects and 1.658% with fixed effects for high-foreign-sales firms, versus only about 0.292% and 0.261% for low-foreign-sales firms. Across customer-return quintiles for high-foreign-sales firms, the top-minus-bottom spread for high-trade-credit firms is about 2.039% without FE and 1.954% with FE. The paper presents this concentration among high-foreign-sales firms as supporting its identification of the cross-border trade-credit mechanism.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the predictability is especially prevalent among firms with high foreign sales. This conditional analysis is central to the paper’s claim that trade credit links between international firms drive the effect rather than unrelated firm characteristics.
Settings.H216: Section 4.2 discussion of conditioning on foreign sales; Table 4 (PDF pp. 604–606; Table 4 on PDF p. 605).
Settings.G217:
Treatment: Joint exposure composed of lagged customer-country return quintile, lagged trade-credit tercile, high foreign sales status, and whether producer-country trading volume relative to market capitalization is high or low. The substantive contrast is the effect of customer-country returns on high- versus low-trade-credit firms during low-volume versus high-volume periods. This is a nonbinary interacted treatment environment.

Method: This robustness/specification extends the baseline pooled firm-month WLS panel regression for the subsample/interaction of high-foreign-sales firms by further interacting the customer-return quintile × trade-credit tercile terms with a high trading volume indicator in the producer country. The authors interpret the total stock trading volume to market capitalization ratio as a proxy for uninformed trading volume, following Campbell, Grossman, and Wang (1993). The regression includes the same lagged firm and return controls as before, and in some columns country and industry fixed effects. The estimator is linear FE/WLS, not a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: The identifying variation is temporal variation in producer-country trading volume states interacted with the existing customer-return and trade-credit exposures, especially among high-foreign-sales firms. The concern is that low volume may coincide with other market conditions affecting expected returns. The paper addresses this with the baseline control set and fixed effects and relies on the model-based prediction that uninformed-volume periods should amplify the trade-credit channel. The key assumption is that, conditional on controls, the volume interaction captures the strength of information-versus-rebalancing trading rather than unrelated omitted states.

Setting: Table 5 tests the model prediction that customer-country returns affect producer-firm returns more strongly through trade credit when trading volume is low. For high-foreign-sales firms in low-volume periods, the bottom-customer-quintile low-minus-high trade-credit spread is 1.560% per month without fixed effects and 1.664% with fixed effects; the long low-trade-credit/top-customer minus high-trade-credit/bottom-customer strategy yields 3.530% per month without FE and 3.516% with FE. In contrast, the corresponding spread is about 1.518% and 1.491% in high-volume periods, and the across strategy falls to about 0.974% and 0.948%. The authors interpret this as supportive evidence that the trade-credit channel is stronger when uninformed trading volume is low.

Main role: This is a mechanism-testing robustness tied to a model prediction that predictability should be stronger when uninformed trading volume is low. It supports, but does not itself define, the paper’s central empirical claim.
Settings.H217: Section 4.2 discussion of trading volume; Table 5 (PDF pp. 606–607; Table 5 on PDF p. 607).
Settings.G218:
Treatment: Joint exposure given by lagged customer-country return quintile, lagged trade-credit tercile, and whether the month is classified as high emerging-market financial stress. The core contrast is how the trade-credit-conditioned effect of customer-country returns differs between high-stress and low-stress periods. This is nonbinary.

Method: This robustness/specification further augments the baseline pooled firm-month WLS panel regression by interacting the customer-return quintile × trade-credit tercile indicators with an emerging-market financial stress indicator. Financial stress periods are defined as months in which the IMF World Economic Outlook Financial Stress Indicator for any emerging market exceeds one. The regressions include the same lagged firm-level and return controls as in the main specification and, in some columns, country and industry fixed effects. The implemented estimator remains linear panel WLS with FE.

Identification: The design exploits time variation in financial stress states and asks whether the interaction between customer-country returns and firm trade credit is stronger in stressed periods. Endogeneity concerns are that financial stress may proxy for many omitted global shocks affecting returns. The paper addresses this using the comprehensive return and firm controls and fixed effects, and interprets the stronger interaction during stress as consistent with the financing-cost-spread mechanism from the model. The identifying assumption is that conditional on controls, the incremental stress interaction reflects asymmetry in access to external finance relevant to trade credit rather than unrelated crisis premia.

Setting: In Table 6, the authors interpret stronger predictability in high financial-stress periods as evidence that customer-country return shocks are transmitted to producer-firm returns through trade credit when financing-cost differences are larger. Within the bottom customer-return quintile, the low-minus-high trade-credit spread is 0.488% per month without fixed effects and 0.545% with fixed effects in low-stress periods, but 2.172% and 2.236% in high-stress periods. The long low-trade-credit/top-customer minus high-trade-credit/bottom-customer strategy is 0.796% to 0.798% in low-stress periods versus 4.129% to 4.145% in high-stress periods. The paper concludes that virtually all of the trading-strategy returns are earned during high financial stress, consistent with the model’s financing-frictions mechanism.

Main role: This is another substantive robustness/mechanism analysis testing a key theoretical prediction: trade-credit-based predictability should be strongest when financing conditions are most unequal, proxied by financial stress. It supports the central mechanism but is not the paper’s main baseline result.
Settings.H218: Section 4.2 discussion of financial stress; Table 6 (PDF pp. 606–608; Table 6 on PDF p. 608).
Settings.G219:
Treatment: Placebo treatment using randomized firm-level trade credit assigned within industry-month, interacted with lagged customer-country return quintiles in the same way as the baseline analysis. The substantive contrast remains low- versus high-'trade-credit' groups under random reassignment. Because the randomized measure is still sorted into groups and interacted with customer-return quintiles, the treatment is nonbinary overall.

Method: This placebo robustness repeats the baseline pooled firm-month WLS panel regression after randomly reassigning firm-level trade credit within industry-month cells across firms. The same empirical steps are rerun—sorting on customer-country returns, sorting on randomized trade credit, and estimating panel regressions with controls and country and industry fixed effects. The implemented estimator is still linear WLS with FE, but the treatment is a placebo version intended to assess whether the original trade-credit measure contains identifying information.

Identification: The strategy is a falsification exercise: if the baseline effect truly arises from the firm’s actual trade-credit position, replacing trade credit with a random within-industry-month assignment should eliminate the differential predictability between low- and high-trade-credit firms. This does not identify the causal effect by itself, but it probes whether the main estimates rely on real trade-credit information rather than spurious group structure or common industry-month factors.

Setting: In Table 7, the authors rerun the baseline customer-momentum regressions after randomizing trade credit within industry-month. Under the actual data, the long low-trade-credit/top-customer minus high-trade-credit/bottom-customer strategy is 1.857% per month without controls and 1.837% with all controls and fixed effects, while the corresponding high-trade-credit strategy is 1.238% and 1.312%. After randomization, the analogous spreads become 0.893% and 0.985% for the low-trade-credit strategy and 0.706% and 0.784% for the high-trade-credit strategy, i.e., the conditioning on trade credit no longer differentiates the results. The paper interprets this as evidence that actual trade credit carries incremental explanatory power and supports its identification strategy.

Main role: This is a placebo/identification robustness check. It is not a central result but supports the paper’s argument that the observed predictability specifically depends on the actual trade-credit measure rather than arbitrary sorting noise.
Settings.H219: Section 4.3 robustness, Table 7 (PDF pp. 608–609; Table 7 on PDF p. 609).
Settings.G220:
Treatment: Portfolio assignment based on lagged customer-country return quintile and lagged firm trade-credit quintile. The economically relevant treatment contrast is belonging to low versus high trade-credit portfolios within a given customer-return quintile, or top versus bottom customer-return portfolios for a given trade-credit group. This assignment is nonbinary and portfolio-based.

Method: The authors also estimate long-short portfolio alpha regressions based on double-sorted portfolios: firms are sorted by customer-return quintile and then by trade-credit quintile (and in the appendix also terciles). They report average excess returns and alphas from linear time-series factor regressions of portfolio returns on the world market factor (MKT), country momentum (MOM), global value factor (HML), and in some appendix specifications a constructed trade-credit factor. This is an asset-pricing time-series regression rather than a panel FE or quasi-experimental design, so it is classified as Other. The design is used to test whether the return spreads survive standard risk adjustment and whether nonlinearities are concentrated in the bottom customer quintile.

Identification: The identification argument is not causal in a quasi-experimental sense; instead, the authors interpret persistent double-sort excess returns and factor-adjusted alphas as evidence that the customer-return × trade-credit predictability is not explained by standard asset-pricing risk factors. The main concern is omitted risk compensation. By showing the spreads survive MKT, MOM, HML, and a trade-credit factor, they argue the effect reflects a fundamentals-based transmission channel rather than conventional factor exposures.

Setting: Table 8 reports portfolio returns and factor-model alphas from double-sorted customer-return × trade-credit portfolios. In the bottom customer quintile, the excess-return spread between high and low trade-credit portfolios is 1.192% per month, and the corresponding three-factor alpha spread is 1.035% per month. The strategy of going long low-trade-credit firms in top-customer-return countries and short high-trade-credit firms in bottom-customer-return countries yields an excess return of 2.467% per month and a three-factor alpha of 2.361% per month. The authors interpret these risk-adjusted portfolio results as confirming that the trade-credit channel generates nonlinear cross-country return predictability not captured by standard factors.

Main role: These portfolio sorts and alpha regressions are robustness analyses used to show the findings survive common risk adjustments and display the model’s predicted nonlinear pattern. They are supportive, not the paper’s principal identification approach.
Settings.H220: Section 4.3 robustness, Table 8 and surrounding discussion (PDF pp. 609–610; Table 8 on PDF p. 610).
Settings.G221:
Treatment: Quarterly firm-level exposure to temperature across establishment locations, measured as sales-weighted hours spent in each 1°C bin over the fiscal quarter. The effective treatment is a continuous, flexible exposure profile to extreme cold/heat rather than a single binary indicator. The paper interprets marginal exposure below/above estimated critical thresholds as temperature shocks.

Method: The core design estimates industry-by-calendar-quarter panel regressions of firm profitability on a flexible function of contemporaneous quarterly temperature exposure across firms’ U.S. establishments. For each 6-digit GICS industry and each calendar quarter, the authors regress log(1+EPS) on a third-order Chebyshev polynomial in hours spent in 1°C temperature bins, plus lagged firm controls (size, market-to-book, leverage, prior loss, dividend yield, no-dividend indicator) and linear and quadratic precipitation. Identification comes from within-firm variation after absorbing firm fixed effects and time fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by firm and quarter. The method is not DiD/IV/RD; it is a nonlinear-in-treatment but linear-in-outcome fixed-effects panel regression interpreted causally as temperature shocks affecting earnings.

Identification: The authors argue that short-run temperature realizations around firms’ established geographic footprints are random and exogenous, and that firm and time fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity and common aggregate shocks. Identification uses within-firm deviations in the distribution of experienced heat around each firm’s mean exposure. Remaining concerns include measurement error in establishment weights, only observing U.S. operations, possible adaptation/hedging, and whether common time effects are sufficient given industry geographic concentration.

Setting: The paper’s main causal claim is that extreme temperature exposure affects firm profitability. Using firm and time fixed-effects panel regressions estimated separately by industry and calendar quarter, the authors find statistically significant earnings sensitivity to extreme temperatures in 24 of 59 industries. Table 2 reports the directions and critical thresholds; e.g., in Q3, construction & engineering, leisure products, capital markets, and gas utilities show negative heat-shock sensitivity, while in Q4 airlines, metals & mining, and capital markets benefit from heat. Economically, the authors state that doubling the frequency of 5% extreme temperatures implies a 37.4 basis point average change in earnings across significant industry-quarter cells, with average +48 bp for positive-response cells and −28 bp for negative-response cells. This design is the primary evidence for the paper’s central contribution.

Main role: This is the paper’s central empirical design supporting the main conclusion that extreme temperatures causally affect firm earnings across many industries, as stated in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H221: Section 2.3 Eq. (2) and Section 3.1; Table 2, Fig. 5, and Appendix Table A.3 (PDF pp. 11–16, 35–36).
Settings.G222:
Treatment: Quarterly sales-weighted firm exposure to temperatures across establishment locations, modeled flexibly through hours spent in each 1°C temperature bin; interpreted as continuous extreme cold/heat exposure.

Method: Using the same industry-by-calendar-quarter firm panel fixed-effects framework as the main earnings regressions, the authors replace EPS with revenue and operating-cost measures to decompose the causal channel through which temperature exposure affects profitability. Regressions use the same flexible Chebyshev function of temperature-bin exposure, firm fixed effects, time fixed effects, lagged controls, and precipitation controls. Standard errors are clustered by firm and quarter.

Identification: Identification is the same within-firm weather-shock variation used in the main specification, now applied to revenue and cost outcomes. The regressions assume that conditional on firm fixed effects, time fixed effects, precipitation, and lagged controls, contemporaneous temperature exposure shifts revenue and/or operating costs. The key concern is still whether temperature exposure is exogenous and properly measured at firms’ economically relevant locations.

Setting: To identify how temperature shocks affect profitability, the authors re-estimate their baseline fixed-effects temperature regressions with revenues and operating costs as outcomes. They conclude that in most significant cases the earnings effects are revenue-driven: for example, hot Q3 temperatures reduce revenues in construction & engineering, capital markets, and gas utilities more than costs fall, lowering earnings; in fewer cases costs dominate, such as leisure products in hot Q3 or life science tools under cold Q2 shocks. This setting is central because it underpins the paper’s argument that consumer-demand shifts, rather than only production costs, explain many temperature-earnings relations.

Main role: These regressions materially support a central conclusion about the mechanism—especially that revenue effects drive about three quarters of the profitability responses.
Settings.G223:
Treatment: Quarterly sales-weighted continuous exposure to temperature bins across firm establishments, with emphasis on exposure below/above critical cold/heat thresholds.

Method: Again using the baseline industry-by-quarter firm fixed-effects panel regression with flexible temperature-bin exposure, the authors further decompose operating costs into cost of goods sold and SG&A. The same firm FE, time FE, lagged controls, precipitation controls, and clustering by firm and quarter apply. This is a channel/mechanism extension of the main FE design.

Identification: Same as the main FE design: within-firm temporal variation in weather exposure, conditional on firm and time fixed effects and observed controls, is treated as exogenous. The additional assumption is that accounting subcomponents like COGS and SG&A respond contemporaneously to the same shocks without major confounding from omitted time-varying cost factors beyond common shocks and precipitation.

Setting: The authors further ask whether temperature-induced operating-cost effects run through production costs or nonproduction overhead. Re-estimating their baseline fixed-effects temperature regressions with COGS and SG&A as outcomes, they find that most operating-cost sensitivities are driven by COGS rather than SG&A; examples with significant SG&A sensitivity include personal products and pharmaceuticals in cold Q2, construction materials in hot Q2, IT services in cold Q4, and machinery in hot Q4. These results help distinguish labor/material-cost and heating/cooling channels from broader revenue-based mechanisms.

Main role: These are mechanism-decomposition results supporting interpretation of operating-cost channels, but they are not the paper’s headline finding.
Settings.G224:
Treatment: Indicator for an extreme temperature day, defined as a day when temperature falls below 4°C, the critical threshold from the Q2 Hotels & Restaurants profitability results. In Panel B, the treatment is interacted with a weekend indicator (Friday-Sunday in the baseline weekend-interaction test).

Method: The authors directly test the consumer-demand mechanism using daily SafeGraph establishment visits matched to daily PRISM weather. They estimate Poisson fixed-effects regressions of daily visits on an indicator for extreme cold days, controlling for mean daily temperature and linear/squared precipitation, with quarter-by-establishment fixed effects and place-by-day-of-week fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the quarter-by-establishment level. Panel B adds an interaction between the shock-day indicator and a weekend indicator.

Identification: Identification comes from within-establishment day-to-day variation in extreme cold exposure during April–June, after controlling for establishment-quarter fixed effects, place-by-day-of-week fixed effects, mean temperature, and precipitation. The paper treats local daily temperature realizations as plausibly exogenous shocks to consumer foot traffic. Remaining concerns are other coincident local shocks and the post-2018 sample being outside the main earnings sample period.

Setting: To test the consumer-demand channel directly, the authors examine whether unusually cold spring days reduce visits to consumer-facing establishments. In Poisson fixed-effects regressions, they find that a sub-4°C day lowers daily visits by 5.08% in the full sample of NAICS 71–72 establishments, with similarly negative effects across spectator sports, museums/historical places, gambling establishments, beverage drinking places, and restaurants. The negative visit effect is larger on weekends: in the full sample, the baseline shock coefficient is −0.0356 and the additional weekend interaction is −0.0373. These results support the interpretation that temperature affects firm earnings partly by shifting local consumer demand.

Main role: These are mechanism tests that substantively support the consumer-demand interpretation but are not the main firm-profitability result.
Settings.H224: Section 3.2.1; Table 5 Panels A and B (PDF pp. 24–25).
Settings.G225:
Treatment: Quarterly sales-weighted weekday-only exposure to temperature bins across firm establishments; continuous flexible exposure to extreme cold/heat based only on Monday–Friday weather realizations.

Method: The authors estimate the same baseline industry-by-quarter firm fixed-effects temperature-exposure regressions as in the main specification, but using only weekday weather exposures (Monday to Friday) to differentiate labor-productivity from consumer-demand channels. The regressions retain firm FE, time FE, controls, precipitation, and clustered standard errors.

Identification: Same as the main FE setting, but variation is restricted to weekdays to emphasize shocks likely to matter through labor productivity rather than weekend consumer activity. The identifying assumption remains that weekday temperature fluctuations conditional on FE and controls are exogenous within firms.

Setting: As a channel test, the authors re-estimate their baseline earnings-temperature regressions using only weekday weather exposures. They report that some labor-intensive industries, such as paper & forest products, machinery, and technology hardware, show sensitivities that are more apparent with weekday-only exposure, while hotels & restaurants no longer exhibits sensitivity, consistent with weekend demand being central there. These weekday-only results support the view that labor-productivity channels are more important in some industries and consumer-demand channels in others.

Main role: This is a substantive mechanism robustness test used to distinguish channels, not a headline baseline result.
Settings.H225: Section 3.2.2 and Appendix Table A.6 (PDF pp. 25, 38).
Settings.G226:
Treatment: Doubling exposure to the left or right 5% tails of each industry’s temperature distribution, derived from the continuous flexible temperature-exposure function estimated in the baseline FE regressions.

Method: The paper jointly estimates industry-by-industry extreme-temperature earnings sensitivity functions for each calendar quarter and then tests whether the economic impacts of doubling the 5% tails differ between tradable and non-tradable industries. The underlying estimates come from the baseline fixed-effects earnings regressions; reported results are Wald-type tests comparing estimated impact magnitudes across industry groups classified using Mian and Sufi (2014).

Identification: The underlying identification is inherited from the baseline within-firm FE weather-shock design. The additional inference step compares estimated extreme-temperature effects across ex ante industry groups classified as tradable or non-tradable; causal interpretation relies on the baseline identifying assumptions plus the argument that greater non-tradable sensitivity is informative about local-demand exposure.

Setting: To probe the consumer-demand channel, the authors compare the economic impact of extreme temperatures across tradable and non-tradable industries. Using Wald tests on impacts implied by the baseline fixed-effects earnings response functions, they find that non-tradable industries are more sensitive to both extreme heat and cold in all quarters, with statistically significant differences for cold and heat extremes in spring and autumn—for example, the Wald statistics are 36.929 (Q2 left tail), 57.424 (Q4 left tail), 8.064 (Q2 right tail), and 32.773 (Q4 right tail). This pattern is interpreted as evidence that local demand links amplify temperature effects in non-tradables.

Main role: This is an auxiliary mechanism test supporting the consumer-demand channel through greater sensitivity in non-tradables.
Settings.H226: Section 3.2.3; Table 6, row “Tradables vs. Non-Tradables” (PDF pp. 25–26).
Settings.G227:
Treatment: Doubling exposure to the left or right 5% tails of an industry’s temperature distribution, with estimated effects compared between the first and second halves of the sample to assess adaptation.

Method: The authors estimate baseline industry-by-quarter fixed-effects temperature-earnings functions separately in the first and second halves of the sample (1990–2002 vs. 2003–2015), then compare the economic impacts of doubling the 5% temperature tails across subperiods using Wald tests. The reported estimator is a comparison of derived impacts from the same FE design across time subsamples.

Identification: The setting uses the same baseline within-firm FE weather-shock identification separately by subperiod, then tests whether estimated temperature sensitivities decline over time. Causal interpretation requires that differences in estimated effects across halves primarily reflect adaptation rather than major changes in composition, measurement, or other confounders.

Setting: The authors test for adaptation by comparing estimated extreme-temperature earnings sensitivities between 1990–2002 and 2003–2015. They report that profits are less sensitive to temperature shocks in the latter half of the sample across all seasons and both tails, with Wald statistics ranging from 79.618 to 2762.749 and all p-values at 0.038 or better. They interpret these declines as strong evidence that firms adapt over time to extreme temperatures.

Main role: This is an important substantive extension showing adaptation over time, but not the primary headline result.
Settings.H227: Section 3.2.4; Table 6, row “First vs. Second Half” (PDF pp. 25–26).
Settings.G228:
Treatment: Doubling the left or right 5% tails of each industry’s temperature distribution, derived from continuous temperature exposure functions estimated in the baseline FE panel.

Method: The authors jointly estimate baseline industry-by-quarter FE earnings response functions and compare derived extreme-temperature impacts between heat-sensitive and non-heat-sensitive industries classified following Graff-Zivin and Neidell (2014). The reported results are Wald-type tests on differences in impact magnitudes for doubled 5% temperature tails.

Identification: Identification inherits the baseline within-firm FE temperature-shock design. The additional comparison relies on ex ante industry classifications of heat sensitivity; larger estimated impacts in heat-sensitive sectors are interpreted as evidence consistent with labor-productivity channels.

Setting: Using the baseline fixed-effects earnings-temperature estimates, the authors compare impact magnitudes across industries classified as heat-sensitive or not. They find greater sensitivity in heat-sensitive industries in nearly all cases; for right-tail extremes, Wald tests are significant at 1% or better in Q2–Q4 (33.358, 7.128, 9.645) and marginal in Q1 (2.849, p=0.091). This comparative evidence is interpreted as consistent with labor-productivity based climate exposure documented by Graff-Zivin and Neidell (2014).

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism test linked to the labor-productivity interpretation rather than a main standalone result.
Settings.H228: Section 3.2.5; Table 6, row “Heat Sensitive vs. Non-Sensitive” (PDF pp. 25–26).
Settings.G229:
Treatment: Quarterly continuous sales-weighted exposure to temperature bins across firm establishments, interpreted as extreme cold/heat shocks.

Method: The authors re-estimate their baseline flexible temperature-exposure fixed-effects regressions using alternative profitability outcomes: EPS including extraordinary items, EPS including extraordinary and special items, and operating cash flow (EPS including extraordinary and special items plus depreciation/amortization and deferred taxes). These are robustness extensions of the same within-firm FE design with firm FE, time FE, controls, and precipitation.

Identification: Same as the baseline FE strategy: within-firm weather variation conditional on firm/time FE and controls is interpreted as exogenous. The robustness exercise checks whether accounting exclusions in baseline EPS understate temperature effects.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors re-estimate their temperature-effect regressions using broader profitability measures that include extraordinary items, special items, and operating cash flow. They report that the results are generally stronger and uncover more sensitive industries than the baseline EPS specification, implying the baseline estimates may be a lower bound on the profitability effects of extreme temperatures. This supports the substantive robustness of the main causal interpretation.

Main role: These are robustness analyses showing the main profitability findings are, if anything, stronger with broader earnings measures.
Settings.H229: Section 3.2.6; Appendix Tables A.8, A.9, and A.10 (PDF pp. 26, 40–41).
Settings.G230:
Treatment: Quarterly sales-weighted continuous exposure to temperature bins across firm establishments, interpreted as extreme cold/heat shocks affecting expected earnings.

Method: To test whether analysts incorporate temperature effects by quarter-end, the authors estimate the same industry-by-quarter fixed-effects temperature-exposure specification as the main earnings model but replace EPS with analysts’ mean consensus earnings forecasts measured as of earnings announcement dates. The regressions use the flexible Chebyshev temperature function, firm FE, time FE, controls, and precipitation.

Identification: The authors apply the same exogenous-within-firm weather-variation argument from the baseline FE design, now with analyst consensus forecasts as the dependent variable. A significant forecast-temperature relation in the same direction as earnings is interpreted as analysts understanding temperature effects; flat relations imply underreaction.

Setting: The paper examines whether analysts understand how temperature affects earnings by regressing consensus forecasts on firm temperature exposure using the same fixed-effects climate specification as for actual earnings. Table 7 shows that for most temperature-sensitive industry-quarter cells, forecasts move in the same direction as earnings—for example, analysts anticipate cold-Q1 effects in aerospace & defense and software and hot-Q3 effects in electric utilities and leisure products. The authors conclude that analysts anticipate at least part of the earnings shocks in many industries by quarter-end.

Main role: This setting materially supports one of the paper’s central conclusions: analysts often account for temperature by quarter-end, though not always.
Settings.G231:
Treatment: Quarterly sales-weighted continuous exposure to temperature bins across firm establishments, interpreted as extreme cold/heat shocks whose effects may or may not be reflected in analysts’ expectations.

Method: Using the same industry-by-quarter fixed-effects temperature-exposure framework, the authors replace the dependent variable with standardized unexpected earnings (SUE), defined as actual EPS minus the mean analysts’ forecast as of quarter-end, scaled by end-of-quarter share price. The flexible temperature-response function, firm FE, time FE, controls, and precipitation remain as in the baseline design.

Identification: Identification again relies on the same within-firm weather-shock variation. If temperature shocks significantly predict SUE, the authors interpret this as evidence analysts did not fully incorporate the causal effects of temperature on earnings by quarter-end.

Setting: The authors test whether temperature shocks generate predictable earnings surprises by estimating the baseline fixed-effects temperature specification with SUE as the outcome. They find that analysts miss or only partially account for temperature effects in seven industries, including leisure products, personal products, life science tools, construction & engineering, trading companies & distributors, commercial services & supplies, and machinery. For example, Table 7 shows positive surprise sensitivity for leisure products in cold Q2 and trading companies & distributors in hot Q1, and negative surprise sensitivity for construction & engineering in hot Q3 and machinery in hot Q4. These results show that temperature shocks remain informative for earnings surprises in some industries.

Main role: This directly supports the paper’s central analyst-learning conclusion by showing where temperature effects generate predictable earnings surprises.
Settings.G232:
Treatment: Occurrence of an extreme temperature event day for a firm, defined as a day on which the sales-weighted average maximum (heat shock) or minimum (cold shock) temperature across the firm’s establishments crosses the industry-quarter-specific critical threshold from Table 2. The treatment is binary at the event-day level.

Method: The authors conduct an event-study style before-after comparison around firm-specific extreme temperature events. For each event window, they compare average analysts’ consensus quarterly EPS forecasts in pre- versus post-event windows after multiplying events associated with positive earnings effects by −1 and demeaning within each event window. Events are defined using critical temperature thresholds from the baseline earnings results. This is not a standard linear FE regression or DiD; it is an event-study mean-comparison design on forecast revisions around extreme weather events.

Identification: The design assumes the timing of extreme temperature events relative to analyst forecast revisions is exogenous and that comparing pre- and post-event consensus forecasts reveals immediate analyst response. Event dates vary with local weather and firms’ geographic footprints. The main threat is other contemporaneous information arrivals within the event windows.

Setting: The authors study whether analysts promptly update expectations when temperature shocks occur within the quarter. Around 8,584 extreme temperature events, they compare consensus forecasts before and after the event and find no meaningful response: mean post-minus-pre forecast differences are 0.003 over [−20,+20], 0.007 over [−10,+10], 0.005 over [−5,+5], and 0.007 over [−1,+1], all statistically insignificant. They interpret this as evidence that analysts do not immediately react to observable intra-quarter temperature shocks, even though they often account for them by quarter-end.

Main role: This is a central result for the paper’s second main theme: analysts do not immediately react to observable intra-quarter temperature shocks.
Settings.H232: Section 3.4; Table 8 column 1 and Fig. 10 (PDF pp. 31–32).
Settings.G233:
Treatment: Binary indicator for an extreme temperature event day, defined using the industry-quarter-specific critical heat/cold thresholds crossed by the firm’s sales-weighted establishment temperatures.

Method: The authors perform a stock-return event study around firm-specific extreme temperature events. For each event, they estimate a Carhart (1997) four-factor model over days −50 to −21, compute abnormal returns over −20 to +20, multiply returns by −1 when the underlying temperature event implies positive earnings news, and cumulate CARs over several event windows. This is an event-study abnormal-return design rather than FE/DiD/IV.

Identification: Identification relies on the exogeneity of extreme temperature event timing and the event-study assumption that abnormal returns around the event capture investor response after removing expected returns via the Carhart model. Remaining concerns include overlapping information events and whether the factor model fully captures normal returns.

Setting: The authors examine whether investors immediately price intra-quarter temperature shocks using a factor-model event study. Across 8,584 extreme temperature events, they find economically small and statistically insignificant CARs over all windows: 0.003 over [−20,+20], 0.001 over [−10,+10], 0.001 over [−5,+5], and 0.001 over [−1,+1]. They therefore conclude that stock prices, like analyst forecasts, do not promptly react to observable extreme temperature shocks.

Main role: This is the paper’s core investor-reaction result: stock prices do not immediately respond to temperature shocks.

Settings.G234:
Treatment: Two-year growth in CZ total wages and salaries (local income growth), measured as a continuous rate. In the IV setting this is the endogenous treatment whose causal effect is estimated; the Bartik manufacturing shock serves as the instrument.

Method: Baseline 2SLS/Bartik design at the commuting-zone (CZ) × year × firm-age-category level for the nontradable sector. The endogenous regressor is two-year CZ income growth (growth in total wages and salaries). It is instrumented with a Bartik-style predicted change in manufacturing employment: the CZ's lagged industry mix across 4-digit manufacturing industries interacted with contemporaneous national employment growth in those industries, excluding the focal CZ from the national shock calculation. Regressions use the nonoverlapping sample of 2001, 2003, 2005, and 2007, include year fixed effects and baseline 2000 controls (log labor force, % high school educated, log total CZ wages). Separate second-stage estimates are reported for aggregate nontradable net job creation and for four age bins. The design aims to isolate plausibly exogenous local demand shocks affecting nontradables through local income, though identification still relies on the exclusion restriction that manufacturing shocks affect nontradable employment only through local income.

Identification: Cross-sectional differences in preexisting manufacturing composition make some CZs more exposed than others to national manufacturing employment shocks. The authors argue these shocks shift local income exogenously relative to nontradable-sector opportunities. Because nontradables depend mainly on local demand, instrumented income growth is interpreted as a local demand/investment-opportunity shock. Key assumptions are: (i) national manufacturing shocks affect nontradable employment only through local income, not via other direct channels; (ii) excluding the focal CZ from the national component helps prevent local shocks from mechanically entering the instrument; and (iii) remaining omitted local trends are captured by baseline controls and year fixed effects.

Setting: Using a Bartik instrument for two-year local income growth, the authors estimate that a one-percentage-point increase in income growth raises aggregate nontradable net job creation by 0.306 percentage points of 2000 nontradable employment (Table III, col. 3). The startup coefficient is 0.274 (col. 5), implying startups account for about 90% of the total net employment response, while firms aged 2-3 and 4-5 years show small insignificant effects (-0.035 and -0.011 in cols. 7 and 9), and firms aged 6+ years show a small insignificant 0.079 effect (col. 11). Elasticity estimates reported at the bottom of the table are 0.371 for aggregate employment, 1.195 for startups, 0.298 for 2-3 year-olds, 0.388 for 4-5 year-olds, and 0.290 for 6+ year-olds. This setting directly underpins the paper's central claim that local demand shocks create jobs mainly through entry of new firms rather than expansion of existing ones.

Main role: This is the paper's core identification strategy and main empirical result: exogenous local-income shocks increase nontradable employment primarily through startup job creation rather than expansion of incumbent firms.

Settings.G247:
Treatment: Average number of daughters among existing partners at the VC firm, measured at the year before a hiring event; in preferred specifications, average number of daughters among senior partners, conditional on average number of children. This is a continuous treatment intensity (roughly replacing one son with one daughter on average across partners).

Method: Linear probability regressions at the hire-event level relate whether a new hire is female to the average number of daughters and total children among existing partners at the firm in the year before the hire. Specifications add firm-level controls (VC firm age, average partner age, partner count, log capital per partner) and year fixed effects; some columns split children variables by senior versus junior partners, where senior partners are those with investment tenure above three years. Standard errors are clustered by venture capital firm and year. The authors interpret the coefficient on daughters conditional on total children as the causal 'daughter effect' from quasi-random child gender, though this remains regression adjustment rather than IV/RD/DiD.

Identification: Identification comes from the authors' argument that, conditional on total number of children, the number of daughters among partners is as-good-as-random because child sex is assigned by nature. They discuss and test threats from sex selection and gender-based stopping rules, and interpret the daughters coefficient as the relative effect of having a daughter rather than a son. The remaining concern is that even with these arguments, the specification is still a linear regression relying on the exogeneity of child gender and adequate control for total children and observed firm characteristics.

Setting: Using hire-level linear probability models, the paper argues that having more daughters among existing partners causes venture capital firms to hire more female investors. In Table 7, column (4), the coefficient on Avg Daughters (Senior) is 0.051 with standard error 0.017, implying that one additional daughter on average among senior partners, holding total children fixed, raises the probability that a new hire is female by 5.1 percentage points. Because the sample female-hire rate is 9.9%, the authors interpret this as a large increase in female hiring and as evidence that daughters debias senior partners' hiring decisions.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize as a central contribution that having more daughters reduces hiring bias and increases female partner hiring; Table 7 is the core evidence for that claim.
Settings.H247: Section 4.1 'Effects on venture capital hiring', Table 7 columns (1)-(6), especially col. (4); PDF page 9.
Settings.G248:
Treatment: Alternative continuous measures of daughter prevalence among senior partners at the firm at the hiring date: daughter ratio, average daughter ratio, daughter-heavy partner fraction, first-daughter partner fraction, and at least one daughter fraction.

Method: Alternative hire-level linear probability regressions use different continuous measures of daughter intensity among senior partners instead of the average number of daughters: daughter ratio, average daughter ratio, daughter-heavy partner fraction, first-daughter partner fraction, and at-least-one-daughter fraction. Controls include average children among senior partners, firm characteristics, and year fixed effects; standard errors are clustered by venture capital firm and year. These are robustness specifications for the same causal hiring claim using alternate treatment codings.

Identification: Same identification argument as the main hiring regressions: conditional on total children, the gender composition of partners' children is treated as exogenous. These columns probe whether the inferred debiasing effect is robust to nonlinear or alternative codings of daughters intensity among senior partners.

Setting: The authors report robustness regressions showing that the causal hiring interpretation is not sensitive to how daughters are measured among senior partners. In Table 8, several alternative daughter-intensity measures are positively related to female hiring, including Daughter Ratio (0.066, s.e. 0.032), Average Daughter Ratio (0.059, s.e. 0.031), and Daughter-Heavy Partner Fraction (0.036, s.e. 0.014), while the first-daughter and at-least-one-daughter measures are weaker. These results are used to support the claim that greater daughter exposure among senior partners causally increases the likelihood of hiring women.

Main role: These are substantive robustness checks supporting the main hiring result by showing it is not driven by one specific daughters measure.
Settings.G249:
Treatment: Average number of daughters among the relevant prior partners whose children are linked to current active partners' hiring, especially average number of daughters among senior partners, conditional on average number of children. Continuous treatment.

Method: Deal-level reduced-form linear regressions relate investment success to the average number of daughters and total children among partners who were present when currently active partners were hired. Controls include firm age, partner count, average partner age, log capital per partner, year fixed effects, and deal-level industry, round, and country fixed effects/controls. Some columns use all partners; others use only senior partners' children. Standard errors are clustered at VC firm and year.
