The paper applies the same linear estimators—sorted portfolio high-minus-low return spreads and univariate Fama-MacBeth slopes—to trading-frictions and market-microstructure characteristics such as size, volatility, turnover, dollar volume, Amihud illiquidity, zero-trading-day measures, short-term reversal, downside beta, bid-ask spreads, liquidity betas, intermediary leverage beta, Pastor-Stambaugh beta, and PIN. The paper especially emphasizes preferred NYSE-VW sorts and FM-WLS regressions, while also reporting All-EW and FM-OLS to show that even microcap-heavy procedures do not rescue most trading-frictions anomalies.

Identification: Identification is observational through return differences across firms with different trading-friction or microstructure characteristics. The authors stress microcap overweighting as one source of inflated original results but also note that many trading-frictions anomalies fail even when microcaps are heavily weighted. Their preferred replication procedures aim to test whether the apparent expected-return effects survive under more economically relevant weighting and breakpoint choices. No exogenous variation is used, and model dependence or omitted-risk concerns remain unresolved.

Setting: Trading-frictions anomalies largely fail to predict returns under the paper’s preferred procedures. With NYSE-VW, 102 of 106 trading-frictions variables do not replicate, and many famous effects shrink dramatically: idiosyncratic volatility and total volatility are mostly insignificant; Amihud illiquidity earns only 0.25%-0.39% per month depending on horizon; short-term reversal shrinks to -0.27% per month versus Jegadeesh’s -1.99%; Acharya-Pedersen and Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity betas are broadly insignificant; maximum daily return, intermediary leverage beta, and PIN also fail. Even All-EW or FM-OLS, which overweight microcaps, leave most trading-frictions effects unreplicated. The authors conclude that these variables are especially fragile and often economically unimportant.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all highlight trading frictions as the 'biggest casualty' of replication, with 96% failing under preferred procedures. This panel is therefore a central main-result setting.
Settings.H424: Section 3.2.6 'Trading Frictions'; Table 3 Panel F; PDF pages 39-44 and 49-51.
Settings.G425:
Treatment: Interaction between mandated post-CD&A disclosure regime (indicator equal to one after a firm's required adoption year) and the firm's pre-CD&A average market share, measured as ln(Share). The causal contrast is that the CD&A disclosure mandate increases the strategic value of using revenue-based pay more for higher-share firms, especially in Cournot industries. Treatment is not binary because the focal estimand varies continuously with ln(Share) in the post period.

Method: The main design is a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences estimated separately in Cournot and Bertrand samples with firm and year fixed effects. The estimating equation is Revenue-Based Pay_i,t = beta ln(Share_i) x PostCD&A_t + firm FE + year FE + error, where Share is a firm's pre-CD&A average 4-digit SIC market share and PostCD&A turns on at the firm's mandated CD&A adoption date. The author interprets this as within-firm, within-year evidence that the mandated disclosure shock changed the relation between market share and use of revenue-based CEO pay. Firm FE absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity; year FE absorb common time shocks and sample-composition changes. Standard errors are clustered by firm. Identification concerns discussed by the paper include whether absent CD&A the slope relating revenue-based pay to share would have evolved similarly across competition types, and whether changes reflect actual pay practices rather than only improved disclosure.

Identification: Identification comes from a regulatory timing shock: the SEC's CD&A disclosure mandate plausibly increased the salience/credibility of executive pay disclosures. The regression compares within-firm changes after adoption and asks whether these changes are steeper for firms with larger pre-period market shares, separately by competitive mode. The author argues that firm FE remove time-invariant confounding, year FE remove aggregate shocks, and the key triple-difference intuition is that absent CD&A the slope of revenue-based pay on share would have moved in parallel across Cournot and Bertrand industries. Remaining concerns include endogenous measurement of competition type and the possibility that disclosure quality, not underlying contracts, changed.

Setting: Using a TWFE DiD-style design around the mandated CD&A disclosure adoption, the paper finds that in Cournot industries higher-share firms became more likely to use revenue-based CEO pay after the rule change, while Bertrand firms did not. In Table 3, the coefficient on ln(Share) x PostCD&A is 0.034 (t=2.754) for Cournot firms and -0.016 (t=-1.308) for Bertrand firms; the cross-sample difference is 0.050 (t=2.881). The author interprets this as evidence that the disclosure mandate increased the viability of strategic commitment through compensation, especially where firms have enough market share to influence rivals.

Main role: This is the paper's central empirical test of whether the 2006 CD&A disclosure mandate caused higher-share Cournot firms to add revenue-based CEO pay, the main claim emphasized in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H425: Section 5.3 Main analysis, Eq. (3), Table 3, PDF pp. 11-12.
Settings.G426:
Treatment: Post-CD&A interaction with pre-CD&A market-share-related exposure measures: either ln(Share) x PostCD&A controlling for ln(Sales) x PostCD&A, or ln(Sales) x PostCD&A together with ln(SIC Sales) x PostCD&A. The focal causal treatment remains increased strategic benefit from disclosure for firms with larger product-market influence, not a binary treatment.

Method: A refinement of the main DiD specification adds ln(Sales) x PostCD&A and alternatively decomposes ln(Share) into ln(Sales) and ln(SIC Sales), still with firm and year fixed effects estimated separately by competition type. This remains a conventional DiD/TWFE design because identification comes from the post-CD&A interaction with pre-period cross-sectional exposure measures. The purpose is to distinguish strategic market-share effects from pure firm-size effects.

Identification: Same disclosure-shock DiD logic as the main analysis, with additional structure to separate firm size from strategic position. The decomposition relies on the identity ln(Share)=ln(Sales)-ln(SIC Sales). If the effect were just firm size, ln(SIC Sales) should not matter; if it is strategic market position, own size and industry size should enter with opposite signs. The identifying assumption remains that absent CD&A these exposure gradients would not differentially shift in ways correlated with omitted factors after conditioning on firm and year FE.

Setting: Table 4 shows that the post-CD&A shift toward revenue-based CEO pay in Cournot industries is linked to market share rather than firm size. In the Cournot sample, controlling for ln(Sales) x PostCD&A leaves the ln(Share) x PostCD&A coefficient essentially unchanged at 0.035 (t=2.818), while the size interaction is -0.003 (t=-0.179). When replacing ln(Share) with its components, ln(Sales) x PostCD&A is 0.032 (t=1.899) and ln(SIC Sales) x PostCD&A is -0.035 (t=-2.819), with significant cross-sample differences versus Bertrand industries. The author interprets this as stronger evidence that strategic market share, not generic scale, drives compensation changes.

Main role: The paper explicitly uses these refinements to support the core strategic-commitment interpretation by showing the effect is about market share rather than firm size.
Settings.H426: Section 5.4.1 Firm size versus market share, Eqs. (4)-(6), Table 4, PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G427:
Treatment: Exposure to the CD&A disclosure mandate in a firm's own adoption year, interacted with pre-CD&A ln(Share), with staggered timing by fiscal year-end. Early Adopter x ln(Share) x Post2006 and Early Adopter x ln(Share) x Post2007 capture whether larger-share firms shift toward revenue-based pay precisely when their own disclosure mandate takes effect. Treatment is continuous because it varies with ln(Share).

Method: A staggered-adoption triple-difference/event-timing refinement estimated over 2005-2007. The regression interacts Early Adopter (December year-end firms) with ln(Share) and Post2006/Post2007 indicators, plus analogous ln(Sales) interactions, firm FE, and year FE. The design exploits that December year-end firms had to comply in fiscal 2006 while September-November year-end firms complied in fiscal 2007. It remains a conventional DiD/DDD rather than modern heterogeneous DiD because the paper implements linear interacted FE regressions rather than a named heterogeneity-robust estimator.

Identification: The design uses plausibly exogenous variation in compliance timing driven by fiscal year-end. If CD&A caused the compensation change, early adopters should adjust in 2006 and late adopters in 2007. Firm FE absorb permanent differences across firms, and year FE absorb common shocks. The author notes a caveat that fiscal year-end is not random, so differential reactions to omitted factors by year-end type cannot be fully ruled out.

Setting: In the 2005-2007 staggered-adoption test, higher-share Cournot firms shift toward revenue-based CEO pay in their own adoption year. Table 5 reports for Cournot firms a coefficient of 0.107 (t=2.083) on ln(Share) x Post2006 x Early Adopter and -0.126 (t=-1.991) on ln(Share) x Post2007 x Early Adopter, consistent with December year-end firms moving first in 2006 and later adopters catching up in 2007. Comparable Bertrand coefficients are small and insignificant (-0.012 and -0.036). The author interprets this timing pattern as evidence that the CD&A, rather than coincident trends, caused the pay-practice shift.

Main role: The paper highlights staggered rollout evidence as an important refinement showing the effect occurs tightly around firms' own adoption dates, directly reinforcing the core causal story.
Settings.H427: Section 5.4.2 Staggered adoption, Eq. (7), Table 5, PDF pp. 13-15.
Settings.G428:
Treatment: ln(Share) x PostCD&A after matching Cournot and Bertrand firm-years on observed determinants of revenue-based pay. The focal treatment remains the differential post-CD&A effect of market share on use of revenue-based CEO pay.

Method: The author re-estimates the main post-CD&A interaction model on coarsened exact matched samples of Cournot and Bertrand firm-years, matching on R&D intensity, advertising intensity, firm age, and market share by year, then applying weights and estimating the same firm-FE/year-FE regression. Because matching is preprocessing and the implemented identifying estimator is still the interacted FE DiD regression, this is classified as conventional DiD rather than matching/weighting.

Identification: The matching step improves comparability of treatment and control industries on observables thought to affect revenue-based pay, while the DiD regression uses within-firm changes around CD&A adoption. Identification still relies on the assumption that, conditional on matching, firm FE, and year FE, there were no differential post-CD&A changes in the share gradient except through the disclosure shock.

Setting: On matched Cournot-Bertrand samples, the main result remains: larger-share Cournot firms become more likely to adopt revenue-based CEO pay after CD&A, unlike Bertrand firms. In Table 6, the quintile-matched sample gives 0.050 (t=3.420) for Cournot and -0.014 (t=-0.771) for Bertrand, with a difference of 0.064 (t=2.721). The decile-matched sample gives 0.035 (t=1.698) for Cournot and -0.042 (t=-1.500) for Bertrand, difference 0.077 (t=2.225). The paper treats this as robustness supporting a strategic interpretation rather than differences in observed firm characteristics.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis used to show the main finding is not due to differences in observable agency-theory determinants across Cournot and Bertrand samples.
Settings.H428: Section 5.4.3 Coarsened exact matching, Table 6, PDF p. 16.
Settings.G429:
Treatment: ln(Share) x PostCD&A, the interaction of pre-CD&A market share with post-CD&A disclosure adoption. Treatment is continuous.

Method: Placebo DiD regressions parallel to the main specification but with alternative outcomes capturing other supplemental CEO performance metrics. The specification is Metric_i,t = beta ln(Share_i) x PostCD&A_t + firm FE + year FE + error, estimated separately for Cournot and Bertrand industries. These are interpreted causally as tests of whether CD&A differentially changed use of non-revenue metrics for large-share firms.

Identification: Same DiD logic as the main analysis, but now the outcomes test alternative channels. If the revenue-based-pay findings just reflected a general post-CD&A increase in metrics for large-share Cournot firms, similar patterns should appear for other-financial or non-financial metrics. Firm and year FE absorb persistent heterogeneity and common shocks.

Setting: The placebo outcomes show the strategic result is specific to revenue-based pay rather than a broad post-CD&A overhaul of all metrics. Table 7 reports no significant effect on Other-Financial metrics: ln(Share) x PostCD&A is 0.014 (t=0.849) for Cournot and 0.005 (t=0.397) for Bertrand. For Non-Financial metrics, both Cournot and Bertrand firms show positive share-related increases, 0.053 (t=2.820) and 0.045 (t=3.414), with an insignificant difference of 0.008. The author interprets this as inconsistent with a revenue-metric result driven solely by a general increase in the number of disclosed metrics.

Main role: These are placebo/supporting analyses to assess whether the main revenue-based-pay result merely reflects a broad expansion in disclosed metrics after CD&A.
Settings.H429: Section 5.5.1 Other performance metrics, Eq. (8), Table 7, PDF pp. 15-16.
Settings.G430:
Treatment: ln(Share) x PostCD&A, the continuous interaction of pre-period market share with post-CD&A disclosure adoption; controls absorb contemporaneous presence or counts of other metric types.

Method: Re-estimation of the main DiD model for Revenue-Based Pay while controlling either for indicators of Other-Financial and Non-Financial metrics or for the logged counts ln(1+#Other-Financial) and ln(1+#Non-Financial), still with firm and year fixed effects and separate Cournot/Bertrand samples. This is a robustness DiD assessing whether changes in revenue-based pay survive controls for broader metric usage.

Identification: Same within-firm post-CD&A identifying variation as the main analysis. By conditioning on other-financial and non-financial metric usage, the author tests whether the share-related post-CD&A change in revenue-based pay reflects strategic use of revenue incentives specifically rather than broader contract expansion.

Setting: Controlling for other supplementary metrics leaves the core result intact. In Table 8, with indicator controls the Cournot coefficient on ln(Share) x PostCD&A is 0.032 (t=2.590) versus -0.019 (t=-1.600) for Bertrand; with logged-count controls it is 0.033 (t=2.773) versus -0.020 (t=-1.691), and the cross-sample differences are 0.051 and 0.054. The paper interprets this as evidence that the CD&A-induced strategic shift is specifically about revenue-based pay, not a general proliferation of performance metrics.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness check showing the main result is not explained by simultaneous increases in other metrics.
Settings.H430: Section 5.5.1 Other performance metrics, Eqs. (9)-(10), Table 8, PDF p. 17.
Settings.G431:
Treatment: Interaction of raw pre-CD&A market share Share with PostCD&A, estimated separately in subsamples below and above threshold market shares (33.3% and 50%). Treatment is continuous.

Method: A non-monotonicity robustness DiD splits the sample by market-share thresholds and estimates Revenue-Based Pay_i,t = beta Share_i x PostCD&A_t + firm FE + year FE + error separately above and below thresholds, and separately for Cournot and Bertrand industries. The treatment dose is raw pre-CD&A Share rather than ln(Share), because the author wants to study sign changes in the marginal effect at high shares.

Identification: Identification again comes from post-CD&A within-firm changes interacted with pre-period market share, but the design now asks whether the slope is positive for oligopolistic firms and negative for near-monopolists in Cournot industries. The argument is that strategic commitment matters only when firms both influence rivals and still face enough competition.

Setting: The non-monotonicity tests support the strategic theory: in Cournot industries, higher share predicts more post-CD&A adoption of revenue-based pay up to moderate concentration, but less adoption in the far right tail where firms approach monopoly. In Table 9 Panel A, below 33.3% share the coefficient is 0.984 (t=3.141) for Cournot versus -0.248 for Bertrand; above 33.3% share it is -0.290 (t=-1.992) for Cournot versus 0.292 for Bertrand. Panel B shows a similar sign reversal around 50% share: 0.614 (t=3.215) below the cutoff and -0.591 (t=-1.949) above it for Cournot firms. The author argues this difficult-to-explain inverted-U pattern is especially consistent with strategic commitment.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis used to test the theory's predicted non-monotonic strategic effect of market share, supporting the central strategic-commitment interpretation.
Settings.G432:
Treatment: Triple interaction of pre-CD&A industry concentration ln(HHI), post-CD&A period, and being in a Cournot industry. The focal treatment captures greater exposure to disclosure-induced strategic delegation in highly concentrated Cournot markets. It is continuous because ln(HHI) is continuous.

Method: Product-market-outcomes DiD/DDD regressions estimate Outcome_i,t = beta1 ln(HHI_i) x PostCD&A_t x Cournot_i + beta2 ln(HHI_i) x PostCD&A_t + firm FE + year-mode FE + error. HHI is a pre-CD&A 4-digit SIC Herfindahl measure of concentration. Outcomes are ln(COGS), ln(Margin), and ln(Markup), estimated on the full 2002-2009 sample and on a 2005-2007 window. Year-mode fixed effects allow common time shocks to differ by competition type. The design is interpreted as testing whether the disclosure-induced compensation changes affected product-market equilibria in concentrated Cournot industries.

Identification: The strategy uses the CD&A mandate as an exogenous shock to the viability of strategic delegation and asks whether highly concentrated Cournot industries differentially shift product-market outcomes after adoption. Because theory predicts effects where strategic substitution is strongest and market concentration high, the triple interaction isolates that exposure. Firm FE absorb stable firm traits; year-mode FE absorb common shocks by competition type. Key assumptions are that, absent CD&A, concentrated Cournot industries would not have had differential post-period shifts in output or margins relative to the comparison groups, conditional on FE.

Setting: The product-market regressions indicate that after CD&A, highly concentrated Cournot industries move toward more aggressive equilibria: higher production-related spending and lower margins/markups. In Table 10, the coefficient on ln(HHI) x PostCD&A x Cournot is 0.154 (t=2.903) for ln(COGS) in the full sample and 0.098 (t=3.036) in 2005-2007; for ln(Margin) it is -0.140 (t=-3.471) and -0.154 (t=-3.826); for ln(Markup) it is -0.111 (t=-2.459) and -0.127 (t=-3.038). The author interprets these patterns as evidence that disclosure-induced strategic delegation through revenue-based pay made firms expand output and compress margins, consistent with Fershtman and Judd (1987).

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that the compensation shift coincides with more aggressive product-market equilibria, making these outcome regressions a key second pillar of the paper's central claim.
Settings.H432: Section 5.5.3 Product market outcomes, Eq. (11), Table 10, PDF p. 18.
Settings.G433:
Treatment: Exposure to the Knight Capital glitch for a stock, implemented as binary indicators for parent-order executions on 'glitch-affected' stocks during specific post-event windows: day 0, next week, Aug. 9–31, and post-Aug. 31. Glitch-affected stocks are identified from abnormally high trading in the first 30 minutes on Aug. 1, 2012. This is a binary exposure at the stock-execution level within each event window.

Method: The main institutional-trading-cost design estimates difference-in-differences style panel regressions at the parent-order-execution level around the August 1, 2012 Knight Capital glitch. The authors regress execution-cost outcomes on indicators for executions in glitch-affected stocks on the glitch day, the next five business days, Aug. 9–31, and post-Aug. 31, plus analogous indicators for non-glitch stocks for which Knight Capital was the designated market maker (DMM). They include stock fixed effects and calendar-day fixed effects, making the specification equivalent to a standard DiD with stock and day dummies, and add execution- and stock-level controls: participation rate, fraction of daily volume, relative daily volume, interval turnover, interval and day volatility, execution duration, day return and absolute day return, earnings-day indicator, and VWAP-algorithm indicator. Standard errors are double-clustered by day and stock. Identification comes from comparing changes in execution costs for affected stocks relative to unaffected stocks before versus after the exogenous glitch.

Identification: The authors argue the Knight Capital glitch is an exogenous technical failure unrelated to fundamentals of the underlying stocks, creating plausibly exogenous supply shocks and inventory imbalances. The DiD-style identification compares execution costs for glitch-affected stocks before versus after the event relative to unaffected stocks, controlling for stock fixed effects, day fixed effects, and known determinants of trading costs. The key assumption is that absent the glitch, treated and untreated stocks would have followed similar within-stock changes in institutional execution costs conditional on controls and day effects.

Setting: Using a stock-by-day fixed-effects DiD specification on institutional parent-order executions, the paper finds that the Knight Capital glitch sharply increased execution costs for glitch-affected stocks. In Table 4, VWAP slippage rises by 6.35 bps on the glitch day and 6.48 bps in the following five business days; implementation shortfall rises by 18.15 bps on the glitch day and 16.66 bps in the next week. VWAP slippage remains elevated by 1.11 bps through Aug. 31. The authors interpret these as causal effects of an exogenous inventory/supply shock on institutional liquidity, central to the paper’s slow-moving-capital argument.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize the causal impact of the exogenous glitch on institutional trading costs and their persistence as a central contribution of the paper.
Settings.H433: Section 5.1 'Institutional trading costs,' Eq. (7), Table 4 columns 'VWAP slippage' and 'Implementation shortfall' (PDF pp. 934-937, especially PDF pp. 934-936).
Settings.G434:
Treatment: Binary indicator for a parent-order execution being in a non-glitch stock for which Knight Capital was the designated market maker, in event windows around the glitch (day 0, next week, Aug. 9–31, post-Aug. 31). This captures exposure to the market-making-capital shock rather than direct glitch trading.

Method: Using the same parent-order-execution panel DiD framework as Eq. (7), the authors estimate causal effects of Knight Capital’s capital shock on institutional execution costs for stocks where Knight was the DMM but that were not directly glitch-affected. The regression includes stock and day fixed effects and the same control vector as in the main specification. The treatment is the DMM exposure interacted with event windows around the glitch.

Identification: The identifying variation is the exogenous capital shock to Knight Capital caused by the glitch, combined with cross-stock exposure via Knight’s role as DMM. By comparing execution costs for Knight-DMM stocks that were not directly glitch-affected to other stocks before and after the glitch, with stock and day fixed effects and controls, the authors argue they isolate the effect of reduced market-making capital. The main assumption is that, absent Knight’s capital shock, DMM stocks would not have experienced differential changes in execution costs relative to controls after conditioning on fixed effects and covariates.

Setting: In the same DiD framework as the main analysis, the paper finds that non-glitch stocks for which Knight Capital was the DMM experienced higher institutional trading costs on the glitch day. Table 4 reports DMM0 coefficients of 5.04 bps for VWAP slippage and 32.92 bps for implementation shortfall. The authors interpret this as causal evidence for a market-making-capital channel: Knight’s capital loss reduced its liquidity provision even in stocks not heavily traded during the glitch. Post-glitch coefficients are not significant, which the paper partly attributes to limited power and the transfer of DMM duties to Getco.

Main role: The paper highlights the market-making-capital channel as one of its two main mechanisms, and these DMM results are presented as evidence that a capital shock to Knight reduced liquidity even in stocks not directly glitch-traded.
Settings.H434: Section 5.1.1 'Market-making capital channel,' Eq. (7), Table 4 columns 'VWAP slippage' and 'Implementation shortfall' (PDF pp. 934-937, especially PDF pp. 936-937).
Settings.G435:
Treatment: KnightSameSide indicator: equals one for executions between Aug. 1 and Aug. 8 in stocks with extreme glitch-period returns (±2.5%) where the institutional order is on the same side as Knight Capital’s expected liquidation trade; e.g., after a positive glitch return implying Knight bought stock, a subsequent sell order is same-side. Binary indicator.

Method: To test asymmetric supply-shock effects, the authors run parent-order-execution regressions of institutional execution costs on a binary indicator KnightSameSide, plus the same glitch, DMM, control, stock fixed effect, and day fixed effect structure used in the main specification. KnightSameSide equals one when a stock had an extreme return during the glitch (±2.5%) and the institutional investor traded in the same direction as Knight Capital would when liquidating the implied inventory imbalance. This is a linear regression adjustment design, not a separate DiD interaction estimator.

Identification: The design exploits cross-execution variation in whether an institutional order is on the same side as Knight’s inferred post-glitch liquidation need, using extreme glitch-period stock returns to proxy for Knight’s inventory direction. Conditional on stock fixed effects, day fixed effects, and rich controls, the authors interpret higher same-side execution costs as evidence that persistent inventory imbalances causally raise liquidity demand on one side of the market. The key assumption is that the inferred inventory direction from glitch returns captures exogenous supply pressure rather than omitted information effects.

Setting: Table 5 shows that institutional orders expected to be on the same side as Knight Capital’s liquidation needs faced materially higher trading costs. KnightSameSide raises VWAP slippage by 8.68 bps and implementation shortfall by 30.52 bps. The paper interprets this as causal evidence that the glitch-induced supply shock affected liquidity asymmetrically: trades that competed with Knight’s need to offload inventory became especially costly. This mechanism supports the paper’s argument that post-glitch illiquidity reflects persistent inventory pressure rather than only transient market disruption.

Main role: The asymmetric same-side trading-cost result is used as direct evidence for the supply-shock mechanism, one of the paper’s central causal channels.
Settings.H435: Section 5.1.2 'Asymmetric impact of supply shock on liquidity,' Table 5 (PDF pp. 937-938).
Settings.G436:
Treatment: Binary indicators for parent-order executions on glitch-affected stocks in event windows around the Knight Capital glitch (day 0, next week, Aug. 9–31, post-Aug. 31).

Method: The authors apply the same stock-and-day fixed-effects event-window DiD regression at the parent-order level to matched standard microstructure liquidity measures computed over the exact execution interval of each institutional order. Outcomes are effective spread, realized spread, and price impact. Controls mirror the institutional-cost regressions, allowing side-by-side comparison of how the glitch affected spread-based liquidity versus institutional costs.

Identification: The same exogenous-glitch event study/DiD logic is used as for institutional costs: compare matched spread outcomes for glitch-affected versus unaffected stocks before and after the glitch, controlling for stock and day effects plus execution-interval covariates. The causal interpretation relies on the glitch generating exogenous inventory/supply shocks while untreated stocks provide the counterfactual evolution of spreads absent the glitch.

Setting: Using matched execution-interval spread measures in the same DiD design, the authors find a much smaller and less persistent liquidity effect than with institutional trading costs. In Table 4, effective spread for glitch-affected stocks rises by 0.86 bps on the glitch day, with no significant increase in the following week; realized spread does not rise significantly, while price impact increases by 1.31 bps on the glitch day and 1.47 bps in the next week (both only weakly significant). The paper interprets this as evidence that standard spread-based measures quickly revert and miss the persistent illiquidity faced by institutional investors.

Main role: A central conclusion is that standard spread-based measures revert quickly and fail to capture the persistent liquidity deterioration seen in institutional costs.
Settings.H436: Section 5.2 'Spreads,' Table 4 columns 'Effective spread,' 'Realized spread,' and 'Price impact' (PDF pp. 936-939).
Settings.G437:
Treatment: Binary indicators for parent-order executions in non-glitch stocks for which Knight Capital was the designated market maker, during event windows around the glitch.

Method: The paper uses the same parent-order-level DiD/event-window regression to estimate the effect of Knight’s DMM exposure on matched spread-based liquidity measures for non-glitch DMM stocks. Outcomes are effective spread, realized spread, and price impact computed over each institutional execution interval. Stock and day fixed effects and the full control vector are included.

Identification: Identification comes from exogenous variation in Knight’s risk-bearing capacity after the glitch and cross-stock exposure through Knight’s DMM assignments. The regression compares changes in matched spread outcomes for Knight-DMM stocks relative to others before and after the glitch, holding constant stock and day effects and interval controls. The assumption is that absent the capital shock, these DMM stocks would not have experienced differential spread changes.

Setting: In Table 4, non-glitch DMM stocks do not show an increase in effective spreads on the glitch day, but they do show a significant fall in realized spreads (-0.99 bps) and a rise in price impact (0.90 bps). The paper treats these as limited-power supporting evidence and notes that stronger spread effects appear only in an extended sample of smaller DMM stocks outside the S&P 500. Thus, matched spread measures provide only weak support for a market-making-capital effect in the benchmark institutional-execution sample.

Main role: These DMM spread results are supporting evidence for the market-making-capital mechanism and are more limited in power than the institutional-cost results.
Settings.H437: Section 5.2 'Spreads' and discussion in Section 5.3, Table 4 DMM rows for spread outcomes (PDF pp. 936-939).
Settings.G438:
Treatment: Binary exposure of a stock to being glitch-affected, interacted with event days 0 through 5 after Aug. 1, 2012, and an Aug. 9–31 post window. The treatment is stock-level glitch exposure, not continuous intensity.

Method: At the stock-day level, the authors estimate event-window DiD regressions of daily effective spread, log turnover, and total dollar depth on separate indicators for glitch-affected stocks on the glitch day and each of the next five trading days, plus an Aug. 9–31 indicator, with analogous DMM indicators. They include stock fixed effects, day fixed effects, and controls for log market capitalization, log price, log turnover (except when turnover is the outcome), and Parkinson volatility. Standard errors are clustered by stock.

Identification: The exogenous Knight glitch creates stock-level treatment for the set of glitch-affected stocks. The event-window DiD compares daily liquidity metrics for affected versus unaffected stocks before and after the event, controlling for stock fixed effects, day fixed effects, and time-varying stock characteristics. The identifying assumption is that, absent the glitch, affected and unaffected stocks would have evolved similarly conditional on those controls.

Setting: At the daily stock level, the paper finds that the glitch caused sharp but heterogeneous changes in standard liquidity metrics for glitch-affected stocks. Table 7 shows effective spreads increase by 3.26 bps on the glitch day but not thereafter; log turnover rises by 0.17 on the glitch day and by about 0.10 to 0.13 on several of the next four days; total depth falls by about $172 thousand on the glitch day, with negative but mostly imprecise post-glitch coefficients. The authors interpret the elevated turnover and reduced depth as evidence that the glitch had persistent effects on dimensions of liquidity more relevant for institutional investors than quoted spreads.

Main role: These results help explain a core paper conclusion: spread-based measures miss the persistent liquidity effects because turnover and depth change materially after the glitch.
Settings.H438: Section 6.3 'Turnover and depth around the glitch,' Eq. (8), Table 7 columns for ES, log turn, and depth (PDF pp. 940-943).
Settings.G439:
Treatment: Binary indicator that a stock was assigned to Knight Capital as DMM but was not glitch-affected, interacted with event days around the glitch and a later Aug. 9–31 window.

Method: Using the same stock-day event-window DiD specification as Table 7, the authors estimate effects of Knight’s DMM exposure on daily effective spread, log turnover, and total dollar depth for non-glitch stocks where Knight was the DMM. The regression includes stock and day fixed effects and controls for price, market cap, turnover, and volatility.

Identification: Identification uses the exogenous reduction in Knight’s market-making capital after the glitch and Knight’s pre-existing DMM assignments across stocks. Comparing DMM stocks to non-DMM stocks before and after the glitch with stock and day effects is intended to isolate the causal effect of reduced DMM liquidity provision. The assumption is no coincident differential shock to Knight-assigned stocks unrelated to the glitch.

Setting: In Table 7, the stock-day DiD results for Knight DMM stocks show little effect on effective spread or turnover immediately after the glitch, but depth becomes significantly lower three to five trading days later, with coefficients around -$20 thousand to -$24 thousand. The authors view this as suggestive evidence that Knight’s impaired market-making capacity, and later the transfer of those duties to Getco, reduced available depth in assigned stocks even without direct glitch trading.

Main role: These are supporting daily-liquidity results for the market-making-capital channel, secondary to the main institutional-cost evidence.
Settings.H439: Section 6.3 'Turnover and depth around the glitch,' Table 7 DMM rows (PDF pp. 941-943).
Settings.G440:
Treatment: Binary indicator that a non-glitch stock had Knight Capital as designated market maker, interacted with event days around the glitch and Aug. 9–31. In this robustness setting, treatment specifically captures DMM exposure in the extended stock sample.

Method: As a robustness test using an extended sample of NYSE/Amex common stocks from July to September 2012, the authors estimate stock-day event-window DiD regressions of daily effective spread, realized spread, price impact, and log turnover on glitch and DMM indicators. The specification includes stock and day fixed effects and controls for log market capitalization, log price, log turnover, and volatility. This larger sample is used especially to test whether Knight’s DMM capital shock affected smaller assigned stocks not in the S&P 500.

Identification: The exogenous Knight glitch generates a capital shock to Knight, and pre-glitch DMM assignments determine exposure. The DiD/event-window regression compares assigned versus unassigned stocks before and after the glitch while controlling for stock fixed effects, day fixed effects, and observables. The identifying assumption is that, absent the Knight shock, these assigned stocks would not have had abnormal post-event spread or turnover changes relative to controls.

Setting: In the extended stock sample, the market-making-capital channel appears more clearly in spread data. Table 8 shows that for non-glitch DMM stocks, effective spread rises by 5.45 bps on the day after the glitch, while turnover falls by 0.08 log points on day 2. The authors interpret this as causal evidence that Knight’s capital shock reduced liquidity provision more strongly in less actively traded, non-S&P 500 DMM stocks than in large S&P 500 names.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis extending the market-making-capital evidence beyond the benchmark S&P 500 sample.
Settings.H440: Section 7.1 'Extended sample of designated market maker stocks,' Table 8 (PDF pp. 943-945).
Settings.G441:
Treatment: Binary stock-level indicator that a stock was glitch-affected, interacted with event days 0 through 5 and Aug. 9–31 in the extended NYSE/Amex sample.

Method: In the same extended-sample robustness design as Table 8, the authors estimate stock-day event-window DiD regressions for glitch-affected stocks on daily effective spread, realized spread, price impact, and log turnover. Stock and day fixed effects plus controls for size, price, turnover, and volatility are included.

Identification: Identification is the same exogenous-glitch DiD logic: compare liquidity metrics for glitch-affected stocks relative to unaffected stocks before and after Aug. 1, 2012, controlling for stock and day fixed effects and stock characteristics. The causal claim rests on the glitch being unrelated to stock fundamentals and thus generating exogenous inventory shocks.

Setting: In the extended stock sample, Table 8 confirms that glitch-affected stocks experienced a large day-0 liquidity shock and persistent abnormal trading. Effective spread rises by 8.33 bps on the glitch day, realized spread by 28.01 bps, price impact falls by 19.10 bps, and log turnover increases by 0.33 on day 0; turnover remains significantly elevated for several subsequent days. These results support the paper’s interpretation that the exogenous glitch created substantial supply-shock-driven dislocations in trading conditions.

Main role: This is a robustness extension of the paper’s main supply-shock findings, confirming them in a broader stock universe.
Settings.H441: Section 7.1 'Extended sample of designated market maker stocks,' Table 8 glitch rows (PDF pp. 943-945).
Settings.G442:
Treatment: State variable used to summarize business-cycle conditions in the second-step cyclicality regression of the estimated price of consumption risk. The authors run separate regressions using standardized detrended stock market wealth-to-aggregate consumption ratio (detrended sc), stock market wealth-to-aggregate consumption ratio (sc), default yield spread dfy, and labor income-to-aggregate consumption ratio yc; each is standardized to unit standard deviation. The substantive focal exposure is an increase in the state variable and how it shifts the estimated price of consumption risk implied by aggregate consumption.

Method: For the aggregate equity market portfolio, the authors first nonparametrically estimate the conditional covariance between 3-month market excess returns and 3-month consumption growth using local linear kernel regression (Epanechnikov kernel; bandwidth selected by bias-corrected AIC) after residualizing returns and consumption growth on conditioning information. They then estimate the conditional price of consumption risk by linear time-series regression of market excess returns on the pre-estimated conditional covariance interacted with conditioning variables, imposing a linear specification for the price of risk: Re_m,t+1 = alpha + (gamma0 + gamma1 z_t) Cov_t(Re_m,t+1,C_t+1/C_t) + error. They then assess the cyclicality of the estimated price of risk by separate OLS time-series regressions on each state variable (sc, detrended sc, dfy, yc). This is a regression-adjustment design, not a quasi-experiment; identification is model-based and depends on the conditional CCAPM structure and the adequacy of conditioning variables.

Identification: The identifying variation is time-series covariation between estimated conditional prices of risk and observed state variables. The authors assume the conditional CCAPM pricing equation is correctly specified for the chosen consumption measure, that the nonparametric first-step adequately captures the conditional covariance (amount of risk), and that the first three principal components of 162 macro-financial variables span investors' conditioning information sufficiently to avoid spurious conditional moments. Endogeneity is not resolved by an external shock; instead, the interpretation is structural/model-based: variation in business-cycle state variables is read as revealing whether the implied price of risk is pro- or countercyclical.

Setting: Using the CRSP value-weighted aggregate equity market, the authors estimate a conditional CCAPM in which expected excess returns equal the product of a time-varying price of risk and a nonparametrically estimated conditional covariance with consumption growth. They then regress the estimated price of risk on state variables. With NIPA aggregate consumption, a one-standard-deviation increase in detrended sc is associated with a 67.71 lower estimated price of risk (t = -7.38), while dfy is associated with a 40.65 higher price of risk (t = 2.39), implying countercyclical aggregate consumption risk pricing. With CEX asset holders' consumption, the signs reverse: detrended sc loads 4.45 (t = 2.93) and dfy loads -8.95 (t = -13.41), implying a procyclical price of asset holders' consumption risk. This setting is central to the paper's claim that asset holders' consumption produces puzzling procyclical risk prices.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize the paper's central finding that the price of asset holders' consumption risk is procyclical whereas aggregate consumption risk is countercyclical; the aggregate equity market evidence is one of the headline demonstrations of this puzzle.
Settings.H442: Section 4.1.1; Fig. 4; Table 2 row 'CRSP Equity Market', Panels A and B (PDF pp. 13-14).
Settings.G443:
Treatment: Business-cycle state variable in the cyclicality regression of estimated price of consumption risk, run separately for detrended sc, sc, dfy, and yc, each standardized to unit standard deviation. The exposure of interest is a continuous change in macro-financial state conditions.

Method: For multiple portfolios, the authors estimate conditional prices of risk using the nonparametric cross-sectional procedure of Roussanov (2014). They first nonparametrically estimate each asset's conditional covariance with 3-month consumption growth and conditional expected excess return as functions of the first three principal components of 162 macro-financial variables. At each date, they then estimate the price of consumption risk from a cross-sectional weighted least squares regression of conditional expected returns on conditional covariances across 25 size/book-to-market portfolios and across all 100 equity portfolios. They then regress the time series of estimated prices of risk on each standardized state variable separately. The design is model-based regression rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional and time-series variation in estimated conditional expected returns and conditional covariances across equity portfolios and over time, under the conditional CCAPM. The authors rely on nonparametric estimation to reduce misspecification of conditional moments and on broad conditioning information summarized by principal components. The causal interpretation is that changes in macro state variables move the equilibrium price of consumption risk; this is inferred from estimated risk-price dynamics, not from exogenous treatment variation.

Setting: Using Roussanov's cross-sectional nonparametric conditional pricing method, the authors estimate time-varying prices of consumption risk from 25 size/book-to-market equity portfolios and from 100 equity portfolios. For NIPA aggregate consumption, the price of risk is countercyclical: for FF25, detrended sc loads -40.58 (t = -4.71) and dfy loads 33.12 (t = 1.76); for all 100 equities, detrended sc loads -20.12 (t = -2.36). For CEX asset holders' consumption, the price of risk becomes procyclical: for FF25, detrended sc loads 4.09 (t = 2.29) and dfy loads -2.73 (t = -2.15); for all 100 equities, detrended sc loads 3.71 (t = 3.78) and dfy loads -2.91 (t = -3.97). These results extend the paper's central puzzle beyond the single market portfolio to the equity cross-section.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly say the procyclical price of asset holders' consumption risk appears in equity portfolios and across multiple asset classes, using alternative empirical methodologies. These equity portfolio tests are therefore part of the main evidence.
Settings.H443: Section 4.1.1; Table 2 rows 'Equity - FF25 portfolios' and 'Equity - 100 portfolios', Panels A and B (PDF p. 14).
Settings.G444:
Treatment: Standardized macro-financial state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, or yc) used one at a time in a time-series regression of the estimated price of consumption risk for each equity portfolio family.

Method: The authors repeat the nonparametric cross-sectional risk-price estimation separately within each equity portfolio family: 25 size/book-to-market, 25 size/investment, 25 size/operating profitability, and 25 size/long-term reversal portfolios. For each family, they estimate conditional expected returns and conditional covariances nonparametrically, recover the time-varying price of consumption risk from cross-sectional weighted least squares, and then regress the estimated price of risk on standardized state variables. This remains a model-based regression design.

Identification: The authors exploit time-varying cross-sectional relations between estimated conditional expected returns and estimated conditional consumption covariances within each portfolio family. The cyclicality results require the conditional CCAPM structure, sufficient conditioning information, and accurate nonparametric estimation of conditional moments. No external source of exogenous variation is used; the equilibrium interpretation is imposed by the asset-pricing framework.

Setting: Estimating conditional prices of consumption risk separately within equity portfolio families, the authors find that NIPA aggregate consumption generally delivers weakly countercyclical or insignificant prices of risk, while CEX asset holders' consumption delivers procyclical prices of risk for several families. For asset holders' consumption, detrended sc loads 4.09 for size/book-to-market portfolios (t = 2.29), 3.45 for size/investment (t = 2.72), and 3.37 for size/reversal (t = 3.91); dfy loads -2.73, -2.25, and -3.14 respectively. Size/operating-profitability portfolios are not significantly related to state variables. The authors interpret this as showing that the procyclical price of asset holders' consumption risk is broadly present within equity styles, not only in pooled equity tests.

Main role: The introduction and Section 4.1.2 stress that procyclical asset-holder risk prices are consistently observed for subsets of equity portfolios, supporting the generality of the paper's central finding within equities.
Settings.H444: Section 4.1.2; Table 3, Panels A and B (PDF pp. 15-16).
Settings.G445:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc), entered one at a time in time-series regressions explaining the estimated price of consumption risk for each non-equity asset class.

Method: The authors extend the same nonparametric cross-sectional conditional asset-pricing procedure to non-equity asset classes: bonds (10 corporate spread-sorted portfolios plus 8 Treasuries), commodities (5 basis-sorted portfolios), and currencies (6 forward-discount portfolios). For each class and each consumption measure, they estimate conditional expected returns and conditional covariances nonparametrically, recover the date-specific price of consumption risk from cross-sectional weighted least squares, and regress the resulting price of risk on standardized state variables. This is a structural regression test of conditional CCAPM implications.

Identification: Identification relies on the cross-section of conditional expected returns and conditional consumption covariances within each asset class and on the maintained conditional asset-pricing model. The cyclicality regressions interpret state variables as proxies for business-cycle conditions that shift equilibrium prices of risk. There is no quasi-experimental variation; assumptions center on correct measurement of consumption, sufficient investor information in the principal components, and robustness of the nonparametric first stage.

Setting: Applying the conditional CCAPM to non-equity assets, the authors find little systematic cyclicality in NIPA aggregate-consumption risk prices for bonds and commodities, but strong countercyclicality for currencies: for currencies, detrended sc loads -130.38 (t = -3.40) and yc loads 161.82 (t = 5.70). With CEX asset holders' consumption, bond and commodity risk prices are procyclical: for bonds, detrended sc loads 9.98 (t = 4.06) and dfy loads -8.10 (t = -2.66); for commodities, dfy loads -9.97 (t = -3.06). Currency risk prices remain less countercyclical than with aggregate consumption, with detrended sc -10.96 (t = -2.27). The authors interpret this as showing that the puzzling procyclical pricing of asset holders' consumption risk is not confined to stocks.

Main role: The abstract explicitly highlights that the procyclical price of asset holders' consumption risk is observed in multiple asset classes including bonds and commodities, making these tests part of the main contribution.
Settings.H445: Section 4.1.1; Fig. 5; Table 2 rows 'Bonds', 'Commodities', and 'Currencies', Panels A and B (PDF pp. 14-16).
Settings.G446:
Treatment: Standardized business-cycle state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, or yc), each used separately to explain the conditional covariance between market returns and consumption growth.

Method: To study the 'amount of risk' rather than the 'price of risk,' the authors nonparametrically estimate the conditional covariance between CRSP market excess returns and consumption growth and then regress that estimated conditional covariance on each standardized state variable separately. They do this for NIPA aggregate consumption and for CEX asset holders' consumption. The estimator is a linear time-series regression with a generated dependent variable produced by local linear kernel methods in the first step.

Identification: The authors infer the cyclicality of the amount of consumption risk from time-series associations between estimated conditional covariances and state variables. Identification is model-based: conditional covariances are assumed to summarize the relevant amount of risk in the CCAPM, and state variables proxy for economic conditions. The interpretation depends on accurate nonparametric estimation of the covariance process and on the state variables capturing the cycle rather than unrelated trends.

Setting: For the aggregate equity market, the authors examine whether business-cycle states shift the conditional covariance between returns and consumption growth. Using NIPA aggregate consumption, the estimated amount of risk appears weakly procyclical but statistically insignificant: detrended sc has coefficient 0.21 × 10^5 (t = 0.35), sc 0.23 × 10^5 (t = 0.47), and yc -0.46 × 10^5 (t = -0.63). Using CEX asset holders' consumption, the amount of risk appears countercyclical, with yc loading 15.85 × 10^5 (t = 4.26), though other state variables are insignificant. The authors conclude that the main puzzle is not procyclical quantities of asset-holder risk but the procyclical price assigned to that risk.

Main role: The paper argues that the puzzle lies in the procyclical price of risk rather than in the amount of risk. This section directly supports that central interpretation by comparing the cyclicality of amounts of risk across consumption measures.
Settings.G447:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc) used one at a time in time-series regressions for the conditional value premium and for the conditional covariance of value-minus-growth returns with consumption growth.

Method: To revisit the conditional value premium puzzle, the authors estimate conditional expected long-short value-minus-growth returns within small and large size groups nonparametrically, and separately estimate conditional covariances of those long-short returns with consumption growth. They then regress the conditional value premium and the conditional covariance on each standardized state variable separately. This is a regression-based conditional asset-pricing exercise using generated dependent variables.

Identification: The identifying variation is time-series movement in estimated conditional value premia and in their conditional consumption covariances across business-cycle states. The authors assume their nonparametric conditional moments are correctly estimated and that differences between aggregate and asset-holder consumption exposures are informative about the economic source of the value premium's cyclicality. No exogenous shock is used; the claim is structural within the CCAPM framework.

Setting: Revisiting Roussanov's conditional value premium puzzle, the authors find that the conditional value premium itself is weakly procyclical: for small stocks, detrended sc loads 19.23 × 10^4 (t = 1.34) and dfy loads -57.61 × 10^4 (t = -1.90); for large stocks the signs are similar but imprecise. With NIPA aggregate consumption, the covariance of value-minus-growth returns with consumption is countercyclical: for SV-SG, detrended sc is -0.13 × 10^4 (t = -2.51) and dfy is 0.16 × 10^4 (t = 2.72). With CEX asset holders' consumption, the covariance flips to procyclical: for LV-LG, detrended sc is 1.60 × 10^4 (t = 1.71), sc is 1.97 × 10^4 (t = 3.33), and yc is -1.52 × 10^4 (t = -3.67). The authors interpret this as asset holders' consumption resolving the conditional value premium puzzle because the amount of risk now moves in the same direction as the value premium.

Main role: The introduction frames explaining the conditional value premium puzzle as a major contribution. This section is therefore central, not merely ancillary.
Settings.G448:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc), used one at a time to explain the estimated price of consumption risk when consumption is measured as CEX aggregate consumption.

Method: As a substantive robustness analysis, the authors repeat the multi-asset-class conditional price-of-risk cyclicality regressions using CEX aggregate consumption instead of NIPA aggregate consumption or CEX asset holders' consumption. Estimation follows the same structure as the main analysis: nonparametric first-step conditional moments, cross-sectional risk-price estimation for multiple portfolios or linear market-level regression for the aggregate equity market, followed by OLS regressions of the estimated price of risk on standardized state variables.

Identification: Same model-based identification as in the main price-of-risk settings, but here the robustness question is whether changing the aggregate consumption data source changes the inferred cyclicality. The interpretation depends on the same conditional CCAPM assumptions and on CEX aggregate consumption being a comparable aggregate measure aside from sampling and measurement differences.

Setting: When the authors replace NIPA aggregate consumption with CEX aggregate consumption, the estimated prices of consumption risk remain countercyclical rather than becoming procyclical. For the CRSP aggregate equity market, detrended sc loads -109.72 (t = -3.10), sc -101.17 (t = -3.64), and dfy 218.78 (t = 14.33). Similar countercyclical patterns appear for several portfolio sets, including commodities where detrended sc is -28.46 (t = -3.70) and yc is 28.48 (t = 3.89). The authors interpret this as evidence that the procyclical asset-holder result is not an artifact of using CEX data per se.

Main role: The paper explicitly uses this exercise to rule out that the main result is driven by differences between CEX and NIPA data sources. Because it validates the central conclusion, it materially supports the main result.
Settings.G449:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc), entered separately in regressions explaining the estimated price of consumption risk using NielsenIQ aggregate or NielsenIQ asset-holder-proxy consumption measures.

Method: As an out-of-sample validation, the authors re-estimate the conditional prices of consumption risk using NielsenIQ Consumer Panel Dataset measures: aggregate consumption and an asset-holder proxy based on households living in counties whose dividend income to adjusted gross income is in the top 10% nationally. Estimation otherwise follows the main nonparametric conditional moment procedure and subsequent cyclicality regressions on standardized state variables.

Identification: Same model-based identification as in prior price-of-risk settings, with an additional maintained assumption that the geographic top-dividend-income-county proxy captures households likely to hold financial assets. The robustness interpretation depends on this proxy being informative about asset ownership and on NielsenIQ purchases providing a valid alternative consumption measure.

Setting: Using NielsenIQ consumer purchases, the authors again find countercyclical aggregate-consumption risk prices and procyclical asset-holder risk prices. For NielsenIQ aggregate consumption, the CRSP market price of risk loads -82.62 on detrended sc (t = -3.79), -95.51 on sc (t = -4.89), and 108.14 on dfy (t = 15.14). For NielsenIQ asset holders' consumption, the CRSP market price of risk loads 51.78 on detrended sc (t = 3.44), 34.78 on sc (t = 2.50), and -79.56 on yc (t = -10.83). Similar, though sometimes weaker because of the shorter 2004-2019 sample, procyclical patterns appear in FF25, bonds, and especially commodities. The authors treat this as out-of-sample confirmation of their main puzzle.

Main role: The abstract explicitly mentions robustness to high-frequency retail shopping data. This out-of-sample validation materially supports the paper's central conclusion that procyclical asset-holder risk prices are not specific to CEX measurement.
Settings.H449: Section 4.5.2; Table 7 Panels B and C (PDF pp. 20-21).
Settings.G450:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc), entered separately in regressions of the estimated price of consumption risk under the alternative GCV bandwidth choice.

Method: Robustness analysis re-estimating the main multi-asset price-of-risk cyclicality results using generalized cross-validation (GCV) rather than the bias-corrected Akaike Information Criterion to select the bandwidth in the local linear nonparametric first-step estimators. The remainder of the procedure is unchanged: conditional expected returns and covariances are estimated nonparametrically, prices of risk are recovered from market-level or cross-sectional regressions, and cyclicality is assessed by OLS regressions on each standardized state variable.

Identification: Same as the main price-of-risk specifications; the robustness concern is nonparametric smoothing choice rather than core endogeneity. The causal interpretation remains structural and model-based.

Setting: Under generalized cross-validation bandwidth selection, the cyclicality results are nearly unchanged. Aggregate consumption still implies countercyclical prices of risk, while CEX asset holders' consumption still implies procyclical prices of risk for aggregate equity, multiple equities, bonds, commodities, and less countercyclical currencies. For example, the CRSP market coefficients are identical to the baseline to reported precision: with NIPA, detrended sc is -67.71 (t = -7.38); with CEX asset holders, detrended sc is 4.45 (t = 2.93). The authors interpret this as evidence that their main conclusions are not driven by the automatic bandwidth-selection procedure.

Main role: This is a methodological robustness check showing that the main cyclicality findings do not depend on one bandwidth-selection rule.
Settings.G451:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc), one at a time, in regressions of the estimated price of consumption risk under the alternative ex-post covariance specification.

Method: Robustness analysis altering the construction of ex-post covariances by omitting the first three principal components of the 162 state variables when computing residuals of consumption growth and asset returns before forming realized covariance products. The subsequent steps—nonparametric estimation of conditional covariances, market-level or cross-sectional estimation of prices of risk, and cyclicality regressions on state variables—remain the same.

Identification: The maintained identification is unchanged, but this robustness probes possible misspecification in the covariance-construction step. The interpretation still rests on the conditional CCAPM and the adequacy of conditioning information later in the process.

Setting: When ex-post covariances are constructed without first residualizing returns and consumption on the principal components, the main qualitative finding survives. NIPA aggregate-consumption prices of risk remain generally countercyclical for the aggregate equity market, FF25 portfolios, and currencies; CEX asset-holder prices remain strongly procyclical for the aggregate market, FF25, 100 equity portfolios, bonds, and commodities. For example, under this alternative, CEX asset-holder prices load 7.89 on detrended sc for FF25 (t = 4.37), 7.89 for 100 equities (t = 6.38), and 11.25 for bonds (t = 4.36), while dfy coefficients are strongly negative. The authors conclude that omission of the conditioning PCs in the residualization step does not overturn their puzzle.

Main role: This is a robustness exercise addressing sensitivity to how ex-post covariances are formed, not a separate core empirical contribution.
Settings.G452:
Treatment: Standardized state variable (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc), entered separately in regressions of the estimated price of consumption risk under the nonnegative-expected-return restriction.

Method: Robustness analysis imposing a theoretically consistent sign on conditional expected excess returns by setting estimated conditional expected returns to zero whenever they are negative, following Campbell and Thompson (2008). The authors then re-estimate prices of risk from multiple asset classes using the constrained conditional expected returns and regress the resulting price of risk series on standardized state variables. The aggregate market specification is omitted because it does not rely on pre-estimated conditional expected returns.

Identification: The design remains a conditional asset-pricing regression framework. This robustness changes the support of the estimated conditional expected returns to better match theory but does not introduce exogenous variation. The interpretation still depends on the maintained model structure.

Setting: After forcing conditional expected excess returns to be nonnegative, the paper's main cyclicality findings persist. Aggregate consumption generally continues to imply countercyclical prices of risk—for example FF25 detrended sc = -34.40 (t = -4.52)—while CEX asset holders' consumption still yields procyclical prices for several asset classes, including 100 equities (detrended sc = 2.47, t = 2.85) and bonds (detrended sc = 9.41, t = 4.04; dfy = -6.89, t = -2.48). The authors interpret this as showing that negative fitted risk premia are not driving the procyclical asset-holder result.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness test that addresses a potential theoretical inconsistency in the estimated conditional expected returns.
Settings.G453:
Treatment: Two related continuous treatments are discussed in this subsection: (i) standardized consumption growth (NIPA aggregate or CEX asset holders') in regressions explaining UMVE portfolio returns, and (ii) standardized state variables (detrended sc, sc, dfy, yc) in regressions explaining the estimated price of currency risk implied by the UMVE portfolio. The substantive causal interpretation concerns how consumption and macro states relate to the priced component of currency returns.

Method: To understand the currency exception, the authors analyze the unconditional mean-variance efficient (UMVE) currency portfolio from Chernov et al. (2022). They regress UMVE portfolio returns on standardized NIPA aggregate or CEX asset holders' consumption growth to assess how consumption relates to the priced component of currency returns, and they estimate the price of currency risk implied by the UMVE portfolio and study its cyclicality using the same type of time-series regressions on state variables. This is not the main CCAPM estimator but a supporting regression-based analysis.

Identification: The authors use auxiliary regressions to relate currency-pricing components to consumption and state variables. Identification is purely observational and interpretive: if aggregate consumption is more tightly linked to the priced component of currency returns than asset-holder consumption, that may explain why currency results differ from other asset classes.

Setting: To rationalize why currency portfolios do not show the same procyclical asset-holder pattern as stocks, bonds, and commodities, the authors show in the online appendix that a one-standard-deviation increase in NIPA aggregate consumption growth raises UMVE currency-portfolio returns by about 0.9 percentage points, whereas the corresponding loading for CEX asset holders' consumption is about 0.3 percentage points and statistically insignificant. They further report that the price of currency risk implied by the UMVE portfolio is countercyclical. The paper interprets this as evidence that aggregate consumption is more closely tied to the priced component of currency returns than household asset-holder consumption, helping explain the currency exception.

Main role: This subsection is an interpretation of the currency-market exception rather than part of the paper's central estimation strategy.
Settings.H453: Section 4.6; Online Appendix Table OA.3 and Table OA.4 referenced in text (PDF p. 24).
Settings.G454:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country, implemented as Post × Treat where Treat identifies firms in countries that ever adopt a takeover law during the sample and Post indicates years after that country’s law passage. The substantive causal effect of interest is the increase in takeover threat induced by the law; the reported key parameter is its interaction with continuous lagged firm performance.

Method: The paper’s headline CEO-turnover tests implement probit difference-in-differences models around staggered country-level adoption of takeover laws. The treatment group is firms in 12 countries that first pass takeover laws during 1992–2003; controls are firms in countries that never adopt such laws during the sample period plus pre-law observations from treated countries. The estimating equation includes country fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects, with firm-clustered standard errors. The key estimand is the triple interaction Post × Treat × firm performance in a nonlinear probit, and the authors also report Ai-Norton-corrected interaction effects to interpret the change in the sensitivity of CEO turnover to poor performance. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear probit rather than a linear DiD, it is classified as Other, though the underlying design is conventional DiD.

Identification: Identification comes from staggered cross-country passage of takeover laws, which the authors argue exogenously raise the threat of takeover relative to firm-level governance choices. The DiD logic compares changes in CEO-turnover-performance sensitivity after law adoption in treated countries to contemporaneous changes in untreated countries and pre-law treated observations, while country, year, and industry fixed effects absorb time-invariant country differences and common shocks. The key assumption is that absent takeover laws, treated and control countries would have followed parallel trends in turnover-performance sensitivity; the authors point to pre-trend evidence and additional country-level controls to address concerns that other contemporaneous legal, governance, or macro changes drive results.

Setting: Using a staggered-adoption DiD implemented via probit, the paper finds that takeover-law enactment increases disciplinary CEO turnover by making turnover more sensitive to poor firm performance. In the full sample, the Post × Treat × firm performance coefficient is -0.851 (z=-2.89), with an Ai-Norton mean interaction effect of -0.119 (z=-2.73). The paper interprets this as evidence that laws increasing takeover threat causally strengthen managerial discipline. This is a main result and the central empirical link between takeover threats and governance.

Main role: This is the paper’s central causal test: whether takeover laws increase managerial discipline by raising the sensitivity of CEO turnover to poor performance. It is emphasized in the abstract, introduction, main results, and conclusion.
Settings.G455:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in a treated country (Post × Treat), with the substantive effect captured by the interaction of this law exposure with continuous lagged firm performance. Estimation is done separately for civil-law and common-law country subsamples as proxies for weak versus strong investor protection.

Method: This setting uses the same probit DiD design as the main CEO-turnover specification but estimated separately by legal-origin subsamples to study heterogeneity by investor protection. The sample is split into civil-law versus common-law countries. Country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects are included; standard errors are clustered by firm; and the nonlinear interaction is interpreted using Ai-Norton corrected interaction effects. Because the implemented model is probit, the method is classified as Other rather than linear conventional DiD.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same staggered takeover-law adoption as in the main design, now evaluated within legal-origin subsamples to test whether the effect is concentrated where alternative governance mechanisms are weaker. The paper argues that if takeover threats substitute for internal governance, effects should be larger in civil-law countries. Causal interpretation still relies on parallel trends within subsamples and on the exogeneity of law timing to firm-level CEO-turnover shocks.

Setting: In subsample probit DiD tests, takeover laws increase the sensitivity of CEO turnover to poor performance in weak-investor-protection countries but not in strong-protection countries. In civil-law countries, the corrected triple-interaction effect is -0.269 (z=-4.03), while in common-law countries it is 0.075 and insignificant; the difference across subsamples is significant at p<0.01. The paper interprets this as evidence that takeover threats discipline managers primarily where internal governance is weaker.

Main role: Heterogeneity by investor protection is a central substantive conclusion: the disciplinary effect of takeover laws is strongest in weak-investor-protection countries.
Settings.G456:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with the main causal parameter being the interaction of that law exposure with continuous lagged firm performance. The sample is split into low-ASDI versus high-ASDI countries using the sample median.

Method: This setting again uses probit difference-in-differences around staggered takeover-law adoption, but the sample is split by the anti-self-dealing index (ASDI) to examine heterogeneous treatment effects by investor protection. The specification includes country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors; the key nonlinear interaction is summarized with Ai-Norton corrected effects. Because the estimator is probit, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification relies on staggered passage of takeover laws, with heterogeneity tested across low- versus high-ASDI environments. The authors’ causal argument is that where minority-shareholder protections are weaker, takeover laws represent a larger governance shock. The assumption remains that absent the laws, turnover-performance sensitivity would have evolved similarly within each protection group, conditional on fixed effects and controls.

Setting: Using the same probit DiD design split by anti-self-dealing protections, the paper finds that takeover laws raise disciplinary CEO turnover only in weak-protection countries. The corrected triple-interaction term is -0.182 (z=-2.32) in low-ASDI countries and -0.054 (z=-1.05) in high-ASDI countries, implying that the governance effect of takeover laws is concentrated where investor protection is weak. This materially supports the paper’s substitution-of-governance interpretation.

Main role: This is another main heterogeneity analysis supporting the paper’s core claim that takeover threats matter most where investor protection is weak.
Settings.G457:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with causal interpretation centered on the Post × Treat × continuous lagged firm performance term after controlling for other regulatory and macro changes.

Method: This robustness setting augments the main probit DiD CEO-turnover regressions with a broad set of potentially confounding country-level changes: labor-union regulation, corporate-governance-code adoption, stock-price informativeness, short-selling restrictions, insider-trading-law enforcement, financial reforms, and GDP growth, plus interactions of these variables with firm performance where applicable. Regressions retain country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear probit, classification is Other.

Identification: The same staggered-law DiD variation identifies the effect, but now the authors explicitly address a threat to identification: takeover-law passage could coincide with other legal or economic reforms that independently alter CEO-turnover sensitivity. By controlling for these channels and their interactions with firm performance, the paper argues that the remaining takeover-law interaction more plausibly isolates the causal effect of heightened takeover threats.

Setting: After controlling for a wide set of country-level regulatory and macro confounders, the probit DiD results remain consistent with takeover laws causing more disciplinary CEO turnover in weak-investor-protection countries. In the full sample the mean interaction effect is -0.139 (z=-2.232), in civil-law countries it is -0.316 (z=-3.371), and in high-protection/common-law groups it is insignificant. The paper treats this as evidence that the main result is not driven by contemporaneous reforms or aggregate economic changes.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis meant to defend the main causal claim against omitted contemporaneous country-level reforms and macro shocks.
Settings.G458:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), interacted with continuous lagged firm performance; additional controls include the annual change in foreign institutional ownership and its interaction with performance.

Method: This robustness analysis re-estimates the probit DiD CEO-turnover specification after adding the annual change in foreign institutional investor (FII) ownership from Thomson Reuters Global Share Ownership. The regressions are run separately for civil-law and common-law samples, include country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects, and retain the nonlinear treatment-performance interaction interpreted via mean interaction effects. Since the implemented estimator is probit, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: The core identification remains the law-adoption DiD. The specific concern addressed is that takeover laws may coincide with increased foreign institutional ownership, which itself could improve monitoring and CEO discipline. Conditioning on changes in FII holdings and their interaction with performance is intended to show that the takeover-law effect is not merely proxying for this alternative governance channel.

Setting: When directly controlling for changes in foreign institutional ownership, the paper still finds that takeover laws increase the sensitivity of CEO turnover to poor performance in civil-law countries. The corrected mean interaction effect remains -0.269 (z=-3.204) in civil-law countries and is 0.102 (insignificant) in common-law countries. The authors conclude that their main result is not explained solely by changing foreign institutional ownership around law passage.

Main role: This is a robustness test against an alternative mechanism—changes in foreign institutional ownership rather than takeover threats per se.
Settings.H458: Section 4.1, Table 4 Panel A cols. (1)–(2), PDF pp. 18–19.
Settings.G459:
