Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with the key causal parameter being the interaction of law exposure with continuous 1-year-lagged excess stock returns rather than accounting performance.

Method: This robustness setting re-runs the probit DiD CEO-turnover analysis using lagged excess stock returns, measured relative to the local market index, instead of the accounting earnings ratio as the firm-performance variable. The estimations are reported separately for civil-law and common-law samples with country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Because the implemented model is probit with interaction effects, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification still comes from staggered takeover-law adoption. The change here is measurement of the moderator that captures poor performance. By showing similar law effects when performance is measured with market-based excess returns, the authors argue the causal claim is not an artifact of the accounting-based performance metric.

Setting: Using excess stock returns as the performance measure, the paper finds that takeover laws still increase disciplinary CEO turnover in weak-investor-protection countries. In civil-law countries, the mean interaction effect is -0.047 (z=-2.473), while in common-law countries it is -0.023 and insignificant. This supports the robustness of the main claim to an alternative performance definition.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis checking whether the main causal inference depends on using accounting-based performance rather than market-based performance.
Settings.H459: Section 4.2, Table 4 Panel A cols. (3)–(4), PDF pp. 18–20.
Settings.G460:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with the causal effect captured by its interaction with continuous industry-adjusted lagged firm performance.

Method: This robustness setting estimates the probit DiD CEO-turnover specification using relative industry performance—firm performance minus the median for the corresponding global 2-digit SIC industry—as the performance measure. Regressions are reported separately for civil-law and common-law samples with country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Since the estimator is nonlinear probit, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: The identifying shock is unchanged: staggered law adoption. The robustness check addresses whether boards evaluate CEOs on relative industry performance rather than absolute performance, and whether the estimated governance effect of takeover laws survives that alternative benchmark.

Setting: Replacing absolute accounting performance with industry-adjusted performance leaves the main pattern intact: takeover laws increase CEO-turnover sensitivity to poor performance in weak-investor-protection countries. In civil-law countries, the mean interaction effect is -0.257 (z=-4.029), while in common-law countries it is 0.074 and insignificant. The paper interprets this as further support for a causal governance effect of takeover threats.

Main role: This is a performance-measure robustness test tied to the paper’s main CEO-discipline result.
Settings.H460: Section 4.3, Table 4 Panel A cols. (5)–(6), PDF pp. 18–20.
Settings.G461:
Treatment: Exposure to first-time antitrust-law adoption in the firm’s country, implemented analogously to takeover laws via Post × Treat, with the main parameter of interest interacting this exposure with continuous lagged firm performance. The law is interpreted as an alternative shock raising takeover activity/threat.

Method: As an alternative source of variation in takeover threat, the paper estimates probit DiD models replacing takeover-law adoption with first-time adoption of antitrust laws, using nine adopting countries and fifteen never-adopting countries. The regressions are reported separately for civil-law and common-law countries and include country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects with firm-clustered standard errors. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear probit, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification now uses staggered adoption of antitrust laws, which prior literature argues promotes M&A by reducing information asymmetries and creating a level playing field. The paper’s argument is that if its mechanism is truly takeover threat rather than features unique to takeover statutes, a similar increase in CEO discipline should appear after antitrust reforms, especially where investor protection is weak.

Setting: Using antitrust-law adoption as an alternative proxy for an exogenous rise in takeover threat, the paper again finds stronger disciplinary CEO turnover in weak-investor-protection countries. In civil-law countries the mean interaction effect is -0.068 (z=-1.974), while in common-law countries it is -0.112 and insignificant. The authors read this as corroborating evidence that takeover threats, not just a particular legal reform, increase managerial discipline.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness/alternative-treatment analysis supporting the claim that exogenous increases in takeover threat discipline CEOs.
Settings.H461: Section 4.4, Table 4 Panel B cols. (1)–(2), PDF pp. 19–20.
Settings.G462:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with the key parameter being the interaction of law exposure with continuous lagged firm performance; inference is altered by clustering at the country level.

Method: This robustness analysis re-estimates the main probit DiD CEO-turnover specification but clusters standard errors by country instead of by firm. The underlying sample splits by civil-law versus common-law countries and retains country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects. Because the model is still probit with nonlinear interaction interpretation, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: The causal variation remains staggered law adoption. This setting specifically addresses whether inference may be overstated because treatment varies at the country-year level; clustering by country makes significance robust to within-country dependence in shocks.

Setting: When the main CEO-turnover probit DiD is re-estimated with country-clustered standard errors, the conclusion remains: takeover laws raise the turnover sensitivity to poor performance in weak-investor-protection countries. The civil-law mean interaction effect is -0.269 (z=-4.039), while the common-law effect is 0.075 and insignificant. This supports the robustness of the paper’s causal inference to alternative error clustering.

Main role: This is an inferential robustness test to show the main finding does not depend on firm-level clustering.
Settings.H462: Section 4.5, Table 4 Panel B cols. (3)–(4), PDF pp. 20–21.
Settings.G463:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment within the subset of 12 adopting countries only, implemented as post-law years relative to pre-law years in the same countries; the main causal term is the interaction of this exposure with continuous lagged firm performance.

Method: This robustness setting limits the CEO-turnover probit DiD analysis to the 12 countries that actually adopt takeover laws during the sample, using firms from the same countries in the pre-law period as controls. Regressions are reported separately for civil-law and common-law countries, with country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Because the estimator is probit, classification is Other.

Identification: Identification relies on within-adopting-country before-versus-after comparisons rather than including never-adopting countries. This addresses concerns that cross-country differences between adopters and nonadopters drive the results. The assumption is that, absent the law, the turnover-performance relationship would have remained stable within adopting countries up to year effects and controls.

Setting: Restricting the sample to the 12 takeover-law adopters, the paper still finds that takeover laws increase disciplinary CEO turnover in weak-investor-protection countries. The mean interaction effect is -0.283 (z=-4.206) in civil-law countries and 0.066 (insignificant) in common-law countries. The authors interpret this as evidence that the main finding is not driven by the choice of external control countries.

Main role: This is a sample-selection robustness test for the main CEO-discipline result.
Settings.H463: Section 4.5, Table 4 Panel B cols. (5)–(6), PDF pp. 20–21.
Settings.G464:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with the key causal effect captured by its interaction with continuous lagged firm performance; the substantive treatment is the increase in takeover threat generated by the law.

Method: The paper estimates probit difference-in-differences models for acquisition likelihood around takeover-law adoption. The dependent variable is an indicator for whether the firm is acquired, and the key regressor is Post × Treat × firm performance, interpreted through Ai-Norton-style corrected interaction effects. The regressions include country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects, firm-clustered standard errors, and a standard set of M&A determinants from Ferreira et al. (2010), including exchange-rate change, market return, size, R&D intensity, foreign sales, leverage, insider ownership, cross-listing, global industry Q, GDP per capita, and domestic credit/GDP. Because the implemented estimator is probit, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification again exploits staggered country-level adoption of takeover laws. The mechanism claim is that if the laws intensify disciplinary takeover threat, then poorly performing firms should become more likely takeover targets after adoption relative to better performers and relative to control observations. Fixed effects and M&A covariates absorb general differences across countries, years, industries, and firm characteristics; the interpretation still relies on DiD-style parallel-trends reasoning.

Setting: In probit DiD tests of acquisition likelihood, the paper finds that takeover laws increase the probability that poorly performing firms are targeted. For all acquisitions in the full sample, the corrected Post × Treat × firm performance interaction effect is -0.120 (z=-3.021). The authors interpret this as direct evidence that takeover laws raise disciplinary takeover threats, which underpins the observed increase in CEO-turnover discipline.

Main role: This is a core mechanism test showing that takeover laws actually increase the takeover threat faced by poorly performing firms, supporting the main CEO-discipline interpretation.
Settings.G465:
Treatment: Exposure to takeover-law enactment in the firm’s country (Post × Treat), with the main parameter being the interaction of this exposure with continuous lagged firm performance; the effect is interpreted as a change in cross-border takeover threat.

Method: This setting is the cross-border-acquisition counterpart to the prior acquisition-likelihood tests, estimated as probit DiD around takeover-law adoption. The dependent variable is an indicator for being acquired by a foreign acquirer. The model includes country, year, and 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects, firm-clustered standard errors, and the same M&A determinants used in the all-acquisitions specification. Because the estimator is nonlinear probit with corrected interaction effects, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The design uses staggered takeover-law adoption to capture changes in cross-border takeover threat. The authors argue that if these laws reduce barriers and improve disclosure/shareholder protection, foreign acquirers should become more likely to target poorly performing firms after adoption. Identification rests on the same exogeneity and parallel-trends logic as the main DiD-style setup.

Setting: For cross-border acquisitions, the paper finds that takeover laws increase the likelihood that poorly performing firms are targeted by foreign acquirers. The corrected triple-interaction effect is -0.032 (z=-1.71) in the full sample, with stronger evidence in civil-law countries than in common-law countries. This supports the mechanism that takeover laws intensify the threat of control contests, including from foreign bidders.

Main role: This is part of the paper’s mechanism evidence, showing that the increase in takeover threat also operates through cross-border acquisitions.
Settings.G466:
Treatment: Exposure of a director to a control contest targeting the director’s firm, measured by binary event indicators T0 (year of deal), T1, T2, and T3 (1, 2, and 3 years after the M&A deal). The focal estimand is the combined effect of these event indicators on director replacement probability.

Method: The paper estimates director-firm-year probit regressions relating takeover events to the probability that a board member is replaced. The treatment is a series of event-time indicators T0, T1, T2, T3 for the deal year through three years after a completed M&A involving the director’s firm. Specifications include firm performance, firm size, director characteristics (chair status, age, directorial experience, CEO experience, gender, awards, committee chairs), plus country, year, and industry fixed effects, with firm-clustered standard errors. The authors report results for the full BoardEx country sample and for civil-law/common-law subsamples. Because this is a nonlinear event-study-style probit rather than linear DiD/FE, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification is based on within-sample variation in whether and when a director’s firm is targeted in an M&A deal. The paper’s mechanism argument is not that takeovers are randomly assigned, but that conditional on firm performance, size, director characteristics, and fixed effects, greater post-targeting director turnover reflects labor-market discipline imposed by control contests. The staggered event-time indicators allow the paper to trace replacement over several years because staggered boards may delay turnover.

Setting: Using BoardEx data and event-time probit models, the paper shows that directors of targeted firms are more likely to lose their board seats after a takeover. In the full sample, coefficients on T0, T1, and T2 are positive and significant, and the summed average marginal effect over T0–T3 is 0.071. The paper interprets this as evidence that directors suffer direct labor-market penalties when their firms are taken over, supporting the board-incentives mechanism behind stronger CEO discipline.

Main role: This is a central mechanism test: if directors face penalties when their firms are taken over, boards have stronger incentives to discipline poorly performing CEOs.
Settings.H466: Section 5.2.1, Table 6 Panel A cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 24–26.
Settings.G467:
Treatment: Director exposure to a completed M&A targeting the director’s firm, measured by binary event indicators T0, T1, T2, and T3 for the deal year and the following three years, estimated on a matched sample of target and control firms.

Method: For robustness, the paper matches target firms to non-target firms using nearest-neighbor matching with the Mahalanobis metric based on firm performance and size in the year before acquisition, plus country and 1-digit SIC industry membership. It then re-estimates director-turnover probit models on the matched sample using the same event-time takeover indicators T0–T3, controls for firm performance and size and director characteristics, country/year/industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. Matching determines the comparison group and is therefore the primary identifying method.

Identification: The matching strategy attempts to construct a more comparable control group by balancing target and non-target firms on observable pre-acquisition performance, size, country, and industry. Conditional on this matched design and regression controls, higher director turnover after takeover is interpreted as the causal effect of control contests on directors’ job loss, though unobserved differences may still remain.

Setting: In matched-sample probit regressions, directors of targeted firms remain significantly more likely to be replaced than comparable directors at non-target firms. The summed average marginal effect over T0–T3 is 0.085 in the full matched sample, with larger effects in civil-law countries (0.096) than common-law countries (0.032). This robustness result reinforces the paper’s mechanism that takeover exposure disciplines directors as well as CEOs.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis designed to show that the director-turnover mechanism is not driven by target firms differing from non-target firms on observable characteristics.
Settings.H467: Section 5.2.1, Table 6 Panel A cols. (4)–(6), PDF pp. 24–27.
Settings.G468:
Treatment: Exposure of a director to an M&A targeting one of the director’s firms, measured by binary event indicators T0, T1, T2, and T3 for the acquisition year and the subsequent three years.

Method: The paper estimates OLS event-time regressions at the director-year level to examine whether directors of targeted firms lose seats at other firms after an M&A event. The treatment is a set of binary indicators T0–T3 for the deal year through three years after the takeover. Controls include the average firm performance, average firm size, and average chair status across the firms employing the director, plus director characteristics, country and year fixed effects, and clustered standard errors by firm. This is a regression-adjustment design without a stronger quasi-experimental method, so it is classified as OLS / WLS / Regression Adjustment.

Identification: The paper compares directors before and after their firms are targeted, controlling for observable director and firm characteristics and fixed effects. The intended causal interpretation is that takeovers reduce future outside board opportunities for target directors. However, assignment to takeover is not random, so this evidence is suggestive regression adjustment rather than a more credible quasi-experiment.

Setting: OLS event-time regressions show that directors of targeted firms hold fewer outside board seats in the years after a takeover. In the full sample, coefficients on T1, T2, and T3 are negative and significant, and the summed effect over T0–T3 is -0.528 seats within three years. The paper interprets this as evidence that directors incur broader labor-market penalties after control contests, strengthening their incentives to monitor CEOs ex ante.

Main role: This is a key mechanism result showing reputational/labor-market penalties for directors beyond the immediate target firm, which supports the board-monitoring channel.
Settings.H468: Section 5.2.2, Table 6 Panel B cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 26–28.
Settings.G469:
Treatment: Director exposure to a completed M&A targeting one of the director’s firms, measured by event indicators T0, T1, T2, and T3, estimated on the matched sample of target and control firms.

Method: As a robustness check for outside-board-seat losses, the paper first constructs a matched sample of target and control firms using nearest-neighbor Mahalanobis matching on pre-acquisition firm performance and size, country, and 1-digit SIC industry, then estimates OLS event-time regressions of directors’ outside seats on takeover-event indicators T0–T3 and controls. Because the matched sample defines the comparison and is central to the design, the method is classified as Matching / Weighting.

Identification: Matching is used to reduce observable differences between target and control firms before estimating the effect of takeover exposure on directors’ outside board seats. The causal claim is that, among observably similar firms, directors of targets lose more outside seats after an acquisition. As with other matching designs, identification rests on selection on observables plus the regression controls.

Setting: In the matched-sample outside-directorship regressions, the negative labor-market effect of being targeted remains. Directors lose 0.556 seats on average in the three years after an M&A event, and the effect is larger in civil-law countries (-0.808) than in common-law countries (positive and insignificant). This robustness check supports the paper’s claim that control contests impose meaningful career costs on directors.

Main role: This is a robustness version of the director labor-market mechanism using a more comparable matched control group.
Settings.H469: Section 5.2.2, Table 6 Panel B cols. (4)–(6), PDF pp. 26–28.
Settings.G470:
Treatment: Fund characteristics interpreted as causal drivers of CDS use, especially flow volatility (standard deviation of estimated monthly fund flows over the prior 24 months), return volatility, portfolio turnover, log fund size, and fund maturity style (long-term or intermediate-term fixed-income funds versus short-term funds). Treatments are continuous except the style dummies.

Method: Fund-quarter-level logit regressions for whether a fund uses CDS, with separate binary outcomes for any CDS sell and any CDS buy, plus a multinomial logit distinguishing buy-only, both buy-and-sell, and sell-only relative to no CDS use. Regressors are lagged fund characteristics: flow volatility, return volatility, portfolio turnover, log fund size, log fund age, performance rank, and maturity-style dummies (long-term and intermediate-term; short-term omitted). The sample includes all mutual funds in Lipper categories where CDS use is feasible, not only actual CDS users. Regressions include quarter and Lipper-category fixed effects; standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust and clustered at the fund level. The paper interprets coefficients as the effect of funding-liquidity-related characteristics on the propensity to use CDS, while acknowledging this is observational and not a clean quasi-experiment.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional and time-series variation in fund characteristics, especially proxies for liquidity needs, conditional on quarter and Lipper style effects. The endogeneity concern is that unobserved manager sophistication, strategy, or omitted fund traits may jointly affect both liquidity proxies and CDS use. The paper argues that flow volatility and portfolio maturity capture ex ante liquidity-management needs, but the estimates remain associative regression-adjusted evidence rather than design-based causal estimates.

Setting: Using fund-quarter logit and multinomial logit regressions, the paper argues that greater liquidity-management needs cause more CDS use by mutual funds. A one-standard-deviation increase in flow volatility is described as raising the odds of CDS selling or buying by about 32% to 40%, and long-term or intermediate-term bond funds are more likely to use CDS than short-term funds. Larger and higher-turnover funds are also more likely to use CDS. These regressions provide central evidence for the paper’s claim that CDS help funds manage liquidity frictions.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that funds invest in CDS when facing unpredictable liquidity needs; Table III Panel A is a core empirical test of that central claim.
Settings.H470: Section II.A, Table III Panel A, columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 556–558 (article pp. 554–558).
Settings.G471:
Treatment: Fund characteristics interpreted as affecting CDS intensity: flow volatility, return volatility, portfolio turnover, log fund size, log fund age, performance rank, duration-style dummies, and in some specifications cash holdings (% of TNA). Main treatment emphasis is again on flow volatility and cash as liquidity-management proxies.

Method: Fund-quarter-level tobit regressions for the intensity of CDS usage, estimated separately for gross sell intensity and gross buy intensity. The dependent variable is the total notional amount of CDS selling or buying scaled by fund total net assets, censored at zero because most funds hold no CDS in a given quarter. Regressors are lagged fund characteristics analogous to the logit specification, with some columns additionally including cash holdings as a percentage of TNA. Quarter and Lipper-category fixed effects are included; standard errors are clustered at the fund level. The paper treats these as causal evidence that liquidity needs and lower cash buffers increase CDS intensity.

Identification: Identification relies on regression-adjusted variation across funds and over time in measured liquidity needs and cash holdings. The main concern is simultaneity and omitted variables: cash and CDS can be jointly chosen, and sophisticated managers may differ on unobservables. The paper interprets negative cash coefficients as substitution between cash and CDS, but it does not offer an external instrument or quasi-experimental source of variation.

Setting: In fund-quarter tobit regressions, the paper argues that higher funding-flow volatility increases how intensively mutual funds use CDS, while cash buffers substitute for CDS. A one-standard-deviation increase in flow volatility is associated with a 1.63 percentage point increase in CDS selling intensity and a 1.69 percentage point increase in CDS buying intensity, both relative to fund TNA. When cash is included, a 1-percentage-point decrease in cash holdings is associated with a 6 to 7 basis point increase in both CDS selling and buying. These results support the claim that funds use CDS as a liquidity-management tool.

Main role: These intensity regressions are part of the paper’s central liquidity-management results, complementing the propensity regressions and highlighted in the text and abstract.
Settings.H471: Section II.A, Table III Panel B, columns (1)–(4), PDF pp. 555, 558–559 (article pp. 555, 558–559).
Settings.G472:
Treatment: Reference-entity and contract characteristics interpreted as treatments affecting fund use of CDS: % bond days traded (bond liquidity), number of CDS contracts (CDS trading capacity/liquidity), log reference-entity assets, CDS spread (bps), and CDS-bond basis (bps). Main focus is the relative liquidity and pricing of CDS versus bonds for a given issuer.

Method: Fund-reference entity-quarter-level logit regressions for whether a fund holds CDS on a given reference entity, separately for any sell and any buy, plus a multinomial logit breaking out buy-no-sell, both buy-and-sell, and sell-no-buy relative to no position. Key regressors are lagged reference-entity characteristics: percentage of bond trading days, number of CDS contracts quoted by Markit, log firm assets, CDS spread, and CDS-bond basis, alongside lagged fund controls from Table III. Regressions include quarter and Lipper-category fixed effects; standard errors are clustered at the fund level. The paper interprets these coefficients as causal evidence on how relative liquidity and yield opportunities affect funds’ decisions to use CDS on particular issuers.

Identification: Identification comes from within-sample variation in issuer-level CDS and bond liquidity and pricing, controlling for observed fund characteristics, time, and fund style. The concern is selection into issuers and omitted issuer attributes correlated with both liquidity and investor demand. The paper argues that the measured contract availability, bond trading days, spread level, and basis capture the trading environment that shapes whether funds use CDS rather than bonds.

Setting: At the fund-reference entity-quarter level, the paper argues that mutual funds’ decision to use CDS on a given issuer is shaped by issuer-specific liquidity and pricing. More CDS contract availability increases both selling and buying, but much more strongly for selling; a one-standard-deviation increase in the number of CDS contracts is said to more than double the likelihood of CDS selling and raise the likelihood of CDS buying by about 27%. Funds are also more likely to sell CDS when bond liquidity is higher and when CDS spreads and CDS-bond basis are higher, while they are more likely to buy CDS when spreads and basis are lower. These results support the paper’s central claim about liquidity substitution and yield-seeking between bonds and CDS.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion stress that funds sell more when CDS is liquid relative to bonds and buy more when basis is more negative; Table IV Panel A is a central test of that claim.
Settings.H472: Section II.B, Table IV Panel A, columns (1)–(7), PDF pp. 563–567 (article pp. 563–567).
Settings.G473:
Treatment: Reference-entity and contract characteristics affecting CDS intensity: % bond days traded, number of CDS contracts, log firm assets, CDS spread, and CDS-bond basis. The main treatment highlighted in the text is the CDS-bond basis as a continuous pricing wedge in basis points.

Method: Fund-reference entity-quarter-level tobit regressions for the intensity of CDS positions, estimated for gross sell intensity and gross buy intensity, with further decomposition of buy intensity into speculative buy and basis buy. Outcomes are ratios of notional CDS exposure to fund TNA, censored at zero. Regressors include the same lagged fund controls as above and issuer-level bond liquidity, CDS contract counts, firm size, CDS spreads, and in some columns CDS-bond basis. Quarter and Lipper-category fixed effects are included; standard errors are clustered at the fund level. The authors interpret these estimates as showing how liquidity and the CDS-bond basis causally affect selling, buying, and especially basis trading.

Identification: Identification uses conditional variation in issuer-specific liquidity and the CDS-bond basis, controlling for observed fund traits and time/style effects. Endogeneity remains because basis and liquidity may reflect unobserved issuer risk or supply-demand shocks that also influence fund trading. The paper’s argument is that these variables capture the relative attractiveness of CDS versus bonds and thereby drive intensive-margin position choices.

Setting: The paper argues that relative liquidity and the CDS-bond basis causally shape how intensively funds use CDS on particular issuers. A one-standard-deviation increase in the number of CDS contracts is associated with a 2.58 percentage point increase in gross selling intensity and a 0.77 percentage point increase in gross buying intensity, both economically large relative to typical issuer-level exposures. More importantly for yield, a more negative CDS-bond basis is associated with stronger CDS buying, especially basis buying, while a higher basis is associated with more CDS selling. These regressions support the claims that funds use CDS both as a more liquid substitute for bond exposure and as a vehicle for negative-basis trades.

Main role: These intensity results underpin the abstract claims on liquidity, yield, and negative basis trading, so they materially support the paper’s main conclusions.
Settings.H473: Section II.B and Section III.A, Table IV Panel B, columns (1)–(6), PDF pp. 564–568 (article pp. 564–568).
Settings.G474:
Treatment: CDS selling intensity, defined as total notional amount of CDS selling scaled by fund TNA; measured either for single-name CDS only or all CDS including index CDS. Continuous treatment in percentage points of TNA.

Method: Fund-quarter linear regressions of portfolio spread over the five-year Treasury rate on CDS selling intensity. The dependent variable is the fund’s portfolio spread, using CRSP-reported yield or an imputed yield from return minus NAV return when missing. The key regressor is CDS selling intensity measured either using only single-name CDS or all CDS positions including indices. Controls include log fund size, broad fund-type dummies (Treasury, high-yield, corporate investment grade), and maturity dummies; some columns include fund fixed effects, and all include time and Lipper-category fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the fund level. The paper interprets the coefficient as the effect of heavier CDS selling on portfolio yield enhancement.

Identification: Identification comes from conditional variation in CDS selling intensity across funds and within funds over time, after controlling for observed fund category, size, maturity, time effects, and in some columns fund fixed effects. The key concern is reverse causality and omitted risk appetite: funds seeking high yield may simultaneously choose both higher-yield portfolios and more CDS selling. The paper interprets the within-fund positive relation as evidence that increasing CDS selling contributes to higher portfolio yield, but causal exogeneity is unresolved.

Setting: The paper uses fund-quarter linear regressions to argue that selling more CDS raises mutual fund portfolio yields. In Table V, CDS selling intensity enters positively and significantly in cross-sectional and, more weakly, fund fixed-effects regressions. The text also states that the average difference between the value-weighted spread on a fund’s CDS sell positions and the equivalent spread on the rest of its portfolio is 93 basis points, and that for heavy CDS users the average (median) portfolio yield is 14 (13) basis points higher with CDS than without CDS. This evidence supports the paper’s main claim that CDS are used to enhance yield.

Main role: Yield enhancement is a central theme in the abstract and conclusion; Table V provides a main piece of evidence that CDS selling raises portfolio yield.
Settings.H474: Section III.B, Table V columns (1)–(6), PDF pp. 569–570 (article pp. 569–570).
Settings.G475:
Treatment: Indicator Top 20% entity in finance, equal to one if the reference entity is in the top quintile by asset size among finance-industry firms (SIC 6000–6999) covered by Markit in 2006. Binary treatment indicating potential systemic importance of the issuer.

Method: Fund-reference entity-quarter tobit regressions of CDS sell and buy intensity, run separately for precrisis (2006–2007), crisis (2008–2009), and postcrisis (2010–2012) subsamples, adding an indicator for whether the reference entity is a top-20% by asset size financial firm in 2006. The specification otherwise follows Table IV Panel B, including fund controls, issuer characteristics, time/style controls, and clustering at the fund level. The paper interprets this as testing whether systemically important financial institutions caused greater CDS selling or buying by mutual funds, especially during the crisis.

Identification: Identification is based on cross-sectional differences between potentially systemically important financial reference entities and other entities within period-specific tobit regressions, controlling for observed issuer and fund characteristics. The main concern is that top financial firms differ along many unobserved dimensions besides systemic importance. The paper treats the coefficient as revealing funds’ preference for betting on large financial institutions, particularly during crisis conditions.

Setting: In period-specific tobit regressions, the paper argues that potentially systemically important financial institutions attracted disproportionately more mutual fund CDS trading during the crisis. During 2008–2009, the likelihood that a mutual fund would sell CDS on a top financial institution is reported to be 5.1 times the likelihood for other entities, and the corresponding likelihood for CDS buying is 2.8 times. The authors interpret this as evidence that funds increased exposure to large financial firms during the crisis, possibly reflecting beliefs about bailouts. This is an important but secondary causal application focused on systemic-risk-taking.

Main role: This is a substantive secondary analysis about systemic risk exposure during the crisis, not the paper’s main liquidity/yield result.
Settings.H475: Section IV.A, Table VI Panel A, columns (1)–(6), PDF pp. 574, 577 (article pp. 574, 577).
Settings.G476:
Treatment: Either a binary indicator for being a CDS user during the sample/current quarter, or CDS intensity equal to total notional amount of all CDS positions divided by fund TNA. Continuous in intensity specifications, binary in user-indicator specifications.

Method: Cross-sectional and panel linear regressions of fund performance on CDS usage. In the cross section, fund-level average two-factor alpha or ten-factor alpha is regressed on a CDS-user indicator or CDS intensity, with fund size and sometimes category fixed effects. In the panel, monthly alpha is regressed on CDS intensity separately for precrisis, crisis, and postcrisis subsamples, including either category fixed effects or fund fixed effects. Performance measures are standard linear factor-model alphas for bond funds. The paper interprets these regressions as testing whether CDS use improves fund performance.

Identification: Identification relies on comparing performance across funds with different CDS usage and within funds over time as CDS intensity changes. The key endogeneity problem is selection: better-managed or more sophisticated funds may both use CDS and perform better. Fund/category fixed effects and size controls reduce some confounding, but no exogenous variation in CDS use is provided. The paper therefore presents these as suggestive causal-performance relations.

Setting: The paper examines whether using more CDS improves fund performance. In cross-sectional regressions, CDS-using funds have 4 to 8 basis points higher monthly alpha before category fixed effects, but the premium mostly disappears once investment style is held constant. In monthly panel regressions, CDS intensity is negatively associated with performance during the 2008–2009 crisis but positively associated in some postcrisis specifications. The authors conclude that CDS-using funds tend to be stronger funds overall, but the sheer intensity of CDS use does not robustly predict better full-sample performance.

Main role: Performance consequences are a major theme but not the paper’s first-order identification contribution; the paper treats these as follow-on consequences of CDS use.
Settings.H476: Section IV.C, Table VI Panels B and C, PDF pp. 574–582 (article pp. 574–582).
Settings.G477:
Treatment: CDS sell intensity, defined as total notional amount of CDS selling (single-name and index) averaged over the four quarters of the year and scaled by fund TNA. Continuous treatment.

Method: Fund-year panel regressions of downside performance on CDS sell intensity. The dependent variable is an indicator for whether the fund falls into the bottom decile of return performance within its Lipper category in a given year. The key regressor is average CDS sell intensity over the year; specifications include fund size and either category fixed effects or fund fixed effects, and are estimated for the full sample and separately by subperiod. Although the outcome is binary, the table reports linear regressions rather than a nonlinear limited-dependent-variable model. The paper interprets the coefficient as the effect of heavier CDS selling on downside tail risk.

Identification: Identification uses panel variation in annual CDS selling intensity across and within funds, controlling for size and either fund category or fund fixed effects. Main concerns are omitted time-varying risk appetite and reverse causality if struggling funds take more CDS risk. The paper interprets stronger within-fund estimates as evidence that increasing CDS selling raises downside risk, especially during crisis periods.

Setting: In fund-year panel regressions, the paper argues that heavy CDS selling increases downside tail risk. A 1 percentage point increase in CDS selling intensity is associated with a 31 basis point higher probability of falling into the bottom performance decile in the cross section and 45 basis points with fund fixed effects. The effect is concentrated in the 2008–2009 crisis period, when hidden tail risk from selling CDS materialized. This supports the paper’s claim that yield-enhancing CDS sales come with increased downside risk.

Main role: This is a consequence/risk analysis supporting the paper’s discussion of hidden tail risk from CDS selling, but it is not the main headline result.
Settings.H477: Section IV.C, Table VI Panel D, PDF pp. 574, 582–583 (article pp. 574, 582–583).
Settings.G478:
Treatment: Firm financial condition measured alternatively as Book leverage = (DLTT + DLC)/AT; Market leverage = (DLTT + DLC)/(DLTT + DLC + market equity); or Altman Z score based on profitability, sales, retained earnings, working capital, and market equity relative to liabilities, all measured in year t-1. These are continuous treatments, not binary. Higher leverage indicates weaker financial condition; higher Altman Z indicates lower distress likelihood.

Method: The authors estimate cross-sectional probit models of recall incidence at the firm-year level for 2006–2010. The dependent variable is an indicator for whether firm i has a recall in year t. Key treatments are lagged financial condition measures—book leverage, market leverage, or Altman Z—entered one at a time, with lagged controls for free-cash-flow shock, unionization, number of suppliers, vertical integration, R&D intensity, total factor productivity, Herfindahl index, and size. Specifications alternatively include year dummies only, year plus 2-digit SIC dummies, or year plus 3-digit SIC dummies. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear probit, it is classified as Other rather than OLS/regression adjustment. Identification relies on conditional selection on observables plus industry/time controls; the paper interprets these coefficients causally but also acknowledges omitted-variable concerns and later supplements them with quasi-experiments and IV.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional and over-time variation in lagged leverage/distress across recalling and nonrecalling firms within industries. The main endogeneity concern is omitted factors, such as managerial quality or industry conditions, that may affect both financing and product quality. The authors mitigate this by using lagged regressors, same-industry control firms, rich observable controls, and year/industry dummies, but they do not claim this baseline probit fully resolves endogeneity; instead it establishes the main conditional association they interpret in light of theory and later causal tests.

Setting: In baseline probit regressions, firms in weaker financial condition are more likely to experience product recalls. With year and 3-digit SIC fixed effects, the reported marginal effect is 0.0579 for book leverage, 0.1279 for market leverage, and -0.0033 for Altman Z (all p=0.001 or better), implying that higher leverage and higher distress likelihood increase recall probability. The authors further state that moving book leverage from the 25th to 75th percentile raises the implied recall probability by 1.68 percentage points relative to an unconditional recall probability of 22.09%, while the analogous increase for market leverage is 3.05 percentage points; Altman Z lowers recall probability by 1.42 percentage points over its interquartile range. These baseline nonlinear regressions are a central part of the paper’s argument, though the paper recognizes potential remaining endogeneity.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all emphasize the basic finding that higher leverage/distress likelihood raises the probability of recalls; Table 3 provides the core baseline evidence supporting the paper’s central claim.
Settings.H478: Section 3.1, Equation (1), Table 3 cols. (1)–(9), discussion on PDF pp. 12–15.
Settings.G479:
Treatment: Interaction between lagged firm financial condition (Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z, all continuous) and a binary industry-year shock indicator Tariff cut equal to 1 when the annual percentage drop in the industry tariff rate is at least two times the industry median level and not reversed the next year. The focal causal treatment is exposure of financially weaker firms to an exogenous tariff-cut shock that increases foreign competition and reduces domestic cash flows.

Method: The authors implement a nonlinear difference-in-differences style probit specification around exogenous tariff cuts. They add to the baseline recall-incidence probit a Tariff cut dummy and its interaction with financial condition (book leverage, market leverage, or Altman Z). Tariff cut equals 1 for industry-years with a large drop in tariff rates, following a Fresard-style rule based on annual percentage tariff declines relative to the industry median. Models include two-digit SIC and year dummies plus the standard controls. The paper interprets the interaction as showing that exogenous adverse industry cash-flow shocks amplify the effect of leverage/distress on recalls. Because the implemented estimator is probit, this is classified as Other rather than conventional DiD.

Identification: The strategy exploits plausibly exogenous large reductions in industry tariffs that increase competition and reduce cash flows for domestic firms. If leverage/distress causally constrains quality investment, the leverage–recall relation should strengthen in shock years. Identification therefore comes from differential sensitivity of recalls to leverage among firms exposed to tariff-cut shocks versus nonshock observations, conditional on controls and fixed effects. The main assumption is that tariff cuts are exogenous to firm-specific recall risk except through the financial-constraint channel, though the authors note a limitation that tariff cuts may also directly affect competition and product quality.

Setting: Using a probit interaction design centered on large industry tariff cuts, the paper finds that adverse competitive shocks amplify the effect of weak financial condition on recalls. In Table 4, the marginal effect on the interaction term Tariff cut × Book leverage is 0.1430 (p=0.009), Tariff cut × Market leverage is 0.1826 (p=0.001), and Tariff cut × Altman Z is -0.0038 (p=0.080). The authors interpret these estimates as evidence that exogenous negative industry cash-flow shocks make leverage- and distress-related constraints more binding, increasing the probability of subsequent product recalls. This quasi-natural experiment is one of the paper’s main causal pillars.

Main role: The abstract and introduction specifically highlight one quasi-natural experiment based on sharp import tariff cuts as key evidence for a causal interpretation.
Settings.H479: Section 3.2.1.1, Equation (2), Table 4 cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 17–21.
Settings.G480:
Treatment: Interaction between lagged financial condition (Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z; continuous) and a binary Negative input price shock indicator equal to 1 if the geometric average growth rate in industry input prices over the prior three years is 5% or more. The treatment captures financially weaker firms’ exposure to exogenous supplier-cost shocks that reduce cash flow.

Method: The authors estimate a nonlinear probit interaction model analogous to a difference-in-differences design, using adverse input price shocks as the exogenous industry cash-flow shock. They interact a Negative input price shock dummy with lagged financial condition (book leverage, market leverage, or Altman Z), controlling for the same firm and industry characteristics as in the baseline model and including two-digit SIC and year dummies. Negative input price shock equals 1 when the geometric average growth rate in weighted supplier input prices over the prior three years is at least 5%. Because the implemented estimator is probit rather than linear DiD, this is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification comes from plausibly exogenous increases in supplier input prices that lower downstream firms’ cash flows. The authors argue these shocks originate in supplier industries rather than downstream demand and document no pre-shock revenue-growth differences between treated and control industries. If financial weakness causally impairs quality investment, leverage/distress should matter more when such cost shocks hit. The core assumption is that input price shocks affect recalls differentially through financial constraints rather than through omitted channels correlated with both leverage and recall risk.

Setting: In probit interaction regressions using adverse input price shocks as quasi-experiments, the paper generally finds that weak financial condition becomes more strongly associated with recalls after exogenous cost shocks. Table 5 reports a marginal effect of 0.1011 on Negative input price shock × Book leverage (p=0.076), -0.0109 on the interaction with Market leverage (p=0.819), and -0.0104 on Negative input price shock × Altman Z (p=0.000). The strongest evidence is for distress likelihood and, more weakly, book leverage. The authors interpret this pattern as further evidence that exogenous negative cash-flow shocks intensify the causal effect of financial weakness on recall incidence.

Main role: The abstract and introduction mention input price shocks as a second quasi-natural experiment central to the paper’s causal case.
Settings.H480: Section 3.2.1.2, Equation (2), Table 5 cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 21–23.
Settings.G481:
Treatment: Debt due at onset of crisis, a continuous maturity-structure variable equal to debt due during the next year divided by debt due during the next year plus long-term debt, measured at end of fiscal year 2007 for firms with 2007 fiscal year-end in Sep/Oct/Nov/Dec/Jan. Higher values indicate more debt coming due when liquidity conditions tightened in the financial crisis.

Method: To exploit the 2008 credit crisis, the authors estimate cross-sectional probit models for recall propensity over crisis horizons as a function of Debt due at onset of crisis, measured at fiscal year-end 2007 for firms with fiscal year-end months in September–January. This debt-maturity share is defined as DD1/(DD1+DLTT), following Almeida et al. (2012). The outcome varies across horizons: any recall from Feb–Dec 2008, from Feb 2008–Dec 2009, or from Feb 2008–Dec 2010. Models include two-digit SIC dummies and firm/industry controls. Because the estimator is probit, the setting is classified as Other.

Identification: The idea is that, if the 2008 crisis was unanticipated when firms chose debt maturities, then the share of debt maturing at the crisis onset is plausibly exogenous. Firms with more debt coming due faced tighter liquidity constraints during the crisis. The paper argues that if weak financial condition causes quality-cutting, then higher crisis-maturity exposure should increase later recall likelihood. Assumptions are that debt maturity structure is predetermined with respect to crisis-period recall shocks and that controls plus industry dummies absorb remaining confounders.

Setting: Using crisis-period debt maturity as an exogenous liquidity-shock measure, the authors find that firms with more debt coming due at the onset of the 2008 financial crisis were more likely to experience recalls afterward. In Table 6 probit models, the coefficient on Debt due at onset of crisis is 0.3848 for recalls in Feb–Dec 2008 (p=0.045), 0.3707 for recalls in Feb 2008–Dec 2009 (p=0.035), and 0.3616 for recalls in Feb 2008–Dec 2010 (p=0.036). The paper interprets these results as evidence that tighter refinancing pressure during the crisis causally increased recall propensity by worsening firms’ financial constraints.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly highlight debt maturing at the onset of the crisis as a third exogenous shock central to the causal argument.
Settings.H481: Section 3.2.1.3, Equation (3), Table 6 cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 17–25.
Settings.G482:
Treatment: Debt due at onset of crisis, measured as DD1/(DD1+DLTT) at end of fiscal year 2007 for the specified fiscal-year-end sample. Continuous exposure to refinancing pressure during the 2008 financial crisis.

Method: The authors estimate Poisson count models for recall frequency over crisis horizons as a function of Debt due at onset of crisis, measured at fiscal year-end 2007 for firms with fiscal year-end months in September–January. Outcomes are the number of recalls from Feb–Dec 2008, Feb 2008–Dec 2009, or Feb 2008–Dec 2010. The same controls and two-digit SIC dummies are included. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear Poisson rather than linear regression, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: As in the crisis-propensity setting, identification relies on plausibly predetermined debt maturity structure at the start of an unexpected aggregate liquidity shock. Greater debt due at crisis onset should tighten financing constraints and, under the paper’s mechanism, lead firms to cut quality-related investments, increasing the number of subsequent recalls. The validity of the strategy requires that crisis-period maturity shares are not chosen in anticipation of future recalls and that included controls absorb other determinants of recall counts.

Setting: The crisis debt-maturity test also indicates that refinancing pressure increased the frequency of product recalls. In Table 6 Poisson models, the coefficient on Debt due at onset of crisis is 0.2533 for the number of recalls in Feb–Dec 2008 (p=0.036), 0.2467 for Feb 2008–Dec 2009 (p=0.009), and 0.2529 for Feb 2008–Dec 2010 (p=0.007). The authors interpret this as evidence that tighter crisis-era liquidity constraints not only raised the probability of a recall but also increased how often recalls occurred, reinforcing the causal role of financial condition in product failures.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that financially weaker firms experience more frequent recalls; the crisis-debt-maturity test is one of the paper’s headline quasi-experimental results for recall frequency.
Settings.H482: Section 3.2.1.3, Equation (3), Table 6 cols. (4)–(6), PDF pp. 17–25.
Settings.G483:
Treatment: Endogenous financial condition, measured alternatively as Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z. These are continuous receipt variables instrumented by Local firm leverage (average market leverage of geographically proximate nonrival firms).

Method: The authors estimate exactly identified 2SLS linear probability models for recall incidence. The endogenous treatment is one of three financial condition variables: Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z. The instrument is Local firm leverage, defined as the average market leverage of firms headquartered within 250 kilometers of the focal firm, excluding the firm itself and industry rivals. The first stage regresses the endogenous financial condition measure on local leverage and controls; the second stage is a linear probability model for the recall indicator with two-digit SIC and year dummies plus the standard controls. The paper motivates the instrument using geographic spillovers in corporate policies and argues exclusion because leverage of nearby firms in other industries should not directly affect the firm’s product quality.

Identification: Identification comes from geographic variation in local firms’ leverage that is presumed to influence a focal firm’s own leverage through local culture and social interactions in financing choices, but not to affect the focal firm’s product quality directly once controls, industry dummies, and year dummies are included. The endogeneity concern is omitted latent factors, such as managerial ability or time-varying firm quality, that jointly determine leverage and recalls. The exclusion restriction requires local nonrival leverage to shift the firm’s leverage without having an independent causal effect on its recall probability.

Setting: In 2SLS linear probability models instrumenting firm financial condition with leverage of geographically proximate nonrival firms, the authors continue to find that weaker financial condition increases recall incidence. Table 7 reports second-stage coefficients of 2.1759 on Book leverage (p=0.000), 1.6200 on Market leverage (p=0.041), and -0.0485 on Altman Z (p=0.038). First-stage instrument coefficients are significant, and the reported relevance and under-identification tests support the instrument’s strength. The paper interprets these IV estimates as evidence for a causal link from leverage/distress to product recalls rather than a mere correlation driven by omitted variables.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion specifically mention 2SLS as part of the collection of tests supporting a plausible causal link; it is a central identification exercise rather than a minor robustness check.
Settings.G484:
Treatment: Firm financial condition measured alternatively as Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z, all continuous and measured prior to the recall outcome.

Method: The authors also report linear probability OLS regressions for recall incidence using the same specification as the baseline models but implemented linearly rather than probit. The dependent variable is the recall indicator; key treatments are Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z, entered separately. Controls include free-cash-flow shock, unionization, number of suppliers, vertical integration, R&D intensity, total factor productivity, Herfindahl index, size, plus two-digit SIC and year dummies. These OLS models are presented mainly to show that the linear probability estimates are similar in spirit to the probit results and as a benchmark for the IV second stage.

Identification: The identification logic is regression adjustment using lagged financial condition, rich controls, and industry/year dummies. The authors interpret the coefficients as the effect of weaker financial condition on recall probability but recognize potential endogeneity; these OLS estimates do not independently solve omitted-variable bias and are mainly used as a linear benchmark alongside IV.

Setting: Linear probability models produce the same qualitative conclusion as the baseline probit regressions: weaker financial condition predicts more recalls. In Table 7, OLS coefficients are 0.0936 on Book leverage (p=0.001), 0.1798 on Market leverage (p=0.000), and -0.0049 on Altman Z (p=0.000). These estimates are not the paper’s strongest identification results, but they show that the central relation between leverage/distress and recall incidence is not an artifact of the probit functional form.

Main role: These OLS linear probability estimates are supportive and primarily motivate comparability with the IV framework; the paper’s main causal claims rely more heavily on the probit baseline, quasi-experiments, and 2SLS.
Settings.G485:
Treatment: Firm financial condition measured alternatively as Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z (continuous). In expanded specifications, the treatment is the interaction of these financial condition measures with Tariff cut or Negative input price shock dummies, capturing how exogenous shocks amplify the impact of weak financial condition on recall severity.

Method: The authors estimate ordered probit models of recall severity for FDA recalls only. Recall severity is coded 3 for FDA class I recalls, 2 for class II, 1 for class III, and 0 for control firms. They regress this ordered outcome on financial condition measures (book leverage, market leverage, or Altman Z), standard controls, and two-digit SIC plus year dummies. Additional specifications interact financial condition with Tariff cut or Negative input price shock to test whether exogenous cash-flow shocks strengthen the effect on severity. Because the estimator is ordered probit, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: For the baseline severity models, identification rests on conditional variation in lagged financial condition across firms, controlling for observables and fixed effects. For the interaction models, the authors use exogenous tariff cuts and input price shocks as plausibly external cash-flow shocks that should magnify the effect of leverage/distress if financial constraints causally worsen product quality. The main assumptions mirror those in the incidence quasi-experiments, with the added assumption that FDA’s recall classes validly rank severity.

Setting: Ordered probit estimates on FDA recalls indicate that weaker financial condition increases the severity of product failures, and that exogenous negative cash-flow shocks further strengthen this effect. In Table 8 baseline models, the coefficient is 0.2115 on Book leverage (p=0.029), 0.6926 on Market leverage (p=0.000), and -0.0171 on Altman Z (p=0.000). In interaction models, Tariff cut × Book leverage is 1.0184 (p=0.000), Tariff cut × Market leverage is 1.0867 (p=0.003), Tariff cut × Altman Z is -0.0168 (p=0.062), Negative input price shock × Book leverage is 1.0083 (p=0.069), and Negative input price shock × Altman Z is -0.0812 (p=0.000), while the interaction with Market leverage is not significant. The paper treats these results as reinforcing the causal interpretation that financial constraints worsen not just whether recalls occur, but how serious they are.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly state that financial weakness increases severity as well as incidence and frequency of recalls; these ordered probit results materially support that central conclusion.
Settings.G486:
Treatment: Firm financial condition measured at the beginning of the sample period (year 2005) as Book leverage, Market leverage, or Altman Z; each is continuous.

Method: The authors estimate Poisson models for the total number of recalls a firm experiences over 2006–2010, collapsing each firm to one observation and measuring explanatory variables at the start of the sample in 2005. The treatment is book leverage, market leverage, or Altman Z, entered separately, along with controls and two-digit SIC dummies. This design is intended to capture longer lags between financial condition and eventual product failures. Because the outcome model is Poisson, the method is classified as Other.

Identification: The authors use pre-sample financial condition measured in 2005 to predict total recall frequency over the next five years, arguing this can capture delayed manifestation of quality problems. The endogeneity concern remains omitted firm traits correlated with both 2005 leverage and later recalls; controls and industry dummies mitigate but do not eliminate this concern. The design mainly addresses timing rather than identification from exogenous variation.

Setting: When firms are collapsed to one observation and 2005 financial condition is used to predict total recalls over 2006–2010, weaker initial financial condition predicts more subsequent recalls. Table 9 shows Poisson coefficients of 0.9441 on Book leverage (p=0.047), 2.1103 on Market leverage (p=0.000), and -0.0357 on Altman Z (p=0.017). The authors interpret these findings as evidence that financial weakness has effects on product quality that can persist for several years, although this timing exercise is more supportive than definitive for causal identification.

Main role: This is an additional lag-structure exercise supporting the persistence of the main mechanism, not a primary identification design highlighted in the abstract.
Settings.G487:
Treatment: Exposure to being a larger firm size category during the COVID period, implemented as interactions between firm-size-category indicators (assets: $50–250m, $250–1000m, $1000–5000m, >$5000m; omitted group <$50m) and a COVID indicator for 2020Q1/2020Q2. This is not a literal treatment assignment but the paper interprets the post-COVID differential by size as reflecting the effect of loan-term regimes associated with firm size.

Method: Loan-level difference-in-differences regressions of revolving-credit-line drawdown rates during the COVID period. The dependent variable is the utilization rate (utilized/committed credit). The design compares changes from pre-COVID quarters to 2020Q1 and 2020Q2 across firm-size classes, with loan fixed effects and time fixed effects in the baseline, and then bank×time, state×time, and industry×time fixed effects plus borrower financial controls and rating×time fixed effects in richer specifications. Additional specifications interact maturity and collateral controls with the COVID indicator to assess how these contract terms explain the size gradient. The authors interpret remaining size differences in drawdowns as reflecting causal effects of loan terms that grant lender discretion, while acknowledging potential demand-side confounds.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from before-versus-during-COVID changes in drawdown rates across firm-size classes, after absorbing loan fixed effects and increasingly rich time-varying controls for banks, industries, states, ratings, and borrower financials. The endogeneity concern is that large firms may have experienced larger liquidity demand shocks, not better access per se. The paper argues against this using controls for industry/state, bond-market access, financials, and by showing that adding maturity and collateral terms attenuates the size gradient. The core assumption is that, conditional on included fixed effects and controls, residual differential changes by size reflect differences in effective credit-line commitment induced by loan terms rather than omitted demand shocks.

Setting: Using loan-level DiD regressions on pre-existing revolving credit lines, the authors find that drawdown rates in 2020 rose much more for larger firms than for small SMEs. In Table 11, column (1), relative to firms with assets below $50 million, the incremental COVID-period drawdown is 4.1 percentage points for $50–250 million firms, 10.5 points for $250–1000 million firms, 13.5 points for $1000–5000 million firms, and 14.1 points for firms above $5 billion. With bank-time, state-time, industry-time, borrower financial, and rating controls, the largest-firm coefficient remains 9.2 percentage points (col. 6). Adding maturity and collateral controls reduces the largest-firm coefficient to 5.3 points (col. 8), which the authors interpret as evidence that stricter loan terms on small firms causally constrained their access to liquidity during COVID.

Main role: A central claim of the paper is that small firms were less able to access bank liquidity during the COVID shock because their loan terms gave lenders more discretion. The introduction, abstract, and conclusions emphasize the COVID drawdown evidence as a main empirical test of the paper’s theory.
Settings.H487: Section 5.1 'Drawdowns by firm size,' Eq. (1), Table 11 cols. (1)-(9), PDF pages 16-18.
Settings.G488:
Treatment: Continuous industry-level COVID shock exposure, measured as abnormal 3-digit-industry employment decline between 2019Q2 and 2020Q2 (or abnormal sales decline in robustness), interacted with the COVID period and with firm-size classes. The focal estimand is the differential effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure on drawdowns across size groups.

Method: Triple-difference/event-study style regressions of revolving-credit-line drawdowns interacting a continuous industry COVID-exposure measure with the COVID period and firm-size categories. The exposure is the abnormal decline in national employment (or in robustness, sales) in the firm’s 3-digit industry from 2019Q2 to 2020Q2, detrended by pre-2020 Q2-to-Q2 averages. Specifications include loan fixed effects, time or bank×time fixed effects, state×time fixed effects, and controls for borrower financials, rating×time fixed effects, and loan terms interacted with COVID/exposure. The authors use this heterogeneous DiD/DDD approach to argue that large firms, but not small firms, drew more when hit by similar demand shocks.

Identification: The design exploits within-size-class differences in exposure to the COVID recession, then compares how exposure translated into drawdowns across size classes before and during COVID. The main endogeneity concern is that observed size differences in drawdowns could be driven by heterogeneous demand. By showing that industry exposure strongly predicts drawdowns for large firms but not for small firms, while the same exposure predicts revenue declines similarly for both size groups, the authors argue that loan-term-related credit constraints muted the response of small firms. Identification requires that abnormal industry employment/sales decline is a valid proxy for firm cash-flow shocks and that remaining confounders are absorbed by fixed effects and controls.

Setting: To separate credit constraints from demand, the authors estimate DDD regressions of drawdowns on industry COVID exposure interacted with the COVID period and firm size. In Table 13 column (2), a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure has essentially no effect for the omitted smallest firms (coefficient on Exposure×COVID = -0.4 percentage points), while the incremental sensitivity rises with size: 3.5 points for $50–250 million firms, 4.4 points for $250–1000 million, 7.2 points for $1000–5000 million, and 9.5 points for firms above $5 billion. With bank-time, state-time, financial, rating, and loan-term controls, the large-firm differential remains substantial though attenuated (e.g., 4.0 points for >$5 billion in col. 6). The authors interpret this as causal evidence that small firms could not draw even in response to similar cash-flow shocks, consistent with lender discretion embedded in their loan terms.

Main role: This is the paper’s main strategy to address the principal alternative explanation that small and large firms faced different credit demand shocks. The introduction specifically highlights the differential sensitivity of drawdowns to industry exposure as key causal evidence.
Settings.H488: Section 5.2 'Drawdowns by firm size and industry exposure,' Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Eq. (2), Table 13 cols. (1)-(6), PDF pages 18-20.
Settings.G489:
Treatment: Continuous endogenous treatment: industry-level abnormal employment decline between 2019Q2 and 2020Q2 (standardized exposure measure). Instrument: industry physical proximity needs from the ONET question 'How physically close to other people are you when you perform your current job?' aggregated to industry level.

Method: Cross-sectional IV regressions of the change in credit-line drawdown between 2019Q4 and 2020Q1 on the firm’s industry COVID exposure, instrumenting abnormal 3-digit-industry employment decline with industry physical-proximity requirements from ONET. The paper reports pooled and size-specific 2SLS coefficients and first-stage effective F-statistics following Montiel Olea and Pflueger. The purpose is to purge industry exposure of confounding shocks and strengthen the causal interpretation of exposure-induced drawdowns differing by firm size.

Identification: The exclusion restriction is that industry physical-proximity requirements affect drawdowns only through their effect on the industry’s COVID-related employment decline, not via other direct channels. The endogenous variable is industry exposure, which may contain omitted industry shocks. By instrumenting exposure, the paper seeks cleaner causal estimates of how cash-flow shocks translated into drawdowns across firm sizes. The interpretation still relies on comparing IV coefficients across size groups to infer differential access to liquidity.

Setting: Using 2SLS, the authors instrument industry COVID exposure with physical-proximity requirements to isolate exogenous variation in cash-flow shocks. Table 14 shows a strong first stage (effective F-statistics around 10-17.5). The pooled IV coefficient of exposure on the 2019Q4-to-2020Q1 drawdown change is 2.6 percentage points, but the size-specific estimates reveal near-zero or negative effects for the smallest firms (-0.8 for firms below $50 million, 0.9 for $50–250 million) and increasingly positive effects for larger firms (4.2, 7.3, and 12.8 percentage points across higher size bins). The authors interpret this as confirming that similar shocks translated into borrowing for large firms but not for small firms, consistent with tighter effective credit constraints on SMEs.

Main role: The introduction and Section 5.2 describe the IV exercise as confirming the key heterogeneous-response pattern and as additional evidence that small firms were constrained rather than merely less exposed to shocks.
Settings.G490:
Treatment: Continuous industry exposure measure: abnormal 3-digit-industry employment decline between 2019Q2 and 2020Q2, standardized to unit variance, interacted with broad firm-size categories.

Method: Cross-sectional regressions at the size-industry-cell level using Compustat to validate the paper’s industry exposure proxy. Mean or median 2020Q1-Q3 year-over-year revenue growth is regressed on the abnormal industry employment decline interacted with broad size classes (0-250 million vs. 1000+ million in assets). This is a linear regression adjustment design rather than DiD in the main estimating equation, used as supporting causal evidence that the exposure variable captures comparable cash-flow shocks across small and large firms.

Identification: The strategy is to test whether the abnormal employment-decline exposure measure predicts actual revenue declines similarly across size groups. The concern is that industry exposure might proxy different underlying cash-flow shocks for small and large firms. If the slopes are similar across size classes, then differential drawdown responses are less likely to be driven by demand differences. This is not the paper’s main identification design but a regression-adjustment validation step.

Setting: To validate its shock measure, the paper regresses size-industry-cell revenue growth on industry exposure separately for small and large firms. In Table 12, a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure predicts roughly 13-16 percentage point lower revenue growth for both broad size groups: for example, Exposure×0–250 equals -13.22 (mean) and -14.14 (median), while Exposure×1000+ equals -16.28 and -16.19. The authors note that the data do not reject equality of intercepts or slopes across size groups, supporting the causal interpretation that the main size differences in drawdowns reflect credit access rather than systematically different cash-flow shocks.

Main role: This setting is a supporting validation exercise rather than a central result. It is used to show that the exposure proxy maps into similar revenue shocks for small and large firms, supporting the interpretation of the main drawdown regressions.
Settings.G491:
Treatment: Receipt of a PPP loan and PPP loan amount, matched from SBA data to Y-14 borrowers. The substantive treatment is government-provided PPP liquidity; Table 15 reports aggregate PPP amount in billions and contrasts non-PPP borrowing before and after receipt.

Method: Descriptive aggregate comparison of PPP recipients’ non-PPP borrowing before and after PPP receipt, using matched Y-14 and SBA PPP data. The implemented evidence is a before/after level comparison in aggregate non-PPP credit outstanding and calculation of repayment ratios relative to PPP disbursements, by firm-size class and overall. There is no explicit control group or panel regression in the main table, but the authors interpret changes in non-PPP balances as the effect of PPP on borrowers’ liquidity and bank borrowing.

Identification: The paper uses within-recipient before/after changes in non-PPP borrowing after PPP disbursement to infer that PPP funds substituted for private bank borrowing. The key concern is that repayments in 2020Q2 could also reflect easing precautionary demand or other concurrent shocks, and the paper does not present a formal untreated counterfactual in the main specification. The interpretation relies on the timing of PPP rollout and the concentration of repayments among matched PPP recipients.

Setting: Matching Y-14 borrowers to SBA PPP records, the authors show that recipients reduced non-PPP borrowing after receiving PPP funds, which they interpret as PPP bolstering liquidity and offsetting small-firm credit constraints. In Table 15, total non-PPP credit outstanding for matched recipients falls from $237.0 billion in 2020Q1 to $189.7 billion in 2020Q2 while PPP disbursements total $50.0 billion, implying an aggregate repayment ratio of 94.7%. For small SMEs (assets below $50 million), non-PPP credit falls from $103.0 billion to $79.5 billion against $32.8 billion of PPP funds, a 71.7% repayment ratio. The authors conclude that PPP substantially, if not fully, counteracted the liquidity shortfall faced by eligible SMEs.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly state that PPP recipients reduced non-PPP borrowing, and the conclusion interprets this as evidence that government-provided liquidity overcame small-firm credit shortfalls. It is one of the paper’s headline policy results.
Settings.H491: Section 5.4 'Paycheck protection program,' Table 15 and Fig. 5, PDF pages 22-23.
Settings.G492:
Treatment: Bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, defined as the percentage difference between the spline-model-implied price and the actual market mid-price, expressed in basis points: Cheapness_tj = (P_tj(theta_t) - P_tj)/P_tj. A one standard deviation increase is about 23 basis points in the purchased sample. This is a continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate linear panel regressions at the auction-CUSIP level relating the Fed’s purchase quantity of a bond in a QE auction to the bond’s pre-auction cheapness measure and other pre-auction controls. Their baseline specification includes CUSIP fixed effects and auction fixed effects, with two-way clustered standard errors by auction and CUSIP. The identifying variation is within-CUSIP over time and within-auction across eligible bonds after absorbing common auction factors and time-invariant bond heterogeneity. The design is not DiD, IV, or RD; it is a causal fixed-effects regression interpreted as evidence that bonds appearing cheaper to the Fed are purchased more. Remaining concern is that cheapness is an estimated proxy for the Fed’s unobserved relative valuation and may still correlate with omitted dealer supply conditions or measurement error.

Identification: The paper argues that the Fed uses an internal yield-curve-based relative value model to rank bonds in purchase auctions, so pre-auction cross-bond and time-series variation in estimated cheapness should map into the Fed’s purchase decisions. Auction fixed effects absorb auction-wide demand/size conditions; CUSIP fixed effects absorb time-invariant bond characteristics. Controls include volatility, repo specialness, outstanding balance, and bid-ask spread. The causal interpretation relies on the estimated cheapness proxy being correlated with the Fed’s actual proprietary relative value metric and not being fully driven by omitted dealer supply or liquidity conditions after controls and fixed effects.

Setting: Using auction-CUSIP panel regressions with auction and CUSIP fixed effects, the authors conclude that the Fed buys more of bonds that look undervalued relative to a spline-model benchmark.
