In their baseline quantity regression, the coefficient on cheapness is 0.012, implying that a 1 basis point increase in cheapness raises the bond’s purchase quantity by about $12 million par value; they summarize this as a one standard deviation increase in cheapness (about 23 bps) increasing purchases by about $276 million. This setting is one of the paper’s two main causal results and is interpreted as evidence that the Fed harvests gains from trade by favoring undervalued bonds.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all emphasize as a central finding that bonds appearing cheaper are purchased more by the Fed in QE auctions.
Settings.H492: Section 5, Eq. (9), Table 8 columns (1)–(7), especially column (3), PDF pp. 12–13.
Settings.G493:
Treatment: Bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, measured as the spline-model-implied price minus the market mid-price divided by market mid-price, in basis points. This is a continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate linear panel regressions at the auction-CUSIP level for purchased bonds, relating the Fed’s auction cost (price markup over secondary market ask prices) to pre-auction cheapness and other pre-auction controls. Their main specification includes CUSIP and auction fixed effects with two-way clustered standard errors by auction and CUSIP. They report costs relative to the closest ask and, as an alternative horizon, relative to the 3:30 p.m. ask. Identification comes from within-CUSIP and within-auction variation in cheapness, interpreted through auction theory as allowing dealers to extract greater markups on bonds the Fed values more. Remaining concerns include measurement error in cheapness and omitted dealer supply conditions.

Identification: The authors’ strategy is that, because the Fed evaluates offers using a proprietary relative-value model, bonds with higher estimated cheapness should command higher dealer markups if dealers can infer the Fed’s preferences. Auction and CUSIP fixed effects absorb common auction conditions and time-invariant bond traits; controls absorb volatility and liquidity/scarcity proxies. The causal claim relies on parallel interpretation of residual cheapness variation as shifting the Fed’s willingness to buy that bond rather than merely reflecting omitted determinants of costs.

Setting: Using auction-CUSIP fixed-effects regressions for purchased bonds, the authors conclude that bonds appearing cheaper to the Fed impose higher execution costs. In the baseline markup regression relative to the closest ask, the cheapness coefficient is 0.115, so a one standard deviation increase in cheapness (23 bps) raises the Fed’s cost by about 2.6 cents per $100 par value. Relative to the 3:30 p.m. ask, the coefficient is 0.142, implying about 3.3 cents higher cost per $100. This is a central paper result and is interpreted as evidence that strategic dealers extract profits on bonds the Fed is more eager to buy.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion present the effect of cheapness on auction costs as a core result alongside the quantity result.
Settings.H493: Section 6, Eq. (11), Table 9 and Table 10 columns (1)–(7), especially column (3) and column (7), PDF pp. 14–15.
Settings.G494:
Treatment: Alternative continuous measures of bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, each based on a different yield-curve fitting or price input method. All are nonbinary continuous treatments in basis points or yield-basis-point differences, depending on specification.

Method: As a robustness exercise, the authors re-estimate the auction-CUSIP quantity regressions using multiple alternative constructions of the cheapness variable: positive smoothing penalty, a denser cubic-spline knot structure, yield-based cheapness, ask-price-based fitting, inclusion of short-maturity bonds, using previous-day prices, and a Svensson yield-curve model. The regressions remain linear panel FE models with CUSIP and auction fixed effects and two-way clustered standard errors. This robustness is substantive because the paper explicitly treats it as checking whether the inferred causal effect of cheapness on purchases depends on the proxy design.

Identification: The identification logic is the same as in the main quantity setting: residual variation in estimated bond cheapness after auction and bond fixed effects and controls proxies for variation in the Fed’s relative valuation. Here the emphasis is on robustness to measurement choices in constructing that proxy.

Setting: In robustness panel FE regressions, the authors show that the positive effect of cheapness on purchase quantity survives many alternative cheapness proxies. In Table A1, the coefficient on cheapness ranges from 0.009 under the Svensson model to 0.015 under the denser cubic-spline model, while the yield-based measure gives 0.076 on its own scale. The authors interpret this as confirming that the Fed’s preference for cheap bonds is not an artifact of the baseline spline specification.

Main role: These are robustness checks intended to show the main quantity result is not sensitive to how cheapness is measured.
Settings.G495:
Treatment: Alternative continuous measures of bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, based on alternative spline penalties, knot sets, yield-based cheapness, ask-price fitting, broader maturity inclusion, previous-day prices, and the Svensson model.

Method: As a robustness exercise, the authors re-estimate the auction-CUSIP cost regressions using multiple alternative cheapness measures generated from different yield-curve specifications or price inputs. These remain linear panel regressions with CUSIP and auction fixed effects and two-way clustered standard errors. The setting is distinct because it reports the sensitivity of the cost effect to alternative treatment measurement approaches.

Identification: Same as the main cost setting: with auction and CUSIP fixed effects and controls, variation in alternative cheapness proxies is interpreted as shifting the Fed’s relative willingness to buy specific bonds, which strategic dealers exploit through higher markups. The robustness aim is to show this does not depend on one particular proxy construction.

Setting: In robustness fixed-effects regressions, the authors find that the positive relation between bond cheapness and auction cost remains across alternative cheapness measures. Table A2 reports coefficients from 0.057 under the Svensson model to 0.147 under the denser cubic-spline model; the yield-based measure gives 0.799 on its own scale. The paper interprets this as showing the main inference—that cheaper bonds cost the Fed more—is robust to how cheapness is measured.

Main role: These are substantive robustness analyses supporting the core cost result.
Settings.G496:
Treatment: Bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, interacted with an indicator for whether the dealer belongs to the top five dealers ranked by aggregate profits. The focal treatment is continuous cheapness; top-five status is binary heterogeneity, not the main treatment itself.

Method: The authors estimate dealer-level auction-CUSIP panel regressions of each dealer’s sales quantity to the Fed on bond cheapness, liquidity/scarcity controls, and interactions with an indicator for being one of the top five most profitable dealers. The baseline includes auction and CUSIP fixed effects, plus interactions of the top-five indicator with auction and CUSIP fixed effects in the most saturated specification, and two-way clustered standard errors by auction and CUSIP. This design is used to infer whether top dealers are more responsive in supplying bonds that the Fed prefers.

Identification: The strategy compares how dealer-level accepted quantities covary with cheapness across top-five and other dealers, holding constant auction and CUSIP effects and standard controls. The authors interpret stronger sensitivity among top dealers as evidence of comparative advantage in sourcing bonds the Fed values. The main assumption is that conditional on controls and fixed effects, the interaction between cheapness and top-five status captures supply responsiveness rather than omitted dealer-specific confounds.

Setting: At the dealer-CUSIP-auction level, the authors find that top dealers supply more of the bonds that appear cheapest to the Fed. In Table 12, column (1), the non-top-five slope on cheapness is 0.0002 and the interaction 1(Top 5)×Cheapness is 0.0023, implying roughly 2.5 million more dealer sales per 1 bp increase in cheapness for top-five dealers versus only 0.2 million for others; the separate-sample regressions in columns (3) and (4) similarly show 0.0026 for top dealers and 0.0003 for others. The paper interprets this as top dealers having a comparative advantage in finding and selling the bonds the Fed prefers.

Main role: This dealer-heterogeneity exercise is important to mechanism but is secondary to the paper’s central quantity and cost results.
Settings.H496: Section 7, Eq. (14), Table 12 columns (1)–(4), PDF pp. 16–17.
Settings.G497:
Treatment: Bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, interacted with dealer top-five status. The main treatment is continuous cheapness; the top-five indicator defines heterogeneous effects.

Method: The authors estimate dealer-level auction-CUSIP panel regressions of each dealer’s markup on selling a bond to the Fed, as a function of bond cheapness, liquidity/scarcity controls, and interactions with an indicator for belonging to the top five dealers by aggregate profits. The regressions include auction and CUSIP fixed effects and in the most saturated specification top-five interactions with those fixed effects, with two-way clustered standard errors by auction and CUSIP. This is used to infer whether non-top dealers charge larger markups on the bonds the Fed appears to prefer.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-dealer heterogeneity in markup sensitivity to bond cheapness after controlling for auction and CUSIP effects and observables. The paper’s interpretation is that if dealers can infer the Fed’s relative valuation, markup sensitivity to cheapness reveals strategic pricing power, and differences between top-five and other dealers reveal heterogeneity in business models or comparative advantage.

Setting: In dealer-level markup regressions, the authors find that non-top-five dealers charge somewhat more for bonds that are cheap to the Fed. Table 12, column (5), shows a cheapness slope of 0.0705 for non-top-five dealers and an interaction of -0.0303 for top-five dealers, implying about 0.04 cents per $100 per 1 bp for top dealers versus about 0.07 for others; separate regressions in columns (7) and (8) show 0.0412 for top-five dealers and 0.0673 for others. The authors interpret this as non-top dealers having a moderate comparative advantage in charging higher prices, though not enough to offset top dealers’ quantity advantage.

Main role: This is a mechanism result on dealer heterogeneity rather than one of the headline paper-wide causal estimates.
Settings.H497: Section 7, Eq. (15), Table 12 columns (5)–(8), PDF pp. 16–17.
Settings.G498:
Treatment: Winsorized versions of the continuous cheapness measure, trimmed at the top and bottom 0.5% or 1% of the cheapness distribution.

Method: As an additional robustness exercise, the authors re-estimate the main quantity and cost regressions after winsorizing the cheapness variable at the top and bottom 0.5% and 1%. These remain linear panel FE models with CUSIP and auction fixed effects and two-way clustered standard errors. The exercise is intended to show that the main causal interpretations are not driven by outliers in the cheapness proxy.

Identification: Same FE identification as the main settings, but applied to winsorized cheapness to reduce influence of extreme observations. The paper uses this to argue that outliers in the estimated cheapness proxy do not drive the results.

Setting: After winsorizing cheapness, the main FE regressions remain essentially unchanged. In Table A3, the purchase-quantity coefficient on cheapness is 0.013 under both winsorization rules, while the auction-cost coefficient is 0.117 when winsorized at 0.5% tails and 0.120 when winsorized at 1% tails. The paper interprets this as evidence that the positive effects of cheapness on both purchases and costs are not driven by outliers.

Main role: This is an outlier-robustness check supporting the main quantity and cost findings.
Settings.G499:
Treatment: Bond cheapness at the auction-CUSIP level, measured continuously in basis points, estimated separately within maturity-based subsamples (>10 years versus <=10 years by remaining or original maturity).

Method: As a maturity-based heterogeneity robustness analysis, the authors split the sample by time to maturity and by original maturity at a ten-year cutoff, then re-estimate the main auction-CUSIP quantity and cost regressions separately within subsamples. These are linear panel FE regressions with CUSIP and auction fixed effects and two-way clustered standard errors. The exercise tests whether the main causal relations differ between shorter- and longer-maturity securities.

Identification: Within each maturity subsample, the same FE identification is used as in the main regressions. The authors interpret persistent positive cheapness coefficients across subsamples as evidence that the main mechanism applies across notes and bonds, though more strongly for longer maturities.

Setting: In maturity-split FE regressions, the positive effects of cheapness on purchase quantity and auction cost remain, with larger point estimates for longer-maturity securities. Table A4 shows, for example, by remaining maturity, a purchase-quantity coefficient of 0.017 and markup coefficient of 0.128 for bonds with more than 10 years to maturity, versus 0.002 and 0.094 for shorter-maturity bonds; by original maturity, the coefficients are 0.024 and 0.220 for >10-year securities versus 0.002 and 0.074 for <=10-year securities. The paper interprets this as robustness with stronger effects among longer-duration bonds.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness/heterogeneity analysis rather than a headline design.
Settings.G500:
Treatment: Exposure to the post-April 1, 2012 integrated fee model (Fee=1 on or after April 1, 2012; 0 before). In this DiD-style before/after design, the causal exposure is the regulatory regime that raised the cost of sending messages to Canadian marketplaces and thereby reduced HFT activity. Binary post-policy indicator.

Method: The authors estimate a conventional difference-in-differences style regression around IIROC's April 1, 2012 integrated fee model, which they interpret as an exogenous negative shock to HFT activity. The estimating equation is linear OLS at the institutional-trade level with a post-fee indicator (Fee), log trade size, and their interaction, plus stock fixed effects and double-clustered standard errors by stock and date. The post indicator captures the change in average fixed execution cost ('spread'), while the interaction with log trade size captures the change in marginal price impact after the regulation. Main implementations include a 6-month window around the reform, specifications with additional controls (trade aggressiveness, time to completion, stock dollar volume), the full sample, and subsamples redefining institutional trades by minimum size thresholds of $500,000 and $1 million. Identification relies on before/after comparisons induced by the regulatory fee change and the interpretation that the fee disproportionately affected HFTs, not institutions.

Identification: The paper treats the integrated fee model as plausibly exogenous variation that raised message costs and disproportionately reduced HFT order activity, while leaving institutional order arrivals largely unchanged. Comparing institutional execution costs before versus after the fee change, and allowing effects to vary with trade size via Fee×log(trade size), is intended to identify how impaired HFT order adjustment changes spread and price impact. Key assumptions are that no other coincident shocks differentially altered institutional execution costs in ways loading on trade size, and that stock fixed effects plus controls absorb stable cross-stock differences and some market-wide execution determinants. The authors partly probe alternative explanations through additional controls, wider sample periods, and subgroup heterogeneity.

Setting: Using a conventional before/after DiD-style regression around IIROC's April 1, 2012 integrated fee model, the authors conclude that a policy-induced reduction in HFT activity increased the fixed-cost component of institutional execution but reduced the price-impact component. In Table 4 column 1, the coefficient on Fee is 3.002 bps, interpreted as a rise in average spread cost, while Fee×ln(T Size) is -0.981, implying a 14.5% decline in the price-impact slope relative to the pre-fee ln(T Size) coefficient of 6.742. They calculate a break-even institutional trade size of about $2.1 million, above which lower price impact dominates wider spreads. Similar patterns hold with added controls, over the full sample, and in larger-trade subsamples, making this a central causal result of the paper.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all foreground the regulatory-change evidence as the paper's main causal link between HFT activity and institutional trading costs.
Settings.H500: Section 3.1 'Baseline results,' Equation (3), Table 4 columns (1)-(5), PDF pp. 15-16.
Settings.G501:
Treatment: Exposure to the post-April 1, 2012 integrated fee model (Fee=1 after the regulation). In this setting the treatment is still the post-fee regime, but the estimand is allowed to differ by institutional trader type defined by historical profitability/informativeness terciles.

Method: The authors estimate subgroup-specific and pooled conventional DiD regressions around the same April 1, 2012 fee reform, splitting institutional trades by trader 'informativeness' terciles based on out-of-sample profitability of past trades. The linear regressions use the post-fee indicator, log trade size, and their interaction, with stock fixed effects and standard errors double-clustered by stock and date. Columns 1-3 run the specification separately for high-, medium-, and low-informed groups; column 4 pools groups and adds interactions with group indicators to compare differential post-fee changes in spread and price impact across groups.

Identification: The strategy combines the fee-change before/after variation with cross-group heterogeneity in institutions' inferred informativeness. The paper argues that if HFTs especially compete against informed institutions, then the fee-induced impairment of HFT order adjustment should reduce price impact most for the historically most informed group. This differential response is interpreted as strengthening causality because broad market-condition changes around the reform are less likely to differentially affect informed versus uninformed institutional traders. Assumptions include that the historical-profitability grouping proxies for information-based trading and that other contemporaneous shocks do not differentially change execution costs by these groups in the same pattern.

Setting: Using DiD regressions by trader informativeness group, the authors find that the fee-induced reduction in HFT activity lowers price impact most strongly for informed institutions. In Table 5 column 1, for the high-informed group the Fee×ln(T Size) coefficient is -2.693 relative to a baseline ln(T Size) coefficient of 9.790, which they summarize as a 27.5% reduction in price impact. The medium-informed group shows a smaller 10.1% reduction (-0.889 relative to 8.797), and the low-informed group shows no statistically significant reduction. In the pooled interaction regression, the high-informed group experiences a significantly more negative price-impact change than the other groups. This is a major causal result because it links HFT particularly to the trading costs of informed institutional orders.

Main role: This heterogeneity analysis directly supports a central conclusion in the introduction and conclusion that HFT especially raises execution costs for informed institutional traders.
Settings.H501: Section 3.2 'Price impact analysis by institutional trader type,' Equation (4), Figure 2, Table 5 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 17-21.
Settings.G502:
Treatment: Presence of a large institutional trade during the 15-minute interval, coded via L: 1 if an institutional buy is being executed, -1 if an institutional sell is being executed, and 0 otherwise. For the interaction coefficients, the effective treatment is whether an institutional trade is underway (|L|=1) versus not underway, conditional on HFT inventory state.

Method: The authors estimate linear inventory-dynamics regressions adapted from Hansch, Naik, and Viswanathan (1998), relating a primary HFT market maker's normalized 15-minute inventory change to its lagged normalized inventory interacted with bins for inventory extremeness. They then add an indicator for whether a large institutional trade is underway and interactions between that indicator and lagged inventory-bin terms. The implementation is pooled OLS with double-clustered standard errors by stock and date; no high-dimensional FE battery is reported for these regressions. Columns 1-3 estimate mean reversion in the full sample and separately when institutional buys or sells are underway; column 4 formally pools and interacts lagged inventory-bin terms with an institutional-trade indicator and includes institutional-trade controls (aggressiveness, time to completion, trade size).

Identification: Identification is observational and comes from within-HFT/stock/time variation in whether a large institutional trade is underway and from the HFT's lagged inventory state. The paper interprets faster mean reversion during institutional trade execution as evidence that HFTs infer information from institutional order flow and actively manage inventory in response. The main concern is that institutional-trade periods differ from other periods in other ways correlated with HFT trading; the authors partially address this by conditioning on inventory bins and including institutional-trade characteristics, but the design remains correlational rather than based on an external quasi-experiment.

Setting: Adapting the HNV inventory model, the authors conclude that institutional trade execution causes market-making HFTs to revert inventory faster. In Table 6 column 1, HFTs mean-revert 27.6% of a nonextreme inventory position in the next 15 minutes and 37.7% of an extreme position, corresponding to half-lives of 32.2 and 22.0 minutes. In column 4, the interaction terms with |L| show that when a large institutional trade is underway, the mean-reversion rate rises by 0.109 for nonextreme inventories and 0.069 for extreme inventories; the authors summarize this as reversion increasing from 21.6% to 32.4% for nonextreme positions and from 34.7% to 41.6% for extreme positions. They interpret roughly one-third of nonextreme-period reversion during institutional-trade execution as attributable to information inferred from the institutional trade. This mechanism evidence materially supports the paper's central story.

Main role: The paper's second core contribution is the mechanism evidence on how HFTs interact with institutional orders; the inventory-reversion results are emphasized in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H502: Section 4.1 'HFT inventory and quote dynamics,' Equation (5), Equation (6), Table 6 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 21-25.
Settings.G503:
Treatment: Presence and direction of a large institutional trade in the prior/current interval, summarized by L=1 for institutional buy, -1 for institutional sell, 0 otherwise; interaction results focus on whether a large institutional trade is underway (|L|=1) and how that changes quote behavior given HFT inventory state.

Method: The authors estimate linear regressions of normalized net HFT order submission activity (Qm,j,t) on lagged normalized HFT inventory interacted with inventory-state bins, an institutional-trade indicator L, and interactions between the institutional-trade indicator and lagged inventory-bin terms. The sample is 15-minute stock-period observations for the primary HFT market maker. Reported specifications add institutional-trade controls and use double-clustered standard errors by stock and date. These are identifying FE-style panel regressions without a three-way absorbed FE structure.

Identification: Identification is from observational variation in institutional-trade presence and HFT inventory state within the panel. The authors argue that if HFTs infer information from institutional order flow and actively manage inventory, they should shift quote submissions toward the same direction as the institutional trade and toward unwinding risky inventory positions. The necessary assumption is that, conditional on controls and inventory state, periods with institutional trades are otherwise comparable for quote-submission behavior; this remains a correlational mechanism analysis.

Setting: The quote-dynamics regressions suggest that institutional trade execution causes HFTs to tilt their submitted limit orders in the same direction as the institutional trade and to do so more aggressively when inventory is extreme. In Table 7, lagged positive inventory predicts more net sell order submission, and the coefficient on L is positive, meaning HFTs submit more same-direction limit orders when institutional buys are underway and more sell-side orders when institutional sells are underway. In column 4, the interaction terms between inventory-state variables and |L| are all negative, implying stronger same-direction quote adjustment during institutional-trade execution at every inventory level. These results support the paper's mechanism that HFTs compete with large institutional trades rather than simply passively accommodating them.

Main role: This is supporting mechanism evidence extending the inventory results; the paper emphasizes it, but less centrally than the regulatory-cost and inventory-reversion findings.
Settings.H503: Section 4.1 'HFT inventory and quote dynamics,' Table 7 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 25-27.
Settings.G504:
Treatment: Institutional trade direction underway in the interval: institutional buy indicator (1B) and institutional sell indicator (1S), effectively binary treatment contrasts for presence of a buy or sell institutional trade versus no such trade.

Method: The authors run linear panel regressions of abnormal HFT buy trade volume, abnormal HFT sell trade volume, abnormal HFT buy limit-order volume, and abnormal HFT sell limit-order volume on lagged HFT inventory-bin interactions and indicators for whether an institutional buy (1B) or sell (1S) order is underway, with controls for institutional trade aggressiveness, time to completion, trade size, and abnormal stock dollar volume. Standard errors are double-clustered by stock and date. The objective is to decompose net HFT responses into same-direction versus opposite-direction trading and order activity.

Identification: The paper uses within-panel variation in whether an institutional buy or sell is underway to see whether HFT abnormal activity shifts in the same or opposite direction. The causal interpretation is that institutional trades induce HFT response. Assumptions are that, conditional on inventory state and included controls, the institutional-trade indicators capture the relevant directional shock; remaining endogeneity from common information shocks is not fully ruled out.

Setting: The abnormal-activity regressions imply that institutional trade execution induces HFTs to increase same-direction trading and order submission more than opposite-direction activity. In Table 8, an institutional buy raises abnormal HFT buy volume by 0.061 while raising sell volume only 0.026; the buy-minus-sell differential is 0.039 (p=.000). Likewise, an institutional sell raises abnormal HFT sell volume by 0.056 more than buy volume, with a buy-minus-sell differential of -0.030 (p=.000). For limit orders, institutional buys raise abnormal buy-order activity by 0.048 versus sell-order activity by 0.027, producing a 0.032 differential (p=.000), while the sell-order differential is smaller and not significant. The authors interpret this as stronger support for back-running/same-direction competition than for a pure reduction in opposite-side liquidity supply.

Main role: These are substantive mechanism decompositions supporting the paper's interpretation that HFTs back-run/compete with institutional orders, but they are not the headline causal design.
Settings.H504: Section 4.2 'Abnormal HFT buying and selling activity,' Table 8 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 27-29.
Settings.G505:
Treatment: Predicted component of the signed large institutional trade indicator L, where L=1 for institutional buy, -1 for institutional sell, 0 otherwise, predicted from publicly observable lagged returns, trade imbalances, and limit-order imbalances. In column 5, the treatment is the predicted component of aggressive institutional trades only. This is a continuous signed predicted exposure, not a binary treatment.

Method: The authors first estimate nonlinear probit models for whether an institutional buy or sell occurs in the upcoming 15-minute interval as a function of lagged returns, trade imbalances, and limit-order imbalances with stock fixed effects and double-clustered standard errors. They then use the predicted component of the signed institutional-trade indicator L from that first-stage prediction in linear OLS regressions of normalized HFT inventory change and, in one specification, aggressive-trade-only predicted L. Because the key implemented causal predictor comes from a nonlinear prediction step and is then used to study HFT response rather than as a standard linear IV/2SLS design, this setting fits 'Other.'

Identification: The argument is that publicly observable variables predict large institutional trades, and the predicted component of those trades should then move HFT inventories if HFTs use that information to compete with institutions. This is not a clean exogenous design: the predicted institutional-trade component may proxy for broader momentum or order-flow conditions. The authors acknowledge this concern and sharpen the argument by focusing on aggressive institutional trades, which are more likely information-based and more likely to generate the observed public signals.

Setting: Using a probit-plus-OLS prediction framework, the authors provide suggestive evidence that HFTs use publicly observable signals to infer and trade with institutional orders. Table 9 columns 1-2 show that lagged returns, trade imbalances, and limit-order imbalances predict institutional buys and sells. In columns 4-5, the predicted component of the signed institutional-trade indicator is positively related to HFT inventory changes: the coefficient on Pred. L is 0.161 using all institutional trades and 0.338 using only aggressive institutional trades. The stronger coefficient for aggressive trades supports the paper's interpretation that HFTs use public information to compete with likely information-based institutional orders, though the authors treat this as suggestive rather than definitive causal evidence.

Main role: This is suggestive supporting evidence about the information HFTs use; the paper explicitly labels it as suggestive rather than core identification.
Settings.H505: Section 4.3 'Large trade predictors and HFT dynamics,' Equation (7), Table 9 columns (1)-(5), PDF pp. 29-32.
Settings.G506:
Treatment: Continuous market-condition measures: relative bid-ask spread, TED spread, FX VIX or its uncertainty/risk-aversion components, realized volatility, trading volume, and a U.S. dollar appreciation indicator depending on the column. The central interpreted treatment for the main liquidity claim is the relative bid-ask spread (percent change in transaction costs) affecting realized Amihud.

Method: Pooled linear time-series/panel-style regressions of daily FX outcomes across 29 currency pairs over November 2011–September 2021. The authors regress daily trading volume, realized volatility (RPV), realized Amihud illiquidity, and relative bid-ask spread on contemporaneous market-condition variables and a lagged dependent variable. Regressors include RPV or volume, relative bid-ask spread, TED spread, FX VIX or its decomposition into uncertainty and risk aversion, a U.S.-dollar-appreciation dummy, and day-of-week dummies. Standard errors are reported as robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. The paper explicitly says this exercise is aimed at documenting correlation patterns rather than causation, but it also interprets coefficients substantively as determinants/associations of liquidity and trading impact.

Identification: No quasi-experimental source of variation is used. Identification comes from conditional linear regression relationships in pooled daily data, controlling for lagged outcomes and observed market conditions. The paper acknowledges likely mutual endogeneity among some regressors and states that the focus is on novel correlation patterns rather than causation. The intended interpretation is still that worsening market conditions are associated with larger trading impact and lower liquidity.

Setting: Using pooled daily regressions across 29 FX pairs, the paper relates trading volume, realized volatility, realized Amihud illiquidity, and bid-ask spreads to transaction costs and market-stress variables. The principal substantive claim is that FX price impact rises with transaction costs, money-market strain, uncertainty, and risk aversion. For example, the authors state that a 1% increase in transaction costs is associated with a 0.20% increase in realized Amihud illiquidity. They also find that volume rises with volatility, while higher spreads and uncertainty reduce trading activity. These regressions are central to the paper’s claim that thinner, more stressed markets have higher trading impact.

Main role: A core aim of the paper is to study what determines FX price impact/liquidity. The abstract and introduction highlight that price impact increases with transaction costs, money market stress, uncertainty, and risk aversion; Table 2 provides those central estimates.
Settings.H506: Section 4.1 'Determinants of trading volume, volatility, and liquidity', Eq. (2), Table 2, PDF pp. 9–11 (journal pp. 867–869).
Settings.G507:
Treatment: Lagged daily relative bid-ask spread (BASt-1) and lagged realized Amihud (At-1) as dynamic treatments, with the key interpreted treatment being yesterday’s relative bid-ask spread affecting today’s realized Amihud.

Method: A two-variable VAR-X in logs with daily realized Amihud and daily relative bid-ask spread as endogenous variables, plus exogenous controls (USD, TED, VXY, and day-of-week dummies). The design uses lagged endogenous variables to study dynamic propagation between transaction-cost liquidity and price-impact liquidity. This is a standard dynamic linear specification without multi-way absorbed fixed effects.

Identification: Identification is from temporal ordering in a daily VAR-X: past spread predicts current realized Amihud conditional on lagged Amihud and observed controls. Endogeneity is mitigated only by using lagged variables and conditioning variables; no external instrument or natural experiment is used. The paper interprets the directional lag from spreads to future trading impact as suggestive that quote setting shapes subsequent market depth.

Setting: In a daily VAR-X for realized Amihud and relative bid-ask spread, the authors find that lagged spreads positively predict current realized Amihud, while lagged realized Amihud does not similarly predict spreads. Table 4 reports a coefficient of 0.044 on BASt-1 in the At equation and -0.007 on At-1 in the BASt equation. The paper interprets this as dealers’ quote-setting and spreads subsequently determining market depth and trading impact, providing a dynamic mechanism linking transaction costs to future price impact.

Main role: This VAR-X is a supporting dynamic analysis clarifying the interaction between the two liquidity dimensions. It is not the paper’s headline identification strategy, but it substantively supports the mechanism that spreads precede price impact.
Settings.H507: End of Section 4.2, Table 4, PDF p. 13 (journal p. 871).
Settings.G508:
Treatment: Average realized Amihud illiquidity of the two indirect currency pairs in a EURUSD triangular-arbitrage triplet, Ā^{x|y;z}; in interacted specifications, a holiday dummy (bank holiday in the United States or euro area) and its interaction with illiquidity. Illiquidity is continuous; holiday is binary but supplementary.

Method: OLS regressions of triangular-arbitrage mispricing on average realized Amihud illiquidity of the two indirect legs forming the synthetic exchange rate for EURUSD triplets. The basic specification regresses RPVE on average illiquidity, and an augmented specification adds holiday dummies (U.S. or euro-area bank holidays) and interactions between holidays and illiquidity. Newey-West robust standard errors are used. This is a linear reduced-form analysis exploiting plausibly exogenous holidays but implemented as regression adjustment rather than a formal DiD design.

Identification: The identifying idea is that higher average illiquidity in the indirect trading legs limits arbitrage and raises deviations from triangular no-arbitrage. Holidays are argued to exogenously reduce trading activity and liquidity, shifting the mispricing-illiquidity relation. The specification assumes conditional linearity and that holiday indicators capture exogenous thinning of markets rather than omitted shocks. This is not a formal causal design, but the paper interprets the results causally as thinner markets impairing price efficiency.

Setting: The paper regresses triangular-arbitrage pricing errors for EURUSD triplets on the average illiquidity of the two indirect FX legs and finds a systematically positive relation: more trading impact implies more no-arbitrage violations. In Table 5, the baseline coefficient β is positive and significant across triplets—for example 0.097 for CHF, 0.073 for GBP, 0.304 for NOK, 0.186 for SEK, 0.074 for AUD, 0.055 for CAD, and 0.071 for JPY. When adding U.S.-holiday interactions, the slope often changes and U.S. holidays shift the relationship, which the authors interpret as evidence that exogenous reductions in liquidity worsen or reconfigure price efficiency. This is a core result supporting the paper’s thesis that illiquidity impedes arbitrage and market efficiency.

Main role: A central contribution of the paper is that liquidity begets price efficiency. The holiday-augmented mispricing-on-illiquidity regressions are a main empirical pillar for that claim and are highlighted in the introduction and conclusions.
Settings.H508: Section 5.1 'Holidays', Eq. (4), Fig. 7, Table 5, PDF pp. 13–15 (journal pp. 871–873).
Settings.G509:
Treatment: Continuous illiquidity of each indirect leg in the triangular parity: A^{x|z} and A^{z|y}. With EURUSD as the direct pair, one regressor corresponds to euro-based indirect-pair illiquidity and the other to dollar-based indirect-pair illiquidity.

Method: OLS regressions of triangular-arbitrage mispricing on the separate realized Amihud illiquidity measures of the two indirect legs in the EURUSD triangle: one euro-based leg and one dollar-based leg. The paper also includes controls for illiquidity and relative bid-ask spread of the direct EURUSD rate to mitigate omitted-variable bias. Newey-West robust standard errors are used. This is the non-IV version of the paper’s disentangling exercise.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-time variation in the separate illiquidity of the euro-based and dollar-based indirect legs, conditional on direct-pair controls. The paper explicitly worries that these regressors are endogenous because of omitted variables, measurement error, and simultaneity from common global trading factors. Thus OLS is treated as suggestive, motivating the IV strategy that follows.

Setting: In OLS regressions separating the two indirect legs’ illiquidity in EURUSD triangles, the paper asks whether euro-leg or dollar-leg liquidity frictions generate triangular-arbitrage deviations. Table 6 shows that at least one coefficient is usually positive and significant, and the euro-leg coefficient is often positive and sizable—for example 0.092 for CHF, 0.074 for GBP, 0.558 for NOK, 0.363 for SEK, 0.082 for AUD, and 0.056 for JPY—while the dollar-leg coefficient is often small or negative. The authors interpret this as suggestive evidence that euro-based pairs, traded in thinner markets, concentrate the illiquidity frictions linked to mispricing, whereas dollar vehicle pairs are less connected to arbitrage deviations.

Main role: Disentangling whether euro-side or dollar-side liquidity drives price efficiency is one of the paper’s central questions. The OLS specification is part of that main analysis, though the IV version is the preferred attempt to address endogeneity.
Settings.H509: Section 5.3 'Disentangling the mispricing and illiquidity relation', Eq. (5), Table 6 columns labeled OLS, PDF pp. 17–20 (journal pp. 875–878).
Settings.G510:
Treatment: Endogenous continuous illiquidity of the separate indirect triangular-arbitrage legs, especially euro-based-leg illiquidity and dollar-based-leg illiquidity for EURUSD triplets. These are instrumented with granular illiquidity shocks derived from cross-sectional heterogeneity in currency-pair illiquidity.

Method: Two-stage least squares using granular instrumental variables (GIV) to instrument the illiquidity of the separate indirect legs in EURUSD triangular-arbitrage regressions. Instruments are constructed as the difference between volume-weighted and equally weighted aggregate illiquidity measures for a given base currency (e.g., EUR_t and USD_t), following Gabaix and Koijen (2020). In some specifications, lags of the endogenous illiquidity regressors are added as further instruments to address errors-in-variables in realized Amihud. The second stage regresses triangular mispricing RPVE on instrumented euro-leg and dollar-leg illiquidity, controlling for the direct pair’s illiquidity and relative bid-ask spread. The paper reports first-stage F statistics and Wu-Hausman tests.

Identification: The paper argues that separate leg illiquidity measures are endogenous due to omitted variables, measurement error, and common global trading factors simultaneously affecting illiquidity and mispricing. The GIV approach extracts idiosyncratic illiquidity shocks for a base currency by differencing volume-weighted and equally weighted aggregate illiquidity measures across many currency pairs, purging the common systematic illiquidity component under the maintained factor-structure assumptions. Relevance is shown by strong first-stage F statistics in most cases; exclusion requires that these idiosyncratic granular shocks affect triangular mispricing only through the targeted currency-leg illiquidity. Lagged illiquidity instruments are additionally used in some columns to mitigate errors-in-variables.

Setting: Using granular 2SLS, the paper instruments the euro-leg and dollar-leg illiquidity entering EURUSD triangular-arbitrage mispricing equations. Across triplets, the instrumented euro-leg coefficient is typically positive and significant—e.g., for CHF 0.196, GBP 0.145, NOK 0.637, SEK 0.470, AUD 0.128, CAD 0.066, and JPY 0.149 in the GIV columns—whereas the dollar-leg coefficient is often small, zero, or negative (e.g., NOK -0.284, SEK -0.168, AUD -0.075, JPY -0.055). The authors conclude that euro-based indirect pairs concentrate the illiquidity frictions behind arbitrage deviations, while dollar vehicle pairs are mostly disconnected, implying that dollar liquidity is especially important for FX price efficiency. This is one of the paper’s most important causal interpretations.

Main role: The introduction explicitly highlights this granular IV exercise as the paper’s method to mitigate endogeneity when asking whether dollar liquidity rather than euro liquidity supports price efficiency. It is a central identification strategy for a main claim.
Settings.H510: Section 5.3.1 'Granular instrumental variables', Eq. (6)–(7), Figs. 10–11, Table 6 columns labeled GIV and Lags, PDF pp. 18–20 (journal pp. 876–878).
Settings.G511:
Treatment: Deviation of illiquidity and mispricing from their long-run cointegrating equilibrium; the substantive treatment interpretation emphasized by the paper is shocks to illiquidity affecting future mispricing and the equilibrium adjustment process.

Method: Bivariate fractional vector error-correction model (FVECM) for mispricing (RPVE) and average realized Amihud illiquidity in EURUSD triangular-arbitrage triplets. The model allows fractional integration and cointegration and estimates a long-run equilibrium relation with error-correction speeds. This is not one of the listed linear reduced-form causal categories; it is a dynamic cointegration/error-correction system.

Identification: Identification is based on time-series cointegration between mispricing and illiquidity and on estimated error-correction coefficients in a fractional VECM. The maintained assumption is that these two series share a stable long-run equilibrium for a given triplet. Causal interpretation is limited and dynamic: shocks moving the system away from equilibrium are followed mainly by adjustment in liquidity rather than mispricing, according to the estimated α coefficients.

Setting: The FVECM analysis finds that mispricing and illiquidity are positively tied in a long-run equilibrium across EURUSD triplets. Table 7 reports cointegration rank tests that do not reject rank 1, cointegration coefficients β2 positive and near one (for example 0.927 for SEK, 1.002 for NOK, 0.872 for JPY, 0.776 for GBP), and significant adjustment coefficients on illiquidity but not on mispricing. The authors interpret this as showing that illiquidity and price inefficiency move together in equilibrium and that, after shocks, liquidity adjustment rather than mispricing adjustment restores equilibrium. This dynamic result reinforces the broader claim that liquidity begets FX price efficiency.

Main role: This is an additional dynamic analysis deepening the main liquidity-efficiency link. It supports the paper’s conclusions but is not the main reduced-form identification design.
Settings.H511: Section 5.4 'Long-term equilibrium between mispricing and illiquidity', Eq. (8), Table 7, PDF pp. 20–21 (journal pp. 878–879).
Settings.G512:
Treatment: High-frequency quotation activity measured by quote updates: any change in the prevailing best bid or offer price or displayed size at the best bid or offer across all exchanges, counted within a half-hour interval. Implemented as a binary contrast between high and low update groups defined by the median number of updates in the prior half-hour within size × trade quintiles.

Method: In the main US cross-sectional design, the authors sort stocks within size quintiles and trade-frequency quintiles into low- versus high-quote-update groups using the median number of quote updates in the prior half-hour, then compare subsequent half-hour market-quality outcomes across these groups. This is a grouped regression-adjustment/stratification design rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental design. Identification comes from conditioning on firm size and contemporaneous trading activity, and from lagging the update measure by one half-hour, but the authors explicitly note remaining endogeneity because quote updates, prices, and trading are jointly determined. Outcomes reported together at this location are deviations of variance ratios from one, higher-frequency variance-ratio deviations for large-cap stocks, and effective half-spreads.

Identification: The intended identifying variation is cross-sectional and within-size/within-trade-frequency variation in prior-half-hour quote-update intensity. By comparing high- versus low-update stocks after conditioning on size and trade intensity, and by measuring updates before outcomes, the paper aims to isolate the effect of quotation speed on price efficiency and trading costs. The key endogeneity concern is selection: more liquid or more informationally efficient stocks may attract more high-frequency quoting. The authors explicitly state that these cross-sectional tests do not imply causation because quote updates and prices are jointly determined.

Setting: Using the full US stock cross section from 2009 to 2011, the authors compare subsequent market quality for stocks with high versus low prior-half-hour quote updating, after grouping by size and trading activity. They interpret the evidence as showing that higher quotation activity improves market quality: the average difference in the absolute deviation of variance ratios from one is negative in every size × trade quintile, ranging from about -0.017 to -0.037 for the 15-second/five-minute variance-ratio measure, and effective half-spreads are generally lower in high-update groups by roughly 0.06 to 6.10 basis points. For large-cap stocks at sub-second horizons, differences in variance-ratio deviations are also mostly negative in trade quintiles 2-4. The paper treats these as evidence consistent with beneficial effects of high-frequency quoting, while cautioning that the design remains endogenous.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize the paper's core finding that higher quote activity is associated with prices closer to a random walk and lower trading costs in the full US cross section. This cross-sectional design is a central empirical pillar, even though the authors acknowledge it is not fully causal.
Settings.H512: Section 3.2-3.4, Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Table 3 Panels A-C, PDF pp. 8-10.
Settings.G513:
Treatment: High-frequency quotation activity, measured as the number of quote updates in the prior half-hour, implemented as a binary high-versus-low update group within size × trade quintiles.

Method: This setting decomposes the effective spread results from the US cross-sectional sorting design into realized spreads and price impact across short horizons from 1 to 20 seconds after each trade. Stocks are first sorted by size, trade quintile, and low/high prior-half-hour quote updates, and the authors compare cross-sectional averages between high- and low-update groups. The design remains observational regression adjustment/stratification with no external quasi-experimental source of variation. The sample for computation is two randomly selected trading days per month in 2010-2011.

Identification: As in the main cross-sectional US tests, identification relies on comparing stocks with differing lagged quote-update intensity after stratifying on size and trading activity. The endogeneity concern remains that more liquid or otherwise different stocks may have both more updates and lower spreads. The decomposition is descriptive-causal in intent, used to infer whether quote updates reduce liquidity-provider rents or adverse-selection losses.

Setting: In a spread-decomposition robustness exercise using US millisecond data, the authors interpret differences between high- and low-update stocks as showing how faster quote updating affects trading costs. Effective-spread differences are usually negative, and most of the reduction is attributed to lower realized spreads rather than lower price impact. For example, Table 4 reports mostly negative realized-spread differences across size and trade quintiles, leading the authors to conclude that increased competition among liquidity providers in higher-update environments compresses realized spreads and thereby lowers effective spreads. This is a supportive causal interpretation rather than the paper's primary identifying evidence.

Main role: This decomposition supports the central claim about lower trading costs by showing where the effective-spread reduction comes from, but it is a mechanism/subcomponent analysis rather than the paper's headline design.
Settings.G514:
Treatment: Occurrence of a large aggregated liquidity drawdown ('collapsed sweep') of at least 10,000 shares, separately for buyer-initiated and seller-initiated sweeps. The implemented treatment contrast is post-sweep versus pre-sweep around the event window.

Method: The authors identify large buyer- and seller-initiated liquidity drawdowns in US millisecond data by first finding same-millisecond trades across multiple venues ('sweeps'), collapsing nearby same-side sweeps when the time between adjacent sweeps is less than the stock's expected trade interval, and restricting to aggregated sweeps of at least 10,000 shares. They then compare variance-ratio deviations and effective spreads in 300-second windows before versus after the drawdown. This is a before/after event comparison without a separate control group or formal DiD, so it is best classified as regression adjustment/mean-contrast observational analysis. The intended causal interpretation is about the effect of a large liquidity drawdown on subsequent price efficiency and trading costs.

Identification: The design treats large, rapid liquidity drawdowns as shocks to liquidity demand and examines whether market quality worsens immediately afterward. The identifying idea is temporal comparison within the same stock around an extreme event, with 300-second pre/post windows. Threats include event selection, time-varying confounders, and the fact that sweeps are endogenous to market conditions; there is no untreated control group. The paper argues that this approach is representative and avoids cherry-picking specific crashes.

Setting: Using 4.4 million aggregated US liquidity sweeps of at least 10,000 shares, the authors study whether large, extremely rapid liquidity extractions harm subsequent market quality. They find little evidence of deterioration after the event. In Table 5 Panel A, post-minus-pre changes in the absolute deviation of variance ratios from one are slightly negative for both buyer- and seller-initiated sweeps across size quintiles (for example, -0.0047 for large-cap buyer-initiated sweeps and -0.0039 for large-cap seller-initiated sweeps). In Panel B, post-minus-pre effective spreads are also negative, such as -0.36 basis points for large-cap buyer-initiated sweeps and -0.38 basis points for large-cap seller-initiated sweeps, even though the intra-sweep total effective spread is large. The paper interprets this as evidence that markets are resilient: large liquidity drawdowns incur trading costs but do not degrade the subsequent price formation process or increase later trading costs.

Main role: Market resiliency during stressed conditions is one of the two major conditional tests highlighted in the introduction, abstract, and conclusion. The before/after liquidity-drawdown analysis materially supports the central claim that even extreme low-latency activity does not degrade market quality afterward.
Settings.H514: Section 3.5, Fig. 4, Table 5 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 12-14.
Settings.G515:
Treatment: Daily percentage change in quote updates, i.e., changes in the number of quote updates per firm-day averaged within size quintiles. The causal interpretation also runs in reverse in discussion, but the paper uses lagged updates as the focal explanatory variable for market quality and lagged market-quality innovations as tests of reverse causality.

Method: The authors estimate reduced-form daily vector autoregressions separately by size quintile over 2009-2011. Daily percentage changes in quote updates, VIX, and one market-quality variable are regressed on four lags of each variable. Two market-quality outcomes are studied in separate systems: daily changes in the absolute deviation of variance ratios from one, and daily changes in effective spreads. This is a dynamic regression framework used to argue about direction of causality/Granger-causality rather than a quasi-experiment. No high-dimensional fixed effects are reported in the VAR implementation.

Identification: Identification comes from dynamic time-series ordering: if improved liquidity or efficiency merely attracts high-frequency quoting, lagged market-quality improvements should predict subsequent increases in updates. Instead, the paper finds that lagged deteriorations in market quality predict higher subsequent updates, and that VIX innovations predict updates but not vice versa. This is not a full causal design; it relies on Granger-causality logic and assumes omitted persistent shocks are adequately captured by lags.

Setting: In daily US time-series VARs, the authors test whether high-frequency quoting responds to or drives market quality. Across size quintiles, lagged increases in effective spreads and lagged increases in the deviation of variance ratios from one tend to be followed by higher quote updating rather than the reverse pattern expected under a simple habitat story. They also find that changes in VIX Granger-cause changes in updates, while updates do not Granger-cause VIX. The authors interpret this as evidence that high-frequency traders step in when market quality worsens and that lagged updates can be used to mitigate, though not eliminate, endogeneity in the main cross-sectional analysis.

Main role: These VARs are presented as identification-supporting evidence against a habitat/selection explanation and as motivation for lagged-update sorts. They are substantively important but secondary to the headline US cross-sectional and TSE-shock evidence.
Settings.H515: Section 4.1, Eq. (11)-(13), Fig. 5, Table 6 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 15-17.
Settings.G516:
Treatment: Previous day's quote-update intensity, measured using the number of quote updates and used to sort securities into low and high update groups for the next day's tests.

Method: Motivated by the VAR results, the authors re-sort US stocks into low and high update groups using the previous day's quote updates rather than the prior half-hour's updates, then replicate the market-quality comparisons from the main cross-sectional analysis. This remains an observational stratification/regression-adjustment design, but uses lagged treatment assignment to reduce contemporaneous endogeneity. The paper reports that the conclusions are the same, though the estimates are not presented in tables.

Identification: The idea is that if quote updates respond to fundamentals or inventory needs, using previous day's updates to assign stocks to update groups should reduce simultaneity between today's omitted shocks and today's measured updates. The remaining assumptions are still strong because lagged updates may correlate with persistent unobservables.

Setting: As a robustness test against contemporaneous endogeneity, the authors use the previous day's quote updates to sort US stocks into low- and high-update groups and then re-estimate the relation with market quality. They report that the same conclusion obtains: higher updates remain associated with variance ratios closer to one. No numerical estimates are reported in the excerpt, but the paper treats this lagged-sort exercise as evidence that omitted contemporaneous factors are less likely to fully explain the main cross-sectional findings.

Main role: This is an identification-oriented robustness check supporting the main US result that higher updates are associated with variance ratios closer to one.
Settings.H516: Section 4.1, prose discussion following Table 6, PDF p. 17.
Settings.G517:
Treatment: Exposure to the post-arrowhead trading regime on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, i.e., the exogenous technological change that reduced posting/execution latency from one to two seconds to less than ten milliseconds and allowed co-location. Implemented as a binary post-versus-pre contrast for the same stocks.

Method: In the Tokyo Stock Exchange analysis, the authors exploit the January 4, 2010 introduction of arrowhead, a technological redesign that sharply reduced latency and enabled co-location. They compare the same stocks over three months before versus three months after the introduction, restricting to 229 securities that did not experience tick-size changes so that variance ratios and spreads are not mechanically affected by price-grid changes. They compute per-stock pre/post averages by half-hour and report cross-sectional averages of the paired after-minus-before differences. This is a conventional before/after same-unit comparison, akin to a simple two-period DiD without an untreated control group.

Identification: Identification relies on an exogenous exchange-level technological shock that materially reduced latency and facilitated high-frequency quotation. By comparing the same stocks before and after arrowhead, and excluding stocks with tick-size changes, the authors argue that changes in variance ratios and trading costs reflect the new faster market environment rather than mechanical pricing-grid effects. Threats include other concurrent TSE rule changes and time-varying information conditions, but the paper treats arrowhead as the central exogenous driver.

Setting: The paper's strongest causal evidence comes from the Tokyo Stock Exchange's January 4, 2010 arrowhead launch, which sharply reduced latency and allowed co-location. Using 229 stocks with no tick-size changes, the authors compare three-month pre- and post-arrowhead averages by half-hour. They find that variance-ratio deviations move closer to zero in every half-hour, with after-minus-before changes from -0.015 to -0.037. Effective spreads also fall sharply, by about 0.88 to 2.69 basis points across half-hours. Realized spreads decline by roughly 5.07 to 8.89 basis points, while measured price impact increases by about 4.14 to 7.73 basis points, which the paper attributes to reduced special-quote smoothing rather than worse market quality. The authors interpret this exogenous shock as showing that faster, high-frequency quotation improves the price-discovery process and lowers trading costs.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight the TSE arrowhead change as the paper's out-of-sample exogenous test, and the conclusion uses it as key causal support for the claim that faster quoting improves price efficiency and lowers trading costs.
Settings.H517: Section 4.2.1-4.2.2, Fig. 6, Fig. 7, Table 7, PDF pp. 17-20.
Settings.G518:
Treatment: Larger versus smaller decline in special price quote dissemination following arrowhead, implemented as a binary split based on whether the percentage increase in special quote dissemination is above or below the median (equivalently, whether the decline is larger versus smaller).

Method: Within the TSE arrowhead analysis, the authors study a mechanism related to price-continuity rules by comparing changes in price impact after arrowhead across two groups of stocks split by whether the percentage increase in special quote dissemination is above or below the median. This is a cross-group observational comparison following the technological shock, not a separate quasi-experimental design. The intended interpretation is that reductions in special quote dissemination caused part of the increase in measured price impact.

Identification: The argument is that TSE rules governing special quote dissemination smoothed prices before arrowhead; when such dissemination declined after arrowhead, measured price impact mechanically rose. The comparison of stocks with larger versus smaller declines in special-quote dissemination is used to support this mechanism, but it remains observational and may reflect other stock characteristics.

Setting: To explain the post-arrowhead increase in measured price impact, the authors compare TSE stocks with larger versus smaller declines in special quote dissemination after the system change. They report that in each half-hour interval, the increase in price impact is significantly larger by about 1 to 2 basis points for stocks with the larger decline in special-quote dissemination. The paper interprets this as evidence that the rise in measured price impact after arrowhead reflects reduced price-smoothing rules rather than a worsening of market quality.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism analysis used to explain why measured price impact rose after arrowhead despite lower effective spreads.
Settings.H518: Section 4.2.2, prose discussion after Table 7 and Fig. 7, PDF pp. 19-20.
Settings.G519:
Treatment: Junior overcollateralization (OC) ratio slack of the CLO, measured as the difference between the reported junior OC ratio and its threshold, in percentage points, measured at m0-1. In alternate columns it is coded as indicators for being in the bottom or middle tercile of OC slack, with the top tercile omitted. Lower slack means the CLO is more constrained.

Method: The authors estimate event-window logit models for whether a given CLO sells a loan that has just been downgraded from B or above to CCC or below. The dependent variable is a sale dummy over windows [-3,-1], [0,2], or [3,5] months around the downgrade month. The key regressor is junior OC-ratio slack measured one month before the event window; specifications use either continuous slack or tercile indicators. Controls include pre-downgrade loan rating and maturity, CLO time to reinvestment date, CLO size, manager age, manager total AUM, CCC-loan share, and calendar year-quarter fixed effects. The implemented estimator is nonlinear logit MLE with misspecification-robust standard errors, so it is classified as Other rather than linear OLS/FE. The design is observational event-study-style regression adjustment intended to isolate the effect of tighter leverage/OC constraints on forced sales, though the paper acknowledges this is not a randomized design.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-CLO variation in ex ante junior OC-ratio slack among CLOs holding downgraded loans, within event windows around the downgrade to CCC or below. The endogeneity concern is that CLOs with low slack may differ in unobserved ways correlated with sale propensity or loan quality. The authors argue that focusing on downgraded loans and controlling for loan and CLO characteristics, plus time fixed effects, helps isolate sales induced by binding leverage constraints rather than discretionary information-based sales. The causal interpretation relies on the institutional mechanism that CCC downgrades change valuation treatment and make sale-and-deleveraging attractive when OC slack is low.

Setting: Using logit regressions around downgrade events, the authors interpret lower junior OC-ratio slack as causing more forced sales of newly downgraded loans. In the main 0-to-2 month window, the marginal effect of continuous slack is -0.48 percentage points per 1 percentage-point increase in slack; equivalently, a one-standard-deviation decrease in slack raises the sale probability by 1.56 percentage points, and moving from the top to the bottom slack tercile raises sale probability by 3.53 percentage points. The unconditional sale probability over this window is 13.27%. Effects are weaker before the downgrade and remain negative after, supporting the paper's central fire-sale mechanism.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize as a central finding that constrained CLOs are forced to sell loans downgraded to CCC or below; this setting provides the paper's direct micro evidence for that claim.
Settings.G520:
Treatment: Junior OC-ratio slack, measured as the percentage of junior OC-ratio slack to the CLO's asset in month t.

Method: The authors run linear OLS regressions of future senior tranche redemption on contemporaneous junior OC-ratio slack and CLO controls, with year-quarter fixed effects. The left-hand side is the negative percentage change in senior tranche outstanding over horizons h = 3, 6, and 12 months. Controls include time to reinvestment date, CLO size, manager age, manager size, and CCC ratio. Hansen-Hodrick standard errors adjust for overlapping observations. The design is observational regression adjustment intended to show that low OC slack leads CLOs to redeem senior debt, consistent with the mechanism behind fire sales.

Identification: The strategy uses cross-CLO and time variation in junior OC slack before reinvestment dates, controlling for observable CLO characteristics and time effects. The key endogeneity concern is omitted CLO condition correlated with both low slack and future redemptions. The authors use the result as mechanism-consistent evidence rather than a definitive clean identification design. The causal claim relies on the contractual structure that low slack makes redeeming senior tranches an effective way to restore compliance.

Setting: As a mechanism test, the paper estimates that lower junior OC-ratio slack causes more future senior tranche redemption by CLOs. In OLS regressions, the coefficient on slack is -0.01 at the 3-month horizon, -0.03 at 6 months, and -0.04 at 12 months (all in percentage points of senior tranche redemption per 1 percentage-point higher slack, with the latter two statistically stronger). The authors interpret this as confirming that constrained CLOs delever by redeeming senior tranches, which explains why selling downgraded loans can improve the OC ratio.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism test reinforcing why constrained CLOs sell loans: they use proceeds to pay down senior tranches and improve OC ratios. It is not the paper's headline result.
Settings.G521:
Treatment: Exposure of a downgraded loan to constrained CLO ownership before downgrade, operationalized in the main comparison as an indicator for being held by an above-median number of constrained CLOs (CLOs with below-median junior OC-ratio slack at month t-2) versus a below-median number.

Method: The authors estimate abnormal weekly returns on downgraded loans from a linear factor model of transaction-price returns on the leveraged-loan index return, T-bill rate, S&P 500 return, and transaction-direction/microstructure controls, estimated separately by loan groups before and after the downgrade event. They cumulate residuals into CARs from week -20 to +20 around downgrade and compare loans widely held by constrained CLOs to those not widely held by constrained CLOs, where constrained CLOs are those with below-median junior OC slack two months before downgrade. The causal claim is based on event-study-style regression adjustment and a random-walk/fundamentals assumption rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing downgraded loans with greater versus lesser pre-downgrade ownership by constrained CLOs, after netting out aggregate market returns and transaction-related noise in the abnormal-return model. The endogeneity concern is that constrained CLOs may hold worse loans; the paper argues against this using post-event convergence of CARs to zero, interpreting mean reversion as evidence of temporary mispricing under the maintained assumption that fundamentals follow a random walk over short horizons. The key assumption is that, absent fire-sale-induced illiquidity, the two groups would not show persistent differential abnormal returns.

Setting: The paper interprets greater ownership of a downgraded loan by constrained CLOs as causing a temporary fire-sale price depression. Loans held by an above-median number of constrained CLOs have MCARs of -8.49% by downgrade week versus -5.13% for loans with below-median constrained ownership, a difference of -3.35 percentage points (t=-2.93). The gap shrinks after downgrade and is -0.33 percentage points by weeks 11-15 and +0.76 percentage points by weeks 16-20, both insignificant. The authors take this temporary divergence and subsequent convergence as evidence that collective sales by constrained CLOs move prices away from fundamentals but only temporarily.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight that loans widely held by constrained CLOs suffer temporary price depreciation that later dissipates; this is a core result establishing the market price impact of fire sales.
Settings.H521: Section 4.1, Eq. (7), Table 6, Fig. 3, Table 7, pp. 1130-1134 (PDF pp. 11-14).
Settings.G522:
Treatment: Alternative continuous measures of a downgraded loan's exposure to constrained CLOs: (i) log number of constrained CLOs owning the loan; (ii) log share of loan face value held by constrained CLOs; (iii) log share of the loan sold by constrained CLOs over the event window; and (iv) log sale-probability-weighted sum of CLO holdings, measured relative to loan face value.

Method: Using cross-sectional OLS regressions, the authors regress cumulative abnormal returns at different event times on alternative continuous measures of pre-downgrade constrained-CLO ownership, plus controls for loan maturity, pre-downgrade rating, log loan size, log borrower loan amount outstanding, and year fixed effects. Alternative ownership measures are: number of constrained CLOs holding the loan, constrained CLO holding share, constrained CLO sale share over the event window, and sale-probability-weighted holdings of all CLOs. This is regression adjustment supporting the price-impact interpretation and robustness to alternative treatment definitions.

Identification: The strategy uses cross-loan variation in pre-downgrade exposure to constrained CLO ownership, conditional on observed loan characteristics and year effects. The endogeneity concern is omitted borrower or loan characteristics correlated with both constrained CLO ownership and price declines. The authors argue robustness across ownership measures and disappearance of effects by week 20 support a fire-sale mechanism rather than persistent fundamental differences.

Setting: In cross-sectional OLS regressions, greater constrained-CLO ownership is interpreted as causing larger temporary abnormal price declines upon downgrade. For the main ownership count measure, a one log-unit increase in the number of constrained CLOs holding the loan predicts a 2.17 percentage-point lower CAR by week 0; for constrained CLO holding share the analogous estimate is -2.64 percentage points; for constrained CLO sale share it is -2.38 percentage points; and for sale-probability-weighted holdings it is -1.20 percentage points. Across specifications, the coefficients are negative around downgrade and fade toward zero by week 20, reinforcing the temporary fire-sale interpretation.

Main role: These are substantive robustness analyses showing that the temporary price-effect result does not depend on the exact ownership measure; they support but do not replace the main comparison in Table 6/Figure 3.
Settings.G523:
Treatment: Quarter-level macro conditions affecting market liquidity and price impact: buyers' capital (loan mutual fund assets plus distressed hedge fund assets scaled by leveraged loan market size), LoanBond issuance difference, FX basis, new CLO issuance relative to outstanding CLO assets, and negative leveraged-loan default rate. In the paper's interpretation these variables proxy for buyers' capital and policy support channels.

Method: The authors run panel OLS regressions of loan-level price impact, defined as minus the downgrade-week CAR, on macro variables intended to capture buyers' capital and channels of Federal Reserve intervention, plus loan controls. Regressions are estimated on loans downgraded in or before 2019, using either each macro proxy separately or all jointly. Macro proxies include buyers' capital, leveraged-loan minus high-yield bond issuance, FX basis, new CLO issuance, and the negative default rate. This is regression adjustment used to interpret time variation in fire-sale price impact, especially why 2020 was milder than the financial crisis.

Identification: The paper exploits time-series variation in macro liquidity conditions and policy-related proxies across downgrade episodes. Endogeneity is substantial: the authors explicitly note buyers' capital is endogenous and policy proxies are indirect. The interpretation is therefore mechanism-based and suggestive rather than sharply identified. The implicit assumption is that these macro variables capture broad liquidity supply conditions that shift the severity of fire-sale price impacts conditional on loan characteristics.

Setting: The authors interpret greater buyers' capital and stronger policy-support channels as reducing the price impact of fire sales on downgraded loans. In univariate regressions, higher buyers' capital, more loan-to-bond substitution, a higher FX basis, more new CLO issuance, and a lower default rate are all associated with smaller downgrade-week price impacts; for example, the coefficient on buyers' capital is -0.602 and on LoanBond is -0.037. Using these estimates, the paper argues such factors can explain much of why 2020 downgrade price impacts were far smaller than during the 2008-2009 crisis. Because the regressions are reduced-form and macro variables are endogenous or indirect proxies, this evidence is suggestive rather than cleanly identified.

Main role: This is a secondary analysis explaining variation in the strength of fire-sale effects over time, particularly during COVID-19, not the core existence-of-fire-sales result.
Settings.H523: Section 4.3, Fig. 4, Eq. (9), Table 9, pp. 1135-1138 (PDF pp. 16-18).
Settings.G524:
Treatment: Counterfactual stress shock to CLO collateral pools: either default of the ten largest borrowers in a month with LGD 50%, or simulated portfolio credit losses corresponding to 95% or 99% VaR from a one-factor Gaussian default model. These are scenario shocks rather than observed treatments.

Method: The authors conduct counterfactual stress tests rather than standard reduced-form regressions. For each CLO-month they compute OC-ratio slack and then simulate how shocks to underlying borrower defaults would change junior and senior OC slack and insolvency slack. Scenarios include (i) default of the ten largest borrowers with 50% loss-given-default, and (ii) one-year 95% and 99% VaR shocks generated from a one-factor Gaussian asset-value/default model calibrated to rating transition probabilities. They report the implied percentage of CLOs that would fail junior OC tests, fail senior OC tests, or become insolvent. This is a structural/counterfactual exercise, so it is classified as Other.

Identification: This is a model-based counterfactual identification strategy. The authors use observed CLO holdings and contractual OC thresholds, then impose hypothetical borrower-default shocks to trace how losses propagate into CLO constraint violations. The main concern is scenario dependence and modeling assumptions (LGD, Gaussian one-factor default structure, default correlations, constant fair value for CCC loans). The exercise identifies a causal mechanism under the maintained stress-test model rather than from quasi-experimental variation in realized data.

Setting: In counterfactual stress tests, the paper concludes that idiosyncratic borrower defaults can cause widespread binding CLO constraints because CLO portfolios overlap heavily.
