In the Fama-French three-factor model, SMB and HML are significant without characteristics (0.213% and 0.225% per month) but become insignificant once SIZE and BM/logBM are added (-0.073% and 0.136%, or -0.064% and 0.124%). The authors treat these as supporting evidence that factor premiums disappear after controlling for characteristics, while emphasizing that OLS is contaminated by EIV bias.

Main role: These OLS results are presented mainly for comparison to show that substantive conclusions are similar after adding characteristics, despite the paper's argument that OLS is biased by errors in variables.
Settings.H591: Section 4.2; Table 6 Panel A columns (6)-(10), with related subperiod OLS columns in Panels B-C. PDF pp. 283-284.
Settings.G592:
Treatment: Continuous stock-level exposures to the Fama-French five factors (market, SMB, HML, RMW, CMA), estimated from daily returns over the prior 36 months. In richer specifications, continuous characteristics SIZE, BM, OP, and INV are also included as regressors.

Method: The authors apply the same monthly cross-sectional IV/Fama-MacBeth design to the Fama-French five-factor model. For each month, they estimate stock betas to MKT, SMB, HML, RMW, and CMA from daily returns over the prior 36 months; odd- and even-month beta estimates from disjoint subsamples supply the endogenous regressors and instruments. Monthly excess returns are regressed on selected factor betas, in some columns one factor at a time and in others jointly; the full specification also adds SIZE, BM, operating profitability (OP), and investment (INV) characteristics. Slopes are averaged over time with Fama-MacBeth t-statistics.

Identification: Identification again comes from using disjoint odd/even daily-return subsamples to estimate two noisy measures of the same underlying betas, with uncorrelated measurement errors under their assumptions. One beta measure instruments for the other in monthly cross-sectional regressions, aiming to purge the EIV bias that would attenuate or distort risk-premium estimates. The key maintained assumption is that these estimated betas capture systematic exposure and that no remaining omitted pricing variable jointly drives returns and included characteristics beyond the authors' control set.

Setting: Using the IV individual-stock estimator, the paper tests whether exposures to the Fama-French five factors command higher expected returns. In the 1967-2012 sample, none of the five factor premiums is significant even without characteristics, and in the full specification with all five betas plus SIZE, BM, OP, and INV, the premiums remain insignificant: MKT 0.367, SMB -0.095, HML 0.354, RMW -0.051, and CMA 0.049 percent per month. In contrast, SIZE (-0.153), BM (0.178), OP (0.649), and INV (-0.709) are significant. The authors conclude that factor risk in the FF5 model is not priced in individual-stock returns once corresponding characteristics are controlled for.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion claim that premiums under the Fama-French five-factor model are insignificant after controlling for characteristics; this table is a central empirical application of the proposed IV method.
Settings.H592: Section 4.3; Table 7 Panels A-C, especially Panel A column (6) and related columns (1)-(5). PDF pp. 284-285.
Settings.G593:
Treatment: Continuous stock-level q-factor exposures: market beta, size-factor beta (ME), investment-factor beta (I/A), and profitability-factor beta (ROE), estimated from daily returns over the prior 36 months. Some specifications also include SIZE, operating profitability (OP), and investment (INV) characteristics as additional regressors.

Method: The paper next applies the same IV/Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional procedure to the Hou-Xue-Zhang q-factor model. Betas to MKT, ME, I/A, and ROE are estimated from daily returns over the previous 36 months, separately in odd and even months to create disjoint-sample explanatory and instrumental beta measures. Monthly excess returns are then regressed on these factor betas, first one at a time, then jointly, and finally jointly with SIZE, OP, and INV characteristics. Time-series averages of monthly slopes and Fama-MacBeth t-statistics are reported.

Identification: Identification is via IV correction for beta measurement error: separate odd/even daily-return subsamples produce two noisy but error-independent measures of each stock's underlying factor exposure. Instrumenting one beta estimate with the other should recover consistent ex post risk-premium estimates in large cross sections. The substantive challenge is distinguishing priced factor risk from characteristic-based return patterns; the authors address this by adding SIZE, OP, and INV controls and interpreting remaining factor slopes as risk premiums.

Setting: In IV tests of the q-factor asset-pricing model on individual stocks from 1975-2012, none of the q-factor betas predicts higher returns once the full model is estimated. In the joint factor regression, MKT, ME, I/A, and ROE premiums are -0.247, 0.222, 0.001, and -0.400 percent per month, all insignificant; with SIZE, OP, and INV controls they are 0.437, -0.118, -0.547, and -0.632, still insignificant. Meanwhile SIZE (-0.202), OP (3.734), and INV (-0.579) are significant. The authors interpret this as no support for the q-factor model's priced factor risks in the cross-section of individual-stock returns.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly mention the Hou et al. four-factor model among the central models whose factor premiums become insignificant under the authors' IV approach with characteristics.
Settings.H593: Section 4.4; Table 8 Panels A-C, especially Panel A columns (5) and (8). PDF pp. 286-287.
Settings.G594:
Treatment: Continuous liquidity-adjusted market beta (LMKT) for each stock, constructed as beta_1 + beta_2 - beta_3 - beta_4 from return and illiquidity innovations under the LCAPM. In some specifications, firm-specific Amihud illiquidity is included as an additional continuous regressor.

Method: For the liquidity-adjusted CAPM (LCAPM), the authors estimate liquidity-adjusted market beta (LMKT) and then run monthly cross-sectional IV regressions on individual NYSE/Amex stocks. Illiquidity cost is based on an Amihud-type measure using daily returns and dollar volume, with market-wide illiquidity innovations estimated from AR models; beta components are estimated by time-series GMM with Dimson-type corrections over the previous 36 months. Odd- and even-month daily data within the rolling window are used to form separate explanatory and instrumental LMKT betas. Monthly cross-sectional regressions relate returns to LMKT, with and without firm-specific Amihud illiquidity as an additional regressor.

Identification: The pricing claim is that higher liquidity-adjusted systematic risk should raise expected return. Estimated LMKT betas are noisy because they depend on estimated return and illiquidity covariances; the authors therefore use disjoint odd/even subsamples of daily data to form separate beta estimates whose measurement errors should be uncorrelated, instrumenting one with the other. They also argue that portfolio-based tests are confounded because LMKT is highly correlated with size and book-to-market in standard test portfolios; using individual stocks and controlling for Amihud illiquidity is intended to better isolate systematic liquidity risk from firm characteristics.

Setting: Applying the IV individual-stock method to the liquidity-adjusted CAPM from 1959-2012, the authors find no evidence that liquidity-adjusted market beta commands a return premium. The LMKT premium is 0.150% per month without Amihud illiquidity and 0.085% with it, both insignificant. By contrast, the slope on firm-specific Amihud illiquidity is 0.220% and highly significant. The authors conclude that characteristic-level illiquidity is positively related to returns, but systematic liquidity-adjusted market risk under the LCAPM is not priced in individual-stock returns.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion list the liquidity-adjusted CAPM among the main models whose factor premiums are insignificant after controlling for characteristics. This section is one of the principal empirical applications of the IV method.
Settings.H594: Section 4.5; Eq. (18) and Table 9. PDF pp. 287-288.
Settings.G595:
Treatment: Continuous estimated past factor betas for each model (MKT; MKT/SMB/HML; MKT/SMB/HML/RMW/CMA; MKT/ME/I/A/ROE; LMKT) plus lagged average characteristics such as SIZE, BM, OP, INV, and Amihud illiquidity, used both as controls and as additional instruments to test whether characteristics proxy for future betas.

Method: As an additional test motivated by the hypothesis that characteristics proxy for future betas, the authors modify their IV design into an 'IV mean-estimator.' They run cross-sectional IV regressions where the dependent variable is the average return over the current and next 12 months, regressors include past betas and past 12-month average characteristics, and instruments include both disjoint-sample past beta estimates and the characteristics themselves. They report results for CAPM, Fama-French three- and five-factor models, the q-factor model, and the LCAPM. Tm=12 columns use Hansen-Hodrick standard errors with 12 lags; Tm=1 columns report comparable one-month IV regressions where characteristics also serve as instruments.

Identification: The concern is that characteristics may forecast future beta changes better than past beta estimates, so significant characteristic slopes could still reflect priced risk. The modified IV strategy instruments past beta estimates with disjoint-sample beta estimates and also uses characteristics as instruments, while lengthening the horizon so characteristics' informational advantage about near-future beta innovations should dissipate in the limit. Under the maintained stationarity/ergodicity assumptions in Proposition 2, the IV mean-estimator consistently estimates the risk premium on beta and should drive the characteristic slope to zero if characteristics matter only because they proxy for future betas.

Setting: In this robustness design, the paper tests whether firm characteristics affect returns only because they proxy for future betas. Using the IV mean-estimator with 12-month average future returns and characteristics as additional instruments, factor risk premiums remain insignificant across all models: for example, with Tm=12 the CAPM MKT premium is 0.056, FF3 MKT/SMB/HML are 0.053/0.042/0.106, FF5 MKT/SMB/HML/RMW/CMA are 0.165/0.123/0.141/0.090/0.653, q-factor MKT/ME/I-A/ROE are 0.335/0.140/-0.242/-0.354, and LCAPM LMKT is 0.021, none significant except CMA is marginal at 1.88 t-statistic. Many characteristic slopes remain significant, such as SIZE, BM, and Amihud illiquidity. The authors interpret this as rejecting the view that characteristics are priced merely because they are better proxies for true future betas than past betas.

Main role: This is an important robustness and interpretation test, not the primary baseline design. It supports the paper's central conclusion by arguing that significant characteristic slopes are not just proxying for future beta information.
Settings.H595: Section 5.1; Proposition 2, Eq. (25), and Table 10 (Tm=1 and Tm=12 columns). PDF pp. 289-291.
Settings.G596:
Treatment: Contemporaneous excess market return, measured as the CRSP value-weighted index return minus the risk-free rate in month t. Continuous return variable.

Method: Monthly time-series OLS regression of the winner-minus-loser (WML) momentum portfolio return on the contemporaneous excess market return over 1927:01–2013:03. The reported parameterization is an unconditional market model, interpreted as estimating market beta and CAPM alpha for momentum. No fixed effects, instruments, or quasi-experimental variation are used; identification is purely regression adjustment using contemporaneous market returns.

Identification: The authors interpret the market-model slope and intercept as measuring the effect of market movements on momentum returns and the abnormal return net of market exposure. Identification comes from time-series covariation between contemporaneous market excess returns and WML returns. Endogeneity is not resolved in a causal-policy sense; this is an asset-pricing regression relying on the maintained linear factor-model interpretation.

Setting: Using monthly data from 1927:01–2013:03, the authors regress the WML momentum portfolio on the contemporaneous excess market return and find an unconditional market beta of -0.576 and an intercept of 1.852% per month (Table 3, regression 1). In Table 1 they report the corresponding annualized CAPM alpha as 22.2% (22.3% in text) with t-statistics around 7.3–8.5. The intended interpretation is that momentum has negative market exposure yet earns large abnormal returns, a central starting point for the paper’s later argument that conditional market exposure helps explain momentum crashes.

Main role: The paper’s central claims begin from the behavior of momentum returns and their market exposure; the unconditional market-model alpha and beta are foundational benchmark causal/risk-interpretation results used throughout the paper.
Settings.H596: Section 2.2, Table 1 and Section 3.2 Eq. (1), Table 3 column (1), PDF pp. 224, 227–229.
Settings.G597:
Treatment: Ex ante bear-market state and its interaction with contemporaneous excess market return. The bear indicator equals one if the cumulative CRSP value-weighted index return over the past 24 months is negative. The effective focal treatment is being in a bear market, affecting both alpha and market sensitivity.

Method: Monthly time-series OLS regression of WML returns on the contemporaneous excess market return interacted with an ex ante bear-market indicator (lagged two-year market return negative), plus the bear indicator itself: a conditional CAPM/market-timing style regression. This is a linear regression adjustment design using observed state variables to estimate how bear markets change momentum alpha and beta.

Identification: Identification uses time-series variation in whether the prior two-year market return is negative. The authors argue that this ex ante state predicts the conditional beta and expected return of momentum. The design addresses the concern that unconditional regressions mask state dependence, but it remains observational and depends on the maintained interpretation that lagged market declines proxy for panic states rather than omitted state variables.

Setting: In a conditional monthly market-model regression, the authors find that when the past two-year market return is negative, WML’s market beta is 1.131 lower (t = -13.4) and WML alpha is 2.040% per month lower (t = -3.4) relative to non-bear periods (Table 3, regression 2). The point estimate for bear-market alpha is near zero. This supports the paper’s central claim that momentum performs poorly after market declines because its conditional market exposure turns strongly negative in those states.

Main role: A main claim of the paper is that momentum crashes occur following market declines; the conditional bear-market regression provides direct evidence that beta becomes much more negative and alpha falls in bear states.
Settings.H597: Section 3.2 Eq. (2), Table 3 column (2), PDF pp. 227–229.
Settings.G598:
Treatment: Contemporaneous excess market return under bear-market and up-market states: specifically, the interaction IB,t−1 × IU,t × market excess return, where IB,t−1 indicates a lagged-two-year bear market and IU,t indicates a positive contemporaneous excess market return. The focal treatment is a market rebound in a prior bear state.

Method: Monthly Henriksson-Merton style OLS regression of WML returns on the contemporaneous excess market return, an ex ante bear-market indicator, and a contemporaneous up-market indicator interacted with the bear-market state. This estimates different market betas in bear/down and bear/up states and is used to infer option-like payoff asymmetry.

Identification: Identification uses time-series interactions between lagged bear states and contemporaneous positive market realizations. The authors interpret the interaction coefficient as capturing the additional effect of market rebounds on momentum returns after prior market declines. This is observational and rests on the linear state-dependent beta specification and exogeneity of the market-state partition.

Setting: Using a monthly market-timing regression, the authors estimate that in bear markets WML’s beta is -0.742 when the contemporaneous market return is negative and -1.796 when the contemporaneous market return is positive, with the differential captured by an additional bear-up-market loading of -0.815 (t = -4.5) in Table 3 column (3). They interpret this as WML being effectively short a call option on the market in bear states, a central mechanism behind momentum crashes during sharp rebounds.

Main role: The option-like asymmetry of momentum in bear markets is one of the paper’s core mechanisms for explaining crashes; this specification delivers the key evidence.
Settings.H598: Section 3.2 Eq. (3), Table 3 column (3), PDF pp. 228–229.
Settings.G599:
Treatment: Bear-market rebound exposure: contemporaneous excess market return and its interactions with lagged bear-market indicator and contemporaneous up-market indicator. The implicit treatment varies continuously with market return but is state contingent.

Method: Monthly time-series OLS regressions of each momentum decile portfolio return and the WML portfolio return on contemporaneous market excess return interacted with ex ante bear-market and contemporaneous up-market indicators, reported separately by portfolio. This is the portfolio-level extension of the Henriksson-Merton style specification.

Identification: Identification comes from the same state-dependent time-series variation as in s3, but applied across decile portfolios. The authors infer that the loser side drives the asymmetric rebound sensitivity because loser betas rise sharply in bear/up states while winner betas do not. This remains model-based observational inference.

Setting: Table 4 Panel A shows that in bear markets the loser decile has a down-market beta of 1.560 (=1.338+0.222) and an up-market beta of 2.160 (=1.560+0.600), while the winner decile’s up-market beta increment is slightly negative (-0.215). The authors conclude that the loser portfolio is the predominant source of WML’s option-like payoff and that momentum crashes are mainly driven by the short side—past losers crashing up during market rebounds.

Main role: The decomposition showing that optionality and crash risk come mainly from the loser leg is substantively central to the paper’s explanation of momentum crashes.
Settings.H599: Section 3.2–3.3, Table 4 Panel A (and comparison to Panel B), PDF p. 230.
Settings.G600:
Treatment: Ex ante market stress, measured by lagged bear-market indicator, lagged market return variance over the previous 126 trading days, and their interaction. Variance is continuous; bear indicator is binary.

Method: Monthly forecasting regressions of WML returns on an ex ante bear-market indicator, lagged estimated market variance over the prior 126 trading days, and their interaction. This is linear regression adjustment used to argue that market stress predicts lower future momentum returns.

Identification: Identification relies on ex ante variation in lagged market declines and lagged realized market variance. The authors argue these variables proxy for panic states that lower the ex ante expected return of momentum. Because the regressors are predetermined, reverse causality is limited mechanically, but omitted-state-variable concerns remain.

Setting: In monthly forecasting regressions, the authors show that both lagged bear-market status and lagged market variance predict lower future WML returns, and that momentum returns are especially poor in bear markets with high volatility. For example, Table 5 reports a coefficient of -0.330 on lagged market variance alone, -2.626 on the bear indicator alone, and interaction terms of -0.397 and -0.323 in specifications that include bear×variance interactions. This evidence motivates the paper’s claim that crashes are partly forecastable using panic-state indicators.

Main role: Forecastability of momentum crashes using bear markets and volatility is a headline finding in the abstract and introduction and underlies the dynamic strategy construction.
Settings.H600: Section 3.5 Eq. (4), Table 5 columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 230–232.
Settings.G601:
Treatment: Panic-state exposure and variance-swap return: IBσ2 is a normalized interaction of the ex ante bear-market indicator and lagged market variance; the variance-swap return is the inferred daily excess return on an S&P 500 variance swap. Treatments are continuous/state-dependent.

Method: Daily time-series OLS regressions of WML returns on a normalized panic-state variable (IBσ2), contemporaneous excess market return and its interaction with IBσ2, and variance-swap returns and their interaction with IBσ2. This specification estimates conditional exposure of momentum to variance risk and market risk in panic states.

Identification: Identification uses daily time-series covariation between WML returns, variance-swap returns, and a normalized ex ante panic-state indicator. The specification asks whether momentum’s exposure to variance risk changes in panic states. It is observational and factor-model based, not a quasi-experiment.

Setting: Using daily data from 1990–2013, the authors estimate that outside panic states WML has mean return 31.48% per year, but weighted-average return in panic periods is about 59% per year lower (Table 6, regression 1). Controlling for the market, WML beta falls by 0.52 in panic states (regression 2). Adding variance-swap returns, they find no significant loading outside panic states but a significant panic-state interaction of -0.10 (t = -4.7), indicating WML is effectively short volatility in panic periods; however, the panic-state premium remains negative, so variance risk does not explain momentum crashes fully.

Main role: This is an important mechanism/robustness exercise, but the paper uses it mainly to show that variance risk exposure does not fully explain the crash pattern rather than as the principal result.
Settings.G602:
Treatment: Dynamic scaling weight on the WML portfolio, varying continuously over time according to estimated conditional Sharpe ratio (forecast mean divided by forecast variance). Not binary.

Method: Dynamic portfolio strategy constructed from estimated conditional mean and variance of momentum returns. The implemented estimator is a model-based strategy weight w*t = (1/2λ)(μt−1/σ²t−1), where expected return is forecast from earlier regressions using bear-market and volatility measures and volatility is forecast using a GJR-GARCH model plus lagged realized volatility. Performance is evaluated by time-series Sharpe ratios and cumulative returns; this is not a standard linear causal estimator.

Identification: The strategy uses predicted mean and variance of WML returns from earlier observational forecasting relations. The intended interpretation is interventionist: changing the portfolio weight on momentum according to forecast panic-state conditions improves performance. This is not identified by exogenous treatment assignment; it is a model-based, implementable trading-rule comparison relying on stability of the forecasting relationships.

Setting: Using the optimal weight formula based on forecast mean and variance, the authors show that the dynamic momentum strategy materially outperforms both static WML and constant-volatility momentum. In the full-sample figure, the dynamic strategy’s Sharpe ratio is nearly twice that of static WML; Table 7 later reports annualized Sharpe ratios of 1.194 out-of-sample and 1.202 in-sample versus 0.682 for static WML and 1.041 for constant volatility. This is one of the paper’s headline results and operationalizes the earlier evidence that momentum crashes are forecastable in panic states.

Main role: A central conclusion of the paper is that an implementable dynamic momentum strategy approximately doubles the alpha and Sharpe ratio of static momentum.
Settings.H602: Section 4, Eq. (6), Fig. 5 and Fig. 6, PDF pp. 233–235.
Settings.G603:
Treatment: Out-of-sample dynamic scaling weight on WML computed each month using recursively estimated expected return and lagged realized variance. Continuous treatment intensity.

Method: Out-of-sample implementation of the dynamic strategy where the conditional mean forecast is estimated recursively with an expanding window and the conditional variance is based on recent realized WML variance. Strategy performance is compared via Sharpe ratios and appraisal ratios across static WML, constant volatility, variance-scaled, and dynamic strategies.

Identification: No exogenous variation is used. The comparison identifies the performance consequences of implementing the dynamic weighting rule in real time under recursively estimated forecasting parameters. The crucial maintained assumption is that the predictive relation between panic states, volatility, and momentum returns is stable enough out of sample.

Setting: In the out-of-sample comparison over 1934:01–2013:03, the static WML strategy has a Sharpe ratio of 0.682, the constant-volatility strategy 1.041, the variance-scaled strategy 1.126, the out-of-sample dynamic strategy 1.194, and the in-sample dynamic strategy 1.202 (Table 7). The authors conclude that moving from constant volatility to the out-of-sample dynamic strategy still yields a substantial performance improvement, consistent with their claim that forecasting both mean and variance improves implementable momentum investing.

Main role: The out-of-sample performance addresses overfitting concerns and is used by the authors to argue the dynamic strategy is implementable and robust.
Settings.G604:
Treatment: Exposure to factor sets used in spanning tests: market, SMB, HML, static WML, constant-volatility momentum, and their panic-state interactions. Continuous factor-return treatments.

Method: Daily time-series spanning regressions of the dynamic momentum portfolio return on the market, Fama-French factors, static WML, and constant-volatility momentum, with and without interactions of these factors with the panic-state indicator IBσ2 to allow conditional betas. The reported coefficient of interest is the intercept (alpha).

Identification: Identification is via time-series factor regressions. The intercept is interpreted as abnormal return unexplained by benchmark factors and competing momentum strategies, including state-dependent exposures. This is observational factor-model evidence rather than quasi-experimental identification.

Setting: Table 8 shows that the dynamic portfolio earns large positive alphas even after controlling for the market and static momentum (23.74% per year, t = 11.99), for conditional market exposure (23.23%, t = 11.76), and for conditional Fama-French factors plus WML (22.04%, t = 11.60). Relative to constant-volatility momentum, dynamic alpha remains about 6–7% per year and significant. Conversely, constant-volatility momentum has near-zero alpha when regressed on the dynamic portfolio. The authors interpret this as evidence that the dynamic strategy is not spanned by standard factors or constant-volatility momentum and in fact spans the latter.

Main role: These spanning tests support the paper’s headline claim that dynamic momentum is not explained by other factors or by constant-volatility momentum, and that it spans the latter.
Settings.H604: Section 4.4, Table 8 Panels A and B, PDF pp. 237–238.
Settings.G605:
Treatment: Local market stress indicators for each region: bear-market indicator based on prior local market return, local market variance, contemporaneous positive market return, and related interactions. Treatments are binary/continuous state variables depending on panel/specification.

Method: Monthly time-series regressions for international equity momentum strategies (Europe, Japan, UK, US, and global equity) on market excess returns, bear-market indicators, up-market indicators, lagged market variance, and bear×variance interactions. Reported in Table 9 Panels A–D, these are direct analogues of the US equity regressions earlier in the paper.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-time variation within each regional market in lagged bear states, local market variance, and local rebounds. The authors interpret these state variables as predicting lower future momentum returns and more negative conditional betas. Because the evidence is observational and factor-model based, interpretation depends on the validity of the same panic-state mechanism across markets.

Setting: Across Europe, Japan, the UK, the US, and a global equity composite, Table 9 shows that momentum betas are more negative in bear markets, optionality in bear/up states is generally present, higher market variance predicts lower future momentum returns, and the bear×variance interaction is negative in all markets. In Panel D, the coefficient on IBσ2 is negative and statistically significant in all markets and for the global strategy (e.g., -6.509 Europe, -9.910 Japan, -11.408 UK, -11.055 US, -8.704 global, all annualized percent units). This supports the paper’s claim that momentum crashes and their predictability are robust across international equity markets.

Main role: Cross-market robustness is emphasized repeatedly in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion; these regressions show the main crash mechanism generalizes beyond US equities.
Settings.H605: Section 5.2, Table 9 Panels A–D, PDF pp. 238–239.
Settings.G606:
Treatment: Asset-class-specific market stress variables: bear-market indicator, local/asset-class market variance, contemporaneous positive market return, and their interactions. Depending on the regressor, treatment is binary or continuous.

Method: Monthly time-series regressions for non-equity asset-class momentum strategies (fixed income, commodities, currencies, equity index futures, global non-equity composite, and global all-asset composite) on market excess returns, bear-market indicators, up-market indicators, lagged market variance, and their interactions, paralleling Table 9.

Identification: Identification uses time-series state variation within each asset class. The authors argue that following bear markets and during high volatility, momentum portfolios in many asset classes also have more negative market exposure and lower abnormal returns. As before, this is observational factor-model inference.

Setting: Table 10 extends the state-dependent momentum regressions to fixed income, commodities, currencies, equity futures, and global composites. In Panel A, bear-market interactions with market returns are negative in all asset classes, implying more negative momentum betas after market declines. In Panel D, the bear×variance interaction is negative in every asset class except fixed income and is statistically significant for FX (-4.655) and GAll (-4.056), both in annualized percent units. The authors interpret this as broadly consistent evidence that momentum crashes and their predictability are not unique to equities.

Main role: Robustness across asset classes is a central contribution emphasized in the abstract and conclusion; these regressions extend the crash mechanism beyond equities.
Settings.H606: Section 5.3, Table 10 Panels A–D, PDF pp. 240–241.
Settings.G607:
Treatment: Strategy-specific dynamic scaling of the local/asset-class momentum portfolio, using forecast conditional Sharpe ratios (dynamic) or forecast volatility alone (constant volatility). Continuous treatment intensity; in fully dynamic composite strategies, component strategies are also volatility scaled ex ante.

Method: Dynamic and constant-volatility momentum strategy comparisons across international equity markets and multiple asset classes. Strategies are constructed using ex ante forecasts of momentum mean and variance from market-stress indicators and GARCH-style volatility forecasts; performance is summarized by Sharpe ratios, skewness, and spanning-regression alphas within each market/asset class.

Identification: This is a model-based trading-rule comparison rather than a quasi-experimental design. The causal claim is that dynamically adjusting momentum exposure using predicted crash states and volatility improves Sharpe ratios and spans simpler strategies. Identification depends on the out-of-sample stability and implementability of the forecasting model across markets and asset classes.

Setting: Table 11 shows that moving from static WML to constant-volatility momentum to the dynamic strategy improves Sharpe ratios in nearly every market and asset class except fixed income. Examples include Europe (0.462 → 0.886 → 1.130), Japan (0.067 → 0.160 → 0.416), UK (0.465 → 0.751 → 0.891), US (0.283 → 0.519 → 0.646), commodities (0.587 → 0.686 → 0.803), and global all assets (0.754 → 0.942 → 1.139; fully dynamic 1.223). Panel B shows positive alphas of the dynamic strategy relative to static WML and usually relative to constant-volatility momentum, while constant-volatility momentum has near-zero alpha relative to the dynamic strategy. The authors use this as major evidence that their dynamic crash-aware momentum strategy robustly outperforms static and constant-volatility alternatives across markets and asset classes.

Main role: The paper’s main practical contribution is that dynamic momentum improves performance robustly across time periods, markets, and asset classes; Table 11 is the key synthesis.
Settings.H607: Section 5.4, Table 11 Panels A and B, PDF pp. 241–242.
Settings.G608:
Treatment: Cross-sectional variation in valuation ratios: primarily log book-to-market, log retained-earnings-to-market, log contributed-capital-to-market, and log accumulated-other-comprehensive-income-to-market. These are continuous logged ratios; for non-positive values the log term is set to zero and accompanied by an indicator for non-positive observations.

Method: Monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth (1973) linear regressions predicting individual stock returns using book-to-market and its components. The main U.S. sample runs from July 1964 to December 2017, excludes financial firms and microcaps, requires positive book equity and non-missing retained earnings and contributed capital, trims variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles, and includes controls for log market equity, prior one-month return, and prior one-year return skipping a month. The focal regressors are log(BE/ME), log(RE/ME), log(CC/ME), and log(AOCI/ME); when a component is non-positive its log is set to zero and an indicator for non-positive values is included. The paper interprets slope differences as evidence about whether these accounting components cause higher expected returns in the cross section, while acknowledging this is an asset-pricing cross-sectional regression rather than a clean quasi-experiment.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional covariance between accounting ratios measured from lagged financial statements and subsequent monthly stock returns, conditional on standard controls. The endogeneity concern is that valuation ratios may proxy for omitted risk, mispricing, or other firm characteristics rather than a distinct causal effect of retained earnings content. The paper's argument is interpretive: if book-to-market predicts expected returns only through its retained-earnings component, then the source of the value premium is accumulated past earnings rather than contributed capital or intrinsic-value book assets. This relies on the maintained assumption that these predictive slopes reveal expected-return-related information rather than spurious correlation.

Setting: In monthly Fama-MacBeth regressions for U.S. nonfinancial stocks from 1964 to 2017, the authors find that higher retained-earnings-to-market predicts higher subsequent monthly returns, while contributed-capital-to-market has no standalone predictive power and accumulated other comprehensive income is insignificant. In Panel A, Column 1, log(BE/ME) has a slope of 0.22 (t=3.17). In Column 2, log(RE/ME) has a slope of 0.18 (t=4.39). In Column 3, when both are included, log(BE/ME) falls to 0.05 (t=0.69) while log(RE/ME) remains 0.17 (t=4.60), implying retained earnings subsumes book-to-market. Contributed capital is insignificant on its own in Column 4 (0.00, t=0.09) and turns negative when book-to-market is included in Column 5 (-0.12, t=-4.11). In the full specification, Column 8, only retained-earnings-to-market remains significant (0.18, t=4.84). These results are the paper's main evidence that book-to-market predicts returns because retained earnings accumulate and average past earnings.

Main role: This is the paper's central empirical design in the introduction and Section 4: showing that retained earnings-to-market predicts expected returns and subsumes book-to-market, while contributed capital-to-market does not.
Settings.H608: Section 4, Table 2 Panels A-B, especially Panel A Columns 1-8 and Panel B Columns 1-4 (PDF pp. 236-239 / article pp. 236-239).
Settings.G609:
Treatment: Continuous logged ratios, mainly log book-to-market and log retained-earnings-to-market, with sample treatment of negative book equity or retained earnings varied across specifications.

Method: Alternative-sample Fama-MacBeth (1973) monthly cross-sectional regressions for the same return-prediction framework as the main specification, but changing sample inclusion rules for negative book equity and negative retained earnings. Columns 1-2 add firms with negative book equity by setting log(BE/ME) to zero when BE<=0 and including an indicator. Columns 3-4 restrict to firms with positive retained earnings. Controls remain log size, prior one-month return, and prior one-year return skipping a month.

Identification: Same cross-sectional predictive identification as the main Fama-MacBeth design, but testing sensitivity to nonlinear handling of negative book equity and negative retained earnings. The concern is that coding negative values via indicator variables or excluding them may mechanically drive results.

Setting: Using alternative samples, the authors show the main return-prediction result is not driven by how negative book equity or negative retained earnings are handled. When firms with negative book equity are included, log(BE/ME) is 0.22 (t=3.17) alone but falls to 0.05 (t=0.73) once log(RE/ME) is added, while log(RE/ME) remains significant at 0.16 (t=4.51). Restricting the sample to positive retained earnings yields the same pattern: log(BE/ME) is 0.16 (t=2.46) alone but -0.01 (t=-0.15) with log(RE/ME), and log(RE/ME) is 0.18 (t=4.85). The authors interpret this as evidence that retained earnings-to-market robustly predicts expected returns and subsumes book-to-market regardless of the treatment of negative accounting values.

Main role: These are robustness checks supporting the main claim that retained earnings-to-market, not book-to-market alone, drives return predictability.
Settings.H609: Section 4, Table 2 Panel C Columns 1-4 (PDF pp. 238-239 / article pp. 238-239).
Settings.G610:
Treatment: Continuous valuation/profitability signals: log(E/P), log(BE/ME), and log(RE/ME), including a specification with one-year-lagged retained earnings in the numerator. These are continuous logged ratios plus indicators for non-positive values.

Method: Monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth (1973) regressions comparing earnings-to-price, book-to-market, and retained-earnings-to-market as predictors of subsequent stock returns. The sample is the same main U.S. sample. Specifications include controls for log market equity, prior one-month return, and prior one-year return skipping a month; negative earnings and negative retained earnings are handled with indicators. One specification lags retained earnings by one year while keeping the market equity denominator current.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in current earnings yield versus accumulated historical earnings yield proxies, conditional on standard return-prediction controls. The central concern is whether retained earnings predicts returns because it averages past earnings rather than because of a functional-fixation mispricing story. The paper interprets the relative coefficients as evidence about which signal better captures expected returns.

Setting: In Fama-MacBeth regressions, retained-earnings-to-market subsumes current earnings-to-price as a predictor of subsequent monthly returns. Earnings-to-price alone is positive and significant at 0.18 (t=3.30). With book-to-market, E/P remains significant at 0.13 (t=3.14) and BE/ME is 0.14 (t=2.37). But with retained-earnings-to-market included, RE/ME is significant at 0.15 (t=4.32) while E/P drops to 0.07 (t=1.50). When retained earnings are lagged one year, RE/ME rises to 0.16 (t=4.61) and E/P stays insignificant at 0.07 (t=1.38). The authors interpret this as evidence that accumulated past earnings in retained earnings provide a better proxy for underlying earnings yield than current earnings alone.

Main role: This comparison directly supports the paper's core mechanism claim that retained earnings works as an accumulated-earnings proxy and subsumes current earnings-to-price.
Settings.H610: Section 4, Table 2 Panel D Columns 1-4 (PDF pp. 238-239 / article pp. 238-239).
Settings.G611:
Treatment: Assignment to high versus low quintiles of book-to-market, retained-earnings-to-market, or contributed-capital-to-market, based on annual NYSE breakpoint sorts. The focal interpreted contrast is typically the high-minus-low portfolio spread for each sorting variable.

Method: Value-weighted portfolio sorts into quintiles based on NYSE breakpoints for book-to-market, retained-earnings-to-market, and contributed-capital-to-market at the end of each June, with portfolios held for the following year. The reported estimands are mean excess returns, CAPM alphas, and Fama-French three-factor alphas for high-minus-low spreads and individual quintiles. This is not a linear regression treatment effect design; it is a portfolio-sort asset-pricing design using treated-versus-control style sorting comparisons.

Identification: Identification is by nonparametric comparison of returns across portfolios sorted on accounting ratios measured before the holding period. The main concern is whether the return spread arises from nonlinearities or functional form assumptions in regressions; the sort approach is used as a robustness check. Interpretation still relies on asset-pricing assumptions that sorted spread returns reveal expected-return differences associated with the treatment variable.

Setting: In annual quintile portfolio sorts, high retained-earnings-to-market stocks earn higher subsequent returns than low retained-earnings-to-market stocks, whereas contributed-capital-to-market shows little predictive power. The high-minus-low spread in excess returns is 0.45 percentage points per month for retained earnings (t=2.81), versus 0.35 for total book-to-market (t=2.43) and 0.12 for contributed capital (t=0.91). CAPM alphas show the same pattern: 0.58 for retained earnings (t=3.68), 0.40 for book-to-market (t=2.83), and 0.09 for contributed capital (t=0.67). Under the three-factor model, the retained earnings spread is near zero at 0.12 (t=1.16), book-to-market is -0.10 (t=-1.36), and contributed capital is -0.23 (t=-2.18), which the authors read as showing that the return-predictive content in book-to-market comes from retained earnings, not contributed capital.

Main role: These portfolio results are presented as a robust nonparametric complement to the Fama-MacBeth regressions and materially support the headline claim that retained earnings drives the value premium.
Settings.G612:
Treatment: Within conditional sorts, assignment to high versus low book-to-market quintiles holding retained-earnings-to-market fixed (Panel A), or assignment to high versus low retained-earnings-to-market quintiles holding book-to-market fixed (Panel B). These are binary high-minus-low contrasts within each conditioning portfolio.

Method: Two-way conditional portfolio sorts. Panel A first sorts stocks into retained-earnings-to-market quintiles and then, within each retained-earnings quintile, into book-to-market quintiles. Panel B reverses the ordering. Portfolios are rebalanced annually at the end of June using NYSE breakpoints, and CAPM alphas are reported for within-cell high-minus-low spreads plus averages of the five conditional spread strategies.

Identification: Identification uses conditional sorts to isolate whether book-to-market contains predictive power once retained earnings is held fixed, and vice versa. The concern is that simple one-way sorts could confound the two highly related variables. The design seeks to show that only retained earnings has incremental return-predictive information.

Setting: Conditional portfolio sorts show that book-to-market has little incremental predictive power once retained-earnings-to-market is held fixed, while retained-earnings-to-market retains predictive power within book-to-market groups. In Panel A, the average retained-earnings-neutral strategy that buys high-BE/ME and sells low-BE/ME earns a CAPM alpha of only 0.15 percentage points per month (t=1.41). In Panel B, the average book-to-market-neutral strategy that buys high-RE/ME and sells low-RE/ME earns a CAPM alpha of 0.45 percentage points per month (t=4.31). The authors interpret this as direct evidence that retained earnings-to-market contains information about expected returns holding book-to-market constant, whereas book-to-market does not add much once retained earnings is known.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis reinforcing the decomposition result rather than the first-line main evidence.
Settings.H612: Section 5 discussion of Appendix Table A.2, Panels A-B (PDF p. 240 and Appendix p. 253 / article pp. 240, 253).
Settings.G613:
Treatment: Exposure to alternative long-short factors formed from high-minus-low sorts on retained-earnings-to-market (HMLRE), contributed-capital-to-market (HMLCC), book-to-market (HML/HML*), or earnings-to-price (E/P). The focal treatment is inclusion of one factor versus another in the spanning set; economically these are binary long-short factor constructions.

Method: Linear spanning regressions of monthly factor returns on other factor returns. The dependent variable is one of HML, HMLRE, HMLCC, or E/P; regressors include MKT, SMB, and one alternative value-related factor. Monthly data run from July 1964 to December 2017. The intercept (alpha) is interpreted as incremental priced information in the left-hand-side factor beyond the spanning set. Although implemented as time-series factor regressions, the paper gives them a causal asset-pricing interpretation about which accounting-based factor carries the economically relevant return-premium information.

Identification: Identification comes from time-series comovement of factor returns. If the intercept remains significant after controlling for market, size, and an alternative value-related factor, the authors interpret the left-hand-side factor as containing incremental expected-return information not subsumed by the controls. The main concern is whether HML's premium is really driven by retained earnings or by other components such as contributed capital or current earnings yield.

Setting: Spanning regressions indicate that retained-earnings-based factor returns contain the useful information in standard HML and earnings-to-price, while contributed-capital-based factor returns do not. When HML is regressed on MKT, SMB, and HMLRE, the intercept is 0.02 (t=0.29), implying no incremental value in HML beyond HMLRE. But when HMLRE is regressed on MKT, SMB, and HML, the intercept is 0.21 (t=2.83), and with HMLCC instead of HML it is 0.57 (t=4.93). HMLCC has a negative alpha relative to HML of -0.17 (t=-2.08). E/P has a positive alpha relative to HML of 0.22 (t=2.82), but not relative to HMLRE, 0.08 (t=1.33). The authors interpret these results as showing that retained earnings-to-market captures the economically relevant value information better than book-to-market, contributed capital, or current earnings-to-price.

Main role: These factor-spanning tests are an important mechanism and robustness exercise, but the main paper result is first established in the cross-sectional regressions and portfolio sorts.
Settings.H613: Section 6, Table 4 Panel C, with supporting factor means in Panel A and correlations in Panel B (PDF pp. 241-242 / article pp. 241-242).
Settings.G614:
Treatment: Continuous logged accumulated-earnings-to-market over windows [t,t] through [t-4,t], plus log(BE/ME) in horse-race specifications. The treatment is the amount of backward-accumulated earnings scaled by current market equity.

Method: Separate sets of monthly Fama-MacBeth (1973) regressions that add a backward-accumulated earnings measure to book-to-market. The accumulated earnings measure sums earnings over windows from the current year back up to five years, divides by the most recent market value of equity, takes logs, and includes an indicator for negative accumulated earnings. Panel A uses either net income or income before extraordinary and special items. The sample runs July 1967-December 2017 to avoid initial Compustat backfill concerns and requires at least five years of earnings data.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in multi-year accumulated earnings yields versus book-to-market, conditional on standard controls. The concern is whether retained earnings predicts returns because it averages past earnings, not because of other balance-sheet features such as repurchases or contributed capital. If extending the earnings accumulation window strengthens the earnings measure and weakens BE/ME, that supports the proposed mechanism.

Setting: Horse-race Fama-MacBeth regressions show that as the authors accumulate earnings over longer windows, the accumulated-earnings signal becomes stronger and book-to-market loses significance. Using accumulated net income, log(BE/ME) falls from 0.16 (t=2.53) with only current earnings to 0.07 (t=1.24) when five years are accumulated, while log(accumulated earnings/ME) rises from 0.11 (t=2.52) to 0.19 (t=3.63). Using income before extraordinary and special items strengthens the pattern further: by the [t-4,t] window, log(BE/ME) is 0.04 (t=0.65) and log(accumulated earnings/ME) is 0.23 (t=3.90). The authors interpret this as strong evidence that book-to-market predicts returns because retained earnings embed accumulated past earnings that average away transitory accounting noise.

Main role: This is a central mechanism test for the paper's thesis that retained earnings works because it accumulates and averages past earnings.
Settings.H614: Section 7, Table 5 Panel A (PDF pp. 242-243 / article pp. 242-243).
Settings.G615:
Treatment: Continuous logged cumulative earnings minus cumulative dividends, and continuous logged cumulative dividends, each scaled by current market value of equity over windows [t,t] to [t-4,t].

Method: Monthly Fama-MacBeth (1973) regressions using accumulated earnings net of dividends and accumulated dividends, each deﬂated by the most recent market value of equity, over windows up to five years backward. Logs are used, with indicators for non-positive accumulated earnings net of dividends and zero dividends. The goal is to separate whether retained-earnings-to-market predicts returns because of accumulated earnings or because of dividend payout policy.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional differences in accumulated earnings retained inside the firm versus dividends paid out, conditioning on standard controls. The concern is that retained earnings could reflect dividend payout policy rather than underlying earnings yield. The design compares the two accumulated components directly within the same return-prediction regressions.

Setting: When the authors separate accumulated earnings net of dividends from accumulated dividends, both enter positively in return-prediction regressions and with similar magnitudes, which they read as evidence that the retained-earnings effect is driven by accumulated earnings rather than payout policy. For example, over [t,t], log(cum. earnings - cum. dividends)/ME has a coefficient of 0.13 (t=4.04) and log(cum. dividends/ME) has 0.12 (t=2.62); over [t-4,t], the corresponding coefficients are 0.14 (t=3.64) and 0.09 (t=2.42). The paper states that for all five windows the differences between the two estimated coefficients are within one standard error of zero, supporting the interpretation that accumulated earnings content, not dividend policy differences, explains retained earnings' predictive power for returns.

Main role: This is a substantive mechanism test supporting the interpretation that accumulated earnings, not payout policy, drive the retained-earnings effect.
Settings.H615: Section 7, Table 5 Panel B (PDF pp. 243-244 / article pp. 243-244).
Settings.G616:
Treatment: Continuous retained-earnings-to-market, book-to-market, and earnings-to-price ratios measured at year t. The focal treatment for the paper's mechanism claim is retained-earnings-to-market as a proxy for underlying earnings yield.

Method: Annual Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions predicting one-, two-, and three-year earnings growth. The dependent variable at horizon k is (IB_{t+k} - IB_t)/ME_t, where IB is income before extraordinary items and ME is December market value of equity in year t. Regressors include log size, E/P, an indicator for negative earnings, BE/ME, and RE/ME. Standard errors are Newey-West adjusted for multi-year horizons.

Identification: Identification is from cross-sectional relation between current accounting ratios and subsequent earnings growth. The concern is whether retained-earnings-to-market reflects mean-reverting current earnings or a more persistent underlying earnings yield. A positive slope on RE/ME alongside negative slopes on E/P is interpreted as evidence of persistence rather than pure mean reversion.

Setting: Retained-earnings-to-market positively predicts future earnings growth, consistent with it proxying for underlying earnings yield. In one-year growth regressions including BE/ME and RE/ME, E/P is -0.52 (t=-12.81), BE/ME is -0.02 (t=-2.66), and RE/ME is 0.02 (t=5.12). At the two-year horizon, RE/ME remains 0.02 (t=3.82), and at the three-year horizon it is 0.02 (t=3.06). By contrast, E/P is negative and significant at all horizons, which the authors interpret as mean reversion in current earnings yields. These findings support the paper's mechanism that retained earnings-to-market captures persistent earnings power linked to expected returns.

Main role: These earnings-growth regressions are a mechanism validation exercise, showing retained earnings-to-market behaves like a proxy for persistent underlying earnings yield.
Settings.G617:
Treatment: Lagged continuous book-to-market or lagged retained-earnings-to-market measured up to five years earlier; the focal treatment is the level of the stale accounting ratio available to investors.

Method: Monthly Fama-MacBeth (1973) regressions that replace current book-to-market and retained-earnings-to-market with increasingly stale lagged values, while updating the standard controls monthly. The figure plots t-statistics for the lagged book-to-market and lagged retained-earnings-to-market coefficients for horizons from the current value out to five years of lag. Regressions include log size, prior one-month return, prior one-year return skipping a month, and for RE/ME an indicator for RE<=0.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional persistence in accounting signals. The concern is whether retained earnings merely captures short-lived noise or instead a persistent expected-return proxy. If stale RE/ME continues to predict returns longer than stale BE/ME, that supports the accumulated-earnings interpretation.

Setting: Lagged-signal regressions show retained-earnings-to-market predicts returns farther ahead than book-to-market. The paper does not report individual coefficients in the figure, but states that book-to-market has significant explanatory power for approximately three years, while retained-earnings-to-market is stronger and persists for about four years. The authors interpret this as consistent with accumulated earnings in retained earnings washing out transitory accounting issues, though predictive power eventually declines because valuation ratios deﬂated by current market values become stale over long horizons.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism exercise showing retained earnings-to-market predicts returns farther into the future than book-to-market.
Settings.G618:
Treatment: High versus low quintile assignment on book-to-market, retained-earnings-to-market, or contributed-capital-to-market in different subsamples: U.S. pre-1990, U.S. post-1990, and developed markets excluding the U.S.

Method: Subsample and international portfolio sorts into annual quintiles on book-to-market, retained-earnings-to-market, and contributed-capital-to-market, reporting CAPM alphas for each quintile and high-minus-low spreads. U.S. subsamples split pre-1990 and post-1990. The international sample covers developed markets excluding the U.S., using a large-stock cutoff rather than NYSE microcap breakpoints. This is a portfolio-sort design rather than a regression-based causal estimator.

Identification: Identification uses sorted return spreads across different eras and markets to test whether the retained-earnings effect is stable and not a statistical artifact. The main concern is data mining or a sample-specific relation. Consistency across subperiods and countries strengthens the interpretation that retained earnings, not contributed capital, is the relevant component behind value-related expected return differences.

Setting: Across time periods and countries, retained-earnings-to-market consistently predicts higher subsequent CAPM-adjusted returns, while contributed-capital-to-market does not. In the U.S. pre-1990 sample, the high-minus-low CAPM alpha is 0.55 percentage points per month for book-to-market (t=2.67) and 0.60 for retained earnings (t=2.96), with contributed capital only 0.15 (t=0.86). Post-1990, book-to-market weakens to 0.26 (t=1.32), but retained earnings remains strong at 0.62 (t=2.68), while contributed capital is -0.06 (t=-0.30). In developed markets outside the U.S., the CAPM alpha is 0.49 for book-to-market (t=3.06), 0.55 for retained earnings (t=3.64), and 0.06 for contributed capital (t=0.45). The authors interpret this stability as evidence that retained earnings drives the value premium across regimes.

Main role: These subsample and international tests are emphasized in the introduction and conclusions to show stability across eras and countries, directly supporting the paper's central conclusion.
Settings.G619:
Treatment: High versus low quintile assignment on total book-to-market, a proxy for retained-earnings-to-market (the fitted value from regressing book-to-market on accumulated past income), or a proxy for contributed-capital-to-market (the residual).

Method: Pre-1964 portfolio sorts using historical accounting data merged from Moody's manuals, Compustat, and Ken French historical book equity data. Because retained earnings are unavailable, the authors proxy for retained-earnings-to-market by regressing book-to-market on income accumulated up to 20 years in the past and using the fitted value; the residual proxies for contributed-capital-to-market. Stocks are sorted into quintiles on total book-to-market and these proxies, with annual rebalancing and CAPM alphas reported for quintiles and high-minus-low spreads.

Identification: Identification comes from historical sorted return spreads using proxies designed to decompose book-to-market into accumulated-earnings-related and residual components before retained earnings are directly observed. The concern is whether the main result is an artifact of the Compustat period. Similar patterns in earlier data support external validity.

Setting: In pre-1964 U.S. data, only the retained-earnings proxy produces a significant high-minus-low CAPM alpha. The high-minus-low alpha is 0.28 percentage points per month for total book-to-market (t=1.39), 0.49 for the retained-earnings proxy (t=3.11), and 0.18 for the contributed-capital proxy (t=0.97). The authors interpret this as further corroboration that the predictive content in book-to-market historically came from accumulated earnings rather than contributed capital.

Main role: This is an external historical corroboration test supporting the paper's main conclusion across a pre-Compustat sample.
Settings.G620:
Treatment: Continuous logged book-to-market and its components—retained-earnings-to-market, contributed-capital-to-market, and AOCI-to-market—within the subsample of financial firms.

Method: Monthly Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions on a sample restricted to financial firms, otherwise mirroring the main Table 2 Panel A design. The sample runs July 1964-December 2017, includes all but microcap financial firms with positive book equity and non-missing retained earnings and contributed capital, trims variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles, and includes controls for size and past returns. Non-positive component ratios are handled by setting logs to zero and adding indicators.

Identification: Same cross-sectional predictive logic as the main regressions, but applied to financial firms to address concern that excluding them drives the findings. The authors note accounting ratios may differ in interpretation for financials, so this is a holdout-style robustness exercise.

Setting: Among financial firms, the same general pattern holds: retained-earnings-to-market drives the predictive power of book-to-market. In Appendix Table A.1, log(BE/ME) alone has a coefficient of 0.24 (t=2.37). log(RE/ME) alone is 0.18 (t=3.29). When both are included, log(BE/ME) declines to 0.14 (t=1.19) and log(RE/ME) is 0.12 (t=1.90). In the full specification with all three components, log(RE/ME) is 0.20 (t=3.42), log(CC/ME) is 0.10 (t=1.70), and log(BE/ME) is 0.28 (t=2.75) when used with AOCI in another column; the text summarizes that retained earnings remains the main source of predictive power, though contributed capital is marginally significant for financials. This supports, but does not replace, the paper's main nonfinancial result.

Main role: This appendix analysis is a substantive robustness check because the main sample excludes financials; it supports generalization of the core result.
Settings.H620: Appendix discussion in footnote 14 and Table A.1 (PDF pp. 239, 252 / article pp. 239, 252).
Settings.G621:
Treatment: Continuous current bottom-line net income to book value of equity ratio (E/BE), with some specifications also controlling for retained-earnings-to-market. The paper uses this as a test of the alternative functional-fixation interpretation.

Method: Monthly Fama-MacBeth (1973) regressions and horizon plots examining whether current bottom-line earnings scaled by book equity predict returns, with and without controlling for retained-earnings-to-market. The figure plots t-statistics for the coefficient on E/BE as the horizon of predicted monthly returns extends out to five years. Regressions include prior one-month return, prior one-year return skipping a month, and log size; when RE/ME is included, a RE<=0 indicator is added and log(RE/ME) is set to zero for those observations.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional relation between current earnings scaled by book equity and future returns, conditional on retained earnings. The key concern is whether investors overweight transitory current earnings components; under functional fixation, the slope on current earnings conditional on retained earnings should be negative. The figure is used to show that it remains positive instead.

Setting: The functional-fixation interpretation predicts that current bottom-line earnings, once retained-earnings-to-market is controlled for, should negatively predict future returns. The authors instead report in Fig. 4 that the coefficient on E/BE is positive for predicting returns out to five years ahead both when included alone and when controlling for retained-earnings-to-market. The figure does not report exact coefficients, only t-statistics, but the stated sign pattern is used as evidence against the view that retained earnings predicts returns because investors initially overweight transitory current earnings components.

Main role: This is a discriminating robustness/mechanism test aimed at rejecting a functional-fixation explanation rather than establishing the main result.
Settings.G622:
Treatment: Exposure to factor returns based on negative-versus-positive special items relative to assets (SPI, SPIsmall, SPIbig) or retained-earnings-to-market (HMLRE). These are long-short factor treatments constructed from portfolio sorts.

Method: Time-series spanning regressions of monthly returns on special-items-based factors and retained-earnings-based factors. Special-items factors are formed by independent size and special-items-to-assets sorts, creating SPIsmall, SPIbig, and SPI. Dependent variables are SPI, SPIsmall, SPIbig, or HMLRE; explanatory variables include MKT, SMB, and either HML/HMLRE or SPI factors. The intercept alpha is interpreted as incremental priced information.

Identification: Identification comes from time-series factor spanning: if HMLRE keeps a large positive alpha after controlling for SPI factors, then the retained-earnings premium is not subsumed by the Dechow-Ge special-items mechanism. The concern is that retained earnings may merely wash out transitory negative special items that investors initially overweight.

Setting: Spanning regressions show that the retained-earnings factor contains distinct return information not explained by special-items factors. Replicating Dechow and Ge, SPIbig has positive alpha: 0.28 relative to HML (t=2.17) and 0.32 relative to HMLRE (t=2.41), while SPI and SPIsmall are not significant. But when HMLRE is the dependent variable, its alpha is 0.57 (t=4.93) with only MKT and SMB, 0.59 (t=5.15) after adding SPI, and 0.58 (t=5.04) after adding SPIsmall and SPIbig. The authors conclude that retained-earnings-to-market's return premium is distinct from special-items-based functional-fixation effects.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis showing the retained-earnings effect is distinct from special-items-based mispricing.
Settings.G623:
Treatment: Equity cash-flow duration, measured at the firm-year level by the author’s Dur metric from Eq. (7), then operationalized as portfolio assignment across duration deciles. The focal implemented treatment contrast is generally short-duration versus long-duration portfolio membership (decile 1 vs decile 10), based on annually formed June sorts. Because the estimand is a decile/rank contrast rather than a literal binary firm treatment, coding as binary is uncertain.

Method: The paper forms annual decile portfolios sorted on the author’s firm-level equity duration measure (Dur) each June and then interprets differences in subsequent portfolio returns as the effect of cash-flow duration on expected returns. The implemented estimator is a portfolio-sort mean-contrast/regression-adjustment design: average annualized excess returns, Sharpe ratios, and long-minus-short return spreads are computed for value-weighted and equal-weighted portfolios, including variants with five-year holding horizons, stale duration sorts, large-firm subsamples, and delisting-adjusted returns. This is not an experimental or quasi-experimental design; the intended causal reading is that shorter equity duration raises required returns/premia. Identification rests on interpreting duration sorts as isolating systematic cash-flow-duration exposure rather than omitted characteristics.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in firms’ estimated equity duration. The paper argues that sorting firms by Dur isolates exposure to short- versus long-maturity cash flows, and then interprets systematic return differences as a duration premium. Endogeneity concerns remain substantial: duration is endogenous to firm fundamentals and may proxy for other expected-return determinants. The paper addresses this by validating the duration measure, examining persistence, large-firm subsamples, and later multivariate controls, but this setting itself is still an observational return-spread design relying on the asset-pricing interpretation that duration differences map to differences in required returns.

Setting: Using annual decile sorts on the author’s Dur measure from 1973–2018, the paper argues that shorter equity duration causes higher expected returns: in value-weighted portfolios, the short-minus-long duration spread is 8.6% per year over the next year, 7.1% per year when held for five years, 4.1% per year even when duration is measured four years earlier, and 6.6% per year among only the largest firms; equal-weighted estimates are similar or slightly larger. These return-spread results are the paper’s starting point and core empirical fact motivating the later reinvestment-risk interpretation.

Main role: The abstract and introduction center the paper on documenting a large short-duration premium, its persistence, and its presence among large firms. Table 2 is the main empirical evidence for that central claim.
Settings.H623: Section 3.3, Table 2 Panels A and B, and Figs. 2–3 (PDF pp. 9–12).
Settings.G624:
Treatment: The focal treatment is the portfolio’s lagged duration decile (or associated short-vs-long duration contrast) constructed from the firm-level Dur measure. In multivariate specifications, the treatment is the duration decile coefficient conditional on book-to-market, profitability, asset growth, and/or size deciles. This is an ordered decile exposure, not a binary treatment.

Method: The paper estimates linear panel regressions of portfolio returns on lagged portfolio-level average decile ranks for duration, book-to-market, profitability, asset growth, and size. The data are constructed from characteristic-sorted decile portfolios; columns 1.1–1.8 include only decile portfolios for included covariates, and columns 2.1–2.7 retain all 50 decile portfolios. Inference uses Driscoll–Kraay standard errors. The coefficients are interpreted causally as characteristic premia after controlling for other firm characteristics, particularly whether duration subsumes value and profitability.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-portfolio variation in lagged characteristic deciles. The design attempts to isolate the marginal return effect of duration versus value, profitability, investment, and size by using multivariate regressions on portfolio returns rather than stock-level regressions. The causal concern is omitted correlated characteristics and functional-form issues; the paper motivates the portfolio-regression approach as a compromise between portfolio sorts and panel regressions. Still, the design is observational and relies on interpreting decile coefficients as characteristic-premium effects conditional on included controls.

Setting: In panel regressions of portfolio returns on lagged characteristic deciles, the paper concludes that duration drives the value and profitability premia. In value-weighted portfolios, the univariate duration premium is 8.6% per year; after controlling for book-to-market it is 9.7%, after controlling for profitability 12.3%, after jointly controlling for value and profitability 12.7%, and in the full five-variable specification 14.4% (t = 2.44). By contrast, the value premium falls from 4.9% univariately to 0.9% when controlling for duration, and from 12.7% with profitability controlled to -0.4% when duration is also included; the profitability premium similarly turns negative once duration is included. This setting materially supports the paper’s claim that value and profitability are proxies for short-duration exposure.

Main role: A central conclusion in the abstract and introduction is that after controlling for duration, value and profitability premia disappear, and joint tests make this result stronger. Table 3 is the main evidence for that claim.
Settings.H624: Section 3.4, Table 3 Panels A and B (PDF pp. 12–13).
Settings.G625:
Treatment: Exposure to reinvestment risk associated with short-duration versus long-duration equity portfolios. Operationally, the treatment is higher short-duration exposure, reflected in the long-minus-short difference in beta to shocks in expected market returns (βEr), or equivalently membership in shorter-duration portfolios that load less negatively on expected-return shocks. This is a continuous risk exposure rather than binary treatment.

Method: The paper estimates an intertemporal CAPM pricing equation using annual returns on duration-sorted portfolio spreads relative to the shortest-duration portfolio, plus in some specifications the aggregate equity premium. Risk prices are estimated from pooled panel regressions of returns on covariances with market-return shocks and expected-return shocks, under CAPM restrictions, ICAPM restrictions, or unrestricted ICAPMU pricing. The substantive causal interpretation is that exposure to reinvestment risk causes the short-duration premium; Table 4 shows the relevant betas and Table 5 the implied pricing errors.

Identification: Identification is structural/asset-pricing rather than reduced-form causal inference. The paper uses the ICAPM to interpret covariation between duration-portfolio returns and shocks to expected market returns as priced reinvestment risk. Expected-return shocks are estimated from predictive-state-variable models. The endogeneity concern is that these shocks and betas are model-dependent and may capture other omitted risks. The paper addresses this by showing monotonic beta patterns across duration deciles, contrasting CAPM versus ICAPM pricing errors, and showing the mechanism also implies an upward bond term structure of premia rather than a counterfactual short-duration bond premium.

Setting: The paper argues that short-duration stocks earn higher expected returns because they expose investors to reinvestment risk. In Table 4, value-weighted annual excess returns fall from 13.3% in the shortest-duration decile to 4.5% in the longest, while βEr falls from -0.41 to -2.30, so the short-minus-long strategy has βEr = -1.89 (t = -7.73). In Table 5, a CAPM cannot explain the short-duration premium, leaving α10−1 = -8.8% when matching the slope of the equity term structure and -13.2% when also matching the equity premium. By contrast, the ICAPM reduces this alpha to -0.9% and -3.0%, respectively, with estimated risk aversion 3.5 or 10.5 depending on whether the equity premium is imposed. This is the paper’s core causal mechanism linking duration to expected returns through priced reinvestment-risk exposure.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that earning the short-duration premium requires exposure to variation in expected returns and that this reinvestment-risk exposure is large enough to explain the premium. Tables 4 and 5 are the main evidence for that central mechanism.
Settings.H625: Sections 4.1–4.2, Tables 4 and 5, and Fig. 4 (PDF pp. 15–18).
Settings.G626:
Treatment: High versus low cross-sectional dispersion in equity duration, σ(Dur), where low is the bottom 25% of annual observations and high is the top 25%. This is implemented as a state split of the time series rather than a firm-level treatment; the focal contrast is high-σ(Dur) periods versus low-σ(Dur) periods.

Method: The paper splits the sample by the cross-sectional standard deviation of log equity duration, σ(Dur), and computes average market returns, short-minus-long duration returns, and risk exposures separately for low-, medium-, and high-dispersion states. This is a state-contingent portfolio-sort comparison rather than an experimental design. The intended causal interpretation is that greater cross-sectional duration dispersion increases the reinvestment-risk exposure of the short-duration strategy and therefore raises its premium.

Identification: Identification comes from time variation in the cross-sectional dispersion of duration. The paper’s mechanism predicts that when the duration spread across firms is larger, the short-duration strategy mechanically has a larger duration gap and therefore greater exposure to expected-return shocks. The causal claim requires assuming σ(Dur) is not merely proxying for some other state variable that jointly changes expected returns and portfolio composition. The paper partially addresses competing stories by showing that aggregate market premia do not vary much across states, market beta variation goes the wrong way for a conditional CAPM explanation, and dividend-growth-risk exposure peaks in the moderate rather than high-dispersion state.

Setting: The paper argues that larger cross-sectional duration dispersion causes a larger short-duration premium by increasing reinvestment-risk exposure. In value-weighted portfolios, the short-duration premium is 3.1% after low-σ(Dur) periods and 20.3% after high-σ(Dur) periods, while the corresponding reinvestment-risk beta moves from -1.02 to -2.56. Aggregate equity premia remain similar across states, which the paper interprets as evidence that the slope, not the level, of the equity term structure varies with σ(Dur). This time-series state-split analysis supports the paper’s reinvestment-risk explanation and is presented as inconsistent with alternative CAPM or cash-flow-risk accounts.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight a time-series fact: the short-duration premium is much higher in periods with higher cross-sectional dispersion in equity duration, and reinvestment risk is also larger during those periods. Table 6 is the central evidence for that time-series mechanism.
Settings.H626: Section 4.3, Table 6 (PDF pp. 19–20; introductory summary on PDF p. 2).
Settings.G627:
Treatment: Alternative equity-duration exposure measured by expected payback period (EPP), then implemented via duration-decile portfolio assignment; focal contrast is shortest-EPP versus longest-EPP portfolios. The treatment is an ordered ranking rather than a literal binary indicator.

Method: The paper repeats the main duration-premium and risk-exposure analyses using an alternative duration metric, expected payback period (EPP), defined in Eq. (14) as the horizon that solves expected cumulative payouts equal to market equity. The empirical implementation mirrors the baseline design: annual decile portfolio sorts, average return spreads, large-firm subsamples, long holding horizons, and ICAPM alpha and beta calculations.

Identification: Same observational identification logic as the baseline portfolio-sort setting, but using EPP as the duration metric.
