The role of this setting is robustness: if similar return spreads and reinvestment-risk exposures arise with a duration measure that does not require discount-rate estimation, that supports the claim that duration itself, rather than a particular measurement procedure, drives the results.

Setting: Using expected payback period (EPP) instead of Dur to sort firms, the paper finds essentially the same causal pattern: in value-weighted portfolios the short-minus-long EPP spread is 8.4% per year, remains 6.9% over five-year holdings, is 7.3% among large firms, and has an ICAPM alpha of only 1.2% while the long-short strategy has βEr = -2.37. The paper interprets this as robustness that short cash-flow duration, not quirks of the baseline duration measure, raises expected returns through reinvestment-risk exposure.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis in Section 5.1 showing the main short-duration premium and reinvestment-risk results are not driven by the baseline duration measure’s discount-rate estimation.
Settings.G628:
Treatment: Alternative equity-duration exposure measured by log-linear duration llDur, then implemented through duration-decile portfolio assignment; focal contrast is lowest versus highest llDur portfolios. This is an ordered nonbinary treatment.

Method: The paper repeats the main duration-premium and risk-exposure analyses using a second alternative duration metric, the log-linear duration approximation llDur from Eq. (15). As with the baseline and EPP analyses, firms are sorted into annual deciles and subsequent returns, large-firm subsample returns, and ICAPM pricing quantities are computed.

Identification: Same observational strategy as other duration-sort settings, but using llDur. The robustness logic is that similar results with llDur suggest the causal interpretation is linked to duration ranking itself rather than to the exact nonlinear Dur calculation or estimated discount-rate input.

Setting: Replacing Dur with the log-linear duration measure llDur, the paper again finds a large short-duration premium and strong reinvestment-risk exposure. In value-weighted portfolios, the short-minus-long spread is 9.4% per year, 7.2% over five-year holdings, and 7.7% among large firms; the ICAPM alpha is only 0.1% and the long-short strategy has βEr = -2.25. The paper uses this as robustness evidence that shorter cash-flow duration increases expected returns because it carries reinvestment risk.

Main role: This is another substantive robustness analysis in Section 5.1, used to show the main results survive when duration is measured with a log-linear approximation that also avoids explicit discount-rate estimation.
Settings.G629:
Treatment: Placebo ‘duration’ pDur, defined as the fitted value from a cross-sectional regression of firm-name alphabetical rank on the state vector s_t; implemented as annual decile portfolio assignment. This is not a real economic treatment but a placebo ordered score.

Method: As a placebo test, the paper constructs a pseudo-duration variable pDur by projecting firm-name alphabetical rank on the same state variables used in Dur and then sorting firms into deciles on that placebo score. It then computes average return spreads, large-firm subsample spreads, long-horizon spreads, Sharpe ratios, and factor-model alphas exactly as in the baseline duration-sort design. The substantive interpretation is that if arbitrary functions of the same characteristics generated return spreads, the main results could be spurious; finding no placebo premium supports the causal relevance of actual duration.

Identification: The identification logic is falsification: if a placebo score built from the same underlying characteristics but unrelated to duration produced similar premia, the main causal interpretation would be undermined. Instead, the placebo sorts generate no meaningful return spreads or alphas, which the paper interprets as evidence that the main effect is specific to duration rather than generic characteristic combination.

Setting: The placebo-duration test yields no premium: sorting on pDur, the value-weighted long-minus-short spread is only 2.8% per year over the next year, 1.2% over five years, and 4.2% among large firms, with insignificant factor-model alphas. The paper interprets this null result as evidence that the baseline duration premium is not an artifact of combining the same state variables in arbitrary ways, strengthening the claim that true cash-flow duration drives expected returns.

Main role: This is a placebo robustness exercise in Section 5.2 used to support the main interpretation by showing the return patterns are not mechanically produced by arbitrary combinations of the same firm characteristics.
Settings.H629: Section 5.2, Table 8 Panels A and B (PDF pp. 21–22).
Settings.G630:
Treatment: Equity duration measured by DSS Dur from Eq. (16), implemented as annual decile portfolio assignment; focal contrast is short-duration versus long-duration DSS Dur portfolios. This is an ordered duration ranking, not binary.

Method: The paper replicates the baseline duration-sort analysis using the Dechow, Sloan, and Soliman (2004) implied equity duration measure (DSS Dur), measured from Eq. (16). Firms are sorted into annual deciles on DSS Dur and the paper computes average return spreads, large-firm subsample spreads, long-horizon spreads, Sharpe ratios, and factor-model alphas. The intended causal reading is still that shorter duration increases expected returns, but the exercise is comparative, assessing whether the older duration measure captures the same premium and factor-model abnormal performance.

Identification: Same observational portfolio-sort logic as the baseline, but with duration measured by DSS Dur. The comparison is meant to assess whether a weaker duration proxy produces weaker return spreads and whether its apparent premium is subsumed by standard factor models. The causal interpretation is therefore comparative: a better duration measure should more cleanly isolate duration-related expected-return variation.

Setting: Sorting on DSS Dur still produces a short-duration premium, but weaker than the baseline and largely explained by standard factors. In value-weighted portfolios, the short-minus-long spread is 6.1% per year over the next year and 5.4% over five years, but the Fama-French five-factor alpha is only 0.4% and the q-factor alpha is -2.0%, both economically small relative to the baseline Dur results. The paper uses this to argue that its own duration measure better captures the causal return effect of cash-flow duration.

Main role: This is a comparative robustness/substantive benchmarking exercise in Section 5.3. It is not the main design but is used to argue that the author’s Dur measure improves on DSS Dur empirically as well as theoretically.
Settings.H630: Section 5.3.2, Table 9 Panels A and B and Fig. 5 (PDF pp. 23–25).
Settings.G631:
Treatment: Fund Herding (FH), a continuous fund-level measure of the tendency of a mutual fund to imitate past institutional trades, constructed as a rank inverse-weighted average of quarterly slope coefficients from fund-specific cross-sectional trade regressions of current fund trades on lagged aggregate institutional trades. Units are approximately proportion/percentage-point-style coefficients; portfolio sorts compare higher-herding versus lower-herding funds, especially decile 10 versus decile 1.

Method: The authors estimate predictive linear portfolio sorts and time-series factor-model regressions to interpret mutual fund herding as affecting subsequent mutual fund performance. Each quarter, funds are sorted into deciles on the continuous fund-level herding measure FH, then equally weighted portfolio returns are computed over the next quarter. They report raw net and gross returns and alphas from linear time-series regressions under CAPM, Fama-French 3-factor, Carhart 4-factor, Pastor-Stambaugh 5-factor, and Ferson-Schadt conditional models. This is not a randomized or quasi-experimental design; identification is based on observed cross-sectional variation in lagged herding and interpreted predictively/causally as reflecting skill differences, with concern remaining about omitted variables and selection.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional heterogeneity in lagged fund herding. The paper argues FH isolates imitation of past institutional trades after controlling for stock momentum, size, and book-to-market in the underlying trade regressions, so differences in subsequent performance are interpreted as reflecting skill rather than common styles. However, this remains observational and relies on the assumption that remaining omitted fund traits do not fully explain both herding and future performance.

Setting: Using quarterly decile sorts on the continuous herding measure FH, the authors find that funds with stronger herding tendencies subsequently perform worse than antiherding funds. In Table II, the top-decile herding portfolio underperforms the bottom-decile antiherding portfolio by 0.19% per month in both net and gross returns, or 2.28% annualized. Risk-adjusted underperformance ranges from 0.14% to 0.21% per month depending on the factor model, including a Carhart alpha spread of -0.16% per month net and gross. The authors interpret this as evidence that greater herding reveals lower managerial skill, and this setting carries the paper’s main causal claim.

Main role: This is the paper’s headline evidence from the abstract, introduction, and conclusion: herding funds underperform antiherding funds by about 2% per year, before and after expenses, and this is the central empirical fact motivating the skill interpretation.
Settings.H631: Section II.A, Table II, panels 'Net Return' and 'Gross Return' (PDF pp. 10-12, especially p. 11).
Settings.G632:
Treatment: Continuous fund herding FH measured at the end of quarter t, based on the inverse-weighted average of fund-specific trade-regression coefficients relating current fund trades to lagged aggregate institutional trades.

Method: The authors estimate predictive panel regressions of future mutual fund performance on lagged fund herding with time fixed effects and fund-clustered standard errors. The dependent variable is next-quarter monthly Carhart four-factor alpha, computed using rolling three-year factor loadings. Controls include fund size, age, expense ratio, turnover, lagged flows, past alpha, and in alternative specifications active share, reliance on public information, similarity to successful funds, and tracking error. Time fixed effects absorb aggregate movements in fund returns, but there are not three separately absorbed FE dimensions, so this is standard FE rather than HDFE.

Identification: Identification comes from within-time cross-sectional differences in lagged fund herding after adjusting for observed fund characteristics and absorbing common time shocks with time fixed effects. The main endogeneity concern is omitted fund-level determinants of both herding and future alpha; the paper argues robustness to controls such as active share, public-information reliance, similarity to successful funds, and tracking error mitigates this concern, but it is not eliminated.

Setting: In panel regressions with time fixed effects, higher lagged fund herding predicts lower future risk-adjusted performance. A univariate regression yields a coefficient of -0.466 on FH for net four-factor alpha; adding standard fund controls gives -0.438, and including other skill-related controls leaves the coefficient between about -0.439 and -0.543. Gross-alpha results are nearly identical. The authors interpret these coefficients causally as showing that herding behavior reveals lower managerial skill rather than merely proxying for past performance or benchmark deviation.

Main role: These regressions are a main supporting specification showing the herding-performance relation survives observable controls and time fixed effects, directly supporting the central claim that herding predicts performance beyond other fund characteristics and skill proxies.
Settings.G633:
Treatment: Continuous stock-level measure of exposure to antiherding versus herding fund ownership, SFH, constructed from portfolio weights of mutual funds rescaled by transformed herding decile ranks; higher values indicate stocks held more by antiherding funds, lower values indicate stocks held more by herding funds. Sample restricted to stocks with small prior-quarter institutional-ownership changes.

Method: The authors construct a stock-level exposure measure SFH by aggregating stock positions across mutual funds with weights based on each fund’s herding tendency, restricting the sample to stocks in the bottom tercile of absolute lagged institutional-ownership changes. They then sort stocks into quintiles on SFH and estimate subsequent monthly returns and linear factor-model alphas. This is an observational portfolio-sorting design intended to isolate whether antiherding funds make better stock-picking decisions even for stocks not heavily traded by institutions.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-sectional differences in which stocks are held by antiherding versus herding funds, while restricting attention to stocks with small institutional-trade shocks to reduce confounding by the same trades used to construct herding and by price-pressure/reversal mechanisms. The remaining assumption is that, within this restricted sample, SFH primarily captures superior stock-picking rather than omitted stock characteristics.

Setting: To test whether antiherding funds make better investment decisions even away from crowded trades, the authors sort stocks with small past institutional-trade changes by an ownership-weighted measure of antiherding versus herding fund exposure. Stocks most heavily held by antiherding funds outperform those held by herding funds by 0.49% per month in raw returns and by 0.38% per month in Carhart alpha. The authors interpret this as evidence that antiherding funds have superior stock-picking skill rather than simply benefiting from reversals in institutionally crowded stocks.

Main role: This is a central skill-mechanism test in Section III, used to support the paper’s main interpretation that antiherding funds are more skilled stock pickers, not merely beneficiaries of price pressure on crowded stocks.
Settings.H633: Section III.A, Table V (PDF pp. 16-18, especially p. 17).
Settings.G634:
Treatment: Continuous fund herding FH, interacted with continuous measures of investment opportunities: CrossVol, IV, and Sentiment, measured contemporaneously or lagged. The focal treatment is the marginal effect of herding conditional on these state variables.

Method: The authors estimate predictive panel regressions of future net four-factor alpha on fund herding, interactions between fund herding and time-varying proxies for investment opportunities, standard fund controls, and time fixed effects, with fund-clustered standard errors. The interaction terms use contemporaneous and lagged cross-sectional stock return dispersion, average idiosyncratic volatility, and investor sentiment. This is a standard FE regression used to interpret heterogeneity in the causal effect of herding on performance when skill is more valuable.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional differences in herding combined with time variation in aggregate opportunity measures, with time fixed effects absorbing common return shocks and controls for standard fund characteristics. The key assumption is that the interaction between herding and the opportunity proxies captures times when skill matters more, rather than omitted state-dependent confounders that jointly affect herding funds’ relative performance.

Setting: The authors test whether the negative effect of herding on future performance intensifies when investment opportunities are greater. In panel regressions with time fixed effects, the coefficient on FH remains negative, and interactions of FH with return dispersion and investor sentiment are significantly negative: for example, FH × CrossVol is -0.322 and FH × Sent is -0.358 in net-alpha regressions. They interpret this as showing that antiherding managers outperform especially when opportunities for active skill are more valuable, reinforcing the view that herding reveals lower skill.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the herding–antiherding performance gap is wider when skill is more valuable. This interaction design is a central mechanism result supporting the skill interpretation.
Settings.H634: Section III.B, Table VI Panel B (PDF pp. 18-21).
Settings.G635:
Treatment: Continuous aggregate investment-opportunity proxy: CrossVol, IV, or Sentiment (current or lagged), interpreted as changing the magnitude of the return effect of herding. The effective outcome contrast is the monthly return spread between top-herding and bottom-herding fund portfolios.

Method: The authors estimate time-series regressions of the monthly return differential between herding and antiherding fund portfolios (decile 10 minus decile 1) on contemporaneous and lagged proxies for investment opportunities: cross-sectional stock return dispersion, average idiosyncratic volatility, and investor sentiment. This is an aggregate observational regression used to interpret how the performance effect of herding varies over time.

Identification: Identification comes from time-series covariation between aggregate opportunity proxies and the return spread between herding and antiherding funds. The concern is that macro conditions correlated with these proxies may mechanically affect the spread through channels other than differential skill. The paper interprets significant negative slopes as evidence that skill-related performance differences matter more in high-opportunity periods.

Setting: Using monthly time-series regressions, the authors show that the return spread between herding and antiherding funds becomes more negative when return dispersion, idiosyncratic volatility, or investor sentiment is high. For example, the coefficient on contemporaneous CrossVol is -0.206 and on contemporaneous Sentiment is -0.256. These results support the interpretation that the cost of herding is larger when the value of managerial skill is higher.

Main role: This is a supporting time-series version of the broader heterogeneity claim that the performance gap widens when skill is more valuable; the panel interaction regressions are the paper’s more comprehensive evidence.
Settings.H635: Section III.B, Table VI Panel A (PDF pp. 18-20).
Settings.G636:
Treatment: Fund Herding (FH), continuous herding measure used to sort funds into deciles; focal contrast is decile 10 minus decile 1 maintained over longer horizons K=6 to 24 months.

Method: The authors perform long-horizon portfolio sorts by fund herding and compute the monthly performance spread between the highest-herding and lowest-herding deciles for holding horizons from 6 to 24 months. They report raw net and gross returns and factor-model alphas. This is an observational portfolio design used to interpret persistence of the performance effect of herding as evidence against luck.

Identification: Identification again uses cross-sectional differences in lagged herding and examines whether associated performance differences persist over longer holding horizons. The interpretive assumption is that persistent spreads are less consistent with random luck; nevertheless, omitted persistent fund characteristics remain a concern in this nonexperimental setting.

Setting: When the authors track herding-sorted mutual fund portfolios for up to two years, the underperformance of herding funds persists. At K=6 months, the decile-10 minus decile-1 spread is -0.15% per month in raw net returns and -0.11% per month in Carhart alpha; even at K=24 months, the spread remains about -0.10% in net returns and -0.06% in Carhart alpha. The authors interpret this persistence as evidence that herding reveals skill differences rather than transitory luck.

Main role: This is a substantive mechanism/robustness analysis supporting the main claim by arguing the herding-performance relation reflects persistent skill rather than short-run luck.
Settings.G637:
Treatment: Current-quarter stock-level change in the fraction of shares owned by antiherding funds or by herding funds, where antiherding and herding funds are defined as the bottom and top 10% of funds based on lagged FH. Treatments are continuous stock-level trading measures.

Method: The authors estimate Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of future aggregate institutional trading in a stock on current trades by antiherding funds and herding funds, with and without controls for lagged institutional trades, size, book-to-market, momentum, and turnover. They interpret the coefficients as testing whether antiherding funds can anticipate later trades of the institutional crowd. This is an observational linear regression design.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional covariation between trades of herding-type funds and subsequent aggregate institutional trading, controlling for lagged aggregate trades and stock characteristics. The main concern is that omitted stock-level information visible to antiherding funds but not controlled for could drive both their trades and subsequent institutional demand; the paper interprets significant positive coefficients for antiherding funds as evidence of earlier information acquisition.

Setting: The trades of antiherding funds predict subsequent institutional crowd trades, while the trades of herding funds do not. For next-quarter institutional trading, the coefficient on antiherding-fund trades ranges from about 1.120 to 1.297 without controls and remains 1.140 with controls; for institutional trading over the next year, the coefficient ranges from about 1.747 to 2.420. The authors interpret this as evidence that antiherding funds are earlier informed and use that advantage in ways consistent with superior skill.

Main role: This is a mechanism test supporting the idea that antiherding funds are earlier informed and more skilled because their trades forecast the crowd’s later trades.
Settings.G638:
Treatment: Fund Herding (FH), a continuous measure of a manager/fund’s tendency to follow past institutional trades. In split-sample specifications the focal treatment remains FH within low- versus high-experience or tenure groups.

Method: The authors estimate logit models of the probability that a mutual fund manager is terminated as a function of fund herding, manager experience or tenure, and fund controls, reporting both logit coefficients and marginal effects. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear binary-response regression, it is classified as Other rather than linear OLS/FE. They also estimate subsample logit models split by manager experience or tenure. The design is observational and intended to interpret herding as reducing career-termination risk, especially for less experienced managers.

Identification: Identification relies on observational variation in herding and manager experience/tenure across single-manager funds, controlling for fund characteristics. The authors interpret negative herding coefficients as evidence that imitating the crowd reduces adverse career outcomes. The main concerns are endogenous manager behavior and unobserved fund-family or manager quality characteristics that jointly influence both herding and retention.

Setting: In nonlinear logit regressions, greater herding is associated with a lower probability of manager termination, and this protective effect is concentrated among less experienced managers. In the whole sample, the coefficient on FH is about -0.075 to -0.080. The authors further compute predicted probabilities: holding other variables at their means, an antiherding manager faces a 5.5% termination probability versus 4.2% for a herding manager; among low-experience managers, the probabilities are 7.4% versus 5.1%. They interpret this as evidence that reputational incentives encourage herding, especially early in managers’ careers.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight stronger effects among managers with stronger career concerns. These termination regressions are central to the reputational-herding mechanism and show why herding may be a rational response to career incentives.
Settings.H638: Section IV, Table IX Panels A and B (PDF pp. 24-27).
Settings.G639:
Treatment: Fund Herding group (four bins from low to high FH), interacted through independent double-sorting with manager experience or tenure groups (low/medium/high). The focal contrast is high-FH versus low-FH within experience groups.

Method: The authors use double sorts of mutual funds by herding and by managerial experience (general experience or fund-specific tenure), then compute subsequent monthly net and gross returns and Carhart four-factor alphas for each portfolio. This observational portfolio design is used to interpret heterogeneity in the performance effect of herding across managers with different career concerns.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional variation in herding within bins of managerial experience or tenure. The authors interpret stronger underperformance of herding funds among inexperienced managers as evidence that herding reveals lower skill more strongly when career concerns are greater. Remaining concerns are endogenous sorting of managers and omitted manager or fund traits correlated with both herding and future performance within experience groups.

Setting: The performance penalty associated with herding is much larger among less experienced managers. In Table XI Panel A, among low-general-experience managers, high-FH funds underperform low-FH funds by 0.16% per month in net returns and 0.18% per month in net Carhart alpha, whereas the spread is insignificant among highly experienced managers. In Panel B using fund-specific tenure, the corresponding low-tenure spreads are 0.23% per month in net returns and 0.22% per month in net alpha, fading to near zero for high-tenure managers. The authors interpret this as evidence that among career-concerned managers, herding is especially informative about lower skill.

Main role: The paper emphasizes that the herding–antiherding gap is larger among managers with stronger career concerns. These double sorts are the main evidence for that heterogeneity claim in the career-concerns section.
Settings.H639: Section IV, Table XI Panels A and B (PDF pp. 28-30).
Settings.G640:
Treatment: Alternative continuous Fund Herding measure based on past orthogonalized institutional trades rather than raw institutional trades, then used to sort funds into deciles.

Method: As a robustness analysis, the authors re-estimate the herding measure after orthogonalizing institutional trades with respect to a large set of stock characteristics—momentum, size, book-to-market, turnover, idiosyncratic volatility, analyst forecast revisions, share issuance, bid-ask spread, Amihud illiquidity, and industry dummies—then repeat decile portfolio sorts and factor-model performance estimation. The implemented estimator remains linear portfolio sorting/time-series regression.

Identification: The design uses the same observational variation as the main portfolio sorts but purges lagged institutional trades of many stock characteristics before constructing herding. The argument is that if the relation persists, it is less likely to be driven by common preferences for liquid, volatile, or certain-industry stocks.

Setting: After redefining herding using institutional trades orthogonalized to many stock characteristics, herding funds still underperform antiherding funds. In Table XII, the decile-10 minus decile-1 spread is -0.16% per month in both net and gross returns, with a net Carhart alpha spread of -0.15% per month. The authors interpret this as robustness of the causal skill interpretation to richer controls for correlated trading induced by stock characteristics.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness check showing that the central herding-performance relation does not depend on a particular herding construction or omitted stock-characteristic comovement.
Settings.G641:
Treatment: Alternative continuous Fund Herding measure based on trade regressions controlling for a fund’s own past trade, then used to sort funds into deciles.

Method: As another robustness analysis, the authors re-estimate the fund-level herding measure from trade regressions that additionally control for the fund’s own lagged trade in the stock, then repeat the decile portfolio sorts and factor-model performance estimation. This remains an observational linear portfolio/time-series regression design.

Identification: Identification again comes from cross-sectional variation in the alternative herding measure, now net of own-trade persistence. The paper’s argument is that controlling for lagged own trades removes a mechanical source of autocorrelation due to fund flows or order splitting, making the remaining relation more plausibly about imitation of the crowd.

Setting: When the herding measure is re-estimated controlling for each fund’s own lagged trades, the negative performance relation remains. In Table XIII, herding funds underperform antiherding funds by 0.17% per month in both net and gross returns, and by 0.14% per month in Carhart alpha. The authors interpret this as evidence that the main herding-performance effect is not driven by serial dependence in a fund’s own trades or flow-related price pressure.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness test addressing whether serially correlated own trading, persistent flows, or stealth trading explain the main result.
Settings.G642:
Treatment: Continuous Fund Herding FH measured at the end of quarter t.

Method: The authors estimate predictive panel regressions with time fixed effects of several alternative future mutual fund performance measures based on holdings or trades on lagged fund herding and standard fund controls, with standard errors clustered by fund. The dependent variables are the DGTW characteristic-selectivity measure for quarter t+1, the Grinblatt-Titman trade-based measure for quarter t+1, and a future-trades GT measure for quarter t+5. Because the regressions include time fixed effects but not three absorbed FE dimensions, this is standard FE.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional differences in lagged herding with time fixed effects and standard controls, applied to alternative performance metrics that more directly reflect stock selection and trading decisions. The argument is that persistence across distinct outcome constructions reduces concern that the main result is an artifact of a particular performance measure.

Setting: Higher herding predicts worse future performance even when performance is measured from holdings and trades rather than fund returns. In Table XIV, the coefficient of FH is -0.251 to -0.276 for the DGTW characteristic-selectivity measure, -0.208 to -0.244 for the contemporaneous Grinblatt-Titman trade measure, and -0.173 to -0.197 for the future-trades GT measure. The authors interpret this as further evidence that herding identifies inferior stock-picking and trading skill.

Main role: These are substantive robustness analyses showing that the negative association between herding and future performance holds using holdings- and trades-based performance metrics, not only return-based alpha measures.
Settings.G643:
Treatment: Continuous Fund Herding FH measured at the end of quarter t.

Method: The authors estimate predictive regressions of future fund flows on lagged fund herding and standard fund controls with time fixed effects and fund-clustered standard errors. This linear FE specification tests whether investors causally respond to information in fund herding by reallocating capital.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional differences in lagged herding and subsequent flows, with time fixed effects absorbing aggregate flow shocks and controls for observed fund characteristics and past performance. The main concern is that omitted determinants of fund demand may mask or confound investor responses to herding.

Setting: The authors test whether investors move money away from herding funds and toward antiherding funds. In Table XV, fund herding has a negative coefficient in a univariate flow regression (-0.033) but becomes smaller and statistically insignificant with controls (-0.019). They interpret this as evidence that investors do not strongly respond to the information in herding, which may help explain why herding retains predictive power for future performance.

Main role: This is a secondary substantive analysis in Section VI, asking whether investors react to the performance information in herding; it is not part of the core claim that herding reveals skill.
Settings.G644:
Treatment: Net Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t: the bank’s net increase in holdings of the GIIPS sovereign debt to which it had the highest preexisting exposure (‘risk-shifting asset’) during the crisis. Continuous measure; examples in text use a one-SD increase of 0.34 and contrasts between 10th and 90th percentiles.

Method: Bank-year-firm-cluster panel regressions implementing a modified Khwaja and Mian (2008) lending-channel design for the subsample of non-GIIPS banks during 2010–2012. The unit of observation is bank × year × firm cluster, where firm clusters are formed by borrower country, industry, and precrisis rating category. The treatment is the bank’s net increase in its risk-shifting sovereign asset. Regressions include bank controls, firm-cluster×year fixed effects to absorb common demand shocks within cluster-year, and firm-cluster×bank fixed effects to absorb time-invariant relationship heterogeneity. Identification comes from within-firm-cluster differences across banks in crisis-period sovereign portfolio reallocation; the paper argues non-GIIPS banks are not subject to GIIPS governments’ moral suasion, so the estimated crowding-out is interpreted as risk shifting affecting loan supply.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-bank heterogeneity in crisis-period increases in the bank’s risk-shifting sovereign holding, compared within the same firm-cluster-year so borrower demand and common shocks are differenced out. Firm-cluster×bank fixed effects absorb persistent relationship differences. For non-GIIPS banks, the authors argue moral suasion by GIIPS governments cannot explain the sovereign purchases, strengthening the interpretation as risk shifting. Remaining concerns are that sovereign portfolio changes may still correlate with unobserved bank shocks affecting lending, though bank controls are included.

Setting: For non-GIIPS banks, a larger crisis-period net increase in the bank’s risk-shifting sovereign asset is interpreted as crowding out corporate lending. In the bank-year-firm-cluster fixed-effects design, the coefficient on Net Change Risk-Shifting Asset is -2.683 for loan volume, 0.040 for the loan-decrease dummy, and 10.762 for loan spreads (Table 2, col. 1). The paper states that a one-SD larger net change (0.34) led to a 0.93 percentage-point reduction in loan volume and a 1.4 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease, and moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile implies a 2.6 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease. This is a main mechanism result supporting the claim that risk shifting by non-GIIPS banks tightened loan supply.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that risk-shifting behavior of weak banks reduced firms’ probability of being granted new syndicated loans and is a central mechanism of the paper.
Settings.H644: Section 3.1 Non-GIIPS banks test; Table 2 Panels A–C, columns (1), PDF pages 16–18 (paper pp. 2870–2872).
Settings.G645:
Treatment: Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010_t: change in value of the bank’s preexisting (March 2010) sovereign debt holdings, using crisis-period sovereign bond price changes, normalized by bank equity. Continuous; more negative values are larger losses. Text discusses a one-SD-larger loss of 3.61 and 90th-to-10th percentile comparisons.

Method: Same modified Khwaja-Mian bank-year-firm-cluster lending regressions for non-GIIPS banks during 2010–2012, but with the treatment defined as the value loss on the bank’s precrisis GIIPS sovereign portfolio, normalized by equity. Includes bank controls, firm-cluster×year fixed effects, and firm-cluster×bank fixed effects. This setting isolates the hit-on-balance-sheet channel.

Identification: Within the same borrower-cluster-year, banks suffered different mark-to-market losses on preexisting sovereign holdings because of heterogeneous March 2010 portfolios. The firm-cluster×year fixed effects absorb common loan demand and macro shocks, while firm-cluster×bank fixed effects absorb persistent relationship characteristics. The causal interpretation relies on these precrisis sovereign portfolios generating quasi-exogenous variation in bank balance-sheet hits rather than borrower-specific credit demand.

Setting: For non-GIIPS banks, larger losses on preexisting GIIPS sovereign holdings are interpreted as weakening bank balance sheets and reducing loan supply. In Table 2 column (2), Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010 has coefficients of 0.329 on loan volume, -0.004 on the loan-decrease dummy, and -1.145 on loan spreads; because the variable is negative for losses, the text interprets this as larger losses causing tighter lending. A one-SD larger loss (3.61) led to a 1.2 percentage-point reduction in loan volume and a 1.4 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease; moving from the 90th to the 10th percentile caused a 3.6 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease. This is a core causal channel in the paper.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize value impairment on banks’ sovereign exposures as a key cause of the credit crunch, making this a central mechanism result.
Settings.H645: Section 3.1 Non-GIIPS banks test; Table 2 Panels A–C, column (2), PDF pages 16–18 (paper pp. 2870–2872).
Settings.G646:
Treatment: Two continuous treatments entered jointly: Net Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t and Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010_t. The estimand is the partial effect of each holding the other fixed.

Method: Horse-race version of the modified Khwaja-Mian bank-year-firm-cluster lending regression for non-GIIPS banks during 2010–2012, including both the net increase in the risk-shifting asset and the value loss on preexisting GIIPS sovereign holdings. Includes bank controls, firm-cluster×year FE, and firm-cluster×bank FE. The purpose is to assess the independent contributions of risk shifting and the balance-sheet hit.

Identification: Identification is the same within-cluster cross-bank variation as in the prior bank-lending settings, with both sovereign-loss and sovereign-purchase measures included together. The interpretation requires that residual unobserved bank shocks are not jointly driving both sovereign exposures and lending, conditional on fixed effects and bank controls.

Setting: In the non-GIIPS bank subsample, the paper jointly estimates the lending effects of crisis losses on preexisting sovereign holdings and crisis increases in the risk-shifting asset. In Table 2 column (3), both Net Change Risk-Shifting Asset and Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010 remain statistically and economically significant across loan volume, loan decrease, and spread outcomes. The authors interpret this as evidence that both the hit-on-balance-sheet channel and the risk-shifting channel independently contributed to the lending contraction, with an add-on effect of risk shifting beyond pure balance-sheet impairment. No separate new percentile or SD magnitudes are reported here beyond the earlier single-treatment specifications.

Main role: The conclusion stresses both sovereign losses and risk-shifting incentives as important determinants of the lending contraction; this joint specification directly supports that conclusion.
Settings.H646: Section 3.1 Non-GIIPS banks test; Table 2 Panels A–C, column (3), PDF pages 16–18 (paper pp. 2870–2872).
Settings.G647:
Treatment: Gross Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t or Net Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t: crisis-period increase in holdings of the GIIPS sovereign debt to which the bank had the highest preexisting exposure. For GIIPS banks this is domestic sovereign debt. Continuous. Text reports one-SD larger gross change of 1.94, one-SD larger net change of 1.73, and 10th-to-90th percentile contrasts for net change.

Method: Modified Khwaja and Mian (2008) bank-year-firm-cluster lending-channel regressions for the GIIPS-bank subsample during 2010–2012, with treatment equal to the gross or net increase in the bank’s risk-shifting asset (domestic sovereign debt for GIIPS banks). Regressions include bank controls, firm-cluster×year fixed effects, and firm-cluster×bank fixed effects. The text interprets gross increases as potentially reflecting risk shifting or moral suasion, and net increases as more indicative of risk shifting.

Identification: Within a given firm-cluster-year, GIIPS banks differ in crisis-period purchases of domestic/risk-shifting sovereign debt. Firm-cluster×year FE absorb borrower demand and common shocks; firm-cluster×bank FE absorb persistent relationship heterogeneity. The interpretation of gross increases is complicated by moral suasion, while net increases are argued to be more consistent with deliberate risk shifting. The setting thus identifies a lending effect of sovereign portfolio reallocation, with the paper using additional tests to separate risk shifting from moral suasion.

Setting: For GIIPS banks, larger crisis-period increases in domestic sovereign holdings are interpreted as crowding out corporate lending, especially when measured as net increases. In Table 3 columns (1) and (2), the gross-change coefficients are -1.010 on loan volume, 0.012 on loan decrease, and 4.268 on spreads, while the net-change coefficients are -1.501, 0.019, and 6.195. The paper states that a one-SD-larger gross change (1.94) led to a 1.96 percentage-point reduction in loan volume and a 2.3 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease; a one-SD-larger net change (1.73) implied a 2.6 percentage-point reduction in loan volume and a 3.3 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease. Moving net change from the 10th to the 90th percentile raised the likelihood of a loan decrease by 9.5 percentage points, and the authors say this implies a 53% reduction in the probability of loan contraction when borrowing from a bank at the 10th rather than 90th percentile. This is a central paper result.

Main role: The abstract highlights that risk-shifting behavior of weakly capitalized banks reduced firms’ probability of obtaining new syndicated loans by up to 53%; this is that main result.
Settings.H647: Section 3.2 GIIPS banks test; Table 3 Panels A–C, columns (1) and (2), PDF pages 18–20 (paper pp. 2872–2874).
Settings.G648:
Treatment: Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010_t: crisis-period change in value of the bank’s preexisting March 2010 GIIPS sovereign holdings, normalized by equity. Continuous; larger negative values indicate larger losses. Text reports one-SD larger reduction of 11.51 and percentile contrasts.

Method: GIIPS-bank modified Khwaja-Mian lending regressions with treatment equal to the value loss on the bank’s preexisting GIIPS sovereign portfolio, normalized by equity. Bank-year-firm-cluster panel, 2010–2012, with bank controls, firm-cluster×year FE, and firm-cluster×bank FE. This captures the hit-on-balance-sheet channel for GIIPS banks.

Identification: Identification uses differential losses on banks’ precrisis sovereign portfolios, compared within firm-cluster-year across GIIPS banks, while absorbing relationship fixed effects. The causal claim relies on these balance-sheet hits being a source of loan-supply variation rather than borrower-demand variation; borrower-cluster-year FE and bank controls are used to support that claim.

Setting: For GIIPS banks, larger losses on preexisting sovereign holdings are interpreted as weakening balance sheets and reducing credit supply. In Table 3 column (3), the coefficient on Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010 is 0.152 for loan volume, -0.002 for loan decrease, and -0.615 for spreads; because the variable becomes more negative when losses are larger, the text interprets larger losses as reducing lending and raising spreads. A one-SD-larger reduction in value (11.51) led to a 1.75 percentage-point loan volume reduction and a 2.4 percentage-point higher likelihood of a loan decrease, corresponding to 19% of the SD of precrisis loan growth. Moving from the 90th to the 10th percentile of the balance-sheet-hit distribution raised the likelihood of a loan decrease by 6.6 percentage points, which the paper says corresponds to a 47.3% decrease in the probability of loan contraction when borrowing from a bank at the 90th instead of 10th percentile.

Main role: The paper’s headline mechanism includes value impairment in banks’ sovereign debt exposures; this GIIPS-bank version materially supports that central conclusion.
Settings.H648: Section 3.2 GIIPS banks test; Table 3 Panels A–C, column (3), PDF pages 18–20 (paper pp. 2872–2874).
Settings.G649:
Treatment: Two continuous treatments entered jointly: Value Change GIIPS Sov Debt 2010_t and either Gross Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t (col. 4) or Net Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t (col. 5).

Method: GIIPS-bank horse-race lending regressions including both sovereign balance-sheet-hit and sovereign purchase measures. Implemented as bank-year-firm-cluster regressions with bank controls, firm-cluster×year FE, and firm-cluster×bank FE. Columns (4) and (5) compare the balance-sheet-hit channel jointly with gross or net risk-shifting-asset changes.

Identification: Uses within-firm-cluster-year cross-bank variation in sovereign losses and sovereign purchases, netting out common borrower shocks and persistent relationship heterogeneity. Interpretation rests on conditional exogeneity of bank-specific sovereign-loss and sovereign-purchase variation after controls and fixed effects.

Setting: In Table 3 columns (4) and (5), the authors jointly include the bank’s losses on preexisting sovereign debt and its gross or net increase in the risk-shifting asset. Both variables remain significant across lending outcomes, which the paper interprets as evidence that both the hit-on-balance-sheet channel and the sovereign-purchase crowding-out channel contributed to the reduction in lending by GIIPS banks during the sovereign debt crisis. No additional standalone percentile or SD comparisons are reported for these joint specifications.

Main role: This joint specification underpins the paper’s conclusion that both the balance-sheet-hit and risk-shifting channels contributed to the credit crunch among GIIPS banks.
Settings.H649: Section 3.2 GIIPS banks test; Table 3 Panels A–C, columns (4) and (5), PDF pages 18–20 (paper pp. 2872–2874).
Settings.G650:
Treatment: Gross Change Risk-Shifting Asset_t interacted with No Hedge, where No Hedge equals one if the bank increases gross and net holdings by at least the same amount. The focal treatment effect is the differential effect of gross sovereign accumulation for nonhedgers relative to hedgers.

Method: GIIPS-bank lending regression distinguishing hedgers from nonhedgers by interacting the gross increase in the risk-shifting asset with a No Hedge indicator. Bank-year-firm-cluster panel, 2010–2012, with bank controls, firm-cluster×year FE, and firm-cluster×bank FE. The design is used as a refinement test to separate risk shifting from moral suasion: nonhedged sovereign accumulation is interpreted as deliberate risk taking, while hedged accumulation is interpreted as more consistent with coerced moral suasion.

Identification: The design compares lending effects of gross sovereign accumulation between banks that did and did not hedge the additional exposure. Conditional on fixed effects and controls, only nonhedged exposure increases are interpreted as reflecting genuine risk shifting. The assumption is that hedging status reveals the economic intent/true exposure behind gross purchases rather than other omitted bank traits.

Setting: Using the hedger-versus-nonhedger refinement in Table 3 column (6), the paper finds that only GIIPS banks that increased gross sovereign holdings without hedging the extra exposure tightened lending. The interaction Gross Change Risk-Shifting Asset × No Hedge is -1.730 for loan volume, 0.036 for the loan-decrease dummy, and 6.900 for loan spreads, while the main effect of gross change alone is insignificant. The authors interpret this as showing that behavior consistent with risk shifting, not moral suasion, drove the lending contraction.

Main role: The paper’s central narrative contrasts risk shifting with moral suasion; this refinement test is key evidence that lending contraction is attributable to risk shifting rather than moral suasion.
Settings.H650: Section 3.2 GIIPS banks test; Table 3 Panels A–C, column (6), PDF pages 18–20 (paper pp. 2872–2874).
Settings.G651:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk: firm-level continuous measure of the GIIPS sovereign risk to which a firm is exposed via its lenders, built from banks’ CDS-weighted GIIPS sovereign holdings and precrisis loan-syndicate weights, with 2009 syndicate composition held fixed during the crisis. In the cash regression it also enters interacted with Cash Flow.

Method: Firm-year fixed-effects regressions relating firms’ indirect exposure to GIIPS sovereign risk through precrisis bank relationships to financial-policy outcomes during the crisis. Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk is constructed from bank sovereign holdings/CDS-weighted risk and the firm’s precrisis syndicated-loan syndicate composition, held constant at 2009 to limit endogenous switching. Regressions include firm fixed effects, firm controls, industry×country×year fixed effects, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year fixed effects. The first column estimates a cash-flow sensitivity of cash specification; columns (2)–(5) estimate effects on net debt, interest coverage, and credit-line usage.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-firm differences in exposure to bank sovereign risk through precrisis lending relationships, with the syndicate composition frozen at the last precrisis year to mitigate endogenous rematching to weak banks. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity; industry×country×year FE absorb country-industry demand and macro shocks; foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE address concerns that borrowing from banks headquartered in GIIPS countries proxies for the firm’s own business exposure to those countries. Remaining concerns are time-varying firm-bank matching or omitted shocks correlated with lender choice.

Setting: The paper argues that firms more exposed to crisis-hit banks through their precrisis lending relationships became financially constrained. In Table 4, column (1), the interaction Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk × Cash Flow is 0.007, implying that a one-SD-higher indirect exposure makes firms save 5.3 cents more per euro of cash flow. In columns (2)–(5), higher indirect exposure reduces net debt (-0.008), lowers ICR (-0.656), and lowers the fractions of outstanding credit lines (-0.012) and undrawn credit lines (-0.016). The authors interpret these results as showing reduced external financing, deteriorating credit quality, and a shift from credit lines toward cash among firms exposed to lender sovereign stress.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion argue that firms linked to affected banks became financially constrained during the crisis; these firm-policy results are part of that central claim.
Settings.H651: Section 4.1 Empirical results for main specification; Equation (4), Equation (5), Table 4 columns (1)–(5), PDF pages 25–28 (paper pp. 2879–2882).
Settings.G652:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk: continuous firm-level measure of GIIPS sovereign risk faced indirectly via its lenders, based on CDS-weighted bank GIIPS sovereign holdings and fixed precrisis syndicate composition.

Method: Firm-year fixed-effects regressions of real firm outcomes on Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk using the main specification. The treatment is firm exposure to sovereign-risk-affected lenders based on precrisis loan syndicates held fixed. Regressions include firm fixed effects, firm controls, industry×country×year FE, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE. This is the central design for estimating the real effects of the credit crunch on firms’ employment, investment, and sales.

Identification: Cross-firm variation in exposure to bank sovereign risk is generated by precrisis lending relationships, with the composition of syndicates fixed at 2009 to reduce endogenous switching to weak banks. Firm FE absorb fixed heterogeneity. Industry×country×year FE absorb local demand and macro shocks that vary by industry and country over time. Foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE are added to address the concern that firms borrowing from GIIPS banks may themselves be exposed to those countries through business ties. The causal interpretation is that lender-side sovereign distress reduced credit supply and thereby affected real activity.

Setting: The main firm-level real-effects regressions show that firms more exposed to sovereign-risk-affected lenders experienced worse real outcomes during the crisis. In Table 4 columns (6)–(8), the coefficient on Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk is -0.007 for employment growth, -0.009 for CAPX, and -0.008 for sales growth. The paper translates a one-SD-higher indirect exposure into 4.7 percentage points lower employment growth, 5.9 percentage points lower investment, and 5.6 percentage points lower sales growth. These are the headline results supporting the claim that the sovereign-debt-induced credit crunch depressed firm employment, investment, and sales.

Main role: These are the paper’s headline real-effects estimates highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H652: Section 4.1 Empirical results for main specification; Table 4 columns (6)–(8), Figure 5, PDF pages 28–30 (paper pp. 2882–2884).
Settings.G653:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk: continuous firm-level exposure to GIIPS sovereign risk through lenders, constructed from precrisis syndicate links and bank sovereign-risk measures. Sample restricted to non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS or other non-EU subsidiaries; links to GIIPS banks are mainly due to presample bank M&A or Bank of Ireland’s UK presence.

Method: Alternative-identification firm-year fixed-effects regressions on a restricted sample of non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS or other non-EU subsidiaries and whose GIIPS-bank links are argued to arise for reasons unrelated to geographic business exposure. Regressions include firm FE, firm controls, industry×year FE, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE because of smaller sample size. The treatment is Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk measured from precrisis lending relationships. This design follows Peek and Rosengren (1997)-style logic to isolate foreign bank-supply shocks.

Identification: The restricted sample is intended to remove direct exposure of firms to GIIPS-country macro conditions: only non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS or other non-EU subsidiaries are kept, and the paper further argues many GIIPS-bank relationships arose through presample bank acquisitions or the Bank of Ireland’s UK presence. Firm FE and industry×year FE absorb fixed firm heterogeneity and common industry shocks across non-GIIPS countries; foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE absorb possible exposure to the bank-headquarter country. The core assumption is that within this sample, higher lender GIIPS risk reflects bank-supply shocks rather than firms’ own demand exposure to GIIPS downturns.

Setting: In the alternative-identification sample of non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS or other non-EU subsidiaries, the paper finds that higher indirect exposure to sovereign-risk-affected lenders still worsened firms’ financial and real outcomes. Panel A of Table 6 shows coefficients of -0.005 on net debt, -0.407 on ICR, -0.005 on employment growth, -0.009 on CAPX, and -0.008 on sales growth; the cash-flow sensitivity interaction is 0.006. The authors interpret this as confirming that the decline in bank loan supply caused negative real effects even among firms with no direct business exposure to crisis countries.

Main role: The introduction and results discussion present this as a key robustness that addresses loan-demand and macro-shock alternative explanations for the main real-effects results.
Settings.H653: Section 4.2 Alternative identification strategy using firms’ business exposure; Table 6 Panel A, Figure 6, PDF pages 32–35 (paper pp. 2886–2889).
Settings.G654:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk, continuous, measured via precrisis lender relationships; sample restricted to non-GIIPS firms whose GIIPS-bank relationships arose through bank acquisitions before the sample period.

Method: Further restricted firm-year FE robustness on the subsample of non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS subsidiaries where the relationship to a GIIPS bank is due specifically to presample bank M&A. Controls and FE follow the reduced-sample alternative-identification design: firm FE, firm controls, industry×year FE, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE.

Identification: Identification relies on presample acquisitions as an exogenous source of firm exposure to GIIPS banks, unrelated to the firm’s geographical business exposure. Within this sample, higher Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk is interpreted as supply-side variation from lender sovereign stress rather than endogenous matching. Firm FE and time-varying industry and foreign-bank-country FE support this claim.

Setting: Restricting the sample further to non-GIIPS firms whose GIIPS-bank relationship came from presample bank M&A leaves the real-effects estimates qualitatively unchanged. In Table 6 panel B, higher Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk is associated with lower net debt (-0.007), lower ICR (-0.393), lower employment growth (-0.006), lower CAPX (-0.008), and lower sales growth (-0.008), while the cash-flow sensitivity interaction remains positive (0.006). The paper interprets this as evidence that its results are not driven by endogenous firm-bank matching on geographic exposure.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness used to strengthen the interpretation of the main real-effects results by leveraging arguably exogenous bank-link formation via M&A.
Settings.H654: Section 4.2 Alternative identification strategy using firms’ business exposure; Table 6 Panel B, PDF page 35 (paper p. 2889).
Settings.G655:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk, continuous, measured through precrisis lenders; sample restricted to non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS subsidiaries and active in nontradable sectors.

Method: Alternative-identification robustness restricted to non-GIIPS firms without GIIPS subsidiaries operating in nontradable sectors. Firm-year FE regressions with firm controls, firm FE, industry×year FE, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE. This is intended to rule out that results are driven by export or tradable-sector exposure to crisis countries.

Identification: By restricting to nontradable sectors and firms without GIIPS subsidiaries, the design seeks to eliminate direct demand effects from international trade or foreign operations in crisis countries. The remaining variation in Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk is attributed to lender-side sovereign distress. Firm FE and industry×year plus foreign-bank-country×year FE further absorb confounds.

Setting: In the nontradable-sector robustness, the paper continues to find negative financial and real effects of exposure to sovereign-risk-affected lenders. Table 6 panel C reports coefficients of -0.007 on net debt, -0.462 on ICR, -0.006 on employment growth, -0.007 on CAPX, and -0.008 on sales growth, with a positive 0.007 interaction in the cash equation. This supports the view that the main real effects do not simply reflect tradable-sector exposure to GIIPS demand shocks.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis addressing alternative explanations related to trade exposure rather than a headline result.
Settings.H655: Section 4.2 Alternative identification strategy using firms’ business exposure; Table 6 Panel C, PDF page 35 (paper p. 2889).
Settings.G656:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk, continuous, measured through precrisis lenders; sample consists of non-GIIPS firms with at least one GIIPS subsidiary/business exposure.

Method: Firm-year FE heterogeneity design comparing firms with versus without direct GIIPS business exposure. The paper reruns the alternative-identification regressions for non-GIIPS firms with GIIPS subsidiaries (panel D of Table 6) to test whether the bank-lending channel matters less when firms themselves faced large demand shocks. Controls are firm FE, firm controls, industry×year FE, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE.

Identification: The comparison exploits the idea that firms with GIIPS business exposure likely suffered larger direct demand shocks, so a lender-supply shock should matter less for them. Within this exposed sample, the estimated effect of Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk is expected to attenuate. The identifying assumption is not a clean causal design on its own, but a heterogeneity pattern consistent with the bank-supply interpretation of prior results.

Setting: For non-GIIPS firms with GIIPS subsidiaries, the paper finds no significant impact of Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk on financial or real outcomes in Table 6 panel D. Coefficients are near zero and insignificant across cash, net debt, ICR, employment growth, CAPX, and sales growth. The authors interpret this attenuation as evidence that when firms’ own loan demand collapsed because of direct exposure to GIIPS macro shocks, the additional lender-side credit-supply contraction had little detectable incremental effect.

Main role: This is a mechanism/heterogeneity test used to show the bank-lending channel is less important when firms’ own demand shocks dominate.
Settings.H656: Section 4.3 Supply and demand factors of bank lending; Table 6 Panel D, PDF pages 35–36 (paper pp. 2889–2890).
Settings.G657:
Treatment: Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk interacted with indicators for Private/Unlisted, No Rating, or No Bond Outstanding. The focal treatment is the differential effect of indirect lender sovereign risk for more bank-dependent firms.

Method: Firm-year FE heterogeneity regressions interacting Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk with firm financing-friction indicators: unlisted/private status, unrated status, and inability to issue bonds. The baseline main-specification controls are retained: firm FE, firm controls, industry×country×year FE, and foreign-bank-GIIPS-country×year FE. These tests examine whether the real effects of lender sovereign distress are stronger for firms less able to substitute away from bank credit.

Identification: These interaction designs test whether the estimated effect of lender sovereign distress is amplified for firms with fewer alternative financing sources. The interpretation is that if the main estimates reflect a bank-credit-supply shock, effects should be stronger among unlisted, unrated, and non-bond-issuing firms. Fixed effects and controls mirror the main design, but the heterogeneity itself is an interpretive rather than standalone quasi-experimental source.

Setting: The paper finds that the negative effects of indirect lender sovereign risk are concentrated among firms less able to replace bank credit. In Table 7, the interaction of Indirect GIIPS Sov Risk with Private/Unlisted is significantly negative for net debt, ICR, employment growth, CAPX, and sales growth, and the triple interaction with cash flow is positive in the cash regression. Parallel results hold for No Rating and No Bond Outstanding. The authors interpret this as evidence that firms with alternative funding sources could offset bank-credit contraction, whereas bank-dependent firms suffered the real effects of the credit crunch.

Main role: These are supporting heterogeneity analyses showing the main real effects are concentrated among firms with limited outside financing options.
Settings.H657: Section 4.3 Supply and demand factors of bank lending; Table 7 Panels A–C, PDF pages 37–38 (paper pp. 2891–2892).
Settings.G658:
Treatment: The latent/constructed pricing kernel specification: inclusion and estimated loading on three factors in the affine SDF m = a(1 − δ_p f_p − δ_c f_c − δ_d f_d), where f_p is the market return, f_c nondurable consumption growth, and f_d durable consumption growth. The treatment is not a binary policy or exposure; it is continuous factor pricing exposure within the estimated SDF.

Method: Continuously updated GMM (CU-GMM) estimation of a one-dimensional admissible stochastic discount factor (SDF) set for Yogo (2006)'s linearized three-factor consumption CAPM. The authors estimate a single affine SDF in market return, nondurable consumption growth, and durable consumption growth using quarterly moments E(mr)=0 and E(m)=c on the 25 Fama-French size and book-to-market portfolios, 1951–2001. The implemented estimator is single-step GMM with Newey-West weighting matrix with one lag; they report overidentification J tests and distance-metric tests for parameter restrictions and the SDF mean. This is not a standard causal design; it is structural asset-pricing/GMM evaluation of whether factor exposures price expected returns.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional asset-pricing moment restrictions linking test-asset excess returns to the affine SDF. Under d=1, standard GMM point identification is maintained if the relevant moment matrix has rank k. The concern emphasized by the paper is that apparent nonrejection of pricing restrictions can be misleading if the model is underidentified or if the admissible SDF is economically meaningless (mean zero / uncorrelated with returns).

Setting: Using CU-GMM on Yogo's linearized three-factor consumption CAPM with 25 quarterly size and value portfolios from 1951 to 2001, the authors find that the usual one-dimensional SDF specification is not rejected by the standard overidentification test (criterion 20.743, p=0.537). In this single-SDF specification, only durable consumption has a statistically significant price-of-risk loading (92.229, p=0.035), while the SDF mean is 0.014 (p=0.790). The authors treat this conventional d=1 result as the benchmark that had supported Yogo (2006), but they argue it is not reliable unless point identification truly holds.

Main role: The paper's central empirical purpose is to reassess prominent asset-pricing models for overspecification/underidentification. The one-dimensional Yogo specification is the benchmark model that previous literature had viewed favorably, so this setting is central even though the authors argue it is insufficient by itself.
Settings.H658: Section 5.1, Table 1, first block 'One-dimensional set' (PDF p. 8 / journal p. 345).
Settings.G659:
Treatment: A two-dimensional continuous SDF basis spanning admissible pricing kernels for the Yogo model, with one basis element loading on market and nondurable consumption growth and the other on market and durable consumption growth. Not a binary treatment.

Method: CU-GMM estimation of a two-dimensional admissible SDF set for Yogo (2006)'s linearized three-factor model. The authors replicate the moment conditions to estimate a basis of two SDFs, normalized as (δ_p, δ_c, 0) and (δ_p, 0, δ_d), interpretable as two linearized Epstein-Zin variants using market+nondurable and market+durable consumption factors. They estimate the basis jointly with exactly identified SDF-mean moments on the 25 quarterly Fama-French portfolios, 1951–2001, and use a J test for whether a two-dimensional admissible set exists plus a distance-metric test of whether both SDF means are zero.

Identification: The identifying variation is the cross-sectional covariance structure between test-asset excess returns and the three proposed factors. By estimating d=2 replicated moment systems, the authors test whether the admissible SDF set is two-dimensional rather than point identified. Economic meaningfulness requires that the vector of expected returns lies in the span of return-factor covariances; if the two SDF means are jointly zero, the admissible SDFs are uncorrelated with returns, implying complete overspecification.

Setting: For the same 1951–2001 Yogo sample, the authors estimate a two-dimensional admissible SDF set and obtain a J-test p-value of 13.4% (criterion 56.687), which they interpret as evidence that the model is likely underidentified rather than point identified. The estimated basis loads heavily on the two consumption measures (nondurables 222.902 in one basis element; durables 99.333 in the other), while the market plays a limited role. Crucially, the joint test that the admissible SDF means are zero is not rejected: the reported SDF means are -0.099 and 0.034, with the second mean's DM p-value 0.494, and the constrained criterion gives p=0.151. The authors conclude that the seeming pricing ability comes from SDFs that are essentially uncorrelated with returns, i.e., complete overspecification.

Main role: This is one of the paper's headline results: the Yogo model is likely underidentified with admissible SDFs lying on a two-dimensional subspace, and those SDFs are economically meaningless because their means are jointly indistinguishable from zero.
Settings.H659: Section 5.1, Table 1, second block 'Two-dimensional set' and surrounding discussion (PDF p. 8-9 / journal pp. 345-346).
Settings.G660:
Treatment: Three separate continuous factor-pricing SDF basis elements, each isolating market, nondurable consumption growth, or durable consumption growth within the affine pricing kernel. Nonbinary.

Method: CU-GMM estimation of a three-dimensional admissible SDF set for Yogo (2006)'s linearized three-factor model, with basis normalized as (δ_p,0,0), (0,δ_c,0), and (0,0,δ_d), effectively testing whether each factor can separately explain risk premia. The model is estimated on quarterly 25 size-book/market portfolios, 1951–2001, using replicated moment conditions and J tests.

Identification: The authors test whether the asset-pricing moments admit a three-dimensional null space. Rejection implies the admissible SDFs cannot span three independent directions, supporting the inference that the model's admissible set is smaller, namely two-dimensional.

Setting: In the three-dimensional Yogo specification on the 1951–2001 sample, the overidentification test is strongly rejected (criterion 215.144, p=0.000). This rules out a three-dimensional admissible SDF space in which each of the three factors separately explains risk premia and reinforces the paper's main inference that the model's admissible SDFs instead lie on a two-dimensional subspace.

Main role: This is a supporting specification used to reject an even larger admissible set and thereby sharpen the conclusion that the admissible Yogo SDF set is two-dimensional, not three-dimensional.
Settings.H660: Section 5.1, Table 1, third block 'Three-dimensional set' (PDF p. 8 / journal p. 345).
Settings.G661:
Treatment: One-dimensional continuous affine SDF in market, nondurable consumption growth, and durable consumption growth under alternative GMM estimators (2S-GMM and IT-GMM).

Method: Two-step and iterated GMM robustness analysis for Yogo (2006)'s one-dimensional admissible SDF set on the 1951–2001 sample. The authors re-estimate the single affine SDF and associated mean/J statistics using two-step GMM and iterated GMM instead of CU-GMM to verify whether conclusions depend on the GMM variant.

Identification: Same asset-pricing moment restrictions as the main Yogo model, but assessed with alternative GMM estimators. The purpose is to show that the inference is not driven by the CU-GMM implementation.

Setting: Using two-step GMM and iterated GMM for the one-dimensional Yogo model on 1951–2001 quarterly 25 portfolios, the model again is not rejected: criterion p-values are 0.633 (2S-GMM) and 0.581 (IT-GMM). The estimated SDF means are 0.053 (p=0.230) and 0.055 (p=0.206), respectively. These robustness results align with the CU-GMM benchmark that a single-SDF specification appears acceptable on conventional tests alone.

Main role: This is a robustness check showing that the benchmark one-dimensional nonrejection persists across GMM implementations, but the paper's central contribution rests on the broader underidentification/overspecification diagnosis.
Settings.H661: Section 5.1, Table 2, first block 'One-dimensional set' (PDF p. 9 / journal p. 346).
Settings.G662:
Treatment: Two-dimensional continuous SDF basis for the Yogo model, estimated with 2S-GMM and IT-GMM rather than CU-GMM.

Method: Two-step and iterated GMM robustness analysis for Yogo (2006)'s two-dimensional admissible SDF set on the 1951–2001 sample. The authors jointly estimate two basis SDFs and test whether a two-dimensional set can price returns and whether the basis means are jointly zero, using 2S-GMM and IT-GMM.

Identification: Same replicated asset-pricing moments as the main two-dimensional Yogo setting. Identification concern is underidentification of risk prices and whether apparent pricing arises from SDFs uncorrelated with returns. Alternative GMM implementations assess robustness of that conclusion.

Setting: Under two-step and iterated GMM, the two-dimensional Yogo model on 1951–2001 data remains nonrejected, with criterion p-values 0.145 and 0.081, respectively, while the zero-mean constrained criteria give p-values 0.138 and 0.068. The reported SDF means are 0.059 and 0.062 (DM p=0.276) for 2S-GMM, and 0.088 and 0.060 (DM p=0.180) for IT-GMM. The authors interpret these results as qualitatively similar to CU-GMM: a two-dimensional admissible SDF set exists and remains close to completely overspecified.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis confirming the main CU-GMM finding that the Yogo model is underidentified and the two-dimensional admissible SDF set remains economically weak/mean-zero-like under alternative GMM procedures.
Settings.H662: Section 5.1, Table 2, second block 'Two-dimensional set' (PDF p. 9 / journal p. 346).
Settings.G663:
Treatment: Continuous three-factor affine SDF based on market return, nondurable consumption growth, and durable consumption growth, estimated over the longer 1949–2012 quarterly sample. Nonbinary.

Method: CU-GMM robustness exercise for Yogo (2006)'s model using a longer sample, 1949–2012, on 25 size and book-to-market portfolios. The authors estimate one-, two-, and three-dimensional admissible SDF sets as in the main analysis, with emphasis on whether the earlier underidentification and complete overspecification findings persist in a larger time sample.

Identification: Same cross-sectional asset-pricing moment restrictions, but with more time-series observations. The goal is to rule out that earlier results were artifacts of limited sample size relative to the number of moments. Underidentification is assessed via the d=2 J test and complete overspecification via the zero-SDF-mean test.

Setting: With quarterly real returns from 1949 to 2012 on the 25 size and value portfolios, the Yogo model continues to exhibit the same pattern. The one-dimensional SDF is not rejected (criterion 18.278, p=0.689), the two-dimensional admissible set is also not rejected (criterion 54.818, p=0.175), and the three-dimensional set is rejected (criterion 165.053, p=0.000). For d=2, the reported SDF means are 0.052 and 0.008 (second mean DM p=0.757), and the constrained criterion yields p=0.216, so the authors again conclude the admissible SDFs lie on a two-dimensional subspace and are completely overspecified.

Main role: The authors explicitly present this as a key robustness check for the paper's headline Yogo result. It materially supports the conclusion that the model remains underidentified and completely overspecified in a longer sample.
Settings.H663: Section 5.2, Table 3 Panel A (PDF p. 10 / journal p. 347).
Settings.G664:
Treatment: Continuous three-factor affine SDF in market, nondurable consumption growth, and durable consumption growth, evaluated on an alternative test-asset set combining 6 size/value portfolios and 5 industry portfolios. Nonbinary.

Method: CU-GMM robustness exercise for Yogo (2006)'s model using a smaller but more varied test-asset cross-section: 6 size and book-to-market portfolios plus 5 industry portfolios, 1949–2012. The authors estimate one-, two-, and three-dimensional admissible SDF sets and test SDF means as before.

Identification: Identification again comes from cross-sectional pricing moments, now with more varied test assets as recommended by Lewellen et al. (2010). The authors assess whether adding industries restores point identification or economic meaningfulness; they find it does not.

Setting: Using 6 size/value portfolios plus 5 industry portfolios over 1949–2012, the Yogo model remains underidentified and overspecified. The one-dimensional set is not rejected (criterion 5.941, p=0.654), the two-dimensional set is also not rejected (criterion 22.165, p=0.225), while the three-dimensional set is rejected (criterion 85.715, p=0.000). For d=2, the SDF means are 0.079 and 0.093 (second mean DM p=0.142), and the constrained criterion gives p=0.164. The authors conclude that even with a more varied test-asset cross-section, the admissible SDFs still lie on a two-dimensional subspace whose elements all have zero means, indicating complete overspecification.

Main role: This robustness setting addresses a key external-validity concern emphasized in asset-pricing tests—whether results depend on the narrow size/value portfolio test set. It supports the paper's main Yogo conclusion on a broader cross-section.
Settings.H664: Section 5.2, Table 3 Panel B (PDF p. 10 / journal p. 347).
Settings.G665:
Treatment: Continuous three-factor affine Yogo SDF under alternative GMM estimators across the longer-sample and expanded test-asset robustness samples. Nonbinary.

Method: Two-step and iterated GMM robustness analyses for Yogo (2006)'s longer-sample and alternative-cross-section exercises in Table 4. The authors re-estimate one-, two-, and three-dimensional admissible SDF sets for both Panel A (25 size/value portfolios, 1949–2012) and Panel B (6 size/value plus 5 industries, 1949–2012) under 2S-GMM and IT-GMM.

Identification: Same moment-condition identification as in the CU-GMM robustness settings; the alternative GMM procedures assess whether underidentification and overspecification findings are estimator-specific.

Setting: Table 4 shows that the longer-sample and broader-cross-section Yogo robustness results are qualitatively similar under two-step and iterated GMM. In Panel A (25 portfolios), the d=2 criterion p-values are 0.467 and 0.343; in Panel B (11 portfolios), they are 0.300 and 0.269. The constrained d=2 criteria are likewise nonrejected in all cases shown (0.258, 0.132, 0.176, 0.146), although the authors note one DM test of c=0 can reject in some implementations.
