Overall, they interpret these results as reaffirming persistent underidentification and near-complete overspecification.

Main role: These are robustness checks confirming that the longer-sample and broader-cross-section Yogo conclusions are not peculiar to CU-GMM.
Settings.H665: Section 5.2, Table 4, Panels A and B (PDF p. 11 / journal p. 348).
Settings.G666:
Treatment: Continuous three-factor Jagannathan-Wang pricing-kernel specification involving market excess return, per-capita labor-income growth proxy, and lagged default spread within the affine SDF. Nonbinary.

Method: CU-GMM evaluation of Jagannathan and Wang (1996)'s three-factor CAPM extension on monthly excess returns for 25 Fama-French size and book-to-market portfolios, 1959:02–2012:12. The affine SDF is m = a(1 − δ_p f_p − δ_l f_l − δ_s f_s), where factors are market excess return, labor income growth proxy, and lagged default premium. The authors estimate one-, two-, and three-dimensional admissible SDF sets, with d=2 normalized as (δ_p,δ_l,0) and (δ_p,0,δ_s).

Identification: The authors exploit cross-sectional pricing moments between monthly test-asset excess returns and the three proposed factors. By comparing d=1, d=2, and d=3 admissible SDF sets, they assess whether the model is point identified or underidentified. They then test whether all admissible SDF means are zero, which would imply the SDFs are uncorrelated with the returns they are supposed to price.

Setting: For Jagannathan and Wang's three-factor model on 25 monthly size/value portfolios from 1959:02 to 2012:12, the authors find evidence of underidentification and economic meaninglessness similar to the Yogo case. The one-dimensional set is not rejected (criterion 22.964, p=0.404), the two-dimensional set is also not rejected (criterion 53.847, p=0.199), and the three-dimensional set is rejected (criterion 188.792, p=0.000). In the two-dimensional set, the market loading is not significant (-0.745, p=0.119), while labor and default premium loadings are large; the reported SDF means are -0.217 and 0.033, and the constrained criterion gives p=0.150. The authors conclude that the admissible SDFs form a two-dimensional set that is effectively uncorrelated with the 25 test assets, indicating complete overspecification.

Main role: The Jagannathan-Wang application is the paper's second main empirical application and provides core evidence that overspecification/underidentification problems extend beyond consumption-based models.
Settings.H666: Section 5.3, Table 5 Panel A (PDF p. 11 / journal p. 348).
Settings.G667:
Treatment: Continuous Jagannathan-Wang affine SDF with market, labor-income growth proxy, and default premium, evaluated on an alternative monthly test-asset cross-section including industries. Nonbinary.

Method: CU-GMM evaluation of Jagannathan and Wang (1996)'s three-factor model on an expanded monthly test-asset set: 6 size and book-to-market portfolios plus 5 industry portfolios, 1959:02–2012:12. The authors estimate one-, two-, and three-dimensional admissible SDF sets and test SDF means; this sample is meant to add identifying information from industries.

Identification: By expanding the cross-section of test assets, the authors seek stronger identifying variation in the return-factor covariance structure. Rejection of d=2 indicates the model becomes point identified on this broader asset set. They then assess whether the resulting one-dimensional admissible SDF has nonzero mean; failure to reject zero mean implies the identified SDF is still uncorrelated with returns and therefore economically unattractive.

Setting: When the Jagannathan-Wang model is estimated on 6 size/value portfolios plus 5 industry portfolios, the authors reject the existence of a valid two-dimensional admissible set (criterion 41.588, p=0.001), so the extended cross-section appears to identify a one-dimensional SDF. The one-dimensional model itself is not rejected (criterion 12.570, p=0.128), and the estimated SDF depends on labor income and especially the default spread (premium loading 72.463, p=0.001). However, the normalized SDF mean is 0.002 (p=0.968), and the constrained criterion is also nonrejected (p=0.183), so the identified SDF is interpreted as uncorrelated with the returns it prices. Thus, identification is restored, but only for an economically unattractive, completely overspecified SDF.

Main role: This is a central comparative application: adding industry portfolios changes the identification result for Jagannathan-Wang, but the identified SDF remains economically unattractive. That distinction is emphasized in the abstract and conclusions.
Settings.H667: Section 5.3, Table 5 Panel B and surrounding discussion (PDF pp. 11-12 / journal pp. 348-349).
Settings.G668:
Treatment: Continuous Jagannathan-Wang three-factor affine SDF under alternative GMM estimators across the 25-portfolio and expanded 11-portfolio monthly samples. Nonbinary.

Method: Two-step and iterated GMM robustness analyses for Jagannathan and Wang (1996)'s model across both monthly samples in Table 6: Panel A with 25 size/value portfolios and Panel B with 6 size/value plus 5 industry portfolios. The authors re-estimate one-, two-, and three-dimensional admissible SDF sets under 2S-GMM and IT-GMM and re-test zero-SDF-mean restrictions.

Identification: Same pricing-moment identification as the main Jagannathan-Wang settings, but evaluated using 2S-GMM and IT-GMM to confirm robustness of inferences about dimensionality and zero-SDF-mean restrictions.

Setting: Table 6 shows that the Jagannathan-Wang findings are qualitatively robust to two-step and iterated GMM. For the 25-portfolio sample (Panel A), the d=2 criterion p-values are 0.095 and 0.159 and the constrained d=2 criteria are 0.061 and 0.119, supporting the CU-GMM conclusion of a nonrejected two-dimensional, economically weak admissible set. For the expanded 11-portfolio sample (Panel B), the d=2 criterion is strongly rejected under both estimators (p=0.001), while the one-dimensional set remains nonrejected with means near zero (e.g., 0.020, p=0.611 under 2S-GMM; 0.023, p=0.555 under IT-GMM). The authors therefore conclude that the broader cross-section identifies only a mean-zero, uncorrelated SDF.

Main role: These are substantive robustness checks showing that the Jagannathan-Wang conclusions—underidentification for the 25 portfolios and identified but mean-zero SDF for the broader test-asset set—are not driven by CU-GMM alone.
Settings.H668: Section 5.3, Table 6, Panels A and B (PDF p. 12 / journal p. 349).
Settings.G669:
Treatment: Calendar year of the speech, treated as a continuous time trend. In columns 1-2 the sample is all SEC speeches 1930-2019; in columns 3-4 it is speeches from 1990-2019. Units are years.

Method: The authors run speech-level linear regressions of SEC speech partisanship on a linear time trend (calendar year), first without and then with Commissioner fixed effects. The dependent variable is the speech-level Congress-based partisanship score derived from the GST-style phrase-probability mapping from Congress to regulator speech. The key identifying comparison is whether the year coefficient survives after absorbing time-invariant Commissioner heterogeneity. No quasi-experimental shock is used; this is a regression-adjustment design with a causal interpretation about whether rising SEC partisanship comes from within-Commissioner changes versus turnover across Commissioners. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust. Remaining concerns are nonrandom timing/composition of speeches and omitted time-varying forces correlated with year.

Identification: The intended identification is comparative: if the positive time trend in speech partisanship disappears once Commissioner fixed effects are included, then the rise in average SEC partisanship is attributed to changes in Commissioner composition rather than within-Commissioner drift. The endogeneity concern is that time trends in speech content could reflect both changing people and changing behavior by the same people. Commissioner fixed effects absorb time-invariant individual speaking style/ideology, so remaining variation comes from within-Commissioner changes over time. The interpretation relies on assuming year captures secular change and that fixed effects sufficiently isolate turnover from within-person change, though time-varying omitted factors within Commissioner tenure remain possible.

Setting: Using speech-level OLS regressions, the authors argue that the rise in SEC partisanship is driven by turnover rather than incumbents becoming more partisan. Without Commissioner fixed effects, the year coefficient is positive and significant: beta=0.0002 (t=7.67) over 1930-2019 and beta=0.0009 (t=9.07) over 1990-2019. After adding Commissioner fixed effects, the year trend becomes statistically insignificant: beta=0.0003 (t=0.87) over the full sample and beta=-0.0003 (t=-0.80) over 1990-2019. The authors interpret this as evidence that less-partisan Commissioners were replaced by more-partisan ones, a key mechanism behind the paper's main finding of rising SEC partisanship.

Main role: A central conclusion of the paper is that rising SEC partisanship is driven by more-partisan Commissioners replacing less-partisan ones rather than incumbent Commissioners becoming more partisan. Table 4 is the direct evidence for that claim and is highlighted in the abstract/introduction/conclusion.
Settings.H669: Section 2.5 'Where did the rise in SEC partisanship come from?', Table 4, columns 1-4, PDF pp. 27-28.
Settings.G670:
Treatment: Observable Commissioner characteristics: indicator for male; indicator for prior political background (worked for a congressperson or president); indicator for law background; indicator for MBA; indicator for graduate degree in economics. These are binary regressors, reported in separate and joint OLS specifications.

Method: The authors regress an estimated Commissioner-specific partisanship measure—the Commissioner fixed effect recovered from the speech-level regression in Table 4, column 2—on observable Commissioner characteristics. Specifications are cross-sectional OLS with each characteristic entered separately and then jointly: male, political background, lawyer, MBA, and graduate degree in economics. The design is correlational regression adjustment, but the text interprets coefficients as indicating whether these observable traits explain heterogeneity in Commissioner partisanship. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust.

Identification: The strategy is observational cross-sectional comparison across 90 SEC Commissioners. The paper's motivating concern is whether observable background variables explain the heterogeneity in Commissioner partisanship that underlies turnover-driven increases in SEC partisanship. The causal content is weak and largely suggestive: no exogenous variation in characteristics is used, and estimates may reflect selection into education/careers and omitted traits. The paper's practical conclusion is mostly negative—that these observables do not explain much of the variation.

Setting: In cross-sectional OLS regressions, the authors assess whether observable Commissioner traits explain heterogeneity in estimated SEC Commissioner partisanship. They find no significant relationship with gender, political background, law degrees, or MBAs, and only weak evidence that a graduate degree in economics predicts lower partisanship: in the univariate specification the coefficient is -0.0109 (t=-1.92), and in the joint specification it is -0.0097 (t=-1.68). The authors interpret this as evidence that rising SEC partisanship through turnover is mostly not explained by these basic observable characteristics.

Main role: This is a supporting analysis about what observable traits correlate with Commissioner partisanship, not a central identification result of the paper.
Settings.G671:
Treatment: Monthly average Congress-based regulator speech partisanship, pi_t, with contemporaneous value and up to two monthly lags. This is a continuous probability-like index between 0 and 1 summarizing regulator speech partisanship in that month.

Method: The authors estimate monthly linear regressions of RegisterPartisanship on contemporaneous and lagged monthly averages of speech-based Congress-partisanship, separately for the SEC and Fed. RegisterPartisanship is computed from Federal Register text, assigning each day's text to the majority party controlling the agency that day, then averaging daily scores within month. Specifications include one contemporaneous monthly speech-partisanship measure and up to two lags. The design is time-series regression adjustment, interpreted as whether higher regulator speech partisanship spills over into rulemaking language. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust.

Identification: The identifying variation is month-to-month fluctuation in speech partisanship within agency, related to month-to-month fluctuation in partisan content of Register text. The endogeneity concern is that both speech and rule text may respond to common shocks, agenda changes, party control, or underlying issues being considered. The paper interprets the contemporaneous and lagged positive coefficients as spillovers from regulator speech partisanship into written rules, but this rests on a conditional-association argument rather than a quasi-experiment. Lag structure is used to probe persistence, not to secure causal identification.

Setting: Using monthly OLS regressions, the authors argue that greater speech partisanship among regulators leads the Federal Register text of their agencies to sound more like the congressional language of the agency's majority party. At the SEC, the contemporaneous coefficient of speech partisanship on Register partisanship ranges from 0.1054 to 0.2002 across specifications (t=2.58 to 4.96), which the authors summarize as about 10.54%-20.02% of speech partisanship spilling over into Register language in the same month. At the Fed, contemporaneous coefficients range from 0.1951 to 0.2280 (t=2.69 to 3.15), with lagged coefficients also positive and often significant. This setting materially supports the paper's claim that partisanship in speech affects actual regulatory outputs.

Main role: A central substantive conclusion is that observed speech partisanship extends to real regulatory behavior, including rulemaking language. Table 6 is one of the main pieces of evidence for that implication and is emphasized in the abstract/introduction/conclusion.
Settings.H671: Section 3.1 'Rulemaking language', Table 6, columns 1-6, PDF pp. 30-32.
Settings.G672:
Treatment: Two related treatments are analyzed jointly: (i) category indicators for proposed/finalized rules versus notices, and finalized rules versus proposed rules; (ii) interactions between those category indicators and monthly speech partisanship pi_t. Rule and Final rule are binary indicators; pi_t is continuous.

Method: The authors estimate linear regressions on an unbalanced month-year-category panel of Federal Register text categories (notices, proposed rules, finalized rules), with monthly RegisterPartisanship as the outcome. Regressors include monthly speech partisanship pi_t, indicators for Rule and Final rule, and interactions between category indicators and speech partisanship. Some specifications absorb month-year fixed effects, so identification comes from within-month-year differences across categories. This is a standard FE setup with one absorbed FE dimension, interpreted as whether more-partisan regulator speech has stronger effects on more consequential rule categories than on notices. Standard errors are clustered at the month-year level.

Identification: The strategy compares partisan content across document categories within the same month-year, especially in specifications with month-year fixed effects. This absorbs common monthly shocks, agency-wide political environment, and time-varying average speech partisanship when only category comparisons are targeted. The causal concern is that category composition and issue salience may differ systematically, and interactions with speech partisanship may still reflect omitted category-specific shocks. The paper interprets significant positive interaction coefficients as evidence that regulator partisanship exerts greater influence on proposed/finalized rules than on notices.

Setting: In month-year-category regressions, the authors argue that regulator speech partisanship has stronger effects on the partisan language of consequential rule documents than on notices. At the SEC, proposed/finalized rules have higher RegisterPartisanship than notices, and the interaction Rule×pi_t is positive and significant in specifications with and without month-year fixed effects: 0.1457 (t=2.36) and 0.1462 (t=2.41), respectively, when proposed and finalized rules are pooled. At the Fed, category levels differ—especially finalized rules versus proposed rules—but the interaction estimates are positive and not statistically significant. The SEC evidence supports the claim that partisan speech disproportionately affects proposed and finalized rules relative to notices.

Main role: This extends the paper's main 'real effects' argument by showing that speech partisanship is especially reflected in consequential rulemaking text, not just overall Register text. It is an important substantive extension, though somewhat more granular than Table 6.
Settings.H672: Section 3.1 'Rulemaking language', Table 7, columns 1-11, PDF pp. 33-35.
Settings.G673:
Treatment: Indicators for whether, on the same voted item, at least one other regulator from the voter's own party dissented (DissentOwnParty) and whether at least one regulator from the opposite party dissented (DissentOtherParty). These are binary indicators.

Method: The authors estimate linear probability models at the individual-vote level for SEC non-Chair Commissioners and Fed non-Chair Governors. The dependent variable is an indicator that the regulator casts a dissenting vote. Regressors are indicators that another regulator from the same party cast a dissenting vote (DissentOwnParty) and that a regulator from the opposite party cast a dissenting vote (DissentOtherParty); some specifications add year fixed effects. The design is observational regression adjustment meant to test whether dissents cluster along party lines. Standard errors are clustered by the rule/decision being voted on.

Identification: The intended identification is within-vote association between a regulator's dissent decision and whether same-party or opposite-party colleagues also dissent. Year fixed effects absorb broad time trends in dissenting propensity, but no exogenous variation is used. Endogeneity concerns include common vote-specific controversy, strategic coordination, and simultaneity because votes are jointly determined. The authors nonetheless interpret the pattern—positive same-party and negative opposite-party association at the SEC—as evidence of partisan voting behavior. For the Fed, positive own-party and weaker/insignificant opposite-party effects are interpreted as less clearly partisan.

Setting: Using individual-vote linear probability regressions, the authors argue that SEC dissenting behavior is partisan. For SEC non-Chair Commissioners, a Commissioner is 45.4 percentage points more likely to dissent when another member of her own party dissents (t=14.31), while the probability of dissent falls by 0.55 percentage points when someone from the opposite party dissents (t=-2.12); with year fixed effects, the estimates are 42.79 percentage points (t=13.07) and -3.17 percentage points (t=-9.19). For Fed non-Chair Governors, own-party dissent also raises dissent probability—14.97 percentage points (t=5.63) and 10.73 percentage points (t=3.65) with year fixed effects—while opposite-party dissent is positive without year effects and insignificant with them. This evidence underpins the paper's claim that SEC votes disproportionately occur together along party lines.

Main role: A major conclusion is that partisanship appears in SEC voting behavior. Table 8 provides direct evidence that dissents align with party lines and is highlighted in the introduction and conclusion.
Settings.H673: Section 3.2 'Voting activity', Table 8 columns 1-4 and accompanying prose, PDF pp. 35-37.
Settings.G674:
Treatment: Continuous standardized ideological distance between the regulator and (i) the average of other regulators voting on the issue, or (ii) the Chair, measured either from Congress-based speech similarity or from a dictionary-based benefits-vs-costs speech measure. Each regressor is normalized to mean zero and unit standard deviation.

Method: The authors estimate individual-vote linear regressions of a dissent indicator on measures of ideological distance between the regulator and either the other regulators voting on the issue or the Chair. They construct ideological distance two ways: using speech-based Congress-partisanship similarity (IdeologicalDistance, IdeologicalDistanceChair) and using dictionary-based regulatory cost/benefit speech shares (DBIdeologicalDistance, DBIdeologicalDistanceChair). All regressions include fixed effects for the rule/decision being voted on, so identification comes from within-decision differences across voters. Standard errors are clustered by the voted rule/decision. This is a standard FE design with one FE dimension.

Identification: By including rule/decision fixed effects, the regressions compare regulators voting on the same issue, holding constant all item-specific controversy and timing. The remaining variation is cross-regulator ideological distance for that same voted item. The endogeneity concern is that ideological distance may proxy for unobserved regulator traits or strategic positioning, and speech-based ideology is itself measured with error. Still, the paper interprets positive within-item associations as evidence that ideological dissimilarity causes more dissenting behavior, especially at the SEC.

Setting: Within the same voted item, regulators whose speech is more ideologically distant from colleagues or the Chair are more likely to dissent. In the SEC sample with rule fixed effects, a one-standard-deviation increase in Congress-based IdeologicalDistance raises dissent probability by 0.0021 (t=2.93), and distance from the Chair raises it by 0.0032 (t=6.33). Using the dictionary-based ideology measure, the effects are larger: 0.0087 (t=15.36) for distance from the rest of the Commission and 0.0062 (t=13.54) for distance from the Chair. For the Fed, the corresponding coefficients are weaker and not always significant, though distance from the Chair is significant in some specifications (e.g., 0.0081, t=2.57, and dictionary-based 0.0091, t=2.37). The authors use this to argue that partisan/ideological differences reflected in speech help explain dissenting votes.

Main role: This is part of the paper's central argument linking speech-based partisanship to actual behavior. It shows that regulators whose speech is more ideologically distant are more likely to dissent, reinforcing the behavioral relevance of the speech measure.
Settings.H674: Section 3.2 'Voting activity', Table 9 columns 1-8 and accompanying prose, PDF pp. 38-40.
Settings.G675:
Treatment: Investor information-production proxies and related bid/bidder characteristics: indicators for largest bid quartile, second-largest bid quartile, price-sensitive bid, money bid, early bid, revised bid, meeting attendance during bookbuilding, pilot-fishing meeting attendance, frequent bidder, and one-time bidder. These are binary indicators rather than a single treatment; the focal causal interpretation is that changing these bid or bidder characteristics affects normalized rationing.

Method: Pooled linear regressions at the investor-by-IPO-bookrunner level relate normalized rationing to bid characteristics and bidder characteristics, with IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects included as controls. Standard errors are clustered at the IPO level because some IPOs have more than one book. The implemented estimator is a linear regression adjustment design rather than a difference-in-differences or identifying fixed-effects design; the authors interpret coefficients as determinants of allocation and as evidence on information revelation. The baseline specification excludes investor-revenue variables and is reported in Table VI column (1), with related discussion in Section II.B.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-investor variation within IPOs and across banks after conditioning on IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects. The design aims to compare otherwise similar investors participating in the same IPO while absorbing IPO-level demand and supply conditions and average bank allocation policies. The endogeneity concern is that unobserved investor attributes or bank-investor relationships may correlate with both bid characteristics and allocations; this setting does not fully solve that concern and is therefore associational/selection-on-observables, though the authors interpret it substantively as evidence on information revelation.

Setting: In pooled OLS regressions of investor-level normalized rationing on bid and bidder characteristics, the authors find that larger bids, price-sensitive bids, meetings, pilot-fishing participation, frequent bidding, and one-time bidder status are associated with more favorable IPO allocations. In Table VI column (1), the coefficient is 0.256 for the largest bid quartile, 0.137 for the second-largest quartile, 0.072 for price-sensitive bids, 0.266 for meeting attendance, 0.266 for pilot fishing, 0.224 for frequent bidders, and 0.137 for one-time bidders; early and revised bids are not significant. The authors interpret these estimates as evidence consistent with information revelation theories of IPO allocation, though the design relies on regression adjustment with IPO and bank fixed effects rather than a quasi-experimental source of exogenous variation.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion state that a central contribution is testing whether allocations reward information production. The baseline allocation regressions provide key evidence for that central claim, even though the revenue/quid-pro-quo results are also central.
Settings.H675: Section II.A–II.B; Table VI, column (1), PDF pp. 2321–2326 (esp. p. 2324–2326).
Settings.G676:
Treatment: Investor revenue rank with the bookrunner in the year of the IPO, coded as indicators for 1st (top), 2nd, 3rd, and 4th revenue quartiles; omitted category is investors generating no revenue for that bookrunner. The paper constructs quartiles separately for each IPO and bookrunner based on total revenues from all services. Treatment is effectively a multi-valued categorical exposure represented by binary indicators.

Method: Pooled linear regressions at the investor-by-IPO-bookrunner level add investor revenue-quartile indicators to the baseline normalized-rationing specification, still including IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects and clustering standard errors at the IPO level. The key design feature is comparing investors within IPOs by their revenue rank with the bookrunner. This remains a regression-adjustment design rather than an identifying fixed-effects design, because the fixed effects used are IPO and bank controls rather than investor or bank-investor absorption. Reported in Table VI column (2), with subgroup versions in columns (3)–(6).

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-investor variation in revenue rank within IPOs, conditional on IPO fixed effects, bank fixed effects, and observable bid/bidder characteristics. The endogeneity concern is that high-revenue investors may differ in unobserved informativeness, sophistication, or bank relationships. The paper argues the rich controls make the revenue-allocation relationship informative but acknowledges unobserved factors as a challenge, later addressed with investor and investor-bank fixed effects in subsequent settings.

Setting: Adding investor revenue quartiles to the pooled allocation regression, the authors find a strong monotonic relationship between bookrunner revenues from an investor and the investor's IPO allocation. In Table VI column (2), relative to investors generating no revenue, normalized rationing is higher by 0.514 for top-quartile revenue investors, 0.272 for second-quartile, and 0.095 for third-quartile investors; the fourth quartile is near zero and insignificant. The paper interprets this as evidence consistent with a quid pro quo in which investors generating more revenue for the bank receive more generous IPO allocations, alongside separate evidence that some information-related behaviors also matter.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize 'strong support for the existence of a quid pro quo whereby broking revenues are a significant determinant of investors’ IPO allocations.' Table VI column (2) is a main result supporting that central conclusion.
Settings.H676: Section II.B; Table VI, column (2), PDF pp. 2324–2326; related verbal summary on PDF pp. 2306 and 2339.
Settings.G677:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators and information-related bid characteristics in subsamples split by whether the IPO had a corporate finance advisor. The substantive treatment of interest is again investor revenue rank with the bookrunner, with separate estimation in advised and nonadvised IPOs.

Method: Subsample pooled linear regressions identical to the main revenue-allocation specification but estimated separately for IPOs with and without a corporate finance advisor. Regressions include IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects, with clustered standard errors at the IPO level. The authors use these to test whether corporate finance advisors alter how information-related bidding and revenue relationships affect allocations. Reported in Table VI columns (3) and (4).

Identification: Within advised and nonadvised IPO subsamples, identification uses cross-investor variation in revenue rank and bidding characteristics conditional on IPO and bank fixed effects. The concern is that advised IPOs differ systematically from nonadvised IPOs in size or complexity, so these are heterogeneity patterns rather than clean causal effects of advisors. The paper interprets differences in coefficients as suggestive of how advisors shape allocation choices.

Setting: When the pooled allocation regressions are split by whether an IPO has a corporate finance advisor, the revenue-allocation relationship remains similar across advised and nonadvised IPOs, while price-sensitive bids appear to be rewarded more in advised IPOs. In Table VI, the top revenue quartile coefficient is 0.492 in advised IPOs and 0.528 in nonadvised IPOs, both highly significant; price-sensitive bids have coefficient 0.116 in advised IPOs but only 0.031 and insignificant in nonadvised IPOs. The authors interpret this as suggesting that corporate finance advisors may help reward more informative bidding, but they do not materially reduce the apparent quid-pro-quo relationship between investor revenues and allocations.

Main role: This is a substantive heterogeneity analysis supporting the main allocation results by examining whether corporate finance advisors mitigate conflicts or change information rewards. It is not the single headline identification design.
Settings.H677: Section II.B; Table VI, columns (3) and (4), PDF pp. 2324–2326.
Settings.G678:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators and information proxies estimated separately by investor type; the main treatment remains investor revenue rank with the bookrunner within long-only and hedge-fund subsamples. Investor type itself is a sample split based on classifications from a leading corporate finance advisor.

Method: Subsample pooled linear regressions of normalized rationing run separately for long-only investors and hedge funds, otherwise using the same regression-adjustment setup with IPO fixed effects, bank fixed effects, and IPO-clustered standard errors. The authors use these to study heterogeneity in how revenue rank and information proxies affect allocations by investor type. Reported in Table VI columns (5) and (6).

Identification: Within each investor-type subsample, the design compares investors with different revenue ranks and bidding characteristics while controlling for IPO and bank fixed effects. Remaining concerns are misclassification of investor type and unobserved differences within type. The authors use these regressions descriptively/causally to infer whether allocation rules differ between long-only investors and hedge funds.

Setting: Separate pooled regressions indicate that the positive relationship between investor revenues and allocations is stronger in absolute terms for long-only investors than for hedge funds, though hedge funds start from lower mean normalized rationing. In Table VI, the top revenue quartile coefficient is 0.673 for long-only investors and 0.265 for hedge funds; price-sensitive bids are also rewarded in both groups. The authors interpret these results as showing heterogeneous allocation practices across investor types, with long-only investors receiving relatively stronger rewards from high bank-revenue relationships.

Main role: This is a substantive heterogeneity analysis used to characterize which investors benefit most from the allocation mechanisms, supporting but not defining the paper's central conclusions.
Settings.H678: Section II.B; Table VI, columns (5) and (6), PDF pp. 2324–2327.
Settings.G679:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators with the bookrunner, plus information-related bidding variables, estimated separately for each bank. The main treatment is an investor's revenue quartile relative to other investors in that IPO for that bank.

Method: Separate bank-level linear regressions of normalized rationing on bid characteristics, bidder characteristics, and investor revenue quartiles, with IPO fixed effects included and standard errors clustered at the IPO level. The authors estimate the specification separately for the top nine bookrunners and a pooled 'others' group to study heterogeneity across banks. Because these are bank-specific regressions with IPO FE only, they remain regression-adjustment designs rather than identifying FE designs. Reported in Table VII.

Identification: Identification comes from within-bank, within-IPO cross-investor variation in revenue ranks and bid features after absorbing IPO fixed effects. The authors use the bank-by-bank estimates to assess whether different banks implement different allocation rules. Remaining endogeneity concerns from unobserved investor or bank-investor factors remain unresolved in this setting and motivate later fixed-effects models.

Setting: Bank-by-bank regressions show that the pooled revenue-allocation relationship is not universal but holds for most major bookrunners. In Table VII, six banks have top-revenue-quartile coefficients between 0.56 and 0.72, another bank and the smaller-bank group have smaller but significant coefficients, one bank has only marginal significance, and one bank shows no evidence that investor revenues influence allocation. The authors interpret this as strong but heterogeneous support across banks for the claim that higher-revenue clients receive more generous IPO allocations.

Main role: These regressions are robustness and heterogeneity analyses showing whether the main pooled patterns are driven by particular banks. They materially support the paper's claims but are not the primary pooled result highlighted in the abstract.
Settings.H679: Section II.C; Table VII, PDF pp. 2327–2330.
Settings.G680:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators with the bookrunner, varying across IPOs for a given investor; omitted category is no revenues. The focal treatment is a change in an investor's relative revenue rank across IPOs. Other bid and meeting indicators are included as covariates, also interpreted causally.

Method: Linear regressions of normalized rationing include investor fixed effects in addition to IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects, so identification comes from within-investor variation across IPOs and banks. The estimator absorbs investor-specific time-invariant unobservables but does not meet the HDFE threshold of three separately absorbed FE dimensions discussed as an identification battery, because the core identifying design is standard FE rather than a high-dimensional FE design emphasized as such. Standard errors are clustered at the IPO level. Reported in Table VIII column (1).

Identification: Identification uses within-investor changes in revenue quartile across IPOs, netting out any time-invariant investor characteristics such as size, sophistication, or persistent informativeness. The endogeneity concern is that unobserved investor traits may drive both revenues and allocations; investor fixed effects address such constant traits but not bank-specific relationships or time-varying unobservables. The paper interprets the remaining positive revenue coefficients as evidence that the pooled results are not solely artifacts of investor heterogeneity.

Setting: With investor fixed effects added, the positive relation between investor revenue rank and IPO allocation remains, though with smaller coefficients because only within-investor variation identifies the effect. In Table VIII column (1), normalized rationing rises by 0.133 for the top revenue quartile and 0.068 for the second quartile relative to no revenues; pilot fishing and meetings remain positive, while the largest-bid indicator turns negative within investor. The authors interpret this as evidence that, for a given investor, higher revenue importance to the bookrunner across IPOs still leads to more favorable allocations, supporting the quid-pro-quo interpretation beyond simple investor selection.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly highlight that the revenue-allocation relationship remains when controlling for unobserved investor characteristics. This fixed-effects setting is therefore a central robustness analysis supporting the main quid-pro-quo conclusion.
Settings.H680: Section III.A; Table VIII, column (1), PDF pp. 2331–2333.
Settings.G681:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators with the same bank across different IPOs run by that bank; the focal treatment is a change in the investor's revenue ranking relative to other investors for that bank across IPOs. Treatment is represented by binary indicators for revenue quartiles.

Method: Linear regressions of normalized rationing include bank-investor fixed effects (investor-bank pair fixed effects), along with IPO fixed effects, so identification comes from within investor-bank-pair variation across IPOs. Standard errors are clustered at the IPO level. This is a standard fixed-effects design targeting time-invariant aspects of a particular investor-bank relationship. Reported in Table VIII column (2).

Identification: Identification comes from within investor-bank-pair changes in revenue rank across IPOs run by the same bank, controlling for time-invariant relationship quality between that investor and bank. The design addresses the concern that close, persistent investor-bank ties, rather than quid pro quo, explain allocations. The remaining assumptions are that time-varying investor-bank shocks correlated with both revenue rank and allocations are limited after controls.

Setting: Even after absorbing investor-bank pair fixed effects, the paper finds that an investor receives more favorable allocations in IPOs where it is more important to the same bank in revenue terms. In Table VIII column (2), the top and second revenue quartiles increase normalized rationing by 0.179 and 0.095, respectively, relative to no revenues, while meetings and pilot fishing remain positive. The authors interpret this as especially strong evidence that the revenue-allocation relation is not merely an artifact of stable investor-bank relationships and is consistent with a quid pro quo.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion stress that the quid-pro-quo relation survives even after controlling for specific investor-bank relationships. This is one of the paper's strongest central robustness settings.
Settings.H681: Section III.A; Table VIII, column (2), PDF pp. 2331–2333.
Settings.G682:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators with the bookrunner, estimated separately in hot and cold IPO subsamples; hotness is an IPO-level sample split based on time to full subscription. The key treatment remains revenue quartile, with interest in whether its effect differs by IPO hotness.

Method: Pooled and investor-fixed-effects linear regressions of normalized rationing are estimated separately for hot and cold IPO subsamples. Regressions include IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects in the pooled versions; the later columns also add investor fixed effects. The split is based on whether time until full subscription at the lower end of the initial price range is below or above the median. Reported in Table IX. This is a regression-adjustment heterogeneity analysis rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: Within hot and cold IPO subsamples, identification uses cross-investor variation in revenue rank and other covariates after fixed effects. The concern is that hotness is endogenous and correlated with unobserved deal characteristics; the authors treat this as heterogeneity evidence rather than a clean causal effect of hotness itself. In investor-FE versions, within-investor variation across IPOs is used separately in hot and cold deals.

Setting: Splitting IPOs by hotness, the authors find that higher-revenue investors are much more favored in hot IPOs than in cold IPOs. In pooled regressions (Table IX columns (1) and (2)), the top revenue quartile coefficient is 0.653 in hot IPOs versus 0.278 in cold IPOs. With investor fixed effects (columns (3) and (4)), the top and second revenue quartiles remain significant only in hot IPOs, not in cold IPOs. The paper interprets this as showing that changes in investor revenue importance affect allocations primarily in hot, presumably more attractive IPOs.

Main role: This is an important substantive extension showing that quid-pro-quo style allocation is concentrated in likely more profitable deals, but it is a secondary analysis supporting the main allocation and profitability conclusions.
Settings.H682: Section III.B; Table IX, PDF pp. 2333–2335.
Settings.G683:
Treatment: Investor revenue quartile indicators with the bookrunner in the year of the IPO, plus information-related bid and bidder indicators. The focal treatment for the quid-pro-quo claim is being in a higher revenue quartile versus no revenues.

Method: The authors first estimate a linear model of IPO underpricing to generate fitted expected first-day returns, then compute investor-level expected profitability of bids as allocated shares times expected return divided by bid size. They then regress expected profitability on bid characteristics, bidder characteristics, and investor revenue quartiles, including IPO fixed effects and bank fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the IPO level. Table X presents baseline, revenue-augmented, investor-FE, and investor-bank-FE versions. Because the final reported treatment-effect regressions on expected profitability are linear regressions on a generated outcome and not FE-identified in the baseline specification, the method is classified as regression adjustment.

Identification: Identification uses cross-investor variation in revenue rank and bidding characteristics within IPOs after IPO and bank fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is again that high-revenue investors may differ in unobservable ways; subsequent investor and investor-bank FE variants probe this. A further limitation is generated-regressor uncertainty because expected profitability uses fitted underpricing rather than observed ex ante expectations, but the paper treats this as the relevant empirical measure of expected rents.

Setting: Using a constructed measure of expected profitability, the authors find that high-revenue investors earn more profitable IPO allocations. In Table X column (2), relative to investors generating no revenue, expected profitability is higher by 0.491 for top-quartile revenue investors, 0.340 for second-quartile investors, and 0.170 for third-quartile investors; in the investor fixed-effects specification (column (3)), the top and second quartiles remain significant at 0.265 and 0.196. The authors interpret these results as showing that the allocation advantages given to higher-revenue investors translate into higher expected profits, reinforcing the quid-pro-quo interpretation.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion state that broking revenues are a significant determinant of investors' IPO profits, not only allocations. These expected-profitability regressions therefore support a core substantive conclusion.
Settings.H683: Section III.B; Table X and equation (2) discussion, PDF pp. 2335–2337.
Settings.G684:
Treatment: County Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate, measured as total subscribers divided by 1920 county population, in percentage points. In this DiD/event-study setting, treatment intensity is continuous and interacted with year indicators.

Method: Annual event-study/difference-in-differences regressions at the county-year level estimate interactions between a county’s Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate and year indicators. Outcomes are commercial-bank aggregates. The specification includes county fixed effects, year fixed effects, Federal Reserve District-by-year fixed effects, time-varying county controls (population, farms, urbanization, race, immigrant shares, illiteracy, crop-price index, and Federal Reserve Bank/branch presence interacted with year), and county-clustered standard errors. Identification comes from differential post-drive changes across counties with higher versus lower subscription rates, with the timing of coefficients used to argue against pre-existing trends.

Identification: The authors compare annual changes in commercial-bank outcomes across counties with different Liberty Bond subscription rates before and after the 1917–1919 drives. County fixed effects absorb time-invariant county differences; year and Fed-district-by-year effects absorb common shocks and district-specific annual shocks; covariates absorb observed evolving county characteristics. The key assumption is that absent the Liberty Bond drives, counties with higher subscription rates would not have experienced differential trends in commercial bank assets/deposits. The absence of pre-1917 differential coefficients is offered as supporting evidence, though the authors note remaining endogeneity because subscription demand may correlate with unobserved financial sophistication or income.

Setting: Using county-level annual event-study DiD regressions, the authors argue that higher Liberty Bond subscription rates caused a relative contraction in commercial banking after the drives. They report that 'A ten percentage point (about a 1 standard deviation) increase in Liberty Bond subscriptions led to an 8.2% decrease in commercial bank assets by 1920 and an 11.6% decrease by 1929, relative to other counties,' and that deposits show a similar pattern. The design relies on county, year, and Federal Reserve District-by-year fixed effects plus time-varying controls, and is used to show the timing of the effect and the lack of pre-trends, but the paper treats IV as the stronger causal evidence.

Main role: The paper presents these annual DiD estimates as suggestive evidence on timing and pre-trends before turning to IV as the main causal design. They support the central narrative but are not the headline identification strategy.
Settings.H684: Section 4, Eq. (1), Fig. 4 Panels A and B, PDF pp. 9–11.
Settings.G685:
Treatment: County Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate, measured as subscribers divided by 1920 county population, in percentage points; continuous treatment intensity interacted with year indicators.

Method: Annual event-study/difference-in-differences regressions at the county-year level estimate interactions between county Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rates and year indicators for investment-bank outcomes. The specification includes county fixed effects, year fixed effects, Federal Reserve District-by-year fixed effects, time-varying county controls, and county-clustered standard errors. Because investment-bank directory data exist only for selected years (1914, 1916, 1918, 1919, 1920, 1922, 1923, 1925, 1929), the event-study is on this irregular panel.

Identification: Identification uses differential changes over time in investment-bank outcomes across counties with higher versus lower Liberty Bond subscription rates. County fixed effects absorb fixed differences; year and Fed-district-by-year effects absorb aggregate and regional annual shocks; time-varying county controls absorb observed confounders. The main assumption is parallel trends conditional on these controls. The lack of differential pre-1918 growth in investment banks is used as evidence against pre-existing trends.

Setting: In county-level event-study DiD estimates, the authors conclude that higher Liberty Bond participation caused later expansion of investment banking. They report that there was 'no ongoing differential growth of investment banks in the counties with high Liberty Bond subscription rates up to 1918,' but 'beginning in 1919 and especially in 1920, there was a positive effect on the number of investment banks,' which then persisted through the 1920s. The outcomes are the log number of investment banks and an indicator for having any investment bank, identified from annual differences across counties with different subscription intensities under a conventional DiD/event-study design.

Main role: These results substantively support the main claim that Liberty Bonds expanded investment banking, but they are presented as timing evidence before the main IV analysis.
Settings.H685: Section 4, Eq. (1), Fig. 5 Panels A and B, PDF pp. 11–12.
Settings.G686:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 if the county had at least one investment bank in that year; 0 otherwise. The variable varies over time within county.

Method: County-panel fixed-effects regressions relate commercial bank assets to the presence of at least one investment bank, interacted with year indicators, to study whether competition between the two sectors changed over time. The model includes county fixed effects, year-varying Fed-district interactions, time-varying county controls, and county-clustered standard errors. This is not DiD around a policy treatment but a FE/event-study association the authors interpret causally as changing competitive effects.

Identification: The regression uses within-county variation over time in whether investment banks are present and how that association changes by year, after absorbing county fixed effects and observed county shocks. The intended causal interpretation is that the competitive effect of investment-bank presence on commercial banks became more negative after the Liberty Bond drives. The paper does not claim this fully resolves endogeneity, since investment banks may enter where banking prospects differ for other reasons.

Setting: As mechanism evidence, the authors estimate county fixed-effects event-study regressions showing that the relationship between investment-bank presence and commercial bank assets became negative after the Liberty Bond drives. They report that 'A county that had an investment bank would have had 10.4% more commercial bank assets in 1916, but 7.0% and 7.7% less commercial banks assets in 1920 and 1925, respectively.' This supports the claim that Liberty Bonds intensified competition between securities markets and commercial banks.

Main role: This is supporting evidence for the mechanism of stronger competition between investment banks and commercial banks, not the core Liberty Bond treatment effect.
Settings.H686: Section 4, Eq. (2), Fig. 6 Panel A, PDF p. 11.
Settings.G687:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 for counties that gained at least one investment bank between 1916 and 1920, and 0 otherwise; interacted with year indicators to trace effects over time.

Method: County-panel event-study DiD regressions compare counties that gained at least one investment bank during 1916–1920 with other counties, interacting this indicator with year fixed effects. The model includes county fixed effects, Fed-district-by-year fixed effects, time-varying county controls, and county-clustered standard errors. The treatment is the county-level adoption/entry indicator for investment banks during the Liberty Bond period.

Identification: Identification compares the evolution of commercial bank assets in counties that gained an investment bank during or just after the Liberty Bond drives with those that did not, before and after 1916–1920. County fixed effects absorb permanent differences and the event-study coefficients are used to assess pre-trends. The assumption is that absent this entry, treated and untreated counties would have had similar trends in commercial bank assets conditional on included controls.

Setting: In a DiD/event-study focused on counties that gained an investment bank during 1916–1920, the authors argue that such entry reduced commercial bank assets, consistent with stronger post-drive competition. They report that a county that gained at least one investment bank had an 'insignificant 5.8% less commercial bank assets in 1916, but a significant 18.7% and 20.7% less commercial banks assets in 1920 and 1925 respectively, relative to 1910.' The finding is used as supporting evidence for the competition mechanism linking Liberty Bonds to commercial-bank contraction.

Main role: This is additional mechanism evidence about competition and entry timing, not the main treatment-effect design.
Settings.H687: Section 4, Eq. (3), Fig. 6 Panel B, PDF pp. 11–13.
Settings.G688:
Treatment: County Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate (subscribers divided by 1920 county population, in percentage points), interacted with post-1918 in the panel. This is the endogenous continuous treatment intensity; actual participation rather than the allotment-system instrument.

Method: Main 2SLS county-panel IV specification. The endogenous regressor is the county Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate interacted with a post-1918 indicator. The instrument is an indicator for use of the allotment system in the Fourth Liberty Bond drive, also interacted with post-1918. The panel includes county and year fixed effects, time-varying county controls, and state-clustered standard errors. Because allotment adoption is strongly correlated with Federal Reserve districts, district-by-year fixed effects are omitted here. Weak-instrument diagnostics reported include Kleibergen-Paap and Montiel Olea–Pflueger effective F-statistics, plus weak-IV robust confidence sets.

Identification: The key endogeneity concern is that Liberty Bond demand may correlate with unobserved county characteristics, such as financial sophistication, income, or risk preferences, that also affect later banking development. The instrument exploits supply-side variation from whether state/Federal Reserve District Liberty Loan committees imposed the allotment system, which made subscription the default for property owners and centralized collection. The authors argue adoption was made at the state or district level rather than in response to local financial conditions. Exclusion requires that allotment-system adoption affect later county financial outcomes only through raising Liberty Bond subscriptions, conditional on county fixed effects and time-varying controls. Independence is supported with state-level balance tests and no evidence of pre-trends in outcomes.

Setting: In the paper’s main 2SLS county-panel design, higher Liberty Bond subscription rates are instrumented with use of the allotment system. The first stage is strong: 'Allotment System for 4th × Post-1918' is 8.143 percentage points for the commercial-bank regressions and 8.983 for the investment-bank regressions. The IV estimates imply that Liberty Bond participation reduced commercial banking and expanded investment banking after 1918: coefficients are -0.021 on log commercial bank assets, -0.025 on log commercial bank deposits, 0.005 on log number of investment banks, and 0.003 on investment-bank presence. The text summarizes the magnitudes as: 'A one standard deviation increase in Liberty Bond subscription rates (10.2%) led to a decrease in log commercial bank assets of 0.21, an increase in the log number of investment banks of 0.05, and an increase in the rate at which investment banks were present in a county of about 3% in the post-1918 period.' This is central evidence that Liberty Bonds transformed local finance.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, Section 5 heading ('Main results'), and conclusion all emphasize the IV evidence using the allotment-system instrument as the paper’s principal causal design for county financial outcomes.
Settings.H688: Section 5, Eqs. (4A) and (4B), Table 5 cols. (1)–(8), PDF pp. 16–18.
Settings.G689:
Treatment: Increase in county Liberty Bond subscription rate from the third to the fourth bond issue, in percentage points, interacted with post-1918. The specification also includes the county third-bond subscription rate separately. The focal endogenous treatment is continuous.

Method: Alternative 2SLS county-panel IV specification decomposes Fourth Liberty Bond subscriptions into the Third Liberty Bond subscription rate and the increase from the third to the fourth issue. The endogenous regressor of interest is the change in subscription rate from the third to the fourth, interacted with post-1918; the instrument is an indicator for switching to the allotment system for the fourth drive, interacted with post-1918. The regressions include county and year fixed effects, time-varying county controls, and state-clustered standard errors. The first stage also includes the third-bond subscription rate. Weak-IV robust confidence sets are reported.

Identification: The strategy isolates the component of Fourth Bond participation associated with increased marketing effort, beyond baseline take-up reflected in Third Bond subscriptions. Conditional on Third Bond subscriptions, the increase from Third to Fourth is instrumented by switching to the allotment system for the Fourth drive. The exclusion restriction is that switching to the allotment system affected later county financial outcomes only through the incremental rise in Liberty Bond participation, not through other channels. This design also addresses concerns that overall subscription levels proxy for baseline county traits. A limitation acknowledged by the authors is that only Idaho among switching states has the necessary county-level data, so identification relies heavily on comparisons involving Idaho.

Setting: Using an alternative IV design that instruments the increase in county subscription rates from the Third to the Fourth Liberty Bond drive with a switch to the allotment system, the authors again find that greater Liberty Bond participation contracted commercial banking and expanded investment banking. Table 6 reports coefficients of -0.049 on log commercial bank assets, -0.050 on log commercial bank deposits, 0.010 on log number of investment banks, and 0.006 on the probability an investment bank is present, all for 'Liberty Bond Diff × Post-1918' in the IV columns. The text summarizes that 'a one standard deviation increase in the change in subscription rates from the third bond issue to the fourth (6.54%) led to a decrease in log commercial bank assets of 0.32, an increase in the log number investment banks of 0.07, and an increase in the likelihood that an investment bank was present in the county of about 4%.' This robustness analysis reinforces the paper’s core causal claim.

Main role: The paper presents this as an important alternative IV specification to address weak-instrument concerns and sharpen identification of marketing-driven variation in subscriptions. It materially supports the central conclusion.
Settings.H689: Section 5, Eqs. (5A) and (5B), Table 6 cols. (1)–(8), PDF pp. 18–19.
Settings.G690:
Treatment: State-level Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate, measured in percentage points; in the alternative OLS specification, the state Third Bond subscription rate and the increase from Third to Fourth are included separately. Continuous treatment intensity.

Method: Cross-sectional linear probability models at the individual respondent level relate ownership of stocks or bonds in 1937–1938 Gallup surveys to state-level Liberty Bond subscription rates. The models include poll fixed effects, survey weights, demographic controls (age, age squared, gender, race), occupation controls, and location controls (farm/small town). Standard errors are clustered by state. The paper interprets the coefficients causally but treats IV variants as stronger evidence.

Identification: The design exploits cross-state variation in Liberty Bond subscription rates and conditions on a rich set of respondent observables and poll fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is omitted persistent state characteristics correlated with both Liberty Bond take-up and later financial asset ownership. Without an instrument, causal interpretation relies on selection-on-observables and the claim that observed respondent and location controls capture important confounders.

Setting: In weighted linear probability regressions using pooled Gallup surveys from 1937–1938, the authors find that residents of states with higher Liberty Bond subscription rates were more likely to report owning stocks or bonds. Table 7 shows an OLS coefficient of 0.004 on the state Fourth Bond subscription rate, and in the decomposition specification coefficients of 0.004 on the Third Bond subscription rate and 0.004 on the increase from Third to Fourth. The paper uses these estimates as supportive evidence of a long-run effect of Liberty Bond exposure on household financial participation.

Main role: These OLS cross-sectional results support the long-run ownership channel, but the authors rely more on IV estimates for causal interpretation because cross-state persistent differences may confound OLS.
Settings.H690: Section 6, Eqs. (6A) and (6B), Table 7 cols. (1) and (3), Fig. 9, PDF pp. 20–21.
Settings.G691:
Treatment: Primary IV treatment: state Fourth Liberty Bond subscription rate in percentage points. Alternative IV treatment: increase in state subscription rate from the Third to the Fourth Liberty Bond issue, with Third Bond rate included as a control. Continuous treatment intensity at the state level.

Method: State-level individual-survey 2SLS/linear probability models estimate the effect of state Liberty Bond participation on whether respondents owned stocks or bonds in 1937–1938. In one IV specification, the endogenous regressor is the state Fourth Bond subscription rate and the instrument is an indicator for use of the allotment system. In the alternative IV specification, the endogenous regressor is the increase in state subscription rate from the Third to the Fourth Bond and the instrument is an indicator for switching to the allotment system in the Fourth drive, while controlling for the Third Bond rate. Regressions include poll fixed effects, respondent demographics, occupation and location controls, survey weights, and state-clustered standard errors. Weak-IV robust confidence sets are reported; the first IV has a weak-IV robust interval excluding zero, while the alternative specification’s interval includes zero.

Identification: The central concern is that cross-state Liberty Bond subscription rates may proxy for persistent state differences in wealth, financial culture, or sophistication. The IV strategy uses state adoption of the allotment system, or switching to that system, as an exogenous supply-side determinant of subscriptions. The exclusion restriction is that the allotment system affected 1930s household stock/bond ownership only through raising earlier Liberty Bond participation. The authors note weak-instrument concerns are more serious here than in county outcomes; effective F-statistics are below 10, so weak-IV robust intervals are emphasized. The first IV specification remains informative because its weak-IV robust confidence set excludes zero, whereas the alternative IV does not.

Setting: In weighted IV linear probability models using Gallup surveys from the late 1930s, the authors find that higher state Liberty Bond participation increased later stock/bond ownership. Table 7 reports an IV coefficient of 0.004 on the state Fourth Bond subscription rate when instrumented by allotment-system use, with weak-IV robust confidence set [.002, 0.007]. In the alternative decomposition IV, the coefficient on the increase from the Third to Fourth Bond is 0.003 with weak-IV robust confidence set [-0.003, 0.009], so that version is less conclusive. The text interprets the main IV estimate as implying that 'a one standard deviation increase in state Liberty Bond subscription rate (8.3%) led to a 3.3% increase in the rate at which households owned stocks.' This is key evidence that Liberty Bonds had long-lasting effects on household financial participation.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly highlight the finding that individuals in states with higher Liberty Bond subscriptions were more likely to own stocks or bonds in the late 1930s. The IV version is the paper’s causal evidence for this long-run household outcome.
Settings.H691: Section 6, Eqs. (6A) and (6B), Table 7 cols. (2) and (4), Fig. 9, PDF pp. 20–21.
Settings.G692:
Treatment: Indicator for whether the supplier’s lead credit officer is a minority, defined as either female or Black based on name-based gender/race assignment. The estimated treatment effect is the post-March-2020 differential for minority-led suppliers relative to non-minority-led suppliers.

Method: Baseline difference-in-differences regressions estimate whether overdue payments rose more after the onset of COVID-19 (After = 1 from March 2020 through May 2020) for suppliers whose lead credit officer is classified as a minority (female or Black) relative to non-minority suppliers. The paper implements linear OLS at the supplier-customer-month transaction level. Across columns, the design adds seller fixed effects and month fixed effects, then interacts After with supplier industry and size quartiles, then adds seller×buyer fixed effects, and finally buyer×month fixed effects following Khwaja and Mian (2008) to absorb time-varying buyer shocks. The authors interpret the After×Minority coefficient causally as the differential change in late payment behavior during COVID. Identification relies on parallel pre-trends and on controls/FE absorbing supplier, buyer, and relationship heterogeneity, though the paper notes remaining concerns about omitted time-varying supplier or relationship-level factors.

Identification: The identifying variation is the differential change in overdue payment outcomes from pre-COVID to post-COVID for minority-led versus non-minority-led suppliers. The endogeneity concern is that minority suppliers may differ systematically in size, industry, customers, or bilateral relationships, and that these differences may have changed with COVID. The paper addresses this by interacting After with industry and size controls and by absorbing seller, month, seller×buyer, and buyer×month fixed effects, so the tightest specification compares how a given buyer changes payment timing to minority versus non-minority suppliers in the same month. The key assumptions are parallel trends absent COVID and that remaining time-varying omitted factors at the supplier or relationship level do not fully explain the differential post-COVID shift.

Setting: Using conventional DiD around the onset of COVID-19, the paper estimates that suppliers with minority lead credit officers experienced larger increases in customer payment delays than suppliers with non-minority officers. In Table 3 Panel A, with the fullest specification including seller×buyer and buyer×month fixed effects, the After×Minority coefficient is 0.205 on log(1+past due dollars), which the authors interpret as a 21% larger increase in overdue accounts. In Table 3 Panel B, the corresponding coefficient is 0.091 on % Past 30 Days, implying a 9% larger increase in the share of recent purchases becoming overdue; across specifications the effect ranges from 9% to 15%. These estimates are central to the paper’s claim that discrimination affects customers’ willingness to pay suppliers during financial stress.

Main role: This is the paper’s core empirical design supporting the abstract’s central claim that customers delay payments more to suppliers with female or Black lead credit officers during COVID.
Settings.H692: Section 5.2 'Multiple regression results'; Eq. (1); Table 3 Panels A and B, cols. (1)-(5), PDF pp. 6-8.
Settings.G693:
Treatment: Two binary treatment indicators are estimated separately: whether the supplier’s lead credit manager is female, and whether the lead credit manager is Black, both based on name classification. The causal contrasts are the post-COVID differential changes for female-led and Black-led suppliers relative to omitted non-female/non-Black lead-credit-officer suppliers.

Method: A refinement of the baseline DiD splits the minority treatment into separate indicators for Female and Black lead credit officers. The paper estimates linear OLS difference-in-differences at the supplier-customer-month transaction level over the same pre/post-COVID design. Specifications sequentially include seller and month fixed effects, After×industry and After×size controls, seller×buyer fixed effects, and buyer×month fixed effects. The implemented estimator remains conventional DiD because identification comes from post-COVID differential changes for treated groups relative to controls, not from a separate FE-only design.

Identification: Identification is the same DiD logic as in the baseline design, but now separately estimates differential post-COVID changes for female-led and Black-led suppliers. The core concern is confounding by correlated supplier, buyer, or relationship characteristics that differ by gender or race and evolve during COVID. The specifications attempt to mitigate this using the same rich fixed effects and post interacted controls as the baseline. The assumptions remain parallel counterfactual trends and no remaining unobserved time-varying relationship factors that differentially affect female-led or Black-led suppliers after COVID.

Setting: The paper separately estimates post-COVID payment-delay effects for female and Black lead credit officers. In Table 4 Panel A column 5, After×Female equals 0.189 and After×Black equals 0.435 on log(1+past due dollars), indicating both groups saw larger increases in overdue accounts, with the Black-officer effect more than twice the female effect in magnitude. In Table 4 Panel B column 5, After×Female equals 0.090 on % Past 30 Days, while After×Black equals 0.016 and is statistically insignificant, which the authors attribute partly to low power in the continuing-transactions subsample for Black officers. These estimates strengthen the paper’s interpretation that both gender and race contribute to discriminatory payment behavior.

Main role: These split-by-demographic results directly support a central conclusion that both gender and race discrimination matter, with larger effects for Black credit officers in the full sample.
Settings.H693: Section 5.2.1 'Baseline results split by female and black credit officers'; Table 4 Panels A and B, cols. (1)-(5), PDF pp. 8-9.
Settings.G694:
Treatment: Continuous triple-difference style exposure: the post-COVID period interacted with supplier minority status (female or Black lead credit officer) and the customer’s continuous county/city/state-level general bias index (BiasPCA). This is not a simple binary treatment; the focal estimand is how a one-unit or one-standard-deviation increase in customer bias changes post-COVID payment delays to minority-led suppliers within a relationship.

Method: The within-relationship estimator is a linear regression with three separately absorbed fixed-effect dimensions: supplier×buyer relationship fixed effects, supplier×month fixed effects, and buyer×month fixed effects. The treatment variable is the triple interaction After×Minority×BiasPCA, where customer bias is measured by a principal component of five location-based proxies (historical lynchings, Sundown Town status, universalist attitudes, implicit gender-career bias, and relative female earnings). This HDFE specification is explicitly motivated as identifying within-relationship changes in payment behavior during COVID while absorbing all time-varying supplier shocks and time-varying buyer shocks. Some columns also add After interacted with quartiles of pre-COVID relationship sales volume to proxy for bilateral importance. The authors note the design is still vulnerable to omitted time-varying relationship-level factors.

Identification: Identification comes from within a given supplier-customer pair, comparing how payment behavior changes after COVID as a function of customer bias when the supplier has a minority lead credit officer, netting out relationship fixed effects and all supplier-month and buyer-month shocks. This addresses supplier-level concerns such as time-varying collection capacity and buyer-level concerns such as liquidity or demand shocks. The remaining threat, acknowledged by the authors, is omitted time-varying bilateral relationship importance or other pair-specific shocks correlated with biased customers and minority suppliers. The paper partially addresses this by interacting pre-COVID relationship sales-volume quartiles with After.

Setting: Using a high-dimensional fixed-effects within-relationship design, the paper finds that the largest increases in payment delays during COVID occur when more biased customers are matched to suppliers with minority lead credit officers. In Table 5 Panel A column 1, the After×Minority×BiasPCA coefficient is 0.100 on log(1+past due dollars); the authors interpret this as a one-standard-deviation increase in customer bias increasing delayed payments to minority suppliers by 10%. In column 3, the coefficient is 0.036 on % Past 30 Days, interpreted as a 3.6% increase for relationships that continue to transact. These estimates remain similar when controlling for relationship importance, and they are central to the paper’s claim that discriminatory preferences, not only broad economic shocks, shape payment behavior in the supply chain.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion emphasize the within-relationship evidence as especially important because it more convincingly isolates discriminatory behavior from economic confounds.
Settings.H694: Section 6 'Within-relationship estimation'; Eq. (2); Table 5 Panel A, cols. (1)-(4), PDF pp. 10-12.
Settings.G695:
Treatment: Continuous interaction treatment: post-COVID exposure interacted with either Female or Black lead-credit-officer indicators and the customer’s continuous gender-bias principal component. The treatment varies continuously with bias intensity and discretely by supplier officer demographic group.

Method: This within-relationship HDFE specification estimates whether customers with stronger gender-bias proxies differentially delay payments after COVID to suppliers with female versus Black lead credit officers. The linear regression includes supplier×buyer, supplier×month, and buyer×month fixed effects, and some columns additionally interact After with quartiles of relationship importance. The focal coefficients are After×Female×GenderBiasPCA and After×Black×GenderBiasPCA, where GenderBiasPCA is the first principal component of county-level universalist attitudes, gender-career IAT scores, and state-level relative female earnings.

Identification: The estimator uses within-relationship post-COVID variation, net of supplier-month and buyer-month shocks, to test whether gender-biased customers differentially worsen payment delays to female-led suppliers. The endogeneity concern is that bias proxies may correlate with unobserved relationship-level shocks or importance. Relationship fixed effects absorb time-invariant matching, and importance quartile interactions with After are added in some columns, but the authors still caution that omitted time-varying pair-specific factors may remain.

Setting: Table 5 Panel B shows that gender-biased customers increase payment delays primarily to suppliers with female lead credit officers, not to those with Black lead credit officers. In column 1, After×Female×GenderBiasPCA equals 0.079 on log(1+past due dollars), and in column 3 it equals 0.020 on % Past 30 Days; both remain similar when relationship importance controls are added. By contrast, the corresponding After×Black×GenderBiasPCA coefficients are small and statistically insignificant. This pattern supports the mechanism that gender-linked discriminatory preferences contribute to delayed payments in the supply chain.

Main role: These results support the paper’s central mechanism claim that the strongest late-payment effects align with the type of customer bias—here, gender bias toward female suppliers.
Settings.H695: Section 6.3 'Within-relationship tests'; Table 5 Panel B, cols. (1)-(4), PDF pp. 11-12.
Settings.G696:
Treatment: Continuous interaction treatment: post-COVID exposure interacted with either Black or Female lead-credit-officer indicators and the customer’s continuous race-bias principal component. The estimand captures how stronger local race bias amplifies post-COVID payment delays toward demographic groups, especially Black officers.

Method: A parallel within-relationship HDFE specification tests whether race-biased customers differentially delay payments after COVID to suppliers with Black versus female lead credit officers. The regression includes supplier×buyer, supplier×month, and buyer×month fixed effects, with optional controls for After interacted with relationship-importance quartiles. The focal coefficients are After×Black×RaceBiasPCA and After×Female×RaceBiasPCA, where RaceBiasPCA is the first principal component of county/city-level lynchings, Sundown Town status, and universalist attitudes.

Identification: Identification comes from within-relationship post-COVID changes interacted with customer race-bias intensity and supplier demographic status, while absorbing all buyer-month, supplier-month, and relationship fixed effects. This is meant to net out general buyer distress, supplier distress, and persistent matching differences. The remaining concern is unobserved relationship-specific shocks during COVID correlated with race bias and officer race; the authors partially address this with importance controls and caution that identification is not bullet-proof.

Setting: Table 5 Panel C indicates that race-biased customers increase delayed payments most strongly to suppliers with Black lead credit officers.
