The After×Black×RaceBiasPCA coefficient is 0.088 in columns 1-2 for log(1+past due dollars) and 0.014 in columns 3-4 for % Past 30 Days, while the corresponding coefficients for female officers are smaller, especially in the percentage-past-due specifications. The paper interprets this as evidence that race-linked bias, above and beyond general COVID shocks, contributed to worse collection outcomes for Black-led suppliers.

Main role: These results materially support the paper’s central claim that race-based discriminatory preferences are especially important for Black lead credit officers.
Settings.H696: Section 6.3 'Within-relationship tests'; Table 5 Panel C, cols. (1)-(4), PDF pp. 11-12.
Settings.G697:
Treatment: Customer default status in month t for a given supplier-customer pair: DefaultingCustomer equals one if any portion of the previous month’s receivable due to supplier s is late, while TimelyCustomer denotes full payment. The causal contrast is defaulting versus timely payment status as a trigger for later relationship termination, reported separately by supplier minority status and period.

Method: The punishment analysis compares the probability that a supplier-customer relationship terminates within six months after a customer defaults versus remains timely, separately for the pre-COVID and COVID periods and for minority versus non-minority suppliers. The table reports mean comparisons rather than a DiD or FE regression. The authors interpret these contrasts causally/substantively as evidence on whether defaulting customers are punished by being 'fired' by suppliers, and how this changed during COVID. Because the implemented estimator is a level contrast in means without a sharper quasi-experimental design, it is best classified as OLS/regression adjustment style descriptive causal comparison.

Identification: The analysis uses timing of default and subsequent relationship cessation to infer punishment. The concern is that relationship terminations are not randomly caused by default and may reflect many other forces, including shifts in supply and demand, relationship quality, or market conditions. The paper therefore interprets the comparison cautiously, emphasizing it as suggestive evidence that defaulting customers were more likely to be dropped before COVID but not during COVID. The implicit assumption is that timely and defaulting relationships are otherwise comparable enough for the difference in termination rates to reflect punishment intensity.

Setting: To examine whether suppliers could punish late-paying customers, the paper compares six-month relationship termination rates for defaulting versus timely customers before and during COVID. In the pre-COVID period, defaulting customers are substantially more likely to be terminated: for non-minority suppliers, the firing probability is 0.092 for defaulters versus 0.038 for timely customers (difference -0.054), and for minority suppliers it is 0.119 versus 0.038 (difference -0.081). During COVID, these differences disappear: 0.293 versus 0.290 for non-minority suppliers and 0.280 versus 0.282 for minority suppliers. The authors use this as supporting evidence that market-based punishment weakened during COVID, allowing discriminatory late-payment behavior to rise.

Main role: This section is used to bolster the proposed mechanism about weakened market-based punishment during COVID rather than to establish the paper’s main discrimination result.
Settings.G698:
Treatment: Coworker peer participation intensity: the mean ESPP participation rate among other employees in the same firm-CBSA-month (firm location-window), measured from a randomly excluded half-sample. It is a continuous share/rate from 0 to 1; the paper often interprets a 10 percentage point increase in this local participation rate.

Method: Baseline peer-effects linear probability model for ESPP participation at the employee-by-firm-by-biannual-window level. The dependent variable is an indicator for whether employee i participates in the firm's ESPP in window t. The key regressor is the average participation rate among the employee's coworkers in the same firm and CBSA in that month, measured in an excluded random half-sample to avoid mechanical reflection bias. The regression includes firm-month fixed effects to absorb firm-wide shocks such as company-stock fundamentals and CBSA-month fixed effects to absorb local economic shocks, plus employee controls for age bins, gender, income bins, and holdings of company options/restricted stock. Standard errors are clustered at the firm-month level.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm, across-location differences in coworker participation after absorbing firm-month shocks common to all employees in the same firm and CBSA-month shocks common to all employees in the same metro area. The design addresses the reflection problem by measuring peer averages in an excluded random half-sample. The remaining concern is office-level unobservables or sorting across offices within firms; the paper treats this as a threat and provides supplementary IV and robustness analyses.

Setting: Using a linear probability model with firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects, the authors estimate that higher coworker participation in a firm's ESPP raises an employee's own participation probability. In Table IV column (1), the coefficient on mean local participation is 0.1420 (SE 0.009), implying that a 10 percentage point increase in participation among local coworkers is associated with about a 1.5 percentage point increase in an employee's probability of participating. This is the paper's main baseline causal setting for peer effects on investment-plan participation.

Main role: This is the paper's core baseline evidence for the central claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that coworkers' ESPP choices causally influence employees' own participation decisions.
Settings.H698: Section II.A 'Baseline Peer Effects,' equation (1), Table IV column (1), PDF pp. 146-148.
Settings.G699:
Treatment: Endogenous treatment is coworker peer participation intensity: the mean ESPP participation rate in the employee's firm-CBSA-month, instrumented by the local demographic composition (age-bin, gender, and income-bin shares) of that firm location-month. Continuous share/rate from 0 to 1.

Method: 2SLS version of the employee participation peer-effects model. The endogenous regressor is the firm-location-month average ESPP participation rate among peers. Instruments are firm-location-month averages of employee demographics: seven age-bin shares, female share, and four income-bin shares. The second stage includes the same employee-level demographic and holdings controls as the baseline model, plus firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects. Peer averages are measured in the excluded random half-sample; standard errors are clustered at the firm-month level.

Identification: The authors argue that cross-office differences in demographic composition predict average local ESPP participation but, conditional on an employee's own demographics, firm-month FE, and CBSA-month FE, should affect that employee's participation only through peers' choices. This is intended to purge office-level participation of common shocks and sorting-related confounds. The key assumption is the exclusion restriction: office demographic composition does not directly affect individual participation after controlling for own traits.

Setting: Using demographic composition of offices as instruments for local coworker participation, the authors find an even larger peer effect on ESPP participation. In Table IV column (3), the second-stage coefficient on mean participate is 0.2706 (SE 0.094), so a 10 percentage point increase in local participation is associated with about a 2.7 percentage point increase in an employee's participation probability. The first stage is strong (Cragg-Donald F-statistic 124.698), and the result is used to reinforce the baseline causal interpretation that coworkers influence participation decisions.

Main role: The IV estimates are a principal supplementary identification strategy repeatedly emphasized in the text and conclusion to support a causal interpretation of peer effects on participation.
Settings.H699: Section II.A 'Baseline Peer Effects,' Table IV columns (2)-(3), PDF pp. 148-150.
Settings.G700:
Treatment: Coworker peer participation intensity in the employee's firm-CBSA-month, plus its interaction with an indicator for whether the focal employee is female. The focal causal contrast is the marginal effect of local participation on own participation and how that slope differs for women versus men.

Method: Interaction LPM for heterogeneous peer effects in ESPP participation by employee gender. The baseline peer participation rate in the firm-CBSA-month is interacted with an indicator for female employees. Column (1) uses firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects; column (2) instead uses firm-CBSA-month fixed effects so identification comes from within-office differences in responsiveness to the same peer environment. Standard employee controls from earlier participation regressions are included; peer averages use the excluded random half-sample.

Identification: The design compares the responsiveness of otherwise similar employees to the same local peer participation environment, with fixed effects absorbing either firm-month and CBSA-month shocks or, more stringently, firm-CBSA-month shocks. The within-office specification is used by the paper to mitigate concerns that worker sorting across offices drives the heterogeneity estimates.

Setting: The authors find that female employees are less responsive than male employees to coworker participation when deciding whether to enroll in the ESPP. In Table V column (1), the baseline peer-effect coefficient is 0.1515 and the Female × Mean Participate interaction is -0.0382, implying a 10 percentage point increase in local participation raises male participation by about 1.5 percentage points but female participation by about 1.1 percentage points. The within-office specification in column (2) yields a similar interaction (-0.0440), which the authors use to argue the heterogeneity result is not driven by office sorting.

Main role: These are substantive heterogeneity results supporting the broader interpretation of who is most influenced by peers, but they are secondary to the central existence-of-peer-effects finding.
Settings.H700: Section II.B 'Cross-Sectional Differences by Worker Demographics,' Table V columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 153-154.
Settings.G701:
Treatment: Coworker peer participation intensity in the employee's firm-CBSA-month, interacted with employee age-bin indicators. The treatment is continuous local participation, and the estimand is how the participation peer effect varies by employee age.

Method: Interaction LPM for heterogeneous peer effects in ESPP participation by employee age groups. The firm-location-month mean participation rate is interacted with age-bin indicators. Column (3) uses firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects; column (4) replaces them with firm-CBSA-month fixed effects to identify within-office variation in responsiveness by age. Standard employee controls are included, and peer averages come from the excluded random half-sample.

Identification: Identification comes from differential slopes of own participation on local peer participation across age groups, while absorbing common firm and metro shocks or, in the stricter specification, office-month shocks. The within-office specification is meant to reduce concerns about endogenous sorting across offices.

Setting: Peer effects on ESPP participation are strongest for younger workers and decline with age. In Table V column (3), the baseline effect of local participation is 0.1861 for workers under 30, while interactions for age 40-45, 45-50, 50-55, 55-60, and 60+ are -0.0466, -0.0696, -0.0797, -0.1305, and -0.1450, respectively; column (4) with firm-CBSA-month fixed effects gives similar estimates. The authors interpret this pattern as consistent with younger or less informed employees learning more from peers.

Main role: These age heterogeneity estimates are substantive supporting analyses showing peer influence is stronger for younger workers, consistent with the paper's learning interpretation.
Settings.H701: Section II.B 'Cross-Sectional Differences by Worker Demographics,' Table V columns (3)-(4), PDF pp. 153-154.
Settings.G702:
Treatment: Coworker peer participation intensity in the firm-CBSA-month, interacted with indicators for high lagged ESPP gains from participating in the previous period. Treatment remains continuous local participation; the heterogeneity dimension is whether recent realized/estimated gains made peer experiences more salient.

Method: Interaction LPM examining whether peer effects on ESPP participation vary with the salience of coworkers' prior ESPP gains. The key regressor is the local mean participation rate interacted with indicators for whether lagged estimated ESPP gains from participating were above the median (Q2) or above the third quartile (Q3). Firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects and standard controls are included. The analysis is run in the full analysis sample and separately among employees who had never previously participated in the ESPP.

Identification: The authors test a cross-sectional implication of peer influence: if peers communicate or employees pay more attention when prior ESPP gains were high, the slope of own participation on local peer participation should be larger following high gains. Identification relies on within-firm, within-CBSA comparisons with firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects; the threat is omitted heterogeneity correlated with high-gain periods.

Setting: The effect of coworker participation on own ESPP participation is stronger when previous-period ESPP gains were high. In Table VI, column (1), the baseline coefficient on Mean Participate is 0.114 and the interaction with LagESPPgains > Q2 is 0.106; in column (2), the interaction with gains above Q3 is 0.090. Among never-before participants, the interactions are even larger in columns (4) and (5): 0.151 and 0.145. The authors interpret this as evidence that salient successful peer experiences amplify peer influence, consistent with learning or endogenous peer effects.

Main role: This is a robustness/mechanism analysis used to support that the estimated peer effects reflect endogenous influence and information transmission rather than contextual effects.
Settings.H702: Section II.C 'Cross-Sectional Differences by the Salience of Peer Experiences,' Table VI columns (1)-(5), PDF pp. 155-156.
Settings.G703:
Treatment: Coworker peer participation intensity in the employee's firm-CBSA-month, interacted with indicators for whether the employee's CBSA has high population density. Treatment is continuous local participation; the heterogeneous exposure is office location in more versus less densely populated metro areas.

Method: Interaction LPM examining whether peer effects on ESPP participation are stronger in denser metro areas, where employee interactions may be more frequent. The local mean participation rate is interacted with indicators for whether CBSA population density is above the median (Q2) or above the third quartile (Q3). The model includes firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects and standard employee controls.

Identification: The strategy tests a predicted moderator of peer transmission rather than a new identification design. With firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects, the authors compare whether the slope of participation on local peer participation is larger in high-density CBSAs, where social contact is presumed greater. The identifying assumption is that density primarily moderates interaction intensity rather than proxying for omitted office traits that also alter responsiveness.

Setting: Peer effects on ESPP participation are stronger in more densely populated metro areas. In Table VI column (6), the coefficient on Mean Participate is 0.127 and the interaction with Density > Q2 is 0.038; in column (7), the interaction with Density > Q3 is 0.040. The authors interpret the larger peer slope in denser areas as evidence that greater coworker contact increases the transmission of investment behavior.

Main role: This is a secondary mechanism/robustness test used to support the interpretation that more contact among coworkers strengthens peer influence.
Settings.H703: Section II.C 'Cross-Sectional Differences by the Salience of Peer Experiences,' Table VI columns (6)-(7), PDF pp. 156-157.
Settings.G704:
Treatment: Among low-information employees, the treatment is the participation rate of low-information coworkers in the same firm-CBSA-month, with heterogeneous effect depending on whether the office-month contains any high-information employees (defined by high-information occupation, good/excellent prior investment experience, or income > $200K). The local participation rate is continuous.

Method: Mechanism regressions focusing on low-information employees only. The outcome is own ESPP participation. The key regressor is the participation rate of low-information coworkers in the firm-location-month, interacted with an indicator for whether there are no high-information types present in that office-month. Separate specifications define high-information workers by occupation (HO), self-reported investment experience (HE), or top income bin (HI). The regressions include firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects, standard controls, and peer averages measured in an excluded random half-sample; robustness variants drop very small/large offices and offices in the headquarters state.

Identification: The design asks whether the responsiveness of low-information employees to low-information peers differs depending on whether at least one high-information coworker is present in the same office-month. The assumption is that office presence of informed types affects low-information employees' slope with respect to peer participation because informed peers seed the information network, rather than through other omitted office characteristics; fixed effects absorb firm-wide and metro-wide shocks, and the paper adds sample restrictions as robustness checks.

Setting: The authors find that low-information employees are much less influenced by low-information coworkers when no high-information employee is present in the office, consistent with informed coworkers seeding learning. In Table VIII column (1), the participation rate of low-information influencers has coefficient 0.1238, while its interaction with 'No High-Information Types at Firm-Location-Month' is -0.0565; columns (2) and (3) using alternative high-information definitions show interactions of -0.1145 and -0.0383. Similar patterns hold after excluding very small/large offices and headquarters-state offices (columns (4)-(9)).

Main role: These are central mechanism tests underpinning the paper's learning interpretation: peer effects are weaker when no informed coworkers are present to seed information transmission.
Settings.H704: Section II.D 'Identifying the Peer Learning Mechanism,' Table VIII columns (1)-(9), PDF pp. 158-162.
Settings.G705:
Treatment: Participation rates of high-information and low-information coworkers in the employee's firm-CBSA-month, with interactions by whether the focal employee is high-information. These are continuous subgroup-specific peer participation rates.

Method: Mechanism regressions decomposing peer participation by informed versus uninformed subgroups. The outcome is employee ESPP participation. Regressors are participation rates of high-information and low-information coworkers in the same firm-location-month, plus interactions of each subgroup participation rate with an indicator that the responder is herself high-information. High-information is alternatively defined by occupation (HO), self-reported prior investment experience (HE), or income > $200K. Peer subgroup averages are measured in an excluded random sample; the model includes firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects and standard controls.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in participation rates of high- and low-information coworkers across firm locations within the same firm-month and metro-month, with own observables controlled. The paper interprets positive effects from high-information peers on low-information responders as evidence of information transmission through workplace networks. Threats include differential within-office interaction patterns and remaining office-level confounds.

Setting: When peer participation is split by informed and uninformed subgroups, the authors find that high-information employees' choices significantly affect low-information coworkers' ESPP participation, while also documenting 'like influencing like.' In Table IX column (1), the participation rate of high-information influencers has coefficient 0.0490 for low-information responders and low-information influencers have coefficient 0.0993; column (3) similarly shows 0.0241 and 0.1588 using income-based information. The authors treat the positive effect of informed peers on uninformed employees as direct evidence for peer learning rather than pure mimicry.

Main role: These subgroup-peer regressions are a core mechanism result because they directly test whether informed employees' choices influence uninformed coworkers, which is central to the paper's learning claim.
Settings.H705: Section II.D 'Identifying the Peer Learning Mechanism,' Table IX columns (1)-(3), PDF pp. 162-164.
Settings.G706:
Treatment: Coworker peer trading intensity: the fraction/rate of ESPP participants in the employee's firm-CBSA-month who sell their acquired shares within two weeks of purchase, measured in an excluded random half-sample. Continuous share/rate from 0 to 1.

Method: Baseline peer-effects linear probability model for post-participation trading behavior. The sample is ESPP participants only. The dependent variable is an indicator equal to 1 if the employee sells ESPP shares acquired in the window within two weeks of purchase. The key regressor is the fraction of ESPP participants in the same firm-CBSA-month who sell within two weeks, measured in an excluded random half-sample. Controls mirror earlier specifications, and the model includes firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects with standard errors clustered at the firm-month level.

Identification: As in the participation baseline, identification uses within-firm, across-location differences in local peer trading after absorbing firm-month shocks and CBSA-month shocks. The excluded-half-sample construction addresses reflection bias. Remaining concerns are office-level unobservables and sorting; the paper addresses these with IV and some robustness checks, though it notes the smaller trading sample reduces power.

Setting: Among employees who participate in the ESPP, the authors find that coworkers' quick-selling behavior increases an employee's own propensity to sell shares shortly after purchase. In Table XI column (1), the coefficient on Mean Sell 2Weeks is 0.0731 (SE 0.014), implying that a 10 percentage point increase in the local quick-sale rate raises an employee's probability of selling within two weeks by roughly 0.73 percentage points. This supports the paper's broader claim that peer networks shape not just participation but also trading behavior.

Main role: The trading regressions are highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as a second major substantive result showing peer effects extend beyond participation to trading decisions.
Settings.H706: Section II.E 'Peer Effects on the Timing of Participators’ Stock Sales,' Table XI column (1), PDF pp. 165-166.
Settings.G707:
Treatment: Endogenous treatment is coworker quick-sale intensity: the fraction of ESPP participants in the employee's firm-CBSA-month who sell within two weeks of purchase, instrumented by local office demographic composition. Continuous share/rate from 0 to 1.

Method: 2SLS model for peer effects on quick ESPP share sales. The endogenous regressor is the firm-location-month fraction of participants who sell within two weeks. Instruments are the office demographic shares used earlier: age-bin shares, female share, and income-bin shares. The second stage includes employee-level demographics and holdings controls plus firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects; peer averages are measured in an excluded half-sample. Standard errors are clustered at the firm-month level.

Identification: The authors use predictable cross-office demographic variation as an instrument for local quick-selling rates, assuming office demographic composition affects an employee's own sale timing only through peers' trading decisions after controlling for own traits and fixed effects. This is intended to isolate exogenous variation in local peer selling and reduce concerns about office-level confounds. The first-stage F-statistic is reported as 53.861.

Setting: Instrumenting the local quick-sale rate with office demographics, the authors find a larger peer effect on trading timing. In Table XI column (3), the second-stage coefficient on Mean Sell 2Weeks is 0.2562 (SE 0.147), implying that a 10 percentage point increase in the local fraction of coworkers who sell within two weeks is associated with about a 2.5 percentage point increase in an employee's own likelihood of selling within two weeks. The result is used to bolster the causal interpretation that peers influence trade timing conditional on participation.

Main role: This IV specification is the key supplementary identification strategy for the paper's second central result on peer effects in trading behavior.
Settings.H707: Section II.E 'Peer Effects on the Timing of Participators’ Stock Sales,' Table XI columns (2)-(3), PDF pp. 166-167.
Settings.G708:
Treatment: Coworker quick-sale intensity in the firm-CBSA-month, plus its interaction with an indicator for whether the focal employee is female. Treatment is continuous local quick-sale rate; the estimand is how its effect on own quick sale differs by gender.

Method: Interaction LPM for heterogeneous peer effects in quick-sale behavior by employee gender. The key regressor is the local firm-CBSA-month fraction of participants who sell within two weeks, interacted with a female indicator. Column (1) includes firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects; column (2) uses firm-CBSA-month fixed effects to compare within-office differences in responsiveness. Standard controls are included.

Identification: Identification comes from differences by gender in the slope of own quick-sale behavior on local peer quick-sale behavior, with either firm-month plus CBSA-month fixed effects or office-month fixed effects. The latter helps address concerns that gender-specific office sorting drives the result.

Setting: Women are less responsive than men to coworkers' quick-selling behavior. In Table XII column (1), the baseline coefficient on Mean Sell 2Weeks is 0.0979 and the Female × Mean Sell 2Weeks interaction is -0.1108; column (2) with firm-CBSA-month fixed effects gives -0.1171. The authors interpret this as evidence that peer effects in trading timing, like participation, are substantially weaker for women.

Main role: These are secondary heterogeneity results for the trading outcome, reinforcing the broader narrative that men and younger workers are more influenced by peers.
Settings.H708: Section II.E 'Peer Effects on the Timing of Participators’ Stock Sales,' Table XII columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 167-168.
Settings.G709:
Treatment: Coworker quick-sale intensity in the employee's firm-CBSA-month, interacted with employee age-group indicators (30-50 and 50+). Treatment is continuous local quick-sale rate; the estimand is how responsiveness differs by age.

Method: Interaction LPM for heterogeneous peer effects in quick-sale behavior by age category. The local quick-sale rate is interacted with age-group indicators for ages 30-50 and over 50 (younger than 30 omitted). Column (3) uses firm-month and CBSA-month fixed effects; column (4) uses firm-CBSA-month fixed effects. Standard controls are included.

Identification: The design compares age groups' slopes of own quick-sale behavior on local peer quick-sale behavior, holding constant firm-wide and metro-wide shocks or, in the stricter version, office-month shocks. The paper uses the similarity across fixed-effect specifications to argue against office sorting explanations.

Setting: Peer effects on selling within two weeks decline with age. In Table XII column (3), the baseline effect of Mean Sell 2Weeks is 0.1436 for workers under 30, while interactions are -0.0575 for ages 30-50 and -0.2082 for ages over 50; column (4) gives similar or larger attenuations (-0.0720 and -0.2435). The authors interpret this as consistent with younger workers being more susceptible to peer influence in trading decisions.

Main role: These are supporting heterogeneity analyses for the trading outcome, used to show peer influence declines with age similarly to the participation setting.
Settings.H709: Section II.E 'Peer Effects on the Timing of Participators’ Stock Sales,' Table XII columns (3)-(4), PDF pp. 167-168.
Settings.G710:
Treatment: Household-level dummy for expecting higher inflation over the next 12 months compared with the previous 12 months; equals 1 when the respondent answers that prices 'will increase more,' 0 otherwise. This is a binary expectation measure, not an exogenous policy assignment.

Method: The authors estimate multinomial logit models for repeated cross-sections of households, interpreting the marginal effect of higher inflation expectations on the probability that respondents say it is a good time to buy durable goods. The outcome has three unordered categories (good time / neither / bad time), so despite rich controls this is a nonlinear specification and is classified as Other. They report average marginal effects from maximum-likelihood multinomial logit, clustering standard errors at the quarter level. Specifications progressively add demographics, inflation perceptions, and other household expectations; some columns split the sample by period (VAT period, forward-guidance period, no-policy periods) and by country. The intended interpretation is that higher household inflation expectations causally increase readiness to spend on durables, though the paper acknowledges repeated-cross-section limitations and residual endogeneity.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional and time-series variation in individual inflation expectations within repeated cross-sections, controlling for perceived past inflation, demographics, and expectations about personal and macroeconomic conditions. The endogeneity concern is that unobserved traits or shocks may jointly affect inflation expectations and spending propensity. The authors argue the relationship is robust to extensive controls and broadly similar across countries and demographics, but they do not claim a clean quasi-experiment for this setting; thus the causal interpretation remains associational-with-controls.

Setting: Using multinomial logit regressions on household survey microdata, the authors interpret higher inflation expectations as increasing households’ willingness to purchase durables. For German households, the average marginal effect of expecting higher inflation is 5.82 percentage points in the baseline specification and 8.76 percentage points with controls; during the VAT period the marginal effect is 19.09 percentage points, versus 5.08 percentage points in the forward-guidance period and 5.40 percentage points in periods without those announcements. They treat this as empirical support for the mechanism that inflation expectations stimulate durable spending, though the design relies on regression adjustment rather than exogenous variation.

Main role: The paper's central mechanism is that higher inflation expectations raise household consumption propensity. The abstract states the authors 'first show theoretically and empirically that higher inflation expectations increase households’ consumption' before evaluating policies.
Settings.H710: Section 3.1–3.2, Equation (7), Table 2 columns (1)–(8), PDF pages 1611–1612 (article pp. 1611–1612).
Settings.G711:
Treatment: Household-level dummy equal to 1 if the respondent expects inflation to increase over the next 12 months relative to the previous 12 months, and 0 otherwise.

Method: The authors estimate multinomial logit models for households’ readiness to save, again using a nonlinear response model and reporting average marginal effects. The key regressor is the same binary measure for expecting higher inflation, with demographics and individual expectations included as controls and standard errors clustered at the quarter level. They interpret the coefficient causally as evidence that higher inflation expectations reduce saving propensity, consistent with the Euler-equation mechanism behind their broader analysis.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in households’ inflation expectations, net of demographics and other expectations. The concern is omitted variables and reverse causality in repeated cross-sections. The paper uses this as supportive evidence rather than a standalone quasi-experimental causal design.

Setting: As a supporting channel test, the authors regress households’ readiness to save on higher inflation expectations in a multinomial logit model. They find that expecting higher inflation raises the probability respondents say it is 'not at all' a good time to save by 2.82 percentage points and lowers the probability they say it is a 'good time' to save by 2.97 percentage points, consistent with higher expected inflation discouraging saving. This result is interpreted as reinforcing the mechanism that inflation expectations shift households away from saving and toward current spending.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism test. The paper's main conclusions focus on consumption propensity and policy-induced changes in inflation expectations and durable spending; saving plans are used to corroborate the Euler-equation channel.
Settings.H711: Section 3.2, Table 3 columns (1)–(3), PDF page 1613 (article p. 1613).
Settings.G712:
Treatment: Household-level dummy equal to 1 when the respondent expects higher inflation over the next 12 months than over the previous 12 months.

Method: The authors estimate multinomial logit models separately by demographic and preference-related subsamples to study heterogeneity in the effect of higher inflation expectations on readiness to buy durables. The estimator remains the same nonlinear multinomial logit as in the baseline specification, with average marginal effects reported and z-tests for equality across subsamples. Subsamples include education, income, age, gender, income expectations, socioeconomic status, and a patience-versus-constraints proxy based on saving behavior among high-income households.

Identification: Within each demographic subsample, the authors use controlled cross-sectional variation in inflation expectations to estimate differences in spending propensity. The purpose is not to claim clean causal identification within each split, but to assess whether omitted changing sample composition could explain their broader findings and whether patience/constraints mediate the mechanism.

Setting: The authors estimate heterogeneous multinomial-logit marginal effects of higher inflation expectations on readiness to buy durables across demographic groups. Effects are similar across education, income, age, gender, income-expectation, and socioeconomic-status splits—for example 6.9 percentage points for low education versus 10.8 percentage points for college, and 9.0 versus 9.4 percentage points across low versus high income—while among high-income households the effect is materially larger for rich savers (10.6 percentage points) than rich nonsavers (6.0 percentage points), with a z-statistic of 2.072. They interpret this as showing limited heterogeneity except where patience/financial constraints plausibly matter.

Main role: These are substantive heterogeneity analyses supporting the mechanism and the later DiD interpretation by showing limited demographic heterogeneity, except for the patience/constraints proxy.
Settings.H712: Section 3.3, Table 4 columns (1)–(14), PDF pages 1614–1615 (article pp. 1614–1615).
Settings.G713:
Treatment: Exposure to the unexpected November 2005 German announcement of a 3-percentage-point VAT increase (from 16% to 19%) to be implemented in January 2007. In the DiD, treatment is being a German household exposed to this preannounced unconventional fiscal policy shock, versus matched foreign households not exposed directly to the German VAT announcement.

Method: This is the paper’s core difference-in-differences/event-time design for unconventional fiscal policy. The authors first match German households to similar foreign households using nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching on demographics within month, then compare changes from a baseline month (June 2005) to each subsequent month between treated Germans and control foreigners. The estimating equation is a sequence of cross-sectional regressions of the change in outcomes between month m and the base month on an indicator for exposure to the German VAT shock plus changes in observables; the coefficient β_m is an event-time DiD estimate. For the VAT setting, France is the preferred control because it shared ECB-set nominal rates but was not exposed to the German VAT preannouncement; some figures also use a broader European control group. This is a conventional DiD/event-study design rather than a modern heterogeneity-robust staggered-adoption estimator.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing pre/post changes for German households around the unexpected VAT announcement to contemporaneous changes for matched foreign households not exposed to the announcement. The authors argue the VAT increase was unexpected, driven by inherited fiscal deficits and EU pressure, and did not trigger offsetting German monetary tightening because the ECB set common euro-area policy and excluded reacting to the one-off VAT effect. The key assumption is parallel trends: absent the announcement, German households’ inflation expectations and spending plans would have evolved like those of matched foreign households. The paper presents pre-trend graphs, matching balance checks, and placebo outcomes on other expectations as support, but remaining concern is time-varying Germany-specific shocks coincident with the announcement.

Setting: Using a matched difference-in-differences event-study around Germany’s November 2005 preannouncement of a VAT increase effective January 2007, the authors conclude that unconventional fiscal policy raised both German households’ inflation expectations and their willingness to buy durables relative to matched foreign households. There are no visible pre-trend differences before the announcement; after it, Germans become 3.8 percentage points more likely to say it is a good time to buy durables by December 2005 (s.e. 1.5 percentage points), and the effect rises through 2006, peaking at 34 percentage points in November 2006 before returning to zero after implementation. Inflation expectations show a similar buildup. The paper treats this as core causal evidence that preannounced consumption-tax increases can stimulate demand by managing expectations.

Main role: This is one of the central empirical designs in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The main conclusion is that unconventional fiscal policy increased both inflation expectations and spending plans.
Settings.H713: Section 4.2–4.4 and Section 5.1, Equations (8) and (9), Figures 2–5, Table 5, PDF pages 1618–1625 (article pp. 1618–1625).
Settings.G714:
Treatment: Exposure of German households to ECB forward-guidance announcements by President Draghi on July 4, 2013, and January 9, 2014, versus matched households in the United Kingdom and Sweden not directly exposed because their countries were outside the euro area.

Method: This setting applies the same matched difference-in-differences/event-time framework to ECB forward-guidance announcements. German households are compared with matched households from the United Kingdom and Sweden, which were not in the euro area and thus were not directly exposed to ECB forward guidance. Using March 2013 as the baseline month, the authors estimate month-by-month post-minus-baseline outcome changes on an exposure indicator plus changes in observables, yielding event-time DiD coefficients β_m around the July 2013 and January 2014 announcements.

Identification: Identification uses DiD variation from exposure to ECB forward-guidance announcements for German euro-area households relative to matched non-euro-area households in the UK and Sweden. The maintained assumption is parallel trends in expectations and spending absent the announcements. The authors show similar pre-trends and no changes in controls’ outcomes around the announcements. A key interpretive issue is that even if financial markets and professional forecasters reacted, households may not have understood or trusted the policy; the null estimates are interpreted as the policy failing to move household expectations/spending rather than as invalid identification.

Setting: Applying the same matched DiD/event-study design to ECB forward-guidance announcements in 2013 and 2014, the authors find no detectable effect on German households’ inflation expectations or willingness to buy durables relative to matched households in the UK and Sweden. Pre-trends are parallel, but after both the July 2013 introduction and January 2014 reiteration of forward guidance, the event-time coefficients remain near zero for both outcomes. This null finding is a central result of the paper and supports the claim that, unlike unconventional fiscal policy, forward guidance did not manage household expectations or spending in this setting.

Main role: This is the second central policy comparison in the paper. The abstract and conclusion emphasize that forward guidance announcements did not increase households’ expectations or spending.
Settings.H714: Section 4.1–4.4 and Section 5.1, Equations (8) and (9), Figures 2–5, Table 5, PDF pages 1617–1625 (article pp. 1617–1625).
Settings.G715:
Treatment: Exposure to the German November 2005 preannouncement of a future VAT increase, estimated separately within demographic or constraint-related subgroups. Treatment remains being a German household exposed to the VAT announcement versus matched foreign households.

Method: The authors extend the matched DiD/event-time analysis of the German VAT announcement by estimating the treatment effect separately within demographic groups. Within each month, German and foreign households are matched within demographic categories, and then average treatment effects on readiness to buy durables are estimated over event time using the same change-from-baseline regression framework as in Equation (9). This is a conventional heterogeneous DiD robustness/substantive analysis, not a separate estimator class.

Identification: Identification is the same DiD comparison as in the baseline VAT design, now executed within matched subgroup samples. The goal is to test whether treatment effects vary with education, gender, expected income, age, socioeconomic status, and proxies for financial constraints. Parallel-trend and no-concurrent-shock assumptions are required within each subgroup; sample sizes are smaller, so the exercise is mainly supportive.

Setting: The subgroup DiD analysis shows that the German VAT announcement raised durable-spending readiness broadly similarly across education, gender, income expectations, age, and socioeconomic-status groups, but the effect was smaller for households more likely to be financially constrained. Figure 6 shows overlapping positive event-time effects across demographic groups, while Figure 7 shows economically and statistically weaker responses for respondents unable to save, for lower-income households, and for renters relative to their less constrained counterparts. The authors interpret this pattern as reinforcing the expectations/intertemporal-substitution mechanism rather than a purely demographic or mechanical explanation.

Main role: These are important substantive heterogeneity results for understanding the mechanism, but the central headline result is the average positive effect of unconventional fiscal policy, not subgroup-specific treatment effects.
Settings.H715: Section 6, Figures 6 and 7, PDF pages 1626–1629 (article pp. 1626–1629).
Settings.G716:
Treatment: Exposure to the November 2005 German VAT preannouncement, estimated within demographic and financial-constraint subgroups; treated units are German households exposed to the announcement versus matched foreign households.

Method: The authors repeat the matched DiD/event-time analysis of the German VAT announcement using inflation expectations, rather than durable-spending readiness, as the dependent variable and estimate subgroup-specific dynamic treatment effects. German and foreign households are matched within demographic groups and compared before and after the VAT announcement using the same change-from-baseline regression framework. This is a conventional DiD heterogeneity/placebo-mechanism analysis.

Identification: This uses the same DiD identifying variation as the main VAT setting, now with inflation expectations as the outcome. The argument is that if unconventional fiscal policy works through inflation expectations, effects on expectations should be broadly homogeneous across demographics, including for constrained households whose spending response is muted. The assumptions mirror the main DiD design within each subgroup.

Setting: When inflation expectations are used as the dependent variable, the VAT-announcement DiD effects are broadly similar across demographic groups and also similar between constrained and unconstrained households. Figures 8 and 9 show that the dynamic rise in Germans’ inflation expectations relative to matched foreign households around the VAT announcement does not vary much by education, gender, age, socioeconomic status, or most proxies for constraints. The authors interpret this as evidence that the policy broadly changed beliefs, while spending responses were weaker only where financial constraints limited households’ ability to act on those beliefs.

Main role: These are supporting mechanism and placebo-style analyses. They bolster the interpretation of the main VAT DiD findings by showing that inflation expectations move similarly across demographics and, unlike spending, do not exhibit the same financial-constraint heterogeneity.
Settings.H716: Section 6, Figures 8 and 9, PDF pages 1630–1632 (article pp. 1630–1632).
Settings.G717:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, where PO_t is total purchase obligations at fiscal year-end scaled by total assets; alternative treatment decomposition uses PO^{t+1}_t (change in the portion due during year t+1, scaled by assets) and PO^{rest}_t (change in the remainder). Treatment is continuous.

Method: OLS panel regressions of future abnormal stock returns on predisclosure changes in purchase obligations (POs), with firm fixed effects and either year fixed effects or industry-year fixed effects; standard errors are clustered at the firm level. The main specifications in Table II regress BHAR_{t+1} on PO_t, or separately on the next-year-due component PO^{t+1}_t and the residual maturity component PO^{rest}_t, sometimes adding earnings surprises as a control. The author interprets these regressions as testing whether predisclosed POs predict future price changes and therefore proxy for managers' private information; identification comes from within-firm changes in POs net of common time or industry-year shocks, but the design is not presented as fully eliminating all endogeneity.

Identification: The paper uses within-firm variation in year-end changes in undisclosed purchase obligations to test whether managers' private information predicts future stock-price adjustment. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity, while year or industry-year fixed effects absorb common shocks. The endogeneity concern is that POs may reflect changing fundamentals rather than private information; the author's interpretation relies on PO changes containing information not yet incorporated into prices and on controls such as earnings surprises and contemporaneous/lagged returns in related settings. Causal language here is limited but the paper treats a change in POs as implying future price increases because it proxies for manager-perceived undervaluation.

Setting: As a first validation of the mispricing proxy, the paper estimates firm fixed-effects regressions showing that higher predisclosure changes in purchase obligations predict higher abnormal stock returns in the following year. In Table II, the coefficient on PO_t is positive and significant; in the preferred specification with industry-year fixed effects and earnings-surprise controls, a one-standard-deviation increase in PO_t is associated with a 1.8 percentage point increase in BHAR_{t+1}, about 5.1% of the outcome's standard deviation. When decomposed, a one-standard-deviation increase in PO^{t+1}_t is associated with a 2.7 percentage point increase in BHAR_{t+1}, about 7.7% of the outcome SD. These results are used to argue that managers' private information embedded in POs predicts future price corrections.

Main role: This is a validation exercise supporting the paper's proxy for information-asymmetry-driven mispricing, rather than the core issuance outcome. It materially underpins the paper but is not itself the central corporate-financing result emphasized in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H717: Section II.A 'Do Predisclosed POs Predict Future Stock Prices?'; Table II, cols. (1)-(8), PDF pp. 3411-3412 (PDF pages 11-12).
Settings.G718:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, alternatively decomposed into PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t; each scaled by assets and continuous.

Method: OLS panel regressions of short-window abnormal stock returns around 10-K filing dates on predisclosure changes in purchase obligations, with firm fixed effects and either year fixed effects or industry-year fixed effects; standard errors clustered by firm. Table III uses BHAR(-1,1) as the dependent variable and PO_t, or PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t, as regressors, sometimes controlling for earnings surprises. The design is interpreted as showing the stock-price response when private PO information is disclosed.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-firm changes in predisclosed POs, with firm fixed effects and common time controls. The paper argues that if POs are genuinely private before disclosure, stock prices should react upon 10-K filing. The main assumption is that this filing-window abnormal return captures new information revelation from POs rather than omitted coincident news; earnings surprises are included in some columns to address one alternative channel.

Setting: The paper next tests whether the market reacts when PO information becomes public. In firm fixed-effects regressions of three-day abnormal returns around 10-K filing dates, higher predisclosure PO changes predict more positive filing-window returns. In Table III, a one-standard-deviation increase in PO_t is associated with about a 28 basis point increase in BHAR(-1,1), equal to 7.6% of the outcome standard deviation, while a one-standard-deviation increase in PO^{t+1}_t is associated with about 33 basis points, or 8.9% of the outcome SD. The author interprets these estimates as evidence that POs were private information before disclosure and that their release causes contemporaneous price adjustment.

Main role: This is another proxy-validation exercise, important for the paper's interpretation that POs are private information, but not the headline issuance or leverage result.
Settings.H718: Section II.B 'Are POs Private Information Prior to Disclosure?'; Table III, cols. (1)-(8), PDF pp. 3412-3414 (PDF pages 12-14).
Settings.G719:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, or its components PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t, each scaled by assets. The author interprets higher PO changes as greater manager-perceived undervaluation and lower PO changes as greater overvaluation. Continuous treatment.

Method: Linear firm-panel regressions of contemporaneous net security issuance on changes in purchase obligations, including firm fixed effects and either year fixed effects or industry-year fixed effects plus lagged firm controls and contemporaneous and one-year-lagged abnormal stock returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Panel A of Table IV reports separate regressions for net equity issuance and net debt issuance, using either aggregate PO_t or the decomposition into PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t. The paper treats these coefficients as the main causal evidence on the effect of information-asymmetry-driven mispricing on financing choices.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm changes in undisclosed POs, interpreted as shifts in manager-perceived mispricing due to information asymmetry. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity in issuance propensity, and year or industry-year fixed effects absorb macro and industry shocks. Lagged controls proxy for financing determinants, while contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns are included so the PO coefficient captures information beyond what is already in prices. The main threat is omitted time-varying fundamentals correlated with PO changes; the paper addresses this later via heterogeneity tests, quarterly timing, financing-deficit tests, and public-vs-private debt splits.

Setting: The paper's main result is that manager-private information captured by changes in purchase obligations affects contemporaneous financing. In Table IV Panel A, higher PO changes—interpreted as more perceived undervaluation—reduce both net equity and net debt issuance, with much larger effects for equity. In the industry-year fixed-effects specification, a one-standard-deviation decrease in PO_t increases net equity issuance by 1.1% of total securities outstanding (8.7% of the outcome SD) and net debt issuance by 0.23% (2.3% of the outcome SD). Using the next-year-due PO component, a one-standard-deviation decrease in PO^{t+1}_t raises net equity issuance by 1.8% (13.8% of the outcome SD) and net debt issuance by 0.35% (3.5% of the outcome SD). The author interprets this as evidence that overvaluation causes issuance, especially equity issuance.

Main role: These are the paper's central corporate-financing results highlighted in the abstract, introduction, Section III, and conclusion: managers issue more securities when firms are overvalued and avoid issuance when undervalued, with stronger effects for equity than debt.
Settings.H719: Section III.A 'Security Issuance'; Table IV Panel A, cols. (1)-(8), PDF pp. 3414-3419 (PDF pages 14-19).
Settings.G720:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets. Higher PO changes are interpreted as more manager-perceived undervaluation; lower changes as more overvaluation. Continuous treatment.

Method: Linear probability-style OLS regressions of issuance/repurchase indicators on PO_t with firm fixed effects, year or industry-year fixed effects, lagged controls, and contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Panel B of Table IV reports separate models for the probability of equity issuance, equity repurchase, debt issuance, and debt reduction. The author treats these as causal evidence on extensive-margin financing responses to mispricing.

Identification: As in the net-issuance setting, identification relies on within-firm changes in PO-based private information after absorbing firm and time/industry-year effects and controlling for standard issuance determinants and past/current abnormal returns. The author interprets the PO coefficient as information-asymmetry-driven mispricing affecting extensive-margin issuance and repurchase decisions. Remaining concern is omitted time-varying fundamentals, addressed elsewhere in the paper via cross-sectional, timing, and alternative-outcome tests.

Setting: On the extensive margin, the paper finds that changes in POs affect whether firms issue or repurchase securities. In Table IV Panel B, lower PO_t increases the probability of equity issuance and debt issuance, while higher PO_t increases the probability of equity repurchases; debt reduction is not significantly affected. In the industry-year fixed-effects specifications, a one-standard-deviation decrease in PO_t raises the probability of equity issuance by 3.1 percentage points, equal to 22.7% of the sample mean, and raises the probability of debt issuance by 0.9 percentage points, equal to 4.5% of the sample mean. A one-standard-deviation increase in PO_t raises the probability of equity repurchase by 2.7 percentage points, or 14.6% of its sample mean. The author interprets this as further evidence that overvaluation causes issuance while undervaluation causes repurchases, especially for equity.

Main role: These extensive-margin issuance results directly reinforce the central conclusion that perceived undervaluation discourages issuance and encourages repurchases, with stronger effects for equity than for debt.
Settings.H720: Section III.A 'Security Issuance'; Table IV Panel B, cols. (1)-(8), PDF pp. 3416-3419 (PDF pages 16-19).
Settings.G721:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, alternatively decomposed into PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t; continuous and scaled by assets.

Method: Linear firm-panel regressions of leverage on changes in purchase obligations, with firm fixed effects and either year fixed effects or industry-year fixed effects, plus lagged firm controls and contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table V reports specifications using PO_t or its decomposition into PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t. The paper interprets these coefficients as the effect of information-asymmetry-driven under- or overvaluation on capital structure.

Identification: The paper uses within-firm variation in PO changes, absorbing firm and year or industry-year effects, and controlling for standard leverage determinants and abnormal returns. The interpretation is that PO-based private information shifts perceived mispricing, which changes the composition of financing and thus leverage. The identifying assumption is that conditional on fixed effects and controls, changes in PO capture mispricing rather than omitted leverage shocks; this is supported by stronger equity than debt responses and by ancillary heterogeneity/timing tests.

Setting: Consistent with equity issuance responding more strongly than debt issuance, the paper finds that PO-based perceived undervaluation raises leverage. In Table V, the coefficient on PO_t is positive and significant with firm and industry-year fixed effects, and both PO^{t+1}_t and PO^{rest}_t also load positively when entered together. The author interprets these estimates as showing that information-asymmetry-driven undervaluation causes higher contemporaneous leverage, while overvaluation lowers leverage, making leverage an equilibrium consequence of security-specific timing responses. No standardized effect relative to the mean or SD of leverage is verbally reported here.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly highlight leverage consequences: undervaluation increases leverage and overvaluation decreases leverage because equity issuance responds more strongly than debt issuance.
Settings.H721: Section III.B 'Financial Leverage'; Table V, cols. (1)-(4), PDF pp. 3420-3421 (PDF pages 20-21).
Settings.G722:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets; continuous.

Method: Subsample firm fixed-effects OLS regressions of net equity issuance and net debt issuance on PO_t, estimated separately across groups defined by information asymmetry: firms that regularly report POs on 10-Qs, high vs. low analyst coverage, old vs. young firms, and low vs. high R&D intensity. All regressions include year fixed effects, lagged controls, and contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table VI uses these heterogeneity patterns as substantive tests of the information-asymmetry mechanism.

Identification: The author tests the mechanism by comparing the same within-firm FE specification across groups where information asymmetry should differ. If PO-based mispricing drives issuance, the PO coefficient should be more negative in higher-information-asymmetry samples and attenuated when POs are disclosed more frequently. This is not a separate quasiexperimental design; it is a structured robustness/mechanism analysis relying on the maintained FE identification within each subsample.

Setting: The paper shows that PO-based mispricing effects on issuance are stronger when information asymmetry should be more severe. In Table VI Panel A, the negative PO_t coefficient for net equity issuance is insignificant among firms that regularly disclose POs in 10-Qs, but much more negative among low-analyst-coverage firms, young firms, and high-R&D firms. Panel B shows broadly similar, though weaker, patterns for net debt issuance. The author interprets this heterogeneity as evidence that the baseline negative PO-issuance association reflects information asymmetry rather than generic financing needs or fundamentals.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion state that effects are more pronounced for firms associated with greater information asymmetry. These heterogeneity tests substantively support the paper's central mechanism, though they are secondary to the baseline issuance regressions.
Settings.H722: Section IV.A 'Cross-Sectional Analyses'; Table VI Panels A-B, cols. (1)-(7), PDF pp. 3421-3426 (PDF pages 21-26).
Settings.G723:
Treatment: Annual predisclosure change in purchase obligations PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}; in placebo-style checks, lagged PO_{t-1}. Continuous treatment scaled by assets.

Method: Firm fixed-effects OLS regressions of quarterly net equity issuance and quarterly net debt issuance on annual PO_t, with year fixed effects, lagged controls, and contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table VII estimates separate quarterly outcome regressions for Q1-Q4 of year t and placebo-style regressions of Q1_t issuance on lagged PO_{t-1}, sometimes alongside current PO_t. The author uses these timing patterns as substantive evidence that the effect operates while information asymmetry is unresolved and fades after disclosure.

Identification: The design exploits within-firm differences in when PO information should be most private: information asymmetry should accumulate through the fiscal year until the annual 10-K release and then dissipate afterward. By estimating separate quarterly issuance regressions and comparing current versus lagged POs in Q1, the paper argues that stronger Q4 effects and null PO_{t-1} effects after disclosure isolate the information-asymmetry channel rather than persistent financing-demand shocks.

Setting: Using quarterly issuance timing, the paper finds that the negative PO-issuance relation is strongest when private information should be most severe. In Table VII, the coefficient of PO_t on quarterly net equity issuance is negative in all quarters of year t but largest in Q4, and the relation disappears for lagged PO_{t-1} in Q1 of year t when that information is already public. Quarterly net debt issuance shows a similar but weaker pattern, with the largest negative effect also in Q4 and no meaningful lagged-PO effect after disclosure. The author interprets these timing results as strong evidence that unresolved information asymmetry, rather than persistent fundamentals, drives the issuance response.

Main role: The abstract and text emphasize that effects are stronger in periods with greater information asymmetry and disappear after disclosure. These timing tests directly support that central mechanism.
Settings.H723: Section IV.B 'Time-Varying Information Asymmetry'; Table VII Panels A-B, cols. (1)-(6), PDF pp. 3426-3429 (PDF pages 26-29).
Settings.G724:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets; continuous.

Method: Firm fixed-effects OLS regressions on a Capital IQ-covered subsample, relating PO_t to net equity issuance, net debt issuance, public debt issuance, and private debt issuance, with year fixed effects, lagged controls, and contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table VIII separates public debt from private debt to test whether more information-sensitive debt responds more strongly to PO-based mispricing.

Identification: Within the Capital IQ subsample, the author compares PO effects across financing instruments differing in information sensitivity. The identifying argument is comparative: if information asymmetry is the mechanism, public debt issuance should respond more than private debt because banks obtain and process private information better. The FE structure removes time-invariant firm heterogeneity, but this remains a robustness/mechanism analysis rather than a distinct exogenous design.

Setting: Among debt types, the paper finds that PO-based mispricing primarily affects public debt issuance, not private debt issuance. In Table VIII, the negative PO_t coefficient remains for the overall net equity and net debt outcomes on the Capital IQ sample, but when debt is decomposed, PO_t significantly reduces public debt issuance while having no meaningful effect on private debt issuance. The author interprets this as evidence that the baseline debt-issuance response is concentrated in the more information-sensitive public debt market, reinforcing the information-asymmetry mechanism.

Main role: The abstract notes that effects are more pronounced for securities associated with greater information asymmetry. The public-versus-private debt split is a key substantive mechanism result supporting that claim.
Settings.H724: Section IV.C 'Public Debt versus Private Debt'; Table VIII, cols. (1)-(4), PDF pp. 3429-3430 (PDF pages 29-30).
Settings.G725:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets; continuous.

Method: Firm fixed-effects OLS regressions of financing deficit on PO_t, with year fixed effects and in some columns lagged controls; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table IX regresses contemporaneous DEF_t and future DEF_{t+1} on PO_t to test an alternative causal channel whereby PO changes proxy for financing needs rather than mispricing. Although framed as ruling out an alternative explanation, the setting still interprets PO as potentially affecting financing deficit and thus qualifies as a substantive causal robustness test.

Identification: The author examines whether within-firm PO changes predict contemporaneous or future financing deficits after absorbing firm and year effects, with and without standard controls. The logic is that if PO is merely capturing financing demand, it should load on DEF; finding no relation weakens that competing explanation. The maintained assumption is that the same FE specification is informative about the financing-needs channel.

Setting: To address the possibility that PO changes simply proxy for firms' financing needs, the paper regresses contemporaneous and future financing deficits on PO_t. In Table IX, the coefficients on PO_t are statistically insignificant for both DEF_t and DEF_{t+1}, with or without additional controls. The author concludes that changes in POs do not meaningfully affect financing deficit, undermining the alternative explanation that the main issuance results are driven by time-varying external financing demand rather than mispricing.

Main role: This is an alternative-explanation test, used to argue that PO effects on issuance are not driven by financing demand. It is supportive but not a central headline result.
Settings.H725: Section V.A 'PO_t and Demand for External Financing'; Table IX, cols. (1)-(4), PDF pp. 3430-3432 (PDF pages 30-32).
Settings.G726:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets; continuous.

Method: Firm fixed-effects OLS regressions using alternative equity-issuance outcomes from SDC and Compustat, with year fixed effects, lagged controls, and contemporaneous and lagged abnormal returns; standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table X reports SEO minus repurchases using SDC or Compustat repurchase data and an SEO indicator, both in the full sample and after excluding firms that never conduct SEOs. The author uses these as robustness checks against the concern that passive equity activities drive the baseline results.

Identification: The identification is the same within-firm FE framework as the baseline issuance regressions, but with alternative outcomes that strip out passive equity changes. The argument is that if the PO effect persists for SEO-based measures, then the baseline relation is not an artifact of scheduled employee grants or other inactive equity adjustments. This addresses outcome-measurement endogeneity rather than introducing a new causal design.

Setting: Using cleaner equity-issuance measures, the paper again finds that lower PO_t predicts more external equity issuance. In Table X, PO_t negatively predicts SEO-minus-repurchase measures based on SDC and Compustat and also lowers the probability of an SEO, with larger coefficients when the sample is restricted to firms that ever conduct SEOs. The author interprets these results as evidence that the baseline equity-issuance effect is not driven by passive or mechanical equity-account changes, but by active financing choices consistent with mispricing-based market timing.

Main role: These are robustness checks confirming the main equity-issuance findings with cleaner issuance measures. They support but do not independently carry the paper's main conclusion.
Settings.H726: Section V.B 'Alternative Measures of Equity Issuance'; Table X, cols. (1)-(6), PDF pp. 3432-3433 (PDF pages 32-33).
Settings.G727:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets; continuous.

Method: Manager-level and firm-level OLS panel regressions of insider trading outcomes on PO_t, including manager or firm fixed effects and year fixed effects; some specifications add lagged firm controls, and standard errors are clustered at the manager level (manager panel) or firm level (firm aggregates). Table XI reports NetSell, Sell, Buy, and Sell/(Sell+Buy) outcomes at both the manager and firm levels. The author interprets these as evidence that managers' private trading responds to perceived mispricing signaled by POs.

Identification: The paper exploits within-manager or within-firm variation in PO changes while controlling for year effects, abnormal returns, and sometimes firm characteristics. Manager fixed effects absorb time-invariant trading propensities. The author's mechanism claim is that when PO_t indicates overvaluation, insiders should sell more and buy less; because POs reflect private information not yet public, these trades reveal managers' beliefs. The main concern is that insider trading covaries with other firm conditions, partially addressed by controls and fixed effects.

Setting: The paper finds that insider trading moves in the direction predicted by PO-based mispricing. In Table XI, higher PO_t—interpreted as undervaluation—reduces net insider selling and gross selling, raises insider buying, and lowers the share of trades that are sales, both at the manager level and in firm-level aggregates. For example, at the manager level, a one-standard-deviation decrease in PO_t increases net sales by about 4.6%, increases sales by about 4.0%, and a one-standard-deviation increase raises purchases by about 6.2%. The author interprets these patterns as evidence that managers believe PO changes predict mispricing and act on that belief in private trading.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly cite managers' trading patterns as evidence that they perceive mispricing. These results are a central complementary piece linking private beliefs to both personal and firm decisions.
Settings.H727: Section VI 'Do Managers Believe that PO_t Predicts Mispricing?'; Table XI Panels A-B, cols. (1)-(8), PDF pp. 3434-3438 (PDF pages 34-38).
Settings.G728:
Treatment: Predisclosure change in purchase obligations, PO_t = PO_t - PO_{t-1}, scaled by assets; continuous.

Method: Manager-level and firm-level OLS panel regressions of executive option-exercise rates on PO_t, with manager or firm fixed effects and year fixed effects, abnormal returns, and in some columns lagged firm controls; standard errors clustered at the manager or firm level. Table XII reports CEO-only, all-executive, and firm-average option exercise regressions. The paper treats these as causal evidence that managers act on PO-implied mispricing in their personal option exercise decisions.

Identification: Within-manager or within-firm variation in PO changes is used to explain option-exercise intensity, controlling for fixed effects and return-based controls. The mechanism is that executives exercise more when PO_t signals overvaluation because exercises are typically followed by sales. Identification depends on the assumption that, conditional on fixed effects and controls, PO changes capture private valuation beliefs rather than omitted determinants of option exercise timing.

Setting: Executive option exercises also line up with the mispricing interpretation. In Table XII, the coefficient on PO_t is negative and significant for CEOs, all executives, and firm-level averages, implying more option exercise when PO_t signals overvaluation and less exercise when it signals undervaluation. For CEOs, a one-standard-deviation decrease in PO_t increases the exercise rate by about 1.9 percentage points, equal to 8.1% of the outcome standard deviation and 14.3% of the mean. The author interprets these estimates as additional evidence that managers believe PO changes reveal mispricing and adjust private actions accordingly.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions cite managers' option exercises alongside stock trading as evidence that perceived mispricing matters for private decisions, making this a central complementary result.
Settings.H728: Section VI 'Do Managers Believe that PO_t Predicts Mispricing?'; Table XII, cols. (1)-(6), PDF pp. 3438-3439 (PDF pages 38-39).
Settings.G729:
Treatment: Estimated exposure to the predicted systematic skewness factor (PSS) in the cross-sectional asset-pricing regression; the reported estimand is the monthly price of PSS risk / risk premium. PSS is a tradable long-short factor formed each month by buying value-weighted stocks in the bottom 30% of predicted coskewness ranks and shorting the top 30%. This is not binary.

Method: The paper estimates linear two-pass asset-pricing regressions to interpret factor exposures as causing differences in expected portfolio returns. In the first pass, monthly excess returns of test portfolios are regressed on factor returns to estimate betas. In the second pass, average portfolio excess returns are regressed on estimated betas (GLS and OLS fit measures reported) to estimate factor risk premia; model-misspecification-robust t-ratios follow Kan et al. (2013). This setting is the CAPM augmented with the predicted systematic skewness factor (PSS), using 25 size and book-to-market sorted portfolios as test assets. Identification is cross-sectional regression adjustment from factor-model structure rather than an external quasi-experiment.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional covariance structure: portfolios with different estimated PSS betas should earn different average returns if systematic skewness is priced. Method: Asset-pricing estimation using the Giglio and Xiu (2017) methodology, which uses principal components of a large test-asset cross section to account for omitted factors and measurement error, then maps those components to the risk premia of named factors such as MKT and PSS. The maintained assumption is that the principal components span the relevant stochastic discount factor space sufficiently well.

Treatment: Membership in the high predicted coskewness portfolio relative to the low predicted coskewness portfolio within a given size quintile; effectively a binary long-short contrast on predicted coskewness sorts.

Method: Time-series linear factor regression of the return on a high-minus-low predicted coskewness portfolio on the CAPM to estimate abnormal performance (alpha). Settings.G749:
Treatment: Lagged valuation conditions in debt and equity markets at the firm level. Depending on the column, treatment is a continuous change in average firm credit spread (%), average firm term spread (%), credit premium (%), term premium (%), predicted next-12-month excess bond return (%), V/P ratio, or predicted next-12-month excess stock return (%). These are not policy assignments but continuous market-valuation shocks interpreted as affecting financing behavior.

Method: Firm-level panel regressions relate quarterly net equity repurchases and net debt issuance to lagged firm-specific debt-market valuation measures and equity valuation measures, with firm fixed effects and double-clustered standard errors by firm and time. The key estimating equations are (1) and (2). The authors use three alternative valuation implementations reported in Table III: (i) lagged average firm credit spread, lagged average firm term spread, and lagged V/P; (ii) lagged credit premium and term premium plus predicted credit-spread and term-spread components and lagged V/P; and (iii) lagged predicted 12-month excess bond returns and predicted 12-month excess equity returns. Controls include lagged cash holdings, contemporaneous profits and CAPX, lagged deviation from target leverage, lagged size, lagged asset growth, and lagged output gap. Identification is within-firm time-series variation after absorbing time-invariant firm heterogeneity; the paper interprets coefficients causally as valuation conditions affecting financing choices, while acknowledging broader endogeneity concerns.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-firm changes over time in lagged debt and equity valuation proxies, after controlling for observable financing determinants and firm fixed effects.
