Key assumptions are that the rulings were at least partly unanticipated and that, absent the rulings, treated and control firms would not have systematically different event-window abnormal returns.

Setting: Using pooled cross-sectional regressions of two-day risk-adjusted stock returns around two Delaware Airgas rulings, with six-digit GICS fixed effects, the authors estimate that firms more affected by the rulings experienced higher abnormal returns when the rulings weakened staggered boards and lower abnormal returns when the rulings restored their protection, implying markets view staggered boards as value reducing. In Table 1 Panel A, the Treat coefficient is 96.116 basis points with Method 1/Treat-1, 95.045 basis points with Method 2/Treat-1, 97.249 basis points with Treat-2, and 120.052 basis points with Treat-3. Panel B reports event-specific treatment effects of about +83 to +94 basis points for Event-1 and -104 to -146 basis points for Event-2, with simulated p-values from 0.0092 to 0.0003 under Methods 2 and expanded treatment definitions. This is the paper’s main evidence that market participants perceive staggered boards to reduce shareholder value on average.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all frame the paper’s central contribution as showing that the Airgas-ruling event-study results remain significant under multiple robustness checks. Table 1 is the baseline replication/extension of CW2013 and is the anchor for the paper’s main causal claim that staggered boards are perceived as value reducing.
Settings.H813: Section 2.1-2.2; Table 1, Panel A columns (1)-(4) and Panel B; PDF pp. 3-5 (esp. PDF p. 4-5).
Settings.G814:
Treatment: Binary treated-firm indicator capturing exposure to the Airgas rulings through staggered boards and late annual meeting timing. Definitions vary by row: Treat-1 = September-December meetings; Treat-2 = July-December; Treat-3 = July-November excluding December. Controls are January-March meeting firms. The treatment remains binary.

Method: This setting re-estimates the same pooled event-study cross-sectional FE regression as the baseline, but on samples excluding subsets of small firms or additionally trimming extreme returns. The dependent variable is Method 2 two-day risk-adjusted ruling-announcement return in basis points. Regressions include the treatment indicator, Event-2 dummy, and six-digit GICS industry fixed effects, with cluster-robust standard errors by six-digit GICS. The paper varies the treatment definition (Treat-1, Treat-2, Treat-3) and exclusion rules: market capitalization below $10 million, below $500 million, below $1 billion, and versions that additionally exclude OTC firms, penny stocks, and/or top and bottom 1% of treatment and control return distributions. These are robustness versions of the same causal event-study estimator.

Identification: Identification is the same differential-exposure event-study logic as the baseline: late-meeting staggered-board firms are more affected by the Airgas rulings than early-meeting staggered-board firms. These robustness exercises test whether the inference depends on very small firms or one-sided outliers. The maintained assumptions remain partial surprise of the rulings, exogeneity/predetermination of annual meeting timing within staggered-board Delaware firms, and no omitted industry news after conditioning on GICS-6 FE. By excluding small-cap firms and by symmetrically trimming extreme returns, the authors argue the estimated treatment effect is not driven by tiny firms or asymmetric outliers.

Setting: Table 2 shows that the estimated positive effect of weakening staggered boards on treated firms’ abnormal returns remains economically large and usually statistically significant when excluding small firms or trimming outliers. Excluding firms with market cap below $10 million yields Treat coefficients of 46.894 basis points for Treat-1, 65.964 for Treat-2, and 73.727 for Treat-3; the latter two are significant at 5%. Excluding firms below $500 million gives 99.471, 98.793, and 109.529 basis points, and excluding firms below $1 billion gives 136.581, 135.666, and 148.098 basis points. Additional symmetric trimming of top and bottom 1% returns still delivers positive coefficients such as 68.991 to 81.889 basis points for the $10 million screen and up to 148.255 basis points for the $1 billion screen plus other exclusions. The authors interpret these results as evidence that their causal conclusion is not driven by very small firms and in fact appears stronger among normal-size firms.

Main role: A major purpose of the paper is to rebut AS2016’s claim that results disappear after excluding small firms. Section 3 is described in the introduction as central, and the conclusion cites the wide array of significant results from these robustness tests as reinforcing the main conclusion.
Settings.G815:
Treatment: Binary treated-firm indicator for staggered-board Delaware firms whose annual meeting timing makes them more affected by the Airgas rulings. Treat-1 = September-December, Treat-2 = July-December, Treat-3 = July-November excluding December; control firms are January-March meeting firms. Binary treatment.

Method: This setting re-estimates the same pooled event-study FE regression after excluding particular observations flagged by AS2016 or after symmetric trimming. The dependent variable is the Method 2 two-day risk-adjusted ruling-announcement return in basis points; regressors are the treated-firm indicator and Event-2 dummy; six-digit GICS industry FE are included and standard errors are clustered by six-digit GICS. Sample modifications include excluding firms with outstanding M&A offers, excluding the ASB observation(s), excluding both ASB and EONC, excluding Airgas (ARG), and versions that add exclusion of top and bottom 1% of returns on each event date. Treatment definitions Treat-1, Treat-2, and Treat-3 are each reported.

Identification: The identifying variation again comes from differential exposure of late- versus early-meeting staggered-board firms to the court rulings. The concern addressed is whether the estimated treatment effect is driven by a few idiosyncratic firms or firm-event observations. By rerunning the same FE event-study estimator after excluding M&A targets, a specific extreme-return firm (ASB), both tails symmetrically, or the focal takeover target Airgas, the authors argue that the causal interpretation does not hinge on a handful of special observations. Assumptions are unchanged apart from robustness to sample composition.

Setting: Table 3 reports that excluding particular observations leaves the inferred value-reducing effect of staggered boards largely intact. Excluding M&A firms yields Treat coefficients of 94.754, 97.270, and 120.122 basis points for Treat-1/2/3. Excluding ASB alone gives 75.860, 85.017, and 106.087 basis points; excluding ASB and EONC gives 86.604, 92.376, and 106.087 basis points. Symmetric trimming together with ASB exclusion raises estimates to 100.094, 92.724, and 117.674 basis points. Excluding Airgas produces 83.573, 88.513, and 111.240 basis points, and excluding Airgas plus top/bottom 1% yields 88.486, 83.625, and 108.574 basis points. The authors interpret these robustness results as showing the event-study treatment effect is not an artifact of a few special observations and continues to support the view that markets perceive staggered boards as value reducing.

Main role: Section 4 is one of the paper’s substantive rebuttals to AS2016, and the conclusion explicitly states that systematic, two-sided handling of outliers reinforces the main conclusion. These are not mere diagnostics; they are presented as important robustness evidence for the paper’s central claim.
Settings.G816:
Treatment: Binary treated-firm indicator for Delaware staggered-board firms with late annual meetings relative to early-meeting staggered-board firms. Treat-1 = September-December; Treat-2 = July-December; Treat-3 = July-November excluding December; controls are January-March meeting firms. Binary treatment.

Method: This setting re-estimates the event-study treatment regression under alternative industry fixed-effect specifications or with no industry FE. The specification remains a pooled cross-sectional regression of Method 2 two-day risk-adjusted ruling-announcement returns on the treated-firm indicator and Event-2 dummy, with second-event returns multiplied by -1 in pooled regressions. Rows 1-3 use four-digit GICS fixed effects and cluster by GICS-4; rows 4-6 exclude industry FE entirely and cluster by GICS-6; rows 7-12 repeat these after excluding top and bottom 1% of returns. Treatment definitions Treat-1, Treat-2, and Treat-3 are each reported. This remains a standard/non-HDFE FE design because at most one FE dimension is absorbed, and some specifications omit FE altogether but are grouped here as separately reported identification variants centered on the role of FE in causal interpretation.

Identification: The identifying logic is still differential exposure to unexpected Airgas rulings across late- and early-meeting staggered-board firms. This section addresses whether results depend on the particular industry-control structure used to absorb confounding industry news. The authors argue GICS-6 is reasonable, but show that using broader GICS-4 FE or no industry FE still yields positive and often significant treatment effects, especially under expanded treatment definitions and symmetric trimming. Assumptions remain that the rulings were at least partly unanticipated and that, conditional on the comparison design, omitted contemporaneous shocks do not differentially affect treated firms.

Setting: Table 4 shows that the estimated treatment effect is robust to alternative industry-control specifications. With GICS-4 fixed effects, the Treat coefficient is 76.876 basis points for Treat-1, 90.607 for Treat-2, and 112.628 for Treat-3; the latter two are conventionally significant, and Treat-1 is significant by the simulation metric. With no industry fixed effects, the coefficients are 71.822, 79.879, and 110.718 basis points, all positive and conventionally significant. After excluding top and bottom 1% of returns, GICS-4 specifications yield 73.744, 71.296, and 91.753 basis points, while no-FE specifications yield 63.922, 62.719, and 93.078 basis points. The authors interpret these estimates as showing that the causal conclusion that staggered boards reduce value is not an artifact of using six-digit industry fixed effects.

Main role: These are substantive robustness analyses about sensitivity to six-digit versus four-digit industry FE or to omitting industry FE. They support the paper’s central conclusion but are secondary to the baseline and the main rebuttals on sample restrictions/outliers.
Settings.G817:
Treatment: Exposure to later rather than earlier resolution of uncertainty, operationalized within matched stock pairs by having lower 30-day implied volatility conditional on nearly equal 365-day implied volatility. Implemented as the long-short contrast late minus early within pairs; effectively binary at the pair level.

Method: The authors implement a linear return-spread comparison from a portfolio-sorting strategy based on matched stock pairs. Each month they form pairs of stocks such that 365-day implied volatility (IV365) differs by at most 1 percentage point while 30-day implied volatility (IV30) differs by at least 25 percentage points; they go long the lower-IV30 stock ('late') and short the higher-IV30 stock ('early') and compute the average subsequent 12-month return difference across pairs. Returns are equal-weighted across pairs; Newey-West t-statistics with 12 lags are reported. Although this is not a regression-based causal design, the paper interprets the resulting contrast as the effect of later versus earlier uncertainty resolution on expected returns, conditional on similar long-run uncertainty.

Identification: The identifying argument is cross-sectional matching on long-horizon implied volatility: by pairing stocks with nearly identical IV365, the authors aim to hold fixed total long-run uncertainty while using differences in IV30 to isolate timing of uncertainty resolution. The endogeneity concern is that short-horizon IV differences could proxy for other return predictors or risk exposures; the paper argues the effect reflects timing of uncertainty resolution rather than total uncertainty, and later shows factor models and other characteristics do not explain the spread. The key assumption is that conditional on similar long-run IV, variation in short-run IV primarily captures earlier versus later uncertainty resolution relevant for expected returns.

Setting: Using matched stock pairs with nearly identical 365-day implied volatility but at least a 25-percentage-point gap in 30-day implied volatility, the authors interpret lower short-run IV as later uncertainty resolution and higher short-run IV as earlier resolution. The 12-month late-minus-early trading strategy earns 5.17 percentage points per year (t=3.10), with the late stock returning 10.86% and the early stock 5.70%. The paper treats this spread as compensation investors require for holding stocks whose uncertainty resolves later, making this a main empirical basis for the claim that investors prefer early resolution of uncertainty.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that portfolio sorts and matched-stock comparisons indicate investors demand over 5% per year to hold late-resolution stocks; this is a core empirical result supporting the paper's central claim about preference for early resolution of uncertainty.
Settings.H817: Section 3.1 'Pairs of stocks', Table 1, PDF p. 4.
Settings.G818:
Treatment: Return on the late-minus-early matched-pair strategy based on lower versus higher IV30 conditional on similar IV365; the focal regressor interpretation is the strategy's exposure to later uncertainty resolution versus earlier uncertainty resolution. Binary long-short contrast at the portfolio level.

Method: The authors run linear time-series regressions of the 12-month return on the matched-pair investment strategy on overlapping 12-month factor returns: first market excess return only, then Fama-French three factors, then Fama-French five factors. The intercept (alpha) is interpreted as abnormal return attributable to late versus early uncertainty resolution after adjusting for standard risk factors. Newey-West standard errors with 20 lags are used.

Identification: Identification relies on linear factor adjustment rather than a quasi-experiment. The concern is omitted risk-factor exposure: the raw late-minus-early return spread could reflect known priced factors rather than timing of uncertainty resolution. By regressing strategy returns on market, size, value, profitability, and investment factors, the paper argues that a large positive alpha after controlling for these exposures supports an independent premium related to late uncertainty resolution. This requires the maintained assumption that the included factors span conventional risk compensation relevant to the strategy.

Setting: To test whether the matched-pair late-minus-early return spread is explained by standard risk factors, the authors regress the strategy's 12-month return on factor returns. The estimated alpha is 6.42 percentage points with only market control, 6.54 percentage points with Fama-French three factors, and 7.71 percentage points with Fama-French five factors; loadings are generally small, with a negative market beta. The paper interprets these positive alphas as evidence that the premium for later uncertainty resolution is distinct from standard factor exposures, reinforcing the main conclusion.

Main role: These factor-adjusted regressions are used to support the central claim that the return spread is not explained by standard risk factors and therefore reflects compensation for timing of uncertainty resolution.
Settings.G819:
Treatment: Later versus earlier uncertainty resolution measured by high versus low implied volatility duration (IVD) within a given IV365 quintile. In the focal LME contrast the treatment is belonging to the highest rather than lowest IVD portfolio; binary at the contrast level.

Method: The authors form 5x5 portfolios by independently sorting stocks monthly on 365-day implied volatility (IV365) and implied volatility duration (IVD), then compute value-weighted and equally weighted 12-month portfolio returns. Within each IV365 quintile they form a late-minus-early (LME) portfolio by going long the highest-IVD quintile and short the lowest-IVD quintile. This portfolio-sorting contrast is interpreted as the effect of later versus earlier uncertainty resolution on expected returns, conditional on total uncertainty. Newey-West t-statistics with 12 lags are reported.

Identification: The strategy uses cross-sectional conditioning on IV365 to hold fixed the overall amount of uncertainty while using IVD to capture the timing of uncertainty resolution. The main concern is that IVD may correlate with other risk or mispricing characteristics; the paper argues that within IV365 quintiles IVD is largely orthogonal to IV365 and many observed characteristics, so the LME spread can be interpreted as compensation for later resolution timing rather than total uncertainty. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on IV365, differences in IVD isolate timing-of-resolution variation relevant for expected returns.

Setting: In monthly 5x5 double sorts on IV365 and IVD, the authors compare high-IVD ('late') and low-IVD ('early') stocks within the same total-uncertainty bucket. For 12-month value-weighted returns, the late-minus-early spread in the highest IV365 quintile is 7.17 percentage points per year (t=1.97); for equally weighted returns it is 6.51 percentage points (t=2.97). The paper interprets these positive LME returns as a premium investors demand for holding stocks whose uncertainty resolves later, especially when overall uncertainty is high.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight the double-sort evidence and especially the roughly 7% LME return in the highest IV365 quintile as a central empirical result.
Settings.H819: Section 4.2 'Portfolio sorts', Table 4 Panels A-B, PDF p. 8.
Settings.G820:
Treatment: Later versus earlier uncertainty resolution measured by high versus low IVD within a given option-implied beta quintile; binary high-IVD versus low-IVD contrast in the LME portfolio.

Method: The authors repeat the portfolio-sort return analysis using 5x5 monthly independent sorts on option-implied beta and implied volatility duration (IVD), then compute value-weighted and equally weighted 12-month returns. Within each beta quintile they form a late-minus-early portfolio (highest minus lowest IVD). This linear contrast is used as a robustness exercise to show that the timing-of-resolution premium is present even conditioning on systematic risk measured by beta.

Identification: By conditioning on option-implied beta instead of IV365, the authors assess whether the late-minus-early return spread simply reflects cross-sectional differences in systematic risk. The identifying logic is observational conditioning: within beta quintiles, variation in IVD proxies timing of uncertainty resolution. The assumption is that sorting on beta sufficiently partials out broad market-risk exposure so that residual return differences across IVD portfolios are informative about timing preferences rather than beta-related compensation.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors sort stocks on option-implied beta and IVD and ask whether later uncertainty resolution still predicts higher returns among stocks with similar beta. In the highest beta quintile, the 12-month late-minus-early spread is 4.78 percentage points for value-weighted portfolios (t=1.78) and 5.83 percentage points for equally weighted portfolios (t=3.24). The paper interprets this as evidence that the timing premium is not just a manifestation of systematic market beta.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis supporting the main claim that the IVD effect is not merely systematic-risk variation tied to beta.
Settings.H820: Section 4.2, Table 5 Panels A-B, PDF p. 9.
Settings.G821:
Treatment: Later versus earlier uncertainty resolution measured by high versus low IVD within a given IV365 quintile; binary high-IVD versus low-IVD contrast in the short-horizon LME portfolio.

Method: The authors estimate the same monthly independent 5x5 double-sort design on IV365 and IVD but evaluate one-month holding-period returns instead of 12-month returns. They report value-weighted and equally weighted portfolio means and the late-minus-early spread within each IV365 quintile, with Newey-West t-statistics using 12 lags. This is interpreted as a short-horizon test of whether later uncertainty resolution raises expected returns.

Identification: The identification logic mirrors the 12-month double sorts: condition on IV365 to hold fixed total uncertainty and use cross-sectional differences in IVD to capture timing of uncertainty resolution. The short-horizon design additionally addresses the concern that the 12-month result might be driven by long-horizon dynamics unrelated to timing. The maintained assumption is that within IV365 buckets, high versus low IVD primarily shifts the timing of risk resolution rather than other omitted return determinants.

Setting: Using the same IV365-by-IVD double sorts but measuring one-month returns, the authors find that later uncertainty resolution predicts higher short-horizon returns among high-uncertainty stocks. In the highest IV365 quintile, the one-month late-minus-early spread is 1.01 percentage points for value-weighted portfolios (t=2.16) and 0.70 percentage points for equally weighted portfolios (t=2.16). The paper interprets this as further evidence that the relevant pricing force is the timing of uncertainty resolution, not merely the level of short-term risk.

Main role: This is an important robustness result showing the timing premium appears even at a one-month horizon, but it is not the single headline result emphasized in the abstract.
Settings.H821: Section 4.2, Table 6 Panels A-B, PDF p. 10.
Settings.G822:
Treatment: Return on the late-minus-early IVD strategy within the high-IV365 quintile, i.e., exposure to later rather than earlier uncertainty resolution among highly uncertain stocks. Binary long-short portfolio contrast.

Method: The authors run linear time-series factor regressions of one-month returns on the LME portfolio formed within the highest IV365 quintile. Regressions include market excess return alone, then market/SMB/HML, then the Fama-French five factors. The intercept alpha is interpreted as abnormal performance of the late-minus-early timing-of-resolution strategy after controlling for standard factor exposures; Newey-West t-statistics with 12 lags are reported.

Identification: The concern is that the LME return within high-IV stocks may simply reflect exposure to conventional priced factors. The factor-regression approach partials out market, size, value, profitability, and investment factor returns; a positive intercept is interpreted as evidence of an independent premium linked to later uncertainty resolution. This relies on the assumption that the included factors adequately capture standard sources of systematic compensation.

Setting: For the late-minus-early portfolio constructed among stocks in the highest IV365 quintile, the authors regress one-month returns on standard factors and find positive alphas: 1.19 percentage points with market only, 1.06 percentage points with three factors, and 0.90 percentage points with five factors. The market loading is negative. The paper treats these intercepts as evidence that the pricing effect of later uncertainty resolution is not subsumed by standard factor models.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis used to argue that standard asset-pricing factors do not explain the LME return in the key high-IV subsample.
Settings.G823:
Treatment: Continuous stock characteristic equal to implied volatility duration multiplied by squared 365-day implied volatility, IVD × IV365^2. Higher values represent later expected resolution of uncertainty especially when overall uncertainty is high. Nonbinary continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate monthly Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of individual stock returns on standard characteristics and the interaction term IVD × IV365^2, reporting time-series averages of the monthly slope coefficients. Specifications add CAPM-style market beta only, then Fama-French three characteristics, then Fama-French five-style characteristics (log market equity, log book-to-market, operating profitability, investment), with all characteristics cross-sectionally demeaned and Newey-West t-statistics using four lags. This two-step panel estimator is used to interpret the effect of later uncertainty resolution, scaled by total uncertainty, on expected returns.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional month-by-month variation in the interaction of uncertainty-timing (IVD) and total uncertainty (IV365^2), after controlling for standard return-predictive characteristics. The endogeneity concern is omitted firm characteristics such as size, value, profitability, or investment, plus possible variance risk premium or idiosyncratic volatility effects; the paper argues robustness to such controls elsewhere. The maintained assumption is that after conditioning on these observables, higher IVD × IV365^2 captures a pricing effect of later uncertainty resolution rather than unrelated omitted predictors.

Setting: In Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions, the authors find that stocks with higher IVD interacted with higher total implied variance earn higher expected returns. The coefficient on IV^2 × IVD is 0.05 in the CAPM-style specification, 0.06 with Fama-French three controls, and 0.06 with five controls, all statistically significant. The authors interpret this as strong cross-sectional evidence that later uncertainty resolution raises expected returns, particularly when overall uncertainty is high.

Main role: The introduction and Section 4.4 present the Fama-MacBeth evidence as showing that IVD has strong explanatory power for the cross-section of expected returns, which materially supports the paper's central empirical claim beyond portfolio sorts.
Settings.H823: Section 4.4 'IVD and the cross-section of returns', Table 11, PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G824:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 in the period after decimalization implementation and 0 in the period before decimalization. This is a binary before/after treatment capturing exposure to the switch to decimal pricing around 2001.

Method: The authors estimate linear before/after regressions of monthly institutional trading costs on a post-decimalization indicator around the 2001 tick-size change. The core specification is Eq. (2): Price impact_i,t = alpha + beta*Decimalization_i,t + delta*C_i,t + error_i,t, where the sample uses the 30 days before and 30 days after decimalization, variables are first built at the firm-day level and then averaged within firm-month, and controls include log(order size), log(dollar volume), log(market value equity), market-to-book, and idiosyncratic volatility. They report full-sample, NYSE-only, and Nasdaq-only estimates. This is a regression-adjustment design relying on the timing of decimalization as an exogenous shock, but without a separate untreated control group in the reported specification.

Identification: Identification comes from the market-wide switch to decimalization, which the paper treats as an exogenous tick-size reduction. The regression asks whether institutional trading costs changed after the regime shift, conditional on changes in firm characteristics and trading conditions. The main concern is confounding time-varying factors around the event window, which the paper addresses with a narrow before/after window and controls, but the setting still relies on the assumption that no other contemporaneous shocks explain post-minus-pre changes in institutional price impact.

Setting: Using a linear before/after regression around decimalization, the authors test whether the exogenous switch to decimal pricing changed institutional trading costs measured by Price impact. In Table 6, the post-decimalization indicator is 0.073 (t=2.16) in the full sample, -0.011 (t=-0.35) for NYSE stocks, and 0.144 (t=2.61) for Nasdaq stocks, all in percentage-point units of Price impact. The authors interpret these results as showing that institutional trading costs do not dramatically improve following decimalization and may even rise for Nasdaq stocks, a central claim used to question decimalization as an instrument for institutional liquidity in prior studies.

Main role: A central paper conclusion is that decimalization does not materially improve institutional trading costs, which underpins the paper's challenge to prior finance research using decimalization as an exogenous liquidity shock.
Settings.H824: Section 6.3, Eq. (2), Table 6, cols. 'Full sample', 'NYSE stocks', and 'Nasdaq stocks' (PDF pp. 11-12).
Settings.G825:
Treatment: Change in stock liquidity surrounding decimalization, alternatively measured as change in Percent effective spread, change in Percent effective spread 1, or change in Price impact 1 from the month before to the month after decimalization. These are continuous treatment intensities, with lower values corresponding to improved liquidity/lower trading costs.

Method: The authors run linear regressions following Fang et al. (2009) to estimate the effect of decimalization-induced liquidity changes on firm value. The dependent variable is the change in market-to-book from the month before to the month after decimalization; the key regressor is a change in liquidity over the same period. They estimate separate specifications using change in Percent effective spread, change in Percent effective spread 1, and change in Price impact 1, with controls for change in S&P 500 membership, log(assets), idiosyncratic volatility, log(analysts), lagged monthly returns, plus industry fixed effects using two-digit SIC codes. The paper refers to this as using decimalization as an instrument/exogenous shock to liquidity, but the implemented estimator reported in Table 8 is a linear regression adjustment of change in firm value on change in liquidity.

Identification: The intended identification uses decimalization as an exogenous liquidity shock: cross-firm variation in liquidity changes around decimalization is interpreted as plausibly exogenous to firm value. The regression controls for concurrent changes in observables and industry fixed effects. The paper's own contribution is to question this strategy when liquidity is measured by institutional Price impact, arguing that if decimalization did not materially shift institutional trading costs, the causal interpretation linking liquidity to firm value is weakened.

Setting: Replicating Fang et al. (2009), the authors regress the change in market-to-book around decimalization on alternative liquidity changes. With Percent effective spread, the coefficient is negative and significant: -0.047 (t=-1.91) in the full sample, -0.178 (t=-3.33) for NYSE stocks, and -0.032 (t=-2.29) for Nasdaq stocks, implying that improved liquidity is associated with higher firm value. But with the institutional measure Price impact 1, the estimates are insignificant in the full sample and NYSE sample and only marginally negative for Nasdaq (-0.032, t=-1.94). The authors interpret this as no compelling evidence that liquidity, measured using institutional trading costs, has a positive causal effect on firm value.

Main role: The paper's abstract and conclusion emphasize that prior causal conclusions are altered when liquidity is measured using institutional trading data; the replication/extension of Fang et al. (2009) is one of the paper's three main demonstrations of that broader point.
Settings.G826:
Treatment: Being in the treatment tercile with the largest improvement in stock liquidity measured by Percent effective spread around decimalization, versus being in the control tercile with the smallest liquidity improvement (including worsened liquidity). This is a binary treated-versus-control exposure based on liquidity improvement intensity.

Method: The authors implement a conventional difference-in-differences design, closely following Fang et al. (2014), to estimate liquidity's effect on innovation around decimalization. For each sample (full, NYSE, Nasdaq) and each liquidity measure, firms are sorted into terciles by the change in liquidity from the month before to the month after decimalization. The tercile with the largest liquidity improvement is the treatment group; the tercile with the smallest improvement is the control group. The authors estimate propensity scores using a probit on pre-decimalization firm characteristics, match treated and control firms one-to-many (5), then compare the change in innovation from the three years before to the three years after decimalization across treated and control firms. The reported estimand is the treated-minus-control change difference.

Identification: The design treats decimalization as an exogenous shock to liquidity and uses cross-sectional differences in liquidity improvement to define treated and control groups. The DiD assumption is that, absent the liquidity shock, matched treated and control firms would have had similar innovation changes from pre to post periods. Matching on pre-event observables is used to improve comparability, but causal interpretation still depends on parallel trends in innovation across the matched groups and on liquidity changes capturing exogenous exposure induced by decimalization.

Setting: Using a matched DiD design with treatment defined by the largest drop in Percent effective spread around decimalization, the authors find that firms with the biggest spread improvement experience larger declines in innovation. In Table 9, full-sample treated-control differences are -0.801 in log(1+cites) (t=-3.10) and -0.214 in log(1+patents) (t=-1.84); the effect is concentrated in Nasdaq stocks, where differences are -0.883 (t=-2.63) for cites and -0.313 (t=-2.20) for patents, while NYSE effects are insignificant. The authors interpret this as replicating Fang et al. (2014)'s conclusion when liquidity is measured with effective spread.

Main role: This is one of the three highlighted replications/extensions used to show that prior causal conclusions based on decimalization and effective spreads can change when institutional liquidity is measured differently.
Settings.G827:
Treatment: Being in the treatment tercile with the largest improvement in stock liquidity measured by Price impact around decimalization, versus being in the control tercile with the smallest liquidity improvement. Because lower Price impact implies lower institutional trading cost, this binary treatment captures relative improvement in institutional liquidity.

Method: This is the same matched conventional DiD innovation design as in the preceding setting, but treatment is defined using the institutional liquidity measure Price impact rather than Percent effective spread. Firms are sorted into terciles by change in Price impact from the month before to the month after decimalization; the largest improvement group is treated and the smallest-improvement group is control. The authors estimate propensity scores from a probit on pre-decimalization firm characteristics, perform one-to-many (5) matching, and compare changes in innovation from three years before to three years after decimalization between treated and control groups.

Identification: As with the prior DiD setting, identification relies on decimalization as an exogenous shock and on parallel innovation trends between matched treated and control firms absent the shock. Here the treatment intensity is based on institutional Price impact changes, which the paper argues are the relevant liquidity changes for institutional-trading theories. The authors' interpretation is that because Price impact did not improve materially around decimalization, the DiD yields no evidence that institutional liquidity affected innovation.

Setting: When the same matched DiD design defines treatment using institutional Price impact instead of effective spread, the innovation result disappears. Table 9 shows full-sample treated-control differences of 0.218 for log(1+cites) (t=1.04) and 0.094 for log(1+patents) (t=0.97), with similarly insignificant effects for NYSE stocks and only weak positive, not negative, differences for Nasdaq stocks. The authors conclude that stock liquidity measured by institutional trading costs does not negatively impact firm innovation, undermining the causal mechanism based on easier institutional exit.

Main role: This extension using institutional trading costs is central to the paper's contribution because it shows that the prior innovation result disappears when liquidity is measured in a way the authors argue better captures institutional traders' costs.
Settings.G828:
Treatment: Being in the treatment tercile with the largest improvement in stock liquidity measured by Percent effective spread around decimalization, versus being in the control tercile with the smallest liquidity improvement. This is a binary treated-versus-control classification based on effective-spread improvement.

Method: The authors implement a conventional matched DiD following Brogaard et al. (2017) to estimate liquidity's effect on default risk around decimalization. For each sample (full, NYSE, Nasdaq), firms are sorted into terciles by the change in Percent effective spread from the month before to the month after decimalization; firms with the largest improvement form the treatment group and those with the worst improvement form the control group. Propensity scores are estimated via probit on pre-decimalization default-risk-related firm characteristics, treatment and control firms are matched one-to-many (5), and the change in expected default frequency (EDF) from the year before to the year after decimalization is compared across groups.

Identification: The design interprets decimalization as an exogenous liquidity shock and uses cross-firm variation in spread improvement to assign treatment intensity. Identification requires that matched treatment and control firms would have had similar changes in default risk absent the differential liquidity improvement induced by decimalization. Matching on pre-period observables seeks to address confounding, but the causal interpretation hinges on the DiD parallel-trends assumption.

Setting: Replicating Brogaard et al. (2017) with effective spreads, the authors find that firms with the largest effective-spread improvement around decimalization have larger reductions in default risk. In Table 10, the full-sample treated-control difference in EDF is -0.026 (t=-1.83), with the effect mainly coming from Nasdaq stocks (-0.031, t=-1.66) and little effect for NYSE stocks (-0.005, t=-0.25). The authors interpret this as confirming the original finding when liquidity is measured by Percent effective spread.

Main role: This is another of the three headline replication/extension exercises showing that prior decimalization-based causal conclusions depend on how liquidity is measured.
Settings.G829:
Treatment: Being in the treatment tercile with the largest improvement in institutional liquidity measured by Price impact around decimalization, versus being in the control tercile with the smallest improvement. This is a binary treatment based on relative improvement in institutional trading costs.

Method: This setting uses the same matched conventional DiD default-risk design as the prior setting, but treatment is defined using the institutional liquidity measure Price impact. Firms are sorted into terciles by the change in Price impact from the month before to the month after decimalization; the largest-improvement tercile is treated and the smallest-improvement tercile is control. Propensity scores are estimated using pre-decimalization firm characteristics, matching is one-to-many (5), and the treated-minus-control difference in the change in EDF from the year before to the year after decimalization is the reported estimand.

Identification: Identification again relies on decimalization as an exogenous liquidity shock and on parallel counterfactual EDF trends between matched treated and control firms. By defining treatment using institutional Price impact, the authors target the institutional-liquidity mechanism emphasized in prior theory. Their argument is that because institutional Price impact did not materially improve at decimalization, there is no corresponding causal effect on default risk.

Setting: When treatment is based on Price impact improvements instead of effective-spread improvements, the matched DiD finds no relation between liquidity changes and default risk. Table 10 reports a full-sample treated-control difference in EDF of 0.013 (t=0.85), with similarly insignificant estimates for NYSE stocks (0.008, t=0.44) and Nasdaq stocks (-0.001, t=-0.07). The authors interpret these estimates as evidence that changes in institutional liquidity surrounding decimalization are not related to default risk.

Main role: This extension is central because it shows that the default-risk result also vanishes when the paper substitutes its preferred institutional-liquidity measure for effective spread.
Settings.G830:
Treatment: Indicator Sponsor_ij for whether treatment arm i in trial j was financially sponsored by that drug’s manufacturer or marketer, including direct funding, author affiliation, company-provided data, or company listed in conflicts/acknowledgments. This is arm-specific sponsorship status, not trial-level randomization. Binary sponsored vs. not sponsored.

Method: The paper’s core design is a difference-in-differences style linear regression at the treatment-arm level. The outcome is drug-arm efficacy, and the treatment is whether that arm is sponsored by the drug’s manufacturer/marketer. Identification comes from comparing the same drug tested against the same comparator drug pair across different randomized clinical trials with different sponsorship status. The implemented regression is y_ij = a + b Sponsor_ij + X_ij g + G_{drug,drug-pair} + e_ij, where G_{drug,drug-pair} are fixed effects for each unique drug within each drug pair, absorbing all time-invariant differences in the efficacy of a given drug against a given comparator. Controls include publication-year bins and efficacy-scale fixed effects; standard errors are clustered at the trial level. The paper explicitly motivates this as analogous to a difference-in-differences comparison within drug sets/pairs. Remaining concerns include nonrandom timing of sponsorship over the drug life cycle and potential unobserved trial-design differences.

Identification: The identifying variation is within the same drug and same comparator drug pair across different RCTs where the focal drug arm is sometimes sponsored by its manufacturer and sometimes not. Drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects hold constant the molecule being evaluated and its comparator(s), addressing confounding from firms selectively funding more effective drugs or choosing weaker comparison drugs. The causal claim requires that, conditional on these fixed effects and controls, sponsored and unsponsored trials are comparable tests of efficacy absent sponsorship. The main threats discussed by the paper are life-cycle timing/mean reversion, unobserved trial-design differences, and publication selection.

Setting: Using arm-level difference-in-differences style regressions with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects on published psychiatric RCTs, the paper estimates that manufacturer sponsorship increases a drug arm’s reported relative efficacy by 0.171 standard deviations (SE 0.052) compared with the same drug tested against the same comparator(s) without sponsorship (table 1, col. 2). Sponsored arms also have 0.259 SD higher absolute efficacy (SE 0.103), are 0.104 more likely to be statistically significantly better at the 5% level (SE 0.040), are 0.283 more likely to be the most effective arm in the trial (SE 0.055), and have a 0.019 higher relative percent decline in psychiatric scores (SE 0.007). These are the paper’s main causal results and are interpreted as evidence that financial sponsorship materially inflates reported drug efficacy.

Main role: This is the paper’s central causal design and directly underlies the headline conclusion in the abstract, introduction, main results section, and conclusion that sponsorship causally raises reported drug efficacy.
Settings.H830: Section III.B–D, figure 3, equation (1), table 1 columns 1–6, PDF pp. 3310–3314 (article pp. 13–17).
Settings.G831:
Treatment: Binary indicator for whether the treatment arm is sponsored by the drug’s manufacturer/marketer. In one robustness column, sponsorship excludes cases identified only through conflicts-of-interest statements; in others the same binary treatment is retained.

Method: This setting uses the same arm-level difference-in-differences regression with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects as the main design, but reports substantive robustness analyses addressing timing, sponsorship coding, and weighting. The estimator remains linear DiD-style regression with clustering at the trial level. Variants add controls for trial order within drug pair or year relative to FDA approval, restrict to postapproval trials, redefine sponsorship to exclude conflicts-of-interest-only cases, or weight by arm enrollment.

Identification: Identification remains within-drug-by-drug-pair comparisons of sponsored versus unsponsored arms. The robustness variants strengthen the case that the main estimate is not driven by sponsorship appearing earlier in the drug life cycle, by preapproval trials, by conflicts-of-interest coding, or by equal weighting of small and large arms. The key assumptions are still comparability of sponsored and unsponsored trials within drug pair conditional on added timing controls/fixed effects and absence of important unobserved differential trial design.

Setting: In robustness versions of the main DiD-style design using relative efficacy as the outcome, the estimated sponsorship effect remains positive and statistically significant. Relative to the baseline 0.171 SD estimate, adding controls for trial order within the drug pair yields 0.160 (SE 0.052), controlling for year relative to approval yields 0.135 (SE 0.052), restricting to postapproval trials yields 0.145 (SE 0.054), excluding conflicts-of-interest-only sponsorship cases yields 0.147 (SE 0.057), and weighting by arm enrollment yields 0.100 (SE 0.041). The paper interprets these results as evidence that mean reversion and coding choices cannot explain most of the sponsorship effect.

Main role: These robustness estimates materially support the main causal interpretation by addressing the paper’s leading alternative explanation, mean reversion/drug life-cycle timing, and by showing robustness to sponsorship definition and weighting.
Settings.H831: Section III.E, table 2 columns 1–6, PDF pp. 3314–3315 (article pp. 17–18).
Settings.G832:
Treatment: Binary indicator for whether the focal drug arm is sponsored by its manufacturer/marketer. The treatment is the same across subsamples, but the identifying sample differs by comparator type, drug class, or source of sponsorship variation.

Method: This setting estimates the same linear DiD-style regression with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects separately across substantive subsamples: active-versus-placebo versus active-versus-active drug pairs, antidepressants versus antipsychotics, industry-versus-nonindustry comparisons, and within-industry sponsorship variation. Standard errors are clustered at the trial level; controls include publication year and psychiatric score type.

Identification: Within each subsample, identification still comes from sponsored-versus-unsponsored comparisons for the same drug in the same drug pair. The heterogeneity results test whether the sponsorship effect differs by comparator structure, drug class, and whether the comparison is between industry and unsponsored trials or across industry-sponsored trials with opposing interests.

Setting: The sponsorship effect on relative efficacy is positive across major subsamples. In active-versus-placebo drug pairs, the estimate is 0.124 (SE 0.103) with mean outcome 0.49; in active-versus-active pairs it is 0.124 (SE 0.058) with mean 0.25. By drug type, the estimate is 0.215 (SE 0.068) for antidepressants and 0.092 (SE 0.061) for antipsychotics. Restricting to industry-versus-unsponsored variation yields 0.159 (SE 0.059) with mean 0.41, while within-industry variation yields a larger 0.250 (SE 0.107) with mean 0.30. The paper interprets the larger within-industry effect as consistent with opposing financial incentives on both sides of the comparison.

Main role: These are heterogeneity analyses that deepen interpretation of the main finding but are not themselves the singular core estimate highlighted in the abstract.
Settings.H832: Section III.F, table 3 columns 1–6, PDF pp. 3315–3316 (article pp. 18–19).
Settings.G833:
Treatment: Binary indicator for whether the arm is sponsored by the drug’s manufacturer/marketer.

Method: This setting studies whether controlling for or conditioning on observable trial and patient characteristics changes the estimated sponsorship effect, using linear DiD-style regressions. Columns 2–4 of table 4 add trial and/or patient covariates to the baseline regression with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects. Columns 5–7 estimate a more saturated version with fixed effects for each drug-by-drug-pair-by-characteristic-group cell, effectively estimating the sponsorship effect within dosage and patient-characteristic strata. Standard errors are clustered at the trial level.

Identification: The identifying comparison remains within the same drug and drug pair, with additional adjustment for observable trial characteristics (length, enrollment, dosage) and patient characteristics (age, sex, baseline severity, dropout). In the most saturated specifications, identification comes from sponsorship variation within drug-by-drug-pair cells sharing dosage and coarse patient-characteristic bins. The paper uses these results to argue against observably different trial design as the main driver.

Setting: Adding controls for trial and patient characteristics does not materially reduce the estimated sponsorship effect on relative efficacy. The coefficient rises slightly to 0.178 (SE 0.052) with trial controls, falls to 0.158 (SE 0.052) with patient controls, and is 0.163 (SE 0.051) with both. Estimating within drug-by-drug-pair-by-dosage cells gives 0.160 (SE 0.073); within dosage, age, and gender cells gives 0.163 (SE 0.076); and within dosage, age, gender, and baseline-severity cells gives 0.194 (SE 0.095). The paper interprets these results as evidence that observable trial design and patient selection do not explain the sponsorship effect.

Main role: These are mechanism-oriented robustness analyses supporting the conclusion that observable trial design and patient composition do not explain the main sponsorship effect.
Settings.H833: Section IV.A.1, equations (2), table 4 columns 1–7, PDF pp. 3318–3319 (article pp. 21–22).
Settings.G834:
Treatment: Binary indicator for whether the arm is sponsored by the drug’s manufacturer/marketer.

Method: To test whether sponsored trials select observably more favorable designs or populations, the paper first predicts drug-arm efficacy from observable trial and patient characteristics using linear regressions of efficacy on drug-specific interactions with each characteristic, plus year and scale controls. It then uses the resulting predicted efficacy as the dependent variable in a regression of predicted efficacy on sponsorship with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects. This is a linear regression-adjustment design rather than DiD on realized outcomes, because the causal object is whether sponsorship causes more favorable observables that would predict higher efficacy.

Identification: The strategy asks whether, within the same drug and drug pair, sponsored arms have higher predicted efficacy solely because they choose more favorable observable trial or patient characteristics. Identification relies on conditioning on drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects and comparing sponsorship status across arms, with predicted efficacy constructed from separate linear models. The interpretation is limited to observables and does not address unobserved design differences.

Setting: Using predicted efficacy from observable trial and patient characteristics as the dependent variable, the paper finds no evidence that sponsored arms systematically choose observably more favorable designs or populations. The sponsor coefficient is approximately zero across predictions based on enrollment (-0.01, SE 0.04), length (-0.01, SE 0.04), dose (0.02, SE 0.03), baseline severity (-0.03, SE 0.03), dropout (0.04, SE 0.03), age (0.01, SE 0.01), gender (-0.02, SE 0.02), and all characteristics combined (0.01, SE 0.04). The paper concludes that observable trial design explains little of the sponsorship effect.

Main role: This is a secondary mechanism test used to argue that observable trial design does not generate the main effect.
Settings.H834: Section IV.A.2, equations (3)–(4), table 5 columns 1–8, PDF pp. 3319–3320 (article pp. 22–23).
Settings.G835:
Treatment: Continuous relative efficacy of a given arm within a trial. The coefficient of interest is on efficacy, estimated separately in sponsored-arm and unsponsored-arm samples; sponsorship here defines subsamples rather than entering as the focal treatment in the reported specifications.

Method: This setting examines publication bias by estimating linear probability models for whether a trial is published as a function of the arm’s relative efficacy, separately for sponsored and unsponsored arms. The regressions include drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects and controls for the efficacy scale. Because the key identifying feature is fixed-effects comparison within drug and drug pair, and the design is not framed as a post-treatment DiD contrast, this is best classified as standard FE. Standard errors are clustered at the trial level.

Identification: Within the same drug and drug pair, the model relates higher relative efficacy to a higher probability of publication, separately for sponsored and unsponsored arms. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects and scale controls, cross-trial variation in efficacy reflects the types of results that may be selectively published. The paper interprets a stronger efficacy-publication gradient among sponsored arms as evidence of publication bias rather than random reporting.

Setting: In linear probability models of publication status with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects, relative efficacy strongly predicts publication for sponsored arms but not for unsponsored arms. For sponsored arms, a one-unit increase in relative efficacy is associated with a 0.149 higher probability of publication (SE 0.029); for unsponsored arms, the coefficient is 0.029 (SE 0.033). The paper interprets this stronger publication gradient among sponsored arms as evidence that publication bias is an important mechanism behind the sponsorship effect.

Main role: This is a mechanism result supporting the interpretation that publication bias helps drive the main sponsorship effect.
Settings.H835: Section IV.B.1, equation (5), table 6 columns 1–2, PDF pp. 3320–3323 (article pp. 23–26).
Settings.G836:
Treatment: Binary sponsorship indicator, interacted either with an indicator for publication after 2005 or with an indicator for whether the trial was preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov. The substantive treatment of interest is sponsorship, with separate estimands before/after preregistration policy or by preregistration status.

Method: This setting interacts the sponsorship indicator with publication-year bins or preregistration status in the same arm-level linear DiD-style efficacy regression with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects. Equation (6) estimates time-varying sponsorship effects by year bins; table 7 reports parsimonious interactions with a post-2005 indicator and a preregistered indicator. Controls include efficacy-scale indicators, and standard errors are clustered at the trial level. The design tests whether the sponsorship effect changed after required trial preregistration and whether it is lower among preregistered trials.

Identification: Identification compares sponsored and unsponsored arms for the same drug and drug pair, while allowing the sponsorship effect to differ by time period or preregistration status. The policy interpretation requires that, absent preregistration and related transparency changes, the sponsorship effect would have evolved similarly across these groups conditional on fixed effects and controls. The paper acknowledges that preregistration coincided with broader norm and reporting changes, so the estimates are suggestive rather than clean policy effects.

Setting: Using interacted versions of the main DiD-style efficacy regression, the paper finds that the sponsorship effect declines after the introduction of required preregistration and is smaller among preregistered trials. In table 7 column 2, the sponsorship coefficient before 2005 is 0.221 (SE 0.059), and the interaction Sponsor × post-2005 is -0.155 (SE 0.068), implying a substantially smaller post-2005 sponsorship effect; the difference is statistically significant. In column 3, the sponsorship coefficient for non-preregistered trials is 0.190 (SE 0.053), and Sponsor × preregistered is -0.190 (SE 0.103), implying a much lower sponsorship effect among preregistered trials. The paper interprets these findings as suggestive evidence that preregistration and related transparency reforms mitigate sponsorship bias.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion highlight preregistration as a key policy implication and evidence that publication bias explains the sponsorship effect; these interacted DiD estimates are central to that policy conclusion.
Settings.H836: Section V.A, equation (6), figure 5B, table 7 columns 1–3, PDF pp. 3324–3327 (article pp. 27–30).
Settings.G837:
Treatment: Binary indicator for whether the arm is sponsored by the drug’s manufacturer/marketer, interacted with drug indicators to estimate a separate sponsorship effect for each drug.

Method: The paper estimates drug-specific sponsorship effects by interacting the sponsorship indicator with drug indicators in the main arm-level linear regression with drug-by-drug-pair fixed effects. Equation (7) yields a separate sponsorship coefficient for each drug. These coefficients are then related descriptively in figures 6 and 7 to years since first approval in drug class and to postapproval prescriptions, respectively. The causal setting is the interacted efficacy regression that recovers heterogeneous sponsorship effects across drugs.

Identification: Identification of each drug-specific effect still comes from within-drug-by-drug-pair sponsored-versus-unsponsored comparisons in the main regression framework. The subsequent plots against novelty or sales proxies are interpretive correlations across estimated treatment effects, not separate causal designs. The paper uses them as consistency checks with scaling theory rather than standalone causal claims about novelty or market size.

Setting: By interacting sponsorship with drug indicators in the main efficacy regression, the paper estimates a separate sponsorship effect for each drug and shows graphically that these effects are larger for more novel drugs within a class and for drugs with larger prescription markets. Figure 6 plots the estimated drug-specific sponsorship coefficients against years since the first drug in class was approved and shows a negative relationship; figure 7 plots the same coefficients against average annual prescriptions in the first five postapproval years and shows a positive relationship. These results are presented as theory-consistent heterogeneity in the magnitude of the sponsorship effect rather than as separate causal effects of novelty or sales on efficacy.

Main role: These are theory-motivated heterogeneity exercises linking the sponsorship effect to novelty and market size, not the core causal estimate of sponsorship on efficacy.
Settings.H837: Section V.B, equation (7), figures 6 and 7, PDF pp. 3327–3330 (article pp. 30–33).
Settings.G838:
Treatment: Random assignment to receive a subsidized electricity connection offer: low subsidy (29% discount; effective price $284), medium subsidy (57% discount; effective price $171), or high subsidy (100% discount; effective price $0), versus control/no subsidy at the regular $398 price. Treatment is implemented as arm indicators at the community level.

Method: The authors estimate intention-to-treat effects of randomly assigned grid-connection subsidy offers on household take-up of an electricity connection. Transformer communities were randomized into control or one of three subsidy arms (29%, 57%, or 100% subsidy), stratified by county, market status, and early transformer installation status. Estimation uses linear regressions of a take-up indicator on treatment-arm indicators, with standard errors clustered by community and controls for stratification variables plus prespecified household covariates. This is a direct randomized assignment design for subsidy offers, not IV for receipt.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized variation in connection prices induced by subsidy assignment across transformer communities. Because subsidy arms were randomly assigned, differences in take-up across arms identify the causal effect of lower connection price on take-up, assuming successful randomization and limited interference beyond the design. The main concern is external validity and the temporary nature of the offer window rather than internal validity.

Setting: Using randomized subsidy offers for grid connections, the paper estimates the demand response of rural Kenyan households to connection prices. Relative to the control-group take-up rate of 1.3%, the 29% subsidy increases take-up by about 5.9 percentage points, the 57% subsidy by 22.9 percentage points, and the 100% subsidy by 95.0 percentage points in the preferred specification with controls. These RCT estimates underpin the paper’s claim that demand for grid connections is sharply downward sloping and substantially lower than policymakers expected, a core ingredient in the paper’s welfare analysis of rural electrification.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize randomized price offers to identify demand for connections and show that demand falls sharply with price; this is a central contribution of the paper.
Settings.H838: Section V.A, Figure 2, equation (1), and Table 2 (PDF pp. 17-19 / article pp. 1537-1541).
Settings.G839:
Treatment: Project scale, measured as the number of connected households in a community construction project (Mc) or corresponding community coverage rate Q from 0 to 100 percent. This is a continuous treatment intensity, not a binary assignment.

Method: The authors estimate how project scale affects average and marginal connection costs using nonlinear regression/curve fitting of average total cost on the number of household connections in a community project. The key variation in project scale is argued to be experimentally induced by randomized price offers affecting take-up, but the implemented estimator reported here is a cost-function regression rather than an IV or RCT outcome regression. They impose ATC = b0/M + b1 + b2 M and derive marginal cost from the estimated total-cost function. Cost data combine actual project budgets/invoices for realized projects and designed-cost projections for higher-coverage levels in a subset of communities.

Identification: The paper argues that randomized subsidy offers shift demand and thus exogenously vary the number of households connected within a community, allowing the cost curve to be traced out. The main identification assumption is that scale variation induced by the experiment is orthogonal to latent cost determinants. Remaining concerns include functional-form assumptions, the use of designed rather than realized costs for some higher-coverage points, and possible implementation inefficiencies or leakage affecting measured costs.

Setting: The paper uses experimentally induced variation in the number of connections per community to estimate economies of scale in rural grid extension. In the preferred nonlinear specification, estimated average total cost is ATC = 2453.4/M + 999.4 - 3.2M, implying a fixed cost of about $2,453 and declining marginal cost MC = 999.4 - 6.5M. The estimated average cost falls sharply with coverage but remains high, reaching about $739 per connection at universal coverage. These estimates support the paper’s central claim that grid-extension projects exhibit strong scale economies, yet costs remain too large relative to household demand.

Main role: Estimating substantial scale economies in grid extension is one of the paper’s main contributions, highlighted in the abstract and introduction as experimental variation in the number of connections revealing considerable scale economies.
Settings.H839: Section V.B, equations (2) and (3), Figure 3A, Table B5 discussion (PDF pp. 20-24 / article pp. 1542-1545).
Settings.G840:
Treatment: Household electrification status in follow-up survey round r, measured as a binary indicator for whether the household is connected to the electricity grid. This is actual treatment receipt, instrumented by the randomized subsidy offers.

Method: The authors estimate treatment-on-treated effects of household electrification status using 2SLS, instrumenting actual grid connection status with the three randomized subsidy-arm indicators. Follow-up survey rounds 1 and 2 are pooled, survey-round fixed effects are included, and regressions also control for prespecified household, student, and community covariates. Standard errors are clustered by community. This is a linear IV design where randomized subsidy assignment shifts actual receipt of electricity connections.

Identification: Randomized subsidy assignment shifts the probability of being connected to the grid, creating exogenous variation in actual electrification status. The IV estimand captures the local average treatment effect of electrification for compliers induced by the subsidy offers, under standard exclusion, independence, and monotonicity assumptions. The key endogeneity concern is that households choosing to connect differ systematically from others; instrumenting connection status with randomized subsidy assignment addresses this. Remaining issues are external validity, medium-run horizon, and potential weak take-up in lower-subsidy arms for some outcomes, though the first stage is substantively strong overall.

Setting: Using 2SLS with actual household grid connection instrumented by randomized subsidy offers, the paper estimates the causal effects of electrification on energy use and broader welfare outcomes 16 and 32 months after connection. Electrification raises monthly electricity spending by $2.17 and the probability electricity is the main lighting source by 86.8 percentage points, increases ownership of some appliances such as televisions by 11.6 percentage points and irons by 3.8 percentage points, and lowers monthly kerosene spending by $1.00 and solar-home-system main-lighting use by 16.1 percentage points. But the authors find little evidence of broader gains: effects on employment/business ownership, earnings, asset value, consumption, health symptoms, student test scores, and the grouped economic and noneconomic indices are close to zero; only life satisfaction shows a positive statistically robust effect of 0.19 SD. This IV setting delivers the paper’s headline conclusion that rural household electrification had limited medium-run economic and social impacts in this context.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight that the authors exploit exogenous variation in grid connections induced by randomized subsidies to estimate electrification impacts and conclude they do not find meaningful medium-run impacts on economic and noneconomic outcomes.
Settings.H840: Section V.D, equations (4) and (5), Table 3 (PDF pp. 24-27 / article pp. 1546-1549).
Settings.G841:
Treatment: Assignment to the high-subsidy treatment arm (100% subsidy, effective price $0, plus free ready-board) versus control group facing the standard $398 price.

Method: The authors estimate intention-to-treat effects of assignment to the high-subsidy arm versus control on follow-up outcomes, pooling rounds 1 and 2. Linear regressions include survey-round fixed effects and prespecified household, student, and community controls, with standard errors clustered by community. The low- and medium-subsidy groups are excluded from these ITT regressions because of limited take-up. This is a direct randomized assignment effect of receiving a near-free connection offer, not an IV receipt effect.

Identification: Because high-subsidy assignment was randomized at the community level, comparisons between high-subsidy and control households identify the causal effect of being offered a free connection opportunity. This ITT parameter captures assignment effects that bundle the offer, induced connection, and any related implementation frictions. Key assumptions are successful randomization and limited interference. The design does not isolate receipt effects separately; those are estimated in the IV setting.

Setting: The paper also reports direct ITT effects of assignment to the free-connection arm versus control. The high-subsidy assignment increased actual grid connection by 82.8 percentage points and monthly electricity spending by $1.80, shifted 72.0 percentage points more households to electricity as their main lighting source, and reduced kerosene spending by $0.90. Yet most broader economic and noneconomic outcomes remain close to zero: no detectable effects on employment/business ownership, earnings, asset value, consumption, health symptoms, student scores, or the grouped indices, while life satisfaction rises by 0.16 SD. These RCT assignment effects reinforce the paper’s conclusion that even removing the connection price did not generate substantial medium-run gains in this setting.

Main role: The ITT estimates are used to show that even eliminating the connection price via the high subsidy generated little medium-run change in broader outcomes; the paper explicitly emphasizes this interpretation in discussing credit constraints and impacts.
Settings.H841: Section V.D, equation (4), Table 3 column 2 (PDF pp. 24-27 / article pp. 1546-1549).
Settings.G842:
Treatment: Annual DI cash payments to the beneficiary, measured in dollars per year; the reported causal effect is scaled as the change in annual mortality from a $1,000 increase in annual DI payments. At the lower BP, the treatment is the primary beneficiary’s DI income induced by the kink in the PIA formula around the lower bend point.

Method: The paper’s main design is a fuzzy regression kink design (RKD), which falls under IV because a kink-induced change in DI benefit generosity instruments actual disability insurance income. The running variable is average indexed monthly earnings (AIME), and the instrument is the statutory change in the slope of DI payments with respect to AIME at the lower bend point (BP), where the marginal replacement rate in the primary insurance amount formula changes from 90% to 32%. The authors estimate local linear regressions on either side of the kink using MSE-optimal bandwidths from rdrobust, a uniform kernel, and Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik bias correction with robust standard errors; they also report conventional local linear estimates and versions with local covariate adjustment for age, sex, race, DI award channel, and disability type. The estimand is the ratio of the change in the slope of mortality with respect to AIME to the change in the slope of DI payments with respect to AIME, interpreted as the local causal effect of DI income on mortality around the lower BP.

Identification: Identification comes from the statutory kink in the DI benefit formula at the lower bend point, which changes the marginal mapping from AIME to DI income while other program rules remain unchanged. The main endogeneity concern is that AIME could be manipulated or correlated with unobservables changing discretely in slope at the kink; the paper argues manipulation is implausible because AIME depends on long earnings histories, lagged wage indexing, and dropped low-earnings years, making precise sorting around bend points difficult. The fuzzy RKD assumption is that, conditional on unobserved type, the density of AIME is continuously differentiable around the BP, so any change in the slope of mortality with respect to AIME is attributable to the change in DI income generosity. The paper also reports smooth covariates/densities and placebo tests to support this interpretation.

Setting: Using a fuzzy regression kink design at the lower DI benefit-formula bend point, the authors estimate that more DI income lowers mortality for low-income beneficiaries. In Table 1, the first-stage kink in DI pay with respect to AIME is about 2.51–2.53 dollars of annual DI pay per $1 of AIME slope change, and the estimated effect of a $1,000 increase in annual DI income on the average annual mortality rate over the first 4 years is between -0.209 and -0.371 percentage points depending on bias correction and covariate adjustment; the preferred covariate-adjusted bias-corrected estimate is -0.346 pp. With a mean annual mortality rate near the BP of 3.86%, the authors interpret this as a substantial mortality reduction among low-income DI recipients and as core evidence that DI income saves lives.

Main role: This is one of the central estimates highlighted in the abstract, introduction, main results, magnitudes, and conclusion: the paper’s main claim is that higher DI income reduces mortality among lower-income beneficiaries.
Settings.H842: Sections III.A–III.C and V.A; Figure 2 (lower BP, PDF p. 12); Table 1 lower BP panel/rows, columns 1–4 (PDF p. 14); Section VI magnitudes (PDF pp. 21–23).
Settings.G843:
Treatment: Annual DI cash payments in dollars per year, including the primary beneficiary’s payment and dependent payments relevant at the family BP; reported as the effect of a $1,000 increase in annual DI payments. This is nonbinary treatment intensity.

Method: A fuzzy RKD uses the statutory family maximum bend point in DI rules as an instrument for total annual DI payments to the beneficiary/dependent family unit. The running variable is AIME, and the instrument is the change in the slope of family DI benefits with respect to AIME at the family BP, where the binding rule switches from 85% of AIME to 150% of PIA, changing the marginal replacement rate from 85% to 48% of AIME. Estimation uses separate local linear regressions above and below the kink with MSE-optimal bandwidths, uniform kernel, bias correction and robust standard errors from Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik, and versions with and without local covariates. The sample at this BP is limited to beneficiaries whose dependent benefit starts at the same time as their own payment, to avoid contamination from later changes in dependent eligibility.

Identification: Identification relies on the statutory kink in total family DI payments at the family bend point. Around this threshold, the marginal relationship between AIME and total family benefits changes sharply because the maximum family benefit rule switches from 85% of AIME to 150% of PIA. The identifying assumption is that absent the benefit-formula kink, the slope of mortality in AIME would evolve smoothly through the bend point; this requires no sorting/manipulation of AIME and smoothly varying predetermined characteristics. The authors restrict the sample to those with dependents whose benefits start immediately to hold dependent eligibility rules fixed and present density, covariate, and placebo checks.

Setting: Using a fuzzy regression kink design at the family bend point, the authors estimate that higher annual DI income for beneficiaries with dependents reduces mortality. In Table 1, the first-stage kink in annual DI pay is about 2.369–2.370, and the estimated impact of a $1,000 increase in annual DI payments on the average annual mortality rate during the first 4 years on DI ranges from -0.184 to -0.319 percentage points; the preferred covariate-adjusted bias-corrected estimate is -0.255 pp. Given a mean annual mortality rate near this BP of 3.65%, the paper interprets these results as strong evidence that extra DI income lowers mortality for lower-income beneficiaries affected by family benefit rules.

Main role: This is another principal estimate emphasized in the abstract, introduction, results, magnitudes, and conclusion as evidence that higher DI income reduces mortality among lower-income beneficiaries, especially beneficiaries with dependents around the family bend point.
Settings.H843: Sections II, III.A–III.C, and V.A; Figure 2 (family BP, PDF p. 12); Table 1 family BP panel/rows, columns 1–4 (PDF p. 14); Section VI magnitudes (PDF pp. 21–23).
Settings.G844:
Treatment: Annual DI cash payments to the primary beneficiary, measured in dollars per year and interpreted as a continuous treatment; effects are reported per $1,000 increase in annual DI payments around the upper BP.

Method: The authors implement a fuzzy RKD at the upper bend point of the DI benefit formula. The running variable is AIME, and the instrument is the statutory change in the slope of the primary beneficiary’s DI payments with respect to AIME at the upper BP, where the marginal replacement rate changes from 32% to 15%. They estimate local linear regressions on either side of the kink, using MSE-optimal bandwidths, a uniform kernel, Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik bias correction and robust standard errors, and versions with and without local covariate adjustment. The ratio of the outcome-slope kink to the first-stage payment-slope kink identifies the local causal effect of DI income on mortality around the upper BP.

Identification: Identification uses the exogenous statutory kink in DI benefit generosity at the upper BP. The logic is the same as at the lower and family BPs: absent sorting or other slope changes in unobservables around the kink, any discontinuous change in the slope of mortality with respect to AIME at the threshold can be attributed to the change in DI income generosity. The authors support this with smooth density/covariate evidence and placebo checks, and the result is interpreted as a local causal effect around a relatively high-income region of the DI schedule.

Setting: At the upper bend point, the fuzzy RKD estimates show no robust mortality effect of higher DI income.
