Table 1 reports a substantial first stage of about 2.161 to 2.169, but the estimated effect of a $1,000 increase in annual DI payments on the average annual mortality rate during the first 4 years ranges from -0.113 to +0.097 percentage points and is statistically insignificant in all specifications. With a mean annual mortality rate near the BP of 4.92%, the paper interprets this as evidence that additional DI income does not measurably reduce mortality for higher-income beneficiaries around the upper BP.

Main role: Although this setting yields a null result, it is central to the paper’s main conclusion that mortality effects appear for lower-income beneficiaries but not for higher-income beneficiaries around the upper bend point.
Settings.H844: Sections II, III.A–III.C, and V.A; Figure 2 (upper BP, PDF p. 12); Table 1 upper BP panel/rows, columns 1–4 (PDF p. 14).
Settings.G845:
Treatment: Annual DI cash payments, measured in dollars per year; subgroup-specific effects are reported per $1,000 increase in annual DI payments around the lower BP.

Method: This is the heterogeneity analysis of the fuzzy RKD estimates at the lower bend point. The authors keep the same local linear RKD estimator with quadratic bias correction, local covariate adjustment, and robust standard errors, but estimate the causal effect separately across substantively defined subgroups: DI award channel, sex, race, age at filing, year started on DI, primary disability category, and time on DI. Table 2 also reports versions restricted to DDS examiner awardees only. These are subgroup-specific IV/RKD estimates of the effect of DI income on mortality.

Identification: The identification strategy remains the statutory lower-BP fuzzy RKD, with subgroup analyses assuming the same smoothness/no-sorting conditions within each subgroup. Endogeneity concerns are the same as in the main RKD. By estimating effects within groups such as DDS examiner awardees, diagnosis categories, and early versus later DI years, the paper assesses how the local causal effect varies across beneficiary types and timing while relying on the same kink-induced variation in DI income.

Setting: Table 2 shows that the lower-BP mortality effect of DI income is concentrated in higher-risk subgroups. Using the preferred bias-corrected, covariate-adjusted RKD, a $1,000 increase in annual DI payments reduces annual mortality by 0.373 pp for DDS examiner awardees (mean 5.00%) but shows a positive, imprecise 0.294 pp estimate for hearings-level awardees (mean 1.36%); the p-value for equality is 0.09. Large negative point estimates also appear for females (-0.422 pp), non-Black beneficiaries (-0.321 pp), cancers (-1.505 pp), ‘all other disabilities’ (-0.541 pp), and during years 1–2 on DI (-0.503 pp), though subgroup differences are often imprecisely estimated. The authors interpret this pattern as consistent with stronger life-saving effects of DI income among beneficiaries with higher baseline mortality.

Main role: These heterogeneity results materially support a central substantive conclusion: mortality effects are strongest among groups with higher baseline mortality, especially initially awarded beneficiaries and certain diagnosis groups.
Settings.H845: Section V.C, Table 2 lower BP columns 1–4 (PDF pp. 17–18); discussion on PDF pp. 16 and 19.
Settings.G846:
Treatment: Annual DI cash payments including dependent payments, measured in dollars per year; subgroup-specific effects are reported per $1,000 increase in annual DI payments around the family BP.

Method: This setting is the family-BP heterogeneity analysis using the same fuzzy RKD framework as the main analysis. The authors estimate local linear, quadratic-bias-corrected, covariate-adjusted RKD effects with robust standard errors separately by award channel, sex, race, age, year started on DI, primary disability type, and time on DI. Table 2 also shows parallel estimates for a sample restricted to DDS examiner awardees only.

Identification: Identification continues to come from the statutory family-BP kink in DI payments, now estimated within subgroups. The same assumptions apply: no precise manipulation of AIME around the BP and smooth evolution of potential outcome slopes absent the payment-formula kink. The subgroup analysis probes external validity and mechanisms while preserving the same local RKD design.

Setting: At the family BP, subgroup-specific RKD estimates again suggest larger mortality reductions in higher-risk groups. In Table 2, a $1,000 increase in annual DI payments lowers annual mortality by 0.227 pp for DDS examiner awardees (mean 4.29%) but only 0.062 pp for hearings-level awardees (mean 1.04%), with p = 0.01 for equality. Other estimates include -0.142 pp for females, -0.148 pp for males, -0.181 pp for non-Black beneficiaries, -0.047 pp for Black beneficiaries, -0.171 pp for cancers, -0.211 pp for ‘all other disabilities,’ and -0.107 pp in years 1–2 versus -0.145 pp in years 3–4. The authors interpret these patterns as broadly consistent with stronger mortality effects where baseline mortality is higher, though most subgroup contrasts are imprecise.

Main role: These heterogeneity estimates support a central substantive interpretation of the paper: DI income’s mortality effects are larger for groups with higher baseline mortality and are especially evident among initially awarded beneficiaries.
Settings.H846: Section V.C, Table 2 family BP columns 5–8 (PDF pp. 17–18); discussion on PDF p. 19.
Settings.G847:
Treatment: Annual DI cash payments, measured in dollars per year; the treatment effect is interpreted as the causal effect of higher DI income on beneficiaries’ earnings around each bend point.

Method: As a mechanism analysis, the paper applies the same fuzzy RKD design to labor earnings outcomes at each bend point, reusing the DI payment kinks as instruments for DI income. The outcome is earnings rather than mortality, and the authors present estimated changes in earnings at each BP in appendix table B6. This is a substantive causal analysis because the paper uses it to argue that changing labor supply is not the mechanism behind the main mortality findings at the lower and family BPs.

Identification: The same statutory benefit-formula kinks instrument DI income, and the identifying assumptions are the same as in the mortality RKD. By examining whether higher DI income changes earnings around each BP, the authors assess whether labor-supply effects are a plausible mediating channel. The core endogeneity concern—selection on AIME or unobservables varying non-smoothly at the BP—is addressed using the same RKD logic and validation exercises as for mortality.

Setting: In a mechanism analysis using the same RKD variation, the authors examine whether higher DI income affects beneficiaries’ earnings. They report that, as in their earlier paper, DI income reduces earnings at the upper BP but has no statistically significant effects on earnings at the lower or family BPs. The paper uses these causal earnings estimates to argue that changes in labor supply are unlikely to explain the mortality reductions found at the lower and family bend points, though no numerical coefficients are reported in the provided main-text discussion.

Main role: This is a mechanism/supporting analysis rather than a central mortality result. It is used to rule out labor-supply responses as the explanation for the mortality effects.
Settings.H847: Section V.D, paragraph beginning “To explore DI’s impacts on labor supply…”; appendix Table B6 referenced on PDF p. 19.
Settings.G848:
Treatment: Annual combined disability cash payments (DI and, where relevant, SSI interactions) measured in dollars per year; the causal effect is interpreted per $1,000 increase in disability income among DI/SSI beneficiaries after the waiting period. At the lower BP, the first stage is nearly zero because SSI top-ups flatten the AIME-payment relationship; at the family BP there remains a strong first stage.

Method: The paper applies its fuzzy RKD to the sample of DI/SSI dual eligibles, excluded from the main sample, to assess whether mortality effects differ when beneficiaries also receive SSI-linked in-kind benefits such as Medicaid and SNAP. The authors focus on mortality after the DI waiting period, when family and upper-BP payments match the DI formula. Estimation follows the main empirical approach and is presented in figure B11 and table B8. This is a substantive robustness/mechanism exercise using the same kink-based IV design in a different sample.

Identification: The same identification logic applies: statutory kinks in DI payment formulas generate exogenous changes in the slope of disability income with respect to AIME. In the dual-eligible sample, however, SSI top-ups weaken or eliminate the first stage at some bend points, especially the lower BP, because ongoing total payments no longer vary much with AIME. The analysis therefore tests whether mortality responses are smaller where recipients also receive Medicaid, SNAP, and related supports, consistent with these benefits partially substituting for DI cash income in protecting health.

Setting: In the dual-eligible DI/SSI sample, the fuzzy RKD estimates are used to assess whether in-kind benefits weaken the mortality effects of disability income. The lower-BP first stage is essentially absent (about 0.001 per dollar of AIME), so the mortality estimate of -0.42 pp per $1,000 is very imprecise, with a 95% confidence interval of -4.2 to 3.3 pp. At the family BP, there is a strong first stage, and the estimated mortality reduction is -0.05 pp per $1,000, compared with -0.26 pp in the main sample; the p-value for equality is 0.12. The authors interpret this as suggestive evidence that Medicaid, SNAP, and related SSI-linked benefits may attenuate the mortality effect of DI cash income.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism/robustness analysis intended to probe whether in-kind benefits attenuate the mortality-income relationship; it is not the paper’s headline result.
Settings.H848: Section V.D, paragraphs discussing DI/SSI beneficiaries; figure B11 and table B8 referenced on PDF pp. 20–21.
Settings.G849:
Treatment: Indicator for whether a city post office is covered by civil service reform in a given reform wave (reformed city in 1883 or 1893 major rollout waves) versus not yet reformed comparison cities within that stacked subexperiment. This is the onset of Pendleton Act civil service protections in the local post office.

Method: The main design is a stacked event-study / stacked difference-in-differences exploiting two major rollout waves of postal civil service reform (1883 and 1893). Following recent heterogeneous-treatment DiD guidance, the authors treat each reform wave as a separate subexperiment and stack them, citing de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020), Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), and Roth et al. (2023). The estimating equation includes reform-wave-by-city fixed effects and reform-wave-by-year fixed effects; in preferred specifications it also includes state-by-year fixed effects and time-interacted baseline controls, including a control-function style interaction of baseline postal employment with year, plus post-double-selection (PDS) selected interacted controls. The outcome is log delivery errors at the city-year level, over a common event window around reform. Identification concerns are nonrandom assignment by city size and correlated time-varying confounders; the implementation addresses these with stacked untreated comparison cities, rich interacted controls, and event-study pretrend checks.

Identification: Identification comes from staggered expansion of civil service protections across cities in two major waves, comparing reformed cities to cities not changing reform status within each wave-specific event-study window. The main endogeneity concern is that larger or otherwise different cities were targeted first, and those differences may correlate with changing postal performance. The authors argue that the federal rollout followed institutional size rules, use city fixed effects to absorb time-invariant differences, include time-interacted baseline postal employment as a control function for the assignment rule, add PDS-selected time-interacted baseline controls, and show no apparent pretrends in event studies. The causal claim therefore relies on conditional parallel trends within the stacked subexperiments.

Setting: Using a stacked modern DiD/event-study around the 1883 and 1893 rollout waves, the authors estimate that extending civil service protections to city post offices reduced log delivery errors by 0.194 to 0.220 in the full sample, which they interpret as a 19–22 percent decline in delivery errors. In Table 2, column 1, the coefficient is −0.220 (SE 0.058); with time-interacted baseline postal employment it is −0.194 (0.063); and with preferred PDS-selected interacted controls it is −0.200 (0.080). Event-study figures show little evidence of pretrends and a postreform decline that grows then levels out. This is the paper’s main evidence that depoliticizing the bureaucracy improved postal service quality.

Main role: This is the paper's central causal result in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion: civil service reform improved public service delivery by reducing postal delivery errors.
Settings.H849: Section III.A–III.B, equation (1), Table 2 columns 1–3, Figures 2 and 3 (PDF pp. 2364–2369).
Settings.G850:
Treatment: Indicator for city post office becoming covered by civil service reform in the 1883 wave or, separately, in the 1893 wave, relative to cities unreformed within that wave’s event-study comparison set.

Method: This is the same stacked event-study / stacked DiD framework as the main specification, but estimated separately by major reform wave to study dynamic effects and pooled post effects for the 1883 and 1893 expansions. The specification remains linear with reform-wave-by-city fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year fixed effects, state-by-year fixed effects, and preferred time-interacted PDS controls; the authors present event-study plots separately by wave and pooled coefficients in Table 2 columns 4 and 5.

Identification: The identifying variation is the separate timing of the two major reform waves. By estimating each wave-specific stacked DiD separately, the authors assess whether the decline in delivery errors appears in both episodes, reducing concern that the main result is driven by a single coincident shock. The assumptions are the same conditional parallel-trends assumptions within each wave-specific stacked sample, conditional on fixed effects and interacted controls.

Setting: Breaking the main design by reform wave, the authors find similar postreform declines in postal delivery errors in both the 1883 and 1893 expansions. In Table 2, the Reform × Post coefficient is −0.517 (SE 0.239) for the 1883 wave sample and −0.181 (0.084) for the 1893 wave sample, with event-study graphs showing similar postreform dynamics and little sign of pretrends. The authors use this as evidence that the productivity gains from civil service reform are not driven by one particular historical episode and that the main result is externally and internally valid.

Main role: These wave-specific results materially support the main conclusion by showing similar effects in both reform waves and helping validate the main causal interpretation.
Settings.H850: Section III.B, Table 2 columns 4–5 and Figure 3 (PDF pp. 2367–2369).
Settings.G851:
Treatment: Indicator for a city being covered by civil service reform in the initial 1883 Pendleton Act rollout, in the subsample with free-delivery service statistics.

Method: For a smaller sample of 512 larger cities with free-delivery statistics over 1875–1891, the authors estimate a stacked event-study that effectively collapses to a simple DiD around the 1883 reform wave. The regressions include city fixed effects and year fixed effects; depending on the column they add time-interacted postal employment or time-interacted PDS controls. They study productivity outcomes rather than delivery errors. Because only one reform wave is used here, the stacked design simplifies, but the interpretation remains a DiD comparing 1883-reformed to unreformed cities before and after reform.

Identification: Identification uses before-after differences between 1883 reform cities and cities not reformed in that wave within the free-delivery sample. The key concern is nonrandom targeting of larger cities; the authors therefore include city and year fixed effects and time-interacted baseline controls, especially postal employment and PDS-selected covariates. The causal interpretation relies on conditional parallel trends in productivity outcomes absent reform.

Setting: Using free-delivery administrative statistics for the 1883 wave, the authors find that civil service reform raised postal productivity and improved cost efficiency. In Table 3, log volume per carrier rises by 0.084 (SE 0.046) with postal-employment controls and by 0.137 (0.068) with preferred PDS controls, which the text summarizes as an 8–14 percent increase. Log cost per volume falls by 0.100 (0.043) and 0.129 (0.068), interpreted as a 10–13 percent gain in cost efficiency. These results are a substantive robustness and mechanism-support result reinforcing the main claim that reform improved public-sector performance.

Main role: These are key corroborating performance results used in the introduction and main text to show the delivery-error findings reflect genuine productivity gains, not reporting artifacts.
Settings.H851: Section III.B, Table 3 and Figure 4 (PDF pp. 2370–2371).
Settings.G852:
Treatment: Indicator for city post office civil service reform coverage in the major rollout waves, comparing reformed cities to unreformed cities within stacked subexperiments.

Method: The authors use the stacked event-study / stacked DiD framework on personnel and derived performance measures at the city-year level. The regressions include reform-wave-by-city fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year fixed effects, state-by-year fixed effects, and either time-interacted postal employment or PDS-selected interacted controls. They estimate effects on total postal employment and on delivery errors per worker, treating these as mechanism and scaling tests.

Identification: Identification is the same stacked rollout timing as in the main analysis. The main concern is that changing staffing or city trends could confound delivery-error improvements. By estimating employment and errors per worker under the same design, the authors test whether reform worked mainly through labor quantity rather than improved organization. Assumptions are conditional parallel trends for these outcomes.

Setting: Applying the main stacked DiD design to staffing and scaled performance outcomes, the authors find little evidence that reform increased the size of the postal workforce, but they do find fewer delivery errors per worker. In Table 4, log total postal staff rises by only 0.014 to 0.017 and is statistically insignificant, while delivery errors per worker fall by 0.081 (SE 0.018) or 0.057 (0.022). The authors interpret this as evidence that the reform improved performance without materially expanding labor inputs.

Main role: These are mechanism and interpretation checks, used to rule out staffing expansion as the source of performance improvements and show error reductions persist per worker.
Settings.G853:
Treatment: Indicator for being hired into a city post office after civil service reform took effect in that city-wave, relative to hires in unreformed cities or prereform periods within the stacked design.

Method: The authors estimate stacked DiD models at the individual-worker level on characteristics of newly hired civil servants. The specification includes reform-wave-by-city fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year-by-state fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year-by-job fixed effects, and time-interacted controls including total postal employment and log city population. One panel uses all hires observed in the personnel records; another uses the subset linked to decennial census records. The design is linear probability/linear regression by outcome and interpreted causally as whether civil service reform changed bureaucratic selection.

Identification: The identifying variation is the timing of reform across cities in the stacked design, applied to observable characteristics of new hires. The causal question is whether exam-based merit procedures changed who entered the postal workforce. By using city, state-year, and job-year controls plus interacted baseline controls, the authors seek to compare comparable hiring environments across reformed and unreformed places over time. The interpretation still relies on conditional parallel trends in these applicant/entrant characteristics.

Setting: The individual-level hiring analyses provide little evidence that civil service reform meaningfully changed the observable composition of new postal workers. In Table 5 panel A, Reform × Post is small and insignificant for same-state hires (−0.014), foreign-born (0.007), German (0.007), and Irish (−0.001). In panel B, the census-linked estimates for age (0.826), literacy (−0.002), female (−0.015), and white (−0.000) are also statistically insignificant. The authors use these null results to argue that improved worker selection is unlikely to be the main channel behind the performance gains.

Main role: These are mechanism tests used to assess whether reform improved performance by changing worker selection rather than by reducing political interference and turnover.
Settings.G854:
Treatment: Indicator for city being covered by the 1883 civil service reform in the free-delivery sample.

Method: In the free-delivery sample for the 1883 wave, the authors estimate DiD regressions of total mail volume and its components on reform status, with city and year fixed effects and either time-interacted postal employment or PDS-selected interacted controls. This is presented as a mechanism test for whether improved performance reflects reduced workload rather than greater efficiency.

Identification: Identification uses before-after changes in 1883 reform cities relative to unreformed cities in the free-delivery sample, under the same conditional parallel-trends logic as the productivity regressions. The causal question is whether reform changed demand/workload. If lower errors were caused by less mail rather than more efficient processing, total volume should fall after reform.

Setting: The workload mechanism tests show no evidence that postal performance improved because reformed cities handled less mail. In Table 6, log total volume rises by 0.122 or 0.129 after reform, while log collected mail rises by 0.257 and log delivered mail by 0.104, though these estimates are imprecise. The authors interpret these results as inconsistent with a demand-reduction story and instead as supportive of a productivity improvement under civil service reform.

Main role: These are mechanism checks used to reject declining demand/workload as the explanation for lower errors.
Settings.H854: Section IV.A, Table 6 and Figure 5 (PDF pp. 2375–2377).
Settings.G855:
Treatment: Indicator for city post office being under civil service reform in a given reform wave, with some specifications additionally interacting with presidential election timing to estimate whether reform differentially affects turnover in election years.

Method: The authors estimate stacked DiD regressions on city-year turnover measures and experience measures using personnel records. The specification includes reform-wave-by-city fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year-by-state fixed effects, and either time-interacted postal employment or PDS-selected interacted controls. Some columns restrict to a balanced panel and interact reform with election timing to test whether effects are concentrated in presidential election years.

Identification: Identification again comes from staggered reform timing across cities. The endogeneity concern is that changing turnover patterns could reflect other city-specific shocks. The authors compare reformed and unreformed cities within the stacked framework and show that reductions are concentrated in presidential election years, consistent with the historical mechanism that patronage staffing turned over with political cycles. The causal interpretation relies on conditional parallel trends in turnover and experience absent reform.

Setting: Using personnel records, the authors find that civil service reform substantially reduced bureaucratic turnover and increased tenure, especially by dampening election-related churn. In Table 7, the exit rate falls by 0.037 to 0.040 from a mean of 0.173, a decline the authors describe as 21–23 percent. In balanced-panel election-interaction results, Reform × Post × Election is −0.130 (SE 0.053), indicating that the turnover reduction is concentrated in presidential election years. Mean experience rises by 0.779 to 0.967 years from a mean of 1.727. These mechanism results underpin the interpretation that separating politics from administration stabilized careers and improved state capacity.

Main role: These are the paper's primary mechanism results, central to the claim that reform improved performance by reducing politically driven turnover and creating stable careers.
Settings.H855: Section IV.B, Table 7 and Figure 6 (PDF pp. 2377–2379).
Settings.G856:
Treatment: Civil service reform indicator interacted with a presidential election-year indicator, capturing whether reform changes performance more in election years than in nonelection years.

Method: This setting interacts reform with presidential election timing in stacked DiD regressions to test whether performance gains are larger in election years, when patronage-related disruption was historically strongest. Column 1 uses all reform waves with delivery errors at the city-year level; columns 2–3 use the 1883 free-delivery sample for productivity outcomes. Specifications include city fixed effects, year/state-year fixed effects as available, and time-interacted PDS controls, with some balanced-panel restrictions.

Identification: The identifying variation is differential postreform performance in election versus nonelection years for reformed relative to unreformed cities. The paper's mechanism is that patronage disruptions were especially severe around presidential elections, so reform should matter most then. The causal claim requires that absent reform, election-year shocks would have affected treated and comparison cities similarly conditional on the included fixed effects and controls.

Setting: The election-year heterogeneity tests show that the performance benefits of civil service reform were concentrated in the years when patronage turnover would otherwise be most disruptive. In Table 8, the triple interaction Reform × Post × Election equals −0.075 (SE 0.041) for delivery errors per worker, 0.194 (0.072) for log volume per carrier, and −0.157 (0.073) for log cost per volume. The authors interpret this as direct evidence that reform improved performance by dampening election-related bureaucratic disruption.

Main role: These are central mechanism heterogeneity tests linking the reduced political cycles in turnover directly to improvements in service quality and productivity during election years.
Settings.G857:
Treatment: Civil service reform exposure at the worker’s city and year, plus in some specifications an indicator for belonging to a post-reform entry cohort (entered after reform implementation).

Method: The authors estimate stacked individual-level DiD models of worker exit with reform-wave-by-city fixed effects, reform-wave-by-experience fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year-by-job fixed effects, reform-wave-by-year-by-state fixed effects, and time-interacted controls. They examine the full sample, pre-reform entrants only, post-reform period only with a post-reform entry cohort indicator, and a combined model. The goal is to distinguish a general retention effect of reform from a cohort-specific selection effect due to exam-based hiring.

Identification: The identifying variation is reform timing across cities applied at the worker-year level, combined with comparisons across entry cohorts. By holding selection constant among pre-reform entrants and examining whether post-reform entrants are differentially retained, the authors seek to isolate whether reform's retention effects are broad-based or selection-driven. The causal claim relies on the same conditional parallel-trends logic and on the cohort interactions capturing differential effects of the new exam regime.

Setting: The individual-level turnover decomposition shows that the reform-induced retention gains were not limited to workers hired under the new merit system. In Table 9, Reform × Post is −0.032 in the full sample and −0.160 among pre-reform entrants only; by contrast, the post-reform entry cohort effect is small and statistically insignificant (0.014 or 0.026). The authors interpret this as evidence that civil service reform mainly reduced arbitrary political firing for all serving bureaucrats, rather than working primarily through improved selection of new entrants.

Main role: This is a deeper mechanism decomposition supporting the interpretation that reduced arbitrary firing, rather than improved selection, drove the retention gains.
Settings.G858:
Treatment: Indicator for a city post office being under civil service reform in a given wave, measured against unreformed cities in election-year newspaper panels.

Method: The authors apply the stacked event-study / stacked DiD design to downstream local newspaper outcomes measured at the city-election-year level using Gentzkow, Shapiro, and Sinkinson (2011) data. The regressions include reform-wave-by-city fixed effects, reform-wave-by-state-by-year fixed effects, and time-interacted PDS controls. Outcomes are the number of newspapers, circulation, and circulation share, each split by political versus independent status. This is a downstream political-effects analysis of civil service reform.

Identification: Identification uses reform timing across cities in the stacked DiD framework, applied to local newspaper outcomes observed in election years. The endogeneity concern is that trends in media partisanship could differ systematically between cities chosen for early reform and others. The authors address this with city fixed effects, state-by-year fixed effects, and time-interacted controls. The causal interpretation requires that, conditional on these controls, treated and untreated cities would have had similar newspaper trends absent reform.

Setting: In downstream political outcomes, the authors find suggestive evidence that civil service reform weakened local partisan politics. Table 10 shows that reform reduced the number of political newspapers by 0.195 from a mean of 1.821, while increasing independent newspapers by 0.085 from a mean of 0.191. Political newspaper circulation falls by 0.266 thousand and independent circulation rises by 0.800 thousand, and the circulation share of political newspapers declines by 0.044 from a mean of 0.907. The authors interpret these results as consistent with reform reducing the strength of local party machines and fostering the rise of independent media.

Main role: Although framed as suggestive, these downstream results support a central concluding claim of a 'double dividend': reform not only improved state performance but also weakened local partisan politics.
Settings.G859:
Treatment: Importer-country contractual enforcement, measured alternatively by: common law legal origin dummy; contract viability; payment delay; enforceability of contracts; confidence in legal system; duration of legal procedure; private credit; and stock market capitalization. Depending on the specification this is binary (common law dummy) or continuous/nonbinary.

Method: Multinomial logit regressions model the choice among three financing modes—cash in advance, letter of credit, and postshipment terms—as a function of one contractual-enforcement proxy at a time. Each specification includes year fixed effects, product fixed effects, log distance to destination, and log GDP per capita; standard errors are clustered by country. Because the implemented estimator is multinomial logit rather than a linear regression, it falls in Other. The authors interpret coefficients and implied marginal effects causally/structurally as evidence that weaker contract enforcement in importer countries causes exporters to rely more on secure payment terms.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-country variation in institutional proxies for contract enforcement, controlling for distance, destination income, product, and year. The intended causal interpretation is that weaker enforcement raises default risk and therefore shifts optimal trade-finance choice toward cash in advance or letters of credit. Endogeneity concerns remain because country institutions may proxy for other destination characteristics; the paper argues robustness to additional controls, but the design is observational and relies on selection-on-observables/structural interpretation rather than an exogenous shock.

Setting: Using multinomial logit specifications, the authors argue that weaker importer-country contract enforcement causes a shift away from postshipment terms toward cash in advance and, to a lesser extent, letters of credit. In table 4, the common-law dummy enters negatively for cash in advance versus postshipment (-3.3423, SE 0.4633) and for letter of credit versus postshipment (-3.0340, SE 0.8000), while it is insignificant for cash in advance versus letter of credit (-0.3083, SE 0.9612). They report large implied marginal effects: moving from a common-law to a civil-law country raises the predicted probability of cash in advance use from 4.0% to 31.7%, raises letters of credit from 0.4% to 4.1%, and lowers postshipment from 95.6% to 64.2%. Similar patterns appear for most other institutional proxies. This is a core empirical setting supporting the paper’s main conclusion that weak institutions increase importer financing of trade.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that importers in weak-contract-enforcement countries more often finance transactions through cash in advance, and table 4 is the main econometric evidence for that central claim.
Settings.H859: Section V.B, Table 4, columns (1)-(3), PDF pp. 883-886 (article pp. 883-886).
Settings.G860:
Treatment: Joint treatment is importer-country contractual enforcement interacted with destination remoteness from the United States (long-distance dummy equal to one for destinations farther from Washington, DC, than the mean international transaction). Enforcement is measured using the same alternative proxies as in table 4. Treatment is not a single binary variable because the focal estimand is the interaction pattern between distance and institutional quality.

Method: The authors estimate multinomial logit specifications similar to those in table 4 but replace continuous log distance with a long-distance dummy and interact that dummy with contractual-enforcement measures. They then graph predicted probabilities of postshipment use for nearby versus remote destinations across levels of institutional quality, with clustered standard errors at the country level. Because the implemented estimator is multinomial logit, this setting is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-country variation in institutional quality and geographic distance, plus their interaction, controlling for product, year, and destination income. The authors' causal story is that distance worsens the exporter’s ability to recover value in default states, so weak enforcement has stronger negative effects on postshipment financing for remote destinations, while proximity mitigates those effects. This remains observational and depends on controls adequately absorbing confounders correlated with both remoteness/institutions and financing choices.

Setting: In multinomial logit interaction specifications summarized in figure 8, the authors argue that distance amplifies the effect of weak importer-country enforcement on financing choice. The focal outcome is the predicted probability of postshipment use. For example, they state that the propensity to use postshipment terms is 61.0 percentage points higher for customers in common-law versus civil-law countries when those countries are remote, but only 13.4 percentage points higher when they are nearby. Across multiple enforcement proxies, stronger enforcement raises postshipment use much more for remote than for nearby destinations, which the authors interpret as evidence that proximity mitigates the effects of weak contractual enforcement. This interaction test directly supports a central theoretical prediction.

Main role: The interaction between weak enforcement and distance is highlighted in the introduction and theory propositions as a key prediction; figure 8 is the main empirical test of that prediction.
Settings.H860: Section V.B, Figure 8, PDF pp. 887-889 (article pp. 887-889).
Settings.G861:
Treatment: Relationship development with a given customer, measured alternatively by log previous sales to that customer location or log number of previous transactions with that customer location, each interacted with a common-law dummy to test weaker effects where institutions are stronger. The focal treatment is continuous/nonbinary relationship intensity.

Method: Linear probability models explain whether a transaction uses cash in advance, letter of credit, or postshipment terms as a function of relationship-development measures. Specifications include fixed effects for each customer-country pair, product fixed effects, and year fixed effects, with standard errors clustered by customer. Because there are identifying customer-country fixed effects plus product and year effects, but not three separately absorbed dimensions in the HDFE sense emphasized in the coding rules, this is standard FE rather than HDFE. The authors interpret within-customer changes in prior transactions/sales as revealing the causal effect of relationship development on financing terms.

Identification: Identification uses within-customer-country variation over time in accumulated past sales or transactions, controlling for time-invariant customer-country heterogeneity, product effects, year effects, transaction value, transaction volume, and destination income. The paper’s endogeneity concern is that cross-customer differences could reflect selection rather than changing terms within a relationship; customer-country fixed effects are intended to show that financing terms change for a given customer as the relationship matures. The causal interpretation assumes no omitted time-varying shocks correlated with both relationship accumulation and payment-term changes.

Setting: Using customer-country fixed-effect linear probability models in table 5, the authors argue that relationship development causes a shift away from cash in advance toward postshipment terms, especially in weaker institutional environments. In column 1, the coefficient on log previous sales is -0.0228 (SE 0.0081) for cash in advance, with an offsetting interaction of 0.0216 (SE 0.0092) for common-law countries; they interpret this as the relationship effect operating in civil-law countries but not common-law countries. They note that a one-standard-deviation increase in log previous sales implies a 3.7 percentage point decrease in cash-in-advance use. In columns 5-6, the mirrored positive effects on postshipment are 0.0186 (SE 0.0087) using log previous sales and 0.0151 (SE 0.0068) using log previous transactions, again offset in common-law countries. Letter-of-credit use shows no significant relationship effect. This is a central causal setting for the paper’s claim that repeated interaction substitutes for formal institutions.

Main role: A main conclusion of the paper is that relationships let firms in weak institutional environments overcome enforcement problems; table 5 is the paper’s core econometric evidence for that claim.
Settings.H861: Section V.C, Table 5, columns (1)-(6), PDF pp. 889-891 (article pp. 889-891).
Settings.G862:
Treatment: Two-valued exposures: (i) new customer indicator equal to one for the first transaction of a customer, and (ii) crisis-period indicator equal to one during the last quarter of 2008 and first two quarters of 2009, with focus on the interaction new customer × crisis. The substantive treatment is being a new customer during the crisis.

Method: Linear probability models compare financing terms for new versus existing customers and test whether that difference changes during the crisis. Specifications include a new-customer dummy, crisis-period dummy, and their interaction, plus country fixed effects, product fixed effects, and year fixed effects; some columns also control for transaction sales value, sales volume, and destination GDP per capita. Standard errors are clustered by customer. The estimator is linear FE/LPM rather than linear DiD because the paper does not invoke a parallel-trends research design; instead it interprets the interaction as showing how the crisis changed terms for new customers relative to others.

Identification: Identification compares new versus established customers within countries, products, and years, and how that gap changes in the crisis period. The authors interpret this as evidence that heightened default/liquidity risk during the crisis caused exporters to demand safer terms from new customers. The design is observational, with possible selection into being a new customer during crisis; the paper argues controls for value and volume help mitigate this concern, but no explicit parallel-trends or exogenous shock design is implemented.

Setting: Table 7 estimates suggest that the crisis caused the exporter to require more secure payment terms from new customers. In columns 1-2, new customers are more likely to use cash in advance (0.0963, SE 0.0116; 0.0962, SE 0.0121), and the additional crisis effect for new customers is positive and significant (0.0799, SE 0.0330; 0.0673, SE 0.0340). Mirroring this, columns 5-6 show that new customers are less likely to receive postshipment terms (-0.1172, SE 0.0118; -0.1181, SE 0.0120), with a further crisis-period reduction for new customers (-0.1031, SE 0.0338; -0.0898, SE 0.0348). New customers are also more likely to use letters of credit, but that effect does not intensify in the crisis. The authors interpret these patterns as consistent with crisis-induced increases in perceived importer liquidity/default risk.

Main role: These crisis/new-customer terms are important supporting evidence for the crisis mechanism, but the central conclusions of the paper are broader and rely primarily on the institutional and relationship results.
Settings.H862: Section V.D, Table 7, columns (1)-(6), PDF pp. 893-896 (article pp. 893-896).
Settings.G863:
Treatment: Share of a customer's precrisis sales that occurred on postshipment terms, measured from 0 to 1. This is a continuous treatment capturing greater reliance on exporter financing before the crisis.

Method: Cross-customer OLS regressions relate crisis-period sales performance to the precrisis share of transactions on postshipment terms. Outcomes are (i) growth including exit, (ii) growth among continuing customers only, and (iii) an indicator for remaining active during the crisis. Controls include destination-country GDP growth, local currency depreciation, and a local banking-crisis dummy; some columns also include log precrisis sales value and volume. The authors interpret the precrisis financing mix as affecting how severely customers cut purchases during the crisis.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-customer differences in precrisis financing composition, conditioning on observed macro shocks in the customer’s country and initial size measures. The authors argue that customers relying more on postshipment terms had more established/trustworthy relationships and therefore were less exposed to crisis-related liquidity/default shocks. Endogeneity remains because precrisis financing choice may reflect unobserved customer quality or relationship strength that also predicts crisis resilience; this is an observational regression adjustment rather than a quasi-experiment.

Setting: In table 8, the authors argue that the way trade was financed before the 2008-09 crisis causally shaped the decline in trade. The key treatment is the share of precrisis sales on postshipment terms. For overall growth including exit, the coefficient is 0.1687 (SE 0.0425) without size controls and 0.1734 (SE 0.0422) with controls, implying that customers with all purchases on postshipment terms reduced sales less than customers with none on such terms. The authors summarize the magnitude as customers with no postshipment use decreasing sales by 17.3 percentage points more than customers with only postshipment use. Intensive-margin growth coefficients are 0.0999 (SE 0.0425) and 0.0688 (SE 0.0396), and remaining-active coefficients are 0.1199 (SE 0.0373) and 0.1322 (SE 0.0341). They interpret this as evidence that customers previously transacting on cash in advance were hit harder in the crisis.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion emphasize that how trade is financed shapes the impact of crises; table 8 provides the main regression evidence for that central claim.
Settings.H863: Section V.D, Table 8, columns (1)-(6), PDF pp. 895-897 (article pp. 895-897).
Settings.G864:
Treatment: Indicator for village assignment to the high-intensity external hiring shock (treated village) versus low-intensity control. In treated villages, external jobs employ on average 24% of the male labor force; controls hire only 1–5 workers (about 3% shock). The treatment is assignment to a larger village-level labor-supply removal shock, not individual job receipt.

Method: Matched-pair, stratified village-level randomized experiment in 60 Odisha villages. Villages were randomized to a large external hiring shock versus a negligible hiring shock: in treated villages the researchers hired on average 24% of the male casual labor force into temporary external jobs, while control villages had only 1–5 hires. Outcomes are estimated from linear regressions of worker-day wages on a treatment indicator, its interaction with a semi-peak-month indicator, round fixed effects, and sometimes baseline controls for worker mean employment and wages; SEs clustered by village. This is an ITT design on assignment to a higher hiring-shock village. The causal interpretation is that removing workers from the local labor market changes equilibrium local wages. The paper emphasizes separate effects in lean versus semi-peak months to diagnose labor rationing.

Identification: Random assignment of large versus negligible village-level external hiring shocks identifies the effect of reducing the local labor supply available to village employers. The main endogeneity concern is that labor demand, worker composition, or other village characteristics could differ across villages or seasons; randomization within matched-pair strata plus round fixed effects addresses cross-village confounding, while the interaction with semi-peak timing isolates heterogeneity by market slack. Interpretation requires that treatment changes local labor supply meaningfully and that observed wage changes reflect equilibrium responses in the local labor market rather than composition or wealth effects; the authors discuss and test these threats.

Setting: The village-level hiring-shock experiment shows sharply different wage responses by season. In lean months, the high hiring-shock treatment has no detectable effect on local wages: in the preferred spillover-sample regression with controls, the coefficient on Hiring shock is -0.0183 log points for log total wages (SE 0.019). In semi-peak months, the additional interaction is 0.0684, so the total semi-peak treatment effect is about 5.0% and statistically significant (p = 0.0256 for shock + shock×semi-peak). In wage levels, the implied semi-peak effect is Rs. 12.94 (= -5.632 + 18.57), p = 0.0472. The authors interpret the zero lean-season wage response and positive semi-peak response as central evidence that labor is rationed in lean months but not when markets are tighter.

Main role: The abstract and introduction center on whether hiring shocks raise wages in peak months but not in lean months, using this contrast to infer labor rationing. These wage effects are a core experimental result supporting the paper’s main conclusion.
Settings.H864: Section V.B. Wages; Figure 4 panels 1A–1B; Table 3 columns 1–5, especially column 3; PDF pp. 3202–3205.
Settings.G865:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to a treated village with a large external hiring shock versus control village with negligible hiring. This is village-level assignment to removal of local labor supply via external jobs.

Method: Same matched-pair, stratified village-level randomized hiring-shock experiment, but outcomes are alternative wage-contract measures. Linear regressions compare treatment and control villages, interacting treatment with semi-peak months, with round fixed effects and clustered village SEs. The outcomes capture hourly total wage and nonprice job attributes to assess whether the hiring shock changed compensation margins other than the daily wage.

Identification: Random village-level assignment to high versus low hiring shocks identifies how the external labor-supply removal affects alternative dimensions of compensation and job contracts. The authors use these estimates to test whether lean-season zero wage effects are hiding offsetting changes in hours or nonwage amenities. Identification rests on the experimental assignment and the assumption that treatment affects these outcomes only through equilibrium labor-market responses.

Setting: Using the same randomized hiring shock, the paper finds that compensation adjustments occur mainly through hourly wages in semi-peak months, not through nonprice job attributes in lean months. The hourly total wage effect is -0.653 in lean months with an additional 4.422 in semi-peak months, implying a significant positive semi-peak effect (p = 0.0464 for the sum). By contrast, there is little evidence of treatment effects on hours per day, expected future work, expected loans, immediate payment, or advances. These results support the interpretation that the main daily-wage findings reflect genuine wage adjustment rather than hidden changes in contract amenities.

Main role: These are supporting robustness results used to show that the main wage findings are not driven by other compensation margins or contract terms, rather than the central result themselves.
Settings.H865: Section V.B. Wages; Table 4 columns 1–6; PDF p. 3206.
Settings.G866:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to the village-level high-intensity external hiring shock versus low-intensity control hiring shock. The treatment removes a sizable fraction of workers from the local labor market.

Method: Village-level matched-pair randomized hiring-shock experiment estimated by linear regressions on worker-day hired-wage-employment indicators for the spillover sample, with a treatment indicator, treatment interacted with semi-peak month, round fixed effects, baseline controls in preferred specifications, and village-clustered SEs. This is an ITT estimate of employment spillovers on workers who signed up but were not offered external jobs.

Identification: Random assignment of villages to a large versus negligible external hiring shock creates exogenous variation in how many competitors are removed from the local labor market. Among workers who remain in the village but are comparable to those hired externally, the design tests whether local employment opportunities improve. The identifying assumption is that assignment is random and affects spillover-sample employment through local labor-market equilibrium rather than other confounds such as household substitution or wealth effects; the paper discusses and probes these mechanisms.

Setting: For workers left in the village, the hiring shock generates substantial positive employment spillovers in lean months but not in semi-peak months. In the preferred specification with controls (Table 5, col. 2), the lean-month effect on hired wage employment is 0.0544 (SE 0.019) on a control mean of 0.145, which the authors describe as a 38% increase. The interaction with semi-peak is -0.0735, so the semi-peak total effect is near zero (p = 0.427 for shock + shock×semi-peak). The authors interpret this as evidence that, in lean months, previously rationed workers fill job slots vacated by externally hired workers.

Main role: Positive employment spillovers in lean months are one of the paper’s three key predictions under labor rationing and are highlighted in the abstract and introduction as core evidence that over a quarter of labor supply is rationed.
Settings.H866: Section V.C. Individual-Level Employment Spillovers; Figure 4 panels 2A–2B; Table 5, especially column 2; PDF pp. 3205–3206.
Settings.G867:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to the high-intensity village-level external hiring shock versus low-intensity control. This treatment creates a large labor-supply removal from the local village labor market.

Method: Village-level matched-pair randomized hiring-shock experiment estimated on the full village sample, using weighted linear regressions of worker-day local hired-employment indicators on treatment, treatment interacted with semi-peak, round fixed effects, and baseline controls; clustered by village. The purpose is to estimate the effect of the external hiring shock on aggregate local employment levels, excluding the external jobs themselves.

Identification: Random village assignment to high versus low external hiring shocks exogenously varies how many workers are removed from local labor supply. By measuring employment across the full village labor force, the design identifies whether aggregate local employment changes, rather than only employment of specific remaining workers. Identification requires representative sampling/weights and that treatment does not differentially affect outcome measurement. The authors argue that under rationing, aggregate local employment should remain unchanged because rationed workers replace removed workers.

Setting: At the aggregate level, the experiment shows that removing roughly a quarter of the labor force leaves local employment unchanged in lean months but reduces it in semi-peak months. In the full-village worker-day regression (Table 6, col. 1), the lean-month effect on local hired wage employment is 0.0141 (SE 0.020; p = 0.483), while the semi-peak interaction is -0.0559, implying a total semi-peak effect of -0.0418 with p = 0.00477 for the sum. Relative to the semi-peak control mean of 0.195, the authors describe this as a 4.2 percentage point or 22% decline in aggregate employment. This contrast is a core part of their revealed-preference test for labor rationing.

Main role: No change in aggregate local employment in lean months but a decline in semi-peak months is one of the paper’s central equilibrium tests for labor rationing and is emphasized in the abstract and introduction.
Settings.H867: Section V.D. Aggregate Employment; Figure 4 panels 3A–3B; Table 6 columns 1–3; PDF pp. 3206–3208.
Settings.G868:
Treatment: Actual employment in the external jobsites at the village-day level (hiring-shock employment), instrumented by assignment to the high-intensity hiring-shock village. This is a continuous dose: share/amount of external-job employment created by the experiment.

Method: Village-day linear IV using assignment to the village-level hiring shock as an instrument for actual employment in the external jobsites. The reduced form regresses village-day aggregate local hired employment on treatment and its interaction with semi-peak; the first stage regresses external-job employment on the same; the second stage estimates how one additional day of external-job employment affects local hired wage employment. Regressions use village-day observations, round fixed effects, baseline controls, analytical weights, and village-clustered SEs. This is effectively a treatment-on-treated crowd-out estimate of local employment displacement per external workday.

Identification: Random assignment to a large hiring shock provides exogenous variation in actual external-job employment. Using assignment as an instrument isolates the causal effect of experimentally created external workdays on local village employment, netting out endogenous take-up or compliance. The identifying assumption is that assignment affects local employment only through actual external-job employment, not through other channels. The seasonal interaction allows crowd-out to differ with labor-market slack.

Setting: Instrumenting actual external-job employment with randomized village assignment, the paper estimates how much one created external workday displaces local private employment. In semi-peak months, the IV coefficient on hiring-shock employment is -0.252 with an additional lean baseline of -0.0301, so each external workday crowds out about 0.282 days of local employment (reported in text; p < 0.001 for the semi-peak total effect). In lean months, crowd-out is near zero and statistically insignificant. The authors interpret this as showing no private crowd-out when slack is high, but substantial crowd-out when labor markets are tighter.

Main role: The crowd-out calculation translates the experimental employment effects into an interpretable equilibrium displacement parameter, directly supporting the paper’s claim that lean-season crowd-out is zero while semi-peak crowd-out is substantial.
Settings.H868: Section V.E. Crowd-Out; Table 6 columns 3–5; PDF pp. 3207–3208.
Settings.G869:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to the high-intensity village-level hiring shock versus low-intensity control, measured in post-shock follow-up when the shock has ended.

Method: Post-intervention follow-up in the same randomized village hiring-shock experiment. Linear regressions analogous to the main specification estimate effects two weeks after the external hiring shock ends, with treatment, treatment interacted with semi-peak, round fixed effects, baseline controls in preferred specifications, and village-clustered SEs. This assesses persistence of treatment effects after all workers return to the village labor force.

Identification: Random assignment still identifies post-shock differences after the intervention ends. The design tests whether earlier lean-season effects persist, which would be expected under wealth effects but not under a pure temporary rationing mechanism. Identification relies on the original randomization and comparable post-shock measurement across treatment and control villages.

Setting: Two weeks after the hiring shock ends, the lean-season treatment effects disappear, while some semi-peak wage effects persist. In Table 7, the post-shock lean-month effects are close to zero for log total wage (0.00410 with controls), hired wage employment (-0.00846), and self-employment (-0.0177), with no evidence of continued lean-season spillovers. By contrast, the semi-peak interaction for wages remains positive, consistent with wage ratcheting. The authors use this to argue that the lean-season during-shock results reflect temporary relief of labor rationing rather than wealth or demand expansions.

Main role: These are supporting dynamics results used to reinforce the rationing interpretation and rule out wealth effects, rather than the paper’s primary treatment effects during the shock.
Settings.H869: Section V.F. Persistence after the End of the Shock; Table 7 columns 1–4; PDF pp. 3208–3209.
Settings.G870:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to the high-intensity village-level external hiring shock versus low-intensity control hiring shock.

Method: Same village-level randomized hiring-shock experiment, estimated by linear regressions on spillover-sample worker-day self-employment indicators, with treatment, treatment interacted with semi-peak, round fixed effects, and baseline self-employment controls. The authors interpret declines in self-employment during lean months as revealed-preference evidence that some self-employment is disguised unemployment caused by rationing in wage labor markets.

Identification: Random village assignment to large hiring shocks creates exogenous job openings in the local wage labor market. If self-employed workers move into wage work when competition is reduced, that reveals they preferred wage employment at the prevailing wage, indicating disguised unemployment. Identification requires that assignment affects self-employment through labor-market opportunities rather than other shocks to household businesses; the paper bolsters this with the transitory nature of effects and household-level analyses.

Setting: In lean months, the randomized hiring shock reduces self-employment among workers left in the village, implying that part of self-employment is disguised unemployment. In Table 8 column 1, the lean-month effect on any self-employment is -0.0336 (SE 0.019) on a control mean of 0.139; the authors describe this as a 3.4 percentage point or 24% decline. Nonagricultural self-employment falls by 0.0333 in lean months (Table 8 col. 2), and agricultural self-employment also declines on average though less precisely (col. 3). The paper interprets these patterns as evidence that at least 24% of lean-season self-employment among the spillover sample arises because workers are rationed out of wage jobs.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that at least 24% of lean self-employment among casual workers occurs because they cannot find jobs. This is a central substantive implication of the experiment.
Settings.H870: Section VI.A. Self-Employment and Separation Failures; Figure 4 panels 4A–4B; Table 8 columns 1–3; PDF pp. 3210–3211.
Settings.G871:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to the high-intensity village-level external hiring shock versus low-intensity control. Heterogeneity is reported by above-median per capita landholdings for farm households.

Method: Village-level randomized hiring-shock experiment estimating heterogeneous self-employment responses by landholdings and broader village-sample impacts. Linear regressions include treatment, interactions with above-median land per capita and semi-peak, round fixed effects, baseline self-employment controls, and clustered village SEs. Outcomes include agricultural and nonagricultural self-employment among all potential workers and total farm labor at the household level. The design is used to trace labor-rationing effects into household farm production and separability failures.

Identification: Random assignment of villages to large hiring shocks identifies how exogenous reductions in local labor-market rationing affect farm and business labor allocation. Heterogeneity by land per capita is motivated by theory: small farms should be most distorted if the household’s own land cannot fully absorb labor. Identification assumes treatment is randomized and that landholding groups are pre-determined, so differential responses reflect causal heterogeneity rather than endogenous selection.

Setting: The experiment shows that lean-season rationing especially distorts labor allocation on small farms. Across all potential workers, nonagricultural self-employment falls by 3.5 percentage points in lean months (Table 8 col. 5). For agricultural self-employment, the average lean effect among smallholders is -0.105, while the differential for above-median land households is +0.196 (col. 6), implying the decline is concentrated among smaller farms. The authors summarize this as small landholders reducing labor supply to their farms by 10.5 percentage points (64%), meaning more than half of lean-season self-employment on small farms is driven by rationing. At the household level, total farm labor falls by 3.656 worker-days for small farms in lean months, with the interaction offsetting this for larger farms (Table 8 col. 7), which the authors interpret as evidence that labor rationing causes separation failures.

Main role: The paper highlights that effects are concentrated among small landholders and that more than half of small-farm self-employment is driven by rationing; this is a substantive extension of the main claim about disguised unemployment and separation failures.
Settings.H871: Section VI.A. Self-Employment and Separation Failures; Table 8 columns 4–7; PDF pp. 3210–3212.
Settings.G872:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment to the high-intensity village-level external hiring shock versus low-intensity control hiring shock.

Method: Same village-level randomized hiring-shock experiment, estimated by linear regressions on worker-day indicators for any work and two survey-based involuntary-unemployment measures, with treatment, treatment interacted with semi-peak, round fixed effects, and baseline controls in preferred specifications; village-clustered SEs. The authors interpret treatment effects on these outcomes as evidence about how standard survey measures capture labor-market slack under disguised unemployment.

Identification: Randomized hiring shocks create exogenous improvement in labor-market opportunities. Comparing how survey-based unemployment measures respond reveals whether those measures capture rationing when workers can substitute into self-employment. Identification relies on the experimental assignment affecting the underlying labor market rather than survey response behavior alone, and on comparable elicitation across treatment and control villages.

Setting: The hiring shock reveals that traditional survey unemployment measures miss lean-season labor rationing. In Table 9, the treatment has little detectable effect on 'any work' or on the traditional involuntary-unemployment measure in lean months (-0.0322 with controls for the traditional measure; p = 0.242). By contrast, the alternate measure falls by 0.0611 to 0.0699 in lean months, with the no-control estimate significant at p = 0.008, and the authors state that this magnitude closely matches the revealed-preference employment spillovers. They interpret this as evidence that standard surveys understate involuntary unemployment when rationed workers are self-employed rather than openly jobless.

Main role: These are important implications for measurement, but they are secondary to the paper’s central experimental demonstration of labor rationing and disguised unemployment.
Settings.H872: Section VI.B. Measuring Involuntary Unemployment in Surveys; Table 9 columns 1–6; PDF pp. 3212–3213.
Settings.G873:
Treatment: Indicator for assignment of the employer’s village to the high-intensity external hiring shock versus low-intensity control.

Method: Employer-side analysis within the same village-level randomized hiring-shock experiment. Linear regressions compare employers in treated and control villages on survey outcomes, with treatment, treatment interacted with semi-peak, round fixed effects, and clustered village SEs. The sampled employers are not necessarily representative, so the paper treats these findings as suggestive causal evidence about employer impacts of the labor-supply shock.

Identification: Village randomization exogenously changes local labor supply facing employers. Employer survey responses then capture whether the shock constrained production or hiring. Because the employer sample is not guaranteed representative, external validity and even internal precision are weaker; the paper explicitly labels these results suggestive. Still, the causal logic is the same experimental contrast between treated and control villages, differentiated by season.

Setting: Suggestive employer-side evidence matches the worker-side rationing results. In lean months, the randomized hiring shock does not appear to disrupt agricultural work, make hiring harder, or reduce perceived worker ability. In semi-peak months, employers are more likely to hire from outside the village and report difficulties with cultivation timing, while wages are also higher. The authors interpret this as consistent with surplus labor in lean periods but meaningful employer-side scarcity in semi-peak periods.

Main role: The paper presents employer outcomes as supplementary suggestive evidence reinforcing the surplus-labor interpretation, not as the main proof.
Settings.H873: Section VI.C. Effects on Employers; online Appendix Table B.9 discussed in text; PDF pp. 3213–3214.
Settings.G874:
Treatment: District-level NREGA program exposure indicator equal to 1 in districts that had already received the program in NSS round 64, with heterogeneity by whether the district-month had above-median baseline casual employment (low slack) prior to NREGA. The focal treatment is program rollout, not actual program participation.

Method: Suggestive triple-differences analysis of India’s NREGA phased rollout using NSS worker-level data from pre- and post-rollout rounds. The implemented linear specification regresses outcomes on an NREGA district indicator, its interaction with a high-baseline-employment district-month indicator, the high-employment indicator itself, district fixed effects, month-by-year fixed effects, and controls. This is a conventional DDD/DiD-style reduced-form design exploiting cross-district rollout timing and heterogeneity by pre-program labor-market slack. The authors explicitly caution that the size of NREGA exposure in a district-month is endogenous, so these should be viewed as suggestive rather than strong causal claims.

Identification: The design compares districts before/after NREGA rollout and between earlier- and later-rollout districts, while also contrasting high- versus low-slack district-months using pre-program baseline employment. District and month-year fixed effects absorb permanent district differences and common shocks. The main concern is endogenous program intensity within treated district-months, which the authors note prevents strong causal interpretation. The intended identifying idea is that phased rollout is quasi-exogenous and heterogeneity by pre-period slack reveals when the same policy should crowd out private work versus absorb slack labor.

Setting: In a suggestive DDD exercise on NREGA rollout, the paper finds that program effects depend on baseline labor-market slack in ways that mirror the experiment. Where baseline district-month employment is lower (higher slack), NREGA has no detectable effect on wages or private employment, but it reduces self-employment. Where baseline employment is above median (lower slack), wages rise and agricultural employment falls by almost 20 percent. The authors interpret this as external supportive evidence that workfare can absorb rationed workers when slack is high but crowd out private work when markets are tighter, while cautioning that the estimates are not cleanly causal because program intensity is endogenous.

Main role: The NREGA analysis is presented in Section VIII as a suggestive extension linking the experimental insights to policy. It is not part of the paper’s core identification strategy.
Settings.H874: Section VIII. Extension: Labor Market Shocks and Labor Market Slack; equation (2); online Appendix Table B.12 discussed in text; PDF pp. 3218–3220.
Settings.G875:
Treatment: Lagged share of workers from minority group g in firm j in year τ-1, measured as a proportion (0 to 1) of the firm's workforce before hiring. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors regress the minority-group-specific share of new hires in a firm-year on the lagged share of incumbent workers from that same minority group in the firm, using linear regression. The purpose is to show that firms with more incumbent workers from group g are more likely to hire from group g later, consistent with referral-based hiring. Specifications add minority-group-by-year fixed effects, firm demand-side controls, local/industry/occupation-based supply controls, and in one specification the lagged share of other minorities. Standard errors are clustered at the firm level and observations are weighted by the number of hires per year. This is interpreted as evidence on the effect of prior coethnic presence on subsequent hiring of the same minority group.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-firm, within-minority-group over time, in the lagged own-group workforce share. The concern is that persistence in hiring coethnics may reflect demand, labor supply, or general openness to minorities rather than referrals. The authors address this by adding minority-group-by-year fixed effects, demand and supply controls, and controls for other minorities, but this remains regression adjustment rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Setting: Using equation (5), the paper interprets a higher lagged share of workers from minority group g in a firm as causing a higher subsequent share of hires from that group, consistent with referrals by incumbent coethnics. In Munich, the preferred specification with controls reports a coefficient of 0.498 on the lagged own-group share (Table 2, cols. 2–3), implying that a 10 percentage point increase in the prior coethnic share raises the share of hires from that group by about 4.98 percentage points. This result supports the paper’s proxy that coethnic workforce share predicts referral hiring, but it is ancillary to the main causal claims about wages and turnover.

Main role: This is a substantive validation exercise for the proxy-referral mechanism, not a central wage/turnover result emphasized in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H875: Section 5.1.1, equation (5), Table 2 columns (1)–(3), PDF pp. 527–528 (article pp. 528–529).
Settings.G876:
Treatment: Share of workers from the worker's own minority background in the firm one year before hire, measured as a proportion. In PASS–IEB the authors also report the analogous German share for German workers. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors run linear probability models relating whether a worker reports having obtained the job through a referral to the lagged share of workers from the worker's own minority background in the firm before hiring. Using linked PASS–IEB and IAB–SOEP/social security data, they estimate OLS with minimal controls and richer controls; in PASS–IEB they also add pre-estimated worker and firm fixed effects from earlier windows as regressors to proxy for worker and firm heterogeneity. This is used as direct evidence that own-group share predicts actual referral use.

Identification: Identification comes from observed differences in prior coethnic workforce shares across firms for otherwise similar workers. The main concern is confounding from worker sorting and firm heterogeneity. The authors mitigate this with demographic, industry, and firm-size controls and, in PASS–IEB, pre-estimated worker and firm fixed effects from earlier periods. The setting remains observational regression evidence supporting the proxy interpretation.

Setting: The paper interprets a higher prior own-group share in the firm as increasing the probability that a minority worker found the job through a referral. In PASS–IEB, a 10 percentage point increase in own-group share is associated with about a 9.8 to 10.9 percentage point higher referral probability; the preferred PASS–IEB specification with pre-estimated worker and firm effects reports a coefficient of 0.982 (Table 3, col. 3). In the IAB–SOEP Migration Sample, corresponding estimates are 0.550–0.585 (Table 3, cols. 4–5). These findings are used to justify the proxy-based main analysis.

Main role: This is another proxy-validation result establishing that own-group share predicts direct referral reports; it supports the main design but is not itself the headline conclusion.
Settings.H876: Section 5.1.1, Table 3 columns (1)–(5), PDF p. 529 (article p. 529).
Settings.G877:
Treatment: Share of workers from the worker's own minority group in the firm one year before the worker was hired, measured as a proportion of firm employment. It is intended as a proxy for referral exposure rather than direct observed referral status. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate linear wage and turnover regressions on matched employer–employee panel data in which the key treatment is the share of workers from the same minority group in the firm one year before the worker was hired, used as a proxy for referral hiring. They report specifications progressing from OLS to controls, worker fixed effects, firm fixed effects, and their preferred model with both worker and firm fixed effects. Outcomes are log daily wages and an indicator for leaving the firm in t+1. Controls include tenure, log firm size, age and age squared, industry, education, gender, and year fixed effects. The identifying role emphasized by the paper is the inclusion of worker and firm fixed effects to account for non-random sorting of workers into firms and differential use of referrals across workers and firms.

Identification: The paper argues that own-group share before hire affects wages and turnover through a higher probability of referral. Endogeneity concerns are that lower-ability workers may rely more on referrals and sort into certain firms, and lower-productivity firms may both hire more coethnics and pay less or have higher turnover. Worker fixed effects absorb time-invariant worker heterogeneity; firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity; year effects and controls absorb observed confounders. The required additional assumption is exclusion: conditional on worker and firm fixed effects and controls, lagged own-group share has no direct effect on wage and turnover dynamics except through referrals.

Setting: In the matched employer–employee data, the paper interprets a higher lagged coethnic share in the firm as improving match quality via referrals, thereby raising wages and lowering turnover. In the preferred specification with both worker and firm fixed effects (Table 4, Panel A, col. 5), a 10 percentage point increase in own-group share increases wages by 0.43% and lowers the probability of leaving the firm by 0.22 percentage points (the turnover estimate is significant at 10%, as stated in the text). These average effects are part of the paper’s central evidence that referral-based hiring improves worker-firm matches once sorting is accounted for.

Main role: These fixed-effects proxy regressions are a core empirical pillar in the paper and are directly tied to the abstract, introduction, and conclusion claims that referral hires earn more and are less likely to leave, especially early in tenure.
Settings.H877: Section 5.1.2, Table 4 Panel A columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 530–531 (article pp. 530–531).
Settings.G878:
Treatment: Share of workers from the same minority group in the firm one year before hiring, and its interaction with tenure in the firm. The underlying treatment is continuous referral exposure proxied by lagged coethnic share.
