Method: The authors extend their matched employer–employee fixed-effects regressions by interacting the lagged own-group share treatment with tenure to test whether referral effects fade with time in the firm. The preferred implementation includes both worker and firm fixed effects, plus year dummies and controls for tenure, firm size, age, industry, education, and gender. Outcomes are log daily wage and annual turnover. This is the main dynamic estimand implied by their model.

Identification: Identification uses within-worker and within-firm variation, with fixed effects absorbing permanent worker and firm heterogeneity and the interaction with tenure tracing how treatment effects evolve over job duration. The key assumption is again that, conditional on fixed effects and controls, lagged own-group share affects wage and turnover trajectories only through referral-driven match quality. The dynamic pattern is interpreted as learning about productivity over tenure rather than remaining confounding.

Setting: The paper’s preferred dynamic fixed-effects specification shows that referral exposure proxied by lagged coethnic share has particularly strong initial effects that fade with tenure. In Table 4 Panel B column 5, a 10 percentage point increase in own-group share raises wages by 0.66% at the start of the job and reduces annual turnover by 0.52 percentage points; the interaction terms imply wage gains decline by 0.20 percentage points per year and turnover effects converge by 0.26 percentage points per year. These results are central to the claim that referrals reduce informational uncertainty and that learning erodes the initial match-quality advantage over time.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly emphasize that referral effects are strongest at the beginning of the employment relationship and decline with tenure; this panel is a direct test of that central prediction.
Settings.H878: Section 5.1.2, Table 4 Panel B columns (1)–(5); magnitude discussion in Section 5.1.3 and Table 6, PDF pp. 530–534 (article pp. 530–534).
Settings.G879:
Treatment: Lagged share of workers from the same minority group in the firm before hire, interacted with indicators for first year at the firm and subsequent years. Continuous treatment proxying referral exposure.

Method: Using the same matched employer–employee framework as the baseline proxy regressions, the authors estimate separate effects of lagged own-group share for the worker's first year at the firm versus subsequent years. The preferred specification includes both worker and firm fixed effects, plus standard controls and year effects. This is an alternative dynamic parameterization to capture learning and the fade-out of referral effects over tenure.

Identification: Identification again relies on conditional exogeneity of lagged own-group share given worker and firm fixed effects and controls. Splitting the effect between first-year and later years is meant to isolate the stage at which referral-driven information matters most. Remaining concern is that coethnic share may affect wages or separations through channels other than referrals, but the paper argues fixed effects and controls remove sorting-based bias.

Setting: As an alternative to linear tenure interactions, the paper shows that the positive wage and retention effects of referral exposure are concentrated in the first year of employment. In Table 4 Panel C column 5, a 10 percentage point increase in own-group share raises first-year wages by 0.69% versus 0.10% in subsequent years, and lowers first-year turnover by 0.64 percentage points while turnover is higher in subsequent years. The authors interpret this as evidence that referrals improve initial matches and that learning about true productivity quickly erodes the advantage.

Main role: This is a substantive alternative dynamic specification that reinforces the central message that referral advantages are concentrated at the start of the match and dissipate thereafter.
Settings.H879: Section 5.1.2, Table 4 Panel C columns (1)–(5), PDF p. 531 (article p. 531).
Settings.G880:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 if the worker obtained the job through a referral (acquaintances, friends, or relatives) in the PASS–IEB survey; compared against non-referral hires or, in the augmented specification, relative to unknown-referral spells with reported referral-vs-nonreferral differences. Binary treatment.

Method: With linked PASS–IEB survey and administrative data, the authors estimate linear wage regressions where the treatment is direct reported referral status rather than the coethnic-share proxy. They use two implementations: (i) only spells with known referral status, adding pre-estimated worker and firm fixed effects from earlier 6-year windows as controls; and (ii) augmenting those spells with all other full-time social security spells from 2002–2012 and jointly estimating worker and firm fixed effects, with unknown-referral spells as the omitted category and reported coefficients as the difference between referral and non-referral indicators. Controls include tenure (cubic), log firm size, age, age squared, industry, education, gender, and year effects. This is a linear fixed-effects/adjustment design with direct referral measurement.

Identification: The authors seek to identify the effect of actual referral hiring on wage trajectories while addressing non-random worker and firm selection into referrals. Because the survey sample is small and sparse over time, they either include pre-estimated worker and firm effects from earlier windows as proxies for unobserved wage heterogeneity or jointly estimate worker and firm fixed effects in an augmented administrative sample. Identification therefore comes from conditional comparisons of referred and non-referred spells after absorbing persistent worker and firm wage components, assuming no remaining time-varying confounding correlated with referral status.

Setting: Using direct survey information on referrals linked to social security records, the paper finds that referred workers start at higher wages but have slower wage growth with tenure. In the preferred augmented fixed-effects specification (Table 5 Panel A, second sub-panel, col. 5), the referral coefficient is 0.034 and the referral×tenure coefficient is −0.023; the text summarizes this as referrals increasing starting wages by around 3.3% with the effect declining by roughly 1.7 to 2.3 percentage points per year. This directly measured-referral evidence materially supports the paper’s main claim that referrals improve initial matches.

Main role: Direct referral estimates are one of the two central empirical approaches highlighted in the introduction and abstract; they corroborate the proxy-based main findings using observed referrals.
Settings.H880: Section 5.2, Table 5 Panel A columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 533–534 (article pp. 533–534).
Settings.G881:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 if the worker obtained the job through a referral (acquaintances, friends, or relatives) in the PASS–IEB survey, interacted with tenure. Binary treatment.

Method: Using linked PASS–IEB data with direct referral status, the authors estimate linear turnover regressions for full-time workers in which the dependent variable is separation from the firm and the treatment is referral status interacted with tenure. Because monthly tenure is only available for PASS–IEB spells, they use the restricted PASS–IEB sample and include pre-estimated worker and firm fixed effects from earlier 6-year windows as controls rather than jointly estimating fixed effects in the turnover regressions. Additional controls include a cubic in tenure, log firm size, age, age squared, industry, education, gender, minority status, and year effects.

Identification: Identification compares referred and non-referred workers after controlling for observed characteristics and pre-estimated worker and firm turnover propensities from past windows. The endogeneity concern is non-random worker and firm selection into referral hiring. The strategy assumes that these pre-estimated fixed effects, plus controls, sufficiently proxy for persistent heterogeneity and that remaining differences in turnover by referral status reflect improved initial matches that fade with learning.

Setting: With direct referral information from PASS–IEB, the paper finds that referred workers are less likely to leave their firms initially, with the retention advantage shrinking over tenure. In Table 5 Panel B column 5, the referral coefficient is −0.016 and the referral×tenure coefficient is 0.012; the text interprets this as an initial reduction of about 1.6 percentage points, or 24.6% of the baseline monthly turnover rate of 6.5%, with rapid convergence thereafter. This is a central substantive result supporting the claim that referrals generate better initial matches.

Main role: This is direct evidence for the paper’s central retention claim using observed referrals, complementing the proxy-based matched employer–employee results.
Settings.H881: Section 5.2, Table 5 Panel B columns (1)–(5); summary Table 6, PDF pp. 533–534 (article pp. 533–534).
Settings.G882:
Treatment: Counterfactual reduction in uncertainty from hiring through referrals, operationalized structurally as a lower variance of the productivity signal in the referral market (σ_R^2 < σ_E^2) versus a counterfactual with σ_R^2 = σ_E^2. This is not a simple observed binary treatment; it is a structural parameter change.

Method: The authors perform a structural calibration/simulation exercise based on their search-and-learning model. They use model-implied wage gaps between referral and external hires at entry and in subsequent periods to match empirical moments from the fixed-effects matched employer–employee analysis. Over a grid of values for the learning rate α and the referral-market signal variance σ_R^2, they minimize the squared distance between model and data moments, given calibrated values for other structural parameters. They then compute counterfactual welfare by re-solving the model under σ_R^2 = σ_E^2, i.e., no informational advantage from referrals. This is a structural counterfactual, not a linear reduced-form design.

Identification: Identification is model-based rather than quasi-experimental. The authors infer structural parameters by matching empirical moments for wage differences between referral and external hires at entry and in later periods. The welfare effect is then obtained from a counterfactual simulation setting referral-market uncertainty equal to external-market uncertainty. Validity depends on the structural model, calibration choices, and the assumption that observed wage patterns are generated by informational advantages of referrals.

Setting: The paper uses a calibrated structural model to quantify how much referral hiring reduces uncertainty and increases welfare. Matching model moments to the empirical wage gaps from the matched employer–employee analysis, the authors estimate σ_R^2 = 0.62 and α = 0.50, implying that referrals reduce uncertainty about worker productivity by 41.4% relative to the external market. In a counterfactual that removes the informational advantage of referrals (σ_R^2 = σ_E^2), welfare falls; equivalently, the paper reports that referrals increase total welfare by 0.62% (standard deviation 0.15%). This is a structural interpretation extending the main reduced-form evidence.

Main role: The welfare calibration is important for interpretation but secondary relative to the core reduced-form evidence on wages and turnover.
Settings.H882: Section 5.4 and Appendix A.5, PDF pp. 535–541 (article pp. 535–541).
Settings.G883:
Treatment: Exposure to the 1967 federal minimum-wage coverage extension: indicator for working in an industry covered for the first time in 1967 versus an industry already covered in 1938. Implemented as Covered in 1967_j interacted with post/reform-year indicators. Binary industry-level treatment assignment.

Method: Baseline cross-industry difference-in-differences/event-study using March CPS 1962–1981 microdata. The authors compare workers in industries first covered by the federal minimum wage in 1967 (treated: agriculture, hotels, restaurants, schools, hospitals, nursing homes, laundries, other services) to workers in industries covered since 1938 (control), before and after 1967. Regressions include industry and year fixed effects plus worker controls: gender, race, schooling, cubic in experience, occupation, marital status, full-time/part-time status, weeks worked, and hours worked. Standard errors are clustered at the industry level. Identification relies on parallel pretrends in annual earnings between newly covered and previously covered industries absent the reform.

Identification: Identification comes from differential timing/exposure across industries: newly covered industries receive the federal minimum wage in 1967 while previously covered industries serve as controls. The key concern is confounding industry-specific shocks or regional trends; the paper argues in favor of the design using parallel prereform trends and robustness to controls and alternative specifications. The causal claim assumes that absent the reform, annual earnings in treated and control industries would have evolved similarly.

Setting: Using CPS microdata and a cross-industry DiD, the authors estimate that the 1967 minimum-wage coverage expansion increased annual earnings in newly covered industries by about 5.3% in 1967 relative to already covered industries, with effects peaking around 6.7% by 1971 and averaging 6.5 log points over 1967–1972. The result is interpreted causally as the effect of extending federal minimum-wage coverage to previously uncovered sectors. This finding is central to the paper’s argument that the reform substantially raised low-end pay and contributed to the decline in racial earnings inequality.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion center on showing that the 1967 minimum-wage extension raised earnings in newly covered industries and helped reduce racial inequality. This CPS cross-industry DiD is the paper’s baseline wage design.
Settings.H883: Section IV.A–IV.B; equation (1); Figure V (PDF p. 21 / article p. 189); Table I col. (1) (PDF p. 23 / article p. 191); Table III (PDF p. 27 / article p. 195).
Settings.G884:
Treatment: Indicator for employment in industries first covered by the federal minimum wage in 1967, interacted with post-1967 period indicators; binary treated-versus-control industry exposure.

Method: Cross-industry DiD robustness specifications for CPS annual earnings, all reported in Table I. Same treated and control industries and same linear model as the baseline, with variants adding state linear trends, state-by-year fixed effects, excluding agriculture, restricting to full-time workers, adding 1961 industries to controls, winsorizing data, and two-way clustered standard errors. These are substantive robustness exercises around the baseline causal wage effect.

Identification: Same cross-industry parallel-trends strategy as the baseline. These variants address concerns about differential state trends, state-specific shocks, agriculture-specific shocks, sample composition, outliers, and inference. The identifying assumption remains that absent the reform, treated and control industries would have followed similar wage paths conditional on the added controls.

Setting: A battery of CPS DiD robustness checks yields wage effects between roughly 5.6 and 6.5 log points over 1967–1972, very close to the baseline estimate. Adding state linear trends gives 6.0 log points; adding state-by-year fixed effects gives 6.1; excluding agriculture gives 5.6; restricting to full-time workers gives 6.5; including 1961 industries in controls gives 5.8; winsorizing gives 6.3; and two-way clustering leaves the point estimate at 6.5. These results reinforce the paper’s claim that the 1967 coverage extension causally raised annual earnings in newly covered industries.

Main role: These specifications support the credibility of the main wage result by checking sensitivity to alternative trends, samples, controls, and inference, but they are not the headline design.
Settings.H884: Section IV.C; Table I cols. (2)–(8) (PDF p. 23 / article p. 191).
Settings.G885:
Treatment: Indicator for working in an industry first covered by the federal minimum wage in 1967 versus industries covered in 1938, interacted with post/reform-year indicators. Binary treatment exposure.

Method: Cross-industry DiD heterogeneity analysis in CPS by education. The authors estimate the same industry-by-post/event-time DiD separately for low-education workers (11 years of schooling or less) and high-education workers (more than 11 years), with industry and year fixed effects and the standard worker controls. This is a subgroup treatment-effect analysis under the same identification strategy.

Identification: Same cross-industry DiD with subgroup-specific estimation. The argument is that if the reform is the source of the wage response, effects should be concentrated among low-education workers who are more likely to earn near the minimum wage. Parallel trends within subgroup-specific treated and control industries are assumed.

Setting: Estimating the CPS cross-industry DiD separately by education, the authors find that the 1967 reform increased annual earnings by about 10.1% in 1967 for workers with 11 years of schooling or less, versus only 2.5% for workers with more than 11 years. They interpret this concentration at the lower-skill end as evidence that the policy raised wages where the minimum wage should bind most strongly, supporting the paper’s central wage mechanism.

Main role: This heterogeneity result substantively supports the interpretation that the estimated wage effects reflect minimum-wage mechanics concentrated among low-wage/low-education workers, but it is ancillary to the headline average effect.
Settings.H885: Section IV.B.2; Figure VI Panel A (PDF p. 28 / article p. 196); Table III (PDF p. 27 / article p. 195).
Settings.G886:
Treatment: Indicator for working in industries first covered in 1967 versus industries covered in 1938, interacted with post/reform-year indicators. Binary industry treatment exposure.

Method: Cross-industry DiD heterogeneity analysis in CPS by race. The authors estimate separate DiD/event-study regressions for black and white workers, comparing newly covered to previously covered industries before and after 1967. Industry and year fixed effects and worker controls are included; robustness variants add state fixed effects and state-by-year fixed effects.

Identification: The identifying variation is again industry coverage status interacted with the post-1967 period, now estimated separately by race. The key endogeneity concern is that other civil-rights-era shocks may differentially affect black workers, especially in Southern states. The authors address this by showing robustness to state-by-year fixed effects and by emphasizing the sharp timing in 1967 and the treated-versus-control industry contrast within race.

Setting: In race-specific CPS DiD regressions, the 1967 minimum-wage extension raised annual earnings much more for black workers than for white workers. Over 1967–1972, the estimated increase is 9.5 log points for black workers and 5.4 log points for white workers in the baseline specification; with state-by-year fixed effects, the corresponding estimates remain 7.4 and 4.8 log points. The authors interpret this as causal evidence that the reform disproportionately boosted black workers’ earnings and thereby reduced racial wage inequality, a central claim of the paper.

Main role: A core contribution of the paper is that the minimum-wage expansion had much larger wage effects for black workers than white workers, helping explain falling racial inequality. This race-specific DiD directly supports that central conclusion.
Settings.H886: Section IV.D; Figure VI Panel B (PDF p. 28 / article p. 196); Table V (PDF p. 33 / article p. 201); Table III (PDF p. 27 / article p. 195).
Settings.G887:
Treatment: Indicator for being in an industry newly covered by the federal minimum wage in 1967 versus previously covered manufacturing industries; in the DDD specification this is additionally interacted with post and South indicators. The underlying treatment is binary coverage exposure.

Method: BLS industry-wage-report difference-in-differences and triple-differences on hourly wages. The authors compare newly covered industries to previously covered manufacturing industries before versus after 1967 using aggregated industry-region-year cells. They estimate (i) a cross-industry DiD with industry, region, and year fixed effects; and (ii) a cross-industry triple-difference adding South interactions to test for larger Southern effects. Standard errors are clustered at the industry level; they report both a full sample and a stricter sample with balanced pre/post industry availability.

Identification: The identifying variation is differential exposure of industries to the 1967 federal minimum-wage extension, comparing newly covered sectors with already covered manufacturing sectors before and after the reform. The DDD adds South versus non-South variation to examine whether effects were larger where the bite was greater and black workers were more concentrated. Assumptions are that absent the reform, treated and control industries would have followed similar hourly-wage trends, and in the DDD that any differential South trends are common across treated and control absent treatment.

Setting: Using newly digitized BLS hourly wage distributions, the authors estimate that the 1967 reform raised hourly wages in newly covered industries by about 8.3 log points relative to previously covered industries in 1967–1969 in the full-sample DiD, and by 11.7 log points in the strict sample. In the DDD, the treated-industry South interaction implies an additional Southern wage increase of 7.5 log points in the full sample. These estimates are interpreted causally as the effect of extending minimum-wage coverage and help validate the CPS annual-earnings results on a cleaner hourly-pay measure.

Main role: The BLS hourly-wage analysis is one of the paper’s major complementary designs and is emphasized in the introduction as confirming large wage effects using newly digitized wage distributions. It materially supports the main substantive conclusions.
Settings.H887: Section IV.B.4; equation (2); Table IV (PDF p. 30 / article p. 198).
Settings.G888:
Treatment: Indicator for residing/working in a strongly treated state with no minimum wage law as of January 1966 versus a weakly treated state with a preexisting minimum wage law. Treatment reflects more binding exposure to the 1967 federal reform. Binary treatment at the state level.

Method: Alternative cross-state difference-in-differences on wages using March CPS, exploiting variation in whether states had preexisting state minimum wage laws before the 1967 federal expansion. The authors compare strongly treated states (no state minimum wage law as of January 1966) to weakly treated states (states with such laws), pooling estimates over pre and post periods. Regressions include state and time fixed effects plus worker controls; standard errors are clustered at the state level.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-state differences in how binding the federal reform was because some states already had state minimum wage laws covering these sectors and others did not. The causal assumption is that absent the reform, wages in strongly and weakly treated states would have evolved similarly conditional on state and time fixed effects and covariates. The main concern is differential regional trends, especially because strongly treated states are concentrated in the South; the paper argues prereform parallel trends and consistency with other designs support the interpretation.

Setting: Under a cross-state DiD comparing states without preexisting minimum wage laws to states with them, the authors find that annual wages in strongly treated states rose by about 4.1% more than in weakly treated states over 1967–1972 after the federal expansion. They interpret this as causal evidence that where the 1967 reform was more binding, wages rose more. This design is secondary for wages but important because it provides the framework later used for employment outcomes.

Main role: This is an alternative wage design used partly to motivate the employment analysis by geography. It corroborates the wage findings but is not the headline causal specification for wages.
Settings.H888: Section IV.E; equation (3); discussion and Online Appendix Table E2 referenced on PDF p. 35 / article p. 203.
Settings.G889:
Treatment: Indicator for strongly treated state (no state minimum wage law as of January 1966) versus weakly treated state. Binary exposure to a more binding 1967 reform.

Method: Cross-state DiD for employment-intensive-margin outcomes using March CPS. The authors use the same strongly-treated-versus-weakly-treated state design as in the alternative wage analysis, with state and time fixed effects and worker controls, to estimate effects on log annual hours worked conditional on employment. Standard errors are clustered at the state level.

Identification: The design relies on differential bite of the reform across states with and without preexisting state minimum wage laws. The key concern is that strongly treated states, many in the South, could have different labor-market trends. The authors argue that annual hours evolved similarly before 1967 and that the postreform estimates are close to zero, supporting the causal interpretation under parallel trends.

Setting: Using a state-level DiD, the authors find no detectable effect of the 1967 federal minimum-wage reform on annual hours worked conditional on employment. Figure VIII Panel A shows no post-1967 divergence between strongly and weakly treated states, and the authors report that they can rule out annual-hours elasticities with respect to the average wage below about −0.16 for all workers and −0.21 for black workers over 1967–1972. This supports the paper’s main claim of limited labor-demand responses.

Main role: The absence of substantial disemployment is a central conclusion of the paper. Intensive-margin hours effects are part of that main employment evidence, though less central than extensive-margin employment probabilities.
Settings.H889: Section V.A.1; Figure VIII Panel A (PDF p. 38 / article p. 206); discussion on PDF p. 37 / article p. 205 and Online Appendix Table E4 referenced there.
Settings.G890:
Treatment: Indicator for strongly treated state lacking a state minimum wage law as of January 1966, versus weakly treated state with such a law. Binary state-level treatment intensity.

Method: Cross-state DiD for extensive-margin employment outcomes using March CPS. The authors compare strongly treated states (no state minimum wage law as of January 1966) to weakly treated states before and after the reform. Linear probability models include state and time fixed effects and controls. Outcomes include employment versus unemployment and employment versus unemployment-or-not-in-labor-force; wage effects from the same cross-state design are used to form implied elasticities. Standard errors are clustered at the state level.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-state heterogeneity in how binding the federal expansion was, due to preexisting state minimum wage laws. The paper’s key assumption is that, absent the reform, employment outcomes in strongly and weakly treated states would have followed similar trends. Concerns include region-specific shocks and contemporaneous policy changes; the authors present prereform parallel-trend evidence and consistency across alternative state-treatment-intensity measures.

Setting: In the main CPS employment design, the 1967 reform has essentially zero estimated effect on the probability of employment. The difference-in-differences coefficient for employment versus unemployment over 1967–1972 is −0.001 for all workers, with a wage effect of 0.040 log points in the same design, implying an employment elasticity around −0.03 and allowing the authors to rule out elasticities more negative than −0.16. For employment versus unemployment or nonparticipation, the coefficient is 0.002, again near zero. These results are central evidence that the wage gains from the reform did not come with large aggregate employment losses.

Main role: Showing that the reform did not generate large employment losses is one of the paper’s headline findings in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. This cross-state DiD is the main CPS employment design.
Settings.H890: Section V.A.2; Table VI first panel/first three columns (PDF p. 40 / article p. 208); Figure VIII Panel B (PDF p. 38 / article p. 206).
Settings.G891:
Treatment: Indicator for being in a strongly treated state with no state minimum wage law as of January 1966 versus a weakly treated state with such a law. Binary state-level treatment intensity.

Method: Cross-state DiD employment heterogeneity by race in March CPS. The authors estimate the same strongly-treated-versus-weakly-treated state design separately for black and white individuals, for extensive-margin employment outcomes, and pair those estimates with race-specific wage effects from the same cross-state framework to compute implied elasticities. State and time fixed effects and demographic controls are included; standard errors are clustered at the state level.

Identification: Same cross-state treatment-intensity strategy as the main employment design, now estimated separately by race. The concern is that black labor markets, particularly in the South, may have different secular trends or be differentially affected by civil-rights-era shocks. The authors rely on prereform parallel trends and alternative state-intensity measures to support the interpretation that the estimated employment effects remain near zero for black workers despite larger wage gains.

Setting: Race-specific cross-state DiD estimates show no statistically significant disemployment for either black or white workers. For black workers, the employment-versus-unemployment coefficient over 1967–1972 is −0.012, while the wage effect is 0.123 log points, implying an elasticity of about −0.10 and allowing the authors to rule out elasticities more negative than −0.24. For white workers, the employment coefficient is −0.001 with a 0.025 log wage effect, again near zero. These results underpin the paper’s claim that the reform reduced racial earnings and income gaps without materially harming black employment.

Main role: The paper’s contribution is specifically about racial inequality. The finding that black workers experienced large wage gains without significant employment losses is a central headline result.
Settings.H891: Section V.A.3; Table VI first panel, Black and White columns (PDF p. 40 / article p. 208).
Settings.G892:
Treatment: Two nonbinary state-level treatment intensity measures: (a) the 1966 Kaitz index, a weighted minimum-to-median wage ratio incorporating state-, demographic-, and industry-specific minimum wages; and (b) the 1966 share of workers with wages below $1.60 in each state. Each is interacted with post-period indicators.

Method: Alternative cross-state DiD employment and wage analyses using continuous treatment-intensity measures: (i) the 1966 state-level Kaitz index and (ii) the 1966 fraction of affected workers in each state. The authors estimate the effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in each treatment measure on employment and earnings over 1967–1972, with state and time fixed effects and controls. These are robustness versions of the cross-state causal design.

Identification: Identification uses continuous cross-state variation in prereform minimum-wage bite rather than a binary strong/weak treatment indicator. The key assumption is parallel trends across states conditional on the treatment intensity and fixed effects. These designs address concern that the binary strong/weak split may misclassify treatment intensity or throw away useful variation.

Setting: Using alternative state-level measures of treatment intensity, the authors again find large wage effects and small employment effects. A one-standard-deviation increase in the 1966 Kaitz index raises earnings by 0.014 log points and changes employment-versus-unemployment by −0.001 for all workers; using the fraction of affected workers, the corresponding effects are 0.022 and −0.001. For black workers, wage effects are larger (0.051 and 0.064) while employment effects remain modest (−0.008 and −0.010). These robustness results reinforce the paper’s conclusion that the 1967 reform had limited disemployment effects even where its bite was larger.

Main role: These are robustness exercises showing the main cross-state employment conclusions are not driven by the binary state classification. They support, rather than define, the main result.
Settings.H892: Section V.A.5; Table VI columns under “Alternative design 1: Kaitz index” and “Alternative design 2: Fraction of affected workers” (PDF p. 40 / article p. 208).
Settings.G893:
Treatment: Introduction of the federal minimum wage in newly covered industries in 1967, operationalized through the new wage floor in hourly wage distributions. In the case study, the relevant treated setting is laundries in the U.S. South facing a $1 nominal minimum in 1967. Treatment is effectively a binary policy change at the industry-region level.

Method: Bunching estimator using BLS hourly wage distributions to infer employment effects of the newly introduced minimum wage within treated industries. The authors construct a counterfactual 1967 wage distribution absent the reform by inflating 1966 nominal wages by national income growth, then compare observed versus counterfactual employment below the minimum wage (‘missing jobs’) and at/slightly above it (‘excess jobs’). They define total employment effect as excess minus missing jobs, normalize by pretreatment employment, and divide by the percent change in average wages to obtain an employment elasticity. This is not a standard linear DiD estimator and is therefore classified as Other.

Identification: Identification assumes that, absent the reform, the wage distribution in treated laundries in the South would have shifted according to aggregate nominal income growth from 1966 to 1967. Deviations from this counterfactual around the new minimum wage are attributed to the policy. The main concern is counterfactual misspecification—e.g., industry-specific or regional shocks changing the wage distribution independently of the minimum wage. The case study is chosen because the reform was highly binding there and the bunching pattern is visually stark.

Setting: In the illustrative case of Southern laundries, the observed 1967 hourly wage distribution shows substantial bunching at the new $1 minimum relative to a counterfactual distribution without reform. Excess jobs just above the minimum roughly offset missing jobs below it, implying an employment elasticity of 0.02 under the baseline assumption that spillovers extend to 115% of the minimum wage, and 0.16 under a 120% spillover assumption. The authors interpret this as near-zero employment impact in a sector-region cell where the reform was especially binding and black workers were overrepresented.

Main role: The bunching design is a central second employment design, highlighted in the abstract and introduction as showing no aggregate employment effect and near-zero employment effects in highly affected treated industries.
Settings.H893: Section V.B.2; Figure IX Panel A (PDF p. 45 / article p. 213); Table VII row “Laundries, South” (PDF p. 46 / article p. 214).
Settings.G894:
Treatment: Introduction of the federal minimum wage in newly covered industries in 1967, applied within treated industry-by-region cells. The treatment is a binary policy shock to each covered industry-region cell, though effect magnitude varies with the prereform wage distribution.

Method: Generalized bunching-estimator analysis across 16 treated industry × region cells from the BLS wage reports (laundries, hotels, restaurants, nursing homes across South, Midwest, Northeast, West). For each cell, the authors compare observed and counterfactual 1967 wage distributions to estimate missing and excess jobs around the new minimum wage, then compute employment elasticities with respect to average wages under alternative spillover assumptions (115% and 120% of the minimum wage).

Identification: As in the case study, identification assumes the counterfactual no-reform wage distribution can be generated by inflating prereform wages by aggregate income growth (plus a special adjustment for nursing homes). Differences between observed and counterfactual low-wage employment near the minimum are attributed to the reform. Threats include industry-region-specific shocks or incorrect assumptions about spillovers and counterfactual growth. The authors address this by showing broadly similar results across many cells and under alternative spillover cutoffs.

Setting: Applying the bunching design across 16 industry-region cells, the authors find that excess jobs just above the new minimum roughly match missing jobs below it, with the fitted relationship lying close to the 45-degree zero-employment-effect line. Elasticities range from about −0.70 to 0.45 across cells, and when aggregated across all industries the implied elasticity is 0.06 under the baseline 115% spillover assumption and −0.21 under a 120% spillover assumption. The authors interpret these results as evidence of low employment responses overall in newly covered industries, consistent with the CPS employment analysis.

Main role: This generalized bunching evidence is a major pillar of the paper’s claim that the reform had little aggregate employment effect in treated industries and is emphasized in the abstract and introduction.
Settings.H894: Section V.B.3; Figure IX Panel B (PDF p. 45 / article p. 213); Table VII all rows and bottom aggregate row (PDF p. 46 / article p. 214).
Settings.G895:
Treatment: Being a black worker relative to a white worker within treated industries and within control industries, traced over time around the 1967 reform. The substantive treatment of interest is the racial earnings gap and how it changes after minimum-wage extension in covered industries. Binary race indicator in interacted year regressions.

Method: Adjusted racial-gap regressions estimated separately within treated and control sectors. The authors regress log annual earnings on a black-worker indicator interacted with year indicators, plus controls for gender, schooling, experience, full-time/part-time status, weeks and hours worked, occupation, marital status, and industry controls, to trace the evolution of the adjusted black-white earnings gap over time. This is a regression-adjustment design used to interpret the effect of the minimum-wage reform on racial wage inequality, rather than a DiD with a single treatment coefficient.

Identification: The authors interpret the sharper post-1967 decline in the adjusted racial gap within treated industries, relative to control industries and relative to prereform trends, as evidence of a causal role for the minimum-wage extension. The main endogeneity concern is that other contemporaneous factors may differentially affect black-white gaps in treated sectors; the paper argues against this by showing parallel prereform trends and concentration among low-education workers in treated industries. Still, this setting is implemented as regression adjustment tracing subgroup gaps rather than a formal single-coefficient DiD.

Setting: Separate adjusted-gap regressions show that before 1967, white workers earned about 20%–25% more than observably similar black workers in both treated and control industries. After the minimum-wage extension, the adjusted racial earnings gap in treated industries falls sharply and is close to zero by the mid-1970s, while a roughly 10% adjusted gap remains in control industries. The authors interpret this as causal evidence that the reform substantially compressed within-industry racial pay disparities, a key part of the paper’s explanation for the decline in racial inequality.

Main role: A central paper conclusion is that within treated industries the adjusted racial earnings gap fell from about 25 log points to roughly zero after the reform. This result is highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H895: Section VI.B; equation (7); Figure XI Panels A–B (PDF pp. 52–53 / article pp. 220–221).
Settings.G896:
Treatment: The 1967 extension of the federal minimum wage to previously uncovered industries, assessed through its contribution to the economy-wide black-white earnings gap. Treatment is a binary policy reform, but implemented through counterfactual decomposition rather than a regression treatment variable.

Method: Decomposition-based counterfactual analysis of the economy-wide unadjusted racial earnings gap. The authors algebraically decompose the total black-white earnings gap into within-control, within-treated, and between-industry components, then project a counterfactual path absent the 1967 reform by assuming that (i) the treated-industry racial gap would have evolved like the control-industry racial gap and (ii) the black control-treatment earnings gap would have evolved like the white control-treatment gap. This is not a standard regression estimator but a structured counterfactual accounting exercise built from observed gap series.

Identification: The counterfactual rests on extrapolating pre-1967 relationships: absent the reform, the racial gap in treated industries would have tracked the racial gap in control industries, and the black control-treatment earnings differential would have tracked the corresponding white differential. The main concern is that these extrapolated paths might not hold without the reform because of other shocks. The paper argues that prereform parallelism and the timing of the 1967 break support the interpretation.

Setting: Using a decomposition of the total racial earnings gap and a counterfactual path without the reform, the authors estimate that the 1967 minimum-wage extension explains about 20% of the decline in the economy-wide unadjusted black-white earnings gap between 1965 and 1980. In the counterfactual, the gap would have been 31 log points instead of 25 log points in 1980, with 82% of the explained decline arising from within-industry convergence in treated sectors. This quantification is a central causal claim of the paper about minimum-wage policy’s role in reducing racial inequality.

Main role: Quantifying how much of the decline in racial inequality the reform explains is one of the paper’s most important substantive conclusions and is emphasized in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H896: Section VI.A; equation (5) and equation (6); Figure X (PDF p. 50 / article p. 218).
Settings.G897:
Treatment: Foreign minus US short-term nominal interest rate differential, annualized, measured at monthly frequency; specifically r_f,t* - r_f,t. Continuous spread, not binary.

Method: Panel linear predictability regressions of one-month annualized 10-year foreign-minus-US bond dollar excess return differentials, currency excess returns, and local-currency bond excess return differentials on the foreign-minus-US short-term interest rate differential. The panel includes country fixed effects and Driscoll-Kraay standard errors with fixed-b inference; individual-country versions are also reported with Newey-West errors, but the panel FE specification is the main implemented panel estimator at this location. Identification is interpretive/predictive rather than quasi-experimental: the authors treat changes in interest-rate differentials as affecting expected returns/risk premia, with country FE absorbing time-invariant country heterogeneity, but they do not claim a clean exogenous shock design.

Identification: The paper uses within-country-over-time variation in short-rate differentials relative to the US, with country fixed effects removing time-invariant cross-country differences. The intended interpretation is that higher foreign short rates predict higher currency excess returns but lower local bond return differentials, so the net effect on dollar long-bond returns is near zero. Endogeneity is unresolved: short rates may reflect omitted state variables, measurement error, or equilibrium responses rather than exogenous treatment. The identifying assumption for a causal reading is that conditional on country FE and the predictive-regression setup, movements in the interest-rate differential capture variation in expected carry and term premia rather than confounding shifts unrelated to risk premia.

Setting: In Table 1 panel A, the authors interpret the foreign-minus-US short-rate differential as changing expected returns. In the country-FE panel, a 1-unit increase in the annualized short-rate differential predicts a 1.98 increase in annualized currency excess returns (y2) and a -1.34 change in annualized local-currency bond return differentials (y3), leaving only a 0.65 effect on 10-year dollar bond return differentials (y1), which is statistically insignificant. This pattern is central to the paper's claim that currency carry premia at the short end are offset by local term premia for long bonds.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize the time-series finding that predictability of foreign bond returns in dollars declines with maturity and that local term premia offset currency risk premia. Table 1 panel regressions are core evidence for that claim.
Settings.H897: Section I.C, Table 1 Panel A, row 'Panel' (PDF pp. 4146-4149, especially PDF p. 4148-4149).
Settings.G898:
Treatment: Foreign minus US yield-curve slope differential, where slope is 10-year yield minus 1-month rate; annualized monthly predictor. Continuous, not binary.

Method: Panel linear predictability regressions of one-month annualized 10-year foreign-minus-US bond dollar excess return differentials, currency excess returns, and local-currency bond excess return differentials on the foreign-minus-US yield-curve slope differential. The panel includes country fixed effects and Driscoll-Kraay standard errors with fixed-b inference; individual-country regressions are also shown. This is a fixed-effects predictive regression rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: Identification comes from within-country time variation in foreign-minus-US slope differentials in a country-FE panel. The authors interpret steeper foreign yield curves as changing expected currency and local bond returns. Country FE absorb invariant country characteristics, but there is no exogenous source of slope movements; the design relies on the predictive content of the slope conditional on fixed effects. The causal interpretation assumes slope differentials summarize state variables that govern expected carry and term premia rather than omitted confounders.

Setting: In Table 1 panel B, a higher foreign-minus-US yield-curve slope differential predicts lower currency excess returns but higher local-currency long-bond excess returns. In the country-FE panel, the coefficient is -2.02 for currency excess returns (y2) and 3.96 for local-currency bond return differentials (y3), implying a net 1.94 effect on 10-year dollar bond return differentials (y1), only marginally significant and in the opposite direction from the short-bond carry logic. This is core evidence that variation in local term premia offsets or more than offsets currency carry premia for long bonds.

Main role: The paper stresses that the slope of the yield curve is a strong predictor and that local term premia more than offset currency premia as maturity rises. Table 1 Panel B is a main empirical result supporting the core argument.
Settings.H898: Section I.C, Table 1 Panel B, row 'Panel' (PDF pp. 4147-4150, especially PDF p. 4148-4150).
Settings.G899:
Treatment: Assignment to high versus low short-term interest rate-deviation portfolios; focal contrast is Portfolio 3 minus Portfolio 1 after sorting countries each month by short rates relative to their own 10-year rolling mean. Implemented as a binary long-short contrast between top and bottom portfolio groups.

Method: Monthly portfolio-sort long-short strategy based on short-term interest rates in deviation from each country's past 10-year rolling mean ('conditionally' low/high rates). Countries are sorted into three portfolios and rebalanced monthly; outcomes are average annualized portfolio returns and Sharpe ratios. This is not a regression-based design and not a quasi-experiment; it is a nonparametric cross-sectional sorting exercise interpreted as showing the effect of being in high- versus low-interest-rate currencies on currency, local-bond, and dollar-bond returns.

Identification: The strategy compares countries with relatively high versus low short-term rates conditional on their own past means. The intended identifying variation is cross-country sorting on a predictor known to forecast returns; the authors interpret membership in high-rate currencies as generating higher currency premia but lower local long-bond premia. This does not solve endogeneity or selection concerns: sorted countries may differ on many state variables. The maintained assumption is that the sorting variable captures the relevant exposure driving expected carry and term premia.

Setting: In the cross section, sorting countries by short-term interest rates relative to their own 10-year mean produces the standard carry premium in currencies but not in long bonds. The long-short currency strategy (high minus low portfolio) earns 2.65 percent per year (y1), while the corresponding local-currency 10-year bond excess return is -3.78 percent (y2), so the long-short 10-year dollar bond excess return is -1.12 percent per year (y3), not statistically significant. This is a central result: high-rate currencies deliver positive short-bond carry premia, but local term premia offset them for long bonds.

Main role: The abstract and introduction center on the cross-sectional fact that carry-trade returns decline with bond maturity and go to zero for long bonds. The interest-rate-sorted portfolio evidence in Table 3 is one of the paper's main empirical demonstrations.
Settings.H899: Section I.D, Table 3, columns 'Sorted by short-term interest rates,' Panels B-D, especially Portfolio 3−1 (PDF pp. 4152-4154, especially PDF p. 4153).
Settings.G900:
Treatment: Assignment to low- versus high-yield-curve-slope portfolios; focal contrast is Portfolio 1 minus Portfolio 3 after monthly sorting on the slope (10-year yield minus 1-month rate). Binary long-short portfolio contrast.

Method: Monthly portfolio-sort long-short strategy based on yield-curve slope. Countries are sorted into three portfolios by the slope of their yield curves and rebalanced monthly; the focal estimand is the annualized average return and Sharpe ratio of the long-short portfolio that goes long flat-slope currencies and short steep-slope currencies (Portfolio 1 minus Portfolio 3). This is a nonparametric sorting design, not a regression or quasi-experiment.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-country differences in yield-curve slope used as a sorting variable each month. The maintained interpretation is that flatter foreign curves raise currency carry premia but reduce local term premia less, while steeper curves do the opposite. The design is not quasi-experimental and leaves open omitted-variable and equilibrium-selection concerns; it relies on the slope summarizing conditional expected returns across countries.

Setting: When countries are sorted by yield-curve slope, investing in flat-slope currencies and shorting steep-slope currencies generates a positive currency excess return of 3.65 percent per year (y1), but local-currency 10-year bond excess returns move in the opposite direction by -5.61 percent (y2). The resulting 10-year dollar bond excess return is -1.96 percent per year (y3), not statistically significant. This is one of the paper's most important findings: slope-based currency carry premia are more than offset by local bond term premia at long maturities.

Main role: The paper repeatedly highlights the slope sort as particularly informative and uses it to show the downward term structure of currency carry trade risk premia. Table 3 slope-sorted portfolios are a key main result.
Settings.H900: Section I.D, Table 3, columns 'Sorted by yield curve slopes,' Panels B-D, especially Portfolio 1−3 (PDF pp. 4152-4154, especially PDF p. 4153).
Settings.G901:
Treatment: Assignment to low- versus high-yield-curve-slope country portfolios, with the same slope carry strategy applied to zero-coupon bonds of varying maturities. Binary long-short contrast between flat and steep yield-curve groups.

Method: Maturity-by-maturity zero-coupon portfolio-sort evidence: countries are sorted by yield-curve slope, the strategy goes long flat-yield-curve countries and short steep-yield-curve countries, and the paper plots annualized dollar excess returns for zero-coupon bonds across maturities using a three-month holding period in an unbalanced panel. This is a nonparametric portfolio design over the full term structure, not a regression or quasi-experiment.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-country sorting on yield-curve slope combined with comparison across bond maturities. The authors interpret this as showing the causal role of maturity in attenuating currency carry premia because local term premia increasingly offset them. The design is observational and non-experimental; it assumes the sort captures the relevant state variable and that changing bond maturity within the same strategy isolates the maturity dimension of risk premia.

Setting: Using zero-coupon bonds over maturities from short bills to 15 years, the slope carry strategy's annualized dollar excess return declines monotonically with maturity. The short end yields 2.67 percent per year with a standard error of 1.50 percent, while at the 15-year maturity the return is -2.18 percent with a standard error of 2.28 percent. The short-minus-long difference equals a local term-premium offset of -4.85 percent with a standard error of 1.82 percent. This figure is the paper's clearest evidence that carry-trade risk premia vanish as foreign bond maturity rises.

Main role: This figure directly visualizes the paper's headline result from the abstract: fixing the investment horizon, carry-trade returns decrease as the maturity of the foreign bonds increases and approach zero or negative values. It is central to the article.
Settings.H901: Section I.D, subsection 'Looking across Maturities,' Figure 2 (PDF pp. 4155-4157, especially PDF p. 4156-4157).
Settings.G902:
Treatment: Indicator for whether a steel plant uses the older vertically integrated technology rather than minimill technology. Binary plant technology classification based on census steel-mill questionnaires/materials/products data.

Method: The authors run descriptive cross-sectional/time-pooled linear regressions of plant characteristics on an indicator for being a vertically integrated (VI) steel plant versus a minimill, using log specifications so the technology coefficient is interpreted as a percentage premium. These are ordinary least squares regressions with year fixed effects in some specifications and time-specific coefficients in the online appendix. The intended interpretation is that technology type is associated with differences in plant size, labor productivity, wages, and related outcomes, but the paper presents these as descriptive comparisons rather than a fully identified causal design; endogeneity from sorting of technologies across firms/plants remains.

Identification: The regressions compare observed plant outcomes across technology types, sometimes with year controls. The endogeneity concern is that technology choice is not randomly assigned and may correlate with firm quality, product mix, geography, or other omitted factors. The authors use these results as descriptive evidence about differences across technologies, not as their main identification strategy.

Setting: In descriptive OLS regressions, vertically integrated plants are compared with minimills on plant characteristics. The authors report that VI plants are on average much larger and ship 144 percent more than minimills, generate about 20 percent more shipments per worker, and pay about 6 percent higher wages; they also note that these gaps narrow over time. These comparisons motivate the later causal/reallocation analysis but are not the paper's main identified estimates.

Main role: These regressions provide motivating facts about differences between minimills and vertically integrated plants, but the paper's central conclusions rely on production-function-based productivity estimation and decomposition rather than these descriptive OLS comparisons.
Settings.H902: Section IIB 'A New Production Technology: Minimills,' PDF pp. 136-137; online Appendix Table B.2 discussed in text.
Settings.G903:
Treatment: Indicator for vertically integrated technology versus minimill technology at the plant level; in the 'VI premium' regression, the coefficient measures the productivity difference associated with being a VI plant. Binary technology classification.

Method: The authors estimate plant-level production functions using an Olley-Pakes (1996) investment-control-function approach with selection correction, separately considering output and input price deflators and pooling or splitting by technology. This is a structural productivity-estimation procedure rather than a standard linear causal estimator. They estimate Cobb-Douglas gross-output production functions, use investment to proxy for unobserved productivity, allow survival to depend on state variables, and then construct plant TFP. They subsequently regress estimated productivity on a VI technology indicator with year effects to recover the 'VI premium.' The design addresses simultaneity of inputs and non-random exit but does not rely on external quasi-experimental variation in technology adoption.

Identification: The authors aim to isolate technology-related productivity differences by estimating production functions that correct for endogenous input choices, plant exit, and plant-specific output/input price variation. Identification comes from Olley-Pakes timing assumptions: investment responds monotonically to productivity, capital adjusts slowly, materials/labor respond to contemporaneous shocks, and survival depends on state variables. The endogeneity concern is that simple OLS revenue production functions confound productivity with output prices, input prices, simultaneity, and selection. The key assumption for interpreting the VI/minimill premium is that after these corrections, residual productivity differences reflect true efficiency differences rather than price or selection artifacts.

Setting: Using an Olley-Pakes-style production-function estimator with plant-level output and input price deflators, the authors estimate that minimills are more productive than vertically integrated plants. In their preferred specification, the VI premium is −0.075, implying minimills have about a 7.5 percent TFP advantage; without plant-level output price deflators the gap is only 3.8 percent, and under OLS it is about 1.8 percent and insignificant. The authors interpret these corrected productivity estimates as evidence that the new minimill technology was genuinely more efficient and that correcting for simultaneity, selection, and price heterogeneity is crucial for the paper's main reallocation results.

Main role: The paper's core conclusions depend on estimating minimill versus vertically integrated productivity differences, and these TFP estimates feed directly into the central decomposition and reallocation results emphasized in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H903: Section IIIA 'Productivity Differences across Technology,' equations (6)-(11), Tables 3 and 4, PDF pp. 143-148.
Settings.G904:
Treatment: Indicator for whether the plant is vertically integrated rather than a minimill. Binary technology status.

Method: The authors regress estimated plant productivity on the VI technology indicator under several fixed-effect structures: year FE, firm-year FE, state-year FE, and firm-year-state FE. These are linear fixed-effects regressions using the previously constructed TFP residual as the dependent variable. The purpose is to assess whether the technology premium survives controls for firm-level ownership/management and geography. There are one or two absorbed FE dimensions depending on specification, but not three separately absorbed FE sets; thus this is standard FE rather than HDFE.

Identification: Identification comes from within-cell comparisons after absorbing increasingly fine fixed effects: within firm-year, within state-year, and within firm-state-year. The endogeneity concern is that technology status may proxy for firm management, organizational form, or regional factors. The authors argue that if the minimill premium persists within firms and within locations, these omitted factors are less likely to explain the result. Remaining concerns include within-firm plant-level selection and unobserved plant-specific factors correlated with technology.

Setting: As a robustness exercise, the authors compare estimated productivity across minimill and vertically integrated plants within increasingly narrow fixed-effect cells. The minimill productivity advantage remains: the VI coefficient is −0.074 with year effects, −0.084 with firm-year fixed effects, −0.102 with state-year fixed effects, and −0.178 with firm-year-state fixed effects. They interpret this as evidence that the minimill productivity premium is not explained by firm ownership/management or geography and therefore materially supports the paper's central technology mechanism.

Main role: These fixed-effect regressions are substantive robustness analyses supporting the central claim that minimills were more productive and that the premium is not driven by firm ownership/management or geography.
Settings.H904: Section IIIB 'Alternative Productivity Drivers,' Table 5, PDF pp. 149-151, 153.
Settings.G905:
Treatment: Change in industry import penetration ratio from 1972 to 1996 at the four-digit SIC87 industry level. Continuous treatment measured in proportion/rate points.

Method: The authors run cross-industry regressions of long-difference productivity growth on long-difference import penetration across four-digit SIC manufacturing industries, weighted by industry shipment shares. This is a linear regression-adjustment design using industry-level changes from 1972 to 1996. It is used to gauge whether rising import competition can explain steel's productivity growth, but the authors acknowledge endogeneity and reverse causality issues in such trade-productivity regressions.

Identification: The regression exploits cross-industry variation in changes in import penetration and productivity growth. The endogeneity concern is substantial: import penetration may respond to domestic productivity changes, omitted industry shocks, or other factors. The authors explicitly note that such estimates are subject to biases and measurement problems and use them only to show that import competition is unlikely to explain most of the steel result.

Setting: Using weighted long-difference regressions across manufacturing industries, the authors estimate how much productivity growth would be predicted by steel's increase in import penetration. They report that this exercise predicts only an 8 percent increase in productivity in the steel industry, implying import competition could explain at most about one-third of actual steel productivity growth. This is presented as suggestive evidence against imports being the main driver of the paper's main findings.

Main role: This is an auxiliary comparison used to argue that imports cannot fully account for steel's productivity growth; it is not a central identification strategy of the paper.
Settings.H905: Section IIIB 'International Trade,' discussion of regression ΔΩ_I = γ0 + γ1 Δimport penetration_I + ν_I; online Appendix Table B.7 referenced, PDF p. 152.
Settings.G906:
Treatment: Sheet specialization ratio: share of plant revenue accounted for by sheet products (hot and cold rolled sheet). Continuous treatment on [0,1]. In some specifications a VI indicator is also included as an additional regressor, but the focal treatment for this setting is sheet specialization.

Method: The authors regress estimated plant productivity on a VI technology indicator and a sheet-specialization ratio under several fixed-effect structures: year FE, state-year FE, firm-year FE, and plant FE for the VI-only sample. These are linear FE regressions using estimated TFP as the outcome. The substantive goal is to test whether product specialization—especially producing sheet rather than bar steel—explains productivity differences and the catching-up of vertically integrated producers.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing plants with different sheet-specialization shares while controlling for time, geography, firm-year, and in one specification plant fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that more productive plants may choose sheet specialization rather than sheet specialization causing productivity. The authors use these regressions as evidence on the mechanism linking product-market competition to observed productivity patterns, not as a clean quasi-experiment.

Setting: To study why vertically integrated producers 'caught up,' the authors regress estimated productivity on a plant's sheet-specialization share. They find a robust positive association: among all plants, the coefficient on sheet specialization ranges from 0.073 to 0.119, and among vertically integrated plants it ranges from 0.099 to 0.168 in specifications with state-year, firm-year, or plant fixed effects. The authors interpret this as evidence that sheet-focused producers were more productive, consistent with minimills intensifying competition in bar products and pushing less efficient bar-oriented VI plants out of the market.

Main role: This is a substantive mechanism test for one of the paper's core conclusions: increased minimill competition in bar products induced reallocation among vertically integrated plants toward more productive sheet producers.
Settings.H906: Section IVD 'Catching Up of the Old Technology,' Table 9, PDF pp. 159-160.
Settings.G907:
Treatment: Primary focal treatment is sheet specialization ratio, the share of revenue accounted for by sheet products. Continuous from 0 to 1. In all-plants specifications a VI indicator is also included as an additional regressor.

Method: The authors estimate survival/exit relationships using nonlinear binary-response models and report marginal effects for whether a plant active in 1963 still exists in 2002. Regressors include the VI technology indicator, sheet-specialization ratio, log capital, and productivity. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear for a binary outcome and the paper reports marginal effects, this belongs in Other rather than linear OLS/FE. The purpose is to test whether sheet-specialized plants were more likely to survive, consistent with minimill competition reshaping the incumbent technology through exit.

Identification: The design uses cross-plant variation in initial sheet specialization to predict long-run survival, controlling for technology, capital, and productivity. The endogeneity concern is that specialization may proxy for unobserved profitability or product-demand conditions. The authors interpret the strong survival premium for sheet producers as evidence that competition from minimills in bar products drove exit among bar-oriented VI plants. Causal interpretation relies on the argument that specialization captures exposure to minimill competition rather than omitted plant quality alone.

Setting: In nonlinear survival regressions, the authors show that plants specialized in sheet products were substantially more likely to survive through 2002. For all plants, a fully sheet-specialized plant had about a 31 to 39 percentage point higher survival probability than a fully bar-specialized plant, on a baseline survival probability around 0.33; among vertically integrated plants, the sheet-specialization effect is about 0.31 in parsimonious specifications. The authors use this to argue that minimill competition in bar products caused exit among less efficient incumbent producers, a central mechanism in the paper.

Main role: These exit/survival results are a key piece of the paper's mechanism showing that minimill expansion induced reallocation among vertically integrated plants by pushing out less productive bar producers.
Settings.H907: Section IVD 'Catching Up of the Old Technology,' Table 10, PDF pp. 160-161.
Settings.G908:
Treatment: Random assignment to watch one of three short income-tax video courses: Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist, relative to no-video control. Each treatment is an indicator for assigned video arm in the survey experiment.

Method: In the income-tax survey, respondents were randomly assigned to one of three instructional video treatments—Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist—or to no video control. The paper estimates intention-to-treat effects using linear regressions of post-treatment reasoning outcomes on treatment indicators, with controls for respondent characteristics (sex, age, race, income class, children, education, economics-related major, employment status, self-reported policy knowledge, self-reported social class, political affiliation, and question/treatment indicators as applicable). Outcomes here are perceived behavioral responses to an increase in the federal personal income tax for high-income and middle-class earners. Identification comes from random assignment of the videos; the estimated effects are direct assignment effects on beliefs, not treatment-on-treated or IV effects.

Identification: Because video assignment is randomized across representative survey respondents, differences in post-video perceived behavioral responses across treatment arms identify causal ITT effects of the pedagogical content on beliefs, assuming successful randomization and no differential post-assignment measurement problems. The paper interprets these as experimentally induced changes in reasoning about efficiency channels of income taxation.

Setting: Using random assignment to short income-tax instructional videos, the paper estimates causal effects on beliefs about how people respond to higher income taxes. Relative to no video, the Efficiency treatment raises the share saying taxes would increase evasion by 0.08 for high earners and 0.07 for the middle class, reduce work by 0.16 and 0.27, increase spouse nonwork by 0.14 and 0.20, and reduce entrepreneurship by 0.14 and 0.19; the Economist treatment produces similar increases. The Redistribution treatment has much smaller effects. These first-stage experimental results support the paper’s central claim that beliefs about tax mechanisms are malleable and can be shifted causally by pedagogical explanations.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, Section VI, and conclusion emphasize that the experiments are used to establish causal links between reasoning and tax-policy views; first-stage belief shifts are part of that central experimental evidence.
Settings.H908: Table III, Panels A-B-C, columns (1)-(12), PDF pp. 2335-2338; discussion in Section V.A.1, PDF pp. 2337-2340.
Settings.G909:
Treatment: Random assignment to an income-tax video arm (Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist) versus no-video control.

Method: In the income-tax survey experiment, respondents were randomly assigned to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist videos or a no-video control, and the paper runs linear regressions of belief outcomes on treatment indicators plus respondent controls. This setting focuses on broader perceived efficiency-cost outcomes of higher income taxation rather than individual behavioral margins. The effects are ITT effects of assignment to explanatory videos.

Identification: Randomized assignment of video content identifies causal effects of receiving efficiency-focused or balanced pedagogical explanations on respondents’ beliefs about macro efficiency consequences of income taxation. The identifying assumption is standard experimental exogeneity of assignment.

Setting: The randomized income-tax videos causally shift beliefs about whether higher taxes on top incomes hurt the economy. Relative to control, the Efficiency video increases the probability of believing that taxing high incomes hurts economic activity by 0.14, and the Economist video by 0.06; neither video significantly changes beliefs in Laffer effects for high incomes or the middle class. These estimates show that efficiency-focused explanations can move perceived macro costs of taxation, even though later policy-support effects are weak for the Efficiency treatment.

Main role: These experimental first-stage effects on perceived efficiency costs are used directly in Section VI.D to compare redistribution versus efficiency channels and are part of the paper’s main causal argument.
Settings.H909: Table IV, Panel B, columns (1)-(3), PDF p. 2339; discussion in Section V.A.1 and VI.D, PDF pp. 2338-2364.
Settings.G910:
Treatment: Random assignment to one of three estate-tax videos—Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist—versus no-video control.

Method: In the estate-tax survey, respondents were randomly assigned to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist instructional videos or no-video control. Linear regressions with respondent controls estimate ITT effects on belief outcomes about behavioral responses to a higher federal estate tax, for wealthy households and for currently young people. Identification rests on random assignment.

Identification: Random assignment of estate-tax video treatments creates exogenous variation in explanatory content. Comparing post-treatment responses across assigned arms identifies causal ITT effects on perceived behavioral responses to estate taxation, under standard RCT assumptions.

Setting: The estate-tax video experiment shows that pedagogical explanations causally change beliefs about behavioral responses to estate taxation. Relative to control, the Efficiency treatment raises the share believing that wealthy people would work less by 0.26, stop working by 0.08, become less entrepreneurial by 0.24, and save less by 0.22; the Economist treatment yields similar increases, including 0.27 for wealthy people working less and 0.20 for saving less. Effects on beliefs about the young are smaller. These estimates provide first-stage evidence that respondents’ views about estate-tax efficiency channels are causally malleable.

Main role: These are experimental first-stage outcomes for the estate-tax part of the paper and underpin the main conclusion that information can shift reasoning, especially about efficiency channels.
Settings.H910: Table V, Panels A-B-C, columns (1)-(14), PDF pp. 2341-2342; discussion in Section V.A.2, PDF pp. 2341-2342 and VI.D, PDF pp. 2362-2364.
Settings.G911:
Treatment: Random assignment to an estate-tax video arm (Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist) relative to no-video control.

Method: In the estate-tax survey experiment, the paper estimates linear ITT effects of randomized assignment to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist videos on broader perceived efficiency-cost outcomes of estate taxation, controlling for respondent covariates. These are direct assignment effects on beliefs about economic harm and Laffer effects from estate taxes.

Identification: The experimental design randomly assigns respondents to estate-tax video content, so differences in post-treatment beliefs about economic effects can be interpreted causally as ITT effects of the information framing, subject to standard RCT assumptions.

Setting: Randomly assigned estate-tax videos modestly affect beliefs about the macroeconomic costs of estate taxation. Relative to control, the Economist treatment increases the probability of saying a higher estate tax would hurt the economy by 0.07, while the Efficiency treatment raises it by 0.05 but not significantly; neither treatment meaningfully changes belief in estate-tax Laffer effects. The paper uses these results to show that efficiency-oriented instruction can shift perceived costs, but less powerfully than redistribution-oriented content shifts policy support.

Main role: These belief shifts are part of the experimental comparison between efficiency and redistribution narratives, central to the paper’s argument about what moves tax support.
Settings.H911: Table IV, Panel B, columns (4)-(5), PDF p. 2339; discussion in Section V.A.2 and VI.D, PDF pp. 2341-2342, 2363-2364.
Settings.G912:
Treatment: Random assignment to one of the income-tax instructional video arms—Redistribution, Efficiency, Economist—or no-video control.

Method: In the income-tax survey experiment, respondents are randomly assigned to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist videos or control, and the paper estimates linear ITT effects on social-preference and fairness outcomes. Regressions include treatment indicators and respondent covariates. This setting groups the fairness/social-preference outcomes reported together for the income-tax module.

Identification: Random video assignment identifies causal effects of pedagogical explanations about redistribution or trade-offs on fairness-related beliefs about inequality and tax entitlement. The main assumption is exogenous assignment across otherwise comparable respondents.

Setting: The income-tax experiment shows that redistribution-oriented explanations causally move some social-preference beliefs. Relative to control, the Redistribution treatment increases the probability of saying inequality is a serious issue by 0.10, and the Economist treatment by 0.06; the Economist treatment also raises by 0.05 the probability of saying people are rich because of advantages rather than effort. Effects on views that wealth should be more evenly distributed or that high-income people are entitled to keep their income are small. These experimental shifts support the paper’s central claim that redistributive reasoning, more than efficiency reasoning, drives support for progressive taxation.

Main role: The paper’s core experimental mechanism is that Redistribution and Economist treatments shift redistributive concerns and inequality seriousness, which then map into greater support for progressive taxes.
Settings.H912: Table VI, Panels A-B-C, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 2345; discussion in Sections V.C.1 and VI.D, PDF pp. 2345-2346, 2363-2364.
Settings.G913:
Treatment: Random assignment to one of the estate-tax instructional video arms—Redistribution, Efficiency, Economist—or no-video control.
