Method: In the estate-tax survey experiment, respondents are randomly assigned to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist videos or to control, and the paper estimates ITT effects on social-preference and fairness outcomes concerning wealth inequality, parental estates, children's inheritances, and the explicit parent-child fairness trade-off. Linear regressions include standard respondent controls.

Identification: Random assignment to estate-tax video treatments generates exogenous variation in explanatory content about redistribution, efficiency, and trade-offs. Differences in post-treatment fairness responses identify causal ITT effects on normative reasoning about estate taxation.

Setting: The estate-tax video experiment causally shifts some fairness judgments. Relative to control, the Redistribution treatment reduces by 0.09 the probability of saying it is fair that wealthy children inherit more and by 0.06 the probability of siding with parents in the parent-child trade-off; the Economist treatment reduces the same trade-off outcome by 0.08. Effects on broader wealth-inequality views are smaller. The paper interprets these experimental changes as evidence that estate-tax support is shaped importantly by fairness considerations about inherited advantage, not mainly by efficiency concerns.

Main role: These treatment effects are part of the paper’s central experimental evidence that redistributive explanations and parent-child fairness framing causally alter support for estate taxation.
Settings.H913: Table VII, Panels A-B-C, columns (1)-(8), PDF pp. 2347-2348; discussion in Sections V.C.2 and VI.D, PDF pp. 2348-2350, 2363-2364.
Settings.G914:
Treatment: Random assignment to one of the three income-tax instructional video treatments—Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist—relative to no-video control.

Method: The paper constructs an income-tax policy index from several standardized post-treatment policy outcomes and estimates linear regressions of this index on randomized assignment to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist videos, with respondent covariates. This is a direct assignment/ITT design. The index averages z-scored components and is then standardized again.

Identification: Random assignment of income-tax videos identifies causal ITT effects on policy support. Because assignment is exogenous, differences in the standardized income-tax policy index across arms capture the effect of being shown a redistribution-focused, efficiency-focused, or balanced tax explanation. Remaining concerns are limited to survey implementation and interpretation of an index outcome.

Setting: The income-tax experiment finds that explanatory content emphasizing redistribution causally raises support for progressive income taxation. Relative to no video, the Redistribution treatment increases the income-tax policy index by about 0.23 standard deviations and the Economist treatment by about 0.18 standard deviations, while the Efficiency treatment has no significant effect. The paper states that the Redistribution effect is around 23% of the Democrat-Republican gap in the index and the Economist effect around 18%, supporting the central conclusion that redistributive concerns dominate efficiency concerns in shaping tax-policy views.

Main role: This is one of the paper’s headline causal results, emphasized in the abstract, introduction, Section VI.D, and conclusion: Redistribution and Economist treatments increase support for progressive income taxation, while Efficiency does not.
Settings.H914: Figure V, Panel A, 'Treatments' rows, PDF p. 2356; definition of the income tax policy index in Section VI.B, PDF p. 2352; experimental interpretation in Section VI.D, PDF pp. 2361-2364.
Settings.G915:
Treatment: Random assignment to one of the three estate-tax instructional videos—Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist—versus no-video control.

Method: The paper constructs an estate-tax policy index from standardized post-treatment policy outcomes and regresses it on randomized assignment to Redistribution, Efficiency, or Economist estate-tax videos, with respondent covariates. The design estimates ITT effects of assignment to pedagogical content on policy support.

Identification: Random assignment to estate-tax video treatments creates exogenous variation in the pedagogical framing of estate taxation. The causal effect on policy support is identified by comparing the standardized policy index across assigned arms under the usual RCT assumptions.

Setting: In the estate-tax experiment, redistribution-oriented and balanced videos causally increase support for the estate tax, while the Efficiency video does not. The paper reports that the Redistribution and Economist treatments improve support for the estate tax by amounts equivalent to roughly 30% of the control-group Democrat-Republican gap in support. Because the index is standardized, these are effect sizes in outcome-SD units. These estimates are central evidence for the paper’s conclusion that fairness and redistribution concerns matter more than efficiency arguments for estate-tax preferences.

Main role: This is the other headline causal result highlighted in the abstract and conclusion: Redistribution and Economist treatments increase support for the estate tax; Efficiency does not.
Settings.H915: Figure V, Panel B, 'Treatments' rows, PDF p. 2356; definition of the estate tax policy index in Section VI.B, PDF p. 2352; experimental interpretation in Section VI.D, PDF pp. 2363-2364.
Settings.G916:
Treatment: Reasoning/attitude variables thought to affect support for progressive income taxes: overestimating tax levels; perceived behavioral-response index; belief that higher taxes hurt the economy/Laffer beliefs index; trickle-down beliefs index; trust in government/belief in broad scope of government index; inequality-seriousness index; belief that high-income people are entitled to keep their income; and belief that luck is the main reason people become rich. These are standardized continuous indices or indicators, not a single binary treatment.

Method: The paper runs cross-sectional linear regressions of the income-tax policy index on a full set of reasoning variables capturing the factors in the authors’ conceptual tax formula, plus respondent covariates and treatment indicators. This is a regression-adjustment/correlational decomposition rather than a quasi-experimental design. The authors explicitly interpret these variables as shaping policy views, while acknowledging that causality is unclear and using the experiment separately to support causal claims.

Identification: Identification is associational rather than design-based. The regression partials out a rich set of demographic and political covariates and treatment indicators to relate policy support to perceived efficiency costs, distributional beliefs, social preferences, and views of government. The endogeneity concern is that reasoning may itself be caused by policy views or partisanship; the paper acknowledges this and supplements with randomized video evidence.

Setting: In cross-sectional regressions, support for progressive income taxation is most strongly associated with social preferences and views of government rather than efficiency concerns. Respondents are more supportive of progressive taxes if they think inequality is a serious problem, trust the government, do not believe high-income people are entitled to keep their income, and do not believe in trickle-down economics. The paper notes that even respondents who think taxes hurt the economy are still more likely to support progressive taxes if they see inequality as serious or trust government. These OLS decomposition results are central to the paper’s substantive claim, though the author emphasizes that causal direction is not fully identified here.

Main role: Although correlational, this decomposition is one of the paper’s two main pillars, prominently summarized in the abstract, introduction, Section VI.C, and conclusion as showing that social preferences and government views matter more than efficiency concerns.
Settings.H916: Figure V, Panel A, 'Mechanisms' rows, PDF p. 2356; discussion in Section VI.C, PDF pp. 2355-2358.
Settings.G917:
Treatment: Reasoning/attitude variables interpreted as affecting support for the estate tax: overestimating estate-tax levels; perceived behavioral-response index; belief that higher taxes hurt the economy/Laffer beliefs index; trust in government index; perceived share of wealth inherited; belief it is unfair to tax parents; belief it is fair that children from wealthy families inherit more/have better opportunities; and siding with parents in the explicit parent-child trade-off. These are standardized continuous indices or indicators.

Method: The paper estimates cross-sectional linear regressions of the estate-tax policy index on standardized reasoning variables and respondent covariates. The regressors map to the conceptual determinants of desired estate taxation: perceived tax levels, behavioral responses and economic costs, trust in government, perceived inherited wealth, and multiple fairness variables from the parents’ and children’s perspectives. This is associational regression adjustment, not an identified quasi-experiment.

Identification: The regression exploits cross-respondent variation in beliefs and fairness judgments, conditioning on a rich set of observables and treatment indicators. The key limitation is endogeneity: policy views, partisan identity, and fairness beliefs may be jointly determined. The paper therefore treats these as decomposition/correlation results and uses experiments for causal support.

Setting: For estate taxes, the OLS decomposition shows that support is strongly associated with social preferences and fairness trade-offs, not mainly with efficiency concerns. Respondents are more supportive of the estate tax if they perceive inequality as serious and trust government, and less supportive if they think estate taxation is unfair to parents, fair that wealthy children inherit more, or if they side with parents when confronting the parent-child fairness trade-off. Perceiving more wealth as inherited also modestly raises estate-tax support. These regressions form a central part of the paper’s substantive claim about why people support or oppose estate taxation, despite the author noting unresolved causality in this nonexperimental setting.

Main role: This correlational decomposition is a core result used to argue that fairness and social-preference considerations dominate efficiency concerns in estate-tax support.
Settings.H917: Figure V, Panel B, 'Mechanisms' rows, PDF p. 2356; discussion in Section VI.C, PDF pp. 2357-2358.
Settings.G918:
Treatment: Eligibility for the employer payroll tax cut based on being below the age threshold in the reform period: ages 19–25 in 2007–2008 and ages 26 or less in 2009 onward, measured as an indicator 1(a<=a_eligible) interacted with post-reform period. This is an age-based binary exposure, not receipt uncertainty, because take-up was near universal and automatic.

Method: Market-level difference-in-differences on aggregate age-by-period cells estimating whether workers below the statutory youth age cutoff experience different wage changes after the reform than slightly older ineligible workers. The authors estimate equation (1) on cohort-period averages, with age fixed effects and period fixed effects, separately for short run (2007–2008 vs pre) and medium run (2009–2013 vs pre). Outcomes are monthly full-time-equivalent net wages and gross wages from the Structure of Earnings Survey. Identification comes from comparing adjacent age groups around the policy eligibility cutoff before vs after the reform, assuming parallel age profiles absent the reform; the paper emphasizes graphical smoothness pre-reform and the sharp policy age cutoff.

Identification: The identifying variation is the discontinuous age eligibility rule for the payroll tax cut, combined with before-after changes. Slightly younger eligible and slightly older ineligible cohorts are treated as close substitutes, so absent the reform their wage profiles would evolve smoothly across age. The endogeneity concern is differential age trends or confounding contemporaneous reforms; the paper argues these other reforms did not create sharp age discontinuities and shows smooth pre-reform age profiles and no discontinuity in net wages but a sharp post-reform discontinuity in gross wages.

Setting: Using age-by-period difference-in-differences around the statutory youth eligibility cutoff, the paper finds no pass-through of the employer payroll tax cut to young workers’ net wages. In Table 1 panel A, the estimated treatment effect on net monthly wages is -1.551 US$ in the short run and -31.625 US$ in the medium run, while the effect on gross monthly wages is -209.154 US$ and -404.698 US$, respectively. The implied pass-through to firms is about 1.007 in the short run and 1.085 in the medium run, meaning essentially all incidence falls on firms through lower labor costs. This is a core finding motivating the paper’s move from market-level to firm-level mechanisms.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight the null effect on net wages of treated young workers and the corresponding labor-cost incidence on firms as a central result of the paper.
Settings.H918: Section II.B, Figure 2, Table 1 panel A (and discussion of equation (1)); PDF pp. 1726–1731 (PDF pages 10–15).
Settings.G919:
Treatment: Binary post-reform eligibility for the youth payroll tax cut based on age/birth cohort, applied in alternative subsamples (monthly birth cohorts, top wage quintile, and new hires).

Method: Same market-level DD design as s1, but substantive robustness/heterogeneity analyses using alternative samples: monthly birth-cohort cells around the cutoff, top 20 percent of the wage distribution, and new hires. The estimator remains the aggregate age-period DD in equation (1) with age and period effects, reported in Table 1 panels B–D. These are used substantively to rule out mismeasurement of the cutoff, minimum-wage floors, and implicit-contract explanations.

Identification: Same age-threshold DiD logic as in s1. The robustness samples target specific threats: monthly birth cohorts sharpen the running age classification; top-20-percent earners reduce concern that minimum wages bind; new hires eliminate implicit wage-contract explanations. Identification still relies on smooth age/cohort wage trends absent reform within each sample.

Setting: In robustness analyses using the same age-based difference-in-differences framework, the paper continues to find essentially zero effect of the payroll tax cut on net wages and near-complete incidence on firms. With monthly birth data, pass-through to firms is 0.994 in the short run and 1.013 in the medium run; for the top 20 percent of earners, pass-through is 0.910 and 0.971; for new hires, pass-through is 1.097 and 1.081. These exercises are important because they argue the main incidence result does not reflect cutoff aggregation, binding minimum wages, or preexisting implicit wage contracts.

Main role: These robustness settings materially support the central incidence claim by showing the wage null is not due to coarse age bins, minimum wage constraints, or implicit contracts.
Settings.H919: Section II.B, Table 1 panels B–D and accompanying text; PDF pp. 1728–1733 (PDF pages 12–17).
Settings.G920:
Treatment: Eligibility for the youth payroll tax cut based on being age 26 or below in the post-2009 reform period (and analogously younger ages during the first reform step in graphs), implemented as an indicator for treated age groups after the reform.

Method: Market-level difference-in-differences on aggregate age-by-period cells estimating employment effects of the youth payroll tax cut. The authors use equation (1)-style DD regressions on cohort-period aggregates with age fixed effects and period fixed effects, excluding 2007–2008 when the reform was partially phased in. Outcomes are employment-related rates and flows constructed from administrative population and unemployment records. The key specification compares ages 20–26 to 27–35 before vs after 2009.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing employment changes for eligible young cohorts to slightly older ineligible cohorts around the reform’s age cutoff, under the assumption that absent the reform age-specific employment profiles would have changed similarly. The main endogeneity concern is differential age trends or aggregate cyclical shocks; the paper emphasizes closely overlapping pre-trends, excludes the transition years 2007–2008, and argues no labor-supply response should confound the employment effect because net wages did not rise.

Setting: Using age-based difference-in-differences on aggregate cohort data, the paper finds that the payroll tax cut increased youth employment. The estimated effect on the employment-to-labor-force ratio is 0.021 (2.1 percentage points), implying an elasticity of 0.21 with respect to the 12.1 percent labor-cost reduction. Alternative definitions produce similar results: 0.023 for employment over labor force plus students and 0.014 for employment over population. Transition estimates suggest increases in unemployment-to-employment transitions and decreases in employment-to-unemployment transitions. This market-level employment response is a central policy result and contrasts with the standard model prediction of wage pass-through with little employment response.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly state that youth employment increased by 2–3 percentage points; this is one of the headline policy effects.
Settings.H920: Section II.C, Figure 4, Table 2; PDF pp. 1733–1737 (PDF pages 17–21).
Settings.G921:
Treatment: Firm exposure to the payroll tax cut measured by the pre-reform share of total wage earnings paid to young workers aged 19–25 in 2006 ('share young'). The main treatment contrast is high-share-young firms (top quartile among firms with positive young share) versus medium-share-young firms (middle two quartiles). This is a binary treatment contrast built from a continuous underlying exposure.

Method: Firm-level DD using pre-reform treatment intensity: firms are grouped by the share of payroll paid to young workers in 2006, and outcomes are traced annually from 2003 to 2013 for a balanced panel of firms. The implemented estimator compares high-share-young firms (top quartile) to medium-share-young firms (middle two quartiles) before vs after the reform using equation (2) on group-year averages normalized to 2006. Additional dosage analyses split the top quartile into fairly high and very high groups. Identification concerns are addressed through graphical pre-trends and the persistence of pre-reform youth shares.

Identification: The reform generated firm-specific tax windfalls proportional to the payroll share of treated young workers. The identifying assumption is that, absent the reform, highly exposed and moderately exposed firms would have followed parallel trends. The authors justify this with extensive pre-reform event-style graphs, note that medium-share-young firms are a better control than firms with few or no young workers, and use the persistence of pre-2006 youth shares as a first stage for continuing exposure. Remaining concerns include differential shocks by firm type, mean reversion in youth shares, and macro shocks like the Great Recession; the paper argues pre-trends and dosage patterns strongly support causality.

Setting: Using a firm-level difference-in-differences design based on pre-reform youth payroll shares, the paper shows that firms more exposed to the payroll tax cut expand significantly after the reform. Comparing high-share-young firms to medium-share-young firms, the estimated effects are 4.6 percent higher employment, 5.8 percent higher total assets, 3.1 percent higher sales, 6.1 percent higher value added, and 8.1 percent higher EBIT profits. The treatment contrast corresponds to a 19.8 percentage point difference in 2006 youth payroll share, which implies an initial tax-windfall differential of 2.4 percent of payroll. Dosage analyses show larger effects for very-high-exposure firms, reinforcing the paper’s central claim that firms used the windfall to expand rather than merely pocketing it.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that firms employing many young workers received larger tax windfalls and expanded in employment, capital, sales, and profits; this is a central substantive result.
Settings.H921: Section III.A–B, Figure 5, Figure 6, Table 3, Table 4; PDF pp. 1737–1746 (PDF pages 21–30).
Settings.G922:
Treatment: Binary high versus medium pre-reform firm exposure to the youth payroll tax cut, within subsamples defined by financial-constraint proxies (young vs old firms, low vs high liquid-assets share, low vs high sales).

Method: Firm-level DD heterogeneity analysis by financial constraints, still based on pre-reform firm exposure (share young) but estimated separately for more versus less financially constrained firms using proxies: firm age, liquid assets/total assets, and sales. The estimator compares high-share-young to medium-share-young firms within each financial-constraint split before vs after the reform on group-year averages. This is a substantive mechanism analysis rather than a new design.

Identification: Identification remains the same DD comparison of high- vs medium-exposure firms over time, now within subsamples that proxy for ex ante financial constraints. The mechanism claim is that if cash injections matter, more constrained firms should respond more. Threats include measurement error in financial-constraint proxies and potentially different first-stage exposure across subsamples; the paper reports that first-stage differences in youth payroll shares are similar across constrained and unconstrained groups.

Setting: To assess whether liquidity matters for the firm response, the paper estimates the same firm-level DD separately by proxies for financial constraints. Employment effects are larger for more constrained firms in all three splits: for example, 5.4 percent versus 1.7 percent when constrained firms are younger than the median age, and 6.0 percent versus 3.2 percent when constrained firms have below-median liquid assets relative to assets. Asset responses are also generally larger for constrained firms, though not always significantly so. The evidence is presented as consistent with, but not definitive proof of, a credit-constraint channel amplifying the tax windfall’s effect on firm growth.

Main role: These results are used to probe the cash/credit-constraint mechanism behind the main firm-expansion findings rather than establish the main effect itself.
Settings.H922: Section III.C, Table 5 and online Appendix Figures A18–A19 referenced in text; PDF pp. 1747–1748 (PDF pages 31–32).
Settings.G923:
Treatment: Binary high-share-young versus medium-share-young firm exposure based on the share of payroll paid to young workers in 2006.

Method: Firm-level DD on average wages and payroll-tax payments per worker, using the same pre-reform firm exposure groups as in the main firm analysis. Outcomes are group-year averages of net wage per worker, payroll tax per worker, and gross wage per worker, each normalized to 2006. The estimator compares high-share-young to medium-share-young firms before vs after the reform, with dosage splits into fairly high and very high exposure firms.

Under parallel trends, differential changes in average wages per worker between high- and medium-exposure firms after the reform are attributed to the tax windfall. A key concern is composition bias from hiring and workforce changes; the paper acknowledges this and follows with worker-level analyses to isolate wages for incumbent ineligible workers.

Setting: At the firm level, more exposed firms use part of the tax windfall to raise workers’ average net pay. Settings.G924:
Treatment: Being employed in 2006 at a firm with high pre-reform exposure to the payroll tax cut (high share of payroll paid to young workers) versus a medium-exposure firm. The treatment is assigned at the worker level based on the employer just before the reform, and all sampled workers are ages 25–60 in 2006 so they are never directly eligible themselves.

The paper interprets this as strong evidence of within-firm rent sharing of the payroll tax windfall.

Main role: These worker-level estimates are the paper’s key evidence for rent sharing: wages of always-ineligible workers rise when their firms receive larger tax windfalls.
Settings.H924: Section IV.B, Figures 8 and 9, Table 6 first rows; PDF pp. 1751–1755 (PDF pages 35–39).
Settings.G925:
Treatment: Being employed in 2006 at a high-share-young rather than medium-share-young firm, in subsamples defined by worker age, initial within-firm earnings rank, gender, or earnings percentile.

Settings.G926:
Treatment: Entrepreneur schooling, measured as average years of schooling of the firm's entrepreneurs, operationalized here as five schooling-group indicators interacted with firm age: [0,6), [6,9), [9,12), [12,15), and 15+ years. The focal contrast emphasized is top group (15+) versus bottom group (<6 years).

Method: Baseline life-cycle regressions estimated by OLS using equation (1): log firm outcome on interactions between entrepreneur-schooling-group indicators and firm-age indicators, plus controls for non-entrepreneur schooling-group dummies, quadratic controls for average entrepreneur and non-entrepreneur experience, and year fixed effects; standard errors clustered at the firm level. The author interprets the schooling-by-age coefficients as evidence on the effect of entrepreneur schooling on firm size at entry and growth over the life cycle, while acknowledging possible omitted-ability bias addressed later.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-firm variation in entrepreneur schooling interacted with firm age, conditional on observed worker-human-capital controls, experience controls, and year fixed effects. The main endogeneity concern is omitted entrepreneur ability correlated with schooling, as well as selection into sectors or differential survival; the paper treats this as a baseline associational/causal specification and later probes ability bias, within-sector variation, and survivor selection in separate analyses. A causal interpretation requires that, conditional on controls, remaining differences in firm dynamics by entrepreneur schooling reflect schooling rather than omitted factors.

Setting: Using OLS regressions of log firm outcomes on entrepreneur-schooling-group-by-age interactions for the 2004–2007 cohorts, the paper argues that higher entrepreneur schooling causes larger entry size and faster early-life growth. These results are a main empirical pillar of the paper’s argument that entrepreneurial human capital drives firm dynamics, though the author notes possible omitted-ability bias and investigates it later.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that firms started by more educated entrepreneurs are larger at entry and exhibit higher life-cycle growth; this baseline regression is the core empirical evidence for that central claim.
Settings.H926: Section 3.1, equation (1), Figure 1, and accompanying text on PDF pp. 2066–2067 (PDF pages 6–7).
Settings.G927:
Treatment: Entrepreneur schooling group interacted with firm age, with focal comparison between 15+ years and <6 years of schooling.

Standard errors are clustered at the firm level. This specification is used to assess whether the baseline effect of entrepreneur schooling on firm dynamics is explained by within-sector variation rather than sector sorting.

The concern addressed is endogenous sorting of more educated entrepreneurs into higher-growth sectors. Main role: The introduction explicitly claims that differences are 'almost fully explained by within-sector variation at the 5-digit level'; this robustness materially supports the paper’s main conclusion that entrepreneurial human capital, not sector selection, drives firm dynamics.
Settings.H927: Section 3.1, Figure 2a and accompanying text on PDF p. 2068 (PDF page 8).
Settings.G928:
Treatment: Entrepreneur schooling group interacted with firm age, focusing on differences between top (15+) and bottom (<6) schooling groups among firms surviving to age 10.

Method: Survivor-only robustness version of equation (1), estimated by OLS on log sales with entrepreneur-schooling-group-by-age interactions, baseline controls, and year fixed effects, restricting the sample to firms that survive until age 10. The survivor-only coefficients are compared with full-sample coefficients to distinguish differential survivor growth from differential selection through firm exit.

Identification: This analysis uses conditioning on eventual survival to age 10 to examine whether the baseline schooling-growth pattern is due to differential firm growth among survivors or compositional change from more exit among low-performing firms. Remaining concerns include endogenous survival conditioning and omitted ability within survivor samples.

Setting: Restricting the sample to firms that survive until age 10, the paper finds that the gap in sales trajectories between high- and low-schooling entrepreneurs remains, implying that the baseline relationship is driven mainly by faster survivor growth rather than by selective exit of smaller firms. This robustness is presented as important evidence that entrepreneurial schooling affects firm growth itself, not just survival composition.

Settings.H928: Section 3.1, Figure 2b and accompanying text on PDF p. 2068 (PDF page 8).
Settings.G929:
Treatment: Average non-entrepreneur schooling of the firm's workers, grouped into the same five schooling bins and interacted with firm age.

Method: Alternative life-cycle OLS regression replacing entrepreneur-schooling-by-age interactions in equation (1) with non-entrepreneur-schooling-by-age interactions, using the same controls and year fixed effects and clustering at the firm level. The comparison is meant to isolate whether the schooling-growth relationship is specific to entrepreneurs. The author interprets this as evidence that it is specifically entrepreneurs’ human capital, not worker schooling generally, that drives firm dynamics.

Settings.H929: Section 3.1, Figure 3 and accompanying text on PDF p. 2068–2069 (PDF pages 8–9).
Settings.G930:
Treatment: Average years of entrepreneur schooling, entered linearly and interacted with firm age; treatment increment is one additional year of entrepreneur schooling.

Method: Linearized baseline OLS regression using equation (2): log firm outcome on continuous entrepreneur schooling interacted with firm-age indicators, with age fixed effects, year fixed effects, continuous non-entrepreneur schooling, and experience controls. The specification is used to summarize the relationship as approximately log-linear and becomes the basis for the omitted-ability analysis in the next subsection.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-firm variation in average entrepreneur years of schooling interacted with age, conditional on observed controls. The author argues the relationship is approximately linear in schooling, which justifies a parsimonious causal interpretation per additional year. Endogeneity concerns from omitted ability remain and are explicitly addressed in the next section.

Setting: Using a linearized OLS specification, the paper finds that the relationship between entrepreneur schooling and firm sales at ages 1, 2, 5, and 10 is approximately log-linear, with the slope increasing with firm age. This supports interpreting each additional year of entrepreneur schooling as increasing firm size more strongly later in the life cycle and provides the empirical backbone for the subsequent ability-bias correction and structural model.

Settings.H930: Section 3.1, equation (2), Figure 4, and accompanying text on PDF p. 2069 (PDF page 9).
Settings.G931:
Treatment: Average years of entrepreneur schooling, interacted with firm age; focal estimates reported at firm ages 0 and 10. In the bias-corrected interpretation, treatment is one additional year of entrepreneur schooling net of ability proxied by prior wage.

Method: Ability-accounting OLS regressions based on equation (6) in the switcher sample: log sales on entrepreneur schooling-by-age interactions plus interactions of entrepreneur’s prior non-entrepreneur log wage with firm age, with year and age fixed effects, experience controls, non-entrepreneur schooling, and in some columns the number of prior occupations by age. This is still a regression-adjustment approach rather than IV.

Settings.H931: Section 3.2, equations (3)–(6), Table 1 columns (1)–(4), PDF pp. 2070–2072 (PDF pages 10–12).

Treatment: Average years of entrepreneur schooling, interacted with firm age; focal bias-corrected estimates at ages 0 and 10.

Method: Same ability-accounting regression-adjustment framework as in Table 1, but with log value added as the dependent variable instead of log sales, estimated in the switcher sample with prior-wage-by-age controls and number-of-prior-occupations robustness. Settings.G933:
Treatment: Average years of entrepreneur schooling, entered linearly; treatment increment is one additional year of entrepreneur schooling.

Method: Cross-sectional quantile regression of log sales on continuous entrepreneur schooling and controls for every percentile of the size distribution, plus an additional regression at the 99.9th percentile. Settings.G934:
Treatment: Average years of entrepreneur schooling, entered linearly and interacted with firm age; treatment increment is one additional year of entrepreneur schooling.

Settings.G938:
Treatment: Change in pollution abatement intensity, measured as the change in log(1 − a_it), where a_it is the abatement cost share of production costs. Economically, higher abatement spending means a lower value of log(1 − a_it). The endogenous treatment is continuous, not binary. Although the instrument is based on binary nonattainment regulation interacted with pollutant intensity, the IV estimand concerns abatement expenditure share.

Method: The paper estimates the pollution-abatement elasticity parameter using linear instrumental variables regressions on a county × industry × year panel (about 3,500 observations). The second stage regresses changes in log pollution intensity on changes in log(1 minus the abatement cost share), with county-NAICS fixed effects. The endogenous regressor is the abatement expenditure share; the instrument is an interaction between whether a county became newly regulated/nonattainment under the Clean Air Act and whether the industry is pollution-intensive for the relevant pollutant. Table 1 reports first-stage, reduced-form, and IV estimates separately by pollutant and for pooled total pollution. The authors motivate IV by concerns about reverse causality (dirtier plants may be forced to spend more on abatement), measurement error in PACE/ASM variables, and endogenous exit.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from differential increases in local Clean Air Act regulatory stringency: counties newly designated nonattainment after the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments should face stronger abatement requirements, especially in industries that are more pollution-intensive for the relevant pollutant. The instrument interacts county nonattainment status with pollutant-specific industry pollution intensity, so identification is difference-in-differences-like across counties, industries, and time but implemented as IV for abatement expenditure shares. The key assumption is exclusion: newly regulated nonattainment status affects pollution intensity only through induced changes in abatement spending, after fixed effects and lower-order terms. The paper explicitly notes threats from reverse causality, measurement error, and endogenous exit, which motivate IV and aggregation to county-sector-year cells.

Setting: Using county × industry × year IV regressions, the authors estimate how greater pollution abatement effort causally lowers emissions intensity. The pooled IV estimate in Table 1, panel C is 91.604 (SE 25.373) for the effect of the abatement expenditure ratio on log total pollution intensity; after the model's nonlinear transformation this implies a pollution elasticity α = 0.011 (SE 0.003) in panel D. Pollutant-specific α estimates range from 0.008 for CO and VOC to 0.017 for PM2.5. Identification relies on county nonattainment designations under the Clean Air Act, interacted with industry pollution intensity, as an instrument for abatement spending. This is a central empirical setting because these parameter estimates feed directly into the model-based inference that environmental regulation tightened substantially and explains most of the emissions decline.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusions emphasize that the paper estimates a key pollution-abatement elasticity parameter and uses it to infer rising implicit pollution taxes and to quantify regulation's role in the emissions decline. Table 1 is therefore a core empirical input supporting the paper's central conclusions.
Settings.H938: Section IV.A 'Estimating Parameters,' equations (16)–(17), Table 1 panels A–D, PDF pp. 3833–3835 (article pages 3833–3835; supplied PDF pages 20–22).
Settings.G939:
Treatment: Exposure to the NOx Budget Trading Program, implemented as a binary triple interaction: being in an NBP region, in an NBP-regulated sector, and in years after 2002 when the program began. In the event study, treatment varies by event-time dummies for the same treated group.

The design compares regulated sectors in NBP states after the policy against nonregulated sectors and/or non-NBP regions.

The key assumption is that absent the NBP, treated region-sector cells would have followed the same trend in implied taxes as the comparison cells. The event study in Figure 6 shows little evidence of differential pretrends and a sharp post-policy rise in implied taxes for treated sectors. This is a substantive but supporting causal setting because it bolsters the claim that the inferred regulation shock corresponds to real environmental regulation.

Main role: The NBP DDD/event-study is presented in the alternative explanations/validation section as a test that the model-implied regulation measure tracks a known real-world regulation. It supports interpretation of the main model output but is not itself the main decomposition result highlighted in the abstract or conclusion.

Settings.G940:
Treatment: Leader punishment type measured from the third-party punishment game and entered as weighted leader-type variables: LEQ equals the number of punishment points a leader spent exclusively on deviations from the equality norm; LEQEF analogously captures punishment points spent by leaders who punish deviations from equality and efficiency norms; LAS equals punishment points spent on cooperators by antisocial leaders; omitted category is non-punishing leaders (LNP). Units are punishment points from the experiment. In some discussion the implied contrast is groups headed by each leader type versus non-punishing leaders.

Method: Cross-sectional OLS regressions relate group forest-management performance to experimentally measured leader punishment types, first without controls and then with extensive regression adjustment. The core specification regresses potential crop trees per hectare (PCT) on indicators or weighted measures of leader types (equality-driven, equality-and-efficiency-driven, antisocial; non-punishers omitted), adding group-level controls, leaders' characteristics, and village fixed effects in some columns. The weighted implementation uses the actual number of punishment points spent in the experiment within each motive category. Estimation is in the cross section of 51 groups; the paper discusses remaining reverse-causality and omitted-variable concerns and argues these are mitigated because leaders were elected before the outcome assessment, groups are similar on many observables, and rich controls including village fixed effects are included. This is not an experimental estimate of forest outcomes; it is an observational regression interpreted causally/associationally by the authors.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-group variation in experimentally elicited leader punishment motives linked to later-observed forest outcomes. The main endogeneity concerns are omitted group traits and selection of leader type by higher- or lower-performing groups. The authors argue reverse causality is limited because leaders were elected at the program outset before outcomes were assessed; groups are similar in ethnicity, religion, occupation, geography, and institutions; and the regressions control for many group and leader covariates, including the share of conditional cooperators and village fixed effects. Still, with cross-sectional observational data, causal interpretation remains vulnerable to unobserved confounding.

Setting: The paper's main observational specification interprets experimentally measured leader punishment motives as affecting group forest outcomes. Using cross-sectional OLS on 51 groups, the authors find that, relative to non-punishing leaders, equality-and-efficiency-driven leaders are associated with substantially better forest management while antisocial leaders are associated with substantially worse performance. In the preferred weighted specification with village fixed effects, each punishment point by an LEQEF leader is associated with about 2.494 more young trees per hectare; because such leaders spent 11.5 points on average, the authors summarize this as roughly 28.68 more trees per hectare. Each antisocial punishment point on cooperators is associated with about 7.404 fewer trees per hectare; with 2.75 such points on average, this implies about 20.36 fewer trees per hectare. Equality-only leaders are not significantly different from non-punishers in the first assessment. These results are central to the paper's claim that leader punishment style shapes cooperation outcomes in commons management.

Main role: This is the paper's central empirical link between experimentally revealed leader punishment motives and real-world commons performance, emphasized in the abstract, introduction, Section V, and conclusion.
Settings.H940: Section V.B 'Econometric Results,' equation (5), Table 6 cols. 1-3 and surrounding text; summary also in abstract/introduction. PDF pp. 768-774.
Settings.G941:
Treatment: Leader type as mutually exclusive indicator variables for equality-driven leaders (LEQ), equality-and-efficiency-driven leaders (LEQEF), and antisocial leaders (LAS), with non-punishing leaders (LNP) omitted. Treatment is implemented as separate binary contrasts versus the omitted leader type.

Method: Cross-sectional OLS robustness regressions re-estimate the relationship between leader punishment type and forest outcomes using leader-type dummies instead of weighted punishment-point measures, plus the same family of covariates and village fixed effects. The reported coefficients compare groups led by LEQ, LEQEF, and LAS leaders with groups led by non-punishing leaders. This is a robustness estimator of the main cross-sectional design rather than a separate identification strategy.

Identification: Same cross-sectional identification logic as the main specification: leader types are experimentally elicited and compared across observationally similar groups, with controls and village fixed effects used to reduce confounding. The authors note that cross-sectional data cannot fully eliminate omitted-variable bias.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors replace weighted leader-type intensities with simple leader-type dummies in the cross-sectional OLS with village fixed effects. The results closely match the main weighted findings: groups led by equality-and-efficiency-driven leaders have about 24.732 more young trees per hectare than groups led by non-punishing leaders, while groups led by antisocial leaders have about 19.820 fewer young trees per hectare; equality-only leaders are not significantly different from non-punishers. The authors interpret the similarity to the weighted results as evidence that punishment motives, not just intensity, matter for forest outcomes.

Main role: The dummy specification is a substantive robustness check for the paper's core conclusion and is discussed as confirming the main leader-type effects.
Settings.H941: Table 6, col. 4 and accompanying text in Section V.C 'Robustness Analysis.' PDF pp. 772-774.
Settings.G942:
Treatment: Being a group led by an equality-driven leader (LEQ) rather than a non-punishing leader (LNP), interacted with the post/second-assessment period in a two-period DiD for the subsample with second-round data. The paper also notes using the weighted LEQ measure in places, but Table 7 presents LEQ as the focal treatment contrast versus LNP over time.

Method: For the subsample of 25 groups with a second forest assessment, the paper estimates a conventional difference-in-differences with group fixed effects by interacting an LEQ leader measure with an assessment-period dummy. The comparison is between groups led by equality-driven leaders and groups led by non-punishing leaders over two assessment rounds (PCT-I and PCT-II). One specification includes no additional controls beyond group fixed effects; another adds interactions of the assessment-period dummy with important covariates. Standard errors are clustered on the group.

Identification: The DiD uses within-group changes between two forest assessments for groups headed by LEQ versus LNP leaders. Group fixed effects absorb time-invariant group heterogeneity; the identifying assumption is that absent leader-type differences, LEQ and LNP groups would have had parallel changes in forest outcomes across assessment rounds. The authors also verify that the assessed subsample appears similar to the original sample on most observables except program timing. The sample is small and only includes LEQ and LNP groups, limiting generalizability.

Setting: Using the subset of 25 groups with a second forest assessment, the authors estimate a two-period difference-in-differences comparing equality-driven leaders with non-punishers. They find that outcomes decline from about 78 to 56 trees per hectare in LNP groups but rise slightly from about 72 to 75 in LEQ groups. In the DiD with group fixed effects, the LEQ × post coefficient is 5.619 without added control interactions and 4.611 with them, both statistically significant, which the authors interpret as evidence that equality-driven leaders eventually have a positive effect on forest performance relative to non-punishing leaders. They further summarize that, because LEQ leaders in this subsample spent 4.46 punishment points on average, LEQ-led groups have about 20.56 more trees than LNP-led groups in the second assessment.

Main role: This is additional evidence on dynamics and timing, supporting the claim that equality-driven leaders eventually improve outcomes, but it is secondary to the main cross-sectional evidence.
Settings.H942: Section V.D 'Additional Results: Second Forest Assessment and Leader Turnover,' Table 7 cols. 3-4 and surrounding text. PDF pp. 775-776.
Settings.G943:
Treatment: Exposure to the sharp increase in marginal out-of-pocket price when annual total drug spending reaches the plan's kink/initial coverage limit and the beneficiary enters the gap. The treatment is effectively a price jump at the kink, averaging about a 60 cent increase in out-of-pocket price per $1 of total spending for the baseline sample; treatment intensity varies across plans.

Method: The authors use a bunching/excess-mass design around the Medicare Part D initial coverage limit (the 'donut hole' kink) to infer the causal effect of a sharp increase in marginal out-of-pocket price on annual drug spending behavior. They compare the observed distribution of annual total drug spending near the year-specific kink to a counterfactual no-kink distribution obtained by fitting a cubic CDF to spending bins below the kink. The implemented estimator is not a standard linear RD or regression design; it is a reduced-form bunching calculation based on excess density within +/-$200 of the kink. Identification comes from the movement of the kink across years and from excess mass concentrating at plan-specific kink locations, with the maintained assumption that absent the kink the local spending distribution would be smooth.

Identification: Identification uses the nonlinear Part D contract: at the initial coverage limit the marginal out-of-pocket price rises sharply. Under the assumption that the counterfactual annual spending distribution would be smooth around the kink absent the price jump, excess mass near the kink is interpreted as a behavioral response to the price increase. Supporting evidence is that the bunching location moves with the year-specific kink and appears around nonstandard plan-specific kinks as well.

Setting: Using the distribution of annual drug spending around the Medicare Part D donut-hole kink, the authors interpret excess mass near the kink as evidence that a higher marginal out-of-pocket price reduces drug spending. Pooling 2007-2009 and fitting a cubic counterfactual distribution below the kink, they estimate excess mass of 29.1% (s.e. 0.3%) in the +/-$200 range around the kink, which they interpret as rejecting the null of no behavioral response to price. This is a reduced-form descriptive causal result that motivates the structural model used for the paper's main counterfactual analysis.

Main role: This descriptive bunching evidence is an important empirical motivation for the paper's dynamic model and supports the claim that beneficiaries respond to nonlinear price schedules, but the headline policy results come from the structural counterfactual model rather than the excess-mass estimate itself.
Settings.H943: Section III.A, Figure IV and accompanying text, PDF pp. 14-16.
Settings.G944:
Treatment: Approaching/reaching the donut-hole kink, which raises the marginal out-of-pocket price for additional drug spending. The relevant treatment is the higher price associated with being near/at/above the kink relative to remaining below it.

Method: The authors use a nonparametric descriptive event pattern around the kink, plotting the share of individuals with at least one drug purchase in a month as a function of end-of-year spending relative to the kink. They compare actual monthly claim propensities near the kink with a counterfactual fitted line estimated from bins below the kink. This is a reduced-form bunching/timing design rather than a standard regression estimator. The outcome is monthly claim propensity, studied separately by month and by drug type, to infer how the higher price in the gap changes within-year purchase timing.

Identification: The authors exploit the same nonlinear budget-set kink: if the higher price in the gap depresses utilization, monthly purchase propensity should fall as individuals approach/reach the kink relative to the smooth counterfactual pattern expected absent the kink. The argument is qualitative and reduced form, relying on the assumption that absent the kink claim propensity would vary smoothly with annual spending. Drug-type heterogeneity is interpreted as differential responsiveness to the same price jump.

Setting: The authors interpret the decline in monthly claiming near the donut-hole kink as evidence that the higher out-of-pocket price reduces drug purchases, especially late in the year and especially for branded drugs. In December, the probability of any drug purchase for individuals within $200 of the kink is 0.846 versus a predicted 0.923 absent the kink, implying an 8.3% decline in purchase probability; for branded drugs the decline is 19.9%, versus 8.5% for generics. These descriptive reduced-form results support the paper's claim that beneficiaries respond to dynamic incentives created by the nonlinear contract.

Main role: These timing patterns are central descriptive evidence used to motivate dynamic incentives in the model, but they are not the paper's headline quantitative policy estimates.
Settings.H944: Section III.B, Figure V and Table IV, PDF pp. 18-23.

Settings.G950:
Treatment: Algorithmic prediction of judge detention based on the defendant's mug shot alone, produced by a convolutional neural network trained on raw facial images. In Table III this is a continuous scalar predicted probability; a one-unit change refers to moving the prediction from 0 to 1 on the model's detention-risk scale. The underlying substantive treatment is facial appearance as summarized by the algorithm, not a binary treatment.

Method: Linear probability / linear regression specifications on the validation sample relate the judge's detention decision to the algorithmic mug-shot-based prediction and to observed defendant features. The core implementation is an OLS regression adjustment with detention as the dependent variable and regressors including the CNN prediction from mug shots alone, demographics, skin tone, psychology ratings, and human guesses. The paper interprets these coefficients causally only tentatively or suggestively, but does use the regressions to argue that facial appearance affects judge detention decisions and that the mug-shot prediction captures novel signal beyond known covariates. No fixed effects, IV, RD, DiD, or experimental assignment are used in these table specifications; remaining confounding and measurement concerns are acknowledged, especially regarding whether face proxies for risk.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional covariation between the face-based algorithmic score and judge detention decisions in held-out validation data, with regression adjustment for measured demographics, skin tone, prior psychology-based facial ratings, and human guesses. The endogeneity concern is that facial appearance may proxy for omitted determinants of legally relevant risk or other unobserved case characteristics. The paper argues novelty by showing the coefficient survives conditioning on known factors, but does not claim a clean causal design here; causal interpretation requires assuming remaining omitted variables are not driving the association or that the face-based score captures the relevant appearance channel.

Setting: In validation-sample linear probability regressions, the mug-shot-based algorithmic prediction strongly predicts whether judges detain defendants. With the algorithmic prediction alone, the coefficient is 0.6963 (s.e. 0.0383); after controlling for gender, age, race, skin tone, attractiveness, competence, dominance, trustworthiness, and incentivized human guesses, it remains 0.6171 (0.0434). The paper uses these OLS associations to argue that facial appearance affects judicial detention decisions and that the algorithm has uncovered facial signal beyond previously known features, while acknowledging unresolved endogeneity and risk-proxy concerns.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that defendants' faces strongly shape jailing decisions and that the algorithm's face-based prediction explains a large share of predictable variation. Table III is central evidence that facial appearance matters for judge decisions beyond known demographics and psychology features.
Settings.H950: Introduction, pp. 754, 758 [PDF pp. 4, 8]; Section IV.A–IV.C and Table III, cols. (1) and (6)–(7), pp. 776–786 [PDF pp. 26–36].
Settings.G951:
Treatment: Facial appearance summarized by the mug-shot-based algorithmic prediction of the judge's detention decision; continuous score. In the risk-bounding comparison, the paper also compares a one-unit change in predicted rearrest risk as an alternative regressor, but the focal substantive treatment is still the mug-shot facial score.

Method: Linear regressions in Section IV.B and Table III/related text regress measured rearrest before trial and judge detention decisions on the mug-shot-based algorithmic prediction and on predicted rearrest risk. These are regression-adjustment exercises used for a bounding argument about whether facial appearance merely proxies for legally relevant risk. The design is observational and cross-sectional, with no quasi-experimental source of variation. The paper explicitly notes severe interpretation problems because rearrest is observed only for released defendants and because measured rearrest depends on police behavior.

Identification: The paper compares observational associations of the mug-shot score with measured rearrest and of predicted rearrest risk with judge detention. The endogeneity concerns are central: measured rearrest may reflect police bias, and rearrest is observed only for released defendants, creating selection issues if judges use private information. The paper therefore does not claim identification, instead using a bounding logic: if judges were using the face solely because it proxies for risk, the face-risk relationship would need to be much larger than what is observed among released defendants. This relies on strong assumptions and is presented as suggestive only.

Setting: To assess whether facial appearance might simply proxy for defendant risk, the paper reports observational regressions linking the mug-shot score to measured rearrest and linking predicted rearrest risk to detention. Regressing rearrest on the mug-shot score yields coefficients of 0.6127 (0.0460) without additional controls and 0.5735 (0.0521) with all controls, while a one-unit change in predicted rearrest risk changes judge detention by 0.6103 (0.0213). Because the mug-shot score changes detention by 0.6963, the authors argue that if judges were using the face only as a proxy for rearrest risk, the implied face-risk relationship would need to be 1.141, exceeding the observed 0.6127; they treat this as tentative evidence that facial appearance likely reflects judicial error rather than lawful risk assessment.

Main role: These regressions are ancillary and used to motivate the claim that the face likely reflects judicial error rather than a valid proxy for risk. The paper presents them as tentative and caveated, not as the main contribution.
Settings.H951: Section IV.B, pp. 777–779 [PDF pp. 27–29], with reference to Table III col. (1).
Settings.G952:
Treatment: Independently coded facial traits from mug shots: (i) well-groomed on a 9-point scale, and (ii) heavy-faced on a 9-point scale, each averaged from human ratings. These are continuous doses rather than binary treatments. In some discussion the paper also compares top versus bottom quartiles of these traits.

Method: Linear regressions in Table VI relate judge detention decisions to independently labeled novel facial features, well-groomed and heavy-faced, alone and with controls for demographics, skin tone, psychology ratings, human guesses, and the algorithmic mug-shot prediction. The estimator is a linear probability model on the validation sample. The paper interprets the coefficients as evidence that these newly generated hypotheses are empirically plausible and potentially causal determinants of judge decisions, while acknowledging confounding remains unresolved.

Identification: Identification is based on observational variation in independently rated facial features across defendants in the held-out validation sample, with regression adjustment for a rich set of known covariates. The key concern is omitted-variable bias: these facial traits may proxy for socioeconomic status, substance abuse, mental health, or other unobservables, and the paper later explores but does not eliminate such confounding. Thus the regressions support hypothesis generation and empirical plausibility rather than clean causal identification.

Setting: In linear probability models, independently rated well-groomed and heavy-faced facial features predict actual pretrial detention decisions. Heavy-faced alone has a coefficient of -0.0234 (0.0036), well-groomed alone -0.0198 (0.0043), and together they explain an adjusted R2 of 0.0061. The paper notes that one-standard-deviation increases are associated with 2.8 and 2.0 percentage point lower detention rates, respectively, and that heavy-faced remains significant even after controlling for the algorithmic mug-shot prediction, consistent with these new hypotheses capturing substantively important appearance-based determinants of judges' decisions.

Main role: The introduction and abstract highlight the discovery of the well-groomed and heavy-faced hypotheses and state that these features predict actual judge behavior. Table VI is the main empirical link from the machine-generated hypotheses to judicial decisions.
Settings.H952: Introduction, p. 758 [PDF p. 8]; Section VI.A and Table VI, pp. 808–812 [PDF pp. 58–62].
Settings.G953:
Treatment: Random assignment of synthetic mug-shot images morphed toward higher versus lower values of well-groomedness or heavy-facedness. The text describes these as randomly morphed directions; effectively an experimental contrast between higher and lower feature values, separately for each facial trait. Coding in the appendix is not reproduced in the main text, but the assignment is binary by design within each manipulated feature.

Method: Laboratory-style experiment with human subjects (Prolific workers) who are asked to act like judges making hypothetical pretrial detention decisions. Synthetic mug-shot images are randomly morphed in the direction of higher or lower well-groomedness or heavy-facedness, and structured case variables such as current charge and prior record are also randomly assigned across image pairs. Subjects choose which defendant they would detain. Because appearance manipulations are randomly assigned, the design identifies direct causal effects of these manipulated facial features on subjects' detention recommendations in the experimental setting. The paper reports the results in Online Appendix Table A.XVII and discusses them in the main text, without emphasizing exact main-paper coefficient values.

Identification: Identification comes from random assignment of appearance manipulations in synthetic mug-shot images, shutting down confounding from defendants' actual traits and isolating the causal effect of manipulated appearance on subjects' choices in the lab. The paper notes that this is not a field experiment with actual judges, so external validity to real court settings remains limited. The experiment also aims to isolate appearance per se rather than channels operating through defendants' own confidence or oral communication.

Setting: In a lab experiment, subjects making hypothetical pretrial release decisions see criminal-record information alongside synthetic mug shots randomly morphed toward higher or lower well-groomedness or heavy-facedness. Subjects respond to structured risk variables as expected, but are also more likely to detain defendants who are less heavy-faced or less well-groomed, even though those facial features were randomly assigned. The paper treats this as suggestive causal evidence that the newly discovered facial traits can directly influence detention decisions, while emphasizing that only a field experiment with actual judges could establish real-world causality conclusively.

Main role: The introduction explicitly states that subjects are more likely to detain defendants who are less heavy-faced or well-groomed even though these features were randomly assigned. This experiment is used as suggestive causal evidence supporting the substantive importance of the discovered hypotheses.
Settings.H953: Introduction, p. 758 [PDF p. 8]; Section VI.C, pp. 816–818 [PDF pp. 66–68], referring to Online Appendix Table A.XVII.
Settings.G954:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office: 1 if the incumbent political party loses the municipal election (incumbent vote margin < 0), 0 if the incumbent party barely wins and remains in office. This is a binary treatment defined at the municipality-election level.

Method: The paper’s core design is a sharp regression discontinuity using close mayoral elections in Brazil. The running variable is the incumbent party’s vote margin, defined as the incumbent party vote share minus the strongest opponent’s vote share; treatment equals one when this margin is below zero, i.e., the incumbent party barely loses and a new party takes office. The authors estimate local linear regressions on either side of the cutoff with an interaction in slope, using Calonico et al. (2016) optimal bandwidths and also reporting fixed alternative bandwidths (0.07 and 0.11). Outcomes here are municipality-level labor-contract flows from RAIS, measured over the 12 months after the election and, in a secondary horizon, over months 12–24 after the election. Standard errors are clustered at the municipality level. Identification relies on continuity of potential outcomes around zero incumbent margin in close elections; the paper presents density and covariate-balance evidence in support.

Identification: Close-election RD compares municipalities where the incumbent party barely loses to those where it barely wins, treating party turnover as as-good-as-random near the zero margin threshold. The endogeneity concern is that municipalities changing party may differ systematically in underlying service trends or competence. The RD addresses this by exploiting quasi-random electoral outcomes in close races, under continuity of potential outcomes and no manipulation of the running variable at the cutoff; the paper reports smooth density and no discontinuities in baseline covariates or baseline personnel outcomes.

Setting: Using a sharp RD around close mayoral elections, the paper finds that political party turnover causes substantial municipal bureaucratic upheaval. A new party in office raises the share of municipal personnel contracts that are new over the following year by about 0.069–0.072, with the preferred estimate 0.0693 (s.e. 0.0188), while the corresponding increase in personnel exits is smaller and statistically weak at 0.0233 (s.e. 0.0168). The increase in new hires is short-lived: between years 1 and 2 after the election, the effect on new personnel falls to 0.0169 and is not statistically significant. These results support the paper’s main claim that political turnover directly disrupts the bureaucracy.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that political turnover causes upheaval in the municipal bureaucracy. These municipal personnel effects are one of the paper’s two central causal findings, alongside education effects.
Settings.H954: Section IV.A, Figure 3 and Table 2 panels A and B, PDF pp. 461–463.
Settings.G955:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office, equal to one when the incumbent party loses the election and a new party takes office.

Method: This is the same close-election sharp RD design, applied to municipality-level labor-contract outcomes disaggregated by contract type, hierarchical level, and service sector using RAIS. The authors estimate local linear regressions around the zero incumbent-party-margin cutoff, with political turnover as the treatment. These are substantive heterogeneity/robustness results rather than diagnostics, aimed at characterizing the scope of the causal bureaucratic disruption across temporary versus civil-service contracts, managers versus nonmanagers, and sectors such as education, health, construction, and other/multiple-service positions.

Identification: Same close-election RD as in the main design. The concern is that observed personnel composition changes could reflect nonrandom differences between municipalities changing party and those not changing party. By focusing on municipalities near the win/loss threshold for the incumbent party, the design attributes discontinuous differences in hiring and termination across categories to political turnover, under continuity and no sorting at the cutoff.

Setting: Using the close-election RD, the paper shows that the personnel shock from political turnover is broad-based. The increase in new hires is concentrated in temporary contracts, which rise by 10.7 percentage points, with temporary-contract terminations also rising by 7.4 percentage points; civil-servant contracts show no comparable effect. Across hierarchy levels, high-manager new contracts rise by 7.9 percentage points, low-manager contracts by 5.7 percentage points (imprecise), and nonmanager contracts by 5.4 percentage points. Across sectors, new hires rise in education, health, construction, and especially multiple-service categories, supporting the claim that political turnover causes wide bureaucratic reshaping rather than a narrow sectoral change.

Main role: These estimates materially support the paper’s central conclusion that political turnover broadly reshapes the bureaucracy, affecting many types of positions and sectors, not just schools.
Settings.H955: Section IV.A discussion of scope; online Appendix Tables A.11 and A.12 referenced on PDF pp. 463–464.
Settings.G956:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office, equal to one if the incumbent party loses and a new party assumes office.

Method: The authors use the same sharp RD around close mayoral elections, but with individual student test scores as outcomes. They estimate local linear regressions around the zero incumbent-party-margin cutoff, controlling for school-level baseline average test scores and, in some columns, school characteristics, individual demographics, and an election-cycle indicator. Outcomes are fourth-grade and eighth-grade Prova Brasil standardized test scores, measured one year after the election. Bandwidths are outcome-specific optimal bandwidths and fixed alternatives. Standard errors are clustered at the municipality level.

Identification: The core endogeneity concern is that municipalities that replace the ruling party may have different preexisting education trends or underlying governance quality, so simple comparisons would confound causality. The sharp RD uses quasi-random variation in whether the incumbent party barely wins or barely loses. Identification requires continuity of potential test-score outcomes around the vote-margin cutoff and no precise manipulation of the running variable. The paper reports no discontinuity in baseline test scores or many other predetermined covariates, supporting the design.

Setting: The paper’s main public-service result is that political party turnover causally lowers student achievement. In the close-election RD, a new party in office reduces fourth-grade test scores by about 0.082 standard deviations (s.e. 0.028) and eighth-grade test scores by about 0.054 standard deviations (s.e. 0.023) one year after the election, with estimates robust to covariates and alternative bandwidths. Because these outcomes are standardized against the no-turnover distribution, the effects are directly interpretable in student-SD units. This evidence underpins the central claim that political turnover harms the quality of public education.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion present the negative effect of political turnover on education quality as a headline finding. This setting is the core public-service quality result of the paper.
Settings.H956: Section IV.B, Figure 4 and Table 3, PDF pp. 465–467; benchmark discussion on PDF pp. 468–469.
Settings.G957:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office, equal to one when the incumbent party loses and a new party wins.

Method: Same close-election sharp RD, applied to student composition and enrollment-related outcomes to assess whether the main education result could be driven by selection into testing or schooling rather than learning. The authors estimate local linear RD models around the zero incumbent-party-margin cutoff for school-level dropout rates, school-level enrollment counts, and student composition variables from surveys and administrative data. These are substantive robustness outcomes because the paper interprets them causally to rule out an alternative mechanism.

Identification: Using the same close-election RD, the paper asks whether political turnover changes who remains enrolled or takes the test, which could mechanically lower scores without reducing school quality. If turnout-induced changes in enrollment, dropout, or demographics were responsible, these outcomes should shift discontinuously at the cutoff. The identifying assumptions are the same continuity assumptions as in the main RD design.

Setting: As a robustness exercise with causal interpretation, the paper finds no evidence that the drop in test scores after political turnover is driven by changes in student composition or access. Political turnover does not affect observable student characteristics, does not affect student enrollment, and does not significantly reduce dropout; if anything, dropout is estimated to be 12 percent higher, but insignificantly so. The authors interpret these results as ruling out a compositional explanation in which new parties broaden access and thereby lower average scores by bringing in marginal students.

Main role: These are supporting robustness checks used to reject a compositional-selection explanation for the main test-score findings, not the headline result themselves.
Settings.H957: Section IV.B discussion and online Appendix Table A.13, Figure A.6, Table A.15, and Table A.14, PDF pp. 466–467 and 476.
Settings.G958:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office, equal to one when the incumbent party loses and a new party takes office in the municipality.

Method: This setting applies the close-election sharp RD to school personnel outcomes in municipal schools. The treatment is party turnover in the mayor’s office. Outcomes are whether the headmaster is new to the school and the shares of teachers new to or leaving the school. Headmaster status comes from Prova Brasil surveys administered roughly 11 months after the new party takes office; teacher flows come from the School Census in May, roughly 5 months after the new party takes office. Regressions are local linear RD specifications around the incumbent-party-margin cutoff with alternative bandwidths and school controls in some specifications.

Identification: The RD leverages quasi-random partisan turnover in close elections to identify the causal effect on school personnel assignments. This addresses the concern that schools in municipalities that change party may differ systematically in underlying personnel trends or education problems. Identification requires continuity of potential personnel outcomes around the zero incumbent-margin cutoff. The paper also shows baseline balance and absence of discontinuities in personnel outcomes prior to the election.

Setting: Political turnover sharply disrupts staffing in municipal schools. In the close-election RD, a new party in office increases the probability that a school has a new headmaster by about 0.278 (s.e. 0.027), or roughly 28 percentage points, and raises the share of teachers new to a school by about 0.117 while also raising the share who leave by about 0.114. The near one-for-one increase in teacher entries and exits suggests reshuffling rather than school-staff expansion. These school personnel effects are a core mechanism for the paper’s main finding that political turnover harms education quality.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion stress that political turnover causes upheavals in school personnel—headmasters and teachers—which is central to the paper’s mechanism linking political turnover to lower educational quality.
Settings.H958: Section IV.B, Figure 5, Table 4, and Table 5 panels A and C, PDF pp. 469–473.
Settings.G959:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office, equal to one if the incumbent party loses the election.

Method: This setting uses the same sharp RD but estimates heterogeneous effects of political turnover on school personnel by prior appointment rules and municipal income. The paper splits the sample by whether the baseline headmaster was politically appointed versus not politically appointed, and by low- versus high-income municipalities, then estimates the same local linear RD around the incumbent-margin cutoff. These are substantive mechanism analyses, not diagnostics.

Identification: The same close-election RD identifies local causal effects within subgroups. The motivation is to test whether political turnover causes larger staffing changes where political discretion is easier to exercise or politically cheaper. Under the same continuity assumptions, subgroup-specific discontinuities at the vote cutoff reveal causal heterogeneity. The baseline headmaster appointment type is measured before treatment to avoid post-treatment bias in subgroup definition; income is predetermined from Census data.

Setting: The heterogeneity analysis suggests a political component to personnel replacement. Political turnover increases headmaster replacement by about 35 percentage points in schools whose baseline headmaster was politically appointed, versus only about 3 percentage points and statistically insignificant in schools whose baseline headmaster was not politically appointed. Teacher replacement is also larger in schools with politically appointed headmasters. By municipal income, political turnover raises headmaster replacement by about 39 percentage points in low-income municipalities and 13 percentage points in high-income municipalities, with similar larger effects on teacher turnover in low-income areas. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that politicians exercise more discretion where disruption is easier or politically less costly.

Main role: These are important mechanism and heterogeneity analyses supporting the interpretation that personnel changes are politically motivated, but they are secondary to the paper’s headline average effects.
Settings.H959: Section IV.B discussion; online Appendix Table A.20, Figures A.14–A.16, Tables A.21–A.22, PDF pp. 474–475.
Settings.G960:
Treatment: Indicator for political party turnover in the mayoral office, equal to one if a new party replaces the incumbent party.

Method: The authors use the close-election sharp RD to estimate the effect of political turnover on municipal finances and school-reported financial constraints. Local linear regressions around the incumbent-party-margin cutoff are run for total municipal expenditures, education expenditure shares, personnel expenditure shares, school-level reports of financial problems, and enrollment. These are substantive mechanism tests about whether resource changes, rather than personnel disruptions, explain lower test scores.

Identification: Same RD identification as the core design. The question is whether municipalities with new parties experience discontinuous changes in funding or financial constraints that could mechanically reduce educational quality. If such resource changes drove the main effect, these budget and school-finance measures should jump at the electoral cutoff.
