Specifications add adviser controls and, in the preferred version, firm × year × county fixed effects. The interaction coefficient is the key estimand.

Identification: The model uses within-firm, within-county, within-year comparisons and asks whether the misconduct-separation slope is flatter at firms with higher misconduct rates. Fixed effects absorb the level of firm employee misconduct and local common shocks. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on controls and FE, variation in the interaction reflects true differences in firm tolerance rather than omitted adviser-case composition.

Setting: The authors find that firms employing more advisers with misconduct records are less likely to punish new misconduct with separation. In table 12 panel A, the interaction coefficient between adviser misconduct and firm employee misconduct is about -3.10, implying that at a firm with a misconduct rate one standard deviation above average, the increase in separation following misconduct is about 9 percentage points smaller than at the average firm. They interpret this as evidence that some firms are more tolerant of misconduct, helping explain why advisers with misconduct can remain in the industry.

Main role: This is a core mechanism result in Section V, used to argue that high-misconduct firms are more tolerant and thus sustain misconduct in equilibrium.
Settings.H997: Section V.A.1 'Differences in Separation,' equation (9), Table 12 panel A, PDF pp. 272-274.
Settings.G998:
Treatment: Firm employee misconduct rate in year t, measured as the percentage of current advisers at the firm reprimanded for misconduct. Continuous treatment in percentage points.

Method: Weighted firm-year linear regression of the share of new hires previously disciplined for misconduct on the firm’s current employee misconduct rate and firm controls, with year and state fixed effects (equation (10)). The sample is firm-year observations with new hires. Observations are weighted by the square root of adviser count and SEs clustered by firm. The authors interpret the coefficient as measuring whether high-misconduct firms are more tolerant in hiring.

Identification: The regression relates a firm’s composition of new hires to its current misconduct environment, controlling for observed firm traits and year/state effects. Endogeneity concerns remain because unobserved firm culture or business model may drive both current misconduct and hiring. The paper nonetheless interprets the strong association as evidence of greater hiring tolerance for misconduct at high-misconduct firms.

Setting: Firms with higher existing misconduct rates hire disproportionately more advisers who were recently disciplined for misconduct. The coefficient in table 12 panel B implies that a 1 percentage point increase in a firm’s current employee misconduct rate is associated with a 0.68–0.72 percentage point higher share of misconduct-tainted new hires in the next year. This is one of the paper’s central mechanism results, supporting the view that some firms specialize in misconduct and match with advisers who have misconduct records.

Main role: This hiring result, together with differential firing, is central to the mechanism of matching between misconduct advisers and misconduct-tolerant firms.
Settings.H998: Section V.A.2 'Differences in Hiring,' equation (10), Table 12 panel B, PDF pp. 274-275.
Settings.G999:
Treatment: Main treatment is Retail_Firm_jt, a binary indicator for whether firm j services retail clients (non-high-net-worth individuals/families/households) in year t. The same regressions also include binary indicators for compensation structures: assets-under-management fees, hourly fees, fixed fees, commissions, and performance fees.

Method: Firm-year linear regressions relating firm employee misconduct to whether the firm serves retail investors and to its compensation structure (equation (11)). Two outcome specifications are reported: stock of misconduct and flow of new misconduct. The sample is firms matched to SEC Form ADV filings over 2011-2014. Some specifications add firm controls, year fixed effects, and state fixed effects; observations are weighted by the square root of adviser count and standard errors clustered by firm. The paper interprets the retail-client coefficient as evidence that misconduct is more common where firms serve less sophisticated customers.

Identification: The design uses cross-firm variation in client base and fee structures among Form ADV filers. Controls, year FE, and state FE address some observable differences, but selection into serving retail clients is a major endogeneity concern. The authors present these results as suggestive evidence consistent with market segmentation by consumer sophistication rather than definitive causal identification.

Setting: Among investment advisory firms filing Form ADV, those serving retail clients have higher misconduct. The authors estimate that retail-serving firms have about 3.4 to 4.2 percentage points more advisers with misconduct records and about 0.21 to 0.32 percentage points higher annual new misconduct rates. Relative to the mean annual misconduct rate of 0.6 percentage points, the 0.2 percentage point increase is substantial. These results support the paper’s interpretation that misconduct is more common where firms cater to less sophisticated investors, though the evidence is observational.

Main role: The link between misconduct and unsophisticated/retail clients is part of the paper’s central interpretation for why misconduct-specializing firms can survive in equilibrium.
Settings.H999: Section V.B.1 'Retail Clients, Fee Structure, and Misconduct,' equation (11), Table 13, PDF pp. 276-277.
Settings.G1000:
Treatment: County demographic measures: log population, log median household income, rural share, college-educated share, share age 65 or older, and labor force participation. These are continuous county-level covariates rather than binary treatments.

Method: County-year linear regressions of county misconduct on county demographic characteristics with year and state fixed effects (equation (12)). Two outcome variants are estimated: stock of misconduct and flow of new misconduct. Observations are county-year cells for counties with at least 50 advisers over 2010-2013, weighted by the square root of adviser count and clustered by county. The authors interpret these relationships as evidence that misconduct is more prevalent where populations are older and less educated, consistent with targeting less financially sophisticated consumers.

Identification: The variation is cross-county over time, with state and year fixed effects removing common regulation at the state level and aggregate shocks. Omitted county characteristics and measurement of detected rather than total misconduct remain concerns. The paper presents the evidence as suggestive and consistent with targeted misconduct rather than making a sharp causal claim.

Setting: At the county-year level, misconduct is more prevalent in places with older and less educated populations. In the specification with state and year fixed effects, a 10 percentage point increase in the share age 65+ is associated with about a 0.34 percentage point increase in annual new misconduct, while a 10 percentage point increase in the college-educated share is associated with about a 0.19 percentage point decrease. Relative to the mean new misconduct rate of 0.6 percentage points, these are sizable differences. The authors use these results to argue that misconduct is concentrated in markets with less financially sophisticated and more vulnerable consumers, though the evidence is observational.

Main role: Geographic evidence on misconduct being higher in wealthy, elderly, less educated counties is highlighted in the introduction, abstract, and conclusion as support for the consumer-sophistication mechanism.
Settings.H1000: Section V.B.2 'Firm Location and Customer Base,' equation (12), Table 15, Figure 7, PDF pp. 278-281.
Settings.G1001:
Treatment: Assignment of a CEMS firm to a private citizen-appeal arm (T1, pooling private message to regulator, website appeal, hotline appeal, and/or phone appeal to firm) or a public citizen-appeal arm (T2, Weibo public appeal), relative to control. Treatment is a randomized assignment indicator at the firm level; actual appeals occur when assigned firms violate standards.

Method: Nationwide field experiment on China’s universe of 24,620 CEMS firms. Firms were randomly assigned to control, private-appeal treatment arms (T1A–T1D, aggregated here as T1), or public Weibo-appeal treatment arms (T2A–T2B, aggregated here as T2). The authors estimate intention-to-treat effects with firm fixed effects and day fixed effects or province-by-day fixed effects in equation (1): outcome on treatment-arm × post interactions, firm FE, and time FE. Appeals are triggered only when a treated firm violates standards during the experimental period, so reported coefficients are ITT effects of assignment. Outcomes reported together in Table 3 are daily firm violation status and daily SO2/COD emission concentrations. Standard errors are two-way clustered by prefecture and week.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized assignment of firms to control, private-appeal, and public-appeal arms before the treatment period. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity, and day or province-by-day fixed effects absorb common shocks and regional time-varying enforcement differences. The causal question is whether citizen appeals cause improved environmental compliance. The key assumption is valid randomization and no differential confounding trends across arms; balance tests support this. Because appeals are triggered by post-randomization violations, coefficients are interpreted as ITT effects of assignment rather than treatment-on-the-treated effects.

Setting: Using firm-level random assignment in a nationwide field experiment, the authors estimate that private appeals modestly reduce daily violations, while public Weibo appeals have much larger effects. In Table 3, preferred specifications with firm and province-by-day fixed effects show private appeals reduce the daily violation probability by 0.002 relative to a control mean of 0.009 (about 24 percent), whereas public appeals reduce it by 0.006 (about 62 percent). Public appeals also reduce daily SO2 emission concentration by 16.2 mg/m3 relative to a control mean of 132.5 mg/m3 (12.2 percent) and COD concentration by 2.2 mg/L relative to 59.1 mg/L (3.7 percent); private-appeal concentration effects are small and not conventionally significant. These estimates are the paper’s main direct causal results.

Main role: This is the paper’s core experimental evidence supporting the central claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that public appeals substantially reduce violations and emissions, while private appeals have more modest effects.
Settings.H1001: Section III.A, equation (1), Table 3 columns (1a)-(3b), PDF pp. 833-836.
Settings.G1002:
Treatment: Assignment of a firm to private-appeal treatment T1 or public-appeal treatment T2 versus control, with coefficients allowed to vary by week relative to the experiment start.

Method: Same nationwide firm-level randomized experiment as the main analysis, but the authors estimate dynamic treatment effects by interacting treatment assignment with week indicators in event-study-style regressions of violation outcomes on treatment-by-week terms, firm fixed effects, and week fixed effects. Figure 3 reports separate paths for aggregated private appeals (T1) and public appeals (T2). The estimator remains an experimental ITT regression; the event-study display traces weekly post-assignment impacts and checks for pre-treatment differences.

Identification: Random assignment identifies weekly ITT effects under the same assumptions as the main experiment. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity, and week fixed effects absorb aggregate time shocks. The event-study serves to show no pre-treatment differences and the evolution of effects over time rather than introducing a new source of identification.

Setting: Figure 3 shows that both private and public appeal assignments reduce violations over time, with effects emerging a few weeks after the experiment begins and growing before stabilizing. The authors interpret the absence of pre-treatment effects as evidence that randomization was well executed and the increasing post-treatment effects as indicating that firms and regulators adjust over time rather than reacting only temporarily. No single summary coefficient is reported in the figure text for each week, but the dynamic pattern is used causally to argue that longer-run partial-equilibrium effects are larger than the average effects in Table 3.

Main role: This dynamic specification supports the interpretation and persistence of the main experimental findings, but the central quantitative results are anchored in Table 3.
Settings.G1003:
Treatment: Assignment of a firm to the public Weibo-appeal treatment arm (T2) versus control.

Method: Using the same firm-level randomized experiment, the authors re-estimate equation (1) on indicator outcomes for bins of a firm’s daily pollutant concentration relative to its emissions standard: 0–40%, 40–80%, 80–100%, 100–200%, and >200%. Figure 4 reports coefficients for public appeals (T2) from specifications with firm fixed effects and province-by-day fixed effects. This is an experimental ITT analysis of how assignment to public appeals shifts the distribution of emissions intensity relative to the legal standard.

Identification: Because assignment to public appeals is randomized, differences in the probability of falling into each standardized emissions bin after treatment are causally identified, conditional on firm fixed effects and province-by-day fixed effects. The analysis addresses whether the treatment merely shifts firms just below the standard or causes larger improvements across the distribution.

Setting: Figure 4 indicates that public appeals causally shift firms away from violation bins, especially extreme violations above 200 percent of the legal limit, and toward high-compliance bins below 40 percent of the limit. The authors interpret this as evidence that public appeals reduce severe excess emissions rather than merely nudging firms to become barely compliant. No single summary coefficient is reported in the text for each bin, but the figure is used as causal evidence about the distributional pattern of emissions reductions.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness/interpretation exercise showing where in the emissions distribution the main public-appeal effects arise, but it is not the headline result.
Settings.G1004:
Treatment: Assignment to private appeals (T1) or public appeals (T2), interacted with firm characteristics: SOE status, final-goods producer status, and pretreatment violation status ('Frequent' in the table notes/text).

Method: Heterogeneity analysis within the same randomized field experiment. The authors estimate regressions analogous to equation (1), using firm and province-by-day fixed effects, and interact private-appeal and public-appeal treatment indicators with firm characteristics: state ownership, final-goods producer status, and whether the firm violated during the seven-week pre-treatment period. Table 4 reports effects on daily violation status and daily SO2/COD concentrations. The estimand remains heterogeneous ITT effects of assignment.

Identification: Randomized assignment identifies average treatment effects, and interactions with predetermined firm characteristics identify treatment-effect heterogeneity under the same randomization assumptions. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences, while province-by-day fixed effects absorb time-varying local shocks. The authors use this to assess whether effects differ by ownership, product type, or pre-existing compliance patterns.

Setting: Table 4 shows that the main treatment effects are concentrated among firms with pre-treatment violations, with little evidence of effects among firms that did not violate before the experiment. Public-appeal effects are somewhat larger for SOEs than private firms, though not significantly so, and there is little consistent evidence of larger effects for final-goods firms. The authors interpret this as suggesting that the treatments mainly work on frequent prior violators and that corporate-image concerns are unlikely to be the main mechanism.

Main role: These analyses are supporting evidence about which firms drive the main experimental effects and possible mechanisms, not the paper’s primary headline estimates.
Settings.G1005:
Treatment: Assignment to specific private appeal channels: direct message to regulator, 12369 website appeal, 12369 hotline appeal, phone call to firm, and the T1C×T1D interaction indicating joint private appeals to regulator and firm.

Method: Within the private-appeals arm of the nationwide experiment, firms were randomized into specific private channels: private message to regulator (T1A), website appeal to regulator (T1B), hotline appeal to regulator (T1C), and phone appeal to firm (T1D), with cross-randomization of T1C and T1D for some firms. Online Appendix Table A6 estimates effects of these subarms and their interaction on firm violations and emission outcomes using the experimental design. This is an RCT analysis of private-appeal mechanisms.

Identification: Randomization across private channels and the cross-randomization of some private channels identify the causal effect of delivery method and complementarities within private appeals. The design addresses whether the modest private-appeal effect works through appealing to the regulator versus the firm or through jointly informing both.

Setting: In Online Appendix Table A6, the authors find little evidence that private appeals to regulators are more effective than private appeals to firms, little evidence that the private delivery channel matters, and no significant complementarity from privately informing both the regulator and the firm. They interpret these null differences as making it difficult to pin down the mechanism behind the relatively modest private-appeal effects.

Main role: This is a mechanism-focused decomposition of the private treatment effect and not central relative to the headline comparison of public versus private appeals.
Settings.H1005: Section IV.A discussing Online Appendix Table A6, PDF p. 838-839.
Settings.G1006:
Treatment: Experimental visibility promotion of a public Weibo appeal by adding roughly 10 likes/shares (T2B) versus no added promotion (T2A). Treatment is assigned at the appeal level.

Method: Appeal-level randomization within the public Weibo arm. Half of public appeals received experimentally added Weibo likes/shares (T2B), while half did not (T2A). Table 5 estimates cross-sectional regressions of regulator-response outcomes on the visibility-promotion indicator, with month fixed effects and optionally province fixed effects. Outcomes are whether the government responded on Weibo, response length in words, and whether the response included proof of an on-site audit. This is a direct RCT of appeal visibility/publicity.

Identification: Appeal-level random assignment of visibility promotion identifies the causal effect of increased social-media salience on regulatory responsiveness within public appeals. Because the promotion changes likes/shares but not the underlying violation information, the key assumption is that randomized promotion affects regulator responses only through the altered visibility/publicity of the appeal. Month and province fixed effects absorb timing and location differences.

Setting: Table 5 shows that experimentally boosting a public Weibo appeal’s visibility substantially increases regulator responsiveness. Adding about 10 likes/shares raises the probability of a regulator reply by 0.06 from a control mean of 0.16 (roughly 40 percent), increases response length by about 34 words from a mean of 33.1 (about a doubling), and raises the probability that the response includes proof of an on-site audit by 0.05 from a mean of 0.07 (roughly 65 percent). The authors use this as key causal evidence that public appeals work because visible public dissatisfaction changes regulators’ incentives.

Main role: The paper highlights this experiment as especially important mechanism evidence showing that increased public visibility makes regulators more responsive, supporting the central interpretation that public appeals work by shifting regulators’ incentives toward avoiding public unrest.
Settings.G1007:
Treatment: Whether a firm’s first violation during the sample period received a promoted public Weibo appeal (T2B) versus a generic non-promoted public Weibo appeal (T2A).

Method: Within the public-appeal arm, the authors use appeal-level randomization of visibility promotion and then compare firm-level subsequent violation outcomes based on whether the first observed violation during the experiment received a promoted or non-promoted public appeal. Reported in Online Appendix Table A8 and discussed in Section IV.B, this is still rooted in randomized assignment, though the authors note some contamination because later violations may receive the other treatment status.

Identification: Because T2B versus T2A is randomized at the appeal level, comparing firms by the treatment status of their first violation gives causal suggestive evidence on later violations. The authors caution that some control firms later receive promoted appeals, so estimates are attenuated and not clean firm-level treatment contrasts over the full period.

Setting: The authors report that firms whose first violation received a promoted Weibo appeal committed about 0.34 fewer violations during the experiment and were 8–9 percentage points less likely to commit any subsequent violation than firms whose first violation received a generic public appeal. They describe these effects as qualitatively large—around 50 percent and 25 percent of the mean among public-appeal firms—but only marginally statistically significant because later treatment contamination attenuates estimates.

Main role: This is supplementary mechanism evidence on whether extra public visibility affects firms’ later compliance, but the authors present it cautiously and not as a primary result.
Settings.H1007: Section IV.B discussing Online Appendix Table A8, PDF p. 840.
Settings.G1008:
Treatment: Regulator career-stage indicator: whether the head environmental regulator is in years 3–5 of the current five-year term versus years 1–2; in some specifications, this is interacted with private/public appeal assignment.

Method: Cross-sectional/regression-adjusted observational analysis linking prefectural environmental-bureau chiefs’ career stage to baseline violations and to treatment responsiveness. Following Guo (2009), the authors collect regulator resumes and compute years remaining in the current five-year term. Online Appendix Table A7 relates baseline violations and treatment interactions to whether the regulator is in years 3–5 versus the first two years. The paper interprets these coefficients causally/mechanistically as evidence on political incentives, but assignment to career stage is not randomized.

Identification: Identification relies on regression adjustment using observed variation in regulators’ time in office. The endogeneity concern is that prefectures with regulators later in their terms may differ systematically in unobserved ways correlated with environmental enforcement. The paper treats the relationship as informative about incentives but does not resolve these concerns experimentally; thus this is best classified as regression adjustment with causal interpretation.

Setting: The authors report that in prefectures where the head environmental regulator is in years 3–5 of a five-year term, pre-experiment firm violation likelihood is 2.7 percent higher than in prefectures where the regulator is in the first two years, and both private and public appeals have larger post-treatment effects there as well. They interpret this as evidence that local regulators’ career incentives influence environmental enforcement and help explain why public appeals are effective. Because this analysis is observational, it is weaker than the experimental mechanism evidence.

Main role: This is supportive mechanism evidence about political incentives, not part of the core identification strategy.
Settings.H1008: Section IV.B discussing Online Appendix Table A7, PDF p. 841.
Settings.G1009:
Treatment: Randomly added threat in a private Weibo appeal stating that unresolved issues would be brought to the central government, versus no such threat.

Method: Mechanism test within the private-Weibo direct-message arm (T1A): in half of these private appeals, the message randomly threatened escalation to the central government if the issue was not resolved. Section IV.B discusses Online Appendix Table A13, which estimates effects of this randomized threat on measures of regulatory effort. This is a randomized variation in message content, not an IV or DiD design.

Identification: Random assignment of escalation language identifies whether threatening upper-level oversight changes regulatory responses. The design addresses an alternative mechanism: that public appeals work because they reduce information asymmetry between local and central authorities, rather than because they create visible public pressure.

Setting: The authors find that randomly threatening to escalate a private Weibo appeal to the central government has no statistically meaningful effect on regulatory effort. They interpret this null result as evidence against the idea that the main public-appeal effects are driven by informing higher-level officials about local violations.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism falsification exercise meant to rule out an information-to-central-government channel.
Settings.H1009: Section IV.B discussing Online Appendix Table A13, PDF p. 841-842.
Settings.G1010:
Treatment: Randomly added threat in a private appeal to contact local newspapers about the violation, versus no such threat.

Method: Another mechanism test within private Weibo appeals: in some appeals, the authors randomly threatened to contact local newspapers about the violation. Section IV.B discusses Online Appendix Table A13 and interprets the results as evidence on whether fear of mainstream media exposure explains regulator responsiveness. This is a direct randomized content variation.

Identification: Randomized addition of newspaper-escalation language identifies whether regulators respond more when mainstream-media exposure is threatened. The key assumption is straightforward random assignment of message content within the relevant appeals.

Setting: The authors report no significant impact of randomly threatening local newspaper exposure on regulatory effort. They use this as evidence that the superior effectiveness of public social-media appeals is unlikely to arise simply because they signal possible mainstream media escalation.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness/mechanism exercise that helps rule out media-escalation explanations.
Settings.H1010: Section IV.B discussing Online Appendix Table A13, PDF p. 842.
Settings.G1011:
Treatment: Assignment of a prefecture to high treatment intensity (95 percent of firms assigned to treatment arms) versus lower treatment intensity (70 percent of firms assigned to treatment arms). The treatment is at the prefecture level.

Method: General-equilibrium analysis using cross-randomized treatment intensity at the prefecture level. Sixty percent of prefectures were assigned 95% of firms into treatment arms; the rest were assigned 70%. Table 6 estimates effects of High Intensity × Post on firm-level outcomes separately for control-group firms and treatment-group firms, with firm FE and day FE or province-by-day FE. This is an RCT exploiting regional randomization of treatment saturation to identify spillovers and indirect effects.

Identification: Identification comes from random assignment of prefectures to different treatment intensities (95% vs 70% of firms treated). By comparing firms in high- versus lower-intensity prefectures, separately within control and treatment groups, the paper tests whether increased appeals shift scarce regulatory effort away from some firms or instead create deterrence/greater overall enforcement. Firm fixed effects and day or province-by-day fixed effects absorb stable firm differences and common shocks. The main assumption is valid prefecture-level randomization of treatment intensity.

Setting: Table 6 uses randomized prefecture-level treatment saturation to estimate spillovers. Among control firms, the authors find no evidence that high-intensity prefectures experience worse compliance or higher emissions, which argues against offsetting crowd-out of enforcement. Among treated firms, the preferred specification shows daily violation probability is 0.003 lower in 95 percent prefectures than in 70 percent prefectures, about 20 percent below the control mean of 0.009, while SO2 and COD concentrations show no meaningful differences. The authors conclude that partial-equilibrium gains are not undone by other firms and that spillovers may even be positive for treated firms.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly highlight the absence of offsetting general-equilibrium effects based on prefecture-level random variation in treatment intensity. This is one of the paper’s three primary findings.
Settings.G1012:
Treatment: Assignment of a prefecture to the high-intensity treatment regime where 95 percent of CEMS firms are assigned to treatment arms, versus the lower-intensity 70 percent regime.

Method: General-equilibrium analysis at the prefecture-day level using the same prefecture-level cross-randomization of treatment intensity. Table 7 estimates equation (2), regressing average ambient SO2 concentration in a prefecture on High Intensity × Post with prefecture and day fixed effects or province-by-day fixed effects. This is a reduced-form experimental estimate of the effect of higher treatment saturation on ambient air quality.

Identification: Random assignment of prefectures to 95% versus 70% treatment intensity identifies the reduced-form causal effect of more widespread appeals on ambient SO2 pollution. Prefecture fixed effects absorb time-invariant local differences, while day or province-by-day fixed effects absorb common or regional time-varying shocks. The endogeneity concern is that firm-level reductions could be offset by spillovers elsewhere; this design directly tests that at the ambient pollution level using an independent monitoring network.

Setting: Table 7 shows that prefectures assigned to the higher treatment intensity experienced lower ambient SO2 concentrations after the experiment started. The estimated effect is about -0.37 relative to a control mean of 10.06, which the authors describe as a decline of more than 3.5 percent in the 95 percent prefectures relative to the 70 percent prefectures. They interpret this as evidence that general-equilibrium effects do not offset the firm-level treatment effects and as corroboration that measured emissions reductions are real rather than data manipulation.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight this ambient-pollution result as evidence that accounting for general equilibrium, pollution declines rather than being offset elsewhere. It materially supports one of the paper’s main conclusions.
Settings.H1012: Section V, equation (2), Table 7, and Figure 5, PDF pp. 843-845.
Settings.G1013:
Treatment: Assignment of a prefecture/city to the high-intensity treatment-saturation regime, interacted with event-time week indicators.

Method: Dynamic event-study version of the prefecture-level saturation experiment for ambient SO2. Figure 5 regresses ambient SO2 on High-Intensity × Week interactions with city fixed effects and province-by-week fixed effects, plotting coefficients over event time. This remains an experimental reduced-form analysis of the dynamic general-equilibrium effect of high treatment saturation on ambient air quality.

Identification: Randomized saturation at the prefecture level identifies dynamic post-treatment differences under the same assumptions as Table 7. City fixed effects absorb permanent differences, and province-by-week fixed effects absorb evolving regional shocks. The event-study is used to visualize timing and potential growth of spillover effects.

Setting: Figure 5 suggests that the reduction in ambient SO2 in high-intensity prefectures grows over time after the experiment begins. The authors interpret this dynamic pattern as consistent with positive general-equilibrium or deterrence effects as firms learn about increased public scrutiny, though they emphasize that statistical imprecision prevents definitive conclusions.

Main role: This figure supports the general-equilibrium interpretation by showing the time path of ambient pollution effects, but the main quantitative evidence is in Table 7.
Settings.G1014:
Treatment: High-frequency monetary policy news shock: the first principal component of unanticipated changes over a 30-minute window around scheduled FOMC announcements in five interest-rate futures (current-month Fed funds rate after the meeting, expected Fed funds rate after next meeting, and expected 3-month eurodollar rates at 2, 3, and 4 quarters). Rescaled so its effect on the 1-year nominal Treasury yield is 1 (roughly a 100 bp effect on that outcome scale, not a literal 100 bp shock in the underlying futures). Continuous shock measure.

Method: The authors estimate linear OLS regressions of the form s_t = alpha + gamma i_t + epsilon_t, where the dependent variable is the one-day change in Treasury yields, TIPS real yields, or breakeven inflation, and the regressor is their high-frequency 'policy news shock' measured as the first principal component of unexpected changes in five short-horizon interest-rate futures over a 30-minute window around scheduled FOMC announcements. The shock is rescaled so its effect on the 1-year nominal Treasury yield equals 1. Identification relies on the assumption that unexpected interest-rate movements within the 30-minute window reflect monetary policy news from the announcement, with scheduled meetings used to avoid contamination from unscheduled reactions to contemporaneous shocks. Separate OLS regressions are run for each maturity/outcome.

Identification: Identification comes from high-frequency variation in interest-rate futures within a 30-minute window surrounding scheduled FOMC announcements. The authors argue that all earlier public information is already priced in, so unexpected movements in this window are monetary policy news. Endogeneity concern is that policy rates usually respond to macro conditions; the narrow event window is meant to purge slower-moving confounders. The key assumption is that no other shocks materially affect the policy indicator during the 30-minute window, or at least that such contamination is negligible in the baseline OLS specification.

Setting: Using OLS event-study regressions around scheduled FOMC announcements, the authors estimate that a positive monetary policy news shock raises nominal Treasury yields and TIPS-based real yields strongly and persistently across maturities. In Table I, the 2-year nominal Treasury yield rises by 1.10 and the 2-year real yield by 1.06; the 3-year values are 1.06 and 1.02; the 5-year values are 0.73 and 0.64; and the 10-year values are 0.38 and 0.44. Forward rates show similar persistence for real rates, while breakeven inflation moves little at short horizons and turns modestly negative at longer horizons, e.g. the 5-year and 10-year forward breakeven responses are -0.21 and -0.20. These estimates are central to the paper’s claim that FOMC announcements have large effects on real rates, implying monetary non-neutrality or, alternatively, important information effects.

Main role: These are core empirical results emphasized in the abstract, introduction, Section III, and conclusion: policy news raises nominal and real rates roughly one-for-one, while expected inflation responds little or only with delay.
Settings.H1014: Section III.A, equation (1), Table I, PDF pp. 1293-1297 (article pp. 1293-1297).
Settings.G1015:
Treatment: High-frequency monetary shock proxy in three variants reported in Table II: (i) 30-minute change in the policy news shock around FOMC announcements; (ii) one-day change in the policy news shock; and (iii) one-day change in the 2-year nominal yield used as a policy indicator. All are continuous measures.

Method: The authors re-estimate the effect of high-frequency monetary shocks on interest rates using Rigobon's (2003) heteroskedasticity-based estimator, comparing the covariance structure on FOMC announcement windows ('treatment' days) with otherwise similar non-FOMC Tuesdays and Wednesdays ('control' days). Outcomes are one-day changes in selected nominal and real instantaneous forward rates; treatments are either 30-minute or one-day policy-news-shock changes, and in an additional panel the one-day 2-year nominal yield. This estimator allows for background noise from other shocks during the event window under the identifying assumption that the variance of monetary shocks rises on FOMC days while the variance of nonmonetary background shocks is unchanged.

Identification: The estimator exploits heteroskedasticity: monetary shock variance is higher in windows containing scheduled FOMC announcements than in similar non-announcement windows, while background-noise variance is assumed unchanged. This relaxes the stricter OLS assumption that no other shocks occur in the event window. The design addresses the endogeneity concern that nonmonetary shocks may contaminate event-window interest-rate changes, especially over one-day windows.

Setting: Using Rigobon’s heteroskedasticity-based estimator, the authors show that 30-minute-window estimates are nearly identical to OLS, implying little background noise at that horizon: for example, the 2-year real forward response is 0.96 under Rigobon versus 0.99 under OLS, the 5-year real forward response is 0.46 versus 0.47, and the 10-year real forward response is 0.11 versus 0.12. In contrast, when the policy shock is measured over a one-day window, OLS and Rigobon estimates diverge sharply and Rigobon confidence intervals widen dramatically, indicating substantial contamination from other shocks. With the one-day 2-year nominal yield as policy indicator, OLS suggests a positive 10-year real forward response of 0.20, but the Rigobon estimate is -0.04 with very wide confidence intervals. This robustness setting underpins the paper’s claim that causal inference is credible only with very narrow high-frequency windows.

Main role: This robustness/alternative identification is substantively important because the paper uses it to validate the 30-minute OLS design and to argue that longer windows are contaminated by background noise.
Settings.H1015: Section III.B, Table II, PDF pp. 1298-1301 (article pp. 1298-1301); related full-results robustness in Appendix Table A.3, PDF p. 1326.
Settings.G1016:
Treatment: Monthly monetary policy news shock aggregated from scheduled FOMC announcement shocks occurring in the month, excluding first-week meetings because the authors cannot determine whether the shock occurred before or after the survey response. Continuous measure based on the same 30-minute high-frequency policy news shock.

Method: The authors estimate monthly OLS regressions of changes in Blue Chip survey expectations about output growth on the monthly policy news shock, using the same baseline linear specification as equation (1) but at monthly frequency. The dependent variable is the month-to-month change in expected output growth over the next year (and, in Appendix Table A.5, at each horizon from current quarter through seven quarters ahead). The treatment is the policy news shock occurring within the month, excluding shocks in the first week when timing relative to the survey is unclear. Identification requires the monthly policy shock to be orthogonal to other confounders affecting changes in survey expectations over the month, a stronger assumption than in the same-day financial-market regressions.

Identification: The identifying variation is the within-month high-frequency policy news shock from FOMC announcements. The endogeneity concern is that policy surprises may correlate with other within-month news affecting private forecasts. The paper argues that the shock is identified from narrow windows around announcements, but acknowledges the identifying assumptions are stronger here because the outcome is a monthly change in expectations rather than a same-window financial-market change. The causal interpretation is that surprise monetary tightenings affect expectations about output growth.

Setting: In monthly OLS regressions, the authors find that surprise contractionary monetary news increases, rather than decreases, expected output growth. In Table III, the coefficient on the policy news shock is 1.01 (s.e. 0.32) for 1995-2014, 1.04 (0.35) for 2000-2014, 0.95 (0.32) for 2000-2007, and 0.79 (0.63) for 1995-2000. Appendix Table A.5 shows positive responses across horizons: 1.38 for current-quarter growth, 1.56 one quarter ahead, 0.66 two quarters ahead, 0.82 three quarters ahead, 0.51 four quarters ahead, 0.54 five quarters ahead, 0.48 six quarters ahead, and 0.90 seven quarters ahead. This positive response of expected output growth to a monetary tightening is a core empirical finding leading the authors to argue that FOMC announcements contain an information effect about economic fundamentals.

Main role: This is a central substantive result in the abstract, introduction, Section IV, and conclusion: a contractionary surprise raises expected output growth, motivating the paper’s information-effect interpretation.
Settings.H1016: Section IV, Table III and Figure II, PDF pp. 1303-1306 (article pp. 1303-1306); horizon-specific results in Appendix Table A.5, PDF p. 1327.
Settings.G1017:
Treatment: Two related continuous treatments in the appendix exercises: (i) the Green Book minus Blue Chip output-growth forecast gap as an explanatory variable for the sign/magnitude of the policy news shock; and (ii) the policy news shock as an explanatory variable for subsequent narrowing of the Green Book–Blue Chip forecast gap. Exact units are forecast percentage-point differences / policy-shock units as defined in the paper.

Method: In Online Appendix G, the authors run linear regressions relating their policy news shock and subsequent forecast revisions to the difference between the Fed’s Green Book output-growth forecast and the Blue Chip private forecast. First, they test whether surprise contractionary shocks occur when the Fed is more optimistic than the private sector; second, they test whether the Green Book–Blue Chip forecast gap narrows after policy news shocks. Although reported in the appendix, these regressions are used substantively to support the information-effect interpretation.

Identification: The paper interprets these linear associations causally/supportively: if FOMC announcements reveal Fed information, positive shocks should occur when the Fed has more optimistic internal forecasts than private forecasters, and private forecasts should move toward Fed forecasts after the announcement. The main concern is omitted factors correlated with both forecast disagreement and policy surprises; the evidence is presented as suggestive support for the information mechanism rather than a standalone design with sharp identification.

Setting: As supporting evidence for a Fed information effect, the authors report in Online Appendix G that positive policy news shocks tend to occur when the Fed’s Green Book forecast for current and future real GDP growth exceeds the corresponding Blue Chip forecast, and that the Green Book–Blue Chip gap tends to narrow after policy news shocks. The paper does not report these appendix results numerically in the main text excerpt provided, but interprets them as evidence that private forecasters update toward the Fed’s informational advantage after FOMC announcements.

Main role: These appendix regressions are supporting evidence for the information channel, not the main headline causal estimates.
Settings.H1017: Section IV discussion referring to Online Appendix G and Table G.1, PDF p. 1306 (article p. 1306).
Settings.G1018:
Treatment: A surprise FOMC monetary tightening shock in the structural model, affecting the path of the policy rule component r-bar_t; a fraction 1-psi operates as a conventional tightening relative to the natural rate and a fraction psi is interpreted as information about the natural rate/fundamentals. The shock is continuous and calibrated/scaled in model units to match empirical impulse responses.

Method: The authors estimate a structural New Keynesian model with habits and a backward-looking Phillips-curve component by simulated method of moments (SMM). They choose four structural parameters—the two AR roots of the monetary shock process, the Fed-information parameter psi, and the slope of the Phillips curve—to match the empirically estimated responses of real rates, breakeven inflation, and expected output growth to high-frequency FOMC policy news shocks. The model explicitly decomposes an FOMC announcement into a conventional monetary policy component and an information component that shifts beliefs about the natural rate. This is a structural causal model rather than a reduced-form linear design.

Identification: Identification comes from matching the model to reduced-form high-frequency moments that the paper argues are causally identified from FOMC announcement windows. The structural endogeneity problem is how to separate conventional monetary tightening from information about fundamentals embedded in the same announcement. The authors impose a model in which announcements shift beliefs about the natural rate by fraction psi of the policy shock, and use moments from real rates, inflation expectations, and output-growth expectations to pin down psi and the Phillips-curve slope. The causal interpretation depends on the validity of the model structure and moment-matching restrictions.

Setting: Using simulated method of moments, the authors estimate a structural model in which surprise FOMC tightenings affect both policy and beliefs about fundamentals. Their baseline estimates imply psi = 0.68, so roughly two-thirds of the real-rate response is interpreted as a response of the natural rate of interest and one-third as a conventional tightening relative to the natural rate; they also estimate a very flat Phillips curve with kappa zeta-hat × 10^-5 = 11.2. The estimated model matches the persistent rise in nominal and real rates, the small delayed fall in inflation, and the increase in expected output growth after a tightening. This setting is central because it translates the reduced-form evidence into the claim that both Fed information effects and conventional monetary non-neutrality are important.

Main role: This structural estimation is central to the paper’s interpretation of the reduced-form evidence: it quantifies the Fed information effect and the conventional monetary channel, both emphasized in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1018: Section V.B-V.C, Table IV and Figures III-V, PDF pp. 1310-1315 (article pp. 1310-1315).
Settings.G1019:
Treatment: Surprise FOMC monetary tightening/announcement in the structural model, including both its conventional policy component and information revelation component; compared against a counterfactual without the announcement but with the same underlying fundamentals eventually realized. Continuous model shock.

Method: The authors use their estimated structural model to compute the causal effect of a surprise FOMC monetary tightening relative to a counterfactual in which the same underlying productivity/fundamental changes occur and are learned by the private sector later even without the Fed announcement. This is a model-based causal decomposition rather than a reduced-form regression. They compare actual model-implied output responses with counterfactual output paths under alternative information timing and policy tracking assumptions.

Identification: The causal estimand is defined within the estimated structural model. The core issue is that Fed announcements reveal information about fundamentals that would likely become known later even absent the announcement. The authors therefore construct a counterfactual in which the path of productivity/fundamentals is unchanged, the private sector learns about changes when they occur and assumes a random walk, and monetary policy tracks the natural rate. The causal effect of the announcement is the difference between actual and counterfactual output paths. Validity depends on the model and the chosen counterfactual timing assumptions.

Setting: In Section VI, the authors argue that the raw positive response of expected output to a surprise tightening is not itself the causal effect of monetary policy because much of the revealed good news would have emerged later anyway. Using their estimated structural model, they compare actual output to a counterfactual with the same fundamentals but no early Fed revelation. Figures VII and VIII show that most of the increase in output expectations would have occurred even without the announcement; the model-based causal effect is much more modest and reflects a negative conventional output-gap effect offset by a positive information-timing effect on natural output. No single numerical coefficient is reported for this causal effect in the text; it is conveyed graphically and conceptually.

Main role: This section reframes the paper’s main causal interpretation: once information effects are present, the relevant causal effect of monetary policy must be defined relative to a counterfactual with the same fundamentals but different timing of revelation.
Settings.H1019: Section VI, Figures VI-VIII, PDF pp. 1316-1319 (article pp. 1316-1319).
Settings.G1020:
Treatment: High-frequency policy news shock around scheduled FOMC announcements, measured over a 30-minute window as in the baseline specification. Continuous shock measure.

Method: The authors estimate the response of stock prices to monetary announcements using a linear regression of one-day changes in the S&P 500 index on the high-frequency policy news shock around FOMC announcements. This is an event-window OLS design analogous to equation (1), with the policy shock measured over 30 minutes and stock prices over one day. They then compare this reduced-form estimate to model-implied responses with and without Fed information effects.

Identification: Identification parallels the baseline high-frequency design: unexpected changes in the policy news shock within a 30-minute FOMC announcement window are treated as exogenous monetary news. The endogeneity concern is confounding by other same-day news, mitigated by the narrow shock window. The stock-price response is then interpreted as the causal effect of the announcement shock on equity valuations.

Setting: Using an OLS event-window regression, the authors estimate that the S&P 500 falls by 6.5% in response to a policy news shock that raises the 2-year nominal forward rate by 1%, with standard error 3.9 according to Table V. They interpret this as broadly consistent with their structural model including information effects, which predicts a -6.8% stock-price response, whereas a no-information-effect model predicts a much larger -11.1% decline. This supporting result suggests that FOMC announcements contain positive information about future fundamentals that partially offsets the usual negative effect of tighter policy on stock prices.

Main role: This is an additional piece of evidence at the end of the paper, used to support the information-effect interpretation rather than to establish the core results.
Settings.H1020: Section VI.B, Table V, PDF pp. 1321-1322 (article pp. 1321-1322).
Settings.G1021:
Treatment: Assignment to reduced property-tax liability relative to the status quo liability. Four-arm randomized treatment: status quo rate (control) vs 17%, 33%, or 50% reduction. Liabilities are fixed annual amounts in Congolese Francs: for low-value properties 3000 CF (control), 2500, 2000, 1500; for high-value properties 13,200 CF (control), 11,000, 8800, 6600. The implemented causal contrast is binary within each arm-versus-control coefficient, though the overall treatment is multi-armed.

Method: Property-level randomized tax abatements embedded in the 2018 Kananga property-tax campaign. Nonexempt properties were randomly assigned, within neighborhood strata, to the status quo annual tax liability or to a 17%, 33%, or 50% reduction, with collectors delivering pre-populated tax letters. The estimating equation is an OLS regression of outcomes on treatment-arm indicators, controlling for property-value-band fixed effects and, in the preferred specification, neighborhood (randomization-stratum) fixed effects; robust standard errors are used because treatment is assigned at the property level. This is a direct ITT design: assignment to lower statutory liability is interpreted as affecting tax compliance and tax revenue.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized assignment of tax liabilities at the property level, stratified by neighborhood, with pre-populated tax letters limiting manipulation. Because treatment is randomized, differences in compliance and revenue across treatment arms identify causal ITT effects of lower assigned tax liability under standard randomization assumptions. The authors discuss and probe threats including knowledge of others’ rates, anchoring on past rates, expectations about future rates, and differential collector effort.

Setting: In the paper’s main experiment, randomly lowering assigned property-tax liability causally increased both compliance and, at sufficiently large abatements, revenue. Relative to a 5.6% compliance rate in the status-quo group, compliance rose to 6.7%, 10%, and 13% under 17%, 33%, and 50% abatements. In Table I with neighborhood fixed effects, the treatment effects on compliance are 0.011, 0.044, and 0.073, and the revenue effects are -20.202 CF, 34.069 CF, and 24.711 CF for 17%, 33%, and 50% abatements, respectively. The 33% and 50% reductions significantly increase revenue, implying status-quo rates are above the revenue-maximizing level. This randomized evidence is central to the paper’s claim that weak enforcement can place tax rates above the revenue-maximizing tax rate in this low-capacity setting.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize the randomized tax-abatement experiment as the paper’s core evidence that status quo tax rates lie above the revenue-maximizing rate because lower rates increase compliance and revenue.
Settings.H1021: Section 5.2; Table I columns 1-8, Figure A2 panels A-B (PDF pp. 12-13).
Settings.G1022:
Treatment: Assigned property-tax liability entered continuously as log(Tax Rate in CF), where Tax Rate takes values {1500, 2000, 2500, 3000} CF in the low-value band and {6600, 8800, 11,000, 13,200} CF in the high-value band. This is a continuous treatment dose derived from the randomized tax-abatement assignment.

Method: Using the randomized tax-rate variation, the authors summarize treatment effects with a linear regression of outcomes on log assigned tax liability: outcome = alpha + beta log(Tax Rate) + controls + neighborhood fixed effects. This is not IV; it is a reduced-form regression adjustment on experimentally assigned tax rates, interpreted causally as the marginal effect of a 1 log-point change in tax liability on compliance or revenue, then converted into elasticities using the sample mean outcome. Outcomes are tax compliance and tax revenue. Robust standard errors are used, and elasticity standard errors are bootstrapped.

Identification: The causal interpretation relies on exogenous randomized variation in assigned tax liability. By regressing outcomes on log tax liability, the authors impose a linear-in-logs summary of the randomized treatment-response schedule. The identifying assumption is that, because tax liability is randomly assigned conditional on strata and controls, beta captures the causal marginal effect of the assigned tax-rate change on outcomes on the reported scale.

Setting: The authors use randomized tax-rate variation to estimate causal elasticities of compliance and revenue with respect to tax liability. In the preferred specification with neighborhood fixed effects, a 1 log-point increase in the tax rate lowers compliance by 0.110 and revenue by 55.870 CF; converted using sample means, this implies an elasticity of compliance of -1.246 (SE 0.062) and an elasticity of revenue of -0.243 (SE 0.081). They interpret these estimates as evidence that a 1% increase in the tax rate reduces compliance by 1.246% and revenue by 0.243%, directly supporting the paper’s conclusion that status-quo rates are above the revenue-maximizing rate.

Main role: The elasticities of compliance and revenue with respect to tax rates are explicitly highlighted in the abstract and introduction and are key inputs for inferring that the status quo rate exceeds the revenue-maximizing tax rate.
Settings.H1022: Section 5.1-5.2; equation (2), equation (3), Table I Panel B-C columns 1-8 (PDF pp. 10-13).
Settings.G1023:
Treatment: Assigned property-tax rate, expressed continuously as a percentage of the status quo rate. The treatment dose varies over the randomized liability levels corresponding to 50%, 67%, 83%, and 100% of the status quo rate, depending on value band. The reported estimand is the revenue-maximizing tax rate implied by the compliance schedule.

Method: The authors estimate the revenue-maximizing tax rate (RMTR) by regressing tax compliance on the assigned tax rate expressed as a percentage of the status quo rate, with property-value-band controls and optionally neighborhood fixed effects. Under a linear compliance function, the RMTR is computed as -beta0/(2*beta1); under a quadratic specification, the RMTR is derived from the estimated polynomial. This is a regression-adjustment/parametric extrapolation exercise built on randomized tax-rate assignment, aimed at the estimand ‘tax rate that maximizes revenue.’ Standard errors for the RMTR use the delta method.

Identification: Randomized tax liability provides exogenous variation in the tax rate. The authors assume a parametric relationship between compliance and the tax rate (linear, with quadratic and cubic robustness), estimate that relationship, and then use the theoretical revenue expression R(T)=T*P(T) to compute the tax rate that maximizes revenue. Identification of the compliance schedule is experimental; identification of the RMTR additionally relies on the functional-form assumption used to interpolate/extrapolate between rate points.

Setting: Using experimental tax-rate variation and a linear compliance specification, the authors estimate that the revenue-maximizing tax rate is about 66% of the status quo rate; with neighborhood fixed effects Table III reports 0.665 (SE 0.014), implying a 33.50% reduction in the tax rate would maximize revenue. Under a quadratic specification, the RMTR is even lower at 0.553 (SE 0.046), implying a 44.71% reduction. These RMTR estimates operationalize the paper’s main claim that, in this low-enforcement environment, statutory tax rates are above the revenue-maximizing level.

Main role: Estimating the RMTR is a central purpose of the paper. The introduction and conclusion emphasize that the status quo rate is above the RMTR and quantify that a roughly one-third cut would maximize revenue.
Settings.H1023: Section 6.2-6.3; equations (4)-(6), Table III columns 1-4, Figure A3 (PDF pp. 19-21).
Settings.G1024:
Treatment: Assignment to an enforcement message on the tax letter, pooled across two variants (central enforcement and local enforcement), versus assignment to an active control message. The treatment is whether the taxpayer was exposed to an enforcement-framed message during registration.

Method: Within the tax campaign, a subset of properties was randomly assigned tax-letter messages: an active control message (‘paying the property tax is important’) or enforcement messages warning that refusal to pay could trigger audit/investigation by the provincial tax ministry or local chief. The authors pool the two enforcement-message arms for power and compare them to the active control. They estimate direct ITT effects on tax compliance and tax revenue, and then estimate separate RMTRs by message group using the same parametric compliance-on-rate approach as before. This is a direct randomized assignment design, not IV.

Identification: Random assignment of letter messages identifies the causal effect of enforcement framing on compliance, revenue, and the estimated compliance schedule. The RMTR comparison across message groups is identified by random assignment of enforcement-message exposure combined with randomized rate variation within groups; additional assumptions are the parametric form used to estimate compliance as a function of rates and that messages shift perceived enforcement rather than other omitted channels.

Setting: Randomly assigned enforcement messages on tax letters increased tax payments and shifted up the revenue-maximizing tax rate. Relative to the active control message, enforcement messages increased tax compliance by 1.6 percentage points and tax revenue by 36 CF per property. More importantly for the paper’s central claim, the estimated RMTR under the linear specification is 55.4% of the status quo rate for the control-message group and 77.9% for the enforcement-message group, implying an RMTR about 41% higher under stronger enforcement messaging; the quadratic specification gives 35.4% versus 77.2%. This randomized evidence supports the claim that stronger enforcement raises the revenue-maximizing tax rate.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly use randomized enforcement letters as one of the two key sources of exogenous enforcement variation showing that greater enforcement raises the RMTR.
Settings.H1024: Section 7.1; Figure 1 panels A-B; Table A13, Table A15 (PDF pp. 22-24).
Settings.G1025:
Treatment: Exposure to a tax collector with higher estimated enforcement capacity, proxied by collector fixed effects from random neighborhood assignment. In the RMTR analysis, treatment intensity is collector-specific enforcement capacity and collector-specific slope/intercept of the compliance-tax-rate schedule; continuous rather than binary.

Method: The authors exploit random assignment of tax collectors to neighborhoods and estimate collector fixed effects in a linear regression of taxpayer compliance on collector indicators, plus a property-value-band indicator and neighborhood-intervention controls. They interpret these collector fixed effects as causal estimates of collector-specific enforcement capacity because assignment is random. They then estimate collector-specific RMTRs from a second fixed-effects regression interacting collector indicators with the assigned tax rate (linear and quadratic versions). This is a standard FE design with one absorbed FE dimension for collectors, not HDFE.

Identification: Collector teams were randomly assigned to neighborhoods each month, so differences in average compliance across assigned neighborhoods identify causal differences in collector enforcement capacity, assuming randomization and no systematic sorting. The second step uses randomized tax-rate variation within collectors’ assigned neighborhoods to estimate collector-specific compliance-rate schedules and RMTRs. The main identifying claim is that higher collector fixed effects reflect causal enforcement capacity rather than neighborhood composition; the authors show balance and robustness, including sample splitting and controls, and cluster standard errors at the collector-pair level.

Setting: Using random assignment of tax collectors to neighborhoods, the authors estimate collector-specific enforcement capacity and show that higher-enforcement collectors have higher revenue-maximizing tax rates. In log-log terms, a 1% increase in collector enforcement capacity is associated with a 0.623% increase in the RMTR under the linear specification and 0.347% under the quadratic specification. In a policy counterfactual, replacing collectors in the bottom quartile of enforcement capacity with average collectors would increase the RMTR by 42%. This fixed-effects/random-assignment evidence reinforces the paper’s central claim that tax rates and enforcement are complementary levers.

Main role: Random assignment of tax collectors is the paper’s second main source of exogenous enforcement variation and is prominently featured in the abstract and introduction to show that stronger enforcement capacity raises the RMTR.
Settings.H1025: Section 7.2 and 7.3; equations (7)-(8), Figure 1 panels C-D, Table A16, Figure 2 panel B (PDF pp. 24-29).
Settings.G1026:
Treatment: Hypothetical increase in enforcement capacity implemented as replacing tax collectors in the bottom quartile of enforcement capacity with average collectors; combined with choice of tax rate (RMTR before or after enforcement change). The enforcement component is a continuous/counterfactual policy change, not a binary realized treatment in the sample.

Method: A substantive policy-counterfactual analysis combines the experimentally estimated compliance schedule with enforcement variation from randomly assigned collectors. The authors predict tax revenue as T*P(T,alpha) under baseline enforcement and under a hypothetical increase in enforcement capacity from replacing bottom-quartile collectors with average collectors, then compare revenue under a naive sequential policy versus a sophisticated joint optimization of rates and enforcement. This rests on previously estimated linear compliance/revenue models and collector FE-based enforcement capacity estimates.

Identification: This setting is a structural/prediction exercise built from experimentally and quasi-experimentally identified components: randomized tax rates identify compliance responses to tax rates, and random collector assignment identifies enforcement-capacity differences. The revenue counterfactual assumes the estimated compliance function and enforcement shifts can be used to predict revenue under alternative policy combinations, and that replacing low-capacity collectors with average ones changes enforcement as modeled without other equilibrium changes.

Setting: The authors use their identified tax-rate and enforcement estimates to predict revenue under alternative policy bundles and argue causally that jointly optimizing rates and enforcement yields larger revenue gains than adjusting them separately. A naive government that first implements the RMTR and then raises enforcement by replacing bottom-quartile collectors with average collectors would increase revenue by 61% relative to the status quo, whereas a sophisticated government that anticipates the higher post-enforcement RMTR would increase revenue by 77%. They summarize this as joint optimization delivering 10% higher revenue gains than optimizing the two levers independently, quantifying the practical importance of complementarity between tax rates and enforcement.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight the complementarity of rates and enforcement in revenue terms, especially the claim that joint optimization yields 10% higher revenue gains than optimizing independently.
Settings.H1026: Section 7.3; Figure 2 panels A-B and accompanying text (PDF pp. 28-29).
Settings.G1027:
Treatment: Indicator for whether the auction title contains the word 'new' and the corresponding low-price BIN title does not, contrasted with other title-word configurations, especially the reverse case where the BIN contains 'new' and the auction does not. This is an implemented discrete title-wording exposure interpreted as changing search visibility/frictions.

Method: The paper's main empirical test in Section II uses cross-sectional mean comparisons/regression-style contrasts based on observed auction-BIN pairs from Malmendier and Lee's (2011) cross section. The implemented design relates overbidding outcomes to wording asymmetry between auction and Buy-It-Now (BIN) titles, especially whether the auction title contains the word 'new' while the BIN title does not, versus the reverse. No fixed effects, IV, RCT, RD, matching, or DiD design is implemented. The author interprets these contrasts causally/substantively as evidence that wording differences generate search frictions that increase the probability and magnitude of overbidding. Remaining concerns include omitted product heterogeneity and title wording correlating with unobserved quality or seller reliability.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in auction-versus-BIN title wording within matched auction-BIN comparisons. The author argues that because eBay's default search algorithm requires search-string words to appear in the listing title, title-word asymmetries plausibly affect whether buyers see auctions and BINs together. If wording asymmetry makes the auction easier to find than the BIN, search frictions should raise overbidding. The main endogeneity concern is that title wording may proxy for other factors, such as perceived seller quality or title descriptiveness, rather than search visibility alone; the author acknowledges these alternatives but notes they are still standard-behavior explanations and often themselves reflect search frictions.

Setting: Using Malmendier and Lee's cross section, Schneider tests whether listing-title wording that should make auctions easier to find than BIN listings increases overbidding. He reports that when only the auction title contains 'new,' 60 percent of auctions are overbid and the mean auction-BIN percentage difference is +11.81 percent; when only the BIN contains 'new,' 37 percent are overbid and the mean percentage difference is -3.17 percent, with both differences reported as statistically significant at p < 0.01. The paper interprets this as evidence that wording-driven search frictions can causally increase overbidding, undermining the claim that overbidding necessarily reflects nonstandard behavior or limited attention.

Main role: This is one of the central pieces of evidence in the comment. The paper's main contribution is to argue that overbidding can be explained by search frictions; the title-wording evidence in the ML cross section is presented as direct empirical support for that reinterpretation.
Settings.H1027: Section II, Table 3, PDF p. 8-9 (article pp. 1188-1189).
Settings.G1028:
Treatment: Exposure to the auction mechanism relative to the low contemporaneous BIN price, examined separately by product to assess whether auctions causally produce overpayment/overbidding for homogeneous items. The treatment is not a separately coded binary regressor; it is the auction-versus-BIN comparison within product.

Method: In Section II, the paper reports product-level contrasts in the ML cross section, tabulating overbidding rates and mean auction-BIN price differences by product. Although descriptive in form, the author uses these product-level estimates to support a causal interpretation that search frictions, rather than nonstandard behavior, explain the pooled overbidding pattern, emphasizing that for most products the mean auction price does not exceed the low BIN price. No stronger identification design is used.

Identification: The author uses within-product tabulations to argue that if auctions inherently caused irrational overpayment relative to BIN options, one would expect positive average auction-BIN gaps broadly across products. Instead, most products do not show such a pattern. This strategy is limited because it does not isolate exogenous variation and may reflect composition differences across products; the author's use is interpretive rather than based on a formal causal design.

Setting: Schneider tabulates overbidding separately for 89 products in the ML cross section and argues that the evidence does not broadly support the causal claim that auctions lead buyers to overpay relative to available BIN options. He states that 66 of 89 products have at least one case of overbidding, but the mean overbidding rate per product is 30 percent and the mean percentage price difference is positive for only 22 of 89 products. He interprets this as showing that the pooled result in ML is not typical across products and is therefore consistent with search frictions rather than a general nonstandard-bidding effect.

Main role: This table supports the paper's broader argument by showing heterogeneity across products and weakening the pooled-overbidding interpretation, but it is not the main identifying evidence compared with the wording-friction tests.
Settings.H1028: Section II, Table 4, PDF pp. 9-10 (article pp. 1189-1190).
Settings.G1029:
Treatment: Title-wording asymmetry between auction and BIN listings in the new DVD data, especially whether the auction contains words such as 'new,' 'disc,' 'special,' or 'dvd' that the BIN does not, or the summed difference in words between auction and BIN titles. This treatment captures a nonrandom search-visibility friction.

Method: In Section III, the author applies the same cross-sectional comparison design to a new dataset of 552 new movie-DVD auctions. He compares auction outcomes to the lowest-price BIN available at the time the winning bid was placed and visually verifies item matches. The implemented estimator is again a set of mean contrasts and grouped comparisons by wording differences in titles, interpreted as the effect of search-friction-inducing wording asymmetry on overbidding. No FE, IV, or quasi-experimental design is used.

Identification: The identifying argument is that eBay's search algorithm depends heavily on title words, so ex post title-word asymmetries between auction and BIN listings generate differential search visibility and thus search costs. The author compares overbidding rates across these wording configurations and interprets higher overbidding when the auction is easier to find than the BIN as evidence of causal search frictions. Key assumptions are that the matched auction-BIN pairs refer to the same item and that title wording differences primarily affect search rather than unobserved quality; the author attempts to mitigate mismatch by restricting to new DVDs and visually inspecting titles.

Setting: Using a new dataset of 552 new movie-DVD auctions, Schneider finds that 23 percent of auctions end above the low BIN price even though the mean auction price is 17 percent below the mean low BIN price. He then shows that title-word differences strongly predict overbidding: for example, the overbidding rate is 35 percent when only the auction contains 'new' but 15 percent when only the BIN contains 'new' (p < 0.01). He interprets these contrasts as evidence that wording-induced search frictions causally raise overbidding, reinforcing the paper's central claim that observed overbidding is consistent with standard behavior once search costs are allowed.

Main role: This new-dataset exercise is a major empirical contribution of the comment. It materially supports the central conclusion that overbidding is linked to search frictions created by listing wording and therefore need not imply nonstandard behavior.
Settings.H1029: Section III, Table 1 and Figure 1, PDF pp. 11-12 (article pp. 1192-1193).
Settings.G1030:
Treatment: Auction purchase mechanism relative to the available low BIN option in the DVD sample, compared overall and by movie version. The paper interprets the auction-versus-BIN price gap as the effect of buying through auction rather than immediate purchase.

Method: Also in Section III, the paper reports level comparisons between mean auction prices and mean low BIN prices for the new DVD sample, overall and by movie version. This is a cross-sectional regression-adjustment/mean-contrast style design without exogenous variation. The author uses these contrasts substantively to argue that auction purchase does not generally cause higher prices than BIN purchase in this setting.

Identification: The strategy compares observed transaction prices in auctions with the lowest BIN prices for the same item at the relevant time. The author argues that if overbidding reflected a general causal tendency for auctions to induce irrational high prices, mean auction prices should exceed low BIN prices. Instead, they are usually lower. This is limited by selection into auctions and potential remaining unobserved differences, though item matching is tightened by restricting to new DVDs and visually inspecting titles.

Setting: In the new DVD data, Schneider compares auction prices with contemporaneous low BIN prices for the same DVD version. He reports an overall mean auction price of $10.04 versus a mean low BIN price of $12.17, implying an average auction-BIN gap of -$2.12 and stating that the mean auction price is 17 percent below the mean low BIN price (p < 0.01). He also notes that the mean auction price is below the mean low BIN price for 22 of 24 movie versions. These results are used to argue against a general causal claim that auctions systematically induce higher prices than available fixed-price alternatives.

Main role: These comparisons are supportive background for the main argument about search frictions. They show that average auction prices are typically below BIN prices in the new dataset, but the stronger substantive contribution comes from the wording-friction analysis.
Settings.H1030: Section III, Table 1, PDF pp. 5-6 and 11 (article pp. 1186-1187, 1192).
Settings.G1031:
Treatment: Exposure to technological change in the worker's pre-displacement occupation, measured by the change between 2007 and 2017 in the share of online vacancies listing a computer or software skill requirement in that occupation. In regressions this variable is normalized to mean zero and unit standard deviation, so coefficients represent the effect of a one-SD increase in occupation-level technological change exposure.

Method: Cross-sectional linear regression on a sample of displaced workers from the CPS Displaced Workers Supplement. The authors regress the change in log real weekly earnings after displacement on occupation-level exposure to technological change, measured as the 2007–2017 change in the share of vacancies in the worker's pre-displacement occupation listing computer or software requirements, normalized to mean zero and unit standard deviation.
