Reported specifications include controls for change in occupation employment share, age, log unemployment duration, pre-layoff tenure, the 2007 level of computer requirements in the occupation, education, gender, survey year, displacement year, and full-time indicators before and after displacement; some columns restrict to full-time workers only and some use an alternative occupation classification (Autor-Dorn) instead of 4-digit SOC. Standard errors are clustered by occupation. The design is observational regression adjustment rather than a quasi-experimental design; the paper interprets the coefficient causally as the impact of exposure to technological change on earnings losses, while acknowledging the need to control for changing labor demand via occupation employment share.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-occupation variation in changes in computer/software requirements over time, linked to workers' pre-displacement occupations. The main endogeneity concern is that occupations with more technological change may simultaneously face changing labor demand or other confounders that also affect post-displacement earnings. The paper argues against a pure demand-shift story by controlling for occupation employment-share changes and the initial level of computer requirements, plus worker characteristics and timing controls. The causal interpretation relies on these controls sufficiently absorbing confounding differences across occupations and displaced workers; no exogenous instrument or natural experiment is used.

Setting: Using CPS displaced workers linked to occupation-level changes in computer and software skill requirements from online vacancies, the authors estimate that greater technological change in a worker's prior occupation causes larger post-displacement earnings losses. In Table 3, column 1, a one-standard-deviation increase in technological change lowers the change in log earnings by 0.0354, and the paper states that comparing a worker one SD above versus one SD below the mean implies an earnings decline over 7 percentage points larger. The estimate remains similar after controlling for occupation employment-share changes (column 2: -0.0345), among full-time workers only (column 3: -0.0315), and with Autor-Dorn occupations (columns 4-5: -0.0259 to -0.0228). This setting directly supports the paper's central claim that technological change is an important source of earnings losses after job loss.

Main role: This is a core empirical result emphasized in the abstract, introduction, Section IV.C, conclusion, and motivation for the quantitative decomposition: workers more exposed to technological change suffer larger earnings losses after job loss.
Settings.H1031: Section IV.C 'Earnings Following Displacement'; Figure 2 and Table 3, cols. 1-5 (PDF pp. 294-296).
Settings.G1032:
Treatment: Exposure to technological change in the pre-displacement occupation, measured as the normalized 2007–2017 change in the share of vacancies in that occupation listing computer or software requirements.

Method: Linear probability regressions on displaced workers from the CPS Displaced Workers Supplement. The dependent variable is an indicator for switching occupations after displacement, and the treatment is the normalized occupation-level change in computer/software requirements in the worker's pre-displacement occupation from 2007 to 2017. Specifications add the same worker controls as the main earnings regressions, optionally include occupation employment-share change, and use either 4-digit SOC or Autor-Dorn occupation definitions. Standard errors are clustered at the occupation level. The paper interprets the coefficient as the causal effect of technological change exposure on the probability of occupational switching after job loss.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-occupation heterogeneity in growth of computer/software requirements. The concern is that occupations with more technological change may also be shrinking or otherwise changing in ways that mechanically push workers into other occupations. The paper addresses this by controlling for occupation employment-share changes and worker characteristics, and by showing robustness to alternate occupation classifications. The causal interpretation assumes conditional exogeneity of occupation-level technological change exposure for displaced workers.

Setting: The paper estimates that workers displaced from occupations with greater technological change are more likely to switch occupations after job loss. In Table 4, column 1, a one-standard-deviation increase in technological change raises the occupation-switching probability by 0.0847; the text translates a comparison of one SD above versus one SD below the mean into nearly 17 percentage points higher switching. The estimate remains similar after controlling for employment-share changes (column 2: 0.0801) and under Autor-Dorn occupation coding (column 3: 0.0682). This setting provides direct evidence for the paper's proposed mechanism that technological change works through occupational reallocation.

Main role: Occupation switching is the main mechanism highlighted by the theory and emphasized in the abstract, introduction, Section IV.D, and conclusion.
Settings.H1032: Section IV.D 'Mechanism: Occupation Switching'; Figure 3 panel A and Table 4, cols. 1-3 (PDF pp. 296-298).
Settings.G1033:
Treatment: Primary causal regressor is exposure to technological change in the pre-displacement occupation interacted with whether the worker switches occupations after displacement. Exposure is the normalized 2007–2017 change in the occupation's share of vacancies listing computer/software requirements; switching is a binary indicator for re-employment in a different occupation.

Method: Linear regression on displaced workers' change in log earnings, adding an interaction between technological change exposure and an occupation-switching indicator. The treatment of interest is the interaction of the normalized change in computer/software requirements in the pre-displacement occupation with whether the worker switches occupations after displacement; specifications also include main effects for switching and technological change, the change in occupation employment share, and the same demographic and timing controls as earlier regressions. Reported results use both 4-digit SOC and Autor-Dorn occupation definitions, with occupation-clustered standard errors. The design is an observational regression decomposition used to argue that the earnings effect of technological change is concentrated among switchers.

Identification: The strategy uses heterogeneity across both technological-change exposure and post-displacement occupation switching to decompose where earnings effects arise. Endogeneity concerns remain substantial because switching is itself an outcome and may correlate with unobserved worker quality or job opportunities. The paper nevertheless interprets the interaction causally as evidence that technological change harms earnings by forcing workers out of their prior occupations. Controls include employment-share changes and worker characteristics; the interpretation relies on conditional comparisons across displaced workers with differing prior-occupation technological change exposure.

Setting: The authors find that the negative earnings effect of technological change is concentrated among workers who switch occupations after displacement. In Table 5, column 3, the interaction between change in computer requirements and occupation switching is -0.0494, while the main effect of technological change for stayers is near zero (0.000532) and the main effect of switching becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero (-0.0175). Using Autor-Dorn occupations yields a similar interaction estimate of -0.0363 (column 4). The paper interprets this as evidence that technological change lowers earnings after job loss mainly by pushing displaced workers into different, lower-paying occupations.

Main role: This is the key mechanism result showing that technological change lowers earnings primarily through occupation switching, a central substantive conclusion of the paper.
Settings.H1033: Section IV.D 'Mechanism: Occupation Switching'; Figure 3 panel B and Table 5, cols. 1-4 (PDF pp. 298-299).
Settings.G1034:
Treatment: Exposure to technological change in the worker's occupation, measured by the normalized change between 2007 and 2017 in the occupation's share of vacancies listing computer or software requirements.

Method: Linear probability regressions on a broader CPS sample comparing displaced and non-displaced workers, where the dependent variable is an indicator for being a displaced worker and the treatment is occupation-level technological change exposure. The key regressor is the normalized 2007–2017 change in computer/software requirements in the worker's occupation. Specifications progressively add occupation employment-share changes, year fixed effects, and controls for age, education, gender, and the initial 2007 computer-requirements level; results are shown under 4-digit SOC and Autor-Dorn occupation coding. Standard errors are clustered by occupation. The paper treats this as a causal test of whether technological change increases displacement risk.

Identification: The paper uses cross-occupation variation in technological change exposure to test whether workers in more rapidly changing occupations are more likely to be displaced. The key alternative explanation is that technological change may directly raise displacement risk by reducing labor demand. By including changes in occupation employment share and basic controls, the authors argue that any remaining association captures the effect of technological change itself. The finding is null, so the paper uses this as evidence consistent with the model assumption that technological change affects displaced workers' post-loss outcomes rather than the probability of displacement.

Setting: In Table 6, the authors estimate that technological change does not materially affect the probability of becoming displaced. The coefficient on change in computer requirements is -0.00125 without controls (column 1) and remains close to zero after adding employment-share changes and controls (e.g., column 4: -0.00401; column 5 with Autor-Dorn occupations: -0.00164). By contrast, declining occupation employment share raises displacement probability. This supporting setting helps the paper argue that technological change mainly worsens outcomes conditional on job loss rather than causing the layoffs measured in the DWS.

Main role: This is a supporting result used to rule out an alternative mechanism—technological change causing displacement itself—rather than the paper's main claim about post-displacement earnings losses.
Settings.H1034: Section IV.E 'Technological Change and the Probability of Displacement'; Table 6, cols. 1-5 (PDF pp. 300-301).
Settings.G1035:
Treatment: Exposure to technological change in the occupation, measured as the normalized change between 2007 and 2017 in the occupation's share of vacancies listing computer or software skill requirements.

Method: Linear regression using CPS Outgoing Rotation Group data on occupation stayers, where the dependent variable is the change in log earnings over 12 months and the treatment is technological change exposure in the occupation. The treatment is the normalized 2007–2017 change in the share of vacancies listing computer/software requirements in the worker's occupation. Specifications include year and gender fixed effects plus controls for age, education, and the initial 2007 computer-requirements level, with optional control for change in occupation employment share and alternative occupation coding (4-digit SOC or Autor-Dorn). Standard errors are clustered by occupation. The paper interprets this as the causal effect of technological change on earnings gains for workers who remain in their occupations.

Identification: The paper exploits cross-occupation differences in technological change exposure among workers who stay in the same occupation over 12 months. The concern is that high-tech-change occupations may differ in wage growth trends or labor demand for other reasons. The authors include employment-share changes and worker controls, and interpret the coefficient as evidence that technological change raises the earnings of workers with skills suited to remain in their occupations. The design remains observational regression adjustment.

Setting: Among workers who stay in their occupations, the paper finds that greater technological change raises earnings growth. In Table 7, column 1, a one-standard-deviation increase in technological change increases the 12-month change in log earnings by 0.00270; the text states that a worker one SD above the mean experiences an earnings increase over 0.5 percentage points higher than a worker one SD below the mean. The estimate is virtually unchanged with employment-share controls (column 2: 0.00272) and somewhat smaller but still positive with Autor-Dorn occupations (column 3: 0.00205). This supports the theory that technological change benefits workers who have the skills to use the new technology, even while hurting displaced workers.

Main role: This is an important supporting result showing that technological change benefits some workers, but it is not the main displaced-worker result emphasized in the abstract's headline claim.
Settings.H1035: Section IV.F 'Gains from Technological Change'; Table 7, cols. 1-3 (PDF pp. 302-303).
Settings.G1036:
Treatment: Model-imposed technological change and related mechanisms. The principal treatment contrast is the presence versus removal of technological change in the calibrated model (setting the technology growth rate g to zero); subsequent contrasts also remove occupation-specific human capital. This is effectively a binary counterfactual feature switch in the model environment.

Method: Calibrated structural quantitative search model of the labor market with occupation choice, embodied technological change, general and occupation-specific human capital, job destruction, and wage ladders. The authors set/estimate model parameters to match aggregate labor market moments and then conduct counterfactual decompositions by removing technological change, then removing occupation-specific human capital, to attribute the average earnings loss after displacement to different mechanisms. The causal estimand is the model-implied contribution of technological change to earnings losses after job loss, not a reduced-form linear coefficient. Because this is a structural/counterfactual decomposition rather than a linear regression or standard quasi-experimental design, it belongs in Other.

Identification: Identification is model-based rather than design-based. The calibrated search model is disciplined by aggregate moments and qualitative fit to empirical patterns on earnings losses and occupation switching by exposure to technological change. The causal contribution of technological change is identified through counterfactual simulations: compare the baseline model to an otherwise identical model with zero technology growth, and then to versions removing occupation-specific human capital. The validity of the decomposition depends on the structural assumptions, calibration targets, and the model's ability to reproduce key untargeted empirical moments.

Setting: In the calibrated structural model, technological change is estimated to account for over 45 percent of earnings losses after job loss. The baseline model produces an average earnings decline of 7.63 percent two years after displacement among re-employed workers; removing technological change lowers the decline to 4.16 percent, implying that technological change explains 45.5 percent of the baseline loss. Removing occupation-specific human capital as well further reduces the loss to 1.53 percent, so occupation-specific human capital explains 34.5 percent and moving lower on the wage/job ladder explains the remaining 20 percent. This decomposition is one of the paper's central contributions and underlies the headline claim in the abstract and conclusion.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion headline that technological change accounts for about 45 percent of earnings losses after job loss; this claim comes from the structural decomposition.
Settings.H1036: Section V.E 'Decomposing Earnings Losses after Displacement'; Figure 5 (PDF pp. 312-313).
Settings.G1037:
Treatment: Exposure to studying at a university that eventually became Protestant, interacted with post-Reformation periods. Implemented as an indicator for an eventually Protestant university in the DiD design; effectively a binary treated-versus-control contrast in university denomination/exposure.

Method: The authors estimate linear difference-in-differences models at the individual graduate level comparing students from universities that eventually adopted Protestantism with students from universities that remained Catholic, before versus after the Reformation. The main specifications are equations (1) and (2): OLS regressions of a church-occupation indicator on university fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-university dummy and either decade dummies or broader period dummies. Standard errors are clustered at the university×decade level. Identification comes from differential changes in occupational sorting around 1517/after 1520 across universities by eventual denomination; the authors emphasize lack of differential pretrends but acknowledge the historical, nonexperimental setting.

Identification: The identifying variation is the change in occupational outcomes after the Reformation for graduates of eventually Protestant universities relative to graduates of Catholic universities. The endogeneity concern is that universities adopting Protestantism may differ in unobserved ways correlated with career outcomes. The paper argues for causal interpretation using parallel pre-Reformation trends: it reports no differential pre-Reformation occupational trend between eventually Protestant and Catholic universities. The design still relies on the assumption that absent the Reformation, relative occupational trends would have evolved similarly.

Setting: Using graduate-level DiD regressions with university and decade fixed effects, the authors argue that the Reformation caused graduates from Protestant universities to shift away from church employment. In the pooled post-1520 specification, Protestant-university graduates were about 11.8 percentage points less likely to take a first job in the church sector than graduates from Catholic universities, relative to the 1510s baseline. The authors present this as evidence that religious competition and the changed political economy of the Reformation reallocated skilled labor away from religious uses and toward secular ones.

Main role: Occupational reallocation of upper-tail human capital from church to secular work is one of the paper's central substantive claims in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H1037: Section III.B, equation (1) and equation (2), Figure V Panel A (PDF pages 30-32).
Settings.G1038:
Treatment: Exposure to studying at an eventually Protestant university, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treated-versus-control contrast.

Method: This is the companion individual-level DiD occupational-choice specification for administrative careers. The authors estimate linear OLS models analogous to equations (1) and (2), with university fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-university indicator and decade or broader post-Reformation period dummies. Standard errors are clustered at the university×decade level. The estimand is the differential post-Reformation change in the probability that graduates sort into administrative occupations.

Identification: Identification again comes from comparing changes after the Reformation for graduates of eventually Protestant universities versus Catholic universities. The key concern is nonrandom adoption of Protestantism by universities and correlated shocks to administrative labor demand. The authors appeal to the absence of pre-Reformation differences and trends in occupational choice between treatment and control universities. Causal interpretation requires parallel counterfactual trends absent the Reformation.

Setting: In DiD regressions of first-job outcomes, the authors argue that the Reformation increased sorting of Protestant-university graduates into administrative careers. Figure V Panel B shows essentially no pre-Reformation gap, then a positive post-Reformation differential. The pooled estimate is about a 5 percentage point increase in the probability of taking an administrative job for graduates of Protestant universities after 1520, an economically large change relative to the low baseline rate of administrative employment.

Main role: The paper's introduction highlights a shift especially toward administrative occupations, so this is a central mechanism/result rather than a peripheral robustness check.
Settings.H1038: Section III.B, Figure V Panel B, discussion immediately following Figure V (PDF pages 32-34).
Settings.G1039:
Treatment: Exposure to enrollment at a university that eventually became Protestant, interacted with post-Reformation timing. Binary university-denomination treatment contrast.

Method: The authors estimate individual-level linear DiD models for degree subject choice, using equations (3) and (4). They regress an indicator for receiving a theology degree on university fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-university dummy and decade or broader post-Reformation period dummies. Standard errors are clustered at the university×decade level. The design compares differential changes in theology study in Protestant versus Catholic universities after the Reformation.

Identification: The identifying variation is the post-Reformation differential change in theology study between eventually Protestant and Catholic universities. The main threat is that universities destined to become Protestant may already have had different trajectories in subject mix. The authors argue against this using small and statistically insignificant pre-Reformation differences and no sustained differential pretrend just before 1517. The DiD interpretation requires parallel trends absent the Reformation.

Setting: Using graduate-level DiD models with university and decade fixed effects, the authors argue that the Reformation sharply reduced investment in church-specific human capital at Protestant universities. In the aggregated post-1520 specification, graduates from Protestant universities were about 4.5 percentage points less likely to receive a theology degree than graduates from Catholic universities, relative to the 1510s baseline. They interpret this as causal evidence that the Reformation redirected students away from theology and thus away from church-sector human capital.

Main role: A shift away from theology toward secular subjects is one of the headline results in the abstract and introduction, directly supporting the paper's secularization argument.
Settings.H1039: Section III.C, equations (3) and (4), Figure VII Panel A (PDF pages 37-38).
Settings.G1040:
Treatment: Exposure to enrollment at an eventually Protestant university, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment contrast.

Method: This is the parallel individual-level DiD specification for more secular, administration-oriented subjects. Using equations (3) and (4), the authors estimate OLS models with university fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-university indicator and decade or broader period dummies, but with an indicator for law or arts degree as the dependent variable. Standard errors are clustered at the university×decade level.

Identification: Identification relies on differential changes after the Reformation between eventually Protestant and Catholic universities in students' degree choices. The concern is endogenous Protestant adoption correlated with unobserved determinants of subject choice. The authors argue there was essentially no pre-Reformation difference or trend in law/arts study between the two groups, supporting a parallel-trends interpretation.

Setting: The authors estimate DiD models showing that the Reformation shifted students at Protestant universities toward more secular subjects, particularly law and the arts. Figure VII Panel B shows little pre-Reformation difference and a positive post-Reformation gap. The pooled post-1520 estimate is about a 2 percentage point increase in the likelihood that a Protestant-university graduate earned a law or arts degree, which the authors interpret as evidence that changing political economy incentives redirected human-capital investment toward skills useful in administration.

Main role: The introduction emphasizes increased study of secular subjects, especially law and the arts, as part of the paper's main evidence on reallocation of human capital.
Settings.H1040: Section III.C, Figure VII Panel B and accompanying text (PDF pages 38-39).
Settings.G1041:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment at the territory level.

Method: The authors estimate territory-level linear DiD models for church construction counts by decade, using equations (5) and (6). The outcome is the number of church-sector construction events in a territory×decade. Regressions include territory fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-territory indicator and decade or broader post-Reformation period dummies. Standard errors are clustered at the territory level. Counts are analyzed with OLS after aggregating to territory×decade because town-year data are sparse.

Identification: Identification comes from differential post-Reformation changes in construction in territories that became Protestant relative to those that remained Catholic. The main concern is that territories differed systematically before 1517 or experienced other time-varying shocks correlated with Protestant adoption. The authors show no differential pre-Reformation trend immediately before 1517 and interpret the relative post-1520 decline in church construction as causal under parallel trends.

Setting: At the territory-by-decade level, the authors argue that the Reformation reduced church construction in Protestant regions relative to Catholic ones. In Figure IX Panel A, post-Reformation interaction coefficients are negative, and the aggregated 1550–1599 interaction is about -1.68 church construction events per territory-decade (p = .05), with a negative but less precise estimate for 1520–1549. They interpret this as evidence that the Reformation shifted fixed investment away from religious uses, especially after secular rulers' claims over church property became consolidated.

Main role: The reallocation of fixed investment away from church construction is one of the three main empirical domains in the abstract and introduction.
Settings.H1041: Section III.D.1, equations (5) and (6), Figure IX Panel A left frame (PDF pages 40-44).
Settings.G1042:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment at the territory level.

Method: This is the same territory-level DiD for church construction as s5, but augmented with flexible controls for pretreatment outcomes: interactions between the stock of construction in 1470 and decade dummies, plus interactions between each territory's construction level in each pre-Reformation decade and decade dummies. The estimating equation remains linear OLS at the territory×decade level with territory and decade fixed effects; standard errors are clustered by territory. This robustness is designed to absorb pre-Reformation construction-level differences and differential mean reversion.

Identification: The strategy is the same post-versus-pre comparison across Protestant and Catholic territories, but now conditional on very flexible functions of pretreatment construction stocks and flows. This aims to address the concern that post-Reformation differences merely reflect reversion to earlier territorial construction levels rather than a causal effect of Protestantism. Causal interpretation still relies on no remaining differential shocks after conditioning on these pretreatment patterns.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors re-estimate the church-construction DiD allowing pre-Reformation construction stocks and flows to shape later outcomes flexibly. In Figure IX Panel A right frame, the post-Reformation church-construction interactions remain negative, though smaller and statistically imprecise (for example, -0.65 for 1550–1599, p = .33). The authors treat this as broadly consistent with the Reformation reducing religious construction even after accounting for pretreatment differences across territories.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis supporting the main construction reallocation claim by addressing concerns about preexisting differences and mean reversion.
Settings.H1042: Section III.D.1, Figure IX Panel A right frame, discussion of controls for pretreatment outcomes (PDF pages 44-46).
Settings.G1043:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment at the territory level.

Method: The authors estimate territory-level OLS DiD models for secular construction counts by decade using equations (5) and (6). The dependent variable is the number of secular construction events in a territory×decade. Regressions include territory fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-territory indicator and decade or broader post-Reformation period dummies, with territory-clustered standard errors.

Identification: The identifying variation is the relative change after the Reformation in secular construction in Protestant versus Catholic territories. The key concern is endogenous Protestant adoption correlated with construction trajectories. The authors note some pre-Reformation level differences, but emphasize that the decade immediately before the Reformation shows movement opposite the post-1520 pattern, and the large post-1550 increase exceeds simple mean reversion. The design assumes that absent the Reformation, relative construction trends would not have diverged as observed.

Setting: The authors use territory-by-decade DiD regressions to argue that the Reformation increased secular construction in Protestant territories. Figure IX Panel B shows positive post-Reformation interactions, especially after 1550 when rulers' claims over church property had consolidated. The aggregated 1550–1599 estimate is about 2.06 additional secular construction events per territory-decade in Protestant regions (p = .07), while the 1520–1549 estimate is 0.81 and less precise. The result supports the paper's claim that fixed investment was reallocated from religious to secular uses.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly highlight the shift of construction from religious to secular purposes as a main result.
Settings.H1043: Section III.D.1, equations (5) and (6), Figure IX Panel B left frame (PDF pages 40-45).
Settings.G1044:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment at the territory level.

Method: This is the secular-construction DiD with very flexible controls for pretreatment outcomes. The authors estimate OLS territory×decade regressions with territory and decade fixed effects, interactions between an eventually-Protestant-territory indicator and post-Reformation periods, plus interactions of decade dummies with the territory's construction stock in 1470 and with each pre-Reformation decade's construction level. Standard errors are clustered by territory.

Identification: This robustness keeps the same DiD logic but conditions flexibly on pretreatment construction stocks and flows, attempting to rule out explanations based on differential initial levels or mean reversion. The identifying assumption is that, after conditioning on those pretreatment patterns, no other differential shocks drove both Protestant adoption and later secular construction. The authors view persistence of positive post-1550 estimates as support for causality.

Setting: Controlling flexibly for pretreatment construction outcomes, the authors still find that Protestant territories experienced more secular construction after the Reformation. In Figure IX Panel B right frame, the 1550–1599 Protestant interaction is about 1.51 additional secular construction events per territory-decade (p = .02), while the 1520–1549 estimate is smaller and insignificant. The authors interpret the robustness of the post-1550 increase as evidence that the Reformation causally redirected fixed investment toward secular uses rather than merely reflecting mean reversion or fixed territorial differences.

Main role: This is an important substantive robustness analysis for the main construction result, addressing preexisting cross-territory differences in construction.
Settings.H1044: Section III.D.1, Figure IX Panel B right frame and discussion (PDF pages 44-46).
Settings.G1045:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment at the territory level.

Method: The authors estimate territory-level DiD models for a narrower secular-construction outcome: counts of palace and administrative building construction events by territory×decade. The baseline specification follows equations (5) and (6), with territory fixed effects, decade fixed effects, and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-territory indicator and decade or period dummies; standard errors are clustered by territory.

Identification: Identification relies on relative post-Reformation changes between Protestant and Catholic territories in construction specifically favored by secular rulers. Concerns mirror those for aggregate construction: preexisting level differences and endogenous Protestant adoption. The authors emphasize no pre-Reformation trend toward the observed pattern immediately before 1517 and larger post-1550 increases consistent with property-rights consolidation after the Schmalkaldic War.

Setting: The authors argue that the Reformation not only increased secular construction overall but specifically redirected investment toward buildings associated with empowered rulers. In Figure IX Panel C left frame, palace and administrative building counts rise relatively more in Protestant territories after the Reformation, especially after 1550. The aggregated 1550–1599 interaction is about 1.47 additional palace/administrative constructions per territory-decade (p = .06), which the authors interpret as evidence that reallocation within the secular sector reflected territorial lords' interests.

Main role: The paper stresses that construction shifted especially toward palaces and administrative buildings, making this a key mechanism/result rather than a minor ancillary outcome.
Settings.H1045: Section III.D.1, Figure IX Panel C left frame (PDF pages 44-45).
Settings.G1046:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, interacted with post-Reformation periods; binary treatment at the territory level.

Method: This is the palace/administrative-construction DiD augmented with flexible pretreatment controls. The authors estimate territory×decade OLS regressions with territory and decade fixed effects, post-Reformation interactions with an eventually-Protestant-territory dummy, and interactions of decade dummies with pretreatment construction stock and pre-Reformation construction flows. Standard errors are clustered by territory.

Identification: The same DiD comparison is sharpened by flexibly conditioning on pretreatment construction, to reduce concerns that post-Reformation increases simply reflect reversion to earlier territorial construction patterns. Causal interpretation requires that, conditional on these controls, no omitted shocks jointly drove Protestant adoption and later palace/administrative construction.

Setting: With flexible controls for pretreatment construction, the authors still find a post-Reformation increase in palace and administrative building activity in Protestant territories. Figure IX Panel C right frame shows an estimated 0.72 additional palace/administrative events per territory-decade in 1550–1599 (p = .05), while the 1520–1549 estimate is small. The authors read this as especially persuasive evidence that the Reformation shifted resources toward fixed investments valued by secular rulers.

Main role: This is a robustness specification reinforcing the main claim that secular-lord-favored investment increased after the Reformation.
Settings.H1046: Section III.D.1, Figure IX Panel C right frame and discussion (PDF pages 44-46).
Settings.G1047:
Treatment: Territory eventually adopting Protestantism, contrasted either with Catholic border territories (high competition) or Catholic nonborder territories (low competition), interacted with post-Reformation periods. Binary Protestant-versus-Catholic comparison within each subsample.

Method: The authors run a heterogeneity DiD for construction by splitting Catholic comparison regions according to exposure to Protestant neighbors, intended to proxy the intensity of religious competition. They estimate OLS territory×decade regressions like the pretreatment-controlled construction models, with territory and decade fixed effects and interactions between an eventually-Protestant-territory indicator and period/decade dummies. Panel A of Figure X compares Protestant territories to Catholic border regions ('high competition'); Panel B compares Protestant territories to Catholic nonborder regions ('low competition'). Standard errors are clustered at the territory level.

Identification: The identification is still difference-in-differences, but now heterogeneity is assessed by comparing Protestant territories to Catholic territories facing different intensities of religious competition, defined by border proximity. The concern is that border and nonborder Catholic regions differ for other reasons; the authors partly address this with the same pretreatment-construction controls used in Figure IX. Their mechanism claim requires that border proximity primarily captures competition intensity rather than omitted confounders.

Setting: To test whether religious competition itself mattered, the authors compare Protestant territories separately to Catholic regions near Protestant borders and to Catholic regions farther away. Figure X shows that Protestant regions differ little from high-competition Catholic border regions, but differ much more from low-competition Catholic nonborder regions, especially in secular construction after 1550. The authors interpret this pattern as evidence that the Reformation's effects on construction operated through greater religious competition altering the bargain between secular and religious elites.

Main role: This is a substantive heterogeneity test supporting the proposed mechanism that religious competition, not just Protestant doctrine per se, drove reallocation.
Settings.H1047: Section III.D.1, Figure X Panels A and B (PDF pages 47-49).
Settings.G1048:
Treatment: Assignment to the complex-numbers version of the risky-choice task, where objective payout probabilities are represented as mathematical expressions rather than plain percentages. This is a binary treatment contrast: complex-numbers treatment versus baseline presentation.

Method: In the main A experiments, subjects first completed six baseline risky-choice tasks and were then randomized in a between-subject design to either another set of baseline tasks or to a higher-complexity treatment in which lottery payout probabilities were displayed as algebraic expressions ('complex numbers'). The authors estimate direct intention-to-treat effects of assignment to the more complex presentation on lottery valuations, primarily by comparing baseline versus complex-number treatment responses and by regressions/interacted response functions. The design is experimental and linear in the reported outcomes; no IV is used because assignment itself is the treatment of interest. Identification relies on random assignment of subjects to the post-baseline complex-number condition.

Identification: Random assignment to the complex-number presentation creates exogenous variation in task complexity. The causal concern is whether more compressed responses merely correlate with self-reported cognitive uncertainty; the experiment addresses this by directly manipulating complexity. Identification assumes randomization balances subject characteristics so that differences in certainty equivalents and cognitive uncertainty across treatment arms are attributable to the more complex presentation.

Setting: In the risky-choice A experiment, assignment to a more complex probability presentation causally increased cognitive uncertainty and made certainty equivalents more compressed toward intermediate values relative to baseline lotteries. The paper states that the complex-numbers manipulation increased cognitive uncertainty by 45% in risky choice, and Figure V shows substantially more compressed normalized certainty equivalents under the complex treatment. This randomized treatment is core to the paper's argument that complexity raises cognitive noise and thereby attenuates responses to objective probabilities.

Main role: A central claim of the paper is that greater complexity causally raises cognitive uncertainty and makes decisions more compressed/regressive to intermediate options. The randomized complexity manipulations are the paper's main causal evidence for that claim.
Settings.H1048: Section III.D.1 and Section VI; Figure V top-left; Online Appendix Tables 10–13 referenced in Section VI (main text PDF pp. 2040, 2056–2057).
Settings.G1049:
Treatment: Assignment to the complex-numbers version of the balls-and-urns belief-updating task, where relevant probabilities are presented as algebraic expressions instead of simple numerical percentages. Binary indicator for complex treatment versus baseline.

Method: In the main A experiments, subjects first completed six baseline belief-updating tasks and were then randomized in a between-subject design to either another set of baseline tasks or to a more complex version where base rates and/or signal diagnosticities were displayed as algebraic expressions ('complex numbers'). The authors interpret differences in beliefs and cognitive uncertainty between treatment and baseline as direct causal effects of complexity. Estimation is through direct comparison of treatment versus baseline response functions and accompanying regressions; identification comes from random assignment.

Identification: Randomization to the complex-number treatment provides exogenous variation in decision-problem complexity. The identification challenge is separating complexity's causal effect from endogenous variation in uncertainty or ability. Under random assignment, differences in posterior beliefs and cognitive uncertainty can be attributed to the more complex presentation, assuming no differential attrition or other protocol violations by treatment arm.

Setting: In the belief-updating A experiment, assignment to a more complex numerical presentation causally increased cognitive uncertainty and made stated posterior beliefs more compressed toward 50:50. The paper reports that the complex-numbers manipulation increased cognitive uncertainty by 48% in belief updating, and Figure V shows substantially more compressed posteriors under complex-number problems than under baseline problems. This experimental result is central to the paper's claim that complexity generates cognitive noise and thereby belief-updating biases.

Main role: The paper's headline mechanism is that complexity causally raises cognitive uncertainty and amplifies compression/base-rate insensitivity. The randomized complexity manipulation in belief updating directly supports this central conclusion.
Settings.H1049: Section III.D.1 and Section VI; Figure V bottom-left; Online Appendix Tables 10–13 referenced in Section VI (main text PDF pp. 2040, 2056–2057).
Settings.G1050:
Treatment: Assignment of a given risky-choice trial to the compound-lottery format rather than the baseline simple-lottery format. In the compound format, the payout probability itself is randomly drawn from a known interval around the baseline probability. This is a binary treatment at the task level: compound versus baseline.

Method: In the earlier B risky-choice experiment, the authors manipulated complexity within subjects by randomly interspersing compound lotteries among baseline lotteries. The compound lottery is normatively equivalent to the baseline lottery in expected-utility terms, so the direct comparison identifies the causal effect of added problem complexity. Outcomes are elicited certainty equivalents/normalized certainty equivalents and cognitive uncertainty. Estimation is via comparisons of response functions and referenced regressions for baseline versus compound tasks.

Identification: Within-subject random assignment of some tasks to the compound format creates exogenous variation in complexity while leaving the normative benchmark unchanged. Identification assumes the random interspersion of compound and baseline tasks isolates the effect of added complexity from stable subject traits. Because the compound manipulation does not change expected utility, differences in responses are interpreted as causal effects of complexity-induced cognitive noise.

Setting: In the B risky-choice experiment, randomly making a lottery compound rather than simple causally increased cognitive uncertainty and yielded more compressed certainty equivalents. The paper reports that the compound manipulation increased cognitive uncertainty by 23% in risky choice, and Figure V shows median normalized certainty equivalents under compound lotteries are more regressive to an intermediate value than in baseline lotteries. This provides experimental robustness for the paper's central complexity-to-noise-to-compression mechanism.

Main role: The compound-problem manipulation is a substantive experimental robustness and extension of the main complexity mechanism, showing similar causal effects in a distinct design and elicitation environment.
Settings.H1050: Section III.D.2 and Section VI; Figure V top-right; Online Appendix E and Online Appendix Tables 10–13 referenced in Section VI (main text PDF pp. 2040, 2056–2057).
Settings.G1051:
Treatment: Assignment of a given belief-updating trial to the compound-updating format rather than the baseline format. In the compound format, signal diagnosticity is itself random over a known interval but constructed so the Bayesian posterior is unchanged. Binary treatment: compound versus baseline task.

Method: In the earlier B belief-updating experiment, baseline updating problems and compound updating problems were randomly interspersed within subjects. The compound version varies signal diagnosticity over a known interval while preserving the same Bayesian posterior as the baseline problem, so the authors interpret differences in responses as the causal effect of greater complexity. Estimation is by comparing posterior-belief response functions and reported regressions for baseline versus compound tasks.

Identification: Random within-subject assignment of belief-updating trials to compound versus baseline conditions provides exogenous complexity variation while preserving the normative posterior benchmark. The identification argument is that any systematic difference in stated beliefs or cognitive uncertainty across conditions is caused by the more complex compound representation, not by differences in underlying Bayesian incentives or subject characteristics.

Setting: In the B belief-updating experiment, random assignment to compound rather than simple updating problems causally increased cognitive uncertainty and made stated beliefs more compressed toward 50:50. The paper reports that the compound manipulation increased cognitive uncertainty by 33% in belief updating, and Figure V shows median posterior beliefs are more compressed in the compound condition. This bolsters the article's central claim that complexity causes cognitive noise and thereby standard belief-updating biases.

Main role: This is an important experimental robustness and extension of the paper's main mechanism, demonstrating that exogenous complexity in belief updating causally increases uncertainty and compression in a distinct design.
Settings.H1051: Section III.D.2 and Section VI; Figure V bottom-right; Online Appendix E and Online Appendix Tables 10–13 referenced in Section VI (main text PDF pp. 2040, 2056–2057).
Settings.G1052:
Treatment: Cognitive uncertainty in risky choice, measured as the subject's stated percent chance that their true lottery valuation lies outside/within a $1 window around their stated certainty equivalent; operationally enters continuously and interacted with payout probability. The focal 'treatment' is higher cognitive uncertainty / cognitive noise, not experimentally assigned in this setting.

Method: Using observational variation across decisions in the baseline risky-choice tasks of Risk A, the authors run linear regressions of normalized certainty equivalents on payout probability, cognitive uncertainty, and their interaction; some specifications add demographic controls. They interpret the interaction causally/structurally as indicating that greater cognitive uncertainty (their proxy for cognitive noise) reduces sensitivity to objective probabilities and thereby generates probability weighting and the flipping pattern of risk attitudes. This is not randomized and does not use FE or IV; it is regression adjustment with a causal interpretation informed by the paper's theoretical framework.

Identification: Identification is associational rather than design-based: the authors treat within-sample variation in self-reported cognitive uncertainty as informative about latent cognitive noise, and regress certainty equivalents on payout probabilities and CU. The main endogeneity concern is that CU may correlate with other respondent traits or measurement error; the paper discusses these concerns and later presents experimental complexity manipulations and repeated-elicitation IV checks as support. In this setting, the causal interpretation relies on the paper's argument that CU proxies awareness of cognitive noise affecting decisions.

Setting: In baseline risky-choice data, higher cognitive uncertainty is interpreted as causing more probability weighting/compression in lottery valuation. Table III shows that the interaction between payout probability and cognitive uncertainty is -0.67, implying that raising cognitive uncertainty from 0% to 50% lowers the slope of normalized certainty equivalents with respect to payout probabilities by 33.5 percentage points; the raw cognitive-uncertainty term is positive (25.1 without controls; 22.7 with controls), consistent with a higher intercept and the 'flipping' pattern. This result is central to the paper's claim that boundedly rational, cognitively noisy decisions underlie apparent probability-dependent risk attitudes.

Main role: A core contribution is that measured cognitive uncertainty strongly predicts compression/probability weighting in risky choice. These regressions are among the paper's central empirical results.
Settings.H1052: Section V.B.1; Table III cols. (1)–(6) (main text PDF pp. 2048–2050).
Settings.G1053:
Treatment: Cognitive uncertainty in belief updating, measured as the participant's stated percent chance that the Bayesian-optimal guess lies within a 2-percentage-point band around their reported posterior belief; enters continuously and interacted with Bayesian posterior.

Method: Using observational variation in the baseline Beliefs A tasks, the authors estimate linear regressions of stated posterior beliefs on Bayesian posteriors, cognitive uncertainty, and their interaction; some specifications add demographic controls. They interpret these coefficients as evidence that greater cognitive uncertainty/cognitive noise attenuates the mapping from objective to subjective probabilities and raises the intercept, producing compression toward 50:50. This is a regression-adjustment design without random assignment, IV, or FE.

Identification: The identifying variation is observational variation in elicited cognitive uncertainty across belief-updating decisions. The endogeneity concern is that CU may reflect other respondent attributes or measurement error rather than causal cognitive noise. The paper's interpretation relies on theory linking CU to latent noise and on separate randomized complexity manipulations that move CU and beliefs in the predicted direction. In this setting, the results remain correlational but are presented as evidence about the effect of cognitive noise on beliefs.

Setting: In baseline belief-updating data, higher cognitive uncertainty is interpreted as causing more compression of stated beliefs toward 50:50. Table IV columns (1)–(2) show that the interaction between Bayesian posterior and cognitive uncertainty is -0.43, so moving from 0% to 50% cognitive uncertainty lowers the slope of beliefs with respect to Bayesian posteriors by about 21 percentage points; the raw cognitive-uncertainty term is about 12.8. The authors interpret this as evidence that what looks like extreme-belief aversion reflects cognitive noise rather than preferences.

Main role: The paper's main message is that cognitive uncertainty predicts belief compression and classic belief biases. These regressions are a central piece of that evidence.
Settings.H1053: Section V.B.2; Table IV cols. (1)–(2) (main text PDF pp. 2050–2052).
Settings.G1054:
Treatment: Cognitive uncertainty in belief updating, measured continuously as the respondent's stated uncertainty about whether the Bayesian-optimal guess lies within a narrow band around their stated belief. The treatment is higher CU / cognitive noise, entering directly and through interactions with log prior odds and log likelihood ratio.

Method: In the same baseline Beliefs A data, the authors estimate Grether-style linear regressions in log-odds space. One specification regresses log posterior odds on log Bayesian odds, cognitive uncertainty, and their interaction; another decomposes the Bayesian benchmark into log prior odds and log likelihood ratio, each interacted with cognitive uncertainty. These are standard linear regressions used to argue that higher cognitive uncertainty causes greater base-rate insensitivity and conservatism (likelihood-ratio insensitivity).

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-decision variation in cognitive uncertainty. The main concern is omitted variables or measurement error in CU; the paper argues that if CU captures awareness of cognitive noise, then stronger CU should mechanically imply lower responsiveness in log-odds updating. The interpretation is supported, but not fully identified, by the theory and by separate randomized complexity manipulations.

Setting: Using Grether regressions, the paper argues that higher cognitive uncertainty causes standard belief-updating biases. In Table IV columns (3)–(4), the interaction between log Bayesian odds and cognitive uncertainty is -0.42, indicating lower sensitivity of posterior log-odds to the Bayesian benchmark when uncertainty is higher. In columns (5)–(6), the interaction of cognitive uncertainty with log prior odds is -0.52 and with log likelihood ratio is -0.21; the authors state these magnitudes imply, for example, base-rate sensitivity falls from 0.69 at CU = 0% to 0.43 at CU = 50%. They interpret this as showing that base-rate insensitivity and conservatism arise from cognitive noise-induced compression.

Main role: A headline contribution is to tie together base-rate neglect, conservatism, and extreme-belief aversion as manifestations of cognitive noise. These Grether regressions directly support that central synthesis.
Settings.H1054: Section V.B.2.i; Table IV cols. (3)–(6) (main text PDF pp. 2050–2052).
Settings.G1055:
Treatment: Sample size in the balls-and-urns updating problem, specifically the number of randomly drawn balls M ∈ {1, 3, 5}. This is a discrete, nonbinary treatment representing greater informational/problem complexity rather than a simple treated-versus-control indicator.

Method: The authors analyze observational variation within Beliefs A to show that, holding sample difference and Bayesian posterior fixed, greater sample size raises cognitive uncertainty, which they interpret as why beliefs respond less strongly in larger samples even when the Bayesian posterior is unchanged. The setting is not anchored on a numbered main-text table but is described in text with a reference to Online Appendix Table 6. The estimator is a linear regression/adjustment framework linking cognitive uncertainty and belief responses to sample-size variation.

Identification: The authors exploit within-experiment variation in sample size while conditioning on sample difference and Bayesian posterior. The causal claim is that larger samples are cognitively more complex, raising cognitive uncertainty and thereby reducing responsiveness. This is observational within the randomized task structure rather than a separately emphasized randomized treatment in the main text; interpretation relies on the maintained complexity/noise mechanism.

Setting: The paper argues that sample-size effects in belief updating are partly caused by complexity-induced cognitive uncertainty. In Section V.B.2.ii, the authors state that cognitive uncertainty significantly increases in sample size, holding sample difference and the Bayesian posterior fixed, and therefore subjects respond more to the sample difference when sample size is smaller. No main-text coefficient is reported there, but the claim is used to reinterpret sample-size insensitivity as another manifestation of cognitive noise.

Main role: This is a substantive secondary mechanism result that extends the main compression argument to sample-size effects in belief updating, but it is not one of the paper's headline results relative to the main CU and complexity findings.
Settings.H1055: Section V.B.2.ii, with evidence referenced to Online Appendix Table 6 (main text PDF p. 2053).
Settings.G1056:
Treatment: Cognitive uncertainty about the stock market forecast, measured as the respondent's stated percent chance that the statistically optimal guess, given their information, lies within a 1-percentage-point band around their reported forecast. Treated as a continuous dose.

Method: For stock market expectations, the authors use cross-sectional observational variation to regress subjective probability forecasts on historical probabilities, cognitive uncertainty, and their interaction (reported in Online Appendix Table 9 and summarized visually in Figure III). They interpret the interaction causally/structurally as showing that greater cognitive uncertainty makes expectations less responsive to objective historical probabilities and more compressed toward 50:50. This is a linear regression design without randomization for the treatment of interest.

Identification: Identification is correlational: respondents differ in cognitive uncertainty and in how closely their forecasts track historical probabilities. The concern is omitted variables such as information or sophistication. The paper interprets CU as a proxy for noise in recalling/processing information and uses the strong monotonic relation in Figure III, alongside experimental evidence from other domains, to motivate a causal reading. No exogenous variation in CU is provided within the stock-forecast setting itself.

Setting: For stock market forecasts, higher cognitive uncertainty is interpreted as causing more compressed expectations: respondents with high CU overestimate small historical probabilities and underestimate large ones. Figure III shows a markedly flatter relationship between subjective forecasts and historical probabilities for higher-CU responses, and the text states that Online Appendix Table 9 confirms this regression pattern. This result extends the paper's main compression mechanism from laboratory risk and belief tasks to economically relevant expectations data.

Main role: The paper emphasizes that cognitive uncertainty predicts compression not only in laboratory tasks but also in real-world economic forecasts. This broad external-domain result materially supports the central contribution.
Settings.H1056: Section V.A and V.B.3; Figure III bottom panels; Online Appendix Table 9 referenced in text (main text PDF pp. 2046–2048, 2053).
Settings.G1057:
Treatment: Measured cognitive uncertainty in risky choice, specifically the interaction of payout probability with the main elicitation of cognitive uncertainty, instrumented by the analogous interaction using cognitive uncertainty from the repeated elicitation of the same decision problem. The underlying treatment is continuous cognitive uncertainty/cognitive noise.

Method: To address measurement error in elicited cognitive uncertainty, the authors implement 'obviously related instrumental variable' analyses in the repeated tasks of Risk A. They re-estimate the risky-choice OLS regressions but instrument the endogenous interaction term between payout probability and cognitive uncertainty using the corresponding interaction between payout probability and cognitive uncertainty measured in the repeated elicitation of the same problem. This is a linear IV design aimed at recovering the effect of cognitive uncertainty on sensitivity to probabilities under classical measurement-error concerns.

Identification: The concern is attenuation bias from measurement error in self-reported cognitive uncertainty. Because the same decision problem was elicited twice, the authors use the repeated measure as an instrument for the main CU interaction, assuming the repeated CU response is strongly related to latent true CU but has independent measurement error conditional on the latent construct. This yields an IV correction for the effect of CU on the slope of certainty equivalents with respect to payout probabilities.

Setting: As a robustness check in risky choice, the authors instrument the payout-probability × cognitive-uncertainty regressor with the same interaction built from repeated CU elicitation on the identical problem. They report that repeated CU is highly correlated across repetitions (r = 0.70) and that the IV results are 'almost identical' to the OLS estimates, suggesting measurement error in CU is not driving the main risky-choice findings. No main-text coefficient is printed in the article body; evidence is referenced to Online Appendix Table 7.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis addressing measurement error, not the primary identification strategy for the paper's main claims.
Settings.H1057: Section V.D; Online Appendix Table 7 referenced in text (main text PDF pp. 2054–2056).
Settings.G1058:
Treatment: Measured cognitive uncertainty in belief updating, particularly the interaction between the objective probability term (Bayesian posterior/log-odds terms) and the main CU elicitation, instrumented by the analogous interaction using repeated-task CU. The underlying treatment is continuous cognitive uncertainty/cognitive noise.

Method: Analogous to the risky-choice robustness check, the authors use repeated elicitations in Beliefs A to instrument for measurement error in cognitive uncertainty. They replicate the belief-updating OLS regressions but instrument the interaction between objective probabilities and cognitive uncertainty using the interaction built from repeated CU elicitations of the same problem. This is a linear IV robustness analysis focused on the effect of cognitive uncertainty on belief responsiveness.

Identification: The authors use repeated CU elicitation on identical problems as an instrument for the potentially noisy main CU measure, assuming common latent CU but independent measurement error across repetitions. This addresses attenuation bias in the effect of CU on the responsiveness of beliefs to Bayesian benchmarks and updating components.

Setting: In belief updating, the authors instrument CU-based regressors with repeated-task CU interactions to address measurement error. They note that repeated CU is highly correlated across repetitions (r = 0.68) and that the resulting IV estimates are 'almost identical' to the OLS results, implying measurement error is unlikely to explain the main compression findings in beliefs. The main text does not report numerical IV coefficients; evidence is referenced to Online Appendix Table 8.

Main role: This is a robustness exercise to show the belief-updating results are not artifacts of measurement error in cognitive uncertainty, rather than a headline design.
Settings.H1058: Section V.D; Online Appendix Table 8 referenced in text (main text PDF pp. 2054–2056).
Settings.G1059:
Treatment: Log geographic (great-circle) distance from the centroid of each district to the nearest top-four port (Buenos Aires, Rosario, La Plata, or Bahía Blanca), used as inverse access to world markets. Continuous variable in logs; a reported contrast is typically a doubling of distance (100% increase).

Method: Cross-sectional OLS regressions of district outcomes on log geographic distance to world markets, implemented as equation (1): Y_lt = a_t + b_t ln(distance_l) + u_lt. The authors interpret Argentina's late-19th-century integration into world markets as a natural experiment and use distance to the nearest of the top-four ports (Buenos Aires, La Plata, Rosario, Bahía Blanca) as a measure of access to world markets. They estimate separate cross sections for baseline 1869 levels and for changes/growth over 1869–1914, without fixed effects beyond year-specific intercepts. This is a regression-adjustment design rather than a panel DiD or FE design. Identification is argued from quasi-exogenous external integration and cross-sectional variation in remoteness, but the authors do not claim full experimental identification for these OLS gradients.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-district differences in remoteness from Argentina's main ports, interpreted in light of externally driven reductions in transatlantic transport costs from steamship technology. The endogeneity concern is that locations near ports may differ systematically for other reasons. The paper argues the historical external integration shock was plausibly exogenous to Argentina's geography, but these OLS specifications do not fully eliminate omitted-variable bias; they are presented as reduced-form evidence consistent with a causal interpretation of access to world markets affecting development outcomes.

Setting: Using district-level OLS regressions, the paper argues that better access to world markets caused higher population density and urbanization in Argentina. In 1869, a one-unit increase in log distance to the nearest top-four port is associated with a 0.414 lower log population density and a 0.046 lower urban population share; over 1869–1914, the corresponding gradients are -0.445 for log population growth and -0.059 for the increase in urban share (table 1, cols. 1–4). The authors summarize these as: when distance doubles, log population density falls by about 41%, urban share by about 5 percentage points, log population growth by about 45%, and urban-share growth by about 6 percentage points. These results are a core reduced-form pillar of the paper's claim that external integration reshaped the spatial distribution and sectoral composition of economic activity.

Main role: These reduced-form gradients are part of the paper's central evidence for the spatial Balassa-Samuelson effect discussed in the introduction, section IV, and conclusion.
Settings.H1059: Section IV.B, equation (1), table 1 columns (1)–(4), PDF pp. 1263–1265 (article pp. 1263–1265).
Settings.G1060:
Treatment: Log geographic (great-circle) distance from the centroid of each district to the nearest top-four port, measuring remoteness from world markets. Continuous log treatment; authors often discuss a doubling of distance.

Method: Cross-sectional OLS regressions of additional district outcomes on log geographic distance to world markets using equation (1), reported in table 1 columns (5)–(7). Outcomes are observed in single cross sections or late-period data: log wage-rental ratio around 1895, log relative price of tradeables around 1895, and the 1914 share of cereals in cultivated area. The design remains reduced-form OLS using access to ports as the explanatory variable, with no fixed effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

Identification: The paper exploits cross-district variation in distance to world markets under the historical argument that late-19th-century external integration was driven by exogenous declines in transatlantic transport costs. The main threat is omitted spatial heterogeneity correlated with port proximity. The results are interpreted causally as evidence that better market access changes prices, factor rewards, and specialization, but the authors acknowledge these are reduced-form regressions rather than fully instrumented estimates.

Setting: The paper uses cross-sectional OLS to argue that locations closer to world markets experienced structural transformation consistent with a spatial Balassa-Samuelson effect. Table 1 reports that higher log distance to a top-four port raises the log wage-rental ratio by 1.158, raises the log relative price of tradeables by 0.153, and lowers the cereal cultivated-area share by 0.085. The authors interpret this as meaning that when distance doubles, the wage-rental ratio more than doubles, the relative price of tradeables rises about 15%, and the cereal land share falls by 8.5 percentage points, implying that locations closer to world markets have higher land prices relative to wages, higher relative prices of nontraded goods, and greater specialization in trade-cost-sensitive cereals. These results are central evidence for the mechanism the model is built to rationalize.

Main role: These are central reduced-form stylized facts supporting the paper's spatial Balassa-Samuelson mechanism: land prices relative to wages, relative nontraded prices, and specialization in transport-cost-sensitive goods.
Settings.H1060: Section IV.B, equation (1), table 1 columns (5)–(7), PDF pp. 1263–1265 (article pp. 1263–1265).
Settings.G1061:
Treatment: Railroad access by 1914, capturing expansion of the railroad network from 1869 to 1914. In column 1 this is a binary indicator equal to one if a district has one or more railroad stations in 1914 and zero otherwise; in column 2 it is continuous rail length within district boundaries in 1914.

Method: The authors estimate equation (2) in long differences from 1869 to 1914, regressing district log population growth on a 1914 railroad-access measure plus controls for log land area, latitude, longitude, and initial log population in 1869. Because the outcome is a long difference and treatment captures expansion from negligible rail access in 1869 to 1914 access, this is a conventional long-difference DiD-style comparison rather than pure cross-sectional OLS. They report OLS estimates using either a binary indicator for any rail connection in 1914 or rail length within the district in 1914.

Identification: The identifying variation is differential railroad expansion across districts over 1869–1914 in a long-difference setup that differences out time-invariant district-level heterogeneity in population levels. Controls absorb district size, broad geography, and initial population. The main concern is nonrandom railroad placement: private railroads may target high-growth places while the state may promote low-growth remote areas. Because this concern remains unresolved in OLS, the authors treat these as suggestive and move to IV for causal identification.

Setting: In long-difference regressions from 1869 to 1914, the paper finds that districts receiving railroad access grew faster in population, consistent with a causal effect of internal integration. Table 2 shows a coefficient of 0.650 on an indicator for a rail connection in 1914 and 0.514 on rail length in 1914, both statistically significant, with controls for land area, latitude, longitude, and initial population. These OLS estimates support the idea that railroad expansion increased local economic activity, but the authors stress that nonrandom rail placement motivates the IV analysis that follows.

Main role: The OLS long-difference railroad regressions are supporting evidence; the paper emphasizes the IV estimates to address nonrandom railroad placement.
Settings.H1061: Section IV.C, equations (2)–(3), table 2 columns (1)–(2), PDF pp. 1266–1269 (article pp. 1266–1269).
Settings.G1062:
Treatment: Rail length in 1914 within district boundaries, used as the endogenous measure of railroad access in the IV columns of table 2; this captures expansion of the railroad network from negligible 1869 levels to 1914. Continuous treatment.

Method: Two-stage least squares estimates of the effect of railroad access on district log population growth from 1869 to 1914. The second stage is equation (2), a long-difference regression of log population growth on rail access plus controls for log land area, latitude, longitude, and initial log population. The endogenous treatment is rail access/rail length in 1914. Instruments are: (i) a 'port' instrument equal to the fraction of a district's area covered by least-cost paths from all district centroids to the top-four ports, and (ii) a 'colonial post' instrument equal to the length of Spanish colonial postal routes within the district. The paper reports IV estimates using both instruments jointly and each separately. This design addresses nonrandom railroad placement.

The port instrument exploits least-cost paths to Buenos Aires-centered ports that existed as the trade hub before railroads. The colonial-post instrument exploits routes shaped by Spanish colonial trade orientation toward the northwest, predating late-19th-century growth patterns. The core exclusion restriction is that, conditional on controls for land area, latitude, longitude, and initial population, these instruments affect later population growth only through railroad connection. First-stage relevance is strong, and overidentification is not rejected when both instruments are used.

Setting: Using 2SLS, the paper concludes that railroad expansion causally increased district population growth in Argentina between 1869 and 1914. In table 2, the IV coefficient on rail length is 0.633 using both instruments, 0.717 using only the port instrument, and 0.608 using only the colonial-post instrument; all are statistically significant. First-stage F-statistics are 34.39, 21.02, and 59.31, and the overidentification test p-value is 0.465 when both instruments are used. The authors interpret the similarity of the OLS and IV estimates, despite opposing private and public siting forces, as supporting a causal impact of the railroad network on the spatial distribution of economic activity. This is a core causal setting for the paper's internal-integration claim.

Main role: The introduction and section IV explicitly highlight use of instruments for the railroad network to address nonrandom placement; these IV estimates are the main reduced-form causal evidence on internal integration.
Settings.H1062: Section IV.C, equations (2)–(3), table 2 columns (3)–(5), PDF pp. 1266–1270 (article pp. 1266–1270).
Settings.G1063:
Treatment: Log relative price of tradeables, measured as the log tradeables consumption price index minus the log overall consumption price index for each district. Continuous endogenous regressor instrumented by travel time to the nearest top-four port based on colonial postal routes.

The second stage is linear; no fixed effects are included because the data are a cross section of 63 districts around 1895.

This setting is central because it pins down inelastic demand between sectors, a key driver of the model's causal mechanism and counterfactual effects.

Main role: This is part of the paper's core structural estimation: it identifies the elasticity of substitution between traded and nontraded goods, a central model parameter used for counterfactuals and the mechanism.
Settings.H1063: Section VI.B, equation (40), table 3 columns (2)–(3), PDF pp. 1287–1289 (article pp. 1287–1289).
Settings.G1064:
Treatment: Log real income in each district, a model-based continuous variable using observed agricultural employment share, land value per hectare, and overall price index; instrumented by travel time to the nearest top-four port based on colonial postal routes.

Method: IV estimation of the domestic population mobility condition using equation (41). The endogenous regressor is log real income, constructed from the model using the agricultural employment share, land values, and the overall price index. The instrument is log IV travel time to the nearest top-four port, computed from a transport network based on colonial postal routes, coast/navigable rivers, and land, for a cross section of 63 districts in 1895. The second stage regresses log population density on instrumented log real income.

The exclusion restriction is that this travel-time measure affects population density only through real income in the population mobility equation.

Table 4, column 2, reports a coefficient of 0.826 of log population density on log real income, implying a preference-dispersion/population-mobility parameter of ε = 4.733. The first stage in column 3 shows a coefficient of -1.078 of log real income on log IV travel time to the top-four port and an F-statistic of 43.69. These estimates support substantial mobility within Argentina and are central to the model's claim that better market access raises density and shifts factor rewards through migration.

Settings.H1064: Section VI.C, equation (41), table 4 columns (2)–(3), PDF pp. 1289–1291 (article pp. 1289–1291).
Settings.G1065:
Treatment: Travel time to the nearest top-four port. In column 1 this is actual lowest-cost travel time using the 1914 transport network with weights railroads=1, navigable rivers/coast=3, land=4.5. In column 2 this travel time is instrumented with travel time computed from colonial postal routes plus rivers/coast and land. Continuous treatment.
