Because PPML is nonlinear, the task rules place this in Other. In column 2, the authors instrument actual travel time with travel time implied by colonial postal routes, yielding an IV-PPML specification. The estimates are used as part of the structural recovery of technology-adjusted prices and agricultural productivity changes.

Identification: The intended causal interpretation is that lower travel time to ports changes relative technology-adjusted prices and thereby district specialization across agricultural goods. Main threats are endogenous railroad placement and correlation between transport access and agroclimatic suitability. The paper addresses these with agricultural land shares (which difference out overall agricultural level effects), latitude/longitude controls with good-specific coefficients, and IV-PPML using colonial-route-implied travel time. The exclusion restriction is that colonial-route-based travel time affects land shares only through actual transport access and resulting prices.

Setting: The paper estimates how internal market access affects specialization within agriculture. In table 5, PPML estimates show that longer travel time to a top-four port lowers the land shares of cereals (-0.421 OLS; -0.253 IV-PPML) and purebred/mixed-breed cattle (-0.355 OLS; -0.340 IV-PPML), while raising the shares of native-breed cattle (0.473 OLS; 0.298 IV-PPML) and native-breed sheep (1.544 OLS; 1.412 IV-PPML); effects for other crops and purebred/mixed-breed sheep are not significant. The authors interpret this as evidence that rail access and lower transport costs shift districts toward more transport-cost-sensitive goods, and they use these estimates to back out agricultural productivity changes for counterfactuals.

Main role: These estimates are an important component of the structural estimation of specialization patterns and the later counterfactual decomposition of external and internal integration.
Settings.H1065: Section VI.F.1, equation (48), table 5 columns (1)–(2), PDF pp. 1294–1297 (article pp. 1294–1297).
Settings.G1066:
Treatment: Log travel time to the nearest top-four port using the transport network. Continuous measure of remoteness from world markets.

Method: Cross-sectional OLS regression of the log tradeables price index on log travel time to the nearest top-four port, with latitude and longitude controls, reported in table 6 column 1. This linear regression is used to recover how transport access affects traded-goods prices as an input to the structural decomposition. Column 2 instruments travel time, but this setting captures the direct OLS implementation in column 1.

Identification: The paper interprets higher travel time as raising local traded-goods prices through transport costs. The main concern is endogenous railroad placement. In OLS this remains unresolved, so the specification is primarily descriptive/structural input, with IV shown separately. Latitude and longitude partially absorb geography and agroclimatic differences.

Setting: As part of the structural decomposition, the paper estimates that greater remoteness from the nearest top-four port raises local tradeables prices. Table 6, column 1, reports a coefficient of 0.063 on log travel time, implying a positive elasticity of the tradeables price index with respect to remoteness. This estimate is then used to recover how changes in the railroad network affect the tradeables price index in later counterfactual calculations, though the authors rely more on the IV version to address endogenous rail placement.

Settings.H1066: Section VI.F.3, equation (51), table 6 column (1), PDF pp. 1299–1300 (article pp. 1299–1300).
Settings.G1067:
Treatment: Log travel time to the nearest top-four port using the actual transport network, instrumented with travel time computed from colonial postal routes plus coast/navigable rivers and land. Continuous endogenous treatment.

Method: IV regression of the log tradeables price index on log travel time to the nearest top-four port, with latitude and longitude controls, using colonial-route-implied travel time as an instrument for actual travel time. Reported in table 6 column 2 with first-stage F-statistic. This linear IV estimate is used to recover how internal transport costs affect tradeables prices in the structural decomposition and counterfactuals.

The paper argues this isolates exogenous variation in transport access from route geometry and historical colonial paths rather than endogenous late-19th-century rail siting. The exclusion restriction is that colonial-route-implied travel time affects local tradeables prices only through actual transport access. Strong first-stage relevance is reported.

Setting: Instrumenting actual travel time with colonial-route-implied travel time, the paper estimates that worse internal transport access causally increases local traded-goods prices. Table 6, column 2, reports a coefficient of 0.061 on log travel time, statistically significant, with a first-stage F-statistic of 129.83. This estimate underpins the later calculation of how removing the railroad network would raise traded-goods prices and lower adjusted agricultural productivity in the counterfactual analysis.

Settings.H1067: Section VI.F.3, equation (51), table 6 column (2), PDF pp. 1299–1300 (article pp. 1299–1300).
Settings.G1068:
Treatment: log(goal factor), a continuous measure of food bank need/size based on relative poverty and population in the service area. In this setting it is interpreted as food bank size/need; lower goal factor corresponds to smaller food banks.

Method: The paper uses linear regressions on food-bank-level annual or panel outcomes to interpret how food bank size/need, measured by log(goal factor), affects engagement with the Choice System. The key example discussed in the main text is an online-appendix regression where bids per client are regressed on log(goal factor), with standard errors clustered at the food bank level. This is not presented as a quasi-experimental design; rather, it is a regression-adjustment relationship interpreted substantively to assess whether smaller food banks were disadvantaged in adapting to the market mechanism.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-food-bank variation in goal factor within the post-Choice data. The endogeneity concern is that goal factor may correlate with other food-bank characteristics such as sophistication or local food richness, so this is not a clean causal design. The paper nonetheless uses the regression substantively to argue that smaller food banks engaged at least as much as larger ones.

Setting: To address concerns that the new auction mechanism might disadvantage smaller food banks, the paper reports regression evidence that smaller food banks bid more intensively: in the online appendix, a 1% reduction in goal factor is associated with a 0.66% increase in bids per client. This is an OLS-style regression interpretation rather than a quasi-experiment, so causality rests on the paper's substantive reading of size/need differences across food banks. The result is used as supporting evidence that the Choice System offered at least weak benefits to all participants, especially small food banks.

Main role: This supports the paper's equity/participation argument that small food banks were not harmed by the new mechanism, but it is not one of the headline welfare or allocation results emphasized in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1068: Section IV, “Weak Benefits and Engagement,” p. 2003–2004 (PDF pp. 11–12), referring to online appendix regression results.
Settings.G1069:
Treatment: log(goal factor), a continuous food-bank-level measure of relative need/size. The focal contrast is how a 1% higher goal factor affects pounds received before versus after the Choice System.

Method: The paper estimates annual regressions of log(total pounds of food received) on log(goal factor), separately by year and summarized in Figure 5, to compare the pre-2005 queueing system with the post-2005 Choice System. Standard errors are clustered at the food bank level. The coefficient is interpreted as the elasticity of food received with respect to goal factor; the post-2005 decline in this elasticity is used to argue that the new mechanism reallocated food away from strict proportionality to need/size and toward smaller food banks.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-food-bank variation in goal factor, compared across years before and after introduction of the Choice System. This is not framed as a formal DiD estimator; instead, the paper reads the annual elasticity changes as evidence that the mechanism altered the mapping from measured need/size to food allocations. Remaining concerns are that other time-varying factors could also affect the relation between goal factor and pounds received.

Setting: A central empirical result is that the Choice System changed how food was allocated across food banks of different sizes. Under the old regime, a 1% increase in goal factor translated into roughly a 1% increase in pounds received, as intended. After 2005, Figure 5 shows that this elasticity falls below 0.5 in every year and averages 0.43 from 2005 to 2011, which the paper interprets as large food banks getting much less additional food than before relative to small food banks. This OLS regression evidence underpins the paper's claim that the market mechanism reallocated quantity toward smaller, food-poorer food banks.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that small food banks obtained substantially more pounds per client under Choice and that the old 1-for-1 relation between goal factor and pounds fell to 0.43 after 2005. This is a core allocation result.
Settings.G1070:
Treatment: log(goal factor), a continuous measure of food bank size/need. The paper interprets higher goal factor as larger, relatively food-richer food banks.

Method: Using food-bank-level comparisons and regressions in the post-2005 period, the paper studies how log(goal factor) predicts the average annual price per pound paid by a food bank and annual shares spent per goal factor. Table 3 reports linear regressions of log(average annual price per pound) and log(annual shares spent/goal factor) on log(goal factor), with year interactions in some specifications and standard errors clustered at the food bank level. These regressions are interpreted as showing mechanisms through which the Choice System led to differential food quantities across small and large food banks.

Identification: The strategy is cross-sectional/panel regression using variation in goal factor across food banks after adoption of Choice. The endogeneity issue is that goal factor proxies for several characteristics, especially food richness and size, so the estimates are associative. The paper nonetheless interprets them causally as reflecting how the new market mechanism induced vertical sorting between quantity and quality and differential spending behavior.

Setting: Table 3 shows the main channels behind the post-Choice redistribution toward smaller food banks. First, a 1% increase in goal factor raises the average annual price paid per pound by about 0.396%, indicating that larger food banks systematically choose more expensive, higher-quality food. Second, while the overall shares-spent elasticity is fragile in the pooled specification, the interacted results show that relative to the initial 2005 benchmark, a 1% increase in goal factor reduced the marginal propensity to consume shares by about 0.2% in later years. The paper interprets these OLS regressions as evidence that larger, food-richer banks traded quantity for quality and were more willing to leave shares unspent, thereby freeing food for smaller banks.

Main role: These regressions provide the paper's main mechanism for why small food banks received more pounds: larger food banks bought more expensive food and, over time, spent fewer shares per client. This mechanism is central to the paper's interpretation of the reallocation.
Settings.G1071:
Treatment: Food bank size group under the Choice System: below-median goal factor (small food banks) versus above-median goal factor (large food banks). This is an explicit binary contrast based on the median of goal factor.

Method: The paper reports a substantive comparison of nutritional quality between the bundles purchased by small and large food banks under the Choice System, using a Weight Watchers points-based nutrition index. This is not a quasi-experimental estimator but an interpreted treatment-control style comparison by food bank size group. The comparison is used to assess whether the quantity gains for small food banks came at the cost of substantially lower nutrition.

Identification: The evidence comes from comparing outcomes for small and large food banks defined by goal factor. The paper interprets the contrast as the consequence of choice in the new market design, not as a randomized or quasi-experimental estimate. The main concern is selection: small and large food banks differ on many dimensions. The paper's argument is descriptive-causal, aimed at showing that the mechanism reallocated quantity toward smaller banks without meaningfully sacrificing nutrition.

Setting: A headline result of the paper is that smaller food banks used the Choice System to obtain much more food without materially worsening nutritional quality. The paper reports that small food banks acquired 72% more pounds of food per client than large food banks, while the nutrition index of the bundle consumed by small food banks was only 1.8% lower. This comparison is based on grouping food banks by whether goal factor is below or above the median and valuing bundles with a Weight Watchers-based index. It supports the central claim that the market reallocated food toward food-poor banks at little nutritional cost.

Main role: The abstract highlights that small food banks acquired 72% more pounds per client at little nutritional cost, making this a headline substantive result.
Settings.H1071: Section VI, paragraph “Nutrition,” p. 2008 (PDF p. 16); also summarized in abstract and introduction on PDF pp. 1 and 3.
Settings.G1072:
Treatment: Allocation mechanism: observed Choice System allocation versus simulated old queueing allocation applied to the same realized post-2005 donations. This is effectively a binary mechanism contrast.

Method: The paper uses a structural simulation based on the pre-2005 queueing algorithm and observed post-2005 donations to estimate what travel distances would have been under the old mechanism. Starting on July 1, 2005, food banks are randomly assigned an initial queue position, loads are sequentially assigned according to the old algorithm, the queue is recomputed after each assignment, and scenarios incorporate assumed rejection of distant offers (the preferred benchmark assumes each food bank rejects the farthest 10% of offers, with loads discarded after three rejections). ArcGIS computes donor-to-winner distance, and external trucking-cost estimates convert distance differences into dollars. This is not a linear regression but a simulation-based counterfactual exercise.

Identification: Identification comes from a model-based counterfactual: hold the realized set of donations fixed and compare observed distances under Choice with simulated distances under the old queueing algorithm. The concern is that the old system also involved offer refusals and other behavior not fully observed; the paper addresses this by simulating rejection thresholds and using a conservative 10% rejection rule. The causal claim relies on the assumption that the simulation accurately approximates what the old mechanism would have generated on the same donation stream.

Setting: To estimate the geographic benefits of the Choice System, the paper compares observed travel distances under Choice to a simulated counterfactual under the old queueing algorithm using the same post-2005 donations. The mean one-way distance traveled under Choice was 1,034 kilometers, while the preferred conservative simulation implies 1,720 kilometers under the old system, after allowing each food bank to reject its farthest 10% of offers. Using trucking costs of $0.99 per kilometer, the paper calculates that Choice reduced average round-trip travel enough to save about $15.7 million per year. This simulation-based mechanism comparison is one of the paper's central welfare results.

Main role: Transportation savings are a major headline result in the abstract and introduction, where the paper claims food was sourced much closer, saving about $16 million annually.
Settings.G1073:
Treatment: Introduction of the Choice System in July 2005, contrasted with the pre-2005 queueing system; effectively a post-adoption mechanism change in the time series.

Method: The paper interprets the before/after time-series increase in total food donations as an effect of the Choice System on supply. The evidence is descriptive time-series variation shown in Figure 1 and discussed in Section VIII, supplemented by qualitative arguments about improved liquidity and maroon pounds. No formal quasi-experimental design is implemented, and the paper explicitly cautions that causality should be interpreted carefully.

Identification: The strategy is an interrupted time-series comparison around the introduction of Choice. The endogeneity concern is that other contemporaneous trends could affect food donations, and the paper explicitly notes that the variation is time series and causality should be inferred cautiously. The paper's causal interpretation rests on institutional arguments that greater liquidity, faster pickup, and the ability to trade maroon pounds increased supply.

Setting: The paper argues that the Choice System increased the supply of donated food by making placements faster and more liquid and by allowing food banks to sell maroon pounds. Figure 1 shows total donations rising from about 200–225 million pounds before 2005 to roughly 320–350 million pounds soon after Choice was introduced, an increase of about 100 million pounds. Section VIII also reports that maroon pounds added an average of 14.7 million pounds and sold at a 30.5% premium over the average pound. The author explicitly cautions that this is based on time-series variation, so causal attribution is suggestive rather than cleanly identified.

Main role: The abstract highlights that donations of food rose by over 100 million pounds, making supply expansion a key conclusion, though the paper is more cautious about causal attribution here.
Settings.H1073: Section VIII, Figure 1 and Table 2, p. 2010 (PDF p. 18).
Settings.G1074:
Treatment: Distance from donor warehouse to winning food bank, measured in kilometers for a given load. The focal treatment is continuous; an extra kilometer of travel distance.

Method: To translate shares into dollars, the paper regresses total winning bids on distance traveled for loads deemed relatively homogeneous, controlling for load size, number of losing bidders, and transportation subsidies. The preferred specifications in Table 4 absorb a three-way fixed-effect structure: food bank × disaggregated food type × year, or food bank × disaggregated food type × bimonthly period. These interacted FE absorb heterogeneity on both the food and food-bank sides, and the coefficient on distance is interpreted as the marginal reduction in bids due to transport cost for otherwise identical loads. Although implemented as interactions rather than separately listed FE sets, the design is high-dimensional and explicitly intended to address omitted heterogeneity.

Identification: Identification comes from within-food-bank × food-type × time variation in distance across otherwise similar loads, especially among 28 relatively homogeneous goods with low bid dispersion. The main endogeneity concern is positive selection: more desirable loads may both attract higher bids and induce longer travel. The paper attempts to purge this by narrowing to homogeneous foods and absorbing rich interacted fixed effects, so remaining variation in distance is interpreted as capturing transport-cost tradeoffs. The causal assumption is that conditional on these controls, distance affects winning bids only through transportation costs.

Setting: To estimate the dollar value of a share, the paper studies how much farther distance reduces bids for otherwise similar loads. In the preferred Table 4 specification using 28 homogeneous goods and food bank × food type × year fixed effects, each additional kilometer lowers the winning bid by 0.111 shares; with bimonthly interacted fixed effects the estimate is 0.093 shares and still similar. The paper summarizes this as an extra 9–10 kilometers traveled reducing bids by one share. Combining this with estimated marginal trucking costs of $0.66 per additional round-trip kilometer implies that one share is worth about $5.97. This HDFE regression is a core building block for the paper's dollar-valued welfare calculations.

Main role: This estimate is central because it underpins the conversion of shares into dollars, which is then used to value welfare gains in dollar terms, a key headline contribution.
Settings.G1075:
Treatment: Reallocation of food under the Choice System relative to the old equal-pounds-per-client queueing allocation, holding total food supply fixed. This is a mechanism/policy contrast rather than a single observed scalar regressor.

Method: The paper uses a structural welfare-calculation framework rather than a reduced-form causal estimator. It assumes quadratic utility over food categories, exogenous outside-food endowments with food-richness heterogeneity, linear transport costs, and that the Choice System achieves the first best. It then calibrates curvature parameters using external own-price elasticity estimates from Andreyeva et al. (2010) and Cornelsen et al. (2015), observed post-2005 prices, and observed allocations, to compute the welfare gain from reallocating a fixed food supply across food banks relative to the old random/queueing allocation. The resulting welfare change is reported in shares, pounds, percentages of food allocated, and dollars.

Identification: The causal claim is model-based. The paper assumes the Choice System implements the first-best reallocation across food banks, that utility is quadratic, and that external price elasticity estimates can recover diminishing returns by food category. Using observed differences between actual post-Choice allocations and the old equal-pound benchmark, the model attributes welfare gains to reallocating food toward food-poor banks and smoothing consumption over time. The main concerns are the strong structural assumptions and the use of external elasticities rather than experimentally identified demand curves.

Setting: The paper's culminating exercise is a structural estimate of how much welfare was gained purely from reallocating a fixed supply of food under the Choice System. Under the benchmark calibration using Andreyeva et al. elasticities, the annual gain is 19.28 million shares, equivalent to 68.9 million pounds of food. Because the Choice System allocated about 330 million pounds annually, this implies that reallocation increased the value of allocated food by 20.8% (described in the paper as about 21%). Using the estimated share value of $5.97, this equals $115.1 million per year, and adding transport savings raises the total to $130.8 million. The paper also reports that permanent differences in food purchases account for 9.79 million shares, or $58.4 million, about 51% of total gains. This structural setting is the main basis for the paper's headline welfare conclusions.

Main role: The abstract and introduction prominently emphasize the estimated 21% increase in value and $115 million annual gain from reallocation, making this the paper's central welfare result.
Settings.H1075: Section X, equations (2) and surrounding text, pp. 2013–2015 (PDF pp. 21–23).
Settings.G1076:
Treatment: Identified positive versus negative government-spending shocks for euro-area countries, derived from the first-stage sign-restricted panel VAR. The shock is an exogenous innovation to real government spending; in the second-stage local projections the authors separately include positive shocks (shock if >=0, else 0) and negative shocks (shock if <0, else 0). The treatment is thus a continuous shock size, signed and split by sign, not a binary treatment.

Method: Two-step macro time-series/panel design for euro-area countries. In step 1, the authors estimate a panel VAR with country fixed effects, time fixed effects, and country-specific linear trends, using Bayesian estimation with four lags and a weak Minnesota prior. Structural government-spending shocks are identified by sign restrictions following Mountford and Uhlig (2009) / Caldara and Kamps (2017), with controls for fiscal foresight via government-spending-growth forecasts and for default-risk spreads. In step 2, they estimate linear local projections that allow asymmetric responses to positive and negative identified spending shocks by including separate shock variables for positive and negative shocks, plus four lags of key macro controls; standard errors are Driscoll-Kraay robust to heteroskedasticity, serial correlation, and cross-sectional dependence. This is not a standard IV/DiD/FE design but a structural VAR plus local-projection impulse-response design.

Identification: The identifying variation is sign-restricted structural fiscal shocks from a panel VAR that isolates government-spending innovations from forecast shocks, business-cycle shocks, and tax shocks while allowing contemporaneous feedback from output to fiscal variables. The second-stage local projections treat these identified shocks as exogenous and estimate separate impulse responses for positive and negative shocks. The key assumptions are the validity of the VAR sign restrictions and orthogonality conditions, linear fiscal rules in observables, and that conditioning on fixed effects, trends, and lags plus the identified shock isolates causal dynamic responses.

Setting: Using euro-area panel data from 1999–2017, the authors identify exogenous government-spending shocks in a sign-restricted panel VAR and then estimate asymmetric local projections. Their main finding is that under an exchange-rate peg-like environment, negative spending shocks reduce output while leaving the real exchange rate and wages largely unchanged, whereas positive spending shocks appreciate the real exchange rate and raise wages while leaving output roughly unaffected. They formally reject symmetry for the real exchange rate on impact and quarter 1 and for output at quarters 1 and 2. They also state that a 1% change in government spending affects output by about 0.3%, implying a multiplier of about 1.5 given average government consumption of about 20% of GDP. This setting is central to the paper's contribution.

Main role: This is the paper's core empirical specification supporting the main claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that under exchange-rate pegs positive and negative government-spending shocks have asymmetric effects: cuts affect output, increases affect the real exchange rate and wages.
Settings.H1076: Section V.A, figures 3 and 4, table 1; discussion on PDF pp. 26-31 (journal pp. 1667-1671).
Settings.G1077:
Treatment: Identified positive and negative government-spending shocks under the Blanchard-Perotti-style predetermined-spending identification, with fiscal foresight controls. Continuous shock size split by sign.

Method: Robustness analysis using the same two-step panel-VAR plus asymmetric local-projection framework as the baseline, but changing the first-stage shock identification to a Blanchard-Perotti-style assumption that government spending is predetermined, extended to control for fiscal foresight. The second stage remains local projections with separate positive and negative shock terms.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from assuming government spending is predetermined contemporaneously, rather than estimating its output elasticity via sign restrictions. By retaining fiscal-foresight controls and using local projections, the authors argue that identified shocks remain plausibly exogenous innovations to spending. The design addresses concern that the baseline asymmetry might be an artifact of the Mountford-Uhlig/Caldara-Kamps identification.

Setting: As a robustness exercise, the authors reidentify fiscal shocks using a Blanchard-Perotti-style predetermined-spending assumption, still controlling for fiscal foresight, and reestimate asymmetric local projections. They report that the resulting output and exchange-rate responses are very similar to the baseline, because the estimated output elasticity of government spending in the baseline is only 0.07. This supports the paper's main conclusion that the asymmetry under fixed exchange rates is not sensitive to the first-stage identification approach.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness check to show the main asymmetry is not driven by the particular sign-restriction identification scheme.
Settings.H1077: Section V.A robustness discussion, figure D1 and figure C1; PDF p. 30 (journal p. 1671).
Settings.G1078:
Treatment: Annual change in military spending, measured in percent of the prior year's output, separated into positive and negative changes. This proxies for exogenous government-spending variation. Continuous treatment split by sign.

Method: One-step local-projection design on annual panel data for 125 countries with fixed exchange rates, following Miyamoto, Nguyen, and Sheremirov (2019). Rather than using first-stage identified shocks, the authors directly regress future outcomes on annual changes in military spending, split into positive and negative changes, with controls for lagged government spending, output, the real exchange rate, a war dummy, and the lagged policy rate. Clustered standard errors are used.

Identification: Identification relies on treating changes in military spending as plausibly exogenous to the business cycle, following prior literature. By estimating asymmetric local projections with controls and fixed exchange-rate samples, the authors argue they can recover the differential effects of positive and negative spending changes without relying on the panel VAR shock extraction. Remaining concern is that military spending changes may still correlate with conflict or monetary conditions, which they address using war and policy-rate controls.

Setting: Using annual military-spending changes for 125 countries with fixed exchange rates, the authors estimate asymmetric local projections directly. They find a similar qualitative pattern to the euro-area baseline: cuts in military spending reduce output immediately while leaving the exchange rate largely unchanged, whereas spending increases appreciate the real exchange rate, with significance emerging after about a year, and produce a more muted initial output response than cuts. This supports the main mechanism beyond the euro area and beyond the paper's baseline two-step method.

Main role: This is an important external-validity robustness check showing the baseline asymmetry also appears in a broader sample and without the paper's two-step identification.
Settings.H1078: Section V.A robustness discussion, figure 5; PDF pp. 31-32 (journal pp. 1671-1673).
Settings.G1079:
Treatment: Identified positive and negative government-spending shocks in countries with floating exchange rates, continuous shock size split by sign.

Method: Panel local-projection robustness comparing exchange-rate regimes. For the float sample, government-spending shocks are identified in a first-stage panel VAR using a Blanchard-Perotti-style predetermined-spending assumption because spending-forecast and tax-revenue data are unavailable. Second-stage local projections split positive and negative shocks. The authors compare these responses to the baseline euro-area peg sample.

Identification: The identifying variation is structural spending shocks for floaters from a panel VAR that assumes spending is predetermined contemporaneously. The comparison exploits cross-regime differences: the authors interpret different impulse responses under pegs versus floats as evidence that exchange-rate flexibility changes the transmission mechanism. The causal assumption is that within each regime the identified shocks are exogenous and that differences across samples reflect regime differences rather than compositional confounding, though this remains a concern.

Setting: Comparing the baseline peg sample to a panel of countries with floating exchange rates, the authors find that under floats the real exchange rate depreciates sharply after a spending cut and that responses to positive and negative shocks are basically mirror images. Output still declines after cuts, but somewhat less than under pegs after 3–4 quarters. They interpret this as evidence that exchange-rate flexibility makes fiscal transmission more symmetric and shifts more adjustment onto the exchange rate, consistent with the model's prediction that the exchange-rate regime matters for the effects of spending shocks.

Main role: The contrast between pegs and floats is one of the paper's central theoretical and empirical dimensions; the abstract and introduction emphasize that the exchange-rate regime matters for fiscal transmission.
Settings.H1079: Section V.B, figure 6; PDF pp. 32-33 (journal pp. 1673-1674).
Settings.G1080:
Treatment: Identified positive and negative government-spending shocks, interacted with indicators for high/low slack (unemployment above country median) and high/low inflation (inflation above 3%). The underlying shock is continuous; the state interactions create state-contingent treatment effects rather than separate treatment codings.

Method: Extended asymmetric local projections in the euro-area sample that interact identified positive and negative government-spending shocks with state indicators for high versus low slack and high versus low inflation. This is a state-dependent local-projection design based on the baseline identified shocks, with coefficient-difference tests across states reported in table 1.

Identification: The same identified government-spending shocks from the baseline are used, but the local projections allow their effects to vary with macroeconomic state. Identification assumes the first-stage shocks are exogenous and that interacting them with predetermined state indicators reveals causal heterogeneity. The paper's mechanism is that slack should matter mainly for positive shocks and inflation mainly for negative shocks because DNWR binds only in certain states.

Setting: In state-dependent euro-area local projections, the authors find that slack and inflation alter fiscal transmission in ways broadly consistent with the model. For positive shocks, output effects tend to be stronger and exchange-rate appreciation smaller when there is slack; the impact difference for the real exchange rate is statistically significant. For negative shocks, slack does not significantly change responses. High inflation does not significantly alter responses to positive shocks, but for negative shocks it makes the real exchange rate appreciate more (equivalently, depreciate less), with significant differences across several horizons. These heterogeneity results materially reinforce the paper's mechanism based on downward nominal wage rigidity.

Main role: The abstract states that economic slack and inflation matter for the fiscal transmission mechanism in the way predicted by the model, so these state-dependent estimates support central substantive claims.
Settings.H1080: Section V.B, table 1 and figure D5; PDF pp. 33-34 (journal pp. 1674-1675).
Settings.G1081:
Treatment: Identified government-spending shocks in the euro-area sample, imposed to have symmetric effects rather than separate positive and negative coefficients. Continuous shock.

Method: Restricted symmetric local-projection specification estimated on the same euro-area sample and same identified shocks as the baseline, but constraining positive and negative government-spending shocks to have the same effect. This is used to assess the bias from imposing symmetry ('depreciation bias').

Identification: Using the same identified shocks and sample as the baseline, the authors change only the second-stage estimating equation by imposing symmetric responses. The comparison with the asymmetric baseline is interpreted causally as model misspecification from restricting heterogeneous effects to be equal. The key assumption is that the asymmetric baseline better captures the true causal response, so deviations in the symmetric estimate reflect bias from functional-form restriction.

Setting: When the authors estimate a symmetric euro-area specification that forces positive and negative spending shocks to have the same exchange-rate effect, they find a 'depreciation bias': the symmetric model predicts too little appreciation after positive spending shocks and too much depreciation after spending cuts relative to the asymmetric baseline. This result is central to the paper's claim that much of the earlier literature's depreciation finding may stem from imposing symmetry when the true transmission is asymmetric.

Main role: The abstract and introduction stress that estimates failing to distinguish positive and negative shocks are subject to a depreciation bias. This symmetric-specification result directly substantiates that central claim.
Settings.H1081: Section V.C, figure 7 top panels; PDF pp. 34-35 (journal pp. 1675-1676).
Settings.G1082:
Treatment: Identified government-spending shocks for the United States, continuous and then modeled either symmetrically or with separate positive/negative effects in the local projections.

Method: US quarterly time-series structural VAR plus local-projection comparison. The authors estimate a parsimonious VAR for real tax revenues, government spending, output, and the real exchange rate over 1983–2019, identify spending shocks using the same sign restrictions as above, then compare a symmetric response specification with their asymmetric baseline local-projection specification.

Identification: The identifying variation is sign-restricted spending shocks from a US VAR. The comparison between symmetric and asymmetric response models asks whether allowing for sign asymmetry changes the inferred causal response of the real exchange rate. Assumptions mirror the baseline VAR identification plus the view that the asymmetric local projection better captures the underlying response than the symmetric model.

Setting: Using US quarterly data from 1983 to 2019, the authors show that a symmetric specification reproduces the classic finding that positive government-spending shocks depreciate the real exchange rate. But once they allow for asymmetric effects of positive and negative shocks, positive US spending shocks instead appreciate the exchange rate in the short run, and negative shocks no longer generate short-run appreciation. The authors interpret this as additional evidence that imposing symmetry can distort estimated fiscal transmission even in a flexible-exchange-rate economy.

Main role: This is an external comparison showing the depreciation-bias logic may extend beyond fixed-exchange-rate economies, but the paper's main empirical focus remains cross-country evidence under pegs.
Settings.H1082: Section V.C, figure 7 bottom panels; PDF pp. 35-36 (journal pp. 1676-1677).
Settings.G1083:
Treatment: Constructed balanced-budget government-spending shock: a spending cut/increase combined with an immediate tax cut/increase such that the budget remains balanced for four quarters. The underlying treatment is a continuous joint fiscal package, not binary.

Method: Balanced-budget impulse-response exercise based on an extended version of the baseline local projections that includes both identified government-spending shocks and identified tax shocks. The authors then construct a linear combination of the two shocks, following Mountford and Uhlig (2009), to keep the government budget balanced for four quarters after a spending cut or increase and compute the implied impulse responses. Confidence intervals are obtained by bootstrap.

Identification: The design first identifies separate spending and tax shocks, then constructs the combination needed to keep the budget balanced for four quarters after a spending change. Causal interpretation relies on the exogeneity of the identified fiscal shocks and on the linearity used to combine their estimated impulse responses. The exercise addresses the endogeneity concern that observed spending changes may be accompanied by endogenous tax changes that alter transmission.

Setting: In a constructed balanced-budget experiment for euro-area countries, a spending cut is paired with an immediate tax cut and a spending increase with an immediate tax increase so that the budget remains balanced for four quarters. Under this joint fiscal package, the real exchange rate depreciates after spending cuts and appreciates after spending increases, with responses that are fairly symmetric—matching the model's prediction once financing is changed from lump-sum/debt-like to immediate tax adjustment. Output rises after a spending-tax cut package and falls after a spending-tax increase package, unlike the stylized model's zero output response but consistent with prior evidence on strong tax effects. This financing channel is a core substantive result of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that how spending is financed matters. The balanced-budget experiment provides central evidence that asymmetric effects disappear when taxes immediately offset spending changes.
Settings.H1083: Section V.D, figure 8; PDF pp. 36-38 (journal pp. 1677-1679).
Settings.G1084:
Treatment: Initial occupation choice, i.e., the occupation for which training is acquired at labor market entry (around age 15–16), grouped into routine, abstract, and manual occupations. In the IV moment, this is an endogenous occupational-choice variable rather than a binary treatment; exact coding in the linear IV regression moment is not fully shown in the main text.

Method: As part of the simulated method of moments estimation of a dynamic structural model, the authors include an implemented linear IV regression moment relating fertility to initial occupation. Initial occupation is treated as endogenous, and it is instrumented using interactions between region of residence at age 16 and year of birth, motivated by temporary or local shortages of apprenticeship training positions in particular occupations. The IV regression is not presented as a stand-alone table of final reduced-form estimates but is explicitly listed among the moments used to identify the model. The estimand is the effect of initial occupation on fertility, used to discipline the structural parameters governing occupational sorting and fertility preferences. Identification relies on the exclusion restriction that region-by-cohort variation in apprenticeship availability shifts initial occupation choice but affects later fertility only through occupation, after removing regional means and aggregate time trends from moments.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from region-by-birth-cohort differences in the availability/cost of apprenticeship positions across occupations, which shift initial occupational choice before fertility decisions are made. The endogeneity concern is that women sort into occupations based on unobserved ability and fertility preferences. The paper argues these local/time-specific shortages serve as instruments for occupational choice. Validity requires that, after removing regional means and aggregate trends and conditioning as specified, these instrument interactions affect later fertility only through initial occupation.

Setting: Within the structural estimation, the authors use an IV regression moment to identify the causal effect of initial occupation on fertility. Initial occupation is instrumented by interactions between region of residence at age 16 and year of birth, intended to capture exogenous variation in access to different apprenticeship occupations. No stand-alone IV coefficient is reported in the main text, but the setting is substantively important because it underpins the paper’s claim that expected fertility affects occupational sorting and that occupation in turn shapes fertility and career costs.

Main role: This IV regression is used as an identifying moment within the structural estimation rather than being a headline causal result in the abstract or conclusions. It supports the central structural analysis but is not itself the main reported causal finding.
Settings.H1084: Table 2, panel D, row 'Instrumental variable regression of fertility on age and initial occupation (instrumented)'; description of occupational cost shifters/instruments in eq. (7) and accompanying text, PDF pages 17 and 15.
Settings.G1085:
Treatment: Years of uninterrupted work experience/skills while working full-time within a given occupation, entering the wage equation linearly and quadratically. This is a continuous treatment, occupation-specific in effect.

Method: The paper reports structural wage-equation parameters from the estimated dynamic model and explicitly interprets them as average treatment effects of working full-time in a given occupation. The wage equation is linear in log wages as a function of skills (uninterrupted work experience), its square, occupation-specific intercepts, and person-specific productivity. These parameters are estimated jointly with the rest of the model by simulated method of moments rather than by a stand-alone regression table, but the authors give them a causal interpretation as returns to human capital/work in each occupation after accounting for selection within the structural model.

Identification: Identification is model-based. The paper uses observed wage profiles by age and occupation, regressions of log wages on experience by occupation, wage dynamics, interruption-related wage changes, and other moments to recover occupation-specific wage intercepts and returns to uninterrupted work experience. The key endogeneity concern is selection into occupations and labor supply paths by unobserved ability and fertility preferences. The structural model addresses this by jointly modeling occupational choice, fertility, labor supply, and unobserved heterogeneity.

Setting: The authors interpret the estimated structural wage equation as capturing the causal return of uninterrupted full-time work experience on women’s log daily wages within each occupation. They report that wage constants are 3.39 in routine, 3.60 in abstract, and 3.32 in manual occupations; linear skill coefficients are 0.100, 0.090, and 0.123, with negative quadratic terms. They conclude that abstract occupations have higher wage levels and less concave wage profiles, so interruptions are especially costly there because women forgo steeper wage growth. These parameters are central to the paper’s explanation of children’s career costs.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions emphasize decomposition of career costs into lost earnings, skill depreciation, and occupational sorting. The occupation-specific wage returns are central inputs to those headline decompositions.
Settings.H1085: Section IV.B, Table 3 panel B, PDF pages 20–22.
Settings.G1086:
Treatment: A work interruption/out-of-work spell, summarized as a 1-year interruption, with effects varying by occupation (routine/abstract/manual) and prior uninterrupted work experience (3, 6, 10 years). This is effectively a binary interruption exposure for the reported quantities, though duration also enters identifying regressions elsewhere.

Method: The paper estimates occupation- and career-stage-specific atrophy parameters within a dynamic structural model and interprets them causally as the effect of being out of work on skill loss. Skills evolve according to an occupation-specific depreciation function that depends on prior skill level; reported quantities are annual depreciation rates implied by a 1-year work interruption at different uninterrupted-experience levels. Estimation uses simulated method of moments, including regression moments based on wage changes around career interruptions, together with the full structural model to address nonrandom selection into interruptions and returns to work.

Identification: The key variation comes from observed wage changes around interrupted work spells, interacted with interruption duration, experience level, and occupation, embedded in a joint dynamic model of fertility, labor supply, occupation, and wages. The endogeneity problem is that interruptions are chosen nonrandomly and return-to-work workers are selected. The paper argues that the structural model, by matching interruption-related wage moments and other dynamic moments, identifies the underlying causal atrophy parameters despite this selection. This requires correct model specification of choices and shocks.

Setting: The paper estimates that a 1-year interruption causes much larger skill loss in abstract than routine occupations, with annual depreciation rates at 3, 6, and 10 years of uninterrupted experience of 0.06%, 0.50%, and 0.61% in routine jobs; 0.11%, 6.90%, and 2.65% in abstract jobs; and 0.03%, 3.45%, and 3.08% in manual jobs. The authors interpret these as causal effects of career interruptions on skills, stressing that depreciation peaks in midcareer and is highest in abstract occupations. This is a core mechanism behind the estimated career costs of children.

Main role: A central conclusion is that children generate career costs through skill depreciation during interruptions, and that atrophy differs by occupation and career stage. These atrophy estimates are highlighted in the abstract, results, and conclusion.
Settings.H1086: Section IV.B, Table 3 panel A; discussion of identifying wage-interruption moments in Section III.B, PDF pages 18 and 20–22.
Settings.G1087:
Treatment: Working in a given occupation when children are present, especially abstract or manual versus routine occupations; and, for the second parameter, working part-time in a given occupation when children are present. These are categorical occupation treatments rather than purely binary overall.

Method: Within the estimated dynamic structural model, the authors estimate occupation-specific amenity parameters and interpret them as the causal effect of occupation on the utility cost of combining work and children. They report utility-of-work-if-children and utility-of-part-time-work-if-children parameters, normalized to zero for routine occupations, and then simulate counterfactual changes in occupational and part-time choices if abstract/manual jobs had routine-job amenity values. These are model-based causal contrasts rather than reduced-form regressions.

Identification: Identification is through the structural model’s fit to differences in labor supply and occupational choices across women with and without children and across occupations. The paper argues these variation patterns cannot be explained solely by atrophy, opportunity costs, or selection, so the model attributes the residual systematic differences to occupation-specific amenity values with children. This is a model-based identification claim and depends on correct specification of preferences and constraints.

Setting: The authors estimate that, relative to routine jobs, work with children present has lower amenity in abstract occupations (-0.056) and manual occupations (-0.014), and part-time work with children has especially low amenity in abstract jobs (-0.42 versus 0 in routine; manual -0.08). They then simulate that if abstract and manual jobs had the same child-related amenity value as routine jobs, the proportion of women choosing abstract or manual occupations would rise by 5%, and if abstract jobs had routine-job part-time amenity, part-time work in abstract jobs would be 7% higher by age 30. These model-based causal effects support the claim that some careers are less child-friendly and thus shape fertility and sorting.

Main role: The paper’s main contribution is to show that occupational choice and fertility interact through not just wages and atrophy but also child-related job amenity. These amenity effects are emphasized as a core mechanism.
Settings.H1087: Section IV.B, Table 3 panel C and accompanying discussion, PDF pages 21–22.
Settings.G1088:
Treatment: Having children/fertility over the life cycle, implemented by comparing the baseline model to a counterfactual no-fertility scenario in which conception probability is set to zero and known ex ante. This is effectively a binary treatment contrast: fertility allowed versus no fertility.

Method: The authors conduct counterfactual simulations from the estimated dynamic structural model comparing the baseline estimated fertility process with a scenario in which conception probability is set to zero, so the woman knows ex ante she will not have children. They then compare life-cycle labor supply, occupational choice, wages, work experience, and net present value of income across the two scenarios. This is a model-based causal estimand rather than quasi-experimental reduced form.

Identification: The causal interpretation comes from the fully specified and estimated life-cycle model linking fertility, occupational choice, labor supply, wages, savings, marriage, and unobserved heterogeneity. By simulating the same women under baseline fertility and under an ex ante known no-fertility state, the model isolates the effect of children on career outcomes. The main concern is model dependence: causal validity rests on correct functional-form, state-transition, and unobserved-heterogeneity assumptions and on the moments used to fit the model.

Setting: Using structural counterfactual simulations, the authors estimate large career effects of children. If a woman knows ex ante she will remain childless, she is about 5 percentage points more likely to enter abstract occupations and 3 and 2 points less likely to choose routine and manual occupations; her employment rate is about 10 percentage points higher in her early 20s and up to 30 points higher in her mid-30s; her conditional daily wage is about 0.03 log points higher at age 20 and 0.22 log points higher by age 40, with the full-time wage about 10% higher by age 40. By retirement, mothers have on average 22% less work experience per child. Overall, children reduce the net present value of lifetime income by 35.3% relative to the no-fertility scenario. This is the paper’s main causal result.

Main role: Quantifying the career costs of children is the paper’s headline contribution, stated in the title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion. These counterfactual comparisons deliver the core substantive results.
Settings.H1088: Section IV.E, Figure 3 panels a–d and related text; Table 6 headline total cost, PDF pages 25–29.
Settings.G1089:
Treatment: Having children/fertility over the life cycle, comparing the baseline model to the ex ante known no-fertility counterfactual. Binary contrast.

Method: This setting is the Oaxaca-style decomposition, applied to model-generated counterfactual outcomes, of the total career cost of children into labor-supply and wage components, and of wage components into atrophy, occupation, and residual factors. The decomposition compares the baseline fertility scenario to the no-fertility counterfactual and alternates reference scenarios as in standard Oaxaca decompositions, averaging the two reference choices.

Identification: The decomposition inherits identification from the estimated structural model and the fertility versus no-fertility counterfactual. The authors compute the net present value of income under each scenario and then attribute differences to labor supply versus wages, and within wages to atrophy and occupation. The underlying concern is again model dependence rather than sampling variation from a quasi-experiment.

Setting: The model implies that children reduce the net present value of income by 35.3%. Of this total career cost, 27 percentage points are attributed to labor-supply differences and 8.5 points to wage differences. Within the wage component, atrophy contributes 1.8 percentage points of total NPV loss and occupational choice 1.6 points, with the remainder due to other wage-related factors. The authors summarize this as about three-quarters of the career cost coming from lost earnings due to intermittency or reduced labor supply, with the rest due to wage responses, and they emphasize that some wage costs arise before children are born through occupational sorting.

Main role: The decomposition of children’s career costs into lost earnings from lower labor supply versus wage effects, and into atrophy versus occupational sorting, is explicitly highlighted in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1089: Section IV.E, Table 6 panels A and B and accompanying discussion, PDF pages 28–29.
Settings.G1090:
Treatment: Childbearing profile: one child at a specified age, or two children with specified ages/birth spacing. This is a nonbinary treatment because timing and spacing vary across multiple scenarios.

Method: The authors use structural counterfactual simulations to estimate the career cost of having one or two children at different ages and birth spacings, measured as the net present value at age 15 relative to a no-children scenario. This is a model-based causal exercise holding the dynamic decision environment fixed while imposing births at specified ages.

Identification: The treatment effect is identified by structural simulation of alternative birth-timing and spacing scenarios using the estimated model of fertility and careers. The main assumption is that the model correctly captures how timing of births causally alters labor supply, skill depreciation, occupational consequences, and discounted income.

Setting: The model predicts that the career cost of children depends strongly on timing and spacing. A first child at age 20 lowers the net present value of income by 31.4% relative to no children; with a second child at age 22 the total loss becomes 36.4%. A first child at age 28 lowers NPV by 24.0%, and two children at ages 28 and 30 lower it by 27.0%. The authors conclude that the first child is much more costly than the second, wider spacing raises the cost of the second child, and later births reduce discounted career costs because women have accumulated more human capital and face lower depreciation.

Main role: Timing and spacing of births are central to the paper’s dynamic perspective on career costs and fertility decisions, though this table is more of a mechanism/result extension than the single headline estimate.
Settings.H1090: Section IV.E, Table 7 and accompanying discussion, PDF pages 29–30.
Settings.G1091:
Treatment: Female fertility/children over the life cycle, operationalized as the difference between the baseline female path and a counterfactual path in which the woman remains childless and knows this from the start of her career. Binary contrast.

Method: Using the estimated structural model, the authors compare observed/predicted female wage profiles to a counterfactual female no-fertility profile and to male wages for similar men. The focal causal estimand is the effect of fertility on women’s contribution to the gender gap in daily wages conditional on working. This is a model-based counterfactual decomposition rather than a reduced-form quasi-experiment.

Identification: The identification is structural and comparative: the model is used to generate what women’s wage profiles would be absent fertility, while male wage profiles are observed for similarly qualified men. Endogeneity concerns are women’s selection into occupations and labor force participation and the dynamic effects of fertility on experience and wages; the model is intended to account for these mechanisms.

Setting: The authors conclude that fertility explains a substantial portion of the gender wage gap. Comparing observed male wages to female wages and to the model-predicted female no-fertility path, they find that the gender gap closes by about 0.2 log points when women are counterfactually childless in their 30s, which they describe as about one-third of the overall gap. The mechanism is that fertility reduces hours, labor-force attachment, and accumulated skills, lowering women’s daily wages conditional on working.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state that fertility explains an important part of the gender wage gap, especially in the mid-30s. This is one of the paper’s central substantive conclusions.
Settings.H1091: Section IV.F, Figure 3f and accompanying discussion, PDF pages 30–31.
Settings.G1092:
Treatment: Introduction of a cash transfer at birth of €6,000 (child premium/child benefit increase). This is a binary policy treatment: policy versus no policy.

Method: The paper simulates the effect of a pro-fertility policy consisting of a €6,000 cash transfer at birth using the estimated dynamic structural model. The authors compare baseline and policy scenarios for birth probabilities by age, aggregate births over time in an overlapping-cohorts setup, and cohort-specific long-run outcomes. This is a policy counterfactual from a structural model, not a reduced-form DiD even though the paper discusses DiD studies in the literature.

Identification: The treatment effect is generated by the estimated structural model under a counterfactual policy regime. The model captures how women of different ages adjust fertility timing, total fertility, labor supply, savings, and occupations when faced with a birth subsidy. The main identifying assumption is that the model’s behavioral structure is valid for this policy intervention and for dynamic cohort responses; no quasi-experimental policy variation from the data is used here.

Setting: The model predicts that a €6,000 birth transfer primarily shifts fertility timing rather than substantially increasing completed fertility. The policy raises birth probabilities at younger ages and lowers them later, implying earlier childbearing. In aggregate, births rise by 4.5% in the first year after implementation, then the effect declines to about half that size after 8 years and is close to zero after 20 years; the implied short-run elasticity with respect to benefits is about 0.04. For women aged 15 when the policy starts, childlessness falls by 0.8 percentage points, the share with two or more children rises by 0.2 points, age at first birth falls by 0.4 years, skills fall by 0.29%, years working fall by 0.08, years in part-time work rise by 0.04, and routine/manual occupation shares rise slightly. The authors conclude that long-run fertility effects are much smaller than short-run effects, while career and savings responses can be important, especially for young cohorts.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that long-run effects of fertility-promoting policies are much smaller than short-run effects and that policies affect labor supply, skills, and occupational choice. This is a key application of the model.
Settings.H1092: Section IV.G, Figure 4 panels a–c, Table 8, and accompanying discussion, PDF pages 31–34.
Settings.G1093:
Treatment: Indicator(s) for the judge handling the case, summarized substantively as assignment to harsher versus more lenient judges through estimated judge effects. In the reported regression, treatment is implemented as a vector of judge dummies; later these estimates are used to classify judges into lenient/harsh groups. Because the focal regressor in the regression is multi-valued judge identity rather than a single binary contrast, treatment is coded nonbinary.

Method: The paper estimates a linear OLS regression of incarceration sentence length on judge indicators and case controls to interpret cross-judge sentencing heterogeneity as reflecting judges' causal sentencing harshness. The specification is sentence_i = X_i'ϑ + Judge_i'ζ + ε_i, using the sample of non-homicide violent-crime cases with observed incarceration sentences. Controls include defendant gender, race/ethnicity, criminal record level, age and age squared, settlement indicator, attorney type, county dummies, year-of-disposition dummies, and offense-severity dummies. The estimated judge coefficients/fixed effects are then used to classify judges as lenient versus harsh. Although the author is careful to motivate exogeneity using judicial rotation, the implemented estimator here is OLS rather than an IV/FE panel design.

Identification: The intended identification argument is that North Carolina's rotating-judge system exposes judges within a division to similar case pools, so systematic conditional differences in observed sentences across judges can be interpreted as judge sentencing behavior rather than case composition. Endogeneity concern is nonrandom case assignment or omitted case severity; the regression addresses observables via extensive controls, and the paper informally argues exogeneity from institutional rotation. The causal interpretation therefore relies on conditional comparability of cases across judges within divisions.

Setting: Using OLS with rich controls, the paper estimates judge-specific sentencing effects and finds substantial cross-judge heterogeneity in incarceration sentence length. Table IV reports that the estimated judge fixed effects have mean 31.58 months, median 31.51 months, standard deviation 6.26 months, and range 16.28 to 64.63 months; average estimated effects are 25.97 months for lenient judges and 36.21 months for harsh judges. The author interprets this as evidence that judge assignment affects sentence length and uses it as the empirical foundation for the structural analysis and policy counterfactuals, but it is not itself the paper's headline causal result.

Main role: This regression is a supporting reduced-form exercise used to motivate the structural identification strategy by documenting cross-judge sentencing heterogeneity, not a central substantive conclusion of the paper's abstract or conclusion.
Settings.H1093: Section 3.3 'Lenient and Harsh Judges,' equation (3.1), Table III column (1), and Table IV, PDF pp. 425-428.
Settings.G1094:
Treatment: Observable case characteristics (age, gender, race/ethnicity, attorney type, offense severity, criminal record, division, year) whose causal effect on assignment to a harsh judge is probed to assess whether cases differ across harsh and lenient judges. Because treatment is a vector of multiple covariates rather than a single binary intervention, coding is nonbinary.

Method: The paper estimates an OLS linear probability model/regression of an indicator for being assigned to a harsh judge on predetermined case characteristics: harsh_i = X_i'ϑ + ε_i. Controls include age, age squared, gender, race/ethnicity, attorney type, Superior Court division dummies, disposition year, offense severity, and criminal record controls. This is presented as a test of whether assignment to harsh judges depends on observables, supporting the exclusion restriction needed for the structural design. The estimator is OLS; no fixed effects beyond division dummies are central to identification.

Identification: The paper uses this regression to assess whether observed case characteristics predict assignment to a harsh judge. The concern is that cross-judge sentencing differences might reflect nonrandom sorting of cases rather than judges' sentencing behavior. Small, mostly insignificant coefficients are taken as evidence consistent with random-like assignment induced by judicial rotation within divisions. Any causal interpretation is secondary and diagnostic.

Setting: As a diagnostic, the paper regresses assignment to a harsh judge on predetermined observables and finds little relationship, supporting the claim that judicial rotation generates quasi-exogenous variation in sentencing harshness. In Table III column (2), all point estimates are near zero and only the female coefficient is significant at the 10% level; the author concludes that cases do not differ considerably across harsh and lenient judges. This diagnostic underpins the later structural interpretation of judge-induced sentence variation but is not itself a substantive main result.

Main role: This is a diagnostic support exercise for the structural identification assumptions, not a central causal claim about plea bargaining outcomes.
Settings.H1094: Section 3.3 'Lenient and Harsh Judges,' equation (3.2), Table III column (2), PDF pp. 427-428.
Settings.G1095:
Treatment: Potential incarceration sentence that would be assigned if the defendant were convicted at trial; measured in months. In the structural model this trial sentence varies continuously, can be zero with some probability (non-incarceration sentence), and is the key causal variable whose effect on plea bargaining outcomes is studied.

Method: Main structural causal setting. The paper nonparametrically identifies and estimates a structural screening/bargaining model of plea negotiations based on Bebchuk (1984). Exogenous variation comes from cross-judge heterogeneity in the distribution of potential trial sentences generated by rotating judges classified as lenient versus harsh. The author first nonparametrically recovers the prosecutor's offer function from density-ratio restrictions comparing trial-sentence densities and accepted-plea densities across judge types, then estimates trial-cost parameters and the latent distribution of defendants' conviction probabilities by maximum likelihood. The resulting estimated model is then used to interpret how potential trial sentences causally affect plea offers, conviction probabilities, and expected assigned incarceration.

Identification: Identification uses judicial rotation across North Carolina Superior Court divisions. The author assumes judge type shifts the distribution of potential trial sentences but does not affect defendants' latent conviction-probability distribution or bargaining costs, conditional on observables. A key exclusion restriction is that F(.), c_d, and c_p do not depend on judge type; a relevance/inclusion restriction is that the ratio of trial-sentence densities across harsh and lenient judges is piecewise strictly monotone. Selection is central because settlement offers are observed only in settled cases and trial sentences only in trial convictions; the paper derives density-ratio equalities using the censored distributions to recover the prosecutor's offer function, then uses the model's first-order conditions and acceptance cutoff equations to recover latent primitives. The design is structural and relies on the bargaining model being correctly specified.

Setting: The paper's main structural result is that harsher potential trial sentences causally change plea bargaining outcomes. Using judge-induced exogenous variation in potential trial sentences and a nonparametrically identified bargaining model, the author estimates that reducing trial sentences tends to increase settlement and slightly increase the probability of incarceration conviction, while substantially lowering expected incarceration time through shorter plea offers. The fitted model for representative covariate groups reproduces overall conviction probabilities reasonably well: for group 1, model versus data are 36.59% versus 38.35% for any incarceration conviction, 34.86% versus 34.60% for settlement conviction, and 1.73% versus 3.75% for trial conviction; for group 2, 42.22% versus 44.11%, 37.50% versus 36.66%, and 4.71% versus 7.45%, respectively. These structural relationships are the basis for the policy counterfactuals that form the paper's central conclusions about sentencing reform and plea bargaining.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize the structurally estimated effects of trial sentences/sentencing reforms on plea bargaining outcomes, conviction rates, and incarceration time. These are the paper's core contributions.
Settings.H1095: Sections 5-6, especially Proposition 1, Proposition 2, Figures 2-4, Tables VI-VII, PDF pp. 431-445.
Settings.G1096:
Treatment: A policy-induced 20% reduction in the potential trial sentence length for all cases, measured as a proportional decrease in the continuous trial-sentence variable in months. This is intended to simulate lowering mandatory minimum sentences across the board.

Method: Structural counterfactual policy experiment using the estimated bargaining model. The author lowers every case's potential trial sentence by 20% and recomputes equilibrium plea offers, settlement behavior, conviction probabilities, and expected assigned incarceration. This is not a reduced-form estimator but a model-based simulation from the nonparametrically estimated structural model.

Identification: The causal claim comes from the estimated structural model: once the prosecutor's offer function, defendant-type distribution, and trial-sentence distribution are identified using judge-induced variation, the author simulates a counterfactual reduction in potential trial sentences holding the estimated primitives otherwise fixed. The key assumptions are the structural bargaining model, valid exclusion of judge type from non-sentence primitives, and policy invariance of estimated behavioral relationships under the counterfactual.

Setting: In the main policy experiment, the paper simulates a 20% reduction in all potential trial sentences and finds that this lowers expected incarceration time substantially while slightly raising conviction probabilities through more settlement. For covariate group 1, the probability of any incarceration conviction rises from 36.59% to 37.28%, with settlement convictions rising from 34.86% to 35.91% and trial convictions falling from 1.73% to 1.37%; expected sentence conditional on conviction falls from 57.12 to 41.23 months and unconditional expected sentence from 20.90 to 15.37 months. For group 2, any-conviction probability rises from 42.22% to 42.49%, settlement from 37.50% to 37.94%, trial from 4.71% down to 4.55%, while conditional expected sentence falls from 45.08 to 35.63 months and unconditional from 19.03 to 15.14 months. This is a headline substantive result about lowering mandatory minimums.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly emphasize this sentencing-reform counterfactual: lower mandatory minimum sentences greatly reduce total assigned incarceration time but may increase conviction rates.
Settings.H1096: Section 7.1 'Reducing Mandatory Minimum Sentences,' Table VIII, PDF pp. 445-446.
Settings.G1097:
Treatment: Policy that sets the incarceration trial sentence to zero for the 10% of cases with the lowest positive potential trial sentence, i.e., a broadened use of non-incarceration/alternative punishments for mild cases. Implemented as a discrete policy change affecting a subset of cases defined by the lower tail of the continuous trial-sentence distribution.

Method: Structural counterfactual policy experiment using the estimated bargaining model. The author replaces the 10% of cases with the lowest positive potential trial sentence by cases with zero potential trial sentence, effectively setting short incarceration trial sentences to zero, and recomputes equilibrium outcomes. This is a model-based simulation rather than a reduced-form regression.

Identification: The effect is generated by the structurally estimated bargaining model. After identifying the model from judge-induced trial-sentence variation, the author changes the support/distribution of potential trial sentences by setting the mildest positive incarceration cases to zero and resolves the model counterfactually. The causal interpretation depends on the same model-specification and policy-invariance assumptions as the other structural simulations.

Setting: The second policy experiment evaluates broader use of non-incarceration sentences for mild cases by setting the lowest 10% of positive potential trial sentences to zero. The model predicts a sizable decline in incarceration conviction rates but very little reduction in expected incarceration time. For group 1, the probability of any incarceration conviction falls from 36.59% to 32.74% (settlement from 34.86% to 31.04%, trial from 1.73% to 1.70%), while conditional expected sentence rises from 57.12 to 63.64 months and unconditional expected sentence is nearly unchanged at 20.90 versus 20.84 months. For group 2, any incarceration conviction falls from 42.22% to 37.94% (settlement 37.50% to 33.38%, trial 4.71% to 4.56%), while conditional expected sentence rises from 45.08 to 49.95 months and unconditional expected sentence barely changes from 19.03 to 18.95 months. This supports the paper's conclusion that alternative punishments reduce convictions but have small effects on total assigned incarceration time.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight this second reform as a central comparison: broader use of alternative punishments can reduce conviction rates substantially but has little effect on total incarceration time.
Settings.H1097: Section 7.2 'Assigning Alternative Punishments for Mild Cases,' Table VIII, PDF pp. 446-447.
Settings.G1098:
Treatment: Ban on plea bargaining: all cases are forced to be resolved at trial rather than through negotiated settlement. This is a binary policy intervention on the bargaining institution.

Method: Structural counterfactual policy experiment eliminating plea bargaining entirely. Using the estimated model, the author forces all cases to go to trial and computes bounds on the resulting incarceration-conviction probability and expected sentence because the latent defendant-type distribution is not identified over its full support. The resulting estimates are partial-identification bounds from the structural model, not reduced-form estimates.

Identification: Starting from the structurally estimated model, the author removes the settlement option so each defendant's expected trial outcome depends on her latent conviction probability and trial sentence. Because the defendant-type distribution is only identified on part of its support, the paper imposes two extreme assumptions for the unidentified tails to construct lower and upper bounds for conviction probabilities and expected sentences. Causal interpretation relies on the validity of the structural model and these bounding assumptions for the unidentified tails.

Setting: When the paper simulates a ban on plea bargaining, it finds that incarceration conviction rates would fall substantially but expected sentences for those convicted would rise sharply. For group 1, the current incarceration-conviction probability of 36.59% falls to a bound of [25.31%, 30.21%], while expected sentence rises from 20.90 months to [36.81, 43.86] months; for group 2, the conviction probability falls from 42.22% to [33.09%, 39.69%], and expected sentence rises from 19.03 to [24.36, 29.22] months. The paper interprets this as showing that a large share of defendants currently incarcerated via plea bargains would be acquitted at trial, while average defendants also lose the informational rents that make negotiated sentences shorter.
