Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly stress this counterfactual, noting that over 20% of defendants currently receiving incarceration through plea bargaining would be acquitted if plea bargains were forbidden.
Settings.H1098: Section 7.3 'Eliminating Plea Bargaining,' Table IX, PDF pp. 447-448.
Settings.G1099:
Treatment: Change in the unemployment rate, included with one lead and one lag as bi(L)Δu_t in the cyclical-adjustment regression for GDP growth. This is a continuous macro covariate, measured in percentage-point changes in unemployment.

Method: The paper first cyclically adjusts aggregate and sectoral growth rates using linear OLS regressions on a short distributed lead-lag polynomial in the change in the unemployment rate, following Fernald et al. (2017). Specifically, GDP growth and sectoral labor or TFP growth are regressed on a constant and leads/lags of the unemployment-rate change (Δu_{t+1}, Δu_t, Δu_{t-1}), and the residualized series are interpreted as growth purged of business-cycle utilization effects. The fitted relationships are not a treatment-effect design in the experimental sense, but the paper uses the regression-adjusted change in unemployment as a causal cyclical control to isolate longer-run variation in GDP growth. Identification is therefore based on a linear regression adjustment rather than quasi-experimental variation, and remaining concerns are that the unemployment-rate changes may not span all cyclical forces.

Identification: The identifying idea is that short leads/lags of changes in the unemployment rate proxy for cyclical resource utilization, so regressing GDP growth on these terms isolates a residual interpreted as cyclically adjusted growth. The endogeneity concern is contamination of long-run growth by business-cycle movements; the assumption is that the specified unemployment-change controls absorb the relevant cyclical component without removing the secular trend of interest.

Setting: Using an Okun's-law style OLS adjustment, the authors interpret changes in the unemployment rate as capturing cyclical movements in GDP growth and remove those effects to study trend growth. They regress GDP growth on a constant and Δu_{t+1}, Δu_t, and Δu_{t-1}, then use the residualized series as cyclically adjusted GDP growth. The paper reports that this cyclical adjustment eliminates much of the short-run variability and helps reveal the long-run decline in GDP trend growth central to the paper, but it is not itself the main substantive result.

Main role: This regression adjustment is a preprocessing step to remove cyclical variation before the paper's main decomposition and model-based aggregate implications. It supports but does not itself carry the central conclusion about sector-specific trend forces.
Settings.H1099: Section II, discussion of Figure 1C–1D and Table 1, PDF pp. 5–7.
Settings.G1100:
Treatment: Change in the unemployment rate and its one lead and one lag, used as cyclical shifters in sector-level regressions for labor-growth and TFP-growth series. Continuous percentage-point changes.

Method: For each sector and for each input series (labor growth and TFP growth), the authors estimate an OLS cyclical-adjustment regression of raw growth on a constant and leads/lags of the change in the unemployment rate, bi(L)Δu_t with one lead and one lag. They then define the cyclically adjusted series as the raw growth rate minus the fitted unemployment component. This is a linear regression-adjustment design used to interpret unemployment changes as affecting measured sectoral labor and TFP growth through cyclical utilization.

Identification: Variation in unemployment changes is treated as capturing cyclical resource utilization common to sectoral series. The main concern is that raw input-growth series mix business-cycle fluctuations with secular movements; the regression-adjusted residual is interpreted as purged of cyclical effects. This requires the short distributed lead-lag in unemployment changes to span the cyclical component relevant for sectoral labor and TFP growth.

Setting: The authors use sector-level OLS regressions to remove the cyclical effect of unemployment changes from labor and TFP growth, interpreting these unemployment movements as affecting observed sectoral growth through utilization. The resulting cyclically adjusted labor and TFP series are then used to estimate low-frequency trends and factor decompositions. No single pooled causal coefficient is emphasized; instead, the adjustment is a common first-step input into the paper's central long-run analysis.

Main role: These regressions are part of the empirical preprocessing that underlies the trend decomposition and structural accounting. They are not the paper's headline causal estimates but are used to justify the interpretation of the remaining low-frequency variation.
Settings.H1100: Section III.B.1 “Cyclical Adjustment,” equation under that subsection, PDF p. 10.
Settings.G1101:
Treatment: Common low-frequency trend factors in labor growth and TFP growth, ft^ℓ and ft^z, entering sectoral trend growth via sector-specific loadings. These are latent continuous factors, not binary treatments.

Method: The authors estimate a low-frequency Bayesian factor model for sectoral labor and TFP growth trends. First, each series is projected by OLS onto a constant and low-frequency cosine basis functions with q=8, capturing periodicities longer than 17.25 years. Then the vector of low-frequency coefficients is modeled as driven by common factors for labor and TFP plus sector-specific disturbances. The paper interprets common trend factors as affecting aggregate labor and TFP trends, and sector-specific components as affecting sectoral trends. This is neither standard FE nor DiD/IV/RD; it is a structural time-series/factor decomposition estimated with Bayesian methods.

Identification: The strategy uses deterministic low-frequency basis functions to isolate long-run components and a latent-factor structure to separate common from sector-specific trend variation. The endogeneity issue is not standard treatment selection but attribution of trend movements to common versus idiosyncratic sources. The maintained assumptions are that long-run variation is well summarized by the q low-frequency coefficients and that the factor structure with priors on loadings provides a meaningful decomposition.

Setting: The paper estimates a Bayesian low-frequency factor model and interprets common labor and TFP trend factors as drivers of aggregate trend movements. The aggregate row of Table 3 reports that common factors explain about 0.67 of the variation in aggregate labor trend growth and about 0.30 of the variation in aggregate TFP trend growth, with the common labor and TFP trends negatively correlated (median correlation −0.29). These empirical results are central because they motivate the later claim that, once sectoral multipliers are applied, sector-specific rather than common sources dominate long-run GDP growth fluctuations.

Main role: A central empirical claim of the paper is that common trend factors explain only a minority of trend variation in aggregate TFP and a limited share of trend GDP growth once propagation is considered. This factor-decomposition setting is core to that argument.
Settings.H1101: Section III.B.3 and III.C, Table 3 and Figure 5, PDF pp. 14–18.
Settings.G1102:
Treatment: Common low-frequency labor and TFP factors entering each sector's trend growth through sector-specific loadings; the paper interprets these common factors as causing part of each sector's labor- and TFP-trend movement. Continuous latent factors.

Method: Using the same Bayesian low-frequency factor model, the authors estimate sector-specific trend components in labor and TFP growth for each of 16 sectors and quantify how much common factors explain each sector's overall trend variation. The implemented estimator is a Bayesian latent-factor decomposition of low-frequency trend coefficients, with posterior medians and credible intervals reported by sector.

Identification: The authors rely on a latent common-factor model for low-frequency sectoral trends. Identification comes from covariance in the low-frequency cosine coefficients across 32 time series (labor and TFP for 16 sectors), combined with priors normalizing the aggregate factor loadings. The assumption is that common forces load across sectors while residual long-run movements are sector specific.

Setting: At the sector level, the factor model attributes only a small share of many sectors' trend variation to common factors. For example, the paper states that in Durable Goods only 3% of the overall trend variation in labor and TFP growth is explained by their respective common trend factors, while some service sectors show larger common-factor shares for labor. These estimates are central evidence that sector-specific forces, not economy-wide common trends, are the main raw ingredients in the later GDP-growth decomposition.

Main role: The sectoral decomposition is used directly to support the paper's central claim that sector-specific forces are quantitatively dominant and that some important sectors, such as Durable Goods and Construction, are driven mostly by idiosyncratic trends.
Settings.H1102: Section III.C, Table 3 and Figures 6–7, PDF pp. 16–20.
Settings.G1103:
Treatment: Sectoral trend growth rates of TFP and labor, by sector, entering the balanced-growth accounting equations. These are continuous percentage-point growth rates; the effective sectoral source term is g_j^a = g_j^z + (1−a_j)g_j^ℓ.

Method: The paper derives balanced-growth accounting equations from a dynamic multisector general-equilibrium model with input-output linkages in materials and investment goods, then applies these equations quantitatively using BEA input-output and capital-flow matrices. The implied linear mapping from sectoral trend TFP and labor growth to sectoral value-added and aggregate GDP growth is g^V_t = s^{v'}(I + a_d Ω' Ξ') [g^z_t + (I−a_d)g^ℓ_t]. This is a structural accounting/multiplier exercise rather than a reduced-form causal estimator.

Identification: Identification is model-based rather than quasi-experimental. The strategy takes estimated sectoral trend TFP and labor growth as inputs and uses a dynamic multisector balanced-growth model with competitive markets, unit-elastic technologies, observed input-output and capital-flow matrices, and sectoral capital shares to infer the causal effect of changes in sectoral trends on aggregate GDP growth. The key assumptions are validity of the balanced-growth approximation at low frequencies, accurate measurement of production linkages, and that transitional dynamics are negligible at the long periodicities studied.

Setting: Applying the derived sectoral multipliers to low-frequency sectoral TFP and labor trends, the authors conclude that trend GDP growth fell by nearly 3 percentage points between 1950 and 2018 and that the model-implied indirect effects from production linkages are substantial. Figure 9 shows that the full-model trend is materially different from the direct-effect-only series based on value-added shares alone, which the paper interprets as evidence that capital accumulation and production networks causally amplify sectoral trend changes into aggregate GDP growth. This structural accounting exercise is the paper's main causal engine.

Main role: This is the core quantitative setting that maps sectoral trends into aggregate trend GDP growth and delivers the headline conclusion that sector-specific factors account for about three-fourths of long-run GDP-growth changes.
Settings.H1103: Section V.D, equation for g_t^v and g_t^V, Figure 9, PDF pp. 34–36.
Settings.G1104:
Treatment: Common trend components versus sector-specific trend components of sectoral TFP and labor growth, propagated to GDP through sectoral multipliers. These are continuous decomposed trend components, not binary treatments.

Method: Using the same structural balanced-growth model combined with the estimated factor decomposition, the authors decompose trend GDP growth into the portion caused by common trend factors in labor and TFP and the portion caused by sector-specific trend components. The implemented estimator is a model-based historical decomposition with posterior distributions carried through from the Bayesian factor model.

Identification: The causal interpretation relies on combining two maintained structures: a latent-factor decomposition of long-run sectoral labor and TFP growth into common and idiosyncratic parts, and a structural mapping from those sectoral trend components into GDP growth through sectoral multipliers. The main assumptions are correct decomposition of common versus idiosyncratic trends and validity of the balanced-growth propagation formula.

Setting: The main quantitative conclusion is that sector-specific rather than common trend components drive long-run GDP growth. Figure 10 and the accompanying text report that sector-specific factors in trend labor and TFP growth have historically accounted for roughly three-fourths of long-run changes in GDP growth, while only about one-fourth comes from common sources; the posterior median for the fraction of variance explained by common sources is 0.26. This decomposition is a central causal claim of the paper.

Main role: This setting directly produces the headline estimate that sector-specific factors explain roughly three-fourths of low-frequency variation in GDP growth and common factors about one-fourth.
Settings.G1105:
Treatment: A change in a given sector's source of growth g_j^a, combining sectoral TFP growth and labor growth as g_j^a = g_j^z + (1−a_j)g_j^ℓ. Continuous change in annual growth-rate points for a sector.

Method: The paper computes sectoral multipliers from the structural model using observed value-added shares, the input-output matrix, the capital-flow matrix, and sectoral capital shares. It decomposes each sector's total effect on GDP growth into a direct effect equal to its value-added share and an indirect network effect ΞΩa_d s^v. The estimator is a calibrated structural multiplier calculation, not a reduced-form regression.

Identification: The strategy is fully structural: observed production-linkage matrices and capital shares determine how a sectoral growth-rate change propagates to GDP. The endogeneity concern is not treatment assignment but whether the calibrated network and balanced-growth assumptions correctly describe propagation. The causal claim rests on the model's equations and measured network parameters.

Setting: Table 4 reports sectoral multipliers that quantify how changes in sectoral trend inputs affect aggregate GDP growth. Durable Goods has the largest total multiplier at 0.42, PBS the second largest at 0.25, and Construction 0.17, with Construction's multiplier exceeding three times its value-added share in GDP. These estimates are central because they show that the aggregate effects of sectoral trend changes are much larger than simple value-added shares would imply.

Main role: Sectoral multipliers are fundamental to the paper's claim that network linkages and capital accumulation amplify sectoral trend shocks, especially for Durable Goods, PBS, and Construction.
Settings.G1106:
Treatment: Sector-specific components of a given sector's trend TFP and labor growth, propagated through the model's multiplier structure. Continuous annual growth-rate components.

Method: The authors use the structural model and estimated sectoral trends to compute historical sector-specific contributions to trend GDP growth by sector. This is a model-based historical decomposition: each sector's idiosyncratic labor and TFP trend components are multiplied by its sectoral multiplier to produce its contribution to the aggregate GDP-growth trend over time.

Identification: The decomposition assumes the balanced-growth propagation formula and the factor-model separation of idiosyncratic trend components. It attributes changes in aggregate trend GDP growth to sector-specific TFP and labor growth in each sector, scaled by the sector's multiplier. Validity depends on the structural model and accurate measurement of sectoral trends and network parameters.

Setting: Figure 12 attributes the aggregate slowdown to particular sectors' idiosyncratic trend changes. The paper states that, comparing the beginning and end of the sample, Durable Goods alone contributed around 1 percentage point of the decline in trend GDP growth and Construction about 0.75 percentage points; Construction contributed roughly a 1 percentage point decline between 1950 and 1980, while Durable Goods contributed an almost 2 percentage point decline after 2000. This setting is central because it translates the abstract multiplier framework into the specific sectors responsible for the slowdown.

Main role: These sector-by-sector historical contributions identify the substantive sectors behind the aggregate slowdown, especially Construction before 1980 and Durable Goods after 2000.
Settings.G1107:
Treatment: Higher measured productivity growth in PBS induced by lower assumed IPP price growth, plus partial reclassification of PBS IPP output from intermediate materials to investment in the capital-flow matrix. This is not binary; it is a measurement/coding change to sectoral TFP growth and network linkages.

Method: As a substantive robustness exercise, the authors alter measurement and classification in Professional and Business Services (PBS). They modify observed price measures for two IPP-related PBS subsectors to align more closely with NIPA price indices, implying higher measured productivity growth, and they also construct a modified capital-requirement matrix that reclassifies 50% of the value of certain PBS intellectual property products from materials to investment. They then recompute sectoral contributions to trend GDP growth under the structural model.

Identification: The robustness exercise changes the measured sectoral price path and the classification of some PBS output in the capital-requirement matrix, then uses the same structural accounting equations to infer counterfactual GDP-growth contributions. The identifying assumption is that NIPA IPP prices better capture true price growth and that some PBS IPP output is more appropriately treated as investment than as intermediate input.

Setting: In a measurement robustness exercise, the authors show that assigning faster productivity growth to PBS and allowing PBS to contribute more to investment production raises PBS's estimated contribution to trend GDP growth and increases its sectoral multiplier from 0.25 to 0.36. Under this alternative specification, contributions from PBS to trend GDP growth become higher overall than those from Construction, while Construction and Durable Goods contributions do not change much. The exercise supports the broader conclusion that sectors with large multipliers can have outsized aggregate effects, even if exact attribution across sectors is sensitive to measurement.

Main role: This is a robustness and measurement exercise rather than a headline baseline result. It checks whether mismeasurement in PBS changes the sectoral-contribution conclusions.
Settings.G1108:
Treatment: Time trend / post-1972 period exposure in national water pollution trends. Implemented as year indicators or a linear year trend and a Year × 1[Year>=1972] interaction. This is not a policy assignment at the unit level but an over-time exposure used to discuss whether pollution changed after the Clean Water Act.

Method: The authors estimate within-monitoring-site fixed-effects regressions of annual water pollution trends using individual pollution readings from 1962–2001. Equation (1) regresses each reading on year indicators, monitoring-site fixed effects, and cubic polynomials in day-of-year and hour-of-day; equation (2) uses a linear time trend and a post-1972 trend break. Identification comes from within-site changes over time after absorbing time-invariant site heterogeneity. The authors interpret post-1972 changes descriptively in relation to the Clean Water Act, but they explicitly note that these national time-series FE regressions are not sufficient to identify the Act’s causal effect because many other forces changed over time.

Identification: Identification is from within-monitoring-site changes over time after controlling for fixed site differences and season/time-of-day patterns. The endogeneity concern is that many contemporaneous national or local changes besides the Clean Water Act could affect pollution, so these regressions do not isolate the Act’s causal effect. The paper uses them to document changes in pollution levels and trend breaks rather than as its primary quasi-experimental policy design.

Setting: Using monitoring-site fixed effects and flexible controls for season and time of day, the authors estimate that U.S. water pollution declined substantially from 1962 to 2001. In linear trend regressions, dissolved oxygen deficits fell by 0.240 percentage points per year, the share of waters not fishable fell by 0.005 per year, and the implied 1972–2001 decline in not-fishable waters is 11.8 percentage points. The authors interpret these results as evidence that water quality improved after 1972, but they emphasize that national trend regressions alone cannot identify the causal effect of the Clean Water Act because other factors also changed over time.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state as a main finding that water pollution concentrations fell substantially since 1972, including a 12 percentage point increase in waters safe for fishing. These FE trend estimates materially support that central descriptive-causal conclusion about long-run changes, though the paper cautions they are not by themselves a clean policy evaluation.
Settings.H1108: Section IV.A and V.A; equation (1) and equation (2); Figure II; Table I, Panel A and Panel B (PDF pp. 18, 25–27).
Settings.G1109:
Treatment: Cumulative number of Clean Water Act municipal wastewater treatment plant grants received by plant p by year y, interacted with an indicator for downstream waters. The causal contrast is the effect of an additional grant on downstream relative to upstream water quality near the same plant. Treatment is a count/intensity measure, not just a binary ever-treated indicator.

Method: The main pollution-effects design is a triple-difference regression (equation (3)) comparing water quality before versus after treatment-plant grants, downstream versus upstream of recipient plants, and across plants with different grant timing/intensity. The estimating equation includes plant×downstream fixed effects, plant×year fixed effects, downstream×basin×year fixed effects, weather controls, and GLS weighting by the number of underlying pollution readings. The treatment is the cumulative number of grants received by a plant, modeled as a durable capital stock. Event-study estimates relative to grant receipt (equation (4)) are also reported as dynamic versions of this same conventional DiD/DDD framework.

Identification: The identifying variation is differential changes in downstream versus upstream pollution around plants as grants accumulate, netting out plant-specific time-invariant upstream/downstream differences, any plant-year shocks common to upstream and downstream reaches, and downstream-specific basin-wide annual shocks. The main endogeneity concern is that grants may respond to unobserved local shocks, such as changes in population or industry, that also alter pollution. The paper argues for validity using event-study pretrends, pollutant-specific responses, spatial concentration within 25 miles downstream, and additional controls for industrial sources, air regulations, and population.

Setting: In the paper’s main triple-difference design, Clean Water Act grants to municipal wastewater treatment plants reduce downstream water pollution. Each additional grant lowers dissolved oxygen deficits by 0.681 percentage points and lowers the downstream share of waters not fishable by 0.007 (0.7 percentage points); BOD falls by 0.104 mg/L, fecal coliforms by 204 MPN/100 mL, and the not-swimmable share by 0.004. Event studies show little evidence of pretrends, effects build over roughly 10 years after grant receipt, are concentrated within 25 miles downstream, and persist for around 30 years. These estimates underpin the paper’s central conclusion that the Clean Water Act grants program caused part of the observed improvement in water quality.

Main role: The abstract and introduction identify the causal effect of Clean Water Act grants on water pollution as one of the paper’s three main findings. This triple-difference design is the core policy-evaluation method supporting that claim.
Settings.H1109: Section IV.B.1; equation (3) and equation (4); Figure III; Table II; Table III; Section VI.A–VI.B (PDF pp. 19–22, 29–33).
Settings.G1110:
Treatment: Event time relative to a Clean Water Act grant for a wastewater treatment plant, interacted with downstream status. Indicators denote years before and after grant receipt, with bins for 10 or more years before and 25 or more years after.

Method: As a supporting specification, the paper reports dynamic event-study regressions around the year a treatment plant receives a grant, using the same triple-difference structure as the main pollution design. Equation (4) includes year-since-grant indicators interacted with downstream status, plus plant×downstream, plant×year, and downstream×basin×year fixed effects and weather controls. These estimates trace the timing and persistence of grant effects and test for pretrends. Because they are separately reported dynamic estimands in a figure and discussed substantively, they constitute a distinct causal setting.

Identification: Identification is the same upstream-versus-downstream difference-in-differences/triple-differences logic as the main grant design, but with separate coefficients by event time relative to grant receipt. The key assumption is that absent grants, upstream-downstream differences near a plant would have followed similar trends. Pre-grant coefficients are used as an indirect test of that assumption.

Setting: Event-study estimates show that before a Clean Water Act grant, downstream and upstream pollution near a plant evolve similarly, while after a grant downstream waters become cleaner. The graphs indicate dissolved oxygen deficits and fishability violations fall gradually over roughly the first 10 years after grant receipt and remain lower for about 30 years. The authors use these dynamics to support the causal interpretation of the main triple-difference estimates and to show that grant benefits persist over the plausible lifespan of treatment-plant capital.

Main role: These dynamic estimates mainly validate and elaborate the main grant-effects result by showing no pretrends, gradual buildup, and persistence. They are important robustness and interpretation evidence rather than the headline average treatment-effect estimates.
Settings.H1110: Section IV.B.1 and VI.A; equation (4); Figure III, panels A–B (PDF pp. 21–22, 29).
Settings.G1111:
Treatment: Cumulative Clean Water Act grant dollars received by a city since 1970. In Panel A the treatment is cumulative federal grant funds; in Panel B it is cumulative grant project costs including both federal funds and required local capital expenditure. Measured in dollars (nominal or real, depending on specification).

Method: To study fiscal pass-through, the authors estimate city-level difference-in-differences regressions of cumulative municipal sewerage capital expenditures on cumulative Clean Water Act grant dollars. Equation (5) includes city fixed effects and year fixed effects, with some specifications adding basin×year fixed effects and inverse-propensity-score reweighting for representativeness. The paper reports versions where the treatment variable is federal grant funds alone and where it is total grant project costs including required local capital contribution. This is a conventional DiD design exploiting differential timing and amounts of grants across cities.

Identification: Identification comes from within-city changes in municipal sewerage capital spending as grant dollars accumulate, relative to other cities and years, with city fixed effects absorbing time-invariant city differences and year or basin-year fixed effects absorbing common shocks. The endogeneity concern is that grant receipt may correlate with city growth or other time-varying factors affecting spending. The paper treats this as supportive evidence and notes limitations, including the inability to use the upstream/downstream comparison and the restricted sample of 198 balanced-panel cities.

Setting: The city-level DiD analysis suggests near-complete pass-through of Clean Water Act grants into municipal sewerage capital spending. When the treatment is total grant project costs including required local contributions, estimated pass-through ranges from 0.84 to 1.09, and the authors state these estimates are within a standard deviation of one, implying little crowding out or in. This result supports the paper’s cost-effectiveness and benefit-cost calculations by suggesting that recorded grant project costs closely track actual wastewater investment induced by the program.

Main role: The abstract highlights that the authors find little displacement of municipal expenditure due to a federal grant. This pass-through estimate is one of the paper’s three headline findings because it matters for interpreting policy costs and grant incidence.
Settings.H1111: Section IV.B.2 and VI.C; equation (5); Table IV (PDF pp. 22–23, 33–35).
Settings.G1112:
Treatment: Cumulative number of Clean Water Act grants received by a wastewater treatment plant by census year, applied to homes near river segments up to 25 miles downstream of the plant. The treatment is a count/intensity measure rather than binary treatment assignment.

Method: For willingness to pay, the authors estimate difference-in-differences hedonic-style regressions relating housing outcomes near downstream river segments to cumulative grants received by nearby treatment plants. Equation (6) includes plant fixed effects and basin×year fixed effects; richer specifications add dwelling characteristics and interactions of baseline covariates with year fixed effects. The preferred design uses only downstream areas within 0.25, 1, or 25 miles of downstream river segments because upstream homes may also benefit from downstream water quality, making triple differences less appropriate for housing. The treatment is cumulative grants, treated as durable capital investment.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing changes in housing outcomes near downstream river segments around plants receiving grants earlier versus later, while absorbing plant fixed effects and basin-wide year shocks. The main concern is nonrandom grant timing and omitted local trends; because the preferred housing design lacks the upstream counterfactual, it requires the stronger assumption that places with different grant timing would have had similar housing trends absent the grants. The authors partially address this with basin×year fixed effects, controls for dwelling characteristics, and baseline-covariate×year interactions, and by showing event-study graphs with limited pretrends.

Setting: The preferred difference-in-differences housing estimates find weak evidence that Clean Water Act grants raised nearby housing values. In the richest specification for homes within 25 miles of downstream rivers, the coefficient on cumulative grants is 0.00024 for log mean home values, close to zero and statistically insignificant; corresponding rent and housing-stock effects are also near zero. The authors interpret these results as implying measured housing-value benefits are substantially smaller than program costs, a key ingredient in the paper’s benefit-cost discussion.

Main role: The abstract identifies grants’ effects on housing values being smaller than grant costs as the third main finding. These DiD housing regressions are the core empirical basis for that welfare conclusion.
Settings.H1112: Section IV.C.2 and VII.A–VII.B; equation (6); Table V; Table VI (PDF pp. 23–24, 35–39).
Settings.G1113:
Treatment: Event time relative to a treatment plant’s receipt of a Clean Water Act grant in the housing difference-in-differences design, for homes near downstream river segments.

Method: The paper also reports event-study graphs for housing values around grant receipt, corresponding to the difference-in-differences housing design. These dynamic regressions use year-since-grant indicators with plant fixed effects and basin×year fixed effects, and in the preferred versions include dwelling characteristics and baseline covariates interacted with year effects. They are used to assess timing and pretrends for homes within 0.25 miles and 25 miles of downstream river segments.

Identification: Identification mirrors the housing DiD setting, relying on differential changes in housing values near downstream river segments around grant timing after absorbing plant and basin-year effects. The key assumption is parallel trends in the absence of grants. Pre-grant coefficients are used as an informal test of this assumption.

Setting: Dynamic housing event studies show at most modest post-grant increases in home values very near affected rivers and essentially no detectable change within 25 miles. The authors emphasize that most year-by-year estimates are statistically insignificant, reinforcing the paper’s conclusion that measured capitalization of water-quality improvements into housing values is limited relative to grant costs.

Main role: These figures are supporting dynamic evidence for the main housing-results setting. They assess pretrends and show the temporal pattern of any housing response rather than provide the headline average estimate.
Settings.H1113: Section VII.A; Figure IV, panels A–B (PDF p. 37).
Settings.G1114:
Treatment: Assignment to timing protocol: Perfectly Continuous time with the freeze-time protocol eliminating inertia versus Perfectly Discrete time with 15 subperiod grid points. This is a two-valued treatment contrast at the session/treatment level.

Method: Between-subject laboratory experiment comparing assignment to Perfectly Discrete time (PD) versus Perfectly Continuous time (PC) protocols in a 60-second timing game. Subjects were randomly invited, assigned to sessions, and each treatment was run in separate sessions with random anonymous rematching within periods. The substantive estimator is a treatment-group comparison of observed entry-time distributions, summarized with kernel densities and CDFs of subject-wise median product-limit estimates of intended entry times. The authors interpret differences across assigned timing protocols causally as the effect of continuity versus discreteness of time on behavior.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized assignment of subjects/sessions to the PD versus PC protocol. Because treatment assignment determines whether subjects can move on a discrete grid or in continuous time with freeze-time eliminating natural inertia, cross-treatment differences in entry timing are attributed to the timing protocol itself. The main assumptions are successful randomization and no systematic confounds across sessions other than the protocol. The product-limit construction addresses censoring of intended entry times from preemption but does not alter the randomized design.

Setting: Using randomized assignment to the timing protocol, the authors show that Perfectly Continuous interaction causes much later market entry than Perfectly Discrete interaction in an otherwise identical 60-second game. In PD, subjects "virtually always enter immediately," whereas in PC they "virtually always delay entry until t*"; the text states that in PC subjects enter about 40% of the way through the period, tightly clustered near the joint-profit-maximizing time, while PD behavior is centered near 0. This treatment contrast is the paper's primary direct test of continuous-time game theory.

Main role: This is a central result of the paper: the abstract, introduction, Result 1, and conclusion all emphasize the causal effect of perfectly continuous versus discrete interaction on entry behavior.
Settings.H1114: Section 4.1, Figure 3, Result 1; treatment design in Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 10-12).
Settings.G1115:
Treatment: Severity of inertia in continuous time interaction, induced by the timing protocol/game duration: zero inertia in PC via freeze time, moderate inertia in IC60, high inertia in IC10, and low inertia in IC280. The focal treatment is a nonbinary dose/category of inertia level.

Method: Laboratory treatment variation in Inertial Continuous time (IC) protocols, comparing zero, low, moderate, and high inertia. IC60 was run between subjects relative to PD/PC; IC10 and IC280 were implemented within subjects in blocks. The causal claim comes from experimentally varying the severity of inertia by changing game duration while holding the underlying payoff structure fixed, and comparing resulting subject-wise median product-limit entry times across treatments. The paper interprets these differences as the effect of inertia on continuous-time behavior.

Identification: Identification comes from experimental manipulation of inertia through the timing protocol and period length. Removing freeze time introduces natural reaction-lag inertia; changing period length from 10 to 60 to 280 seconds changes the fraction of the game represented by a given human reaction lag. Because these protocol features are assigned by design while payoff functions are held fixed, differences in entry timing are interpreted as caused by the severity of inertia. The within-subject implementation for IC10 and IC280 increases precision but raises possible order/learning concerns; the paper nevertheless treats these as causal treatment effects.

Setting: The experiment shows that increasing inertia causes earlier entry in continuous-time games, while reducing inertia moves behavior toward the Perfectly Continuous benchmark. Figure 4 and Result 2 report median entry times of about 0.184 in IC60, 0.323 in IC280, and 0.393 in zero-inertia PC, while high-inertia IC10 collapses to near-immediate entry, close to PD. The authors interpret this as evidence that high inertia pushes continuous-time play toward discrete-time behavior, but small inertia preserves much of the efficient delay predicted for perfectly continuous play.

Main role: This is one of the paper's main findings: the abstract, introduction, Section 4.2, Result 2, and conclusion all stress that changing inertia causally shifts behavior from discrete-like to continuous-like levels.
Settings.H1115: Section 4.2, Figure 4, Result 2; treatment design in Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 10, 12-13).
Settings.G1116:
Treatment: Payoff-function treatment changing the temptation to preempt, specifically lowering the monopoly/preemption premium parameter Pi_F from 4 to 1.4. The implemented contrast is binary within each protocol pair (PD vs L-PD, PC vs L-PC).

Method: Additional laboratory validation treatments comparing L-PD and PD, and L-PC and PC, where the preemption temptation parameter Pi_F is experimentally lowered from 4 to 1.4 while holding the timing protocol fixed. The design is between subjects. The causal claim is based on treatment assignment to alternative payoff functions and is evaluated using median product-limit entry times and their relation to risk dominance benchmarks. The paper interprets differences as the effect of changing temptation/preemption incentives on entry behavior.

Identification: Identification comes from exogenous experimental variation in the payoff parameter Pi_F across treatments while the timing protocol is held fixed within PD/L-PD and PC/L-PC comparisons. This isolates the causal effect of changing temptation to preempt on entry timing. The key interpretation is that Pi_F changes strategic risk in PD but not in PC, so differential behavioral responses across protocols are attributed to the strategic-risk channel induced by the payoff manipulation.

Setting: In validation treatments, lowering the temptation to preempt causes later entry in Perfectly Discrete time but not in Perfectly Continuous time. The authors report that reducing Pi_F from 4 to 1.4 changes strategic risk in PD and leads to later entry there, whereas in PC the same manipulation does not affect risk dominance and behavior remains essentially unchanged; a Mann-Whitney test rejects equality of PD and L-PD distributions (p=0.02) but not PC and L-PC (p=0.183). These treatments substantively support the paper's claim that strategic uncertainty shapes behavior.

Main role: These are validation/diagnostic treatments supporting the strategic uncertainty interpretation rather than the headline continuity-versus-discreteness result.
Settings.G1117:
Treatment: Assignment of the school to the pedagogical intervention: teachers in treated schools received seminar training and toolkit materials encouraging curiosity-nurturing, learner-centered, inquiry-based teaching throughout the academic year. Control schools were assigned to later training. Binary school-level assignment.

Method: Clustered randomized controlled trial at the school level, pooled across two independent trials (Mersin 2018–2019 and Adana 2021–2022). Schools were randomized to immediate teacher training in a curiosity-focused pedagogy or delayed training control, stratified by district and grade level in Study 1 and by district in Study 2. The reported estimating equation is OLS of outcomes on a treatment indicator with district and grade fixed effects and baseline covariates selected by post-double-selection LASSO; standard errors are clustered at the school level and wild-cluster bootstrap p-values are also reported. The estimand is the ITT effect of assignment to the pedagogical intervention on teacher beliefs and teaching styles.

Identification: Identification comes from random assignment of schools to treatment versus control in two clustered trials. Under randomization, treatment assignment is exogenous to potential teacher outcomes; the ITT compares average teacher beliefs/practices across assigned groups, conditioning on prespecified/selected baseline covariates and strata fixed effects to improve precision. The key assumption is that school-level assignment generates comparable treated and control teachers absent the intervention.

Setting: Using school-level randomized assignment to a teacher-training pedagogy, the authors estimate that treated teachers became more learner-centered and psychologically different from controls. Figure 2 reports treatment effects of 0.199 SD on teacher curiosity, 0.159 SD on modern teaching, 0.168 SD on warmth, and 0.278 SD on growth mindset, with near-zero effects on several other beliefs/practices. These results are interpreted as evidence that the intervention changed classroom pedagogy in the intended direction, helping explain downstream student learning effects, but they are not the paper’s principal causal endpoints.

Main role: These teacher outcomes support the mechanism that the intervention changed pedagogy, but the paper’s core conclusions in the abstract and conclusion emphasize effects on children’s curiosity, knowledge retention, science achievement, and peer learning rather than teacher outcomes as the main endpoint.
Settings.G1118:
Treatment: Assignment of the student’s school to the curiosity-focused pedagogical teacher-training intervention versus control/delayed training. Binary assignment at the school level.

Method: Clustered school-level randomized controlled trial pooled across two studies, estimated by OLS ITT regressions of standardized subject test scores on school treatment assignment, baseline covariates selected by post-double-selection LASSO, and district/grade fixed effects, with school-clustered standard errors and wild-cluster bootstrap p-values. The same design is used for short-term endline outcomes in the pooled sample and long-term follow-up outcomes for Study 1 only, with inverse probability weights in the long-term analysis to address attrition.

Identification: Because schools were randomly assigned to treatment, differences in student achievement across treated and control schools identify the ITT effect of the pedagogical intervention. Covariates and district/grade fixed effects improve precision but are not the source of identification. For long-term outcomes, the authors use inverse probability weights to address attrition, relying on the argument that remaining attrition is balanced across treatment status conditional on observables.

Setting: The school-level randomized intervention increased science achievement but not math or verbal scores. In Table 1, treated students score 0.073 SD higher on short-term science tests (SE 0.030; wild-bootstrap p = 0.033), with coefficients near zero for math (0.013 SD) and verbal (0.032 SD). In the Study 1 long-term follow-up, the science effect remains 0.073 SD (SE 0.043; wild-bootstrap p = 0.124), while long-term math and verbal effects are approximately zero or negative. These estimates support the paper’s core claim that curiosity-oriented pedagogy improves science learning and that gains persist into middle school.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all highlight that the intervention increased science achievement and that these effects persisted into middle school. This is one of the paper’s central causal claims.
Settings.G1119:
Treatment: Assignment of the child’s school to the teacher-training pedagogy intended to nurture curiosity. Binary school-level treatment assignment.

Method: Clustered school-level randomized controlled trial pooled across the two studies, with OLS ITT estimation of treatment effects on children’s choices and willingness to pay in the incentivized curiosity task. Regressions include school treatment assignment, post-double-selection LASSO baseline covariates, and district/grade fixed effects; standard errors are clustered at the school level and wild-cluster bootstrap p-values are reported. Outcomes come from the first visit of the endline curiosity task and are interpreted as causal effects of the pedagogy on topic interest and curiosity.

Identification: Random assignment of schools to the pedagogical intervention provides exogenous variation in exposure to curiosity-focused teaching. Under the RCT design, differences in task choices and WTP between treated and control students identify ITT effects on stated interest and incentivized willingness to sacrifice tokens for information. The authors argue the task is incentive compatible and measure WTP before booklet-test outcomes.

Setting: The randomized pedagogy increased both interest in science topics and children’s incentivized willingness to pay for information. In Table 4 panel A, treatment raises the probability of choosing a science-related booklet by 0.038 and lowers choosing no booklet by 0.029, with no meaningful change for non-science booklet choice. In panel B, treatment increases overall WTP by 0.109 SD and science-booklet WTP by 0.098 SD, while the non-science WTP effect is essentially zero. These estimates are key evidence for the paper’s claim that the intervention causally nurtured curiosity, especially scientific curiosity.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that the intervention increased children’s curiosity, measured by willingness to pay for information, making this a central result rather than a peripheral mechanism.
Settings.H1119: Section IV.C, Figure 3 and Table 4, PDF p. 19–20.
Settings.G1120:
Treatment: Assignment of the child’s school to the curiosity-focused pedagogical intervention versus control. Binary school-level treatment assignment.

Method: Clustered school-level randomized controlled trial, with analysis restricted to classrooms assigned to the half-half booklet-distribution regime of the endline curiosity task. Within these classrooms, exactly half of students received booklets randomly irrespective of WTP or booklet choice, balancing information availability across treatment status. The authors estimate OLS ITT regressions of standardized booklet-test scores on treatment assignment with LASSO-selected baseline covariates plus district/grade fixed effects, clustering at the school level and reporting wild-cluster bootstrap p-values. Long-term results use Study 1 follow-up and inverse probability weights for attrition. Panel B further reports scores excluding questions from the child’s preferred booklet; the authors treat those as suggestive because question composition differs by treatment.

Identification: The primary identification combines school randomization into treatment with the half-half classroom regime that randomizes booklet receipt independent of WTP and topic choice, thereby equalizing the amount and composition of information circulating in treated and control classrooms. This addresses a key confound: treated classrooms in the market-price regime would otherwise have more booklets because treatment raises WTP. Under this design, differences in booklet-test scores across treated and control schools identify the causal effect of the pedagogy on knowledge retention. The authors note that the 'excluding preferred booklet' outcomes are suggestive rather than fully causal because the set of remaining questions can differ across treatment groups when preferences shift.

Setting: Restricting to half-half classrooms where booklet availability was balanced by design, the randomized pedagogy substantially increased knowledge retention. Table 5 panel A shows short-term effects of 0.114 SD on overall booklet-test performance, 0.102 SD on science retention, and 0.086 SD on non-science retention; in the long-term follow-up, effects are 0.137 SD overall, 0.156 SD for science retention, and 0.056 SD for non-science retention. Panel B shows similarly sized positive effects even when excluding questions from each child’s preferred booklet, though the authors caution these are suggestive because treatment changes preferences and thus the test composition. This setting provides core evidence that stimulating curiosity translates into deeper and persistent learning.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that the intervention increased knowledge retention, including persistent effects. This is a central headline result alongside curiosity and science achievement.
Settings.G1121:
Treatment: Assignment of the child’s school to the curiosity-focused pedagogical intervention. Binary school-level assignment.

Method: Clustered school-level randomized controlled trial analyzing peer-learning and information dissemination outcomes from the curiosity-task environment. The authors estimate OLS ITT regressions of standardized booklet-test scores on treatment assignment for selected subsamples: booklet recipients in the half-half regime, nonrecipients, and nonrecipients whose preferred booklet was received by at least one student in their friendship network. Regressions include LASSO-selected baseline covariates and district/grade fixed effects, with school-clustered standard errors and wild-cluster bootstrap p-values. Friendship networks are built from in-degree and out-degree nominations within classrooms.

Identification: Identification comes from school-level randomization into the pedagogy, combined with exogenous half-half booklet allocation for recipient analyses and observed friendship-network exposure for nonrecipient analyses. For booklet recipients, treated-control comparisons estimate whether pedagogy improves learning conditional on receiving information. For the network sample, the key comparison is among students who did not receive a booklet but were exposed through friends who received their preferred booklet. The causal claim relies on random treatment assignment and the authors’ evidence that this restricted sample is balanced on baseline characteristics; however, conditioning on realized network exposure is more design-based supportive evidence than a separate randomized exposure treatment.

Setting: The randomized pedagogy appears to improve classroom information sharing and peer learning. In Table 6 panel A, treated booklet recipients score 0.150 SD higher overall, 0.129 SD higher in science retention, and 0.119 SD higher in non-science retention than control recipients. Panel B shows smaller, statistically weaker positive effects for students who did not receive a booklet. Most notably, panel C shows that nonrecipients whose preferred booklet was available within their friendship network score 0.170 SD higher overall, 0.145 SD higher in science retention, and 0.138 SD higher in non-science retention in treated versus control classrooms. The authors interpret this as evidence that curiosity-oriented pedagogy strengthens information dissemination and peer learning.

Main role: The abstract and summary emphasize that the intervention led to more information sharing and peer learning in classrooms. These peer-learning estimates materially support that central claim.
Settings.H1121: Section IV.C, Table 6 and Figure 4, PDF p. 23–24.
Settings.G1122:
Treatment: Assignment of the child’s school to the curiosity-focused pedagogical intervention versus control. Binary school-level assignment.

Method: Clustered school-level randomized controlled trial, estimated by OLS ITT regressions of aspiration outcomes on treatment assignment with baseline covariates selected by post-double-selection LASSO and district/grade fixed effects; school-clustered standard errors and wild-cluster bootstrap p-values are reported. Short-term estimates use the pooled trials; long-term estimates use Study 1 follow-up with inverse probability weights for attrition. Although the outcomes are binary, the implemented estimator is linear OLS and is interpreted causally as an ITT from random assignment.

Identification: Randomization of schools to the pedagogy identifies ITT effects on aspirations by comparing average aspiration indicators in treated versus control schools. Covariate adjustment and district/grade fixed effects improve precision. Long-term analyses further rely on inverse probability weighting to mitigate attrition bias.

Setting: The randomized intervention modestly increased educational aspirations toward science-related study. Table 7 shows a short-term effect of 0.008 on intending to go to university and 0.023 on aspiring to major in science, with near-zero effects on engineering and medicine and a -0.021 effect on non-STEM aspirations. Long-term coefficients are similar in sign for science aspirations but are imprecisely estimated. These results suggest the pedagogy may shift future educational ambitions toward science, though the evidence is weaker than for learning and curiosity outcomes.

Main role: The paper mentions aspirations as an additional outcome and notes these effects are less precise in the long run. They are not as central as curiosity, knowledge retention, science scores, or peer learning.
Settings.G1123:
Treatment: Assignment of the child’s school to the curiosity-focused pedagogical intervention. Binary school-level assignment.

Method: Clustered school-level randomized controlled trial estimating ITT effects on student socioemotional skills, attitudes, and survey-based curiosity measures using OLS with LASSO-selected baseline covariates, district/grade fixed effects, and school-clustered standard errors. Short-term estimates use the pooled trials; long-term estimates use Study 1 follow-up with inverse probability weights. These outcomes are explored as possible mechanisms through which the pedagogy affects achievement and retention.

Identification: Random assignment of schools to the pedagogical intervention identifies causal ITT effects on these student attitudes and socioemotional outcomes by comparing treated and control schools. Because these are secondary mechanism outcomes, the interpretation is that any differences are downstream consequences of the treatment-induced change in pedagogy. Long-term results additionally rely on inverse probability weighting to handle attrition in Study 1.

Setting: As potential mechanisms, the randomized intervention increased several student attitudes and traits linked to learning. Figure 5 reports positive effects of 0.065 SD on risk tolerance, 0.087 SD on ambiguity tolerance, 0.078 SD on critical thinking, 0.207 SD on survey-measured curiosity, and 0.161 SD on survey-measured scientific curiosity, with little short-term effect on grit and impulsivity. In the long run, the authors report persistence in general curiosity and a 0.070 SD increase in grit. These estimates support the interpretation that the pedagogy changed students’ dispositions in ways consistent with stronger learning, though they are secondary to the main outcomes.

Main role: These are mechanism and supporting outcomes. The paper uses them to discuss channels but does not center the paper’s contribution on these measures compared with curiosity task outcomes, knowledge retention, and science achievement.
Settings.G1124:
Treatment: Exposure to a positive growth-opportunity shock generated by the exit/closure of a large industry competitor. Event date 0 is the first year in which the large competitor is no longer active in the firm's industry. The treatment is effectively an event-time exposure indicator for being in a shocked industry at relative time τ around closure.

Method: The authors estimate a pooled event-study difference-in-differences specification on shocked business-group (BG) firms operating in industries that experience a large competitor closure. Treatment timing varies by industry across 100 large closure events in 84 French industries between 2002 and 2010. The estimating equation includes firm fixed effects and calendar-year fixed effects, with event-time indicators from -3 to +3 relative to the closure; coefficients are interpreted relative to the omitted counterfactual outside the event window and often discussed as changes relative to event date -1. Standard errors are clustered by industry and destination group. This is a conventional TWFE/event-study DiD; the paper later reports robustness to Sun-Abraham and de Chaisemartin–D’Haultfœuille estimators, but the implemented main estimator here is conventional event-study DiD.

Identification: Identification comes from staggered timing of unexpected closures of large competitors across industries, interpreted as exogenous positive shocks to surviving firms' growth opportunities. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity in firm/group structure; year effects absorb aggregate shocks. The key assumption is parallel trends in outcomes for treated firms relative to their counterfactual path absent the closure. The authors argue lack of pre-trends alleviates concern that expanding BG firms caused competitor closure. Remaining concerns include nonrandom closure timing and any industry-specific shocks coincident with closure.

Setting: Using a pooled event-study DiD around 100 closures of large competitors in 84 French industries, the authors find that shocked business-group firms expand and rely more on internal labor markets after the shock. Relative to event date -1, employment rises by about 10 workers, hiring rises similarly, investment also increases with some imprecision, and market share rises by about 0.06 percentage points. Most centrally, the share of internal hires increases by 0.01 at τ=+1 and 0.015 at τ=+2, which the authors describe as 17% and 26% increases over the pre-shock baseline of 0.057. These results support the paper’s main claim that positive shocks trigger greater use of internal labor markets and allow affiliated firms to exploit growth opportunities.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that following large competitor exits, group-affiliated firms expand, gain market share, and increase reliance on internal labor markets. This event-study DiD is the core design establishing those central claims.
Settings.H1124: Section 5.1, Figures 4 and 5, equation (3), PDF pp. 2697-2700 (PDF pages 23-25).
Settings.G1125:
Treatment: Exposure to a large-competitor closure interacted with predetermined ILM Access. The focal treatment is effectively the positive shock for firms with greater versus lower access to same-group workers in the same local labor market and different industries. ILM Access itself is a continuous measure but implemented as binary high/low groups in figures (above median, top quartile, top decile, top 5% versus below median).

Method: The authors estimate a pooled event-study DiD that interacts event time around large competitor closures with predetermined categories of ILM Access among shocked BG firms. The specification includes firm fixed effects and year fixed effects, with separate event-time coefficients for firms with high ILM Access and for firms with below-median ILM Access. ILM Access is measured at τ=-1 as the employment in same-group affiliates located in the same local labor market but in different four-digit industries. Standard errors are clustered by industry and group. This is a conventional interacted event-study DiD, not a modern heterogeneity-robust DiD in the main specification.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from staggered competitor closures across industries combined with cross-sectional heterogeneity in predetermined ILM Access measured before the shock. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences across firms/groups; year effects absorb common macro shocks. The maintained assumption is that, absent the shock, high- and low-ILM-access shocked firms would have parallel outcome trends. The authors discuss threats such as ILM Access correlating with external labor market thickness or internal capital market scope; they argue against these by showing high-access firms increase the share of internal hires and by showing industry diversification or group cash do not explain the response in the same way.

Setting: The authors show that access to same-group workers in geographically proximate affiliates substantially amplifies firms’ responses to positive shocks. After a large competitor closure, firms with above-median ILM Access increase the share of internal hires by 0.019 at τ=+1 and 0.024 at τ=+2, while firms with below-median access do not; they also expand the number of active internal partners by 12.5% relative to baseline. Employment, investment, and market-share gains are concentrated among high-access firms, with effects strengthening as ILM Access moves from above median to top quartile/decile/5% of the distribution. For example, firms in the top quartile of ILM Access gain almost 0.3 percentage points of market share (21.7% relative to their 1.38% pre-event share), while top-decile firms gain 0.57 percentage points (26% relative to 2.2%). The authors interpret these results as evidence that geographic proximity within the group facilitates internal labor reallocation and helps firms exploit growth opportunities.

Main role: A central claim of the paper is that firms with better access to affiliates’ human capital expand more and gain more market share after positive shocks. These heterogeneous DiD results are highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusions.
Settings.H1125: Section 5.2, equation (4), Figures 6-10, PDF pp. 2700-2704 (PDF pages 25-29).
Settings.G1126:
Treatment: Exposure of bilateral origin-destination pairs to a large competitor closure affecting the destination firm’s industry, with emphasis on whether the origin is an internal (same-group) versus external partner. The treatment is event-time exposure around closure for internal-flow pairs; in the local restriction, all origins are in the same local labor market as the shocked firm.

Method: The authors estimate a pair-level pooled event-study DiD on bilateral worker flows between firms, where the destination firm is a shocked BG firm and the origin firm is a labor-market partner. The specification includes pair fixed effects and separate year effects for internal and external flows, with event-time indicators around the large competitor closure. The main estimand is the change in internal bilateral flows after the shock, relative to event date -1 and to the counterfactual outside the event window. They also estimate a restricted sample where all origins are in the same local labor market as the shocked firm. Standard errors are clustered by industry and destination group.

Identification: Identification comes from within-pair changes in bilateral flows around staggered closure events. Pair fixed effects absorb all time-invariant origin-destination pair characteristics and time-invariant group characteristics; separate year effects for internal and external flows allow different aggregate cyclicality. The causal assumption is that, absent the shock, bilateral internal flows would have followed their counterfactual path. Restricting to pairs where all origins are in the same local labor market helps rule out the concern that the post-shock increase in internal hiring is just a shift toward local hiring rather than an ILM effect.

Setting: At the bilateral pair level, the paper finds that worker flows from same-group origins to shocked firms rise significantly after large competitor closures. Relative to the year before the event, average internal bilateral flows increase by about 6.8% at τ=0, 15% at τ=+1, and 20% at τ=+2 and τ=+3, using a pre-event average internal flow of 7.4% as benchmark. The same qualitative pattern holds even when comparing only origin firms located in the same local labor market as the shocked firm, which the authors interpret as evidence that same-group status itself facilitates mobility and that the results are not simply due to local hiring after the shock.

Main role: This pair-level analysis supports and sharpens the main mechanism by showing where the increase in internal hiring comes from and addressing compositional/local-hiring concerns, but the core headline results are at the firm level.
Settings.H1126: Section 5.3, equation (5), Figure 11, PDF pp. 2706-2708 (PDF pages 31-33).
Settings.G1127:
Treatment: Exposure to a large-competitor closure for bilateral internal-flow pairs, interacted with indicators for origin-firm characteristics: low versus high pre-event value added per worker and low versus high pre-event CapEx.

Method: Using the same pair-level event-study DiD framework as equation (5), the authors allow treatment effects on internal bilateral worker flows to vary by characteristics of the origin firm, especially pre-event value added per worker and pre-event capital expenditures. The specification retains pair fixed effects and year effects, and compares the dynamic response of internal flows from lower- versus higher-productivity/growth-opportunity affiliates after a closure shock.

Identification: Identification uses within-pair changes in flows around staggered closure events, comparing origins with different predetermined characteristics. Pair fixed effects absorb time-invariant pair heterogeneity; origin characteristics are measured pre-event. The causal interpretation requires that absent the shock, bilateral flows from low- and high-productivity origins would have evolved similarly conditional on the fixed effects and event-study structure. This setting directly tests the model prediction that labor is reallocated from less productive/less promising affiliates.

Setting: The pair-level evidence indicates that internal labor reallocation after a positive shock comes disproportionately from weaker affiliates. Following a competitor closure, worker flows from lower-value-added-per-worker affiliates rise more than flows from higher-productivity affiliates, and flows from low-CapEx affiliates increase while flows from high-CapEx affiliates do not. The authors interpret this as evidence that business-group internal labor markets reallocate workers from less productive and poorer-expansion-opportunity units toward the shocked unit, reducing within-group labor misallocation in line with the model.

Main role: These results substantively support the mechanism that groups reallocate labor from lower-productivity and weaker-growth affiliates toward positively shocked units, but they are presented as a deeper mechanism test rather than the primary headline design.
Settings.G1128:
Treatment: Exposure to a large-competitor closure interacted with whether the least productive same-group affiliate within the same local labor market (and in non-shocked sectors) has below- versus above-median value added per worker. This captures stronger versus weaker scope for within-group local labor reallocation after the shock.

Method: The authors estimate firm-level event-study DiD specifications, similar to equation (4), where treatment effects of competitor closures vary by the pre-shock productivity of the least productive same-group affiliate located within the same local labor market and operating in non-shocked sectors. The regressions include firm fixed effects and year dummies and compare dynamic responses for shocked firms whose least productive nearby affiliate is below versus above the median of that productivity distribution.

Identification: Identification exploits closure timing across industries and cross-sectional predetermined heterogeneity in the productivity of local same-group affiliates. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences across firms/groups; year effects absorb common shocks. The intended causal interpretation is that firms with poorer nearby affiliates have more scope to reallocate workers internally when hit by the same positive shock, and absent the shock their employment and market-share paths would have evolved similarly to those of firms with more productive nearby affiliates.

Setting: Consistent with internal reallocation from weaker affiliates, the authors find that shocked BG firms expand more when the least productive nearby same-group affiliate has lower pre-shock value added per worker. Employment growth after the shock is significantly larger for firms below the median productivity of the least productive affiliate, and market-share growth is also higher, though less precisely estimated. The interpretation is that local low-productivity affiliates provide a nearby labor pool that allows the shocked firm to exploit the opportunity more effectively.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism result linking firm-level expansion to the productivity of nearby affiliates, reinforcing the ILM reallocation channel rather than introducing the main claim.
Settings.G1129:
Treatment: Exposure to a large-competitor closure for internal bilateral origin-destination flows, with separate treatment effects by worker occupation category. The treatment is event-time exposure of the destination firm’s industry to competitor closure.

Method: The authors estimate a pair-level event-study DiD by worker occupation category using equation (6). The dependent variable is the bilateral flow of workers in a given occupation category from origin firm k to shocked BG destination j, scaled by total hiring of j. The model includes firm-pair-by-occupation fixed effects, year dummies, and event-time indicators around the closure, estimated separately for internal and external flows. They analyze four broad occupations and then finer categories such as STEM-skilled managers and skilled blue-collar workers.

Identification: Identification uses within-firm-pair-by-occupation changes in bilateral flows around staggered closure events. Fixed effects absorb time-invariant pair-occupation heterogeneity, while year effects capture aggregate changes. The key assumption is that, absent the closure, occupation-specific bilateral internal flows would follow their counterfactual path. The occupation breakdown is used to test whether the ILM is especially valuable where external hiring frictions are most severe.

Setting: The authors show that the increase in internal labor-market hiring after positive shocks is concentrated in occupations for which external hiring is likely more difficult. Internal flows of managers/high-skill workers rise by 0.34 percentage points at τ=+1 and by 0.44 percentage points at τ=+2 and τ=+3; with a pre-event average internal flow of 2.1%, these correspond to roughly 16% and 21% increases. Blue-collar internal flows also rise by 0.39 percentage points at τ=0 and by 0.49 and 0.43 percentage points at τ=+1 and τ=+2, about a 20% increase over pre-event levels. Finer results in the appendix show especially strong responses for STEM-skilled managers/professionals and skilled blue-collar workers, supporting the claim that ILMs help firms overcome hiring frictions in technical and skilled occupations.

Main role: The abstract specifically highlights that ILM use is mainly driven by technical managers and skilled blue-collar workers. This occupation-level pair DiD provides direct evidence for that central mechanism.
Settings.H1129: Section 5.3.2, equation (6), Figure 14, and Table A25 discussed in text, PDF pp. 2710-2711 (PDF pages 35-36).
Settings.G1130:
Treatment: Counterfactual relaxation of the ILM constraint by one additional worker redeployed from a non-shocked affiliate to the shocked unit. This is a discrete one-worker change in internal labor reallocation generated by the model-based exercise.

Method: This is not a reduced-form regression design but a model-based calibration/quantification exercise. For shocked BG firms with below-median ILM Access and at least one affiliate in non-shocked sectors, the authors compute a within-group labor-misallocation wedge λ using equation (2b) from their model. They approximate marginal revenue products with value added per worker under a Cobb-Douglas production function and assumed labor shares of 1/2 or 2/3, and calculate how much consolidated group profits would rise if one additional worker were redeployed to the shocked unit. The exercise is descriptive-structural rather than a standard linear causal estimator.

Identification: The exercise takes the paper’s structural model as given and uses observed value added per worker to proxy marginal revenue productivity. The intended causal interpretation is the model-implied profit effect of relaxing constrained ILM access by one worker for shocked units. Its validity depends on the production-function assumptions, measurement of MRPL, and the model’s mapping from wedges to profit gains rather than on quasi-experimental variation.

Setting: Using a model-based calibration, the authors estimate the profit gains from slightly relaxing ILM constraints after a shock. For shocked firms with below-median ILM Access, redeploying one additional worker to the shocked unit would increase one-year group profits by about €124,000 to €165,000 in more diversified groups, depending on the assumed labor share. Compared with average consolidated group profits, this corresponds to roughly 0.2% to 0.3%, which the authors describe as economically meaningful and between one-fifth and one-ninth of the estimated contribution of a CEO’s continued employment to firm profits. The exercise supports the paper’s claim that constrained geographic access to group human capital creates real within-group labor misallocation.

Main role: This quantification exercise is used to gauge economic magnitude and illustrate how group structure affects ILM value; it is not one of the main reduced-form identification strategies.
Settings.H1130: Section 5.2.1, Table 3, equation (2b) discussion, PDF pp. 2704-2706 (PDF pages 29-31).
Settings.G1131:
Treatment: Local tourism attractiveness, measured either as (i) a nearby-island dummy, (ii) a continuous municipality fraction of coastline/shoreline covered by white-sand beach pixels, (iii) a pre-Hispanic ruins dummy, (iv) joint inclusion of these measures, or (v) a continuous standardized attractiveness index equal to the average z-score of inverse distance to nearest island, white-sand share, and inverse distance to nearest pre-Hispanic site. Coding depends on column; because this setting groups outcomes reported together in the reduced-form design, treatment is best described as ex ante tourism-attractiveness exposure rather than realized tourism activity.

Method: Cross-sectional reduced-form regressions of municipality-level economic outcomes in two pooled cross sections (population-census outcomes in 2000 and 2010; economic-census outcomes in 1998 and 2008) on measures of ex ante tourism attractiveness. The estimating equation is equation (1): outcome logs on tourism-attractiveness measures, coast-by-period fixed effects, and predetermined municipality controls, with standard errors clustered at the municipality level in the main tables. The three tourism-attractiveness measures are: nearby offshore island within 5 km, fraction of shoreline within 100 m covered by white-sand pixels matched to top-ranked beaches, and presence of pre-Hispanic ruins; authors also use a standardized average z-score and joint inclusion. Identification is argued from geological/oceanographic/archaeological variation affecting local outcomes only through tourism attractiveness, with controls and placebo pre-1960 population tests used to support the claim.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional ex ante tourism attractiveness along Mexico’s coastline from natural/cultural features: nearby islands, white-sand beaches, and archaeological ruins. The endogeneity concern is that attractive places may differ in other determinants of economic development or residential amenities. The paper argues exclusion by conditioning on predetermined geography and historical-location controls, using coast-by-period fixed effects so identification is relative to other coastal locations, and presenting placebo pre-1960 population regressions before beach tourism mattered. The causal interpretation still relies on the assumption that these features do not affect local outcomes except through tourism attractiveness.

Setting: Using reduced-form cross-sectional regressions, the paper interprets ex ante tourism attractiveness as causing long-run local economic gains. A one-standard-deviation increase in standardized attractiveness is associated with a 33.2 percent increase in municipality employment, a 23.7 percent increase in population, an 81.8 percent increase in labor income, a 73.6 percent increase in GDP, a 67.7 percent increase in GDP excluding hotels, a 45.1 percent increase in manufacturing GDP, and a 7.59 percent increase in Mincerized wages; the effect on agricultural GDP is positive but not statistically significant. These results, identified from geological, oceanographic, and archaeological variation plus controls and placebo tests, support the paper’s core claim that tourism generates substantial local development and positive manufacturing spillovers.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize reduced-form evidence that tourism attractiveness causes higher local employment, population, GDP, wages, and manufacturing activity. These regressions are a central empirical pillar motivating the model and the tourism-as-causal claim.
