Setting: Using observed LIS microdata for single-male, single-earner households in OECD countries during 1994–2007, the OLS relationship between openness and relative labor tax burdens remains qualitatively similar to the main results: higher trade openness lowers the relative tax burden in the upper tail of the wage distribution. The figure is presented to show that the hollowing-out pattern is not driven by wage-distribution imputation. No specific percentile coefficients are reported in the text for this robustness setting, but the authors state that the shape and magnitude are consistent with the larger imputed-wage dataset.

Main role: This is a robustness check intended to show that the main findings are not artifacts of imputing wage distributions. It supports but does not itself anchor the central identification.
Settings.G1169:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), instrumented with Instrument I (model-based bilateral trade-cost measure) or Instrument II (oil-price-by-port-distance measure). Continuous endogenous treatment.

Method: In the same LIS microdata robustness exercise for single-male, single-earner households, the authors estimate 2SLS versions of the percentile-specific relative tax-burden regressions for OECD countries in 1994–2007, using the same two instruments for trade openness as in the main analysis. Outcomes are percentile-specific relative employee-borne labor tax burdens computed from observed LIS wage data rather than imputed wages.

Identification: Same IV exclusion restrictions as in the main specification, but implemented on the smaller LIS-based sample. Validity requires the instruments to shift openness without directly affecting percentile-specific tax burdens except through openness, conditional on controls and FE.

Setting: The 2SLS results using observed LIS wage microdata for OECD countries in 1994–2007 show the same qualitative pattern as the main IV estimates: greater trade openness reduces the relative labor tax burden in the right tail of the wage distribution. Because top incomes may be capped or under-sampled in LIS data, the authors note that these estimates likely understate the effect at the very top. The figure-based evidence is offered as robustness rather than as a new main estimate, and no specific coefficient values are stated in the text.

Main role: This IV specification is a robustness check confirming the main IV results with observed microdata, not the primary presentation of the paper’s main findings.
Settings.G1170:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), based on manufacturing trade openness. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors use full LIS microdata for all household types, not only single-male single-earner households, to recompute percentile-specific effective average labor income tax burdens accounting for main and secondary earner incomes, marital status, and children. They then estimate OLS versions of the relative tax-burden regression for OECD countries in 1994–2007. Because results are noisy across percentiles, they report both original estimates and a polynomial-smoothed response function.

Identification: Same conditional-exogeneity logic as the baseline OLS design, but with broader household coverage. The identifying variation is across countries, years, and percentiles in openness and relative tax burdens, conditional on controls and FE. Endogeneity concerns remain those of OLS.

Setting: For OECD countries in 1994–2007, OLS estimates using all household types in LIS microdata indicate that globalization generally lowered relative tax burdens in the right tail of the wage distribution, similar to the benchmark results for single-male, single-earner households. Because household composition varies across percentiles and countries, the unsmoothed estimates are noisy, so the authors emphasize the smoothed pattern. The result is presented as evidence that the main effect is not limited to one household archetype.

Main role: This is a robustness exercise demonstrating that the main pattern extends beyond the benchmark household archetype. It is supportive rather than central.
Settings.G1171:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), instrumented by Instrument I or Instrument II. Continuous endogenous treatment.

Method: For the all-households LIS robustness exercise, the authors also estimate 2SLS versions of the relative tax-burden regression for OECD countries in 1994–2007, instrumenting log trade openness with the same two instruments as in the main analysis. Outcomes are percentile-specific relative employee-borne labor tax burdens constructed from LIS household microdata and tax calculators; reported curves are noisy and also shown smoothed.

Identification: Same IV identification as in the main analysis, applied to the all-households LIS sample. The instruments must affect relative tax burdens only through openness, conditional on controls and FE.

Setting: The IV estimates for all household types in OECD countries during 1994–2007 continue to show that greater openness lowered relative labor tax burdens toward the top of the wage distribution. Although the percentile-specific estimates are noisy and therefore shown with polynomial smoothing, the qualitative pattern matches the benchmark finding that globalization reduced the relative burden on upper-tail earners. This robustness result supports generalizability across household structures.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness check extending the IV result to all household types in the available LIS sample.
Settings.G1172:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), from manufacturing trade openness. Continuous treatment.

Method: To decompose mechanisms, the authors first regress the log average gross wage in a country-year on log trade openness, with the same controls and country/year fixed effects as in prior aggregate specifications. This OLS regression isolates the effect of globalization on average wages before taxes; they also estimate IV versions, but the OLS is a distinct causal setting because it is separately interpreted in the text. The sample is the OECD panel split by subperiods as in the main analysis.

Identification: Identification is from cross-country and time variation in openness, conditional on controls and country/year fixed effects. As an OLS decomposition step, it inherits unresolved endogeneity concerns; the authors note only that they find a positive effect and then use it to construct counterfactual wages.

Setting: In the decomposition exercise, the authors estimate that globalization positively affected the average annual gross wage before taxes. They do not report coefficient values in the main text here, only state that OLS and especially IV specifications find a positive effect of openness on the average annual wage. This result is used to net out wage effects when constructing counterfactual tax burdens and to argue that the main findings are driven by tax-calculator changes rather than wage-level changes.

Main role: This decomposition is used to show the main results are driven by changes in tax calculators rather than wage changes. It supports mechanism, not the headline empirical finding.
Settings.G1173:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), based on manufacturing trade openness. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors next regress percentile-specific wage shares s_pit, defined from the decomposition of gross wages into the average wage times a percentile-specific dispersion term, on log trade openness using OLS and the same control structure as in the main panel analysis. This setting is reported as part of the decomposition of globalization effects into wage- and tax-rate-based components.

Identification: Identification again comes from country-year variation in openness with controls and FE. The paper uses the estimates descriptively/causally to determine whether wage dispersion responds to globalization, but notes the coefficients are not statistically significant.

Setting: The decomposition regressions do not find statistically significant effects of globalization on the percentile-specific dispersion of gross wages around country-year averages. The authors interpret this absence of a wage-dispersion effect, together with the positive average-wage effect, as evidence that their main distributional tax results are primarily driven by changes in tax calculators rather than by changes in the underlying wage distribution. No main-text numerical coefficients are reported for this setting.

Main role: This is a decomposition and robustness step meant to assess whether openness changed wage dispersion rather than tax calculators. It is not a headline result.
Settings.G1174:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), based on manufacturing trade openness. Continuous treatment.

Method: Using the decomposition results, the authors construct counterfactual percentile-specific wages that remove the component of wages predicted by trade openness, feed those wages through the tax calculators, and compute counterfactual percentile-specific relative labor tax burdens. They then estimate OLS regressions of these counterfactual relative burdens on log trade openness for OECD countries separately in 1980–1993 and 1994–2007, with the same controls and fixed effects as the baseline.

Identification: The setting inherits the identification of the decomposition-based counterfactual construction and the OLS panel regression. By removing wage changes associated with openness, the regression isolates the component of openness operating through tax calculators. Causal interpretation still relies on conditional exogeneity in the OLS second step.

Setting: When openness-induced wage changes are netted out and counterfactual tax burdens are recomputed, the OLS results remain very similar to the baseline findings. Under the 5% mixture distribution, the coefficients for the 75th, 90th, and 100th percentiles are 0.01, 0.23, and 4.48 in 1980–1993 and 0.18, -0.08, and -3.48 in 1994–2007. The authors interpret this as evidence that the key response to globalization occurred through changes in countries’ labor income tax calculators rather than through changes in gross wages or wage dispersion.

Main role: This is a robustness/mechanism check showing the main findings arise from tax-calculator changes rather than wage effects. It is substantively important but not the main headline estimator.
Settings.H1174: Section III.C, equations (14)–(15), Figure 8, PDF pp. 375–376.
Settings.G1175:
Treatment: Log trade openness, ln(pi_it), treated as endogenous and instrumented with Instrument I or II. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate 2SLS regressions for the counterfactual percentile-specific relative tax burdens constructed after removing openness-induced wage changes. As in the baseline, they instrument log trade openness with Instrument I or Instrument II, using OECD data split into 1980–1993 and 1994–2007. Controls and fixed effects parallel the baseline percentile-level tax-burden specification.

Identification: Identification uses the same two IV strategies as the main analysis, but the outcome is the counterfactual tax burden stripped of openness-related wage changes. Thus the estimated effect is intended to isolate the causal impact of openness through tax calculators, assuming the instruments satisfy the same exclusion restrictions as before.

Setting: The 2SLS results for counterfactual tax burdens closely match the main IV findings, reinforcing the claim that globalization worked through changes in tax calculators. The authors report, under Instrument II and the 5% mixture distribution, coefficients of -0.01, 1.07, and 19.72 for the 75th, 90th, and 100th percentiles in 1980–1993 and -0.10, -0.58, and -5.72 in 1994–2007. The qualitative similarity to the main IV results is taken as evidence that changes in tax schedules, not wage effects, drove the post-1994 reduction in top earners’ relative labor tax burdens.

Main role: This IV decomposition is a mechanism robustness check, not the primary headline specification, though it substantively supports the tax-calculator channel.
Settings.G1176:
Treatment: Log migration openness, defined from bilateral migration stocks as the average immigrant/emigrant stock relative to native population, denoted ln(pi_it^mig). Continuous treatment.

Method: As an alternative globalization measure, the authors estimate OLS regressions of percentile-specific relative employee-borne labor tax burdens on log migration openness, where migration openness is the average immigrant/emigrant stock relative to native population. The specification parallels equation (2), run for OECD countries separately over 1980–1993 and 1994–2007, with the same controls and percentile-country and percentile-year fixed effects.

Identification: Identification follows the OLS panel strategy using migration openness instead of trade openness. The authors caution that migration data are sparse and imprecise and therefore view these estimates as secondary. Causal interpretation relies on conditional exogeneity of migration openness after controls and FE.

Setting: Using migration openness instead of trade openness, OLS results for OECD countries remain qualitatively similar to the main findings: between 1980 and 1993, migration openness increased the relative tax burden of higher-income earners, while between 1994 and 2007 it reduced relative burdens in the right tail. The authors note that magnitudes are smaller than for trade openness, plausibly because migration is measured in stocks rather than flows. This robustness exercise suggests that broader globalization, not only trade, is linked to the same shift in labor tax burdens.

Main role: This is an alternative-measure robustness exercise. The main paper emphasizes trade openness because migration data are scarcer and noisier.
Settings.H1176: Section III.D, equation (17), Figure 10 panels A and B, PDF pp. 377–379.
Settings.G1177:
Treatment: Log migration openness, ln(pi_it^mig), treated as endogenous and instrumented with a bilateral migration-cost-style instrument constructed from normalized bilateral migration shares. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate 2SLS regressions of percentile-specific relative employee-borne labor tax burdens on log migration openness for OECD countries over 1980–1993 and 1994–2007, using a migration-cost instrument constructed analogously to the trade-cost instrument from bilateral normalized migration shares. The specification parallels the main percentile-level model with controls and fixed effects.

Identification: The endogenous regressor is migration openness. Identification uses an instrument based on bilateral migration shares intended to capture relative mobility costs across destinations while being exogenous to country-year-specific labor tax burdens. Validity requires these relative migration-cost components to affect tax burdens only via migration openness, conditional on controls and FE.

Setting: The IV results using migration openness also reproduce the paper’s central qualitative pattern: migration openness increased the relative tax burden on higher earners before 1994 and reduced relative burdens in the upper tail after 1994. The authors stress that these estimates are less precise and generally smaller than the trade-based ones because migration data are weaker. Nonetheless, the IV evidence is presented as corroborating the broader claim that globalization shifts labor tax burdens away from top earners in the later period.

Main role: This is a secondary robustness analysis using a noisier alternative globalization measure. It supports, but does not anchor, the paper’s main claim.
Settings.H1177: Section III.D, Table 5, Figure 10 panels C and D, PDF pp. 378–379.
Settings.G1178:
Treatment: Log interstate migration openness for state-year, based on in- and out-migration of tax returns across US states (including a foreign residual category). Continuous endogenous treatment.

Method: In a US subnational case study, the authors estimate 2SLS regressions of quantile-specific relative state-level income tax burdens on log interstate migration openness for US states over 2000–2007. The outcome is 100 times quantile-q state income tax payments times taxable income divided by the sum across 50 taxable-income quantiles. The treatment is interstate mobility measured from IRS migration flows; it is instrumented with a mobility-cost measure constructed analogously to the migration instrument used in the cross-country setting. Regressions include state-level controls and year and state fixed effects; taxable-income quantiles are used instead of percentiles because of state sample sizes.

Identification: Identification uses variation in interstate mobility across states and time, instrumented with a migration-cost-style measure derived from normalized state-to-state migration flows. The argument is that relative mobility costs shift migration openness but are exogenous to quantile-specific state income tax burdens conditional on controls and state/year fixed effects. The design aims to test whether mobility induces subnational tax competition, especially at the top of the income distribution.

Setting: In the United States, higher interstate mobility causally reduced the relative state-level income tax burden on top earners while increasing it for middle and upper-middle quantiles. The authors state that the estimated coefficients imply that a 1 percent increase in interstate mobility into and out of a state led to a decline of 0.15 percentage points in the relative state-level tax burden of the top-income percentile. The shape of the response is described as strikingly similar to the post-1994 OECD results, supporting the interpretation that mobile high earners induce tax competition at the state level.

Main role: This is an extension showing similar mechanisms at the subnational level in the United States. It reinforces generality but is not the main cross-country evidence.
Settings.H1178: Section III.E, equation (18), Figure 11 panel A, PDF pp. 379–381.
Settings.G1179:
Treatment: Log interstate migration openness for state-year, instrumented using the state-to-state migration-cost-style instrument. Continuous endogenous treatment.

Method: The authors re-estimate the US interstate-migration 2SLS design using as outcome the total relative income tax burden combining state and federal income taxes, again by 50 taxable-income quantiles for single individuals with positive income over 2000–2007. Interstate migration openness is instrumented with the same mobility-cost measure; controls and fixed effects match the state-level-tax specification.

Identification: Same IV identification as the prior US state-level setting, but now the outcome includes the federally imposed tax layer that cannot be avoided by interstate migration. The comparison is used to infer that federal taxation coordinates or constrains tax competition induced by worker mobility.

Setting: When the outcome is the combined state-plus-federal relative income tax burden, higher interstate mobility has much weaker effects than for state taxes alone. The authors report that coefficients are largely insignificant and become negative only at the very right tail of the income distribution, concluding that the federal layer acts as a tax-policy coordination device that mitigates the adverse effect of interstate mobility on state-level income taxation for most of the distribution. This extension supports the paper’s broader mechanism by contrasting subnational and coordinated tax systems.

Main role: This is a supporting extension showing that a federal tax layer can mitigate subnational tax competition. It is not one of the paper’s primary cross-country results.
Settings.H1179: Section III.E, Figure 11 panel B, PDF pp. 380–381.
Settings.G1180:
Treatment: Shared work experience between the proceduralist and the physicians treating the patient during the hospitalization, measured as the weighted average across treating physicians of the number of hospital visits those physicians provided to that proceduralist’s PCI/CABG patients in the prior 730 days; weights are each physician’s share of visits to the current patient. Main regressions scale this variable by its sample standard deviation. It is continuous, not binary.

Method: Emergency-department (ED) admissions only. The author estimates linear probability models of patient outcomes on standardized proceduralist-physician shared work experience, exploiting within-proceduralist variation across unexpectedly arriving ED patients who encounter different physicians on duty. The implemented estimator includes proceduralist fixed effects, then adds hospital-year, admission month, and day-of-week fixed effects, controls for proceduralists’ and physicians’ own recent experience, physician observables, and patient risk controls. Identification is argued to come from predetermined physician schedules combined with unanticipated ED arrivals, which should make assignment to higher- versus lower-shared-experience teams quasi-random within proceduralist. Remaining concerns are patient sorting to on-duty physicians and correlation of shared experience with physician characteristics or match quality; the paper addresses these with balance tests and robustness checks.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-proceduralist variation in team shared experience among ED patients. Because physician work schedules are set in advance while ED admissions for acute heart conditions are unanticipated, the paper argues patients are quasi-randomly exposed to physicians with different prior collaboration with the proceduralist, conditional on proceduralist FE, hospital-year, admission timing, and own experience controls. The main endogeneity concern is nonrandom patient assignment to physicians on duty or omitted physician characteristics correlated with shared experience. The paper supports the assumptions using balance in patient risk measures and physician observables, stability to rich controls, and additional robustness analyses.

Setting: Using ED patients only, the paper estimates within-proceduralist linear FE models and finds that higher proceduralist-physician shared work experience lowers 30-day mortality. In the fully controlled specification, a one-standard-deviation increase in shared work experience reduces 30-day mortality by 0.588 percentage points for PCI patients and 1.242 percentage points for CABG patients. The author interprets this as quasi-experimental evidence from unexpected ED admissions and predetermined physician schedules, making this setting a main pillar of the paper’s claim that past collaboration builds team-specific human capital that saves lives.

Main role: This is one of the paper’s two headline causal strategies described in the introduction, abstract, and Section III, and it underpins the central claim that shared collaboration experience causally reduces mortality.
Settings.H1180: Section III.A ‘Empirical Strategy I: Patients Admitted through the ED,’ especially Table 2 columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 3935–3943 (article pp. 13–21).
Settings.G1181:
Treatment: Shared work experience between the proceduralist and physicians treating the patient, measured as the weighted average across treating physicians of the number of hospital visits those physicians provided to that proceduralist’s PCI/CABG patients in the prior 730 days; weights are each physician’s share of visits to the current patient. In Table 3 it is standardized by the sample standard deviation. Continuous treatment.

Method: All PCI and CABG patients, regardless of ED admission. The author estimates a linear two-way fixed-effects model with proceduralist fixed effects and main-physician fixed effects, plus weighted-average observables of non-main physicians, individual work experience controls, hospital-year and admission-time fixed effects, and patient covariates. Because exact physician groups are hard to repeat, the implemented FE structure uses the physician providing the largest share of hospital visits as the main physician. The design aims to compare patients within proceduralist and within main physician while holding constant observable composition of the remaining physicians.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in shared work experience across patients treated by the same proceduralist and same main physician, after controlling for time-invariant doctor heterogeneity via proceduralist and main-physician fixed effects, admission timing, own experience, and observable composition of other physicians. The strategy is intended to remove doctor-patient sorting and time-invariant doctor quality differences, though the paper acknowledges it cannot fully rule out remaining unobserved physician-group variation. Similarity to the ED results and balance on patient observables are used as supporting evidence.

Setting: In the full sample, the paper estimates a two-way FE model with proceduralist and main-physician fixed effects and finds similar mortality effects to the ED design. A one-standard-deviation increase in shared work experience reduces 30-day mortality by 0.508 percentage points for PCI and 0.754 percentage points for CABG, which the author describes as about 10 percent and 13 percent of the mean, respectively. This setting is a central confirmation that team-specific human capital improves patient survival beyond the ED-only sample.

Main role: This is the paper’s second headline empirical strategy and is emphasized in the introduction and main results as confirming the mortality effect in a larger, more heterogeneous sample.
Settings.H1181: Section III.B ‘Empirical Strategy II: Two-Way Fixed Effects Model,’ Figure 4 and Table 3, PDF pp. 3944–3947 (article pp. 22–25).
Settings.G1182:
Treatment: Shared work experience between the proceduralist and treating physicians, measured as the weighted average prior-730-day collaboration count and standardized by the sample standard deviation. Continuous treatment.

Method: Robustness analysis using the same two-way FE framework as the full-sample strategy, but with different medical resource use outcomes instead of mortality. The specification includes proceduralist fixed effects, main-physician fixed effects, weighted-average characteristics of non-main physicians, doctors’ own experience, hospital-year and admission-time fixed effects, and patient controls. Patients who died during the hospital stay are excluded for these utilization outcomes.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same as in the two-way FE mortality specification: within-proceduralist and within-main-physician variation in shared work experience, net of doctor fixed effects, own experience, timing, and patient controls. The causal interpretation is that if higher shared experience changes resource use while mortality improves, the mechanism is improved productivity. Endogeneity concerns mirror those in the main two-way FE design.

Setting: Using the full-sample two-way FE design, the paper shows that shared work experience lowers resource use even as mortality falls. For PCI, a one-standard-deviation increase in shared work experience reduces length of stay by 0.256 days, tests/exams by 0.315, and the probability of Medicare outlier payments by 0.007. For CABG, the corresponding reductions are 0.460 days, 0.811 tests/exams, and 0.006 in outlier-payment probability. These estimates support the paper’s central mechanism claim that past collaboration raises team productivity rather than merely increasing treatment intensity.

Main role: These mechanism results are central to one of the paper’s major conclusions: shared work experience improves productivity rather than simply increasing inputs.
Settings.H1182: Section IV.A ‘Improved Productivity versus Increased Inputs,’ Table 5, PDF pp. 3952–3954 (article pp. 30–32).
Settings.G1183:
Treatment: Shared work experience between proceduralist and physicians, standardized, interacted with either proceduralist individual work experience or physicians’ weighted-average individual work experience (also demeaned and standardized). The focal treatment is still continuous shared work experience, with heterogeneous marginal effects by own experience.

Method: Heterogeneity analysis in the full-sample two-way FE framework interacting standardized shared work experience with standardized proceduralist or physician individual work experience. The linear model includes the main shared-experience term, the interaction term, doctor fixed effects, weighted non-main-physician observables, doctor own experience controls, hospital-year and admission-time fixed effects, and patient controls. This is intended to test whether general human capital substitutes for team-specific human capital.

Identification: The design uses the same two-way FE identification as the main full-sample analysis, adding interactions to estimate how the mortality effect of shared work experience varies with doctors’ own experience. The main assumption is that conditional on the rich FE structure and controls, variation in the interaction term is not driven by omitted factors correlated with both mortality and the joint distribution of shared and individual experience.

Setting: In the two-way FE heterogeneity specification, the paper finds that the mortality benefit of shared work experience is smaller when doctors have more individual experience, implying limited substitution between general and team-specific human capital. For PCI, the interaction of shared work experience with proceduralist experience is +0.272 and with physician experience is +0.113, relative to baseline shared-experience coefficients around −1.06. For CABG, the interaction coefficients are +0.128 and +0.107. The author interprets these as showing some substitution, but not enough for own experience to eliminate the value of repeated collaboration except at very high experience levels.

Main role: The substitution between shared and individual experience is a substantive conclusion highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, though secondary to the main average treatment effect.
Settings.H1183: Section V.A ‘Heterogeneity by Doctors’ Individual Work Experience,’ Table 6, PDF pp. 3955–3956 (article pp. 33–34).
Settings.G1184:
Treatment: Standardized shared work experience between the proceduralist and physicians, interacted with subgroup indicators capturing patient complexity or whether doctors are from different practices. The underlying treatment remains continuous shared work experience.

Method: Additional heterogeneity analysis in the full-sample two-way FE model, interacting standardized shared work experience with indicators for patient complexity and organizational affiliation: patient age in top quartile, predicted mortality in top quartile, uncommon comorbidities, and whether proceduralist and physicians are from different practices. The linear model includes both the interaction and level terms plus the same two-way FE controls and patient covariates as the main specification.

Identification: Identification follows the same two-way FE logic as the main full-sample design, with causal interpretation attached to interaction terms capturing differential effects of shared work experience across patient complexity and organizational settings. The author uses these patterns to assess whether shared experience matters more where coordination is harder or organizational routines are weaker.

Setting: Using the full-sample two-way FE design with interaction terms, the paper reports that shared work experience reduces 30-day mortality more in settings where care is more complex and where doctors are from different practices. For PCI, the interaction with top-quartile age is −0.458, with top-quartile predicted mortality is −0.508, with uncommon comorbidities is −0.270, and with different practices is −1.062. For CABG, the age interaction is −0.551 and the different-practice interaction is −0.264, with weaker precision for some other interactions. The author interprets these patterns as consistent with collaboration-specific learning being especially valuable when coordination is more difficult or less routinized.

Main role: These are supporting heterogeneity analyses that deepen mechanism interpretation but are not the core average-effect estimates.
Settings.H1184: Section V.B ‘Heterogeneity by Care Complexity and Doctor Practice Affiliation,’ Table 7, PDF pp. 3956–3958 (article pp. 34–36).
Settings.G1185:
Treatment: Indicator for being randomly assigned to the treatment group, i.e., offered access to 1 year of heavily subsidized management consulting services (4 hours/week). This is the ITT treatment assignment, coded as treatment versus control.

Method: The paper’s main short-run estimates are intent-to-treat (ITT) effects from a randomized controlled trial in which 150 of 432 applicant firms were randomly assigned to be offered subsidized consulting services and 282 served as controls. The reported estimator for short-run firm outcomes is cross-sectional OLS comparing treatment assignment to control at follow-up, controlling for stratification variables (sector and firm size), all variables used in the re-randomization procedure, and a survey-month dummy; some columns additionally control for the baseline outcome value using ANCOVA-style adjustment. The treatment is assignment/offer, not actual take-up. The authors also report winsorized and trimmed variants at the same table location as robustness checks, but these are the same randomized ITT design. Identification comes from random assignment, though compliance was imperfect (80 of 150 treated firms took up consulting, and one control firm was mistakenly treated), and some outcomes are self-reported survey measures with possible reporting noise/outliers.

Identification: Because treatment assignment was randomized among applicant firms, differences in follow-up outcomes between assigned treatment and control firms identify the causal ITT effect of being offered subsidized consulting, conditional on the paper’s randomization controls. The design addresses selection into consulting demand among applicants, though not external validity beyond interested firms. Remaining concerns discussed by the paper include imperfect compliance, attrition/nonresponse, and self-reporting bias in survey outcomes; the authors use administrative data and robustness checks to address some of these concerns.

Setting: In the main short-run RCT setting, assignment to receive subsidized consulting is interpreted as improving firm performance after about one year. In table 3, the treatment effect on the productivity residual is 0.270 (SE 0.141) without baseline-outcome control and 0.250 (SE 0.130) with baseline control; the treatment effect on ROA is 0.105 (SE 0.060) and 0.098 (SE 0.064), respectively. Effects on employees, sales, profits, and assets are imprecisely estimated and mostly not statistically different from zero in the main specifications. These results are central to the paper’s claim that relaxing managerial-capital constraints can raise SME productivity in the short run.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion present the randomized consulting intervention’s effects on productivity and ROA as core evidence that managerial capital matters for SME performance.
Settings.H1185: Section IV.A 'Short-Run Business Performance,' Table 3 cols. 1-6, PDF pp. 17-20 (journal pp. 652-655).
Settings.G1186:
Treatment: Indicator for being randomly assigned to the treatment group (offer of subsidized consulting), interacted with the post/follow-up period in a two-period difference-in-differences specification.

Method: For short-run survey outcomes, the paper reports a robustness analysis using a conventional difference-in-differences OLS specification on the baseline and follow-up panel. Each regression includes a treatment-group dummy, a follow-up-period dummy, and their interaction, plus stratification controls, re-randomization variables, and a survey-month dummy. The treatment effect is the coefficient on treatment × follow-up. The underlying source of exogenous variation is still randomized assignment, but the implemented estimator is a conventional DiD on two periods. The authors note these estimates are less efficient than ANCOVA given low outcome autocorrelation. Winsorized and trimmed variants are reported in the same appendix table.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized treatment assignment combined with before-after differencing. The DiD estimator compares changes from baseline to follow-up between treatment and control firms, assuming the random assignment makes the groups comparable; with only two periods, this is a standard treated-versus-control change comparison rather than a modern heterogeneous DiD design. The paper highlights that this approach is less efficient than ANCOVA in their setting.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors estimate treatment effects using a conventional difference-in-differences specification on baseline and follow-up survey data. In appendix table A5, the treatment × follow-up coefficient for the productivity residual is 0.306 (SE 0.217) in the full sample, 0.302 (SE 0.212) in the 1% winsorized sample, and 0.251 (SE 0.190) in the 1% trimmed sample; for ROA the corresponding estimates are 0.272 (SE 0.133), 0.160 (SE 0.094), and 0.062 (SE 0.065). Most other business outcomes remain imprecisely estimated. These results substantively support, but do not constitute, the paper’s main short-run causal findings.

Main role: The paper presents these DiD regressions in the appendix as robustness checks to the main ANCOVA-style RCT results, not as the primary evidence.
Settings.H1186: Appendix Table A5 'ITT Treatment Effect Estimates, Short-Run Business Outcomes, Difference-in-Difference: OLS,' PDF pp. 40-41 (journal p. 675).
Settings.G1187:
Treatment: Indicator for being in the randomized treatment-assignment group, interacted with a post-intervention period dummy (years 2010-2014) in administrative-data difference-in-differences. The causal contrast is assignment to receive the consulting offer.

Method: The paper’s main long-run employment analysis uses administrative IMSS data and a conventional difference-in-differences OLS regression at the treatment-group-by-year level. Because individual firm-level IMSS data were unavailable for confidentiality reasons, the unit of observation is the treatment-assignment group × year average, yielding 14 observations (treatment and control groups over 2 pre years and 5 post years). The regression includes a treatment-group dummy, a post-period dummy for years 2010-14, and their interaction; the interaction identifies the ITT effect of treatment assignment on post-program employment and wage-bill outcomes. This is a standard DiD design rather than a modern heterogeneous DiD estimator.

Identification: The identifying variation is the randomized assignment of applicant firms to treatment versus control, combined with pre/post administrative outcome data. The DiD regression compares how average employment and daily wage bill change from pre-intervention years (2005-06) to post-intervention years (2010-14) in treatment versus control groups. The paper argues pre-period averages were similar, helping support the comparison. Remaining limitations include analysis on only the subset of firms matched to IMSS records and the inability to use firm-level microdata; the authors provide attrition/composition checks and note that under-registration of workers in IMSS could affect levels.

Setting: Using IMSS administrative data, the paper estimates long-run ITT effects of consulting via a conventional difference-in-differences design. The treatment × post coefficient is 5.765 employees (SE 1.332) and US$125.210 in daily wage bill (SE 38.064). The authors state these correspond to a 57% increase in employees relative to an average control-group post-period level of 10.1 employees and a 72% increase in wage bill relative to an average control-group post-period daily wage bill of US$172. This long-run employment growth is a headline finding and is used to argue that consulting had persistent effects on firm scale and performance.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions emphasize the persistent long-run increase in employment and wage bill, even 5 years after the program, as a central result demonstrating lasting effects of consulting.
Settings.H1187: Section IV.B 'Long-Run Business Performance,' Table 4 and Figures 2-3, PDF pp. 22-25 (journal pp. 657-659).
Settings.G1188:
Treatment: Indicator for randomized assignment to the treatment group, i.e., offer of subsidized consulting services.

Method: The paper estimates ITT effects of randomized treatment assignment on short-run business process outcomes using follow-up cross-sectional OLS, with the same experimental design as the main RCT. Regressions include stratification controls, re-randomization variables, and a survey-month dummy; for outcomes observed at baseline, some columns additionally control for the baseline outcome. The treatment is random assignment to be offered subsidized consulting. Outcomes are mainly binary self-reports on business practices and one index combining practices. The authors note these self-reported process outcomes could be upward biased if treated firms wanted to please surveyors.

Identification: Random assignment of firms to consulting offer versus control identifies the ITT effect on reported management-process changes among applicant firms. The argument is that, absent treatment, process outcomes would differ only by chance after conditioning on the randomization controls. Remaining concerns are imperfect take-up and potential self-reporting/experimenter-demand bias in process variables, which the authors explicitly acknowledge.

Setting: In the RCT analysis of business processes, assignment to consulting is interpreted as changing management practices and organizational behavior. The overall process index rises by 0.072 standard deviations (SE 0.104), not statistically significant. Two specific practices do increase significantly: making a new marketing effort rises by 0.129 (13 percentage points; SE 0.055), and keeping formal accounts rises by 0.076 (8 percentage points; SE 0.030) without baseline control and 0.068 (SE 0.029) with baseline control. Other process outcomes are small or imprecisely estimated. These channel results are central to the paper’s claim that consulting improved managerial practices, particularly in marketing and accounting.

Main role: The abstract and introduction frame changes in management practices—especially marketing and formal accounting—as one of the paper’s three primary result sets and as evidence on channels.
Settings.H1188: Section IV.C 'Process Variables,' Table 5 cols. 1-4, PDF pp. 25-27 (journal pp. 660-663).
Settings.G1189:
Treatment: Indicator for randomized assignment to the treatment group, i.e., offer of access to subsidized consulting services.

Method: The paper estimates ITT effects of randomized assignment on entrepreneurial-spirit outcomes using cross-sectional OLS at follow-up, with the same randomized treatment-versus-control design. Regressions include stratification controls, re-randomization variables, and a survey-month dummy, and some columns additionally control for the baseline value of the entrepreneurial-spirit measure when available. Outcomes are composite indices built from survey questions about owners’ confidence, goal setting, and locus of control, plus the individual survey components.

Identification: Random treatment assignment identifies the ITT effect of the consulting offer on entrepreneurial attitudes among applicant firms, after conditioning on the randomization controls. The paper discusses that changes in these attitudes may reflect either a direct effect of consulting on mindset/goal setting or an indirect response to improved business outcomes; randomization identifies the reduced-form causal effect on the reported index but not the mechanism decomposition.

Setting: The RCT shows that assignment to consulting increased owners’ entrepreneurial spirit, measured by survey-based confidence and goal-setting indices. In table 6, the PCA entrepreneurial spirit index rises by 0.237 (SE 0.140), with a similar 0.240 (SE 0.140) when two possibly endogenous components are excluded. The KLK standardized index rises by 0.130 standard deviations (SE 0.103), positive but not statistically significant. Among components, 'I have professional goals' increases by 0.114 (SE 0.060). These results support the paper’s argument that consulting improved owners’ confidence and goal orientation, potentially helping generate longer-run growth.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly highlight an increase in entrepreneurial spirit as one of the primary sets of findings and part of the proposed mechanism behind long-run firm growth.
Settings.H1189: Section IV.D 'Entrepreneurial Spirit,' Table 6, PDF pp. 27-30 (journal pp. 663-664).
Settings.G1190:
Treatment: Indicator for randomized assignment to treatment, i.e., offer of subsidized consulting services.

Method: The paper estimates ITT effects of randomized assignment on firms’ reported responses to the 2008 economic crisis using follow-up cross-sectional OLS. These regressions include the same randomization-control set as other short-run survey analyses: stratification controls, re-randomization variables, and a survey-month dummy. Outcomes are binary indicators for specific adjustments to the crisis and a count of the number of changes made. These questions were asked only at follow-up, so no baseline control is included.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the causal ITT effect of consulting offer on reported coping responses to the crisis among applicant firms. The paper’s interpretation is that consulting may have improved firms’ ability to weather shocks. Since these outcomes are self-reported and measured only at follow-up, identification rests on randomization rather than on pre/post comparisons.

Setting: The paper uses the RCT to test whether consulting changed how firms responded to the 2008 economic crisis. In table 7, treated firms are 0.080 less likely to report cutting production in response to the crisis (SE 0.040), relative to a control-group mean of 0.206. Other crisis-response outcomes are not statistically different between groups, though the estimate for seeking government assistance is positive at 0.056 (SE 0.044). This is presented as suggestive evidence that consulting improved firms’ resilience to adverse shocks.

Main role: The crisis-response analysis is a secondary mechanism/result, not one of the headline core outcomes in the abstract.
Settings.H1190: Section IV.E 'Response to Economic Shocks,' Table 7, PDF pp. 31-32 (journal pp. 665-666).
Settings.G1191:
Treatment: Assigned monetary piece-rate incentive for own earnings in the MTurk task. Main contrasts are no piece rate vs 1 cent per 100 points vs 10 cents per 100 points; also a 4 cent per 100 points treatment used as an additional incentive arm. Treatment is assignment to a discrete piece-rate arm, not actual earnings. Units are cents per 100 points.

Method: Between-subject randomized real-effort experiment on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Subjects were randomly assigned to one of the benchmark piece-rate arms differing only in the incentive paragraph: no piece rate, 1 cent per 100 points, 10 cents per 100 points, and an out-of-sample 4 cent per 100 points arm. The authors interpret mean differences in points completed over a 10-minute button-pressing task as causal effects of monetary incentives on effort. Estimation is by treatment-arm mean comparisons; they also fit a structural costly-effort model to the three benchmark arms and compare its prediction to the 4-cent arm. Sample restrictions exclude noncompleters, likely bots, restarts, and some technical failures; remaining concern is external validity, not internal validity, because assignment is randomized.

Identification: Identification comes from random assignment of participants to piece-rate treatment arms in a between-subject experiment. Because treatment wording is the only designed difference across arms, differences in mean output identify the ITT effect of assigned incentive levels on effort under standard randomization assumptions and minimal interference. The authors use the benchmark arms to estimate nuisance parameters of a structural costly-effort model and assess whether observed effort responds monotonically to incentives.

Setting: In the benchmark randomized experiment, higher assigned private piece rates causally increase effort in the 10-minute task. Average performance rises from 1,521 points with no piece rate to 2,029 with a 1-cent piece rate and 2,175 with a 10-cent piece rate; the 4-cent arm yields 2,132 points. The authors interpret these arm differences as evidence that monetary incentives strongly and monotonically motivate effort, and they use the three benchmark arms to estimate a structural cost-of-effort function that predicts the 4-cent arm closely. This benchmark result is central to the paper’s comparison of behavioural treatments and expert forecasts.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize the causal effect of monetary incentives on effort as a central finding and as the benchmark used to interpret all other treatments and expert forecasts.
Settings.H1191: Section 4.1.1 “Piece rate treatments,” Table 3 columns (3)-(4), Figure 3, and discussion around Figure 2a; PDF pp. 1044-1049 (pages 16-21 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1192:
Treatment: Assignment to a very low private piece rate: 1 cent for every 1,000 points scored, versus benchmark no piece rate and other piece-rate arms. This is a discrete assigned incentive condition.

Method: Between-subject randomized MTurk experiment comparing a very-low-pay arm ('1 cent for every 1,000 points') to the no-piece-rate benchmark and to the structural prediction from the benchmark piece-rate arms. The implemented causal evidence is the randomized arm difference in mean points; the structural model is used to interpret whether there is motivational crowd-out relative to a no-crowd-out counterfactual. Internal validity rests on random assignment; the crowd-out interpretation additionally relies on the costly-effort model estimated from benchmark arms.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the ITT effect of offering a very low piece rate on output relative to other arms. To interpret this as 'no crowd-out,' the authors compare observed effort in the low-pay arm to a counterfactual effort predicted by a structural model fit on the benchmark incentive arms under the assumption of no shift in intrinsic motivation. Thus the causal experiment identifies the arm effect directly, while the crowd-out claim adds model-based interpretation.

Setting: The randomized very-low-pay treatment causes effort to rise relative to no piece rate rather than fall. Mean output is 1,883 points in the 1-cent-per-1,000-points arm versus 1,521 in the no-pay arm, and it is almost identical to the model-predicted 1,893 points under no crowd-out. The authors therefore conclude that, in this setting, a very low monetary incentive does not crowd out motivation. This is one of the paper’s headline contrasts with expert forecasts and part of its central contribution.

Main role: The absence of crowd-out from very low pay is highlighted in the abstract, introduction, expert-forecast discussion, and conclusion as a major substantive finding.
Settings.H1192: Section 4.1.2 “Pay enough or don’t pay at all,” Table 3, Figure 2b, Figure 3; PDF pp. 1047-1049 (pages 19-21 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1193:
Treatment: Assignment to charity-linked incentives where the Red Cross charitable fund, not the worker, receives either 1 cent or 10 cents for every 100 points scored. Treatment is discrete assignment to a charity-return arm.

Method: Between-subject randomized experiment with two charity piece-rate arms: Red Cross receives 1 cent per 100 points or 10 cents per 100 points. The authors compare these arms to no piece rate and to private piece-rate arms, and structurally interpret responses using warm-glow and pure-altruism models. The implemented estimator is treatment-arm mean comparison; the structural parameter interpretation is secondary and model-based.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the causal effect of charity-linked incentive arms on effort. Comparing charity arms to no-pay and private-pay arms identifies whether charitable incentives motivate effort and whether they are weaker than private incentives. Comparing the 10-cent and 1-cent charity arms identifies whether raising the return to charity further changes effort. The warm-glow versus pure-altruism interpretation additionally relies on the structural social-preference model.

Setting: Randomized charity incentives increase effort relative to no private incentives, but increasing the return to charity from 1 cent to 10 cents per 100 points does not materially increase effort. Mean output is 1,907 in the 1-cent charity arm and 1,918 in the 10-cent charity arm, both above the 1,521 no-pay benchmark but below comparable private piece-rate arms. The authors interpret this as evidence that charitable giving motivates workers, yet the motivating effect is largely independent of the return to the charity, favoring a warm-glow interpretation over pure altruism. This is a central behavioural result and an important point of disagreement with expert forecasts.

Main role: Charitable-giving treatments are central to the paper’s evidence on social preferences and to the comparison between MTurker behavior and expert beliefs about altruism versus warm glow.
Settings.H1193: Section 4.1.3 “Social preferences,” Table 3, Figure 3, and structural discussion in Section 7.3/Table 5 Panel B; PDF pp. 1048-1049 and 1061-1064 (pages 20-21 and 33-36 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1194:
Treatment: Assignment to an unconditional 40-cent bonus ('gift exchange') with no performance-contingent pay. This is a discrete treatment arm versus no piece rate and other arms.

Method: Between-subject randomized experiment with a gift-exchange arm: subjects receive an unconditional 40-cent bonus and no piece rate. The causal estimate is the mean difference in output relative to the no-piece-rate benchmark and other no-private-incentive arms. The authors interpret this as a reciprocity/gift-exchange effect. Estimation is by randomized arm means; structural motivation-shift interpretation is supplementary.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the causal ITT effect of receiving an unconditional monetary gift on task effort. The reciprocity interpretation assumes the higher effort relative to the no-pay baseline arises from reciprocal motivation rather than other channels, but internal validity of the arm contrast is experimental.

Setting: The unconditional 40-cent gift-exchange treatment modestly raises effort relative to the no-piece-rate arm, but by much less than experts anticipated. Mean output is 1,602 points in the gift-exchange arm versus 1,521 with no piece rate. The authors interpret this as some evidence of reciprocal gift exchange, though quantitatively small. This result contributes to the paper’s central assessment of behavioural motivators and expert beliefs.

Main role: The paper highlights gift exchange as part of its social-preference findings, noting some but quantitatively small reciprocal response compared with experts' stronger expectations.
Settings.H1194: Section 4.1.3 “Social preferences,” Table 3, Figure 3, and Section 7.3/Table 5 Panel B; PDF pp. 1048-1049 and 1061-1064 (pages 20-21 and 33-36 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1195:
Treatment: Assignment to a 1-cent-per-100-points private piece rate paid after either 2 weeks or 4 weeks, rather than near-immediately. Treatment is a discrete timing-of-payment arm.

Method: Between-subject randomized experiment with delayed-payment piece-rate arms. Subjects receive the same 1 cent per 100 points piece rate as in the benchmark, but payment is delayed by 2 or 4 weeks instead of within 24 hours. Causal evidence is from treatment-arm mean comparisons; the authors also map these means into beta-delta discounting parameters using a structural model.

Identification: Random assignment across payment-delay arms identifies the causal effect of delaying otherwise identical performance pay on effort. Comparison to the immediate-pay benchmark identifies the effect of delay length. The beta-delta interpretation requires the structural mapping from observed effort to discounted incentive value; experimentally, the arm contrasts are internally valid.

Setting: Randomized delays in receiving performance pay reduce effort somewhat relative to immediate pay, but the pattern does not show strong present bias. Mean output is 2,004 points with a 2-week delay and 1,970 with a 4-week delay, compared with 2,029 in the immediate 1-cent benchmark. The authors conclude that delayed payout induces less effort than immediate pay, as expected, but the decline looks closer to exponential than hyperbolic discounting. This is a central behavioural-treatment result, though the structural parameter estimates are noisy.

Main role: The paper’s abstract and introduction emphasize that delayed payments reduce effort but the pattern is more consistent with exponential discounting than with strong present bias.
Settings.H1195: Section 4.1.4 “Time preferences,” Table 3, Figure 3, and Section 7.4/Table 5 Panel B; PDF pp. 1048-1049 and 1064 (pages 20-21 and 36 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1196:
Treatment: Assigned framing and size of threshold-contingent bonus: (i) gain of 40 cents if score at least 2,000 points, (ii) loss framing of a 40-cent bonus unless score at least 2,000 points, or (iii) gain of 80 cents if score at least 2,000 points. Treatment is discrete assigned contract/frame.

Method: Between-subject randomized experiment with threshold bonus treatments designed to test loss aversion: 40-cent gain frame, 40-cent loss frame, and 80-cent gain frame, all contingent on reaching 2,000 points. Causal evidence comes from mean comparisons and distributional shifts around the threshold; the authors use a local approximation to infer a loss-aversion parameter from the three arms. The implemented design is direct treatment assignment, not IV.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the causal effect of bonus framing and size on effort under standard experimental assumptions. Comparing the 40-cent loss and 40-cent gain arms isolates the effect of framing holding expected payoffs fixed; comparing the 80-cent gain and 40-cent gain arms benchmarks the magnitude. The interpretation as loss aversion relies on prospect-theory style framing assumptions and the authors’ local approximation for mapping differences into λ.

Setting: Threshold bonuses causally raise effort substantially, and loss framing yields somewhat higher effort than an equivalent gain frame, though the difference is not statistically significant. Mean output is 2,136 in the 40-cent gain arm, 2,155 in the 40-cent loss arm, and 2,188 in the 80-cent gain arm. The authors interpret the ordering as suggestive of loss aversion, with the 40-cent loss arm roughly halfway between the two gain arms, but the evidence is imprecise. This is a substantive central behavioural analysis.

Main role: Reference dependence and loss aversion are highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as key behavioural mechanisms tested by the experiment.
Settings.H1196: Section 4.1.5 “Reference dependence,” Section 4.2.1 on distributions, Figure 3, Figure 4c, Table 3, and Section 7.6/Table 6 Panel B; PDF pp. 1049-1051 and 1065-1066 (pages 21-23 and 37-38 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1197:
Treatment: Assignment to probabilistic private piece-rate incentives: either a 1% chance of receiving $1 per 100 points, or a 50% chance of receiving 2 cents per 100 points. Treatment is assignment to discrete probabilistic incentive schemes.

Method: Between-subject randomized experiment with probabilistic incentive arms having the same expected value as the deterministic 1-cent benchmark: 1% chance of $1 per 100 points and 50% chance of 2 cents per 100 points. Causal evidence is from arm mean comparisons; the authors structurally interpret these contrasts in terms of probability weighting and utility curvature.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the causal effect of different probabilistic compensation schemes on effort. Comparing each probabilistic arm to the deterministic 1-cent expected-value-equivalent benchmark reveals whether uncertainty and small-probability framing change behavior. The probability-weighting interpretation depends on the prospect-theory mapping from observed effort to transformed probabilities and on assumptions about utility curvature.

Setting: Probabilistic incentives with the same expected value as a deterministic 1-cent piece rate cause lower effort, especially when the reward is concentrated in a 1% chance of a large payoff. Mean output is 1,896 in the 1% chance of $1 arm and 1,977 in the 50% chance of 2 cents arm, versus 2,029 in the deterministic 1-cent benchmark. The authors conclude that the data do not support overweighting of small probabilities; if anything, the 1% treatment underperforms. This is a central test of prospect-theory style probability weighting.

Main role: The paper explicitly highlights probability weighting as a core prospect-theory component and concludes that the data do not support overweighting of small probabilities.
Settings.H1197: Section 4.1.5 “Reference dependence,” Table 3, Figure 3, and Section 7.5/Table 6 Panel A; PDF pp. 1049 and 1064-1065 (pages 21 and 36-37 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1198:
Treatment: Assignment to one of three non-monetary motivational messages with no private performance pay: (i) social comparison message that many previous participants scored more than 2,000 points, (ii) promise to show ranking relative to other participants, or (iii) task-significance message asking participants to do their very best because the researchers care about how fast people press digits.

Method: Between-subject randomized experiment with three non-monetary psychology-based treatments: a Cialdini-style social comparison message, a ranking/relative-performance information treatment, and a task-significance encouragement treatment. Estimation is by treatment-arm mean comparisons against the no-piece-rate benchmark and among no-private-incentive treatments. The treatments differ only in the motivational wording shown to subjects.

Identification: Random assignment identifies the ITT effect of each motivational message on effort relative to the no-piece-rate benchmark. Because no monetary incentives differ across these arms, differences are attributed to the non-monetary framing or social comparison content under standard experimental assumptions. External validity remains context-specific, but internal validity is experimental.

Setting: Psychology-based non-monetary messages causally increase effort relative to no piece rate, but less than monetary incentives. Mean output is 1,848 for the social-comparison message, 1,761 for the ranking treatment, and 1,740 for the task-significance treatment, compared with 1,521 in the no-pay benchmark. The authors summarize these as roughly 15-21% improvements over no pay, with the Cialdini-type comparison the most effective. These treatments support a central conclusion that psychological motivators work, but are weaker than even small monetary incentives in this setting.

Main role: The effectiveness of non-monetary psychological motivators relative to monetary incentives is one of the paper’s headline findings in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H1198: Section 4.1.6 “Psychology-based treatments,” Table 3 and Figure 3; PDF pp. 1049-1050 (pages 21-22 of the supplied PDF).
Settings.G1199:
Treatment: Randomized graphical-representation assignment in phase 1: participants are assigned to one of four combinations of RD-graph parameters crossing bin width (large/IMSE-optimal versus small/MV) with y-axis scaling (normal/Stata default versus large/doubled vertical range). The focal treatment is thus graph construction method, not an economic exposure. This is a multi-arm discrete treatment rather than a single binary indicator.

Method: The paper’s first main design is a set of randomized survey/lab experiments in which nonexpert participants are randomly assigned to view regression-discontinuity graphs constructed with different graphical parameters. Outcomes are participants’ classifications of whether a graph has a discontinuity. The implemented estimates are differences across randomized treatment arms in classification rates, summarized via empirical power functions and, for treatment-effect estimates, regressions of participant responses on treatment indicators with stratum fixed effects, where strata are defined by the 11 DGPs for each discontinuity magnitude. In phase 1 the manipulated factors are bin width (IMSE-optimal ‘large’ bins versus MV ‘small’ bins) and y-axis scaling (Stata default versus doubled range). Identification is by random assignment of participants to graph-treatment arms; remaining concerns are external validity and dependence on the chosen DGPs, not internal validity.

Identification: Because participants are randomly assigned to graphical treatment arms, differences in discontinuity-detection rates across arms identify causal effects of graph-construction choices on visual inference. The design uses simulated graphs from 11 calibrated DGPs and randomizes graph assignments/order. Assumption is standard random assignment of participants to treatment arms and comparable graph sets within strata; causal interpretation pertains to effects of graphical parameters on viewers’ perceptions, with external-validity limits to these DGPs and participant pools.

Setting: In phase 1, the authors causally test whether RD graph construction affects visual inference by randomizing nonexpert participants across four graphing methods that vary bin width and y-axis scaling. Using regressions of binary discontinuity classifications on treatment indicators with stratum fixed effects, they find that large IMSE-optimal bins substantially raise false-positive rates relative to small MV bins, while axis scaling has little effect. The paper summarizes this as both small-bin treatments yielding type I error rates of about 5%, versus roughly 20%–25% for large bins, with large bins also lowering type II error at small discontinuities. This randomized evidence is central to the paper’s recommendation to use small bins as a default.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state that the paper’s first major component is to assess the effects of different graphical representation methods using randomized experiments, and the conclusion highlights the recommendation arising from these experiments.
Settings.H1199: Section III.C and Section IV.A; Table I (phase 1) and Figure V, Phase 1 panel; discussion on PDF pp. 1995, 1999–2000.
Settings.G1200:
Treatment: Randomized graphical assignment in phase 2: one of four combinations crossing bin width (large IMSE-optimal versus small MV) with bin spacing (evenly spaced versus quantile spaced). This is a discrete multi-arm graph-design treatment.

Method: The second randomized experimental setting is phase 2 of the nonexpert experiments. Participants are randomly assigned to view graphs that vary the RD-plot bin width and bin spacing. The implemented estimator is a regression of the participant’s binary discontinuity classification on treatment indicators and stratum fixed effects, where strata are defined by DGP and discontinuity magnitude, and results are visualized as empirical power functions by treatment arm. The design isolates the causal effect of evenly spaced versus quantile-spaced bins, alongside replication of the large-versus-small bin-width comparison under a different sample and holding other graph features fixed.

Identification: Random assignment of participants to graph-design arms identifies the causal effects of bin spacing and bin width on visual discontinuity judgments. The identification argument is purely experimental: treatment arms differ only in graph construction, with other features held fixed and graph sets randomized within the experiment. Remaining limitations concern representativeness of the DGPs and participant population.

Setting: In phase 2, the authors experimentally vary both bin width and bin spacing in RD graphs shown to nonexperts. Randomized comparisons show that the earlier bin-width result is robust—large bins again generate higher false-positive rates than small bins—while evenly spaced and quantile-spaced bins perform very similarly. The paper therefore concludes that bin spacing has a small or null causal effect on visual inference for the tested DGPs, whereas bin width materially affects discontinuity detection. This evidence supports the broader recommendation that practitioners need not be overly concerned about spacing choice but should care about bin width.

Main role: This phase contributes directly to the paper’s main conclusion that bin spacing matters little while small bins perform better on type I error. The conclusion explicitly mentions bin spacing as having little effect.
Settings.H1200: Section III.C and Section IV.A; Table I (phase 2) and Figure V, Phase 2 panel; discussion on PDF pp. 1995, 2000–2001.
Settings.G1201:
Treatment: Randomized graph-format assignment in phase 3 among three discrete arms: (i) no fit line with vertical line, (ii) no fit line and no vertical line, and (iii) fit line with vertical line. The treatment is graph representation choice; multi-arm and nonbinary overall.

Method: The third randomized experimental setting is phase 3 of the nonexpert experiments. Participants are randomly assigned to graphs differing in whether they include parametric fit lines and/or a vertical line at the treatment threshold, while bin width, spacing, and axis scaling are held fixed. The authors estimate treatment effects using regressions of the participant’s binary discontinuity classification on treatment indicators with stratum fixed effects and also compare empirical power functions across arms. This is a direct randomized ITT design for graph features affecting visual inference.

Identification: Random assignment of participants to graph versions identifies causal effects of fit lines and the vertical cutoff line on visual discontinuity classification. The identification assumption is that assignment is random and the only systematic differences across arms are the manipulated graph features. Internal validity is experimental; external validity is limited to studied DGPs and viewer populations.

Setting: In phase 3, nonexperts are randomly assigned to RD graphs that differ in the presence of fit lines and of a vertical cutoff line. The authors find little effect of the vertical line on classification behavior but find that adding fit lines raises type I error in this phase, matching concerns that fit lines can visually suggest discontinuities. This randomized evidence is one of the paper’s key reasons for recommending no fit lines as a default starting point when drawing RD graphs.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize the importance of fit lines; this phase is the main randomized evidence on fit lines and the vertical threshold line.
Settings.H1201: Section III.C and Section IV.A; Table I (phase 3) and Figure V, Phase 3 panel; discussion on PDF pp. 1995, 2001.
Settings.G1202:
Treatment: Randomized assignment to one of four graph-construction treatments crossing bin width (small MV versus large IMSE-optimal bins) and fit-line presence (no versus yes). Discrete multi-arm treatment.

Method: The fourth randomized experimental setting is phase 4 of the nonexpert experiments, which directly crosses the two graph features the earlier phases suggested were most important: bin width and fit lines. Participants are randomly assigned to one of four graphing methods (small/large bins × fit line/no fit line), with other graph parameters held fixed. The authors estimate arm effects via regressions of binary discontinuity classifications on treatment indicators and stratum fixed effects and present the resulting power functions. This is the direct randomized comparison underlying the paper’s preferred-method recommendation and expert-prediction evaluation.

Identification: Random assignment to the four graph-design cells identifies the causal effects of bin width and fit lines, jointly, on visual detection of discontinuities. The design relies on randomized assignment and controlled graph generation. Assumptions concern valid randomization and stable presentation; external validity remains limited to the selected DGPs and sample of viewers.

Setting: Phase 4 randomizes nonexperts across the four combinations of bin width and fit lines, the two graphing choices the prior phases identified as most consequential. The results reaffirm the bin-width finding—small bins again have much lower false-positive rates than large bins—while the fit-line effect is more muted and less stable than in phase 3. Based on this direct randomized comparison and related decision criteria, the authors recommend graphs with small bins and no fit lines as a sensible default for RD practice.

Main role: This phase directly underpins the main recommendation and is used for the expert-prediction exercise. The conclusion emphasizes small bins and no fit lines based on the experiments.
Settings.H1202: Section III.C and Section IV.A; Table I (phase 4) and Figure V, Phase 4 panel; discussion on PDF pp. 1995, 2001–2002.
Settings.G1203:
Treatment: Randomized assignment in supplemental phase 5 to one of four DGP-specification treatments crossing global quintic versus local linear conditional expectation specification with homoskedastic versus heteroskedastic error structure. This is a multi-arm discrete treatment affecting the graph-generating process shown to participants.

Method: A supplemental randomized experimental setting tests whether the visual-inference results are sensitive to the way the authors specify the underlying data-generating processes used to simulate graphs. Participants are randomly assigned to graph sets generated under four combinations crossing global-quintic versus local-linear CEF specification and homoskedastic versus heteroskedastic error structure, while graphing parameters are held at the recommended method. The design is again a direct randomized ITT comparison on participants’ discontinuity classifications, though the article refers readers to the online appendix for details and reports the result qualitatively as robustness.

Identification: Random assignment of participants to alternative graph-generating-process specification arms identifies the causal effect of those underlying graph-simulation choices on measured visual-inference performance. The internal-validity argument is standard randomization; the purpose is robustness, not the main research question.

Setting: In a supplemental experimental phase, the authors randomize nonexperts to graphs generated from alternative DGP specifications—global quintic versus local linear CEFs and homoskedastic versus heteroskedastic errors—to test robustness of their visual-inference findings. They report that the results are remarkably robust to these alternatives, supporting the conclusion that the recommendation for small bins and no fit lines is not an artifact of the original DGP-specification choices. No main-text numerical treatment effects are reported here.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis rather than a core headline result, included to show sensitivity to alternative DGP specifications.
Settings.H1203: Table I (supplemental phase 5) and discussion in Section III.B / IV.A referring to Online Appendix C; PDF pp. 1996, 1994, 2002.
Settings.G1204:
Treatment: True discontinuity magnitude d embedded in the simulated data-generating process, measured as a continuous dose taking values 0, ±0.1944σ, ±0.324σ, ±0.54σ, ±0.9σ, and ±1.5σ; operationally, the right arm of the conditional expectation function is shifted vertically by d·1[X≥0]. The causal estimand is the effect of a discontinuity in the running-variable threshold relationship on the econometric test’s rejection outcome.

Method: The paper’s second major component compares visual inference with formal econometric inference procedures by applying several RD estimators/tests to the same simulated microdata underlying the expert graphs. One reported setting is the ‘correctly specified’ global piecewise quintic regression with homoskedastic standard errors, used to test for a discontinuity at the threshold. This is a linear regression adjustment rather than a local-RD design in the paper’s own classification scheme here because it is implemented as a global parametric regression model on simulated data, and the object of interest is the rejection probability/power function. The authors compare its rejection decisions to expert visual classifications over the same datasets.

Identification: Identification here comes from controlled Monte Carlo variation in the true discontinuity magnitude d within the simulated DGPs. Because the data-generating process is specified by the authors, shifts in d causally change the presence and size of the discontinuity, and the outcome is the regression-based test’s rejection indicator. The main assumption is that the simulation environment and parametric model correspond to the benchmark they seek to study; concerns are about generalizability beyond the calibrated DGPs.

Setting: As a benchmark in the visual-versus-econometric comparison, the authors apply a correctly specified global piecewise quintic regression with homoskedastic errors to the same simulated datasets shown to experts. Increasing the true discontinuity magnitude d raises the probability that this econometric procedure rejects no discontinuity; relative to experts, its type I error is 0.068 versus 0.079 for experts, while its type II error at |d|=0.324σ is 0.395 versus 0.537 for experts and its average type II error is 0.260 versus 0.336. Thus, this benchmark regression slightly improves detection while maintaining a similar false-positive rate.

Main role: The abstract and introduction say the second major component compares visual and econometric inference; the piecewise-quintic benchmark is part of this substantive comparison, though less central than IK/CCT/AK.
Settings.H1204: Section IV.C, Figure VIII, Table II; PDF pp. 2005–2007.
Settings.G1205:
Treatment: True discontinuity magnitude d in the simulated RD data-generating process, a continuous shift at the cutoff measured in multiples of the DGP-specific error SD σ (0, ±0.1944σ, ±0.324σ, ±0.54σ, ±0.9σ, ±1.5σ).

Method: The paper compares visual inference to the conventional Imbens-Kalyanaraman RD procedure: a local linear sharp RD estimator using the IK MSE-optimal bandwidth, with conventional inference that ignores asymptotic bias. Applied to the same simulated microdata as the expert graphs, the outcome is whether the 5% test rejects the null of no discontinuity.
