Although used here as a performance-comparison object rather than to estimate an empirical policy effect, this is an implemented sharp-RD inference procedure on linear outcome models. The authors emphasize that the method enjoys lower type II error but substantially inflated type I error.

Identification: The simulation directly manipulates the true discontinuity size d at the cutoff, so causal effects of d on the RD test’s rejection probability are identified by construction. The econometric design itself is a sharp RD local-linear estimator exploiting the discontinuity at the running-variable threshold. The main issue discussed is that conventional IK inference ignores asymptotic bias, producing excess type I error.

Setting: Using the same simulated datasets shown to experts, the authors apply the conventional IK sharp-RD procedure—local linear estimation with the IK bandwidth and conventional 5% inference—to ask how often it detects a true discontinuity. The procedure is much more aggressive than visual inference: its type I error rate is 0.226 versus 0.079 for experts, but its type II error at |d|=0.324σ is only 0.216 versus 0.537, and its average type II error is 0.145 versus 0.336. The authors interpret this as a type I/type II trade-off driven by bias-ignorant conventional RD inference.

Main role: Comparing visual inference to IK is central to the paper’s second major component and to its conclusion that visual inference has lower type I error than common 5% econometric RD procedures.
Settings.H1205: Section IV.C, Figure VIII, Table II; PDF pp. 2005–2007.
Settings.G1206:
Treatment: True discontinuity magnitude d in the simulated RD design, a continuous treatment intensity at the cutoff measured as multiples of the DGP-specific σ.

Method: Another econometric-inference setting compares visual inference to the Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik robust bias-corrected sharp RD procedure, implemented through rdrobust. This uses local linear RD estimation, estimates and corrects asymptotic bias, and adjusts confidence intervals for bias-estimation uncertainty. Applied to the same simulated microdata, the outcome is whether the 5% test rejects no discontinuity. The authors report both power functions and error rates relative to experts.

Identification: The true discontinuity is manipulated in simulation, which identifies its effect on rejection probabilities. The implemented econometric estimator is a sharp RD local-linear design with robust bias-corrected inference. The paper’s discussion highlights that remaining differences in type I error may partly reflect small-sample performance on the specific 88 datasets used for comparison.

Setting: The authors compare expert visual inference with the CCT robust bias-corrected sharp-RD procedure applied to identical simulated datasets. CCT still rejects too often relative to nominal 5% in this sample—type I error 0.132 versus 0.079 for experts, though the difference is not statistically significant—but has materially lower type II error: 0.342 versus 0.537 at |d|=0.324σ and 0.219 versus 0.336 on average across nonzero discontinuities. The paper concludes that CCT offers better detection power than visual inference but at somewhat higher false-positive rates in these simulations.

Main role: This is one of the headline econometric methods named in the abstract, introduction, results, and conclusion when comparing visual and econometric inference.
Settings.H1206: Section IV.C, Figure VIII, Table II; PDF pp. 2005–2007.
Settings.G1207:
Treatment: True discontinuity magnitude d embedded in the simulated RD data-generating process, continuously varying in multiples of σ.

Method: A further econometric-inference setting uses the Armstrong-Kolesár RDHonest procedure, which constructs honest, minimax-optimal confidence intervals for a local linear sharp RD estimator under a bound on the second derivative of the conditional expectation function. The authors implement the default rule-of-thumb tuning parameter in RDHonest on the same simulated microdata used in the expert study. The outcome is whether the null of no discontinuity is rejected, summarized as power functions and error rates relative to visual inference.

Identification: Within the simulation, the true discontinuity level d is exogenously set, so its effect on rejection probabilities is identified by construction. The implemented econometric design is a sharp RD local-linear estimator with honest inference robust over a Taylor/Hölder-type class via a second-derivative bound. The substantive interpretation hinges on the theoretical coverage guarantee of AK, unlike visual inference.

Setting: Applying the AK RDHonest sharp-RD procedure to the same datasets used for expert visual inference, the authors find performance very close to that of human visual inference on recommended graphs. AK’s type I error is 0.058 versus 0.079 for experts, its type II error at |d|=0.324σ is 0.500 versus 0.537, and its average type II error is 0.321 versus 0.336; none of these differences is statistically significant in Table II. The paper highlights this close match as striking because AK has minimax optimality and honest coverage guarantees while visual inference does not.

Main role: The paper repeatedly emphasizes the close similarity between visual inference and AK, calling it remarkable given AK’s minimax optimality; this is a central substantive result.
Settings.H1207: Section IV.C, Figure VIII, Table II; PDF pp. 2005–2008.
Settings.G1208:
Treatment: True discontinuity magnitude d in the simulated RD DGP, continuously varying in multiples of σ. The separately reported procedure also changes the inferential rule by using adjusted critical t-values (2.46 for IK and 2.28 for CCT) chosen to equate type I error with visual inference in this sample.

Method: The authors also study adjusted versions of the IK and CCT sharp RD procedures where the critical value is increased so that the procedure’s type I error rate matches that of expert visual inference on the tested sample. This remains a sharp RD setting because the underlying estimators are still IK and CCT local-linear RD procedures; the separately reported estimand/performance object is the rejection behavior under alternative, type-I-error-equalized critical values. The paper presents new power functions for these adjusted procedures and compares them with visual inference.

Identification: The same simulation-based identification applies: d is exogenously manipulated, and the outcome is the RD procedure’s rejection decision. The additional adjustment changes only the decision threshold, allowing the authors to isolate how much of the visual-versus-econometric comparison is driven by different type I error rates rather than underlying power. The caveat is that the adjusted critical values are sample-specific and lack the broad coverage guarantee of AK.

Setting: To compare visual inference with econometric methods at the same false-positive rate, the authors raise the critical values of the IK and CCT sharp-RD procedures until each matches visual inference’s type I error in this sample. Even after this adjustment, both procedures’ type II error rates rise only modestly—by about 5 to 10 percentage points according to the text—and remain significantly below those of visual inference at moderate discontinuities. The authors caution that this result is specific to the 11 tested DGPs and does not imply valid general coverage like AK’s honest procedure.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness/interpretive extension within the second major component, not the core baseline comparison.
Settings.H1208: Section IV.C, Figure VIII right panel; PDF pp. 2008–2009.
Settings.G1209:
Treatment: True discontinuity magnitude d in the simulated RD DGP, continuously varying in multiples of σ. The decision rule additionally combines two signals—expert visual classification and econometric rejection—via an AND rule.

Method: The paper reports a combined visual-and-econometric inference rule: infer a discontinuity if and only if both expert visual inference and a given econometric procedure reject no discontinuity. This is not a standard linear estimator category, so it falls under Other. The implemented combinations are experts with the correctly specified piecewise quintic benchmark, with IK, with CCT robust, and with AK. The outcome is the combined procedure’s rejection indicator and corresponding power function on the same simulated datasets. This is presented as an analysis of complementarity between human visual and formal econometric inference.

Identification: The true discontinuity magnitude is experimentally fixed in the simulated DGPs, so its effect on the combined rejection probability is identified by construction. The combined rule exploits potentially nonoverlapping error patterns between visual and econometric procedures. The authors motivate this by examining the joint distribution of tests and showing weak association in type I errors but stronger association in type II errors.

Setting: The authors construct a combined inference procedure that declares a discontinuity only when both expert visual inference and a formal econometric test agree. This lowers type I error because visual and econometric false positives are not strongly associated when the true discontinuity is zero, while keeping type II error from rising too much because the methods’ misses are more positively associated when a discontinuity exists. In particular, the combined IK-and-visual rule has a type I error rate of 2.6% and a power function close to AK’s, leading the authors to argue that visual and econometric inference are complementary and that such informal combination may help explain RD’s credibility in practice.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, results, and conclusion explicitly emphasize complementarity of visual and econometric inference; the combined-inference exercise is one of the paper’s headline findings.
Settings.H1209: Section IV.C.1, Table III, Figure IX; PDF pp. 2009–2012.
Settings.G1210:
Treatment: Receipt of reperfusion therapy within 12 hours of admission for acute myocardial infarction (AMI), defined as receiving thrombolytics/fibrinolytics or angioplasty within 12 hours. In the mid-1990s sample, over 90% of reperfused patients received thrombolytics. Implemented as an indicator for actual treatment receipt.

Method: The paper’s first substantive causal setting is a hierarchical/random-coefficient logit framework used to estimate how reperfusion therapy within 12 hours affects survival, allowing the treatment effect to vary across hospitals and patients. The treatment equation is a random-effect logit of reperfusion on rich chart-based patient covariates plus a hospital random intercept; the survival equation is a random-coefficient logit of 30-day survival on reperfusion, patient covariates, and hospital random intercept/random slope. The authors interpret the reperfusion coefficient as a treatment-on-the-treated causal effect under a selection-on-gains framework: conditional on rich clinical controls, treatment is assumed uncorrelated with unobserved baseline survival factors but may be correlated with unobserved gains from treatment. This is not a standard linear OLS/FE/DiD/IV design and is therefore classified as Other.

Identification: The identifying argument is that the rich CCP chart covariates sufficiently absorb confounding in baseline mortality, allowing the survival logit to recover treatment-on-the-treated effects of reperfusion while permitting selection on gains. Hospital-level and patient-level heterogeneity in treatment rates are estimated from the treatment logit; hospital-level heterogeneity in treatment effects comes from the survival random-coefficient logit. The authors argue credibility by comparing average logit treatment effects with randomized trial evidence and by showing robustness to increasingly rich controls.

Setting: Using CCP chart data on elderly AMI patients, the authors estimate a random-coefficient logit model for 30-day survival and interpret the reperfusion coefficient as the causal benefit of reperfusion conditional on rich clinical controls. Figure I shows substantial hospital-level variation in estimated treatment effects and that aggressive hospitals are more likely to treat low-propensity patients for whom reperfusion is estimated to harm survival. This setting is foundational for the paper’s main claim that variation in treatment rates cannot be interpreted purely as warranted comparative advantage and may reflect allocative inefficiency.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusions emphasize that the paper’s core contribution is to estimate treatment effects and show that aggressive hospitals treat patients with negative treatment effects, motivating allocative inefficiency. The motivating facts from Figure I are central to the paper’s main argument.
Settings.H1210: Section II.C, Figure I Panels A–C, PDF pp. 10–13; supporting discussion in Section IV.B.3, PDF pp. 38–40.
Settings.G1211:
Treatment: Indicator for receiving reperfusion therapy within 12 hours of AMI admission.

Method: The authors estimate local-logistic and local-linear versions of their treatment-on-the-treated equation to examine how reperfusion affects survival as a function of the propensity to receive treatment and hospital aggressiveness. Specifically, they nonparametrically estimate the effect of reperfusion on 30-day survival against the propensity index separately for hospitals in the lowest and highest terciles of hospital treatment intensity, and also against the hospital treatment-rate effect controlling nonparametrically for propensity. This is a semiparametric causal heterogeneity design motivated by their Roy model, not a standard linear estimator.

Identification: The strategy is to use the estimated propensity index from the treatment model as a sufficient index for expected treatment benefit under the Roy model. Conditional on this propensity, differences in treatment effects across hospitals are interpreted as differences in hospital thresholds/allocative inefficiency rather than comparative advantage. Low-propensity patients identify overuse because treatment effects for the lowest-propensity treated patients approach the hospital threshold. Credibility still rests on the same rich-controls assumption underlying treatment-on-the-treated estimation.

Setting: The nonparametric graphical analysis shows that reperfusion’s survival benefit rises with a patient’s propensity to be treated, but conditional on a given propensity the benefit is lower in more aggressive hospitals. For the lowest-propensity patients, estimated survival effects are significantly negative in high-treatment hospitals and near zero in low-treatment hospitals, which the authors interpret as causal evidence of overuse and allocative inefficiency. These plots visually anchor the paper’s central conclusion that many hospitals treat patients who are harmed by reperfusion.

Main role: These figures provide the paper’s main graphical evidence for overuse and allocative inefficiency: low-propensity patients in aggressive hospitals are harmed by reperfusion, and higher hospital treatment intensity is associated with lower treatment benefits conditional on propensity.
Settings.H1211: Section IV.A, Figure IV and Figure V, PDF pp. 28–30, 31.
Settings.G1212:
Treatment: Binary indicator for receiving reperfusion within 12 hours of AMI admission.

Method: The authors estimate linear probability models of 30-day survival on reperfusion, interactions of reperfusion with the patient propensity index and the hospital treatment-rate effect from the propensity equation, patient risk adjusters, and hospital fixed effects. Alternative specifications control for propensity linearly, via an inverse Mills ratio, or nonparametrically using 100 propensity-percentile indicators interacted with reperfusion. The coefficient on reperfusion × hospital treatment rate tests whether more aggressive hospitals have lower treatment returns conditional on propensity, which the paper interprets as allocative inefficiency.

Identification: Identification relies on the authors’ selection-on-gains framework: with rich chart-based controls and hospital fixed effects, OLS of survival on treatment recovers treatment-on-the-treated effects under the assumption that treatment is conditionally uncorrelated with unobserved baseline mortality but may be correlated with unobserved gains. The propensity index summarizes patient and hospital determinants of treatment; conditional on this index, a negative reperfusion × hospital treatment-rate interaction indicates lower hospital treatment thresholds rather than comparative advantage.

Setting: In linear probability models with hospital fixed effects, reperfusion raises 30-day survival for the average treated patient, and its benefit increases strongly with the patient propensity index. But conditional on propensity, hospitals with higher risk-adjusted reperfusion rates have lower returns to reperfusion: the reperfusion × hospital-rate interaction is about −0.031 to −0.037 percentage points per unit of hospital treatment-rate effect across specifications. The authors interpret this pattern as causal evidence that aggressive hospitals use reperfusion too far into the low-benefit tail, generating allocative inefficiency.

Main role: Table II supplies core regression evidence for the central claims: treatment benefits rise with propensity and fall with hospital aggressiveness conditional on propensity, supporting allocative inefficiency.
Settings.H1212: Section IV.A, Table II columns (1)–(4), PDF pp. 31–33.
Settings.G1213:
Treatment: Indicator for reperfusion within 12 hours of AMI admission.

Method: The authors estimate logit survival models analogous to the OLS specifications in Table II. They regress 30-day survival on reperfusion, reperfusion interacted with the propensity index, and reperfusion interacted with the hospital treatment-rate effect, controlling for patient covariates and hospital fixed effects. Alternative specifications control for propensity linearly, via an inverse Mills ratio, or nonparametrically with 100 propensity-percentile interactions. Because the implemented estimator is logistic, this falls under Other.

Identification: Same identification logic as the linear models, but implemented through logistic regression. Rich clinical controls and hospital fixed effects are used so that treatment is assumed conditionally uncorrelated with unobserved baseline survival, while selection on gains is allowed. Conditional on the estimated propensity, a negative interaction of reperfusion with hospital treatment intensity is interpreted as evidence that higher treatment rates reflect lower thresholds rather than higher comparative advantage.

Setting: The logit regressions show that reperfusion increases 30-day survival for the average treated patient and that the treatment benefit rises with patient propensity to be treated. However, conditional on propensity, more aggressive hospitals have significantly lower returns to reperfusion: the reperfusion × hospital-rate interaction is about −0.211 to −0.252 log-odds. The authors interpret this as strong causal evidence of allocative inefficiency in high-treatment hospitals.

Main role: The logit estimates in Table II are one of the paper’s main causal result sets, mirroring the linear models and connecting magnitudes to odds of survival.
Settings.H1213: Section IV.A, Table II columns (5)–(7), PDF pp. 31–33.
Settings.G1214:
Treatment: Indicator for receiving reperfusion therapy within 12 hours.

Method: The authors re-estimate their logit survival specification for alternative horizons: 7-day and 360-day survival. Each regression includes reperfusion, reperfusion interacted with the propensity index, and reperfusion interacted with the hospital treatment-rate effect, with hospital fixed effects and rich CCP controls. Propensity is controlled either linearly or nonparametrically. This is a robustness analysis of the same causal estimand using nonlinear logit models.

Identification: Same selection-on-gains and rich-controls argument as in the 30-day models. The 7-day horizon is intended to isolate the immediate treatment consequences of AMI management; the 360-day horizon tests persistence once post-discharge factors matter more. A negative reperfusion × hospital treatment-rate interaction conditional on propensity continues to indicate allocative inefficiency.

Setting: When the survival window is shortened to 7 days or extended to 360 days, the main pattern persists: reperfusion benefits rise with patient propensity, and hospitals with higher risk-adjusted treatment rates have lower returns to reperfusion conditional on propensity. The hospital-rate interaction is −0.271 to −0.325 for 7-day survival and −0.147 to −0.192 for 360-day survival in log-odds terms. This robustness supports the paper’s interpretation that aggressive hospitals overuse reperfusion rather than merely differing in later care quality.

Main role: These are important robustness analyses supporting the main allocative-inefficiency conclusion across alternative survival windows, but they are not the primary headline results.
Settings.H1214: Section IV.A, Table III, PDF pp. 33–34.
Settings.G1215:
Treatment: Binary indicator for reperfusion within 12 hours after AMI admission.

Method: The authors estimate mixed-effects/hierarchical logit models of 30-day survival with hospital-level correlated random coefficients on the intercept and reperfusion. The first specification includes a hospital random intercept only; the second adds a hospital random coefficient on reperfusion, with reperfusion also interacted linearly with the propensity index. These models directly estimate the variance of hospital-specific treatment thresholds and their correlation with hospital baseline productivity. Because the estimator is nonlinear mixed logit, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification uses the same treatment-on-the-treated framework, but instead of testing allocative inefficiency through observed hospital treatment rates, the model directly estimates hospital-specific random slopes on reperfusion after controlling for propensity. The variance of the hospital-specific reperfusion coefficient is interpreted as variance in hospital treatment thresholds (allocative inefficiency), while the hospital random intercept captures general productivity in usual care. This relies on the hierarchical normality assumptions for random effects and the same rich-controls treatment-on-treated assumption.

Setting: The mixed-logit model directly estimates substantial variation across hospitals in the return to reperfusion after conditioning on patient propensity. The standard deviation of the hospital-specific reperfusion coefficient is 0.313 log-odds, essentially the same size as the average reperfusion effect for the average treated patient (0.314). The authors interpret this as large cross-hospital variation in treatment thresholds/allocative inefficiency, with hospitals that are more conservative in reperfusion tending to have worse outcomes for unreperfused patients.

Main role: Table IV is central because it directly quantifies hospital-level variation in treatment thresholds/allocative inefficiency and shows it is large—one of the main conclusions in the abstract and introduction.
Settings.H1215: Section IV.A, Table IV, PDF pp. 35–36.
Settings.G1216:
Treatment: Indicator for receipt of reperfusion within 12 hours of admission.

Method: This setting uses simple and progressively richer logit regressions of 30-day survival on reperfusion to validate the treatment-on-the-treated causal interpretation. The models add age-sex-race controls, full CCP controls, ZIP-code socioeconomic controls, and AHA/ACC appropriateness criteria. The authors explicitly interpret stability of the reperfusion coefficient across richer covariate sets, and its similarity to randomized trial estimates, as evidence supporting causal identification. Because the estimator is nonlinear logit, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The strategy is indirect validation: if rich clinical controls render treatment conditionally uncorrelated with omitted determinants of baseline survival, then the reperfusion coefficient should be stable as more detailed controls are added and should match randomized-trial treatment-on-treated effects. The authors compare their CCP logit estimates with the Fibrinolytic Therapy Trialists’ RCT synthesis and inspect sensitivity to added observables.

Setting: To support the causal interpretation of their treatment-on-treated estimates, the authors show that the estimated effect of reperfusion on 30-day survival is 0.424 log-odds with no controls but falls to 0.192 with only age-sex-race controls and remains very similar—0.207 with full CCP controls and 0.199 with extra ZIP/AHA-ACC controls. Because the full-controls estimate closely matches the randomized-trial benchmark of 0.20 log-odds, the authors argue that their observational design credibly recovers causal treatment-on-treated effects.

Main role: This is an identification-supporting robustness exercise rather than a standalone headline result, though it is substantively important because the paper’s causal interpretation depends on it.
Settings.H1216: Section IV.B.3, Table VI, PDF pp. 38–40.
Settings.G1217:
Treatment: Indicator for receiving reperfusion therapy within 12 hours of AMI admission.

Method: The paper jointly estimates a hierarchical logit treatment equation and a hierarchical logit survival equation to recover the joint distribution of hospital reperfusion rates, hospital general productivity, and hospital treatment thresholds. The treatment equation is a hospital-random-effect logit for reperfusion; the survival equation is a hospital-random-intercept/random-slope logit for 30-day survival with reperfusion and reperfusion interacted with the propensity index. The joint estimation allows the authors to infer comparative advantage and thresholds simultaneously from correlated hospital random effects. Because this is a nonlinear structural mixed-logit system, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification combines the treatment propensity equation and the survival equation. The hospital effect in the treatment equation equals comparative advantage minus treatment threshold up to a scale parameter; the hospital random slope in the survival equation loads on threshold after conditioning on propensity. Jointly estimating the covariance structure of these hospital effects, together with assumptions about the scale of idiosyncratic gains, allows the authors to infer how much treatment-rate variation reflects thresholds versus comparative advantage. The model depends on the Roy/single-index structure and normal random-effect assumptions.

Setting: The jointly estimated hierarchical-logit system shows that variation in hospital reperfusion rates is related to, but not fully explained by, treatment thresholds. The standard deviation of the hospital reperfusion-rate effect is 0.442, the standard deviation of hospital treatment thresholds is 0.327, and the correlation between the reperfusion-rate effect and thresholds is −0.341. The authors interpret this as evidence that some treatment-rate variation reflects allocative inefficiency, but because the correlation is far from −1, substantial hospital comparative advantage must also be present.

Main role: This structural joint-estimation setting is central to the paper’s headline claim that both allocative inefficiency and comparative advantage contribute to treatment variation.
Settings.H1217: Section IV.C, Table VII, PDF pp. 43–45.
Settings.G1218:
Treatment: Indicator for reperfusion receipt within 12 hours.

Method: To study mechanisms, the authors estimate mixed-logit survival models that interact reperfusion with hospital characteristics such as ownership, teaching status, discharge volume, beds, and resident-bed ratio, while controlling for patient propensity and hospital random effects. The aim is to test whether the causal return to reperfusion varies systematically by hospital type, which would support financial-incentive or learning-by-doing mechanisms for overuse. Because the estimator is a nonlinear mixed logit, the setting is classified as Other.

Identification: The same treatment-on-treated logic applies, but the identifying comparison is whether conditional treatment effects differ systematically with observed hospital characteristics after controlling for patient propensity. If for-profit or teaching hospitals overtreated for financial or learning motives, reperfusion returns would be lower in those hospitals conditional on propensity. The strategy is observational and depends on the same rich-controls assumptions plus the interpretability of treatment-characteristic interactions.

Setting: The mixed-logit mechanism tests find no evidence that the causal survival return to reperfusion differs by for-profit status, church ownership, government ownership, teaching status, size, volume, or safety-net share once patient propensity is controlled for. The authors interpret the jointly insignificant treatment × hospital-characteristic interactions as rejecting simple financial-gain or learning-by-doing explanations for allocative inefficiency. Instead, treatment-rate differences associated with those characteristics are inferred to reflect comparative advantage rather than lower treatment thresholds.

Main role: These are mechanism tests supporting the conclusion that overuse is not primarily driven by for-profit status, teaching status, or similar observable hospital traits.
Settings.H1218: Section V, Table VIII, PDF pp. 46–47.
Settings.G1219:
Treatment: Hospital belief-driven use of reperfusion within 12 hours; the effective treatment margin is still actual reperfusion receipt, but the key causal object is hospital misperception/prediction error in comparative advantage that shifts treatment decisions.

Method: The paper estimates a minimum-chi-square structural learning model that maps reduced-form hospital-level moments from the hierarchical logits into structural parameters governing comparative advantage, baseline productivity, the reliability of hospitals’ signal about comparative advantage, the weight hospitals place on that signal, and the scale of patient-level unobserved gains. Alternative specifications constrain the signal weight to equal reliability or allow reliability to vary by hospital volume. This is a structural causal mechanism model, not a standard reduced-form estimator.

Identification: Identification proceeds by treating the variances and covariances of hospital treatment-rate effects, thresholds, and productivity from the reduced-form hierarchical logits as moments generated by a structural signal-extraction model. In the model, hospitals observe a noisy signal of comparative advantage and choose treatment based on beliefs; allocative inefficiency equals the prediction error. Minimum chi-square estimation recovers structural parameters by matching these reduced-form moments, and overidentifying restrictions test whether optimal weighting of the signal or common reliability across hospital-volume groups fits the data.

Setting: The structural learning model implies substantial variation in hospital comparative advantage—standard deviation about 0.317—and very noisy hospital information about that advantage, with reliability only about 0.065 when all hospitals are pooled. Hospitals are estimated to overweight their noisy signal (weight 0.154 > reliability 0.065), and the restriction of optimal weighting is rejected. When reliability is allowed to vary by volume, high-volume hospitals have more reliable signals than low-volume hospitals, and the model fits the data well. The authors interpret this as causal evidence that allocative inefficiency is driven in part by hospitals’ misperceptions of their own comparative advantage.

Main role: The paper’s conclusion emphasizes that hospitals’ imperfect information and misperceptions about their comparative advantage are a principal mechanism behind allocative inefficiency; Table IX provides the key evidence.
Settings.H1219: Section V, Table IX, PDF pp. 49–51.
Settings.G1220:
Treatment: Hospital-level allocative inefficiency in reperfusion use, operationalized through the treatment threshold/prediction error τ_h that distorts actual reperfusion receipt relative to the efficient rule.

Method: The authors conduct a stylized welfare calculation based on their estimated structural/logit parameters. They treat hospital allocative inefficiency (differences in treatment thresholds or prediction errors) as causally reducing survival benefits by causing too much or too little treatment, and compute average welfare losses from the estimated variance and mean of hospital thresholds. They also calculate counterfactual welfare gains from eliminating allocative inefficiency or standardizing treatment. This is a model-based welfare simulation, so it belongs in Other.

Identification: The welfare analysis takes the estimated variance of hospital thresholds from the hierarchical logits and the estimated responsiveness of treatment probability to the threshold, then applies a triangular-loss formula from the Roy model. One component comes from cross-hospital variance in thresholds; another from systematic overuse if the mean threshold is below zero, proxied using treatment effects for very low-propensity patients. Counterfactuals assume better information can eliminate some or all prediction error. The validity of the welfare claims depends on the structural model and earlier causal identification of treatment effects and thresholds.

Setting: Using their estimated threshold dispersion and treatment-response function, the authors calculate that variation in allocative inefficiency across hospitals reduces log-odds survival by about 0.014 per patient, implying that removing this inefficiency would increase the effectiveness of reperfusion by about 28% relative to the average total treatment benefit of 0.05. Adding systematic overuse—using low-propensity patients’ negative treatment effects to proxy a mean threshold below zero—raises the estimated gain from eliminating allocative inefficiency to about 44%. This welfare simulation is a central quantitative conclusion of the paper.

Main role: The abstract reports a 44% welfare gain from eliminating allocative inefficiency; this stylized calculation is therefore a headline substantive result.
Settings.G1221:
Treatment: Exposure to a police killing during high school, operationalized as an indicator that a student lived within 0.50 miles of an officer-involved killing in a given event-study period relative to the first such nearby killing during grades 9–12. In the treatment/control contrast, treated students lived within 0.50 miles; controls lived 0.50–3 miles from their nearest killing during high school.

Method: The main design is a dynamic difference-in-differences/event-study estimated on student-semester panel data. Treatment is defined as living within 0.50 miles of an officer-involved killing during a student’s LAUSD high school career; controls are students whose nearest killing during high school was between 0.50 and 3 miles away. The regression includes individual fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects (primarily census block group × semester), and cohort-year fixed effects, with leads and lags relative to first nearby killing. Identification comes from comparing changes in GPA over time for students living very close to a killing to students in the same neighborhood living slightly farther away. Standard errors are clustered by ZIP code. The paper discusses threats from nonrandom police killings, local crime/policing shocks, migration, and staggered timing; robustness includes alternative neighborhoods, controls for homicides/crime/arrests, placebo permutations, and cohort-specific event studies.

Identification: The endogeneity concern is that police killings occur disproportionately in disadvantaged areas and may coincide with changing neighborhood crime or policing. The strategy restricts comparisons to students in the same neighborhood and semester, differing only in hyperlocal distance to the killing, and uses within-student changes over time. The identifying assumption is that absent the killing, treated and slightly farther-away control students in the same neighborhood would have followed parallel trends in GPA. The paper supports this with flat pretreatment event-study coefficients, immediate localized attendance responses fading after 0.50 miles, no differential pretrends in local crime/arrests/homicides, and limited evidence that migration biases results.

Setting: Using a dynamic difference-in-differences design with student fixed effects and neighborhood-semester fixed effects, the paper estimates that exposure to a police killing within 0.50 miles lowers nearby students’ semester GPA. GPA falls by 0.04 points in the semester of the shooting and by about 0.07 to 0.08 points in the next two semesters; the paper notes GPA mean = 2.08 and standard deviation = 1, and describes these as declines as large as 0.08 standard deviations. Average posttreatment effects in the simpler post dummy specification are about −0.027 points. These estimates are central to the article’s claim that police violence harms educational outcomes for inner-city youth.

Main role: This is the paper’s core empirical design for the central claim that police killings reduce nearby students’ academic achievement. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all emphasize persistent GPA declines from exposure to police violence.
Settings.H1221: Section IV.A; equation (1) in Section III.B; Figure II (PDF pp. 131–136, especially PDF pp. 135–136).
Settings.G1222:
Treatment: Exposure to a police killing during high school, defined by residence within 0.50 miles of an officer-involved killing relative to students living 0.50–3 miles from their nearest killing during high school.

Method: A conventional DiD/event-study is estimated on student-semester panels with individual fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects, and cohort-year fixed effects, but the dependent variable is an indicator for emotional disturbance (ED). Treatment is living within 0.50 miles of a police killing during high school; controls are students whose nearest killing during high school was between 0.50 and 3 miles away. The event-study uses relative time to first nearby killing. Standard errors are clustered by ZIP code. Robustness mirrors the GPA design, including controls and alternative neighborhood definitions.

Identification: The design uses hyperlocal treatment variation within neighborhoods over time to address confounding from disadvantaged areas and changing neighborhood conditions. The key assumption is parallel trends in ED incidence between very near and slightly farther students within the same neighborhood absent the killing. The paper argues that police killings are difficult to predict at exact dates and locations, shows little evidence of differential pretreatment trends, and includes neighborhood-time fixed effects to absorb broader shocks.

Setting: Applying the same difference-in-differences event-study used for GPA to semester indicators of emotional disturbance, the paper finds that exposure to a police killing increases the probability of an ED classification in subsequent semesters. Posttreatment estimates range from about 0.04 to 0.07 percentage points, and the simpler post-treatment specification is 0.470 per 1,000 students. The paper interprets this as roughly a 15% increase over the mean ED rate of 0.5%, supporting the claim that police violence harms students’ psychological well-being.

Main role: Psychological well-being is one of the paper’s main outcome domains in the abstract and introduction, where increased emotional disturbance is presented as corroborating evidence that police violence traumatizes students.
Settings.H1222: Section IV.B; Figure III; Table II Panel B (PDF pp. 140–141, and Table II on PDF p. 138).
Settings.G1223:
Treatment: Indicator for living within 0.50 miles of a police killing during high school, estimated separately by student race subsample against students 0.50–3 miles from their nearest killing.

Method: This is a heterogeneous-effects version of the main DiD, estimated by student race subsamples using a posttreatment dummy rather than the full event-study. The estimating equation is the baseline student-level DiD with individual fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects, and cohort-year fixed effects. Separate regressions are run for black students, Hispanic students, and pooled white/Asian students, comparing those living within 0.50 miles of a police killing during high school to those 0.50–3 miles away.

Identification: Within each race subsample, identification is as in the main DiD: compare treated and slightly farther-away control students in the same neighborhood over time. The causal contrast depends on parallel trends within race groups, conditional on fixed effects and neighborhood-time controls. The paper uses this to assess whether exposure effects differ by student race and argues the pattern is not explained by family background, prior achievement, school, or cohort composition.

Setting: In race-specific DiD regressions, exposure to a police killing lowers semester GPA for black and Hispanic students but not for white/Asian students. The estimated posttreatment effect is −0.038 GPA points for black students and −0.030 for Hispanic students, versus about −0.003 for pooled white and Asian students. The paper treats this as evidence that the educational spillovers of police violence are racially disparate and concentrated among underrepresented minorities, a central substantive claim.

Main role: Racial heterogeneity is a central conclusion of the paper: the abstract, introduction, and conclusion all stress that effects are driven entirely by black and Hispanic students and not by white or Asian students.
Settings.H1223: Section V.A; Figure IV Panel A (PDF pp. 143–144).
Settings.G1224:
Treatment: Exposure to a nearby police killing during high school, with treatment differentiated by race of the person killed: black/Hispanic versus white/Asian fatality. Exposure is defined as living within 0.50 miles of such an incident; controls are 0.50–3 miles from their nearest killing.

Method: A heterogeneous-effects DiD estimates average posttreatment GPA effects separately by race of the deceased. The design remains a conventional difference-in-differences with individual fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects, and cohort-year fixed effects, either via subsample/event coding or via equation (2), which interacts posttreatment exposure with indicators for whether the deceased was black/Hispanic versus white/Asian, plus additional interacted controls in some specifications. Treatment is living within 0.50 miles of a police killing during high school versus 0.50–3 miles away.

Identification: Identification again relies on hyperlocal treated-versus-control comparisons within neighborhoods over time. The heterogeneity analysis asks whether otherwise similar exposure has different effects depending on the deceased’s race. Because race of the deceased is not random, the paper adds flexible interactions for neighborhood characteristics, media coverage, residence near the incident, and deceased age/gender to assess whether observables explain the pattern. The remaining assumption is that conditional on these controls and fixed effects, differences by deceased race reflect differential causal spillovers rather than omitted correlated incident features.

Setting: The paper finds that nearby police killings of black or Hispanic individuals reduce student GPA, whereas killings of white or Asian individuals do not. In Figure IV Panel B, average posttreatment effects are about −0.031 points for killings of black/Hispanic individuals and about +0.003 for killings of white/Asian individuals. In Table III, treatment effects for black/Hispanic killings remain around −0.028 to −0.034 points across specifications with rich interacted controls, while effects for white/Asian killings remain near zero and insignificant. This supports the paper’s core claim that students respond primarily to police killings of minorities.

Main role: The paper’s abstract and conclusions emphasize that effects are driven by police killings of other minorities; this setting directly underpins that claim.
Settings.H1224: Section V.A; Figure IV Panel B; equation (2); Table III (PDF pp. 143–147).
Settings.G1225:
Treatment: Exposure to a police killing within 0.50 miles during high school, differentiated by weapon status of the deceased: unarmed, armed with a gun, or armed with another weapon. Controls are students 0.50–3 miles from their nearest killing.

Method: This setting is a heterogeneous-effects DiD by incident weapon context. Using a modified version of equation (2), the author interacts posttreatment exposure with indicators for whether the person killed was unarmed, armed with a gun, or armed with another weapon (knife/other). The sample is restricted to incidents with hand-coded contextual information from DA reports or other sources (556 of 627 killings). The regression otherwise follows the main student-semester DiD structure with individual fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects, and cohort-year fixed effects.

Identification: The same hyperlocal DiD variation identifies exposure effects, while heterogeneity by weapon type tests whether contextual severity/perceived reasonableness matters. Because weapon status is not randomized, the paper checks robustness to interacted controls for neighborhood characteristics, media coverage, deceased residence, and demographics. The identifying interpretation is that, conditional on these observables and fixed effects, larger effects for unarmed killings reflect causal differences in spillovers by incident context.

Setting: In a DiD that differentiates exposure by the deceased’s weapon type, police killings of unarmed individuals produce the largest GPA declines. In the full contextual-information sample, the estimated posttreatment GPA effect is −0.047 points for unarmed killings, roughly twice the size of killings involving a knife/other weapon (−0.020) or a gun (−0.024), with the differences versus armed incidents statistically significant at about the 5% level. Restricting to black/Hispanic fatalities yields an even steeper pattern, with −0.053 points for unarmed and −0.020 for gun-armed killings. This is a key result for the paper’s interpretation that students respond to perceived reasonableness or legitimacy of police force, not just violence per se.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that effects are largest for incidents involving unarmed individuals, making this a central mechanism/result rather than a minor robustness check.
Settings.H1225: Section V.B; Figure V; Online Appendix Table A.IV as described in text (PDF pp. 148–150).
Settings.G1226:
Treatment: Counts of nearby lethal violence exposures within 0.50 miles by semester relative time, separately for police killings and nonpolice gun-related criminal homicides. This is not a binary treatment; coefficients represent the effect of exposure to one additional nearby killing of each type.

Method: The paper estimates a modified event-study/DD model comparing contemporaneous and lagged exposure counts to police killings and criminal gun-related homicides on semester GPA. Equation (3) regresses GPA on leads/lags of the number of police killings and nonpolice killings within 0.50 miles, including individual fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects, cohort-year fixed effects, and block-level controls for reported crimes and arrests. The sample is restricted to 2010 onward when crime and arrest controls are available.

Identification: Identification comes from within-student and within-neighborhood timing differences in exposure to nearby police versus criminal killings, controlling for neighborhood-semester shocks and local crime/arrests. The concern is that violence exposures are correlated with local disorder or policing. The design uses hyperlocal exposure counts, fixed effects, and block-level crime controls to isolate marginal effects of police and nonpolice killings. The paper interprets larger police coefficients than criminal-homicide coefficients as evidence that police violence has distinct spillovers beyond generic exposure to violent death.

Setting: Using a modified DiD/event-study that includes exposure counts to both police killings and criminal gun homicides, the paper finds both types of violence reduce semester GPA, but police killings have substantially larger effects. The paper reports that at the peak, the effect of a criminal homicide is only 60% as large as that of a police killing, and the coefficients differ significantly at the 5% level for the current and next two semesters. The author interprets this as evidence that police killings are not simply another violent homicide shock; they generate larger educational spillovers than criminal violence.

Main role: The abstract and introduction stress that police killings have larger and qualitatively different effects than criminal homicides; this comparison directly supports that broader interpretation.
Settings.H1226: Section V.C; equation (3); Figure VI (PDF pp. 150–152).
Settings.G1227:
Treatment: Exposure to a police killing within 0.50 miles in a given expected grade (grades 9–16 in the pooled student × expected-grade data), relative to students living 0.50–3 miles from the nearest killing in that expected grade. For simplified specifications, treatment is interacted with an indicator for expected grade ≤12 (still in high school at event time).

Method: This is the long-run cross-cohort difference-in-differences/event-study for cumulative GPA. Because final GPA is measured once per student, the author constructs a pooled cross-section of student × expected-grade observations around each killing and estimates equation (4). The model includes neighborhood-cohort fixed effects, a treatment indicator for living within 0.50 miles of the nearest killing in that expected grade, interactions between treatment and expected-grade indicators (expected grades 9–16, omitted grade 13), and demographic controls for school, race, sex, free lunch, household language, parental education, and eighth-grade proficiency. Control observations are students 0.50–3 miles from a killing in the same expected grade. Standard errors are clustered by student.

Identification: Because final attainment outcomes are observed once, the strategy compares younger cohorts in a neighborhood who were still in school when a nearby killing occurred to older cohorts from the same neighborhood whose schooling was already complete. Neighborhood-cohort fixed effects absorb area-specific cohort trends, while the event-study across expected grades tests for parallel pretrends using older cohorts (expected grades >12). The identifying assumption is that, absent the killing, attainment differences across expected grades would evolve similarly between treatment and control areas within neighborhoods, conditional on covariates.

Setting: In the long-run cross-cohort DiD, exposure to a police killing while still in high school lowers final cumulative GPA. Older cohorts whose schooling was complete when the killing occurred show near-zero pretrend coefficients, while students exposed in expected grades 9–12 have lower final GPA. The paper notes that the average treatment estimate on cumulative GPA is 0.029 points in absolute value, nearly identical to the 0.027-point average on semester GPA from the main fixed-effects model, and interprets this as validation of the long-run design and evidence of persistent academic harm.

Main role: Long-run educational consequences are a central claim in the abstract and conclusion. The cumulative GPA evidence also validates the long-run identification strategy used for graduation and college enrollment.
Settings.H1227: Section VI.A–VI.B; equation (4); Figure VII Panel A; Table IV Panel A (PDF pp. 153–159, especially PDF pp. 155–159).
Settings.G1228:
Treatment: Exposure to a police killing within 0.50 miles in a given expected grade while still potentially enrolled in high school, compared with students 0.50–3 miles away from a killing in that expected grade.

Method: The long-run pooled cross-section DiD/event-study of equation (4) is estimated on an indicator for receiving a high school diploma or equivalent from LAUSD. The construction, treatment/control definition, neighborhood-cohort fixed effects, and demographic controls match the long-run design. Event-time is expected grade at exposure, with older expected grades serving as placebo/pretrend cohorts. Simplified robustness specifications replace the full expected-grade interactions with a single posttreatment indicator for expected grade ≤12.

Identification: The design compares cohorts within neighborhoods that were differentially exposed during high school because of timing relative to the killing. Older cohorts in the same area provide a control for area-specific cohort patterns; students slightly farther away provide the spatial control group. The key assumption is parallel trends across expected grades between treatment and control areas within neighborhood-cohort cells, conditional on covariates. The paper supports this by showing insignificant coefficients for expected grades above 12 and robustness to bandwidths, neighborhood definitions, standard errors, and transfer-out analyses.

Setting: The long-run DiD/event-study shows that exposure to a nearby police killing during earlier high-school years lowers high school completion. Exposure in expected grade 9 predicts a 1.7 percentage point decline in graduation, exposure in grade 10 a 1.8 point decline, exposure in grade 11 a 1.0 point decline, and exposure in grade 12 about a 0.3 point decline; the paper notes the ninth-grade estimate corresponds to a 3.4% decrease relative to the mean graduation rate of 50%. In the simpler posttreatment specification, exposure in expected grades ≤12 lowers graduation by roughly 1.1 percentage points. This is a central long-run finding of the paper.

Main role: Reduced high school completion is highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as a main long-run consequence of exposure to police violence.
Settings.H1228: Section VI.B; Figure VII Panel B; Table IV Panel B (PDF pp. 155–159).
Settings.G1229:
Treatment: Exposure to a police killing within 0.50 miles in a given expected grade during high school, relative to students living 0.50–3 miles from a killing in that expected grade.

Method: The same long-run pooled cross-section DiD/event-study of equation (4) is estimated on college enrollment, defined using National Student Clearinghouse data for LAUSD graduates/cohorts where available. Treatment and control are based on residence within 0.50 miles versus 0.50–3 miles from the nearest killing in each expected grade; the model includes neighborhood-cohort fixed effects and demographic controls, with older cohorts used to assess pretrends. A simpler posttreatment version is also reported in robustness and racial heterogeneity figures.

Identification: Identification mirrors the graduation setting: compare younger cohorts exposed while in school to older cohorts from the same neighborhoods whose schooling was complete, using slightly farther-away students as the spatial control group. The validity condition is parallel cohort trends in college-going between treatment and control areas absent the killing, conditional on neighborhood-cohort fixed effects and demographics. The paper reports qualitatively similar dynamics to graduation and robustness across alternative specifications.

Setting: In the long-run DiD/event-study, exposure to a nearby police killing during the 9th or 10th grade lowers college enrollment. The paper reports decreases of about 0.09 percentage points for 9th- and 10th-grade exposure in Figure VII Panel C, and then summarizes these as a 2.7% decrease relative to the mean college enrollment rate of 32.6%. In the simpler posttreatment specification, exposure in expected grades ≤12 reduces college enrollment by around 0.6 percentage points. These estimates support the paper’s claim that police violence has lasting effects on educational attainment beyond GPA.

Main role: Lower college enrollment is featured in the abstract and introduction as a principal long-run consequence of police violence.
Settings.H1229: Section VI.B; Figure VII Panel C; Table IV Panel C (PDF pp. 156–159).
Settings.G1230:
Treatment: Indicator for exposure to a police killing within 0.50 miles in expected grades 9–12 (versus 0.50–3 miles from a killing), estimated separately for black/Hispanic students and for white/Asian students.

Method: A simplified long-run DiD based on equation (4) replaces the full set of expected-grade-by-treatment interactions with a single posttreatment indicator for treated observations in expected grade ≤12, and estimates effects separately by student race subsamples. The pooled cross-section of student × expected-grade observations, neighborhood-cohort fixed effects, and demographic controls are retained. Outcomes are final cumulative GPA, high school graduation, and college enrollment.

Identification: The identification is the long-run cross-cohort DiD described above, applied within student-race subsamples. The assumption is that, absent the killing, cohort trends in long-run attainment would be parallel between very near and slightly farther-away students of the same racial subsample within neighborhoods, conditional on fixed effects and controls. The paper uses this to show that the long-run effects are racially concentrated.

Setting: Estimating the long-run DiD separately by student race, the paper finds significant negative effects of police killings on black and Hispanic students’ cumulative GPA, high school graduation, and college enrollment, but no significant effects for white and Asian students. Figure VIII shows this racial pattern across all three outcomes, with black/Hispanic estimates below zero and white/Asian estimates near zero. This extends the paper’s central racial-heterogeneity finding from short-run GPA to long-run attainment outcomes.

Main role: The paper’s main message is that long-run educational harms are borne by black and Hispanic students, not by white and Asian students. This figure directly establishes that pattern for cumulative GPA, graduation, and college enrollment.
Settings.G1231:
Treatment: Log of the household's marginal electricity price (total variable price per kWh, including energy price, grid price, municipality tax, and KEV surcharge). For dual-tariff customers, the effective marginal price is a weighted average of day and night prices using predicted consumption shares. The regression uses lagged prices as the operative price households respond to. Units are log CHF/kWh (table reports price in Rp./kWh descriptively).

Method: The paper estimates residential electricity demand elasticities using a geographical boundary regression discontinuity design. The estimating equation is a linear regression of log annual household electricity consumption on log marginal electricity price, household/building controls, year fixed effects, and border-point fixed effects, restricting the sample to households within 1 km of provider borders. Identification comes from discontinuous changes in assigned local-monopoly electricity tariffs at spatial boundaries between utilities, with households unable to choose providers. The design is sharp because provider assignment changes discretely by location. The authors discuss threats from sorting and compositional differences and address them with border-point fixed effects, rich controls, and balance tests across borders. Dual-tariff households are assigned a predicted weighted marginal price based on household characteristics.

Identification: Households are assigned to local monopoly electricity providers by residence and cannot choose suppliers. Near provider borders, otherwise similar households face different tariffs because of discrete provider assignment. The design assumes households on either side of a border are comparable absent the tariff jump, with no sorting on energy prices; the paper argues energy prices are negligible in location choice and reports no significant differences in observed household and house characteristics across the border sample. Border-point fixed effects absorb local unobservables common within boundary segments; year fixed effects absorb common time shocks. Remaining concerns include imperfect measurement of the relevant marginal price under dual tariffs and any residual spatial differences not captured by controls and border fixed effects.

Setting: Using a sharp geographical RD around electricity-provider borders, the authors estimate how higher electricity prices reduce household electricity demand. In their preferred border-sample specification, the coefficient on log price is -0.224 for the lowest-wealth quintile, with positive interaction terms of 0.072, 0.099, 0.129, and 0.115 for the 2nd through 5th wealth quintiles, implying smaller price sensitivity for wealthier households. The outcome is log annual electricity consumption, and the treatment is log marginal electricity price. These demand elasticities are a central causal input for the paper's structural and welfare analysis of tariffs, solar adoption incentives, and redistribution.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, Section 4, Section 5, and conclusion present identification of electricity demand elasticities as a core empirical input to the structural model and the policy counterfactuals. The paper explicitly highlights using a geographical boundary RDD to estimate demand parameters.
Settings.H1231: Section 4.1 'Energy demand' and Section 5.1 'Energy demand model'; Table 6, especially column (2) RDD model, PDF pp. 3283-3287 (article pages 3283-3287; PDF pages 18-21).
Settings.G1232:
Treatment: Lagged state variable value: prior-year PV revenue under feed-in tariffs, prior-year PV revenue under self-consumption, or prior-year PV installation cost, each entering linearly as the AR(1) regressor. Underlying monetary variables are rescaled by CHF 10,000 in the estimation.

Method: The paper estimates the state transition processes used in the dynamic structural solar-adoption model with linear AR(1) regressions estimated by ordinary least squares. Specifically, it regresses revenue under the feed-in-tariff regime on its lag, revenue under the self-consumption regime on its lag, and fixed installation cost on its lag. These are not merely descriptive in the paper's logic: they are used as the law of motion for the state variables in the adoption Bellman equation and thus given a causal/behavioral interpretation for households' expectations in counterfactual policy analysis. The sample is the counterfactual sample of potential solar adopters, and annual variation in feed-in tariffs, electricity prices, and installation costs identifies persistence.

Identification: Identification comes from annual time variation in the underlying aggregate determinants: declining feed-in tariff revenues, slightly increasing self-consumption revenues through electricity prices, and declining installation costs over time. The paper assumes households have expectations summarized by these AR(1) laws of motion and treats the estimated persistence parameters as the transition process for the dynamic state space. Endogeneity is not the main focus here; rather, the regressions impose a reduced-form dynamic process used for structural simulation.

Setting: To construct the state transition matrix for the dynamic PV-adoption model, the authors estimate AR(1) processes by OLS. They find persistence/decline parameters of 0.873 for feed-in-tariff revenue, 1.016 for self-consumption revenue, and 0.774 for installation costs, all precisely estimated. The intended interpretation is that past policy- and market-driven values causally shape households' expected future PV revenues and costs, thereby affecting current adoption incentives in the structural model. These estimates are supportive ingredients for, rather than the headline results of, the paper.

Main role: These AR(1) estimates are auxiliary but substantively important inputs to the main structural adoption model and counterfactuals; the paper reports them as a supporting causal/behavioral component rather than as a central standalone result.
Settings.H1232: Section 3.3 'Transition probabilities', Section 4.2 'PV adoption and transition probabilities', and Section 5.2 'Transition processes'; Table 7, PDF pp. 3281-3288 (article pages 3281-3288; PDF pages 15-22).
Settings.G1233:
Treatment: PV adoption incentives, primarily (i) net fixed installation cost of a solar panel and (ii) discounted indirect utility from PV revenue, entering the adoption value function. In the preferred estimates, fixed installation cost sensitivity varies by wealth quintile. Installation cost is continuous, measured in CHF 10,000s net of tax deductions and, in 2014, subsidies; PV revenue is continuous and measured in CHF 10,000s of discounted utility-relevant value. The actual choice outcome is whether the household installs a PV in a given year.

Method: The paper estimates a structural dynamic discrete-choice model of household photovoltaic (PV) adoption via maximum likelihood, solving a Bellman optimal stopping problem. Households are forward-looking and decide whether to install a solar panel based on the discounted indirect utility gains from PV revenue versus the disutility from fixed installation costs; the adoption probability is logit because the choice-specific shocks are assumed type-I extreme value. The state variables are total expected discounted PV revenue and installation cost, with transition probabilities estimated separately as AR(1) processes. The sample is restricted to BKW customers who are homeowners in one- or two-apartment buildings, because they are plausible decision-makers over rooftop installation. The model allows installation-cost sensitivity to differ across wealth quintiles and includes additional indicators (2010, middle-aged household head, rural area) in the preferred specification. Because this is nonlinear structural estimation rather than a linear regression design, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification relies on time-series variation in PV installation costs and revenues and cross-sectional variation in roof size, solar exposure, electricity consumption/self-consumption potential, income tax rates affecting tax deductibility, and wealth heterogeneity affecting installation-cost sensitivity. A key source of time variation is the institutional switch from feed-in tariffs to self-consumption plus installation subsidies in 2014, assumed unexpected by households. Restricting the sample to likely decision-makers (homeowners in small buildings) helps align observed adoptions with modeled choices. Remaining concerns include parametric assumptions on expectations, discounting, discrete state-space approximation, and the maintained assumption that adoption affects utility mainly via revenue rather than directly changing electricity consumption.

Setting: In the dynamic structural adoption model, lower installation costs and higher discounted PV revenues increase the probability that a household installs solar panels. In the preferred specification, the coefficient on indirect utility from PV revenue is 0.214, while the baseline coefficient on fixed installation cost is -0.702, with positive interaction terms of 0.148, 0.125, 0.251, and 0.357 for the 2nd through 5th wealth quintiles, implying wealthier households are less deterred by installation costs. The model also finds lower adoption in 2010 (-1.096) and higher adoption for middle-aged (0.310) and rural (0.210) households. This causal behavioral model is central to the paper's analysis of how subsidies and tariffs affect PV uptake, welfare, and redistribution.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions emphasize estimating a structural model of solar panel adoption and using it for tariff/subsidy counterfactuals. The PV adoption model is a core empirical pillar of the paper's main policy claims.
Settings.H1233: Section 3.2 'Dynamic PV adoption', Section 4.2 'PV adoption and transition probabilities', Sections 5.3-5.4 'PV adoption model' and 'PV adoption model fit'; Table 8 and Table 9, PDF pp. 3280-3290 (article pages 3280-3290; PDF pages 14-24).
Settings.G1234:
Treatment: Regulator-set marginal grid price within a two-part tariff, jointly varied with the annual fixed fee and the installation-cost subsidy over a five-year horizon. In Table 10, the marginal grid price is changed by percentages relative to the 2014 baseline grid price of CHF 0.089/kWh. This is a continuous policy dose, not a binary treatment.

Method: The paper performs structural counterfactual policy simulations in which a regulator chooses a constant five-year combination of marginal grid prices, fixed fees, and installation-cost subsidies to achieve a solar-energy target while satisfying a network-financing constraint. This is not a reduced-form empirical design but a model-based policy experiment using the estimated electricity-demand and dynamic PV-adoption parameters. The optimization is solved under four objective functions: minimizing aggregate grid expenditure, minimizing equity-weighted grid expenditure changes, maximizing aggregate welfare, and maximizing equity-weighted welfare. The implemented policy lever of interest in this setting is the marginal grid price, with the fixed fee and subsidy jointly chosen as complementary policy instruments. Outcomes reported together include solar adoption rates, household grid expenditure by income quintile and PV ownership, aggregate welfare change, grid integration cost, and subsidy cost per kWh.

Identification: Identification is entirely model-based. The simulated effects of marginal grid prices on PV adoption and household outcomes are traced through two estimated behavioral channels: the RD-based electricity demand elasticity and the structural dynamic PV-adoption model. A higher marginal grid price raises the value of self-consumption, induces more PV adoption, changes electricity consumption, and alters grid-cost financing. The regulator's optimization additionally imposes the network-financing constraint and the solar-energy-target constraint. Validity depends on the structural assumptions, the estimated demand and adoption responses being stable out of sample, and the assumed five-year constant-policy horizon.

Setting: The structural counterfactuals imply that raising the marginal grid price causally increases PV adoption and helps achieve solar-energy targets more cheaply than relying on subsidies alone, but at larger welfare cost. For the 7.5% target under cost minimization, the optimal policy raises the grid price by 25.8%, cuts the fixed fee by 96.3%, sets a subsidy equal to 20.8% of installation costs, and yields 1.8% PV adoption; grid expenditure falls by 15.5% for the bottom income quintile and rises by 1.8% for the top quintile, while aggregate welfare falls by CHF 12.16 million. For the 9.0% target, the cost-minimizing policy raises the grid price by 34.6%, cuts the fixed fee by 98.5%, sets an 83.3% subsidy, and yields 2.4% PV adoption. These simulations are the central policy results of the paper.

Main role: These counterfactuals directly deliver the paper's headline policy conclusions in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion about whether regulators should rely more on marginal prices or subsidies, and how that affects efficiency, equity, and welfare.
Settings.H1234: Section 6 'Counterfactuals', especially Sections 6.1-6.2; Table 10, Figure 2, and Figure 3, PDF pp. 3290-3298 (article pages 3290-3298; PDF pages 24-32).
Settings.G1235:
Treatment: Installation-cost subsidy for PV adoption, measured as the percentage of the fixed installation cost covered by the regulator. In Table 10 this ranges, for example, from 20.8% to 50.0% for the 7.5% target and from 83.3% to 98.3% for the 9.0% target, depending on the optimization objective. Continuous policy dose.

Method: A second structural counterfactual setting from the same regulator optimization focuses on installation-cost subsidies as the focal policy lever, jointly with fixed fees and marginal grid prices. Using the estimated dynamic PV-adoption and electricity-demand model, the regulator chooses a five-year constant subsidy rate as a percentage of installation costs, along with tariff components, to satisfy network financing and a solar target. The paper interprets these simulations causally as the effect of larger installation subsidies on adoption, expenditure distribution, welfare, and subsidy cost per kWh. This is nonlinear structural policy simulation rather than a reduced-form estimator.

Identification: The simulated effects of subsidies are identified through the dynamic adoption model, where lower net installation costs increase the value of adopting a solar panel, with heterogeneous sensitivity across wealth quintiles. The subsidy changes adoption directly through the installation-cost term and indirectly affects grid expenditure and welfare through the financing instruments required by the network-financing constraint. Validity depends on the structural adoption model and the assumptions on future state transitions and regulator constraints.

Setting: In the policy simulations, higher installation-cost subsidies causally raise PV adoption, but financing them tends to require higher fixed fees or lower welfare than relying on marginal-price incentives. For the 7.5% target under welfare maximization, the regulator sets a subsidy equal to 50.0% of installation costs, cuts the grid price by 69.8%, raises the fixed fee by 257.3%, and obtains 2.0% PV adoption, with aggregate welfare falling by CHF 11.02 million and subsidy cost reaching CHF 0.24 per kWh. For the 9.0% target under welfare maximization, the subsidy rises to 98.3% and PV adoption to 2.5%, with subsidy cost CHF 0.55 per kWh. These results support the paper's main claim that subsidies can preserve welfare better but are less cost-efficient and can be more regressive than marginal-price incentives.

Main role: The contrast between subsidy-based encouragement and marginal-price-based encouragement is a primary substantive conclusion in the abstract and conclusion. The paper explicitly compares subsidies with marginal-price incentives on cost efficiency, progressivity, and welfare.
Settings.H1235: Section 6 'Counterfactuals' and Section 7 'Conclusion'; Table 10, PDF pp. 3290-3299 (article pages 3290-3299; PDF pages 24-33).
Settings.G1236:
Treatment: Primary treatments are continuous measures of income composition/risk: (i) individual's average paycheck share in total income over observed years (unit interval share), where lower values imply greater non-paycheck income exposure; (ii) log variance of annual non-paycheck income; (iii) log variance of annual paycheck income; and (iv) log lagged 'ExcessWit' measuring potential excess withholding from within-year paycheck volatility, constructed from IRS withholding schedules. All are continuous regressors rather than binary treatment contrasts.

Method: The paper estimates individual-year OLS regressions relating log tax refunds to measures of income composition and volatility using the app-based panel. The dependent variable is log(Refund)_it and the key regressors are the individual's average paycheck share, the log variance of annual non-paycheck income, the log variance of annual paycheck income, and a constructed measure of lagged excess withholding induced mechanically by within-year paycheck volatility. Estimation uses pooled person-year observations with robust standard errors; no individual fixed effects are reported in Table 3. The authors interpret these coefficients substantively as evidence on how income sources and income risk affect refunds, while acknowledging the exercise is descriptive/correlational rather than a clean quasi-experiment.

Identification: The intended causal interpretation is that greater exposure to income not subject to withholding, and greater income uncertainty, lead households to overwithhold and therefore receive larger refunds. Identification comes from cross-individual and over-time variation in income composition and income volatility measured from account data. The endogeneity concern is that unobserved household traits, tax sophistication, family structure, and other determinants of withholding may correlate with both income composition/volatility and refund size. The paper argues these patterns are consistent with the model's mechanism rather than claiming a fully exogenous design.

Setting: Using person-year OLS regressions, the authors relate positive tax refunds to the composition and variability of income. They report that refunds are larger for households with lower paycheck income shares and higher annual non-paycheck income volatility, consistent with the model in which uncertain income not subject to withholding causes rational overwithholding. In Table 3, column 1, the coefficient on payshare is -0.903, and in column 2 the coefficient on log variance of non-paycheck income is 0.104; column 3 adds paycheck-income variance with a smaller positive coefficient of 0.0382. They also show a positive but economically modest association between lagged excess withholding from within-year paycheck volatility and refunds. These regressions are central empirical evidence supporting the paper's explanation for refund levels, but they rely on observational variation and not a quasi-experimental source of exogenous shocks.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize as central evidence that larger refunds are associated with greater non-paycheck income shares and income variability; Table 3 provides the main reduced-form empirical support for the model's refund mechanism.
Settings.H1236: Section III.D 'Correlates of Tax Refunds,' Table 3 columns (1)-(7), PDF pp. 2971-2974 (article pages 2971-2974; supplied PDF pages 13-16).
Settings.G1237:
Treatment: Monthly tax refund inflow received by the individual, normalized by total spending in the regression. The underlying treatment is the dollar amount of tax refund arrival; it is continuous and can vary in size across observations.

Method: The paper estimates the average marginal propensity to consume (MPC) out of tax refunds using an individual-month OLS regression of normalized nondurable spending on normalized tax refunds plus month fixed effects. Specifically, equation (20) regresses C_tilde_it on refund_tilde_it, where both spending and refunds are normalized by total spending. The coefficient on refunds is interpreted as the average MPC out of refunds. This is a linear regression adjustment rather than an experimental or instrumental design; the authors motivate refund timing as partially unanticipated and use the coefficient as an empirical MPC estimate.
