Method: Main two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences/event-study design using pre-program eligibility as a proxy for treatment. Equation (6) regresses firm-year outcomes on the interaction of a post-1996 indicator with an indicator for being eligible for autonomy before 1997, with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector-specific linear trends; standard errors are clustered at the firm level. The paper also presents event studies with year-by-year interactions relative to 1996. Because treatment timing in this implementation is not staggered—the treatment proxy is fixed pre-program and interacted with a common post period—the estimator is conventional DiD/TWFE rather than a modern heterogeneous DiD estimator.

Identification: Identification comes from differential changes after 1996 between firms that satisfied autonomy eligibility rules before the program and those that did not. The author’s endogeneity concern is that actual autonomy receipt and timing may be chosen by firms or the government based on expected returns; using pre-program eligibility sidesteps that concern. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity, year fixed effects absorb common shocks, and 2-digit sector linear trends address differential sector growth correlated with eligibility. The design requires parallel trends conditional on these controls; event studies are used to assess this. Because eligibility is only a proxy for actual autonomy, estimates are reduced-form effects of eligibility-based treatment exposure rather than treatment-on-the-treated IV estimates.

Setting: Using a conventional DiD with firm and year fixed effects plus 2-digit sector linear trends, the paper finds that pre-program-eligible SOEs experienced higher post-1996 value added, capital, and labor spending, but no detectable TFPR improvement. Table IV reports that eligibility-based exposure increases value added by 5,431.702 million rupees, capital by 11,035.022 million rupees, and salaries/benefits by 756.027 million rupees, while the TFPR estimate is -0.232 and imprecise. These results are central to the paper’s claim that granting managers greater formal autonomy induced scale expansion and higher value added without productivity gains.

Main role: These are the core firm-performance and mechanism results emphasized in the abstract, introduction, main results, and conclusion: autonomy raises value added and inputs, but not TFPR.
Settings.H1270: Section 5.2; Section 6.2; Table IV cols. (1)-(4); Figure 2(a)-(d); discussion on magnitudes in Section 6.2 and 6.3.1 (PDF pp. 10-16).
Settings.G1271:
Treatment: Proxy for exposure to managerial autonomy: binary indicator for pre-1997 eligibility to apply for autonomy, interacted with a post-1996 indicator. This captures the post-period treatment contrast for firms eligible under the program rules before introduction.

Method: Main two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences/event-study design using pre-program eligibility as proxy for treatment, implemented as in equation (6) with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends; standard errors clustered by firm. This setting groups the consumer and employee welfare outcomes reported together in Table V and Figure 3.

Identification: Same DiD identification as the main specification: compare outcome changes after 1996 between firms eligible before the program and those not eligible, conditioning on firm fixed effects, common year shocks, and sector-specific linear trends. The paper’s argument is that using pre-program eligibility avoids endogenous selection into actual autonomy timing. The identifying assumption is parallel trends conditional on controls; event studies assess this. Estimates are reduced-form effects of eligibility-based exposure to autonomy.

Setting: The paper uses its main DiD design to study outcomes tied to consumer and employee welfare. Table V shows that autonomy exposure increased markups by 2.251, did not significantly change the temporary-worker share (-3.543, imprecise), and reduced the probability of any employee housing construction by 0.145. The author interprets these results as evidence that managerial autonomy shifted SOEs toward manager-valued objectives and away from some government-valued objectives, especially consumer prices and employee amenities.

Main role: These outcomes are central to the paper’s broader conclusion that autonomy improves manager-valued outcomes but worsens some government-valued outcomes such as higher markups and reduced employee housing.
Settings.H1271: Section 6.2; Table V cols. (1)-(3); Figure 3(a)-(c) (PDF pp. 14-15).
Settings.G1272:
Treatment: Binary exposure to autonomy proxied by pre-1997 eligibility, switched on after 1996, estimated separately by subsamples defined by baseline conflict. Baseline conflict is proxied by whether the SOE paid dividends in all profitable pre-1997 years (high conflict) versus not all profitable years (lower conflict).

Method: Conventional DiD with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends, estimated separately within subsamples split by baseline incentive conflict. Treatment is pre-program eligibility interacted with post, as in equation (6); standard errors clustered at the firm level. Table VI reports the same estimator for firms with high baseline conflict and firms with lower baseline conflict.

Identification: Within each baseline-conflict subsample, identification follows the main DiD logic: compare post-1996 changes for pre-program-eligible versus ineligible firms, controlling for firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and sector trends. The heterogeneous-effect interpretation assumes the baseline conflict proxy is measured pre-treatment and captures ex ante disagreement between managers and government rather than post-treatment responses. Remaining concern is that subsamples may differ on other dimensions correlated with treatment effects.

Setting: The paper shows that autonomy’s effects are larger where baseline manager-government conflict was higher, proxied by firms that paid dividends in all profitable pre-1997 years. In the high-conflict subsample, eligibility-based autonomy exposure raises value added by 6,848.441 million rupees, capital by 15,411.270 million rupees, and labor spending by 1,306.009 million rupees, with no significant TFPR change. In the lower-conflict subsample, the corresponding estimates are smaller: 3,588.765 for value added, 5,607.132 for capital, and 156.263 for labor, again with no significant TFPR change. This supports the paper’s agency-conflict mechanism and is one of the paper’s main conclusions.

Main role: Heterogeneity by baseline incentive conflict is highlighted in the abstract and introduction as a key substantive finding about when autonomy has larger returns.
Settings.H1272: Section 6.3.2; Table VI panels A-B, cols. (1)-(4) (PDF pp. 16-17).
Settings.G1273:
Treatment: High baseline conflict indicator, defined using pre-1997 dividends: firms that paid dividends in all profitable years before 1997 are coded as having high conflict. The text interprets this as a determinant of autonomy take-up, conditional on eligibility.

Method: Cross-sectional linear probability regressions of autonomy take-up on baseline conflict conditional on eligibility, discussed in the text and reported in Appendix Table A.8. The author uses both pre-program and ever-eligibility variants, with some specifications additionally controlling for pre-program mean sales, mean profits, and their interactions with eligibility. This is a cross-sectional regression adjustment exercise rather than a panel design.

Identification: The paper interprets the pre-treatment baseline conflict proxy as exogenous to later autonomy take-up, conditional on eligibility and controls. The regression is used to show that firms with stronger baseline conflict were more likely to seek/receive autonomy, consistent with the theory that the value of autonomy rises with conflict. Because this is observational cross-section, causal interpretation is limited.

Setting: As supporting evidence for the agency-conflict mechanism, the paper reports that among eligible firms, those with higher baseline conflict—measured by always paying dividends in profitable pre-1997 years—were 34 to 38 percentage points more likely to take up autonomy, depending on specification (Table A.8, discussed in text). The author interprets this as consistent with the theory that autonomy is more valuable when manager and government preferences diverge more strongly.

Main role: This is supporting evidence for the mechanism that autonomy is more valuable when manager-government conflict is larger; the central claims are about outcome effects, not take-up determinants.
Settings.H1273: Section 6.3.2, discussion of Table A.8 (PDF p. 17).
Settings.G1274:
Treatment: Binary proxy for autonomy exposure: pre-program eligibility indicator interacted with post-1996 period.

Method: Conventional DiD with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends, again using pre-program eligibility interacted with post as treatment proxy, for ownership and managerial-turnover outcomes. Event studies are shown in Figure 4. Standard errors are clustered at the firm level.

Identification: Same main DiD identification based on post-1996 differences between pre-program-eligible and ineligible firms, with firm and year fixed effects and sector trends. The purpose is to test alternative mechanisms, not to establish the main treatment effect. Interpretation assumes no differential trends in ownership or vacancy posting absent the program.

Setting: Using the main DiD design, the paper finds no evidence that autonomy worked through changes in ownership or management turnover. Table VII reports an estimated effect of -0.101 on the percentage of central government ownership and 0.028 on the probability of any board vacancy, both statistically insignificant. The author uses these null results to argue that the same managers under unchanged government ownership behaved differently after autonomy was granted.

Main role: These are mechanism-exclusion tests showing that the main effects are not driven by ownership changes or managerial turnover, rather than primary findings themselves.
Settings.H1274: Section 6.3.3; Table VII cols. (1)-(2); Figure 4(a)-(b) (PDF pp. 17-18).
Settings.G1275:
Treatment: Binary treated indicator for firms that entered the program at the Mini-Ratna Category-I level of autonomy, interacted with the post period. Other treated firms are omitted so the contrast is versus controls. This treatment captures autonomy receipt in a subsample where incentive effects from moving to higher autonomy are argued not to drive results.

Method: Restricted-sample conventional DiD designed to net out incentives from earning higher autonomy tiers. The sample keeps treated firms that entered directly at Mini-Ratna Category-I, for which higher autonomy could not be earned during the first 10 program years, and compares them with control firms. The regression includes firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends, with standard errors clustered at the firm level.

Identification: The author exploits institutional details: for the first 10 years, Mini-Ratna Category-I firms could not earn the top Navratna status, so post-treatment behavior among these firms should be less contaminated by dynamic incentives to climb autonomy tiers. Identification still relies on DiD assumptions comparing these treated firms with controls after the program, conditional on fixed effects and sector trends.

Setting: To show that the main effects are not driven only by firms investing to earn higher autonomy, the paper estimates DiD effects for firms that entered directly at Mini-Ratna Category-I and compares them with controls. Table VIII reports positive and significant effects on value added (3,357.860 million rupees), capital (5,503.472 million rupees), and salaries/benefits (398.221 million rupees), with no significant TFPR effect (-0.220). The author interprets these as autonomy effects net of incentive effects from earning additional autonomy tiers.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis showing that the main effects are not solely due to incentives to earn higher autonomy levels.
Settings.G1276:
Treatment: Binary treatment proxy based on any-year eligibility: 1(Ever Eligible) interacted with 1(Post Eligibility), where Post Eligibility turns on in and after the year a firm becomes eligible for autonomy. This captures staggered eligibility-based exposure to autonomy rather than actual autonomy receipt.

Method: Generalized staggered-adoption DiD using eligibility in any year as a proxy for treatment, implemented with the de Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille (2020) estimator rather than conventional TWFE. Equation (7) uses an ever-eligible indicator interacted with a post-eligibility indicator, with the dependent variable in first differences according to the paper’s description. The text explicitly notes that recent DiD concerns apply here because treatment timing is staggered and states that results are reported from the estimator that corrects for such bias. Firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends are included; standard errors are clustered at the firm level.

Identification: Identification comes from staggered changes in eligibility status over time, comparing outcome changes when firms become eligible versus not-yet-eligible/never-eligible firms. The author explicitly addresses endogeneity concerns in staggered TWFE by using the de Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille (2020) estimator, which avoids contaminated comparisons with already-treated units under heterogeneous treatment effects. The key assumptions are parallel trends in untreated potential outcomes across eligibility-timing groups, conditional on fixed effects and sector trends, and that eligibility timing is a valid proxy for autonomy exposure.

Setting: As a robustness check, the paper estimates a generalized staggered DiD using any-year eligibility as treatment and the de Chaisemartin–d’Haultfoeuille estimator. Table IX reports that post-eligibility exposure raises value added by 4,193.012 million rupees, capital by 10,180.911 million rupees, and salaries/benefits by 692.339 million rupees, while the TFPR estimate is -0.247 and insignificant. The author interprets these similar estimates as reinforcing the main conclusion that autonomy increased scale and value added but not productivity.

Main role: This is an important robustness analysis showing similar results when treatment is defined using any eligibility and estimated with a heterogeneity-robust staggered DiD estimator, but the paper’s headline results rely on the pre-program eligibility design.
Settings.H1276: Section 5.2 discussion of equation (7) and modern DiD estimator; Section 7.1; Table IX cols. (1)-(4) (PDF pp. 11, 19-20).
Settings.G1277:
Treatment: Binary proxy for autonomy exposure: pre-program eligibility indicator interacted with post-1996, estimated after dropping 13 just-eligible firms and 9 just-ineligible firms around the profitability criterion.

Method: Conventional DiD robustness analysis excluding firms just eligible and just ineligible around the profitability threshold ('donut' estimator). The specification otherwise follows the main equation (6): firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, 2-digit sector linear trends, and firm-clustered standard errors. It is meant to address concerns that firms near the rule boundary may have lobbied to shape eligibility rules.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same as in the main pre-program eligibility DiD, but observations closest to the eligibility margin are removed to reduce concern that firms with exactly three profitable pre-program years lobbied for rules favorable to themselves, or that near-threshold firms differ in problematic ways. Interpretation still relies on conditional parallel trends among the remaining firms.

Setting: Dropping firms just eligible and just ineligible around the pre-program profitability rule leaves the main results largely intact. Table X reports effects of 4,853.699 million rupees on value added, 11,694.644 million rupees on capital, and 904.438 million rupees on salaries/benefits, with no significant TFPR effect (-0.245). The author interprets this as evidence that lobbying or rule manipulation by near-threshold firms does not explain the main findings.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness check addressing a specific alternative explanation—lobbying or manipulation of rules around the eligibility margin.
Settings.G1278:
Treatment: Binary proxy for autonomy exposure: pre-program eligibility indicator interacted with post-1996.

Method: Conventional DiD on additional borrowing-related outcomes, using the same main specification with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends, clustering standard errors by firm. These results are reported in Appendix Table A.4 and discussed in Section 7.1.

Identification: Same pre-program eligibility DiD strategy as the main design. The author interprets differential post-1996 changes between eligible and ineligible firms as the effect of autonomy on financing patterns, conditional on firm FE, year FE, and sector trends. Concerns remain those of the main design, especially that eligibility is a proxy rather than actual treatment.

Setting: On additional financing outcomes, the paper finds suggestive evidence that autonomy altered borrowing patterns. The text reports that pre-program-eligible firms increased non-central-government borrowing by 7.3 billion rupees, while government loans fell by 4.5 billion rupees. Using matched banker-name data, the paper also finds that eligible firms became 31.4 percentage points more likely to report a private bank as a lender after 1997, and that this was not driven by a higher likelihood of reporting any banker. These results suggest autonomy shifted firms toward more commercially oriented financing.

Main role: These are additional outcomes that help characterize financing channels but are not among the core headline results in the abstract or conclusion.
Settings.H1278: Section 7.1 discussion of Appendix Table A.4 (PDF p. 19).
Settings.G1279:
Treatment: Binary proxy for autonomy exposure: pre-program eligibility indicator interacted with post-1996. For exit, the sample is restricted to firms present in 1992; for capacity utilization, the sample is manufacturing SOEs with available data.

Method: Conventional DiD for additional/robustness outcomes in Appendix Table A.1, using the same main specification with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and 2-digit sector linear trends, firm-clustered standard errors. The text discusses cumulative exit and capacity utilization as substantive robustness outcomes.

Identification: The design again compares post-1996 changes for pre-program-eligible versus ineligible firms. For cumulative exit, the author uses this to assess differential attrition and then restricts main analysis to the balanced panel. For capacity utilization, the goal is to test whether differential demand shocks could explain investment and value-added results. Interpretation depends on the same parallel-trends logic as the main DiD specification.

Setting: Appendix DiD results show that pre-program-eligible firms were 5.8 percentage points less likely to exit, relative to a mean cumulative exit probability of 0.16, though this estimate is not statistically significant at conventional levels (p = 0.13). The author therefore restricts the main analysis to a balanced panel. The same appendix also shows no effect on capacity utilization among manufacturing SOEs, which the paper uses to argue against differential demand shocks as the driver of the main investment results.

Main role: These are robustness and sample-selection checks, used to motivate the balanced-panel restriction and to assess demand-shock confounding.
Settings.H1279: Section 6.2 discussion of Appendix Table A.1; Section 7.2 discussion of Appendix Table A.1 (PDF pp. 12, 20-21).
Settings.G1280:
Treatment: Indicator for the provider/clinic visited being in the private sector rather than the public sector in the representative sample of clinics. This is a binary sector contrast at the interaction level; the SP visits providers on a walk-in basis.

Method: The authors estimate linear regressions of standardized-patient interaction outcomes on an indicator for whether the visited provider is private, using the representative sample of public and private primary-care clinics. The core estimating equation regresses quality measures on a private-provider indicator with standardized-patient fixed effects and case fixed effects; in preferred specifications they add market fixed effects so comparisons are within the same local health-care market, and in a further specification add provider/practice controls such as age, sex, qualifications, and patient load during the visit. This is a regression-adjustment design rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental design; the authors interpret coefficients as differences in patient experience and quality associated with private versus public provision, while acknowledging that representative-sample comparisons combine sector incentives with provider-composition differences.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-provider variation in whether the visited clinic is private versus public, holding constant SP identity and case, and in preferred columns comparing within the same market. The endogeneity concern is that public and private providers differ in qualifications and other observable and unobservable characteristics, so this representative-sample comparison does not isolate incentives from composition. The authors therefore interpret this setting as the typical-patient comparison across sectors, not a clean causal effect of sector incentives alone; assumptions are that conditioning on fixed effects and controls yields informative adjusted contrasts in care quality across sectors for otherwise comparable SP presentations.

Setting: Using linear regressions on the representative sample of clinics, the authors argue that private-sector practice is associated with substantially greater provider effort than public-sector practice for comparable standardized patients. In their preferred market-fixed-effects specification (Table 3, panel B), private providers spend 1.486 more minutes with patients relative to a public-sector mean of 2.388 minutes, complete 7.352 additional percentage points of checklist items relative to a public mean of 15.287 percent, and score 0.668 higher on the IRT quality index. These representative-sample estimates materially support the paper's core claim that the typical patient receives higher effort in private clinics, while also reflecting both sector incentives and provider composition differences.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that private providers exert more effort than public providers in representative comparisons; this setting is one of the paper's central empirical findings.
Settings.H1280: Section III.B, Table 3 columns 1–3, especially Panel B and Panel C (PDF pp. 3778–3780, article PDF pages 14–16).
Settings.G1281:
Treatment: Indicator for the standardized-patient interaction occurring in the doctor's private practice rather than the same doctor's public practice in the dual-practice MBBS sample.

Method: The authors re-estimate their linear quality regressions in the dual-practice sample of MBBS doctors observed in both their public and private practices. Outcomes are regressed on an indicator for being in the doctor's private practice, with SP fixed effects and case fixed effects; preferred specifications add district fixed effects and practice-level controls. The design compares the same doctor's behavior across public and private practice settings for the same standardized cases, though the main specification does not include doctor fixed effects because the angina case is not observed in both practices for each doctor; the paper notes results are unchanged with provider fixed effects when feasible. This is an identifying fixed-effects/within-provider comparison rather than DiD or IV.

Identification: Identification uses within-doctor variation across practice setting: the same MBBS doctor is observed in public and private clinics, facing the same standardized cases. This addresses confounding from fixed doctor knowledge and many provider characteristics, isolating the role of practice setting and incentives more cleanly than representative-sector comparisons. Remaining concerns include differential case completion due to higher public-sector absence, different practice conditions, and the lack of doctor fixed effects in the main pooled specification for all cases, though the paper argues random assignment of the angina case across practices and robustness with provider fixed effects mitigate these concerns.

Setting: In the dual-practice sample, the authors interpret the same doctor's private practice as causing substantially higher effort than his public practice. In Table 3, panel B, private practice increases consultation time by 1.514 minutes from a public-practice mean of 1.561 minutes, raises checklist completion by 8.977 percentage points from a public mean of 17.720 percent, and increases the IRT quality score by 0.759. The paper summarizes this as doctors doubling consultation length and completing about 60 percent more checklist items in private practice. This setting is core to the paper because it is intended to isolate the effect of market versus administrative accountability holding doctor characteristics constant.

Main role: The paper's second central finding is that the same doctors provide higher quality in their private than public practices; this dual-practice comparison is explicitly highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H1281: Section III.B, Table 3 columns 4–6, especially Panel B and Panel C (PDF pp. 3778–3781, article PDF pages 14–17).
Settings.G1282:
Treatment: Indicator for the visited provider being private rather than public in the representative sample, for unstable angina and asthma SP visits.

Method: The authors estimate linear regressions for diagnosis outcomes in the representative sample, regressing whether a diagnosis was given and whether it was correct on a private-provider indicator, with SP and case fixed effects, market fixed effects in preferred specifications, and additional provider controls in extended specifications. The sample for diagnosis excludes the dysentery proxy case and uses only unstable angina and asthma. This is a regression-adjustment comparison across sectors in representative clinics, not a quasi-experimental design.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-provider sector status in the representative sample, with constant SP and case composition and within-market comparisons in preferred columns. The main endogeneity concern is compositional differences between public and private providers; thus these estimates describe adjusted sector differences in typical diagnostic performance rather than a clean causal effect of sector incentives alone. The authors rely on standardized patients to eliminate patient sorting and use market fixed effects and controls to reduce confounding.

Setting: For diagnosis outcomes in the representative sample, the authors conclude that private providers are more likely to pronounce some diagnosis but are not more likely to pronounce a correct one. In Table 4, panel B, being private increases the probability of giving any diagnosis by 0.188 from a public mean of 0.263, but changes correct diagnosis conditional on diagnosing by only -0.019 and correct diagnosis unconditionally by 0.023, relative to a very low public mean of 0.039. This supports the paper's broader claim that higher private-sector effort in the representative sample does not translate into better diagnosis accuracy.

Main role: A key headline result is that private providers in the representative sample are no better than public providers on correct diagnosis despite greater effort; this diagnosis setting is part of the main comparison across sectors.
Settings.H1282: Section III.C, Table 4 columns 1–3, especially Panel B and accompanying text (PDF pp. 3782–3783, article PDF pages 18–19).
Settings.G1283:
Treatment: Indicator for an SP seeing the doctor in his private practice rather than his public practice in the dual-practice MBBS sample, for unstable angina and asthma cases.

Method: The authors estimate diagnosis regressions in the dual-practice MBBS sample, comparing the same doctor's private and public practices using linear models with SP and case fixed effects, district fixed effects in preferred specifications, and additional controls. The diagnosis sample includes only unstable angina and asthma. This is a within-doctor practice-setting comparison implemented with fixed-effects-style regression adjustment.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing the same doctor's diagnostic behavior across public and private practice settings for standardized cases, which nets out fixed doctor ability and many provider-level confounds. Remaining concerns include non-completion due to public absence and limited power. The paper treats this as more informative about incentive effects than representative-sample comparisons.

Setting: In the dual-practice sample, the same doctor's private practice is not associated with materially higher diagnosis accuracy overall. In Table 4, panel B, private practice changes the probability of giving any diagnosis by 0.092, correct diagnosis conditional on diagnosis by -0.056, and correct diagnosis unconditionally by 0.025, from public-practice means of 0.382, 0.385, and 0.147 respectively. The authors interpret this as showing little overall difference in diagnosis rates or correctness across the same doctor's public and private practices, despite the large private-practice increase in effort.

Main role: The dual-practice diagnosis comparison is substantively important but secondary relative to the central findings on effort and treatment; the paper emphasizes that there is little difference in diagnosis across practices except in some case-specific robustness.
Settings.H1283: Section III.C, Table 4 columns 4–6, especially Panel B and accompanying text (PDF pp. 3782–3783, article PDF pages 18–19).
Settings.G1284:
Treatment: Indicator for the visited provider being private rather than public in the representative sample, for unstable angina and asthma interactions.

Method: The authors estimate linear regressions of treatment outcomes on a private-provider indicator in the representative sample, using only the unstable angina and asthma SP cases. Specifications include SP and case fixed effects, then market fixed effects, and then provider controls. Outcomes include indicators for receiving at least one correct treatment, a palliative treatment, an unnecessary treatment, only a correct treatment, any antibiotic, and the total number of medicines dispensed and/or prescribed. This is a regression-adjusted representative-sector comparison.

Identification: Identification uses sector status across providers in the representative sample, controlling for SP, case, and local market. The main concern is selection/composition: private and public providers differ in qualifications and other traits, so these regressions yield adjusted representative differences in treatment patterns rather than a clean incentive effect. The standardized-patient design eliminates patient case-mix differences, which is the paper's main argument for interpreting these coefficients substantively.

Setting: For treatment outcomes in the representative sample, the authors find little evidence that private providers outperform public providers despite greater effort. In Table 5, panel B, the private-provider coefficient is 0.051 for correct treatment, 0.040 for palliative treatment, 0.095 for unnecessary treatment, -0.020 for correct treatment only, 0.086 for antibiotic use, and 0.894 additional medicines. Public-provider means are 0.211 for correct treatment, 0.526 for palliative treatment, 0.737 for unnecessary treatment, 0.026 for correct treatment only, 0.263 for antibiotic use, and 2.092 medicines. The paper interprets this as private providers performing no better on diagnosis and treatment in representative comparisons, while tending to provide more medicines.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state that private providers in the representative sample recommend correct treatments equally often as public providers and are similarly likely to offer unnecessary treatments; this is a main substantive result.
Settings.H1284: Section III.D, Table 5 columns 1–6, especially Panel B and accompanying text (PDF pp. 3783–3786, article PDF pages 19–22).
Settings.G1285:
Treatment: Indicator for the interaction taking place in the doctor's private practice rather than his public practice in the dual-practice MBBS sample, for unstable angina and asthma cases.

Method: The authors estimate treatment regressions in the dual-practice MBBS sample, comparing a doctor's private and public practices for unstable angina and asthma cases using linear models with SP and case fixed effects, district fixed effects, and optionally practice-level controls. Outcomes mirror the representative-sample treatment outcomes: correct, palliative, unnecessary treatment, correct treatment only, antibiotic use, and number of medicines. This is a within-doctor fixed-effects-style comparison of practice settings.

Identification: Identification relies on within-doctor comparisons across private and public practices for the same standardized cases, intended to isolate incentive effects while holding doctor knowledge fixed. Threats include public-practice non-completion due to doctor absence, potential differences in practice environments, and possible strategic effort diversion, though the paper argues robustness checks support the main interpretation.

Setting: In the dual-practice sample, the authors conclude that practicing privately increases the same doctor's treatment quality. In Table 5, panel B, private practice raises correct treatment by 0.156 from a public-practice mean of 0.373, lowers palliative treatment by 0.127 from 0.637, leaves unnecessary treatment essentially unchanged at -0.022 relative to a public mean of 0.833, raises correct treatment only by 0.018 from 0.020, lowers antibiotic use by 0.139 from 0.490, and has no effect on the number of medicines (-0.002 from a public mean of 2.833). The paper interprets these as private-practice treatment protocols strictly dominating public-practice ones for the same doctors, supporting its claim that market accountability improves quality when administrative accountability is weak.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that the same doctors are more likely to offer correct treatment in private practice and show no greater overtreatment there; this is a central result.
Settings.H1285: Section III.D, Table 5 columns 7–12, especially Panel B and accompanying text (PDF pp. 3783–3786, article PDF pages 19–22).
Settings.G1286:
Treatment: Continuous transaction price/fee charged in rupees by the private provider for the completed interaction, including medicines dispensed. The paper interprets this as the market reward/incentive variable associated with quality.

Method: The authors estimate regressions of prices charged by private providers on quality measures in private-sector interactions. They report bivariate ('binary correlations') and multiple linear regressions with SP, case, and district fixed effects; samples are the representative private sample, the dual private-practice sample, and a pooled private sample. The key substantive interpretation is that market prices reward some dimensions of provider quality and also unnecessary treatment. This is observational regression adjustment, not a causal design, but the paper makes causal/structural claims about what market incentives reward.

Identification: The paper uses cross-interaction variation in fees charged within private-sector visits to estimate which aspects of care are associated with higher prices. The key economic concern is simultaneity and omitted variables: prices and quality are jointly determined by provider type, qualifications, and transaction characteristics. The authors therefore frame these estimates as correlates showing what the market rewards rather than clean causal price effects on quality or vice versa. Fixed effects for SP, case, and district help remove some mechanical differences across cases and locations.

Setting: The pricing regressions are used to argue that unregulated market incentives reward both useful and socially costly aspects of care. In Table 6, the authors show positive associations between fees charged and time spent, checklist completion, and in bivariate regressions correct treatment, while also showing strong positive associations with unnecessary treatment and the number of medicines dispensed, and a negative association with referrals. In the pooled multiple regression, for example, each additional minute is associated with 0.805 Rs higher fees, each percentage point of checklist completion with 0.309 Rs higher fees, unnecessary treatment with 5.545 Rs higher fees, and each additional dispensed medicine with 3.937 Rs higher fees. These results support the paper's central interpretation that market accountability increases effort and some dimensions of quality but also encourages overtreatment.

Main role: A major contribution highlighted in the abstract and introduction is that market prices are positively correlated with checklist completion and correct treatment but also with unnecessary treatments; this pricing analysis is central to the paper's interpretation of market accountability.
Settings.H1286: Section IV.A, Table 6 columns 1–6 and accompanying discussion (PDF pp. 3788–3790, article PDF pages 24–26).
Settings.G1287:
Treatment: Continuous public-sector compensation measure: either log monthly salary or a desirability index of the public posting. The paper interprets these as incentive/reward variables in the public sector.

Method: The authors regress public-sector compensation measures on provider quality measures using public observations only. They estimate bivariate and multiple regressions of log monthly salary, and separately a posting desirability index for PHC/CHC providers, on checklist completion, time spent, and correct treatment, with district fixed effects and provider covariates. The substantive interpretation is that public-sector pay and posting desirability do not reward quality of care. This is observational regression adjustment.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-public-provider variation in salaries and posting desirability, conditional on district and covariates. Endogeneity concerns are substantial because pay and posting reflect seniority, qualifications, and assignment rules rather than experimental incentives; the authors use these regressions descriptively to support a causal interpretation of weak public accountability and lack of quality-linked rewards. The assumptions are that if the public sector rewarded quality, observable positive correlations would appear after controlling for basic covariates.

Setting: The authors use regressions of public-sector pay and posting desirability on quality to argue that public administrative incentives do not reward effort or treatment quality. Table 7 shows essentially zero associations of log salary and posting desirability with checklist completion, time spent, and correct treatment once controls are included. The paper summarizes this as finding no correlation between salaries or desirability of posting and any measure of quality delivered. This is central to the paper's comparison between market accountability in the private sector and administrative accountability in the public sector.

Main role: The absence of any correlation between public salaries/postings and quality is directly highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as a central contrast with private-market incentives.
Settings.H1287: Section IV.A, Table 7 and accompanying discussion (PDF pp. 3790–3791, article PDF pages 26–27).
Settings.G1288:
Treatment: Indicator for the observed clinic/provider being private rather than public in the representative sample of real patient interactions.

Method: As an external-validity and substantive robustness exercise, the authors estimate regressions on direct observations of real patient-provider interactions in the representative sample, regressing interaction characteristics on a private-provider indicator. Specifications move from no controls to market/district fixed effects and then patient and provider controls. Outcomes are time spent, total questions asked, whether a physical examination was done, whether medicines were dispensed/prescribed, and the number of medicines. This is an observational regression-adjustment comparison, used to support causal interpretation of broader sector differences in effort and treatment intensity.

Identification: The identifying variation is again sector status across observed real-patient interactions, with fixed effects and rich controls for patient symptoms and provider characteristics in preferred specifications. The main concern is patient sorting and case-mix differences across sectors; unlike the SP analyses, real-patient regressions cannot fully standardize illness severity. The authors use them as supporting evidence because the patterns match the SP findings.

Setting: Using observed real patient interactions in the representative sample, the authors find similar sector differences to those in the SP data: private providers spend more time, ask more questions, and are more likely to examine patients physically, while also giving more medicines on average. In Table 8, panel C, being private is associated with 1.190 extra minutes, 0.654 more questions, a 0.522 higher probability of physical examination, a near-zero 0.009 change in whether medicines are dispensed/prescribed, and 0.602 more medicines. The authors use this to argue that the higher-effort private-public gap likely extends beyond the three SP cases.

Main role: These are robustness and external-validity analyses supporting the standardized-patient results rather than standalone core evidence.
Settings.H1288: Section V.A, Table 8 columns 1–5, especially Panel C and accompanying discussion (PDF pp. 3791–3793, article PDF pages 27–29).
Settings.G1289:
Treatment: Indicator for the real patient interaction occurring in the doctor's private practice rather than public practice in the dual sample.

Method: As a robustness exercise, the authors estimate analogous regressions on real patient-provider interactions in the dual sample, comparing the same doctors' public and private practices. Specifications include district fixed effects and then patient and provider controls. Outcomes are time spent, total questions asked, physical examination, medicines dispensed/prescribed, and total medicines. This is a within-doctor practice-setting comparison using real-patient data.

Identification: Identification uses within-doctor variation across public and private practices in observed real-patient interactions, which helps address doctor fixed heterogeneity. Remaining concerns include patient sorting and different case mix across the two practices; the paper responds by reporting symptom overlap and similar results after patient controls. The purpose is to validate the SP-based incentive interpretation.

Setting: In the dual sample of real patient interactions, the same providers again exhibit more effort in private practice. In Table 8, panel C, private practice is associated with 1.570 additional minutes, 0.561 more questions, and a 0.072 higher probability of physical examination, with essentially no difference in medicine use (-0.016 for dispensing/prescribing and -0.016 in total medicines). The authors interpret this as remarkably similar to the SP dual-sample results: higher effort in private practice without more medicines, supporting the broader validity of their main findings.

Main role: This is a robustness/external-validity check reinforcing the dual-practice SP findings, not a primary headline result.
Settings.H1289: Section V.A, Table 8 columns 6–10, especially Panel C and accompanying discussion (PDF pp. 3791–3793, article PDF pages 27–29).
Settings.G1290:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: total value of directors’ residential real estate holdings, measured in pounds, holding directors/properties fixed in 2002 and updating via regional house price indices; regressions scale this by lagged firm turnover. The same setting also reports the effect of continuous firm corporate real estate value, measured as 2002 land-and-buildings book value updated by the firm-region house price index, also scaled by lagged turnover.

Method: Baseline linear panel fixed-effects regression of firm investment on directors’ residential real estate and firm-owned corporate real estate, estimated on UK firm-year data from 2002–2014. The specification includes firm fixed effects, region×time fixed effects, and 2-digit industry×time fixed effects, plus lagged cash and profits and additional firm/director controls interacted with the firm-region house price index. Residential real estate is constructed by fixing each firm’s directors and their homes in 2002 and updating values using directors’ regional house-price indices; corporate real estate fixes 2002 land-and-buildings book value and updates using the firm-region house-price index. Standard errors are clustered by firm NUTS3 region. Identification comes from within-firm changes in the values of fixed initial real estate holdings induced by regional house-price movements after absorbing common region-time and industry-time shocks.

Identification: The paper argues that endogenous levels of property holdings are addressed by fixing directors’ homes and firm property at 2002 levels and using only subsequent house-price-driven valuation changes. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm/director heterogeneity; region×time fixed effects absorb local macroeconomic conditions in the firm’s region; industry×time fixed effects absorb common industry shocks; additional director and firm observables interacted with local prices aim to absorb heterogeneity in sensitivity to housing shocks. Remaining concerns are that director house values in 2002 may still correlate with latent traits and that house prices may proxy for local demand or bank credit supply, which motivate later robustness settings.

Setting: In the baseline panel FE design, the authors estimate that a £1 increase in the value of a firm’s directors’ homes raises firm investment by £0.0298, while a £1 increase in corporate real estate raises investment by £0.0511. Investment is measured as change in fixed assets plus depreciation, scaled by lagged turnover. Identification relies on within-firm variation from regional house-price changes applied to fixed 2002 real estate holdings, with firm, region-time, and industry-time fixed effects plus controls. This setting delivers the paper’s central causal claim that directors’ home values relax financing constraints and increase investment.

Main role: This is the paper’s core microeconometric result emphasized in the abstract, introduction, Section IV, and conclusion: £1 more director home value increases firm investment by about £0.03, compared with about £0.05 for corporate real estate.
Settings.H1290: Section IV.A, Table 5 col. (7), physical PDF page(s) 18–20 (article pp. 2242–2244).
Settings.G1291:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value in pounds, constructed by fixing 2002 directors/properties and updating with regional house price indices; scaled by lagged turnover.

Method: Same baseline linear panel FE design as Table 5, but with different outcome variables capturing labor inputs rather than investment. The authors estimate the effect of directors’ residential real estate on the firm’s wage bill and employment using firm fixed effects, region×time FE, industry×time FE, and the same control structure. These results are reported in online Appendix Section A.12 and summarized in the main text.

Identification: Uses the same identification argument as the baseline FE design: within-firm variation from house-price-driven changes in the value of fixed 2002 director real estate, with firm FE and rich region-time/industry-time FE to absorb local and sectoral shocks. Endogeneity concerns are analogous to the investment specification.

Setting: Using the same high-dimensional fixed-effects framework as the investment regressions, the authors report that a £1 increase in directors’ residential real estate increases the firm’s wage bill by £0.033 and employment by 0.0009; they interpret this as about one extra worker for a £1.1 million increase in house values. These are supplementary causal results showing that the collateral channel affects labor inputs as well as fixed investment.

Main role: These are supporting outcomes used to show that higher director home values affect other real firm margins beyond investment, but they are not the headline estimates in the abstract or conclusion.
Settings.H1291: Section IV.A text referring to online Appendix Section A.12, physical PDF page(s) 20 (article p. 2244).
Settings.G1292:
Treatment: Continuous endogenous treatments: directors’ residential real estate value and firm corporate real estate value, both in pounds and scaled by lagged turnover. These are instrumented using predicted regional house-price indices based on interest-rate × housing-supply-constraint interactions.

Method: 2SLS robustness design instrumenting firm-level residential and corporate real estate values with alternative regional house price indices predicted from the interaction of aggregate mortgage interest rates and regional housing supply constraints (share of developable land developed by 1990, following Mian and Sufi 2011; Chaney, Sraer, and Thesmar 2012; Chetty, Sándor, and Szeidl 2017). The IVs are used to reconstruct Residential RE and Corporate RE, and the baseline investment equation with firm, region×time, and industry×time fixed effects is re-estimated on the IV sample.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from exogenous shifts in regional house prices induced by the interaction of aggregate mortgage interest rates with regional housing supply constraints. The paper argues this isolates plausibly exogenous house-price movements unrelated to firm-specific investment decisions. Assumptions are standard IV relevance and exclusion: conditional on fixed effects and controls, the predicted house-price component affects investment only through residential/corporate collateral values.

Setting: In the IV robustness specification, instrumented increases in directors’ residential real estate still raise investment: the IV coefficient is 0.0269, close to the baseline 0.0298, while the IV coefficient on corporate real estate is 0.0467. The design instruments regional house prices using interest-rate × housing-supply-constraint interactions and then reconstructs firm-level collateral values. This setting is used to reinforce the paper’s main causal claim by addressing the possibility that local firm activity itself affects observed house prices.

Main role: The IV is a major robustness analysis highlighted in the introduction and Section IV.B to support the paper’s central causal interpretation against concerns that firm behavior directly moves local house prices or that price changes proxy for omitted shocks.
Settings.H1292: Section IV.B, Table 6 col. (8), physical PDF page(s) 20–21 (article pp. 2244–2245).
Settings.G1293:
Treatment: Continuous treatment variants of directors’ residential real estate value. Depending on column, the treatment assumes all directors have the same initial house value, all live in the firm’s region, all firms have the same number of directors, or uses only the component of directors’ regional house-price variation orthogonal to firm-region house prices; all scaled by lagged turnover.

Method: Decomposition robustness regressions that replace the baseline Residential RE variable with alternative constructed measures that switch off particular sources of variation: same-house, same-region, same-number-of-directors, same-region-and-number, and orthogonalized-price-index measures. All are estimated in the baseline firm FE + region×time FE + industry×time FE framework with controls. The purpose is to isolate whether the causal signal comes from initial house values, regional price dynamics, or number of directors.

Identification: The strategy tests whether the estimated effect depends on initial director home values, spatial price heterogeneity, or director count. If same-house variation yields zero effect while same-region remains similar to baseline, the paper interprets this as showing that price growth alone is not enough absent exposure via initial home values, and that geographic differences in directors’ house prices matter above firm-region prices for firms with at least one director outside the firm’s region.

Setting: When the authors force all directors to have the same initial house value, the estimated investment effect disappears (-0.0001), whereas assuming all directors live in the firm’s region leaves the estimate near the baseline (0.0308). Assuming all firms have the same number of directors yields 0.0277, and the orthogonalized director-region price component is 0.0334 among firms with at least one director living outside the firm region. The authors interpret these decompositions as evidence that exposure through directors’ initial house values is essential and that director-region house price movements matter over and above firm-region prices.

Main role: These are substantive identification robustness checks unpacking the source of identifying variation behind the baseline result rather than standalone headline results.
Settings.H1293: Section IV.B, Table 7 cols. (1)–(6), physical PDF page(s) 21–23 (article pp. 2245–2247).
Settings.G1294:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value, sometimes restricted to homes bought before 1995, or separated into values of current 2002 directors who remain at the firm versus those who have left. Measured in pounds, scaled by lagged turnover.

Method: Additional robustness regressions aimed at the endogeneity of initial director real estate holdings. The baseline FE model is re-estimated on subsamples or with treatment splits: excluding houses purchased 1995–2002; separating real estate of 2002 directors who remain at the firm versus those who later leave; adding controls for director skill based on performance at other firms; and controlling for director remuneration. All use firm, region×time, and industry×time fixed effects.

Identification: Identification remains within-firm house-price-driven variation in fixed initial housing exposure, while the restrictions and controls test whether results survive when initial housing choices are more historically predetermined and whether effects disappear when the relevant director leaves. The leaver test is especially intended to distinguish true collateral effects from omitted firm sensitivity to local housing cycles.

Setting: The investment effect of directors’ home values remains similar when focusing only on houses purchased before 1995 (coefficient 0.0288), when controlling for director skill from other firms (0.0310), and when controlling for director pay (0.0469 on a smaller sample). Splitting 2002 directors by later tenure shows that real estate of directors still present predicts investment (0.0257), while real estate of directors who have left does not (0.0082), with a reported p-value of 0.0791 for equality. The authors interpret this as evidence against omitted firm-level sensitivity stories and in favor of a causal financing channel tied to active directors.

Main role: These are important robustness tests supporting the main interpretation by addressing omitted firm- and director-level heterogeneity and endogenous initial housing choices.
Settings.H1294: Section IV.B, Table 8 cols. (2)–(6), physical PDF page(s) 23–25 (article pp. 2247–2249).
Settings.G1295:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value, measured in pounds via fixed-2002 exposure updated by regional house prices, scaled by lagged turnover.

Method: Dynamic local-projection version of the baseline FE model. For each horizon h, the dependent variable is future investment t+h and the same regressors and FE structure are used: firm FE, region×time FE, and industry×time FE with controls. This traces the impulse response of investment to a contemporaneous, persistent increase in residential real estate.

Identification: Uses the same within-firm collateral-value variation as the baseline but applies local projections to assess dynamic responses. The interpretation assumes the same identifying assumptions as the baseline FE setting and treats the residential real estate shock as effectively permanent because the collateral measure behaves like a random walk in their data.

Setting: The dynamic FE local projections show that the contemporaneous investment response of about £0.03 per £1 rise in director home values persists over roughly the current year and next three years before fading, implying a cumulative investment increase of about £0.12 for a permanent £1 increase in Residential RE. Placebo lead effects at t-2 and t-1 are insignificant. The authors view this pattern as consistent with adjustment costs, time-to-build, or delayed lending responses under collateral constraints.

Main role: This dynamic specification is a substantive follow-up showing timing and persistence of the main effect rather than introducing a separate identification strategy.
Settings.H1295: Section IV.C, Figure 3, physical PDF page(s) 26–27 (article pp. 2250–2251).
Settings.G1296:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value in pounds, scaled by lagged turnover, interacted with indicators for firm financial-constraint groups (low/medium/high within year; low/high within firm over time). Corporate real estate is similarly interacted in the same setting.

Method: Heterogeneity regressions interacting residential and corporate real estate with measures of firm financial constraints based on a re-estimated Whited-Wu index. The baseline FE specification is run by tertiles of the index within year and by above/below the firm’s own median index over time, with firm, region×time, and industry×time fixed effects plus controls.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same as the baseline FE model; the added assumption is that differential slopes by financial-constraint groups reveal whether the collateral channel is stronger when financing frictions are tighter. The Whited-Wu style index is used as a proxy for financing constraints, acknowledging measurement error.

Setting: The authors find that investment is more sensitive to directors’ home values among financially constrained firms. In the within-year split, the Residential RE coefficient rises from 0.0216 in the low-index tertile to 0.0282 in the high-index tertile. Using within-firm variation in constraints gives a sharper contrast: 0.0230 when the firm is below its own median constraint level versus 0.0310 when above, with p-value 0.0003 for equality. These results are interpreted as evidence that the home-value effect operates by easing financial constraints.

Main role: Heterogeneity by financial constraints is central to the paper’s mechanism argument that the effect runs through collateral constraints, highlighted in the abstract and introduction.
Settings.H1296: Section V.A, Table 9 cols. (2)–(6), physical PDF page(s) 27–28 (article pp. 2251–2252).
Settings.G1297:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value in pounds, scaled by lagged turnover, interacted with indicators for firm size (<250 versus >=250 employees; <£10m versus >=£10m assets) and for whether residential real estate divided by lagged total assets is >=15% versus <15%. Corporate real estate is also interacted in the same location for comparison.

Method: Heterogeneity regressions interacting Residential RE and Corporate RE with firm size measures and with an indicator for whether directors’ residential real estate is at least 15 percent of lagged total assets. The same baseline FE estimator with firm, region×time, and industry×time fixed effects and controls is used. Some specifications further split jointly by employment size and Residential RE-to-assets ratio.

Identification: Same within-firm collateral-valuation variation as the baseline FE model, with heterogeneous treatment effects estimated across size and exposure groups. The 15 percent threshold is interpreted as capturing whether directors’ homes are material enough to matter as collateral upon liquidation.

Setting: The effect of directors’ home values on investment is concentrated in firms for which directors’ homes are valuable relative to the firm. When Residential RE is at least 15 percent of lagged total assets, the coefficient is 0.0333; when below 15 percent, it is -0.0136, with p-value 0.0831 for equality. In a four-way split, firms with high residential-real-estate-to-assets ratios respond whether they have fewer than 250 employees (0.0275) or at least 250 employees (0.0753), while low-ratio firms do not. The authors interpret this as evidence that what matters is whether directors’ homes are a meaningful collateral source, not simply firm size.

Main role: This heterogeneity evidence is central to the paper’s mechanism and aggregation arguments, especially the claim that the effect is concentrated where directors’ homes are meaningful collateral relative to the firm’s asset base.
Settings.H1297: Section V.A, Table 10 cols. (1)–(8), physical PDF page(s) 28–30 (article pp. 2252–2254).
Settings.G1298:
Treatment: Continuous treatments: directors’ residential real estate value and firm corporate real estate value, both in pounds and scaled by lagged turnover. In some columns, Residential RE is interacted with joint categories of firm employment size and whether Residential RE/Assets is at least 15%.

Method: Panel FE regressions of financing outcomes on residential and corporate real estate, using the same baseline structure with firm FE, region×time FE, industry×time FE, and controls. Outcomes are changes in issued equity, director loans, short-term debt, and long-term debt. Additional heterogeneity specifications split debt responses by employment size and the Residential RE-to-assets threshold.

Identification: Same within-firm variation in real-estate-based collateral values as in the investment baseline. The financing outcomes are interpreted causally under the same assumptions, with the goal of determining whether the collateral channel operates through external debt, insider finance, or equity injections.

Setting: A £1 increase in directors’ residential real estate raises issued equity by 0.0086 and short-term debt by 0.0210, with negligible effects on director loans (-0.0001) and long-term debt (0.0023). For corporate real estate, the response is mainly debt: 0.0318 in short-term debt and 0.0373 in long-term debt. In heterogeneity splits, debt responses to Residential RE appear only for firms where directors’ homes are at least 15 percent of assets; among such firms, smaller firms respond mainly through short-term debt (0.0222) while larger firms respond mainly through long-term debt (0.0969). The authors interpret this as evidence that rising home values relax financing constraints primarily by expanding debt capacity, likely through increasingly valuable personal guarantees.

Main role: These financing regressions are a central mechanism exercise showing how higher director home values translate into firm funding, especially via short-term debt and some equity issuance.
Settings.H1298: Section V.B, Table 11 cols. (1)–(8), physical PDF page(s) 30–32 (article pp. 2254–2256).
Settings.G1299:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value in pounds, scaled by lagged turnover, separated into Residential RE of shareholder-directors and Residential RE of non-shareholder directors.

Method: Private-firm heterogeneity regressions splitting directors’ residential real estate into holdings of directors who are shareholders versus non-shareholders. Estimated with the baseline FE structure—firm FE, region×time FE, industry×time FE, and controls—on samples where both measures are non-missing or nonzero. This tests whether ownership status governs the collateral effect.

Identification: Uses the same within-firm, house-price-driven variation as the baseline but decomposes exposure by director ownership status. The paper’s argument is that if the mechanism is collateral provided by owners, shareholder-director home values should matter more than non-shareholder managers’ home values; pure omitted-sensitivity stories would not predict this split.

Setting: Among private firms, the investment response is driven by the home values of shareholder-directors rather than non-shareholder directors. On the sample where both components are non-missing, the coefficient is 0.0393–0.0394 for shareholder residential real estate and about 0.0117–0.0139 for non-shareholder residential real estate. On the stricter sample where both are nonzero, the shareholder coefficient rises to 0.0770 while the non-shareholder coefficient is 0.0168. The authors interpret this as evidence that the collateral channel depends on directors’ ownership incentives to support the firm with personal assets.

Main role: This is key mechanism evidence: the paper argues the effect should be stronger for directors with ownership stakes because they have incentives to pledge personal assets; this is highlighted in the abstract and discussion.
Settings.H1299: Section V.C, Table 12 cols. (2)–(8), physical PDF page(s) 32–34 (article pp. 2256–2258).
Settings.G1300:
Treatment: Continuous treatment: directors’ residential real estate value in pounds, scaled by lagged turnover, interacted with indicators for high versus low average director LTV (threshold 85%), with additional interactions by firm financial-constraint group and by whether the residential real estate belongs to shareholder versus non-shareholder directors in private firms.

Method: Heterogeneity regressions interacting Residential RE with directors’ loan-to-value (LTV) ratio on their homes, sometimes jointly with the firm financial-constraint index and with shareholder status. The baseline FE specification with firm FE, region×time FE, industry×time FE, and controls is re-estimated on the subsample where average director LTV can be observed.

Identification: Same identifying variation as the baseline FE model, with heterogeneous slopes by directors’ leverage and firm constraints. The idea is that if home values matter by relaxing collateral constraints, the effect should be strongest when both the firm is constrained and directors have little spare home equity or high leverage.

Setting: Investment responds more strongly to directors’ home values when directors are highly levered. On the LTV-observed sample, the coefficient on Residential RE is 0.0450 for firms whose directors’ average LTV is at least 85 percent versus 0.0335 below that threshold. The contrast sharpens when combined with firm financial constraints: among highly constrained firms the coefficient is 0.0499 for high-LTV directors versus 0.0305 for low-LTV directors. In private firms, the positive high-LTV response is concentrated among shareholder-directors (0.0414 versus 0.0153 for low LTV). The authors interpret this as evidence that directors’ personal balance-sheet tightness amplifies the collateral channel.

Main role: This is core mechanism evidence supporting the collateral-constraint interpretation: the paper predicts stronger effects when directors are personally more levered and thus more constrained.
Settings.H1300: Section V.C, Table 13 cols. (2)–(8), physical PDF page(s) 34–36 (article pp. 2258–2260).
Settings.G1301:
Treatment: Continuous treatment variants: baseline directors’ residential real estate value; residential equity value; or contemporaneous residential real estate instrumented by baseline Residential RE. In the large-sample variant the treatment is Residential RE scaled by lagged total assets rather than turnover. Some specifications also include continuous Corporate RE.

Method: Further robustness FE regressions altering outcome and treatment measurement and sample coverage. Variants include excluding real-estate investment from the investment outcome, replacing Residential RE with Residential Equity, instrumenting contemporaneous director real estate with baseline Residential RE to allow directors/moves after 2002, interacting effects by firm age and by whether local house prices are rising or falling, and estimating on a much larger sample using change in total assets scaled by lagged total assets with firm, region×time, and industry×time FE.

Identification: All variants retain the panel FE identification idea of within-firm changes in collateral values induced by house-price movements after fixing initial exposure, though the contemporaneous-value specification explicitly uses IV to address endogenous director turnover and moves. The maximal-sample regression sacrifices controls for coverage but preserves firm and time-varying regional and industry fixed effects.

Setting: The main effect remains under a wide range of alternative measurements. When the outcome excludes investment in land and buildings, the Residential RE coefficient is 0.0176. Replacing home values with home equity yields 0.0316. Instrumenting contemporaneous director real estate with baseline Residential RE gives 0.0388. The response is similar for younger (<10 years, 0.0338) and older (>=10 years, 0.0290) firms, and during rising (0.0293) and falling (0.0351) house-price periods. In a maximal sample of about 2.07 million firm-years using change in total assets scaled by lagged total assets, the coefficient is 0.0228. These robustness results support the paper’s central claim that higher director home values causally increase firm activity.

Main role: These are broad robustness checks showing the main effect is not an artifact of property revaluation, outcome definition, sample selection, or focusing only on young firms or periods of rising prices.
Settings.H1301: Section VII, Table 14 cols. (1)–(8), physical PDF page(s) 41–42 (article pp. 2265–2266).
Settings.G1302:
Treatment: Experimentally assigned treatment conditions represented by indicator variables in the regression: primarily an indicator for Unstable versus Stable search-parameter environment; additionally indicators for professionals, limited-information conditions, and adjustment-speed categories. The focal treatment carrying the main causal comparison in the table is the Unstable market dummy (1=unstable parameters, 0=stable parameters).

Method: The authors estimate linear OLS regressions at the market-block level in which the dependent variable is the average median posted price across the four periods in a treatment block. Regressors are treatment-condition indicators: an Unstable-market dummy, a Professionals dummy, dummies for limited-information conditions (no counterfactual projection; no information on others’ prices), and fast and slow adjustment-speed dummies, with omitted categories Stable market, students, high information, and medium adjustment speed. Standard errors are clustered by market. The coefficient interpretation is causal because treatment conditions are experimentally assigned within sessions/markets, though the paper does not frame this as a formal RCT estimator.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized/controlled variation in laboratory treatment conditions. Because treatment indicators are assigned by design across blocks and sessions, the OLS coefficients compare outcomes across exogenous environments. The main concern is finite-sample noise and clustering at the market level, not confounding from self-selection. The regression summarizes causal effects of the experimental conditions on market-level median prices.

Setting: Using OLS on block-level averages, the authors interpret treatment assignments as causing changes in median prices. In Table 3, the Unstable-market coefficient is -0.163 (SE 0.008), implying that unstable search parameters reduce median posted price by 0.163 price units relative to stable parameters, holding other assigned conditions constant. Limited information raises median prices: no counterfactual projection by 0.052 and no information on others’ prices by 0.057; fast and slow adjustment speeds each reduce the median slightly relative to medium speed (-0.019 and -0.018). This regression is part of the paper’s core evidence on how search-friction parameters and information conditions affect price levels.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion emphasize treatment effects on central tendency of prices—especially lower median prices under unstable versus stable parameters and higher prices under limited information—as central substantive findings supporting the paper’s comparison of search environments.
Settings.G1303:
Treatment: Experimentally assigned treatment conditions represented by regression indicators, with the main focal contrast the Unstable-market dummy (1=unstable search parameters, 0=stable search parameters). Other treatment indicators in the same regression capture professionals, information conditions, and adjustment speed.

Method: This is the companion OLS regression in Table 3 with market-block average IQR of posted prices as the dependent variable. The same experimentally assigned treatment indicators enter linearly: Unstable market, Professionals, no counterfactual projection, no information on others’ prices, and fast/slow adjustment speed, with standard errors clustered by market. The regression is interpreted causally because these are design-assigned treatment conditions.

Identification: Exogenous experimental assignment of market environment, information, and adjustment-speed conditions identifies the coefficients. The regression compares average price dispersion across assigned conditions, relying on the laboratory protocol rather than observational controls. Remaining issues are sampling variation and clustering, not omitted variables.

Setting: The Table 3 OLS regression treats experimental conditions as causing changes in price dispersion. For the main unstable-versus-stable comparison, the Unstable-market coefficient is -0.008 (SE 0.007), implying no statistically significant causal effect on IQR relative to the stable environment. Professionals increase IQR by 0.045, suppressing information on others’ prices raises IQR by 0.022, and slow adjustment lowers IQR by 0.034. This setting supports the paper’s conclusion that average dispersion differs less across stable and unstable parameter environments than cycle behavior does.

Main role: The abstract and results stress treatment effects on dispersion as one of the paper’s central outcomes, alongside central tendency and cycle properties.
Settings.G1304:
Treatment: Assigned treatment indicators in the laboratory environment; the primary treatment of interest is an Unstable-market indicator (1=unstable parameter vector, 0=stable parameter vector). Other assigned indicators capture professionals, information, and adjustment speeds.

Method: The authors estimate OLS regressions of the cycle rotation index (CRI), averaged across the four periods within each treatment block/session cell, on experimentally assigned treatment indicators: Unstable market, Professionals, no counterfactual projection, no information on others’ prices, and fast/slow adjustment speed. Standard errors are clustered by market. Although CRI is constructed from Poincaré-section counts, the reported estimator is linear OLS.

Identification: The identifying variation is randomized/controlled experimental assignment of the search-parameter environment and other treatment conditions. Because CRI is computed from observed paths within each assigned condition, the OLS coefficient on the Unstable dummy is interpreted as the causal effect of unstable parameters on directional cycling, conditional on the other assigned treatments. Threats are limited to market-level sampling noise and measurement of the derived CRI.

Setting: The authors use OLS to show that assigned unstable search parameters increase the directionality of cycling in price distributions. In Table 6, the Unstable-market coefficient in the CRI regression is 0.080 (SE 0.020), indicating more clockwise cycling under unstable than stable parameters after controlling for information, subject pool, and adjustment speed. Limited information reduces CRI substantially (-0.110 for no counterfactual projection and -0.262 for no information on others’ prices), while professionals also lower CRI (-0.156). This is core evidence for the paper’s main claim that unstable environments generate stronger cyclical dynamics.

Main role: Persistent clockwise cycles and stronger cycling under unstable parameters are a central contribution emphasized in the abstract, results, and discussion.
Settings.G1305:
Treatment: Assigned experimental treatment indicators, primarily the binary Unstable-market indicator contrasting unstable versus stable search-parameter vectors. Additional assigned indicators control for professionals, limited-information conditions, and fast/slow adjustment speeds.

Method: This is the second OLS specification in Table 6, regressing average cycle amplitude on experimentally assigned treatment indicators. Cycle amplitude is the median distance from the cycle center when the (median price, IQR) trajectory crosses the tripwire in the clockwise direction. The same treatment dummies as in the CRI regression are included, with market-clustered standard errors.

Identification: Experimental assignment of the stable versus unstable environment and other treatments identifies the linear effect of those conditions on the derived cycle-amplitude measure. Since treatments are manipulated by design, omitted-variable concerns are minimal; uncertainty comes from finite samples and clustering across markets.

Setting: The Table 6 amplitude regression implies that unstable search parameters causally increase the size of price cycles. The Unstable-market coefficient is 0.034 (SE 0.004), meaning average cycle amplitude is 0.034 units larger in unstable than stable treatments, conditional on other assigned treatments. No information on others’ prices lowers amplitude by 0.024, while professionals and the no-counterfactual-projection condition have small, insignificant effects. This setting underpins the paper’s conclusion that unstable search environments produce larger, persistent cycles.
