Main role: Differences in cycle amplitude between stable and unstable parameterizations are one of the paper’s headline causal findings and directly test the learning-dynamics hypotheses.
Settings.G1306:
Treatment: Exposure of a municipality’s home regiment(s) to direct command by Pétain at Verdun in 1916, measured as the share of regiment(s) raised in the municipality’s recruitment bureau that fought at Verdun during Pétain’s command window rather than under another general. In many cases this is 0/1; in some municipalities it is fractional because the bureau fielded multiple regiments.

Method: The main design estimates cross-municipality regressions of later collaboration outcomes on whether a municipality’s home line regiment(s) were rotated through Verdun while Philippe Pétain held direct command there (February 26 to May 1, 1916), controlling for whether regiment(s) served at Verdun at all, department fixed effects, and pre-1916 controls. The estimating equation is at the municipality level, with the treatment coded as the share of regiment(s) raised by the municipality’s recruitment bureau that served at Verdun under Pétain; in many municipalities this is effectively an indicator because one bureau fielded one regiment. The preferred OLS specifications use log collaborators per capita as the dependent variable; standard errors are clustered by military recruitment bureau. Identification rests on the paper’s claim that regimental rotation timing through Verdun and Pétain’s temporary assignment were effectively arbitrary with respect to municipalities’ prewar political and demographic characteristics, but this remains a regression-adjustment design rather than a quasi-experimental estimator like DiD or RD.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-municipality exposure to regiments rotated through Verdun specifically during the short interval of Pétain’s direct command, versus municipalities whose regiments served at Verdun under other generals or not at Verdun. The endogeneity concern is that regiments or municipalities exposed to Pétain could differ systematically in prior politics, demographics, combat intensity, or later occupation conditions. The paper argues assignment timing was arbitrary because regiment rotation was driven by military exigency and broad strategy, and documents balance on prewar vote shares, population, and many observables. The causal claim therefore depends on unconfoundedness conditional on department fixed effects and pre-1916 controls, plus the historical argument that regimental rotation timing relative to Pétain’s command was as-good-as-random.

Setting: Using municipality-level OLS and Poisson regressions, the paper argues that municipalities whose home regiments served at Verdun under Pétain’s direct command later produced more active Nazi collaborators during 1940–1944. In Table 4, the preferred OLS specification with department fixed effects and prewar vote-share and population controls yields a coefficient of 0.067 on Verdun-under-Pétain exposure for log collaborators per capita; restricting to municipalities rotated at Verdun gives 0.091. Poisson estimates on collaborator counts are 0.190 and 0.221, respectively. The authors interpret these as roughly 7–9 percent higher collaboration rates and about 10,469 additional active collaborators, making this the paper’s main evidence that heroic exposure to Pétain causally shifted communities toward later collaboration.

Main role: This is the paper’s central causal setting: the abstract, introduction, and conclusions emphasize that Verdun-under-Pétain municipalities later raised more Nazi collaborators per capita.
Settings.H1306: Section IV.A 'Main Result', Table 4 columns (1)–(8), PDF pp. 1911–1913 (article pages 1911–1913); empirical strategy equation in Section II, PDF p. 1902.
Settings.G1307:
Treatment: Same treatment as the main setting: share of municipality home regiment(s) rotated through Verdun under Pétain’s direct command in 1916.

Method: Robustness analysis using Poisson count regression at the municipality level, with the number of collaborators as the dependent variable and municipality population included as a control. The treatment remains exposure to Verdun under Pétain, with department fixed effects and prewar controls. Because the task classifies nonlinear estimators such as Poisson outside the linear categories, this specification belongs in Other.

Identification: Same historical as-good-as-random rotation argument as the main setting, but implemented with a Poisson count model instead of OLS on logs. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on department fixed effects and prewar controls, exposure to Pétain at Verdun is exogenous to potential collaboration counts.

Setting: As a substantive robustness check to the main OLS specification, the paper estimates Poisson models for municipality collaborator counts. In Table 4, the coefficient on Verdun-under-Pétain is 0.190 in the full 1914-France sample and 0.221 in the Verdun-only sample. The authors interpret the latter as implying about 10,469 additional active collaborators across Verdun-under-Pétain municipalities, reinforcing the main conclusion that exposure to Pétain causally increased collaboration.

Main role: The paper highlights Poisson estimates as a key robustness for the magnitude of the main collaboration result and uses them to compute additional collaborators.
Settings.H1307: Table 4 columns (5)–(8), Section IV.A, PDF p. 1912–1913.
Settings.G1308:
Treatment: Local exposure of a municipality’s home regiment(s) to Verdun under Pétain, instrumented by crossing regiment catchment boundaries near the boundary cutoff.

Method: Spatial regression discontinuity robustness around regiment catchment boundaries implemented as an IV design. The paper restricts the sample to municipalities near military recruitment-bureau boundaries using the Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik optimal bandwidth, instruments Verdun-under-Pétain exposure with distance to the boundary, and includes the same prewar controls as in the main specification, sometimes with a quadratic polynomial in latitude and longitude. The reported first-stage F-statistics are 50.74 to 54.41. Because treatment receipt changes discretely but not perfectly across boundaries, the paper characterizes this as a local IV-type design around boundaries rather than a sharp RD.

Identification: Identification uses discontinuous changes in regiment assignment across recruitment-bureau catchment borders, comparing municipalities close to opposite sides of a boundary. The endogeneity concern is spatial confounding or omitted regional heterogeneity. The authors argue that near the boundary, municipalities are locally comparable; they instrument exposure with distance to boundary and show no discontinuity in prewar vote shares, WWI fatality rates, or 1911 population. The causal interpretation depends on continuity of potential outcomes at the boundary apart from regiment-assignment exposure and a strong first stage.

Setting: In a hyperlocal robustness design, the paper estimates an IV-style spatial RD around regiment catchment borders. Using an optimal boundary bandwidth and instrumenting exposure with distance to the boundary, the authors find that municipalities just on the side assigned to regiments that served under Pétain at Verdun have 10.2 to 10.8 percent more collaborators. They also report no analogous discontinuities in prewar vote shares, WWI fatality rates, or 1911 population. This supports the claim that the main collaboration result is not driven by broad spatial trends or omitted geography.

Main role: This is presented as a robustness design supporting the main result by leveraging hyperlocal border variation, not as the primary estimator in the paper.
Settings.H1308: Section IV.B 'Robustness', discussion of online Appendix Table A9, PDF p. 1914.
Settings.G1309:
Treatment: Exposure of a municipality’s home regiment(s) to direct command by Pétain at Verdun in 1916, measured as in the main setting.

Method: Municipality-level OLS regressions of interwar legislative vote shares on Verdun-under-Pétain exposure, with department fixed effects and pre-WWI controls analogous to the main collaboration specification. The paper pools evidence across interwar elections and, in party-specific tables, estimates effects on log vote shares for left, right, and extreme-right parties. Standard errors are two-way clustered by military recruitment bureau and electoral district.

Identification: The design exploits the same allegedly arbitrary wartime exposure to Pétain through regiment rotation and examines downstream political behavior before World War II. The key endogeneity concern is that treated municipalities may already have had different political tastes. The paper addresses this by showing similar 1914 prewar vote shares and controlling for them, then interpreting later divergence as caused by the heroic network linked to Pétain.

Setting: To show that exposure to Pétain changed political values before Vichy, the paper regresses interwar municipal vote shares on Verdun-under-Pétain exposure. The authors report that treated municipalities were 18.2 percent more likely to vote for the right and 1.3 percent more likely to vote for the extreme right across the interwar period, and in party-specific estimates they were 11.1 percent less likely to vote for the left as early as 1919 while becoming more supportive of conservative and later extreme-right parties. These patterns are interpreted as evidence that the heroic network forged under Pétain diffused increasingly authoritarian and anti-left values well before WWII.

Main role: The abstract and introduction stress that voting patterns diverged after Verdun in ways matching Pétain’s evolving authoritarian views; these are central mechanism and substantive findings.
Settings.H1309: Section V.A 'Effects on Voting Behavior in Interwar France', online Appendix Tables A11 and A12, discussed on PDF pp. 1916–1917.
Settings.G1310:
Treatment: Exposure of municipality’s home regiment(s) to Pétain’s direct command at Verdun in 1916.

Method: Municipality-level OLS regression of the change in party vote shares between the first and second rounds of the 1936 legislative election on Verdun-under-Pétain exposure, with department fixed effects and the standard pre-WWI controls. The sample is restricted to municipalities where the given party contested both rounds; standard errors are two-way clustered by military recruitment bureau and arrondissement/electoral district. The paper interprets this within-election swing as response to Pétain’s highly publicized anti-left intervention on May 1, 1936.

Identification: The identifying argument is that exposure to Pétain at Verdun created municipalities more responsive to his later political appeals; by examining round-to-round vote shifts within a single election one week apart, the paper seeks to isolate reaction to Pétain’s May 1 public intervention. Remaining concerns are differential local campaigning or other coincident factors, but the paper treats the short horizon plus prewar controls as supportive of a causal interpretation.

Setting: The paper studies whether Verdun-under-Pétain municipalities responded more strongly to Pétain’s public anti-left intervention between the two rounds of the 1936 legislative election. In Table 5, these municipalities show a 7.063 percentage point decline in the Socialist vote share and a 7.524 percentage point increase in the Alliance Démocratique vote share between rounds, with no meaningful turnout change. The authors interpret this as causal evidence that the network created under Pétain at Verdun made communities especially receptive to his authoritarian and anti-left political message.

Main role: The paper highlights this as especially persuasive mechanism evidence because the two election rounds were one week apart and separated by Pétain’s public speech.
Settings.G1311:
Treatment: Two related treatments: (i) Verdun-under-Pétain exposure, defined as municipality home regiments rotated through Verdun under Pétain; and (ii) Pétain-before-Verdun exposure, indicating municipality regiments previously exposed to Pétain’s command before Verdun via his prewar and early-war postings.

Method: Mechanism regressions using municipality-level OLS of collaborator rates for likely line-infantry WWI veterans on exposure to Pétain at Verdun and, separately, exposure to Pétain before Verdun via earlier field/staff commands. Outcomes are constructed from the subset of collaborators for whom age and gender are observed, identifying males born 1890–1898 as likely line infantry veterans. Regressions include department fixed effects, Verdun exposure, and the standard pre-WWI controls; standard errors clustered by recruitment bureau.

Identification: The paper uses the same historical assignment argument as before but narrows outcomes to collaborators likely to have been line infantry veterans, who could personally have served under Pétain. The causal claim is that increased collaboration in this subgroup reflects loyalty induced by direct command, especially at Verdun. This relies on correct age-based classification and on exposure timing being exogenous to municipality traits.

Setting: To test whether direct military exposure to Pétain created later loyalty, the paper examines collaboration among likely WWI line-infantry veterans. In Table 6, Verdun-under-Pétain municipalities have 6.0 percent more likely-veteran collaborators, while exposure to Pétain before Verdun is associated with about 2.9 percent more in the separate specification and 2.2 percent when both exposures are included. The authors interpret this as evidence that soldiers who served under Pétain were more willing to follow him into collaboration decades later.

Main role: This is mechanism evidence about loyalty among exposed veterans, not the headline reduced-form result.
Settings.H1311: Table 6 columns (1)–(3), Section V.B, PDF p. 1920–1921.
Settings.G1312:
Treatment: Exposure of municipality home regiments to Verdun under Pétain and to Pétain before Verdun, measured as in Table 6.

Method: Mechanism regressions using municipality-level OLS of collaborator rates among nonveterans or non-line-veterans on Verdun-under-Pétain exposure and Pétain-before-Verdun exposure. Nonveterans are defined from the subset with age/gender data as women and men too young or too old to have served in the line infantry in WWI. Controls and clustering mirror the main specification. This setting tests whether effects diffuse beyond directly exposed veterans.

Identification: Using the same as-good-as-random exposure argument, the paper compares later collaboration among people unlikely to have personally served under Pétain. The endogeneity concern is that municipalities with Pétain-exposed regiments may differ generally; the paper interprets stronger effects only for Verdun-under-Pétain, but not pre-Verdun Pétain exposure, as evidence that communities were influenced by the heroic status of Verdun veterans rather than by simple direct-command loyalty alone.

Setting: The paper argues that the Pétain-Verdun network diffused authoritarian values beyond the veterans themselves. In Table 6, Verdun-under-Pétain municipalities have 7.1 percent more collaborators among nonveterans in one specification and 7.2 percent when pre-Verdun exposure is added, whereas pre-Verdun Pétain exposure has essentially zero or slightly negative effects on nonveteran collaboration. The authors interpret this pattern as evidence that loyalty among directly exposed veterans translated into broader local influence only when those veterans also possessed Verdun’s heroic credentials.

Main role: This is mechanism evidence supporting diffusion beyond directly exposed soldiers.
Settings.H1312: Table 6 columns (4)–(6), Section V.B, PDF p. 1920–1921.
Settings.G1313:
Treatment: Exposure of municipality home regiment(s) to Verdun under Pétain’s direct command.

Method: Municipality-level OLS regressions by specific collaborationist organization, using the log number of collaborators in each category per capita as the dependent variable. Treatments are Verdun-under-Pétain exposure with department fixed effects, Verdun control, and standard pre-WWI covariates. Outcomes span political parties, paramilitary groups, direct Nazi organizations, economic collaboration, and other pro-Pétain groups. This is a heterogeneous-outcomes extension of the main reduced form.

Identification: Same as the main setting: the timing of regiment rotation under Pétain at Verdun is argued to be arbitrary conditional on controls. The authors use organization-specific outcomes to test whether treatment effects span collaboration types, including older parties reconstituted under Vichy and later, riskier organizations like the Milice and Waffen-SS. The causal claim is that exposure changed values broadly rather than only affecting one channel such as pecuniary collaboration.

Setting: To study persistence and escalation, the paper estimates effects of Verdun-under-Pétain exposure on collaboration in specific organizations. Table 7 shows positive and statistically significant effects across political collaborators (RNP 0.075, PPF 0.062, MSR 0.052, Francisme 0.055), paramilitary groups (SOL 0.052, Milice 0.043, LVF 0.057), direct Nazi collaboration (German Intelligence 0.058, Gestapo 0.052, SS 0.053), economic collaboration (0.056), and Friends of the Marshal (0.049). The authors interpret this breadth as evidence that the heroic network diffused authoritarian values widely and persistently, not just through one organizational channel.

Main role: These are detailed mechanism and heterogeneity results showing the breadth and persistence of the collaboration effect across organizations.
Settings.H1313: Table 7 Panels A and B, Section V.B, PDF pp. 1923–1925.
Settings.G1314:
Treatment: Exposure of municipality home regiment(s) to Verdun under Pétain’s direct command in 1916.

Method: Alternative-data-source regressions using municipality-level collaboration measures built from the OSS list of top Vichy collaborators and an independently collected LVF volunteer dataset, separately and combined, in specifications analogous to the main OLS collaboration regressions. These are substantive robustness checks on the outcome data source, not diagnostics.

Identification: Same historical exposure argument as the main setting, but with alternative outcome datasets collected independently by US intelligence and archival LVF records. The main concern addressed is measurement error or selective coverage in the Paillole list rather than identification of treatment assignment.

Setting: The paper re-estimates the collaboration effect using alternative sources: an OSS dataset on 1,327 high-level Vichy collaborators and a separate dataset on 10,636 LVF volunteers, and then combines these with the main dataset. The authors state that results remain robust and comparable in magnitude, despite these sources capturing distinct forms of collaboration. This supports their claim that the effect of Verdun-under-Pétain exposure on later collaboration is not an artifact of one intelligence source.

Main role: These are robustness analyses showing that the main collaboration effect is not driven by idiosyncrasies of the Paillole dataset.
Settings.H1314: Section IV.C 'Alternative Data Sources', discussion of online Appendix Table A10, PDF p. 1915.
Settings.G1315:
Treatment: Village-level assignment to the gossip-seed arm in the Haryana immunization RCT: in these villages, 17 randomly selected households were asked to nominate villagers who are good at spreading information, and the six most-nominated individuals were recruited as ambassadors receiving regular SMSs/calls to spread information about immunization camps. The estimating coefficient is the contrast of this gossip arm relative to the omitted random-seed arm.

Method: Village-month panel regressions for the Haryana immunization randomized seeding experiment. The estimating equation regresses the number of children immunized in village j and month t on village-level treatment-arm indicators for gossip seeds, trusted seeds, and trusted-gossip seeds, controlling for the other cross-randomized incentive treatments and including district-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the village level. Although treatment is randomized, the implemented estimator is a linear regression with time and district-by-time comparisons rather than a simple difference in means; the district-by-month fixed effects absorb common shocks within district-month cells. The comparison group is villages assigned to random seeds.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized village-level assignment of seeding strategy among 521 villages, with gossip-seed villages compared to random-seed villages while controlling for other cross-randomized interventions and district-by-month shocks. Because seed type is randomly assigned, the coefficient on the gossip arm is interpreted as the causal effect of using nominated gossip seeds instead of random seeds on monthly immunization attendance. The district-by-month fixed effects improve precision by absorbing local time-varying shocks; causal interpretation relies on successful randomization and no differential confounding across treatment arms.

Setting: In the Haryana immunization RCT, villages assigned to use gossip nominees as immunization ambassadors had higher monthly immunization take-up than villages assigned random seeds. In village-month regressions with district-by-month fixed effects and controls for the cross-randomized incentive treatments, the gossip treatment increased the number of children receiving at least one shot by 4.903 per month relative to a random-seed mean of 18.11, with positive effects across vaccine-specific outcomes as well: 1.017 for Penta1, 1.022 for Penta2, 1.030 for Penta3, and 1.078 for measles. The paper interprets this randomized contrast as evidence that asking villagers to identify good information diffusers causally improves the spread of immunization information and resulting take-up.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion present the Haryana immunization experiment as a central empirical contribution showing that seeding information via gossip nominees raises a policy-relevant outcome: immunization. This is a main result of the paper.
Settings.H1315: Section 2.2.3 'Impact on immunization', equation (2.5), Table 3 upper panel and related discussion on PDF pp. 2467-2471 (article pp. 2467-2471).
Settings.G1316:
Treatment: Village-level assignment to an SMS blast treatment in which either 33% or 66% of all households that had previously attended at least one immunization camp were randomly selected to receive targeted SMS reminders of the next vaccine due. The lower-panel coefficients compare each SMS blast arm to villages with no SMS blast.

Method: Same Haryana village-month panel regression framework as equation (2.5), but focusing on the cross-randomized SMS blast arms rather than the seeding-arm coefficients. The lower panel of Table 3 adds indicators for SMS blast to 33% and SMS blast to 66% of previously attending households, alongside the seeding-arm indicators, incentive-treatment controls, and district-by-month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the village level. The authors causally interpret these coefficients because the SMS intensity was randomized.

Identification: Identification comes from randomized assignment of villages to SMS reminder intensity arms within the broader Haryana experiment. Conditional on incentive-treatment controls and district-by-month fixed effects, differences in monthly immunization outcomes across SMS arms are causal intent-to-treat effects of receiving reminder blasts relative to no blast. The authors use these estimates to argue that wider untargeted-ish direct messaging did not outperform targeted gossip seeding.

Setting: In the Haryana immunization experiment, the authors also estimate the causal effect of SMS reminder blasts sent to 33% or 66% of previously attending households. In the lower panel of Table 3, village-month regressions with district-by-month fixed effects show small and statistically insignificant coefficients for both SMS blast arms on all vaccine outcomes; for the broad attendance outcome, the 33% blast coefficient is 3.507 and the 66% blast coefficient is 0.723, versus a random-seed mean of 18.11. The paper interprets these randomized estimates as showing that directly informing many more households did not significantly increase immunization relative to the targeted gossip-seeding strategy.

Main role: The SMS-blast estimates are used as a substantive comparison/robustness benchmark to contrast broad reminders with gossip seeding, but the paper's main causal claim centers on the effectiveness of gossip nominees, not SMS reminders themselves.
Settings.H1316: Section 2.2.3 'Impact on immunization', Table 3 lower panel and surrounding discussion on PDF pp. 2468-2471 (article pp. 2468-2471).
Settings.G1317:
Treatment: Village-level assignment in the Karnataka raffle experiment to have the k seeds selected from the list of gossip nominees rather than from random households (omitted category) or village elders. k was 3 or 5. The focal treatment coefficient is the gossip-treatment dummy relative to the random-seeding arm.

Method: Cross-sectional village-level reduced-form regression for the Karnataka cell-phone raffle RCT, equation (2.1). The outcome is either the number of calls received or calls per seed in village j. Regressors are indicators for assignment to the gossip-treatment arm and elder-treatment arm, with controls for the randomized number of seeds and for the number of gossip and elder nominees in the village. This is a linear regression adjustment version of the randomized intention-to-treat comparison; no fixed effects are used. Robust standard errors are reported.

Identification: Identification comes from random assignment of villages into random-seed, gossip-seed, and elder-seed treatment arms. Because assignment is randomized, the regression-adjusted coefficient on the gossip-treatment indicator is interpreted as the causal intention-to-treat effect of intentionally seeding gossip nominees instead of random households. Controls for the number of seeds and for the counts of nominees by type address design features and conditional chance overlap, improving precision. Remaining concern emphasized by the authors is that even random and elder villages may incidentally include gossip nominees, motivating further 'hit at least one gossip' analyses.

Setting: In the Karnataka cell-phone raffle RCT, villages assigned to seed information through gossip nominees received more calls than villages assigned random seeds, although the reduced-form estimates are imprecise. In equation (2.1) and Table 1 column (1), the gossip-treatment coefficient is 3.651 additional calls relative to the random-treatment mean of 8.077, and 1.053 additional calls per seed relative to a random-treatment mean of 1.967. The authors interpret this randomized reduced-form contrast as the policy-relevant causal effect of first identifying gossips and then seeding them rather than choosing seeds randomly.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion identify the Karnataka RCT as one of the two core experiments establishing that gossip nominees spread information more effectively than random or elder seeds. The reduced-form ITT treatment comparison directly answers the policy question and materially supports the central conclusion.
Settings.H1317: Section 2.1 'Study 1: The cell phone and cash raffle RCT', equation (2.1), Table 1 column (1) and accompanying text on PDF pp. 2459-2462 (article pp. 2459-2462).
Settings.G1318:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 if at least one seed household in the village was a gossip nominee ('GossipReached'), regardless of treatment arm; focal contrast is villages where at least one gossip was hit versus villages where no gossip was hit. This is a two-valued treatment receipt measure at the village level.

Method: Cross-sectional village-level OLS regression for the Karnataka raffle experiment, equation (2.2), relating outcomes to indicators for whether at least one gossip seed was hit and whether at least one elder seed was hit, with controls for the number of seeds and the number of gossip and elder nominees in the village. The authors argue that, conditional on nominee counts, the event of hitting at least one gossip/elder is random, so this OLS specification can be interpreted causally; they also report IV as a robustness/alternative design because hitting at least one gossip is mechanically linked to treatment assignment.

Identification: Identification is based on quasi-random variation in whether at least one gossip nominee is included among the seeds, conditional on the number of potential gossip and elder seeds and the number of assigned seeds. Because seed selection within treatment status is random and because random and elder villages can accidentally include gossips, the authors treat the conditional OLS contrast between villages that did and did not hit at least one gossip as causal, while acknowledging that the event is random only conditional on nominee counts. This motivates the IV version using treatment assignment as an instrument.

Setting: Using the Karnataka raffle experiment, the authors estimate the effect of actually reaching at least one gossip nominee on diffusion. In OLS regressions controlling for village nominee counts and number of seeds, hitting at least one gossip increased total calls by 3.786 relative to villages where no gossip or elder was reached, compared with a control mean of 5.846; on a per-seed basis the effect is 0.952 relative to a mean of 1.451. The paper interprets this as evidence that information seeded to a gossip circulates more widely than information seeded to someone who is not a gossip.

Main role: The paper highlights the effect of actually hitting a gossip seed as a key experimental result about the mechanism and magnitude of diffusion. It is a central substantive result, though complemented by the reduced-form and IV estimates.
Settings.H1318: Section 2.1, equation (2.2), Table 1 column (2) and discussion on PDF pp. 2460-2462 (article pp. 2460-2462).
Settings.G1319:
Treatment: Endogenous village-level treatment receipt: indicator that at least one seed in the village was a gossip nominee. Instrumented by assignment of the village to the gossip-treatment arm; 'at least one elder' is simultaneously instrumented by elder-treatment assignment. This is a binary receipt effect, conceptually a complier effect of actually hitting a gossip seed.

Method: Village-level 2SLS in the Karnataka raffle experiment using randomized village assignment to the gossip-treatment arm and elder-treatment arm as instruments for endogenous receipt indicators 'at least 1 gossip' and 'at least 1 elder'. The second-stage equation is (2.2); first stages are equations (2.3) and (2.4). Controls include number of seeds, number of gossip nominees, and number of elder nominees. Robust standard errors are reported. This estimates the causal effect of actually hitting at least one gossip seed, instrumented by assignment-induced variation in hitting one.

Identification: The endogeneity concern is that the realized event of hitting at least one gossip nominee is not purely random unconditionally, because it depends on village nominee availability and treatment arm. The authors therefore instrument realized 'gossip reached' with randomized assignment to the gossip-treatment arm, and simultaneously instrument 'elder reached' with randomized assignment to the elder-treatment arm. Causal interpretation relies on random assignment, relevance shown in the first stages, and an exclusion restriction that assignment affects calls through whom the village seeds reach rather than through other channels beyond the included controls.

Setting: In the Karnataka raffle experiment, the authors instrument whether a village actually hit at least one gossip seed with randomized assignment to the gossip-treatment arm. The 2SLS estimates in Table 1 show that reaching at least one gossip causes substantially greater diffusion: the second-stage coefficient is 7.436 additional calls per village, and 1.979 additional calls per seed. The IV control-group mean for total calls is 5.805, so the paper emphasizes that seeding at least one gossip yields an extra 7.4 calls and nearly doubles the base rate. This is one of the paper's core experimental findings on causal diffusion effects.

Main role: The IV estimate is highlighted in the introduction and experiment discussion as a key result: seeding at least one gossip yields extra calls and nearly doubles the base rate. It supports the core conclusion about the causal effect of gossip seeds on diffusion.
Settings.H1319: Section 2.1, equations (2.2)-(2.4), Table 1 columns (3)-(5), and discussion on PDF pp. 2460-2462 (article pp. 2460-2462).
Settings.G1320:
Treatment: Two related binary treatment contrasts are reported in Figure 2: (i) assignment to the gossip treatment arm versus the omitted random-seed arm, and (ii) having hit at least one gossip seed versus not. Both are village-level binary exposures; the figure emphasizes the gossip contrasts.

Method: Quantile regressions in the Karnataka raffle experiment estimating treatment effects at different points of the outcome distribution, shown in Figure 2. Panel A reports quantile treatment effects of gossip- versus random-treatment assignment (reduced form); Panel B reports quantile effects of hitting at least one gossip or elder versus not. Because quantile regression is a nonlinear effect estimator, it is classified as Other. The paper interprets these as causal distributional effects using experimental or conditionally random variation.

Identification: For Panel A, identification comes from randomized assignment to gossip versus random treatment arms; for Panel B, from conditional randomness in whether at least one gossip was hit. The quantile-regression framework examines how these causal effects vary across the distribution of calls, addressing concerns that mean effects might be driven by outliers. Interpretation relies on the same randomization arguments as the mean regressions.

Setting: As a robustness check against outlier-driven mean effects in the Karnataka raffle experiment, the authors estimate quantile treatment effects for gossip seeding. Figure 2 shows that the effect of hitting at least one gossip becomes significantly positive starting around the 35th percentile of the calls distribution; the paper states that hitting a gossip increases the 35th-percentile number of calls by 122% and the 80th-percentile number by 71.27%. These results are interpreted as showing that gossip seeding causally shifts the upper part of the diffusion distribution, not merely a few extreme observations.

Main role: The quantile regressions are robustness/distributional analyses supporting the main Karnataka RCT findings by showing that gossip effects arise in the upper part of the calls distribution. They are not the primary headline estimates.
Settings.H1320: Section 2.1, Figure 2 and discussion on PDF p. 2462-2463 (article pp. 2462-2463).
Settings.G1321:
Treatment: Household-level network centrality, especially diffusion centrality DC(1/E[lambda1] g, E[Diam(g)]), normalized by its standard deviation. Alternative centrality measures (degree, eigenvector) and leader/geographic status are also included in some specifications. The focal 'treatment' is a continuous one-standard-deviation increase in diffusion centrality.

Method: Poisson regressions in the Karnataka network-and-nomination data relating the expected number of nominations a household receives to its centrality measures and other characteristics (Tables 6 and 7). Because Poisson is a nonlinear count model, it is classified as Other. The authors interpret these coefficients substantively as evidence that higher diffusion centrality causes or drives a greater likelihood of being nominated as a good information spreader, though identification is observational rather than experimental. Village fixed effects are included conceptually via μv in the discrete-choice setup described in the text; the reported equivalent Poisson regressions use village-level comparisons and clustered standard errors.

Identification: Identification is associational rather than experimental. The authors use detailed network data and regress nomination counts on measured diffusion centrality, degree, eigenvector centrality, leadership status, and geographic centrality to argue that nominations are systematically related to diffusion centrality rather than merely to observable prominence. The key concern is omitted-variable bias: unobserved traits like talkativeness could correlate with both centrality and nominations. The authors therefore frame these estimates as supportive evidence consistent with the theory, not definitive causal identification.

Setting: Using detailed Karnataka network data, the authors estimate whether more diffusion-central households are more likely to be nominated as good information spreaders. In Poisson regressions, a one-standard-deviation increase in diffusion centrality is associated with a 0.607 log-point increase in the expected number of event nominations and a 0.625 log-point increase for loan nominations (Table 6). In specifications adding other centrality measures and observables, diffusion centrality remains predictive; in post-LASSO, it is the only selected predictor for event nominations. The paper uses these observational estimates to support the mechanism that villagers identify globally central individuals when nominating gossips.

Main role: These observational regressions are important supporting evidence for the paper's mechanism—that villagers nominate central people—but the central claims rest on the RCTs, not on these nomination regressions.
Settings.H1321: Section 4.2.2 'Are central individuals more likely to be nominated?', Tables 6 and 7 on PDF pp. 2480-2483 (article pp. 2480-2483).
Settings.G1322:
Treatment: Percentile rank of household j in respondent i's network gossip assessment NG_{j,i}; this is a continuous dyadic measure of how often i is expected to hear gossip originating from j. The focal regressor is not binary.

Method: Linear probability regressions in the Karnataka nomination data examining whether respondent i is more likely to nominate household j when j ranks higher in i's network-gossip assessment, reported in Table 8. The specifications include respondent fixed effects, rankee fixed effects, and in some columns flexible polynomial controls for j's diffusion centrality. This is a panel-style dyad regression with one or two FE dimensions, not HDFE by the schema's three-dimension threshold. Standard errors are clustered at the village level.

Identification: Identification is observational and comes from within-respondent and/or within-rankee variation after absorbing respondent fixed effects, rankee fixed effects, and in some columns flexible controls for j's diffusion centrality. The idea is to test whether a respondent is relatively more likely to nominate those about whom she is predicted to hear more gossip, even holding constant general nominee attractiveness or centrality. Remaining concerns include dyad-level omitted factors and measurement error, so the paper treats this as stronger supportive evidence for the mechanism rather than definitive causal identification.

Setting: To test a sharper prediction of their network-gossip model, the authors regress whether respondent i nominates household j on j's percentile in i's network-gossip ranking. In Table 8, the coefficient remains positive with respondent fixed effects, rankee fixed effects, and flexible controls for j's diffusion centrality. The paper highlights that moving from the 50th to the 99th percentile of NG corresponds to about a 46.6% higher nomination probability in column (4) and a 10.5% higher probability even with both i and j fixed effects in column (6). This supports the mechanism that villagers nominate those they hear about more often through the network.

Main role: This is a more specific supporting test of the theoretical mechanism, not a headline experimental effect. It helps distinguish the network-gossip mechanism from alternative explanations.
Settings.H1322: Section 4.2.2, Table 8 and surrounding discussion on PDF pp. 2483-2484 (article pp. 2483-2484).
Settings.G1323:
Treatment: Indicator that the randomly selected seed set in a random-seed village included at least one 'high DC' seed, where high diffusion centrality means at least one standard deviation above the mean of the centrality distribution. Some specifications also include the indicator that at least one gossip was hit. The focal treatment here is the high-DC indicator, a binary village-level exposure realized by chance in random-seed villages.

Method: Cross-sectional OLS regressions in the subsample of 68 random-seed Karnataka villages with follow-up network data, reported in Table 9. Outcomes are calls received and calls per seed. Regressors indicate whether the realized random seed set included at least one gossip, at least one elder, and/or at least one high-diffusion-centrality (high DC) seed, with controls for total numbers of gossips, elders, and seeds. This is a substantive robustness/mechanism analysis using random variation in which seed types were hit by chance within the random-seed arm.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from chance realization of seed types within the random-seed treatment villages. Since all seeds in this subsample were randomly chosen households, whether at least one realized seed happened to be a gossip or high-DC household is plausibly random conditional on village composition controls. The analysis tests whether diffusion is higher when random seeding accidentally hits more central or gossip-type households. Remaining issues include limited sample size, correlation between gossip and high-DC indicators, and measurement error in network centrality.

Setting: In a follow-up analysis using 68 Karnataka villages from the random-seed arm where network data were later collected, the authors regress diffusion outcomes on whether the random seed set happened to include at least one high-diffusion-centrality household. High-DC seeds increase calls: in Table 9 column (3), hitting at least one high-DC seed raises calls by 5.183 relative to villages with no high-DC seed, and in column (6) raises calls per seed by 1.312. When both high-DC and gossip-hit indicators are included, the gossip coefficient declines only modestly, which the authors interpret as suggesting that diffusion centrality explains only part of why nominated gossips are especially effective seeds.

Main role: This is a follow-up mechanism/robustness analysis used to ask whether diffusion centrality explains the extra diffusion from gossip nominees. It supports interpretation but is not a headline causal result.
Settings.H1323: Section 4.3 'Re-interpreting the cell phone RCT results', Table 9 and discussion on PDF pp. 2484-2486 (article pp. 2484-2486).
Settings.G1324:
Treatment: Crossing the SSO threshold under PPS, which triggers a large discrete increase in Medicare payment for retaining the patient one more day beyond the threshold. This is an eligibility/payment-schedule discontinuity at the threshold day, not actual treatment receipt. Implemented as being at/just to the right of the threshold versus just to the left in the PPS payment regime.

Method: The paper uses a sharp regression discontinuity design around the LTCH short-stay outlier (SSO) threshold, where Medicare reimbursement jumps discretely once a stay reaches the DRG-specific threshold day. The running variable is days relative to the SSO threshold. The substantive reduced-form outcomes are daily discharge hazards, estimated nonparametrically in figures by plotting discharge shares by relative day in pre-PPS versus PPS periods. The design interprets the payment jump as causally affecting discharge behavior at the threshold. Identification relies on smooth potential discharge patterns absent the threshold-induced payment jump; the pre-PPS linear-payment period is used as a descriptive comparison showing no analogous bunching.

Identification: Identification comes from the discontinuous increase in Medicare reimbursement at the DRG-specific SSO threshold under PPS. Comparing stays just before versus just after the threshold isolates the effect of payment incentives on discharge timing, under the assumption that absent the payment jump, discharge hazards would evolve smoothly with stay length around the threshold. The pre-PPS period with a linear schedule provides supportive evidence that bunching is not mechanically driven by underlying patient trajectories at the same relative day.

Setting: Using the sharp payment discontinuity at the LTCH short-stay outlier threshold, the authors show that provider financial incentives substantially increase discharges. In the PPS period, the share of stays discharged rises from about 2% per day just before the threshold to about 9% at the threshold, with the increase driven primarily by downstream discharges. In the pre-PPS linear-payment period there is no analogous bunching. The intended causal claim is that the large payment jump causes LTCHs to discharge more patients precisely when the threshold is reached, a central empirical fact motivating the paper’s dynamic model and contract-design analysis.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that discharges increase substantially after the threshold because of the payment jump. This descriptive causal response to provider incentives is central motivation for the paper’s modeling and policy counterfactuals.
Settings.H1324: Section 3.2 “Discharge Patterns,” Figure 3 (PDF pp. 2174–2175; article pp. 2174–2175).
Settings.G1325:
Treatment: Crossing the PPS SSO threshold that creates a discrete increase in Medicare payment for keeping the patient an additional day. The treatment is threshold exposure to the higher payment schedule.

Method: The paper uses the same sharp RD at the SSO payment threshold to study how the payment jump changes the composition/health of marginal dischargees. Outcomes are discharge destination margins and post-discharge spending by destination plotted against days relative to the threshold. The design is reduced form: threshold eligibility/payment causes changes in who is discharged and where they go. Identification relies on smooth evolution of patient health/composition around the threshold absent the payment discontinuity.

Identification: The authors exploit the discontinuous PPS payment increase at the SSO threshold. If patient health/composition would change smoothly with stay length absent the payment jump, then discontinuities in discharge destination and in post-discharge payments at the threshold can be attributed to the financial incentive changing which patients are discharged and where. Post-discharge payments are interpreted as a proxy for patient health at discharge.

Setting: Around the sharp SSO payment threshold, the authors interpret the payment jump as causing LTCHs to discharge relatively healthier patients. At the threshold, downstream discharges rise much more than upstream discharges, and among downstream dischargees average post-discharge payments jump from roughly $10,000 to $20,000, indicating LTCHs ‘work down the distribution’ and discharge less healthy patients on the downstream margin after the threshold becomes attractive. On the upstream margin, post-discharge payments move slightly in the opposite direction. These reduced-form composition effects are a central input to the paper’s dynamic discharge model.

Main role: The abstract and introduction stress that the marginal discharged patient is in relatively better health. This composition result is part of the paper’s central contribution and motivation for the model.
Settings.H1325: Section 3.2 “Discharge Patterns,” Figure 3 and Figure 4 (PDF pp. 2174–2176; article pp. 2174–2176).
Settings.G1326:
Treatment: Being at or just to the right of the SSO threshold under PPS, which sharply changes the incentive to discharge due to the payment jump. Treatment is threshold-induced change in discharge incentives/location of care, captured by threshold eligibility rather than actual discharge receipt.

Method: The authors estimate sharp RD specifications for mortality hazards around the SSO threshold using linear probability regressions with local bandwidths of 3, 5, and 10 days and either linear or quadratic trends in days relative to the threshold, interacted with a post-threshold indicator. Outcomes are 1-day mortality hazard and 30-day forward mortality hazard, both unconditional on current location of care. This is a reduced-form/ITT cutoff effect of the payment-threshold-induced discharge distortion on mortality.

Identification: The SSO threshold creates a sharp first-stage change in discharge location/timing. The authors compare mortality hazards immediately around the threshold, using flexible local linear/quadratic controls in relative day. Under the assumption that absent the threshold-induced payment change mortality hazards would evolve smoothly through the cutoff, any discontinuity in level or slope at the threshold would be attributable to the discharge distortion induced by provider incentives. Because mortality is observed regardless of location, this avoids selection problems from conditioning on remaining in the LTCH.

Setting: Using the payment threshold as a sharp RD, the authors test whether the threshold-induced change in discharge behavior affects mortality. They find no evidence of a discontinuity in either the same-day mortality hazard or the 30-day forward mortality hazard around the SSO threshold. In their baseline linear specification with a 3-day bandwidth, they estimate a threshold effect on the 1-day mortality hazard of 0.00007 (s.e. 0.00023) and on the 30-day hazard of -0.00005 (s.e. 0.00016), both economically tiny and statistically insignificant. This supports the paper’s central claim that the discharge distortions generated by payment incentives do not produce detectable mortality effects on average.

Main role: A central conclusion in the abstract and introduction is that despite strong provider responses, the paper finds no compelling evidence of effects on patient mortality. The RD mortality analysis is one of the main empirical bases for that claim.
Settings.H1326: Section 3.3 “(Lack of) Mortality Effects,” Figure 5; Appendix C equations (C.1)-(C.2), Table C.I, Figure C.1 (PDF pp. 2177–2178 and 2203–2205; article pp. 2177–2178 and 2203–2205).
Settings.G1327:
Treatment: Average LTCH length of stay for a DRG-year cell, measured in days. This is the endogenous treatment receipt in the IV design, instrumented by the DRG-year SSO threshold (in days).

Method: The paper estimates 2SLS regressions at the DRG-year level using over-time within-DRG changes in the SSO threshold as an instrument for average LTCH length of stay. The first stage regresses average length of stay on the SSO threshold with year and DRG fixed effects; reduced forms regress 30-, 60-, and 90-day mortality on the SSO threshold with the same fixed effects; second stage instruments length of stay with the threshold. This is a linear IV design. The paper also plots the reduced form and first stage using residualized binned scatters.

Identification: Identification comes from changes over time in the DRG-specific SSO threshold, determined by prior-year geometric mean LOS, which shift financial incentives and thereby average LOS within a DRG. With DRG and year fixed effects, the identifying assumption is that within-DRG threshold changes are as good as exogenous to contemporaneous mortality shocks except through induced LOS changes. The paper notes no evidence that admissions or admitted-patient mix change in response to threshold changes. The IV estimand is the effect of a one-day increase in LOS induced by these threshold shifts on mortality.

Setting: Using over-time within-DRG changes in the SSO threshold as an instrument for LTCH length of stay, the authors estimate no meaningful effect of LOS on mortality. The first stage shows that a one-day increase in the threshold raises average LOS by 0.298 days. IV estimates of the effect of an additional day of LOS on mortality are 0.0001 percentage points for 30-day mortality, -0.0045 percentage points for 60-day mortality, and -0.0040 percentage points for 90-day mortality, all statistically insignificant. Relative to the 90-day mortality mean of 30.6%, the 95% confidence interval rules out mortality declines greater than 4.3% and increases greater than 1.8%. This IV evidence materially supports the paper’s conclusion that incentive-induced discharge timing does not measurably harm mortality on average.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize the absence of detectable mortality effects. This IV strategy is the paper’s second major empirical design, supplementing the RD evidence with independent variation in incentives over time.
Settings.H1327: Section 3.3 “(Lack of) Mortality Effects,” equation (1), Figure 6, Table III (PDF pp. 2178–2180; article pp. 2178–2180).
Settings.G1328:
Treatment: Counterfactual LTCH payment schedule parameters, such as removing the jump at the SSO threshold by changing the pre-threshold per diem or cap amount. The focal treatment varies across simulated contracts; for the first pair of counterfactuals reported, treatment is adoption of a 'higher rate per day' schedule or a 'lower cap' schedule instead of the observed PPS schedule.

Method: The paper specifies and estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of LTCH discharge behavior by simulated method of moments. Patient health follows a latent AR(1)-type process; each day the LTCH chooses whether to retain the patient, discharge upstream, or discharge downstream. Choice-specific value functions incorporate Medicare payments, estimated daily cost, and non-monetary value from patient location. The model is estimated to match daily discharge and mortality patterns in pre-PPS and PPS periods plus post-discharge payment moments. The model is then used to simulate counterfactual payment schedules and their effects on length of stay, LTCH payments/profits, post-discharge payments, and total Medicare spending. This is a structural counterfactual causal model rather than a standard reduced-form linear design.

Identification: The model uses the sharp variation created by the SSO payment threshold, plus pre/post PPS differences, to identify discharge incentives, latent health dynamics, costs, and the mapping from discharge timing/location to post-discharge spending. Identification is structural and parametric: the payment jump identifies sensitivity to financial incentives; mortality profiles help identify latent health processes; discharge destination patterns and post-discharge payments help identify how health affects location choice and downstream spending. Counterfactual causal claims require the model structure and maintained assumptions, including stable admission composition under the simulated payment schedules and no mortality effect of counterfactual contracts in the reported exercises.

Setting: The estimated dynamic model implies that changing LTCH payment schedules causally changes discharge timing and Medicare spending. Under the 'higher rate per day' no-jump schedule, average LOS falls from 19.3 to 17.4 days, LTCH payments rise slightly from $27,953 to $28,316, LTCH profits rise from $6,518 to $8,991, and total Medicare payments are essentially unchanged at $47,877 versus $47,796. Under the 'lower cap' no-jump schedule, LOS falls to 14.8 days, LTCH payments drop to $16,024, LTCH profits become negative at -$407, and total Medicare payments fall to $35,399. These structural counterfactuals show that contract design strongly affects provider behavior and spending, forming the backbone of the paper’s policy analysis.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize the model-based counterfactual contract analysis as a central contribution. The paper’s main policy conclusions rely on this structural method.
Settings.H1328: Sections 4.2–4.4 and 5.1–5.3; Figure 9, Figure 10, Table V (PDF pp. 2182–2195; article pp. 2182–2195).
Settings.G1329:
Treatment: Adoption of an alternative no-jump, capped payment schedule from the set of 'LTCH preferred' schedules. The focal reported contract is the one with the payment threshold set 1 day above the current SSO threshold and a pre-SSO per diem of $1,931 with cap amount $32,830.

Method: Using the same estimated dynamic discrete choice model, the paper simulates a family of counterfactual 'win-win' payment schedules with a constant per diem up to a cap but no jump, where the per diem is chosen so that LTCH revenue is held fixed under observed discharge behavior. The authors then let modeled behavior adjust and compare predicted LTCH payments, profits, length of stay, and total Medicare payments across these schedules. This is a structural counterfactual exercise.

Identification: The causal predictions come from the estimated structural model of daily discharge decisions under alternative payment schedules. The key identifying variation is still the observed response to the SSO payment jump and related moments used to estimate the model. The 'hold harmless' design constrains contracts to keep LTCH revenue fixed at observed behavior, so any behavioral response under the model implies providers are weakly better off by revealed preference. Validity depends on the model’s structural assumptions and the maintained assumption that out-of-sample responses not in the model (e.g., entry/exit, quality changes) are limited for these conservative schedules.

Setting: The model predicts that certain no-jump contracts can reduce Medicare spending while making LTCHs at least as well off. The contract with the largest savings among these 'win-win' schedules sets the cap one day later than the current threshold and implies LTCH payments of $26,313 versus $27,953 under the observed contract, total Medicare payments of $45,691 versus $47,796, LTCH profits of $6,876 versus $6,518, and LOS of 17.5 versus 19.3 days. In the text, the authors summarize this as a $2,127 reduction in total Medicare payments, or 4.4%, while LTCH profits rise by $315 per stay, or 4.5%. This setting directly underpins the paper’s main contract-design conclusion.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight the existence of alternative contracts that can reduce Medicare spending while leaving LTCHs harmless or better off. This is the paper’s headline policy result.
Settings.H1329: Section 5.3 “'Win-Win' Payment Schedules,” Figure 11, Table V column (4) (PDF pp. 2195–2197; article pp. 2195–2197).
Settings.G1330:
Treatment: Adoption of a constant-per-diem cost-based payment schedule instead of the observed PPS schedule. Two variants are reported: estimated-cost per diem of $1,109 capped at 60 days, and SNF opportunity-cost per diem of $507 capped at 60 days.

Method: The same structural dynamic model is used to simulate two additional counterfactual cost-based reimbursement schedules: (i) a constant per diem equal to estimated LTCH costs, capped at 60 days, and (ii) a constant per diem equal to the average SNF per diem (reference-based or 'opportunity cost' pricing), also capped at 60 days. The paper compares modeled LOS, LTCH payments, profits, and total Medicare payments under these schedules to the observed contract.

Identification: These causal predictions come from the estimated structural dynamic model. The model maps alternative per diem/cap contracts into discharge incentives and simulated care paths. Identification is inherited from the structural estimation discussed earlier; external validity depends on the assumption that these more aggressive contracts do not induce out-of-model changes such as altered admissions, quality, or provider exit, which the authors explicitly flag as a concern especially when profits fall sharply.

Setting: Under cost-based constant-per-diem reimbursement, the structural model predicts large changes in provider behavior and spending. Paying LTCHs their estimated cost of $1,109 per day increases LOS from 19.3 to 32.9 days, raises LTCH payments from $27,953 to $35,546, and increases total Medicare payments to $51,851 while producing LTCH profits of -$971. Paying LTCHs the SNF opportunity-cost rate of $507 per day reduces LOS to 14.7 days, LTCH payments to $7,392, and total Medicare payments to $25,879, while LTCH profits fall to -$8,865. These exercises illustrate how strongly outcomes depend on payment design, but the paper cautions that large profit reductions could generate unintended out-of-sample consequences.

Main role: These are additional illustrative policy counterfactuals. They support the broader message about incentive design but are not the headline 'win-win' result stressed in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1330: Section 5.3 “Cost-Based Payment Schedules,” Table V columns (5) and (6) (PDF pp. 2197; article p. 2197).
Settings.G1331:
Treatment: Monetary policy surprise measured from federal funds futures around FOMC announcements. In return regressions the treatment is the surprise change in the policy rate (basis points); in volatility regressions the regressor is the squared surprise v_t^2. This is continuous, not binary.

Method: Event-study style linear regressions relate aggregate S&P 500 returns, and separately squared S&P 500 returns, in a 30-minute window around FOMC press releases to high-frequency monetary policy surprises constructed from federal funds futures. The authors estimate simple time-series OLS on event dates, and in some columns split the sample by regular meetings, turning points, and intermeeting announcements. Identification comes from narrow-window high-frequency variation intended to isolate unanticipated monetary policy shocks around announcements rather than broader macro news.

Identification: The identifying variation is the unexpected component of monetary policy changes captured by federal funds futures in a narrow intraday window around FOMC announcements. The endogeneity concern is that scheduled policy changes reflect macro conditions; the futures-based surprise and narrow window are used to isolate the unanticipated component. Assumptions are that little else relevant to stock prices arrives in that window and that the futures change accurately measures the surprise component.

Setting: Using narrow-window OLS event-study regressions, the authors interpret unexpected monetary policy shocks as causing movements in aggregate stock returns and volatility. In Table 3, a 25 basis point unexpected cut raises the S&P 500 by more than 1.3 percent in the pre-2005 sample, while for the full sample the return effect is negative but imprecise. Squared policy shocks significantly raise squared S&P 500 returns; the column 3 coefficient is 84.38, with the effect concentrated in turning points in policy. This setting mainly establishes that monetary policy surprises are a meaningful causal shock for the firm-level analysis.

Main role: These regressions validate that monetary policy surprises move the aggregate market and volatility, supplying the shock source for the paper, but the central contribution is cross-firm heterogeneity by price stickiness rather than aggregate-market effects.
Settings.H1331: Section III.A Aggregate Market Volatility; Table 3, cols. (1)–(6), PDF pp. 179-180.
Settings.G1332:
Treatment: Interaction between continuous monetary policy shock intensity (typically squared federal funds futures surprise around the FOMC announcement) and firm-level price flexibility/stickiness measured by the frequency of price adjustment (FPA, monthly probability of a price change). The causal contrast of interest is how the effect of a monetary shock varies with lower versus higher FPA. FPA is continuous, and the shock is continuous.

Method: Baseline firm-level event-study OLS regressions relate squared stock returns of S&P 500 constituent firms in narrow windows around FOMC announcements to squared monetary policy surprises, the firm-level frequency of price adjustment (FPA) from PPI microdata, and their interaction. Variants include outlier correction, 30- versus 60-minute windows, volume-weighted returns, absolute-return versions, and CAPM- or Fama-French-adjusted returns. The core estimator is linear regression without FE in baseline columns, though some robustness columns add FE; the implemented causal design remains event-study regression adjustment using high-frequency shocks.

Identification: Identification uses high-frequency monetary policy surprises from federal funds futures in tight windows around FOMC announcements, assumed to be exogenous to firm-specific contemporaneous shocks within the event window. Cross-sectional heterogeneity in FPA is measured from confidential PPI microdata. The key endogeneity concern is that FPA may proxy for other firm traits; the baseline assumes that, conditional on controls and the event design, the interaction captures differential causal exposure of firms with stickier prices to monetary shocks. The authors explicitly note they cannot fully rule out unobserved heterogeneity in FPA.

Setting: The paper’s main causal claim is that unexpected monetary policy shocks increase stock-return volatility more for firms with stickier prices. In baseline firm-level event-study regressions, the coefficient on squared shocks is 128.50 and the interaction with FPA is -169.80 in Table 4 column 1; with outlier correction these are 76.95 and -67.26 in column 2. The authors interpret this as a 25 bp surprise causing about an 8 percentage point increase in squared returns for the stickiest-price firms, while the impact for the most flexible-price firms is about one-third as large. Similar negative interaction estimates appear with 60-minute windows, volume-weighting, absolute returns, and factor-adjusted returns, supporting the central conclusion that sticky prices are costly because they amplify the volatility response to nominal shocks.

Main role: This is the paper’s central empirical design: firms with stickier prices exhibit a larger increase in stock-return volatility after monetary policy announcements. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all emphasize this finding.
Settings.H1332: Section III.B Baseline; Table 4 panel A cols. (1)–(8), panel B cols. (1)–(8), and panel C cols. (1)–(8), PDF pp. 180-183.
Settings.G1333:
Treatment: Continuous interaction of squared monetary policy surprise around FOMC announcements with continuous firm-level frequency of price adjustment (FPA). FPA itself is time invariant or near-time-invariant at the firm level in these regressions; treatment is nonbinary.

Method: Firm-level event-study linear regressions identical to the baseline specification but with firm fixed effects and, in some columns, event fixed effects added to absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity and common announcement-specific shocks. The absorbed FE dimensions are one or two sets depending on the column (firm FE; or firm FE plus event FE), so this is standard FE rather than HDFE. The treatment remains the interaction of squared monetary shocks with FPA.

Identification: The design combines high-frequency event-time monetary shocks with within-firm comparisons across announcement dates while absorbing firm fixed effects, and in some specifications event fixed effects. This addresses concerns that time-invariant firm traits correlated with FPA drive the results, and event FE absorb average announcement-specific volatility shifts. Remaining concern is that FPA could still proxy for time-varying omitted characteristics interacting with shocks.

Setting: Adding fixed effects does not overturn the main claim that sticky prices amplify volatility responses to monetary shocks. In Table 4 panel A, with firm fixed effects the squared-shock coefficient is 127.50 and the FPA interaction is -168.00 (col. 3), or 77.00 and -67.82 with outlier correction (col. 4). With firm and event fixed effects, the interaction remains negative and significant at -166.60 (col. 5) and -43.96 (col. 6). The authors interpret this as evidence that the differential effect is not merely due to fixed differences across firms or common event-level volatility shocks.

Main role: The authors use firm and event FE robustness as a key demonstration that the main volatility result does not reflect fixed firm heterogeneity or common event-level shocks. They describe these results as leaving the main conclusion materially unchanged.
Settings.H1333: Section III.B Baseline; Table 4 panel A cols. (3)–(6), PDF pp. 180-181.
Settings.G1334:
Treatment: Continuous interaction between squared monetary policy surprise and continuous firm-level FPA, estimated while conditioning on many interacted covariates. Treatment is nonbinary.

Method: Firm-level event-study regressions of squared firm returns on squared monetary shocks, FPA, their interaction, and an extensive set of observed firm- and industry-level controls interacted with shocks, with firm fixed effects included throughout these specifications. Controls include price-cost margin, concentration, book-to-market, size, sales volatility, durability, labor share, wage adjustment frequency, receivables-payables to sales, investment to sales, depreciation to assets, Engel curve slopes, synchronization, number of products, ratings, financial constraints, leverage, fixed costs, and export share. This is a standard FE regression-adjustment approach used to bolster a causal interpretation of the interaction term.

Identification: The identifying variation remains announcement-window monetary surprises interacted with cross-firm FPA, but now the authors seek to block observed confounders that might make sticky-price firms systematically more sensitive to monetary shocks for other reasons. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity; interacted controls account for differential shock sensitivity via observed firm and industry traits. The remaining assumption is that unobserved time-varying traits correlated with FPA do not explain the interaction coefficient.

Setting: Across a large battery of firm- and industry-level controls, the interaction of FPA and monetary shocks remains negative and significant, reinforcing the claim that stickier prices causally raise the volatility response to monetary policy surprises. For example, with outlier correction and firm FE, the FPA interaction is -45.52 controlling for price-cost margins, -67.68 controlling for concentration, -63.02 controlling for size, -74.70 controlling for sales volatility, -54.57 controlling for durable/nondurable/service/investment/government/net-export exposure, -96.51 controlling for labor share, -76.12 controlling for wage adjustment frequency, -52.22 controlling for synchronization, and -35.33 controlling for number of products. In the full specification with many controls jointly, the interaction is still -188.70 and highly significant. The authors interpret this as strong evidence against alternative confounding explanations.

Main role: These control-heavy FE regressions directly support the paper’s main claim by arguing the differential volatility effect is not explained by alternative mechanisms correlated with FPA, such as firm size, market power, demand volatility, or financial characteristics.
Settings.H1334: Section III.C Additional Controls and Analysis of Subsamples; Table 5 cols. (1)–(22), PDF pp. 183-187.
Settings.G1335:
Treatment: Continuous interaction between squared monetary policy surprise and continuous FPA, estimated separately within agriculture, manufacturing, utilities, trade, finance, service, and in a sample excluding durable-goods producers. Treatment is nonbinary.

Method: Within-industry event-study regressions of squared firm returns on squared monetary policy surprises and the interaction with FPA, estimated separately by broad industry and including firm fixed effects for most columns. One specification excludes durable goods producers. This is a standard FE regression within industry to assess whether the main interaction survives when identification comes from cross-firm variation in FPA inside industry groupings.

Identification: The design leverages the same high-frequency monetary surprises but compares firms with differing FPA within broad industries, thereby reducing concern that cross-industry differences in technology or demand drive the main finding. Firm fixed effects absorb persistent firm-level heterogeneity. Assumptions are similar to the baseline, with added reliance on within-industry comparability.

Setting: The authors show that the differential volatility response by price stickiness generally survives within-industry estimation. In Table 6, the interaction between FPA and squared shocks is negative and significant in agriculture (-106.60), manufacturing (-35.99), and utilities (-125.00), negative but imprecise in trade and finance, and becomes small and insignificant in services after excluding outliers. Excluding durable-goods producers, the interaction is still -112.90. These results are interpreted as evidence that the main effect is broad-based rather than driven by sectoral composition or durable-goods exposure alone.

Main role: These are substantive robustness checks showing the main effect appears within most industries and is not driven solely by durable-goods sectors, but they are not the core headline specification.
Settings.H1335: Section III.C Additional Controls and Analysis of Subsamples; Table 6 cols. (1)–(8), PDF p. 187.
Settings.G1336:
Treatment: Continuous interaction between squared monetary policy surprise and continuous FPA, while controlling for continuous estimated firm-level return sensitivity to monetary policy surprises. Treatment is nonbinary.

Method: Event-study regressions of squared firm returns on squared monetary policy surprises, FPA, and their interaction, augmented with a generated control for each firm’s return sensitivity to monetary policy surprises (beta_vt), in levels, squares, or absolute value interacted with squared shocks. These are linear regression-adjustment robustness checks without FE emphasis in the table. The design remains high-frequency announcement-window OLS.

Identification: The authors first estimate each firm’s return sensitivity to monetary shocks and then include that sensitivity interacted with squared shocks to see whether the FPA interaction survives. The identifying assumption is that conditional on this generic exposure measure, any remaining FPA interaction reflects differential volatility amplification from price stickiness rather than from ordinary return beta to policy shocks.

Setting: Controlling for firms’ general return sensitivity to monetary policy does not eliminate the main effect of price stickiness on volatility responses. In Table 7, the FPA interaction remains negative and significant across specifications: -157.90 and -62.11 when controlling for squared return sensitivity, -160.80 and -61.02 when controlling for return sensitivity, and -170.70 and -62.17 when controlling for absolute return sensitivity. The authors interpret this as evidence that sticky-price firms are not merely firms with higher ordinary exposure of returns to policy shocks; instead, price stickiness specifically increases conditional volatility after monetary surprises.

Main role: This is a targeted robustness exercise against the alternative explanation that sticky-price firms simply have greater generic return sensitivity to monetary shocks, independent of sticky prices. It supports but does not define the main result.
Settings.H1336: Section III.C Additional Controls and Analysis of Subsamples; Table 7 cols. (1)–(8), PDF p. 188.
Settings.G1337:
Treatment: Continuous monetary policy shock interacted with continuous FPA, examined in nonlinear form via subsamples (below/above median) and polynomial terms, or effectively by FPA quintile categories in separate regressions. The treatment of interest remains nonbinary overall.

Method: Nonlinear and subgroup event-study regressions examine whether the effect of monetary policy shocks on squared firm returns varies nonlinearly across the distribution of FPA. The authors estimate the baseline separately below and above the median FPA, a quadratic-in-FPA specification, and separate regressions by FPA quintile. These are linear OLS regressions run on subsamples or with polynomial terms.

Identification: The same narrow-window shock design is used, but the authors test whether the interaction pattern is stronger among stickier-price firms, as New Keynesian logic predicts. The identifying assumptions are unchanged from the baseline; these regressions mainly probe functional form rather than introduce a new identification source.

Setting: The response of stock-return volatility to monetary shocks is strongest among the stickiest-price firms. In Table 8 panel A, splitting the sample at the median FPA shows a larger interaction magnitude in the stickier half than in the more flexible half. In panel B, separate regressions by FPA quintile show the coefficient on squared monetary shocks declines monotonically from 145.60 in the stickiest quintile to 70.67 in the most flexible quintile. The authors interpret this pattern as supporting the theory that firms with stickier prices tolerate wider deviations from optimal prices and therefore exhibit larger volatility responses to nominal shocks.

Main role: These are substantive robustness analyses about heterogeneity across the FPA distribution. They deepen interpretation of the main mechanism but are not the flagship baseline result.
Settings.H1337: Section III.C Additional Controls and Analysis of Subsamples; Table 8 panel A cols. (1)–(6) and panel B cols. (1)–(5), PDF pp. 188-189.
Settings.G1338:
Treatment: Continuous interaction between squared monetary policy surprises and continuous FPA. Treatment is nonbinary; in placebo regressions the same monetary-shock series is assigned to pseudo-event outcomes between adjacent events.

Method: Placebo and relative-volatility event-study regressions use either the ratio of event-window squared returns to pseudo-event-window squared returns, or pseudo-event squared returns themselves, as outcomes. Specifications include firm FE, event FE, or both, plus outlier correction variants. These standard FE regressions test whether the main interaction appears only on true monetary announcement windows rather than on non-event windows.

Identification: The relative-volatility design asks whether monetary announcements disproportionately raise volatility for sticky-price firms relative to their own nonevent volatility. The placebo design tests whether the same interaction spuriously appears in pseudo-event windows where no causal effect of monetary announcements should exist.
