Method: The authors implement calendar-time portfolio sorts and time-series regressions to study whether a trading rule based on k-NN forecasted earnings growth affects investment performance. Each month from 1998 to 2018, firms are assigned to UP or DOWN portfolios depending on whether the latest available k-NN forecast implies positive or negative earnings growth; firms remain in the assigned portfolio for 12 months and are rebalanced monthly. They then compute equal-weighted hedge returns (UP minus DOWN), excess returns over the risk-free rate, and Fama-French three-factor alphas. They also sort independently by MAD quartile and compare hedge returns for k-NN versus portfolios built from HVZ and EP-LIFE forecasts. This is a portfolio-sort/event-study style design rather than a standard causal estimator.

Identification: Identification relies on return differences between stocks sorted on k-NN-implied earnings growth signs, with risk adjustment through excess returns and Fama-French three-factor alphas. The paper interprets positive UP-minus-DOWN returns as evidence that k-NN forecasts identify mispricing or value-relevant earnings information. Assumptions are that factor adjustment adequately captures common risk and that forecast-based portfolio assignment is not merely loading on omitted risk factors. This is not a quasi-experimental causal design and remains vulnerable to omitted-risk and data-mining concerns.

Setting: The paper forms monthly hedge portfolios that are long firms for which k-NN predicts positive earnings growth and short firms for which k-NN predicts negative earnings growth, and interprets the resulting abnormal returns as evidence of the forecasts' usefulness for investors. For all firms, the k-NN hedge portfolio earns a monthly excess return of 0.26 and a Fama-French three-factor alpha of 0.34, both statistically significant. Among low-MAD firms, these rise to 0.91 and 1.10, while high-MAD firms show -0.05 and -0.15, yielding low-minus-high differences of 0.96 and 1.25. Relative to hedge portfolios based on HVZ and EP-LIFE forecasts, the k-NN hedge portfolio generally performs better, especially in the low-MAD subsample. These results materially support the paper's claim that k-NN forecasts are useful in security analysis and that MAD identifies when to rely on them more heavily.

Main role: The abstract states that a trading strategy based on k-NN-predicted earnings growth earns positive risk-adjusted returns exceeding those from alternate forecasts, and that profitability is greater when MAD is low. This is a headline application of the paper.
Settings.H1371: Section VIII, 'Trading Strategy,' Table 10 Panels A and B, PDF pp. 21-22.
Settings.G1372:
Treatment: IRS Audit, an indicator equal to 1 when the firm-year is classified as under IRS audit and 0 otherwise. It is constructed within year and firm-size group by ranking firms on IRS EDGAR-download attention and labeling the top share equal to the TRAC audit rate (subject to at least three IRS downloads) as audited.

Method: Firm-year OLS panel regressions of insider stock gift outcomes on an indicator for whether the firm is classified as under IRS audit in that year, with firm and year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. The authors aggregate gifts by the firm's top five officers (CEO, CFO, COO, President, Chairman) to the firm-year level and estimate Eq. (1). The identifying variation is within-firm changes in gift activity between audited and non-audited years after absorbing time-invariant firm heterogeneity and common year shocks; remaining concerns are time-varying omitted variables and measurement error in the constructed IRS Audit proxy.

Identification: The paper argues that corporate IRS audits raise executives' perceived detection risk and thereby deter manipulated gifting. Identification comes from within-firm changes in gift activity when the firm is under audit versus not under audit, controlling for firm and year fixed effects plus observables. The intended causal interpretation is that audit-induced scrutiny changes insider behavior. Key assumptions are that, conditional on controls and fixed effects, the timing of audit status is not driven by other time-varying factors that also affect gifting, and that the constructed IRS Audit proxy reasonably captures actual audit exposure.

Setting: Using firm and year fixed-effects panel regressions on 33,181 firm-years, the authors estimate that IRS scrutiny reduces overall stock gifting by top executives. In Table 3, IRS Audit is associated with a -0.250 coefficient for Gift Volume and -0.237 for Gift Value (dependent variables scaled by 100), which they interpret as within-firm declines during audit years. They report these imply a 16.6% reduction in gifted share volume, about 3,150 fewer shares relative to an average annual 19,000 shares, and a 15.0% reduction in gifted value, about $135,000 relative to an average annual $900,000. This baseline FE setting is a core test of the paper's claim that corporate tax enforcement deters managerial self-dealing.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that IRS audits reduce insider stock gift volume and value as direct evidence that tax enforcement deters managerial self-dealing. This is the paper's baseline central result.
Settings.H1372: Section 4.1 Baseline results: insider stock gift volume and value; Table 3 columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 11-12.
Settings.G1373:
Treatment: IRS Audit indicator equal to 1 if the firm is classified as under IRS audit in that year, 0 otherwise, based on the paper's composite audit proxy using firm-size-group audit probabilities and IRS EDGAR-download attention.

Method: Firm-year OLS panel regressions with firm and year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors, applied separately to stock gifts with delayed reporting and timely reporting. Delayed reporting is defined as more than 15 trading days between the purported gift date and SEC reporting date; timely reporting is 15 or fewer days. The same IRS Audit treatment is used, and the goal is to isolate effects on gifts more likely to be manipulated/backdated.

Identification: The authors use within-firm changes in audit status to identify the effect of scrutiny on different gift types. By partitioning on reporting delay, they argue delayed gifts are more likely to involve backdating or other manipulation, so larger effects there support the deterrence mechanism rather than a general reduction in all gifting. Assumptions mirror the baseline FE design: no confounding time-varying shocks differentially correlated with audit status and delayed/timely gift outcomes, plus the maintained interpretation of reporting delay as an ex ante manipulation proxy.

Setting: In Table 4, the paper finds the audit effect is concentrated in gifts most likely to be manipulated. IRS Audit is associated with a -0.114 coefficient on Gift VolumeDelay and -0.130 on Gift ValueDelay, but near-zero and insignificant effects for timely gifts (-0.006 for Gift VolumeTimely and -0.019 for Gift ValueTimely). The authors interpret these as 33.3% and 34.5% reductions, respectively, in delayed-reported gift volume and value relative to their sample means, consistent with IRS scrutiny deterring backdated or otherwise manipulated stock gifts rather than all gifts generally. This setting materially supports the mechanism underlying the paper's main claim.

Main role: The paper's central hypothesis concerns manipulated stock gifts specifically. The delayed-vs-timely split is repeatedly highlighted in the introduction, main results, and conclusion as showing that the deterrent effect is concentrated in gifts most likely to be manipulated.
Settings.H1373: Section 4.2 Manipulated stock gifts: gifts with delayed versus timely reporting; Table 4 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 12-13; related event-time discussion in Fig. 2 on PDF p. 13.
Settings.G1374:
Treatment: IRS Audit indicator for whether the firm is classified as under IRS audit in the fiscal year of the stock gift transaction.

Method: Transaction-level OLS regressions of cumulative abnormal returns around stock gifts on IRS Audit, with firm and year fixed effects, controls, and firm-clustered standard errors. Estimated separately for pre-gift and post-gift six-month CARs and for delayed versus timely reported gifts, following Eqs. (2) and (3). CARs are daily returns minus the CRSP equal-weighted market index cumulated over the relevant six-month window.

Identification: The design exploits within-firm changes in audit status across gift transactions. The paper's logic is that manipulated gifts should occur near local price peaks, producing high pre-gift and low post-gift abnormal returns; if IRS audits deter such manipulation, the return pattern should flatten specifically for delayed gifts. Firm and year fixed effects absorb persistent firm traits and common shocks. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on controls and FE, audit status is not itself driven by contemporaneous return dynamics that mechanically create the observed pre/post pattern.

Setting: At the transaction level, the authors show that IRS audits flatten the classic inverse-V return pattern around likely manipulated gifts. In Table 5, for delayed gifts, IRS Audit is associated with a -0.035 coefficient on Pre-Gift CARDelay and a +0.027 coefficient on Post-Gift CARDelay, while effects for timely gifts are insignificant (0.004 and -0.007). The paper interprets these magnitudes as reducing pre-gift CARs from 8.3% to 4.8% and increasing post-gift CARs from 2.3% to 0.4%, implying less opportunistic timing/backdating when the firm is under audit. This is a central mechanism test supporting the paper's claim that tax enforcement deters manipulated insider gifting.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion describe the flattening of the inverse-V return pattern around gifts as key evidence that audits deter manipulative timing/backdating. This transaction-level evidence is central to the mechanism, not merely ancillary.
Settings.H1374: Section 4.3 Abnormal returns around insider stock gifts; Fig. 3 and Table 5 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G1375:
Treatment: IRS Audit indicator equal to 1 when the firm is classified as under IRS audit in the year, 0 otherwise.

Method: Firm-year OLS panel regressions with firm and year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors, using the baseline Eq. (1) but redefining outcomes by whether gifts occurred at suspiciously high stock prices. Manipulated gifts are alternatively identified as gifts made at prices at or above the 90th percentile of all available firm trading prices from the start of the fiscal year to the earlier of the SEC report date or fiscal year-end. Outcomes are estimated separately for suspect and non-suspect gift volume and value.

Identification: The identification mirrors the baseline firm and year FE design, but the key robustness argument is outcome reclassification: if audits truly deter manipulated gifts, effects should appear for gifts at suspiciously high prices and not for other gifts. This alternative outcome construction reduces reliance on possibly manipulated reporting lags. Assumptions remain that within-firm audit timing is conditionally exogenous to other time-varying drivers of suspect gifting and that the price-percentile rule is a reasonable proxy for suspicious timing.

Setting: As a robustness test, the paper redefines manipulated gifts as those made at prices above the 90th percentile of the firm's available same-year price distribution. In Table 8, IRS Audit is associated with -0.215 for Gift VolumeSuspect and -0.233 for Gift ValueSuspect, but insignificant effects for non-suspect gifts (-0.086 and -0.048). The authors interpret this as a 47.8% decline in suspect gift volume and a 44.0% decline in suspect gift value relative to their sample means, reinforcing the view that IRS audits specifically deter manipulated stock gifts rather than ordinary giving.

Main role: This is presented as a robustness analysis to address measurement error in the main delayed-reporting proxy for manipulation. It supports but does not itself constitute the headline result.
Settings.H1375: Section 5.3 Alternative approach to identifying manipulated stock gifts; Table 8 columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 17-18.
Settings.G1376:
Treatment: IRS Audit indicator equal to 1 when the firm is classified as under IRS audit in the year and 0 otherwise.

Method: Firm-year OLS panel regressions with firm and year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors, examining the effect of IRS Audit on insider trading outcomes aggregated annually for top five executives. Trades are classified as opportunistic or routine following Cohen et al. (2012): routine if the insider trades in the same calendar month for at least three consecutive years; otherwise opportunistic conditional on at least one trade in each of three consecutive years. Outcomes include trading volume and profitability for opportunistic and routine trades.

Identification: The authors use within-firm variation in audit status to test whether IRS scrutiny reduces informed insider trading. The mechanism is that audits increase perceived detection risk because the IRS can investigate executives directly and refer suspicious behavior to criminal investigators or other agencies. Routine trades serve as a within-paper contrast group because they are viewed as less information-based. The causal interpretation relies on the same FE assumption that, conditional on firm and year FE and controls, audit timing is not driven by omitted time-varying factors that separately affect opportunistic trading volume/profitability.

Setting: In the paper's secondary setting, IRS audits also deter informed insider trading by top executives. Table 9 shows IRS Audit is associated with -0.019 for Trade VolumeOpp and -0.003 for Trade ProfitOpp, while effects on routine trading are small and insignificant (-0.004 for Trade VolumeRout and approximately 0.000 for Trade ProfitRout). The authors interpret these as a 19.0% decline in opportunistic trading volume, roughly 12,350 fewer shares relative to about 65,000 annual opportunistic shares, and a 37.5% decline in opportunistic trading profitability, about $115,000 relative to average annual opportunistic profits of $306,000. This extends the paper's argument that tax enforcement curbs managerial self-dealing beyond stock gifts.

Main role: The paper labels insider trading as a 'secondary setting' and 'final analysis.' It extends the deterrence argument beyond stock gifts, so it is substantive but not the paper's primary contribution.
Settings.H1376: Section 6 Secondary setting: insider trading; Table 9 Panel B columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 19-20.
Settings.G1377:
Treatment: Ease/difficulty of accessing new data, operationalized qualitatively through topic areas with more versus less readily available archival data (e.g., financial reporting, governance, tax versus auditing, managerial accounting). This is not directly numerically coded in the paper’s reported table; the effective treatment contrast is higher versus lower availability of readily available data.

Method: In Section 2, the authors tabulate counts of published papers across topic areas and methods for four accounting journals from 2003–2013, and interpret the observed cross-topic differences as evidence that data availability affects researchers' method choice. This is not implemented as a formal causal design such as DiD, IV, or RD; instead it is an informal regression-adjustment/association-style causal interpretation based on descriptive comparisons of publication shares across topic areas and journals. The paper explicitly frames the result as being 'consistent with Vatter’s conjecture' that easier access to archival data causes more archival-method publication. No formal estimator, standard errors, or regression coefficients are reported in the excerpted article.

Identification: The intended identifying argument is comparative: topics with greater preexisting, readily accessible archival data should induce more archival research, whereas topics with less readily available data should induce more experiments and field work. The endogeneity concern is that topic differences may correlate with other determinants of method choice, such as journal mission and traditions, which the authors acknowledge by noting cross-journal variation even after controlling for topic. Thus the design provides suggestive causal evidence rather than clean identification; it relies on the plausibility of data availability as the main driver of cross-topic method patterns.

Setting: Using counts of 1,638 papers published in four top accounting journals from 2003–2013, the authors argue that ease of data access affects methodological choice in published accounting research. They report that archival work constitutes over 75% of financial reporting and tax research and is also especially prevalent in governance and compensation, while auditing and managerial topics rely more heavily on experiments and field work. The paper interprets these cross-topic differences as consistent with Vatter’s conjecture that readily available data push researchers toward archival methods, making this an important empirical motivation for the paper’s broader framework about data gathering choices.

Main role: Although the paper is primarily methodological and conceptual, this empirical classification exercise is one of the paper’s substantive central findings, introduced in the abstract and introduction as evidence motivating the framework.
Settings.H1377: Section 2 'The State of the Literature,' especially discussion on PDF pages 344–345 and Table 1, Panels A–E on PDF pages 346–347.
Settings.G1378:
Treatment: Firm or filing characteristics interpreted as affecting scriptability: Size, Age, Distress, OpComplex, FinComplex, Growth, institutional ownership (%IH), high-tech industry indicator (HTI), FileLag, Top25FA, Watermark, and HTML. These are a mix of continuous covariates and binary indicators; the paper highlights especially Top25FA and Watermark as improving scriptability.

Method: The authors estimate linear OLS regressions of scriptability measures on firm and filing characteristics using equation (1), with year-month fixed effects and Fama-French 48-industry fixed effects. The design is cross-sectional/within-time-and-industry association interpreted causally or quasi-causally in places as characteristics that improve or reduce scriptability. Identification comes from within-year-month, within-industry variation after controlling for other observables including HTML and filing-agent indicators. Because there are only two absorbed FE dimensions and the paper discusses them as controls for heterogeneity rather than as a stronger quasi-experiment, this is standard FE rather than HDFE.

Identification: The paper uses conditional cross-sectional variation in firm/filer characteristics, holding constant year-month and industry fixed effects plus other observables. The endogeneity concern is that firms with different reporting resources, complexity, or technology may differ on unobserved determinants of scriptability. The paper interprets coefficients as suggestive evidence that certain factors, especially top filing agents, improve scriptability, but the design remains observational and potentially subject to omitted variables and reverse selection into filing agents.

Setting: Using FE regressions by form type, the authors argue that some firm and filing characteristics affect disclosure scriptability. Their strongest result is that using a top-25 filing agent is associated with materially higher scriptability across all form types and all three scriptability measures: for example, in Table 3 the Top25FA coefficient is 4.793 for 10-K CompScript, 4.749 for 10-Q CompScript, 2.303 for 8-K CompScript, and 3.224 for DEF 14A CompScript, with similarly positive effects on IdentifyData and DataToInformation. Watermark and HTML also often load positively. The paper interprets these patterns as evidence that outside filing providers improve scriptability, helping validate the measure, though the evidence is observational rather than cleanly causal.

Main role: These regressions validate and characterize the new scriptability measure, but the paper’s central conclusions concern capital-market consequences of scriptability, especially market timeliness, Dow Jones dissemination, information asymmetry, and XBRL interactions.
Settings.H1378: Section 2.2, equation (1), Table 3, PDF pp. 13–19 (esp. Table 3 on PDF p. 18).
Settings.G1379:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability, measured alternatively as CompScript, IdentifyData, or DataToInformation for the filed SEC disclosure. These are continuous percentile-rank-based measures, not binary treatments.

Method: To test H1, the authors estimate linear OLS regressions of price-based intraperiod timeliness (IPTP) on scriptability using equation (3), separately by form type and separately for 5-minute, 60-minute, and 24-hour windows. IPTP is a decile-ranked abnormal area-under-the-price-response-curve measure computed from TAQ data relative to a same-time/day benchmark over the prior 52 weeks. Regressions include the scriptability measure (CompScript or task-based measures), a large set of controls, and year-month and industry fixed effects. Despite the fixed effects, the identifying design is regression adjustment rather than a quasi-experiment.

Identification: The intended identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in scriptability across filings, conditional on firm information-environment controls, filing clustering, year-month fixed effects, and industry fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that scriptability may correlate with omitted disclosure quality or firm traits that also affect price response speed. The paper treats the estimates as evidence on whether scriptability facilitates faster price formation, but acknowledges noise in short-window price IPT measures and reports mixed results rather than a strong causal design.

Setting: The authors test whether more scriptable disclosures speed price formation. In Table 4 they find no support in 5-minute price IPT regressions, some support at 60 minutes, and limited support at 24 hours. Examples include a positive coefficient on CompScript for 8-K IPTP60m of 0.283 (t = 2.26), a positive coefficient on DataToInformation for 8-K IPTP60m of 0.270 (t = 2.90), and a positive coefficient on CompScript for 10-K IPTP24h of 0.978 (t = 2.15). They also find some counterevidence, such as a negative coefficient on CompScript for 10-Q IPTP60m of -0.309 (t = -2.60). Overall, the paper interprets these OLS results as mixed but suggestive evidence that scriptability can increase the speed of price formation, especially for some forms and horizons.

Main role: The abstract and introduction state that a core planned hypothesis is that market response speed increases with scriptability. These price-timeliness regressions are one of the main tests of that central claim, even though evidence is mixed.
Settings.H1379: Section 3.2.1 equation (3); Section 4.1; Table 4 panels A-C, PDF pp. 22, 25–32.
Settings.G1380:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability, measured as CompScript, IdentifyData, or DataToInformation for the SEC filing. Continuous percentile-rank-based measures.

Method: The authors estimate OLS regressions of volume-based intraperiod timeliness (IPTV) on scriptability using equation (3), separately by form type and separately for 5-minute, 60-minute, and 24-hour windows. IPTV is a decile-ranked abnormal area-under-the-cumulative-volume-response-curve measure from TAQ, benchmarked to the prior 52 weeks at the same time/day. Models include CompScript or the task-based scriptability measures, extensive controls, and year-month and industry fixed effects.

Identification: Identification relies on conditional cross-sectional variation in scriptability across filings, net of controls for information environment, performance, filing clustering, and year-month and industry fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is omitted correlated disclosure quality and firm characteristics. The paper argues that if scriptability reduces computerized processing frictions, investors should trade more quickly on the information in the filing. Because this remains observational, the claim depends on the adequacy of control adjustment rather than a quasi-experimental source of variation.

Setting: Using volume-based IPT as the outcome, the authors find their strongest evidence that scriptability speeds the market response to filings. In Table 5, effects are especially strong for 8-Ks: for the 5-minute window, CompScript loads 0.577 (t = 5.06) and IdentifyData 0.780 (t = 6.10); for the 60-minute window, CompScript loads 0.642 (t = 6.48), IdentifyData 0.315 (t = 2.62), and DataToInformation 0.325 (t = 3.93); for the 24-hour window, CompScript loads 0.357 (t = 2.24) and IdentifyData 0.218 (t = 2.86). The paper treats this as the clearest evidence that poor scriptability impedes some traders, particularly around 8-K filings.

Main role: The abstract emphasizes that the strongest evidence is that scriptability increases the timeliness of trading (volume IPT), particularly for 8-Ks. This is a central substantive result of the paper.
Settings.H1380: Section 3.2.1 equation (3); Section 4.1; Table 5 panels A-C, PDF pp. 22, 33–40.
Settings.G1381:
Treatment: Individual scriptability components such as TextFromTables, SeparateSections, UsefulHeadings, ExtReferences, BinaryExhibits, %NumTabulate, UnexpectChar, TokenQuality, Typo, TableMarkup, CellConsistency, and UsefulRowNames. These are continuous component measures.

Method: This is an unplanned descriptive component-level analysis using Spearman correlations between individual scriptability components and price-based IPTP measures, reported in Table 4 panel D. It is not a linear causal design with standard regression identification, but the authors use it to explore which components may drive causal effects of scriptability on price formation across form types and horizons.

Identification: There is no strong identification strategy; the analysis simply examines unconditional component-level Spearman correlations to assess whether certain aspects of scriptability appear more relevant to price timeliness than aggregate measures. The authors explicitly present it as exploratory after observing mixed IPTP results.

Setting: In an unplanned descriptive exercise, the authors relate individual scriptability components to price-based IPT measures to see whether specific dimensions of scriptability, rather than the summary indices, matter for price formation. They conclude that they 'fail to observe much consistency in component-level correlations,' suggesting no single component robustly explains the mixed IPTP evidence across forms and horizons.

Main role: The paper labels this analysis unplanned and descriptive, intended to better understand mixed main results rather than to carry a central conclusion on its own.
Settings.G1382:
Treatment: Individual scriptability components such as TextFromTables, SeparateSections, UsefulHeadings, ExtReferences, BinaryExhibits, %NumTabulate, UnexpectChar, TokenQuality, Typo, TableMarkup, CellConsistency, and UsefulRowNames. Continuous component measures.

Method: This is an unplanned descriptive component-level analysis using Spearman correlations between individual scriptability components and volume-based IPTV measures, reported in Table 5 panel D. It is exploratory rather than a standard linear causal estimator.

Identification: No quasi-experimental identification; the analysis inspects unconditional component-level rank correlations to infer which filing features may facilitate faster trading responses. The authors use it to argue that scriptability is context specific and that different components matter for different form types.

Setting: The component-level correlation analysis suggests that scriptability is not a 'one-size-fits-all' construct for trading speed. The authors highlight that ExtReferences and BinaryExhibits correlate with IPTV for 10-Ks, 10-Qs, and proxies but not 8-Ks, while %NumTabulate correlates in the expected direction only for 8-Ks and negatively for other forms. They interpret this as evidence that different scriptability components affect information processing in different settings.

Main role: This is explicitly an unplanned descriptive follow-up used to interpret the main volume-timeliness results, not a primary test.
Settings.G1383:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability, measured as CompScript, IdentifyData, or DataToInformation for the SEC filing. Continuous percentile-rank-based measures.

Method: For H2 the authors estimate a Probit model when the dependent variable is Dissem, an indicator for whether Dow Jones disseminates at least one newswire within 24 hours of filing receipt by the SEC. Equation (4) is estimated separately by form type with scriptability measured by CompScript or task-based measures, a broad control set, and year-month, industry, hour, and day-of-week fixed effects. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear probit, classification falls under Other.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in scriptability across filings conditional on controls for reporting environment, filing intensity, volatility, litigation risk, news coverage, and timing fixed effects. The concern is omitted characteristics of the filing or newsworthiness that correlate with both scriptability and whether Dow Jones chooses to disseminate it. The authors interpret the coefficient as evidence on whether scriptability facilitates intermediary dissemination, but the design is observational and they note low dissemination base rates may limit power.

Setting: The paper tests whether more scriptable disclosures are more likely to be picked up by Dow Jones. Using Probit models, Table 6 shows little support overall. One positive result is for 8-Ks, where CompScript has a positive coefficient of 0.422 (t = 2.66), and in task-based models IdentifyData for 8-Ks is 0.970 (t = 8.26). But there are also opposite-signed findings, such as CompScript for 10-Qs at -1.401 (t = -2.17), CompScript for DEF 14As at -2.198 (t = -2.57), and DataToInformation for 8-Ks at -0.226 (t = -2.36). The authors conclude that they find little evidence that scriptability increases the incidence of Dow Jones dissemination.

Main role: Newswire dissemination is one of the two main planned hypotheses in the paper. The abstract states they find little evidence that scriptability affects the incidence and speed of dissemination by Dow Jones, so these tests are central even though mostly null.
Settings.H1383: Section 3.2.2 equation (4); Section 4.2; Table 6 panel A and panel B Dissem columns, PDF pp. 23–24, 41–46.
Settings.G1384:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability, measured as CompScript, IdentifyData, or DataToInformation. Continuous percentile-rank-based measures.

Method: For H2 the authors estimate OLS regressions when the dependent variable is NewsDelay, the minutes between SEC acceptance and the matched Dow Jones newswire. Equation (4) is estimated separately by form type on the subsample with dissemination, with scriptability measured by CompScript or task-based measures, controls including DJ article length, and year-month, industry, hour, and day-of-week fixed effects.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in filing scriptability among disseminated filings, controlling for filing/news characteristics and timing fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that more newsworthy or complex filings may differ both in scriptability and in the time DJ takes to publish a story. The paper treats coefficients as evidence on whether scriptability speeds intermediary processing, but the design is observational and low dissemination rates reduce precision.

Setting: The authors ask whether greater scriptability reduces the delay before Dow Jones publishes a newswire. OLS results in Table 6 are mostly unsupportive. For 8-Ks, CompScript is associated with longer delay, not shorter, with coefficient 71.962 (t = 6.61); in task-based models, IdentifyData predicts shorter delays for 8-Ks (-36.415, t = -4.19) while DataToInformation predicts longer delays (85.758, t = 14.12). For 10-Qs, IdentifyData is associated with longer delays (411.476, t = 2.99). The paper concludes there is little overall evidence that scriptability speeds Dow Jones dissemination.

Main role: This is part of the paper’s second main planned hypothesis regarding the speed of newswire dissemination, which the abstract says receives little support.
Settings.H1384: Section 3.2.2 equation (4); Section 4.2; Table 6 panel A and panel B NewsDelay columns, PDF pp. 23–24, 41–46.
Settings.G1385:
Treatment: Individual scriptability components such as TextFromTables, SeparateSections, UsefulHeadings, ExtReferences, BinaryExhibits, %NumTabulate, UnexpectChar, TokenQuality, Typo, TableMarkup, CellConsistency, and UsefulRowNames. Continuous component measures.

Method: This is an unplanned descriptive analysis of Spearman correlations between individual scriptability components and the two Dow Jones dissemination outcomes, Dissem and NewsDelay, for 8-K disclosures only, reported in Table 6 panel C. It is exploratory and nonlinear/noneconometric in the causal-design sense.

Identification: No strong identification. The exercise examines unconditional component-level correlations to infer which aspects of scriptability may matter for the specific Dow Jones monitoring and processing workflow. The authors emphasize that this depends on unknown details of DJ’s scripts and procedures.

Setting: The unplanned 8-K component analysis shows that some filing features correlate with more frequent and faster Dow Jones dissemination in the predicted direction, including TextFromTables, SeparateSections, UsefulHeadings, %NumTabulate, TableMarkup, and UsefulRowNames, while others correlate in the opposite direction. The paper uses this to argue that portions of scriptability may capture programmatic impediments relevant to DJ, even though the aggregate measure mostly does not.

Main role: The authors explicitly label this unplanned and use it to interpret the mostly null H2 results rather than as a main design.
Settings.G1386:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability (CompScript), with heterogeneity analyzed by XBRL presence partition (XBRL = 1 if filing has EX-101 XBRL metadata, 0 otherwise). The focal treatment remains continuous scriptability; XBRL partition is a moderator/sample split.

Method: In a planned supplemental analysis, the authors estimate equation (3) and equation (4) separately on 10-K filings with and without XBRL during 2010–2012, comparing the coefficient of CompScript across partitions. The implemented estimators are the same OLS models for IPTP, IPTV, and NewsDelay and Probit for Dissem; because this setting pools the partitioned comparison across outcomes and the paper emphasizes coefficient differences, it is best described as regression adjustment with sample splits. The goal is to assess whether XBRL presence moderates scriptability’s effects.

Identification: The design compares regression coefficients on scriptability across XBRL and non-XBRL 10-K samples. Endogeneity concerns include selection into XBRL adoption and differences across filers beyond XBRL itself. The paper interprets coefficient differences as evidence on whether XBRL provides an alternative machine-readable channel that substitutes for scriptability, but because XBRL presence is not randomized, the evidence is observational.

Setting: To test whether XBRL presence changes how scriptability affects market and dissemination outcomes, the authors split 10-Ks into XBRL and non-XBRL samples and re-estimate their main models. Table 7 panel A shows almost no significant differences in the CompScript coefficient across partitions; the only reported significant difference is for NewsDelay (difference test p = 0.02). The paper concludes that this generally does not support the conjecture that XBRL substitutes for filing scriptability in 10-K processing.

Main role: This is a planned supplemental analysis about whether XBRL substitutes for scriptability. It supports a secondary conclusion in the abstract that there is little evidence XBRL interacts with scriptability meaningfully.
Settings.H1386: Section 5.1; Table 7 panel A, PDF pp. 48–50.
Settings.G1387:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability (CompScript) interacted with XBRL metadata extent/quality: %Tagged (numeric tags divided by unique numbers), StandardTags (one minus share of extended tags), and TagQuality (share of XBRL-quality dimensions marked OK). All are continuous measures; the causal question is whether better XBRL substitutes for scriptability.

Method: The authors estimate equation (5), an interaction model including CompScript, XBRL metadata extent/quality measures (%Tagged, StandardTags, TagQuality), and interactions of those XBRL variables with CompScript, for 10-K filings during 2013–2015. Outcomes include IPTP, IPTV, Dissem, and NewsDelay. Because Dissem is modeled with a nonlinear estimator elsewhere and because this is a mixed interaction design over multiple outcomes centered on moderation by XBRL quality, classification is Other.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-sectional variation in XBRL coverage and quality among 10-K filers, interacted with scriptability, conditional on the same controls and fixed effects as the main models. The main concern is omitted differences in filer sophistication and disclosure systems correlated with both XBRL quality and outcomes. The authors interpret interaction signs as evidence on substitution versus complementarity between XBRL and scriptability.

Setting: In Table 7 panel B, the authors test whether more extensive or higher-quality XBRL metadata changes scriptability’s effects. Results are mixed and mostly insignificant. Examples include a positive CompScript × %Tagged interaction for Dissem of 0.608 (t = 1.93), suggesting complementarity, and a negative CompScript × StandardTags interaction for Dissem of -0.823 (t = -1.74), suggesting substitution; for IPTP24h, CompScript × StandardTags is 17.255 (t = 2.27), opposite substitution. The paper concludes there is little consistent evidence that XBRL meaningfully substitutes for or interacts with scriptability at the aggregate level.

Main role: This planned additional analysis informs a secondary conclusion about XBRL’s limited interaction with scriptability, not the primary contribution.
Settings.H1387: Section 5.1, equation (5), Table 7 panel B, PDF pp. 50–52.
Settings.G1388:
Treatment: Disclosure scriptability, measured as CompScript, IdentifyData, or DataToInformation for the SEC filing. Continuous percentile-rank-based measures.

Method: In a planned additional analysis, the authors estimate equation (6), linear OLS regressions of abnormal bid-ask spread ratios on scriptability, separately by form type and for 5-minute, 60-minute, and 24-hour windows. The dependent variable %AbSpread is the post-filing quoted spread divided by the spread 60 seconds before the disclosure. Models include CompScript or task-based measures, the same controls as in H1, and year-month and industry fixed effects.

Identification: Identification uses conditional cross-sectional variation in scriptability across filings, controlling for firm information environment and filing clustering plus year-month and industry fixed effects. The causal concern is that unobserved disclosure characteristics may affect both scriptability and post-filing spreads. The authors’ conceptual argument is that high scriptability may initially advantage early sophisticated traders, raising asymmetry in very short windows, but lower asymmetry over longer windows as others catch up.

Setting: The information-asymmetry regressions suggest that scriptability can both increase and reduce post-filing asymmetry depending on context. In Table 8 panel A, DataToInformation is positively related to %AbSpread5m for 10-Ks (0.606, t = 1.97) and 8-Ks (0.580, t = 2.08), and CompScript is positive for 8-Ks (0.811, t = 2.56), consistent with early sophisticated traders gaining a short-run advantage. Over longer windows, the 8-K results split: in panel B, IdentifyData is negative (-2.200, t = -1.94) while DataToInformation is positive (3.511, t = 3.77); in panel C, IdentifyData is significantly negative (-3.090, t = -2.86) while DataToInformation remains positive (4.172, t = 3.69). The paper interprets this pattern as evidence that early scriptability can widen asymmetry briefly, but some aspects of scriptability, especially data identification, reduce asymmetry as time passes.

Main role: The abstract highlights additional planned analyses on information asymmetry, noting both positive and negative associations depending on filing, window, and measure. These are important substantive results.
Settings.H1388: Section 5.2, equation (6), Table 8 panels A-C, PDF pp. 52–59.
Settings.G1389:
Treatment: Primary treatment is insider selling intensity, especially GREEN_SALES: total dollar value of director and officer insider sales, scaled by beginning-quarter market value of equity, during the 10-trading-day (14-calendar-day) window after the current quarter's earnings release; also lagged GREEN_SALES and other windows enter. In the same setting the paper also interprets LITIGATION_RISK (predicted probability of 10b-5 litigation next quarter from Kim and Skinner (2012)-style model) as affecting warning likelihood. The focal treatment for the main claim is selling intensity, a continuous scaled variable.

Method: Firm-quarter logistic regressions estimate how insider selling affects the probability that managers bundle a negative earnings forecast with the current quarter's earnings announcement. The dependent variable is N_FORECAST, and the key regressors are insider sales in different within-quarter windows (especially GREEN_SALES and lagged GREEN_SALES) plus an ex ante litigation-risk proxy. Specifications include industry and time effects and controls for prior guidance behavior, current earnings news, analyst environment, size, prior returns, meeting/beat history, and volatility. The design is observational regression adjustment with a nonlinear logit link; because implemented causal estimator is nonlinear rather than linear, it falls in Other. The authors interpret coefficients causally as trading incentives and litigation risk influencing the disclosure decision, but identification relies on selection on observables and timing arguments rather than an external quasi-experiment.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional and intertemporal variation in insider sales intensity around quarterly earnings announcements, conditional on rich controls and fixed industry/time effects, among firms facing impending negative news and especially among recent/committed guiders. The endogeneity concern is that firms or managers inclined not to warn may also differ in unobserved ways correlated with trading. The authors argue timing and sample restrictions mitigate this concern: they focus on impending bad-news quarters, committed guiders, positive-current-surprise cases, and CEO/CFO trades, and show effects are concentrated in low-jeopardy post-announcement trading windows. Nonetheless, causal interpretation still requires no omitted determinants of both selling and warning after controls.

Setting: Using logit regressions on 107,307 firm-quarters and narrower subsamples, the paper argues that insider selling reduces the likelihood of a preemptive bad-news warning. In Table 4 Panel A, GREEN_SALES enters negatively throughout: for the full sample the mean marginal effect is -0.367 (t=-5.80), for impending-bad-news firm-quarters -0.524 (t=-3.95), for recent guiders -1.457 (t=-4.05), for committed guiders -1.949 (t=-4.09), for committed guiders with current positive surprise -2.039 (t=-3.77), and using CEO/CFO trades only -3.369 (t=-3.19). LAG_GREEN_SALES is also negative. LITIGATION_RISK is positive, consistent with higher expected litigation pushing managers to warn. The authors interpret this as evidence that trading incentives contribute to strategic silence, a central paper claim.

Main role: A core contribution of the paper is that insider selling helps explain strategic silence before earnings disappointment; the abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize this result.
Settings.H1389: Section 5.1, Eq. (1), Table 4 Panel A columns [1]-[6], PDF pp. 11-14 (especially p. 12-14).
Settings.G1390:
Treatment: Insider selling intensity, especially GREEN_SALES and lagged GREEN_SALES, measured as total dollar value of director/officer sales scaled by beginning-quarter market value of equity in the low-jeopardy post-earnings-announcement trading window; LITIGATION_RISK is also interpreted as affecting positive disclosure. Treatment is continuous.

Method: Firm-quarter logistic regressions analogous to Eq. (1), but with P_FORECAST as the dependent variable, estimate whether insider selling affects the probability of bundling a positive forecast with the current quarter's earnings announcement while managers face impending bad news next quarter. The model includes the same industry and time effects and disclosure, news, information-environment, size, return, beat-history, volatility, and litigation-risk controls. Because the implemented estimator is logit, classification is Other.

Identification: The paper exploits variation in insider sales and litigation risk across firms and quarters, conditional on extensive controls and industry/time effects, and within samples where managers face impending bad news. The main concern is omitted variables that jointly determine willingness to issue positive guidance and trading; the authors address this by using recent/committed guiders, current positive-surprise subsamples, and CEO/CFO trades. Causal interpretation requires conditional exogeneity of sales and litigation-risk proxies in the logit specification.

Setting: In Table 4 Panel B, the authors show that insider selling increases the likelihood of positive bundled guidance even when managers face impending negative news next quarter. GREEN_SALES is positive across specifications: 0.260 (t=6.78) in the full sample, 0.248 (t=3.73) with impending bad news, 0.538 (t=3.28) for recent guiders, 0.731 (t=3.73) for committed guiders, 0.972 (t=3.34) when current-quarter surprise is positive, and 1.651 (t=3.38) using CEO/CFO trades only. LITIGATION_RISK is negative throughout. The authors interpret this as evidence that selling is linked to selective/tactical silence rather than to a blanket aversion to guidance.

Main role: This complementary analysis is used to argue the silence result is strategic rather than due to a general reluctance to disclose; it materially supports the central interpretation.
Settings.H1390: Section 5.1, Table 4 Panel B columns [1]-[6], PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G1391:
Treatment: Opportunistic insider selling intensity (SALES_OPP), especially green-window opportunistic sales and lagged green-window opportunistic sales, measured as total dollar value of director/officer sales scaled by beginning-quarter market value and classified as opportunistic using Cohen et al. (2012). Routine sales (SALES_ROU) are included for contrast. Treatment is continuous.

Method: Firm-quarter logistic regressions repeat the disclosure-choice analysis using Cohen, Malloy, and Pomorski (2012) trade-level classifications to separate opportunistic from routine insider sales. The dependent variables are N_FORECAST in Panel A and P_FORECAST in Panel B. Specifications include the same industry and time effects and the same control set as Table 4, but key treatments are opportunistic and routine sales by trading window. Because estimation is logit, this qualifies as Other.

Identification: As in the earlier disclosure regressions, identification uses conditional variation in insider trading intensity across firm-quarters, now partitioned into opportunistic versus routine trades based on historical trading patterns. The concern is selection on unobservables and misclassification of motives. The authors argue that finding effects only for opportunistic sales, concentrated in low-jeopardy windows and stronger for CEO/CFO trades and committed guiders, supports the intended causal interpretation that strategic trading incentives affect disclosure choices.

Setting: Table 5 shows that opportunistic rather than routine sales are associated with disclosure choices. For negative warnings (Panel A), opportunistic GREEN_SALES is negative and significant across increasingly targeted samples, reaching -3.107 (t=-3.34) for committed guiders with current positive surprise and -3.020 (t=-2.06) using CEO/CFO trades only, while routine green sales are never significant. For positive forecasts (Panel B), opportunistic GREEN_SALES is positive and significant, ranging from 0.258 (t=5.29) in the full sample to 1.572 (t=2.36) with CEO/CFO trades only. The authors interpret this as evidence that opportunistic selling causes strategic silence about bad news and greater likelihood of positive disclosure, reinforcing the paper's main mechanism.

Main role: The paper highlights that silence is linked specifically to opportunistic, not routine, selling; this sharpens the central mechanism and is emphasized in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1391: Section 5.2, Table 5 Panels A and B columns [1]-[6], PDF pp. 14-16.
Settings.G1392:
Treatment: Preemptive bad-news warning (WARN), an indicator equal to 1 if the firm issues a management forecast of negative news in the 90 days prior to the end of the class period (or a downward revision during the class period/fiscal year, depending on sued/non-sued status). In the second-stage simultaneous-equations specification the treatment is the predicted warning instrument derived from the first-stage WARN model.

Method: Single-equation and simultaneous-equations litigation regressions in the spirit of Field, Lowry, and Shu (2005) examine whether warning affects litigation risk. The implemented models are logistic in the single-stage specifications and a nonlinear two-stage/predicted-value simultaneous-equations approach in which WARN is first modeled using firm characteristics and prior disclosure, then a WARN instrument enters the SUED equation. Controls include size, industry dummies, returns, volatility, turnover, and prior disclosure. Because the implementation is nonlinear rather than linear IV/2SLS, this is classified as Other.

Identification: The authors explicitly address endogeneity between warning and litigation risk: firms with higher litigation risk are more likely to warn, so naive regressions can misleadingly suggest warnings trigger suits. Following FLS, they first show this endogeneity in single-stage logits, then use a simultaneous-equations framework where WARN is predicted from size, industry, return, volatility, turnover, and prior disclosure, and that predicted warning enters the SUED equation. Identification relies on functional-form/exclusion-style structure from prior disclosure appearing in the warning equation and on the assumption that the predicted component of warning captures exogenous variation in disclosure propensity relevant for litigation risk.

Setting: Replicating Field et al. (2005), the paper argues that preemptive warnings deter litigation once endogeneity is addressed. In the naive single-stage regressions, SUED positively predicts WARN (0.249, t=8.75 in Table 7 col. [1]) and WARN positively predicts SUED (0.301, t=8.05 in col. [2]), showing the endogeneity problem. In the two-stage framework, the WARN instrument is significantly negative in the SUED equation: -0.883 (t=-3.87) in the full sample (col. [4]) and -1.016 (t=-3.83) among non-dismissed lawsuits (col. [6]). The authors interpret this as strong evidence that warning lowers litigation risk, a major substantive conclusion of the paper.

Main role: A central contribution is the claim that warnings reduce litigation risk; the paper presents this as the first robust evidence of a litigation benefit from warning.
Settings.H1392: Section 6.2, Eqs. (2)-(5), Table 7 columns [1]-[6], PDF pp. 17-19.
Settings.G1393:
Treatment: Primary treatment is predicted SILENCE (failure to warn; WARN=0) and its interaction with insider selling during the class period, where SALES is total dollar value of insider sales scaled by market value of equity. Variants use CEO/CFO sales, opportunistic sales (SALES_OPP), routine sales (SALES_ROU), abnormal sales (SALES_AB), and GOOD forecasts. The focal treatment for the paper's H3 claim is the interaction between silence and selling. Both silence and good are binary; sales measures are continuous; the interaction is mixed.

Method: A nonlinear simultaneous-equations litigation-risk framework extends Field, Lowry, and Shu (2005) by adding insider selling and its interaction with predicted silence. The first stage models WARN (then reversed to SILENCE) as a function of firm characteristics, prior disclosure, and insider sales; the second-stage SUED regression includes predicted SILENCE, sales, and SILENCE×SALES. Variants use total class-period sales, CEO/CFO-only sales, opportunistic versus routine sales, abnormal sales relative to a pre-class-period benchmark, and good-news forecasts. Because this is a nonlinear predicted-value simultaneous-equations approach rather than linear IV/2SLS, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The identification argument extends the warning-litigation simultaneous-equations design by incorporating insider sales. The paper seeks to isolate the effect of disclosure and selling on lawsuit incidence while addressing the endogenous tendency of high-risk firms to warn. Predicted SILENCE from the first-stage warning equation is used in the second-stage SUED regression together with observed sales and their interaction. Assumptions include adequate control for common determinants of warning, sales, and litigation through size, industry, returns, volatility, turnover, prior disclosure, and extended class-end returns; and that the predicted component of silence captures exogenous disclosure propensity. Remaining concerns are omitted severity/prospect variables jointly affecting sales and litigation.

Setting: Table 8 shows that silence and selling each raise litigation risk and that their interaction raises it further. In Panel A, predicted SILENCE is positive across specifications, e.g. 0.479 (t=2.61) with total class-period sales in col. [2], 0.487 (t=2.60) with CEO/CFO sales in col. [3], and 0.500 (t=2.74) with opportunistic/routine sales in col. [4]. Sales are also positive: 11.010 (t=6.26) in col. [2], 21.800 (t=5.29) for CEO/CFO sales in col. [3], 11.481 (t=6.27) for opportunistic sales in col. [4], and 4.205 (t=2.83) for abnormal sales in col. [5]. Most importantly, the interaction terms are positive and significant: SILENCE×SALES = 10.829 (t=5.89) in col. [2], 21.392 (t=5.07) for CEO/CFO sales in col. [3], SILENCE×SALES_OPP = 11.259 (t=5.91) in col. [4], and SILENCE×SALES_AB = 8.407 (t=2.93) in col. [5]. The authors interpret this as evidence that silence combined with insider selling incrementally increases litigation risk beyond the separate effects.

Main role: The interaction of silence and selling on litigation risk is a headline result in the abstract and conclusions, directly tied to the paper's central contribution.
Settings.H1393: Section 6.3, Eqs. (6)-(7), Table 8 Panel A columns [1]-[6], PDF pp. 19-21.
Settings.G1394:
Treatment: Preemptive warning (WARN=1) interacted with insider sales during the class period scaled by market value of equity. WARN is binary, SALES is continuous, and the focal estimand concerns the interaction/moderation effect of sales on the warning benefit.

Method: A variant of the simultaneous-equations litigation model reverses the first stage back to predicting WARN rather than SILENCE so that the second-stage SUED regression can include WARN, SALES, and WARN×SALES. This directly examines whether selling offsets the litigation-risk reduction associated with warning. Estimation remains the same nonlinear predicted-value simultaneous-equations approach used in Table 8; hence classification is Other.

Identification: Using the same simultaneous-equations framework as the prior setting, the authors estimate the effect of predicted WARN, sales, and their interaction on litigation risk. Identification relies on the same assumptions about exogenous predicted disclosure propensity after controlling for firm characteristics and the exclusion-style structure from the warning equation. The interaction is interpreted as showing whether insider selling moderates the deterrence effect of warning.

Setting: Table 8 Panel B directly assesses whether selling erodes the litigation benefit of warning. The SUED regression reports WARN coefficient -2.552 with mean marginal effect -0.479 (t=2.61), SALES coefficient 58.705 with mean marginal effect 11.010 (t=6.26), and SALES×WARN coefficient 57.742 with mean marginal effect 10.829 (t=5.89). The authors conclude that selling before/within the class period offsets some but generally not all of warning's benefit. They state that, based on these point estimates, insiders would need to sell about 10% of market value in the class period to completely eliminate the warning benefit, a magnitude rarely observed in their sample.

Main role: This specification underpins the paper's conclusion that selling offsets some but not all of warning's benefit, a key substantive claim in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1394: Section 6.4, Table 8 Panel B, PDF pp. 21-22.
Settings.G1395:
Treatment: Executive and firm characteristics interpreted as affecting the probability of winning the current CEO tournament: TopPaid, SecondPaid, ThirdPaid, LogAge, Tenure, COO/President, CFO/Treasurer, Co-CEO, General Counsel, Division Head, measures of generalist skills, incumbent CEO traits, and firm performance/size variables. Treatments are mixed binary and continuous covariates, not a single binary treatment.

Method: Probit selection model used causally/interpreted structurally as estimating executives' ex ante odds of winning the current CEO tournament. The authors estimate a nonlinear binary-response model for Pr(WinCurrentTour=1) on executive characteristics (pay-rank indicators, log age, tenure, title indicators, generalist-skill proxies), CEO characteristics, firm characteristics, and year and industry fixed effects. Because the implemented estimator is probit, it is classified as Other rather than linear OLS/FE. The paper treats the regressors as determinants of promotion odds and uses fitted values to construct the key treatment-like variable Competitiveness for later analyses, but this is not based on an external source of quasi-random variation and remains associational/selection-on-observables.

Identification: The paper argues that observed executive, CEO, and firm characteristics proxy for ex ante promotion prospects in CEO tournaments. Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in these observables conditional on year and industry fixed effects. The concern is omitted determinants of promotion prospects and nonrandom executive assignment to titles/ranks; the paper does not claim quasi-experimental identification.

Setting: As a measurement step underlying the paper's later causal claims, the authors estimate a probit model of which executives win the current CEO tournament. Higher pay rank, tenure, and COO/President or co-CEO status are interpreted as increasing promotion odds, while CFO/Treasurer and General Counsel roles lower odds. The fitted probabilities from this nonlinear model define Competitiveness, the paper's proxy for an executive's ex ante chance of promotion. This setting is important for operationalizing the theory, but is not itself one of the headline causal findings.

Main role: This model is primarily a construction/measurement step for Competitiveness used in the paper's main tests, rather than itself a central substantive result in the abstract or conclusion.
Settings.H1395: Section III, Equation (1), Table 1 Panel B column (1), PDF pp. 6-9.
Settings.G1396:
Treatment: Prior tournament Competitiveness (estimated ex ante probability of winning the current CEO tournament), along with executive, CEO, and firm controls, interpreted as affecting the probability of winning the next CEO tournament in the same firm. Competitiveness is continuous on [0,1].

Method: Second probit model for Pr(WinNextTour=1), again a nonlinear binary-response estimator with year and industry fixed effects, estimated on non-promoted executives from a prior tournament whose firm's next CEO turnover is observed. The key regressor is prior-tournament Competitiveness; the model is interpreted as showing how losing the current tournament changes future promotion prospects. Because the estimator is probit, classification is Other.

Identification: Identification relies on conditional cross-sectional variation in prior Competitiveness and controls among NPEs whose firms later experience another CEO tournament. The authors interpret a negative coefficient on prior Competitiveness as evidence that previously strong contenders who lost are less likely to win the next tournament. Endogeneity remains because prior Competitiveness may correlate with unobserved traits affecting future promotion, and the sample conditions on survival/observability of a later tournament.

Setting: Using a probit model of winning the firm's next CEO tournament, the paper argues that losing the current tournament lowers future promotion prospects for previously strong contenders. In Table 1 Panel B column (2), prior Competitiveness enters negatively (coefficient/marginal effect reported as -0.243, t=-1.704), which the authors interpret as meaning that executives who were ex ante more competitive in the current tournament but lost are less likely to become CEO in the next tournament. This is a core empirical link in the paper's argument that NPEs' promotion-based incentives fall after a tournament ends.

Main role: A central contribution is that losing the current tournament reduces future promotion prospects, especially for previously competitive executives; this model provides the direct evidence cited in the main results discussion.
Settings.H1396: Section V, Table 1 Panel B column (2), discussion around Table 5 Panel A, PDF pp. 13-15.
Settings.G1397:
Treatment: Exposure to the end of a CEO tournament, operationalized as being an NPE in a CEO-change firm-year versus a matched control VP in a no-CEO-change firm-year; comparisons are also split by more versus less competitive NPEs. This is a binary treatment contrast at the executive-year level.

Method: Matched comparison of pay changes for non-promoted executives (treatment firms around CEO changes) versus executives in matched control firm-years without CEO turnover. Control firms are selected on fiscal year, Fama-French 12-industry, size quartile, stock-return quartile, and minimum difference in estimated propensity of CEO turnover. The analysis is primarily descriptive/comparative in medians rather than a regression, but the intended causal interpretation is that CEO tournament completion changes NPE compensation relative to a matched baseline. The authors further stratify by whether executives are above/below the sample median Competitiveness.

Identification: The identifying argument is selection on matched observables: by matching treatment firm-years to no-turnover control firm-years with similar year, industry, size, stock returns, and propensity of CEO turnover, the authors aim to recover the baseline pay growth that would have occurred absent the tournament ending. Remaining concerns are unobserved firm shocks around succession, differential composition of executives, and lack of exact causal isolation beyond matching.

Setting: To test whether firms offset reduced promotion-based incentives with higher explicit pay, the authors compare NPE pay changes around CEO succession to those of matched control executives outside the CEO-change window. For more competitive executives, median total pay rises by $64 thousand for NPEs versus $66 thousand for matched control VPs, implying essentially no extra adjustment; for less competitive executives, NPE total pay rises by $128 thousand versus $76 thousand for controls. The authors interpret this as evidence that firms make only limited compensation adjustments for the executives most affected by the tournament outcome, supporting the paper's central reduced-incentive mechanism.

Main role: The paper's first main conclusion is that firms do not sufficiently adjust explicit compensation to offset the loss in promotion-based incentives; these matched pay-change comparisons are central evidence.
Settings.H1397: Section V, Table 5 Panels B-C and accompanying discussion, PDF pp. 13-15.
Settings.G1398:
Treatment: End of the CEO tournament / losing the current tournament, operationalized through the before-versus-after change in an NPE's estimated odds of winning (current versus next tournament), with separate calculations for more versus less competitive NPEs. Treatment is effectively a before-after exposure, not a simple binary variable in a regression.

Method: Univariate/constructed comparison of promotion-based incentives before versus after CEO change, using fitted promotion odds from probit models and observed CEO-NPE pay gaps. The authors compute changes in winning probabilities for the current versus next tournament and multiply by pay gaps to estimate changes in implicit promotion-based incentives. This is not a formal regression effect and relies on generated regressors from nonlinear models, so it fits Other.

Identification: The paper interprets the change from current-tournament to next-tournament winning odds as the effect of losing the tournament on future promotion prospects, and then maps this into expected compensation losses using CEO-NPE pay gaps. Identification comes from model-based counterfactual construction rather than quasi-experimental variation. Assumptions include validity of the promotion-odds models, stable mapping from pay gaps to promotion prizes, and that observed future-tournament outcomes reveal post-loss promotion prospects.

Setting: The paper's first substantive test estimates how losing a CEO tournament changes implicit promotion-based incentives. Average winning odds fall from 0.161 to 0.077 for more competitive NPEs, a decline of 0.084, while less competitive NPEs' odds rise from 0.020 to 0.049. Combining these odds with CEO-NPE pay gaps, the authors estimate that more competitive NPEs' promotion-based incentives from total pay fall by $225 thousand (median $111 thousand), whereas less competitive NPEs' incentives rise by $101 thousand (median $46 thousand). The authors interpret this as direct evidence that the tournament's end reduces total incentives for the executives who were strongest ex ante contenders.

Main role: This is the paper's direct evidence for H1 that more competitive NPEs lose total incentives after the tournament ends; it is emphasized in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H1398: Section V, Table 5 Panels A-B and accompanying discussion, PDF pp. 13-15.
Settings.G1399:
Treatment: Tournament characteristics and executive competitiveness interpreted as causing NPE turnover: Closed tournament indicator (heir apparent promoted) versus open tournament base group; Outside winner indicator versus open tournament base group; and continuous Competitiveness. These are mixed binary and continuous treatments estimated jointly.

Method: Probit regressions for executive turnover following CEO tournaments, with tournament-type indicators, Competitiveness, Generalist, interactions, and controls plus year and industry fixed effects. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear probit rather than a linear probability model, it is classified as Other. The paper interprets coefficients as causal effects of tournament characteristics and competitiveness on turnover, while acknowledging possible alternative mechanisms such as the new CEO forcing out executives.

Identification: Identification relies on conditional comparisons across NPEs in different tournament types and with different estimated competitiveness, after controlling for executive title/rank, age, tenure, unvested equity, CEO characteristics, firm performance, size, volatility, and year/industry fixed effects. The paper's argument is that tournament design and ex ante competition generate variation in lost promotion-based incentives, which then affects departures. Remaining concerns are unobserved succession circumstances, voluntary versus forced turnover, and omitted factors correlated with tournament type.

Setting: The main turnover regressions indicate that non-promoted executives are more likely to leave when the tournament outcome implies a larger loss of incentives. In Table 7, the marginal effect of Competitiveness is positive and significant (0.566 in column 2; 0.702 in column 3), the Outside indicator is strongly positive (about 0.163-0.180), and the Closed indicator is negative in simpler specifications (-0.045 in column 1). The authors interpret these estimates as showing that turnover is higher for more competitive NPEs, lower after closed than open tournaments, and higher when the winner is an outsider rather than an insider—key evidence for the paper's theory of reduced incentives plus managerial sorting.

Main role: Higher turnover after open tournaments, outsider-winner tournaments, and among more competitive NPEs is a central conclusion featured in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.H1399: Section V, Equation (2), Table 7 columns (1)-(3), PDF pp. 16-18.
Settings.G1400:
Treatment: In pooled models, treatment is being an NPE versus a matched control VP, plus interactions with Competitiveness/Generalist. In alternative-measure models, treatments are continuous measures of lost promotion incentives: D_Competitiveness, Promo_Incentives, and D_Promo_Incentives. Treatments are mixed binary and continuous.

Method: Additional probit turnover analyses: (i) pooled sample of NPEs and matched control VPs with an NPE indicator and interactions, and (ii) alternative turnover specifications replacing Competitiveness with alternative measures of promotion-based incentives such as D_Competitiveness, Promo_Incentives, and D_Promo_Incentives. These are nonlinear probit models with controls and year/industry fixed effects where applicable, used as substantive supporting evidence for the causal mechanism.

Identification: The pooled NPE-versus-control design uses matched control VPs to net out executives' general propensity to leave and asks whether turnover-competitiveness sensitivity is larger specifically at tournament end. The alternative-measure regressions test whether turnover is stronger when the modeled loss in promotion-based incentives is greater. Identification still depends on selection on observables and the validity of the constructed incentive measures; no exogenous shock is used.

Setting: Additional turnover tests bolster the paper's mechanism. In the pooled NPE-control sample, NPEs are more likely to turn over than matched controls, and the interaction NPE × Competitiveness is positive and significant at 0.298, indicating that competitiveness predicts departures especially at tournament end. Using alternative measures, turnover is also higher when executives experience a larger decline in competitiveness after succession (D_Competitiveness = 0.508), had larger pre-change promotion-based incentives (Promo_Incentives = 0.107), or experience larger declines in promotion-based incentives (D_Promo_Incentives = 0.139). These results support the interpretation that reductions in implicit promotion incentives contribute to NPE turnover.

Main role: These analyses reinforce the main turnover mechanism but are framed as additional analyses rather than the primary headline result.
Settings.H1400: Section V, Table 8 columns (1)-(5), PDF p. 19.
Settings.G1401:
Treatment: Tournament type indicators Closed and Outside, with open tournaments as the omitted group, plus executive Competitiveness and Generalist. The focal treatment in the causal interpretation is the type of tournament from which the NPE departs. Tournament-type treatments are binary indicators.

Method: Career-outcome regressions for departed NPEs using probit (FindNewJob), ordered probit (NewJobType), and OLS (LogSizeRatio, LogSalaryRatio). The paper treats tournament type and executive traits as affecting subsequent labor-market outcomes and interprets those outcomes as revealing labor-market assessment of NPE quality. Because the implemented estimators include nonlinear probit/ordered probit, the setting is classified as Other.

Identification: The authors compare departed NPEs across tournament types conditional on observable executive and firm characteristics, year FE, and industry FE where available. The identifying argument is that tournament type reveals why executives left and thus should affect the labor market's assessment of their quality. Remaining concerns include selective observability of new jobs, omitted determinants of departure/job search, and the fact that labor-market outcomes are interpreted as a proxy for quality rather than directly observed quality.

Setting: The paper interprets labor-market outcomes of departed NPEs as evidence about whether turnover reflects reduced incentives or firms weeding out low-quality managers. Relative to open tournaments, the Closed indicator is negative and significant for finding a new job and for better job type, while the Outside indicator is significantly negative for relative new-firm size and relative new salary. The authors conclude that executives departing after open tournaments are viewed more favorably than those leaving after closed tournaments or tournaments won by outsiders, consistent with open-tournament departures including relatively high-quality managers who leave because their incentives fell.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly emphasize that departed NPEs from open tournaments have more favorable labor-market outcomes than those from closed or outsider-winner tournaments.
Settings.H1401: Section V, Equation (3), Tables 9-10, PDF pp. 20-22.
Settings.G1402:
Treatment: Indicator for being in the post-inspection period for a company’s auditor: equals one for fiscal years ending after completion of the first POB inspection of the company’s auditor. Inspection completion is assumed one, two, or three years after the inspection program commences for annually, biannually, or triennially inspected auditors, with timing differing for large (Big-N) versus small auditors. In interacted specifications, treatment intensity is effectively whether this post-inspection indicator occurs in a POB/country with above-median inspector-reported auditor responses such as more documentation, training, scrutiny of estimates, audit/testing effort, checklist changes, procedural-manual changes, independence-control changes, audit-quality review changes, materiality-threshold changes, removing low-quality partners, partner compensation changes, or manager compensation changes.

Method: The paper estimates linear panel regressions at the company-year level relating audit quality to the onset of public oversight board (POB) inspections, with company fixed effects and year fixed effects plus time-varying controls following Carson et al. (2021). Treatment timing varies by country, POB inception year, auditor size, and inspection frequency (annual/biannual/triennial), so POST_INSPECTION turns on after the first likely completed POB inspection of the company’s auditor. The reported specifications interact POST_INSPECTION with country/POB-level indicators derived from inspector survey responses about how auditors respond to inspections (e.g., above-median average inspector agreement that auditors increase documentation or training). Identification is thus a staggered before-after within-company FE design, not branded as DiD by the authors, and the authors note important confounds from concurrent regulatory changes and measurement error in treatment assignment because they cannot observe which engagements were actually inspected.

Identification: Identification comes from within-company changes in audit quality after the likely first inspection of the firm’s auditor, with company FE absorbing time-invariant company differences and year FE absorbing common shocks. Cross-sectional heterogeneity is introduced via country/POB-level above-median survey-response indicators. The intended causal interpretation is that POB inspections improve audit quality, especially where inspectors report certain auditor responses. Endogeneity concerns include staggered but not random treatment timing, inability to observe actual inspected engagements, country-level aggregation of survey measures, and confounding contemporaneous reforms such as IFRS adoption and other EU enforcement changes; the authors explicitly caution that the design may not fully separate POB effects from concurrent regulatory changes.

Setting: Using company- and year-fixed-effects regressions on 169,966 company-years, the authors interpret the onset of POB inspections as reducing unsigned discretionary accruals, especially in countries where inspectors report stronger auditor behavioral responses. In Table 3, the interaction POST INSPECTION × DOCUMENTATION is 0.004 (t=1.88; p-value for sum of coefficients 0.01), POST INSPECTION × FIRM-WIDE TRAINING is 0.006 (t=4.62; p-value for sum 0.00), × SCRUTINY OF ESTIMATES is 0.005 (t=3.32; p-value for sum 0.00), × AUDIT & TESTING EFFORT is 0.004 (t=1.81; p-value for sum 0.00), and × REMOVE LOW QTY PARTNER is 0.004 (t=2.65; p-value for sum 0.01). The paper interprets these positive interaction terms together with significant tests on the sum of coefficients as indicating a stronger post-inspection decrease in |discretionary accruals| where those auditor responses are more prevalent. Other interactions are not significant, except a counterintuitive positive coefficient for manager-compensation changes. This is a central validating analysis, though the authors stress unresolved confounding and treatment-measurement limitations.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize understanding whether/how/why POBs work; these archival FE regressions are used to validate the survey evidence by linking inspector perceptions to an external audit-quality proxy and are discussed in the paper’s main text as important corroborating evidence.
Settings.G1403:
Treatment: Indicator for being in the post-inspection period for a company’s auditor, interacted with whether the company is in a POB/country where inspectors give above-median average ratings that auditors (i) tamper with closed/archived audit files to fix them for inspection or (ii) inappropriately obtain confidential information about upcoming inspections. The post-inspection variable is binary and defined by likely completion of the first POB inspection based on country program start, auditor size, and inspection frequency.
