Method: The paper estimates company-year linear fixed-effects regressions with company and year indicators plus controls, again using POST_INSPECTION as the treatment timing variable, but now interacting it with above-median country/POB-level inspector reports that auditors game the inspection system. The two heterogeneity dimensions are whether inspectors report more tampering with closed files and whether inspectors report more inappropriate access to confidential information about upcoming inspections. The design is the same within-company before-after FE framework as Table 3, with the same acknowledged limitations about confounding reforms and imperfect treatment assignment.

Identification: Within-company variation compares audit quality before versus after likely first auditor inspection, with company and year FE absorbing stable company heterogeneity and common time shocks. The causal heterogeneity claim is that inspections are less effective where auditors can game the system. The main identifying assumption is that absent inspections, treated companies would not have differential within-company audit-quality changes correlated with these survey-based country/POB classifications after controls and FE. The authors note unresolved endogeneity from concurrent regulatory changes, survey aggregation at the country level, and inability to observe actual inspected engagements.

Setting: In Table 4, the authors use company- and year-fixed-effects regressions to assess whether POB inspections have weaker audit-quality effects when inspectors report gaming behavior by auditors. For file tampering, POST INSPECTION is 0.001 (t=1.06) and the interaction with TAMPER WITH CLOSED FILES is 0.001 (t=0.48), with p-value for the sum of coefficients 0.13, yielding no significant post-inspection improvement. For obtaining confidential information, POST INSPECTION is 0.004 (t=4.09) but the interaction POST INSPECTION × OBTAIN CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION is 0.004 (t=1.76), with p-value for the sum of coefficients 0.56; the paper interprets this as inspections becoming ineffective at improving audit quality where inspectors perceive auditors obtain confidential information about upcoming inspections. This supports the paper’s argument that gaming can blunt the effectiveness of public oversight.

Main role: The paper highlights this analysis as corroborating survey evidence on gaming behavior with archival audit-quality outcomes; it materially supports the paper’s central claim about how and why POBs work and when they may be less effective.
Settings.G1404:
Treatment: Indicator for being in the post-inspection period for a company’s auditor, interacted with whether inspectors report that the POB has an evaluation program for inspection quality, especially a formal evaluation process. The base post-inspection treatment is binary and based on likely completion of the first POB inspection of the company’s auditor.

Method: The paper estimates linear company-year regressions with company fixed effects, year fixed effects, and standard controls, interacting the post-inspection indicator with indicators for whether the POB has an inspection evaluation program. One specification uses any evaluation program (formal or informal); another uses a formal evaluation program specifically. This is a within-company before-after FE design intended to assess whether formal internal inspection-evaluation systems make POB oversight more effective.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-company change after likely first auditor inspection, with heterogeneity by presence of inspection-evaluation programs at the POB. Company FE and year FE absorb time-invariant company characteristics and common annual shocks. The authors interpret significant effects for formal programs as evidence that such internal oversight enhances inspection effectiveness, while noting the same limitations as elsewhere: nonrandom treatment timing, concurrent reforms, survey-based and country-level measurement of POB characteristics, and inability to map actual inspections to engagements.

Setting: Table 5 asks whether POBs with inspection-quality evaluation programs generate stronger audit-quality improvements after inspections begin. In the broad evaluation-program specification, POST INSPECTION is 0.002 (t=1.71) and the interaction with EVALUATION PROGRAM is 0.001 (t=0.26), with p-value for the sum 0.204, so there is no clear effect. In contrast, with FORMAL EVALUATION PROGRAM, POST INSPECTION is 0.001 (t=0.28) and the interaction POST INSPECTION × FORMAL EVALUATION PROGRAM is 0.003 (t=2.35), with p-value for the sum 0.013. The authors interpret this as POB inspections being associated with decreases in |discretionary accruals| only where the POB has a formal program to evaluate inspection quality.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism analysis about POB organizational features, not the core descriptive survey evidence about whether/how auditors respond. It nonetheless provides substantive corroboration.
Settings.G1405:
Treatment: Indicator for being in the post-inspection period for a company’s auditor, interacted with whether the relevant POB has above-median inspector-reported use of a given promotion criterion for inspectors (e.g., seniority by duration at the POB, emotional intelligence, ability to diffuse tension, team-member feedback, promotion opportunities). Base post-inspection treatment is binary and based on likely completion of the first POB inspection.

Method: The paper runs a sequence of linear company-year regressions with company and year fixed effects plus controls, interacting the post-inspection indicator with above-median POB-level inspector perceptions of various promotion criteria for inspectors. These criteria include seniority by POB employment, seniority by age, deficiencies detected, quality-control deficiencies detected, positive auditor feedback, perceived moral values, perceived emotional intelligence, work ethic, ability to diffuse tension, team leader feedback, team member feedback, evaluations of inspections, and promotion opportunities. The design remains a within-company before-after FE approach using likely first auditor inspection timing.

Identification: Identification again relies on within-company changes around the likely onset of auditor inspections, with company FE and year FE. Cross-sectional heterogeneity comes from country/POB-level average inspector reports about promotion criteria. The intended causal claim is that certain inspector incentive structures enhance the effectiveness of public oversight. This depends on assuming no omitted time-varying factors jointly drive audit-quality changes and the POB-level promotion-criteria classifications; the authors acknowledge general confounding and measurement issues in these archival validations.

Setting: In Table 6, the authors examine whether the effect of POB inspections on audit quality is stronger when inspector promotions rely on particular criteria. They report that post-inspection decreases in |discretionary accruals| are present when promotions depend more on seniority by duration at the POB (interaction 0.005, t=2.46; p-value for sum 0.00), perceived emotional intelligence (0.006, t=3.71; p-value for sum 0.00), ability to diffuse tension with auditors during inspections (0.006, t=3.21; p-value for sum 0.01), team-member feedback (0.004, t=1.84; p-value for sum 0.01), and availability of promotion opportunities (0.006, t=4.62; p-value for sum 0.00). By contrast, they find no evidence that promoting inspectors based on the number of deficiencies detected strengthens inspection effects, contrary to some auditors’ perceptions that inspectors are rewarded for finding problems. This is a supporting mechanism analysis on inspector incentives.

Main role: This is a secondary, organizational-heterogeneity analysis about inspector incentives and promotion systems. It supports the paper’s broader argument about why POBs work but is not the centerpiece of the paper.
Settings.G1406:
Treatment: Assigned audit quality in Experiment 1, manipulated as whether the auditor tested 10 of 70 inactive quarry sites (low quality) or 50 of 70 sites (high quality) when investigating an identified fraud risk. In this setting, only the late-SOC-assessment conditions are used, i.e., jurors knew audit quality when assessing SOC.

Method: Experiment 1 is a randomized between-participants 2×2 experiment with 125 mock jurors recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk and randomly assigned to audit-quality and timing conditions. The treatment is the experimentally assigned level of audit quality, operationalized as the number of quarry sites tested by the auditor (10 versus 50 out of 70), in the subsample where jurors learned audit quality before assessing standard of care (SOC). The authors estimate treatment effects using mean contrasts, logistic path models/mediation analysis for the binary negligence verdict, and linear models for SOC. They interpret the manipulated audit-quality contrast causally because assignment is randomized. Identification concerns discussed by the paper center not on confounding, but on whether jurors anchor SOC on observed audit quality, producing competitive mediation.

Identification: Because audit quality is randomly assigned across participants, differences in negligence judgments and SOC between high- and low-audit-quality conditions can be interpreted as causal effects of audit quality in this experimental setting. Within the late-SOC-assessment arm, jurors all observe audit quality before stating SOC, so the design isolates whether higher assigned audit quality raises SOC and thereby indirectly increases negligence risk while directly lowering it. The key assumption is successful randomization and that the manipulation changes perceived audit quality as intended.

Setting: In the late-SOC-assessment conditions of Experiment 1, randomly assigning higher audit quality from 10 to 50 tested sites directly reduced jurors' negligence verdicts but indirectly increased them by raising jurors' required standard of care. Descriptively, negligence verdicts fell from 68 percent under low audit quality to 41 percent under high audit quality, while mean SOC rose from 29 to 49 sites. In the path analysis, higher SOC increased negligence judgments (Path B estimate 0.1, z=3.62, p<0.001), higher audit quality reduced negligence conditional on SOC (Path C' estimate -3.73, z=3.48, p<0.001), and higher audit quality increased SOC (Path A estimate 19.46, t62=4.25, p<0.001). A bootstrap mediation test was significant at the 99 percent confidence level, supporting the paper's central claim of competitive mediation.

Main role: The abstract and introduction present Experiment 1 as primary evidence that jurors anchor SOC on audit quality, generating competitive mediation in negligence judgments. This is one of the paper's central findings.
Settings.H1406: Section III, 'Experiment 1,' especially 'Tests of Hypotheses'; Table 1 Panel A and Figure 2 Panel A; PDF pp. 6-9.
Settings.G1407:
Treatment: Assigned audit quality in Experiment 1, manipulated as whether the auditor tested 10 of 70 inactive quarry sites (low quality) or 50 of 70 sites (high quality), in the early-SOC-assessment conditions where jurors did not know audit quality when assessing SOC.

Method: Experiment 1 is a randomized between-participants 2×2 experiment. This setting uses the subsample where jurors assessed SOC before learning audit quality. The focal treatment remains experimentally assigned audit quality, operationalized as 10 versus 50 tested sites out of 70. The authors estimate effects with descriptive contrasts and mediation/path analyses, emphasizing that early elicitation of SOC precludes mediation because audit quality is not yet known at the time SOC is assessed. Causal interpretation rests on randomized assignment of audit quality.

Identification: Random assignment of audit quality ensures causal identification of the effect of higher audit quality on negligence judgments within the early-SOC-assessment arm. Because participants state SOC before learning assigned audit quality, audit quality cannot causally affect SOC in this arm by design. This allows the authors to argue that any stronger effect of audit quality on negligence here reflects the absence of the offsetting mediation channel.

Setting: In the early-SOC-assessment conditions of Experiment 1, randomly assigning higher audit quality from 10 to 50 tested sites sharply reduced negligence judgments without significantly changing SOC, because jurors had not yet learned audit quality when stating SOC. Descriptively, negligence verdicts declined from 77 percent to 23 percent and probability-of-negligence ratings from 61 to 24, while mean SOC changed only from 40 to 44 sites. The path analysis shows a significant direct effect of audit quality on negligence judgments (overall effect z=4.06, p<0.001; direct effect z=3.86, p<0.001), a positive association between SOC and negligence (z=2.63, p<0.005), but no significant effect of audit quality on SOC (t61=0.74, p=0.462). This setting supports the paper's claim that precluding anchoring makes verdicts better discriminate between low- and high-quality audits.

Main role: This setting is central because it supplies the comparison condition for H2: when SOC is set before audit quality is known, negligence verdicts discriminate more strongly between low- and high-quality audits.
Settings.H1407: Section III, 'Experiment 1,' especially 'Effect of Timing of SOC's Assessment'; Table 1 Panel B and Figure 2 Panel B; PDF pp. 7-9.
Settings.G1408:
Treatment: Assigned timing/order condition for SOC assessment in Experiment 1: whether jurors assessed standard of care before learning audit quality (early SOC) or after learning audit quality (late SOC). The reported causal result is the interaction of this timing treatment with audit quality on negligence verdicts.

Method: Experiment 1 includes a randomized 2×2 design with two experimentally assigned factors: audit quality and the timing of SOC assessment. In this setting, the treatment is the timing condition itself, estimated jointly with audit quality in a binary logistic regression of negligence verdicts. The authors interpret the interaction causally because both factors are randomized. The estimand is whether the effect of audit quality on negligence differs depending on whether jurors assess SOC before versus after learning audit quality.

Identification: Both audit quality and timing of SOC elicitation are randomly assigned. The interaction in the logistic regression therefore identifies whether the causal effect of higher audit quality on negligence differs when SOC is assessed before versus after jurors know audit quality. The paper's interpretation relies on the design-based fact that early SOC assessment blocks the channel from audit quality to SOC, whereas late assessment permits it.

Setting: Experiment 1's randomized timing manipulation shows that audit quality is more effective in reducing negligence verdicts when jurors assess SOC before learning audit quality. In the logistic regression, audit quality has a main effect reducing negligence verdicts (χ2=16.46, p<0.01), and the interaction between audit quality and timing is significant (χ2=2.79, p<0.05), indicating that higher audit quality is more effective when jurors did not know audit quality before assessing SOC. Descriptively, the low-high audit-quality gap in negligence verdicts is 54 percentage points in the early-SOC condition (77% vs. 23%) but only 27 percentage points in the late-SOC condition (68% vs. 41%). This is a central causal result because it links the timing of SOC determination to auditors' litigation exposure.

Main role: H2 is one of the paper's main hypotheses, and the randomized timing manipulation is crucial to the paper's core conclusion that the order in which jurors form SOC changes how effectively audit quality shields auditors from negligence verdicts.
Settings.H1408: Section III, 'Experiment 1,' Table 1 Panel C and discussion of H2; Figure 1; PDF pp. 7-9.
Settings.G1409:
Treatment: Assigned audit quality in Experiment 2, manipulated as whether the auditor required the client to correct $108,000 (low quality) or $358,000 (high quality) out of a possible $700,000 overstatement in a Level-3 fair value estimate.

Method: Experiment 2 is a randomized between-participants experiment with 60 mock jurors. All jurors know audit quality at the time they assess SOC. Audit quality is manipulated as the amount of correction required by the auditor for a $700K possible overstatement in a Level-3 fair value estimate: $108K versus $358K. The authors estimate treatment effects using descriptive contrasts and mediation/path analysis, with negligence verdicts as the main dependent variable, SOC as mediator, and probability of negligence as a parallel continuous outcome. Causal interpretation follows from random assignment.

Identification: Random assignment of the amount of required correction identifies the causal effect of higher audit quality on juror SOC assessments and negligence judgments. Because all jurors observe assigned audit quality before stating SOC, the experiment is designed to test whether higher audit quality raises SOC and thereby offsets its direct protective effect against negligence verdicts. The core identifying assumption is that randomization equalizes other case perceptions across conditions.

Setting: In Experiment 2, randomly increasing audit quality from a $108K to a $358K required correction directly reduced negligence judgments but indirectly raised them through a higher assessed SOC. Descriptively, negligence verdicts fell from 53 percent to 40 percent, while mean SOC rose from $235K to $370K. The mediation analysis shows a significant effect of audit quality on SOC (t59=3.12, p<0.001) and of SOC on negligence likelihood (z=2.95, p<0.002). Audit quality significantly reduced negligence conditional on SOC (z=2.37, p<0.009) but was insignificant when SOC was excluded (z=1.03, p<0.302), implying that the indirect effect via SOC offset the direct effect enough to erase the unconditional effect. This is one of the main pieces of evidence that competitive mediation generalizes beyond the sample-size manipulation of Experiment 1.

Main role: The abstract and introduction describe Experiment 2 as a generalization of Experiment 1 to a different audit-quality proxy, again finding competitive mediation. It materially supports the paper's core conclusion.
Settings.H1409: Section IV, 'Experiment 2'; Table 2 Panel A; PDF pp. 10-11.
Settings.G1410:
Treatment: Assigned audit quality in Experiment 3, manipulated as whether the auditor required correction of $108,000 or $358,000 out of a possible $700,000 overstatement, with SOC elicited only after jurors made negligence judgments.

Method: Experiment 3 is a randomized between-participants experiment using the same audit-quality manipulation as Experiment 2, but changing the order of elicitation: participants learn audit quality, render a negligence verdict, justify it, and only then assess SOC. Audit quality is experimentally assigned as a low versus high required correction amount ($108K versus $358K). The authors estimate causal effects via mediation/path analyses, arguing that competitive mediation still appears even when SOC is elicited after verdicts, consistent with jurors using SOC to justify or maintain consistency with verdicts.

Identification: Random assignment of audit quality identifies causal effects of the required-correction amount on verdicts and post-verdict SOC assessments. The paper's claim is that even when SOC is elicited after the negligence decision, jurors' SOC still varies with assigned audit quality and helps sustain a competitive mediation pattern. The main assumption is valid randomization; the substantive concern is external validity about whether post-verdict SOC reflects real juror reasoning, which the authors address with written justifications.

Setting: Experiment 3 shows that competitive mediation persists even when SOC is elicited after jurors first make negligence judgments. Randomly increasing required correction from $108K to $358K raised mean SOC from $175K to $361K but barely changed negligence verdict rates (23% vs. 22%). In the mediation analysis, audit quality significantly increased SOC (t62=4.89, p<0.001), SOC significantly increased negligence likelihood (z=3.80, p<0.001), and audit quality significantly reduced negligence conditional on SOC (z=2.53, p<0.006), though not when SOC was omitted (z=0.07, p<0.945). The bootstrap mediation test was significant at the 99 percent confidence level. This supports the paper's broader claim that jurors use malleable SOC assessments to maintain consistency between audit quality and negligence judgments even when SOC is articulated after the verdict.

Main role: Experiment 3 extends the main competitive-mediation result to a setting closer to actual deliberation, where SOC may be articulated after verdicts. The abstract explicitly highlights this extension.
Settings.H1410: Section V, 'Experiment 3'; Table 2 Panel B; PDF pp. 12-13.
Settings.G1411:
Treatment: Assigned audit quality in Experiment 4, manipulated as whether the auditor required correction of $108,000 or $358,000 out of a possible $700,000 overstatement, in revised case materials designed to make negligence more likely and with SOC elicited after verdicts.

Method: Experiment 4 is another randomized between-participants experiment using the same low-versus-high required-correction audit-quality manipulation as Experiments 2 and 3, again with SOC elicited after negligence verdicts. The case materials are altered to make auditor negligence more plausible and avoid a floor effect in negligence verdicts. The treatment remains assigned audit quality ($108K versus $358K correction). Effects are estimated with descriptive contrasts and mediation/path analysis, and interpreted causally due to random assignment within the experiment.

Identification: Within Experiment 4, random assignment of audit quality identifies the causal effect of higher required correction on SOC and negligence judgments in the revised negligence-prone setting. The design tests whether the competitive mediation result survives when overall negligence rates are pushed upward. The authors caution that cross-experiment comparisons are not randomized, but the within-experiment audit-quality contrast is randomized.

Setting: Experiment 4 replicates the competitive-mediation result in a modified case designed to raise baseline negligence judgments. Randomly increasing required correction from $108K to $358K increased mean SOC from $341K to $445K and lowered negligence verdicts from 71 percent to 55 percent. The mediation analysis shows a significant effect of audit quality on SOC (t61=2.34, p<0.001), a significant positive effect of SOC on negligence likelihood (z=4.13, p<0.001), and a significant direct protective effect of audit quality conditional on SOC (z=2.84, p<0.003), whereas audit quality is not significant when SOC is omitted (z=1.31, p<0.191). The bootstrap mediation test is significant at the 95 percent confidence level. This robustness setting supports the claim that competitive mediation is not an artifact of a floor effect in Experiment 3.

Main role: Experiment 4 is described as a robustness/replication exercise addressing the potential floor effect in Experiment 3. It substantively supports the paper's central conclusion but is not the primary initial evidence.
Settings.H1411: Section VI, 'Experiment 4'; Table 2 Panel C; PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G1412:
Treatment: Exposure to the SEC’s 2006 mandatory RPT-governance disclosure shock for firms that were not previously disclosing such governance: the implemented treatment is the DID interaction Newly-Disclosed × Post, where Newly-Disclosed=1 for firms that did not disclose RPT governance pre-regulation but initiated disclosure post-regulation, and Post=1 after 2006.

Method: The authors implement a conventional difference-in-differences design around the 2006 SEC rule requiring disclosure of related-party-transaction (RPT) governance. They estimate linear regressions of RPT outcomes on Newly-Disclosed × Post, where Newly-Disclosed equals 1 for firms that did not disclose RPT governance before the rule but initiated disclosure after it, and Post equals 1 for fiscal years after 2006. The sample is 892 nonfinancial S&P 1500 firms observed in 2004, 2007, and 2010 (2,676 firm-years). Controls include firm characteristics and governance/monitoring covariates; Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects are included and standard errors are clustered by firm. The design treats Already-Disclosed firms as the comparison group and interprets the interaction coefficient as the regulation’s effect on RPT occurrence, subject to the standard parallel-trends assumption and the concern that treatment status is based on preexisting voluntary disclosure choices rather than random assignment.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing pre/post changes in RPT outcomes for Newly-Disclosed firms versus Already-Disclosed firms. The argument is that the 2006 rule imposed a larger disclosure shock on firms that had not previously disclosed RPT governance, while firms already disclosing serve as a lower-exposure control group. The causal interpretation requires that absent the rule, RPT trends would have evolved similarly across groups after conditioning on observed controls and industry effects. A potential concern is selection into pre-2006 voluntary disclosure status; the paper argues the regulation is an exogenous increase in required disclosure intensity.

Setting: Using a conventional DID around the SEC’s 2006 RPT-governance disclosure rule, the authors find that firms newly induced to disclose governance reduce RPT activity relative to firms already disclosing. In Table 4 Panel A, the interaction Newly-Disclosed × Post is -0.436 (t=-2.98) for the number of RPTs above $120,000 and -0.441 (t=-2.35) for the indicator of any such RPT. The authors interpret this as evidence that mandated governance disclosure reduced the occurrence of RPTs, supporting the paper’s main claim that disclosure regulation has real governance consequences.

Main role: This is the paper’s primary quasi-experimental test of whether the 2006 SEC disclosure regulation changed firms’ RPT behavior, a central question in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.
Settings.H1412: Section III Regression Model (equation (1), PDF p. 7-8); Table 4 Panel A, columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 15-17.
Settings.G1413:
Treatment: Exposure to the SEC 2006 disclosure shock for Newly-Disclosed firms in the post period, estimated separately in low-board-monitoring and high-board-monitoring subsamples based on the median of the principal-component monitoring index.

Method: The authors re-estimate the same conventional DID specification for RPT outcomes after partitioning firms by an aggregate board-monitoring measure, constructed as the principal component of five board characteristics (CEO duality, independent directors, director ownership, director busyness, board size). Separate regressions are run for low- and high-monitoring subsamples, with the same controls, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. This is a heterogeneous-effects DID intended to test whether the regulation’s effect is stronger where ex ante monitoring is weaker.

Identification: This setting uses the same DID comparison as the main design but asks whether the treatment effect differs by ex ante board-monitoring strength. Identification still relies on parallel trends within each monitoring subsample and comparability of Newly- versus Already-Disclosed firms conditional on controls. The partition is motivated by the theory that mandatory disclosure should bite more where prior monitoring was weak.

Setting: In subsample DID tests, the paper reports that the 2006 disclosure rule reduced RPTs primarily among low-monitored firms. In Table 4 Panel B, Newly-Disclosed × Post is -0.796 (t=-3.48) for #RPT and -0.914 (t=-3.08) for DRPT in the low-monitoring subsample, versus -0.127 and -0.090 in the high-monitoring subsample; the cross-subsample difference is significant at the 5 percent level. The authors interpret this as evidence that mandated disclosure strengthened monitoring especially where boards were initially weaker.

Main role: The paper highlights that effects are more pronounced for low-monitored firms in the abstract, hypothesis development, results discussion, and conclusion, so this heterogeneity analysis materially supports a central conclusion.
Settings.H1413: Table 4 Panel B, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 16.
Settings.G1414:
Treatment: Newly-Disclosed × Post exposure to the 2006 SEC rule, estimated separately across subsamples defined by individual board-monitoring characteristics (CEO duality, low/high independence, low/high director ownership, high/low busyness, small/large boards).

Method: The authors run a battery of conventional DID regressions for the same RPT outcomes, partitioning the sample by each of five individual board-monitoring characteristics: CEO duality, percentage of independent directors, director ownership, director busyness, and board size. They estimate separate low/high (or duality/no duality) subsample regressions with the same controls, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. The purpose is to interpret stronger effects in weak-monitoring environments as evidence of a governance channel.

Identification: The identifying logic is the same DID treatment-versus-control, pre-versus-post comparison within each governance-defined subsample. The paper’s claim is that stronger effects under CEO duality, lower board independence or ownership, greater busyness, and smaller boards indicate the regulation mattered most where monitoring incentives were weaker. Assumptions include within-subsample parallel trends and meaningful ex ante classification by monitoring proxies.

Setting: Using partitioned DID regressions by individual board characteristics, the paper finds larger post-regulation RPT reductions among weak-monitoring firms. For #RPT, Newly-Disclosed × Post equals -0.560 with CEO duality, -0.488 for low independence, -0.720 for low director ownership, -0.659 for high busyness, and -0.530 for small boards; DRPT results are directionally similar, with several significant estimates (Table 4 Panels C-D). The authors interpret these patterns as supporting a monitoring-based mechanism rather than a purely mechanical disclosure effect.

Main role: These are substantive heterogeneity analyses reinforcing the governance interpretation, but they are secondary to the main overall DID estimates and aggregate low-monitoring split.
Settings.H1414: Table 4 Panels C and D, columns (1)-(20), PDF pp. 16-17.
Settings.G1415:
Treatment: Exposure of Newly-Disclosed firms to the post-2006 disclosure mandate, estimated separately for business RPT and non-business RPT outcomes.

Method: The authors estimate conventional DID models separately for business and non-business related-party transactions. Outcomes are either counts or indicators of Business RPTs and Non-Business RPTs, where non-business transactions are argued to be more opportunistic. The regressions include the same treatment interaction Newly-Disclosed × Post, the same control set, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. This is a heterogeneous-effects DID by transaction type.

Identification: The strategy is the same DID framework, but the paper tests whether treatment effects concentrate in RPT categories more likely to reflect self-dealing. The key assumption remains differential exposure of Newly-Disclosed firms to the rule and parallel trends in each transaction-type outcome absent treatment. The interpretation relies on the classification of business versus non-business RPTs as informative about opportunism.

Setting: The authors find that the regulation’s effect is concentrated in non-business RPTs, which they view as more likely opportunistic. In Table 4 Panel E, Newly-Disclosed × Post is insignificant for business-RPT counts (0.125) and indicators (0.180), but is -0.285 (t=-3.17) for non-business-RPT counts and -0.554 (t=-2.84) for non-business-RPT indicators. They interpret this as evidence that mandatory RPT-governance disclosure mainly curtailed the more problematic forms of related-party transactions.

Main role: The abstract and conclusions emphasize that effects are stronger for RPTs more likely to be opportunistic, making this heterogeneity result part of the core substantive contribution.
Settings.H1415: Table 4 Panel E, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 17.
Settings.G1416:
Treatment: Occurrence/intensity of RPTs in the post-regulation period for Newly-Disclosed versus Already-Disclosed firms; the focal regressor is RPT × Post, where RPT is either the count of RPTs above $120,000 or an indicator for any such RPT, estimated separately by disclosure-status group.

Method: To study capital-market consequences, the authors estimate linear regressions of implied cost of capital (ICC) on RPT × Post separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms. ICC is the average of four model-based implied cost-of-equity measures. The key coefficients are on either #RPT × Post or DRPT × Post, with controls for risk, firm characteristics, and governance, plus Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Although estimated in separate subsamples rather than a pooled triple interaction, the intended interpretation is a DID-style change in how RPTs are priced after mandated disclosure, with Already-Disclosed firms serving as a placebo/control comparison.

Identification: The design examines whether the association between RPTs and ICC becomes less adverse after the 2006 rule, especially for Newly-Disclosed firms that experienced a larger disclosure shock. Identification relies on comparing pre/post changes in the RPT-ICC slope within each disclosure-status group and informally across groups. The causal interpretation assumes that absent the regulation, the pricing of RPT risk would have evolved similarly and that controls absorb other shifts in risk determinants; the paper acknowledges that the difference in ICC reduction between groups is not always statistically significant.

Setting: Using DID-style regressions of ICC on RPT × Post, the authors conclude that the 2006 SEC disclosure rule reduced the equity-risk premium investors attach to RPTs for firms newly required to disclose governance. In Table 5 Panel A, for Newly-Disclosed firms the interaction is -0.099 (t=-2.51) when RPT is measured as #RPT and -0.292 (t=-1.70) when RPT is measured as DRPT, while the corresponding estimates for Already-Disclosed firms are insignificant. The paper interprets this as evidence that enhanced transparency and improved governance lowered perceived RPT-related risk, though it notes that the between-group difference is not statistically significant.

Main role: A central goal of the paper is to test whether mandated governance disclosure reduced investors’ perceived RPT risk; the ICC analyses are featured prominently in the abstract, introduction, results, and conclusion.
Settings.H1416: Section III Regression Model (equation (2), PDF p. 8); Table 5 Panel A, columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 18-21.
Settings.G1417:
Treatment: RPT occurrence/intensity in the post period (RPT × Post), estimated separately by disclosure-status group and low/high aggregate board-monitoring subsamples.

Method: The authors re-estimate the ICC-on-RPT × Post regressions separately by low versus high board monitoring using the aggregate principal-component monitoring measure, and separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms. These are conventional DID-style heterogeneity analyses with the same controls, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors, intended to show that the post-regulation decline in the pricing of RPT risk is stronger where monitoring was initially weak.

Identification: The setting relies on the same DID-style change in the RPT-ICC association before and after the rule, now within monitoring-defined subsamples. The paper interprets stronger negative RPT × Post coefficients among low-monitoring Newly-Disclosed firms as evidence that mandated governance disclosure particularly reduced investors’ concerns where internal monitoring had been weaker. Identification assumes comparable trends in RPT pricing within subsamples absent the rule.

Setting: The paper reports some evidence that the post-regulation decline in ICC associated with RPTs is concentrated among Newly-Disclosed firms with weak aggregate board monitoring. In Table 5 Panel B, for Newly-Disclosed firms the coefficient on #RPT × Post is -0.107 (t=-1.97) in low-monitoring firms versus -0.072 in high-monitoring firms, and the coefficient on DRPT × Post is -0.436 (t=-2.02) in low-monitoring firms versus -0.120 in high-monitoring firms; corresponding placebo-group estimates are insignificant. The authors view this as consistent with stronger governance effects where boards were initially less effective.

Main role: This is a substantive heterogeneity analysis supporting the claimed monitoring channel for ICC effects, but it is secondary to the main ICC results.
Settings.H1417: Table 5 Panel B, columns (1)-(8), PDF p. 19.
Settings.G1418:
Treatment: RPT occurrence/intensity in the post period, captured by #RPT × Post or DRPT × Post, estimated separately across subsamples defined by individual board-monitoring characteristics and by Newly- versus Already-Disclosed status.

Method: The authors further partition the ICC-on-RPT × Post regressions by each individual board-monitoring proxy, separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms. These linear DID-style regressions use either #RPT or DRPT as the RPT variable, interact it with Post, include the full control set, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. The goal is to show that investor pricing of RPT risk fell more after the rule when governance was ex ante weaker according to specific board characteristics.

Identification: Identification mirrors the main ICC DID setup, within subsamples defined by CEO duality, independence, director ownership, busyness, and board size. The argument is that if the regulation improved monitoring, the RPT-ICC association should decline most where those monitoring traits indicated weakness. This requires within-subsample comparability over time and credible classification of firms by monitoring quality.

Setting: Across individual monitoring characteristics, the paper finds suggestive evidence that the pricing penalty on RPTs declines more after the regulation for Newly-Disclosed firms with weak board structures. Examples in Table 5 Panels C-D include #RPT × Post estimates of -0.121 under CEO duality, -0.117 for low independence, -0.089 for low director ownership, -0.124 for high busyness, and -0.103 for small boards; several DRPT × Post estimates are also negative, such as -0.459 under CEO duality and -0.415 for low independence. The authors interpret these patterns as consistent with disclosure-induced improvements in monitoring reducing investors’ risk assessment of RPTs.

Main role: These results are supplementary heterogeneity analyses used to support the governance-channel interpretation of ICC effects.
Settings.H1418: Table 5 Panels C-F, columns (1)-(20), PDF pp. 19-21.
Settings.G1419:
Treatment: Business or non-business RPT occurrence/intensity in the post period, captured by BusRPT × Post and NonBusRPT × Post, estimated separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms.

Method: The authors estimate ICC regressions that distinguish business and non-business RPTs, again using RPT-type × Post interactions and estimating separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms. The regressions are linear, include the full control set, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. This is a DID-style heterogeneity analysis by transaction type intended to show that the regulation reduced the pricing of especially opportunistic RPTs.

Identification: The strategy compares how the ICC association with non-business versus business RPTs changes after the regulation, especially among Newly-Disclosed firms. The paper argues that non-business RPTs are more likely to represent self-dealing, so a stronger post-regulation attenuation of their ICC association supports a governance mechanism. The same caveats about nonrandom disclosure status and parallel evolution of unobservables apply.

Setting: The paper finds that the 2006 rule mainly reduced the implied cost of capital associated with non-business RPTs for Newly-Disclosed firms. In Table 5 Panel G, NonBusRPT × Post is -0.148 (t=-1.94) in the #RPT specification and -0.338 (t=-1.77) in the DRPT specification for Newly-Disclosed firms, while business-RPT interactions are insignificant and placebo-group estimates are also insignificant. The authors interpret this as evidence that investors had viewed non-business RPTs as especially risky and revised those assessments downward after governance disclosure became mandatory.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize stronger effects for RPTs likely to be opportunistic, making this an important component of the paper’s central claim about governance and investor risk perceptions.
Settings.H1419: Table 5 Panel G, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 21.
Settings.G1420:
Treatment: RPT occurrence/intensity in the post-regulation period, with cross-sectional heterogeneity by whether the firm has a written RPT governance policy. The focal causal interpretation is that written-policy governance attenuates the ICC associated with RPTs.

Method: In post-period-only regressions, the authors relate ICC to RPT measures separately across firms with versus without a written RPT governance policy. The specification is a linear regression of ICC on either #RPT or DRPT plus controls, year fixed effects, and Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, with firm-clustered standard errors. This is not a DID because it uses only the post-regulation period and interprets cross-sectional differences in the RPT-ICC slope by governance-policy choice as evidence that stronger RPT governance lowers investors’ perceived RPT risk.

Identification: Identification is cross-sectional and therefore weaker than the paper’s DID design. The authors compare the association between RPTs and ICC among firms with and without a written RPT policy in the post period, controlling for observables and fixed effects. The causal interpretation rests on the assumption that remaining differences in ICC pricing of RPTs are attributable to governance-policy strength rather than omitted firm traits, which is not fully testable.

Setting: In post-regulation cross-sectional regressions, the authors find that RPTs are associated with lower ICC for firms that have a written RPT governance policy, which they interpret as evidence that stronger formal governance reduces perceived RPT risk. In Table 6 Panel A, the coefficient on #RPT is -0.056 (t=-1.69) and on DRPT is -0.288 (t=-1.95) among firms with written policies, versus small and insignificant estimates among firms without written policies. The paper treats this as supportive evidence that written governance policies benefit firms through lower RPT-related financing costs.

Main role: This is an additional post-period association analysis about governance-policy choices, used to extend rather than anchor the main quasi-experimental results.
Settings.H1420: Table 6 Panel A, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 22-23.
Settings.G1421:
Treatment: RPT occurrence/intensity in the post period, with cross-sectional heterogeneity by whether the firm has a designated committee to review and approve RPTs. The implied treatment of interest is stronger committee-based RPT governance.

Method: The authors estimate post-period-only linear regressions of ICC on RPT measures separately for firms that do or do not designate a formal committee to review and approve RPTs. The regressions include controls, year fixed effects, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. This is a cross-sectional regression-adjustment design used to infer whether having a designated review committee changes the capital-market consequences of RPTs.

Identification: The strategy is cross-sectional comparison of the RPT-ICC association between firms with and without a designated committee, conditional on controls and fixed effects. The paper’s causal language is that assigning committee oversight reduces investors’ perceived RPT risk, but the design cannot rule out omitted differences in governance quality correlated with committee choice.

Setting: The paper reports that firms with a designated RPT-review committee appear to face a smaller ICC penalty from RPTs in the post period. In Table 6 Panel B, the coefficient on #RPT is -0.065 (t=-1.86) for firms with a committee versus -0.121 (t=-1.97) for firms without one, and the between-subsample difference is significant at 1 percent; for DRPT, the estimate is -0.200 (t=-1.68) with a committee and near zero without. The authors interpret this as evidence that formal committee oversight of RPTs lowers investors’ perceived risk.

Main role: This is an additional analysis on post-period governance choices, supporting but not central to the main regulatory-effect results.
Settings.H1421: Table 6 Panel B, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 22.
Settings.G1422:
Treatment: RPT occurrence/intensity in the post period, with cross-sectional heterogeneity by whether the firm’s RPT-governance disclosure length is above or below the median. The intended treatment interpretation is more extensive governance disclosure.

Method: The authors estimate post-period-only linear regressions of ICC on RPT measures separately for firms with long versus short RPT-governance disclosures, where disclosure length proxies for disclosure quality. Regressions include the usual controls, year fixed effects, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. This cross-sectional regression-adjustment setting is used to infer whether more extensive governance disclosure lowers the cost-of-capital consequences of RPTs.

Identification: Identification is based on post-period cross-sectional differences in the RPT-ICC association between firms with longer and shorter governance disclosures, conditional on controls. The paper interprets longer disclosure as better governance transparency, but this relies on strong selection-on-observables assumptions because firms choose disclosure detail endogenously.

Setting: Using post-period regressions split by disclosure length, the authors find that RPTs are associated with lower ICC among firms providing more extensive RPT-governance disclosure. In Table 6 Panel C, the coefficient on #RPT is -0.068 (t=-1.85) for long disclosures versus -0.014 for short disclosures, and the coefficient on DRPT is -0.246 (t=-1.88) versus -0.127. The paper interprets this as evidence that more detailed governance disclosure reduces investors’ perceived RPT-related risk.

Main role: This is another supporting post-period analysis of governance-policy choices rather than one of the paper’s headline quasi-experimental estimates.
Settings.H1422: Table 6 Panel C, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 23.
Settings.G1423:
Treatment: RPT occurrence/intensity in the post-regulation period, captured by #RPT × Post or DRPT × Post in separate regressions for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms.

Method: As an alternative market-outcome test, the authors estimate linear regressions of Tobin’s Q on RPT × Post separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms. They use either #RPT or DRPT as the RPT measure and include controls motivated by prior valuation literature, plus Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Although implemented as separate-group regressions, the intended design is DID-style: whether the valuation association of RPTs changes after the 2006 regulation, especially for Newly-Disclosed firms.

Identification: The design compares the post- versus pre-2006 change in the valuation association of RPTs for Newly-Disclosed versus Already-Disclosed firms. The logic is that if mandated governance disclosure reduced the harmfulness or perceived risk of RPTs, the relation between RPTs and firm valuation should improve after the rule for more affected firms. This requires assumptions similar to the ICC DID analysis about comparable counterfactual trends in RPT valuation slopes.

Setting: Using Tobin’s Q as an alternative market-based outcome, the authors find that the valuation association of RPTs improves after the regulation for Newly-Disclosed firms. In Table 7 Panel A, RPT × Post equals 0.034 (t=1.66) when RPT is measured by #RPT and 0.219 (t=1.87) when measured by DRPT for Newly-Disclosed firms, while estimates for Already-Disclosed firms are insignificant (-0.019 and -0.176). The paper interprets this as consistent with investors valuing RPT firms more highly after mandated governance disclosure reduced perceived RPT risk.

Main role: The paper describes Tobin’s Q as an additional/alternative valuation consequence test rather than a primary outcome, though it supports the broader claim that the regulation improved market assessments.
Settings.H1423: Table 7 Panel A, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 24-25.
Settings.G1424:
Treatment: Business or non-business RPT occurrence/intensity in the post period, captured by BusRPT × Post and NonBusRPT × Post, estimated separately for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms.

Method: The authors decompose the Tobin’s Q DID-style analysis by business versus non-business RPTs. Separate regressions for Newly-Disclosed and Already-Disclosed firms include NonBusRPT × Post and BusRPT × Post, the usual valuation controls, Fama-French 48 industry fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. This heterogeneous-effects DID is intended to test whether valuation gains after the regulation are concentrated in the RPT category more likely to reflect opportunism.

Identification: The strategy mirrors the main Tobin’s Q DID setup, now asking whether valuation effects are stronger for non-business RPTs. The paper argues these transactions are more likely opportunistic, so a stronger positive post-regulation shift in their valuation association for Newly-Disclosed firms would indicate that mandated governance disclosure especially improved market perceptions of high-risk RPTs. Assumptions are the same as for the broader DID analysis.

Setting: In Tobin’s Q decompositions, the authors find that post-regulation valuation improvements are concentrated in non-business RPTs for Newly-Disclosed firms. In Table 7 Panel B, NonBusRPT × Post is 0.069 (t=1.78) in the #RPT specification and 0.230 (t=1.86) in the DRPT specification for Newly-Disclosed firms, while the corresponding Already-Disclosed estimates are insignificant and the between-group differences are significant at 5 percent. The paper interprets this as evidence that investors revised upward their valuation of firms with potentially opportunistic RPTs once governance disclosure became mandatory.

Main role: This is an additional heterogeneity analysis on the valuation outcome, supporting the opportunistic-RPT interpretation but not among the paper’s main headline tests.
Settings.H1424: Table 7 Panel B, columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 25.
Settings.G1425:
Treatment: Exposure to a particular individual manager’s time-invariant style, operationalized through a full set of manager fixed-effect indicators in the MDV sample. This is not a single scalar dose but a many-valued categorical treatment assigning each firm-year to the manager in place; treatment is effectively manager identity/style.

Method: The paper’s primary design is a linear panel fixed-effects regression using the manager mobility method (MDV) on firm-year data for 23,427 observations from 1,040 firms and 907 managers who each work at at least two firms for at least three years per firm. The estimated equation is AQ_it = a + b*EconomicDeterminants_it + Manager_m + Year_t + Firm_i + e_it, where AQ is a five-year rolling standard deviation of abnormal accrual residuals, EconomicDeterminants are eight time-varying controls from Francis et al. (2004), and the regression includes separately absorbed manager fixed effects, firm fixed effects, and year fixed effects. This has three FE dimensions, and the paper explicitly argues these fixed effects absorb time-invariant manager and firm heterogeneity to identify the manager-specific incremental effect on accounting quality. The estimator is used to compare adjusted R-squared across nested specifications, test the joint significance of manager fixed effects, and study the distribution of estimated manager effects. Robust standard errors are used. The paper notes remaining concerns about serial correlation and the large number of fixed effects, and addresses them with placebo/randomization robustness checks rather than a different identification design.

Identification: Identification comes from managers moving across firms in the Execucomp sample, which allows the author to separately estimate manager and firm fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that accounting quality may reflect stable firm traits or sorting of managers to firms rather than manager-specific idiosyncrasies. The argument is that, conditional on firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and time-varying economic determinants of accrual quality, remaining systematic variation associated with manager identity captures a manager-specific incremental effect. This requires that time-invariant manager attributes are portable across firms and that time-varying omitted shocks correlated with manager moves are not driving the results. The author acknowledges limits of FE designs and uses placebo reassignment/bootstrap tests to argue the manager fixed effects are not mechanically significant because of the large number of indicators.

Setting: Using the manager mobility method with firm, manager, and year fixed effects, the paper interprets manager identity/style as causally affecting accounting quality. In the full MDV specification (Table 4, Panel A, column (8)), adding manager fixed effects to a regression that already includes economic determinants, year effects, and firm fixed effects raises adjusted R-squared from 59.50% to 64.04%, a 4.54 percentage point increase (7.63% relative to the comparable model), and the manager fixed effects are jointly significant (F = 5.52, p < 0.001). The Shapley decomposition attributes 12.83% of explained variation to manager fixed effects versus 28.47% to firm fixed effects. The estimated interquartile range of manager fixed effects is 0.0143, which the paper states is 44.62% of mean AQ and 54.17% of the interquartile range of AQ, supporting the central claim that who manages the firm materially affects accrual quality.

Main role: This is the paper’s main empirical design used to support the central claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that individual managers have an incremental effect on accounting quality after controlling for firm and time effects.
Settings.H1425: Section IV, “Individual Managers and the Cross-Sectional Variation in AQ,” Equation (3), Table 4 Panels A-C, and Figure 2 (PDF pp. 10-13).
Settings.G1426:
Treatment: Exposure to a particular individual manager’s time-invariant style, represented by a full set of manager fixed-effect indicators in the AKM connected sample. Treatment is many-valued/categorical manager identity, not binary.

Method: A secondary fixed-effects design implements the Abowd-Kramarz-Margolis manager connectedness method (AKM) in a linear panel regression of AQ on economic determinants with separately absorbed year, firm, and manager fixed effects. The AKM sample includes 90,769 observations, 1,040 firms, and 15,914 managers connected through within-sample mobility, allowing inclusion of non-movers. The estimating equation parallels the MDV specification, and the design is used to assess whether manager fixed effects continue to matter when the sample is expanded. Robust standard errors are used, and the paper reports adjusted R-squared improvements and a Shapley decomposition of explained variance.

Identification: Identification again relies on manager-firm connectedness through labor mobility, which is sufficient in AKM to separately identify manager and firm fixed effects. The concern is that MDV results could be driven by unusual movers; AKM broadens the sample to connected non-movers while preserving separate firm and manager effects. The identifying assumption is that, after conditioning on firm fixed effects, year effects, and observed determinants of AQ, systematic remaining variation tied to manager identity reflects a portable manager-specific component rather than omitted time-varying shocks. The author notes possible limited-mobility bias but treats AKM as a robustness design alleviating concerns about MDV sample selection.

Setting: Using the AKM connectedness method, the paper again interprets manager fixed effects as affecting accounting quality. In Table 5, Panel A, the adjusted R-squared rises from 60.74% without manager fixed effects to 68.85% with them, an 8.11 percentage point increase (13.35% relative increase), and the joint test of manager fixed effects is significant (F = 7.21, p < 0.001). The Shapley decomposition assigns 25.83% of model R-squared to manager fixed effects and 29.43% to firm fixed effects, leading the author to conclude that managers provide nearly as much explanatory power as firms in this broader sample. This materially supports the paper’s central conclusion that managers matter for accounting quality.

Main role: The paper presents AKM as an important alternative methodology to address external-validity limits of the mover-only MDV sample and to show the manager effect persists in a broader sample; the abstract and conclusion reference alternative methodologies supporting the main claim.
Settings.H1426: Section IV, “Individual Managers and the Cross-Sectional Variation in AQ,” Table 5 Panels A-B (PDF pp. 13-14).
Settings.G1427:
Treatment: Exposure to a particular firm-manager spell (manager-firm combination), implemented as a full set of spell fixed-effect indicators. This is a many-valued categorical treatment capturing the joint time-invariant effect of a specific manager at a specific firm.

Method: A further supplementary fixed-effects design uses the spell method (SPELL), estimating a linear regression of AQ on economic determinants, year fixed effects, and firm-manager spell fixed effects, with some specifications also including firm fixed effects. The sample contains 158,164 firm-year observations, 2,396 firms, and 22,542 managers. The spell fixed effect is an indicator for each firm-manager combination, capturing the time-invariant joint firm-manager component. This design is used to show that controlling for unobserved manager-firm heterogeneity in a much larger sample improves explanatory power, though it does not separately identify manager and firm effects. Robust standard errors are used.

Identification: The spell method controls for unobserved time-invariant heterogeneity at the firm-manager combination level, reducing omitted-variable bias when estimating relations between economic determinants and AQ. The paper interprets the increase in fit from adding spell effects as evidence consistent with manager-specific influence, but acknowledges the key limitation that manager and firm effects are not separately identifiable. Thus the strategy is weaker for attribution than MDV/AKM and serves mainly as robustness/generalizability evidence.

Setting: In the supplementary SPELL analysis, adding firm-manager spell fixed effects to regressions of AQ increases explanatory power in a larger sample, which the paper interprets as further evidence that managerial heterogeneity affects accounting quality. Table 6 shows that including spell effects raises adjusted R-squared from 63.40% to 70.22% when compared with a model containing economic determinants, year fixed effects, and firm fixed effects, a 6.82 percentage point increase (10.76% relative to the comparable model). Because SPELL does not separate manager from firm effects, this is supporting rather than primary evidence, but it reinforces the paper’s claim that unobserved manager-related heterogeneity matters for AQ beyond firm characteristics.

Main role: The paper explicitly describes SPELL as supplementary analysis to show generalizability to a larger set of firms and managers, not as the primary method for separately identifying manager effects.
Settings.H1427: Section IV, “Individual Managers and the Cross-Sectional Variation in AQ,” Table 6 (PDF p. 15).
Settings.G1428:
Treatment: A switch in manager AQ-style type at the firm: specifically, positive-AQ-style to negative-AQ-style, negative-AQ-style to positive-AQ-style, or neutral-to-neutral. AQ-style is based on quartiles of estimated manager fixed effects from the main MDV model. The focal treatment contrast is binary within each column (one switch type versus the before period for the same firms).

Method: The paper next studies mean changes in firm outcomes around switches in manager type. Managers are first classified using the estimated manager fixed effects from the full MDV regression: fourth quartile as positive AQ-style, first quartile as negative AQ-style, and middle two quartiles as neutral. The analysis in Table 7 is a univariate difference-in-means/event comparison, reporting the average change in AQ and several other firm measures when firms switch from one manager type to another. No additional regression controls are reported in the table itself; the causal interpretation comes from the prior classification of manager style and the before-after comparison around manager changes.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-firm change in manager AQ-style type. The paper argues that if managers carry portable styles, then firms switching from negative- to positive-style managers should see improved AQ and the reverse for positive- to negative-style switches. The main endogeneity concern is assortative matching and dynamic self-selection: firms may choose managers because of ongoing structural changes that also affect AQ. The author explicitly acknowledges this limitation and presents the analysis as suggestive evidence complemented by later exogenous-turnover evidence.

Setting: The paper interprets switches in manager AQ-style as causing subsequent changes in accounting quality. In Table 7, firms switching from a positive AQ-style manager to a negative AQ-style manager experience a 0.0407 increase in AQ, from 0.0248 to 0.0655, which the paper interprets as a statistically significant 264% decrease in mean accounting quality. Firms switching from a negative AQ-style manager to a positive AQ-style manager experience a 0.0377 decrease in AQ, from 0.0809 to 0.0433, interpreted as about a 50% increase in mean accounting quality. Neutral-to-neutral switches show no significant AQ change (0.0017). Because AQ is coded so larger values are worse quality, these results support the central claim that manager-specific idiosyncrasies affect accounting quality, though the author notes this design cannot fully rule out dynamic self-selection.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion emphasize the finding that firms switching manager type experience changes in AQ, and Table 7 is the paper’s direct test of whether manager style is applied consistently across firms.
Settings.H1428: Section IV, “Change in AQ When Firms Switch Manager-Type,” Table 7 (PDF pp. 14-16).
Settings.G1429:
Treatment: Manager AQ-style classification carried into a third firm: positive, neutral, or negative AQ-style, defined from the manager’s estimated fixed effect based on the first two firms. The treatment is categorical manager type.

Method: As a holdout-sample robustness test against ex post classification bias, the paper examines 31 managers who move to a third firm. Manager AQ-style is classified from the first two firms using estimated manager fixed effects from the MDV model, and then average AQ at the third firm is compared across positive-, neutral-, and negative-style managers. The implemented estimator is a mean comparison rather than a panel FE specification in the holdout sample.

Identification: The identifying idea is out-of-sample portability of manager style: if AQ-style estimated from the first two firms reflects manager-specific attributes rather than overfitting or ex post sorting, then those classified as positive-style should exhibit better AQ at a third firm than those classified as negative-style. The main concern is the very small sample and continuing manager-firm matching issues; the author explicitly notes that generalizability is unknown given the limited sample size.

Setting: In a small holdout test using 31 managers who move to a third firm, the paper interprets prior manager AQ-style classification as causing differences in accounting quality at the new firm. Table 8 shows that positive AQ-style managers have mean AQ of 0.0200 at the third firm, while negative AQ-style managers have mean AQ of 0.0650; the reported difference is 0.0449 and statistically significant. The paper uses this result to argue that cross-sectional variation in manager attributes documented in the first two firms persists out of sample, supporting the portability of manager effects on AQ, though it treats this as limited-sample robustness evidence.

Main role: The paper presents Table 8 as a robustness/holdout test to address ex post bias in Table 7, not as the primary source of the main conclusion.
Settings.H1429: Section IV, “Change in AQ When Firms Switch Manager-Type,” Table 8 (PDF p. 16).
Settings.G1430:
Treatment: The incoming outside CEO’s prior AQ-style/proxy, operationalized as the three-year average AQ of the CEO’s old firm during the manager’s employment. This is a continuous treatment proxy for the manager’s style.

Method: To address selected-style versus idiosyncratic-style hypotheses, the paper studies a sample of 41 exogenous CEO turnover events due to health, death, or natural retirement, followed by an outside CEO hire. The implemented estimator is a Pearson correlation between (i) the change in AQ at the new employer, measured as the difference in three-year average AQ surrounding the old CEO’s departure, and (ii) the three-year average AQ at the new CEO’s old employer. This is not IV or DiD; it is a reduced-form regression-adjustment/correlation design using arguably exogenous turnover timing as the empirical setting.

Identification: The design exploits arguably exogenous shocks to CEO turnover—health events, death, and natural retirement—to mitigate endogeneity in the timing of CEO replacement. The main endogeneity concern is that firms may actively select managers with desired AQ styles; using unexpected turnover aims to weaken that concern. The identifying argument is that if the new CEO carries an idiosyncratic style affecting AQ, then the AQ of the CEO’s old firm should positively correlate with the change in AQ at the new firm after the turnover. The author notes an important remaining limitation: the outside-hire replacement itself is not exogenous, so firms could still choose the replacement CEO based on AQ-style.

Setting: In an exogenous-turnover setting intended to distinguish idiosyncratic manager effects from firm selection, the paper finds that the new CEO’s prior-firm accounting quality predicts changes in accounting quality at the hiring firm. Using 41 cases of unexpected CEO turnover followed by outside hiring, the Pearson correlation between the change in AQ at the new employer and the AQ of the incoming CEO’s old firm is 0.54195 (p = 0.0003). The paper interprets this positive relation as evidence for the idiosyncratic style hypothesis: managers themselves affect accounting quality, rather than the observed effects merely reflecting firms choosing managers to fit desired AQ outcomes.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly highlight the exogenous CEO turnover setting as key evidence that manager effects are not merely firms choosing managers with desired attributes. It materially supports a central identification claim.
Settings.H1430: Section IV, “Exogenous CEO Turnover and the Selected Style Hypothesis” (PDF pp. 16-17).
Settings.G1431:
Treatment: Primary causal regressor is the interaction between output-price inflexibility and input-cost visibility. Inflex is the frequency of price adjustment (FPA) for a 6-digit NAICS customer sector, multiplied by -1; more negative values correspond to more flexible prices and higher values to more inflexible prices. VSBY is sector-year input-cost visibility, a continuous weighted average of supplier-sector publication coverage by the BLS. The paper interprets both the main effect of Inflex and the moderating effect of VSBY causally: greater price inflexibility raises information asymmetry, while greater public visibility of input costs mitigates that effect.

Method: Baseline weighted least squares panel regressions of information-asymmetry outcomes on sector-level output-price inflexibility (Inflex), sector-year input-cost visibility (VSBY), and their interaction, estimated on S&P 1500 firms from July 1997 to June 2013. The specification is Y_{k,t}=alpha+beta Inflex_j+gamma Inflex_j×VSBY_{j,t-1}+delta VSBY_{j,t-1}+controls+year FE+industry FE or firm FE, with observations weighted by firm assets and standard errors clustered at the 6-digit NAICS level. The identifying variation is within industry or within firm over time, with FE intended to absorb time-invariant heterogeneity and year shocks; the paper acknowledges remaining endogeneity of VSBY and later addresses it with IV.

Identification: The paper exploits cross-sectional differences in time-invariant sectoral output-price inflexibility and time-varying cross-sector differences in input-cost visibility created by BLS publication coverage of supplier-sector price indices, with controls plus year and industry or firm fixed effects to absorb common shocks and time-invariant heterogeneity. The concern is that VSBY may still correlate with unobserved customer-sector conditions or firm fundamentals, so these FE regressions are interpreted causally but not as fully immune to endogeneity.

Setting: In the baseline panel FE/WLS regressions, the authors argue that more inflexible output prices causally exacerbate information asymmetry, while more public information about input costs mitigates that effect. In Table 4, when VSBY is held at zero, a one-standard-deviation increase in Inflex is associated with increases of 0.4 percentage points in bid-ask spread, 0.7 percentage points in PIN, and 4.3 percentage points in forecast dispersion, which they state are 12%, 7.4%, and 10% of sample means. The interaction Inflex×VSBY is negative and significant across outcomes; for fully inflexible-price firms, a one-standard-deviation increase in input-cost visibility reduces bid-ask spread by 0.4 percentage points, PIN by 1.85 percentage points, and dispersion by 4.8 percentage points. These estimates are central to the paper’s claim that government-disclosed input-cost information is especially valuable for inflexible-price firms.

Main role: These are the paper’s main baseline tests of the central hypothesis in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion: price inflexibility increases information asymmetry and public information about input costs mitigates it.
Settings.H1431: Section 4.2, equation (5), Table 4 columns (1)-(9), PDF pp. 19-24.
Settings.G1432:
Treatment: Endogenous treatment is input-cost visibility VSBY, and in practice the focal causal estimand is the interaction of VSBY with output-price inflexibility Inflex. VSBY is a continuous sector-year measure of public observability of supplier input prices. Inflex is a continuous sector-level measure (negative of frequency of price adjustment). The instrument exploits exogenous expansion in supplier-sector publication coverage when the BLS moved from SIC to NAICS.

Method: Panel 2SLS using the BLS January 2004 conversion from SIC to NAICS as a quasi-natural experiment. The endogenous regressors are VSBY and Inflex×VSBY; instruments are IV=Post×Rank2004_j and Inflex×IV, where Rank2004_j is the percentile rank of the change in input-cost visibility between December 2002 and January 2004. Regressions are weighted by firm assets, include controls plus year and either industry FE or firm FE, and cluster at the 6-digit NAICS level. First-stage results are in Table 5 and second-stage results in Table 6.

Identification: The identifying shock is the exogenous expansion of BLS publication coverage after the January 2004 switch from SIC to NAICS. Different customer sectors experienced different increases in visibility because their supplier sectors differed in how much publication coverage expanded under NAICS. The exclusion restriction is that supplier-side classification-driven publication expansion affects firms’ information asymmetry only through increased input-cost visibility, not through customer-sector fundamentals. Relevance is demonstrated in strong first stages with F-statistics above 10.

Setting: Using a panel IV strategy based on the BLS’s 2004 SIC-to-NAICS conversion, the authors estimate the causal effect of publicly observable input costs on information frictions, especially for inflexible-price firms. In Table 6, the second-stage coefficient on Inflex×VSBY is negative and significant across all three outcomes: -0.089 and -0.104 for bid-ask spread, -0.114 and -0.142 for PIN, and -1.018 and -0.749 for forecast dispersion, depending on industry-FE or firm-FE specifications. The Inflex coefficient remains positive where reported (0.039 for bid-ask spread, 0.081 for PIN, 0.492 for dispersion). The paper interprets these IV results as showing that the exogenous component of input-cost visibility reduces information asymmetry for inflexible-price firms, reinforcing the main baseline conclusion.

Main role: The abstract and introduction specifically highlight the panel-IV strategy as addressing endogeneity and confirming the main mechanism, so it materially supports the paper’s central claim.
Settings.H1432: Section 4.4, equations (6)-(7), Table 5 Panels A-B, Table 6 columns (1)-(6), PDF pp. 26-32.
Settings.G1433:
Treatment: Exposure to the 2004 BLS publication expansion, measured continuously as Rank_j (the percentile-rank transformed sector-specific change in input-cost visibility from December 2002 to January 2004), with treatment effects allowed to vary by sectoral output-price inflexibility Inflex. The focal treatment is thus differential post-2004 exposure to increased public input-cost visibility for more inflexible-price sectors.

Method: Event-time difference-in-differences style dynamic specification around the January 2004 BLS SIC-to-NAICS conversion. The regression interacts event-time dummies with Inflex and Rank_j, omitting 2004 as the base period, and includes firm and year fixed effects, controls, and clustering at the 6-digit NAICS level. The outcomes are the same information-asymmetry measures as in the main analysis. The design is used to assess pretrends and dynamic treatment effects of the publication-expansion shock that differentially increased input-cost visibility across sectors.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing firms/sectors with larger versus smaller predicted increases in input-cost visibility after the 2004 BLS classification reform, while allowing effects to differ by output-price inflexibility. The key assumption is parallel pretrends across high- and low-exposure sectors absent the reform; the paper argues this is supported by flat pre-period coefficients and lack of anticipation effects.

Setting: The event-time DiD analysis examines whether information frictions fell differentially after the 2004 BLS publication expansion for firms in more inflexible-price sectors with larger exposure to visibility increases. The paper reports that pre-2004 coefficients fluctuate around zero with no discernable pretrends, while coefficients become significantly negative for most post-2004 periods one to two years after the switch. Although no full table of coefficients is printed in the supplied pages, the authors interpret Figure 5 as causal corroboration that exogenously increased input-cost visibility reduces information asymmetry particularly for inflexible-price firms.

Main role: This dynamic analysis is a substantive robustness/interpretation exercise supporting the IV design by showing no pretrends and negative post-shock effects, but the main headline results are carried by the baseline FE and IV tables.
Settings.G1434:
Treatment: Primary treatment is the interaction of sector-level output-price inflexibility Inflex with sector-quarter input-cost visibility VSBY. Inflex is continuous (negative frequency of price adjustment). VSBY is continuous sector-quarter visibility of supplier input prices. The paper interprets these regressors as affecting analysts’ demand for cost information during calls.

Method: Linear probability panel regressions of whether analysts ask at least one cost-related question during a conference call Q&A on Inflex, VSBY, and their interaction, with controls, time fixed effects, and either industry or firm fixed effects. The sample is conference-call transcripts from January 2002 to June 2013, excluding calls with Q&A shorter than 1,000 words; observations are weighted by firm assets and clustered at the 6-digit NAICS level. This is a substantive corroborating analysis using textual measures.

Identification: The paper uses within-industry or within-firm changes over time in input-cost visibility combined with cross-sectional differences in price inflexibility, controlling for firm characteristics and management discussion of costs during the presentation section. The concern is that VSBY may be endogenous, so the paper also estimates IV versions; nevertheless the FE specification is presented as causal corroboration of the proposed mechanism.

Setting: In conference-call regressions, the authors argue that analysts are more likely to ask about production costs when firms have inflexible output prices, and that public visibility of input costs reduces this need. In Table 7 baseline column 1, holding visibility at zero, a one-standard-deviation increase in Inflex raises the likelihood of at least one cost-related question by 4.6 percentage points; under the IV version the effect is nearly doubled. In the firm-FE baseline specification, the interaction Inflex×VSBY is -0.825, indicating that greater public input-cost visibility substantially attenuates analysts’ cost-information demand for inflexible-price firms. This supports the paper’s mechanism that price rigidity suppresses cost revelation and creates informational demand.
