The authors conclude that TCJA, by limiting tax benefits from offshore reinsurance, leveled the playing field in favor of U.S.-owned life insurers. Because this is an event-study rather than a regression-based causal design, the evidence is supportive rather than definitive.

Main role: These tests are presented as a final set of supporting analyses with policy relevance, not the core causal evidence on pre-TCJA income shifting or firm consequences. They reinforce the interpretation that TCJA reduced foreign-owned shadow insurers' advantage.
Settings.H1465: Section VI, 'Shadow Insurance and TCJA,' Figures 3-4 and Table 8 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 27-32.
Settings.G1466:
Treatment: Indicator for whether the firm’s earnings announcement receives WSJ earnings-article coverage because of the restructuring-induced coverage change. In the ERC DiD this is implemented as exposure switched on/off for treatment firms during the broader-coverage year (Treat×TreatYr). Treat is binary; TreatYr marks the period with broader WSJ coverage (the preyear for the 2007 coverage-decreasing event and the postyear for the 2008 and 2013 coverage-increasing events).

Method: The paper’s main price-discovery design is a difference-in-differences/event-study-style ERC regression around three Wall Street Journal (WSJ) restructuring events in January 2007, January 2008, and Summer 2013 that plausibly changed WSJ earnings coverage for some S&P 500 firms. Treatment firms are those whose WSJ earnings coverage changed in the predicted direction around the relevant event; controls are firms with unchanged coverage status matched to treatment firms’ preevent coverage state (always-covered controls for the 2007 coverage decrease; never-covered controls for the 2008 and 2013 coverage increases). The estimating equation regresses announcement-window abnormal returns on earnings surprise and its interaction with Treat×TreatYr, plus lower-order interactions, year-quarter fixed effects, and in some specifications year-quarter fixed effects interacted with surprise, with firm-clustered standard errors. The coefficient of interest is the triple interaction Surprise×Treat×TreatYr, interpreted as the change in the earnings response coefficient (ERC) caused by WSJ coverage. The design addresses endogeneity by exploiting newsroom restructurings, matching on recent newsworthiness proxies, adding controls, and presenting pretrend/pseudo-event evidence, though the paper still describes exogeneity as only plausible.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing treatment firms whose WSJ coverage changed at exogenous-looking WSJ restructuring events with similar control firms whose coverage did not change, before versus after the event-specific broader-coverage year. The key concern is endogenous media coverage of more newsworthy firms. The paper argues the restructuring altered the WSJ’s coverage threshold independently of focal firms’ changing fundamentals; it supports this with evidence that sample coverage changes around the events are not explained by observable changes in firm newsworthiness, while ordinary non-event coverage changes are. The design further uses coarsened exact matching on surprise and prior volatility, year-quarter fixed effects, interactions with surprise, controls, and separate pretrend/pseudo-event analyses. The identifying assumption is parallel trends in the ERC absent the restructuring-induced coverage changes.

Setting: Using DiD around three WSJ newsroom restructuring events, the paper estimates that WSJ earnings coverage increases the earnings response coefficient. In table 4, the coefficient on Surprise×Treat×TreatYr is 0.058 in column 2 and remains positive and significant across specifications (0.048 in columns 3 and 4), implying the ERC is about 39% larger with than without WSJ coverage relative to the baseline ERC of 0.148. The author interprets this as faster or more efficient price discovery at covered S&P 500 earnings announcements, a central causal claim of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that WSJ earnings articles improve price discovery at S&P 500 earnings announcements; the ERC DiD is one of the paper’s central tests supporting that claim.
Settings.H1466: Section 4.1 “earnings response coefficient,” equation (1), Table 4 cols. 1–4, Figure 2 panel A; PDF pp. 17–18, 31–35.
Settings.G1467:
Treatment: Binary exposure to WSJ earnings-article coverage induced by the restructuring events, operationalized as Treat×TreatYr in the IPT DiD. Treatment firms are those whose coverage changed in the expected direction around the event; control firms have unchanged coverage status with matching preevent coverage state.

Method: A conventional DiD with firm and year-quarter fixed effects estimates the effect of WSJ earnings coverage on intraperiod timeliness (IPT), an area-under-the-curve measure of how quickly returns are incorporated over trading days t through t+5. The treatment is the same restructuring-induced coverage change indicator Treat×TreatYr used in the main design. The regression follows equation (2), includes firm and year-quarter fixed effects and controls, and clusters standard errors by firm. This is a separate estimand from the ERC analysis because the dependent variable is IPT rather than returns interacted with surprise.

Identification: The source of identifying variation is the same WSJ restructuring events that changed coverage for treatment but not control firms. Firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity and year-quarter fixed effects absorb common shocks. The paper argues coverage changes around the events are plausibly exogenous to current or anticipated newsworthiness, unlike ordinary coverage changes, and presents matching and pretrend/pseudo-event evidence to support parallel trends. The remaining assumption is that, absent restructuring-induced coverage changes, IPT would have evolved similarly for treatment and control firms.

Setting: In DiD estimates using IPT as the dependent variable, WSJ earnings coverage increases the speed with which earnings news is incorporated into prices. Table 7 panel A reports a baseline Treat×TreatYr coefficient of 0.082 (t=3.02). Using the sample mean IPT of 4.222 and standard deviation of 9.465, the author states this implies an approximately 18% increase in IPT from a WSJ earnings article. This supports the paper’s central claim that journalist editorial content improves price discovery around earnings announcements.

Main role: The abstract states WSJ earnings articles improve price discovery, and IPT is the paper’s second main price-discovery outcome alongside the ERC.
Settings.H1467: Section 4.3 “alternative measures of market reaction,” equation (2), Table 7 panel A, Figure 2 panel B; PDF pp. 18, 43–45.
Settings.G1468:
Treatment: Binary indicator for restructuring-induced WSJ earnings-article coverage, implemented as Treat×TreatYr in the abnormal-volume DiD.

Method: A conventional DiD with firm and year-quarter fixed effects estimates the effect of WSJ earnings coverage on abnormal trading volume around earnings announcements. Using equation (2), the dependent variable is Abnormal Volume, defined as average daily share turnover during t−1 to t+1 minus average daily turnover over the prior 60 trading days, multiplied by 100. Treatment is the restructuring-induced WSJ coverage change Treat×TreatYr; controls and identification mirror the main design. Standard errors are clustered by firm.

Identification: The design compares before-after changes in abnormal volume for firms whose WSJ coverage changed at the restructuring events against matched control firms whose coverage status did not change. Firm and year-quarter fixed effects absorb firm-specific and common time shocks. The paper argues that around the WSJ restructurings, coverage changes are plausibly unrelated to changes in treated firms’ observable fundamentals, unlike normal-time coverage changes, and supplements this with matching and pretrend/pseudo-event evidence. The key assumption is parallel trends in abnormal volume absent the shock-driven coverage changes.

Setting: Using DiD around WSJ restructuring events, the paper finds that WSJ earnings articles raise trading activity at earnings announcements. In Table 7 panel B, the baseline Treat×TreatYr coefficient is 0.054 (t=2.02). The author interprets this as about an 8% increase in abnormal volume relative to the sample mean, supporting the central claim that editorial coverage increases trading around earnings news.

Main role: The abstract states that WSJ earnings articles increase trading volume at S&P 500 earnings announcements; this DiD volume test is a core result.
Settings.H1468: Section 4.3 “alternative measures of market reaction,” equation (2), Table 7 panel B, Figure 2 panel C; PDF pp. 18, 43–45.
Settings.G1469:
Treatment: The focal treatment is the degree of difference in wording between the WSJ article and the firm’s earnings press release, measured as RWordDiff: the quintile rank (scaled 0 to 1) of Word Diff, where Word Diff is negative one times the residual from regressing the Jaccard similarity between the article and release on log lengths of both documents. The causal estimand of interest is how this continuous treatment modifies the effect of WSJ coverage on the ERC, especially via Surprise×Treat×TreatYr×RWordDiff.

Method: For the subset of earnings announcements with a firm-specific WSJ article, the paper estimates how the causal effect of WSJ coverage on the ERC varies with article–press-release word differences, using 2SLS to address endogeneity of content differences. The underlying outcome equation is the DiD ERC regression augmented with interactions involving RWordDiff, the quintile-rank-scaled word-difference measure. All terms containing Word Diff are instrumented with two plausibly exogenous busy-news-day variables—Other Earnings News and Other Industry News—and their analogous interactions with the exogenous regressors (e.g., Surprise×Other Earnings News, Surprise×Treat×TreatYr×Other Earnings News). The overidentification p-value is reported, and first-stage relevance is supported in Table 5.

Identification: The concern is that article differences from the press release are endogenous to firm newsworthiness or unobserved announcement characteristics. The paper instruments word-difference interactions using the amount of competing earnings news and industry news around the focal announcement, arguing busy news days crowd out journalists’ ability to create firm-specific content but are unlikely to be driven by the focal firm’s newsworthiness. Identification requires these instruments to affect the ERC only through their effect on article word difference, conditional on controls and fixed effects. First-stage estimates show strong negative associations and the partial F-statistic exceeds the weak-IV threshold cited by the paper; overidentification tests do not reject.

Setting: In 2SLS ERC regressions, greater article–press-release word difference causally strengthens the effect of WSJ coverage on the market’s immediate earnings response. Table 6 panel A reports a coefficient of 0.061 on Surprise×Treat×TreatYr×RWordDiff (t=2.65), while the coefficient on Surprise×Treat×TreatYr for the lowest-word-difference articles is −0.010 and insignificant. The author interprets this as evidence that the price-discovery effect of WSJ coverage is concentrated in articles that differ more from firms’ releases, consistent with information creation rather than mere dissemination.

Main role: A central contribution in the abstract and introduction is that textual analysis suggests articles that differ more from the firm’s release drive the informational effects. The IV version is a substantive robustness/causal refinement of that core claim.
Settings.H1469: Section 4.2.2–4.2.3, Table 5 panel B (first stage), Table 6 panel A (2SLS column); PDF pp. 37–42.
Settings.G1470:
Treatment: Continuous treatment RToneDiff, defined as the scaled quintile rank of Tone Diff, where Tone Diff is the absolute difference between the percentage of negative words in the earnings release and the WSJ article. The estimand of interest is the interaction effect on the ERC, especially Surprise×Treat×TreatYr×RToneDiff.

Method: For announcements with a firm-specific WSJ article, the paper uses 2SLS in an augmented DiD ERC regression to estimate how the causal effect of WSJ coverage varies with article–press-release tone differences. The endogenous treatment is RToneDiff, the 0–1 scaled quintile rank of the absolute difference between the fraction of negative Loughran-McDonald words in the WSJ article and the earnings release. All terms involving Tone Diff are instrumented using Other Earnings News and Other Industry News and their corresponding interactions with exogenous regressors. The implementation mirrors the word-difference IV design.

Identification: Because tone differences may be endogenous to the firm’s news and omitted announcement characteristics, the paper instruments tone-difference terms with competing earnings and industry news, arguing that busy news days constrain journalists’ capacity to produce differing content but are exogenous to the focal firm. Identification assumes those busy-news-day variables affect the market response only through the induced tone difference in the WSJ article, conditional on controls and fixed effects. First stages are strong and overidentification tests do not reject.

Setting: In the 2SLS ERC heterogeneity tests, larger tone disagreement between the WSJ article and the firm’s earnings release weakens the immediate price response to earnings. Table 6 panel B reports a coefficient of −0.121 on Surprise×Treat×TreatYr×RToneDiff (t=−2.32), while the coefficient on Surprise×Treat×TreatYr for the lowest-tone-difference articles is 0.065 (t=1.93). The paper interprets this as evidence that article content corroborating firm tone speeds price discovery, whereas contradictory tone slows the earnings response.

Main role: The abstract highlights that differences speed up price discovery when they corroborate tone and slow it down when they contradict tone. This IV setting underpins that central nuance.
Settings.H1470: Section 4.2.2–4.2.3, Table 5 panel C (first stage), Table 6 panel B (2SLS column); PDF pp. 37–42.
Settings.G1471:
Treatment: Continuous treatment RWordDiff, the 0–1 scaled quintile rank of the residualized article–press-release word-difference measure, interacted with restructuring-induced WSJ coverage in the IPT DiD.

Method: Using equation (2) with firm and year-quarter fixed effects, the paper estimates via 2SLS how the effect of WSJ coverage on intraperiod timeliness varies with article–press-release word differences. The endogenous treatment is RWordDiff and its interactions with Treat×TreatYr and related terms. Instruments are Other Earnings News and Other Industry News and the analogous interactions with exogenous regressors. This is a separate IV setting because the dependent variable is IPT rather than abnormal returns.

Identification: The endogenous content-difference concern is addressed by instrumenting word-difference interactions with competing earnings and industry news. The logic is that busy news days exogenously reduce journalists’ capacity to create distinctive content. Given firm and year-quarter fixed effects and controls, identification assumes these instruments affect IPT only through word-difference-induced variation in the informational content of the WSJ article.

Setting: In IV DiD estimates for IPT, higher word difference strengthens the price-discovery effect of WSJ coverage. Table 7 panel A reports a coefficient of 0.106 on Treat×TreatYr×RDiff when RDiff is RWordDiff (2SLS column, t=2.16), while the base Treat×TreatYr coefficient is 0.002 and insignificant. The paper interprets this as showing that faster incorporation of earnings news into prices is concentrated in WSJ articles that differ more from the firm’s release.

Main role: This is a key extension of the textual-analysis claim to the paper’s second main price-discovery outcome, reinforcing the core interpretation.
Settings.H1471: Section 4.3, Table 7 panel A, 2SLS column under RWordDiff; PDF pp. 43–45.
Settings.G1472:
Treatment: Continuous treatment RToneDiff, the 0–1 scaled quintile rank of the absolute article–press-release tone-difference measure, interacted with restructuring-induced WSJ coverage in the IPT DiD.

Method: Using equation (2) with firm and year-quarter fixed effects, the paper estimates via 2SLS how the effect of WSJ coverage on intraperiod timeliness varies with article–press-release tone differences. The endogenous treatment is RToneDiff and its interactions; instruments are Other Earnings News and Other Industry News and their analogous interactions with exogenous terms. This is the IPT analogue of the tone-difference ERC IV design.

Identification: Tone-difference interactions are instrumented with competing earnings and industry news under the assumption that busy news days affect IPT only through journalists’ ability to produce more or less tone-differing content, not directly through focal-firm price-discovery dynamics once controls and fixed effects are included. First-stage evidence and overidentification tests are reported in adjacent tables.

Setting: In IV DiD estimates for IPT, greater tone difference between the WSJ article and the firm’s release reduces the price-discovery gains from coverage. Table 7 panel A shows Treat×TreatYr = 0.052 (t=2.40) for the lowest-tone-difference articles and Treat×TreatYr×RDiff = −0.047 (t=−2.16) when RDiff is RToneDiff. The author interprets this as meaning that articles with corroborating tone speed price discovery, while articles with contradictory tone slow it.

Main role: This setting supports the paper’s central nuanced claim that tone corroboration versus contradiction determines whether media differences speed or slow price discovery.
Settings.H1472: Section 4.3, Table 7 panel A, 2SLS column under RToneDiff; PDF pp. 43–45.
Settings.G1473:
Treatment: Continuous treatment RWordDiff, the scaled quintile rank of the residualized word-difference measure, interacted with restructuring-induced WSJ coverage in the abnormal-volume DiD.

Method: Using equation (2) with firm and year-quarter fixed effects, the paper estimates via 2SLS how the effect of WSJ coverage on abnormal trading volume varies with article–press-release word differences. The endogenous treatment is RWordDiff and its interactions with Treat×TreatYr and related terms; instruments are Other Earnings News and Other Industry News and their analogous interactions. This is a separate IV outcome setting because the dependent variable is abnormal volume.

Identification: The paper treats word differences as endogenous and instruments the relevant terms with competing earnings and industry news, arguing such busy-news measures exogenously reduce journalists’ ability to create distinctive content. Conditional on firm and year-quarter fixed effects and controls, these instruments are assumed to affect abnormal trading volume only through the resulting content difference in WSJ coverage.

Setting: In IV DiD estimates of abnormal volume, high word-difference WSJ articles cause larger trading responses to earnings announcements. Table 7 panel B reports a coefficient of 0.095 on Treat×TreatYr×RDiff when RDiff is RWordDiff (2SLS column, t=2.12), while the base Treat×TreatYr coefficient is 0.011 and insignificant. The paper interprets this as evidence that increased trading volume is concentrated in articles that create more information relative to the firm’s own release.

Main role: The abstract emphasizes that articles differing more from the release increase trading volume; this IV setting is the causal version of that core textual-analysis result.
Settings.H1473: Section 4.3, Table 7 panel B, 2SLS column under RWordDiff; PDF pp. 43–45.
Settings.G1474:
Treatment: Continuous treatment RToneDiff, the scaled quintile rank of the absolute difference in negative-word percentages between WSJ article and earnings release, interacted with restructuring-induced WSJ coverage in the abnormal-volume DiD.

Method: Using equation (2) with firm and year-quarter fixed effects, the paper estimates via 2SLS how the effect of WSJ coverage on abnormal trading volume varies with article–press-release tone differences. The endogenous treatment is RToneDiff and its interactions; instruments are Other Earnings News and Other Industry News and their analogous interactions with exogenous regressors. This is the volume analogue of the tone-difference IV design.

Identification: To address endogenous tone differences, the paper uses competing earnings and industry news as instruments for tone-difference interactions, relying on the argument that busy news days constrain journalists’ capacity to produce tone-divergent content while being exogenous to the focal firm’s trading response after controls and fixed effects. Validity is supported by first-stage strength and nonrejection in overidentification tests.

Setting: In IV DiD estimates of abnormal volume, larger tone differences between the WSJ article and the earnings release increase trading around the announcement. Table 7 panel B reports Treat×TreatYr×RDiff = 0.176 when RDiff is RToneDiff (t=2.10), with the base Treat×TreatYr coefficient equal to 0.033 and insignificant. The paper interprets this as showing that both corroborating and contradictory differences can raise trading volume, even though contradictory tone can slow price discovery.

Main role: The abstract states that articles differing more from the release increase trading volume and that tone differences matter; this IV setting supports that core contribution.
Settings.H1474: Section 4.3, Table 7 panel B, 2SLS column under RToneDiff; PDF pp. 43–45.
Settings.G1475:
Treatment: Adoption of a voluntary executive compensation clawback policy. In the DiD, treatment exposure is an adopter indicator interacted with a post-adoption period indicator; the underlying exposure is whether a firm has adopted a clawback policy, turning on in the adoption year and all later years for treated firms relative to matched non-adopters.

Method: The paper’s main design is a propensity-score-matched difference-in-differences estimated by linear OLS on a matched sample of voluntary clawback adopters and non-adopters. First, the authors estimate a logit model of clawback adoption and match each adopter to a non-adopter within the same two-digit SIC industry and fiscal year on the closest predicted probability, without replacement. In the second stage they estimate ETR = a + b0*CLAWBACK + b1*POST + b2*(CLAWBACK×POST) + controls + fixed effects + error, where the coefficient on CLAWBACK×POST is interpreted as the effect of clawback adoption. Reported specifications include year+industry fixed effects and, alternatively, year+company fixed effects; standard errors are clustered by company except in the company-FE specification. Identification relies on parallel trends between matched adopters and matched non-adopters absent adoption, conditional on observed covariates and fixed effects; the paper discusses residual concern about unobservables and performs pseudo-event, Rosenbaum sensitivity, and entropy-balancing checks.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-firm pre/post change in ETR for adopters relative to matched non-adopters observed over the same adoption-centered periods. Matching on predicted adoption within industry-year is intended to construct comparable controls on observables related to adoption. The DiD assumption is that, absent clawback adoption, ETR trends for adopters would have followed those of matched controls after conditioning on controls and fixed effects. The key endogeneity concern is self-selection into voluntary clawback adoption based on governance, risk, or other omitted factors that may also affect tax policy; the authors argue this is mitigated but not eliminated by propensity-score matching, covariates, fixed effects, pseudo-event tests, entropy balancing, and Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis.

Setting: Using a propensity-score-matched DiD, the authors conclude that adopting a voluntary clawback policy causes lower effective tax rates. In Table 3, the coefficient on CLAWBACK×POST is -0.016 with year and industry fixed effects (p<0.05) and -0.017 with year and company fixed effects (p<0.01), implying ETRs about 1.6–1.7 percentage points lower after adoption relative to matched non-adopters. The paper interprets this as economically meaningful, noting that with mean pre-tax income of about $1.1 billion it corresponds to roughly an $18 million reduction in income tax expense. This is the paper’s main causal result and the foundation for its broader claim that clawbacks induce more tax planning.

Main role: This is the central causal test supporting the paper’s headline claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that voluntary clawback adoptions lower firms’ effective tax rates.
Settings.H1475: Section III Empirical Design and Section IV Difference-in-Differences Regressions; Figure 1 (PDF p.12) and Table 3, Panel B, Columns (1)–(2) (PDF pp.13–14).
Settings.G1476:
Treatment: Adoption of a voluntary clawback policy, represented by event-time indicators for the year before adoption, adoption year, year after adoption, and two years after adoption onward among adopters relative to matched non-adopters.

Method: This setting uses the same matched-sample OLS DiD framework as the main specification but estimates dynamic event-time treatment effects by replacing POST with separate indicators for YEAR_BEFORE_ADOPT, YEAR_ADOPT, YEAR_AFTER_ADOPT, and TWOYEARS+_AFTER_ADOPT. The design remains a conventional staggered-adoption DiD/event-study style regression rather than a named modern heterogeneous DiD estimator. The paper uses it to assess timing and persistence of the clawback effect on ETR. Numerical coefficients are described in prose as negative and significant after adoption, with the pre-adoption lead insignificant.

Identification: Identification again comes from comparing event-time changes in ETR for adopters to matched non-adopters, assuming no differential trends absent treatment. The insignificant lead (year before adoption) is used as a validity check against anticipatory effects or differential pre-trends; negative post-adoption coefficients are interpreted as causal and persistent. Remaining concern is staggered-adoption DiD bias and selection on unobservables, not fully resolved because the paper does not implement a modern heterogeneous DiD estimator.

Setting: In an augmented event-time DiD, the paper finds no detectable ETR effect in the year before adoption but negative, statistically significant effects in the adoption year, the year after, and two or more years afterward. Although the paper does not report the exact dynamic coefficients in the text, it interprets the pattern as showing a swift decline in ETR at adoption that persists in later years. This robustness analysis reinforces the main claim that clawback adoption causes sustained reductions in effective tax rates rather than reflecting pre-existing trends.

Main role: This timing specification directly supports the main conclusion by showing no pre-trend and persistent post-adoption ETR declines.
Settings.H1476: Section IV Difference-in-Differences Regressions, paragraph beginning “To assess when subsequent ETRs decreased...” (PDF p.15).
Settings.G1477:
Treatment: AFTER CLAWBACK equals 1 during the year of and all years after a firm adopts a clawback policy, and 0 before adoption, estimated only among clawback-adopting firms.

Method: Within the sample of clawback adopters only, the authors estimate linear OLS regressions of tax-planning proxies on AFTER CLAWBACK, controlling for the same firm characteristics as in Equation (2) and including industry fixed effects; they cluster standard errors by company and note untabulated company-fixed-effect versions for some outcomes. This is not a DiD against non-adopters in the reported table, but a within-adopter before/after design meant to identify channels through which clawback adoption changes tax planning behavior.

Identification: The strategy is a within-adopter before/after comparison: if clawback adoption changes incentives away from accrual-based earnings management and toward tax planning, tax-planning opportunities and investments should rise after adoption. Industry fixed effects absorb time-invariant sector differences, and controls absorb time-varying observables, but there is no separate untreated control group in the reported table, so identification is weaker and relies on the assumption that no other coincident changes among adopters drive these outcomes. The authors accordingly describe this evidence as informative/descriptive about mechanisms rather than definitive.

Setting: Among adopting firms, the paper reports that tax-planning activities rise after clawback adoption. In Table 4, AFTER CLAWBACK is associated with a 0.010 increase in the probability of a new tax-haven subsidiary (p<0.10), a 0.060 increase in the probability of using an industry tax-expert auditor for tax services (p<0.05), a 0.245 increase in log tax fees paid to auditors (p<0.05), and a 0.055 increase in low-tax network ties (p<0.01). The authors interpret these within-firm post-adoption increases as evidence that clawback adoption induces greater investment in tax planning, providing a mechanism for the main ETR decline.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize increased tax planning investments as the mechanism behind lower ETRs; these channel regressions materially support that central interpretation.
Settings.H1477: Section IV Tax Planning Investments; Table 4, Columns (1)–(4) (PDF pp.15–16).
Settings.G1478:
Treatment: AFTER CLAWBACK equals 1 in the adoption year and subsequent years for firms that adopted clawbacks, 0 before adoption.

Method: Within clawback adopters only, the paper estimates OLS regressions of accrual-related outcomes on AFTER CLAWBACK with control variables from Equation (2), industry fixed effects, and company-clustered standard errors. The outcomes are the absolute magnitude of pre-tax discretionary accruals, the absolute magnitude of tax accruals, and an indicator for future tax-related misstatements. The goal is to test whether post-clawback ETR reductions reflect opportunistic accrual reporting rather than tax planning.

Identification: The identifying argument is within-adopter before/after change: if clawbacks raise executives’ costs of aggressive accrual-based reporting, then accrual use and tax-related misstatements should fall after adoption. Industry fixed effects and controls account for observable differences, but absent a control group the design depends on no confounding post-adoption shocks. The paper uses these results as mechanism evidence rather than stand-alone causal proof.

Setting: Table 5 shows that firms reduce accrual-related behavior after adopting a clawback policy. AFTER CLAWBACK is associated with a -0.009 change in the magnitude of pre-tax accruals (p<0.01), a -0.001 change in tax accruals (p<0.10), and a -0.036 change in the probability of a future tax-related misstatement (p<0.01). The paper interprets these declines as evidence that lower post-adoption ETRs are not driven by more opportunistic accrual reporting, but instead by increased tax planning.

Main role: These tests are central to the paper’s argument that lower ETRs come from tax planning rather than opportunistic tax accrual manipulation.
Settings.H1478: Section IV Tax Accruals; Table 5, Columns (1)–(3) (PDF pp.17–18).
Settings.G1479:
Treatment: AFTER CLAWBACK indicator for post-adoption years among clawback adopters, estimated separately by whether the firm decreased accruals after adoption.

Method: The authors estimate within-adopter OLS regressions of ETR on AFTER CLAWBACK separately for two subsamples: firms that decreased accruals following clawback adoption and firms that did not. Regressions include the same controls as Equation (2), industry fixed effects, and company-clustered standard errors. This is a heterogeneity analysis of the within-adopter before/after effect to assess whether ETR declines are concentrated where accrual use falls.

Identification: This analysis relies on within-adopter post-adoption variation and compares heterogeneous treatment patterns across partitions defined by whether accruals decreased after adoption. The intended interpretation is that if firms substitute away from accruals toward tax planning, ETR declines should be larger among firms that reduced accruals. Identification is descriptive/conditional and does not isolate exogenous heterogeneity in accrual changes.

Setting: Partitioning adopters by whether they reduced accruals after adoption, the paper finds larger ETR declines where accruals fell. In Table 6, AFTER CLAWBACK equals -0.023 (p<0.01) for firms with decreased accruals and -0.008 (p=0.170) for firms without decreased accruals; the paper notes an untabulated Welch test showing the difference is significant at p<0.05. The authors interpret this pattern as consistent with clawback adoption causing firms to substitute tax planning for aggressive accruals.

Main role: This is a substantive mechanism heterogeneity test supporting, but not itself establishing, the central claim.
Settings.H1479: Section IV Tax Accruals; Table 6, Columns (1)–(2) (PDF p.19).
Settings.G1480:
Treatment: Post-adoption exposure to a clawback policy among adopters, partitioned by clawback type: robust clawbacks triggered by any restatement versus misconduct clawbacks triggered only by intentional misstatements.

Method: The paper estimates within-adopter OLS regressions of ETR on AFTER CLAWBACK separately for firms adopting robust clawbacks and those adopting misconduct clawbacks. Controls from Equation (2), industry fixed effects, and company-clustered standard errors are included. This is a heterogeneity analysis by clawback type, motivated by theory that broader clawbacks more strongly raise the cost of aggressive reporting.

Identification: The identifying idea is that robust clawbacks should more strongly discourage accrual-based earnings management because they can be triggered by any restatement, not just intentional misconduct. Comparing before/after ETR changes within adopter subsamples tests whether the treatment effect is stronger when clawback incentives are stronger. As with other within-adopter tests, omitted coincident changes remain a concern.

Setting: The paper finds that the post-adoption decline in ETR is stronger when firms adopt more stringent clawbacks. In Table 7, the coefficient on AFTER CLAWBACK is -0.023 for robust clawbacks (p<0.01) and -0.013 for misconduct clawbacks (p<0.05); an untabulated Welch test puts the difference at p=0.104. The authors interpret this as evidence that stricter clawback provisions cause larger shifts toward tax-planning-based reductions in tax expense.

Main role: The abstract specifically notes that decreases are stronger among firms adopting robust clawback policies, making this an emphasized substantive extension.
Settings.H1480: Section IV Clawback Type; Table 7, Columns (1)–(2) (PDF pp.17–20).
Settings.G1481:
Treatment: AFTER CLAWBACK indicator for the adoption year and later years among firms that adopt voluntary clawback policies.

Method: Within clawback adopters only, the authors regress tax outcome volatility and tax disclosure measures on AFTER CLAWBACK using OLS with Equation (2) controls, industry fixed effects, and company-clustered standard errors. Outcomes are CV_ETR, log Gunning-Fog readability index of tax footnotes, and log word count of tax footnotes. These are additional analyses on the consequences of the induced tax-planning changes.

Identification: The within-adopter before/after strategy asks whether the tax consequences associated with clawback adoption are more sustainable and transparent after treatment. Industry fixed effects and controls absorb observable heterogeneity, but there is no explicit untreated counterfactual in the table. The causal interpretation depends on assuming that observed post-adoption changes in volatility and disclosure are attributable to clawback-induced tax policy changes rather than other concurrent shifts.

Setting: The paper reports that clawback adoption improves the nature of subsequent tax outcomes and disclosures. In Table 8, AFTER CLAWBACK is associated with lower ETR volatility (CV_ETR coefficient -0.148, p<0.05), lower FOG (coefficient -0.027, p<0.10, implying more readable tax footnotes), and higher WORD COUNT (coefficient 0.128, p<0.01, implying longer tax disclosures). The authors interpret these results as evidence that clawback-induced tax planning leads to more sustainable tax outcomes and higher-quality tax disclosure rather than more opportunistic behavior.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight lower tax outcome volatility and improved tax disclosure following adoption as part of the paper’s broader central message about positive spillovers of clawbacks.
Settings.H1481: Section V Additional Analyses, Tax Outcome Volatility and Tax Disclosure; Table 8, Columns (1)–(3) (PDF pp.18–21).
Settings.G1482:
Treatment: Change in clawback adoption status (ΔCLAW ADOPT), indicating adoption between periods in the changes specification.

Method: In an untabulated robustness analysis, the authors estimate a first-difference/changes specification where the dependent variable is the change in ETR and the treatment variable is the change in clawback adoption status (ΔCLAW ADOPT), with controls also entered in changes. This is a linear regression adjustment design rather than a panel fixed-effects model as reported in the text. It is used to remove time-invariant unobserved characteristics over the change interval.

Identification: Identification comes from relating within-firm changes in ETR to changes in clawback adoption status while differencing away time-invariant firm characteristics. The paper interprets a negative coefficient on ΔCLAW ADOPT as corroborating the main causal claim. Remaining concerns include time-varying omitted variables correlated with adoption timing.

Setting: As an untabulated robustness test, the authors estimate a changes regression and report that the coefficient on ΔCLAW ADOPT is negative and significant at p<0.05 when ΔETR is the dependent variable. They interpret this as additional evidence that adopting a clawback policy lowers effective tax rates, with differencing helping eliminate static unobserved firm traits.

Main role: This is an untabulated robustness check confirming the main result, not the core design emphasized in the paper.
Settings.H1482: Section V Additional Analyses, paragraph “Changes Design” (PDF p.21).
Settings.G1483:
Treatment: Adoption of a voluntary clawback policy, captured by the interaction CLAWBACK × POST in the same matched DiD framework as the main analysis.

Method: In untabulated robustness analyses, the authors re-estimate their matched-sample difference-in-differences using alternative tax outcome measures: temporary book-tax differences, permanent book-tax differences, and cash taxes paid scaled by total assets. The underlying design is the same conventional OLS DiD as Equation (2), with CLAWBACK×POST as the treatment effect of interest, applied to alternative dependent variables. These robustness tests assess whether the clawback effect appears specifically in tax outcomes associated with permanent, earnings-affecting tax planning and cash tax savings.

Identification: The identification is the same matched DiD parallel-trends argument as the main specification. By changing the dependent variable, the paper tests whether the estimated treatment effect aligns with a tax-planning channel: no effect on temporary differences, positive effect on permanent differences, and lower cash taxes paid. This helps rule out denominator-driven profitability stories and tie the treatment to tax expense reductions.

Setting: Using the same DiD design with alternative tax outcomes, the paper reports no significant effect of clawback adoption on temporary book-tax differences, but a positive and significant effect on permanent book-tax differences and a significant increase in cash tax savings when cash taxes paid over assets is the outcome. Although exact coefficients are not reported, the authors interpret this pattern as showing that clawback adoption affects permanent, earnings-relevant tax planning and real tax cash flows rather than merely shifting temporary differences.

Main role: These are untabulated robustness checks strengthening interpretation of the main ETR result, not separate headline findings.
Settings.H1483: Section V Additional Analyses, paragraphs “Alternative Measures of Tax Outcomes” and related discussion of alternative scalars (PDF p.22).
Settings.G1484:
Treatment: MIS = 1 if the industry in which peer firm i operates has at least one accounting misstatement in year t; 0 otherwise. This is an industry-year exposure indicator for peer firms, based on SEC/DOJ enforcement-action violation periods of other firms in the same Fama-French 48 industry.

Method: The paper estimates linear OLS regressions of peer firms' operating decisions on an indicator MIS that equals 1 when the firm's Fama-French 48 industry has at least one firm in an SEC/DOJ accounting-misstatement period in year t. The specification augments outcome-specific 'fundamental factors' (such as cash, ROA, size, market-share leadership, sales, Tobin's Q, external financing, and lagged R&D where relevant) with industry dummies and year dummies; standard errors are clustered by firm. Identification is regression adjustment using cross-industry and within-industry-over-time variation between misstatement-industry-years and other firm-years, not a formal DiD because there is no treated×post design or unit fixed effects. The authors interpret the MIS coefficient causally as distortion from peers being misled by false financial statements, while acknowledging concerns about selection and undetected misstatements.

Identification: The identifying variation is whether a peer firm's industry-year is experiencing at least one other firm's misstatement period. The paper argues that, conditional on observed fundamentals plus industry and year dummies, remaining differences in peer decisions reflect distorted responses to false signals about demand/cost conditions embedded in misstating firms' reports. The main endogeneity concern is that misstatement industries may differ for reasons also affecting peer operating decisions, or that detected misstatements are selected by regulators. The strategy relies on regression adjustment and the argument that broad controls absorb normal determinants of decisions; causal interpretation requires that conditional on these controls and fixed industry/year effects, MIS is not proxying omitted industry shocks or peer firms' own misconduct.

Setting: In the main regressions, the author interprets industry exposure to accounting misstatements as causing peer firms to distort their operating decisions. Relative to firms in non-misstatement industry-years and peer firms in non-misstatement years, peer firms in misstatement-industry-years have CAPX higher by 0.007 (scaled by lagged assets; t=6.54), R&D higher by 0.002 (t=2.22), advertising higher by 0.002 (t=2.21), and gross profit/sales lower by 0.032 (t=-2.88). The paper states these imply that the median peer firm 'overinvests 14 percent in capital expenditures, 7 percent in R&D, and 10 percent in advertising, and experiences 10 percent lower gross profit during the periods of misreporting.' These results are the core evidence for the paper's main claim that false reports distort peer firms' real decisions.

Main role: These are the paper's primary tests of H1a-H1d and directly support the abstract's central claim that false financial statements distort peer firms' capital investment, R&D, advertising, and pricing decisions.
Settings.H1484: Section IV 'Main Results,' Table 2 Columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 9-10.
Settings.G1485:
Treatment: Exposure to industry-year misstatement periods (MIS), with heterogeneous effect by SIZE RATIO = peer firm's sales divided by misstating firm's sales in year t-1. The focal causal estimand is the interaction MIS × SIZE RATIO, i.e., how the effect of misstatement exposure changes with relative size.

Method: The paper estimates linear OLS regressions that interact the misstatement-industry exposure indicator MIS with SIZE RATIO, defined as peer-firm sales divided by misstating-firm sales in t-1. The models include the same fundamental controls, industry dummies, year dummies, and firm-clustered standard errors as the main specification. This is a cross-sectional heterogeneity analysis of the causal effect of misstatement exposure on peer decisions, with the interaction coefficient interpreted as showing how the distortion varies with peers' size relative to misstating firms.

Identification: The strategy asks whether the estimated effect of misstatement exposure differs systematically with peer size relative to the misstating firm. Conditional on controls plus industry/year dummies, the interaction is interpreted as capturing lower susceptibility of larger peers to false signals. This still relies on selection-on-observables and assumes SIZE RATIO is not proxying omitted heterogeneity in how peer decisions respond to industry shocks during misstatement periods.

Setting: The paper argues that larger peers, relative to the misstating firm, are less distorted by false financial statements. In Table 3, the interaction MIS × SIZE RATIO is -0.002 for CAPX (t=-4.59), approximately zero and insignificant for R&D, -0.001 for ADEX (t=-1.61), and +0.024 for GP (t=6.06). The positive GP interaction means the misstatement-induced decline in gross profit is attenuated for relatively larger peers. These estimates support the paper's central cross-sectional claim that misstatement distortions are smaller when peer firms are larger relative to the misstating firm.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that distortions are smaller for larger peers, making this cross-sectional interaction a central substantive result, not merely a robustness check.
Settings.H1485: Section IV 'Cross-Sectional Tests,' Table 3 Columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 12.
Settings.G1486:
Treatment: Exposure to industry-year misstatements (MIS), with heterogeneity by FRD ANALYSTS, the number of analysts following misstating firms during year t. The focal treatment contrast is the interaction MIS × FRD ANALYSTS, not analyst following alone.

Method: The paper estimates linear OLS models interacting MIS with FRD ANALYSTS, the number of analysts following the misstating firms during year t (set to zero if missing). The regressions include the same operating-decision controls, industry dummies, year dummies, and firm-clustered standard errors. This is a heterogeneous-effects regression-adjustment design where the interaction measures how the effect of misstatement exposure varies with the misstating firms' external information environment.

Identification: The paper uses variation in analyst following of misstating firms to proxy the strength of information transmission. After conditioning on fundamentals and industry/year effects, the interaction coefficient is interpreted as showing that false statements have larger causal spillovers when they are more widely disseminated. This requires assuming analyst following is not simply capturing unobserved industry conditions that themselves alter peer firms' decision responses during misstatement years.

Setting: The author interprets Table 4 as showing that the external information environment of misstating firms amplifies spillovers to peers. The interaction MIS × FRD ANALYSTS is 0.003 for CAPX (t=7.09), about 0.000 and insignificant for R&D (t=1.18), 0.001 for ADEX (t=3.66), and -0.007 for GP (t=-1.57, marked significant at 10 percent in the paper). Thus, when misstating firms are followed by more analysts, peer firms invest more in capital and advertising and experience lower gross profit during misstatement periods. This is presented as evidence that stronger information transmission magnifies the distortive effect of false reports.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight that distortions are larger for more widely followed misstating firms, so this interaction supports a central substantive conclusion.
Settings.H1486: Section IV 'Cross-Sectional Tests,' Table 4 Columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 13.
Settings.G1487:
Treatment: Exposure to industry-year misstatements (MIS), with heterogeneity by peer firms' MA SCORE (managerial ability). The focal estimand is the interaction MIS × MA SCORE.

Method: The paper estimates linear OLS models interacting MIS with MA SCORE, a continuous measure of peer firms' managerial ability from Demerjian et al. (2012), with missing values replaced by industry-year averages. The regressions again include fundamental controls, industry and year dummies, and standard errors clustered by firm. The interaction is interpreted as heterogeneity in the causal effect of misstatement exposure by peer managers' ability to see through false signals.

Identification: The design uses cross-sectional variation in managerial ability among peer firms. Conditional on controls and fixed industry/year effects, the paper interprets the interaction as showing that more able managers are less misled by false statements. This relies on MA SCORE not standing in for omitted determinants of how firms respond to industry shocks specifically in misstatement years.

Setting: The paper finds that peer managerial ability dampens some distortions from false financial statements. In Table 5, MIS × MA SCORE equals -0.020 for CAPX (t=-2.46), 0.008 and insignificant for R&D, 0.012 and insignificant for ADEX, and +0.627 for GP (t=4.90). The author interprets these results as showing that high-ability managers are less likely to overinvest in fixed assets and less likely to suffer the misstatement-related decline in gross profit, though managerial ability does not significantly moderate R&D or advertising responses.

Main role: The abstract concludes that distortions are smaller for peers managed by more able managers, so this interaction is part of the paper's central contribution.
Settings.H1487: Section IV 'Cross-Sectional Tests,' Table 5 Columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 14.
Settings.G1488:
Treatment: CNT = number of misstatements in a given industry and year, measured among peer firms' industries during misstatement years only. This is a continuous treatment intensity, not a binary indicator.

Method: For peer firms in misstatement years only, the paper estimates linear OLS regressions of operating decisions on CNT, the number of misstatements in a given industry-year, controlling for the same fundamental variables plus industry and year dummies and clustering standard errors by firm. This is regression adjustment on the intensive margin of industry misstatement exposure, interpreted as the effect of multiple false statements on the severity of peer distortions.

Identification: The strategy exploits within-misstatement-year differences in the count of misstating firms across industry-years. After controlling for fundamentals and year/industry effects, the paper interprets a higher CNT as increasing the severity of distorted peer responses because more false signals arrive from the industry. The key assumption is that the number of misstatements is not just proxying unobserved industry shocks that independently raise investment or compress gross margins.

Setting: Among peer firms already exposed to at least one industry misstatement, the paper estimates that more simultaneous misstatements intensify distortions. In Table 6, CNT has coefficients of 0.0003 on CAPX (t=2.78), 0.0005 on R&D (t=1.92), 0.0007 on ADEX (t=3.98), and -0.0074 on GP (t=-3.79). The author interprets this pattern as evidence that multiple misstatements magnify peers' overinvestment and pricing distortions relative to years with fewer misstatements.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion state that distortions are larger in industries in which more firms misstate, making this a central cross-sectional finding.
Settings.H1488: Section IV 'Cross-Sectional Tests,' Table 6 Columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 15.
Settings.G1489:
Treatment: Current misstatement exposure MIS and post-revelation timing indicators AFT1-AFT5, where AFTix = 1 if year t is the ith year after the end of misstatements/revelation, 0 otherwise. The substantive treatment in this setting is being in the years after revelation versus the misstatement period.

Method: The paper estimates linear OLS regressions for peer firms only that include MIS and five post-revelation indicators AFT1-AFT5, each equal to 1 for the first through fifth year after the end/revelation of misstatements. The models include the same fundamental controls, industry dummies, year dummies, and firm-clustered standard errors. The author interprets these coefficients and F-tests comparing MIS with post-revelation coefficients as evidence on whether peers reverse earlier distorted decisions once the fraud is revealed.

Identification: The paper examines whether peer decisions move back after revelation of misreporting, using post-event indicators within peer firms and controlling for fundamentals and time/industry effects. The identifying argument is that if misstatements caused distorted decisions, revelation should attenuate or reverse those distortions. This is still observational and may be confounded by other post-revelation industry adjustments occurring around the same time.

Setting: To bolster the causal story, the paper studies whether peers reverse their decisions after misstatements are revealed. Relative to the misstatement-period coefficient MIS, post-revelation CAPX coefficients are negative and increasingly so from AFT1=-0.004 (t=-2.53) to AFT5=-0.017 (t=-10.81); for GP they shift from AFT1=-0.051 (t=-2.81) to AFT5=0.055 (t=3.06), with F-tests showing later post-revelation coefficients are significantly greater than the misstatement coefficient. R&D shows negative AFT1-AFT3 coefficients and advertising also declines relative to the misstatement period according to the authors' discussion. The paper interprets this as peer firms reversing distorted operating and pricing choices once misconduct becomes known.

Main role: These dynamic post-revelation regressions are used to reinforce the interpretation that earlier estimated effects reflect distortions that reverse after truth revelation; they support, rather than constitute, the headline contribution.
Settings.H1489: Section IV 'Additional Tests: Peer Firms' Operating Decisions through Time,' Table 7 Columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 16-17.
Settings.G1490:
Treatment: FRDYR = 1 if year t is a misstatement year for the misstating firm, 0 otherwise.

Method: The paper estimates a linear OLS regression for misstating firms' own management-forecast errors FRD_FE on an indicator FRDYR for whether the firm-year is a misstatement year, controlling for forecast and firm characteristics, year dummies, and clustering by firm. This is not an operating-decision regression for peers, but the authors treat it as substantive evidence that misstaters issue overly optimistic guidance during fraud periods, potentially contributing to peer distortions.

Identification: The design compares misstatement years to other years within the sample of misstating firms, controlling for observable forecast determinants. The paper interprets a more negative forecast error in misstatement years as evidence that management provides more optimistic projections when it is misreporting. Causal interpretation assumes no omitted time-varying factors correlated with both misstatement years and forecast optimism after conditioning on controls.

Setting: As a mechanism test, the author asks whether misstating firms issue more optimistic earnings guidance during misstatement years. Appendix C reports a coefficient of -0.004 on FRDYR (t=-1.96) in a regression where the dependent variable FRD_FE is actual EPS minus management forecast, scaled by lagged price. Because more negative FRD_FE implies more optimistic forecasts, the paper interprets this as evidence that misstating firms make overly optimistic projections during fraud periods, which could further mislead peers.

Main role: This is an ancillary mechanism test used to examine whether optimistic guidance by misstating firms could help explain the main peer effects.
Settings.H1490: Section IV 'Misstating Firms' Management Guidance and Peers' Distorted Decisions,' Appendix C, PDF pp. 16, 27-28.
Settings.G1491:
Treatment: Exposure to industry-year misstatements (MIS), with heterogeneity by CEO PPS, a continuous measure of executive incentive compensation / pay-for-performance sensitivity. The focal estimand is MIS × CEO PPS.

Method: The paper estimates linear OLS models interacting MIS with CEO PPS, the change in value of the CEO's equity wealth in response to a 1 percent stock-price change, with missing values set to industry averages. The regressions include the same fundamental controls, industry dummies, year dummies, and clustered standard errors. The interaction coefficient is interpreted as showing how peer firms' executive equity incentives affect their reaction to misstatement exposure.

Identification: The design uses variation in CEOs' equity incentives among peer firms to see whether compensation sharpens responses to false signals. Conditional on controls and fixed industry/year effects, the interaction is interpreted as causal heterogeneity in the effect of misstatement exposure. This requires that CEO PPS not merely proxy for omitted firm traits that differentially shape responses in misstatement years.

Setting: The paper argues that executive equity incentives can amplify peer reactions to false statements. In Table 9, the interaction MIS × CEO PPS is 0.001 for CAPX (t=5.67), about 0.000 for R&D (t=1.54), approximately -0.000 and insignificant for ADEX (t=-0.73), and -0.005 for GP (t=-2.10). The author interprets this as evidence that when CEOs' wealth is more sensitive to stock price, peers respond more strongly to misstatements by raising capital investment and, to some extent, R&D, while suffering a larger decline in gross profit.

Main role: This is an additional cross-sectional test on managerial incentives rather than a headline contribution emphasized in the abstract.
Settings.H1491: Section IV 'The Effect of Executive Incentive Compensation,' Table 9 Columns (1)-(4), PDF p. 21.
Settings.G1492:
Treatment: REPAT, a continuous proxy for potential repatriation tax costs imposed by the U.S. worldwide tax system. Constructed as foreign pretax income multiplied by the difference between the U.S. statutory tax rate and the firm's three-year average foreign current effective tax rate, scaled by lagged total assets; set to 0 for firm-years with foreign tax rates above the U.S. statutory rate, negative current foreign pretax income, or negative cumulative three-year foreign pretax income.

Method: Main dividend-payout analysis using a Cragg (1971) hurdle model on a panel of 12,444 U.S. multinational firm-years from 1987–2004. The first part is a probit for whether the firm pays a dividend (DivIndicator), and the second part is a truncated normal regression for the dividend level conditional on positive dividends (DivLevel>0). The paper then computes average partial effects on the unconditional dividend level. Regressors include the continuous treatment REPAT and a standard set of payout-policy controls, plus year fixed effects; standard errors are bootstrapped with firm clustering. This is not framed as a quasi-experiment and relies on regression adjustment/selection modeling under the author's argument that conditioning on observables isolates the effect of potential repatriation tax costs; remaining endogeneity from omitted variables and measurement error in REPAT is an identification concern.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional and intertemporal variation in REPAT across U.S. multinationals, after controlling for domestic and foreign profitability, size, growth opportunities, investment, firm age, retained earnings, leverage, cash holdings, earnings volatility, past stock returns, option-related dilution incentives, and year effects. The causal concern is that repatriation tax costs may be correlated with omitted determinants of payout policy; the paper argues that conditioning on standard payout determinants and focusing on potential tax costs imposed by the tax system allows interpretation as the effect of repatriation tax costs on dividends. The hurdle model separately identifies effects on the participation and amount margins but does not itself solve omitted-variable bias.

Setting: Using a Cragg hurdle model on 1987–2004 U.S. multinational firm-years, the paper interprets higher potential repatriation tax costs as causing lower dividend payouts. REPAT is negatively related to both the probability of paying a dividend and the amount paid conditional on paying one, yielding a negative unconditional effect on dividends. The paper states that a U.S. MNC with the mean (median) positive REPAT has a 4.35 (2.00) percentage point lower probability of paying a dividend than a firm with REPAT=0, and an unconditional dividend level 0.17 (0.08) percent of lagged assets lower, equal to 14.32 (6.57) percent of the mean dividend level. This is the paper's core causal claim about how repatriation tax costs constrain shareholder payouts.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize as a central finding that repatriation tax costs constrain U.S. MNCs' dividend payments and that the economic magnitude is substantial.
Settings.H1492: Section IV, 'Results of the Tests of H1,' Table 4 Columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 9–11.
Settings.G1493:
Treatment: REPAT, the continuous repatriation-tax-cost proxy equal to foreign pretax income times the gap between the U.S. statutory corporate tax rate and the firm's three-year average foreign current effective tax rate, scaled by lagged total assets, and set to 0 for firms not expected to face incremental U.S. taxes upon repatriation.

Method: Main share-repurchase analysis using the same Cragg (1971) hurdle model as the dividend tests, on 12,444 U.S. multinational firm-years from 1987–2004. The first part is a probit for whether the firm repurchases shares (RepIndicator), and the second is a truncated normal regression for the repurchase level conditional on positive repurchases (RepLevel>0); the paper also reports unconditional average partial effects. Controls mirror the dividend analysis and include year fixed effects; standard errors are bootstrapped with firm clustering. This is a nonexperimental regression-based design, with causal interpretation resting on conditioning on observables rather than an external source of exogenous variation.

Identification: Identification again uses variation in REPAT across firms and time, controlling for observed payout determinants and year fixed effects. The main endogeneity concern is omitted determinants of repurchases correlated with tax costs; the paper relies on observables and the structure of REPAT as a tax-cost proxy to interpret coefficients causally. The hurdle model distinguishes the decision to repurchase from the magnitude decision, but there is no separate quasi-experimental identification strategy.

Setting: In the paper's main repurchase setting, higher potential repatriation tax costs are interpreted as reducing the likelihood that a U.S. MNC repurchases shares, but not the amount repurchased conditional on repurchasing and not the overall unconditional level of repurchases. The paper reports that a firm with the mean (median) positive REPAT has a 1.74 (0.80) percentage point lower probability of repurchasing than a firm with REPAT=0, equal to 3.74 (1.72) percent of the mean repurchase probability. However, the conditional amount and unconditional repurchase-level effects are insignificant, leading to the substantive conclusion that repatriation tax costs do not reduce share repurchases on average.

Main role: A central conclusion in the abstract and conclusion is that repatriation tax costs do not reduce share repurchases on average, although they do lower the probability of repurchasing.
Settings.H1493: Section IV, 'Results of the Tests of H2,' Table 5 Columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 12–13.
Settings.G1494:
Treatment: REPAT, the continuous measure of potential repatriation tax costs; the setting studies how its effect differs between financially constrained and unconstrained firms, where constraint status is defined by a top-quartile negative-words ratio in the firm's 10-K.

Method: Cross-sectional robustness/substantive heterogeneity analysis for share repurchases using the Cragg (1971) hurdle model estimated separately by financial-constraint status. The sample is partitioned into financially constrained versus relatively unconstrained firm-years using the Bodnaruk, Loughran, and McDonald (2015) text-based 10-K negativity measure; results are compared across groups. The same REPAT treatment and repurchase outcomes are used, with the baseline control set and year fixed effects. This remains a nonexperimental regression design; subgroup comparison is used to support the mechanism that ability to borrow moderates the effect of repatriation tax costs.

Identification: The paper argues that if borrowing helps firms avoid repatriation taxes when funding repurchases, REPAT should matter more where external financing is difficult. Identification comes from comparing regression-estimated REPAT effects across financially constrained and unconstrained subsamples. The key assumption is that the financial-constraint partition proxies for borrowing ability rather than other omitted moderators of repurchase behavior; because the partition is not randomized, confounding in subgroup differences remains possible.

Setting: When the sample is split by a text-based measure of financial constraints, the paper interprets stronger negative REPAT effects among constrained firms as evidence that repatriation tax costs reduce repurchases when firms cannot easily borrow. In Table 6 Panel A, REPAT is significantly negatively associated with both the probability of repurchasing and the conditional repurchase amount among financially constrained firm-years, but not among unconstrained firm-years. The unconditional average partial effect of REPAT on repurchases is significantly negative for constrained firms and insignificant for unconstrained firms, and the cross-group difference is statistically significant. This mechanism analysis supports the paper's claim that borrowing ability attenuates repatriation-tax constraints on repurchases.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight cross-sectional variation in repurchase effects based on firms' opportunities to fund repurchases through external borrowing; this partition is one of the key supporting mechanism analyses.
Settings.H1494: Section V, 'Cross-Sectional Tests for Share Repurchases—External Debt Financing,' Table 6 Panel A, PDF pp. 13–16.
Settings.G1495:
Treatment: REPAT, the continuous proxy for potential repatriation tax costs, with effects compared across firm-years with versus without relatively large positive net debt issuance.

Method: Cross-sectional share-repurchase analysis using the Cragg (1971) hurdle model estimated separately by actual net debt issuance. The sample is partitioned into firm-years with relatively large positive net debt issuance versus others, where net debt issuance is long-term debt issuance minus long-term debt reduction, scaled by lagged assets. The same repurchase outcomes, controls, year fixed effects, and bootstrapped clustered standard errors are used. This is a regression-based heterogeneity design intended to assess whether debt issuance mitigates the impact of repatriation tax costs on repurchases.

Identification: The identifying idea is that if firms borrow to avoid repatriation taxes, REPAT should be less negative or more positive for repurchases among high net-debt-issuance firm-years. The strategy compares estimated REPAT effects across debt-issuance subsamples. This relies on the assumption that the issuance partition captures access to or use of borrowing for payout purposes rather than other correlated shocks to repurchase demand, so causal mechanism interpretation remains suggestive rather than design-based.

Setting: Partitioning firm-years by actual net debt issuance, the paper finds patterns interpreted as evidence that borrowing offsets repatriation-tax frictions for repurchases. The negative association between REPAT and the probability of repurchasing is concentrated among firms without relatively large net debt issues; conditional on repurchasing, REPAT is insignificantly related to repurchase magnitude among low-issuance firms but significantly positively related among high-issuance firms. The unconditional REPAT effect is negative but insignificant for low-issuance firms and positive with p=0.171 for high-issuance firms, with a significant difference across groups. The author interprets this as consistent with U.S. MNCs incurring borrowing costs to fund repurchases while avoiding repatriation taxes.

Main role: The paper highlights evidence based on actual net debt issuance as supporting the interpretation that firms facing repatriation tax costs use debt to fund repurchases.
Settings.H1495: Section V, 'Cross-Sectional Tests for Share Repurchases—External Debt Financing,' Table 6 Panel B, PDF pp. 14–16.
Settings.G1496:
Treatment: REPAT, the continuous potential repatriation tax cost measure, with estimated effects compared between firm-years with and without beginning-of-year net operating loss carryforwards (NOLs).

Method: Cross-sectional share-repurchase analysis using the Cragg (1971) hurdle model estimated separately by the presence of tax loss carryforwards (NOLs) at the beginning of the year. The partition variable equals 1 if Compustat tax loss carryforwards are positive. The model otherwise mirrors the baseline repurchase hurdle model with controls and year fixed effects. This regression-based heterogeneity analysis is used to test whether tax attributes that reduce cash tax liability moderate the effect of repatriation tax costs on repurchases.

Identification: The paper's mechanism argument is that NOLs lower the marginal U.S. cash tax cost of repatriating foreign earnings, so REPAT should be less restrictive for repurchases when NOLs are present. Identification is from comparing estimated REPAT coefficients/effects across NOL and non-NOL subsamples. The main concern is that NOL status may proxy for other firm conditions related to repurchase behavior; the evidence is therefore supportive of, but not a clean causal test of, the tax-attribute mechanism.

Setting: In the NOL partition, the paper interprets cross-group differences as evidence that valuable tax attributes help firms avoid repatriation-tax constraints when repurchasing shares. Table 6 Panel C shows that for firm-years without NOLs, REPAT is negatively associated with the unconditional level of share repurchases (two-tailed p=0.150), whereas for firm-years with NOLs, REPAT is significantly positively associated with the unconditional repurchase level. The difference across groups is statistically significant. The author concludes that NOLs facilitate repurchases by reducing the cash tax cost of repatriation.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion mention cross-sectional variation based on opportunities to minimize the incremental U.S. cash tax cost of repatriations; the NOL partition is a key mechanism result for that claim.
Settings.H1496: Section V, 'Net Operating Loss Carryforwards (NOLs),' Table 6 Panel C, PDF pp. 14–16.
Settings.G1497:
Treatment: REPAT, the continuous measure of potential repatriation tax costs imposed by the U.S. worldwide tax system, interpreted here as shifting the firm's choice of payout form toward repurchases rather than dividends.

Method: OLS regression on the subsample of firm-years with payouts to study whether repatriation tax costs affect the form of shareholder distributions. The dependent variable is RepMix, defined as repurchases minus dividends, scaled by lagged total assets; higher values indicate greater use of repurchases relative to dividends. The treatment is continuous REPAT. Controls are similar to the baseline payout regressions, with additional controls for dividend history and, in some columns, overall payout size indicators/levels; year fixed effects are included, and Huber-White standard errors clustered by firm are used. This is a standard regression-adjustment design without quasi-experimental variation.

Identification: Identification comes from conditional correlations between REPAT and a payout-mix measure after controlling for firm characteristics, payout history, payout size, and year effects. The endogeneity concern is that firms with high repatriation tax costs may differ systematically in unobserved ways that also affect dividend-versus-repurchase choice. The paper interprets the positive OLS coefficient as evidence that repatriation tax costs causally shift payouts toward repurchases because repurchases are more flexible and easier to align with tax-planning or borrowing strategies.

Setting: Using OLS on payout-paying firm-years, the paper concludes that higher repatriation tax costs cause U.S. MNCs to rely more on repurchases than dividends when distributing cash. In Table 7, the coefficient on REPAT is positive and significant in all three specifications. In Column (3), the paper states that a firm with the mean (median) positive REPAT has RepMix 0.0049 (0.0023) higher than a firm with REPAT=0, which equals 58.18 (26.71) percent of the mean RepMix of 0.0085. This supports the paper's broader claim that repatriation tax costs affect the form of shareholder payout, not just its level.

Main role: The conclusion states that repatriation tax costs affect not only the level but also the form of shareholder distributions, and Table 7 provides the main evidence for that claim.
Settings.H1497: Section V, 'Relative Use of Repurchases versus Dividends,' Table 7 Columns (1)–(3), PDF pp. 17–18.
Settings.G1498:
Treatment: REPAT, the continuous proxy for potential repatriation tax costs, examined in the 2009–2014 post-AJCA and post-financial-crisis period.

Method: Post-AJCA-period extension of the main hurdle-model analyses, estimated for years 2009–2014 after excluding 2005–2007 to avoid AJCA-funded payouts and excluding 2008 because of the financial crisis. The paper re-estimates Equations (1) and (2)—the Cragg (1971) hurdle model—for dividends and share repurchases using the post-AJCA sample. Results are described as untabulated. This remains a nonexperimental regression design using the same continuous REPAT treatment and control-based identification logic as the main tests.

Identification: As in the main analyses, identification comes from variation in REPAT across firms and years conditional on controls. The paper uses this extension to test whether the earlier association persists after the AJCA and the financial crisis. The same omitted-variable concerns remain, and no separate quasi-experimental source of post-period variation is introduced.

Setting: In untabulated post-AJCA analyses for 2009–2014, the paper reports no evidence that repatriation tax costs reduce either dividend payments or share repurchases on average. The same hurdle-model framework is applied as in the main sample, but no significant negative association between REPAT and the level of dividends or repurchases is found. This serves as a substantive temporal robustness/contrast showing that the main pre-2005 findings do not generalize to the later period.

Main role: This is a later-period extension and contrast to the main 1987–2004 findings, included to assess external validity over time rather than to establish the principal result.
Settings.H1498: Section V, 'Post-AJCA Period,' untabulated estimates of Equations (1) and (2), PDF pp. 17–19.
Settings.G1499:
Treatment: Bidder financial constraint proxy, alternately: No Credit Rating (indicator = 1 if the acquirer lacked an S&P/Moody's/Fitch/Duff & Phelps rating in the fiscal quarter before announcement), No Dividend Payout (indicator = 1 if no dividend paid in prior fiscal quarter), High SA Index (indicator = 1 if Hadlock-Pierce SA index above sample median), or High WW Index (indicator = 1 if Whited-Wu index above sample median). Each implementation is a binary treatment contrast.

Method: Linear probability models estimated on a propensity-score-matched sample of earnout and non-earnout deals. The dependent variable is an indicator for whether the acquisition includes an earnout. Specifications in Table 3 Panel A include matched-pair fixed effects, target-industry fixed effects (2-digit SIC), and year fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the matched-pair level. The treatment is alternatively measured using four bidder financial-constraint proxies: no credit rating, no dividend payout, high SA index, and high WW index. The authors interpret these coefficients as the effect of bidder financial constraints on earnout use, while acknowledging remaining non-experimental concerns and attempting to absorb transaction heterogeneity via matching and fixed effects.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in bidder financial constraints within a matched sample of similar transactions, after absorbing matched-pair, year, and target-industry fixed effects and controlling for target information-asymmetry proxies. The endogeneity concern is that unobserved deal or target features could jointly affect both financial constraints and earnout use. The paper argues that matching on transaction characteristics plus FE reduces this concern, but the design remains observational and relies on selection-on-observables/absorbed heterogeneity rather than exogenous treatment assignment.

Setting: Using linear probability models on a matched sample with matched-pair, target-industry, and year fixed effects, the authors argue that bidder financial constraints causally increase the likelihood that an acquisition uses an earnout. In Table 3 Panel A, acquirers without a credit rating are 0.175 more likely to use an earnout; non-dividend payers are 0.165 more likely; bidders above the median SA index are 0.181 more likely; and bidders above the median WW index are 0.254 more likely. These effects are interpreted as evidence that earnouts serve as an alternative financing source for constrained acquirers, a central claim of the paper.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion center on the claim that financially constrained acquirers are more likely to finance acquisitions with earnouts; Table 3 Panel A is the paper's core firm-level evidence for that claim.
Settings.H1499: Section 5.1, Table 3 Panel A, columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 9-11 (esp. p. 10-11).
Settings.G1500:
