Treatment: Exposure to the 2007-2009 financial crisis, either as Crisis indicator (=1 in the ten quarters starting in 2007Q4) or interacted with bidder financial-constraint indicators: Crisis × No Credit Rating, Crisis × No Dividend Payout, Crisis × High SA Index, Crisis × High WW Index. Each focal treatment is a binary interaction capturing differential crisis exposure for constrained bidders.

Method: Linear probability models on the matched sample estimating earnout use as a function of a post-2007 financial-crisis indicator and its interactions with bidder financial-constraint proxies. Specifications in Table 3 Panel B include matched-pair fixed effects and target-industry fixed effects; the table notes clustering at the matched-pair level. The authors interpret the crisis-period interaction coefficients as showing that the negative credit-supply shock increased earnout use especially for constrained firms.

Identification: The identifying variation is time-series exposure to the post-2007 crisis period, interacted with cross-sectional measures of bidder financial constraints, in a matched sample with fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that other concurrent shocks could affect earnout use; the authors motivate the crisis as a sudden negative credit-supply shock and interpret larger effects for constrained firms as consistent with a causal credit-supply mechanism. This is still observational FE regression rather than a formal DiD treatment-post design with untreated/treated group means explicitly reported.

Setting: The authors use crisis-period FE regressions to argue that the 2007 credit shock raised earnout use, especially for financially constrained bidders. In Table 3 Panel B, the crisis indicator alone is 0.134 in Model 1, and the interaction Crisis × No Credit Rating is 0.303 in Model 2; Crisis × High SA Index is 0.252 in Model 4, while Crisis × High WW Index is positive but insignificant at 0.154 in Model 5. They interpret these results as showing that earnouts became a more valuable substitute source of transaction liquidity after the crisis reduced external credit supply, reinforcing the paper's central financing story.

Main role: The introduction and conclusion emphasize the financial crisis as a quasi-exogenous shock to credit supply and use the crisis interactions as key evidence supporting a financing interpretation rather than pure contracting frictions.
Settings.H1500: Section 5.1, Table 3 Panel B, columns (1)-(5), PDF pp. 9-12 (esp. p. 12).
Settings.G1501:
Treatment: Market credit conditions, measured either as Percent Tightening (net percentage of loan officers reporting tighter standards in the Fed Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey; continuous) or High C&I Spread (indicator = 1 if the spread between average commercial and industrial loan rate and federal funds rate is above the sample median).

Method: Linear probability models on the matched sample relating market-wide credit conditions to the probability of earnout use. Table 4 includes matched-pair fixed effects and target-industry fixed effects, with clustered standard errors at the matched-pair level. The treatments are the net percentage of loan officers tightening credit standards and an indicator for above-median C&I spread. The authors interpret these coefficients as the effect of tighter/ costlier credit markets on earnout usage.

Identification: Identification relies on time variation in aggregate credit supply/cost conditions matched to acquisition timing, after controlling for matched-pair characteristics and target industry. The concern is that aggregate conditions may correlate with other omitted macro determinants of deal structure. The authors cite prior literature using SLOS tightening as a proxy for credit supply and interpret these variables as plausibly exogenous shifts in access to credit.

Setting: In Table 4, the authors argue that tighter credit markets cause more acquisitions to use earnouts. In Model 1, Percent Tightening has coefficient 0.205, and the text states that a one-standard-deviation increase raises the probability of an earnout by 3.8%. In Model 2, High C&I Spread has coefficient 0.147, which they interpret as acquirers being 14.7% more likely to use an earnout when the C&I spread is above the median. These market-level results are used to support the paper's claim that earnouts substitute for scarce or expensive external financing.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly mention tighter credit market conditions increasing earnout use; Table 4 provides central market-level evidence for that claim.
Settings.H1501: Section 5.1, Table 4, columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 11 and 14.
Settings.G1502:
Treatment: Alternative nonbinary bidder financing-condition measures: Log Proceeds-to-Transaction Value (total public debt and equity issuance proceeds over prior three years, scaled by transaction value, logged), Log Loans-to-Transaction Value (total Dealscan loan packages over prior three years scaled by transaction value, logged), Abnormal Leverage (continuous residual from leverage model), and Equity Overvaluation (continuous Rhodes-Kropf et al. decomposition residual).

Method: Linear probability models on the matched sample relating acquirers' pre-bid financing access and balance-sheet conditions to earnout use. Table 5 includes matched-pair fixed effects, target-industry fixed effects, and year fixed effects, with clustered standard errors at the matched-pair level. Treatments are continuous/log measures of prior public issuance activity, prior loan activity, abnormal leverage, and equity overvaluation. The authors interpret these coefficients causally as showing how greater financing access reduces, and debt overhang increases, reliance on earnouts.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in financing access and leverage within matched deals, with pair, industry, and year FE soaking up observable transaction heterogeneity and common shocks. Endogeneity remains possible because firms' capital-market activity may reflect omitted investment opportunities or deal demand. The paper nonetheless interprets these coefficients as evidence on financing constraints affecting earnout use.

Setting: The authors find that better pre-bid access to capital markets lowers earnout use, while debt overhang raises it. In Table 5, Log Proceeds-to-Transaction Value enters at -0.054 and Log Loans-to-Transaction Value at -0.031; the text interprets one-standard-deviation increases as reducing earnout probability by 5.4% and 3.1%, respectively. Abnormal Leverage is positively related to earnout use (0.055), while Equity Overvaluation is negatively related (-0.081), consistent with overvalued equity reducing demand for earnout financing. These findings support the central claim that earnouts substitute for other financing sources.

Main role: The paper's financing hypothesis also depends on direct evidence that acquirers with better external capital-market access rely less on earnouts; Table 5 is a major supporting result for that mechanism.
Settings.H1502: Section 5.1, Table 5, columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 12 and 14.
Settings.G1503:
Treatment: Bidder financial-constraint proxies after 2009: no credit rating, dividend status, high SA index, and high WW index. The focal treatment discussed explicitly is No Credit Rating (indicator = 1 if no credit rating).

Method: Unreported multivariate analysis after SFAS 141(R) adoption in 2009. The authors estimate the likelihood that the reported fair value of the earnout, scaled by maximum earnout payment, falls in the bottom quartile of the sample, as a function of bidder financial-constraint proxies and transaction/acquirer characteristics. The exact estimator is not fully reported, and the text only summarizes results; because the implementation details and fixed effects are not given, this is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification is observational: cross-sectional variation in bidder financial constraints among post-2009 earnout deals is related to whether reported fair values are unusually low. The concern is reporting discretion and omitted deal complexity. The authors argue that constrained acquirers have incentives to book lower liabilities under SFAS 141(R), but no quasi-experimental source of exogenous variation is provided.

Setting: In unreported post-2009 multivariate tests, the authors argue that financial constraints cause acquirers to book lower reported earnout liabilities. The substantive result discussed is that firms with no credit rating are 10.4% more likely to report a fair-value-to-maximum-payment ratio in the bottom quartile; positive significant results also obtain for other financial-constraint measures. The authors interpret this as evidence that earnouts provide an additional financing-related benefit by allowing constrained acquirers to preserve covenant flexibility through lower reported liabilities.

Main role: This accounting-liability result is supportive rather than central: it extends the financing story by suggesting another benefit of earnouts for constrained acquirers, but it is not one of the headline identification settings in the abstract.
Settings.H1503: Section 5.1 discussion of unreported multivariate analyses following SFAS 141(R), PDF pp. 12-13.
Settings.G1504:
Treatment: Use of an earnout agreement in the acquisition contract, measured by Earnout Indicator = 1 if the bid includes an earnout, 0 otherwise. In the bivariate probit, earnout choice is treated as endogenous and instrumented via accounting-regulation and auditor-based excluded variables, but the focal treatment is still actual earnout use.

Method: Probit and bivariate probit models of acquisition external financing. Table 6 first reports probit marginal effects for the relation between an earnout indicator and the probability the acquisition uses external debt/equity financing, then jointly models earnout choice and financing choice with a bivariate probit. Identification in the bivariate probit uses two excluded instruments for earnout use: Post-Pooling Method (after 2001 elimination of pooling accounting) and Non-Big-N Auditor × Post-SFAS 141. Standard errors are clustered by acquirer and year. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear bivariate probit rather than linear IV/2SLS, this falls under Other.

Identification: The key endogeneity concern is simultaneous determination of earnout use and financing source. The authors address this by jointly modeling the binary earnout and financing choices in a bivariate probit and excluding two variables from the financing equation: a post-2001 indicator capturing the elimination of pooling accounting, which increased the relative attractiveness of earnouts, and a Non-Big-N Auditor × Post-SFAS 141 interaction capturing higher earnout-auditing complexity after 2009 for smaller auditors. The identifying assumption is that these accounting-rule and auditor-cost shifters affect outside financing only through their effect on earnout use.

Setting: Table 6 argues that using an earnout reduces reliance on external acquisition financing. In simple probit models, the earnout indicator is associated with a 6.1%, 6.0%, and 5.2% lower probability of external financing across specifications. In the bivariate probit that treats earnout choice as endogenous and uses accounting-regulation and auditor interactions for identification, the marginal effect of earnout use on external financing is -15.7%. The authors interpret this as causal evidence of a substantial tradeoff between earnout financing and external debt/equity financing, directly supporting the paper's financing thesis.

Main role: A central purpose of the paper is to show that earnouts substitute for outside financing. Table 6 provides the paper's direct selection-corrected evidence on that tradeoff.
Settings.G1505:
Treatment: Bidder financial-constraint proxy, alternately No Credit Rating, No Dividend Payout, High SA Index, or High WW Index; each is binary. The bivariate system jointly accounts for endogenous form of payment via Cash Deal, but the focal treatment in the earnout equation is the bidder's financial constraint status.

Method: Bivariate probit models jointly estimating earnout use and the probability of 100% cash payment. Table 7 reports marginal effects for the earnout equation and the cash-deal equation. Capital gains tax rate is used as an excluded instrument in the cash-payment equation; the models are estimated on the matched sample with industry fixed effects and standard errors clustered by acquirer. Because the estimator is nonlinear bivariate probit, this is classified as Other.

Identification: The endogeneity concern is simultaneous determination of earnout inclusion and cash-versus-noncash payment. The authors jointly estimate both binary choices in a bivariate probit and use the maximum individual capital gains tax rate as an instrument excluded from the earnout equation but included in the cash-deal equation, arguing capital-gains taxation affects cash payment choice more directly than earnout inclusion. The causal interpretation still depends on exclusion of tax-rate variation from the earnout equation except through payment method.

Setting: As a robustness test, Table 7 estimates bivariate probit models to show that bidder financial constraints still increase earnout use after jointly modeling cash payment choice. The marginal effects in the earnout equation are 0.141 for No Credit Rating, 0.127 for No Dividend Payout, 0.144 for High SA Index, and 0.169 for High WW Index. The cash-deal coefficients are negative for these same financial-constraint measures, and Capital Gains strongly reduces cash payment. The authors use this as supporting evidence that their financing-constraint results are not merely driven by simultaneous choice of cash as the acquisition currency.

Main role: These models are robustness analyses showing the financial-constraint/earnout relation survives joint determination with method of payment; they support but do not replace the main FE evidence.
Settings.H1505: Section 5.2, Table 7, Models (1)-(4), PDF pp. 15 and 17.
Settings.G1506:
Treatment: Liquidity of the corporate parent selling a subsidiary target, measured alternatively as Parent Cash-to-Assets (ratio of cash and marketable securities to parent assets), Log of Parent Cash-to-Transaction Value, or Log of Parent Cash. These are continuous treatments.

Method: Linear probability models on the full sample of subsidiary acquisitions only, relating target parent liquidity to earnout use. Table 8 includes year and target-industry fixed effects, with standard errors clustered by acquirer and year. Treatments are parent cash-to-assets, log parent cash-to-transaction value, and log parent cash holdings, with controls for parent assets, transaction size, and deal characteristics. The authors interpret these coefficients as evidence that greater seller liquidity increases the supply of earnout financing.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-sectional variation in liquidity of corporate parents selling subsidiaries, controlling for parent size, transaction characteristics, year, and target-industry fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that liquid parents may differ in unobserved ways correlated with deals suited to earnouts. The paper interprets the positive coefficients as a seller-financing supply effect analogous to trade-credit supply by liquid nonfinancial intermediaries.

Setting: In Table 8, the authors argue that seller liquidity increases the supply of acquisition financing via earnouts. For subsidiary sales, Parent Cash-to-Assets has coefficient 0.069, Log Parent Cash-to-Transaction Value has 0.005, and Log Parent Cash has 0.006, all positive and statistically significant. The text states that a one-standard-deviation increase in parent liquidity raises earnout probability by 1.0% to 1.6% across these measures. This supply-side evidence complements the main demand-side results by showing that more liquid target parents are more willing to accept deferred consideration.

Main role: The paper argues not only that constrained acquirers demand earnouts, but also that liquid sellers supply them; Table 8 is the central evidence for this supply-side channel highlighted in the abstract and conclusion.
Settings.G1507:
Treatment: Primary treatment is Earnout Indicator = 1 if the bid includes an earnout, 0 otherwise. In Model 3, the focal estimand also includes the interaction Earnout Indicator × High C&I Spread, where High C&I Spread = 1 if the commercial-and-industrial loan spread is above the median. Both are binary treatment contrasts.

Method: OLS regressions of target transaction value-to-sales multiples on earnout use and credit-market conditions. Table 9 uses the full sample with available sales data, includes year and target-industry fixed effects, and clusters standard errors by acquirer and year. The dependent variable is the winsorized log transaction value-to-sales ratio, standardized by demeaning and dividing by its standard deviation. Specifications include the Earnout Indicator, High C&I Spread, and their interaction. The authors interpret these coefficients as the effect of earnout financing on target prices and use them to infer an implied 'earnout yield.'

Identification: Identification is observational and cross-sectional: earnout use is related to target pricing after controlling for deal characteristics, target industry, year, and in some specifications credit-market conditions. The endogeneity concern is that earnouts may be chosen in deals with systematically different targets or bargaining environments. The authors interpret the positive earnout coefficient, and its stronger effect when C&I spreads are high, as evidence that merger parties price the financing benefit of earnouts into target valuations.

Setting: Table 9 relates earnout use to higher target price multiples. In Model 1, Earnout Indicator is 0.101 on the standardized log value-to-sales ratio; in Model 3, the unconditional earnout coefficient is 0.039 and the interaction Earnout Indicator × High C&I Spread is 0.133, indicating especially high multiples for earnout deals when credit spreads are elevated. The authors interpret this as evidence that the financing value of earnouts is shared with target shareholders through higher prices. They further transform these coefficients, together with the average earnout share of transaction value and average earnout duration, into an implied average earnout yield of 5.6% per annum and 22.1% in high-spread periods.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight that earnout bids garner higher transaction valuation multiples and use these estimates to compute the implied cost/yield of earnout financing; this is a major paper contribution.
Settings.H1507: Section 5.4, Table 9, Models (1)-(3), and ensuing earnout-yield calculations, PDF pp. 18-19.
Settings.G1508:
Treatment: Auditor speaking up, measured as a composite self-reported scale averaging three 7-point agreement items: providing suggestions without reluctance, being an active participator, and speaking up when having something to say. This is not experimentally assigned; it is a continuous/ordinal composite measure rather than a binary indicator.

Method: Study 1 uses survey-based linear association tests relating individual auditors’ self-reported speaking up to supervisor-assigned performance measures in actual audit teams. The paper reports coefficients and t-statistics from regressions/correlations of supervisor ratings on a composite speaking-up measure constructed as the average of three 7-point Likert items. The authors explicitly interpret this survey as correlational rather than causal, noting vulnerability to reverse causality, omitted variables, and selection bias, but they still use it as initial evidence about whether speaking up affects performance evaluations. Some robustness discussion mentions controls for tenure on team and group size and clustering for team-level influences, but the key reported estimates are simple linear associations.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in auditors’ self-reported speaking up across real audit teams and its association with supervisor ratings. The intended interpretation is that speaking up leads to higher performance evaluations, but the authors explicitly acknowledge that this design does not rule out reverse causality (high performers may speak up more), correlated omitted variables, or selection bias. Thus this is a regression-adjustment/correlational setting used as suggestive evidence rather than clean causal identification.

Setting: In Study 1, the authors survey 143 staff on 41 audit teams and relate a continuous speaking-up composite to supervisor ratings. They report that greater speaking up is associated with higher overall performance evaluations (b = 0.46, t141 = 6.16, p < 0.01), higher ratings for providing perspectives of value (b = 0.37), offering new ideas (b = 0.40), organizational citizenship (b = 0.39), and a global performance composite (b = 0.43), but not cooperation (b = 0.09, p = 0.27). The paper treats this as correlational evidence consistent with the claim that leaders reward speaking up, while noting unresolved endogeneity and motivating the later experiments.

Main role: The paper presents Study 1 as initial survey evidence and explicitly says experiments provide stronger causal evidence. The main causal claims of the paper rely primarily on the experimental Studies 2–4.
Settings.H1508: Section III, “Survey of Interacting Audit Teams,” especially “Hypothesis Test,” PDF pp. 6–7.
Settings.G1509:
Treatment: Primary treatment is whether the evaluated auditor speaks up about a potential audit issue versus does not speak up; implemented as a within-participant binary contrast. Heterogeneity is induced by randomized issue content (effectiveness issue implying more work versus efficiency issue implying less work) and randomized supervisor/team focus (effectiveness versus efficiency).

Method: Study 2 is a randomized vignette experiment with a 2 x 2 mixed design for the performance-appraisal outcome. Audit Issue is randomized between participants (effectiveness issue that would increase audit effort versus efficiency issue that would decrease audit effort), Supervisor Concern is randomized between participants (effectiveness/audit quality focus versus efficiency/audit cost focus), and within participants each respondent rates an auditor who speaks up and an auditor who does not. The reported estimand is the causal effect of speaking up on later performance evaluation, plus heterogeneity by issue-focus alignment, implemented as repeated-measures ANOVA and difference scores. Performance is rated on a 0–100 scale after a distractor task intended to mimic elapsed time before appraisal.

Identification: Because issue content and supervisor concern are experimentally randomized and respondents compare speaking-up and non-speaking auditors within the same scenario, identification of the intended speaking-up effect comes from random assignment and within-subject contrasts. The authors use the non-speaking auditor as a baseline and argue that this captures relative intra-team performance evaluation. The key assumptions are successful randomization and that vignette responses reveal causal reactions supervisors would have in analogous settings; external validity rather than internal validity is the main concern.

Setting: Study 2 experimentally tests whether speaking up causally changes later performance appraisal. Across 217 experienced audit seniors/managers, auditors who speak up receive higher later performance ratings than auditors who do not speak up: M = 69.40 versus M = 53.70, with a repeated-measures effect F1,216 = 194.12 (also reported as F1,213 = 198.35 in the repeated-measures formulation). Using the relative difference score, the reward for speaking up is larger when the issue raised aligns with the supervisor’s focus: under an effectiveness focus, the relative performance advantage is 20.84 for effectiveness issues versus 11.78 for efficiency issues (t108 = 3.01, p < 0.01); under an efficiency focus, 16.62 versus 13.27 (t105 = 1.03, p = 0.31), with interaction F1,213 = 7.82, p = 0.006. This setting is central to the paper’s main claim that leaders reward speaking up in performance evaluations, especially when content aligns with team priorities.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that the experiments establish a causal relationship between speaking up and performance evaluations and that alignment with the team’s effectiveness/efficiency focus moderates this reward. Study 2 is the core causal test.
Settings.H1509: Section IV, “Study 2: Reactions ‘In the Moment’ and at Performance Appraisal,” Table 1 Panel A and B, Figure 1, PDF pp. 7–11.
Settings.G1510:
Treatment: Whether the auditor speaks up about a potential audit issue versus does not speak up, with randomized variation in whether the issue concerns effectiveness (implying increased audit effort) or efficiency (reduced audit effort), and randomized supervisor concern (effectiveness/audit quality or efficiency/audit cost).

Method: Study 2 also experimentally estimates the causal effect of speaking up on supervisors’ immediate irritation. The same 2 x 2 mixed randomized vignette design is used: randomized Audit Issue and randomized Supervisor Concern between participants, with within-participant ratings of a speaking-up auditor and a non-speaking auditor. The outcome is a two-item irritation/frustration scale on 0–100 likelihood ratings, combined and differenced between the speaking and non-speaking auditor. The analysis is repeated-measures ANOVA and 2 x 2 ANOVA on difference scores.

Identification: Immediate reaction effects are identified by random assignment of vignette conditions and within-participant comparison of reactions to otherwise similar auditors who do versus do not speak up. The design isolates whether speaking up, and the type of issue raised, causally affects immediate irritation. Internal validity rests on randomization; the main limitation is external validity of stated reactions in a hypothetical scenario.

Setting: In Study 2, the authors find that supervisors react more negatively in the moment to auditors who speak up. The mean irritation score is 44.77 for the speaking-up auditor versus 23.40 for the non-speaking auditor, with repeated-measures F1,215 = 153.11. The relative irritation effect is larger when the issue raised is an effectiveness issue that implies additional work: mean relative irritation 26.82 versus 15.89 for efficiency issues, F1,212 = 10.49, p = 0.001. By contrast, irritation does not significantly depend on whether the issue aligns with the supervisor’s effectiveness/efficiency focus (interaction F1,212 = 0.30, p = 0.583). This is a principal result supporting the paper’s claim that leaders are irritated in the moment even though they later reward speaking up.

Main role: A central contribution of the paper is the time inconsistency between ‘in the moment’ reactions and later performance appraisal. The abstract and conclusion prominently highlight immediate irritation as a main finding.
Settings.H1510: Section IV, “Study 2: Reactions ‘In the Moment’ and at Performance Appraisal,” Table 2 Panel A and B, Figure 2, PDF pp. 7–13.
Settings.G1511:
Treatment: Whether the subordinate speaks up to challenge the supervisor’s previously set audit budget versus does not speak up. This is a binary within-participant treatment contrast.

Method: Study 3 is a within-participant field-style experiment conducted over three days during firm training. Participants act as supervisors, make budget decisions for audit areas, then one subordinate later challenges the budget by speaking up while another subordinate does not. On day 3 participants themselves rate each subordinate’s performance on a 0–100 scale. This is a direct experimental contrast between a speaking-up subordinate and a silent subordinate, with the speaking-up act operationalized as challenging the supervisor’s own earlier budget decision.

Identification: Identification comes from the experimental setup in which the same supervisor rates one subordinate who challenges the supervisor’s own budget and one who does not. Since the design fixes context and compares the two subordinates within person, the causal interpretation comes from experimental control. Remaining concerns are external validity and whether the specific inventory/receivables setting generalizes broadly.

Setting: Study 3 partially replicates Study 2 by having experienced auditors act as supervisors over multiple days and then rate one subordinate who challenged their budget and one who did not. The subordinate who spoke up receives a substantially higher performance evaluation (M = 72.13) than the subordinate who did not (M = 55.45), with t30 = 6.07, p < 0.01; the same inference appears in repeated-measures ANOVA (F1,23 = 32.87, p < 0.01). The authors interpret this as causal evidence that leaders reward speaking up even when the subordinate challenges a decision the supervisor actually made.

Main role: Study 3 is presented as a partial replication/robustness check showing that the positive appraisal effect survives when participants make decisions for themselves rather than judging what a typical senior would do.
Settings.H1511: Section IV, “Study 3: Effect of Challenge on Performance Appraisals,” PDF pp. 12–14.
Settings.G1512:
Treatment: Within participants, the focal treatment is team-member behavior profile: (i) has insight and speaks up, (ii) has insight but does not speak up, (iii) does not originally speak up but verifies another silent auditor had the same insight, and (iv) no behavioral description control. Between participants, outcome information is randomized: significant material misstatement found, no significant issues found, or outcome unknown. For the main causal comparison, speaking up versus not speaking up is binary, while the broader behavior profile factor is multi-valued.

Method: Study 4 is a mixed experiment with randomized outcome information between participants and randomized/structured within-participant comparison across four team-member behavior profiles. The paper uses this design to isolate whether performance rewards stem from speaking up itself versus merely having insight, and whether those rewards depend on whether speaking up leads to discovery of a material misstatement, no misstatement, or outcome information remains unknown. The implemented estimator is repeated-measures ANOVA for the four behavior profiles and planned contrasts; the between-participant outcome manipulation is also analyzed for the speaking-up auditor in absolute levels and for relative performance differences.

Identification: Random assignment of outcome information identifies whether downstream audit outcomes causally moderate performance ratings. Within-participant manipulation of team-member behavior profiles identifies whether speaking up itself, as opposed to private insight, drives evaluations. The causal interpretation relies on successful experimental control and respondents’ revealed judgment in the vignette context; unresolved issues are external validity rather than internal validity.

Setting: Study 4 shows that supervisors reward speaking up itself, not just the underlying insight, and that this relative reward persists regardless of downstream outcome information. In the repeated-measures results, the speaking-up auditor receives a much higher performance rating (M = 81.02) than the non-speaking control auditor (M = 48.08), F1,96 = 448.32, p < 0.01; the silent auditor who merely had the same insight is rated even lower (M = 42.55), and the silent verifier is rated 45.95. The overall within-participant team-member effect is F3,288 = 253.90, p = 0.001. Across randomized outcome conditions, the average group of ratings does not differ (between-participant outcome F2,96 = 0.04, p = 0.96; interaction F6,288 = 0.83, p = 0.55). In additional between-participant analysis focusing only on the speaking-up auditor, absolute ratings are higher when a material misstatement is found (84.13) than when none is found (79.06), t97 = 1.63, p = 0.05 one-tailed, consistent with outcome bias, but the relative performance advantage of speaking up over the non-speaking control does not significantly vary across outcomes (F2,97 = 0.80, p = 0.45). This setting materially supports the paper’s conclusion that supervisors reward speaking up beyond insight and that relative evaluation benefits persist even when outcomes do not validate the concern.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that leaders reward speaking up rather than mere insight and that speaking-up benefits persist regardless of whether outcomes validate the concern, though absolute ratings show outcome effects. This is central to reconciling their findings with Brazel et al. (2016).
Settings.H1512: Section IV, “Study 4: Effect of Outcomes on Performance Appraisals,” Table 3 Panel A and B and accompanying text, PDF pp. 14–16.
Settings.G1513:
Treatment: Whether a given client engagement in a fiscal year is selected for an internal inspection by the audit firm (INSPECT=1), with a secondary contrast for noninspected engagements of a lead partner whose other engagement is inspected that year (NONINSPECT=1). The focal treatment is inspection selection/anticipated inspection at the engagement-year level.

Method: Generalized difference-in-differences / TWFE-style linear regressions exploiting the staggered timing of audit-firm internal inspections across client-years. The authors estimate OLS models of log audit effort and log audit fees on indicators for whether the engagement is selected for internal inspection (INSPECT) and whether the lead partner has another engagement inspected that year while this engagement is not inspected (NONINSPECT), controlling for engagement risk/complexity covariates. They include client, year, audit-firm, and two-digit SIC industry fixed effects, cluster standard errors by client issuer, and interpret the coefficients as causal effects of anticipated inspection on audit effort. Identification relies on within-client changes over time relative to other clients inspected in different years or never inspected, under a parallel-trends style assumption that absent inspection timing, audit effort for inspected and comparison observations would evolve similarly conditional on controls and fixed effects.

Identification: The paper argues that internal inspections are predictable and staggered across engagements. By using each client as its own control with client fixed effects and comparing inspected years to noninspected years, while also using other clients inspected in different years and never inspected, the authors seek to isolate the effect of anticipated internal inspection on audit effort. Endogeneity concern is that inspections target riskier, larger, or first-year audits; the authors address this with extensive controls and fixed effects. Identification still requires that no omitted time-varying client shocks jointly drive inspection selection and audit effort beyond included controls.

Setting: Using generalized DiD/TWFE regressions with client, year, audit-firm, and industry fixed effects, the authors estimate whether anticipated internal inspections increase audit effort. They report that inspected engagements have 0.012 higher log total hours and 0.044 higher log lead-partner hours, interpreted as about 1.2 percent and 4.4 percent increases, respectively, with weak evidence for EQR hours (0.017) and no significant change in audit fees (0.006). They conclude that auditors strategically increase effort on engagements ultimately selected for inspection, supporting the paper’s core claim that predictable internal inspections deter shirking in the inspection year.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that engagement teams increase effort in anticipation of predictable internal inspections and concentrate effort on selected engagements. This is a central mechanism in the paper.
Settings.H1513: Section V, Equation (1), Table 3 Panel B columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 10-13.
Settings.G1514:
Treatment: Extra audit effort in anticipation of inspection, proxied by Ln(ENGAGE_HOUR)_RESID (residual abnormal log engagement hours) and compared with Ln(ENGAGE_HOUR)_PRED (predicted normal log engagement hours). The focal treatment is continuous extra effort, not binary.

Method: Ordered logit model on the subsample of 2,775 internally inspected engagements, relating internal inspection ratings to predicted normal log engagement hours and residual 'abnormal' log engagement hours from a first-stage hours model that omits INSPECT and NONINSPECT. The outcome RATING is ordinal (1=unsatisfactory, 2=satisfactory with comments, 3=satisfactory), so by the task’s rules this nonlinear causal estimator is classified as Other. The authors interpret the residual component as extra hours spent in anticipation of inspection and test whether those hours causally improve inspection outcomes, including controls plus audit-firm, industry, and year fixed effects, but no client fixed effects because of limited within-client variation in the inspected sample.

Identification: The authors attempt to isolate abnormal effort attributable to anticipated inspection by decomposing log engagement hours into predicted normal hours and residual hours from a model excluding inspection indicators. They then relate these components to inspection ratings within inspected engagements. The endogeneity concern is that residual hours may still capture omitted engagement characteristics correlated with rating; the authors argue such measurement error should bias against finding results. The causal interpretation relies on the assumption that, conditional on controls and fixed effects, residual hours primarily represent effort induced by inspection anticipation rather than unobserved risk that also affects ratings.

Setting: Among internally inspected engagements, the authors use an ordered logit to test whether extra audit effort spent in anticipation of inspection improves the inspection rating. Total log engagement hours are positively associated with better ratings (0.391), and when decomposed, both predicted normal hours (0.273) and abnormal residual hours (0.913) load positively, with the residual effect statistically larger. They interpret this as evidence that auditors rationally work harder before an expected inspection and are rewarded with better internal ratings.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism result showing that added effort helps obtain better inspection ratings, but it is secondary to the paper’s main effort and financial reporting quality analyses.
Settings.H1514: Section V, 'Does the Higher Audit Effort Help in Getting a Better Rating?', Table 4 Panel B columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G1515:
Treatment: Current-year internal inspection status at the engagement-year level, either as INSPECT=1 or decomposed into SAT, SATCMT, and UNSAT depending on the internal inspection outcome category. These are binary indicators relative to noninspected engagements.

Method: Generalized DiD / TWFE-style OLS regressions replacing audit effort with contemporaneous financial reporting quality outcomes. The treatment indicators are INSPECT and, in disaggregated specifications, SAT, SATCMT, and UNSAT for the engagement-year’s internal inspection status and rating. Models include client, year, audit-firm, and industry fixed effects plus outcome-specific controls. The authors treat the coefficients as the effect of being internally inspected in the current year on current reporting quality.

Identification: Identification again uses staggered within-client timing of inspections and comparison to the same client in noninspected years, plus other clients inspected at different times or never inspected. The main endogeneity concern is nonrandom selection of riskier engagements into inspection and possible detection effects for restatements because inspection may uncover problems that otherwise would remain hidden. The authors address selection with controls and fixed effects and use ABSDA as an alternative measure not contaminated by postinspection detection. Causal interpretation requires that, after controls and fixed effects, inspection timing/outcomes are as good as exogenous with respect to contemporaneous reporting quality shocks.

Setting: Using generalized DiD/TWFE OLS models, the authors test whether current-year internal inspections improve clients’ financial reporting quality. They find no significant effect of INSPECT on restatement likelihood (0.005), but ABSDA declines by 0.005 on inspected engagements and by 0.008 on noninspected engagements in the same partner portfolio. When decomposed by outcome, unsatisfactory inspections are associated with a 0.095 higher restatement likelihood, while satisfactory and satisfactory-with-comments inspections are associated with lower ABSDA (0.006 and 0.010, respectively). The authors interpret the ABSDA results as evidence of some reporting-quality improvement in the inspection year, consistent with deterrence of auditor shirking.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion state that there is some evidence of improvement in financial reporting quality in the inspection year. This setting directly tests that central implication of anticipated inspections.
Settings.H1515: Section V, 'Financial Reporting Quality Effects', Table 5 Panels B-C columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 15-17.
Settings.G1516:
Treatment: Lagged internal inspection outcomes for the client engagement: satisfactory, satisfactory with comments, or unsatisfactory in the prior year or two years ago. These are binary indicators for prior exposure to a given inspection outcome category.

Method: Generalized DiD / TWFE-style OLS regressions of future audit effort and audit fees on lagged internal inspection outcome indicators (SATprior year, SATCMTprior year, UNSATprior year, and two-years-ago analogues) plus current INSPECT, with client, year, audit-firm, and industry fixed effects and the same audit complexity/risk controls. This design estimates how prior inspection outcomes causally affect subsequent auditor effort on the same client.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-client over time in whether the same engagement received specific inspection outcomes in prior years, controlling for current inspection and fixed effects. The concern is that poor-quality or riskier clients both receive unfavorable ratings and demand more future effort; the authors use extensive controls and fixed effects to absorb time-invariant client differences and common shocks. The interpretation requires that, conditional on included controls and FE, prior inspection outcomes capture the feedback/treatment effect of internal inspections rather than omitted persistent time-varying client risk.

Setting: The authors estimate how prior internal inspection outcomes change subsequent audit effort. They find that after a satisfactory rating, audit hours revert to baseline: SATprior year is insignificant, and F-tests show current inspection effort exceeds effort one year after a satisfactory rating. By contrast, an unsatisfactory rating increases effort the next year across engagement-team, lead-partner, and EQR hours, and for total and lead-partner hours the higher effort persists two years later. No corresponding increase in audit fees is detected. These findings support the paper’s core claim that favorable ratings induce effort reversal while unfavorable ratings prompt sustained corrective effort.

Main role: A central contribution of the paper is showing effort reverses after favorable ratings but remains elevated after unfavorable ratings. The abstract and conclusion both highlight this dynamic response.
Settings.H1516: Section VI, Equation (2), Table 6 columns (1)-(7), PDF pp. 17-19.
Settings.G1517:
Treatment: Lagged internal inspection exposure and outcomes, especially prior unsatisfactory internal inspection ratings, and their interaction with PCAOB-identified deficiencies in the audit firm’s internal inspection program (QC_DEFICIENT). Treatments are binary indicators at the engagement-year level, with heterogeneous effects by whether the program is deemed deficient.

Method: Generalized DiD / TWFE-style OLS regressions of future financial reporting quality on lagged inspection indicators and lagged inspection-outcome indicators interacted with whether the PCAOB deemed the audit firm’s internal inspection program deficient (QC_DEFICIENTprior year and QC_DEFICIENTtwo years ago). Models include client, year, audit-firm, and industry fixed effects and outcome-specific controls. The authors interpret these regressions as estimating how prior inspection outcomes, conditional on internal inspection program effectiveness, affect later reporting quality.

Identification: The strategy compares within-client changes in later reporting quality following different prior inspection outcomes, while allowing treatment effects to vary by whether the PCAOB identified deficiencies in the internal inspection program. Endogeneity concerns are that unfavorable ratings and deficient QC may proxy for underlying difficult clients or weak audit firms. The authors use client FE, audit-firm FE, year FE, industry FE, and many controls, and interpret the interaction as evidence that only effective inspection programs translate postinspection effort into better reporting quality. This requires that conditional on these controls, lagged inspection outcomes and QC deficiency status are not merely markers of other omitted shocks to future reporting quality.

Setting: The authors test whether internal inspections improve future reporting quality and whether this depends on the quality of the internal inspection program itself. Average prior inspection exposure does not significantly change future restatement risk or ABSDA. But when the prior inspection outcome is unsatisfactory and the program is not deemed deficient, future reporting quality improves: UNSATprior year and UNSATtwo years ago are negative for RESTMT, and UNSATprior year is negative for ABSDA. The positive interactions with QC_DEFICIENT offset these improvements, implying that extra postinspection effort after an unfavorable rating enhances reporting quality only when the internal inspection program is effective. This directly supports the paper’s central conclusion about the importance of effective internal inspections.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that higher effort after an unfavorable rating improves financial reporting quality only when the internal inspection program is not deficient. This is one of the paper’s headline conclusions.
Settings.H1517: Section VI, 'Financial Reporting Quality Effects', Table 7 Panels A-B and Table 8 Panels A-B columns (1)-(4), PDF pp. 19-23.
Settings.G1518:
Treatment: Internal inspection outcome category for the engagement in the current year—satisfactory, satisfactory with comments, or unsatisfactory—with heterogeneity by whether audit-firm tenure is shorter than three years. Treatment is a binary indicator for each outcome category relative to noninspected/other omitted category.

Method: Logit regressions of audit-firm switching on current internal inspection outcome indicators (SAT, SATCMT, UNSAT), with a second specification interacting these outcomes with short audit-firm tenure (SHORT_TENURE). Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear logistic regression, this qualifies as Other under the task rules. The models include controls from Equation (1) plus audit-firm, year, and industry fixed effects, and the authors interpret coefficients as the effect of inspection outcomes on client retention decisions.

Identification: The authors relate internal inspection outcomes to subsequent client switching behavior, arguing that ratings may convey credible information about audit quality to clients. Identification is observational and relies on controls and fixed effects to account for client risk and switching propensity. Remaining concerns are that inspection outcomes may correlate with unobserved client dissatisfaction or other factors driving switching. The paper presents this as suggestive evidence of informational value rather than the primary identification design.

Setting: In supplemental logit analyses, the authors test whether internal inspection outcomes affect the probability that a client switches audit firms within two years. A satisfactory rating is associated with a lower switching likelihood (coefficient -0.286 in column (1); -0.255 in column (2)), while an unsatisfactory rating increases switching only among short-tenure audit relationships, where the sum of UNSAT and UNSAT×SHORT_TENURE is positive with p=0.057. The authors interpret these results as evidence that internal inspection findings have informational value to clients, although this is a secondary analysis.

Main role: This is an additional analysis on informational value to clients, not part of the paper’s main causal chain on effort and reporting quality.
Settings.H1518: Section VII, Table 9 columns (1)-(2), PDF pp. 23-24.
Settings.G1519:
Treatment: Exposure to the post-2007 effective enforcement regime for regulated peers, operationalized by being an unlimited- or limited-liability firm in the post period. The authors' substantive causal interpretation focuses on the increase in mandatory disclosure enforcement for limited-liability firms and its spillover onto unlimited-liability firms' own financial-statement availability. The implemented contrasts are binary post-versus-pre interactions by legal-form group.

Method: In the paper's first main design (the "unlimited versus limited" setting), the authors estimate linear pre/post contrasts around Germany's 2007 disclosure-enforcement reform using indicators for legal form and post-reform period. The key implementation in Table 4 Panel A regresses an indicator for whether Creditreform has a firm's full financial statements on Limited, Unlimited, and their interactions with Post (fiscal year 2006 onward), with some specifications restricting the unlimited-liability sample to comparable OHG/KG firms and adding size controls for log sales and log employees. The authors interpret the post coefficient for limited firms as the reform's direct effect on regulated firms and the post coefficient for unlimited firms as an indirect spillover effect on unregulated firms. This is a conventional DiD-style before/after design rather than a modern heterogeneity-robust DiD estimator.

Identification: The identifying variation is the sharp increase in effective enforcement of limited-liability firms' mandatory disclosure after the 2007 reform, while unlimited-liability firms remained legally unregulated. The key endogeneity concern is that other time-varying shocks could change financial-statement availability in Creditreform at the same time. The authors argue identification from using unlimited firms before the reform as a counterfactual for unlimited firms after the reform, supplemented by similar pre-reform trends and timing evidence in Figure 2. The causal interpretation requires that absent enforcement-induced spillovers from limited firms' public disclosures, unlimited firms' financial-statement availability would not have fallen for confounding reasons around the same time, conditional on the included controls/specification.

Setting: Using Creditreform data from 2000-2011, the authors compare financial-statement availability before and after the 2007 enforcement reform. In Table 4 Panel A, column (3), availability for regulated limited-liability firms rises by 0.282 from a pre-reform level of 0.414, which they describe as a 68 percent increase, while availability for unregulated unlimited-liability firms falls by 0.136 from a pre-reform level of 0.313, which they describe as a 43 percent decrease. They interpret this conventional pre/post DiD-style evidence as showing that stronger mandatory disclosure for regulated firms crowded out unregulated firms' disclosures, likely through intermediaries such as credit bureaus reducing collection of unregulated firms' statements. This is a central result of the paper.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all emphasize that regulated firms' mandatory disclosures crowd out unregulated firms' disclosures. This time-series reform design is one of the paper's two main identification settings and provides core evidence for the central claim.
Settings.H1519: Section VII "Evidence: 'Unlimited versus Limited' Setting," Research Design and Results; Table 4 Panel A columns (1)-(3), Figure 2; PDF pp. 8-13, especially Table 4 on PDF p. 12.
Settings.G1520:
Treatment: Post-reform exposure to stronger local-industry regulatory spillovers, measured either as Share of Limited Peers × Post or # of Limited Peers × Post, where peers are defined in the same county-industry-year. These are continuous treatment intensities reflecting how many regulated firms potentially provide spillover information after enforcement rises.

Method: Still in the "unlimited versus limited" setting, the paper estimates linear regressions of financial-statement availability on spillover-strength proxies interacted with the post-reform period, while including a rich battery of fixed effects: firm fixed effects, county-year fixed effects, and industry-year fixed effects. This gives three separately absorbed FE dimensions and is explicitly motivated as addressing confounding differences across firms and local/industry trends. The treatment variation is differential post-reform exposure to a higher share or number of regulated limited-liability peers in the firm's local industry. The reported specifications also include size controls. Although the paper describes the setup as 'difference-in-differences in the spirit of Berg, Reisinger, and Streitz (2021),' the implemented identification heavily relies on HDFE absorption of firm, county-year, and industry-year heterogeneity while estimating the post interacted spillover term.

Identification: Identification comes from differential changes after the enforcement reform across firms facing different local-industry exposure to regulated peers. The idea is that once regulated peers' public statements become available after enforcement, firms in county-industries with more limited-liability peers should experience stronger spillovers and thus larger declines in own financial-statement availability. Firm FE absorb time-invariant firm differences; county-year FE absorb local shocks over time; industry-year FE absorb industry shocks over time. The causal interpretation requires that, conditional on these controls and FEs, post-reform changes correlated with peer composition are not driven by other omitted changes affecting statement availability.

Setting: In Table 4 Panel B, the authors show that after the 2007 enforcement reform, firms in local industries with more regulated peers experience larger declines in financial-statement availability in Creditreform. With firm, county-year, and industry-year fixed effects and size controls, the coefficient on Share of Limited Peers × Post is -0.105 and on # of Limited Peers × Post is -0.012, while Limited × Post remains about 0.475. The authors interpret these estimates as evidence that information spillovers from newly enforced disclosures of regulated peers crowd out the demand for and supply of firms' own financial statements, strengthening the causal mechanism behind the main result.

Main role: This setting substantively supports the paper's mechanism and heterogeneity claims about stronger crowding-out where spillovers should be larger, but it is secondary to the main average-effect results in the two headline settings.
Settings.H1520: Section VII "Evidence: 'Unlimited versus Limited' Setting," subsection "Cross-Sectional Variation in Strength of Information Spillovers"; Table 4 Panel B columns (1)-(2); PDF pp. 8, 12-13.
Settings.G1521:
Treatment: Regulatory size-class status around the small-medium thresholds, comparing effectively regulated "medium" firms with effectively unregulated "small" firms after the enforcement reform. The substantive treatment is being subject to the more stringent mandatory disclosure requirements that apply to firms classified as "medium" rather than "small" near the thresholds. Implemented analyses are reported separately for the two groups rather than a single binary coefficient in Table 5.

Method: In the paper's second main design (the "small versus medium" setting), the authors construct a predicted voluntary-regime disclosure benchmark for each firm as clicks multiplied by a disclosure/click multiple estimated from larger benchmark firms, then study abnormal disclosure defined as actual mandatory-regime characters minus predicted voluntary-regime characters. Around the small-medium thresholds, they regress abnormal disclosure levels on size controls (log total assets, log sales, log employees centered at thresholds), log age, legal-form indicators, and county-industry-year fixed effects, separately for "small" and "medium" firms, and report the average constant as the estimated abnormal disclosure at the thresholds. This is a linear regression-adjustment design using an externally constructed benchmark rather than RD or DiD.

Identification: The authors exploit the discontinuity in disclosure requirements between otherwise similarly sized "small" and "medium" limited-liability firms around the statutory thresholds, but they do not estimate a formal RD. Instead, identification comes from comparing actual disclosure to a counterfactual voluntary-regime disclosure benchmark derived from larger firms presumed unaffected by disclosure mandates or peer spillovers. Controls for the three size dimensions, age, legal form, and county-industry-year FE are intended to net out size-related disclosure incentives and local-industry conditions. The causal claim requires that the larger firms' disclosure-per-click multiple is a valid benchmark for what small and medium firms would disclose absent stronger medium-firm requirements, and that remaining size-related differences are adequately adjusted by the controls.

Setting: Using Bundesanzeiger and Bureau van Dijk data for 2008-2011, the authors estimate abnormal disclosure around the small-medium thresholds by comparing actual filing characters with characters predicted from a benchmark disclosure/click multiple. In Table 5 Panel A, medium firms around the thresholds have positive abnormal disclosure of about 8,440 characters, while small firms have negative abnormal disclosure of about -3,579 characters; Panel B reports predicted voluntary-regime disclosure of 13,002 and 10,161 characters, respectively. Panel C translates these into a direct effect of about +65 percent of voluntary-regime disclosure for medium firms and an indirect spillover effect of about -35 percent for small firms. The authors interpret this as evidence that tighter mandatory disclosure for medium firms increases their own disclosure while crowding out disclosure by nearby unregulated small firms. This is a core result of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight the finding that medium firms disclose about 65 percent more and small firms about 35 percent less than predicted in a voluntary regime. This is the paper's other headline identification setting and central evidence on firms' actual disclosure behavior.
Settings.H1521: Section VIII "Evidence: 'Small versus Medium' Setting," Research Design and Results; Figures 4-5 and Table 5 Panels A-C; PDF pp. 13-19, especially Table 5 on PDF p. 19.
Settings.G1522:
Treatment: Differential spillover exposure for "small" relative to "medium" firms, implemented through interactions of the Small indicator with (i) High R2 industry comovement, (ii) log number of medium peers in the county-industry-year, and (iii) medium peers' aggregate abnormal disclosure. Small is binary; the interacted spillover measures are binary or continuous intensity variables. The substantive treatment is stronger peer-information spillovers from regulated medium firms.

Method: In the cross-sectional heterogeneity tests for the "small versus medium" setting, the authors estimate linear regressions resembling a difference-in-differences design: abnormal disclosure (or alternative disclosure outcomes) is regressed on a Small indicator and Small interacted with spillover-strength proxies, with county-industry-year fixed effects, legal-form fixed effects, and controls for the three size dimensions and age. Because there are two absorbed FE sets rather than three, this falls under standard FE rather than HDFE. The treatment intensity is stronger expected information spillovers for small firms relative to medium firms within the same county-industry-year.

Identification: Identification uses within county-industry-year comparisons between otherwise similar small and medium firms, asking whether the small-medium disclosure gap is larger where spillovers should be stronger. County-industry-year FE absorb common local-industry shocks; legal-form FE and size/age controls absorb observable differences. The causal logic is a cross-sectional DiD-style interaction: if the medium-firm mandate creates spillovers, then the relative disclosure shortfall of small firms should be greater in high-spillover peer groups. Assumptions are that, conditional on FE and controls, the interaction between small-firm status and the spillover-strength proxies is not picking up other omitted determinants of the small-medium disclosure gap.

Setting: Table 6 shows that the disclosure gap between small and medium firms is larger where peer information spillovers should be stronger. For abnormal disclosure, the Small × High R2 coefficient is -0.394, Small × # of Medium Peers is -0.089, and Small × Medium Abnormal Disclosure is -0.532; similar patterns appear for raw disclosure in the mandatory regime, publication lag, and voluntary sales disclosure. The authors interpret these standard-FE interaction regressions as evidence that small firms reduce disclosure more when fundamentals are more correlated, when there are more regulated medium peers, and when those peers provide more abnormal disclosure, reinforcing the paper's spillover mechanism and headline conclusions.

Main role: These heterogeneity results materially support the paper's central mechanism: the disclosure gap widens exactly where information spillovers should be stronger. The abstract and introduction explicitly mention larger effects in industries with stronger comovement, more medium peers, and more peer disclosure.
Settings.H1522: Section VIII "Evidence: 'Small versus Medium' Setting," subsection "Cross-Sectional Variation in Strength of Information Spillovers"; Table 6 Panels A-B; PDF pp. 19-22.
Settings.G1523:
Treatment: Discrete change in regulatory size class: Up (Small to Medium), Down (Medium to Small), Up (Medium to Large), or Down (Large to Medium). Each is a binary indicator for switching regulatory category between years.

Method: As supplemental/robustness evidence for the necessary conditions in the "small versus medium" setting, Table 7 Panel A estimates first-difference regressions of changes in disclosure in the mandatory regime and changes in number of clicks on indicators for switching regulatory class up or down (small to medium, medium to small, medium to large, large to medium), with legal-form and county-industry-year fixed effects plus controls for changes in firm characteristics. The authors use these regressions causally to assess whether moving into a stricter disclosure class increases disclosure and whether such class changes affect clicks.

Identification: The design uses within-firm changes associated with changing regulatory class, controlling for changes in firm characteristics and county-industry-year conditions. The causal interpretation is that moving from small to medium exposes the same firm to stricter disclosure requirements, so associated changes in filing length identify the direct effect of stricter regulation, while changes in clicks test whether stakeholder breadth itself shifts. Assumptions are that conditional on controls and FE, class changes are not driven by simultaneous omitted shocks that independently alter disclosure or clicks.

Setting: In Table 7 Panel A, firms switching from small to medium increase mandatory-regime disclosure by 0.813 log points, while switching from medium to small is associated with -0.701 log points; by contrast, moving between medium and large has near-zero effects on disclosure (0.006 and 0.031). The corresponding click changes are small and insignificant (e.g., 0.013 for small-to-medium). The authors use these results as causal support that the small-medium threshold meaningfully changes disclosure requirements and filing behavior, while not materially changing clicks, which helps justify the benchmark design in the main small-versus-medium setting.

Main role: These are supplemental validity checks for necessary conditions, not headline evidence on crowding out itself.
Settings.H1523: Section VIII "Evidence: 'Small versus Medium' Setting," subsection "Supplemental Results" under "Necessary Conditions"; Table 7 Panel A columns (1)-(4); PDF pp. 23-24.
Settings.G1524:
Treatment: Regulatory class indicator equal to 1 when the firm is classified as Medium (versus Small) or Large (versus Medium), depending on the sample. Binary treatment reflects exposure to the stricter class's disclosure regime within the adjacent-class sample.

Method: Also as supplemental/robustness evidence, Table 7 Panel B estimates firm fixed-effects regressions of disclosure in the mandatory regime and number of clicks on Medium or Large indicators within samples spanning adjacent regulatory classes (small/medium or medium/large), with year fixed effects, legal-form fixed effects, and controls for levels of firm characteristics. This linear FE design is used to causally interpret the effect of being in a stricter regulatory size class on disclosure and clicks.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm variation in regulatory size class over time. Firm FE absorb time-invariant firm heterogeneity, year FE absorb common shocks, and controls account for changing firm characteristics. The causal interpretation is that when the same firm becomes medium rather than small, stricter disclosure rules increase filing length; the absence of click effects suggests stakeholder counts are not mechanically changed by class. Assumptions are that within-firm class changes are conditionally exogenous to other shocks affecting disclosure or clicks.

Setting: Table 7 Panel B shows that, within firms, being classified as medium rather than small is associated with a 0.768 log-point increase in mandatory-regime disclosure, while being large rather than medium is associated with only 0.029 log points. The analogous coefficients for clicks are small and insignificant (0.015 and 0.012). The authors interpret these FE estimates as showing that the small-medium threshold has a strong direct effect on disclosure but not on clicks, whereas the medium-large threshold does little, supporting the design assumptions behind the main crowding-out analysis.

Main role: These are supporting tests for the paper's maintained assumptions and threshold relevance rather than principal evidence on spillovers.
Settings.H1524: Section VIII "Evidence: 'Small versus Medium' Setting," subsection "Supplemental Results" under "Necessary Conditions"; Table 7 Panel B columns (1)-(4); PDF pp. 23-24.
Settings.G1525:
Treatment: Being a Micro firm (versus Small) and its interaction with spillover-strength proxies in the micro-small placebo setting. Micro is binary; the interactions vary with industry comovement or peer-information intensity.

Method: In placebo tests for the constrained micro-small threshold setting, Table 8 Panel A estimates linear regressions of log disclosure in the mandatory regime on a Micro indicator and its interactions with spillover-strength proxies (High R2, # of Small Peers, Small Abnormal Disclosures), including county-industry fixed effects, legal-form fixed effects, and controls for size and age. The authors interpret these as causal placebo tests: because both micro and small firms are effectively regulated here, there should be no spillover-driven relative disclosure reduction for micro firms.

Identification: The placebo design asks whether the same spillover-interaction patterns arise in a setting where both groups are effectively regulated and thus no unregulated firms should be crowded out. With county-industry FE and controls, the authors test whether relative disclosure of micro firms changes more in high-spillover environments. The identifying logic is falsification: null interaction effects support the main causal interpretation by showing the pattern is not mechanical.

Setting: In Table 8 Panel A, the Micro indicator is positive (around 0.405-0.450), but the interaction terms Micro × High R2 (0.011), Micro × # of Small Peers (0.007), and Micro × Small Abnormal Disclosures (0.001) are insignificant. The authors interpret this placebo evidence as showing no crowding-out pattern around the micro-small threshold, consistent with both groups being effectively regulated and therefore inconsistent with a generic tendency for smaller firms to disclose less in richer peer environments.

Main role: This is a placebo analysis used to validate the interpretation of the main setting by showing absence of effects where the theory predicts none.
Settings.H1525: Section VIII "Evidence: 'Small versus Medium' Setting," subsection "Supplemental Results" under "Placebo Tests"; Table 8 Panel A columns (1)-(3); PDF pp. 25-27.
Settings.G1526:
Treatment: Being a Medium firm (versus Large) and its interaction with spillover-strength proxies in the medium-large placebo setting. Medium is binary; interactions vary with High R2, number of large peers, or large peers' abnormal disclosure.

Method: In placebo tests for the unconstrained medium-large threshold setting, Table 8 Panel B estimates linear regressions of abnormal disclosure, disclosure in the mandatory regime, and publication lag on a Medium indicator and its interactions with spillover-strength proxies (High R2, # of Large Peers, Large Abnormal Disclosures), including county-industry-year fixed effects, legal-form fixed effects, and controls for the three size dimensions and age. The authors use these as placebo and boundary-condition tests because both medium and large firms around this threshold are treated as effectively unregulated on average.

Identification: The placebo logic is that if both medium and large firms are generally unconstrained by mandatory requirements, then relative disclosure between them should not systematically vary with spillover-strength proxies. County-industry-year FE and controls absorb confounders. Null effects for High R2 and weak patterns for peer counts support the main interpretation; a positive interaction with Large Abnormal Disclosures is interpreted by the authors as arising only where large peers are actually pushed above voluntary levels, i.e., a boundary case consistent with the spillover theory.

Setting: Table 8 Panel B shows mostly null placebo effects around the medium-large threshold: Medium × High R2 is 0.051 for abnormal disclosure, 0.003 for mandatory disclosure, and 0.002 for publication lag, all insignificant; Medium × # of Large Peers is insignificant for abnormal disclosure and publication lag, though positive for mandatory disclosure. However, Medium × Large Abnormal Disclosures is positive and significant (0.399 for abnormal disclosure; 0.040 for mandatory disclosure), which the authors interpret not as failure of the theory but as evidence that spillovers can still arise in county-industries where large firms are actually pushed above voluntary disclosure. Overall, this placebo setting is used as supporting validation rather than headline identification.

Main role: These are falsification/placebo results, not main evidence, though they also clarify that spillovers may appear when large firms are actually pushed above voluntary disclosure in particular local peer groups.
Settings.H1526: Section VIII "Evidence: 'Small versus Medium' Setting," subsection "Supplemental Results" under "Placebo Tests"; Table 8 Panel B columns (1)-(9); PDF pp. 25-27.
Settings.G1527:
Treatment: Randomly assigned CAM disclosure condition in the audit report. The focal contrasts reported are Related CAM versus Control (no mention of CAMs), Related CAM versus None (explicitly states there were no CAMs), Unrelated CAM versus Control, and Unrelated CAM versus None. Treatment is assignment to a binary contrast within each planned comparison, though the underlying experiment has four arms.

Method: Between-subjects 4×2 experiment using jury-eligible Mechanical Turk participants. The causal factor is audit-report critical audit matter (CAM) disclosure status, manipulated at four levels: control/no CAM mention, related CAM, unrelated CAM, and explicit statement of no CAMs; misstatement type (inventory overstatement versus environmental restoration liability understatement) is also manipulated. The main reported estimator for the primary outcome is a difference in negligent-verdict rates across randomized conditions, analyzed with a general linear model with logit link and planned pairwise contrasts. This setting covers the direct intention-to-treat effect of CAM disclosure condition on the binary negligence verdict outcome.

Identification: Identification comes from random assignment of participants to CAM disclosure conditions and misstatement types, so average differences in negligence verdicts across arms are interpreted as causal effects of disclosure content on juror judgments. The main assumptions are successful randomization, participant comprehension of the manipulation, and that the experimental materials isolate the intended ex ante risk-disclosure differences. The paper reports high manipulation-check pass rates and analyzes planned contrasts by treatment arm; remaining concerns are external validity to actual juries and legal settings rather than internal identification.

Setting: Using a randomized experiment, the authors estimate how assigning jurors to different audit-report CAM disclosures changes the probability of a negligent verdict against auditors after an undetected misstatement. In Table 1, overall negligent-verdict rates are 42.1% in Control, 32.1% with a Related CAM, 36.4% with an Unrelated CAM, and 50.0% when the report states there were no CAMs. The Related-versus-Control contrast is -10.0 percentage points overall (chi-square 2.87, one-tailed p=0.045), driven by the inventory case (-16.8 points; 39.7% to 23.0%; p=0.021) and not the restoration-liability case (-4.9 points; p=0.281). Related CAMs also lower negligent verdicts versus explicitly stating no CAMs by 17.9 points overall (50.0% to 32.1%; p=0.002). Unrelated CAMs do not differ significantly from Control overall (-5.7 points; p=0.347) but do reduce liability relative to None by 13.6 points (50.0% to 36.4%; p=0.027). This is the paper's main causal setting because it directly tests the central claim that CAM disclosure can reduce, rather than increase, auditor liability judgments.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, results, and conclusion center on whether CAM disclosures change jurors' negligence judgments. The negligent-verdict outcome is explicitly described as the primary measure of auditor liability and underpins the paper's headline conclusions.
Settings.H1527: Section IV, 'Testing of Hypotheses and Research Questions'; Table 1 Panels A-C, PDF pp. 8-9.
Settings.G1528:
Treatment: Random assignment to a Related CAM versus Control (no CAM mention) condition in the experiment; in the controlled variant the same treatment contrast is estimated while including misstatement type as an additional exogenous variable.

Method: Structural path analysis / structural equation modeling on experimental data comparing Related CAM versus Control, with observed variables for Foreseeability, Affect, and binary negligence Verdict. The authors estimate directed paths from CAM assignment to foreseeability, foreseeability to affect, and affect to verdict, and also a variant controlling for misstatement type. This is not a standard linear RCT contrast on the final outcome alone; it is a mediation/path model used to test the proposed causal mechanism. Because the implemented estimator is SEM/path analysis rather than a simple linear mean difference, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The exogenous source of variation is randomized assignment to Related CAM versus Control. The path model assumes that the imposed causal ordering runs from CAM disclosure to foreseeability perceptions to affect to negligent verdicts, and that the SEM is correctly specified. Because the mediator-outcome links are not separately randomized, these mechanism estimates rely on theory and model structure rather than random assignment alone; the paper addresses temporal-order concerns with model-fit checks, reverse-order path models, and subsample analyses.

Setting: To test its mechanism, the paper estimates a path model on the randomized Related-versus-Control comparison. The authors report that assignment to a Related CAM significantly increases foreseeability (standardized coefficient 0.256, p<0.001), higher foreseeability is associated with less negative affect toward the auditors (coefficient 0.195, p<0.001), and more positive affect lowers the probability of a negligent verdict (coefficient -0.484, p<0.001). The model fit is reported as excellent (chi-square 0.584, df=2, p=0.747, CFI>0.999, RMSEA<0.001), and inferences are unchanged when controlling for misstatement type (chi-square 0.933, df=3, p=0.817). This setting supports the paper's main claim that CAM disclosures can reduce liability through increased perceived foreseeability to the plaintiff and reduced negative affect.

Main role: The paper's central contribution includes theory about the mechanism by which related CAMs affect liability judgments. The abstract and conclusion expressly highlight the path analysis as evidence supporting the posited mechanism, so it materially supports a central conclusion.
Settings.H1528: Section IV, 'Supplemental Analyses—Path Analysis—Related CAMs'; Figure 2 and Figure 3 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 9-11.
Settings.G1529:
Treatment: Random assignment to a Related CAM versus Control condition, with heterogeneity examined across the separately randomized misstatement type (Inventory versus Restoration Liability). The focal treatment in the path model remains Related CAM assignment relative to Control.

Method: Multi-group structural path analysis / SEM on the experimental Related-versus-Control comparison, testing whether path coefficients are invariant across the two randomized misstatement types (Inventory versus Restoration Liability). The authors compare a fully constrained model to unconstrained and partially unconstrained models, focusing on whether the CAM-to-Foreseeability path differs by misstatement type.
