Using the sample standard deviation of POLCON (8.271), the paper states that a one-standard-deviation increase in political connections reduces this debt-demand effect by about 47 percent. The corresponding political-connection interactions for managerial ownership and litigation demand are not statistically supportive. This setting is central to the paper’s main claim that political connections substitute for conservatism in debt contracting.

Main role: This is the paper’s core test of H1 and directly supports the headline conclusion in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that political connections moderate the debt contracting demand for conditional conservatism.
Settings.H1561: Section IV, “Political Connections and Conditional Conservatism,” Table 4, plus economic-magnitude discussion on PDF pp. 12–13.
Settings.G1562:
Treatment: Political connections measured by continuous firm-year POLCON as the ownership-contribution association from annual Tahoun-style Tobit regressions. In this setting the focal treatment is the interaction of POLCON with the litigation-demand indicator LIT, and also with PCOST and TAXCOST. LIT and PCOST are binary indicators; TAXCOST is continuous. The main causal emphasis is on whether greater political connections attenuate the effect of litigation demand on unconditional conservatism.

Method: Main unconditional-conservatism specification estimated by pooled OLS on firm-year data for 2005–2011 with firm fixed effects, year fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. The dependent variable is CONACC, Givoly and Hayn’s persistent negative-accruals measure of unconditional conservatism. Regressors are litigation risk, political-cost demand, tax-cost demand, political connections, their interactions, and controls for firm size, market-to-book, and operating cash flow. Identification comes from within-firm changes over time after absorbing firm and year fixed effects; the paper interprets interaction terms as political connections moderating how litigation, political costs, and tax demand affect unconditional conservatism, subject to remaining endogeneity concerns.

Identification: The identification argument is that, conditional on firm FE, year FE, and controls, within-firm variation in political connections changes the extent to which firms in high-litigation-risk industries supply unconditional conservatism. The key confounds are time-varying omitted determinants of conservative reporting, selection into political connections, and reverse causality. Firm FE are meant to absorb persistent firm-specific conservatism; year FE absorb common shocks; controls for size, market-to-book, and CFO capture important determinants of accrual conservatism. The causal interpretation depends on no omitted time-varying shocks jointly affecting POLCON interactions and CONACC. The paper explicitly cautions that unobservable differences could still explain the results.

Setting: Using firm- and year-fixed-effects OLS with CONACC as the dependent variable, the paper examines whether political connections weaken the relation between stakeholder demand proxies and unconditional conservatism. In Table 5, litigation risk (LIT) has a coefficient of 0.010 (p=0.00), implying higher unconditional conservatism among high-litigation firms when POLCON=0. The interaction LIT × POLCON is negative and statistically significant (reported as -0.000 with p=0.04; the text uses -0.0002 for magnitude), which the author interprets as political connections moderating the litigation demand for unconditional conservatism. A one-standard-deviation increase in POLCON is said to reduce this litigation-demand effect by roughly 17 percent relative to the baseline LIT coefficient. Interactions with political-cost and tax-cost demand are insignificant. This setting is a main pillar of the paper’s conclusion that political connections substitute for conservatism in shielding firms from litigation exposure.

Main role: This is the paper’s core test of H2 and underpins the abstract and conclusion that political connections moderate the litigation demand for unconditional conservatism.
Settings.H1562: Section IV, “Political Connections and Unconditional Conservatism,” Table 5, plus economic-magnitude discussion on PDF p. 14.
Settings.G1563:
Treatment: Political connections as a binary treatment in the matching stage: indicator equal to 1 if the firm-year has a positive ownership-contribution association (POLCON > 0), and 0 otherwise. In the matched-sample regression, the interaction term still uses POLCON, but treatment assignment for design purposes is the binary politically connected versus non-connected distinction.

Method: Propensity-score-matched robustness design. First, the paper estimates the probability that a firm-year is politically connected (indicator for positive ownership-contribution association) using observable determinants of conservatism and politicians’ investment decisions, with industry and year fixed effects. Each treated observation is matched to up to four controls using nearest odds with a 0.001 caliper. On the matched sample, the author re-estimates a reduced version of the conditional-conservatism model with firm and year fixed effects, omitting balanced covariates following Erkens et al. (2014). The substantive estimand is whether political connections moderate the leverage-driven demand for conditional conservatism among observably similar firms.

Identification: The matching strategy aims to remove selection on observables into political connections by comparing treated and control firm-years with similar estimated propensity scores based on determinants of conservatism and politicians’ investments. The subsequent fixed-effects regression on the matched sample uses only remaining within-sample variation. The key assumption is conditional independence given observed covariates used in the score and adequate overlap/common support. The paper uses covariate balance checks and reports similar inferences, but does not claim this fully resolves unobservable confounding.

Setting: As a robustness test, the paper matches politically connected firm-years to non-connected firm-years with similar propensity scores and then re-estimates the conditional-conservatism model. In Table 6 Panel C, RET × NEG × LEV is 0.339 (p=0.00), and the four-way interaction RET × NEG × LEV × POLCON is -0.018 (p=0.00), supporting the conclusion that political connections weaken the leverage-related demand for conditional conservatism even after balancing observables. The author interprets this as evidence that observable differences between politically connected and unconnected firms are unlikely to explain the main result.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis intended to mitigate bias from observable confounders, not the paper’s primary identification strategy.
Settings.H1563: Section V, “Additional Analyses—Propensity Score Matching,” Table 6 Panel C, PDF pp. 14–16.
Settings.G1564:
Treatment: Binary political connection treatment in the matching design: indicator for a positive ownership-contribution association (politically connected) versus zero/nonpositive association (not politically connected). The substantive moderation result concerns whether this connection status attenuates the litigation-demand effect through LIT × POLCON in the matched sample.

Method: Propensity-score-matched robustness design for unconditional conservatism. Politically connected firm-years (positive ownership-contribution association) are matched to up to four non-connected controls on estimated propensity scores using observables, industry FE, and year FE in the score model. The author then estimates a matched-sample regression with firm and year fixed effects, focusing on litigation demand and its interaction with political connections, omitting balanced covariates in the outcome regression.

Identification: Identification comes from matching on observables to balance treated and untreated firm-years, then estimating differences in the relationship between litigation risk and CONACC within the matched sample. The design assumes no unobserved confounders after conditioning on the propensity-score covariates and that matched treated and control units are comparable. Firm and year FE are added to reduce remaining bias, but the paper recognizes that unobservables may still matter.

Setting: In the matched-sample robustness analysis for unconditional conservatism, Table 6 Panel D reports a positive coefficient on LIT of 0.011 (p=0.00) and a negative coefficient on LIT × POLCON of approximately -0.000 (p=0.05). The author interprets this as confirming that political connections moderate the litigation demand for unconditional conservatism after conditioning on a rich set of observable firm characteristics. This strengthens the paper’s central claim by showing that observable selection into political connections is unlikely to be the full explanation.

Main role: This is a supporting robustness analysis to address observable selection, not a primary headline specification.
Settings.H1564: Section V, “Additional Analyses—Propensity Score Matching,” Table 6 Panel D, PDF pp. 15–16.
Settings.G1565:
Treatment: Political connections measured continuously by POLCON, interacting with leverage, managerial ownership, and litigation risk. The central treatment contrast is the continuous moderation term LEV × POLCON, interpreted as political connections weakening the debt-contracting demand for conditional conservatism measured by CSCORE.

Method: Alternative-measure robustness analysis using pooled OLS with firm fixed effects and year fixed effects on the Khan and Watts (2009) firm-year C-Score (CSCORE) as the dependent variable. The regression relates CSCORE to leverage, managerial ownership, litigation risk, political connections, their interactions, and controls for size, market-to-book, and cash flow. This is a fixed-effects linear regression on an alternative conditional-conservatism proxy rather than the Basu asymmetric-timeliness regression.

Identification: The paper uses within-firm over-time variation in POLCON and demand proxies after controlling for firm FE, year FE, and standard covariates. The identifying assumption is that time-varying shocks to CSCORE are not jointly driven by omitted factors correlated with POLCON interactions once these controls are included. This robustness is aimed at measurement error in the dependent variable rather than at introducing a stronger quasi-experimental design.

Setting: Using the Khan and Watts C-Score as an alternative measure of conditional conservatism, the paper again finds that political connections weaken the leverage-related demand for conservatism. In Table 7, LEV has a coefficient of 0.095 (p=0.00), LIT has 0.282 (p=0.00), and the interaction LEV × POLCON is -0.001 (p=0.07), while interactions with managerial ownership and litigation are insignificant. The author interprets this as reinforcing the main result that political connections moderate the debt contracting demand for conditional conservatism and that the result is not driven by the specific Basu measure.

Main role: This is an additional robustness analysis using an alternative conservatism measure to show the main conclusion does not depend on Basu’s specification.
Settings.H1565: Section V, “Additional Analyses—Alternative Measure of Conditional Conservatism,” Table 7, PDF pp. 17–18.
Settings.G1566:
Treatment: Firm i's operating cash flows (CFO), scaled by average total assets. In panel A of Table 2 this is contemporaneous CFO in levels; in panel B it is the annual change in CFO. The paper interprets a $1 increase in operating cash flows as causing an offsetting change in accruals via accrual accounting's timing role. Treatment is continuous, not binary.

Method: The authors run annual cross-sectional OLS regressions of total accruals on contemporaneous operating cash flows, following Dechow (1994), separately for each year from 1964 to 2014. They interpret the coefficient on cash flows and the adjusted R-squared as capturing the timing/smoothing role of accrual accounting. They estimate both a levels specification and a changes specification, winsorizing variables annually at the 1st and 99th percentiles. There are no fixed effects, instruments, or quasi-experimental features; the design is a descriptive/associational regression used with causal language about how changes in cash flows affect accruals through the timing role of accounting.

Identification: The paper's identifying argument is conceptual rather than quasi-experimental: if accrual accounting smooths temporary timing fluctuations in cash flows, then higher contemporaneous cash flows should mechanically/causally map into lower accruals. Annual cross-sectional variation in cash flows is used to estimate that mapping, and changes over calendar time in the coefficient and adjusted R-squared are interpreted as changes in the timing role of accruals. Endogeneity is not solved in a causal-inference sense; instead the authors rely on accounting theory that accruals offset timing-related cash-flow shocks. The main assumptions are that the annual regression captures the underlying accrual-cash-flow mapping and that temporal movement in coefficients/R-squared reflects changes in the prominence of that role rather than only sample composition or measurement error.

Setting: Using annual cross-sectional OLS regressions of total accruals on contemporaneous operating cash flows, the authors argue that accrual accounting's timing role causes accruals to offset cash-flow fluctuations. In the levels model, the coefficient on CFO rises from about -0.68 to -0.81 in the 1960s to around -0.02 to 0.01 by 2006-2014, while adjusted R-squared falls from roughly 0.66-0.74 to about 0.00-0.01 (Table 2, panel A). In the changes model, the coefficient rises from about -0.93/-0.94 in the 1960s to about -0.42 in 2014, and adjusted R-squared falls from roughly 0.89-0.92 to 0.09-0.19 in the 2010s (Table 2, panel B). Time-trend regressions in panels C and D show statistically significant attenuation over time. These regressions are central evidence for the paper's main conclusion that the negative accrual-cash-flow relation has largely disappeared.

Main role: This is one of the core empirical designs supporting the paper's central claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that the timing/smoothing relation between accruals and cash flows has dramatically weakened over time.
Settings.H1566: Section 4.1.1, equation (1a) and (1b), Table 2 panels A-D, Figure 1; PDF pp. 12-14.
Settings.G1567:
Treatment: Firm i's operating cash flows from operations, scaled by average total assets: lagged CFO_{t-1}, contemporaneous CFO_t, and future CFO_{t+1}. The focal causal interpretation emphasized by the paper is the effect of contemporaneous CFO_t on current accruals, with lagged and future CFO included to capture mapping into adjacent periods. Treatment is continuous.

Method: The authors estimate annual cross-sectional OLS regressions of total accruals on lagged, contemporaneous, and future operating cash flows, following Dechow and Dichev (2002), separately by year from 1964 to 2013. They interpret the cash-flow coefficients and adjusted R-squared as measuring how accruals map into adjacent cash flows and thus the timing role of accrual accounting. Variables are winsorized annually at the 1st and 99th percentiles. This is a linear regression-adjustment design without experimental or quasi-experimental identification.

Identification: Identification again comes from the accounting-theory mapping between accruals and operating cash flows: current accruals should offset contemporaneous cash-flow timing shocks and map positively into adjacent-period cash flows. The authors use annual cross-sectional variation in lagged, current, and future CFO and interpret temporal declines in the model fit and attenuation of the contemporaneous CFO coefficient as evidence that the timing role of accruals has weakened. The strategy does not resolve endogeneity in a quasi-experimental sense; it relies on the maintained theoretical relation between accruals and cash-flow timing and on the interpretation of calendar-time changes in the estimated mapping.

Setting: In annual OLS regressions of total accruals on past, current, and future cash flows, the authors interpret the cash-flow coefficients as the causal mapping implied by accrual accounting's timing role. The adjusted R-squared of the Dechow-Dichev model falls from about 0.73-0.77 in the mid/late 1960s to 0.06-0.10 in the 2000s-2010s (Table 3, panel A). The contemporaneous CFO coefficient increases from roughly -0.79 to -0.87 in the 1960s to around -0.33 to -0.47 in the most recent years, while coefficients on past and future CFO rise only modestly. Time-trend regressions in panel B show a significant positive trend in the contemporaneous coefficient and a significant negative trend in adjusted R-squared. This is a central empirical setting supporting the paper's conclusion that accruals' timing role has sharply declined.

Main role: This is the paper's second main model, highlighted in the abstract, results, and conclusion as corroborating the decline in the accrual-cash-flow mapping over time.
Settings.H1567: Section 4.1.2, equation (2), Table 3 panels A-B, Figure 2; PDF pp. 14-18.
Settings.G1568:
Treatment: Annual proxies for economic-based and timing-related cash-flow shocks: Std(CFO), the annual cross-sectional standard deviation of cash flows from operations, and Auto CFO, the annual average lag-one autocorrelation in changes in cash flows. Both are continuous annual measures.

Method: The authors run annual time-series regressions across years where the dependent variable is the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow and Dichev (2002) accrual model, and regress it on a linear time trend plus proxies for cash-flow volatility and timing-related cash-flow shocks: the annual cross-sectional standard deviation of CFO and the average lag-one autocorrelation in changes in CFO. Newey-West standard errors with three lags are used. This is a linear time-series regression interpreting whether changes in these proxies explain the decline in the accrual-cash-flow relation.

Identification: The authors exploit time-series variation across years in annual cash-flow volatility and autocorrelation measures and ask whether these variables account for the decline in the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow-Dichev model. The interpretation is that more economic-based volatility or less negative cash-flow autocorrelation changes the need for accrual smoothing. The design is correlational and vulnerable to omitted time-varying factors and multicollinearity; the authors explicitly frame this as exploring possible explanations rather than establishing clean causal identification.

Setting: To assess whether changing cash-flow shocks explain the weakening accrual-cash-flow relation, the authors regress the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow-Dichev model on a time trend, annual cash-flow volatility, and annual cash-flow autocorrelation. In Table 4 column 2, the coefficient on Std(CFO) is -0.080 (t=-0.12) and on Auto CFO is -0.412 (t=-1.68), while the time-trend coefficient remains negative at -0.014 (t=-7.78), only slightly smaller than the baseline -0.016. The authors interpret this as evidence that growth in economic-based cash-flow shocks did not significantly explain the decline, and that reduced timing-related shocks may have played only a limited role. This is a mechanism analysis rather than the paper's main causal setting.

Main role: This is a secondary explanatory analysis investigating mechanisms behind the main decline, not the primary demonstration of the central phenomenon.
Settings.H1568: Section 4.2.1, equation (3a), Table 4 column 2; PDF pp. 19-21.
Settings.G1569:
Treatment: Annual proxies for non-timing-related accrual recognition: Std(OI-PTI), the annual cross-sectional standard deviation of operating income after depreciation minus pretax income, and PctLoss, the annual proportion of firms with negative earnings before extraordinary items. Both are continuous annual measures.

Method: The authors estimate annual time-series regressions of the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow and Dichev (2002) model on a linear time trend plus proxies for non-timing-related accruals: Std(OI-PTI), the annual cross-sectional standard deviation of the difference between operating income after depreciation and pretax income, and PctLoss, the annual frequency of firms reporting negative earnings before extraordinary items. Newey-West standard errors with three lags are used. This is an OLS explanatory regression at the year level.

Identification: The authors use annual time-series variation in proxies for one-time/nonoperating items and loss frequency to explain variation in the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow-Dichev model. The identifying argument is that non-timing-related accruals are not linked to contemporaneous or adjacent operating cash flows, so an increase in such accruals should mechanically reduce the fitted association between accruals and cash flows. The setting is observational and subject to multicollinearity and omitted aggregate trends; the authors acknowledge these issues and interpret results using economic theory plus stand-alone and full-model sign consistency.

Setting: The authors test whether growth in non-timing-related accruals caused the decline in the accrual-cash-flow relation by regressing the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow-Dichev model on annual proxies for one-time/nonoperating items and loss prevalence. In Table 4 column 3, Std(OI-PTI) has coefficient -0.011 (t=-0.01) and PctLoss has coefficient -1.098 (t=-3.77), while the time-trend coefficient shrinks from -0.016 in the baseline to -0.006 (t=-3.54). In the full model (column 6), Std(OI-PTI) is -2.264 (t=-2.05) and PctLoss is -0.657 (t=-2.18), with Time still -0.006. The authors conclude that one-time and nonoperating items and the frequency of loss firm-years explain most of the decline in the accrual-cash-flow correlation, about 63%, making this a central explanatory result.

Main role: Explaining the decline is part of the paper's central contribution, and the abstract and conclusion specifically highlight one-time/nonoperating items and loss frequency as explaining the majority of the decline.
Settings.H1569: Section 4.2.2 and 4.2.4, equation (3b), Table 4 columns 3 and 6; PDF pp. 21-26, especially pp. 22-25.
Settings.G1570:
Treatment: Annual adjusted R-squared from the Dichev and Tang (2008) model, used as a continuous proxy for the degree of matching between revenues and expenses.

Method: The authors regress the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow and Dichev (2002) model on a time trend and the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dichev and Tang (2008) sales-expense matching model. This year-level OLS with Newey-West standard errors is used to test whether declining revenue-expense matching explains the weakening accrual-cash-flow relation.

Identification: The strategy uses annual aggregate variation in a proxy for matching quality to explain annual variation in the accrual-cash-flow mapping. The maintained assumption is that if poor matching were driving the attenuation, then years with lower Dichev-Tang adjusted R-squared would also have lower Dechow-Dichev adjusted R-squared. This is observational time-series evidence with substantial scope for confounding trends, so the interpretation is exploratory rather than tightly identified.

Setting: To test whether deteriorating revenue-expense matching explains the weakening relation between accruals and cash flows, the authors regress the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow-Dichev model on a time trend and the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dichev-Tang matching model. In Table 4 column 4, the coefficient on Adj. R2(Dichev Tang) is -0.226 (t=-0.23), statistically insignificant, while the time coefficient remains -0.017 (t=-9.39). The authors interpret this as evidence that declining matching between revenues and expenses played little role in the observed attenuation of the accrual-cash-flow relation.

Main role: This is a secondary mechanism test used to rule out one proposed explanation; the paper concludes matching explains little of the main decline.
Settings.H1570: Section 4.2.3, equation (3c), Table 4 column 4; PDF pp. 23-24.
Settings.G1571:
Treatment: Annual SG&A intensity, measured as selling, general, and administrative expenses scaled by total expenses, used as a continuous proxy for intangible intensity.

Method: The authors regress the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow and Dichev (2002) model on a time trend and annual SG&A intensity, defined as SG&A expense scaled by total expenses, following Srivastava (2014) as a proxy for intangible intensity. Newey-West standard errors with three lags are used. This is an annual time-series OLS mechanism test.

Identification: The authors use aggregate time-series variation in SG&A intensity to test whether rising intangible intensity reduced the need or ability for accruals to offset cash flows. The logic is that more intangible investment is expensed immediately and therefore generates less contemporaneous accrual smoothing. Identification is correlational and potentially confounded by concurrent trends; the paper treats it as exploratory explanatory evidence.

Setting: The authors examine whether growth in intangible-intensive firms contributed to the weakening accrual-cash-flow relation by regressing the annual adjusted R-squared from the Dechow-Dichev model on a time trend and annual SG&A intensity. In Table 4 column 5, SG&A intensity has coefficient -1.109 (t=-1.32), statistically insignificant, while Time is -0.012 (t=-3.54), compared with -0.016 in the baseline. The authors infer that, when considered alone, intangible intensity is related to about 25% of the decline, but overall it plays only a limited role once other factors are considered.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism analysis; the paper emphasizes that intangible intensity explains only a limited portion of the decline.
Settings.H1571: Section 4.2.4, equation (3d), Table 4 column 5; PDF pp. 24-25.
Settings.G1572:
Treatment: Contemporaneous operating cash flows (CFO), scaled by average total assets, plus an interaction D×CFO where D equals 1 if annual CFO is negative and 0 otherwise. The focal treatment remains continuous CFO, with heterogeneity by negative-CFO states.

Method: The authors estimate annual cross-sectional OLS regressions of total accruals on contemporaneous cash flows, an indicator for negative cash flows, and their interaction, following Ball and Shivakumar (2006), to incorporate asymmetrically timely gain/loss recognition. They plot the annual adjusted R-squared and coefficients through time and compare them with the linear Dechow (1994) model. This is a linear regression with an interaction term, run separately by year.

Identification: The authors augment the accrual-cash-flow regression with a negative-CFO indicator and interaction to allow the mapping from cash flows to accruals to differ when firms have negative cash flows, consistent with asymmetrically timely recognition of gains and losses. The identifying argument is theoretical: if changing timely loss recognition were offsetting the timing role in the linear model, then controlling for this nonlinearity should stabilize the fit over time. This remains a correlational annual cross-sectional regression without exogenous variation.

Setting: Using the Ball-Shivakumar nonlinear extension, the authors test whether increasing asymmetrically timely loss recognition explains the observed attenuation in the accrual-cash-flow relation. They estimate annual regressions of accruals on CFO, a negative-CFO indicator, and the interaction. Figure 3 panel A shows that the adjusted R-squared from this model still declines from about 70% in the 1960s to under 10% in recent years, very similar to the unadjusted Dechow model. Panel B shows the interaction coefficient becomes positive and increases from the mid-1970s to 2000, while the CFO coefficient rises from about -0.67 in 1980 to about -0.35 in recent years. The authors conclude that the decline in the timing role is not mainly driven by an offsetting increase in timely gain/loss recognition.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness/mechanism test used to rule out the alternative explanation that stronger timely loss recognition explains the attenuation in the linear accrual-cash-flow relation.
Settings.G1573:
Treatment: Firm-specific operating cash flows from operations, scaled by average total assets: contemporaneous CFO in equation (1a), and lagged/current/future CFO in equation (2). Continuous treatment variables.

Method: As a robustness analysis, the authors split the sample into four subperiods (1964-1975, 1976-1987, 1988-1999, 2000-2014) and estimate the Dechow (1994) levels model and the Dechow and Dichev (2002) model by firm using firm-specific time-series OLS regressions, requiring minimum numbers of observations per firm. They then summarize the distribution of firm-level coefficients and adjusted R-squared values. This is still linear OLS, but now estimated within firm over time rather than cross-sectionally by year.

Identification: The strategy is the same accounting-theory mapping as in the main models, but estimated within firm over time over subperiods. By using firm-specific time-series regressions, the authors test whether the decline in the accrual-cash-flow relation is driven purely by cross-sectional composition changes rather than within-firm changes. This is not a fixed-effects panel estimator; it is a set of separate time-series OLS regressions within firms.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors estimate the accrual-cash-flow relation separately within firms over four subperiods. In Table 5 panel A, the median coefficient on CFO in the Dechow levels model rises from -0.91 in 1964-1975 to -0.82 in 1976-1987, -0.65 in 1988-1999, and -0.43 in 2000-2014; the median adjusted R-squared falls from 0.84 to 0.71, 0.37, and 0.16. In panel B, the Dechow-Dichev model shows a similar though somewhat weaker decline. The authors interpret this as corroborating evidence that the weakening relation is not an artifact of the annual cross-sectional specification.

Main role: This is a robustness check confirming the main pattern under a different estimation window; it supports but does not anchor the central claim.
Settings.H1573: Section 5.1, Table 5 panels A-B; PDF pp. 28-29.
Settings.G1574:
Treatment: Firm i's contemporaneous operating cash flows (CFO), scaled by average total assets, within each listing cohort and year. Continuous treatment.

Method: The authors estimate annual cohort-specific OLS regressions of the Dechow (1994) levels model separately for five listing cohorts (pre-1970, and firms first listed in the 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, and 2000s) and track the adjusted R-squared over time. This is a robustness/sample-composition analysis using annual cross-sectional OLS within cohorts.

Identification: The authors exploit within-cohort annual variation in the accrual-cash-flow relation to test whether the documented attenuation reflects only the entry of newer firms. The argument is that if cohort-specific adjusted R-squared also declines within older cohorts, then sample composition cannot fully explain the main result. This is an observational robustness design, not a quasi-experiment.

Setting: To assess whether changing sample composition drives the decline in the accrual-cash-flow relation, the authors estimate annual Dechow regressions separately for listing cohorts. Table 6 and Figure 4 show that adjusted R-squared declines markedly within each cohort, not just in the pooled sample. For example, the pre-1970 cohort's adjusted R-squared drops from about 0.66-0.74 in the 1960s to around 0.05-0.14 in the 2000s-2010s. The authors conclude that the attenuation is prevalent among both older and newer cohorts, so the main result is not driven solely by compositional change.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis addressing whether sample composition drives the main finding. It materially supports credibility but is not itself the headline result.
Settings.G1575:
Treatment: Time, measured as the number of years since 1964, in regressions of differences in residual-accrual properties across estimation methods. Continuous annual trend variable.

Method: The authors estimate pooled, annual, and firm-specific OLS versions of the Dechow (1994) and Dechow and Dichev (2002) models, compute residual accruals under each approach, and then run time-trend regressions of differences in the annual mean and annual standard deviation of residual accruals between pooled or firm-specific models and annual regressions. This is an implication analysis using linear time-series regressions to show bias from pooling when the accrual-cash-flow relation changes over time.

Identification: The authors use a linear annual time trend to test whether the discrepancy between residual-accrual properties computed from pooled or firm-specific regressions versus annual regressions systematically changes over time. The logic is mechanical: if the underlying accrual-cash-flow relation changes over time, pooled coefficients become increasingly misaligned with later years, biasing residuals. This is a descriptive regression interpretation rather than a quasi-causal design.

Setting: The paper examines the consequence of a changing accrual-cash-flow relation for residual accrual estimates by regressing differences in mean and standard deviation of residual accruals across estimation methods on a time trend. In Table 7 panel A, for the Dechow model, the time coefficient is -0.0019 for pooled-versus-annual mean residuals, -0.0008 for firm-specific-versus-annual mean residuals, -0.0007 for pooled-versus-annual residual SDs, and -0.0004 for firm-specific-versus-annual residual SDs. In panel B, corresponding coefficients for the Dechow-Dichev model are -0.0016, -0.0005, -0.0004, and -0.0006. The authors interpret these patterns as showing that pooled and firm-specific regressions increasingly understate residual accrual magnitude and variance in recent years.

Main role: This is an implication for later research use of accrual models, not a central test of the paper's main economic claim.
Settings.H1575: Section 5.3, Table 7 panels A-B; PDF pp. 32-34.
Settings.G1576:
Treatment: Employee performance–potential rating combination in year t, implemented as binary indicators for each joint category (TOP-1, TOP-2, TOP-3, TOP-4, STR-1, STR-2, STR-4, MOD-1, MOD-2, MOD-3, MOD-4) relative to omitted STR-3. Conceptually this is categorical rather than a single binary treatment.

Method: Linear OLS regression of next-year promotion on mutually exclusive indicators for each performance–potential rating combination, with STR-3 omitted as the base category and LOW-4 excluded because those employees were never promoted next year. The specification includes employee covariates (tenure, full-time, expat, male, age) and five absorbed fixed-effect dimensions: rank, business unit, function, country of employment, and year. Standard errors are clustered by employee. The paper interprets the coefficients as showing whether the performance–potential system is used as intended in promotion decisions, while acknowledging this is not a quasi-experimental design and remaining selection/endogeneity concerns are unresolved.

Identification: Identification comes from within-cell differences across employees with different current performance–potential combinations after adjusting for observed characteristics and extensive fixed effects for organizational rank, business unit, function, country, and year. The endogeneity concern is that ratings are not randomly assigned and may capture unobserved employee quality or career prospects correlated with promotions. The paper uses the strong FE structure and controls to show ratings are economically associated with later promotions, but causal interpretation is still associational/selection-on-observables conditional on FE.

Setting: To show supervisors use the performance–potential system as intended, the paper estimates an HDFE linear probability model of promotion in year t+1 on current rating combinations. Relative to STR-3, promotion likelihood is much higher for HiPo categories: TOP-1 has coefficient 0.378, TOP-2 0.179, and STR-1 0.268, and the paper states these are statistically higher than any of the other nine non-LOW-4 combinations. For example, 'the likelihood of promotion for a TOP-1 employee is 36.3 percentage points higher than the likelihood of promotion for a TOP-3 employee, all else equal (0.378 vs. 0.015).' This supports the paper’s premise that performance and potential assessments feed into promotion decisions, but it is auxiliary to the main turnover question.

Main role: This is a validating analysis showing the system operates as intended, not the paper’s central turnover claim. The abstract/introduction emphasize voluntary departures, with promotions used mainly as supporting institutional evidence.
Settings.G1577:
Treatment: Employee performance–potential rating combination in year t, coded as a set of joint-category indicators including LOW-4, relative to omitted STR-3. This is a multi-valued categorical treatment rather than a binary treatment.

Method: Linear OLS regression of next-year involuntary termination on indicators for all possible performance–potential rating combinations, with STR-3 omitted as the base category and LOW-4 included. Controls are tenure, full-time, expat, male, and age, with five absorbed fixed-effect dimensions: rank, business unit, function, country, and year. Standard errors are clustered by employee. The specification is used substantively to show poor performers with low potential are most likely to be terminated under the system.

Identification: Variation comes from differences in current ratings across employees, conditional on controls and multiple organizational/time fixed effects. The underlying concern is nonrandom assignment of ratings and unobserved employee problems correlated with termination risk. The paper does not claim exogenous assignment; instead it interprets the adjusted FE coefficients as evidence the system is implemented as intended, assuming conditioning variables absorb major confounders.

Setting: Using an HDFE linear probability model, the paper finds employees with the worst rating combination are far more likely to be involuntarily terminated in the next year. In Table 3 column (2), LOW-4 has coefficient 0.395, much larger than the next highest coefficient, MOD-4 at 0.092, and the paper states MOD-3, MOD-4, and LOW-4 are statistically higher than the other ten combinations. This is interpreted as evidence that poor performers with low potential become termination candidates under the performance–potential system, supporting the paper’s setup but not its main turnover result.

Main role: Like the promotion regression, this is an institutional validation exercise rather than a central contribution. The main conclusions concern voluntary departures and assessed potential.
Settings.G1578:
Treatment: Employee’s year-t performance–potential rating combination, entered as mutually exclusive binary indicators (TOP-1, TOP-2, TOP-3, TOP-4, STR-1, STR-2, STR-4, MOD-1, MOD-2, MOD-3, MOD-4) relative to omitted STR-3; LOW-4 is excluded from voluntary-departure analyses because Clearly Below employees were very likely to be terminated. The focal treatment is categorical rather than binary.

Method: Cox proportional hazards survival model for voluntary departure, stratified by age, with time-varying covariates constructed at the employee-year level. The model includes indicators for all performance–potential rating combinations except LOW-4, controls for tenure, full-time, expat, and male, plus fixed effects for rank, business unit, function, country, and year; standard errors are clustered by employee. Employees exiting involuntarily are censored at exit. The author also reports alternative random probit, logit, and OLS specifications at the same table location, but the Cox model in column (1) is the primary specification. This is not linear and therefore falls under Other.

Identification: The strategy uses within-sample variation in current assessed performance–potential ratings to predict future voluntary departure, controlling for observed employee characteristics and multiple organizational/time fixed effects. The paper’s conceptual endogeneity concern is that ratings may reflect latent match quality, outside options, or other unobservables correlated with turnover. The interpretation relies on the argument that conditional on these controls and FE, differences in departure hazards across same- or different-performance/potential categories reveal how assessed potential and HiPo status relate to departures, but there is no exogenous source of variation.

Setting: The main survival analysis tests whether assessed potential and HiPo status affect next-year voluntary departures. In Table 4 column (1), relative to STR-3, hazard ratios are 0.350 for TOP-1, 0.678 for TOP-2, 0.605 for TOP-3, 1.114 for TOP-4, 0.899 for STR-1, 0.914 for STR-2, 0.973 for STR-4, 1.355 for MOD-1, 1.494 for MOD-2, 1.756 for MOD-3, and 2.380 for MOD-4. The paper interprets these as showing HiPos generally depart at a lower rate than lower-performing non-HiPos, but there is little evidence in the full sample that HiPos depart less than non-HiPos with the same performance. Among non-HiPos, potential matters especially for Moderate performers: MOD-4 departs more than MOD-1, MOD-2, and MOD-3, and MOD-3 departs more than MOD-2. This is a central result supporting the claim that potential can matter to departures beyond performance.

Main role: This is the paper’s core empirical setting. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion all emphasize whether HiPos and higher-potential employees depart at lower rates, above and beyond performance.
Settings.H1578: Section 3.2, Table 4 panel A column (1) with pairwise interpretations from panels B and C, PDF pp. 17–22.
Settings.G1579:
Treatment: Employee’s year-t performance–potential rating combination, coded as mutually exclusive indicators relative to STR-3, estimated separately within shorter-tenured employees (tenure <= 7.54 years) and longer-tenured employees (tenure > 7.54 years). Categorical rather than binary.

Method: Conventional Cox proportional hazards survival models, stratified by age with time-varying covariates, estimated separately for shorter-tenured and longer-tenured employees. The split is based on whether tenure is at or below versus above 7.54 years, the average tenure of employees who voluntarily departed. Specifications include the same rating-combination indicators, controls (male, tenure, full-time, expat), and fixed effects for rank, business unit, function, country, and year, with employee-clustered standard errors. This nonlinear survival design is used to test heterogeneous effects of assessed potential by tenure.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same as in the main survival model but examined separately by tenure group, motivated by theory that shorter-tenured employees have more uncertainty about match quality and may learn more from potential ratings, whereas longer-tenured employees may already know their prospects. Remaining concerns are nonrandom ratings and endogenous tenure-based selection into the subsamples. The interpretation assumes the extensive controls/FE and within-subsample comparisons isolate informative differences in turnover hazards associated with assessed potential.

Setting: Splitting the sample by tenure reveals the paper’s main heterogeneity result. In Table 5 panel A, among shorter-tenured employees hazard ratios are 0.282 (TOP-1), 0.694 (TOP-2), 0.690 (TOP-3), 2.265 (TOP-4), 0.775 (STR-1), 0.840 (STR-2), 0.872 (STR-4), 0.849 (MOD-1), 1.329 (MOD-2), 1.603 (MOD-3), and 2.185 (MOD-4). Pairwise tests show stronger evidence that some HiPos depart less than same-performance non-HiPos and, among Moderate non-HiPos, departure rises as potential worsens. Among longer-tenured employees, hazard ratios are 0.640 (TOP-1), 0.574 (TOP-2), 0.548 (TOP-3), 0.685 (TOP-4), 1.232 (STR-1), 1.024 (STR-2), 1.088 (STR-4), 12.857 (MOD-1), 1.732 (MOD-2), 1.959 (MOD-3), and 2.614 (MOD-4); the main robust pattern is that MOD-1 longer-tenured employees depart especially quickly, suggesting a negative reaction to the extreme mismatch of low performance with highest potential. These results underpin the paper’s claim that potential matters mainly in employees’ early sorting decisions.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion stress that potential matters especially for shorter-tenured employees and much less for longer-tenured employees. These tenure-split hazard models are therefore central, not ancillary.
Settings.H1579: Section 3.3, Table 5 panels A–C, PDF pp. 24–28.
Settings.G1580:
Treatment: Four binary change indicators measured from prior year to current year: POT_DROP equals 1 if current potential is worse than prior-year potential; POT_INC equals 1 if current potential is better; PERF_DROP equals 1 if current performance is worse; PERF_INC equals 1 if current performance is better. These are estimated jointly alongside current rating-combination indicators.

Method: Cox proportional hazards survival regressions of voluntary departure on indicators for changes in potential and changes in performance from the prior year to the current year, controlling for current performance–potential rating combinations, employee controls, and rank/business unit/function/country/year fixed effects, with age stratification and employee-clustered standard errors. The sample excludes 2008, employees without a prior-year rating, and employees promoted or demoted in the current year. The table reports full-sample and tenure-split versions and same- versus different-supervisor subsamples. The nonlinear survival implementation places this under Other.

Identification: This setting exploits within-employee year-to-year changes in assessed potential and performance, conditional on the employee’s current rating combination and extensive fixed effects. The paper’s argument is that a change in potential conveys new information or a shock about match quality/promotion prospects beyond the current level. Endogeneity remains because revisions are not random and may reflect unobserved shocks that also affect departure. The design reduces some confounding by conditioning on current ratings and excluding current-year promotions/demotions, but causal interpretation still relies on selection-on-observables plus the idea that revisions themselves are informative shocks.

Setting: The paper estimates whether revisions in assessments affect next-year voluntary departure, above current ratings. In Table 6 column (1), a drop in potential increases the departure hazard (POT_DROP hazard ratio 1.342), while an increase in potential lowers it (POT_INC 0.869); neither a performance drop nor increase matters (PERF_DROP 1.009, PERF_INC 0.999). In the shorter-tenured subsample, POT_INC is significant at 0.806, while in the longer-tenured subsample POT_DROP is significant at 1.609. The author interprets this as evidence that changes in potential, especially downward revisions for longer-tenured employees, act as negative shocks that increase exits, whereas performance changes are unrelated to departures.

Main role: The conclusion highlights this as a key additional central finding: downward revisions in potential raise departures, especially for longer-tenured employees, whereas performance changes do not. It materially supports the paper’s broader message that potential information matters.
Settings.G1581:
Treatment: Consecutive HiPo status at the same hierarchical level, coded as categorical indicators HIPO 1x (base), HIPO 2x, HIPO 3x, and HIPO 4x, where HiPo means TOP-1, TOP-2, or STR-1 and counts consecutive annual HiPo ratings without a change in management level. This is categorical, not binary.

Method: Cox proportional hazards survival regressions relating next-year voluntary departure to the count of consecutive HiPo ratings at the same hierarchical level (without promotion), with age stratification, employee-clustered standard errors, controls for male, tenure, full-time, expat, and rank/business unit/function/country/year fixed effects. HIPO 1x is the omitted category; HIPO 2x, 3x, and 4x are compared against it, alongside other non-HiPo rating categories. Column (2) additionally controls for promotion or demotion in year t. Because the implementation is a nonlinear survival model, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The strategy compares employees with different lengths of consecutive HiPo status at the same rank, controlling for observed characteristics and extensive fixed effects. The motivation is to test whether repeated high-potential signals without promotion erode retention benefits. Endogeneity concerns remain substantial because employees with multiple consecutive HiPo ratings are selected on underlying talent, opportunity, and promotion timing, and the paper notes limited power because long uninterrupted HiPo spells are rare.

Setting: The paper tests whether the likelihood of voluntary departure rises with repeated HiPo ratings without promotion. In Table 7 panel A, relative to HIPO 1x, the hazard ratios are 0.816 for HIPO 2x, 0.693 for HIPO 3x, and 1.385 for HIPO 4x in column (1), with similar values when controlling for promotion/demotion in column (2). Pairwise tests show no statistically significant differences among the HIPO categories, and no significant differences between HIPO 4x and TOP-3 or TOP-4. The author concludes there is no clear evidence that more consecutive HiPo ratings without promotion increase voluntary departures, though limited power and prompt promotion of many HiPos may explain the null result.

Main role: This is a final exploratory extension about whether repeated unfulfilled HiPo status raises departures. It is discussed as supplementary, not as a primary pillar of the paper’s conclusions.
Settings.H1581: Section 3.6, Table 7 panels A–B, PDF pp. 34–37.
Settings.G1582:
Treatment: Continuous or binary explanatory variables interpreted as shifting firms' choice of short CEO PBEA performance periods: AbnROA (industry-adjusted ROA averaged over prior three years), New (CEO tenure <=3 years indicator), NPeer (number of industry peer firms), Mobility (share of firms in industry with externally hired CEOs), FirmAge (years in Compustat), AdjRetSTD (industry-adjusted daily return volatility), and PaySTD (industry SD of CEO residual compensation). These are not manipulated treatments but are interpreted by authors as causal determinants of short performance periods.

Method: Main tests use logit regressions of an indicator for whether the CEO performance-based equity award (PBEA) has a short performance period (ShortPP=1 if performance period is two years or less) on proxies for CEO expected productivity, alternative employment opportunities, firm operating uncertainty, and dispersion of managerial productivity, plus contractual and firm/CEO controls and year fixed effects. The authors interpret coefficient signs as causal evidence about determinants of firms' chosen performance period length. Sample: S&P 1500 industrial firms granting PBEAs to CEOs, 2009–2013; 2,922 firm-years for all PBEAs and 2,876 for largest PBRS. Standard errors are clustered by firm and year. Because implemented estimator is nonlinear logit, this belongs in Other rather than OLS/regression adjustment.

Identification: Identification is cross-sectional/within-period conditional association from nonlinear regression adjustment. The authors argue that proxies for expected productivity, outside opportunities, uncertainty, and productivity dispersion affect the optimal performance period through a sorting mechanism. Endogeneity remains possible because governance, compensation design, and firm characteristics may be jointly determined with performance periods; the design attempts to mitigate confounding using extensive observed controls, year fixed effects, lagged firm and industry regressors for many variables, and clustered standard errors. The paper does not claim quasi-experimental identification.

Setting: In the paper's main empirical design, the authors causally interpret observed firm, CEO, and industry characteristics as affecting the probability that a CEO PBEA uses a short performance period. In Table 3, Column (1) for all PBEAs, lower prior abnormal ROA, being a new CEO, more peer firms, younger firm age, higher abnormal return volatility, and greater industry dispersion in CEO residual pay are reported to increase the likelihood of short performance periods, with six of seven proxy coefficients in the predicted direction and statistically significant except Mobility. They also report magnitudes relative to a baseline short-period propensity of 26 percent: e.g., a one-standard-deviation decrease in AbnROA raises short-period use by about 4 percentage points (15 percent of base), one-SD increase in NPeer by about 4 points (14 percent), one-SD increase in FirmAge lowers it by about 5 points (20 percent), one-SD increase in AdjRetSTD raises it by 2 points (6 percent), and one-SD increase in PaySTD raises it by 2 points (7 percent). These results are presented as the main evidence that firms choose short performance periods to sort CEO talent more rapidly.

Main role: This is the paper's central empirical test of hypotheses H1-H4 about what causes firms to choose shorter CEO PBEA performance periods, highlighted in the abstract, introduction, Section V, and conclusion.
Settings.H1582: Section V, Equation (10), Table 3 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 11-15.
Settings.G1583:
Treatment: ShortPP indicator equal to 1 if the CEO's PBEA performance period length is two years or less, interacted with lagged performance measures (Idiosyncratic Return and Industry-Induced Return) to test whether short performance periods increase turnover sensitivity to poor performance. ShortPP is binary; the interaction terms combine a binary treatment with continuous performance measures.

Method: Supplementary logit regression of subsequent CEO departure on lagged idiosyncratic return, lagged industry-induced return, short-performance-period indicator, and interactions between performance and short-performance-period status, following a two-stage decomposition of firm returns. First stage regresses firm annual return on industry return to obtain fitted industry-induced and residual idiosyncratic components; second stage is a logit for CEO departure with controls and year fixed effects. The interaction effects are further evaluated using Ai and Norton (2003) average interaction effects and graphed probability differences. Because the implemented second-stage estimator is nonlinear logit, classify as Other.

Identification: Identification comes from conditional differences in turnover-performance sensitivity between firms with short versus long PBEA performance periods, after decomposing returns into industry-induced and idiosyncratic components and controlling for CEO age, executive turnover, labor market thickness, governance, size, Tobin's Q, and year effects. The authors' argument is that if short performance periods are used for sorting, poor performance should lead to more turnover under short periods. This remains observational and vulnerable to endogenous contract choice and omitted differences across firms; no quasi-experimental variation is provided.

Setting: To test a key implication of the sorting theory, the authors examine whether short CEO PBEA performance periods make boards more likely to remove poorly performing CEOs. In Table 4, the coefficient on ShortPP is positive (0.262, p<0.01), and its interactions with lagged idiosyncratic return (-0.601, p<0.05) and lagged industry-induced return (-0.944, p<0.01) are negative in the all-PBEAs sample, indicating stronger turnover sensitivity to poor performance when performance periods are short. Using Ai-Norton interaction calculations, the average interaction effects are -0.085 and -0.118, both significant, and Figure 1 shows that when returns are negative, the probability of CEO departure is significantly higher under short than long performance periods. The paper interprets this as validating the causal sorting role of short performance periods.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that underperforming CEOs are more likely to exit firms with shorter performance periods; this validates the paper's central sorting interpretation.
Settings.H1583: Section VI, 'Effect of Performance Period Length on CEO Turnover,' Equations (11a)-(11b), Table 4, Figure 1, PDF pp. 15-19.
Settings.G1584:
Treatment: Same set of continuous and binary determinants as the main model—AbnROA, New, NPeer, Mobility, FirmAge, AdjRetSTD, PaySTD, plus controls—interpreted as affecting the firm's choice of a short performance period for the overall incentive compensation mix rather than just PBEAs.

Method: Supplementary logit regression analogous to the main specification, but the dependent variable is an indicator for whether the value-weighted performance period of a broader incentive compensation mix—annual bonuses, long-term cash bonuses, and PBEAs, diluted by time-based equity in the denominator—is one year or less. Regressors are the same determinants and controls as in the main model, with year fixed effects and firm/year-clustered standard errors. Implemented estimator is nonlinear logit.

Identification: Observational regression adjustment exploiting cross-sectional variation in CEO, firm, and industry characteristics, with the same causal interpretation as the main analysis. The authors argue that if sorting shapes incentive design more broadly, the same determinants should affect the overall compensation mix's performance period. Endogeneity from jointly determined compensation design remains possible; the design relies on controls and timing conventions rather than exogenous variation.

Setting: As a supplementary analysis, the paper estimates whether the same sorting-related variables that explain short PBEA performance periods also explain short performance periods for a broader incentive compensation mix including annual and long-term cash bonuses. In Table 5, New, NPeer, FirmAge, and PaySTD have predicted signs and are statistically significant, while AbnROA, Mobility, and AdjRetSTD have predicted but insignificant coefficients. The authors interpret these results as evidence that broader incentive pay can also be used to sort CEO talent, although PBEAs appear to be the most important component for sorting.

Main role: This is a supplementary extension testing whether the sorting explanation generalizes beyond PBEAs to a broader compensation mix; it supports but does not replace the main PBEA results.
Settings.H1584: Section VI, 'Performance Periods of Broader Incentive Compensation Mix,' Table 5, PDF p. 20.
Settings.G1585:
Treatment: Within the new-CEO subsample, continuous and binary determinants interpreted as affecting short performance periods, including AbnROA, NPeer, Mobility, FirmAge, AdjRetSTD, PaySTD, and in alternative columns Internal=1 for internally promoted CEO versus external hire.

Method: Supplementary logit regressions of short PBEA performance periods estimated only within the subsample of newly appointed CEOs (tenure <=36 months). The regressors largely mirror the main specification, omitting New and Retirement and in some columns adding Internal, an indicator for internally promoted CEOs. Year fixed effects are included and standard errors are clustered by firms and years. Implemented estimator is nonlinear logit.

Identification: Conditional association within the subsample of newly appointed CEOs. The idea is that sorting should be especially salient for new CEOs, and internal versus external hire could additionally affect required sorting speed. Identification remains observational with controls and year fixed effects; reduced sample size weakens precision and causal certainty.

Setting: Restricting attention to newly appointed CEOs, the authors estimate whether the same proxies for sorting needs explain short PBEA performance periods. In Table 6 for all PBEAs, AbnROA and NPeer are marginally significant with predicted signs, FirmAge is significantly negative as predicted, Mobility and AdjRetSTD are insignificant, and PaySTD is insignificant. Adding Internal, an indicator for internal promotion, yields an insignificant coefficient, which the authors interpret as offsetting sorting and performance considerations. This supplementary evidence suggests the main sorting determinants retain some explanatory power even among new CEOs.

Main role: This is a supplementary subsample analysis aimed at whether sorting determinants also explain design choices for new CEOs; it is not a headline result.
Settings.H1585: Section VI, 'Performance Periods for New CEOs,' Table 6, PDF pp. 18-21.
Settings.G1586:
Treatment: Same sorting-related determinants as in the main model affecting the probability of a short PBEA performance period, while jointly modeling the vesting period. In the companion OLS vesting equation, the focal determinant emphasized is AdjRetSTD and additional lagged firm variables (LTAsset, Ret, Spread, BrdIndp, TobinQ, Size).

Method: Seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) system combining (i) a logit equation for ShortPP, which is the same nonlinear model as the main specification, and (ii) an OLS equation for vesting period length (VestLen) on its own determinants following Cadman et al. (2013). The purpose is to allow for joint determination of performance period and vesting period. The implemented system includes year fixed effects in the ShortPP equation; standard errors are clustered by firms and years. Because the focal causal equation for ShortPP is nonlinear logit within a system, classify as Other.

Identification: The SUR framework addresses concern that performance period and vesting period are jointly chosen contractual features. The authors identify the short-performance-period equation from the same observed determinants as before, while modeling the vesting equation with separate covariates from prior literature. This improves accounting for simultaneous contract design but remains nonexperimental; causal claims rely on observed controls and structural interpretation of contract choice.

Setting: In a robustness exercise, the authors jointly model short PBEA performance periods and vesting period lengths. The logit ShortPP equation in Table 7 continues to show the same pattern as the main results—AbnROA negative and significant, New positive, NPeer positive, FirmAge negative, AdjRetSTD positive, PaySTD positive, and Market and VestLen negative—supporting the sorting interpretation even when vesting is jointly determined. In the companion OLS vesting equation, industry-adjusted return volatility is negatively related to vesting length, consistent with firms choosing shorter vesting periods to realign risk-taking incentives. The paper treats this as reinforcing the main causal story for performance periods.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis reinforcing that the main findings on performance periods are not driven by separate determination of vesting periods.
Settings.H1586: Section VI, 'Performance Period and Other Contractual Features,' Equations (12a)-(12b), Table 7, PDF pp. 20-22.
Settings.G1587:
Treatment: Two related treatments are interpreted causally in this selection framework: (a) granting a CEO a PBEA at all, PA=1, in the selection equation; and (b) among grantors, the same sorting-related determinants affecting use of a short PBEA performance period (ShortPP) in the outcome equation. Most regressors are continuous; PA itself is binary in the first-stage outcome.

Method: Probit-based Heckman selection model that jointly estimates (i) a first-stage selection/granting equation for whether a firm grants PBEAs to the CEO and (ii) a second-stage performance-period equation for ShortPP among grantors. The selection equation uses AdjRet, RetSTD, Invst, Segmt, IH, CEOShr, and Size; the outcome equation mirrors the main ShortPP specification. The paper describes excluded first-stage variables as instrumental variables for estimation purposes. Because the implemented models are nonlinear probit/Heckman, classify as Other.

Identification: The authors worry that observing performance period choice only among firms that grant PBEAs may create selection bias. They therefore estimate a Heckman selection model where excluded first-stage variables (AdjRet, RetSTD, Invst, Segmt, IH) help identify selection into granting PBEAs, and then assess whether the same sorting variables explain ShortPP conditional on grant. The paper explicitly notes that inference depends on the quality of these instruments/exclusion restrictions, so identification is model-based and not experimental.

Setting: To address possible endogeneity of the decision to grant PBEAs, the paper estimates a probit-based Heckman model. In Table 8 Panel B, the second-stage performance-period equation for all PBEAs yields results qualitatively similar to the main Table 3 findings: AbnROA is negative, New positive, NPeer positive, FirmAge negative, AdjRetSTD positive, and PaySTD positive or marginal, implying that selection into granting PBEAs does not materially change the sorting interpretation. In the first-stage grant equation, firms are reported to be more likely to grant PBEAs when operations are more complex (Segmt) or firms are larger (Size), and less likely when return volatility, investment intensity, or CEO shareholding are higher. The authors interpret this as evidence that the short-performance-period results are robust to endogenous PBEA granting decisions.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis addressing selection into granting PBEAs; it supports the main result but is not the primary empirical design.
Settings.H1587: Section VI, 'Performance Period Length and the Choice to Grant PBEAs,' Equation (13), Table 8 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 23-24.
Settings.G1588:
Treatment: Future realized stock return realizations over three horizons—one-month cum-dividend return (RET1), cumulative return months 2–6 (CRET2_6M), cumulative return months 7–12 (CRET7_12M)—and dividend yield (DIVYIELD, prior-year common dividends divided by prior-year market value of equity). All are continuous regressors measured at the firm-month level.

Method: Baseline linear predictive/causal-interpretation regressions estimated cross-sectionally each month from April 1999 to December 2016 using Fama-MacBeth averages of monthly coefficients with Newey-West (11 lags) standard errors. The dependent variable is analyst target price implied return (IMPRET), and the regressors are future realized returns over three non-overlapping post-forecast windows (RET1, CRET2_6M, CRET7_12M) and, in one specification, dividend yield. The authors interpret these coefficients as showing how future realized return realizations and expected dividend distributions determine target price implied returns and as a benchmark for analysts' information versus forecast error. There is no quasi-experimental source of variation; identification is associational/regression-adjustment only.

Identification: The paper uses cross-sectional variation in subsequent realized returns and dividend yields to assess whether analyst implied returns reflect information about future prices versus predictable errors. The key concern is that future realized returns are not exogenous causal treatments but realized outcomes mechanically related to forecast quality; thus the design supports interpreted determinants rather than credible causal effects. Assumptions are limited to linear conditional association and the authors' conceptual model that, absent forecast error, implied returns should equal future ex-dividend returns.

Setting: In the paper's baseline regressions, the authors interpret future realized returns and dividend yield as determinants of analyst target price implied returns. Monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth regressions show that implied returns are only weakly related to short-term future returns and negatively related to longer-horizon future returns, while higher dividend yield lowers implied returns. Specifically, in Table 2 column (2), the coefficient on DIVYIELD is -2.171 (t=6.74), RET1 is 0.012 (t=0.63), CRET2_6M is -0.031 (t=1.97 in absolute value), and CRET7_12M is -0.024 (t=1.73 in absolute value), with adjusted R2 rising from 4.07% to 7.13% when dividends are added. These baseline results materially support the paper's claim that only a small share of implied returns reflects future returns, motivating the search for forecast-error and incentive determinants.

Main role: The baseline decomposition is central to the paper's framework because the paper starts from how much implied returns reflect future realized returns/dividends before adding forecast-error and incentive determinants.
Settings.H1588: Section V, Table 2 columns (1)-(4), Figure 1, PDF pp. 9-10.
Settings.G1589:
Treatment: Perfect-foresight fundamental forecast error proxies: FY1_BIAS, the difference between consensus one-year-ahead EPS forecast and actual EPS scaled by stock price; and LTGREV, current consensus long-term growth forecast minus the consensus forecast 12 months later. Both are continuous measures where higher values indicate more optimistic forecast error.

Method: Monthly cross-sectional linear regressions (Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West 11 lags) relating analyst target price implied returns, future ex-dividend returns, and target price bias to perfect-foresight proxies for fundamental forecast errors: FY1_BIAS and LTGREV. The authors estimate equations with and without the baseline return/dividend controls to interpret whether ex post errors in earnings and long-term growth forecasts cause target price implied returns and target price optimism. No fixed effects or quasi-experimental design are used.

Identification: The paper argues that errors in forecasting earnings and growth feed through valuation models into target price errors. Identification comes from cross-sectional correlation between ex post realized proxy measures of forecast error and contemporaneous implied returns/bias. The main endogeneity limitation is that these perfect-foresight variables use future information and therefore document association with realized target price error rather than ex ante causal effects perceived at issuance. The authors use them to quantify the role of fundamental forecast mistakes, not as a clean exogenous shock design.

Setting: Using perfect-foresight measures of analysts' fundamental forecast errors, the authors conclude that more optimistic earnings and growth forecast errors raise analyst target price implied returns and their bias. In Table 3 Panel A column (1), FY1_BIAS has coefficient 0.015 (t=6.99) and LTGREV 0.005 (t=3.38) in explaining IMPRET, with adjusted R2 of 4.17%. With future returns and dividend yield added (column (2)), coefficients remain positive and significant—0.016 and 0.004, respectively—and adjusted R2 rises to 10.81%. For target price bias (column (4)), FY1_BIAS is 0.058 (t=14.04) and LTGREV 0.017 (t=5.65), with adjusted R2 of 11.67%. These results support the paper's central claim that errors in forecasting fundamentals are a material source of optimistic target prices.

Main role: Fundamental forecast errors are one of the paper's four core determinant groups and are part of the main explanatory framework for target price implied returns and optimism.
Settings.H1589: Section V, Table 3 Panel A columns (1)-(4), Figure 2 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 10-13.
Settings.G1590:
Treatment: Model-based predicted fundamental forecast bias variables available at the time of target price issuance: CO (characteristic forecast optimism from So 2013) and DISPARITY (difference between long-term growth forecast rank and implied short-term earnings growth rank from Da and Warachka 2011). Both are continuous; larger values indicate more predicted optimism in analyst fundamentals.

Method: Monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth regressions with Newey-West corrections using ex ante model-based measures of predictable fundamental forecast bias—CO and DISPARITY—as treatments. Outcomes are IMPRET, CXRET12M, and TP_BIAS. Specifications are estimated both standalone and with baseline realized-return/dividend controls. The design is linear regression adjustment without a separate identification strategy beyond observed covariates and model-based predictors.

Identification: The identifying argument is that if predictable optimism in analysts' earnings and growth forecasts is transmitted into target prices, then cross-sectional ex ante bias proxies should predict implied returns and target price bias but not future realized returns if markets do not price the bias. Endogeneity remains substantial because these are observational correlations based on model-generated measures, not exogenous shocks. The paper relies on timing—variables known at issuance—to interpret these as ex ante determinants of target price bias.

Setting: The paper finds that predictable optimism in analysts' fundamental forecasts translates into predictable optimism in target price implied returns. In Table 3 Panel B column (1), CO has coefficient 0.262 (t=6.44) and DISPARITY 0.012 (t=4.20) for IMPRET, explaining 3.93% of variation. After adding future returns and dividend yield (column (2)), the coefficients remain positive and significant at 0.179 and 0.008, with adjusted R2 of 9.20%. In column (3), neither variable predicts future ex-dividend returns, while in column (4) they positively predict TP_BIAS—CO 0.240 (t=2.67), DISPARITY 0.014 (t=2.87), adjusted R2 2.47%. These estimates are central to the paper's later construction of predicted target-price bias and the claim that investors fail to fully discount it.

Main role: These ex ante predictable-bias measures are important because the paper later uses them to forecast target price bias and assess investor mispricing, a central contribution.
Settings.H1590: Section V, Table 3 Panel B columns (1)-(4), Figure 2 Panels C-D, PDF pp. 10-13.
Settings.G1591:
Treatment: Continuous empirical risk proxies measured at the firm-month level: CAPM beta, idiosyncratic volatility, log firm size, book-to-market ratio, leverage ratio, and Amihud illiquidity. The paper interprets changes in these proxies as affecting analyst target price implied returns by inducing expected-return forecast errors.

Method: Monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth linear regressions with Newey-West corrections where the treatment variables are empirical risk proxies (BETA, IDVOL, SIZE, BM, LEVERAGE, ILLIQ). The authors estimate their effects on IMPRET, CXRET12M, and TP_BIAS, with and without baseline controls for future returns and dividend yield. The implemented estimator is standard linear regression adjustment.

Identification: The paper's strategy is to compare how analysts price risk proxies in implied returns versus how realized returns load on the same proxies. If analysts place positive expected-return weights on risky characteristics but realized returns do not, the difference is interpreted as analyst misunderstanding of the risk-return trade-off. This is an observational comparison of coefficients, not causal identification from exogenous variation. Key assumptions are that these proxies capture the return dimensions analysts use and that conditioning on the included variables is sufficient for the interpreted comparison.

Setting: Risk proxies are the paper's strongest determinant group: analysts assign higher implied returns to riskier firms, but realized returns often do not compensate these risks, which the authors interpret as analyst overestimation of expected returns to risk. In Table 3 Panel C column (1), the risk variables jointly explain 16.90% of variation in IMPRET. Coefficients are positive for BETA (0.051, t=4.93), IDVOL (5.001, t=8.91), BM (0.045, t=3.41), LEVERAGE (0.053, t=3.48), ILLIQ (0.026, t=3.60), and negative for SIZE (-0.015, t=5.48). With baseline controls (column (2)) adjusted R2 is 18.80%. In future-return regressions (column (3)), several signs differ or are insignificant, and TP_BIAS results (column (4)) show that these mistakes explain 10.51% of bias in target prices. This setting directly underpins the paper's headline claim that misunderstanding the risk-return trade-off is the largest source of target price error.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that misunderstanding the expected return to empirical risk proxies has the greatest impact among all determinant groups, making this a core main-result setting.
Settings.H1591: Section V, Table 3 Panel C columns (1)-(4), Figure 3 Panels A-F, PDF pp. 11-15.
Settings.G1592:
Treatment: Continuous proxies for analyst job-related incentives: trading volume percentile measure (VOLUME), external financing scaled by assets (EXT_FIN), and institutional holdings share (IHOLD). Higher values proxy for stronger commission-generation, financing-related optimism, and institutional-monitoring/reputation channels, respectively.

Method: Monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth regressions with Newey-West corrections using analyst job-related incentive proxies—VOLUME, EXT_FIN, and IHOLD—as treatments. Outcomes are IMPRET, CXRET12M, and TP_BIAS, estimated with and without baseline controls for future returns and dividends. The estimator is standard linear regression adjustment.

Identification: The authors exploit cross-sectional differences in proxies for analysts' incentives to encourage trading, support financing clients, and maintain reputation with institutions. The interpretation is that stronger incentives induce optimistic target prices beyond information and fundamentals. This is observational and vulnerable to omitted-variable bias; the authors partially address this by adding future-return and dividend controls, but no exogenous identification is offered.

Setting: The paper interprets analyst incentive proxies as drivers of optimistic target prices, especially for firms raising external financing. In Table 3 Panel D column (1), VOLUME has coefficient -0.038 (t=2.23 in absolute value), EXT_FIN 0.239 (t=8.91), and IHOLD -0.023 (t=0.95) for IMPRET, with adjusted R2 of 6.79%. After adding baseline controls (column (2)), EXT_FIN remains strongly positive at 0.193 (t=9.97) and IHOLD becomes significantly negative at -0.067 (t=2.99). Future returns are lower for firms with more external financing (column (3): -0.079, t=2.43 in absolute value), and TP_BIAS is strongly higher for these firms (column (4): 0.317, t=6.27), with adjusted R2 of 4.64%. These estimates support the paper's main conclusion that incentive-related optimism contributes meaningfully to target price bias.

Main role: Analyst incentives are one of the four broad determinant groups highlighted in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as contributing to target price implied returns and bias.
Settings.H1592: Section V, Table 3 Panel D columns (1)-(4), Figure 4 Panels A-C, PDF pp. 12-15.
Settings.G1593:
