Treatment: Simultaneous continuous determinants from all four channels: dividend yield, future realized returns (RET1, CRET2_6M, CRET7_12M), perfect-foresight fundamental forecast error proxies (FY1_BIAS, LTGREV), risk proxies (BETA, IDVOL, SIZE, BM, LEVERAGE, ILLIQ), and incentive proxies (VOLUME, EXT_FIN, IHOLD).

Method: Full multivariable monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth regressions with Newey-West corrections. Panel A uses perfect-foresight fundamental error variables (FY1_BIAS, LTGREV) together with baseline realized-return/dividend regressors, risk proxies, and incentive proxies. Outcomes are IMPRET, CXRET12M, and TP_BIAS. This is the paper's comprehensive linear regression model.

Identification: Identification is purely observational: the paper estimates a comprehensive cross-sectional determinant model and interprets coefficients as partial effects after controlling for other determinant groups. This is meant to reduce confounding across fundamentals, risk, and incentives, but it does not solve endogeneity or measurement error. The interpretation relies on the authors' valuation framework and on included controls capturing the main joint determinants.

Setting: In the comprehensive model with perfect-foresight fundamental errors, the paper concludes that the four determinant groups jointly explain almost a quarter of the cross-sectional variation in analyst implied returns. Table 4 Panel A column (1) reports adjusted R2 of 22.65% for IMPRET. Key coefficients include DIVYIELD -1.095 (t=8.80), RET1 0.082 (t=7.10), FY1_BIAS 0.009 (t=8.67), LTGREV 0.003 (t=5.25), IDVOL 2.543 (t=9.20), BM 0.041 (t=4.69), LEVERAGE 0.064 (t=4.39), VOLUME 0.177 (t=2.99), EXT_FIN 0.088 (t=10.09), and IHOLD -0.075 (t=3.20). The corresponding TP_BIAS regression in column (3) has adjusted R2 20.12%. This full model is a central result because it summarizes the relative importance of the paper's proposed determinants and shows that target price informativeness improves after accounting for these biases.

Main role: This full model is the paper's main summary specification and underlies the claim that the determinants jointly explain nearly a quarter of the cross-sectional variation in implied returns.
Settings.H1593: Section V, Table 4 Panel A columns (1)-(3), PDF pp. 16-17.
Settings.G1594:
Treatment: Simultaneous continuous determinants from all four channels with ex ante fundamental-bias proxies: DIVYIELD, RET1, CRET2_6M, CRET7_12M, CO, DISPARITY, BETA, IDVOL, SIZE, BM, LEVERAGE, ILLIQ, VOLUME, EXT_FIN, IHOLD.

Method: Full multivariable monthly cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth regressions with Newey-West corrections. Panel B uses predicted-bias fundamental variables (CO, DISPARITY) instead of perfect-foresight variables, together with dividend yield, future realized returns, risk proxies, and incentive proxies. Outcomes are IMPRET, CXRET12M, and TP_BIAS.

Identification: As with the other cross-sectional regressions, the model uses observed covariation and included controls to estimate partial associations. Its special role is ex ante implementability: all non-realized regressors are available at issuance, which the authors exploit in out-of-sample prediction of target price bias. Endogeneity remains unresolved; the paper interprets the specification structurally through the valuation framework rather than through exogenous variation.

Setting: The ex ante full determinant model shows that observable predictors known at issuance explain a large share of target price implied returns and bias. In Table 4 Panel B column (4), the IMPRET regression has adjusted R2 of 21.85%; notable coefficients are DIVYIELD -0.995 (t=8.53), RET1 0.033 (t=3.12), CO 0.072 (t=2.62), DISPARITY 0.003 (t=7.02), IDVOL 2.433 (t=9.00), BM 0.046 (t=5.01), LEVERAGE 0.072 (t=4.73), VOLUME 0.188 (t=3.11), EXT_FIN 0.108 (t=12.32), and IHOLD -0.079 (t=3.40). Column (6) shows adjusted R2 of 12.47% for TP_BIAS. This setting is pivotal because it generates the predicted error component that the paper later links to future stock underperformance.

Main role: This ex ante full model is central because it forms the basis for the predicted-error measure PERROR used in the investor-mispricing tests.
Settings.H1594: Section V, Table 4 Panel B columns (4)-(6), PDF pp. 16-17.
Settings.G1595:
Treatment: Same full-model determinant sets as in Table 4, estimated in two versions: one with perfect-foresight fundamental variables (FY1_BIAS, LTGREV) and one with predicted-bias variables (CO, DISPARITY), alongside dividend yield, future returns, risk proxies, and incentive proxies. Continuous regressors.

Method: Robustness analysis re-estimating the two full IMPRET determinant models annually using only April observations each year from 1999 to 2016 rather than monthly panels. The authors report mean coefficients and Fama-MacBeth t-statistics across 18 annual regressions. This remains linear regression adjustment, with no new identification design.

Identification: The robustness strategy asks whether the cross-sectional determinant relations persist when reducing serial dependence by using only one month per year. It does not improve causal identification beyond the baseline observational design but addresses concerns that monthly overlapping measurements and serial correlation may drive significance.

Setting: As a robustness test, the authors re-estimate the full determinant models annually using only April observations. Table 5 shows that signs are unchanged relative to Table 4 and most coefficients remain significant. The average adjusted R2 is 24.93% for the model with perfect-foresight fundamentals and 24.23% for the model with predicted-bias fundamentals. This supports the stability of the paper's main cross-sectional determinant results but remains an observational robustness analysis rather than a separate identification design.

Main role: This is a robustness check confirming the full-model findings under annual rather than monthly regression timing; it supports but does not independently anchor the paper's main claims.
Settings.H1595: Section V, Table 5 columns (1)-(2), PDF p. 17.
Settings.G1596:
Treatment: Ranked target price implied return components scaled 0 to 1 by monthly deciles: R_IMPRET (ranked IMPRET), R_PURIFIED (ranked purified implied return after removing predicted bias), and R_PERROR (ranked predicted bias component). These are continuous ranking treatments, not binary interventions.

Method: Out-of-sample predictive-bias regressions of future returns on ranked target price implied return and its decomposed components. The authors first estimate a rolling historical version of the ex ante full IMPRET model to construct PERROR (predicted bias) and PURIFIED = IMPRET - PERROR using only information available by month s. They then run monthly Fama-MacBeth regressions of future one-month and six-month returns on ranked IMPRET, ranked PURIFIED, and ranked PERROR, with controls for size, book-to-market, and momentum. This is a linear regression/predictive-return design, not a quasi-experiment.

Identification: The paper's argument is that if investors do not perfectly separate the information and bias components in target prices, stocks with higher predicted bias should earn lower subsequent returns, while stocks with higher purified signal should earn higher short-term returns. Identification comes from cross-sectional predictive return regressions using only lagged, publicly available characteristics in constructing PERROR. The main concern is omitted predictors of returns correlated with PERROR or PURIFIED; the authors include size, book-to-market, and momentum controls, but causal claims about investor overreaction remain observational.

Setting: Using an out-of-sample decomposition of target price implied returns into a purified signal and a predicted-bias component, the authors argue that investors overreact to predictable optimism and underreact to the informative part. In Table 6 Panel A, future one-month returns are weakly related to overall implied returns (R_IMPRET coefficient 0.531, t=1.63), strongly positively related to R_PURIFIED (0.994, t=4.15), and negatively related to R_PERROR (-1.099, t=2.40 in absolute value). In Table 6 Panel B, six-month returns are not positively related to R_IMPRET (-0.320, t=0.31), are positively related to R_PURIFIED when entered alone (2.041, t=3.17), and are strongly negatively related to R_PERROR (-5.370, t=2.74 in absolute value; -5.064, t=2.33 when both components enter). These regressions are a core basis for the paper's claim that predicted bias in target prices leads to future underperformance.

Main role: These regressions are central to the paper's second major contribution: investors fail to fully discount predictable target-price bias, and the purified component predicts returns more cleanly.
Settings.H1596: Section V, equations (8)-(11), Exhibit 2, Table 6 Panels A-B, PDF pp. 18-20.
Settings.G1597:
Treatment: Portfolio assignment based on decile rankings of target price implied return components: highest versus lowest decile of IMPRET, PURIFIED, or PERROR in monthly sorts. The focal treatment contrast in each hedge portfolio is binary at the portfolio level (top decile long minus bottom decile short), though it arises from an underlying ranked continuous signal.

Method: Portfolio-sorting asset-pricing analysis rather than a regression design. Each month the authors sort stocks into deciles based on IMPRET, PURIFIED, or PERROR, form hedge portfolios long the highest decile and short the lowest decile, and compute subsequent monthly Fama-French four-factor alphas for months 1 through 6 after formation. Both equal-weighted and value-weighted strategies are reported. Because this is a factor-model portfolio estimator rather than one of the listed linear causal designs, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The strategy compares future risk-adjusted returns of stocks with high versus low target-price signals or predicted bias. The interpretation is that if investors overreact to predictable target-price optimism, high-PERROR stocks should underperform low-PERROR stocks even after standard factor adjustment. This remains observational because portfolio sorts can load on omitted anomalies; the four-factor alpha is the paper's adjustment for common risk exposures rather than a causal identification device.

Setting: The portfolio evidence indicates economically meaningful mispricing related to predicted target-price bias. Table 7 Panel C shows that a hedge portfolio long low-PERROR stocks and short high-PERROR stocks earns strongly negative alphas for the high-minus-low direction every month from month 1 to month 6: for equal-weighted portfolios, -1.16%, -1.17%, -1.17%, -0.89%, -0.99%, and -0.83%, all statistically significant; value-weighted alphas are similar, from -0.91% to -0.74%. Panel B shows that PURIFIED-based portfolios earn positive alphas, especially in the first two months (equal-weighted 0.94% and 0.70%). The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that investors initially overvalue firms with high predicted target-price bias and that removing predictable bias improves the investment usefulness of target prices.

Main role: The trading-strategy results are explicitly highlighted in the abstract and introduction as evidence of economic significance: a low-bias minus high-bias strategy earns about 6% over six months.
Settings.H1597: Section V, Table 7 Panels A-C, PDF pp. 20-22.
Settings.G1598:
Treatment: EPO: indicator equal to 1 if the controlling shareholder’s last name is part of the firm name, 0 otherwise. This is intended to proxy stronger owner identifiability/exposure through disclosure.

Method: The paper’s main German-sample specification is a cross-sectional linear probability / linear regression design estimated by OLS with industry-by-county fixed effects and county-clustered standard errors. The treatment is whether the firm is eponymous (the controlling owner’s surname appears in the firm name). The authors interpret the coefficient on EPO as the effect of stronger owner exposure on disclosure avoidance after the 2006 German enforcement shift made disclosure mandatory. Controls include leverage, size, tangibility, cash, ownership concentration, age, missing-sales indicator, and industry concentration. This is not DiD because the reported main specification uses only one post-reform cross section and compares eponymous versus noneponymous local-industry peers; identification comes from within county×industry comparisons conditional on observables and FE, with remaining concern that naming is endogenous to unobservables.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-sectional variation in whether a private German firm is named after its controlling owner, compared within narrow county×industry cells after the 2006 enforcement reform. The endogeneity concern is that eponymous naming may correlate with omitted owner, firm, or local characteristics that also affect disclosure. The paper argues that conditioning on local-industry fixed effects and firm controls helps isolate owner privacy concerns, but causal interpretation still relies on selection-on-observables / fixed-effects arguments rather than an exogenous shock to eponymy.

Setting: In the main German sample, the authors interpret eponymy as increasing owner exposure and thereby causing greater disclosure avoidance. Relative to noneponymous local-industry peers, eponymous firms are estimated to be 0.6–0.8 percentage points more likely not to disclose before enforcement (Table 2 cols. 1–2: 0.008 and 0.006), to disclose fewer items once forced to disclose (col. 3: 0.007 on log undisclosed items), and to be 0.4 percentage points more likely to withhold net income information (col. 4: 0.004). These estimates are from OLS/LPM specifications with county×industry fixed effects and controls, and they form the core evidence for the paper’s claim that owner-level privacy concerns dampen firm-level disclosure.

Main role: These are the central results supporting the paper’s headline claim in the abstract, introduction, results, and conclusion that eponymous firms are more opaque and avoid disclosure more.
Settings.H1598: Section IV, “Eponymous Firms’ Disclosure Avoidance,” Table 2 columns (1)–(4), PDF pp. 8–10.
Settings.G1599:
Treatment: EPO: indicator equal to 1 if the controlling shareholder’s surname is in the firm name.

Method: The paper re-estimates the main German extensive-margin result on a propensity-score-matched sample of eponymous and noneponymous firms. Matching is nearest neighbor, no replacement, caliper = 0.0001, based on a propensity score from controls plus county and industry fixed effects; the outcome model then estimates No Disclosure on the matched sample with industry-by-county fixed effects and county-clustered standard errors. The treatment remains eponymy. This is a matching-based causal robustness analysis intended to compare more similar treated and control firms.

Identification: Identification relies on selection on observables: after matching eponymous firms to observably similar noneponymous firms on estimated propensity scores, the remaining disclosure difference is interpreted as due to eponymy/owner exposure. The concern is residual imbalance on unobserved determinants of naming and disclosure.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors match eponymous firms to similar noneponymous peers and still find that eponymy increases disclosure avoidance. In the matched sample, the EPO coefficient on No Disclosure is 0.006 (Table 2, col. 5), very similar to the baseline. This supports the paper’s central claim that the main association is not driven solely by observable differences across firms.

Main role: The authors present this as corroborating robustness for the main finding rather than the primary identification strategy.
Settings.H1599: Section IV, Table 2 column (5) and Table 1 Panel B, PDF p. 9–10.
Settings.G1600:
Treatment: Within-firm variation in EPO over time: indicator equal to 1 when the firm is named after the controlling owner, 0 otherwise, observed in panel years 2001–2006 for firms with constant ownership structure.

Method: The paper estimates a panel regression for years 2001–2006 on firms with constant ownership structure, using firm and year fixed effects and clustering at the firm level. The treatment is time variation in EPO within firm, arising from firm name changes or ownership changes; the sample is restricted to firms without change in control. The dependent variable is a panel nondisclosure indicator equal to 1 if a firm discloses no financial information in a given year. The authors interpret this within-firm FE estimate as evidence that becoming eponymous increases nondisclosure.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm changes in eponymy over time, netting out time-invariant firm heterogeneity with firm FE and common shocks with year FE. The main endogeneity concern is that changes in EPO may themselves be induced by changing disclosure incentives or other time-varying shocks correlated with nondisclosure.

Setting: Using a 2001–2006 panel with firm and year fixed effects, the authors show that within a firm, eponymy is associated with higher nondisclosure. The Table 2, column (6) coefficient is 0.058, implying a 5.8 percentage point increase in the probability of disclosing no financial information when the firm is eponymous. The authors use this within-firm result as stronger corroboration that owner exposure through naming affects disclosure behavior.

Main role: This is a robustness design meant to bolster the main finding by exploiting within-firm variation rather than cross-sectional comparisons.
Settings.H1600: Section IV, discussion of within-firm variation and Table 2 column (6), PDF p. 9–10.
Settings.G1601:
Treatment: EPO interacted with one moderator at a time: common equity (standardized log equity), HIGH GAP indicator for owner firm-specific wealth relative to county income above median, standardized leverage, LOW GINI indicator, LEFTWING vote share, and RURAL indicator.

Method: The paper estimates cross-sectional interaction regressions in the German sample, using the same OLS/LPM framework with county×industry or state×industry fixed effects and county-clustered standard errors, to test whether the effect of eponymy on No Disclosure varies with owner wealth, relative wealth, leverage, local inequality, left-wing political sentiment, and rurality. Each column extends Equation (1) by adding one interaction. The treatment of interest is the interacted effect of eponymy with these moderators.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional comparisons of how the eponymy–nondisclosure relation differs across observable information-sensitivity and local-environment measures, conditional on controls and fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that these moderators may capture other omitted determinants of disclosure; the paper interprets the interaction patterns as consistent with privacy concerns rather than alternative channels.

Setting: The paper argues that eponymy causes more disclosure avoidance especially when disclosure is more personally sensitive or socially costly. In Table 3, the interaction of EPO with firm equity is 0.003, with HIGH GAP is 0.007, with leverage is 0.003, with LOW GINI is 0.009, with LEFTWING is 0.003, and with RURAL is 0.007. The authors interpret these positive interaction coefficients as evidence that owner privacy concerns are stronger when disclosure reveals higher or more salient wealth, higher indebtedness, and in environments where social comparison, anticapitalist sentiment, or identifiability are stronger.

Main role: These heterogeneity results are emphasized in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion as core evidence that privacy concerns intensify when disclosure reveals socially stigmatized information and in social environments where norms matter more.
Settings.H1601: Section IV, “Breadth of the Effect of Owner Privacy Concerns on Firm Disclosure,” Table 3 columns (1)–(6), PDF pp. 10–12.
Settings.G1602:
Treatment: EPO: indicator equal to 1 if the firm is named after a shareholder/controlling owner, following the paper’s international implementation in Amadeus.

Method: The paper estimates international cross-sectional OLS regressions using country-region and industry fixed effects, controls, and clustering at the country-region level. The treatment is EPO, and outcomes are the number of undisclosed items overall and by item category. The design parallels the German intensive-margin analysis but in a 13-country European sample. The authors interpret the EPO coefficient as the effect of owner exposure through firm naming on disclosure opacity internationally.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in eponymy within country-region×industry cells, conditional on controls. The main concern is omitted cross-country and local institutional factors correlated with both naming and opacity; country-region and industry FE absorb some of this, but the design remains observational.

Setting: In the international sample of more than 1.2 million private firms from 13 European countries, the authors find that eponymous firms disclose less information. Table 4 Panel A reports an EPO coefficient of 0.110 on the overall undisclosed-items measure, 0.004 on undisclosed equity items, and 0.120 on undisclosed profit-and-loss items, with little difference for asset items. The paper interprets this as showing that owner exposure through eponymy reduces disclosure internationally, particularly for wealth- and performance-related information.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion highlight international evidence as showing external validity and that privacy concerns are stronger in insider-oriented settings; the base international EPO effect is an important supporting pillar.
Settings.H1602: Section IV, “International Evidence on Privacy Concerns and Firm Disclosure,” Table 4 Panel A columns (1)–(5), PDF pp. 12–13.
Settings.G1603:
Treatment: EPO interacted one at a time with RURAL, FSI (financial secrecy), STOCK MARKET SIZE, ANTI-SELF-DEALING, DISTRUST, and IDENTIFIABILITY in the international sample.

Method: The paper estimates international cross-sectional interaction regressions using the same country-region and industry fixed-effects framework to test whether the effect of EPO on undisclosed items varies with country-level rurality, financial secrecy, stock market size, anti-self-dealing protections, distrust, and public identifiability/searchability of company records. Standard errors are clustered at country-region level. These are interaction-based causal robustness analyses on the intensive disclosure margin.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-sectional heterogeneity in how the eponymy-opacity relation varies with country-level institutions and environments after controlling for country-region and industry fixed effects. Endogeneity concerns remain because institutional variables may proxy for other determinants of private-firm reporting.

Setting: The international heterogeneity tests show that eponymous owners are especially opaque in environments where privacy concerns should be stronger. Table 4 Panel B reports positive interaction coefficients of 0.023 for EPO×RURAL, 0.016 for EPO×FSI, −0.030 for EPO×Stock Market Size (consistent with more opacity in smaller stock-market/outsider-poor settings), −0.011 for EPO×Anti-Self-Dealing, 0.061 for EPO×Distrust, and 0.004 for EPO×Identifiability. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that owner privacy concerns rise in insider-oriented, secretive, distrustful, and more searchable environments.

Main role: These results are highlighted in the abstract and conclusion as showing that privacy concerns are stronger in insider-oriented settings with higher secrecy and distrust.
Settings.H1603: Section IV, “International Evidence on Privacy Concerns and Firm Disclosure,” Table 4 Panel B columns (1)–(6), PDF pp. 13–14.
Settings.G1604:
Treatment: Owner-exposure/privacy variables: SINGLE (single-owner firm indicator), SAME ZIP (majority owner resides in same zip code as firm), OWNER AGE (log age of majority owner), NO ENTRY (majority owner has no telephone-book entry), alongside EPO.

Method: The paper estimates German cross-sectional OLS/LPM regressions with industry-by-county fixed effects to test whether owner characteristics other than eponymy causally affect disclosure avoidance. In Table 5 column (1), No Disclosure is regressed on EPO plus SINGLE, SAME ZIP, OWNER AGE, and NO ENTRY, with the usual firm controls and county-clustered standard errors. The authors treat these owner characteristics as additional proxies for exposure/privacy concerns affecting public disclosure.

Identification: Identification is cross-sectional conditional association with fixed effects and controls. The endogeneity concern is that each owner characteristic may capture other mechanisms besides privacy; the authors acknowledge alternative explanations and present the results as corroborating rather than definitive.

Setting: As corroborating evidence, the authors show that several owner characteristics associated with greater identifiability or stronger privacy preferences also predict more nondisclosure. In Table 5 column (1), SINGLE is 0.012, SAME ZIP is 0.005, OWNER AGE is 0.038, and NO ENTRY is 0.007, all positive and significant, while EPO remains positive. The paper interprets this as evidence that privacy concerns can arise through multiple owner dimensions beyond eponymous firm naming.

Main role: This is corroborating evidence that privacy concerns manifest through multiple owner dimensions, not a primary identifying result.
Settings.H1604: Section IV, “Corroborating Evidence on the Importance of Privacy Concerns for Public Disclosure,” Table 5 column (1), PDF p. 15–16.
Settings.G1605:
Treatment: EPO indicator equal to 1 if the firm is named after the controlling owner.

Method: The paper estimates a cross-sectional OLS/LPM regression with industry-by-county fixed effects where the outcome is private financial-statement availability at a rating agency (FS Availability). The treatment is EPO. This is used to contrast public versus private disclosure responses. The authors interpret the null EPO coefficient as evidence that eponymy does not reduce private disclosure to intermediaries, supporting the privacy-based interpretation of public opacity.

Identification: Identification is from cross-sectional variation in eponymy conditional on controls and industry×county fixed effects. The key assumption is that, absent privacy concerns specific to public exposure, eponymous and noneponymous firms would differ similarly in private disclosure; the null result is interpreted as inconsistent with alternative quality-based explanations.

Setting: To distinguish public from private disclosure, the authors test whether eponymous firms are also less likely to share extensive financial information with a rating agency. In Table 5 column (2), the EPO coefficient on FS Availability is 0.003 and statistically insignificant, indicating no detectable private-disclosure difference. The paper uses this null result to argue that eponymous firms’ greater opacity is specific to public disclosure and thus plausibly rooted in privacy concerns.

Main role: This is a corroborating placebo-style comparison intended to show that privacy concerns are specific to public disclosure rather than all disclosure.
Settings.H1605: Section IV, Table 5 column (2), PDF p. 15–16.
Settings.G1606:
Treatment: Interaction of EPO (eponymous firm indicator) and No disclosure (firm had avoided disclosure pre-enforcement), capturing eponymous firms particularly exposed by the enforcement change.

Method: The paper estimates a cross-sectional linear probability model with industry-by-county fixed effects for majority-owned firms, where the outcome is whether the firm changes its name between 2008 and 2010. The key treatment is the interaction EPO × No disclosure, alongside EPO and controls. The authors interpret this as the effect of being previously eponymous and previously nondisclosing on the probability of changing the firm name after mandatory disclosure enforcement, i.e., avoiding owner exposure by dropping eponymy.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional variation in prior nondisclosure and eponymy after the 2006 enforcement change. The endogeneity concern is that name changes may reflect other contemporaneous firm changes; the paper restricts to firms without owner change and interprets the interaction as avoidance of owner exposure induced by mandatory disclosure.

Setting: The authors show that eponymous firms that had previously avoided disclosure are more likely to change their names after public disclosure becomes effectively mandatory. In Table 5 column (3), the interaction EPO × No disclosure is 0.036, while EPO alone is −0.048 and No disclosure is not separately shown in that column’s coefficient list beyond controls; the text states this positive interaction is consistent with reducing exposure after 2006. This response is central to the paper’s argument that owners actively adjust firm naming to preserve privacy once opacity is no longer feasible.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly highlight that when forced to disclose, eponymous owners more frequently change their firms’ names. This is one of the paper’s central behavioral responses.
Settings.H1606: Section IV, Table 5 column (3), PDF pp. 15–17.
Settings.G1607:
Treatment: POST indicator equal to 1 for years of incorporation after 2006 and 0 otherwise, capturing exposure to the mandatory-disclosure regime at the naming stage for newly founded firms.

Method: The paper studies newly incorporated firms around the 2006 enforcement reform and estimates a linear model where the outcome is EPO and the treatment is POST, an indicator equal to 1 for incorporation years after 2006 and 0 before. The regression includes industry-by-county fixed effects and controls. This is a conventional before/after comparison interpreted as the effect of the post-enforcement regime on the propensity to choose an eponymous firm name for new firms.

Identification: Identification comes from comparing the share of newly incorporated firms that are eponymous before versus after the 2006 enforcement reform, conditional on controls and industry×county fixed effects. The causal concern is that other secular changes in naming practices could coincide with the reform; the authors argue there is no similar pre-trend decline and interpret POST as the effect of mandatory disclosure on naming choices.

Setting: For newly incorporated firms, the paper finds that mandatory disclosure reduced the likelihood of choosing an eponymous name. In Table 5 column (4), the coefficient on POST is −0.017, indicating a 1.7 percentage point lower probability that a new firm is named after its owner in the post-2006 regime. The authors interpret this as direct evidence that anticipated public disclosure leads owners to avoid eponymy ex ante to protect privacy.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that newly founded firms are less likely to be eponymous after the 2006 reform, making this a central behavioral response result.
Settings.H1607: Section IV, Table 5 column (4), PDF pp. 15–17.
Settings.G1608:
Treatment: EPO indicator, and in some columns EPO interacted with standardized ROE or RATING; subsamples restrict governance structure (controlling owners only, single owners, owner-managers).

Method: The paper estimates a series of German cross-sectional OLS/LPM robustness regressions with industry-by-county fixed effects to test whether the main EPO effect survives controls for alternative explanations related to firm quality and agency problems, and in restricted subsamples. These include benchmarking against firms with other personal last names in firm names, interactions EPO×ROE and EPO×RATING, and restricting to controlling-owner, single-owner, and owner-manager subsamples. The treatment remains EPO or its interaction with quality proxies.

Identification: Identification is observational, relying on fixed-effects comparisons and sample restrictions to hold more alternative mechanisms constant. The purpose is not new identification but to test whether the main eponymy effect plausibly survives quality- and agency-based confounds.

Setting: The paper shows that the positive effect of eponymy on nondisclosure survives several robustness tests against alternative mechanisms. In Table 6, EPO remains positive when compared to firms with another personal last name in the firm name (0.005), when interacted with ROE (EPO 0.006; EPO×ROE 0.004), when interacted with credit rating (EPO 0.008; EPO×RATING 0.006), and in subsamples of controlling-owner, single-owner, and owner-manager firms (EPO coefficients 0.008, 0.007, and 0.007). The authors interpret these results as evidence that firm quality and agency-conflict differences do not explain the main opacity finding.

Main role: These are substantive robustness tests used to argue against alternative explanations, not the paper’s main design.
Settings.H1608: Section IV, “Alternative Explanations Related to Firm Quality and Agency Issue Differences,” Table 6 columns (1)–(6), PDF pp. 17–19.
Settings.G1609:
Treatment: Participation in the USPTO telecommuting program (Patents Hoteling Program), coded as an indicator equal to 1 for examiner-months after the examiner starts telecommuting and 0 otherwise. This is a binary switch-on exposure to telecommuting status, not telecommuting intensity.

Method: The main design is an examiner-month panel difference-in-differences estimated by OLS: % New Cites_it = b0 + b1 Treatment_it + examiner fixed effects + year-month fixed effects + GS-level fixed effects + tenure fixed effects + e_it, with standard errors clustered by examiner. Treatment equals 1 for months after an examiner enters the Patents Hoteling Program (PHP) and 0 before; never-telecommuters are always 0. The paper reports the full-sample DiD, a version excluding months t-2 through t+2 around telecommuting, a 6-month pre/6-month post window, dynamic lead-lag event-study coefficients, and a telecommuters-only before/after specification. The identifying argument is parallel trends between telecommuters and nontelecommuters conditional on examiner, calendar-month, rank, and tenure effects; the paper notes remaining endogeneity concerns from nonrandom telecommuting choice.

Identification: Identification comes from within-examiner changes in outcomes when an examiner transitions into telecommuting, compared with nontelecommuting examiners over the same calendar months. Examiner fixed effects absorb time-invariant examiner heterogeneity; year-month fixed effects absorb aggregate shocks; GS-level and tenure fixed effects absorb changes in constraints and experience. The key concern is endogenous selection into telecommuting and possible time-varying omitted variables correlated with telecommuting timing; the paper assesses this with event-study pretrends, matched comparisons, early-adopter subsamples, and IV in separate settings.

Setting: Using examiner-month DiD regressions, the paper estimates that entering telecommuting raises the share of new prior-art citations. In Table 2 Panel A, the Treatment coefficient is 0.013 in the full sample, 0.016 when excluding months t-2 through t+2 around telecommuting, and 0.007 in a +/-6 month window. In Table 2 Panel B, telecommuting raises the count of new citations by 0.753 per examiner-month. The paper interprets these as causal effects of telecommuting on information acquisition under a parallel-trends assumption, and this is the central empirical result of the article.

Main role: This is the paper's core design for the headline claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that telecommuting increases examiners' acquisition of new information.
Settings.H1609: Section III 'Primary Analyses'; Equation (1); Table 2 Panels A and B; Figures 1-3; Table 9 Panel A cols. (1)-(3) and Panel B col. (2); PDF pp. 7-10 and 20-21.
Settings.G1610:
Treatment: Telecommuting status after entry into the PHP, interacted with an above-median Art Unit work-hours indicator to estimate heterogeneity in the telecommuting effect by time pressure.

Method: This setting estimates heterogeneous DiD effects of telecommuting by preexisting Art Unit time pressure. The OLS specification interacts Treatment with High Art Unit Work Hours, where High Art Unit Work Hours is an indicator for above-median Art Unit examining hours per examiner in a year. Two versions use total work hours and overtime work hours. The regression includes examiner fixed effects, year-month fixed effects, GS-level fixed effects, tenure fixed effects, and examiner-clustered standard errors.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-examiner before/after telecommuting compared across Art Units with high versus low work-hour pressure, netting out time-invariant examiner heterogeneity and common time shocks. The interaction is interpreted as showing larger causal telecommuting effects where preexisting time pressure is greater. This relies on the same DiD parallel-trends logic as the main design plus the assumption that differential trends by Art Unit work-hours status are not driving the interaction.

Setting: The paper finds that telecommuting increases information acquisition more for examiners facing greater time pressure. In Table 3, the baseline Treatment coefficient is 0.009 when time pressure is measured using total Art Unit work hours and 0.008 using overtime hours, while the interaction Treatment × High Art Unit Work Hours is 0.009 and 0.010, respectively. The author interprets this as evidence that reduced time pressure is an important channel through which telecommuting raises acquisition of new information.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that telecommuting's effect is greater for employees under greater time pressure; this table directly supports that central heterogeneity claim.
Settings.H1610: Section III 'Time Pressure and New Information Acquisition'; Equation (2); Table 3; PDF pp. 10-12.
Settings.G1611:
Treatment: Telecommuting status after PHP entry, interacted with an above-median Art Unit size indicator capturing larger pre-telecommuting workplace environments and presumed greater workplace distractions.

Method: This setting estimates heterogeneous DiD effects of telecommuting by office distraction exposure proxied by Art Unit size. The OLS regression interacts Treatment with High Art Unit Size, an indicator for above-median number of examiners in the focal examiner's Art Unit-month. The regression includes examiner, year-month, GS-level, and tenure fixed effects, with standard errors clustered by examiner.

Identification: Identification uses within-examiner before/after telecommuting variation and cross-sectional heterogeneity by whether the examiner was in a larger Art Unit, interpreted as a proxy for greater interruptions and background noise at the office. Fixed effects absorb examiner-level and time-level confounds, but the paper notes that Art Unit size is only a noisy proxy and may capture other unobservables such as differences in application mix.

Setting: In Table 4, the telecommuting effect on Percent New Cites is concentrated among examiners in larger Art Units. The coefficient on Treatment alone is 0.003 and statistically insignificant, whereas the interaction Treatment × High Art Unit Size is 0.014 and statistically significant. The paper interprets this as evidence that telecommuting raises information acquisition especially for employees previously exposed to greater workplace distractions.

Main role: The abstract states that the effect is greater for employees experiencing greater workplace distractions before telecommuting; this is the main test of that mechanism.
Settings.H1611: Section III 'Art Unit Size and Information Acquisition'; Equation (3); Table 4; PDF pp. 11-13.
Settings.G1612:
Treatment: Telecommuting status after PHP entry, interacted with Purposefully Unpromoted, a binary proxy for being less responsive to USPTO incentives and potentially more likely to shirk.

Method: This setting estimates heterogeneous DiD effects of telecommuting by examiners' responsiveness to the organization's incentive system. The OLS regression interacts Treatment with Purposefully Unpromoted, an indicator equal to 1 for examiners who remain at GS-12 for two years or more. The model includes examiner fixed effects, year-month fixed effects, GS-level fixed effects, tenure fixed effects, and examiner-clustered standard errors.

Identification: The setting compares within-examiner changes around telecommuting between examiners classified as purposefully unpromoted and others. The interpretation is that telecommuting's effect differs by incentive responsiveness. Identification inherits the DiD assumptions from the main design and additionally assumes the Purposefully Unpromoted classification captures heterogeneity in responsiveness rather than omitted differential time trends.

Setting: Table 5 shows that telecommuting's average positive effect on information acquisition is reversed for examiners deemed least responsive to incentives. The Treatment coefficient is 0.021, but the interaction Treatment × Purposefully Unpromoted is -0.029, implying a total effect of -0.008 for that group. The author interprets this as evidence that telecommuting can reduce information acquisition for a subset of employees likely to shirk or less responsive to organizational incentives.

Main role: The abstract highlights an adverse telecommuting consequence for employees least responsive to incentive systems; this specification directly produces that result.
Settings.H1612: Section III 'Examiners’ Responsiveness to Incentive Systems'; Equation (4); Table 5; PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G1613:
Treatment: Being a telecommuting examiner in the matched treated group, with the post period defined relative to the treated examiner's telecommuting month; the focal causal contrast is telecommuting adoption among matched comparable examiners.

Method: The paper first estimates a propensity score for telecommuting using a logit model with gender, ethnic-minority status, pretreatment averages of # New Cites, % New Cites, # Office Actions, Art Unit Size, and Overtime Art Unit Work Hours, then performs one-to-one nearest-neighbor matching without replacement with a caliper of 0.02, requiring matched controls to share the same USPTO entry year, technology center, and office location. On the matched sample of treatment and control examiners, the author estimates a DiD OLS with Post, Treated Examiner, and their interaction, including examiner, year-month, GS-level, and tenure fixed effects and clustering by examiner.

Identification: Identification relies on balancing observable pretreatment characteristics through propensity score matching and then applying a before/after comparison between matched treated and control examiners. The strategy addresses comparability on observables and some timing concerns but, as the paper notes, does not eliminate omitted-variable bias, self-selection, or endogeneity from unobserved time-varying factors.

Setting: Using a one-to-one propensity-score-matched sample, the paper continues to find a positive telecommuting effect on information acquisition. In Table 6 Panel C, the coefficient on Post × Treated Examiner is 0.030 for Percent New Cites. The result is used as supporting evidence that the main finding is not driven by strong functional-form dependence or poor comparability between telecommuters and nontelecommuters.

Main role: The paper presents this as a robustness check to mitigate concerns that telecommuters differ from nontelecommuters due to functional form misspecification, not as the primary identification design.
Settings.H1613: Section III 'Robustness Tests – Propensity Score Matching'; Equations (5) and (6); Table 6 Panels A-C; PDF pp. 14-17.
Settings.G1614:
Treatment: Telecommuting status after PHP adoption among examiners who elected to telecommute within one or two months of first becoming eligible under the two-year tenure rule.

Method: This robustness setting re-estimates the main DiD specification on restricted samples of telecommuters who adopt the PHP shortly after becoming eligible. The author limits the sample to examiners who telecommute within one month after the two-year tenure requirement, and separately within two months after that requirement, then estimates Equation (1) with examiner, year-month, GS-level, and tenure fixed effects and examiner-clustered standard errors.

Identification: The paper argues that conditioning on adoption shortly after the two-year eligibility threshold makes telecommuting timing more plausibly exogenous because eligibility timing is driven by hire date and all sampled examiners choose telecommuting. Identification still uses before/after and treated/control DiD logic, but on a more homogeneous subset where self-selected timing is constrained by the eligibility rule.

Setting: Restricting attention to early adopters after eligibility, the paper still finds telecommuting increases information acquisition. In Table 7 Panel A, the Treatment coefficient is 0.032 for examiners who telecommute within one month after the two-year requirement and 0.030 for those who telecommute within two months. These estimates are presented as robustness evidence against concerns that the main result is driven by endogenous telecommuting timing.

Main role: This is an endogeneity robustness analysis aimed at making telecommuting timing more plausibly exogenous; it supports but does not replace the paper's main design.
Settings.H1614: Section III 'Robustness Checks for Endogeneity – Plausibly exogenous assignment of examiners to telecommuting'; Table 7 Panel A; PDF pp. 16-18.
Settings.G1615:
Treatment: Actual telecommuting status after entering the PHP, treated as endogenous and instrumented by the number of other telecommuters in the same Art Unit in a given month.

Method: The paper estimates a 2SLS model in which the endogenous treatment is telecommuting status (Treatment) and the instrument is # Art Unit Telecommuter, the number of other telecommuting examiners in the focal examiner's Art Unit-month. The first stage regresses Treatment on # Art Unit Telecommuter; the second stage regresses % New Cites on the predicted Treatment. The specification includes examiner fixed effects, GS-level fixed effects, and tenure fixed effects, but not year-month fixed effects because the instrument has insufficient within-year-month variation; standard errors are clustered by examiner.

Identification: The instrument exploits peer telecommuting intensity within an Art Unit. The paper argues relevance because more telecommuting peers reduce fear of social isolation and stigmatization, making the focal examiner more likely to telecommute. Exclusion is argued from the isolated nature of U.S. patent examination, so other coworkers' telecommuting should affect the focal examiner's information acquisition only through the focal examiner's own telecommuting status. The first-stage F-statistic of 152.12 is reported as evidence against weak instruments.

Setting: The IV results continue to imply a positive effect of telecommuting on information acquisition. In Table 7 Panel B, the first-stage coefficient of # Art Unit Telecommuter on Treatment is 0.002, with an F-statistic of 152.12, and the second-stage coefficient of Treatment on Percent New Cites is 0.326 (t = 1.83, two-tailed p < 0.10). The paper interprets this as supporting the causal claim that telecommuting increases acquisition of new information even when telecommuting choice is treated as endogenous.

Main role: The IV is presented as an additional robustness check to complement the main DiD results and address endogenous telecommuting choice, not as the baseline design.
Settings.H1615: Section III 'Robustness Checks for Endogeneity – Instrumental variable estimation'; Table 7 Panel B; PDF pp. 17-19.
Settings.G1616:
Treatment: Participation in telecommuting (PHP) after adoption, coded as an indicator equal to 1 in examiner-months after telecommuting begins.

Method: In an additional analysis, the paper estimates the same examiner-month OLS DiD framework as Equation (1), but with Percent RCE as the dependent variable. The model includes examiner fixed effects, year-month fixed effects, GS-level fixed effects, tenure fixed effects, and examiner-clustered standard errors. Treatment is the post-telecommuting indicator for adopters and zero otherwise for never-telecommuters.

Identification: Identification again comes from within-examiner changes after telecommuting relative to nontelecommuters over the same months, controlling for examiner, time, rank, and tenure effects. The causal interpretation requires parallel trends in complaint rates absent telecommuting and no time-varying confounds correlated with telecommuting adoption. The paper presents this as a preliminary extension rather than a fully separate identification design.

Setting: As an additional outcome, the paper finds telecommuting improves one dimension of work quality. In Table 8, the Treatment coefficient on Percent RCE is -0.004, which the author describes as a 0.4 percent decrease in the proportion of Requests for Continued Examination. The paper interprets lower RCE incidence as improved quality because RCEs arise when applicants are dissatisfied with the review process and disagree with examiners' cited prior art.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion state that work quality improves following telecommuting; this is the main substantive quality outcome analysis.
Settings.H1616: Section IV 'Additional Analyses'; Equation (7); Table 8; PDF p. 19.
Settings.G1617:
Treatment: Participation in telecommuting (PHP) after adoption, coded as an indicator equal to 1 in examiner-months after telecommuting begins.

Method: This robustness/auxiliary setting uses the same DiD OLS framework as Equation (1) with examiner, year-month, GS-level, and tenure fixed effects and examiner-clustered standard errors, but changes the dependent variable to # Office Actions in one column and then includes # Office Actions as a control in a % New Cites regression in another column. The goal is to assess whether output increases explain the main information-acquisition effect.

Identification: Identification follows the same conventional DiD logic as the main specification. The first regression asks whether telecommuting changes output (# Office Actions). The second asks whether the telecommuting coefficient on % New Cites remains after conditioning on output. This does not fully separate hours worked from information acquisition, but is used to argue the main result captures an independent dimension of work.

Setting: Table 9 Panel B shows telecommuting raises output and still raises information acquisition after conditioning on output. The Treatment coefficient is 0.555 when # Office Actions is the outcome, and in the % New Cites regression that controls for # Office Actions, the Treatment coefficient remains 0.016 while # Office Actions enters at -0.004. The paper interprets this as evidence that telecommuting's effect on information acquisition is not merely a byproduct of increased output.

Main role: These are supporting robustness analyses intended to show that increased output does not mechanically drive the main telecommuting-information-acquisition result.
Settings.H1617: Section IV 'Robustness Tests – Controlling for Output'; Table 9 Panel B; PDF pp. 20-21.
Settings.G1618:
Treatment: Lagged Demand for Prd Mkt Info: the sum of absolute market-adjusted announcement-day returns of product-market announcements made by the focal firm's peer firms during the fiscal quarter, scaled by the total number of peers. Continuous measure; higher values proxy for greater managerial demand for product-market information.

Method: OLS panel regressions of managers' direct conference interactions on lagged proxies for managers' information demand, with firm fixed effects, calendar-year-quarter fixed effects, and fiscal-quarter fixed effects, plus extensive controls for investor information demand, capital-market incentives, firm characteristics, focal-firm announcements, information transfer from linked firms, and conference-peer counts. The implemented estimator is a linear fixed-effects regression on a continuous principal-component measure of interaction intensity (and related underlying interaction proxies discussed in the text). The paper interprets the coefficients as evidence that greater demand for product-market information causes managers to seek more direct interactions with institutional investors, while acknowledging the design is associational and cannot unambiguously establish causality.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm variation over time in peer-firm product-market announcement activity, after absorbing firm fixed effects and common time effects and conditioning on many observables that could affect conference behavior. The endogeneity concern is that peer activities may coincide with higher investor demand, more conferences, or time-varying industry attractiveness rather than managerial learning demand. The paper argues against this using controls, firm and time fixed effects, and supplemental subsamples of regular and non-industry-focused conferences, but explicitly acknowledges the evidence remains associational.

Setting: Using firm, calendar-year-quarter, and fiscal-quarter fixed effects, the paper finds that when managers have greater demand for product-market information—as proxied by peer firms' product-market announcements with larger absolute announcement returns—they engage in more direct interactions with institutional investors at conferences. In Table 3 Panel A, the coefficient on Demand for Prd Mkt Info is positive and significant across all specifications, ranging from 1.356 to 3.144; in conference quarters, column 4 reports 3.047, which the paper states implies that a one-standard-deviation increase in Demand for Prd Mkt Info is associated with a 0.072 standard deviation increase in Direct Interaction. This is a central associational result motivating the interpretation that managers seek interactions in order to learn from investors.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion present managers seeking more interactions when they need information as a core finding supporting the paper's central claim that managers learn from institutional investors through direct interactions.
Settings.H1618: Section 4.4, Table 3 Panel A, columns 1-6, especially column 4; PDF pp. 9-11.
Settings.G1619:
Treatment: Lagged Demand for Supply Chain Info: the sum of absolute market-adjusted announcement-day returns of product-market announcements made by the focal firm's direct suppliers and customers during the fiscal quarter, scaled by the total number of suppliers and customers. Continuous proxy for managerial demand for supply-chain information.

Method: OLS panel regressions of managers' direct conference interactions on lagged proxies for demand for supply-chain information, using firm fixed effects, calendar-year-quarter fixed effects, and fiscal-quarter fixed effects and the same control set as in the product-market specification. The implemented estimator is a linear FE model on the continuous Direct Interaction score. The paper interprets the coefficients as evidence that managers seek more investor interaction when they need information about upstream and downstream industries, while noting unresolved endogeneity and association-based inference.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-firm time-series variation in supply-chain-related announcement activity from suppliers and customers, conditional on firm and time fixed effects and extensive controls. The main threat is correlated shocks that simultaneously affect supply-chain news, investor demand, and conference activity. The paper addresses this through fixed effects, controls, and subsamples of regular and broad-themed conferences, but explicitly treats the evidence as associational rather than cleanly causal.

Setting: In fixed-effects panel regressions, higher demand for supply-chain information predicts more direct manager-investor interactions at conferences. Table 3 Panel B shows positive, statistically significant coefficients on Demand for Supply Chain Info in all specifications, ranging from 0.551 to 1.435; in conference quarters, column 4 reports 1.291, which the paper translates into a 0.031 standard deviation increase in Direct Interaction for a one-standard-deviation increase in treatment. The paper interprets this as evidence that managers seek interactions with institutional investors when they want to learn about supply-chain industries.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that managers seek more interactions when they need information about product markets and supply chains, making this a central finding.
Settings.H1619: Section 4.4, Table 3 Panel B, columns 1-6, especially column 4; PDF pp. 9-11.
Settings.G1620:
Treatment: Demand for Prd Mkt Info, as in the baseline incentive specification, estimated separately in high- versus low-product-market-knowledge investor subsamples defined by the median of Prd Mkt Hldgs.

Method: Cross-sectional heterogeneity version of the baseline firm fixed-effects panel regression: separate FE regressions are estimated in subsamples split by whether managers' institutional investors are more versus less knowledgeable about the focal firm's product market, measured from 13F holdings in peer firms. The estimator remains linear OLS with firm, calendar-year-quarter, and fiscal-quarter fixed effects and the baseline controls. The paper interprets differential coefficients as evidence that managers seek interactions specifically when investors are expected to possess the relevant information.

Identification: The strategy uses cross-sectional variation in the expected knowledge of a firm's current institutional investor base to test the learning mechanism. The underlying assumption is that higher Prd Mkt Hldgs captures expected investor expertise rather than other omitted characteristics that change the sensitivity of conference interactions to information demand. The paper notes endogeneity concerns and provides additional analyses with regular and non-industry-focused conferences and low correlations between demand and knowledge proxies.

Setting: The paper shows that the positive relation between managers' demand for product-market information and direct investor interactions is concentrated among firms whose institutional investors are more knowledgeable about the product market. In Table 4 Panel A, the coefficient on Demand for Prd Mkt Info is 2.446 (t=4.82) in the high-knowledge all-quarter sample versus 0.406 (t=1.21) in the low-knowledge sample, with an F-statistic of 11.573 (p<0.01); in conference quarters, the corresponding coefficients are 4.982 versus 1.632, with an F-statistic of 4.077 (p=0.04). The paper interprets this as mechanism evidence that managers seek interaction in order to learn from knowledgeable investors.

Main role: This heterogeneity test is important to the paper's mechanism: the relation should be stronger when investors are expected to be knowledgeable. The abstract explicitly notes stronger relations when managers expect investors to be knowledgeable.
Settings.H1620: Section 4.5, Table 4 Panel A, columns 1-4; Appendix C robustness using regular and non-industry-focused conferences; PDF pp. 11-12, 24-25.
Settings.G1621:
Treatment: Demand for Supply Chain Info, estimated separately in high- versus low-investor-supply-chain-knowledge subsamples based on the median of Supply Chain Hldgs.

Method: Cross-sectional heterogeneity FE regressions splitting the sample by investor supply of supply-chain information, proxied by institutional investors' holdings in the focal firm's supply-chain industries. The estimator remains linear firm fixed-effects OLS with calendar-year-quarter and fiscal-quarter fixed effects and the baseline controls. The intended interpretation is that learning-motivated interaction should be stronger when investors are likely to know more about supply chains.

Identification: The paper exploits cross-sectional differences in expected investor expertise in supply-chain industries to test whether managerial interaction responds more strongly to information demand in those firms. Identification is limited by possible omitted variables correlated with both investor holdings and conference choices; the paper mitigates concerns with fixed effects, controls, and supplementary subsamples, but treats the design as associational.

Setting: In Table 4 Panel B, the sensitivity of direct interactions to supply-chain information demand is stronger when managers' institutional investors are more knowledgeable about supply-chain industries. The coefficient on Demand for Supply Chain Info is 1.102 (t=4.44) in the high-knowledge all-quarter sample versus 0.278 (t=1.68) in the low-knowledge sample, with an F-statistic of 7.621 (p=0.01); in conference quarters, coefficients are 2.133 versus 0.860, with an F-statistic of 2.909 (p=0.09). The paper interprets this pattern as supporting learning from investors rather than simply responding to investor demand for access.

Main role: This is part of the paper's main mechanism evidence that the incentive result is stronger when managers expect investors to be knowledgeable about the needed information.
Settings.H1621: Section 4.5, Table 4 Panel B, columns 1-4; Appendix C robustness; PDF pp. 11-12, 24-25.
Settings.G1622:
Treatment: Interaction between price informativeness (either Price NonSync or PIN) and Q, estimated separately in high versus low Direct Interaction subsamples; the focal causal moderator is high direct conference interaction, defined as top tercile of Direct Interaction versus bottom two terciles.

Method: Firm-panel fixed-effects regressions of investment (capital expenditures plus R&D scaled by assets) on Tobin's Q, price informativeness, and their interaction, estimated separately in subsamples with high versus low direct conference interactions. The model follows Chen et al. (2007) and includes firm, calendar-year-quarter, and fiscal-quarter fixed effects, controls for firm size inverse, price informativeness, cash flow and its interaction with informativeness, and future stock returns. The paper uses the heterogeneous interaction coefficients across subsamples to argue that direct interactions help managers learn from prices and therefore make investment more sensitive to informative prices.

Identification: Identification follows the learning-from-prices literature: when prices are more informative, investment should be more sensitive to Q if managers learn from those prices. This paper's added step is to compare that sensitivity across high- and low-direct-interaction subsamples. The key assumption is that, conditional on controls and fixed effects, stronger INFO×Q sensitivity in the high-interaction sample reflects better extraction of information from prices through investor interactions rather than other differences across firms or quarters. Because interactions are not randomized, selection into high interaction remains a concern.

Setting: To test whether conference interactions help managers learn from prices, the paper estimates investment-to-price-sensitivity regressions separately for high- and low-interaction subsamples. In Table 5 Panel A, when price informativeness is measured by Price NonSync, the coefficient on INFO×Q is 0.257 (t=3.29) in the high-direct-interaction all-quarter sample versus 0.045 (t=0.59) in the low-interaction sample, with an F-statistic of 4.36 (p=0.04). Using PIN yields 0.919 (t=1.77) versus 0.078 (t=0.23). The paper interprets this as evidence that direct interactions help managers extract decision-relevant information from prices and then translate it into corporate investment.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion explicitly state that direct interactions help managers extract information embedded in stock prices and use it to make investments, making this a core consequence test.
Settings.H1622: Section 5.1.1, Eq. (2), Table 5 Panel A columns 1-8; PDF pp. 13-14.
Settings.G1623:
Treatment: Direct Interaction (continuous component score) or Deal Discussion (count of mentions of the pending acquisition in conference transcripts), each interacted with Ann CAR, the value-weighted bidder-target announcement cumulative abnormal return. These are continuous treatments/moderators of how much announcement returns predict completion.

Method: Cross-sectional linear probability / regression-adjustment style M&A completion regressions that relate whether a pending acquisition is completed to announcement returns, direct conference interactions, and their interaction, with year fixed effects and Luo (2005)-style deal controls. The paper estimates Eq. (3A) on transactions where the bidder attended a conference within 90 days after announcement and before completion/withdrawal. The design is not a panel FE design and does not use an external quasi-experiment; it is a controlled cross-sectional regression interpreted causally as evidence that conference interactions help bidders learn deal-relevant information from prices.

Identification: The identifying variation is cross-deal variation in bidder conference interactions and deal discussion after announcement, conditional on announcement CAR and standard deal controls. The logic is that if interactions help managers extract or obtain deal-relevant information, then announcement returns should better predict eventual completion when conference interaction is stronger. Main concerns are omitted deal quality, managerial discretion, and selection into discussing deals at conferences; the paper provides controlled regression evidence but no exogenous source of interaction intensity.

Setting: For announced acquisitions where the bidder attends an investor conference shortly after announcement, the probability that the deal closes becomes more tightly linked to announcement returns when the bidder interacts more with investors or discusses the deal more at conferences. In Table 5 Panel B, the coefficient on Direct Interaction×Ann CAR is 0.176 (t=1.91) and the coefficient on Deal Discussion×Ann CAR is 0.029 (t=2.37). The paper interprets these estimates as evidence that conference interactions help managers understand investors' valuation of the deal, either through better interpretation of price reactions or through direct feedback, and use that information in the completion decision.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize that conference interactions help managers use information in prices for acquisition decisions; this is one of the two principal 'learn from price' consequence tests.
Settings.H1623: Section 5.1.2, Eq. (3A), Table 5 Panel B columns 1-2; PDF pp. 14-15.
Settings.G1624:
Treatment: Negative Deal-related Qns or Positive Deal-related Qns: counts of investor questions in conference Q&A classified by Loughran-McDonald tone as more negative than positive or vice versa. Continuous count variables.

Method: Controlled cross-sectional regressions in the subsample of M&A transactions whose pending deal is explicitly discussed at investor conferences. The dependent variable is deal completion, and the regressors are counts of negative or positive deal-related investor questions, controlling for announcement CAR and standard deal controls with year fixed effects. The paper interprets these coefficients as evidence that the content of direct interactions provides information used by managers in the completion decision.

Identification: The strategy exploits variation in the tone of investor questions for deals discussed at conferences, conditional on announcement returns and deal controls, to see whether investor concerns predict completion. The causal interpretation is that investor questions reveal information to managers beyond what is already in prices. The key assumption is that question tone captures informative feedback rather than unobserved deal traits fully determining both the questions and the eventual outcome; this remains a correlational mechanism test.

Setting: In the subset of 197 acquisitions discussed at conferences, the paper finds that more negative investor questions predict a lower probability of completion. Table 5 Panel B column 3 reports a coefficient of 0.044 on Neg Deal-related Qns, which the text interprets as one additional negative investor question being associated with a 4.4% lower probability of deal completion; positive questions are not significantly related to completion in column 4 (coefficient 0.013, t=0.62). The paper interprets this as evidence that information conveyed in direct interactions—especially skeptical investor feedback—affects managers' acquisition decisions.

Main role: This is a more specific mechanism refinement within the broader M&A consequence test rather than a stand-alone central result in the abstract.
Settings.H1624: Section 5.1.2, Eq. (3B), Table 5 Panel B columns 3-4; PDF pp. 14-15.
Settings.G1625:
Treatment: Participating Insider: indicator equal to 1 if the insider executing the trade had participated in an investor conference on behalf of the firm before the transaction date, and 0 otherwise.

Method: Trade-level linear probability fixed-effects regressions of whether a trade occurs within seven days after a conference on whether the insider had participated in the conference, with either firm-quarter or firm-month fixed effects and controls for CEO status and conference information content (abnormal return and turnover). The sample contains opportunistic insider trades within two months before or after conferences. The paper interprets the within-firm-month comparison as evidence that conference participation increases the likelihood of using newly acquired information to trade after the conference.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm-quarter or within-firm-month comparisons across insiders and trade timing around the same conference environment. The firm-month fixed effects absorb all firm-level factors constant within a month, such as firm news and conference occurrence. The remaining assumption is that, conditional on controls, participating versus non-participating insiders are comparable apart from information gained at the conference; concerns remain about role differences or pre-existing information advantages, which motivate additional robustness and falsification tests.

Setting: Using opportunistic insider trades within two months of conferences and comparing insiders within the same firm-month, the paper finds that insiders who participated in the conference are more likely to trade in the seven-day post-conference window. Table 6 Panel A column 2 reports a coefficient of 0.065 (t=5.98) on Participating Insider, which the text interprets as participating insiders being 6.5% more likely to trade after the conference than non-participating insiders from the same firm-month. The paper views this as consistent with conference participation generating an information advantage that insiders act on shortly after the interaction.

Main role: The abstract mentions this as part of the insider-trading evidence, but the profitability regressions, not timing alone, carry the stronger substantive claim about expanded private information.
Settings.H1625: Section 5.2.1, Eq. (4), Table 6 Panel A columns 1-2; PDF pp. 16-18.
Settings.G1626:
Treatment: ParInsiderTradePOST: indicator equal to 1 if a trade was executed by an insider within seven days after that insider participated in an investor conference on behalf of the firm, and 0 otherwise. The control group combines trades by non-participating insiders and trades by participating insiders outside the seven-day post-conference window.

Method: Trade-level fixed-effects regressions of insider trading profits on an indicator for trades executed by participating insiders within seven days after attending a conference, with either firm-quarter or firm-month fixed effects and controls for CEO status and conference abnormal return/turnover. Outcomes are linear abnormal-return measures over the 30 days after the trade: Alpha30 and BHAR30. The implemented estimator is linear FE regression on continuous return outcomes. The paper interprets the coefficient as the causal effect of information acquired through direct interactions on insiders' private information and trading profits, while acknowledging broader observational limits.

Identification: The strategy compares post-conference trades by participating insiders to other insider trades within the same firm-quarter or firm-month, absorbing common firm-time shocks. The tight within-firm-month comparison is designed to control for unobserved firm news, operating changes, and conference-level factors. Remaining concerns are that participating insiders may systematically differ from non-participating insiders in rank or baseline information, or that managers time participation around private information. The paper addresses these with alternative control groups, regular-conference samples, and pre-conference falsification tests.

Setting: The paper's main insider-trading consequence test shows that trades executed by conference-participating insiders within seven days after attending a conference are more profitable than other trades of the same firm in the same month. In Table 6 Panel B, the firm-month fixed-effects estimate for Alpha30 is 0.030 (t=2.09), implying an incremental abnormal return of 0.03% per day over the 30 days after the trade; the corresponding BHAR30 estimate is 0.497 (t=1.89). The paper interprets this as evidence that direct interactions with institutional investors expand managers' private information sets.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion prominently feature the result that participating insiders' post-conference trades earn higher abnormal returns, interpreting this as evidence that conference interactions expand managers' private information set.
Settings.H1626: Section 5.2.1, Eq. (5), Table 6 Panel B columns 1-4; PDF pp. 16-18.
Settings.G1627:
Treatment: ParInsiderTradePOST indicator as in the main insider-profit specification, re-estimated under alternative sample definitions and control groups.

Method: Alternative-specification trade-profit regressions re-estimating Eq. (5) on narrower or different comparison samples: regular conferences only, participating versus non-participating insiders only, within participating insiders only, and trades within a (-7,+7) day window. The estimator remains linear fixed-effects regression with firm-quarter or firm-month fixed effects and the Table 6 controls. These are substantive robustness checks for the insider-learning interpretation.

Identification: The same within-firm-time identification logic as the main insider-profit regressions applies, but robustness samples are chosen to address specific threats: regular conferences reduce managerial timing discretion; alternative control groups assess whether the result depends on the control composition; a tight event window reduces contamination from other information arrivals. The design remains observational.

Setting: Robustness analyses in Table 7 show that the positive association between post-conference participating-insider trades and abnormal profits survives several alternative specifications. The coefficient on ParInsiderTradePOST for Alpha30 ranges from 0.018 to 0.093 across variants, and for BHAR30 from 0.543 to 1.725 in most specifications; for example, using only regular conferences, the firm-month estimate is 0.030 for Alpha30 and 0.566 for BHAR30. The paper interprets the persistence of positive post-conference trading profits across these designs as reinforcing the learning-from-investors interpretation.

Main role: These are robustness checks supporting the main insider-profit finding rather than separate headline results.
Settings.H1627: Section 5.2.2, Table 7 specifications A-D; PDF p. 18.
Settings.G1628:
Treatment: Participating Insider in timing regressions and ParInsiderTradePRE in profit regressions: indicators capturing whether the insider participated in the conference and whether the trade occurred within seven days before that participation.

Method: Falsification regressions that mirror the main insider-trading timing and profit specifications but move the treatment window to the seven days before conference participation. Panel A regresses the pre-conference timing indicator on Participating Insider; Panel B regresses Alpha30 or BHAR30 on ParInsiderTradePRE. The estimator remains linear FE regression with firm-quarter or firm-month fixed effects and the same controls. The paper uses these as substantive tests to distinguish learning after conferences from opportunistic pre-conference trading.

Identification: These regressions apply the same within-firm-time comparison as the main insider tests but in the pre-conference window. If results appeared pre-conference, they could reflect opportunistic timing rather than learning from interactions. The identifying assumption is unchanged, but the expected null or opposite sign serves as a diagnostic for the mechanism.

Setting: The pre-conference falsification tests do not support a story that participating insiders already possess superior tradable information before the conference. In Table 8 Panel A, Participating Insider is negatively associated with trading in the pre-conference window (firm-month coefficient -0.095, t=-7.51). In Panel B, ParInsiderTradePRE is not significantly related to Alpha30 or BHAR30 in three of four columns; for example, the firm-month Alpha30 coefficient is 0.012 (t=0.60) and BHAR30 is 0.193 (t=0.57). The paper interprets this pattern as supporting post-conference learning rather than pre-conference opportunism.

Main role: These are falsification tests aimed at ruling out managerial opportunism rather than central findings themselves.
Settings.H1628: Section 5.2.3, Table 8 Panels A-B; PDF pp. 19-20.
Settings.G1629:
Treatment: ParInsiderTradePOST indicator, estimated separately in subsamples split by the median of Demand for Prd Mkt Info or Demand for Supply Chain Info.

Method: Cross-sectional heterogeneity version of the insider-trading profit regression, estimated with firm-month fixed effects after splitting the sample by high versus low manager demand for product-market or supply-chain information. The estimator is the same linear FE regression as Eq. (5), but run in subsamples. The intended interpretation is that if conference learning concerns product-market or supply-chain information, post-conference insider-profit effects should be stronger when such information demand is high.

Identification: The analysis relies on cross-sectional differences in managers' information demand to sharpen mechanism. Within each subsample, firm-month fixed effects absorb common shocks, and differences in the ParInsiderTradePOST coefficient across high- and low-demand groups are interpreted as evidence about what information is learned.
