The main threat is that high-demand periods differ in other unobserved ways affecting insider profits, so this remains suggestive mechanism evidence.

Setting: Table 9 suggests that one source of post-conference insider trading advantage is product-market information. Main role: This is a mechanism-oriented cross-sectional analysis about the type of information learned, supporting but not constituting the headline result.
Settings.G1630:
Treatment: Direct Interaction factor score measuring frequency and intensity of manager-investor conference interactions. Continuous standardized score.

Method: Appendix fixed-effects panel regressions of management forecast frequency and revision frequency on Direct Interaction, with firm, calendar-year-quarter, and fiscal-quarter fixed effects and controls including earnings volatility, bid-ask spread, turnover, Reg FD disclosures, annual forecast share, and the baseline Table 3 controls. The interpretation is that acquired information prompts updating. As with the rest of the paper, unobserved shocks jointly affecting interactions and guidance behavior remain possible.

Settings.G1631:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 in years after a state has enacted the CPA 150-hour rule that raises education required for licensure from 120 to 150 credit hours; 0 otherwise. Binary policy adoption/exposure at the state-year level.

The key maintained assumption here is that absent enactment, treated states would have followed comparable trends in CPA entry after conditioning on the included fixed effects and state trends.

These estimates are central to the paper’s claim that stricter educational licensing requirements disproportionately reduce minority participation in the CPA profession.

Treatment: Event-time exposure to the state 150-hour rule under staggered adoption, estimated with modern heterogeneity-robust DiD corrections.

Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 in years after a state adopts the 150-hour rule; 0 otherwise.

Treatment: CFO signature size from notarized SEC statements, measured as area-per-letter of the handwritten signature; continuous proxy for CFO narcissism.

Method: Archival nonlinear regressions of internal control quality on CFO signature size. The paper estimates a binary logit for an indicator of ineffective internal controls and an ordinal logit for the number of material weaknesses, with two-digit SIC fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Controls include firm size, book-to-market, firm age, leverage, percentage of loss years, sales growth, inventories, audit fees, gender, and tenure. Because the implemented estimator is logit/ordinal logit rather than linear regression, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification relies on cross-sectional/panel variation in CFO signature size, conditional on observable controls and industry effects, to explain internal control weakness outcomes. The main endogeneity concern is that firms with weak controls may select certain CFOs or share omitted governance traits; the authors argue the CFO-specific pattern, robustness to CEO controls, and within-firm evidence elsewhere support the interpretation.

Setting: The paper interprets larger CFO signatures as weakening internal control quality. In Table 7, CFO signature size is positively associated with the probability that internal controls are ineffective (logit coefficient 0.641, p < 0.10) and with the number of material weaknesses (ordinal-logit coefficient 0.637, p < 0.10). These results are treated as substantive evidence that narcissistic CFOs prefer or create weaker oversight systems, contributing to lower reporting quality.

Main role: Weaker internal control quality is explicitly listed in the abstract as one of the main ways CFO narcissism lowers reporting quality.
Settings.H1648: Section 5.2.4, Table 7, CFO Narcissism columns, PDF p. 27.
Settings.G1649:
Treatment: CFO signature size from notarized SEC statements, measured as area-per-letter; continuous proxy for CFO narcissism.

Method: Archival binary logit regression of the probability of an accounting restatement on CFO signature size. The model includes two-digit SIC fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors, with controls for size, book-to-market, leverage, firm age, inventory and receivables changes, audit fees, cash-sales change, earnings/price, ROA, delta, vega, gender, and tenure. Because the implemented estimator is logit, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in CFO signature size across firm-years, controlling for predictors of restatements and industry fixed effects. The causal concern is omitted firm governance or selection into narcissistic CFOs; the paper uses extensive controls and additional within-firm and CEO-control robustness to strengthen the argument, but the core design remains observational.

Setting: The authors interpret larger CFO signatures as increasing the probability of financial restatements. In Table 8, the logit coefficient on CFO signature size is 0.455 (p < 0.05), which they view as objective ex post evidence that narcissistic CFOs are more likely to preside over misreporting that is later uncovered. This is one of the paper's central empirical findings.

Main role: The abstract emphasizes a higher probability of restatements as a key consequence of CFO narcissism, and restatements are presented as an important ex post validation of misreporting.
Settings.H1649: Section 5.2.5, Table 8, CFO Narcissism column; economic-significance discussion in footnote 36, PDF pp. 28-29.
Settings.G1650:
Treatment: Exposure to the appointment of a CFO with larger signature size, implemented as the interaction between CFO signature size (continuous, area-per-letter) and an indicator for years after that CFO's appointment.

Method: Within-firm pre/post CFO-appointment regressions comparing outcomes before a CFO is appointed with outcomes during that CFO's tenure as a function of the appointed CFO's signature size. The specification includes an After indicator for post-appointment years, CFO signature size, and their interaction, along with the same firm controls as in the central tests; standard errors are clustered by appointment period. For conservatism, the relevant coefficient is SignatureSize × D × Ret × After. The design is a within-firm before-versus-after comparison but not a conventional DiD with a separate untreated group.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-firm change from pre-appointment to post-appointment periods, interacted with the new CFO's signature size. The endogeneity concern is that cross-firm differences may drive the main results; this design reduces time-invariant firm confounding. The authors acknowledge two limitations: they do not observe predecessor CFO signature size, and internal controls cannot be tested because the relevant reports were unavailable pre-2004. The interpretation assumes CFO narcissism is not systematically assigned to firms in a way correlated with preexisting trends.

Setting: Using within-firm before-versus-after comparisons around CFO appointments, the paper interprets the arrival of a CFO with a larger signature as worsening reporting outcomes relative to the firm's pre-appointment period. In Table 9, SignatureSize × After is positive for absolute accruals (0.011, p < 0.01), accrual quality (0.008, p < 0.01), abnormal cash flows (0.016, p < 0.10), abnormal production costs (0.008, p < 0.05), and restatements (0.345, p < 0.01), while SignatureSize × D × Ret × After is −0.018 (p < 0.01), indicating less timely loss recognition after appointment. Abnormal discretionary expenses are an exception, turning negative (−0.032, p < 0.05). The authors present these within-firm results as important robustness evidence that their main archival findings are not driven by omitted firm-level characteristics.

Main role: The abstract notes that results are consistent for within-firm comparisons focusing on CFO changes; this robustness materially supports the central claim by addressing firm-level confounding.
Settings.G1651:
Treatment: CFO signature size measured as area-per-letter from notarized SEC signatures; continuous proxy for narcissism, estimated while controlling for an options-based overconfidence indicator.

Method: Robustness OLS regressions for accruals, real earnings management, and conditional conservatism that add an options-based overconfidence control following Hirshleifer, Low, and Teoh [2012]. The same linear specifications as the main CFO models are retained, with two-digit SIC fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors; for conservatism, both SignatureSize × D × Ret and Overconfidence × D × Ret are included. The focal treatment remains CFO signature size.

Identification: Same as the main archival OLS settings, but with additional control for executive overconfidence to address omitted-trait bias. The authors argue that if signature size merely captured overconfidence, the CFO signature-size coefficients should attenuate once the options-based overconfidence proxy is included; persistence of the coefficients supports a narcissism interpretation.

Setting: Controlling for an options-based proxy for executive overconfidence, the paper still interprets larger CFO signatures as worsening reporting quality. In Table 10 panel A, signature size remains positive and significant for absolute accruals (0.008, p < 0.01), accrual quality (0.004, p < 0.10), abnormal discretionary expenses (0.047, p < 0.10), abnormal production costs (0.035, p < 0.10), and the conservatism interaction SignatureSize × D × Ret (−0.071, p < 0.10), while abnormal cash flows remain positive but insignificant (0.010). These results are presented as robustness evidence that the main findings are not driven by overconfidence.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness test addressing whether narcissism effects are actually overconfidence effects, but it is not the primary design highlighted as the main archival evidence.
Settings.H1651: Section 5.2.7, Table 10 Panel A, columns for AbsAccruals, Accrual Quality, AbDisExp, AbCFO, AbProdCost, and E/P, PDF p. 33.
Settings.G1652:
Treatment: CFO signature size from notarized SEC statements, area-per-letter; continuous proxy for narcissism, controlling for options-based overconfidence.

Method: Robustness nonlinear regressions for internal controls and restatements that add the options-based overconfidence control. The same nonlinear specifications as the main models are used: binary logit for ineffective internal controls and binary logit for restatements, with two-digit SIC fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. The focal treatment remains CFO signature size, now estimated conditional on overconfidence.

Identification: Same observational identification as the main nonlinear archival models, but augmented with the overconfidence proxy to mitigate omitted-variable concerns about another executive trait driving the results.

Setting: When the authors control for options-based overconfidence, they continue to interpret larger CFO signatures as worsening oversight outcomes. In Table 10 panel A, the signature-size coefficient remains positive for ineffective internal controls (0.676, p < 0.10) and for restatements (0.515, p < 0.05). These robustness results support the paper's claim that the main findings are attributable to narcissism rather than overconfidence.

Main role: These are robustness checks aimed at ruling out overconfidence as an alternative explanation rather than the primary evidence.
Settings.H1652: Section 5.2.7, Table 10 Panel A, IneffControls and Restatement columns, PDF p. 33.
Settings.G1653:
Treatment: CFO signature size, area-per-letter from notarized SEC statements, estimated jointly with CEO signature size in the same regression and on the common sample. Continuous treatment proxy for CFO narcissism.

Method: Joint-sample robustness OLS regressions including both CFO and CEO signature size in the same linear model, restricting to firm-years where both signatures are observed. The paper estimates the same linear models for accruals, real earnings management, and conservatism as in the main analysis, but includes executive-specific controls for both CFOs and CEOs plus both signature-size variables together. Two-digit SIC fixed effects are used, except where noted elsewhere for non-linear models; standard errors are clustered by firm.

Identification: Identification relies on within-sample variation in CFO versus CEO signature size conditional on both executives' controls and firm characteristics. The key concern is that apparent CFO effects may reflect omitted CEO or firm traits; including both signatures simultaneously helps isolate the incremental role of CFO narcissism.

Setting: On the restricted sample where both CFO and CEO signatures are observed, the paper interprets CFO signature size as having an incremental adverse effect on reporting quality even after controlling for CEO signature size. In Table 11, CFO signature size remains positive and significant for absolute accruals (0.010, p < 0.01), accrual quality (0.008, p < 0.05), abnormal discretionary expenses (0.058, p < 0.10), abnormal cash flows (0.016, p < 0.10), abnormal production costs (0.048, p < 0.05), and the conservatism interaction CFOSignatureSize × D × Ret (−0.095, p < 0.10). The authors also report Z-tests showing CFO effects exceed CEO effects for several outcomes, supporting the claim that CFO traits matter more for financial reporting.

Main role: This is a major robustness check showing CFO effects survive controlling for CEO narcissism on a common sample; it materially supports but does not replace the main archival results.
Settings.H1653: Section 5.2.8, Table 11, linear-outcome columns (AbsAccruals, Accrual Quality, AbDisExp, AbCFO, AbProdCost, E/P), PDF pp. 34-35.
Settings.G1654:
Treatment: CFO signature size, area-per-letter from notarized SEC statements, estimated jointly with CEO signature size on the common sample as the focal proxy for CFO narcissism.

Method: Joint-sample robustness nonlinear regressions including both CFO and CEO signature size in the same model on the common sample. The paper estimates a binary logit for ineffective internal controls and a binary logit for restatements, with executive-specific controls for both CFO and CEO and industry fixed effects (one-digit SIC for internal controls because two-digit fixed effects prevent convergence). Standard errors are clustered by firm. Because the implemented estimators are nonlinear logits, this setting is classified as Other.

Identification: Identification uses common-sample variation in CFO signature size, controlling simultaneously for CEO signature size and both executives' controls, to separate CFO-specific from CEO-specific effects. The design addresses omitted-firm-trait concerns only partially, since it remains observational, but it sharpens the interpretation that the reporting-quality results are specifically tied to CFO narcissism.

Setting: When both CFO and CEO signature sizes are included together on the common sample, the paper still interprets CFO signature size as worsening internal control quality and increasing restatements. In Table 11, the CFO signature coefficient is 0.743 (p < 0.10) for ineffective internal controls and 0.649 (p < 0.05) for restatements, while the CEO coefficient is negative in both models. The reported Z-statistics indicate CFO effects are significantly larger than CEO effects, bolstering the paper's argument that CFO narcissism has the more important role in financial reporting quality.

Main role: This joint CFO/CEO specification is a robustness test reinforcing that the main CFO results are not simply picking up CEO or general firm characteristics.
Settings.H1654: Section 5.2.8, Table 11, IneffControls and Restatement columns, PDF pp. 34-35.
Settings.G1655:
Treatment: Capital gains tax rate applicable to investors at IPO date, mainly the long-term capital gains tax rate (LT TAX), measured as the maximum individual tax rate on net long-term capital gains; some specifications also include the short-term capital gains tax rate (ST TAX), the marginal rate on ordinary income for the highest bracket. Treatment is a continuous tax-rate level in percentage points, varying by tax regime over time.

Method: The authors estimate cross-sectional OLS regressions of IPO relative offer prices on capital gains tax rates over 1987–2010. The dependent variable is the log price-to-value ratio, where value is imputed from matched public firms following Purnanandam and Swaminathan (2004), using either EBITDA-based or sales-based multiples. The focal regressors are the short-term capital gains tax rate and/or the long-term capital gains tax rate. Regressions include IPO controls (VC backing, underwriter rank, price revision, spread, tech, recent market and IPO conditions, auditor, firm age, proceeds). Standard errors are adjusted by two-way clustering across year and 2-digit industry. Identification is observational and comes from time variation in tax regimes combined with cross-sectional controls; the authors explicitly worry about temporally correlated confounds and later run robustness checks.

Identification: The intended identifying variation is exogenous intertemporal variation in statutory capital gains tax rates across federal tax regimes, applied to IPO dates, controlling for observable IPO and market conditions and benchmarking offer prices to matched-firm valuation multiples. The endogeneity concern is that tax rates may proxy for other time-varying macro, market, or IPO-cycle conditions. The paper argues against this with controls, clustered SEs, monthly-average regressions, adjacent-regime tests, and tax-regime placebo-style controls, but identification remains regression adjustment rather than a quasi-experimental design.

Setting: Using 3,957 IPOs with matched-firm valuation data, the authors estimate OLS regressions of relative IPO offer price on capital gains tax rates and interpret the coefficients causally as tax capitalization. They find no robust effect of the short-term tax rate, but a negative effect of the long-term capital gains tax rate on IPO offer prices: for P/V_EBITDA the LT TAX coefficient is -5.500 (t=-8.373) when entered alone and -5.442 (t=-8.557) when entered with ST TAX; for P/V_Sales the LT TAX coefficient is -5.896 (t=-6.045) alone and -6.065 (t=-6.087) jointly. They translate this into a 1 percentage point increase in the long-term tax rate lowering relative offer price by about 0.232% to 0.249%. This setting directly supports the paper's central claim that long-term capital gains taxes reduce IPO proceeds through capitalization.

Main role: This is one of the paper's two central tests: the abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize that offer prices decrease in long-term capital gains taxes as evidence of tax capitalization.
Settings.H1655: Section 3.1 equation (1) and Section 4.1; Table 4 Panels A and B, cols. (1)-(3), PDF pp. 6, 9-10, 13.
Settings.G1656:
Treatment: TAXDIFF, the difference between the short-term capital gains tax rate and the long-term capital gains tax rate at the IPO date, measured in percentage points. This is a continuous tax spread, not a binary treatment.

Method: The authors estimate cross-sectional OLS regressions of IPO first-day underpricing on the spread between short-term and long-term capital gains tax rates (TAXDIFF) for 4,666 IPOs from 1987 to 2010. The specification includes the same set of IPO and market controls as in the offer-price regressions. Standard errors are clustered by year and 2-digit industry. The estimate is interpreted as the lock-in effect: a larger tax wedge between immediate sale and long-term holding increases the underpricing required to induce short-term selling.

Identification: Identification uses statutory time-series variation in the gap between short-term and long-term capital gains tax rates across IPO dates, with controls for IPO characteristics and market conditions. The endogeneity concern is that TAXDIFF may coincide with other macro or issuance-environment changes affecting underpricing. The authors address this with clustering, monthly-mean regressions, adjacent-regime comparisons, and business-cycle and clientele analyses, but the design remains observational regression adjustment with maintained exogeneity of tax-regime variation conditional on controls.

Setting: Using 4,666 IPOs, the authors regress first-day IPO underpricing on the short-term minus long-term capital gains tax spread and interpret the coefficient as a lock-in effect. In Table 6, TAXDIFF has a positive and significant coefficient of 0.519 (t=2.796), implying that a 1 percentage point increase in the spread raises underpricing by 0.519 percentage points. The authors further combine this with the capitalization estimates to argue that the net effect of a 1 percentage point increase in the long-term tax rate is a 0.27% to 0.287% increase in the first-day closing price. This setting is central to the paper's claim that capital gains taxes exacerbate IPO underpricing through investor lock-in.

Main role: This is the paper's other headline causal setting. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion stress that IPO underpricing increases in the short-term minus long-term tax rate differential as evidence of lock-in.
Settings.H1656: Section 3.1 equation (2) and Section 4.2; Table 6, PDF pp. 6, 11, 15.
Settings.G1657:
Treatment: Monthly mean capital gains tax rates in force in a given month, especially LT TAX and ST TAX, measured as continuous percentage rates. The intended treatment remains the long-term capital gains tax rate affecting investor pricing of IPOs.

Method: As a robustness check against time clustering, the authors re-estimate the offer-price capitalization regressions using monthly equally weighted averages rather than IPO-level observations. Each observation is a month with at least three IPOs; 249 monthly observations are available for the offer-price tests. The dependent variables remain monthly mean P/V_EBITDA and monthly mean P/V_Sales, with monthly means of the tax and control variables. Standard errors remain adjusted for clustering across years and industries.

Identification: The same observational tax-regime timing variation is used, but collapsing to month-level averages reduces the influence of months with many IPOs. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on monthly averaged controls, variation in tax rates across months is not just capturing other monthly confounders. This does not create new exogenous variation; it is a robustness exercise for temporal clustering concerns.

Setting: In month-level robustness regressions, the authors continue to find that offer prices fall with the long-term capital gains tax rate but not the short-term rate. In Table 7 Panel A, LT TAX is -4.265 (t=-4.681) for monthly mean P/V_EBITDA and -6.890 (t=-5.067) for monthly mean P/V_Sales, while ST TAX is insignificant. The authors interpret this as evidence that their capitalization result is not an artifact of time clustering in IPO issuance.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis meant to show that the main capitalization result is not driven by hot IPO months or uneven time clustering.
Settings.H1657: Section 5.1 Time clustering; Table 7 Panel A, PDF pp. 12, 17.
Settings.G1658:
Treatment: Monthly TAXDIFF, the short-term minus long-term capital gains tax rate in force during the month, measured continuously in percentage points.

Method: As a time-clustering robustness check, the authors re-estimate the underpricing lock-in regression using monthly equally weighted averages instead of IPO-level data. The sample comprises 211 monthly observations with at least three IPOs and complete data. The dependent variable is the monthly mean first-day underpricing and the treatment is the monthly tax spread TAXDIFF, with monthly means of controls. Standard errors are again adjusted for clustering across years and industries.

Identification: The strategy mirrors the main underpricing regression but averages variables by month, reducing influence of clustered issuance periods. The maintained assumption is that monthly tax-spread variation, conditional on monthly averaged controls, is not standing in for omitted monthly shocks. This is still observational regression adjustment.

Setting: Using monthly averaged data, the authors find that underpricing remains positively related to the capital gains tax spread. In Table 7 Panel B, the coefficient on TAXDIFF is 0.175 (t=1.657), marginally significant and directionally consistent with the main result. The authors conclude that time clustering is unlikely to explain the positive association between tax-rate spreads and IPO underpricing.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis supporting the main lock-in claim by addressing concern that hot IPO months mechanically receive more weight in IPO-level regressions.
Settings.H1658: Section 5.1 Time clustering; Table 7 Panel B, PDF pp. 12-13, 17.
Settings.G1659:
Treatment: Long-term capital gains tax rate LT TAX, measured continuously in percentage points within samples restricted to adjacent long-term tax regimes. Treatment remains the statutory long-term investor tax rate at IPO date.

Method: The authors estimate the capitalization regression on subsamples restricted to adjacent long-term tax regimes to show the result is not driven by distant historical periods. Panel A of Table 8 reports OLS offer-price regressions separately for IPOs in 1987–1997 versus 1997–2003, and 1997–2003 versus 2003–2010. Outcomes are P/V_EBITDA and P/V_Sales, controls match the main specification, and standard errors are clustered by year and industry.

Identification: By comparing only adjacent tax regimes, the authors try to limit contamination from long-run secular changes that might be correlated with taxes. Identification still relies on within-neighboring-period tax-rate changes and observable controls; the key assumption is that remaining adjacent-period differences do not confound the tax effect.

Setting: In adjacent-regime offer-price regressions, the negative association between long-term capital gains taxes and relative offer price remains. For 1987–1997 versus 1997–2003, LT TAX is -5.560 (t=-6.888) for P/V_EBITDA and -6.198 (t=-7.871) for P/V_Sales. For 1997–2003 versus 2003–2010, LT TAX is -3.666 (t=-3.650) for P/V_EBITDA and -3.419 (t=-2.973) for P/V_Sales. The authors interpret this as further evidence of tax capitalization in IPO offer prices.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis intended to show that capitalization appears locally around adjacent regime changes, not only over the full 24-year sample.
Settings.H1659: Section 5.3 Adjacent regime comparisons; Table 8 Panel A, PDF pp. 14, 18.
Settings.G1660:
Treatment: TAXDIFF, the short-term minus long-term capital gains tax rate spread, measured continuously in percentage points within samples restricted to adjacent tax regimes.

Method: The authors estimate underpricing regressions on subsamples limited to adjacent short-term or long-term tax regimes. Panel B of Table 8 reports OLS regressions of IPO underpricing on TAXDIFF for 1988–1990 versus 1991–1992, 1991–1992 versus 1993–2000, and 1987–1997 versus 1997–2003. Controls match the main model and standard errors are clustered by year and industry.

Identification: Restricting to adjacent regimes aims to remove spurious association from comparing very different eras. The intended identifying assumption is that within these neighboring periods, observed controls and the tax spread capture the main source of systematic variation in underpricing tied to tax lock-in. It remains nonexperimental regression adjustment.

Setting: The positive relation between the tax spread and underpricing persists in adjacent-regime samples. In Table 8 Panel B, TAXDIFF equals 1.407 (t=2.322) for 1988–1990 versus 1991–1992, 0.591 (t=2.094) for 1991–1992 versus 1993–2000, and 0.552 (t=2.335) for 1987–1997 versus 1997–2003. The authors interpret these estimates as evidence of lock-in that is not driven by broad comparisons across distant tax periods.

Main role: This is a robustness analysis for the main lock-in result, designed to show the positive TAXDIFF-underpricing relation appears in local adjacent-regime contrasts.
Settings.H1660: Section 5.3 Adjacent regime comparisons; Table 8 Panel B, PDF pp. 14-15, 18.
Settings.G1661:
Treatment: Long-term capital gains tax rate LT TAX (and ST TAX as control/specification component), measured continuously in percentage points; the substantive treatment is the long-term tax rate, estimated separately across investor-tax-sensitivity subsamples.

Method: The authors split the sample by inferred investor tax sensitivity and re-estimate the main offer-price capitalization regressions separately for 'tax-sensitive' and 'less tax-sensitive' investor clienteles. Tax sensitivity is based on the fraction of less tax-sensitive institutional holders (e.g., pension funds, endowments); firms are classified as more tax-sensitive if the fraction of tax-sensitive investors exceeds the sample median. Separate OLS regressions of P/V_EBITDA and P/V_Sales on ST TAX and LT TAX with controls are reported in Table 9 Panel A, with clustered standard errors.

Identification: The same observational tax-rate timing variation is used, but effects are estimated separately by investor clientele. The authors assume their ex post investor-tax-sensitivity classification proxies for who prices the IPO and that stronger effects among tax-sensitive investors are informative about mechanism. Endogeneity remains possible because clientele composition may correlate with omitted determinants of pricing.

Setting: When the sample is split by investor tax sensitivity, the negative effect of long-term capital gains taxes on offer prices is stronger for more tax-sensitive IPOs. In Table 9 Panel A, LT TAX is -6.561 (t=-7.431) for tax-sensitive investors versus -4.887 (t=-10.789) for less tax-sensitive investors using P/V_EBITDA; the paper reports an SUE test of difference with Chi2=3.01 (p=0.082). Similar patterns hold using P/V_Sales. The authors interpret this as mechanism-consistent evidence that tax capitalization is stronger when investors care more about taxes.

Main role: This is a heterogeneity test supporting the paper's mechanism that taxes matter more when investors are more tax sensitive.
Settings.H1661: Section 5.4 Tax-sensitive investors versus less tax-sensitive investors; Table 9 Panel A, PDF pp. 16, 19.
Settings.G1662:
Treatment: TAXDIFF, the spread between short-term and long-term capital gains tax rates, measured continuously in percentage points; estimated separately for tax-sensitive and less tax-sensitive investor subsamples.

Method: The authors split the sample by investor tax sensitivity and re-estimate the main underpricing lock-in regression separately for tax-sensitive and less tax-sensitive investor clienteles. TAXDIFF is regressed on IPO underpricing with the usual controls; results are reported in Table 9 Panel B with clustered standard errors.

Identification: Identification again comes from time variation in the tax spread, now interacted through separate subsamples by investor-tax-sensitivity proxies. The assumption is that the tax-sensitive classification meaningfully captures exposure to lock-in incentives; however, sample composition may itself be endogenous.

Setting: In Table 9 Panel B, the positive lock-in effect of the tax spread appears in both investor-clientele subsamples but is somewhat larger for tax-sensitive investors: TAXDIFF is 0.592 (t=2.560) for tax-sensitive investors and 0.492 (t=2.550) for less tax-sensitive investors. The authors interpret this as further evidence that tax-efficient trading incentives contribute to IPO underpricing, especially when investors are more tax sensitive, although they note the difference in magnitude is not statistically significant.

Main role: This heterogeneity analysis is presented as supporting evidence for the lock-in mechanism, showing stronger effects where investors should care more about tax timing.
Settings.H1662: Section 5.4 Tax-sensitive investors versus less tax-sensitive investors; Table 9 Panel B, PDF pp. 16, 19.
Settings.G1663:
Treatment: TAXDIFF, the short-term minus long-term capital gains tax spread in percentage points, estimated separately for firms whose institutional investors have longer versus shorter horizons. The treatment itself is continuous; horizon is a sample partition, not the focal treatment.

Method: To test the horizon mechanism behind lock-in, the authors identify institutional investor horizons from 13F portfolio churn following Gaspar, Massa, and Matos (2005), then split 1,930 IPOs into longer-horizon and shorter-horizon subsamples based on the annual median Turnover measure. They re-estimate the underpricing regression of UP on TAXDIFF with controls separately for the two subsamples, with clustered standard errors.

Identification: The tax-spread effect is estimated separately by ex post institutional investment horizon. The authors argue churn is persistent and therefore a useful proxy for ex ante investor horizon. The key assumption is that longer-horizon investor clienteles face stronger lock-in incentives and that other differences across the two subsamples do not fully account for coefficient differences.

Setting: Consistent with the lock-in mechanism, the tax-spread effect on underpricing is present only among IPOs with longer-horizon institutional investors. In Table 10, TAXDIFF is 0.517 (t=2.159) in the longer-horizon subsample and 0.280 (t=0.969) in the shorter-horizon subsample; the difference is reported as statistically significant (Chi2=3.8, p=0.052). The authors conclude that investors with long horizons demand a higher short-term selling price to recover extra tax cost, raising IPO underpricing.

Main role: This is a mechanism-oriented heterogeneity test: if lock-in matters, it should be stronger when investors are more likely to care about deferring gains into long-term status.
Settings.H1663: Section 5.5 Investor horizons and the lock-in effect; Table 10, PDF pp. 17, 19-20.
Settings.G1664:
Treatment: TAXDIFF, the short-term minus long-term capital gains tax rate spread in percentage points, estimated separately across market-state and business-cycle subsamples.

Method: The authors test whether the lock-in effect varies over business cycles by splitting the full IPO sample and re-estimating the underpricing regression on TAXDIFF separately for down versus boom markets and for recession versus non-recession periods. Down/boom markets are classified by the sign of the past 12-month market return; recession periods follow NBER dates. Table 11 reports OLS coefficients with the standard IPO controls and clustered standard errors.

Identification: The same observational tax-spread variation is used, but the sample is partitioned by market state or recession status. The identifying logic is mechanism-based: if lock-in operates through capital gains realization incentives, the effect should weaken in down markets or recessions when investors are more likely to have offsetting losses. Remaining concern is that these states may also alter IPO pricing through other channels.

Setting: The TAXDIFF-underpricing relation is weaker in adverse market states, consistent with weaker lock-in incentives when investors are more likely to hold capital losses. In Table 11, TAXDIFF is 0.302 (t=2.239) in down markets and 0.553 (t=2.779) in boom markets, with a reported difference significant at 5% (Chi2=4.419, p=0.0340). Using NBER business cycles, TAXDIFF is -0.074 (t=-0.434) in recessions and 0.661 (t=3.379) in non-recessions, with a strongly significant difference (Chi2=11.32, p=0.0005). The authors interpret these patterns as further support for the lock-in mechanism.

Main role: This is a corollary robustness/mechanism analysis showing the lock-in effect is weaker when investors are more likely to have capital losses and thus weaker incentives to defer gains.
Settings.H1664: Section 5.6 Lock-in effect through business cycles; Table 11, PDF pp. 18, 20.
Settings.G1665:
Treatment: Same Product Market, an indicator equal to 1 if both companies in the pair operate in the same product market based on Hoberg and Phillips (2016) text-based product-market classifications, 0 otherwise.

Method: The authors estimate linear probability/OLS regressions of whether a pair of public-company clients within the same audit office shares the same audit partner on an indicator for whether the pair is in the same product market. Their preferred OLS specification includes audit-office fixed effects, Company1 fixed effects, Company2 fixed effects, and year fixed effects, plus pair-level controls for size, profitability, loss status, fiscal year-end similarity, and office partner count. Because the design absorbs three separately included FE dimensions (office, company1, company2, plus year) and the paper argues these FE help control for time-invariant office and client heterogeneity, this qualifies as HDFE. Identification remains observational and relies on within-office, within-company, over-time residual variation; the authors acknowledge the analysis is not experimental.

Identification: The identifying variation comes from comparing company pairs within the same audit office and across years, while controlling for observed pair characteristics and absorbing audit-office, company, and year fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that similar firms may sort to the same partner for unobserved reasons correlated with product-market proximity. The paper argues that office and company fixed effects mitigate time-invariant office- and client-level confounds, but causal interpretation still depends on no important omitted time-varying pair-level determinants of both product-market overlap and partner sharing after controls.

Setting: Using pairwise data on public clients within audit offices for 2016–2017, the authors interpret the HDFE OLS coefficient on Same Product Market as showing that product-market rivals are more likely to share the same audit partner. In Table 3 Panel B column (2), the OLS coefficient is 0.193 on a binary outcome, and univariate rates in Panel A show partner sharing of 19.2% for same-product-market pairs versus 10.1% otherwise. This baseline result supports the paper’s broader argument that partner sharing can be beneficial on average, before considering how information-spillover concerns attenuate that sharing.

Main role: A core paper claim is that product-market similarity affects the tendency to share audit partners, establishing the baseline from which spillover-concern interactions are interpreted.
Settings.H1665: Section 4.1, Fig. 1, Table 3 Panel A and Panel B col. (2), PDF pages 6–7.
Settings.G1666:
Treatment: Interaction treatment capturing whether a company pair is in the same product market and has high information-spillover concerns. Info Concern is measured separately as: Redacted = 1 if at least one company in the pair redacts 10-K information; Trade Secret = 1 if at least one mentions trade secrets; Prop Info = 1 if at least one mentions proprietary information; R&D High = 1 if at least one has above-median R&D/assets. The focal treatment is the binary interaction Same Product Market × Info Concern.

Method: The authors estimate pair-level OLS regressions of Same Partner on Same Product Market, an information-spillover-concern proxy, and their interaction, using the within-audit-office sample. The preferred OLS models in Table 4 Panel B columns (2), (4), (6), and (8) include audit-office fixed effects, Company1 fixed effects, Company2 fixed effects, and year fixed effects, plus controls for size, profitability, losses, fiscal year end, and office partner count. Separate specifications are reported for four proxies of information-spillover concerns: Redacted, Trade Secret, Prop Info, and R&D High. This is a high-dimensional FE observational design rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental one.

Identification: Identification comes from differential partner-sharing propensities across same-product-market versus different-product-market pairs, interacted with proxies for concern about proprietary information spillovers, within audit offices and net of company and year fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that disclosure choices and R&D may be correlated with unobserved determinants of partner assignment. The authors argue these variables proxy for spillover concerns from prior literature and use rich fixed effects and controls to reduce confounding, but the assumptions remain observational: after controls and FE, the interaction captures concern-driven avoidance of shared partners rather than omitted pair-level sorting forces.

Setting: The paper’s main HDFE regressions indicate that product-market rivals are less likely to share the same audit partner when at least one firm has stronger information-spillover concerns. In Table 4 Panel B OLS columns (2), (4), (6), and (8), the interaction coefficients Same Product Market × Info Concern are -0.262 for Redacted, -0.192 for Trade Secret, -0.125 for Prop Info, and -0.278 for R&D High, all statistically significant. The authors summarize the economic magnitude by stating that partner-sharing probability for same-product-market firms falls from about 25% when unconcerned to 5% when concerned. This setting directly underpins the paper’s central causal claim about client concerns driving partner assignment.

Main role: This is the paper’s principal test of the hypothesis stated in the introduction and theory: concerns about information spillovers causally reduce partner sharing among product-market rivals.
Settings.H1666: Section 4.2, Figs. 2–5, Table 4 Panel A and Panel B cols. (2), (4), (6), (8), PDF pages 7–10.
Settings.G1667:
Treatment: Same Product Market × Info Concern Intensity, where Info Concern Intensity equals the sum of Redacted, Trade Secret, Prop Info, and R&D High divided by 4, so it is a continuous intensity measure from 0 to 1. Same Product Market itself is binary, but the focal interaction includes a continuous component.

Method: The authors estimate pair-level OLS regressions of Same Partner on Same Product Market, the continuous aggregate measure Info Concern Intensity, and their interaction. The preferred OLS model in Table 5 column (2) includes audit-office fixed effects, Company1 fixed effects, Company2 fixed effects, and year fixed effects plus the same pair-level controls as in prior specifications. Info Concern Intensity is the count of four proprietary-cost proxies divided by four, taking values between 0 and 1.

Identification: The model exploits within-office and within-company residual variation in a continuous index of spillover concern interacted with product-market rivalry. The concern is that the index aggregates endogenous disclosure and R&D choices that may correlate with partner assignment. The authors argue the index summarizes multiple proxies from prior literature and that FE plus controls mitigate omitted heterogeneity. Causal interpretation requires that, conditional on FE and controls, the interaction with the intensity measure captures concern-driven avoidance of shared partners.

Setting: As a robustness and summary specification, the authors show that the reluctance of product-market rivals to share the same audit partner increases with the intensity of information-spillover concerns. In Table 5 column (2), the OLS coefficient on Same Product Market × Info Concern Intensity is -0.357, statistically significant, implying that as the concern index rises from 0 to 1, same-product-market pairs become markedly less likely to share a partner. This result reinforces the paper’s central claim that proprietary-cost concerns causally shape partner assignment.

Main role: This aggregate-intensity specification is presented as a key robustness and consolidation of the main information-spillover hypothesis.
Settings.G1668:
Treatment: Interaction treatment Same Product Market × Info Concern in city-level pairwise multinomial logit models. Info Concern is measured separately as Redacted, Trade Secret, Prop Info, or R&D High, each coded 1 if at least one company in the pair exhibits that characteristic. Same Product Market is binary; the focal interaction is also binary.

Method: The authors estimate multinomial logit models on all possible company pairs within the same city as the audit office, with a trichotomous dependent variable indicating: (1) same audit partner, (2) same audit office but not same partner, or (3) neither. They regress each outcome relative to the omitted category on Same Product Market, an information-concern proxy, and their interaction, with observed controls and year fixed effects but without office or company fixed effects because the multinomial model did not converge with those FE. Since multinomial logit is nonlinear, the setting is classified as Other despite being conceptually a regression-adjustment design.

Identification: The model compares pair outcomes within city-level matched markets for audit offices, controlling for observed company-pair and auditor characteristics and year effects. The endogeneity concern is selection of auditors, offices, and partners correlated with unobserved pairwise factors. The paper’s argument is that if spillover concerns matter specifically at the personnel level, the interaction should predict lower partner sharing but not lower office sharing. Causal interpretation relies on the assumption that, after controls, the differential interaction across multinomial outcomes reflects concern-driven avoidance of shared partners rather than omitted city-pair sorting forces.

Setting: In city-level multinomial logit models, the authors interpret the interaction between product-market rivalry and information-spillover concern as causally reducing shared-partner arrangements but not shared-office arrangements. For the Same Partner outcome in Table 7 Panel B, Same Product Market × Info Concern is negative and significant across all four proxies: -0.948 for Redacted, -0.947 for Trade Secret, -0.682 for Prop Info, and -1.105 for R&D High. For the Same Office outcome, the corresponding interaction coefficients are small and insignificant (-0.040, -0.232, -0.122, -0.020). This supports the paper’s central claim that clients particularly object to sharing individual partners, while office-level Chinese walls appear sufficient to avoid office-level deterrence.

Main role: Distinguishing partner sharing from office sharing is a central contribution emphasized in the abstract and conclusion: spillover concerns deter partner sharing but not office sharing.
Settings.H1668: Section 4.4, Table 7 Panel A and Panel B, PDF pages 12–14.
Settings.G1669:
Treatment: Primary treatment is Partner Sharing, an indicator equal to 1 if the focal company shares its audit partner with another company in the same product market, 0 otherwise. A second treatment in the same specification is Office Sharing without Partner Sharing, equal to 1 if the focal company shares its audit office but not its partner with another company in the same product market. Both are binary indicators.

Method: The authors estimate an OLS regression of log audit fees, Ln(AF), on Partner Sharing and Office Sharing without Partner Sharing, with company-year controls, audit-office fixed effects, and year fixed effects in the sample of 2,437 company-year observations. Partner Sharing equals 1 if the focal company’s partner audits another company in the same product market; Office Sharing without Partner Sharing equals 1 if the office audits another company in the same product market but the partner is different. Because the design uses two FE dimensions (audit office and year) rather than three or more, it is standard FE rather than HDFE.

Identification: The regression uses cross-sectional variation in whether a company shares its partner or only its office with another same-product-market client, controlling for firm size, profitability, complexity, internal controls, office size, partner workload, and fixed effects for audit office and year. The endogeneity concern is that partner sharing is chosen based on expected costs and benefits, so lower fees may reflect selection rather than a pure treatment effect. The authors explicitly caution that Partner Sharing is endogenously determined and interpret the result as suggestive of benefits rather than definitive proof of optimality.

Setting: In supplementary standard-FE analyses of company-year outcomes, the authors find that sharing the same audit partner with another company in the same product market is associated with lower audit fees, which they interpret as evidence of audit-efficiency gains from knowledge transfer. In Table 8 Panel B column (1), the coefficient on Partner Sharing is -0.149 on log audit fees, while Office Sharing without Partner Sharing is insignificant at -0.019. The paper translates this into an economically significant 13.8% lower audit fee when same-product-market firms share the same partner. The authors note, however, that the treatment is endogenous and therefore the result is suggestive rather than cleanly identified.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion emphasize supplementary evidence that partner sharing can be beneficial through lower audit fees; this is one of the paper’s main secondary takeaways.
Settings.H1669: Section 4.5, Table 8 Panel A and Panel B col. (1), PDF pages 15–16.
Settings.G1670:
Treatment: Primary treatment is Partner Sharing, an indicator equal to 1 if the focal company shares its audit partner with another company in the same product market, 0 otherwise. A second treatment in the same specification is Office Sharing without Partner Sharing, equal to 1 if the focal company shares its audit office but not its partner with another company in the same product market. Both are binary indicators.

Method: The authors estimate a logit model of accounting misstatements, Misstate, on Partner Sharing and Office Sharing without Partner Sharing, with company-year controls and year fixed effects; they do not include audit-office fixed effects because of insufficient within-office variation in the binary outcome. Big 4 is included as a control instead. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear logit, the setting is classified as Other rather than FE or OLS.

Identification: The model compares misstatement incidence across firms that do and do not share partners with same-product-market peers, holding constant observable determinants of audit risk, complexity, and auditor characteristics, plus year effects. The key endogeneity problem is nonrandom matching of firms to shared partners. The authors explicitly state caution because partner sharing is endogenously determined by perceived costs and benefits. Thus the result is interpreted as suggestive evidence consistent with partner-level knowledge spillovers improving audit quality.

Setting: In a supplementary logit analysis, the authors find that companies sharing the same audit partner with another same-product-market client are less likely to later restate due to a material accounting misstatement. In Table 8 Panel B column (2), the coefficient on Partner Sharing is -0.845, significant, whereas Office Sharing without Partner Sharing is insignificant at -0.268. The paper summarizes the magnitude by stating that the probability of a misstatement falls from 6.6% to 2.6% when same-product-market firms share the same partner. This supports the paper’s claim that partner sharing may improve audit quality, though the authors emphasize that the relation is observational and endogeneity remains.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion stress fewer accounting misstatements as the second main benefit of partner sharing, alongside lower fees.
Settings.H1670: Section 4.5, Table 8 Panel A and Panel B col. (2), PDF pages 15–16.
Settings.G1671:
Treatment: Same Firm, an indicator equal to 1 if both firms in the comment-letter pair have the same Big 4 audit firm and 0 otherwise; interpreted as exposure to a common auditor style at the firm level.

Method: The main design is an OLS regression on a sample of pairwise comment-letter observations formed by pairing all unique combinations of Big 4 client comment letters within the same fiscal year and two-digit SIC industry. The treatment is an indicator for whether both clients in the pair share the same audit firm (Same Firm). Outcomes are three continuous similarity measures between the two letters: cosine similarity of comment-letter text, similarity of significant LDA topics, and similarity of detailed issue keys. The regressions include a large set of pair-level controls constructed as absolute differences and minima of client characteristics related to SEC review propensity and comment-letter features, plus year and two-digit SIC fixed effects; standard errors are clustered by GVKEY pair. The authors interpret the Same Firm coefficient as the effect of auditor style on common disclosure issues, while acknowledging that auditor-client matching cannot be fully eliminated as a limitation.

Identification: Identification comes from cross-sectional variation in whether two same-industry, same-year SEC comment-letter recipients share the same audit firm, conditional on extensive controls for economic similarity, SEC review determinants, comment-letter breadth, and year/industry fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is nonrandom auditor-client matching or common industry/product-market features causing similar disclosure issues even absent auditor style. The paper argues that matching within industry, adding economic-similarity controls, and multiple robustness tests alleviate but do not eliminate this concern; causal interpretation therefore relies on selection on observables plus the auditor-style argument rather than a quasi-experimental shock.

Setting: Using OLS on industry-year comment-letter pairs of Big 4 clients, the authors estimate whether sharing the same audit firm increases the similarity of SEC comment letters. Same Firm is positive and significant for all three outcomes: 0.003 for Similar Text, 0.004 for Similar Topics, and 0.003 for Similar Keys (Table 4, Panel A), which the authors describe as 0.83 percent, 1.70 percent, and 1.74 percent increases relative to the sample means. They interpret these results as evidence that auditor style propagates common disclosure issues across clients. This is the paper’s main causal setting, though the authors note auditor-client matching remains a limitation.

Main role: This is the core test of H1 and directly underpins the paper’s central claim in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion that auditor style is associated with common disclosure issues among Big 4 clients.
Settings.H1671: Section IV, “Auditor Style and SEC Comment Letter Similarity,” Equation (1), Table 4 Panel A, cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 12–16.
Settings.G1672:
Treatment: Same Firm, an indicator equal to 1 if both firms in the comment-letter pair have the same Big 4 audit firm and 0 otherwise.

Method: The authors re-estimate the main relation using logistic regressions where the dependent variable is an indicator for whether a pair’s similarity score falls in the top quartile of the corresponding distribution. The treatment remains Same Firm. The specification otherwise follows the main OLS setting, with the same letter-pair construction, controls, and year and industry fixed effects. Because the implemented estimator is logistic rather than linear, it falls under Other. The reported coefficients are interpreted as marginal effects/probability changes from having the same auditor.

Identification: Same identifying variation as the main setting: within industry-year comment-letter pairs, whether both firms share the same audit firm. The concern is again auditor-client matching and omitted common factors. The interpretation relies on extensive controls and fixed effects, but no quasi-experimental source of exogenous auditor assignment.

Setting: As a nonlinear robustness check, the paper estimates logistic models for whether same-auditor pairs are unusually similar, defined as being in the top quartile of each similarity measure. Same Firm has positive coefficients of 0.054 for Top Similar Text, 0.037 for Top Similar Topics, and 0.041 for Top Similar Keys (Table 4, Panel B), which the authors summarize as roughly 4 percent increases in the likelihood of being in the top quartile. These results support the interpretation that auditor style increases the chance of highly similar disclosure issues.

Main role: These are supporting robustness analyses reinforcing the main conclusion by showing same-auditor pairs are more likely to fall in the top quartile of similarity, but the core paper emphasis is on the linear similarity regressions.
Settings.H1672: Section IV, Table 4 Panel B, cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 14–16.
Settings.G1673:
Treatment: Long Tenure, an indicator equal to 1 if both firms in a same-auditor comment-letter pair have auditor tenure of at least five years and 0 otherwise.

Method: The authors estimate a variation of Equation (1) on the subsample of letter pairs where Same Firm = 1, replacing Tenure Diff and Tenure Min with Long Tenure, an indicator equal to 1 if both clients in the pair have had their auditor for five or more years. OLS is used with the same broad control set and fixed effects structure as the main analysis. This design is intended to test whether long shared auditor tenure causes clients with the same auditor to converge more in disclosure style and issues.

Identification: Identification uses cross-sectional variation within the same-auditor subsample in whether both clients have long auditor tenure. The intended mechanism is accumulation of auditor influence over disclosures over repeated audit engagements. Endogeneity concerns remain because long-tenure clients may differ in unobserved ways from shorter-tenure clients, so the evidence is suggestive rather than quasi-experimental.

Setting: Among letter pairs sharing the same auditor, the authors test whether long common tenure intensifies auditor-style effects. They report that Long Tenure is positive and statistically significant across the three similarity measures in Table 5 columns (1)–(3), interpreting this as evidence that clients with the same auditor converge in style and disclosure issues as tenure increases. Exact coefficients are not visible in the provided excerpt, but the paper treats this as evidence that auditor influence accumulates over time.

Main role: The abstract and introduction explicitly note that clients with the same auditor converge in issues as tenure increases, making this a substantive extension of the central auditor-style mechanism.
Settings.H1673: Section IV, “Auditor Style and the Effects of Tenure,” Table 5 cols. (1)–(3), PDF pp. 17–18.
Settings.G1674:
Treatment: Long Tenure, an indicator equal to 1 if both firms in a different-auditor comment-letter pair have auditor tenure of at least five years and 0 otherwise.

Method: The authors estimate the same tenure-variation model on the subsample of letter pairs where Same Firm = 0. Treatment is Long Tenure, indicating both firms have at least five years with their different auditors. OLS with the main controls and fixed effects is used to test whether long tenure at different auditors causes clients to diverge in disclosure issues, consistent with adopting distinct auditor styles.

Identification: Identification comes from variation in long auditor tenure among pairs with different audit firms. The interpretation is that longer exposure to different auditor styles reduces similarity. As with the other tenure setting, causal threats are unobserved firm differences correlated with long tenure.

Setting: For letter pairs with different auditors, the authors ask whether long tenure with different audit firms makes comment letters less similar. They state that Long Tenure is negative and significant for Similar Text in column (4) and insignificant in columns (5) and (6), which they interpret as partial evidence that clients with long tenure at different auditors diverge in style and issues. Exact coefficient values are not reported in the provided text.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism test that complements the main same-auditor tenure result by showing divergence across different auditors.
Settings.H1674: Section IV, “Auditor Style and the Effects of Tenure,” Table 5 cols. (4)–(6), PDF pp. 17–18.
Settings.G1675:
Treatment: Same Firm, an indicator equal to 1 if both firms in the comment-letter pair have the same audit firm and 0 otherwise, estimated separately in subsamples split by below/above median nonaudit fees, low/high audit-market competition, and both/neither industry-expert auditor status.

Method: The paper re-estimates Equation (1) in cross-sectional subsamples defined by nonaudit fees, audit-market competition, and auditor industry expertise. The implemented estimator remains OLS on letter pairs with the same similarity outcomes, controls, and fixed effects. The causal contrast is still Same Firm, but the estimand is the effect within each subsample, interpreted as showing when auditor style more strongly affects common disclosure issues.

Identification: Within each subsample, identification is the same observational comparison of same-auditor versus different-auditor letter pairs, conditional on controls and fixed effects. The subsample splits are intended to probe mechanisms related to auditor independence, competition, and expertise. Endogeneity concerns from sorting into these environments remain.

Setting: The authors report that auditor-style effects are concentrated where auditors plausibly exert more influence or where quality is weaker: among clients with below-median nonaudit fees, in low-competition audit markets, and among nonindustry expert auditors. Across these subsample OLS regressions, the Same Firm effect is said to be present only in those environments, supporting the interpretation that auditor style causally contributes to common disclosure issues when auditor influence is greater or mitigating expertise is lower. Exact coefficients are not provided in the visible excerpt.

Main role: These are substantive heterogeneity analyses supporting the mechanism that greater auditor independence or lower expertise magnifies the propagation of style-based disclosure issues, but they are not the paper’s primary design.
Settings.H1675: Section IV, “Auditor Cross-Sectional Tests,” Table 6 Panels A–C, PDF pp. 18–19.
Settings.G1676:
Treatment: Post Switch, an indicator equal to 1 for switcher observations after the client changes from one Big 4 auditor to another Big 4 auditor, in samples where switcher letters are paired to nonswitcher letters of the switcher’s subsequent auditor. This captures exposure to the new auditor’s style.

Method: For auditor changes, the authors construct modified letter-pair samples matching switchers to nonswitchers in the same industry and year. In the ‘assume new style’ design, switcher letters are paired with nonswitcher letters audited by the switcher’s subsequent auditor. They estimate regressions with Post Switch equal to 1 after the auditor change and 0 before, using the controls from Equation (1). The design compares the change in similarity of switchers’ letters relative to matched nonswitchers before versus after the switch, which is a conventional DiD-style setup without a named modern heterogeneous estimator.

Identification: The identifying variation is within-switcher before-versus-after changes in similarity to clients of the subsequent auditor, benchmarked using matched nonswitchers from that auditor in the same industry-year. The key assumption is that absent the auditor switch, switchers would not have become similarly closer to the subsequent auditor’s clients. Remaining concerns include endogenous auditor switching and contemporaneous shocks prompting the switch.

Setting: Using a difference-in-differences-style auditor-change design, the paper finds that clients switching Big 4 auditors become more similar in disclosure issues to the clients of their new auditor. In Table 7 Panel A, Post Switch is positive and significant for Similar Topics and Similar Keys (columns (2) and (3)) and not reported as significant for Similar Text, which the authors interpret as evidence that clients assume the disclosure issues of the subsequent auditor. Exact coefficient values are not legible in the supplied excerpt.

Main role: The abstract and introduction highlight that clients changing auditors assume the issues of the subsequent auditor; this is a central dynamic mechanism reinforcing the main auditor-style interpretation.
Settings.H1676: Section IV, “Auditor Changes and Assuming Disclosure Issues,” Table 7 Panel A cols. (1)–(3), Appendix C pairing description, PDF pp. 19–23 and 36.
Settings.G1677:
Treatment: Post Switch, an indicator equal to 1 after a switcher changes auditors, estimated in samples where switcher letters are paired to nonswitcher letters of the switcher’s predecessor auditor. This captures the post-switch loss of exposure to the old auditor’s style.

Method: In the companion auditor-change design, switcher letters are paired to nonswitcher letters from the switcher’s predecessor auditor. The same regression setup uses Post Switch to capture periods after the switch, testing whether similarity to the predecessor auditor’s clients falls after the change. This is again a conventional DiD-style before/after comparison around switching, with matched nonswitchers.

Identification: Identification relies on before/after changes in similarity to predecessor-auditor clients around the switch, relative to matched nonswitchers. The assumption is that similarity to predecessor-auditor clients would have remained stable absent switching. Endogenous switching and other concurrent shocks remain concerns.

Setting: In the full auditor-switch sample, the paper does not find evidence that switchers’ comment letters become less similar to the clients of the predecessor auditor after the change. In Table 7 Panel A columns (4)–(6), Post Switch is not significant, which the authors interpret as no average loss of old style in the full sample, possibly because disclosure practices are sticky or additive. No focal numerical estimate is discussed in the text provided.

Main role: This is a supporting auditor-change analysis. The paper emphasizes some evidence of losing the old style mainly in certain bad-quality subsamples rather than in the full sample.
Settings.H1677: Section IV, “Auditor Changes and Assuming Disclosure Issues,” Table 7 Panel A cols. (4)–(6), PDF pp. 19–23.
Settings.G1678:
Treatment: Post Switch, an indicator equal to 1 after the Big 4 auditor switch. Estimated separately in subsamples where the switch was preceded by a restatement or ICMW, or not, and for both subsequent-auditor and predecessor-auditor pairing designs.

Method: The paper repeats the auditor-change DiD-style designs in subsamples where the switch was preceded in the prior two years by a restatement announcement or an internal control material weakness (ICMW), and complementary subsamples without such events. The implemented estimator remains the same before/after regression using Post Switch on modified matched letter-pair samples. These are substantive heterogeneity analyses of the switching design.

Identification: Same switch-based DiD logic as settings s6–s7, but within subsamples defined by prior restatements or ICMWs. The authors use these splits to argue that revelation of poor prior reporting quality may induce abandonment of old auditor style. Endogeneity of switching and the bad-event subsample remains substantial.

Setting: The paper reports that when the switch was preceded by a restatement or ICMW, clients generally do not assume the new auditor’s style, but there is evidence they lose the old auditor’s style—especially after restatements. In Table 7 Panels B and D, Post Switch is negative and significant in predecessor-style tests; in Panels C and E, when there was no prior restatement or ICMW, clients adopt the style of the new auditor in Similar Topics and Similar Keys but do not lose the old style. The text provides directional and significance conclusions but not readable coefficient values in the excerpt.

Main role: These are nuanced supporting analyses showing when clients lose or assume styles after switching, especially after revelations of poor reporting quality.
Settings.H1678: Section IV, “Auditor Changes and Assuming Disclosure Issues,” Table 7 Panels B–E, PDF pp. 20–23.
Settings.G1679:
Treatment: Same Firm, indicator for both firms in the comment-letter pair having the same audit firm, estimated separately for pairs filing within 30 days of each other and pairs filing more than 30 days apart.

Method: The authors split the main letter-pair sample by whether the two firms’ filing dates are within 30 days of each other and re-estimate Equation (1) separately. The estimator remains OLS with Same Firm as the treatment and the same set of controls and fixed effects. The purpose is to test whether auditor style effects depend on temporal proximity of filings, consistent with learning from others’ disclosure issues.

Identification: Within each filing-proximity subsample, identification again uses cross-sectional variation in same-auditor status, conditional on controls. The interpretation is that if auditors learn from other clients’ issues, common disclosure issues should only appear when filings are temporally close enough that learning has not yet occurred. This remains observational and subject to unobserved differences across close-versus-far filing pairs.

Setting: When the authors split pairs by filing-date proximity, they find the Same Firm effect is positive and significant for all similarity measures only when the two firms filed within 30 days of each other, and insignificant when filings are more than 30 days apart. They interpret this as evidence that auditors and managers learn from previously identified disclosure issues, so common problems persist only when filings are close in time. Exact coefficients are not shown in the provided excerpt.

Main role: The abstract and conclusion mention that style effects are present only when filings are close in time, making this a highlighted mechanism test about auditor learning.
Settings.H1679: Section IV, “Auditor Learning,” Table 8, PDF p. 23.
Settings.G1680:
Treatment: Same Firm, indicator equal to 1 if both firms in the pair share the same audit firm, estimated in subsamples restricted to letters above the sample median in RefGuidance, DeficientAreas, DiscChanges, or Quality.

Method: The paper limits the main OLS Equation (1) sample to letter pairs where both letters are above the sample median on a measure of more warranted or impactful comment letters following Kubic and Toynbee (2023): RefGuidance, DeficientAreas, DiscChanges, or a factor-based Quality measure. The estimator remains OLS with Same Firm as treatment, the same outcomes, controls, and year/industry fixed effects. These are robustness analyses showing whether auditor style affects more substantive comment letters.

Identification: Same observational same-auditor comparison as the main model, but on restricted subsamples intended to capture more warranted SEC comments. This does not solve the main matching concern; it tests whether the relation persists for more substantive comment letters.

Setting: Restricting the sample to more warranted letters, the authors continue to find positive Same Firm effects across all three similarity measures. For example, with letters above the median in RefGuidance, Same Firm is 0.003 for Similar Text, 0.004 for Similar Topics, and 0.003 for Similar Keys; for DeficientAreas, 0.003, 0.008, and 0.004; for DiscChanges, 0.002, 0.003, and 0.003; and for Quality, 0.003, 0.005, and 0.004 (Table 9 Panels B–E). They interpret this as evidence that auditor style is associated not just with any common issues, but with more impactful disclosure issues.

Main role: These are substantive robustness tests showing that the main relation is present for more impactful comment letters, but they are secondary to the headline results.
Settings.H1680: Section V, “Warranted Comment Letters,” Table 9 Panels B–E, PDF pp. 24–25.
Settings.G1681:
Treatment: Audit-firm identity among same-auditor pairs, operationalized through Big 4 auditor fixed effects and pairwise comparisons of which audit firm has the more positive coefficient for each topic-specific outcome. This is effectively a multinomial categorical treatment rather than a single binary regressor.

Method: To study issue-type-specific style, the authors use logistic regressions with auditor fixed effects on a sample restricted to pairs with the same auditor (Same Firm = 1). For each of 20 Ryans (2021) LDA topics, the dependent variable is an indicator equal to 1 if both letters in the pair have that significant topic and 0 otherwise. The paper compares estimated auditor fixed effects pairwise across the Big 4 to infer which audit firm is more likely to propagate each topic. Because the implemented estimator is logistic and centered on auditor fixed effects rather than a single linear treatment coefficient, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The design conditions on the pair already sharing an auditor and uses auditor fixed effects to compare whether certain Big 4 firms are more likely than others to have both clients exhibit a given comment-letter topic. The interpretation is causal in the paper’s discussion of firm-specific styles, but identification is purely observational and vulnerable to audit-firm-specific client composition.

Setting: In topic-specific logistic regressions restricted to same-auditor pairs, the authors argue that each Big 4 firm propagates a distinctive set of common disclosure issues. Table 10 reports pairwise auditor comparisons rather than coefficients; for example, KPMG clients are more likely than other Big 4 clients to receive loan-loss, internal-control, and standardized-language topics, while PwC clients are more likely to receive operating-performance and tax topics. This setting supports the claim that auditor style differs across firms, though no single numeric treatment effect is emphasized.

Main role: These are additional analyses illustrating firm-specific auditor style by disclosure topic, not the paper’s main average-treatment result.
Settings.H1681: Section V, “Auditor Style and SEC Comment Letter Similarity by Firm,” Table 10 and related discussion, PDF pp. 25–26.
Settings.G1682:
Treatment: Audit-firm identity captured by Big 4 auditor fixed effects in client-year logistic regressions for comment-letter receipt. The treatment is categorical auditor affiliation rather than a single binary regressor.

Method: The authors estimate logistic regressions for whether a Big 4 client receives an SEC comment letter (Letter = 1), once without and once with audit-firm fixed effects, using the full Compustat/Audit Analytics Big 4 client-year panel and a restricted panel of firms not reviewed in the prior two years. The goal is to test whether aggregate disclosure quality differs across Big 4 clienteles. Because the estimator is logistic, this qualifies as Other.

Identification: The strategy is cross-sectional comparison of comment-letter receipt across Big 4 clienteles conditional on client controls and year/industry fixed effects. The concern is client sorting across auditors. The authors use this only as a descriptive/causal-style check on aggregate style differences, not as their main identification design.

Setting: Using client-year logistic regressions with auditor fixed effects, the paper tests whether the Big 4 differ in clients’ overall probability of receiving an SEC comment letter. The chi-square test for joint auditor fixed effects is insignificant in both the full and restricted samples (p-values 0.506 and 0.545), and pseudo R-squared values change negligibly, so the authors conclude that Big 4 clienteles do not differ in aggregate likelihood of comment-letter receipt. This supports their claim that style differences concern issue composition rather than average disclosure quality.

Main role: This is an additional analysis used to argue that Big 4 firms do not differ in aggregate disclosure quality even though they propagate different issue types.
Settings.H1682: Section V, “Overall Disclosure Quality and Remediation Costs,” Table 11 Panel A cols. (1)–(4), PDF pp. 28–29.
Settings.G1683:
Treatment: Audit-firm identity captured by Big 4 auditor fixed effects in client-year OLS regressions on comment-letter severity measures.

Method: The paper estimates OLS regressions of comment-letter severity outcomes on client controls, year and industry fixed effects, with and without audit-firm fixed effects, using the comment-letter sample. Severity outcomes are Keys, Rounds, and Days. The purpose is to test whether overall comment-letter severity differs across Big 4 clienteles. The implemented estimator is linear regression for continuous outcomes.

Identification: Cross-sectional comparison across auditor fixed effects conditional on client controls and year/industry fixed effects. The authors interpret insignificant joint tests as evidence of no aggregate severity differences across auditors, but selection into auditors remains a concern.

Setting: In OLS regressions of comment-letter severity, adding Big 4 auditor fixed effects does little to improve fit, and joint F-tests are insignificant for Keys and Rounds, though significant for Days. The authors conclude that clients of different Big 4 firms are not materially more likely to receive more severe letters in aggregate, except that time to resolve letters may vary by auditor, perhaps reflecting style in crafting responses rather than initial severity. This complements the main result that auditor style affects issue composition, not average quality.

Main role: This is an additional analysis to show that Big 4 firms do not differ materially in aggregate comment-letter severity, except possibly response days.
Settings.H1683: Section V, “Overall Disclosure Quality and Remediation Costs,” Table 11 Panel A cols. (5)–(10), PDF pp. 28–29.
Settings.G1684:
Treatment: Style Topics, a count of significant LDA topics in the client’s comment letter that are attributed to the client’s auditor’s style because that auditor has the highest mean value of the topic across clients. This is a nonbinary intensity measure.

Method: The authors regress three remediation-cost outcomes on Style Topics, the count of significant LDA topics in a client’s comment letter for which that client’s auditor has the highest mean prevalence across its clientele. Two models are OLS (Rounds and Days), and one is logistic (Extension); by the classification rule, the nonlinear estimator would normally be Other, but because the table reports both linear and logistic outcomes together in one substantive setting tied to the same treatment and location, this setting is best summarized as a single mixed regression-adjustment robustness setting described explicitly here. Controls are client-year versions of Equation (1) controls plus year and industry fixed effects.
