Political connections may themselves be endogenous, so this remains suggestive rather than fully causal.

Setting: Table 6 Panel F shows that the negative association between political rank and crash risk appears only among firms without political connections. For PC_{t-1}=0, a one-rank increase in Dshi_{t-1} is associated with -0.1121 (z=-2.31) in the Crash specification and -0.0266 (t=-2.09) in the Ncskew regression; coefficients are insignificant for politically connected firms. The authors interpret this as evidence that political rank and political connections can substitute for each other in reducing incentives for risky behavior.

Main role: The abstract emphasizes that the effect is significant only in firms without political connections, so this heterogeneity test supports a main conclusion.
Settings.H1721: Section IV, “Political Connections,” Table 6 Panel F, PDF pp. 15–16.
Settings.G1722:
Treatment: Chairman political rank (Dshi_{t-1}), four-level ordinal measure. The key moderator is whether the observation falls in a promotion period: for local provincial leaders, Promotion_t=1 or Promotion_{t+1}=1; for chairmen, an analogous indicator for the chairman’s own promotion. The paper studies how promotion periods dampen the effect of political rank on crash risk.

Method: Heterogeneity analysis by promotion windows. In Table 6 Panels G and H, the authors split observations into periods with versus without upcoming/current local provincial leaders’ promotions or firm chairmen’s promotions, then re-estimate the baseline Crash logit and Ncskew OLS models with year and industry fixed effects and standard controls.

Identification: The authors argue that promotion windows create incentives to suppress bad news, weakening the ordinarily risk-reducing role of political rank. Identification is from comparing the estimated rank effect in promotion versus non-promotion periods, controlling for observables and year/industry fixed effects. The design assumes that promotion timing captures shifts in incentives rather than unobserved shocks directly affecting crash risk.

Setting: The paper finds that promotion periods dampen the usual negative association between political rank and crash risk. In Table 6 Panel G, for periods with no provincial-leader promotions in t or t+1, a one-rank increase in Dshi_{t-1} is associated with -0.1358 (z=-2.40) for Crash and -0.0270 (t=-1.76) for Ncskew; coefficients are insignificant during promotion periods. Panel H shows a similar pattern for chairmen’s own promotions, with non-promotion-period coefficients of -0.1180 (z=-2.57) for Crash and -0.0249 (t=-2.05) for Ncskew. The interpretation is that distorted promotion incentives can offset the otherwise caution-inducing effects of political rank.

Main role: The abstract states that the effect is significant only during periods with no local government leaders’ or managers’ political promotions, so this is a substantive main-result heterogeneity analysis.
Settings.H1722: Section IV, “Effect of Promotions on the Association between Political Ranks and Crash Risk,” Table 6 Panels G–H, PDF pp. 15–17.
Settings.G1723:
Treatment: Chairman political rank (Dshi), measured as the ordered four-level political-rank variable. The treatment is nonbinary.

Method: Alternative-mechanism regressions replacing crash risk with measures of real benefits or rent-seeking outcomes: bank-loan ratio, financing cost, tax burden, SEO indicator, SEO amount/assets, subsidies/assets, and other payables/assets. The authors state these variables replace Crash in Equation (3), implying regression adjustment with the same controls and likely year/industry fixed effects, though they do not tabulate the coefficients. Some outcomes are binary and may have been estimated linearly or otherwise; because implementation details are sparse and results are summarized textually, this is coded as regression adjustment.

Identification: The paper uses regression adjustment to test whether political rank affects firm resources, financing, taxes, SEO access, subsidies, or propping, which could be an alternative mechanism behind lower crash risk. The identifying assumption is conditional exogeneity of political rank given controls; the authors mostly interpret null results as evidence against the rent-seeking channel. Because results are untabulated and observational, identification is weak.

Setting: As an alternative-mechanism exercise, the authors regress several rent-seeking or preferential-treatment outcomes on political rank. They report that in all seven regressions, the coefficients on Dshi are insignificant, suggesting political ranks do not directly bring real benefits to firms; only in the long-tenure partition do financing fees and tax ratios show negative coefficients. No full numerical estimates are reported in the paper for these regressions. The intended causal claim is that rent seeking is not the main channel through which political rank lowers crash risk.

Main role: These are supporting alternative-mechanism tests intended to assess whether rent seeking or preferential treatment explains the main result, not the core crash-risk finding itself.
Settings.H1723: Section IV, “Alternative Mechanisms—Rent Seeking,” untabulated regressions described in text, PDF p. 17.
Settings.G1724:
Treatment: Chairman political rank (Dshi_{t-1}), the four-level ordered political-rank variable.

Method: Alternative-mechanism regressions of securities-law violations, information-disclosure violations, and non-clean audit opinions on chairman political rank and controls. The authors estimate Equation (5), which is written as a linear regression with rank, size, market-to-book, leverage, ROA, and abnormal accruals as covariates; results are summarized in text and not tabulated.

Identification: The authors examine whether higher-ranked managers are less likely to face regulatory punishment or non-clean audit opinions, which could indicate preferential treatment or better suppression of bad news. The interpretation assumes that conditional on included covariates, political rank shifts the likelihood of these outcomes. Because this is observational and likely subject to omitted variables, it is best viewed as suggestive mechanism evidence.

Setting: In untabulated Equation (5) regressions, the authors report that higher political rank is associated with fewer securities-law sanctions and fewer non-clean audit opinions. Specifically, the coefficient on Dshi_{t-1} is -0.3406 (z=-2.67) for Violation_t, -0.2853 (z=-1.96) for InforViolation_t, and -0.3846 (z=-2.18) for Auditop_t. The paper interprets these results as suggesting that firms with highly ranked managers may receive preferential treatment from authorities or auditors, which could help explain lower crash risk.

Main role: These are supporting analyses probing preferential-treatment mechanisms rather than the paper’s main causal outcome of crash risk.
Settings.H1724: Section IV, “Alternative Mechanisms—Punishment Due to Securities Law Violations and Audit Opinions,” Equation (5) discussion, PDF pp. 17–18.
Settings.G1725:
Treatment: Chairman political rank (Dshi_{t-1}), four-level ordered political-rank measure treated as endogenous in the IV analysis.

Method: Two-stage least squares using province/city public-infrastructure variables from 1998 as instruments for chairman political rank. First stage regresses Dshi_{t-1} on per capita living space (Space), buses per 1,000 residents (Bus), running water usage per capita (Water), gas usage per capita (Gas), plus the usual controls and year/industry fixed effects. The fitted value of political rank is then used in second-stage crash-risk regressions. The paper reports a first-stage OLS table and second-stage results for Crash and Ncskew, with clustered robust standard errors. They discuss minimum eigenvalue statistic and over-identification test to address instrument relevance and validity.

Identification: The IV strategy exploits historical regional population density and infrastructure/public-facility measures in 1998—Space, Bus, Water, and Gas—as instruments for chairman political rank. The paper argues these variables predict where highly ranked firms and managers are located but are unlikely to directly affect current firm-level stock price crash risk except through political rank. Identification requires instrument relevance and exclusion: conditional on controls and fixed effects, historical regional infrastructure must affect crash risk only through manager rank. The paper reports a minimum eigenvalue statistic of 35.38 rejecting weak instruments and an insignificant over-identification test (Chi-square 1.90).

Setting: Using 2SLS to address endogeneity, the paper continues to find that higher political rank lowers crash risk. In Table 7 Panel A, Space strongly negatively predicts rank (-0.0711, t=-6.72), while Bus and Gas positively predict rank. In Panel B, the second-stage coefficient on Dshi_{t-1} is -0.0863 (z=-1.78) for Crash and -0.2142 (t=-2.48) for Ncskew. The authors interpret these IV estimates as supporting a causal effect of political rank on lower crash risk, though the exclusion restriction for historical regional infrastructure is the key identifying assumption.

Main role: This is the paper’s main endogeneity-robustness design and is used to reinforce the central claim that political rank causally reduces crash risk.
Settings.H1725: Section IV, “Dealing with Endogeneity—Instrumental Variable Analysis,” Table 7 Panels A–B, PDF pp. 18–21.
Settings.G1726:
Treatment: Endogenous chairman political rank (Dshi_{t-1}), instrumented using Space, Bus, Water, and Gas. The substantive focus is heterogeneity by age and tenure subsamples.

Method: Subsample 2SLS analyses by manager age and tenure, using the same 1998 regional infrastructure instruments and first-stage approach as the main IV setting. The second stage separately estimates crash-risk effects in older versus younger manager subsamples and longer versus shorter tenure subsamples.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same IV variation as in the main 2SLS design, now within age and tenure subsamples. The paper uses this to ask whether the rank effect is stronger for younger or shorter-tenure managers. Identification again depends on the exclusion of historical regional infrastructure from current crash risk except through political rank, within each subsample.

Setting: The IV subsample results broadly mirror the baseline heterogeneity patterns. In Table 7 Panel B, for younger managers (Age<=51), the second-stage coefficient on Dshi_{t-1} is -0.3665 (t=-2.38) for Ncskew, while Crash is negative but insignificant (-0.0888, z=-1.09); effects are insignificant for older managers. For shorter-tenure managers (Tenure<2), the coefficients are -0.1376 (z=-2.09) for Crash and -0.3705 (t=-2.99) for Ncskew, while effects are insignificant for longer-tenure managers. The authors interpret these results as IV support for stronger political-rank effects among younger and shorter-tenure chairmen.

Main role: These IV subsample estimates are robustness/supporting analyses that reinforce the age and tenure heterogeneity patterns already shown in the baseline regressions.
Settings.H1726: Section IV, “Dealing with Endogeneity—Instrumental Variable Analysis,” Table 7 Panel B columns (3)–(10), PDF pp. 19–21.
Settings.G1727:
Treatment: Changes in chairman political rank between t-2 and t-1. In Panel A the main treatment is Up_{t-1}, an indicator equal to 1 if a manager’s rank in t-1 is higher than in t-2 and 0 if lower. In Panel B the treatments are Up_Chairman_{t-1}, Up_Chain_{t-1}, Up_Other_{t-1}, and Stable_{t-1}, all binary indicators relative to omitted downward-change cases.

Method: Change-specification robustness analysis. The authors difference political rank and controls across years and examine whether changes in rank predict changes in crash risk. For change in Crash they estimate an ordered logit because the differenced crash measure can take multiple integer values; for change in Ncskew they estimate a linear model. Panel A restricts to observations with changes in rank and estimates the effect of an upward versus downward rank change; Panel B expands to the full sample and separates upward changes due to chairman changes, control-chain changes, or other reasons, plus a stable-rank indicator. Year and industry fixed effects are included, and robust firm-clustered standard errors are used.

Identification: By differencing, the authors aim to remove time-invariant omitted firm characteristics and reduce reverse-causality concerns. The interpretation is that upward changes in political rank should reduce subsequent changes in crash risk if rank is causal. Identification requires that year-to-year changes in rank are not driven by omitted contemporaneous shocks that also affect changes in crash risk.

Setting: The change analysis provides weaker but broadly supportive evidence. In Table 8 Panel A, upward rank changes are associated with lower changes in crash risk: for observations with -1<ADshi<+1, Up_{t-1} has coefficient -0.3926 (t=-1.76) for the ordered-change Crash outcome and -0.1588 (t=-1.92) for change in Ncskew; estimates become smaller and often insignificant in wider change windows. In Panel B, the negative change effect appears mainly when political rank rises due to control-chain changes, with Up_Chain_{t-1} coefficients around -0.53 to -0.47 in Crash specifications and insignificant in Ncskew specifications. The authors interpret this as weaker but directionally consistent support for a causal effect of rank on crash risk.

Main role: The change model is an endogeneity-robustness exercise, not the paper’s primary specification.
Settings.H1727: Section IV, “Dealing with Endogeneity—Change Model,” Table 8 Panels A–B, PDF pp. 21–22.
Settings.G1728:
Treatment: Post-retirement exposure interacted with chairman political rank. Two related treatments are analyzed: (i) Postretire_t, an indicator equal to 1 for years 0, 1, and 2 relative to retirement and 0 for years -3, -2, and -1, interacted with Dshi_{t-1}; and (ii) Postyoung_t, equal to 0 before retirement and to the age difference between retiring and succeeding chairmen after retirement, interacted with Dshi_{t-1}. The intended treatment is the age shock induced by retirement while holding political rank constant across outgoing and incoming chairmen.

Method: Retirement-shock robustness test using a six-year event window around chairman retirements where the retiring and successor chairmen have the same political rank. The authors estimate regressions of Crash and Ncskew on either a post-retirement indicator or a continuous measure of the successor’s relative youth (Postyoung), plus interactions with political rank, and standard controls. This combines a before/after event comparison with regression adjustment rather than a formal DiD because there is no untreated control group.

Identification: The authors treat chairman retirement as an exogenous shock to manager age because successors are typically younger, while conditioning on cases where retiring and incoming chairmen have the same political rank. They then test whether the association between rank and crash risk strengthens after retirement or when the successor is much younger. Identification hinges on retirement timing and the resulting age change being unrelated to other shocks to crash risk, conditional on controls.

Setting: Using 88 chairman retirements where successor and predecessor have the same political rank, the authors test whether bringing in a younger manager amplifies the rank effect. In Table 9, the interaction Postretire_t × Dshi_{t-1} is -0.5749 (z=-1.60) for Crash and insignificant for Ncskew. Using the continuous age-gap measure, Postyoung_t × Dshi_{t-1} is -0.0648 (z=-2.63) for Crash and -0.0094 (t=-1.76) for Ncskew. The paper interprets this as evidence that the negative association between political rank and crash risk becomes stronger when retirement brings in a younger chairman.

Main role: This is a secondary endogeneity/age-mechanism robustness test supporting the younger-manager channel.
Settings.H1728: Section IV, “Manager Retirement,” Equation (7) and Table 9, PDF pp. 22–24.
Settings.G1729:
Treatment: Alternative measures of chairman political rank: (i) adjusted Dshi_{t-1} adding 0.5 for principal ranks while leaving deputy ranks unchanged; and (ii) binary indicators Dshi4_{t-1}, Dshi3_{t-1}, and Dshi2_{t-1} for specific political-rank categories relative to the omitted base group.

Method: Robustness regressions remeasuring political rank. Panel A adds 0.5 to Dshi for principal versus deputy rank distinctions; Panel B replaces the single rank measure with separate indicator variables for rank 4, rank 3, and rank 2, omitting the lowest category. The authors re-estimate the same Crash logit and Ncskew OLS models with year and industry fixed effects and the standard controls.

Identification: These specifications test whether the main result is sensitive to how rank is measured. The identifying logic is unchanged from the baseline observational regressions; only the treatment coding differs. The assumption is that alternative codings better capture hierarchy or nonlinear rank effects without introducing major measurement error.

Setting: Table 10 shows that the main negative association is robust to alternative rank codings. With principal/deputy adjustment (Panel A), the coefficient on Dshi_{t-1} is -0.1448 (z=-2.96) for Crash and -0.0258 (t=-2.02) for Ncskew. Using separate indicators (Panel B), coefficients become more negative at higher ranks: Dshi4_{t-1} is -0.5275 (z=-2.66) for Crash and -0.0971 (t=-2.13) for Ncskew; Dshi3 and Dshi2 are smaller in magnitude. The authors interpret this as reinforcing that higher political rank lowers crash risk.

Main role: These are measurement robustness checks, not central identification designs.
Settings.H1729: Section IV, “Robustness Checks—Principal and Deputy Ranks” and “Indicators for Ranks,” Table 10 Panels A–B, PDF pp. 24–25.
Settings.G1730:
Treatment: State ownership and manager-rank group indicators. In columns (1)–(2), SOE_{t-1}=1 if the firm is state-owned and 0 otherwise. In columns (3)–(4), Highdshi_{t-1}=1 if a state-owned firm’s manager rank is at or above department/bureau level and 0 otherwise, and Lowdshi_{t-1}=1 if below department/bureau level and 0 otherwise; the omitted group is non-state-owned firms.

Method: Comparison of state-owned and non-state-owned firms using pooled regressions. In Table 10 Panel C, the authors regress Crash and Ncskew on an SOE indicator, then alternatively on indicators for state-owned firms with high-ranked versus low-ranked managers, with year and industry fixed effects and standard controls. Crash is estimated with logit; Ncskew with OLS.

Identification: The authors compare crash risk across ownership/rank groups, interpreting lower crash risk in state-owned firms—especially those with highly ranked managers—as consistent with their political-incentives story. Identification is purely observational and relies on regression adjustment; substantial omitted differences between SOEs and non-SOEs remain possible.

Setting: In pooled comparisons, the authors find lower crash risk in state-owned firms and particularly in SOEs with highly ranked managers. Table 10 Panel C reports that SOE_{t-1} has coefficient -0.0858 (z=-1.42) for Crash and -0.0437 (t=-2.58) for Ncskew. Relative to non-SOEs, Highdshi_{t-1} has coefficient -0.1616 (z=-2.17) for Crash and -0.0656 (t=-3.24) for Ncskew, while Lowdshi_{t-1} is smaller at -0.0542 and -0.0403. The paper interprets this as further evidence that the state-sector political ranking system is associated with lower stock price crash risk.

Main role: This is a contextual robustness/comparison exercise rather than the main within-SOE causal setting.
Settings.H1730: Section IV, “Robustness Checks—Comparison with Non-State-Owned Firms,” Table 10 Panel C, PDF pp. 24–26.
Settings.G1731:
Treatment: Indicator equal to 1 in tournament months that included a specific prize for the branch manager ('Manager prize'), and 0 otherwise. The treatment is assignment to a monthly contest design with an added leader bonus, not actual receipt of the prize. Prize amount for winning manager: US$1,200 gift card.

Method: Within-subject field experiment at 177 bank branches over four monthly tournaments (September-December 2014). The treatment is whether the monthly tournament included an additional US$1,200 prize for the manager of the top-scoring branch in each zone. The months with manager prize (October and December) were chosen by lottery and described as orthogonal to branch productivity. The authors estimate intent-to-treat effects with linear OLS regressions of branch-month goals on a manager-prize dummy, with and without branch covariates, clustering standard errors at the branch level. Because the same branches appear in treated and untreated months, identification comes from randomized time variation in the prize regime; the paper also emphasizes monthly random reassignment of branches to tournament groups to limit dynamic strategic responses to repeated competition.

Identification: The identifying variation is randomized assignment of the manager-prize regime across months: researchers selected the two months with leader bonus by lottery, claiming orthogonality to branch productivity. Because all branches participate in all months, the design compares the same branches under treated and untreated monthly prize structures. Random monthly regrouping of branches into tournaments is used to reduce confounding from learning and strategic responses to repeated opponents. Remaining concerns are limited time shocks because treatment varies only at the month level, but the paper interprets the lottery-based month assignment as exogenous.

Setting: Using a field experiment in a Latin American bank, the authors estimate the causal effect of adding an explicit manager prize to branch tournaments on branch performance. In OLS regressions of monthly goals, branches score about 1.47 to 1.51 more goals in manager-prize months (Table 4, Panel B, columns 1-2), which the authors describe as economically meaningful. They interpret this as evidence that providing explicit incentives to team leaders increases team performance on average, a core conclusion of the paper.

Main role: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion present the positive average effect of providing explicit incentives to team leaders on team performance as a central finding of the paper.
Settings.H1731: Section V, 'Manager Prizes and Performance'; Table 4 Panel A and Panel B, columns (1)-(2) (PDF pp. 13, 16).
Settings.G1732:
Treatment: Indicator for whether the monthly tournament included a specific prize for the branch manager (1 in October and December, 0 in September and November). The substantive estimand is how the causal effect of this binary treatment varies with the continuous, demeaned Transformational manager factor.

Method: Same field experiment as s1, but the estimand is treatment-effect heterogeneity by pre-measured manager leadership style. The authors estimate linear OLS regressions of branch-month goals on the randomized manager-prize indicator, a demeaned survey-based factor 'Transformational manager,' and their interaction, with clustered branch-level standard errors. In richer specifications they also include manager satisfaction, team-photo factors, branch size, branch controls, and past performance. The causal component is the interaction between randomized treatment assignment and nonrandom leadership style measured before the tournaments; the authors are careful that leadership style itself is not randomized.

Identification: Identification of the heterogeneous treatment effect comes from random assignment of the manager-prize regime across months, interacted with leadership style measured before treatment. Because leadership style is not randomized, the paper does not treat its main effect as cleanly causal for branch performance, but it interprets the interaction with the randomized prize as showing moderation of the treatment effect by leadership style. The key assumption is that the randomized prize months are orthogonal to branch productivity and other branch-specific determinants, so differential performance changes by style reflect differential causal responses to the prize rather than differential treatment timing.

Setting: The paper’s main heterogeneity result is that the positive causal effect of a manager prize on branch goals is substantially weaker for more transformational managers. In Table 6 model 1, the average manager-prize effect is 1.529 goals, while the interaction Transformational manager × Manager prize is -1.348 goals; in models 4-6 the interaction is about -1.796 goals. The authors interpret this as showing that leader incentives are less effective, and can nearly disappear, when managers motivate through transformational appeals rather than more transactional methods.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that leader incentives have heterogeneous effects depending on managers' leadership style, specifically being less effective for transformational leaders. This is a central contribution.
Settings.H1732: Section V, 'Heterogeneous Responses to Manager Prizes'; Table 6 models (1), (4), (5), and (6) (PDF pp. 14-18).
Settings.G1733:
Treatment: Binary indicator for tournament months with a manager prize versus no manager prize. The focal estimands are heterogeneous treatment effects by continuous demeaned team attributes: Team social enjoyment and Team creativity.

Method: Field-experimental heterogeneity analysis using the randomized monthly manager-prize treatment interacted with team characteristics derived from coded branch photos. The authors run linear OLS regressions of monthly goals on the prize dummy, demeaned Team social enjoyment and Team creativity factors, and interaction terms, with clustered branch-level standard errors. They interpret these interactions as moderating the causal effect of the randomized manager-prize treatment. Specifications progressively add leadership-style controls, team size, branch controls, and past performance.

Identification: Because the manager-prize regime is randomized across months, interactions between treatment and pre-existing team characteristics identify differential causal responses to the treatment under the assumption that treatment timing is exogenous. The team characteristics themselves are not randomized and may be correlated with branch productivity, so the authors add controls and past performance to address concerns that these factors merely proxy for underlying ability. The causal claim pertains to moderation of the randomized treatment, not to the standalone causal effect of team characteristics.

Setting: In secondary analyses, the authors argue that the causal effect of leader incentives varies with team characteristics. In Table 6 model 2, the manager-prize effect is stronger for branches with higher Team social enjoyment (interaction 1.085, significant at 10%) and less positive for branches with higher Team creativity (interaction -0.732, not significant there); in fuller models 4-6, the Team social enjoyment interaction remains about 1.076 and the Team creativity interaction about -0.903 (significant at 10%). They interpret this as evidence that leader incentives work better in teams with higher costs of effort and worse in more creative teams, consistent with monitoring-based mechanisms.

Main role: These analyses are presented as supplemental or secondary tests of H3 and H4 about team characteristics moderating the treatment effect, rather than the paper’s primary contribution.
Settings.H1733: Section V, 'Supplemental Analyses' and 'Robustness Tests'; Table 6 models (2), (4), (5), and (6) (PDF pp. 16-18).
Settings.G1734:
Treatment: Binary indicator for whether the monthly tournament included a specific prize for the branch manager. In different Poisson specifications, the treatment is interacted with Transformational manager, Manager satisfaction, Team social enjoyment, Team creativity, and Number of employees.

Method: Nonlinear robustness analysis of the same field experiment, estimated with Poisson regressions because monthly goals are non-negative integers. The treatment remains the randomized monthly manager-prize indicator, with interactions for leadership style and team characteristics. Clustered standard errors are at the branch level. Under the task rules, nonlinear effect estimators are classified as Other even though identification is experimental.

Identification: Identification still rests on randomized assignment of manager-prize months, but the implemented estimator is Poisson rather than linear OLS. The interaction terms are interpreted as heterogeneous treatment effects because they combine randomized treatment variation with pre-measured moderator variables. This is a robustness exercise checking whether conclusions are sensitive to functional-form choice for a count outcome.

Setting: As a robustness check, the authors re-estimate the treatment and heterogeneity effects using Poisson regressions for the count outcome of goals. The average manager-prize effect is about 0.150-0.160 log-count units across models, and the treatment effect is again smaller for transformational managers: the Transformational manager × Manager prize coefficient is about -0.166 in model 1 and about -0.214 to -0.219 in models 4-6. Team social enjoyment positively moderates the treatment effect and Team creativity negatively moderates it in the fuller specifications. The authors state that these results are identical to, if not stronger than, the OLS findings.

Main role: The Poisson models are presented explicitly as a final robustness test to show that the main OLS findings are not driven by the count nature of the outcome.
Settings.H1734: Section V, 'Robustness Tests'; Table 7 models (1)-(6) (PDF p. 19).
Settings.G1735:
Treatment: Current-year indicator ViolAny_t equal to 1 if firm i committed at least one OSHA violation in any state in year t; binary exposure to being sanctioned for any workplace-safety violation in the prior year.

Method: The authors estimate a dynamic linear probability model on a firm-year panel to study whether a prior OSHA violation reduces a firm's subsequent violation likelihood anywhere in the U.S. The specification regresses next year's indicator for any OSHA violation on the current-year indicator for any violation, adding year fixed effects and what the table labels as firm-by-state fixed effects, plus firm-level controls in some columns. Because the empirical unit here is firm-year, the fixed-effects structure is unusual as described in the paper, but the implemented estimator is a linear FE regression with a lagged dependent variable; the paper also reports a split-panel jackknife logit as a bias-corrected robustness check for Nickell/incidental-parameters concerns. The causal interpretation is deterrence from prior enforcement, though the authors acknowledge dynamic panel bias concerns and address them with the SPJ logit.

Identification: Identification comes from within-firm temporal variation in prior violations, controlling for time-invariant heterogeneity through fixed effects and common shocks through year effects, plus firm controls for size and performance. The endogeneity concern is that persistent firm safety culture or shocks could correlate with both current and future violations. The authors argue the fixed-effects structure and controls absorb broad heterogeneity, while the SPJ logit addresses bias from lagged dependent variables in short panels. Causal interpretation relies on remaining within-firm changes in detected violations reflecting sanctions/deterrence rather than omitted time-varying confounders.

Setting: Using a firm-year linear probability model, the paper estimates whether being cited for any OSHA violation in year t affects the chance of any violation in year t+1. In Table 3 column 2, a prior-year violation is associated with a 0.0708 lower probability of any next-year violation; the authors state this is a 7.1 percentage point decline, or 22.5% relative to the 31.5% firm-year violation rate in this sample. A split-panel jackknife logit in column 3 yields a similarly negative coefficient (-0.1982). The authors interpret this as evidence that OSHA sanctions deter future violations firm-wide, a central premise of the paper.

Main role: The abstract and introduction emphasize that firms caught violating subsequently violate less overall, making this deterrence result a central building block for the paper before turning to geographic reallocation.
Settings.G1736:
Treatment: Current-year indicator ViolAny_t equal to 1 if the firm committed at least one OSHA violation in any state in year t.

Method: As a robustness check to the dynamic linear FE model, the authors estimate a fixed-effects logistic model using the split-panel jackknife of Dhaene and Jochmans (2015) on the firm-year panel. This nonlinear dynamic panel estimator is used specifically to reduce bias from the lagged dependent variable and incidental parameters. The outcome is next year's any-violation indicator, and the treatment is the current-year any-violation indicator. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear logit with SPJ correction, it is classified as Other.

Identification: The identifying variation is the same within-firm intertemporal variation as in the baseline, but the estimator explicitly addresses incidental-parameters and dynamic-panel bias in nonlinear binary outcome settings by splitting the panel across time and bias-correcting the fixed-effects logit estimates. Causal interpretation still depends on assuming that remaining within-firm changes in prior violations are conditionally exogenous after controls and fixed effects.

Setting: The paper re-estimates the deterrence specification with a split-panel jackknifed fixed-effects logit to address concerns that the lagged dependent variable in a short panel biases linear FE estimates. In Table 3 column 3, the coefficient on prior-year any violation is -0.1982 (significant at 5%), confirming the negative effect of prior sanctions on subsequent firm-wide violation risk. The result is used as a robustness check supporting the paper's central deterrence claim.

Main role: This is a substantive robustness analysis validating the main deterrence result against dynamic panel bias, but the headline evidence is presented using the linear model.
Settings.G1737:
Treatment: Two focal prior-year binary treatments are estimated jointly: (i) ViolInState_t, an indicator equal to 1 if firm i committed at least one OSHA violation in state j in year t; and (ii) ViolOutOfState_t, an indicator equal to 1 if firm i committed at least one OSHA violation in any state other than j in year t. These capture same-state and cross-state prior sanction exposure.

Method: The authors estimate a firm-state-year linear probability model of next year's in-state violation indicator on current in-state and out-of-state violation indicators, with firm-by-state and year fixed effects, establishment-count and firm controls; one specification further adds firm-by-year and state-by-year fixed effects. This design is meant to separate same-state deterrence from cross-state shifting of violations. The estimator is linear FE, not DiD, because treatment varies continuously across many firm-state-year cells rather than as a single treated/post design. The paper also reports SPJ logit robustness and a linear model on the SPJ sample.

Identification: Identification comes from within firm-state changes in prior in-state versus out-of-state violations, after absorbing all time-invariant firm-state heterogeneity with firm-by-state fixed effects and common annual shocks with year fixed effects; some models also absorb firm-year and state-year shocks. The main endogeneity concern is that violation persistence or concurrent shocks could generate spurious correlation. The authors argue the fixed-effects structure rules out stable cross-state differences in a firm's operations and state enforcement, while firm-year and state-year FE mitigate firm-wide or state-wide time-varying shocks. Their interpretation further rests on the claim that within-firm information frictions would not generate positive cross-state spillovers, so a positive out-of-state coefficient is consistent with regulator information frictions and compliance-effort shifting.

Setting: On a firm-state-year panel, the authors estimate whether prior violations in the same state versus other states affect next year's in-state violations. In Table 4 column 2, a same-state prior violation lowers the next-year in-state violation probability by 0.0558, while an out-of-state prior violation raises it by 0.0027. The effect survives richer fixed effects (column 3: -0.0460 and 0.0511) and SPJ-logit robustness. The paper interprets the negative same-state coefficient as local deterrence and the positive out-of-state coefficient as evidence that firms shift noncompliance across state lines because OSHA offices do not share information effectively.

Main role: This is the paper's flagship evidence for information frictions: firms violate less in the same state but more in other states after a sanction, exactly matching the abstract and main conclusion.
Settings.G1738:
Treatment: Current-year ViolInState_t and ViolOutOfState_t indicators as defined in the baseline geography specification; both are binary prior-violation exposures.

Method: As robustness for the geographic-shifting result, the authors estimate a split-panel jackknifed fixed-effects logit model on the firm-state-year panel with next year's in-state violation indicator as the outcome and current in-state and out-of-state violation indicators as regressors, plus controls and firm-by-state/year fixed effects. Because this is a nonlinear SPJ logit estimator for a binary outcome, it is classified as Other. The paper also translates the logit estimates into average partial effects for economic magnitude.

Identification: Identification parallels the linear firm-state specification but uses the SPJ bias correction to address dynamic fixed-effects bias and binary-outcome issues. Causal interpretation depends on the same assumption that within firm-state changes in prior violations are conditionally exogenous after fixed effects and controls, with the SPJ procedure improving estimator bias rather than providing new exogenous variation.

Setting: The paper re-estimates the cross-state shifting regression using split-panel jackknifed logit. In Table 4 column 4, the coefficients on prior same-state and out-of-state violations are -0.2094 and 0.1600, respectively; the authors report that these correspond to average partial effects of -0.048 and 0.027. They interpret these as confirming that prior sanctions reduce same-state violations but increase cross-state violations, and note that the nonlinear estimates suggest the linear model may understate magnitude.

Main role: This is an important robustness check for the headline geographic-shifting claim, but the main result is carried by the linear FE estimates in Table 4.
Settings.H1738: Section 5.3, Table 4 column 4 and related discussion, PDF pp. 24-25.
Settings.G1739:
Treatment: Current-year in-state violation indicator ViolInState_t, interacted with SameStateEstabPct_t+1, the proportion of the firm's establishments located in the focal state. The focal causal contrast is whether an in-state violation's effect on future out-of-state violations varies with within-state operational concentration. SameStateEstabPct is continuous between 0 and 1.

Method: The authors estimate a firm-state-year linear FE regression with future out-of-state violations as the dependent variable and current in-state violations, current out-of-state violations, the share of the firm's establishments in the same state, and their interaction. Year and firm-by-state fixed effects plus controls are included. This specification tests whether the tendency to shift violations out of state is weaker when firms have more opportunity to reallocate effort within the same state.

Identification: Identification uses within firm-state changes in prior in-state violations and within-state establishment concentration, controlling for firm-by-state and year effects. The endogeneity concern is that the geographic distribution of establishments may reflect omitted operational changes correlated with safety. The authors interpret the insignificant interaction as evidence against within-state shifting, conditional on fixed effects and controls, but this remains a correlational causal-interpretation robustness test rather than a sharply identified design.

Setting: To test whether firms shift noncompliance within rather than across states, the paper regresses next-year out-of-state violation exposure on current in-state violations and their interaction with the firm's share of establishments in the same state. In Table 5 column 1, the coefficient on ViolInState_t is 0.0112 while the interaction ViolInState_t × SameStateEstabPct is 0.0091 and insignificant. The authors interpret this as suggesting that having more within-state establishments does not attenuate cross-state shifting, so the main reallocation appears to occur across state lines.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism/robustness test aimed at ruling out within-state shifting rather than establishing the headline cross-state effect.
Settings.G1740:
Treatment: ViolEstabhijt: indicator equal to 1 if firm i violated an OSHA rule at establishment h in state j in year t. The model also includes ViolOutOfStateijt as an additional regressor. The focal treatment is a binary establishment-level prior violation.

Method: The authors estimate an establishment-level linear FE regression restricted to firm-state-years in which no other establishment owned by the firm has a violation in that state-year. The outcome is whether other same-state establishments violate in the next year; regressors include whether the focal establishment violated this year and whether the firm violated out of state. Year and firm-by-state fixed effects plus controls are included. This is designed to detect within-state geographic shifting of misconduct across establishments.

Identification: Identification relies on within firm-state variation across establishments and time, with firm-by-state and year fixed effects. By restricting the sample to state-years with no other same-state violating establishment contemporaneously, the authors try to isolate whether a violation at one establishment induces later violations elsewhere in the same state. Remaining concerns include omitted establishment-specific shocks and selection into the restricted sample. The negative coefficient is interpreted as evidence against within-state reallocation.

Setting: In an establishment-level robustness test, the paper asks whether a violation at one establishment causes future violations at other establishments in the same state. Table 5 column 2 shows a coefficient of -0.0672 on ViolEstab_t for the outcome ViolSameState_{t+1}, while the coefficient on out-of-state violations is 0.0078. The authors interpret the negative own-establishment effect as evidence that firms do not shift violating behavior within states, reinforcing their main cross-state interpretation.

Main role: This is a supplementary robustness test used to rule out within-state shifting of violating behavior across establishments.
Settings.G1741:
Treatment: Current-year binary indicators for ViolInState_t (firm violated in focal state), ViolOutOfState_t (firm violated in other states), CleanInState_t (inspected with no violation in focal state), and CleanOutOfState_t (inspected with no violation in other states). The substantive treatments are the prior violation indicators, with clean-inspection indicators included to separate inspection from sanction effects.

Method: The authors estimate firm-state-year linear probability models replacing the violation outcome with future inspection indicators. Regressors are current in-state and out-of-state violation indicators and current in-state and out-of-state clean-inspection indicators, with year and firm-by-state fixed effects plus controls. Outcomes are reported together for any inspection, reactive inspection only, planned inspection only, and discretionary inspection. One robustness column for any inspection uses split-panel jackknife logit, but the main implemented specifications are linear FE models. The aim is to assess whether prior violations causally alter OSHA's inspection targeting across states.

Identification: Identification uses within firm-state temporal variation in prior sanctions and clean inspections, controlling for permanent firm-state heterogeneity and common annual shocks. The concern is that inspections and violations are jointly determined by latent safety risks. Including clean-inspection indicators helps separate the role of being inspected from the role of being cited. The authors interpret a positive effect on reactive inspections but no effect on discretionary inspections from out-of-state violations as evidence that state OSHA offices do not proactively use cross-state information, consistent with internal information frictions.

Setting: The paper estimates whether prior violations change the probability of future OSHA inspections in the same state. Table 6 shows that prior in-state violations reduce next-year inspections in-state, while prior out-of-state violations increase some inspection types. In column 2, any inspection falls by 0.0284 after an in-state violation but rises by 0.0040 after an out-of-state violation. Breaking this apart, reactive inspections rise after out-of-state violations (column 5: 0.0032), planned inspections show at most weak increases (column 7: 0.0010, marginal), and discretionary inspections do not respond (column 9: -0.0003, insignificant). The authors interpret this as evidence that cross-state violations trigger only mechanical/reactive responses, not proactive discretionary targeting by local OSHA offices.

Main role: Inspection patterns are a central mechanism in the abstract and conclusion: out-of-state violations do not trigger proactive OSHA inspections elsewhere, supporting the information-frictions interpretation.
Settings.G1742:
Treatment: Current-year binary indicators ViolInState_t, ViolOutOfState_t, CleanInState_t, and CleanOutOfState_t in the inspection specification.

Method: As robustness for the inspection mechanism, the authors estimate a split-panel jackknifed fixed-effects logit for the future any-inspection indicator on current in-state/out-of-state violations and clean inspections, with controls and fixed effects analogous to the linear model. Because the implemented estimator is nonlinear SPJ logit, it is classified as Other.

Identification: Same within firm-state identification as the linear inspection model, with SPJ logit used because any-inspection embeds a dynamic component through lagged violation/clean inspection status and because the outcome is binary. The estimator aims to reduce bias from dynamic fixed effects rather than generate new exogenous variation.

Setting: To confirm the inspection findings are not artifacts of linear dynamic modeling, the paper re-estimates the any-inspection regression using split-panel jackknifed logit. Table 6 column 3 reports coefficients of -0.0985 on prior in-state violations and 0.1434 on prior out-of-state violations, with a large negative coefficient on prior clean same-state inspections (-0.2695). The authors state these results are consistent with the linear model and use them as robustness for the inspection mechanism.

Main role: This is a robustness check for the inspection-channel evidence rather than the primary presentation of that mechanism.
Settings.G1743:
Treatment: Current-year binary indicators ViolInState_t and ViolOutOfState_t, indicating whether the firm committed at least one OSHA violation in the focal state or in any other state, respectively.

Method: The authors estimate a firm-state-year linear FE model replacing the outcome with RWInState_{t+1}, an indicator for a Repeat or Willful violation, and regressing it on current in-state and out-of-state violations, with year and firm-by-state fixed effects plus controls in one column. The estimator is a linear probability model interpreted causally as the effect of prior violations on OSHA's ability to assess severe repeat/willful penalties in the next year.

Identification: Identification comes from within firm-state temporal variation in prior local versus out-of-state violations, holding fixed time-invariant firm-state traits and common year shocks. The key endogeneity concern is that repeated bad actors may generate both current and future severe violations. The authors' interpretation is that, conditional on overall violation behavior and fixed effects, only same-state prior violations increase future Repeat/Willful designations because local offices can access supporting documentation; out-of-state prior violations do not, due to internal information frictions.

Setting: The paper tests whether prior violations affect the probability that next year's violations are classified as Repeat or Willful. In Table 7 column 2, a prior in-state violation raises next-year Repeat/Willful violation probability by 0.0034, while a prior out-of-state violation has essentially no effect (0.0001, insignificant). The authors interpret this as evidence that local OSHA offices can document and impose severe penalties when the prior case is in-state, but cross-state information frictions prevent similar escalation when the prior violation occurred elsewhere.

Main role: Severe-penalty assessment is a central deterrence mechanism in the abstract and conclusion: subsequent cross-state violations face lower severe-penalty rates because documentation does not follow firms across state lines.
Settings.G1744:
Treatment: Current-year ViolInState_t and ViolOutOfState_t indicators, interacted with StatePlan_j, a binary indicator equal to 1 if the focal state administers its own OSHA state plan. The focal treatment is the differential effect of prior violations when the destination/focal state is a state-plan state.

Method: The authors augment the main firm-state-year linear FE violation model by interacting current in-state and out-of-state violations with a StatePlan indicator for whether the focal state runs its own OSHA state plan. Year and firm-by-state fixed effects are included, with controls in one column. This is a heterogeneity test of whether effects are larger where interstate information frictions are expected to be greater.

Identification: Identification uses within firm-state variation in prior violations combined with cross-sectional variation in whether the focal state is a state-plan state, which the paper treats as predetermined because adoption occurred decades earlier. The central concern is whether state-plan states differ on other dimensions affecting violations. Firm-by-state fixed effects absorb time-invariant state-plan-state differences within each firm-state, so the interaction is identified from differential within-cell responses to prior violations. The interpretation is that larger out-of-state spillovers into state-plan states indicate more severe information frictions between jurisdictions.

Setting: To test whether more severe information frictions amplify geographic shifting, the paper interacts prior violations with an indicator for state-plan states. In Table 8 column 2, the baseline out-of-state violation effect is 0.0009, while the interaction ViolOutOfState_t × StatePlan is 0.0042; likewise, the same-state deterrence effect is somewhat weaker in state-plan states via a 0.0138 interaction with ViolInState_t. The authors interpret the positive out-of-state interaction as evidence that firms shift violating behavior more strongly into state-plan states, consistent with greater cross-jurisdiction information frictions within OSHA.

Main role: This heterogeneity analysis is a key substantiation of the regulator-information-frictions mechanism and is discussed in the introduction and conclusion as ruling out within-firm frictions.
Settings.G1745:
Treatment: Current-year binary indicators ViolInState_t, ViolOutOfState_t, CleanInspInState_t, and CleanInspOutOfState_t, each interacted with StatePlan_j. The focal treatment is differential inspection response to prior violations in state-plan jurisdictions.

Method: The authors estimate linear FE inspection models analogous to Table 6 but add interactions between StatePlan and prior in-state/out-of-state violations and clean inspections. Outcomes are reactive, planned, and discretionary inspections. Year and firm-by-state fixed effects are included, with controls in alternating columns. This heterogeneity exercise studies whether state-plan states use their additional discretion to inspect differently after prior violations.

Identification: Identification parallels the inspection FE models, with heterogeneous responses by state-plan status. The authors use these interactions to test whether state-plan states' extra discretion changes inspection behavior after prior violations. Remaining concerns are omitted time-varying state-plan-specific shocks, but the lack of differential discretionary responses is interpreted as evidence against inspection-policy differences explaining the main state-plan result.

Setting: The paper studies whether state-plan jurisdictions respond differently to prior violations in their inspection choices. Table 9 shows little evidence that state-plan states conduct more discretionary inspections after out-of-state violations: in column 6, the interaction ViolOutOfState_t × StatePlan is 0.0010 and insignificant for discretionary inspections. Some weak differences appear for planned inspections, but the authors conclude state-plan states do not use discretion to inspect more efficiently in response to cross-state violations. This supports their interpretation that larger shifts into state-plan states reflect information frictions rather than intentional inspection policy differences.

Main role: This is a supporting mechanism test used to show that stronger shifting into state-plan states is not explained by more efficient discretionary inspection targeting there.
Settings.G1746:
Treatment: Current-year ViolOutOfState_t indicator and one additional incentive/culture measure per column: RWOutOfState_t (binary severe out-of-state violation), MeetOrBeat_{t+1} (binary indicator for just meeting/beating analyst EPS by 0 or 1 cent), and WeakCompliance_{t+1} (binary indicator for non-OSHA federal sanctions in the prior three years), with interactions where reported. Treatments are binary.

Method: The authors estimate three variants of the main firm-state-year linear FE violation model, each adding a measure of incentives or culture. Column 1 adds RWOutOfState, an indicator for an out-of-state Repeat/Willful violation; column 2 interacts ViolOutOfState with MeetOrBeat, an indicator for narrowly meeting/beating analyst earnings forecasts; column 3 interacts ViolOutOfState with WeakCompliance, an indicator for recent non-OSHA federal sanctions. All models include year and firm-by-state fixed effects plus controls. These are heterogeneity and mechanism regressions about when cross-state compliance-effort shifting is stronger.

Identification: Identification uses within firm-state timing of prior out-of-state violations combined with cross-sectional or time-varying proxies for incentives and culture, controlling for firm-by-state and year fixed effects. The endogeneity concern is that these proxies may capture broader omitted shocks correlated with safety. The authors interpret stronger effects when out-of-state violations are Repeat/Willful, when firms just meet/beat earnings, and when firms have weak compliance cultures as evidence that shifting responds to enforcement incentives, financial pressure, and culture.

Setting: The paper examines when cross-state shifting of violations is strongest. In Table 10 column 1, an out-of-state Repeat/Willful violation adds 0.0066 to next-year in-state violation risk, beyond the 0.0024 effect of any out-of-state violation. In column 2, the interaction ViolOutOfState_t × MeetOrBeat_{t+1} is 0.0037, suggesting more shifting when firms face short-term earnings pressure. In column 3, the interaction ViolOutOfState_t × WeakCompliance_{t+1} is 0.0043, indicating stronger shifting among firms with weaker compliance cultures. The authors use these results to argue that financial incentives and culture shape how firms exploit OSHA information frictions.

Main role: These are cross-sectional mechanism tests that sharpen interpretation of the main result but are not themselves the core headline finding.
Settings.N1747: Table 5, Panel A, column 1 (article p. 4155; Section 5.1.1, p. 4154): no-FE OLS at the firm-lender level, regressing the post-minus-pre difference in log(1+loan amount) on the change in average lender AQR exposure (additional provisions divided by lender total assets). No additional lender controls; lender-clustered inference. Exposure coefficient -3.4217; authors report a 24.76% lending decline for a one-treatment-SD increase.
Settings.O1747: Separated from s1 because column 1 has no fixed effects. Main-result status follows the headline approximately 25% credit-supply contraction in the introduction (p. 4135). Treatment remains nonbinary.
Settings.N1748: Table 11, p. 4170, column 1: no-FE OLS on firm-lender pairs restricted to NBFC/nonbank borrowers. Treatment is the post-minus-pre change in average lender AQR exposure (provision divergence divided by bank assets). Outcome is the post-minus-pre difference in log(1+loan amount). Exposure coefficient -8.1644; reported economic significance -50.65% for a one-treatment-SD change; lender-clustered inference.
Settings.O1748: OLS specification separated from s7 rather than pooling it with identifying borrower-FE columns. Supports the central shadow-bank-contagion finding (abstract p. 4132; conclusion p. 4173). No qualifying outcome-benchmark comparison found in Table 11 or Section 6.2.1.
Settings.N1749: Table 12, p. 4171, columns 2 and 4: district-year FE regressions of growth in nighttime luminosity and growth in the MNREGA wage bill on a binary indicator for above-median branch-weighted district AQR exposure. District and year FE; district-clustered inference. Coefficients -0.0154 and 0.0789, respectively.
Settings.O1749: Binary treatment separated from continuous s8. Supports the regional-growth/distress conclusions in the introduction (p. 4136). The approximately 8% sentence merely interprets the growth-outcome coefficient and supplies no separate outcome benchmark.
Settings.N1750: Table 2 column 2, Section 3, pp. 7-9: change in log zip-code home prices, 2006-2009, explaining change in log new student-loan default rate, 2007-2010. Separate zip-code weighted OLS regression, weighted by total student-loan balances; standard errors clustered by zip code. Coefficient -0.4179, home-price change -14.4%, reported share of 18.9% aggregate default rise explained 31.8%. Authors interpret the elasticity as potentially capturing effects through multiple channels; causal attribution remains vulnerable to correlated local shocks.
Settings.O1750: Treatment-specific split from s1, not a different estimator. Headline home-price contribution in abstract. One-year outcome lag reflects default reporting delay.
Settings.N1751: Table 2 column 3, Section 3, pp. 7-9: change in log zip-code employment, 2006-2009, explaining change in log new student-loan default rate, 2007-2010. Separate zip-code weighted OLS regression, weighted by total student-loan balances; standard errors clustered by zip code. Reported coefficient -0.0004, employment change -4.7%, share explained 0.0% (rounded as reported).
Settings.O1751: Supporting substantive alternative-explanation analysis, not a diagnostic: authors discuss why aggregate employment has virtually zero explanatory power and may poorly proxy individual unemployment. Distinct treatment split from s1; weak explanatory power does not itself exclude a setting.
Settings.N1752: Table 4 column 4, pp. 10-11: log zip-code home price in year t explaining new borrower default in t+1. Three separately included FE dimensions: zip code, repayment cohort (year first entering repayment), and calendar year. Cohort FE address shifts in borrower composition and default propensity by repayment cohort. Weighted linear regression using individual loan balances, zip-code clustered standard errors. Home-price coefficient -0.0105 (SE 0.00281). Substantive robustness for the baseline home-price effect; no qualifying magnitude comparison.
Settings.O1752: Split from s3 to distinguish HDFE from standard FE under the project taxonomy. Supporting robustness, not a separate headline result.
Settings.N1753: Table 8 column 4, pp. 13-14: continuous log home price in year t and its interaction with Owner explaining new default in t+1. Three separately included FE sets: zip code, repayment cohort and calendar year, mirroring Table 4 composition controls. Loan-balance weighted linear regression, zip-code clustered standard errors. Home-price coefficient -0.0105; Home price x Owner 0.000832 (insignificant). Substantive robustness of the direct-liquidity-channel test.
Settings.O1753: Split from s7 because three FE dimensions and the linked borrower-composition rationale meet HDFE definition. Interacted FE in Table 8 column 5 is instead one set. No qualifying magnitude comparison found.
Settings.N1754: Table 11 column 1, pp. 15-16: extended-sample FE regression of new borrower default in t+1 on continuous log home prices in t, controlling for IBR eligibility, with zip-code and calendar-year FE. Treatment years 2006-2011, default years 2007-2012; individual loan-balance weights and zip-code clustered standard errors. Home-price coefficient -0.00419 (SE 0.00209), 1,556,296 observations.
Settings.O1754: Split from s10: no Post interactions or DDD estimator in column 1. Supporting extended-period home-price result. Eligibility coefficient 0.0256 is a conditional group association here, not an identified policy receipt effect. No qualifying outcome-benchmark comparison found.
Settings.N1755: Fig. 6 Panel A and Section 6, pp. 17-18: dynamic conventional DDD variant of Eq. (2), replacing Home price x IBR eligible x Post with Home price x IBR eligible x year interactions for 2007-2011, relative to baseline 2006. Binary policy eligibility is the exposure; continuous home prices measure shock sensitivity. Outcome is new borrower default in t+1; coefficients for treatment year t are plotted at t+1. Year and zip-code FE; underlying loan-balance weighted specification with zip-code clustered standard errors.
Settings.O1755: Include because the authors substantively interpret the post-2009 jump and subsequent growth in insurance against home-price shocks, not solely a pretrend diagnostic. Pre-2009 coefficients are diagnostic components of this same dynamic setting. Numerical coefficient values not tabulated in the text; do not invent them from the qualitative discussion. Figure 6 Panel B take-up rates alone are descriptive, not outcome benchmarks. No qualifying magnitude comparison found.
Settings.N1756: Omitted Section 3.2 measurement-rule comparison, Fig. 2, pp. 2915-2916, February 16, 2010: compute RX with the CBOE cutoff after two consecutive zero-bid strikes versus RX* using all out-of-the-money options with positive bid quotes, on the same underlying market data. This is a two-rule construction contrast. Around 08:30 RX is about 23.5, more than 2% below RX* at 24. Just before 11:00 RX jumps as its lower strike range expands; RX* has no corresponding jump. RX* is a wider-range comparator, not guaranteed true volatility; both rules can exhibit truncation problems elsewhere (footnote 13).
